The assumption of the *mishna* is that any female derivative — which cannot itself be brought as an *olah* — must wait until it develops a *mum*, a physical blemish, at which point it is redeemed and the proceeds go toward an *olah*. Crucially, the fact of being female is not itself considered a *mum* — this is not a statement about gender per se, but rather a halakhic point that a *mum* must be a concrete physical defect. The wrong gender, like the wrong gender of a male *chatas*, does not qualify for redemption on its own.

### Female Olah Debate

The *mishna* then addresses a new case: *hamafrish nekeivah l'olah* — one who directly sanctified a female as an *olah*. If it then gave birth to a male, what is the law of that male child? The *mishna* rules that the child is not brought directly as an *olah*; instead, one waits for the child to develop a *mum*, sells it, and uses the proceeds for an *olah* — *yeireh ad sheyista'ev v'yimacher v'yavi bidamav olah*. Rabbi Eliezer disagrees: *hu atzmo yakriv olah* — the male child itself may be brought as an *olah*.

This generates an apparent inconsistency within the *mishna*. In the first half, wherever a male appears in the descendant chain — even after passing through female intermediaries — it may be brought as an *olah*, and there seems to be no debate about this. Yet in the second half, when the top of the chain is a female directly sanctified as an *olah*, the rabbis say that even the male child may not be brought. What distinguishes these two situations?

### Beginning vs. End Debate

The *gemara* puts this question directly: *mai shna reisha d'lo palgi u'mai shna seifa d'palgi*? Why is there no debate in the first clause, but there is in the second?

### Rabbah bar Chana's Posit…

Rabbah bar bar Chana answers: *b'machlokes shnuya* — actually, the first clause is also disputed. The opening of the *mishna*, which seems to permit bringing any male that appears in the descendant chain, reflects only the position of Rabbi Eliezer. The rabbis would actually hold that once a derivative male goes through a female, even in the first scenario, one may never bring the descendant directly — only the proceeds. According to this reading, there is no inconsistency between the two halves; the apparent consensus in the first half is simply Rabbi Eliezer's uncontested position, while the rabbis would contest it there as well.

### Rava's Kedusha Model

Rava disagrees: *afilu teima Rabbanan* — even the rabbis concede the first half of the *mishna*, which represents their view as well. The distinction lies elsewhere.

The rabbis dispute Rabbi Eliezer only in the case of *hamafrish nekeivah l'olah* — where a female was directly sanctified as an *olah*. Why? Because *d'imei lo karva* — the mother could never have been brought as an *olah*. The beginning of the chain was itself unbringable. This is directly analogous to the earlier case of sanctifying an animal with a *mum* and then having an unblemished child — if the original animal could not be brought, its derivatives cannot be brought either, even when a viable animal appears further down the chain.

*Aval temurah d'imei nami karva* — but if you begin with a male *olah* that is duly sanctified, and the *temurah* happens to be female, the top of the chain *could* be brought. *Afilu Rabbanan modu* — even the rabbis agree that when you subsequently hit a male further down that chain, you may bring it. The *kedusha* at the top of the chain was a full, bringable *kedusha*, and the chain retains that character.

Rava's model is thus precise: the rabbis require that the top of the chain be an animal that itself could have been brought. Rabbi Eliezer relaxes that requirement — he does not demand that the mother be bringable, only that there be a consistency of *kedusha* throughout the chain. If you start with a female *olah*, it cannot be brought, but it carries *kedushas olah*, and when the descendant is male and also carries *kedushas olah*, Rabbi Eliezer says you may bring it.

### Asham Case Analysis

The *gemara* now tests Rava's model with a new *beraisa* concerning the *asham*. The *asham*, like the *olah*, is male-only, but it differs in an important respect: the *temurah* or descendant of an *asham* is not brought directly — it must be left to graze, develop a *mum*, and then the proceeds are used. In the case of a standard *asham* that gets "derailed" — whether through death of the owner, prior atonement, or other circumstances — the proceeds go to a communal *olah*. This is not the same as bringing the animal as an *olah*; it is a secondary resolution.

The *beraisa* reads: *tmuras asham u'vlad tmura u'vlad vlad*, all the way to the end of time — *yiru ad sheyista'avu v'yimachru v'yipelu demeihem linedava* — they graze until they develop a *mum*, are sold, and the proceeds go toward *nedava*, i.e., a communal *olah*. Rabbi Eliezer says they must die — consistent with his general position that *ha'asham ke'chatas*, the *asham* follows the laws of a *chatas*, and since the offspring of a *chatas* must die, so must the offspring of an *asham*. Rabbi Elazar (a distinct figure from Rabbi Eliezer) says *yavi bidmeihen olah* — use the money for an *olah* — referring to a private, rather than communal, *olah*.

Crucially, neither the *tanna kamma* nor Rabbi Elazar says to bring the animal itself, even if a male is reached down the chain. This is precisely where the *gemara* asks its pointed question: *bidamim in, gufo lo* — the money, yes; the animal itself, no. But this scenario begins with a male *asham* at the top of the chain. According to Rava, the rabbis should agree that when you hit a male descendant, you can bring it — because the top of the chain *was* bringable. Why then does everyone agree here that you cannot?

Rav Chisda resolves this according to the approach of Rabbah bar bar Chana: he argues that Rabbi Elazar is speaking *lidvreihem d'Rabbanan* — he is engaging the rabbis on their own terms. The rabbis, in his view, would always say you cannot bring a descendant, regardless of whether the chain began with a bringable animal. Rabbi Elazar's own position, as he himself says, is that even the descendant itself could be brought as an *olah* if it is male — *lididi sevira li de'afilu vlad nami karev olah*. He is only challenging the rabbis on whether the proceeds go to a communal or private *olah*.

Rava must answer differently, since his model holds that the rabbis would agree to bring the descendant when the chain began with a bringable animal. The key is this: *ad kan lo ka'amar Rabbi Eliezer hu atzmo yakriv olah ela b'mafrish nekeivah l'olah*, Rabbi Eliezer only permits bringing the descendant in the case of a female *olah* — *d'ika shem olah al imo*, because the mother retains the *shem olah*, the name of *olah*. *Aval gabei tmuras vlad asham*, in the *asham* case, *deleika shem olah al imo* — the mother does not have the name of an *olah* at all.

This is the heart of Rava's refined model. When an *asham* becomes derailed — through *temurah*, through offspring passing through female intermediaries — the proceeds, when they must eventually be realized, go toward an *olah*, not an *asham*. This means the *kedusha* at the point of eventual bringing is *kedushas olah*, while the original sanctification was *kedushas asham*. They do not match. Even Rabbi Eliezer, who permits bringing a descendant that began from an unbringable mother, insists on one condition: that the *kedusha* of the descendant must be the same as the *kedusha* of the original. When the chain begins as *asham* and the descendant would be brought as an *olah*, that condition is not met — *modei Rabbi Eliezer debidmei in hu atzmo lo*.

The resulting picture is nuanced but coherent. According to the rabbis, the top of the chain must have been itself bringable. According to Rabbi Eliezer, the top need not have been bringable, but the *kedusha* must remain consistent throughout the chain. When the *asham* chain is brought as an *olah*, consistency is broken, and even Rabbi Eliezer agrees the animal itself may not be brought.

One might ask whether this creates a practical absurdity: if someone committed a transgression requiring an *asham*, could none of these derived animals serve? The answer is yes — one would need to set aside a third animal as the actual *asham*. The derived animal, once it has a *mum*, generates proceeds that go toward an *olah*, not toward the *asham* obligation.

### Abaye's Motar Model

Abaye challenges Rava's model. *Ve-chi ba'ei Rabbi Eliezer shem olah al imo* — does Rabbi Eliezer truly require that the original animal carry the same *kedusha* as the descendant one seeks to bring? Abaye proposes an entirely different framework. He cites the principle: *lemakom shehaMosar holech haVlad holech* — wherever the *motar* goes, the child goes. The *motar*, the leftover, refers to cases where you have an excess or substitute sanctified animal — where, for instance, you lost your *korban*, designated another, and then found the original. The *halacha* for what is done with that leftover animal is taken as the template for what is done with any descendant.

### Pesach Before/After

To illustrate the *motar* model, Abaye works through the cases. Begin with the *olah*: if you lose an *olah* and designate another, and then find the original, both are brought. Therefore, any descendant of an *olah* is also brought. Now consider the *asham*: if you lose an *asham* and designate another, and then find the original, you have *niskaper baal be'acher ba'asham* — you bring one, and the other must graze and cannot be brought itself. Therefore, the descendant of an *asham* is likewise not brought itself, only its proceeds are used. The *motar* model maps the treatment of leftover substitutes onto the treatment of descendants.

The *pesach* case is particularly instructive. The *mishna* under discussion begins with *hamafrish nekeivah l'pesach* — a female designated as a *korban pesach*, which must be male. She and her children must graze until they develop a *mum*, after which the proceeds go toward a *pesach*. This is the *before-Pesach* scenario. But then: *nish'ar achar Pesach* — if the animal remains after Pesach has passed, it grazes and the proceeds go toward a *shelamim*. Why? Because a *pesach* that passes Pesach without being offered becomes a *shelamim*: *mosar pesach gufa karev shelamim*. And if the child is born after Pesach, Rabbi Eliezer says *hu atzmo yakriv shelamim* — the child itself may be brought as a *shelamim*.

This case is used to challenge Rava's model in a striking way. Here the *kedusha* at the top of the chain is *kedushas pesach*, not *kedushas shelamim*. Yet Rabbi Eliezer permits bringing the child as a *shelamim*. Does he not require, as Rava claims, that the descendant's *kedusha* match the original? The *gemara* responds on Rava's behalf: *shani achar Pesach, demosar Pesach gufia karev shelamim* — the case after Pesach is different precisely because a leftover *pesach* itself becomes a *shelamim*. The *kedusha* of the chain has effectively transformed into *kedushas shelamim*, and therefore the descendant can be brought as a *shelamim*. Rava's requirement of matching *kedusha* is thus satisfied, since by the time the child is to be brought, the *kedusha* throughout the chain is *shelamim*.

But if so, the *gemara* asks, why does Rabbi Eliezer not argue in the *before-Pesach* case — why not allow the male child to be brought as a *pesach*? After all, the mother has *kedushas pesach*, and the male child has the same *kedusha*, which is exactly what Rava requires. Rava responds: *ein hachi nami palig* — actually, Rabbi Eliezer would indeed argue there too. The *braisa* only chose to illustrate his position in the after-Pesach case, but he would equally permit the male child before Pesach to be brought as a *pesach*.

Abaye, however, says *lo palig* — Rabbi Eliezer would not argue in the before-Pesach case. His reasoning invokes the *motar* principle. Abaye says: *midi degamiri*, this is a received tradition — *lemakom shehaMosar holech haVlad holech*. Before Pesach, if you have a leftover or substitute *pesach* that is not brought, what do you do? You use it for *dmei pesach* — the proceeds are used toward a future *pesach*, not the animal itself. Therefore, the same applies to the child: *vlad nami lidmei pesach* — the child is also only for the value of a *pesach*, not the *pesach* itself.

Tosafot, however, while noting that this *motar* language does not fit the words of the *gemara* entirely cleanly, proposes a deeper explanation that he considers to be the heart of Abaye's position. The real reason Rabbi Eliezer would not permit the male child to be brought as a *pesach* before Pesach — even though the *kedusha* matches — is that bringing the child effectively *derails* the mother. When a *korban pesach* has already been brought by someone else, and the original becomes a leftover, the original is genuinely derailed. Here, if the male child is brought as the *pesach*, it is as if to say: the child is the *pesach*, not the mother. But each person may only bring one *korban pesach*, tied to a specific *chabura*. By selecting the child over the mother, you are rejecting the mother's claim entirely.

This stands in contrast to the *olah* case. If a female *olah* cannot be brought, and the male child is brought as an *olah*, no competition or rejection is involved — if the mother had been male, both would have been brought. The mother's inability to be brought is simply a function of gender, not a displacement. But with *pesach*, there is only one per person, and choosing the child necessarily excludes the mother. Tosafot understands Abaye's position as: you cannot bring the child when doing so constitutes a real rejection — an effective stripping of status — from the mother.

The same logic, Tosafot notes, applies to *asham*. Just as there is only one *korban pesach* per person per year, so too there is only one *asham* per specific transgression. To bring the male child as an *asham* when the mother is also an *asham* is to say that the child's *asham* is the real one, and the mother's *asham* is not. That constitutes a derailment of the mother's status, and therefore even Rabbi Eliezer agrees in that case.

The *gemara* concludes by introducing the challenge of Rav Ukva bar Rachma: *umi amrinan mid'imi lidmei vlad nami lidmei* — would we truly say that whenever the mother is only for the proceeds, so too the child? A *braisa* seems to contradict this: it says that one who sets aside a female for *pesach* — she and her children graze until they develop a *mum*, and the proceeds go for a *pesach*. Yet Rabbi Eliezer says *hu atzmo yikrav pesach* — the child itself may be brought as a *pesach*. This directly contradicts Abaye's view that the child could not be brought as a *pesach* in the before-Pesach case.

### Pregnant Animal Case

Ravina resolves the contradiction: *bemafrish beheima me'uberes askinan* — the *braisa* is dealing with a case where the animal was already pregnant at the time of sanctification. Ravina invokes the position of Rabbi Yochanan: *im shiyaro meshuyar*, that the fetus may be sanctified independently of the mother, since *ubar lav yerech imo hu* — the fetus is not considered a limb of the mother and may receive its own independent *kedusha*.

In the *braisa*'s case, the mother was sanctified for the *value* of a *pesach* but the fetus was directly sanctified as a *pesach* itself. There is no question of derivative *kedusha*, no question of rejecting the mother, because the child's *kedusha* does not derive from the mother's at all. It received its own direct sanctification as a *pesach* and may therefore be brought as one.

Mar Zutra son of Rav Mari confirms that this reading is indeed compelling, pointing to the *braisa*'s language: *hi u'veladoseha* — "she and her children" — which implies the children were already present or imminent at the time of sanctification, unlike the other *braisa* which describes a subsequent birth.

The overall framework emerging from Rava and Abaye's positions, as clarified throughout this extended discussion, is as follows. According to the rabbis, a descendant may be brought in its own right only if the top of the chain was itself bringable. According to Rabbi Eliezer, even an unbringable animal at the top of the chain does not disqualify the descendants — provided two conditions are met: first, the *kedusha* must be consistent throughout (*asham* cannot beget an *olah*); and second, bringing the descendant must not constitute a real rejection or derailment of the mother's own claim (*pesach* and *asham* both fail this test). Where neither of these limitations applies — as in the case of a female *olah* giving birth to a male — Rabbi Eliezer permits the child to be brought directly.

---

## Female Asham Case

### Female Asham Agreement

With that framework in place, the *gemara* turns to a directly related statement. Rav Yosef bar Chanina says: *umodeh Rabbi Eliezer b'mafrish nekeivah l'asham she'ein benah karev asham* — even Rabbi Eliezer agrees that if one sets aside a female as an *asham*, the male child may not be brought as an *asham*. This is not an instance where Rabbi Eliezer takes his expansive view; he concedes that the child cannot itself be brought directly.

The case here is subtler than the earlier *asham* discussion. Previously, the reason the descendant could not be brought was that the chain had passed through a *temurah*, at which point the *kedusha* shifted from *kedushas asham* to *kedushas olah*. Once you perform *temurah* on an *asham*, the resulting animal — if it cannot be brought — is treated as derailed, and the proceeds go toward an *olah*, not an *asham*. So the *kedusha* at the bottom of the chain is *olah* while the top is *asham*, and Rava's matching requirement is violated.

But here, no *temurah* has occurred. One simply sanctified a female directly as an *asham* and it gave birth to a male. No lateral move into *olah* territory has taken place. The mother's *kedusha* is *kedushas asham*, the child's potential *kedusha* is *kedushas asham* — the *kedusha* appears to match. Why then does even Rabbi Eliezer agree the child cannot be brought?

### Mother Status in Asham

The *gemara* responds: *peshita* — this is obvious! *Asham lo ka'amar Rabbi Eliezer ela b'mafrish nekeivah l'olah d'ika shem olah al imo* — Rabbi Eliezer permitted bringing the male child only in the case of a female *olah*, because in that case the mother still carries the *shem olah*, the name of *olah* — she simply cannot be brought due to gender. *Aval gabei mafrish nekeivah l'asham deleika shem asham al imo* — by contrast, a female sanctified as an *asham* does not truly carry the *shem asham*, the identity of an *asham*. And therefore *afilu Rabbi Eliezer modeh delo karev asham* — even Rabbi Eliezer agrees the child may not be brought as an *asham*.

### Derailing the Mother

The *gemara*'s language — that the mother "does not have the name of *asham*" — requires explanation, since it is not immediately clear how this differs from the *olah* case. Tosafot addresses this directly, drawing on the principle established through the *pesach* discussion: the reason is that bringing the child as an *asham* would effectively remove the *shem asham* from the mother. An *asham* is brought for a specific transgression; one may only bring one *asham* for a given sin. If the child is presented as the *asham* for that transgression, the mother is thereby cast aside — her status as an *asham* is stripped away by the act of bringing the child. This is precisely the same dynamic as the *pesach* case: choosing the child to be the *korban* necessarily rejects the mother's own claim to that status.

The *gemara* then asks why it was necessary to state this case explicitly. *Ei ashmi'inan olah, hava amina olah hu d'lo karva d'lo akdesha l'imeih kedushas asham* — had we only been told about *olah*, one might have reasoned that the prohibition on bringing the child as an *olah* was due to the mismatch of *kedusha*: the mother carries *kedushas asham* while the child would be an *olah*. *Aval asham, eima vlad karev asham* — but when both the mother and the child are *asham*, perhaps the same *kedusha* throughout the chain should make it permissible. *Ka mashma lan* — it does not. The same mechanism — the derailment of the mother — applies here even when the *kedusha* is identical.

### Kedusha Transfer Rules

To summarize the accumulated rules: according to the rabbis, a descendant may be brought directly only if the top of the chain was itself a bringable animal — that is, if one began with a male for a male-only *korban*, and a male reappears further down the chain. According to Rabbi Eliezer, one need not begin with a bringable animal, but two conditions govern his leniency: first, the *kedusha* must remain consistent from top to bottom of the chain (the *asham*-to-*olah* shift disqualifies the descendant); and second, bringing the child must not constitute a genuine displacement or rejection of the mother's claim (the single-*pesach*, single-*asham* principle). Where both conditions are satisfied — as in the case of a female *olah* with a male child — Rabbi Eliezer permits the child to be brought. Where either condition fails, he concurs with the rabbis that the child may not be brought and the proceeds alone are used.

---

## Female Asham Mishna

### Female Asham Blemish Rule

The final *mishna* of this *daf* returns to the practical resolution of the female *asham* case. If one sets aside a female for an *asham*, she grazes — *tireh ad shetista'ev* — until she develops a *mum*. The gender mismatch is, as noted, not itself sufficient for redemption; a genuine physical *mum* is required. Once she has a *mum* she is sold, and the proceeds are used to bring an *asham* — *vetimacher v'yavi bidmeiha asham*.

This conclusion may initially seem surprising: one might have assumed that since the proceeds of a derailed *asham* typically go toward an *olah*, the same would apply here. The distinction is important: the proceeds go to an *olah* only when the *asham* has been genuinely derailed — through a *temurah*, through the children becoming derivatives, or through the owner having already been atoned by another means (*nitkapru be'aleha be'acher*). When the animal simply has a *mum* — or, in this case, is the wrong gender but otherwise intact in its sanctity — it has not been derailed. It is merely unable to be brought in its current form. In that case, the proceeds are used for a proper *asham*, maintaining the continuity of the original *kedusha*.

### Derailment Case

If, however, the owner has already brought another *asham* — *ve'im kariv ashamo* — then this animal is now genuinely *nitkapru be'aleha be'acher*, the owner has been atoned by a different animal. At that point the female *asham* is fully derailed, and *yiplu dameha l'nedavah* — the proceeds go to *nedavah*, the communal *olah* fund. The distinction between these two outcomes turns entirely on whether genuine derailment has occurred or whether the animal simply requires replacement due to a formal disqualification.

### Rabbi Shimon Opinion

Rabbi Shimon takes a dissenting position: *timacher shelo b'mum* — the wrong gender is itself equivalent to a *mum* for purposes of redemption. In his view, the practical inability of the female to ever be brought as an *asham* functions halakhically like a blemish, and therefore the animal may be redeemed without waiting for a physical defect to develop. The majority position, as reflected in the first clause of the *mishna*, is that gender mismatch is not equivalent to a *mum* and the animal must wait for an actual blemish before redemption is available.

---

---

# Temurah 20

## Female Asham

### Opening & Overview

Daf 20 opens in the middle of the *mishnah* on 19b, which deals with *temurah* and *vladot* — the offspring — of various *korbanot*. The preceding discussion had already covered *zevach todah*, *shelamim*, and *olah*. By *shelamim*, the offspring follows the same *halacha* as the parent animal. By *todah*, things are slightly different: the *lechem* is not brought for the offspring. And by *olah*, the interesting complication is that an *olah* itself cannot directly produce a *vlad* in the ordinary sense, so the discussion there concerned the *vlad* of a *temurah* of an *olah* — whether a male offspring in that position could itself be brought, or whether it follows the original animal's status.

The question turned on whether the animal that originated the chain could itself be brought. If one was *makdish* a female *olah*, the calculus shifts, since the original could not be brought at all. With that background established, the *mishnah* now turns to the *asham* — specifically, a female *asham*.

### Female Asham Problem

The question posed is: what does one do with a female animal designated as an *asham*? An *asham* must be male. This animal is not one of the five *chataot* that die when they cannot be brought; it simply cannot be brought because it is the wrong gender. The *halacha* is that one waits until it acquires a *mum* — a blemish — and only then redeems it, transferring the funds toward a proper *asham*.

The *gemara* presses: why wait for a *mum* at all? The animal cannot be used — *kivan d'lo chazi l'miti haynu mum*, the very fact that it cannot be brought should itself be equivalent to a *mum*, and it should be redeemable immediately. One might add that the question is even sharper here than in a case like a *treifah* that became unfit after sanctification. Here, the animal was never fit from the moment of consecration — it could never have received *kedushat haguf* in the first place.

### Transform Doctrine

Rav Yehuda amar Rav provides the answer: *migu d'nachit lei kedushat damim nachit nami kedushat haguf* — since it descended into *kedushat damim*, it also descended into *kedushat haguf*. The *gemara* takes for granted that because this female animal cannot be brought, its basic *kedusha* is *kedushat damim* — the sanctity of its monetary value — rather than *kedushat haguf*, the sanctity of the body itself that would allow it to be offered on the *mizbe'ach*. *Kedushat damim* means one uses the proceeds; the animal itself is not a *korban*.

If that is so, why does one need a *mum* to redeem it? The answer is that although it starts as *kedushat damim*, it transforms and rises to *kedushat haguf* — and since it has *kedushat haguf*, it requires a *mum* for redemption. One senses a certain circularity in this reasoning: the whole question was why it should need a *mum* if it can never be brought, and the answer essentially says that because it is fit enough, it gets upgraded — but the explanation of why the upgrade occurs in this case is not fully elaborated.

Rashi frames this carefully: the upgrade to *kedushat haguf* is only *l'milsa d'ba'ei mum* — to the degree that it cannot be redeemed without a *mum* — not to the degree that it could actually be offered. So the *kedushat haguf* here is a partial one. The implicit logic seems to be that while a *mum* renders an animal automatically redeemable by Torah law, preventing it from ever reaching *kedushat haguf*, wrong gender is not treated with the same severity. The animal is otherwise fit; it lacks only the required gender. Therefore, although it enters with *kedushat damim*, because it is close enough — being an unblemished animal of the right species — it transforms into *kedushat haguf*. The question of why wrong gender is treated differently from *mum* is, as the lecturer acknowledges, not fully resolved by the *gemara*; it is, to some degree, simply stated as the operative rule.

### Rava's Logic

From this principle, Rava draws a further inference: *hamakdish zachar lidamav kadosh kedushat haguf* — if one consecrates a male animal for its *damim*, intending to use the proceeds toward an *asham* or *olah* rather than bringing the animal itself, the animal automatically acquires *kedushat haguf*. This statement has appeared before in the tractate. The logic seems even stronger here than in the female *asham* case: if you are consecrating a male animal specifically so that its proceeds fund this type of *korban*, and the animal itself is perfectly suited to serve as that *korban*, why would we honor the artificial distinction and not treat the animal as already having *kedushat haguf*?

Yet one might question whether this inference flows naturally from the female *asham* case. There, the *kedushat haguf* arose despite the animal never being fit for the designated use. Here, the animal is entirely fit — the person simply tried to give it the lesser consecration of *kedushat damim*. The *gemara* acknowledges this is something of a logical leap: in the previous case, *kedushat haguf* arose even where the upgrade made the animal no more eligible to be brought; here the upgrade is more intuitive since the animal actually can be brought.

### Rav Kahana vs. Rava

The *gemara* then reveals that this *hamakdish zachar lidamav* principle was actually the subject of a debate. Rav Kahana held: *kadosh kedushat haguf* — it does receive *kedushat haguf*. Rava originally held: *eino kadosh kedushat haguf* — it does not automatically receive *kedushat haguf*. Ultimately, *v'hadar bei Rava legabei d'Rav Kahana mi'd'Rav Yehuda amar Rav* — Rava retracted his position in favor of Rav Kahana's, based on the very teaching of Rav Yehuda amar Rav about the female *asham* and the transformation from *kedushat damim* to *kedushat haguf*.

The underlying difficulty remains: once you grant the upgrade in the female *asham* case, the upgrade in the *hamakdish zachar lidamav* case follows even more naturally. But neither the female *asham* case nor the male *damim* case fully explains, from first principles, *why* a *kedushat damim* that was placed on a fit animal automatically upgrades. The *gemara* simply establishes that it does.

### Rabbi Shimon's View

The *mishnah* records that *Rabbi Shimon* takes a different view. He holds that a female *asham* can be redeemed even without a *mum* — *timacher shelo b'mum*. The *gemara* now challenges this: *migo d'necheta lei kedushat damim necheta lei nami kedushat haguf* — by the same principle that it acquired *kedushat damim*, should it not also acquire *kedushat haguf*, and thereby require a *mum* for redemption?

The *gemara*'s challenge reveals how it is conceptualizing Rabbi Shimon's position. Rabbi Shimon is not saying that wrong gender is equivalent to a *mum* — there is nothing physically wrong with the animal. Rather, the *gemara* understands him as saying: this was the wrong type of thing to consecrate for this purpose, and therefore it never acquired *kedushat haguf* at all. Just as if one consecrated an inanimate object for an *olah*, it would only receive *kedushat damim* with no possibility of *kedushat haguf*, so too an animal of the wrong gender for this *korban* receives only *kedushat damim*.

The *gemara* responds: *Rabbi Shimon l'taamei* — Rabbi Shimon is consistent with his broader position. He holds *kol midi d'la chazi l'gufei lo nechis lei kedushat haguf* — anything that cannot be brought itself does not descend into *kedushat haguf*. A *braita* reinforces this with the case of *asham ben shana v'hevio ben shtayim* — an *asham* requiring a one-year-old animal where the owner consecrated a two-year-old, or vice versa. The *tanna kamma* holds that the animal has *kedushat haguf* and may be offered, though it does not fulfill the owner's obligation. Rabbi Shimon says *kol atzman einan kedoshin* — they fundamentally do not have *kedushat haguf*, only *kedushat damim*, so the proceeds are used but the animal itself cannot be brought.

It is important to note that Rabbi Shimon is not invoking the concept of a *mum* here at all. A two-year-old animal is not blemished in any sense, and if it were designated for a different type of *asham* it could well be brought. The point is simply: if it is not fit for what you tried to consecrate it for, it receives only *kedushat damim*. This case, where the same species of *korban* exists in both one-year and two-year versions, makes even clearer that Rabbi Shimon's principle goes beyond wrong gender and extends to any situation of mismatch between the animal and its designated purpose.

---

## Gender & Category

### Challenge to Shimon

The *gemara* now challenges Rabbi Shimon's position. If his principle is that anything unfit for its designated purpose never receives *kedushat haguf*, how does he handle the case of *mechusar zman* — an animal less than eight days old, which cannot yet be offered? In another context, Rabbi Shimon himself holds that if one consecrated such an animal and then slaughtered it outside the *Beis Hamikdash*, one is liable for *shechutei chutz* — a liability that only applies to animals with *kedushat korban*. This implies that even a *mechusar zman* has *kedushat haguf* according to Rabbi Shimon — so why is it any different from a wrong-gender animal?

The *gemara* answers: *shani mechusar zman dechazi lemachar* — a *mechusar zman* is different because it will naturally become fit in a matter of days. It is not truly outside the category; it will come into the category on its own.

The *gemara* immediately presses: if so, then an *asham ben shtayim* that was supposed to be *ben shana* will also naturally become fit in the future — why should Rabbi Shimon say it lacks *kedushat haguf*? The *gemara* responds: the logic of *mechusar zman* is not a general principle about future fitness; it derives from a specific *pasuk* learned from *bechor*. As the *braita* states, Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda said in the name of Rabbi Shimon: a *mechusar zman* can be included in one's flock when counting *maaser behemah* — just as a *bechor* is sanctified from birth but can only be brought after eight days, so too any animal can be consecrated before it is eight days old. This is a special scriptural exception for *mechusar zman*, not a general principle. Absent that exception, if it cannot presently be brought, it would only receive *kedushat damim*.

The *gemara* emphasizes a crucial point in its framing of Rabbi Shimon's position: nowhere does it treat wrong gender as a *mum*. The framework throughout is that if the thing cannot be brought, it is *like* consecrating an inanimate object — it receives only *kedushat damim*, not *kedushat haguf*. The *chachamim*, by contrast, hold that it always receives *kedushat haguf*. The most satisfying way to understand the *chachamim*'s position — though the *gemara* does not spell this out — is probably that since the animal is otherwise unblemished and could be used for some type of *korban*, it remains sufficiently within the world of *korbanot* to receive *kedushat haguf*. A car, or a *baal mum*, or perhaps a *treifah*, is categorically outside. A female sheep, or a two-year-old when a one-year-old is needed, is not categorically outside — it simply does not fit this particular slot, and that, according to the *chachamim*, is enough for the upgrade.

### Pesach Exception

The *mishnah* now presents the broader application. *Hamakdish nekeiva le'olato lepischo ule'ashamo* — if one consecrates a female animal for one's *olah*, one's *pesach*, or one's *asham* — the *tanna kamma* holds that these animals perform *temurah* (i.e., they have *kedushat haguf* and require a *mum* for redemption). Rabbi Shimon holds: *le'olato oseh tmura lepischo ule'ashamo eino oseh tmura* — a female designated for an *olah* does make *temurah*, but a female designated for a *pesach* or an *asham* does not. His reasoning: *she'ein lecha davar oseh tmura ela haraui lehista'ev* — only something for which one would need to wait for a *mum* before redeeming can make a *temurah*. Since, in his view, a female *asham* and female *pesach* have only *kedushat damim*, they require no *mum* and therefore cannot make *temurah*. His concession of *olah* remains to be explained.

At this point, *Rebbe* — Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi — enters with a comment: *eini ro'eh divrei Rabbi Shimon bePesach* — he cannot agree with Rabbi Shimon regarding *pesach*. A female designated for a *pesach* should receive *kedushat haguf*, because *ho'il umotar pesach karev shelamim* — leftover animals from a *pesach* context (a substitute found after the original was offered, etc.) are brought as *shelamim*. Since a *pesach* can in certain circumstances transform into a *shelamim*, and *shelamim* can be female, a female designated for a *pesach* is not a complete category mismatch. It retains some relevance, and therefore does receive *kedushat haguf*.

The *gemara* then considers: by this same logic, why doesn't Rebbe also challenge Rabbi Shimon regarding *asham*? An *asham* that cannot be brought can in certain circumstances transform into an *olah*. Since Rabbi Shimon concedes the case of *olah* (as we will see), a female *asham* is potentially close enough to a female *olah*, and female *olah* is something Rabbi Shimon grants. Why, then, doesn't Rebbe make the same argument for *asham* as he made for *pesach*?

The answer: *Rebbe savar lah keRabbanan de'amri mosros linedvas tzibur azli* — Rebbe holds that when an *asham* transforms into an *olah*, it becomes a *nedavat tzibur*, a communal *olah*. And *ein temurah betzibur* — there is no *temurah* from communal *korbanot*. Since the entire question in the *mishnah* is framed around the capacity to make *temurah*, not simply whether the animal has *kedushat haguf* in the abstract, there is no way a female *asham* could ever make *temurah* even if we granted it *kedushat haguf* — because any *olah* it might approach the status of would be outside the *temurah* framework entirely.

### Olah Concession

Why does Rabbi Shimon concede the *olah* case? The *gemara* suggests: *d'ha ika shem olah aleiah gabei olas ha'of* — because there is such a thing as a female *olah*, namely the *olat ha'of*, a bird *olah*. The *gemara* establishes that *tamus v'zachrus b'behema v'ein tamus v'zachrus b'of* — the requirements of gender and unblemished status apply to animal offerings but not to bird offerings. Birds can be either gender, and even blemished birds may be offered (the only disqualification for birds being a missing limb). Therefore, a female *olah* is not a category that is entirely nonexistent; a female bird can be an *olah*. This makes a female animal designated as an *olah* close enough to the category that Rabbi Shimon grants it *kedushat haguf*.

The *gemara* now tests this reasoning. If female is relevant for *olah* because of *olat ha'of*, perhaps Rabbi Shimon should also concede other cases where a female version of the same type of *korban* exists in some context. For instance, a *kohen gadol* who consecrated a female cow (*parah*) instead of the required male bull (*par*) for his *Yom Kippur* service — should Rabbi Shimon concede that case, since there is such a thing as *parat chatat* in the form of the *parah adumah*? The *gemara* answers: *kodshei bedek habayit* — the *parah adumah* belongs to the category of *bedek habayit* sanctity, not *korban* sanctity. Since *kodshei bedek habayit lo avdi temurah*, it is outside the framework of *temurah* entirely and cannot make the female category relevant.

Tosafot raises a pointed question here: there are plenty of female *chataot* — individual sin offerings are typically female sheep or goats — so why does the *gemara* reach all the way to *parah adumah*? Tosafot answers that the relevant comparison is not merely whether such an animal type exists in some *korban* category somewhere, but whether *you yourself, in your circumstances*, could have brought such an animal instead. This is what makes the *olat ha'of* so central: any person who is obligated in an *olah* could in theory have discharged that obligation with a bird *olah*. The alternative has to be personally relevant. The *gemara*'s use of *parah adumah* remains somewhat puzzling even within Tosafot's framework, since the *kohen gadol* would not use the *parah adumah* for his *Yom Kippur* service, but that difficulty is noted and left without a fully satisfying resolution.

### Testing Limits

The *gemara* continues to probe. If one takes Rabbi Shimon's logic to its endpoint — that any case where the alternate gender might be personally relevant gives the animal *kedushat haguf* — should not a male animal consecrated for a female *chatat* also be granted *kedushat haguf*, since a *nasi* who sinned brings a male goat (*se'ir*), and female individuals bring female goats (*se'irah*)? Might a male goat be considered relevant to the *chatat* category?

The *gemara* goes through several permutations. What if the *nasi* sinned before his appointment? He must bring a female *se'irah* for that sin, since at the time of sin he was a commoner. If he accidentally designated a male instead, should Rabbi Shimon say it has *kedushat haguf* because now, as *nasi*, he would bring a male? The *gemara* rejects this: *ha lo cheit lo chayav b'se'ir* — he has not sinned as a *nasi*, and the male is not relevant to the sin at hand. What makes something "relevant" in Rabbi Shimon's calculus is whether the alternate gender is relevant specifically to this person for this particular obligation — not whether there exists some other circumstance under which this person might bring the other gender.

### Bird Alternative

This principle of personal relevance is what resolves the *olah* case. The *gemara* asks: even granting that a bird *olah* can be female, when this person consecrates a sheep as an *olah*, he is not bringing a bird. Why should a female *olat ha'of* be considered relevant to him?

The *gemara* answers: *Rabbi Shimon savar lah k'Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah*. As a *mishnah* elsewhere records, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah holds that if one says *harei alai olah* — "I am obligating myself in an *olah*" — one may discharge that obligation by bringing *tor o bnei yonah*, pigeons or turtledoves. Even a person of means, when undertaking a voluntary *olah* obligation, retains the option of fulfilling it with a bird. Therefore, the *olat ha'of* is not an irrelevant category for this person — it is a genuine alternative available to him. A female is relevant to his *olah* obligation because the bird option, which has no gender restriction, is always open to him. This is sufficient for Rabbi Shimon to grant *kedushat haguf* for a female *olah*.

This brings the entire analysis into focus. Rabbi Shimon's position is coherent and consistent: if the animal is not fit for what was intended, it receives only *kedushat damim*. The one case where he concedes is where, for this person in this context, the alternate gender is genuinely relevant — as it is for *olah*, since a female bird *olah* is always an option. The *tanna kamma* holds that any animal within the general category of *korbanot* (not a *baal mum*, not an inanimate object) always receives *kedushat haguf*. The *gemara* never fully articulates why the *chachamim* grant the upgrade, though the implication is that animals which could be used as some type of *korban* — even if not the intended one — retain sufficient connection to the world of *korbanot* to receive *kedushat haguf*.

---

## Property Sanctificat (II)

### Eliezer View

A *mishnah* cited from *Shekalim* now introduces a related question. If someone says *hamakdish nechasav* — "I consecrate all my property to the *beis hamikdash*" — and among his property are unblemished animals fit for the *mizbe'ach*, both male and female, what happens to those animals?

Rabbi Eliezer holds that the *kedusha* is uniform: just as his house, his vessels, and his money all go to the Temple treasury (*bedek habayit*), so too the animals go to the Temple treasury. Nevertheless, because there is a principle that once an animal fit for the *mizbe'ach* comes under *hekdesh* control we seek to ensure it reaches the altar, Rabbi Eliezer says the animals should be sold — males to people who need to bring *olot*, females to people who need to bring *shelamim*. The proceeds revert to the Temple treasury. The *kedusha* on the animals is *kedushat bedek habayit*, not *kedushat korban*, but the principle of ensuring they reach the *mizbe'ach* is honored by directing their sale to those bringing *korbanot*.

---

## Property Sanctificat (II)

### Yehoshua View

Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees. When a person consecrates animals along with his property, the implicit *kedusha* he places on unblemished animals fit for the *mizbe'ach* is *kedushat korban*, not *kedushat bedek habayit*. People naturally associate animals with *korbanot*. Moreover, since an *olah* represents the fullest form of giving to the *beis hamikdash* — unlike a *shelamim*, where the owner retakes most of the meat — the translation of this consecration is that the animals are treated as *olot*. Therefore, *zcharim atzman yikrevu olot* — the males are brought directly as *olot*. As for the females, they are sold to people bringing *shelamim*, and those proceeds are used to purchase an *olah*.

### Female Olah Issue

This immediately raises a difficulty. If the males are brought directly with *kedushat haguf* as *olot*, then the females, by the same logic, also have *kedushat haguf* as *olot*. But if so, how can they be sold without a *mum*? Rabbi Shimon — and even the *tanna kamma* — required a *mum* before redeeming a female *olah*. The *gemara* presses: *ba'aya re'iya* — it needs to graze, it needs to acquire a *mum*. You cannot simply sell an unblemished female with *kedushat haguf* and use the proceeds for something else.

### Yehoshua Agrees Shimon

The *gemara* resolves this: *Rabbi Yehoshua savar lei k'Rabbi Shimon* — Rabbi Yehoshua holds in accordance with Rabbi Shimon's opinion in our *mishnah*, that *kol midi d'lo chazi lei l'gufei lo nachsi lei kedushat haguf* — whatever cannot be brought itself does not receive *kedushat haguf*, only *kedushat damim*. Therefore, the female animals, though consecrated as *olot*, never receive *kedushat haguf* — they have only *kedushat damim* — and can be sold without a *mum*. The proceeds carry the *kedusha* that was on the females and are used to purchase an *olah*. Rabbi Yehoshua thus aligns himself with a particular reading of Rabbi Shimon — specifically the reading that a female *olah* does not receive *kedushat haguf* — which corresponds to the dissenting *tanna* cited earlier: *Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda omer mishum Rabbi Shimon: af le-olah eino oseh temurah*.

---

## Temurah & Vlad

### Mishna Law

The *mishnah* now addresses directly what happens to a *temurah* of an *asham* and its offspring. If one has a *temurah* of an *asham* — or the *vlad* of that *temurah*, or the *vlad* of a *vlad*, down through all generations — the rule is *yiru ad she'yista'avu v'yimachru v'yipelu dmeihem l'nedava*: they graze until they acquire a *mum*, are sold, and the proceeds go to *nedava* — a communal *olah*. This parallels the general treatment of a *temurah* of an *asham*: whereas a *temurah* of a *chatat* is left to die, a *temurah* of an *asham* grazes and the money is used for an *olah*.

### Eliezer Dissent

Rabbi Eliezer dissents: *yamutu* — they die. His position identifies the *asham* with the *chatat* in this respect. The *gemara* will clarify that his reasoning is not a fundamental equation of *asham* and *chatat* but a rabbinic precaution, as we will see shortly.

### Elazar Dissent

Rabbi Elazar dissents in the opposite direction: *yavi bidmei olot* — one brings an *olah* with their proceeds. This, as the *mishnah* itself will immediately clarify, means a private *olah* rather than a communal one.

---

## Asham Derailment

### Five Cases

The *mishnah* then widens the discussion to all the cases in which an *asham* becomes unavailable for its intended purpose — cases that parallel the *chatat* that dies. These include: *asham she'meitu ba'alav* — the owners died; *she'nitkapru ba'alav ba'acher* — they were atoned for by another animal; *temurah*; *vlad*; and an animal that has exceeded its valid age. These five situations present the question of what becomes of a derailed *asham*.

### Default Halacha

The default ruling: *yiru ad she'yista'avu v'yimachru v'yipelu dmeihem l'nedava* — they graze until blemished, are sold, and the proceeds go to a communal *olah* (*nedavat tzibur*). Rabbi Eliezer says they die. Rabbi Elazar says they are used for a private *olah*.

### Private vs. Communal

The *mishnah* itself poses the question: given that both the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Elazar are directing the animal or its proceeds toward an *olah*, what is the practical difference between them?

### Private Olah Details

If it is a private *olah*, as Rabbi Elazar holds: the owner performs *semicha* on it; he must supply the *nesachim* — the wine, oil, and flour libations — at his own expense; if he is a *kohen* and brings his own *korban*, he may perform the *avoda* that day regardless of which *mishmar* is on duty, and the hide of the animal belongs to him.

### Communal Details

If it is a communal *olah* (*nedava*), as the *tanna kamma* holds: there is no *semicha*, since *semicha* applies only to private *korbanot* brought by an individual owner; the *nesachim* are funded from communal resources, not the individual's; and even if the person happens to be a *kohen*, he has no special right to perform the *avoda* — the *kohanim* of the assigned *mishmar* for that week perform the service and retain the hide.

---

## Timing Doctrine

### Eliezer's Logic

The *gemara* now returns to Rabbi Eliezer's position that the *temurah* and *vlad* die, and clarifies that the *mishnah* needed to state his ruling in both contexts — both in the case of *temurah* and *vlad*, and in the case of *meitu ba'alav* and *nitkapru b'acher*.

Had the *mishnah* stated his ruling only in the case where owners died or were atoned for elsewhere, one might have thought that Rabbi Eliezer's concern there is specifically: *mishum degazar achar kapara atu lifnei kapara* — he decrees that the animal must die after atonement as a precaution against doing so before atonement. If we were to permit the original *asham* to be redeemed and its proceeds used for an *olah* after the special circumstances arise, people might come to redeem the original *asham* even before those circumstances arise, conflating "after atonement" with "before atonement." But this concern applies only to the original *asham*. For the *temurah* and *vlad* — which are not the original — one might think Rabbi Eliezer agrees with the *rabbanan* and permits them to graze, since nobody will make any mistake there. Had the *mishnah* stated his ruling only for *temurah* and *vlad*, one might think that there the *rabbanan* perhaps also concede that the original *asham* should die, lest we come to redeem it prematurely. Therefore, *tzericha* — both cases are necessary.

### After Atonement

The *gemara* records a teaching from Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha: *zu machlokes le-achar kaparah* — the three-way debate of the *mishnah* (die, communal *olah*, private *olah*) applies only after the owner has already received his atonement. *Aval lifnei kaparah* — but before the owner has achieved atonement, using the original first *asham* — *divrei hakol hu atzmo yikarev asham*: everyone agrees that the *temurah* or *vlad* itself can be brought as an *asham*.

### Rava Rejects

Rava rejects this emphatically: *shtei teshuvos badavar* — two responses. First: *ein adam miskaper bedavar haba ba-aveira* — one cannot achieve atonement through something that itself came through a transgression. Performing a *temurah* is itself an *aveira*; the *temurah* is a product of sin. To suggest that this product of sin can serve as a proper *asham* to atone for sin is inconceivable. An *asham*'s entire purpose is atonement, and something produced through transgression cannot serve that purpose.

Second, Rava cites the teaching of Rabbi Chanina, brought in support of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who held that a *vlad rishon* — the first-generation offspring — can be brought as a *korban*, but a *vlad sheni* — a second-generation offspring — cannot. Since one of the cases in the *mishnah* involves the *vlad* of the *temurah* — which is two degrees removed from the original — the suggestion that this animal could itself be brought as an *asham* is ruled out on this ground as well.

### Clarification

The *gemara* therefore corrects the formulation: *ela i itmar hachi itmar* — if Rav Nachman's teaching was indeed transmitted, here is how it should be understood. The three-way debate — die, communal *olah*, private *olah* — applies *kodem kapara*, before the owner has used the original *asham* and received atonement. *Aval le-achar kapara* — but once the owner has already used the original *asham* and been atoned for, *hu atzmo karev olah* — the *temurah* or *vlad* itself may be brought directly as an *olah*, rather than the roundabout procedure of grazing until blemished, selling, and using the proceeds.

The reasoning: once the original *asham* has been brought, the animal is no longer under the shadow of an *asham* obligation. The *asham* identity has been discharged. This remaining animal is heading toward an *olah* one way or another — why not use it directly? Before the original *asham* was brought, the animal still exists in an *asham* context and the identity of *temurah* or *vlad* of an *asham* constrains it. But once the original has been offered and the *asham* obligation is fully resolved, the animal can proceed directly to be brought as an *olah*, at least if it is male and otherwise fit.

The *gemara* concludes with *kasha* — a difficulty remains. If the case involves a *vlad* of the *temurah*, that is two degrees removed, and the teaching of Rabbi Chanina cited above indicates that a second-generation offspring cannot be brought. This difficulty stands unresolved.

---

---

# Temurah 21

## Female Asham & Offspring

### Question on Female Asham

The *gemara* picks up five lines from the wide lines on 21b with a question posed by one *amora* to another: *ba'ei minei Rabbi Avin bar Chiya me'Rabbi Avin bar Kahana* — Rabbi Avin bar Chiya asked Rabbi Avin bar Kahana: if one consecrated a female animal for an *asham*, what is the law regarding her offspring? Can the offspring be brought as an *olah*?

The background to this question is as follows. When a female animal is consecrated for an *asham*, it cannot be brought as an *asham*, since an *asham* requires a male. The normal consequence for an *asham* that becomes derailed — whether through *temurah*, through the owner having achieved atonement through another animal, or otherwise — is that one waits for it to acquire a *mum*, redeems it, and uses the proceeds to purchase an *olah*. So the question becomes: once the offspring of this female *asham* happens to be male, why not simply bring the animal itself as an *olah* rather than waiting for a *mum* and using the proceeds?

### Earlier Discussion Refer…

The *gemara* observes that this very question appears to have been addressed in an earlier discussion: *tifshotei mid'Rabbi Yochanan bar Chanina* — the matter can seemingly be resolved from the earlier teaching in which Rabbi Yochanan bar Chanina weighed in on a structurally similar case. The earlier *mishna* discussed the *temurat olah* and its offspring, where Rabbi Eliezer maintained that once you arrive at a male you may bring it as an *olah*. One might assume the same reasoning applies here: a female consecrated for an *asham* produces a male offspring, and since derailed *asham* funds go toward an *olah*, why not bring the thing itself?

But the earlier discussion distinguished between the cases. There, when one consecrated a female for an *olah* — or when a male *olah* produced a *temurah* and then offspring — whenever one ultimately arrives at a male, the *kedusha* one is bringing it under (*olah*) matches the *kedusha* of the original. Here, however, the original *kedusha* was that of an *asham*, and what one now seeks to bring is an *olah*. Since the proposed *kedusha* of the derivative does not match the *kedusha* of its origin, Rabbi Yochanan bar Chanina had implied that even Rabbi Eliezer would agree one cannot bring it.

The *gemara* then explains why the question is being asked afresh: *lo shmi'a lei* — Rabbi Avin bar Chiya was simply not party to that earlier discussion, and wished to reason through the matter himself.

### Avin's Response

Rabbi Avin bar Kahana's response cuts against the earlier reasoning: *benah yikrav olah* — the male offspring may indeed be brought as an *olah*. His reasoning is that Rabbi Eliezer's position should not be read so narrowly as to require that the derivative's *kedusha* match the original. Rather, *mishum d'chazi l'akrava* — the operative principle for Rabbi Eliezer is simply that once the animal is fit to be brought, you bring it. There is no requirement that it carry the identical *kedusha* as the original.

### Challenge from Mishnah

The *gemara* challenges this reading from our own *mishna*. Our *mishna* addressed the case of the offspring of a *temurat asham*, a structurally similar case — the original *kedusha* was *asham*, and now one is dealing with a derivative. In that *mishna*, Rabbi Eliezer says *vlad u'vlad vlad ad sof kol ha'olam yavi bidmeihem olah* — the offspring and their offspring until the end of time: use the proceeds for an *olah*. The *mishna* says *bidmeihen* — their monetary value is used; *atzman lo* — the animals themselves are not brought, even once one arrives at a male.

This appears to directly contradict the position that Rabbi Eliezer would allow bringing the animal itself. One might anticipate a simple resolution: our *mishna* is discussing the case of a *temurat asham*, where the *halacha* of waiting for a *mum* and using the proceeds is already established at the level of the *temurah* itself, and that *halacha* passes down to the offspring. Whereas the original question concerned a female consecrated directly for an *asham*, which never entered that category, and whose offspring might therefore be brought directly. The *gemara*, however, does not pursue this path.

### Resolving Contradiction

Instead, the *gemara* offers a different resolution: *k'gon she'yalda nekeiva* — perhaps our *mishna* is speaking of the scenario where only female offspring were produced. The *gemara* immediately presses: but the *mishna* says *vlad u'vlad vlad ad sof kol ha'olam* — across endless generations, did not even one male appear? The answer given is: *meshanyinan shinuyei d'chika b'Vavel* — this is one of those forced Babylonian-style answers. Yes, the scenario is that females were born for the entire lineage.

It is striking that the *gemara* itself frames this as a strained answer, characteristic of Babylonian *amoraim*, who were sometimes depicted by their colleagues in *Eretz Yisrael* as offering *kvetch* resolutions. Rabbi Avin bar Kahana appears to be an *amora* of *Eretz Yisrael*, and the framing here preserves that ambient tension in the tradition. The *gemara* notes that some versions contain an additional, marginally better answer — found in the *Shita Mekubetzet* — which reads the *mishna* as addressing the case of a female, with the male case simply left unaddressed rather than explicitly excluded. The *Gra* suggests yet another possibility, though the distinction between these resolutions is not dramatic. In either reading, the takeaway is that one cannot straightforwardly resolve the question of the female *asham*'s male offspring from this *mishna*, and Rabbi Avin bar Kahana's position — that the male offspring may be brought directly as an *olah* — retains its standing.

---

## Bechor & Maaser Rules

### Bechor/Maaser Intro

With those intricate discussions behind us, the *perek* concludes with a far more accessible sugya as the *gemara* transitions from *asham* and *olah* to *bechor* and *maaser*. A brief word of background is in order. The *halacha* of *bechor u'ma'aser* is different from all other *korbanot* in a fundamental way. The *pasuk* states *lo yimacher velo yiga'el* — they cannot be sold or redeemed. If they acquire a *mum*, you do not redeem them and transfer the value toward another *korban*. Instead, they retain their *kedusha*, are slaughtered outside the *Beis HaMikdash*, and are eaten — the *bechor* by the *kohen*, and *maaser* by any *Yisrael*.

The same principle extends to *temurah*. If one makes a *temurah* from a *bechor* or *maaser*, that *temurah* is not brought as a *korban*. The *gemara* derives this from *pesukim*, but the underlying logic is compelling on its own terms: *kedushah* of *bechor* and *kedushas ma'aser* cannot be transferred to an animal that is not inherently a firstborn or a tenth. Such a *temurah* can never achieve the full status of *bechor* or *maaser* and therefore cannot be brought on the altar. The resolution is the same as with the original animal: wait for a *mum*, then eat it outside the *Beis HaMikdash*.

### Mishnah Text

The *mishna* states: *temurat habechor ve'hama'aser* — the *temurah* of a *bechor* and *maaser*, along with *vladan u'vlad vladan ad sof ha'olam* — their offspring and the offspring of their offspring until the end of time — *harei elu kebechor u'kema'aser*: they carry the same *kedusha* as *bechor* and *maaser*. This means not that they are brought as *korbanot*, but that they share the same *din*: *veyeachlu bemumam labe'alim* — one waits for a *mum* to appear and they are then eaten by their owners.

One point worth noting: *bechor* is by definition male, so there cannot be direct offspring of a *bechor* itself. But *maaser* can be female, allowing for direct offspring of the *maaser* animal. In either case — whether offspring of the *temurah* or direct offspring of a *maaser* — the same *halacha* applies: they are not brought as *korbanot*.

### Marketplace Restriction

The *mishna* then asks: *mah bein bechor u'maiser levein kol hakodashim* — what distinguishes *bechor* and *maaser* from all other *korbanot*? The answer: *shekol hakodashim nimkarin be'itliz venishchatin be'itliz venishkalin belitra* — all other *kodashim* that acquire a *mum* may be sold in the meat market, slaughtered in the meat market, and weighed out by the pound. *Chutz min habechor vehama'aser* — except for *bechor* and *maaser*.

The reasoning behind permitting the sale of other *kodashim* in the marketplace is essentially one of maximizing the transfer value. When an animal that was consecrated as a *korban* acquires a *mum*, one redeems its monetary value and uses those funds to purchase a replacement *korban*. Retail sale yields a higher price than wholesale, so *chazal* permitted even the indignity of selling it like ordinary meat — slaughtered and weighed in the market — because the proceeds benefit *hekdesh*. The greater the sale price, the greater the value transferred toward the next *korban*.

By contrast, *bechor* and *maaser* are never redeemed and their value is never transferred to another *korban*. The owner simply eats the animal himself. Since *hekdesh* gains nothing from a higher price, there is no basis to permit treating the animal with such disregard; we insist instead that it be sold privately, wholesale, in deference to the *kedusha* it still retains. One might add that unlike other *kodashim* whose *kedusha* has been transferred away at the time of redemption, *bechor* and *maaser* retain their *kedusha* throughout — an additional reason to handle them with greater care.

### No Redemption

The *mishna* continues: *veyesh lahem pidyon utmuratan pidyon* — all other *kodashim* that acquire a *mum* can be redeemed, and so too their *temurah* if it acquires a *mum*. *Chutz min habechor vehama'aser* — but *bechor* and *maaser* cannot be redeemed; a *mum* does not trigger redemption but simply permits eating outside the *Beis HaMikdash*.

### Outside Eretz Yisrael

The *mishna* also states that all other *korbanot* may be brought from *chutz la'aretz*, whereas *bechor* and *maaser* may not be brought from outside *Eretz Yisrael* — though Rashi explains that *bedi'avad*, if they were brought unblemished, they are offered as *korbanot*. If they arrived with a *mum*, one eats them outside the *Beis HaMikdash* as one would in any case.

---

## Rabbi Shimon Explained

### Parnasa Argument

Rabbi Shimon explains why *bechor* and *maaser* should not be brought from *chutz la'aretz*: *shehabechor vehama'aser yesh lahem parnasa mimkomam* — *bechor* and *maaser* can be "sustained" where they are. Since they may be eaten outside the *Beis HaMikdash* once they acquire a *mum*, they can be dealt with locally. If one is in *chutz la'aretz* and possesses a *bechor* or *maaser* that has a *mum*, or waits until it acquires one, there is no need to transport the animal to *Eretz Yisrael*.

### Other Korbanot Transfer

By contrast, all other *korbanot* — even if they acquire a *mum* — must have their value transferred and a replacement *korban* brought. There is no way to "resolve" the matter outside the *Beis HaMikdash*. Since those animals must come to ירושלים in any case, the *halacha* accepts them from *chutz la'aretz*.

This reasoning raises a question that remains somewhat open: it explains why an individual *in* *chutz la'aretz* might personally prefer to handle a *bechor* or *maaser* locally, but it does not fully explain why *we* — as a matter of *halacha* — prefer that they remain in *chutz la'aretz* rather than seize the opportunity to come to *Eretz Yisrael* and bring a *korban*. *Tosafot* addresses this, and one might conjecture a practical concern: during the *regalim*, when pilgrims gathered in *Yerushalayim*, the volume of *bechor* and *maaser* animals arriving from the *diaspora* would have been enormous, and the policy may have been designed to manage that logistical burden. This question will resurface; indeed, the first *mishna* of a later *perek* opens with the striking heading *keitzad maarimin al habechor* — how does one use a legitimate stratagem to avoid the obligation of *bechor* — itself a testament to how seriously *chazal* took finding workable solutions within the framework of *halacha*.

---

## Making Blemish Permitted?

### Rav Aha Question

The *gemara* now records a question posed in *Eretz Yisrael*: *hamatil mum b'tmurat bechor u'maaser mahu* — what is the law if one intentionally makes a *mum* in an animal that is the *temurah* of a *bechor* or *maaser*, or the *vlad* of a *maaser*? There is a well-known prohibition against deliberately blemishing *kodashim*, but in this case the animal cannot be brought as a *korban* under any circumstances. Does the prohibition against *matil mum b'kodashim* apply even where the animal's being brought as a *korban* is entirely foreclosed? Or does the prohibition only apply where blemishing would actually prevent a *korban* from being offered?

This is a practically significant question. If one is left with such an animal and cannot bring it as a *korban*, one would naturally prefer to induce a *mum* and eat it rather than maintaining the animal indefinitely. The question is whether doing so constitutes a transgression.

### Abaye's Daisy-Chain

Abaye responds by redirecting the question: *v'tiba'ei lach hamatil mum b'tshii maaser* — why didn't you ask the same question about the ninth animal counted in *maaser behema*? If one miscounted and declared the ninth animal the tithe, it is *kadosh v'eino karev* — it has *kedushat maaser* but cannot be brought as a *korban*, because it is not the actual tenth. Can one make a *mum* in that animal? If you did not think to ask that question — presumably because you took for granted that since it cannot be brought there is no prohibition — then apply the same reasoning here.

The comparison works in both directions: *d'rachmana miatinhu* — in the case of *tmuras bechor u'maaser*, the Torah excluded their *temurah* from being brought, stating *kodesh hem — hem kreivin v'ein tmuratan kriva*, only the original animals are brought, not their *temurah*. And *ha'asiri v'hotzi et hatshii* — for *maaser*, the Torah specifies the tenth, thereby excluding the ninth. In both cases, the Torah's own language establishes that these animals cannot be offered.

### Conclusion: Permitted

The *gemara* records a second version of this exchange — attributed to Rav Pinchas the son of Rav Chisda — in which the question was actually posed about the ninth animal of *maaser*, and the response redirected to *tmuras bechor u'maaser*. In either direction, the logic is the same: each case takes the other's conclusion for granted, and from that mutual assumption the *gemara* concludes that it is permitted to make a *mum* in these animals, since they cannot be brought as *korbanot* regardless.

The *gemara* itself acknowledges that this reasoning is somewhat circular — the *pesukim* cited establish only that these animals are not brought, not that making a *mum* in them is therefore permitted. The conclusion is essentially reading an assumption back out of itself. Nevertheless, as the *gemara* frames it, that is indeed the operative conclusion: where an animal categorically cannot be brought as a *korban*, the prohibition against making a *mum* does not apply. The practical *nafka mina* is significant: one need not wait indefinitely for a *mum* to appear naturally but may induce one directly.

### Tosafot Distinction

*Tosafot* notes that one might have expected the *gemara* to relate this question to a parallel discussion in *Menachot* concerning whether one may make a *mum* in an animal that already possesses a *mum*. In that case too, the animal cannot be brought as a *korban* — so why doesn't that discussion resolve our question? *Tosafot* explains that the cases are not equivalent, and their answers need not be the same.

Two distinctions are offered. First, in the *Menachot* case, the animal started with a full *kedusha* capable of producing a *korban* and only subsequently became blemished. That original *kedusha* may retain its full protective force even once the animal can no longer be brought. Here, by contrast, the *kedusha* of *tmuras bechor* and *vlad maaser* was never capable of producing a *korban* from the outset, and the prohibition may simply never have applied with full force. Second, from the opposite direction: in the *Menachot* case, adding a *mum* to an already-blemished animal does not transform an unblemished *korban* into a blemished one, so the concern about degrading a *korban* is absent — yet even there it might be prohibited. Here, the animal is unblemished and making a *mum* is a meaningful act — yet it may still be permitted, because the prohibition is tied to the possibility of the animal's being brought. The two cases thus present different profiles, and *Tosafot* concludes that while they raise analogous questions, their outcomes are not interdependent.

---

## Three Tannaic Opini (III)ons

### Contradiction Setup

The *gemara* now addresses an apparent contradiction regarding bringing *bechor* from outside *Eretz Yisrael*. Our *mishna* implies that *bedi'avad*, if a *bechor* was brought from *chutz la'aretz* while unblemished, it is offered as a *korban*. Yet a *mishna* in *Challa* records that a certain Antignos brought *bechorot* up from *Bavel* and they were refused — even *bedi'avad*, they would not accept it. Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction: *ha Rabbi Yishmael ha Rabbi Akiva* — these represent the positions of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva respectively. A *braita* cited in the name of Rabbi Yossi records three traditions he received from three different elders. We now examine each in turn.

---

## Rabbi Akiva (III)

### Akiva's Distinction

Rabbi Akiva's position is: *yachol ya'aleh bechor michutz la'aretz la'aretz bizman sheBeis HaMikdash kayam veyakrivenu* — one might think a *bechor* could be brought from outside *Eretz Yisrael* when the *Beis HaMikdash* stands and offered as a *korban*, even *bedi'avad*. The Torah teaches otherwise from the verse *ve'achalta lifnei Hashem Elokecha maaser degancha tiroshcha ve'yitzharecha u'bechorot bekarcha ve'tzonecha* — you shall eat before God your *maaser* of grain and wine and oil and the firstborn of your cattle and flock. The verse links *bechor* to *maaser dagan*, and from that link Rabbi Akiva derives: *mimakom she'atah maaleh maaser dagan atah maaleh bechor* — only from the place where you bring *maaser* of grain do you bring your *bechor*. And *maaser dagan* is an agricultural obligation tied to *Eretz Yisrael* — one does not bring *maaser dagan* from *chutz la'aretz*. Therefore one does not bring *bechor* from *chutz la'aretz* either, even *bedi'avad*.

---

## Three Tannaic Opini (III)ons…

### Rabbi Yishmael

Rabbi Yishmael's position is that one simply cannot bring a *bechor* nowadays — meaning during the period when the *Beis HaMikdash* does not stand — and the question he explores is whether *maaser sheni* may still be eaten in *Yerushalayim*.

### Logical Derivation

Rabbi Yishmael poses a *kal vachomer*-style derivation: *bechor ta'un hava'at makom u'maaser ta'un hava'at makom* — both *bechor* and *maaser* must be brought to *Yerushalayim*. Just as *bechor* cannot be eaten without the *Beis HaMikdash* — because it must be offered on the *mizbe'ach* — perhaps *maaser sheni* likewise cannot be eaten without the *Beis HaMikdash*. The *braita* considers and rejects two possible analogies. First: learn from *bechor* — but *bechor* requires sprinkling blood and offering *imurim* on the *mizbe'ach*, which distinguishes it. Second: learn from *bikurim* — both *bikurim* and *maaser* require being brought to *Yerushalayim* without necessarily being burned on the *mizbe'ach*. But *bikurim* requires the ritual of *hanacha* — *vehinachto lifnei Hashem Elokecha* — a placement before the altar, connecting it to the *Beis HaMikdash*. *Maaser sheni* has no such ritual; perhaps its eating in *Yerushalayim* is entirely independent of the *Beis HaMikdash*.

The *talmud lomar* — the verse itself — resolves the matter: *ve'achalta lifnei Hashem Elokecha maaser degancha...u'bechorot bekarcha ve'tzonecha*. The Torah places *maaser* and *bechor* side by side. *Hikish maaser le'bechor* — the verse creates an equation: just as *bechor* cannot be eaten without the *Beis HaMikdash*, so too *maaser sheni* cannot be eaten without the *Beis HaMikdash*. The conceptual question this leaves open — whether *maaser sheni*'s connection to *Yerushalayim* is an extension of the *Beis HaMikdash* or something independent that the Torah arbitrarily links to *bechor* — the *gemara* does not fully resolve. But *halachically* the link is firm.

---

## Rabbi Akiva (III)

### Akiva's Derivation

Rabbi Akiva uses the same verse — *ve'achalta lifnei Hashem Elokecha maaser degancha...u'bechorot bekarcha ve'tzonecha* — but reads it in the opposite direction from Rabbi Yishmael. Where Rabbi Yishmael learns about *maaser* from *bechor*, Rabbi Akiva learns about *bechor* from *maaser*: *mimakom she'atah maaleh maaser dagan atah maaleh bechor* — the same place from which you bring *maaser* of grain is the place from which you bring *bechor*. Since *maaser dagan* is not brought from *chutz la'aretz*, neither is *bechor*. The two *tanna'im* thus use the same verse's equation in opposite directions to reach opposite rulings — Rabbi Yishmael concluding that *maaser sheni* follows *bechor* in requiring the *Beis HaMikdash*, Rabbi Akiva concluding that *bechor* follows *maaser dagan* in being limited to *Eretz Yisrael*.

The underlying rationale for Rabbi Akiva's position is conceptual. The obligations of *bechor* and *maaser behema* are not simply about the *kedusha* of the land in a narrow, soil-based sense. They are part of the agricultural cycle — the yearly products of national life in *Eretz Yisrael*. The Torah conceives of *Bnei Yisrael* as engaged in agriculture in their land, and *bechor* and *maaser* are expressions of that national reality. When one is living outside that reality, in *chutz la'aretz*, bringing *bechor* and *maaser* loses its proper context. A regular *korban* may appropriately be brought from anywhere, because its significance is not tied to the land's agricultural life. But *bechor* and *maaser* belong to the yearly product of the nation living in its land — and that is precisely what Rabbi Akiva is expressing when he says: bring *bechor* only from the same place from which you bring *maaser dagan*.

---

## Three Tannaic Opini (III)ons…

### Common Denominator Q

The *gemara* asks: why was the verse necessary at all? Could one not have derived the same conclusion from a *mah hatzad* — a common-denominator argument — between *bechor* and *bikurim*? Each was considered independently and rejected, but their shared features, after eliminating the respective distinguishing qualities, should yield the conclusion.

### Pesuk Necessity

Rav Ashi answers: *mishum de'ika lemeimar mah le'hatzad hashaveh shebahen sheyesh bahen tzad mizbe'ach* — one could argue that what *bechor* and *bikurim* have in common is precisely that they both involve some ritual on or at the *mizbe'ach*. *Bechor* has blood and *imurim* on the *mizbe'ach*; *bikurim* has the *hanacha* ritual before the *mizbe'ach*. *Maaser sheni* has no such ritual whatsoever. One might therefore argue that the *Yerushalayim* eating of *maaser sheni* is genuinely independent of the *Beis HaMikdash*, and the common denominator fails. The verse is therefore necessary to establish the link explicitly.

This analysis crystallizes the conceptual question: how do we think about *Yerushalayim* vis-à-vis *maaser sheni*? Is its status an extension of the *Beis HaMikdash* — such that without a *Beis HaMikdash* it becomes irrelevant — or is *Yerushalayim* for *maaser sheni* a category unto itself, independent of the *Mikdash*? The *gemara* does not provide a full conceptual resolution; it simply establishes *halachically*, via the verse, that *maaser* follows *bechor* in requiring the *Beis HaMikdash*.

### Kedusha Scenario

The *gemara* probes further with a sharper question. Rabbi Yishmael's discussion was premised on a situation where it is taken for granted that one cannot eat *bechor* nowadays but it is not immediately obvious whether the same is true of *maaser sheni*. How is this possible? Either the *kedusha* of *Yerushalayim* and the *makom hamikdash* still exists — in which case one should theoretically be able to bring *bechor* as well, simply by building a *mizbe'ach* — or it does not exist, in which case *maaser sheni* in *Yerushalayim* is obviously irrelevant.

The *gemara* presses: *de'i salka da'atach kedusha rishona kidsha lesha'atah velo kidsha le'atid lavo* — if the *kedusha* has lapsed, then even the question about *maaser sheni* should not arise. And if the first *kedusha* remains *le'atid lavo*, then *afilu bechor nami* — even *bechor* should theoretically be possible. So where exactly is the question located?

The *gemara* resolves this by proposing a specific scenario. We do assume — following the view that the first *kedusha* endures — that *Yerushalayim* and the *makom hamikdash* retain their *kedusha* today. In theory, one could build a *mizbe'ach* and offer *korbanot*, as is well known from the relevant discussion in later authorities.
