But there is a specific *halacha* that prevents eating the meat of a *bechor* even in a case where the blood has already been sprinkled. The scenario: imagine a *bechor* was brought to the *Beis HaMikdash* on the very last day, the blood was sprinkled on the *mizbe'ach* — and then the *Beis HaMikdash* was destroyed. The meat is still present the next day. Why can one not eat it?

### Blood-Meat Unity

*Keivan de'ee issa ledam lavar zvika hu, asi basar yalif midam* — since if one now wanted to slaughter the animal, it could not be done with *zerikat hadam*, and *basar* is derived from *dam*: meat takes its permissibility from the ability to perform the blood service. At the moment when the blood can no longer be sprinkled on a *mizbe'ach*, eating the meat is prohibited, even if the blood was already sprinkled while the *Beis HaMikdash* stood. This establishes a *halacha* — not merely a practical impossibility — that one cannot eat *bechor* at a time when the *mizbe'ach* no longer functions. From that *halacha* regarding *bechor*, one then derives via the verse's equation that *maaser sheni* likewise cannot be eaten when the *mizbe'ach* is absent.

The *gemara* then raises the objection of Rabbi Yochanan's rule: *kol hatorah kulah lemedin lamed min lamed chutz mikodshim* — throughout the entire Torah one may do a "daisy-chain" derivation, learning from B to C because one learned from A to B — except in the case of *kodshim*. Here we have a double derivation: from the inability to do *zerikat hadam* to the prohibition on eating the *bechor*'s meat (*dam* to *basar*), and from there to *maaser sheni*. Since *bechor* is *kodshim*, one cannot daisy-chain within it. The answer: *maaser chullin hu* — *maaser sheni*, for the purposes of this rule, is not considered *kodshim* of the altar. There is a broader debate about whether *maaser sheni* is *mamon gavoah* or *mamon hedyot*, but either way it is not *korbanot hekdesh*, and therefore the daisy-chain prohibition does not apply to the final link. However, the objection can be reformulated: even if C (*maaser sheni*) is not *kodshim*, A and B (*dam* and *basar* of *bechor*) are — and if one says the prohibition on daisy-chaining follows the status of A and B rather than C, the problem remains. The *gemara* resolves this: *basar vedam chada milsa hi* — the blood and the meat of a *bechor* are fundamentally one unit. Deriving the meat's status from the blood's status is not a daisy-chain at all; it is an internal application within a single legal entity. Thus the derivation stands, and the conclusion of Rabbi Yishmael is firmly grounded.

---

## Rabbi Akiva (III)

### Agricultural Basis

Rabbi Akiva's conceptual basis for excluding *bechor* from *chutz la'aretz* reflects a broader understanding of what *bechor* and *maaser behema* represent. These obligations belong to the agricultural cycle — the yearly produce of national life in *Eretz Yisrael*. The Torah conceives of *Bnei Yisrael* as engaged in agriculture within their land, and *bechor* and *maaser* are expressions of that national-agricultural reality. One who is living outside that framework, in *chutz la'aretz*, is not participating in the context that gives these obligations their meaning. A regular *korban* may be brought from anywhere because its significance is not bound to the land's agricultural life. But *bechor* and *maaser* belong to the yearly product of the nation in its land. That is the logic of Rabbi Akiva's derivation: bring *bechor* only from the same place from which you bring *maaser dagan*.

---

## Ben Azzai Position

### Ben Azzai Question

The third tradition cited by Rabbi Yossi is that of Ben Azzai. Ben Azzai addresses yet another question derivable from the verse's equation of *maaser* and *bechor*. He asks: *yachol maaleh maaser sheni yochlenu bechol haroeh* — perhaps when bringing *maaser sheni* to *Yerushalayim*, one need not limit oneself to within the walls but may eat it anywhere visible from *Yerushalayim* — the area known as *kol haroeh*. The concept of *kol haroeh* is familiar in other contexts: cities visible from a walled city read the *Megillah* on the fifteenth. Might *Yerushalayim*'s status for *maaser sheni* extend similarly beyond its walls?

### Logical Derivation

Ben Azzai attempts a logical derivation: *bechor ta'un hava'at makom u'maaser ta'un hava'at makom* — both *bechor* and *maaser* must be brought to *Yerushalayim*. Just as *bechor* is eaten *lifnim min hachoma* — within the walls — perhaps *maaser* follows suit and is also limited to within the walls.

### Mizbe'ach Distinction

The derivation is rejected: *mah l'bechor sheken ta'un matan damim ve'imurim legabei mizbe'ach* — *bechor* has blood and *imurim* on the *mizbe'ach*, which ties it to the walls as an extension of the *Beis HaMikdash*. *Maaser sheni* has no such *mizbe'ach* connection — perhaps its *Yerushalayim* definition is not the same as *bechor*'s.

### Verse Link

The verse connecting *maaser* to *bechor* then resolves the question: *makish maaser le'bechor — mah bechor ne'echal lifnim min hachoma af maaser ne'echal lifnim min hachoma* — just as *bechor* is eaten within the walls, so too *maaser sheni* is limited to within the walls. The Torah's equation forecloses the possibility of extending *maaser*'s domain to *kol haroeh*.

### Walls vs. Kol HaRoeh

The *gemara* asks: what prompted Ben Azzai to even raise the idea of *kol haroeh*? Where does that concept get its foothold? If the *mishna* already establishes that eating within the walls is the rule, why would anyone think to extend it?

### Shilo Precedent

The source is a *mishna* in *Zevachim* which establishes the difference between the period when the *Mishkan* stood at *Shilo* and the period of *Yerushalayim*: *ela shebeShilo ochlin kodashim kalim u'maaser sheni bechol haroeh* — at *Shilo*, one ate *kodashim kalim* and *maaser sheni* wherever visible from the *Mishkan*. *Uvi'Yerushalayim lifnim min hachoma* — in *Yerushalayim*, only within the walls. The reason *Shilo* used *kol haroeh* is that *Shilo* had no walls; *kol haroeh* served as the functional substitute for the walls that did not exist. Since at *Shilo* the extended area was included, one might have thought to apply that same principle to *Yerushalayim* even within the era of walls.

### Wall Limitation

The *gemara* concludes: *kol haroeh* at *Shilo* was a *bedi'avad* substitute for walls that did not exist. In *Yerushalayim*, where walls were consecrated with a formal *hakdashah*, the walls define the parameters — for *maaser* no less than for *korbanot*. The concept of *kol haroeh* served its purpose only where a wall-defined boundary did not exist. Once *Yerushalayim* has walls, the eating of *maaser sheni* follows the *halacha* of *bechor* and is confined to within those walls.

---

## Bechor Year Validity

### Third Opinion Psul

A third opinion (*acherim*) raises yet another question one might derive from the verse's equation of *maaser* and *bechor*: *yachol yehei bechor she'avar shenaso kifsulei hamukdashim veyipasel* — perhaps a *bechor* that has passed its first year becomes *pasul*, like other *psulei hamukdashin*. The Torah says *lifnei Hashem Elokecha tochlenu shana veshana* — you shall eat it before God year by year. This might indicate not merely an obligation to bring the *bechor* within the first year, but a definition: an animal older than one year is no longer a valid *bechor korban*.

### Maaser Connection

This is rejected via the same verse: *makish bechor le'maaser* — the Torah connects *bechor* to *maaser*. Just as *maaser* does not become *pasul* from one year to the next — indeed, the Torah contemplates eating *maaser* over multiple years, including the *biur ma'aser* clearing process every third year — so too *bechor* does not become *pasul* after its first year. The obligation to bring it within the year remains, but failure to do so does not render the animal an invalid *korban*.

### Shana BeShana

The other *tanna'im* in the *braita* — who use the verse's equation for other purposes (establishing the parameters of *Yerushalayim* for *maaser* or the limits of bringing from *chutz la'aretz*) — derive the rule that *bechor* is not *pasul* after a year from a different reading of the same phrase *shana veshana*: *yesh em labechor she'eino nifsal mishana lachaverta* — the *bechor* remains valid from one year to the next.

### Two Days Eaten

Having used *shana veshana* for the *pasul* question, the *acherim* still need a source for the rule that a *bechor* may be eaten for two days. The *gemara* establishes that a *bechor* is *ne'echal lishnei yamim velaila echad* — eaten for two days and one night. The *acherim* derive this from the phrase *shana veshana* itself: *erev Rosh Hashanah ve'Rosh Hashanah* — one can eat a *bechor* across two consecutive years by beginning on the eve of Rosh Hashanah and continuing into Rosh Hashanah itself, thus spanning two days across two calendar years.

### Two Days Source

For the other *rabbanan* — who already used *shana veshana* to teach that *bechor* is not *pasul* after a year — the source for eating over two days comes from elsewhere: *amar kra yiheyeh lach kehazeh* — the Torah says the *kohen* shall receive the *bechor* as he receives the *chazeh hatnufa*, the wave breast of a *shelamim*. Since the *chazeh hatnufa* of a *shelamim* is eaten for two days and one night, the same applies to *bechor*.

*Hadran alach Kol Pesulei HaMukdashin.*

---

---

# Temurah 22

## Chatat Meita Categories

### Five Categories

The new perek begins at the very bottom of 21b and is devoted entirely to the laws of *chatat*, a subject that merits its own chapter precisely because of the unique category of *chatat meita* — the *chatat* that must be left to die. While we are familiar with the idea that there are five categories of *chatat meita*, a close reading of our *Mishna* reveals that the precise contours of those five are considerably less straightforward than one might assume.

The *Mishna* opens with three unambiguous cases: *vlad chatat* (the offspring of a *chatat*), *temurat chatat* (a substitution made for a *chatat*), and a *chatat* whose owners have died, rendering it permanently incapable of fulfilling its atonement purpose. In all three cases the ruling is simply *yamutu* — they are locked away and left to die. The animal cannot be actively killed; since it is *kodashim*, no form of *shechita* is permitted, nor may it be destroyed in any other manner. One simply withholds food and allows it to perish.

### Absolute vs Conditional

Beyond those three clear cases, the *Mishna* introduces two further categories that are conventionally listed among the five, but which are here presented with an important qualification. The *Mishna* speaks of an animal that has passed its first year (*avar shnata*) and of one that was lost and subsequently found to be *ba'alat mum* (blemished). What is striking is that neither of these two cases is stated as an absolute rule. Rather, the *Mishna* frames them as conditional: only under certain circumstances do these animals enter the category of *chatat meita*.

### Manuscript Reading Analy…

There is a significant textual question surrounding the exact *girsa* of the *Mishna*. The printed text reads *im mishe'kiperu ba'alim tamut* — if after the owners have atoned, it must die — which would limit the case to where the animal was found only after the owners had already achieved atonement through a replacement. Both Rashi and Tosafot, however, emend the *girsa* to *im kiperu ba'alim tamut*, meaning: even if the animal was found beforehand, once the owners subsequently went ahead and brought another *korban* for atonement, it must die.

This distinction is not merely textual — it maps onto a major *halachic* debate about the precise moment at which *nitkapru ba'alim b'acher* (atonement through another) creates the status of *chatat meita*. The more obvious case is where the animal was lost, was still missing when the replacement was brought, and was only found afterwards. In that scenario, when the lost animal was being dealt with it already bore the full status of *nitkapru ba'acher*, and everyone agrees it must die. The more complex and debated case is where the animal was found before the replacement was brought. Here there is a dispute — which will be elaborated later in the *Mishna* — between Rabbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) and the *Chachamim*. Rabbi holds that even being lost at the time the replacement was designated is sufficient to create *chatat meita* status; the *Chachamim* hold that only finding it after the owners have actually completed their atonement creates that status.

Rashi's approach is that the *Mishna* here is addressing a case of a "double problem" — the animal was found before the atonement was completed, yet it has an additional deficiency (either *ba'alat mum* or *avar shnata*) on top of having been lost. This double problem, in Rashi's view, is what leads to *tamut* status even according to Rabbi in cases where the animal was found prior to atonement. Tosafot reads the *gemara* differently and we will follow Rashi's approach throughout.

Practically, this means that what the *Mishna* presents is not two separate categories standing independently, but rather a combination: being lost, plus an additional problem preventing the animal from being brought. When both conditions are present and the owners have sought atonement through another animal, the first one must die. Without the combination, there is no *chatat meita*.

It is worth noting that even when an animal does not fall into the *chatat meita* category, the proceeds of a *chatat* that cannot be used (*motar chatat*) go toward an *olah*, as in the case of *nedavat tzibbur*.

### Chatat Meita Implications

Once an animal has acquired the status of *chatat meita*, several important *halachic* consequences follow. First, it cannot serve as a basis for *temura*. The ability to make *temura* is premised on the animal eventually making its way to the *mizbe'ach* — directly or through its proceeds. An animal designated to die will never reach the *mizbe'ach* and therefore cannot generate a valid *temura*. Second, *lo nehenin velo mo'alin* — not only is one prohibited from deriving benefit from it, one does not violate the biblical prohibition of *me'ila* if one does benefit from it. Since the animal's *kedusha* is never destined to reach the *Beit Hamikdash* in any form, it does not carry the full *kedusha* that would trigger *me'ila*.

By contrast, if the owners have not yet atoned through another means — *im ad shelo kiperu ha-ba'alim* — the animal retains its full sanctity. In that case, one waits for it to develop a *mum*, then redeems it and uses the proceeds to purchase a proper *chatat*. It retains the capacity to generate *temura* and is subject to *me'ila*. The status of *chatat meita* is therefore not simply a function of the animal's physical condition; it is a function of the entire complex of circumstances surrounding the owner's path to atonement.

One might note a practical difficulty: where the owner is under time pressure to achieve *kappara* — a *nazir* awaiting purification, a *yoledes* unable to enter the *Beit Hamikdash* — the requirement to wait for the animal to develop a *mum* before redeeming it could impose a significant delay. Whether one may proactively bring a replacement and thereby deliberately create a *chatat meita* status for the original is a subtle question that the *gemara* does not explicitly address, but the straightforward reading of the *halacha* does not appear to prohibit doing so.

---

## Reish Lakish Position

### Cemetery Analogy

With the textual and conceptual framework of *chatat meita* in place, the *gemara* turns to a striking statement by Reish Lakish. He declares that a *chatat* that has passed its first year — *avar shnata* — is to be viewed as though it is standing in a cemetery, where the *kohen* cannot access it. One watches over it, lets it graze, and eventually waits for it to develop a *mum* and be redeemed. In Reish Lakish's formulation, *avar shnata* never actually reaches the status of *tamut*; the problem is external and circumstantial rather than a *halachic* transformation of the animal itself.

### Contradiction Challenge

The *gemara* immediately challenges this position from our very *Mishna*, which teaches that *she'avra shnata v'avda v'nimtze'et ba'alat mum, im achar shekiperu ba'alim, meita* — if an animal passed its first year, was lost, and was found to be *ba'alat mum*, and the owners have already atoned through another means, it must die. This appears to contradict Reish Lakish's categorical assertion that *avar shnata* never leads to *meita* status, since the *Mishna* combines *avar shnata* with the scenario of *nitkapru ba'alim* and concludes that it dies. The *gemara* therefore initially declares this a *tiyuvta* — a refutation — of Reish Lakish's position.

### Reish Lakish Response

Reish Lakish, however, deflects the challenge by reinterpreting the structure of the *Mishna*. He reads the phrase *avar shnata* as a standalone entry whose *halacha* is simply not stated at the end of the *Mishna*. The final ruling — that the animal dies if the owners were atoned after the fact, and grazes if they were not yet atoned — applies only to the last case in the *Mishna*: the animal that was lost and found to be *ba'alat mum*. The case of *avar shnata* appears parenthetically in the list but is not subject to the same conditional ruling at the end. According to Reish Lakish, *avar shnata* is entirely separate and is never in the category of *meita*.

### Rava's Reconciliation

The *gemara* presses further. If the final section of the *Mishna* — dealing with whether the owners were atoned before or after the animal was found — applies only to the case of *ba'alat mum*, then the instruction to "let it graze until it develops a *mum*" is internally incoherent: if the animal already had a *mum*, what does it mean to wait for one? Rava attempts to resolve this by suggesting that the *Mishna* was dealing with a transitory *mum*, not a permanent one. The animal had a temporary blemish when found; if it was found after the owners atoned, it must die, while if it was found before, you wait for the *mum* to become permanent (*mum kavua*) before redeeming it. The *gemara*, however, ultimately rejects this as well, on two grounds: first, the language of "let it graze until it becomes blemished" is inappropriate for an animal that already has some blemish; second, and more fundamentally — *she'ibur shnaso l'mai hilchasa katani*? — if *avar shnata* is excised entirely from the consequential part of the *Mishna*, what is it doing there at all?

### Avar Shnata Status

Rava therefore proposes a complete reinterpretation that preserves Reish Lakish's position: read the *Mishna* as presenting two parallel cases under the conditional ruling. Either the animal passed its first year *and* was lost (*ibur shnaso v'avda*), or it was lost and found to be *ba'alat mum* (*avda v'nimtze'et ba'alat mum*). In both cases, the ruling is: if the owners were atoned afterwards, it dies; if beforehand, it grazes until redeemable.

What emerges from this reading is quite striking. We began by assuming that *avar shnata* is one of five independent categories of *chatat meita*. Our *Mishna* then showed that it requires combination with *nitkapru ba'alim b'acher*. Reish Lakish now shows that even *nitkapru ba'alim b'acher* by itself is insufficient; the animal must also have been *lost*. And not only must it have been lost — it must have had an additional problem beyond the loss alone, such as being *avar shnata* or *ba'alat mum*. *Avar shnata*, then, is not a category in its own right. It is a subset of *nitkapru ba'alim b'acher*, and even that status requires the double combination of being lost plus having an additional disqualifying characteristic.

---

## Double Problem Requireme…

### Separate Listings

The *gemara* now asks: given that *avar shnata* and *ba'alat mum* are functionally parallel — both rendering the animal unfit for this particular *korban* and both requiring the additional element of having been lost in order to generate *chatat meita* status — why does the *Mishna* need to list both cases? Would not one suffice to teach the principle?

### Avar Shnata Combination

The answer is *tzricha* — both are necessary — but for opposite reasons. Each case contributes something the other cannot teach. If the *Mishna* had mentioned only *avar shnata*, we might have concluded: it is *specifically* the combination of loss with *avar shnata* that triggers *meita* status, because being over a year old renders the animal completely irrelevant — *lo chazya l'milsa* — to the category of *chatat* entirely. An animal more than a year old is not merely unusable for this particular *korban*; it has undergone a categorical change of identity (a *keves* becomes an *ayil*), and one might think that this degree of total irrelevance is what gives the loss its consequence.

### Ba'alat Mum Analysis

Conversely, if the *Mishna* had mentioned only *ba'alat mum*, we might have concluded: it is specifically being *ba'alat mum* that, combined with loss, creates *meita* status, because a *ba'alat mum* is entirely unfit for *any* offering — *lo chazya l'hakravah* — even though conceptually a *mum* is an accidental characteristic of the animal rather than an essential one. One might then have thought that *avar shnata*, which is merely irrelevant to *this* offering but could in principle be brought for a *different* offering, does not rise to the level needed to combine with loss and create *meita* status.

### Essential vs Accidental

The distinction the *gemara* is drawing here engages a deep conceptual question about the nature of *psul*. A *ba'alat mum* has what one might call an accidental defect: it is still essentially the same animal, but something external has happened to it that prevents it from being offered. A *avar shnata*, by contrast, represents a categorical identity shift — the passage of time has made it a different type of animal. Yet paradoxically, this identity shift does not render it *completely* irrelevant, since it remains fit for other offerings. The *mum*, despite being accidental, does render it completely unfit for any offering at all.

The result is that each case is both stronger and weaker than the other in different dimensions. One cannot be inferred from the other, and therefore the *Mishna* must state both explicitly.

This analysis, it should be noted, follows Rashi's reading throughout. Tosafot reads the *gemara* in a fundamentally different direction — arguing that the additional problem is not what creates *meita* status but rather that the *chiddush* is that *even* with the additional disqualifying problem the animal is still subject to *tamut*. According to Tosafot the double problem actually argues *against* *meita* status in some sense, and the novelty is that the *halacha* still applies. This reading involves different *girsaot* as well, but the analysis here follows Rashi.

The upshot of all this, stated plainly, is as follows. The *halacha* of *nitkapru ba'alim b'acher* does not apply universally. At one extreme, if one sanctified two animals from the outset intending to use either, brings one, and the other is left over — everyone agrees that is not *chatat meita*; one simply waits for the second to develop a *mum* and uses the proceeds for an *olah*. At the other extreme, if the animal was completely lost, the replacement was brought and the owners fully atoned, and only then was the original found — everyone agrees it is *chatat meita*. The contested middle ground involves an animal that was lost, a replacement was designated (but not yet brought), and the original was then found. In that scenario, Rabbi says it is *meita*; the *Chachamim* say it is not. And even in that contested zone, our *Mishna* teaches that if the animal had a double problem — both being lost and having an additional disqualifying characteristic — even the *Chachamim* might agree it is *meita*. That remains the overall framework as we proceed.

A natural question arises regarding how these *halachot* are ruled upon in practice. The *Rambam* addresses these issues in *Hilchot Pesulei Hamukdashin*, but given the complexity of the *machloket* and the absence of practical *korbanot* today, a definitive review of the *Rambam*'s position is left for separate study.

---

## Lost at Night

### Night Loss Principle

Having established the framework of the double-problem requirement, the *gemara* introduces a related principle in the name of Rava: *aveidah de'laila lav shemah aveidah* — loss that occurs at night does not constitute genuine loss for these purposes. The reasoning is straightforward: since *korbanot* cannot be brought at night, the entire framework of *zman hakrava* (the time relevant for offering) is inapplicable after dark. If an animal was lost during the night and found before daybreak, there was never a meaningful period during which its absence affected anything. It is therefore as though it was never truly lost.

### Rabbi vs Chachamim

The *gemara* asks: according to whom is this principle relevant? If we are speaking according to the *Rabbanan*, the principle seems unnecessary — according to the *Rabbanan*, even a loss that occurred during the day is not a problem as long as the animal is found before the replacement is actually brought (*avuda bi-sha'at hafrasha ro'eh*). If the *Rabbanan* are lenient even for daytime loss, it goes without saying that nighttime loss presents no problem.

The principle is therefore relevant specifically according to Rabbi, who is otherwise strict and says that even loss at the time the replacement was designated (*sha'at hafrasha*) creates *meita* status. According to Rabbi, one might have thought that nighttime loss — which occurred at an irrelevant hour but nevertheless preceded the designation of a replacement — would also create *meita* status. Rava therefore teaches that even Rabbi agrees: if the loss occurred at night and the animal was found before daybreak, it is considered as though both animals were simultaneously before the owner and the designation of the replacement does not trigger *meita* status.

### Day vs Night

Furthermore, the *gemara* advances a second interpretation. Even if one says the principle of *aveidah de'laila* is relevant according to the *Rabbanan*, it is speaking of a case where the animal was lost at night but remained lost into the following day — and was still absent when the atonement was eventually brought. Here the question is whether the *status* of the loss is defined by when it first began or by its ongoing duration. According to this reading, since the initial loss occurred at a time when *zman hakrava* was inapplicable, the loss is never fully "counted" as a genuine *aveidah* — even when the animal remains absent during the day and the replacement is brought. The first occurrence of the loss establishes its character, and since that first occurrence was at night, the *halacha* of *chatat meita* does not apply even according to the *Rabbanan*.

### Irrelevance Principle

What ties together the principle of nighttime loss and the earlier discussion of the double problem is a single underlying idea: *lo chazya lo l'gufa v'lo l'damei* — at night, the animal is completely irrelevant, not only in its physical form but even in terms of its monetary value, since the entire institution of *korbanot* is suspended after dark. This is what distinguishes nighttime loss from the case of a *ba'alat mum* or *avar shnata*, where the animal remains relevant at least for its redemption value (*chazya l'damei*) even if it cannot be offered directly. The *gemara* concludes: complete irrelevance (nighttime) does not create *meita* status; partial irrelevance (a *mum* or advanced age) combined with loss does; and no irrelevance at all (a healthy, in-season animal that was simply lost during the day and found before atonement) creates a dispute between Rabbi and the *Chachamim*.

---

## Definition of Loss

### Lost Not Stolen

Having clarified when loss is significant in terms of *zman hakrava*, the *gemara* turns to the question of what constitutes *aveidah* (loss) in the first place. Abaye states: *aveidah velo gnuva, aveidah velo gezulah* — only genuine loss qualifies, not theft and not robbery. If the animal was taken by a thief or robber, someone knows its whereabouts, and it therefore does not have the status of a truly lost animal.

### Yoshia's Standards

Rabbi Yoshia sets the standard broadly: *afilu achas be'edra, v'afilu achas b'achas* — even if the animal is mixed within the owner's own flock and he cannot identify which one it is, and even if it is mixed up one-to-one with another animal, the owner being unable to identify it constitutes *aveidah*. There is no principle of *bitul b'rov* here; even if the animal is visibly present but unidentifiable, that counts as lost.

### Behind Door Standard

Rabbi Yochanan states that an animal behind a door — *achorei ha-delet* — is considered *aveidah*.

### Visibility vs Knowledge

The *gemara* asks what exactly Rabbi Yochanan means. Is he saying that only when the animal is behind a door — where *no one* can see it — does it constitute *aveidah*, but if it is in the open and visible to passersby, even if the owner cannot identify it, it would not be *aveidah*? Or does he mean that even something behind a door, where one need only turn around to find it, qualifies as *aveidah* — because for practical purposes the owner does not know where it is? The question essentially asks whether *aveidah* is defined by physical invisibility or by the owner's epistemic state, i.e., his inability to locate it. The *gemara* concludes *teiku* — the question remains unresolved.

Rav Pappa adds a further principle: *aveidah mimenu velo mero'eh lo havya aveidah* — if the owner does not know where the animal is but the shepherd does, it is not considered lost. Equally, if the shepherd does not know but the owner does, it is certainly not lost. Only when neither the owner nor the shepherd knows the animal's location is it considered *aveidah*. Whether the presence of some unknown third party who happens to know its location removes the status of *aveidah* also remains *teiku*.

---

## Blood in Vessels

### Post-Shechita Loss

Rav Pappa then poses a more complex question: *aveidah b'kos mai hu* — what is the *halacha* when the "loss" occurs at the level of the blood in a vessel? The scenario here is not about the animal going missing before *shechita*, but about a situation where the replacement animal has already been *shechted* and its blood has been collected in a vessel — yet the original animal has now been found. The question is whether, at this stage, the blood in the vessel constitutes a "brought" replacement in the sense that triggers *chatat meita* for the original.

### Blood Status

The *gemara* frames this as a question that depends on whose opinion we are working with. According to Rabbi, who says *aveidah bi-sha'at hafrasha* is already sufficient to create *meita* status, the question of whether the blood was thrown or merely collected is irrelevant — the original animal's fate was already sealed when the replacement was designated. The question is therefore relevant only according to the *Rabbanan*, who require that the replacement actually be brought before the original is found in order for *meita* status to apply. For the *Rabbanan*, one must ask: does their requirement of "after the replacement was brought" mean after the blood was actually sprinkled on the *mizbe'ach*, or is it enough that the blood was caught in the vessel? The principle of *kol ha'omed lizrok ke-zaruak dami* — whatever is about to be sprinkled is considered as if already sprinkled — might indicate that collecting the blood in the vessel is equivalent to completing the offering. Or one might say: as long as the blood has not actually been thrown, the offering is not yet complete, and the original animal's status is still that of *aveidah bi-sha'at hafrasha* (loss at the time of designation), for which the *Rabbanan* hold *ro'eh* (it grazes). The *gemara* does not resolve this question.

### Multiple Vessels

A second interpretation of the question reframes it entirely. Some say the question is not actually about two animals at all, but about a single animal whose blood was collected into two vessels, one of which was subsequently lost. When the remaining vessel is used for the *zerikat ha-dam* (sprinkling), what is the status of the missing vessel's blood if it is later found? This is a genuine sub-question of the *aveidah* framework: can part of an offering "go lost" in a way that parallels the loss of an entire animal?

### Vessel Rejection

The answer depends on a pre-existing dispute about the rule of *kos oseh chaveiro dichui* — whether using one vessel to perform the *avoda* causes the other vessel to become *nidcheh* (rejected). According to those who hold that it does — that using one cup to throw the blood "rejects" the others — there is no question: even if the missing blood were to reappear, it would be *nidcheh* regardless, since it would have been rejected the moment its companion vessel was used. The question therefore only arises according to those who say that using one cup makes the remaining blood in the other vessels *shirayim* (remnants to be poured at the base of the *mizbe'ach*), which presupposes that the blood remains valid as long as both cups are present. When one is missing, the *gemara* asks: do we still classify the absent blood as *shirayim*-equivalent (valid, merely temporarily absent), or does its absence at the moment of *zerikat ha-dam* render it rejected, analogous to an animal that was absent when the replacement was brought? The *gemara* concludes *teiku*.

---

## Rabbi vs Chachamim

### Unanimous Case

The *Mishna* now sets out the positions of Rabbi and the *Chachamim* in a series of carefully constructed cases. The baseline case on which everyone agrees: *ha-mafrish chatat v'avdah v'hikriv acheret tachteha v'achar kach nimtzet ha-rishonah, tamut* — one set aside a *chatat*, it was lost, a replacement was brought, and then the original was found. The original must die. This is the unambiguous case of *nitkapru ba'alim b'acher* with which the *gemara* began.

### Lost Money Case

The *Mishna* then introduces the case of money. One set aside money for a *chatat*, the money was lost, a replacement *chatat* was brought, and then the money was found. Since money designated for a *chatat* has *kedushat chatat*, it is treated analogously to the animal: *yolichem le-yam ha-melach* — throw it into the Dead Sea. The money must be destroyed.

### Money Mixing

A more complex case: one set aside money for a *chatat*, it was lost, and one then set aside *other* money to replace it — but has not yet purchased a new animal. Before buying the new animal, the original money is found. Now one has two pools of money, each designated as a *chatat*. If one simply uses one pool and ignores the other, the unused pool would be subject to *nitkapru ba'alim b'acher* — according to Rabbi it would have to be destroyed. The solution the *Mishna* provides is *yavi me'elu u-me'elu le-chatato* — mix the two pools of money together and use the combined funds to purchase a single *chatat*. Whatever remains is leftover *chatat* money and is used for an *olah*. Since the money is fungible, combining the two pools eliminates the identity of either as a "rejected" pool; there is no single pile that was "chosen" over another.

### Animal Money Mix

The *Mishna* continues with hybrid cases involving both animals and money. If one set aside money and lost it, then set aside a replacement *chatat* animal, and then found the original money before bringing the animal — the solution, if the *chatat* animal happens to have a *mum*, is to redeem the animal, producing money, and then mix *all* the money together and bring a *chatat* from the combined funds. The remainder goes for an *olah*. The mixing principle that works for money can be extended to an animal by first converting the animal into money through redemption.

Similarly, if one set aside a *chatat* animal that was lost, then set aside money to replace it, and then found the original animal with a *mum* — redeem the animal, mix all the money together, buy a *chatat* from the combined funds, and the remainder goes for an *olah*.

When both the original and replacement are animals without a *mum*, the situation becomes more difficult. If both happen to be *ba'alot mum*, one may sell both, mix all the money, and proceed as above. If both are unblemished, then one brings one as a *chatat* and the other must die, for it has become a case of *nitkapru ba'alim b'acher* — *divrei Rebbi*.

### Finding Before/After

This last ruling encapsulates the central dispute. According to Rabbi, the moment one animal was lost and another was designated in its place, the lost animal became subject to *meita* status — even if it is subsequently found before the replacement is actually brought. In the case of two unblemished animals, since one cannot be converted into money and combined with the other, one must bring one and the second must die, because it has the status of *chatat she-nitkapru ba'aleha b'acher*.

The *Chachamim* fundamentally disagree. Their position: *ein chatat meita ella she-nimtzet me-achar she-kiperu ha-ba'alim* — the status of *chatat meita* applies only when the original animal is found after the owners have completed their atonement through the replacement. If it is found beforehand — at any point before the replacement is actually brought — then no *meita* status applies, the owner may use whichever animal he wishes, and the remainder is treated as an *olah*. Correspondingly, the rule requiring money to be thrown into the *yam ha-melach* also applies only when the money is found after the owners have completed their atonement. All the elaborate mixing of money described above is, according to the *Chachamim*, unnecessary in any case where the original was found before atonement was completed — one simply treats the leftover as an *olah*.

### Sale Creates Meita

The *Mishna* closes with a remarkable ruling by Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon. If one set aside a *chatat* that developed a *mum*, sold it, and used the proceeds to purchase and bring a new *chatat* — and if the second *chatat* was brought before the original purchaser had a chance to *shecht* the animal he bought — then *tamut shekvar kiperu ba'alim b'acher*: the animal that was sold must die. The reasoning is that from the moment the seller brought his replacement *chatat* on the *mizbe'ach*, the sold animal retroactively acquired the status of *chatat she-nitkapru ba'aleha b'acher*, because it had been consecrated as a *chatat* and the original owner has now achieved atonement through another means. The buyer's animal — which had been purchased as an ordinary *ba'al mum* being redeemed — is suddenly subject to *meita* status, apparently regardless of the buyer's expectations. Whether the buyer receives any recourse is not discussed.

---

---

# Temurah 23

## Lost Animal Dispute

### Mishnah Overview

The daf opens in the middle of a large *mishnah* that spans the bottom of 22b into 23a. The subject is a *chatas* whose owner was *niskaper b'acher* — atoned for through another offering — and the question is under what circumstances the original animal is declared *mesa*, consigned to death. According to the *chachamim*, this outcome applies only when the missing animal is found after the owners have already been atoned for through the second offering. According to Rabbi Meir, it applies even if the missing animal is found after the second one has merely been sanctified, before it was actually brought.

### Rabbis' Position

The *gemara* begins its analysis by noting an apparent internal tension within the *mishnah* itself. The opening line of the *mishnah* reads: the reason the first animal must die is that when it was found, the second had already been brought in its stead. The implication is clear — had the second not yet been brought, but only sanctified, the first would merely graze (*ro'eh*) rather than die. This reflects the position of the *rabbanan*: that the animal is *avuda b'sha'as hafrasha* — lost at the time of designation — but is not subject to the death rule unless the replacement was actually brought (*hikriv*). If the animal was found after the second was sanctified but before it was brought, it simply grazes.

### Rabbi Meir Section

The middle section of the *mishnah*, however, appears to operate on entirely different assumptions. It addresses the case where one designated money (*maos*) for a *chatas*, that money was lost, a second pile was designated, and then the first pile was found. The *mishnah* teaches that the solution is *yavi me'elu u'me'elu* — one purchases the *chatas* from both piles together, with the remainder going for a *nedava* in the form of an *olah*. The significance of this solution is that it presupposes there is a fundamental problem even if the money was found before the second pile was used. That is, the very act of designating a second pile has already created a situation requiring remediation — which sounds like the position of Rabbi Meir, not the *rabbanan*.

### Structure Resolution

This creates a structural difficulty: does the first section of the *mishnah* reflect the *rabbanan* while the middle section reflects Rabbi Meir? The *gemara* resolves this by observing that the *mishnah* first presents the straightforward law according to the *rabbanan* and then elaborates the interesting practical *halacha* according to Rabbi Meir — the solution of mixing the money — before concluding explicitly with the full text of the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the *rabbanan*. The explicit statement of their disagreement appears at the end of the *mishnah*, where it states: Rabbi Meir says bring one and the other must die; the *chachamim* say a *chatas* is only put to death if it was found after the owners were atoned for, and similarly the money is only cast into the Dead Sea under those same conditions. The reason for presenting the intermediate cases before stating the dispute openly is to teach the substantive and surprising *halacha* of mixing the money — a solution that would never have been intuited without the *mishnah*'s detailed case presentation.

---

## Rav Huna Approach

### Consensus on Selection

The *gemara* now turns to a detailed examination of the two *amora'ic* approaches that explain when the *chachamim* may agree with Rabbi Meir that the first animal must die even when found before the second has been brought. Rav Huna said in the name of Rav: *hakol modim* — everyone agrees — that if you found both animals present and on your own initiative *mashach* one of them, selected one, and then brought it as the offering, the second must die. The act of selection, made unilaterally, constitutes an effective rejection of the unchosen animal. In this, the *rabbanan* concede entirely to Rabbi Meir's result, even though the second animal had not yet been brought at the moment of finding.

### Beis Din Consultation

The dispute between Rabbi Meir and the *rabbanan*, according to Rav Huna's reading, is confined to a very specific scenario: *b'ba l'imalech* — when one comes to ask *Beis Din* what to do. There are, conceptually, two considerations that might affect the outcome. The first is which animal is ultimately brought: the one that had been lost (*avuda*) or the replacement (*she'eina avuda*). The second is whether the selection was made unilaterally or through consultation with *Beis Din*. When a person approaches *Beis Din* and asks for guidance, the act of selecting is no longer a unilateral rejection of one animal over another — it becomes an attempt to navigate the situation constructively. In that context, the *rabbanan* hold that *Beis Din* can and should advise a path that salvages the outcome.

### Rabbi Rejects Salvage

According to Rav Huna's reading, Rabbi Meir's position is that *lo asu takana b'kodshim* — we do not enact remedial measures in matters of *kodshim*. Even when one comes to ask *Beis Din*, Rabbi Meir's position is that *Beis Din* is not interested in engineering a solution. He would advise: go, bring the second animal — the non-lost one — as the *korban*, and let the first, which had been lost, die. This is a striking position. The person is asking for help, the solution exists, and yet the instruction is to bring the replacement and allow the lost animal to die.

### Rabbis Salvage Effort

The *rabbanan*, by contrast, hold *asu takana b'kodshim* — we do attempt to salvage situations involving *kodshim*. Their advice to *Beis Din* is: tell the person to go and bring the *avuda*, the animal that had originally been lost, as the *korban*. Since that animal is now being brought, and since the replacement animal was never itself lost, the replacement never acquired the stigmatized status that triggers the death rule. It can therefore be allowed to graze, eventually develop a blemish (*mum*), be sold, and the proceeds used for an *olah*. This is the full content of the *rabbanan*'s position: the dispute is exclusively about whether *Beis Din* advises the salvage route. On all other points — including the case where a person acts on their own initiative — the *rabbanan* agree that the second animal must die.

This understanding also illuminates why the middle section of the *mishnah* works even according to the *rabbanan*. The cases there involve someone who did not consult *Beis Din*. Since they acted on their own, the *chachamim* concede to Rabbi Meir that there is a fundamental problem. The only self-help solution available in that posture — that is, without going to *Beis Din* — is to mix the two piles of money, thereby ensuring that neither pile alone is designated as the one that was used while the other was rejected. Mixing creates a situation where both piles are equally implicated in the *korban*, and the remainder is simply *mosar*, leftover funds for a *nedava*. Even a *talmid chacham* who knows the law well enough to realize that *Beis Din* would tell him to bring the *avuda* must still actually go and ask *Beis Din*, because the act of formally consulting them — rather than acting unilaterally — is itself what changes the halachic character of the selection.

### Tosafos Softening

*Tosafos* raises a pointed question against Rabbi Meir's position: how can Rabbi Meir simply not care about salvaging sanctified property, given the general principle that one may not destroy *kodshim* willfully (*ma'avdin kodshim b'yadayim*)? When a solution is readily at hand, why does Rabbi Meir not require that one take it? *Tosafos* answers by suggesting there is some benefit involved in bringing the non-lost animal. If, for example, the *avuda* is thin and weak while the replacement is fat and healthy, Rabbi Meir would instruct to bring the healthier animal as the *korban* — a more fitting offering for the *Beis HaMikdash* — and let the inferior one die. This framing presents Rabbi Meir not as indifferent to *kodshim* generally, but as prioritizing the quality of the offering over the possibility of preserving the rejected animal. This softens what would otherwise be a startling indifference to *takanas kodshim*. The *gemara* itself, however, states Rabbi Meir's position without any such qualification.

### Challenge to Rabbi

A challenge is now raised against the premise that Rabbi Meir never concerns himself with salvaging *kodshim*. A *beraisa* is cited in which a remedial instruction is given regarding the eating of a *mincha*: if there is a great deal of *mincha* and relatively few *kohanim* to eat it, they are told not to eat other foods beforehand, so that when they eat the *mincha* they will not be stuffing themselves (*achila gassa*), which would not constitute valid eating. This instruction is a kind of *takana* — an advisory arrangement to ensure the *kodshim* are handled properly. If Rabbi Meir genuinely held that no such remedial arrangements are ever made, this *beraisa* would appear to contradict him. The *gemara* responds that perhaps this *beraisa* is only according to the *rabbanan*, and Rabbi Meir would indeed not endorse even this kind of practical arrangement. This remains a somewhat difficult position.

### Mincha Eating

The *gemara* works through the *beraisa* in detail. The verse states *yochluha* — they shall eat it — which is apparently a redundant phrase given that eating has already been mentioned. The redundancy teaches that if the *mincha* is plentiful and there are fewer *kohanim*, they should not fill themselves on ordinary food or *teruma* beforehand, so that the *mincha* should not end up being eaten in a state of *achila gassa*. Conversely, if the *mincha* is small and many *kohanim* are present, they may and should eat beforehand so that they have an appropriate appetite and the eating of the *mincha* will be meaningful. The *gemara* then asks: does this *beraisa* not reflect even Rabbi Meir's position? The answer given is that it may reflect only the *rabbanan*. This confirms the difficult implication that Rabbi Meir, at least as the *gemara* reads him here, would not endorse practical measures to ensure the proper treatment of *kodshim* even in simple, uncontested cases.

One further point arises tangentially: the question of whether the *kohanim* could eat non-*kodshim* food within the *azara* in order to prepare themselves to eat the *mincha* there. *Rashi* holds that they should go outside to eat, since bringing *chullin* into the *azara* is problematic. *Tosafos*, however, argues in several places that there is no categorical prohibition against bringing *chullin* into the *azara*; the prohibition concerns treating non-*kodshim* items with the ceremonial character of *avoda*, not merely their physical presence in that space.

---

## Rabbi Abba Approach

### Using Non-Lost Animal

Rabbi Abba said in the name of Rav: *hakol modim b'miskaper b'she'eina avuda she'avuda mesa* — everyone agrees that if you were atoned for through the non-lost animal, the number-two replacement, then the first animal, which had been lost, must die. This is not surprising: the first animal had already acquired the stigmatized status of *avuda*, and if it was not the one brought as the *korban*, that stigma is not remediated.

### Using Lost Animal

The dispute between Rabbi Meir and the *rabbanan*, on this reading, concerns the opposite case: *b'miskaper b'avuda* — when you bring the animal that had been lost as the *korban*. Here the question is what happens to the replacement, number two, which had never been lost at all.

### Quasi-Lost Status

Rabbi Meir holds *muchlefes ke-kedusha dami* — the replacement has a status equivalent to that of the original. Since it was designated specifically to stand in place of the lost animal, it takes on the same halachic character as the one it replaced, including a quasi-lost status. Just as the original, if not brought, would be *mesa* because it was once lost, so too the replacement — by virtue of its substitutive function — carries that same quasi-*avuda* status. Therefore, even if you bring the original lost animal, the replacement must die.

### No Quasi-Status

The *rabbanan* disagree: *lav ke-kedusha dami* — the replacement does not acquire the status of the original. The replacement was never lost. It never experienced the rejection and stigmatization that forms the foundation of the death rule. Designating it as a substitute does not transfer the original's history onto it. Therefore, if you bring the original *avuda* as the *korban*, the replacement — which was always a clean, unstigmatized animal — may simply graze, develop a *mum*, be sold, and the proceeds go toward an *olah*.

This understanding of the dispute is clean and analytically elegant. It explains the debate in terms of whether a substitutive designation transmits status, without invoking the separate question of *Beis Din* consultation at all.

One might then ask how this approach explains the middle section of the *mishnah*, which appears to offer mixing the piles as the only solution — implying there is no simpler alternative such as simply using the pile that had been lost. According to this approach, the *rabbanan* would in fact have a simpler solution available: bring the *chatas* from the pile that had been lost, and the other pile, never having had *avuda* status, may go for a *nedava* without requiring any mixing. The *gemara* raises this as an objection and responds, as before, that the *mishnah* states only the categorical solution — the one that always works under all circumstances. Mixing the piles is the *psika* case, the solution that admits of no complications regardless of which pile is used or how the selection was made. The *mishnah* does not purport to enumerate every possible solution, and the existence of alternative paths does not contradict the teaching that this particular path is always effective.

Regarding the analogy to the *Yom Kippur* goats: the *gemara* elsewhere discusses what happens when one of the two goats designated for *Yom Kippur* dies and a second pair must be brought. Rav rules that *ba'alei chayim einam nidchin* — live animals cannot be halachically rejected — and therefore the surviving goat from the first pair retains its validity. The *kohen gadol* is atoned for using that goat from the first pair. The extra goat from the second pair thus corresponds to one that was designated knowing full well it would not be brought — a case the *gemara* calls *mafrish le'ibud*, designating for non-use from the outset. This is argued to be analogous to the situation where an animal is designated as a replacement from the start. The *gemara* notes that this analogy is actually somewhat stronger than the ordinary *avuda* case, since there the owner intended to use the replacement but here the second-pair animal was always destined not to be brought.

---

## Money Mixing Solution

### Mixing Moneys

The *gemara* now revisits the *mishnah*'s middle section in its own right. The *mishnah* teaches: *hamafrish ma'os l'chataso v'avdu* — one who designated money for a *chatas*, the money was lost, he designated a second pile, and then the first was found — the solution is *yavi me'elu u'me'elu*, to purchase the *chatas* from both piles combined. The remainder goes for a *nedava*, an *olah*. In this way, neither pile is identifiable as the one that was definitively chosen while the other was rejected.

### Apparent Contradiction

One might ask: according to the *rabbanan*, why is mixing necessary at all? Under Rav Huna's approach, you could consult *Beis Din* and be advised to bring from the *avuda* pile, thereby salvaging the replacement pile. Under Rabbi Abba's approach, you could simply use the pile that had originally been lost, and the replacement pile would never have had a problem in the first place. Either way, it appears that the *mishnah* is presenting mixing as if it were the only solution — which seems to contradict both Amoraic approaches.

### Clear vs. Unclear Cases

The *gemara* resolves this by applying the same principle it used earlier: *milta d'psika lei katani, milta d'lo psika lei lo katani*. The *mishnah* teaches only what is categorically true and admits of no exceptions. Mixing the piles always works, regardless of which pile is used for the *korban*, regardless of whether one acted unilaterally or consulted *Beis Din*, regardless of any other circumstance. The *mishnah* is not suggesting that no other solutions exist — it is teaching the one solution that is universally effective. The existence of situationally contingent alternatives is not denied; the *mishnah* simply confines itself to the unambiguous case.

---

## Surety Piles Case

### No Death for Backup

Rabbi Ami introduces a distinct and clarifying case. If a person designated two piles of money *l'achrayos* — for surety, as a backup — meaning from the outset one pile was meant to serve as collateral in case the other was lost, and then one pile was used to purchase the *chatas*: in this case the second pile does not die and is not cast into the Dead Sea. Rather, *niskaper b'echad meihen v'hasheni yiplu l'nedava* — one was used for the *korban* and the other goes for a *nedava*, an *olah*. This is because nothing in this configuration ever had the status of *avud*, lost.

### Agreement Without Loss

The *gemara* asks: according to whom must this ruling be stated? If it is stated according to Rabbi Meir, it is obvious. And if it is stated according to the *rabbanan*, it is even more obviously true.

### Lost Status Principle

The reason it is obvious according to Rabbi Meir is that *ad kan lo ka'amar Rebbi ela b'makom sheyesh ibud* — Rabbi Meir's entire position, including his ruling that the replacement acquires a quasi-*avuda* status, is premised on there having been an actual *ibud* somewhere in the chain of events. The replacement is treated as quasi-lost only because it was designated to stand in for something that was genuinely lost. Here, nothing was ever lost. The two piles were set aside together from the beginning, one as the primary fund and one as backup. Since the foundation of the death rule — *avuda* — is entirely absent, even Rabbi Meir would agree that the second pile simply goes for a *nedava*. The ruling is obvious.

### Rabbi Shimon's View

The *gemara* concludes that the ruling is needed specifically *aliba d'Rabbi Shimon* — according to Rabbi Shimon's position. Rabbi Shimon is the *tanna* who elsewhere treats the *chamesh chatas hamesos* — the five categories of *chatas* that must die — as a unified group, such that if any one of them does not apply in a given context (*tzibbur*), none of them apply. Based on this categorical approach, one might have supposed that Rabbi Shimon holds the death rule operates without exceptions whenever the *halacha* applies at all — that is, once you are in the world of *chatas*, the animal always dies, never grazes, no *nedava* ever applies. Rabbi Ami therefore must state that even Rabbi Shimon agrees that *nedava* applies when the second pile was never in a position of *avuda* to begin with.

### Yehoyada Midrash

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: was it not already obvious that Rabbi Shimon acknowledges *nedava* as a category? For Rabbi Shimon himself is quoted in a *beraisa* about the thirteen *shofros* — the charity boxes in the *Beis HaMikdash*. Thirteen boxes were stationed there, each designated for a different type of contribution. Seven were for specific purposes: *taklin chadatin* (new *shekalim* for the current year contributed late), *atikin* (old *shekalim* from the prior year contributed late), *kinin* (pairs of bird offerings for those obligated in *kinim* such as a *zav*, *zava*, *yoledes*, or *metzora*), *gozlei olah* (individual bird *olah* contributions), *eitzim* (wood for the altar fires), *levona* (frankincense), and *zahav lakapores* (gold for the *kapores* or other Temple vessels). Six were designated simply *l'nedava* — for voluntary contributions — specifically for the *olah* offerings purchased from leftover *chatas* and *asham* funds.

The relevant *beraisa* records a *midrash* taught by Yehoyada the *kohen*, based on the verse *asham hu asham asham laHashem* — the repeated word *asham* teaches that the money goes for *God* and the *kohanim*: the flesh of the *olah* is entirely for God (*olah* is entirely burnt), but the skin goes to the *kohanim*. Rav Nechemya — and some say Rabbi Shimon — objected: if the skins go to the *kohanim*, then you have effectively nullified Yehoyada's *midrash*, which teaches that everything from these leftover funds goes entirely for the *olah* without any priestly benefit. The point for our purposes is that Rabbi Shimon's objection demonstrates his clear acceptance that *nedava* applies in these cases of leftover *chatas* and *asham* funds. That is, Rabbi Shimon does hold that *nedava* is an operative category for leftover *kodshim* funds. Why then was Rabbi Ami's ruling necessary?

### One vs. Two Piles

The *gemara* distinguishes the two scenarios. In the *Yehoyada midrash* case, there is one pile of money designated for a *chatas*, and after the *korban* is purchased, there is leftover money from that single designation. That leftover naturally and obviously goes for a *nedava* — no one would think otherwise. But in Rabbi Ami's case, there are two piles designated from the outset, one as backup for the other. One might have thought — at least according to Rabbi Shimon's categorical approach — that the second pile, having been designated as a correlate to the first, acquires a rejected or quasi-lost status and must be destroyed rather than used for *nedava*. That is the *chiddush* Rabbi Ami comes to teach: even in that case, since nothing was ever actually lost, neither pile ever acquired *avuda* status, and the second pile goes for a *nedava* just like simple leftover funds.

### Lost Status Foundation

The *gemara*'s conclusion thus articulates a foundational principle that has been operative throughout the entire sugya but is stated explicitly only now: the entire *halacha* of *chatas mesa* — including Rabbi Meir's expansive application of it, including his ruling that the replacement acquires a quasi-*avuda* status — is built entirely on the premise that something was *avud*, genuinely lost, at some point in the chain of events. Rabbi Meir does not disagree with this foundation; his innovation is only that *avuda* status can be transmitted derivatively to the replacement through the logic of *muchlefes ke-kedusha dami*. But where no *avuda* ever existed — where two piles were designated together for surety from the start — even Rabbi Meir agrees that *niskaper b'echad meihen v'hasheni yiplu l'nedava*: use one for the *korban* and the other goes simply and cleanly for a *nedava*.

---

---

# Temurah 24

## Two Animals Achrayus

### Rav Hoshaiah's Case

The daf opens at 24a with a statement of Rav Hoshaiah that brings a new dimension to the ongoing discussion of *chatas hameisah*. Until now, the Gemara had been exploring the debate between Rebbe and the *Rabbanan* regarding the conditions under which a sin offering must die — both positions requiring, at minimum, that the original animal had first been lost, with the dispute turning on precisely when the second designation or atonement must occur relative to that loss. Rabbi Shimon had introduced the most stringent view, holding that any *chatas* whose owner achieved atonement through another offering dies, categorically and without nuance, subsumed under his rule of *chamesh chataos meisos*.

The Gemara had earlier established that even Rabbi Shimon would concede one case: where the owner designated two separate piles of money from the outset, one as a backup for the other. In that scenario, since neither pile was ever lost, even Rabbi Shimon would agree that the unused pile does not need to be destroyed. Now the Gemara extends the inquiry: what if, instead of two piles of money, a person designated two animals as a *chatas* from the outset — *hamafrish shtei chataos l'achrayus* — one serving as backup for the other? The owner is then atoned through one of them, while the other grazes. What is the law?

The Gemara immediately asks: *aliba d'man* — according to whom is Rav Hoshaiah's ruling a *chiddush*? If it is according to the *Rabbanan*, the novelty is negligible. The *Rabbanan* require actual loss as a precondition for the *chatas hameisah* designation. They hold that even designating a second animal as a replacement for one that was lost (*mafrish l'ibud*) does not suffice to confer quasi-lost status on the second — *lav k'ibud dami*. How much more so, then, if there was never any loss at all, as in a pure *achrayus* arrangement? The Rabbis would obviously say the second animal simply grazes. The real *chiddush* must therefore be directed at Rabbi Shimon, whose position is the most categorical: *nitkaper b'acher*, atoned through another, is sufficient in all circumstances. Under his view, even in the *achrayus* case, one might have thought the remaining animal must die. Rav Hoshaiah is therefore clarifying that this is not so.

But the Gemara quickly leapfrogs over Rabbi Shimon as well: *ela aliba d'Rebbi* — the statement is addressed to Rebbe. Rebbe occupies the middle position, stricter than the *Rabbanan* but not as absolute as Rabbi Shimon. When does Rebbe say the second animal must die? Only *b'ibud* — when the situation builds on the reality of loss, either because one animal was actually lost or because the second was designated in place of a lost one. But *achrayus* — a backup arrangement that never involved any loss at all — does not trigger the *halacha* of *chatas hameisah* even according to Rebbe. Hence the ruling: the animal grazes, and the proceeds go toward a *nedavah*.

### Rabbi Shimon vs. Rebbe

This ruling clarifies an important distinction that is easily obscured. One might have assumed that Rabbi Shimon's position — *nitkaper b'acher, hi meisah* — is simply an extreme version of Rebbe's, differing only in degree. The Gemara now makes clear that there is a qualitative difference. Both Rebbe and the *Rabbanan* ground the entire *halacha* of *chatas hameisah* in the phenomenon of loss. The owner's atonement through a second animal is not sufficient on its own; it must build on a prior reality of *ibud*. The debate between Rebbe and the *Rabbanan* concerns only the details of that framework — whether the second animal was designated before or after the first was found, and whether one counts from the moment of designation or the moment of *hakrava*. But the essential precondition of loss is shared by both.

Rabbi Shimon stands apart. He requires no *ibud* whatsoever. The sole criterion is *nitkaper b'acher*: once the owner achieves atonement through another animal, the original dies regardless of circumstances. This is true even when the first animal was never lost, as long as actual animals — not money — are involved. By contrast, where the owner designated two piles of money, Rabbi Shimon concedes that the unused pile survives, because the conceptual framework of *chatas hameisah* does not apply to money in the same way. But two animals sanctified as *chataos*, one of which atones — that remaining animal dies according to Rabbi Shimon even absent any loss. This is the structural significance of Rav Hoshaiah's ruling: it delineates precisely where Rabbi Shimon's categorical position ends.

---

## Redeemed Korban Status

### Blemished Sin Offering

The Gemara now pivots to an adjacent *mishnah* discussed earlier in the tractate. The case involves a person who designated a *chatas* that turned out to have a *mum*. The *Mishnah* rules: *hamochrah u'meivi acher tachteha* — you redeem it and bring a different animal in its stead. This is a straightforward application of the laws of redemption. What makes the case interesting is the position of Rabbi Elazar b'Rebbi Shimon appended to this *Mishnah*: *im karva shniya kodem she'nishchata rishona* — if the second *korban* was brought before the first (the redeemed one) was slaughtered, then the first animal acquires the status of *chatas she'nitkapru ba'aleha b'acher*, a sin offering whose owners were atoned by another, and it must be left to die.

### Redeemed Retains Identity

This is a striking position. The first animal had a *mum* and was redeemed — its *kedusha* was transferred. Yet Rabbi Elazar b'Rebbi Shimon holds that it retains the essential identity of a *chatas* to such a degree that a subsequent atonement through another animal can still doom it. The Gemara asks: according to which earlier authority does this align? The initial assumption was that Rabbi Elazar b'Rebbi Shimon follows Rebbe — the position that is comparatively stringent. But the Gemara challenges this. Even according to Rebbe, the *halacha* of *chatas hameisah* requires *ibud*, and this animal was never lost. Its situation is analogous to *achrayus*: it could not be used, another was brought in its stead, but there was never a status of being lost. Why should it die?

The Gemara therefore concludes: *lo, de'Rabbi Elazar b'Rebbi Shimon k'avuhu svara lei* — he holds like his father, Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Shimon holds that *nitkaper b'acher* suffices regardless of circumstance. If this animal retains its identity as a *chatas* even after redemption, then once the owner is atoned through another, it dies — no *ibud* required. The remaining question, which the Gemara defers for the moment, is the threshold condition: why would we say the redeemed animal still retains its *chatas* identity at all?

### Second Before First

The significance of this exchange is that it sharpens the conceptual landscape further. Rabbi Elazar b'Rebbi Shimon's position — that a redeemed *korban* retains its identity — is a distinct and independent claim. It interacts with Rabbi Shimon's ruling to produce a uniquely stringent outcome: the redeemed animal dies even though it was never lost, because (a) it retains its *chatas* identity post-redemption, and (b) Rabbi Shimon does not require *ibud*. Neither premise alone would be sufficient; the ruling requires both.

One might ask whether the person who purchased the blemished animal bears any practical responsibility. If the animal he bought was once a *chatas*, and Rabbi Elazar b'Rebbi Shimon holds it may still be rendered forbidden, he presumably needs to know this. Indeed, minimally one would be obligated to inform the buyer, since it limits his use of the animal: the prohibition on shearing, working, or grazing it applies, and he must slaughter it before the seller's second *korban* is brought.

---

## Two Animals Achrayus (II)

### Achrayus & Loss

The Gemara now returns to the framework of *achrayus* in order to connect it with the larger discussion of *sheir la'azazel*. The key conceptual move is understanding what the status of the second animal in a pair actually is when the first is used. The Gemara had established that the second *sheir lachatas* — the extra one left over when a new pair is brought — is treated as *achrayus*, a backup. But this raises an immediate difficulty: *achrayus* implies the possibility of choosing either one, whereas here one knows from the outset which will be used. If the second *sheir* is definitively going to be unused, how can it be described as mere *achrayus* rather than as *avud*?

The answer emerges in stages. The Gemara previously concluded that Rav holds *ba'alei chaim einan nidchin* — living animals are not rejected — and therefore *mitzvah b'rishon*, there is an obligation to bring the *sheir lachatas* of the first pair. This means it is not merely optional to use the first pair's *sheir*; it is required. Consequently, the second pair's *sheir lachatas* is not in an ambiguous backup position at all — it is known from the very outset that it will not and cannot be used. That status is equivalent to loss, *k'avud dami*, from the moment of designation. And once it has an *avud*-equivalent status, the framework of *nitkaper b'acher* applies, and a *yachid*-equivalent would die.

This explains a surface tension in the Gemara: earlier in the discussion the second *sheir* was described as *achrayus*, implying choice and optionality, yet here it is treated as effectively foreclosed from use. Tosafos notes that the earlier framing may simply represent the stage before the Gemara's conclusion, and the final position is that since *mitzvah b'rishon* is operative, the second *sheir* has *avud*-equivalent status from the beginning.

A student raised an interesting question during the shiur: what if the *sheir lachatas* of the first pair also dies before the second pair is brought? Would you then bring a third pair, or use the surviving *sheir* from the second pair? The answer is that the label of *chatas hameisah* only crystallizes once *nitkaper b'acher* has actually occurred. Before you have brought one of them and achieved atonement, the status is not yet permanent. So in that scenario, where atonement has not yet been achieved through either, you could go back and use the *sheir* of the second pair — which is perhaps part of why one could initially describe it as having a quasi-*achrayus* status. But the resolution remains: once *nitkaper b'acher* is established, the second one's fate is determined.

---

## When Is Lost (Avuda)?

### Lost at Designation

The Gemara introduces a *braita* taught by Rav Shimi bar Zeira before Rav Papa, which presents a striking formulation of the debate between Rebbe and the *Rabbanan*. The *braita* divides the cases as follows. *Avda b'sha'at hafrasha* — if the animal was lost at the time of the initial designation of the second one, but subsequently found before the second *korban* was actually brought: *l'Rebbe meisah*, Rebbe says it must die; *l'Rabbanan tir'eh*, the *Rabbanan* say it grazes. This is the familiar framing: Rebbe is stringent in holding that the loss at the moment of designation is sufficient, while the *Rabbanan* require the loss to persist through the moment of atonement.

### Lost at Atonement

The *braita* then turns to the converse case: *avda b'sha'at kapara* — lost at the time of atonement, meaning it was found only after the second *korban* was brought. Here, says the *braita*: *l'Rabbanan meisah*, the *Rabbanan* say it dies; but *l'Rebbe ro'eh*, Rebbe says it only grazes. This is deeply surprising. According to this *braita*, Rebbe and the *Rabbanan* are not on a continuum where one is simply stricter than the other in all respects. Rather, they are mirror images: Rebbe is stricter when the animal was lost earlier (at designation) but more lenient when it was lost later (at atonement), while the *Rabbanan* are more lenient about the earlier case but stricter about the later one. One can construct a logic for Rebbe's position: when the animal was found before the second one was brought, the owner actively chose to use the second one rather than reclaim the first — a deliberate rejection. Whereas if the animal was only found after the second was already brought, the owner had no opportunity to choose; the first was simply unavailable, so its non-use was not an active rejection.

### Rav Papa's Correction

Rav Papa, however, rejected this *braita* entirely. He argued from a *kal v'chomer*: if even in the case where the animal was found earlier (*b'sha'at hafrasha*) Rebbe says it must die, how much more so should Rebbe agree that it dies when the animal was not found until after atonement was achieved (*b'sha'at kapara*)? The later scenario is unambiguously worse — the atonement was complete, the animal was truly unavailable throughout the entire process. It is logically impossible for Rebbe to be more lenient in the more severe case. Therefore Rav Papa ruled: *ela tani hachi* — emend the *braita* to read as follows. *Avuda b'sha'at hafrasha l'Rebbe meisah l'Rabbanan ro'eh*: when lost at designation and found before bringing, Rebbe says die and the *Rabbanan* say graze — as before. *B'sha'at kapara divrei hakol meisah*: when lost at the time of atonement, everyone agrees it dies. The two positions form a strict continuum; later is always worse, and the earlier disagreement between Rebbe and the *Rabbanan* simply concerns how early a partial status of *ibud* is sufficient for Rebbe's ruling.

---

## Skin Removal Laws

### Margling on Yom Tov

The Gemara now introduces a new *braita*: *ein maraglin b'Yom Tov* — one may not perform the removal of leg skin (*margling*) on *Yom Tov*. The practice of *margling* involves flaying the skin off an animal from the legs upward rather than slitting it lengthwise down the belly. The latter method is simpler but yields a less useful piece of leather, since it is cut open. The leg-based removal is harder but produces a more intact piece suitable for flasks or other whole-leather uses. The reason it is forbidden on *Yom Tov* is straightforward: *d'ka tarach tircha d'la chazi lei* — it involves substantial effort that yields no *Yom Tov* benefit whatsoever. The leather cannot be used on *Yom Tov* itself. *Shechita* is a *tzorech Yom Tov* and therefore permitted, but this ancillary labor-intensive processing is not.

### Beis Shammai Kedusha

The *braita* adds: similarly, one may not perform *margling* on a *bechor* or on *psulei hamukdashin* — animals that were consecrated as *korbanos* but developed a *mum* and were redeemed. The prohibition in these cases, unlike the *Yom Tov* case, requires explanation. The Gemara asks: *bechor man tana* — who is the *tanna* responsible for the *bechor* ruling?

Rav Chisda answers: it is Beis Shammai. The *Mishnah* records a dispute between Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel regarding a *bechor* with a *mum*. Beis Hillel holds that once a *bechor* has a blemish, while certain prohibitions remain (one may not shear it, work it, or sell it by the piece), the meat may be eaten by anyone, not just *Kohanim*. Beis Shammai, however, holds that the *bechor* with a *mum* retains essentially the same *kedusha* as a *bechor* without one — and therefore a non-*Kohen* may not join with the *Kohen* in the eating (*lo yimaneh Yisrael im hakohen al habechor*). Since, according to Beis Shammai, the *kedusha* of the *bechor*'s meat is preserved even with a blemish, it follows that one may not engage in processing that focuses commercial attention on the leather rather than honoring the meat. The Gemara (later in the *sugya*) cites the phrase *nirah k'avodah b'kodashim* — it appears like performing labor with sanctified property. Whatever the precise mechanism of that concern, the underlying principle is that if the meat retains *kedusha*, redirecting one's effort toward the leather rather than the meat is disrespectful.

### Redeemed Even if Cooked

The *braita* turns to the prohibition by *psulei hamukdashin* — a *korban* that had a *mum* and was redeemed. This case is more extreme than *bechor* because unlike a *bechor* (which is never technically redeemed, its *kedusha* simply being reconfigured), a redeemed *korban* has had its *kedusha* explicitly transferred to money. Why should it retain enough of its *korban* identity to prohibit *margling*?

Rav Chisda answers: it is Rabbi Elazar b'Rebbi Shimon. The Gemara cites a *braita* that goes further than the *Mishnah* we have already encountered. The *braita* describes a case where someone had two *chataos* — one with a *mum* and one without — sanctified for the same sin. The unblemished one is brought, and the blemished one is redeemed. The *chachamim* themselves hold that if the blemished animal was slaughtered before the blood of the unblemished one was sprinkled, it is permitted — *muteres*. But once the blood of the unblemished one was sprinkled — *mishenizrak dama shel temima assura* — the blemished animal becomes forbidden.

Rabbi Elazar b'Rebbi Shimon goes further: *afilu basar ba'alas mum b'kdeira* — even if the meat of the blemished animal is already cooking in the pot, once the second *korban*'s blood is sprinkled, the pot's contents must be taken out and burned.
