### First Assumption

The *gemara* initially reads the *baraita* as supporting *Reish Lakish*. The phrase *ba'alei mumim yipadu* — blemished animals may be redeemed — is initially understood as referring to animals that acquired their *mum* after consecration. If that reading is correct, then the *tanna kamma* is permitting the redemption of *korbanot* that died with a *mum* that came upon them later — which is precisely *Reish Lakish*'s position, that *kodshei mizbe'ach* do not require *ha'amadah ve'ha'aracha* according to the *tanna kamma*. This, the *gemara* says, appears to contradict *Rabbi Yochanan*: *tiyuvta de'Rabbi Yochanan meireisha*.

### Ba'al Mum Me'ikaro

*Rabbi Yochanan* responds: the *baraita* is discussing *ba'al mum me'ikaro* — an animal that bore its *mum* from the very beginning. That is the case where everyone, including the *tanna kamma*, agrees the animal may be redeemed even after death. And indeed, this interpretation is confirmed by the logic of *Rabbi Shimon*'s own position. *Rabbi Shimon* holds unambiguously that *kodshei mizbe'ach* must be alive to be redeemed. If the *baraita* were discussing an animal that acquired its *mum* after consecration, *Rabbi Shimon* would have explicitly disagreed with the *tanna kamma*'s permission to redeem it. The fact that *Rabbi Shimon* does not dispute this ruling in the *baraita* demonstrates that the *mum* must be *me'ikaro* — present from the start — since that is the only scenario in which *Rabbi Shimon* concedes that a dead *korban* may be redeemed.

### Alignment

The *gemara* confirms this inference: *ela lav shema mina* — we learn from here that *ba'alei mumim* in the *baraita* means *ba'al mum me'ikaro*, because only then do *Rabbi Shimon* and the *tanna kamma* align. This supports *Rabbi Yochanan*'s framework perfectly.

---

## Alt. Text & Shitur

### Reish Lakish Girsa

At this point, *Reish Lakish* is said to have a different *girsa* — a different version of the *baraita* — which is somewhat more ambiguous about *Rabbi Shimon*'s position. In this alternative text, *Rabbi Shimon* is not explicit about whether the blemished case he permits refers to a *korban* where the blemish came later or where it was present from the start. This ambiguity gives *Reish Lakish* more room to maneuver.

### Reconciliation

With this different version of the text, *Reish Lakish* can argue as follows. The *tanna kamma* permits redeeming a blemished *korban* even when the blemish came later — demonstrating that the *tanna kamma* does not require the living condition for *kodshei mizbe'ach*. And *Rabbi Shimon*, in *Reish Lakish*'s reading of this alternative *baraita*, does not explicitly endorse the *tanna kamma*'s ruling in the *korban* case; he is only distinguishing between blemished and unblemished, which could be a reference limited to *bedek habayis*. Therefore, on this reading, *Rabbi Shimon* is silently disagreeing with the *tanna kamma* about the case where a *korban* acquired its *mum* later. The *gemara* notes, however, that even this alternative version ultimately runs into the same difficulties, and the stronger textual case remains with *Rabbi Yochanan*.

---

## Dead Korbanot Issue

### Rav Yirmiyah Query

*Rav Yirmiyah* poses a pointed question to *Rabbi Zeira*. According to *Reish Lakish*, the *rabbanan* — the *tanna kamma* — permit redeeming *kodshei mizbe'ach* even when dead, since they hold that the living requirement does not apply to sacrificial animals. But this generates a serious problem.

### Keluvim Problem

If a *korban* dies a natural death and then is redeemed, what does the owner do with it? He feeds it to the dogs. And that is precisely the problem of *podim et hakodshim le'ha'akhilam la'klavim* — redeeming sanctified animals for the purpose of feeding them to dogs — which is explicitly prohibited in the context of *korbanot*. So even if we grant that there is no technical requirement of *ha'amadah ve'ha'aracha* for *kodshei mizbe'ach* according to *Reish Lakish*, how do we avoid this problem?

### Shechut Chutz Case

The *gemara* answers: *hacha bemai askinan — beshe'avar ve'shachtan* — we are dealing with a case where the animal was already *shechted*, albeit improperly. The person violated the prohibition and *shechted* the *korban* outside the *Beis HaMikdash*. Now that it has been *shechted*, redeeming it will not result in feeding it to dogs — once redeemed, it can actually be eaten. This is precisely the case discussed in the subsequent *baraita*: *kol hakodashim she'naflu bahem mum ve'shachtan* — a *korban* that acquired a *mum* and was then *shechted* without having been redeemed first. *Rabbi Meir* says it must be buried, likely as a *knas* for the improper slaughter. *Ve'chachamim* say it may be redeemed — and this represents the explicit permission of the *chachamim* to redeem a dead *korban*, which is the view consistent with *Reish Lakish*.

---

## Blemished Korban Baraita

### Ba'al Mum Laws

A further *baraita* is then introduced, spelling out the full set of *halachot* governing an animal that was sanctified as a *korban* while already bearing a permanent *mum* — *ba'al mum me'ikaro*. The *baraita* describes a comprehensive picture of how the complete removal of *kedushas haguf* in this case affects every applicable *halacha*.

### Permissibility Details

Since the *kedusha* in this case was never a genuine *kedushas haguf*, the animal upon redemption sheds its *kedushah* entirely. Therefore: its firstborn is subject to the laws of *bechor*; if *shechted*, the *matanot* — the *zero'a*, *lechayayim*, and *keiva* — are given as usual; it may be shorn and worked (*yotzim le'chulin le'gozez ula'avod*); and its offspring and milk (*velad ve'chalav*) are permitted without restriction. These rules stand in sharp contrast to an animal that was sanctified and later acquired a *mum*, where shearing, working, and the milk and offspring remain bound by the *kedusha* even after redemption.

### Temura & Redemption

The *baraita* further specifies: *ein osim temurah* — such an animal cannot serve as the basis for *temurah*. This is consistent with the principle established throughout *Temurah* that *temurah* requires *bein tov lera bein ra letov* — a genuine *kedushas haguf* that at one point was fit for the altar. Since *ba'al mum me'ikaro* never had such fitness, no *temurah* can be made from it. And then, directly relevant to our discussion: *ve'im meisu yipadu* — if such an animal dies, it may be redeemed.

---

## Attribution Dispute

### Rav Yehuda's Claim

*Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Rav* asserts: *zu divrei Rabbi Shimon* — this is the position of *Rabbi Shimon* alone, not the *tanna kamma*. According to *Rabbi Shimon*, a *ba'al mum me'ikaro* is effectively like *bedek habayis* since it never bore *kedushas haguf*, and it therefore does not require *ha'amadah ve'ha'aracha*. Hence it can be redeemed after death. The *pasuk*'s word *otah*, on *Rabbi Shimon*'s reading, excludes *bedek habayis* from the requirement — and *ba'al mum me'ikaro* falls into that same excluded category.

### Attribution Challenge

This attribution to *Rabbi Shimon* alone raises an immediate question: why is the ruling ascribed only to *Rabbi Shimon*? The *tanna kamma* would equally appear to allow redeeming a dead *ba'al mum me'ikaro*. Should the *baraita* not have said *zu divrei Rabbi Shimon u'machlokto* — the view of *Rabbi Shimon* and the *tanna kamma* together?

### Reish Lakish Reasoning

The answer returns to *Reish Lakish*. The reason the *baraita* attributes the ruling only to *Rabbi Shimon* is that the compiler held like *Reish Lakish*. And according to *Reish Lakish*, the *tanna kamma* permits redeeming *kodshei mizbe'ach* even when dead — even when the *mum* came later. So what the *baraita* says about *ba'al mum me'ikaro* being redeemable is something the *tanna kamma* trivially agrees to in any case, since the *tanna kamma* allows redeeming dead *korbanot* generally. Therefore the ruling in the *baraita* — that a *ba'al mum me'ikaro* may be redeemed when dead — is not distinctive of the *tanna kamma*'s position. It is only *Rabbi Shimon*'s position that requires this specific clause, because *Rabbi Shimon* normally insists that *kodshei mizbe'ach* must be alive — but carves out the exception of *ba'al mum me'ikaro*.

### Tanna Kamma Assumption

The underlying logic of the attribution is thus as follows. Had the *baraita* been written according to *Rabbi Yochanan*'s reading of the *tanna kamma*, the attribution should have covered both opinions. But since the *baraita* is being read through *Reish Lakish*'s lens — where the *tanna kamma* broadly permits redemption of dead *korbanot* — only *Rabbi Shimon*'s position requires the explicit qualifier about *ba'al mum me'ikaro*. Hence the attribution to *Rabbi Shimon* alone.

---

## Temimim Restriction

### Unblemished Burial

With the *ba'al mum* side of the *baraita* now resolved, the *gemara* turns to a new question. Why does the *baraita* prohibit redeeming unblemished animals — *temimim* — even when they were sanctified only for the temple treasury? According to *Rabbi Shimon*, *bedek habayis* does not require *ha'amadah ve'ha'aracha* at all. Why then should an unblemished *bedek habayis* animal that dies be subject to burial?

### Mizbe'ach Domain

The answer, as *Rabbi Zeira* explains to *Rav Yirmiyah*, is: *mishum de'chazu le'hakrava* — because unblemished animals are fit for sacrifice. Even though this particular animal was dedicated to the treasury rather than the altar, its physical fitness for sacrifice means we cannot simply discard it as ordinary property. We treat it as though it were a *korban*, and since a dead *korban* cannot be redeemed according to *Rabbi Shimon*, the same rule applies here.

### Treasury to Korban

This principle is supported by a further *baraita*: *ha'makdish temimim le'bedek habayis* — one who dedicates unblemished animals to the temple treasury. When they are to be redeemed, *einam nifdim ela le'mizbe'ach* — they are sold only to a buyer who will bring them as a *korban*. The treasury does not simply sell them to the highest bidder; they must pass to someone who will use them for sacrifice.

### Perpetual Claim

The *baraita* articulates the principle explicitly: *she'kol ha'ra'uy le'mizbe'ach eino yotzei mi'yedei mizbe'ach le'olam* — anything fit for the altar never completely exits the altar's domain. Once an unblemished animal has been sanctified — even for the treasury — it can never be fully diverted from its potential as a *korban*. It must always be channeled back to the altar. This is the reason that even for *bedek habayis*, an unblemished animal that dies must be buried rather than redeemed: to redeem it for secular use would be to permanently remove from the altar's domain an animal that could have been a *korban*.

---

## Final Resolution

### Challenge

*Rav Pappa* now challenges the assumption that has quietly underpinned the entire preceding discussion. The *gemara* had been working with the premise that everyone — both *Rabbi Shimon* and the *tanna kamma* — agrees that *ba'al mum me'ikaro*, when sanctified as a *korban* and subsequently dying, may be redeemed. *Rav Pappa* challenges this directly.

### Mishna Evidence

The *mishna* in *Temurah* explicitly lists the distinctive *halachot* of an animal sanctified as a *korban* while already bearing a permanent *mum*: its firstborn may be taken, its *matanot* given, it may be shorn and worked, and if it dies — *ve'im meisu yipadu* — it may be redeemed. If this were a unanimous position, why would it need to be stated at all?

### R. Shimon Only

*Rav Yehuda* responds: *zu divrei Rabbi Shimon* — this is only *Rabbi Shimon*'s position. It is *Rabbi Shimon* who holds that *ba'al mum me'ikaro* sanctified as a *korban* can be redeemed after death, because *Rabbi Shimon* limits the *ha'amadah ve'ha'aracha* requirement strictly to genuine *kodshei mizbe'ach* and excludes anything that was never fit for the altar.

### Chachamim Stringency

The *chachamim* — the *tanna kamma* — disagree even in this case. According to the *chachamim*, even a *ba'al mum me'ikaro* that was sanctified as a *korban* requires the living condition. The sanctification, however imperfect, was a *korban*-type dedication, and the *chachamim* do not carve out this exception.

### Tanna d'bei Levi

This stringent *chachamim* position is identified with the *tanna d'vei Levi*, the extreme opinion encountered earlier. *Tanna d'vei Levi* holds that *hakol hayu bichlal ha'amadah ve'ha'aracha* — everything must be alive — and it is this view that insists even *ba'al mum me'ikaro* cannot be redeemed after death. This is not the mainstream *tanna kamma* of the *mishna*, but the outlying, maximalist position.

### Final Agreement

The *gemara* ultimately resolves that *ve'ibayeit eima* — one may also say: *Rav s'veira lei k'Rabbi Yochanan* — Rav holds like *Rabbi Yochanan*. And according to *Rabbi Yochanan*'s reading of the *tanna kamma*, the *tanna kamma* does agree that *ba'al mum me'ikaro* can be redeemed. The ruling in the *mishna* therefore represents the position of *Rabbi Shimon* and *the tanna kamma* together. The difficulty of the attribution — why did it say only *Rabbi Shimon* and not both? — is resolved by noting that the language can simply be adjusted: *eima hachi nami* — so understand it that way too. The only opinion that stands in genuine isolation is the extreme position of *tanna d'vei Levi*, who would not permit any redemption of a dead *korban*, even *ba'al mum me'ikaro*. The normative ruling, consistent with *Rabbi Yochanan* and the *tanna kamma*, is that an animal which bore its *mum* from the very beginning of its consecration as a *korban* may indeed be redeemed after death. With that, the *daf* concludes — and nearly so does the *masechet*.

---

---

# Temurah 34

## Nikbarim Intro

### Kodshim Comparison

The final daf of Maseches Temurah — daf 34 — begins with the Mishnah found at the bottom of 33b. Throughout the preceding discussion, we have been occupied with comparisons between *kodshei mizbe'ach* and *kodshei bedek ha-bayit*. This concluding Mishnah likewise has the character of a summary, yet its scope is considerably broader than the *kedushah*-centered distinctions that preceded it. Rather than focusing narrowly on issues of sanctity, it introduces a comprehensive taxonomy of forbidden objects and the prescribed method for their destruction.

### Miscarriage & Placenta

The Mishnah opens: *ve-elu hen ha-nikbarim* — the following are things that must be buried. The context flows naturally from the preceding Mishnah, which discussed which *kodshim* animals that have died may be redeemed and which may not. When redemption is unavailable, burial is required. Accordingly, the first case is *kodshim she-hipilu* — a *korban* animal that miscarried. Such an animal is treated like a *korban* that died: it cannot be redeemed and must therefore be buried. Underlying this ruling is an implicit assumption about the *kedushah* of a fetus in the womb. If a fetus acquires *kedushah* only upon birth, then a miscarriage would not generate this obligation. The Mishnah may therefore reflect the view that the fetus is *kadosh* while still in the mother's womb, or alternatively it addresses a case where the owner sanctified the animal after it was already pregnant, thereby directly conferring *kedushah* upon the fetus. In any case, the operative principle is *ein podi'in et ha-kodshim le-ha'achilam la-klavim* — one does not redeem *kodshim* in order to feed them to the dogs — and since the animal cannot be made alive again, burial is mandated. Similarly, *hipilah shilya tikaver*: if a consecrated animal produced only a placenta and no visible fetus, the placenta must also be buried, since we presume the presence of a fetus.

### Asurim be-Hana'ah

From the transition case of a dead *korban*, the Mishnah moves to the broader and more general category: things that are *asurim be-hana'ah* — forbidden in benefit. The question with such items is not merely that they cannot be eaten; because one may not derive any benefit from them at all, they cannot simply be left lying around. They must be disposed of. The Mishnah's answer, at least as a default, is burial.

### Forbidden Items List

The Mishnah enumerates: *shor ha-niskal* — an ox that was stoned because it killed a person; *eglah arufah* — the calf whose neck was broken in the ritual performed when a murder victim's killer is unknown; *tzipporei metzora* — the birds used in the purification ritual of a *metzora*. Regarding the birds: only the one that was slaughtered is *asur be-hana'ah*, not the one that was sent free, since the Gemara elsewhere establishes that the Torah would never *shillach le-takalah* — send away an animal into a situation of danger or prohibition. Next: *se'ar nazir* — the hair of a *nazir* that is shaved at the conclusion of his period of *nezirus*, which is also *asur be-hana'ah*; *peter chamor* — the firstborn donkey, which, if the owner refuses to redeem it with a sheep, becomes *asur be-hana'ah* (as this Mishnah assumes, though this was itself a subject of discussion in Maseches Bechoros); *basar be-chalav* — meat cooked with milk, a classic case of *issurei hana'ah*; and finally, *chullin she-nishchatu ba-azarah* — non-consecrated animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard.

### Chullin ba-Azarah

This last case, *chullin she-nishchatu ba-azarah*, is the most legally complex entry in the list, and it is worth dwelling on it. There is an extensive discussion in the Gemara about whether the prohibition of *chullin she-nishchatu ba-azarah* is of biblical or rabbinic origin. Even if one accepts that it is *de-oraisa*, that likely refers to the prohibition of performing such slaughter, not necessarily to the resulting object being intrinsically forbidden. The question of why the *object itself* becomes *asur be-hana'ah* is therefore far from obvious.

Rashi explains: *mishum de-michlefi behu kodshim she-ira behu pasul* — because someone who sees an animal slaughtered within the *azarah* and realizes it is not part of a *korban* will naturally assume that it must be an invalid *korban*. And the general rule for disqualified *korbanot* is that they must be burned. If this *chullin* animal is treated as freely consumable, it will be confused with *psulei kodshim*, leading to improper conduct.

The Mishnah then records a dispute: *Rabbi Shimon omer chullin she-nishchatu ba-azarah yisarefu* — Rabbi Shimon holds that such animals must be burned precisely because they will be confused with invalid *korbanot*, and invalid *korbanot* are burned. The first opinion, the *tanna kamma*, holds only that burial is required, not burning. The Gemara even extends Rabbi Shimon's position: *ve-chen chayah she-nishchatah ba-azarah* — even a non-domesticated animal, or indeed a pig or camel slaughtered in the *azarah*, would according to Rabbi Shimon receive this treatment. Since the governing concern is the act of slaughter in the *azarah*, we treat anything slaughtered there as though it were a *psul korban*, regardless of whether it could ever actually have been a valid *korban*.

A practical question arises: does the obligation of burial mean that one is literally required to dig a hole? The answer is that burial in this context means one should not simply leave the object available; other forms of destruction would be permissible as well, as the Mishnah will clarify shortly.

---

## Nisrafin Overview

### Things Burned Intro

The Mishnah continues: *ve-elu hen ha-nisrafin* — the following are things that must be burned. This is an important counterpoint to the preceding list. While *issurei hana'ah* in general are disposed of by burial, there are specific cases where the Torah mandates burning as the mode of destruction. The Mishnah proceeds to enumerate them.

### Chametz be-Pesach

The first item is *chametz be-Pesach* — leavened bread on Passover — which must be burned: *yisaref*. This reflects the opinion of one school of thought; as discussed in Maseches Pesachim, there is actually a dispute about whether *tashbitu be-chol davar* — "you shall eliminate" leaven by any means — or whether burning specifically is required, learned by analogy from *notar*. The *stam* of this Mishnah follows the view that burning is mandatory.

### Trumah Teme'ah

The next case is *trumah teme'ah* — *terumah* that has become ritually impure. This is a notably unusual category. Unlike the other items on the list, *trumah teme'ah* is not technically *asur be-hana'ah* in the classic sense. What exists here is a *mitzvah* to destroy it by burning, combined with a special allowance: one may derive *hana'ah* — benefit — from the heat and light *as it burns*. One might ask whether a *kohen* could simply feed *trumah teme'ah* to his animals, which would also constitute a form of disposal. The Gemara's position is that feeding it to animals is considered an act of deriving benefit from it rather than an act of destroying it. The technical violation is not the classic *issur hana'ah* but rather a failure to fulfill the *mitzvah* of destruction in the proper manner. The question of why using it as a fuel source — *or* as a type of air freshener, as the Gemara elsewhere establishes regarding *trumah teme'ah* wine — is categorically different from feeding it to animals is admittedly a subtle point that merits further investigation.

### Orlah & Kil'ei

The Mishnah adds *orlah* and *kil'ei ha-kerem* — produce of the first three years of a fruit tree and produce of mixed species planted in a vineyard, respectively — as further instances where the Torah mandates burning. The derivation for *kil'ei ha-kerem* comes from the verse *pen tikdash ha-mele'ah ha-zera asher tizra*, read through the homiletical lens of *tikdash tukad esh* — "it becomes holy" meaning "it must be set ablaze." The connection to *orlah* is derived by the Gemara through a principle that *orlah* and *kil'ayim* are learned from one another — *gamri me-hadadi* — though Rashi notes this linkage.

### Solid vs Liquid

The Mishnah then states: *et she-darkan li-saref yisaref, et she-darkan le-kaver yikaver* — that which is normally burned shall be burned, that which is normally buried shall be buried. One might wonder what practical work this rule performs given what the Mishnah has already stated. The answer is that this clause addresses liquids. One cannot practically burn a liquid that is not flammable. If one has wine of *orlah*, for example, or other non-oil liquid *issurei hana'ah*, burning is not a viable option. Such items are therefore buried. Oil, being flammable, would still be burned. The rule of *et she-darkan* maps the abstract obligation onto the physical reality of what can and cannot be incinerated.

### Bread & Oil Usage

The Mishnah concludes this section: *umadlikin be-fas be-shemen shel terumah* — one may use bread or oil of *trumah teme'ah* as fuel. This is the direct application of the principle just stated: since bread and oil are items that can in practice be burned, they are burned, and by the earlier rule, one may derive benefit from the heat and light produced as they are being consumed. The precise reason the Mishnah adds the case of bread (*pas*) alongside oil is not entirely clear, but the practical teaching is explicit.

---

## Psulei Kodshim

### Chutz mi-Zman

The Mishnah continues: *kol ha-kodashim she-nishchatu chutz mi-zmanam ve-chutz mi-mkomaum* — all sacrifices that were slaughtered with improper intention regarding time or place must be burned. This is somewhat implicit in what was discussed regarding *chullin she-nishchatu ba-azarah*, but here it is stated explicitly as a general rule. The case here is not *shechutei chutz* — animals slaughtered outside the Temple precincts entirely — but rather *korbanot* slaughtered within the *azarah* while the officiant had in mind to eat the sacrifice after its permitted time (*chutz mi-zmano*, the basis of *pigul*) or outside its designated location (*chutz mi-mkomo*). The broader principle, established by the Gemara in Pesachim, is *kol davar she-psulo be-hekdesh nisraf* — anything whose disqualification occurs within the realm of the sacred is burned. The Torah states explicitly about *notar*, *ve-ha-notar ba-esh yisarefu*, and from this the rule is extended to all *psulei korbanot*.

### Asham Talui

The Mishnah proceeds to a more complex and striking case: *asham talui yisaref*. The *asham talui* is a guilt offering brought by one who is uncertain whether he committed a sin for which a *chatat* would normally be required — for example, someone who may have accidentally consumed forbidden *chelev* but is not certain. This offering provides provisional atonement while the matter remains unresolved.

Now suppose this person brought the *asham talui*, the animal was slaughtered and offered, but before the *kohanim* could eat the meat, it became clear that he had *not* in fact sinned. The entire offering was therefore unnecessary. What is the status of the meat? Since there was no sin it corresponded to, retroactively this is *chullin* — non-consecrated meat slaughtered in the *azarah*, the paradigm of *chullin she-nishchatu ba-azarah*.

Yet there is a crucial difference from ordinary *chullin she-nishchatu ba-azarah*: at the time of slaughter, this animal genuinely possessed the *kedushah* of a *korban*. It was only retroactively, upon the clarification of facts, that its necessity evaporated. This proximity to genuine *psulei kodshim* means that even the *tanna kamma*, who in the standard case of *chullin she-nishchatu ba-azarah* required only burial, agrees here that the meat must be burned: it truly resembles a *korban* that became *pasul*. Nevertheless, *Rabbi Yehuda omer yikaver*: Rabbi Yehuda maintains that since it is ultimately *chullin* — the sin never having been committed — it should be buried, not burned.

### Chatat ha-Of

The Mishnah then addresses *chatat ha-of ha-ba'ah al ha-safek* — a bird *chatat* brought on the basis of uncertainty. The case involves a woman who is uncertain whether she gave birth to a viable child that obligates the bringing of a *korban* to permit her re-entry into the Temple and consumption of *kodshim*. Failing to bring the offering would leave her permanently excluded. Bringing it risks the category of *chullin ba-azarah* if no obligation existed. The Gemara learns from a *pasuk* that one may bring such a *korban* under conditions of doubt.

After *melikah* — the ritual nipping of the bird's neck — is performed, if the offering was in fact not obligatory, the bird is a *neveilah* and cannot be eaten. What is to be done with it? The Mishnah rules *tisaref*: it is burned, like a *korban pasul*. Rabbi Yehuda, however, says *yatilena la-amah* — cast it into the *amah*, the water channel that ran through the Temple courtyard, and cut it up limb by limb so that it flows out into Nachal Kidron. The reasoning behind Rabbi Yehuda's position here may be nuanced: since there remains a possibility that this *was* a genuine *korban*, actively destroying it in the manner one would treat *psulei kodshim* might itself be problematic. Disposing of it through the *amah*, a more passive mode of removal, avoids this concern. If the offering was indeed a valid *korban*, one has not actively violated it; if it was not, it has been removed. The question of why Rabbi Yehuda does not simply say *yikaver* here, as he did in the case of the *asham talui*, is left by the Gemara without explicit treatment, though it seems plausible that the *amah* disposal functions as a variant form of burial well-suited to the Temple setting.

---

## Burial/Burning Rule

### Don't Burn Buried

The Mishnah now states the overarching rule: *kol ha-nikbarim lo yisarefu* — everything that must be buried must not be burned. The Gemara asks the reason. The answer that will emerge is: *mishum de-nikbarin afran assur* — because items that must be buried retain forbidden status even after they are reduced to ashes. If one were permitted to burn such items, observers might reason that since they have now been burned, their ashes are surely permissible, applying the leniency that pertains to items that were *required* to be burned. But that leniency does not apply here. Hence: do not burn things that must be buried, lest someone mistakenly treat the resulting ashes as permissible.

### Don't Bury Burned

The converse rule — *ve-kol ha-nisrafin lo yikaveru* — everything that must be burned must not be buried — is, at first glance, more straightforward. If there is a *mitzvah* to burn something, one is obligated to fulfill that *mitzvah*; burying it instead would simply constitute a failure to perform the requisite act of destruction. Rashi, somewhat surprisingly, does not invoke this simple reasoning. Instead, Rashi says: *dilma ati inish ve-ashkechei ve-achlei* — lest someone happen upon the buried item, uncover it, and eat it. Burning is more thorough a mode of destruction than burial, and we are therefore concerned that a buried item will not be fully destroyed and will be misused. This Rashi is admittedly a difficult one, and the *acharonim* find it challenging: if the concern is insufficiency of destruction, why is that concern not equally applicable to items that must be buried? The straightforward reason — there is a *mitzvah* to burn — would seem sufficient.

The underlying logic that emerges from the Mishnah is therefore: items that must be buried have no Torah-mandated act of destruction, so virtually any form of elimination is acceptable, but do not burn them, because then their ashes would be mistakenly treated as *mutar*. Items that must be burned have a specific *mitzvah* to burn, so burning is required and one may not substitute another method.

### Rabbi Yehuda

*Rabbi Yehuda omer: im ratza le-hachmir al atzmo lisrof et ha-nikbar rashai* — Rabbi Yehuda rules that if one wishes to be stringent and subject things designated for burial to the more thorough destruction of burning, one is permitted to do so. The more complete physical destruction eliminates all possibility of misuse. *Amru lo: ein mutar le-shanot* — the Sages respond: it is not permitted to deviate from the established categories. Maintaining clear categorical boundaries prevents confusion between the two regimes. If one blurs the line in one direction, one risks blurring it in the other as well.

---

## Se'ar Nazir Debate

### Contradiction Raised

The Gemara now turns to the Mishnah's ruling that *se'ar nazir* must be buried, and Tavi raises a sharp contradiction before Rav Nachman. The Mishnah teaches *se'ar nazir yikaver* — the *nazir*'s hair is buried. Yet a Mishnah in Avodah Zarah states: *ha-oreg melo ha-sit mi-tzemer bechor be-veged yidaleik ha-veged* — if one weaves into a garment even a *melo ha-sit* (the span from thumbnail to forefinger) of wool from a *bechor* — a firstborn animal whose shearing is forbidden and whose wool is *asur be-hana'ah* — the garment must be burned. The Mishnah in Avodah Zarah then continues: *mi-se'ar ha-nazir u-feter chamor be-sak, yidaleik ha-sak* — if one weaves the hair of a *nazir* or the hair of a firstborn donkey into a sackcloth, the sackcloth must be burned. Here the text says *burn*, not *bury*. Why the discrepancy?

### Nazir Tahor/Tamei

The first answer offered is: *kan be-nazir tamei, kan be-nazir tahor* — the two sources are addressing different cases. When a *nazir* is *tahor* and completes his *nezirus*, the Torah explicitly prescribes what is done with his shaved hair: it is burned beneath the meat of the *korban* being cooked, as part of the ritual in the *Beit HaMikdash*. This means that for a *nazir tahor*, the Torah has positively commanded *sherifah* — burning — of the hair. The *nazir*'s hair therefore possesses an intrinsic obligation of burning. This point is made by Rav Velvel (the Griz), who argues that the *mitzvah* of burning the *nazir tahor*'s hair is not merely a procedural component of the ritual but reflects a *din* of the object itself: the Torah declares this hair to be subject to *sherifah*, even if for some reason it was not burned in the Temple context. When the hair is thus intrinsically obligated in burning, the Mishnah in Avodah Zarah's ruling to burn it makes sense. When, by contrast, the *nazir* is *tamei* and must shave but there is no ritual of burning prescribed by the Torah, the hair falls under the default category of *issurei hana'ah* designated for burial, and that is the case our Mishnah addresses.

### Peter Chamor Issue

The answer regarding *nazir* is acknowledged as a valid distinction. But the questioner presses: *peter chamor a-peter chamor kashya* — what about the firstborn donkey? Our Mishnah says bury it; the Mishnah in Avodah Zarah says burn the sackcloth woven from its hair. There is no *mitzvas sherifah* by *peter chamor* analogous to that of *nazir tahor*. The prohibition on *peter chamor* is simply *issurei hana'ah*, with no Torah-mandated burning. Rav Nachman has no response. He was silent.

### Hair vs Sack

Then Rav Nachman asked Tavi whether he had heard an answer to this, and Tavi reported what Rav Sheshes had told him: *kan be-sak, kan be-se'ar* — the distinction is not about which type of *nazir* or which *issurei hana'ah*, but about whether one is dealing with raw hair or a finished *sak*. If the hair is simply buried as hair, even if it were accidentally uncovered, the likelihood that anyone would derive benefit from loose, forbidden hair is low. But if it has been woven into a usable sackcloth and is then buried, the risk is substantial: someone will uncover a perfectly serviceable sack and use it. Under those circumstances we set aside the normal rule against burning items designated for burial and require burning to ensure genuine destruction. This answer applies to *peter chamor* as much as to *nazir*: in both cases, when the hair has been woven into a *sak*, we require burning.

### Rabbi Yose & Eliezer

This answer is corroborated: *amar Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina* — Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina independently said the same: when it is a *sak*, burn it; when it is mere hair, bury it. Rabbi Eliezer, however, reverts to the first answer — burn when it is *nazir tahor*, bury when it is *nazir tamei* — an answer that, as was noted, leaves the *peter chamor* case unresolved.

### Bitul be-Rov Q

The Gemara then raises a fresh question: *libatel se'ar be-rubba* — why is the forbidden hair not nullified (*batel*) by the majority of permitted material into which it is woven? If one strand of a *nazir*'s hair or a *peter chamor*'s hair is woven among a great many strands of permitted hair, it should be *batel be-rov* and the entire sackcloth should be permitted. The Gra notes that the word *sak* in this passage is textually awkward and removes it; the question is simply why the hair is not nullified in the majority.

### Recognition Pattern

Rav Pappa answers: *be-tzipporta* — because it was woven into a deliberate decorative pattern, such as a bird design. When the forbidden strand is incorporated into a recognizable design, its location is known; it is *nikkar* — identifiable — and therefore cannot be *batel*. The Gemara then asks: if you know exactly where it is, just remove that section — *tzipporta lishlefinhu* — and then only that piece need be destroyed. Why destroy the entire *sak*?

### Rabbi Yirmiya

Rabbi Yirmiya responds: *hani Rabbi Yehuda hi* — this ruling reflects the position of Rabbi Yehuda, who said that if one wishes to be stringent and burn items designated for burial, one may do so. The Gemara immediately challenges this: the prior question was simply why one need destroy the whole sack when one can remove the specific section — invoking Rabbi Yehuda's general *kulah* does not address that. Rabbi Yirmiya clarifies: if it is possible to remove the design, that is indeed the preferred option. But if it is not possible, then on the authority of Rabbi Yehuda one may burn the whole.

This leaves us with three distinct answers to the original question of why the Mishnah in Avodah Zarah prescribes burning rather than burial: first, that it is invoking Rabbi Yehuda's permission to burn rather than a strict obligation; second — and this is the strongest answer applicable to both *nazir* and *peter chamor* — that when forbidden hair has been woven into a functional object like a *sak*, the danger of misuse after burial is severe enough to require burning; and third, applicable only to the *nazir* case, that when a *nazir tahor*'s hair carries an intrinsic *mitzvas sherifah*, burning is mandated.

---

## Nisrafin List

### Chametz Burning

The Gemara now revisits the Mishnah's enumeration of *nisrafin*. The Mishnah's statement that *chametz be-Pesach yisaref* is identified as following the position of Rabbi Yehuda, who rules *ein biur chametz ela sherifah* — the destruction of chametz can only be accomplished through burning, learned by analogy from the laws of *notar*. This reflects a dispute about *biur chametz*, and the *stam* of the Mishnah adopts Rabbi Yehuda's view.

### Trumah Benefit

The Mishnah's inclusion of *trumah teme'ah* among things to be burned is revisited. As established earlier, this is a distinctive category: it is not *asur be-hana'ah* in the classic sense, but there is a *mitzvah* to destroy it by fire, and one may benefit from it in the course of that destruction.

### Orlah Burning

The cases of *orlah* and *kil'ei ha-kerem* are confirmed as instances where the Torah itself mandates burning, drawn from specific scriptural derivations as outlined in the Mishnah.

### Solids & Liquids

The Gemara spells out the practical meaning of *et she-darkan li-saref yisaref, et she-darkan le-kaver yikaver*: *ochlin bi-sreifah* — foods are burned; *mashkin bi-kvurah* — liquids that cannot practically be burned are buried. The Gemara notes that *trumah teme'ah* follows different rules from classic *issurei hana'ah*: wine of *trumah teme'ah* is not buried but rather dispersed as a kind of air freshener, a permitted form of benefit-in-destruction unique to its category.

---

## Ashes Status

### Reason for Rule

The Gemara now investigates the underlying principle stated in the Mishnah: *kol ha-nikbarim lo yisarefu*, and asks *mai ta'ama* — what is the reason?

### Ashes Principle

The Gemara's answer: *mishum de-nikbarin afran assur* — because items that must be buried have forbidden ashes, while items that must be burned have permitted ashes. This is the operative distinction. If one burns something that was designated for burial, observers will mistake the resulting ashes for those of items designated for burning — whose ashes are permitted — and will come to benefit from them improperly. Items that must be burned, once properly burned in fulfillment of the *mitzvah*, produce ashes that are *mutar*; items that must be buried, even if burned, produce ashes that remain *assur*. Hence the rule: do not cross categories.

---

## Mitzvah Principle

### Tosafot Mitzvah

Why should the status of ashes differ based on whether a *mitzvah* of destruction existed? Tosafot addresses this explicitly in the last Tosafot on 33b. Tosafot asks: *tzarich iyun ta'ama mai* — the reason requires investigation. Why should burning produce permitted ashes in the case of *nisrafin* but not in the case of *nikbarim*? Tosafot answers by invoking the concept of *na'asit mitzvato*: *keivan she-tzivah ha-katuv ve-serafan, achar she-asah ke-ilu na'asit mitzvato, ve-ein davar she-na'asit mitzvato mo'alin bo* — since the Torah commanded that it be burned, after the act is performed it is as though the *mitzvah* has been fulfilled, and one does not have the prohibition of *me'ilah* regarding something whose *mitzvah* has been completed.

### Torah Acknowledgment

The conceptual foundation is this: when the Torah prescribes a specific act of destruction — burn this object — the Torah is implicitly declaring that once that prescribed act is performed, the object is legally considered to have been eliminated. The Torah's prescription of the act constitutes a recognition that after the act, *this thing is done with*. What remains — the ashes — is therefore legally a new entity, not a transformed version of the original forbidden object. Conversely, when the Torah issues no command of destruction but merely says "do not derive benefit," it offers no mechanism for the object's legal elimination. If one on one's own initiative burns such an object, the Torah has never acknowledged that act as constitutive of the object's termination. The ashes are therefore treated as a modified form of the original object, and since that original object was *assur be-hana'ah*, the ashes remain so.

### Chemical Change

This conceptual framework connects to a broader question in halachah: how much physical transformation is needed before an object is considered legally distinct from what it was? This question arises, for example, in discussions about gelatin derived from pig bones, where chemical processing may render the substance physically unrecognizable. The question is always whether the degree of change is sufficient to constitute a different object. The principle here adds a further dimension: even radical physical transformation — reduction to ashes — may not be sufficient to create a new legal status unless the Torah itself has endorsed the act of transformation as constitutive. When there is a *mitzvah* of *sherifah*, the Torah endorses the burning as an act of legal termination; when there is not, no physical transformation achieves that result by itself. Some hold that even in the case of *nikbarim*, the prohibition on their ashes is only rabbinic — that biblically, ashes are indeed a different object — but the Gemara's operative framework is as described.

---

## Ashes Status (II)

### Drying Question

The Gemara probes the principle from several angles. It cites a *beraita* regarding *dam ha-niddah* and *basar ha-meit* — the blood of a *niddah* and the flesh of a corpse. Though these items remain *tamei* even if dried, the *beraita* states that if they become so desiccated that they crumble at the touch (*she-nifrechu*), they are *tehorim* — they no longer convey *tumah*. The Gemara asks: does *tehorim* mean they are now considered entirely a different object, such that they would also be *mutar be-hana'ah*? The Gemara responds: no — *tehorim va-asurin*. The law of *tumah* has a threshold based on the physical state of the object, and once that threshold is crossed, the *tum'ah* does not apply. But the prohibition of *hana'ah* is a separate matter; there, the object retains its status regardless of physical change, and it remains *assur be-hana'ah*.

### Sacrifice Remnants

A further challenge comes from the case of *olat ha-of she-nitmatzta dama* — a bird *olah* from which the blood has been fully squeezed out in the proper ritual manner. After this is done, the crop and feathers, which the Torah designates for removal to the side of the *mizbe'ach*, are stated to have gone *midei me'ilah* — out of the category of *me'ilah*. The Gemara asks: does *yatzu midei me'ilah* mean they are now fully permitted? The Gemara answers: *lo yatzu midei me'ilah va-asurin* — they have exited the prohibition of *me'ilah* but remain forbidden in benefit. The completion of the ritual act removes *me'ilah* specifically, but does not render them *mutar*. These remain two distinct legal categories.

### Ashes Exceptions

The Gemara then turns to examine the principle from the opposite direction: is it really true that when there is a *mitzvah* to burn something, the ashes are *mutar*? A *beraita* is cited: *kol ha-nisrafin afran mutar* — all things that are burned, their ashes are permitted. But then exceptions follow: *chutz me-efer asherah ve-efer de-hekdesh le-olam assur* — except for the ashes of an *asherah* and the ashes of *hekdesh*, which are forever forbidden. This contradicts our Mishnah, which addressed *hekdesh* cases where burning was required and whose ashes should accordingly be *mutar*.

The Gemara pauses to ask a parenthetical question: why does the *beraita* list *asherah* and *hekdesh* as two separate entries rather than combining them in a single phrase? The answer: *mishum de-asherah yesh lah bitulah bi-vnei kochavim, hekdesh ein lo bitulah olamit* — because the laws differ. An *asherah* can be nullified if the gentiles who worshipped it formally renounce its status as *avodah zarah*, whereas *hekdesh* that became *pasul* can never be permissibilized through such nullification. Since their legal contours differ, they must be listed separately.

### Hekdesh Accident

The Gemara resolves the contradiction between the *beraita* and our Mishnah through Rami bar Chama: *kegon de-nafla deleika be-heichalei hekdesh me-eleha* — the *beraita*'s ruling that *hekdesh* ashes are forever forbidden refers specifically to a case where a fire broke out accidentally in the Temple treasury. The *hekdesh* was burned, but no human being performed the *mitzvah* of burning it. In such a case, the ashes remain forbidden, because the Torah's transformation-principle — *na'asit mitzvato* — never came into effect. The prescribed act of destruction was not performed; the burning happened on its own. Without the deliberate fulfillment of the *mitzvah* of *sherifah*, the ashes are treated as a modified form of the original object and remain *assur*.

The Gemara frames this with reference to *me'ilah* as well: since nobody performed an act of *me'ilah* — unauthorized benefit — the property did not become *chulin* through that mechanism either. There are thus two pathways by which *hekdesh* could become *mutar*: the transgression of *me'ilah*, which converts it to *chulin*, and the fulfillment of a *mitzvah* of *sherifah*, which renders the resulting ashes *mutar*. When the fire broke out by itself, neither pathway operated. Hence the ashes remain forbidden.

### Special Cases Only

Rav Shemaya offers an alternative resolution: *ki tanya ha-hi be-trumat ha-deshen tanya* — when the *beraita* says that certain *hekdesh* ashes are forever forbidden, it is not speaking about *korbanot* that became *pasul* and were burned in fulfillment of a *mitzvas sherifah*. Those ashes are indeed *mutar*. The reference is specifically to *trumat ha-deshen* — the daily removal of ash from atop the *mizbe'ach*, performed each morning by the *kohen*.

### Trumat Deshen

The ashes of *trumat ha-deshen* are forbidden by their own distinct law. The Torah commands *ve-samo* — he shall place it — referring to the placement of the removed ashes beside the ramp, and the Gemara derives from this verse that the ashes of *trumat ha-deshen* must remain in their designated place and may not be used for benefit. This is categorically unrelated to the general principle about *mitzvas sherifah* and its resulting ashes being *mutar*. *Trumat ha-deshen* represents an independent Torah prohibition on those particular ashes, and this is the case the *beraita*'s exception refers to.

One question left without explicit discussion in the Gemara is why the ashes of an *asherah* remain forbidden even though there is a *mitzvah* to destroy it. One of the *acharonim* offers an explanation based on the principle of *chalifei avodah zarah assur* — that the prohibition of *avodah zarah* extends to objects derived from or exchanged for the idol, not merely the idol itself. Just as money paid for an idol becomes forbidden, so too ashes derived from it — even if not the original object — carry the extended prohibition.

The upshot of the entire sugya: when the Torah mandates an act of destruction and that act is duly performed, the resulting ashes are considered a new entity and are *mutar*. When no such Torah-mandated act exists — whether because the item is simply *assur be-hana'ah* with no prescribed destruction, because the burning occurred without human agency, or because a special law uniquely governs the resulting ashes — the prohibition persists.

*Hadran alach kodshei mizbe'ach, u-selikah lah Maseches Temurah.*

---

---

# Keritot 2

## Intro to Keritot

### Masechet Overview

*Masechet* Keritot is another short *masechet* of roughly 30 *daf*, placing it among the several brief tractates that conclude the *Seder Kodashim*. In many ways, however, it feels quite different from the other *Kodashim* material covered in recent months. The bulk of *Seder Kodashim* focuses either on the mechanics of bringing *korbanot* — the specific *mitzvot* governing the sacrificial process — or on more metaphysical questions of *kedusha*: how holiness inheres in an offering, how it transfers, and what its implications are. Keritot, by contrast, is a *masechet* centered on *mitzvot*, obligations, and transgressions in a far more conventional sense. The animating questions here are: when does one incur an obligation to bring a *korban chatat*? What counts as an unintentional violation? How many *chatatot* must one bring if multiple sins were committed in a single state of forgetfulness?

### Focus on Chatat

The pivot around which the entire *masechet* turns is the *korban chatat*. One brings a *chatat* for sins that carry *karet* when committed intentionally. But the *masechet* ranges more broadly than that. There is the *asham talui*, brought when one is uncertain whether a sin requiring a *chatat* was committed at all. There are forms of *asham* that are sin offerings but not *chatatot* in the classical sense. And there are *chatatot* that are not about sin at all — the most prominent example being the *yoledet*, a woman who has given birth, who brings a *chatat* as part of the completion of her purification. As discussed in an earlier context, *chatat* carries a meaning of cleansing and restoration, not only of atonement for wrongdoing. Part of the *masechet* thus addresses the full range of obligations that fall broadly within the *chatat* category.

A further major theme is the question of multiplicity: if one committed several sins in a single state of forgetfulness — *helem achat* — does one bring a single *chatat* or multiple *chatatot*? And if one forgot *Shabbat* entirely and performed multiple *melachot*, how many offerings does that generate? These are questions about obligations and *aveirot* in a manner that feels far more like a standard *masechet* than the more specialized *Kodashim* material preceding it.

### Text Transmission

One distinctive feature of Keritot is its language. It is among the five *masechtot* whose Aramaic has a distinctly *Yerushalmi* flavor — it does not read like standard Babylonian Aramaic. The scholarly consensus holds that this reflects an earlier redaction or a redaction in a different location within *Bavel*, in a region where the Aramaic was closer to Palestinian Aramaic. That said, the text of Keritot is considerably more stable than that of *Temurah*, where variant readings and brackets proliferated throughout. Here the actual text is relatively settled, likely because the *masechet* was studied more frequently — which makes sense, given its more accessible subject matter.

### Pseudo-Rashi Issue

In terms of *mefarshim*, the first pages of the *masechet* carry no *Tosafot* at all — and indeed *Tosafot* appears only sparsely throughout. This means the pages are quite large in terms of sheer *Gemara* text, but the bulk of *Rashi* on each page compensates by keeping the overall page dimensions manageable.

The *Rashi* here, however, is strikingly verbose. On the very first *mishna*, which lists the 36 categories of *karet*, the commentary proceeds to enumerate each sin individually, cite the *pasuk* that prohibits it, and cite the *pasuk* that establishes it as *karet* — an approach entirely unlike *Rashi*'s characteristic terseness. This raises the obvious question of authenticity. While Strack and Stemberger, the standard reference on the *Talmud*, do not mention Keritot specifically, the Jewish Encyclopedia under the heading of *Rashi* records that scholars have concluded the *Rashi* printed on Keritot is not authentic. Zunz was the first to demonstrate this. The true author is unknown — possibly one of *Rashi*'s students — but the attribution is no longer tenable. Practically speaking, the verbosity of the pseudo-*Rashi* is not a burden for the learner following along in the *shiur*, even if it requires attention during preparation.

---

## 36 Karets List

### Karet Intro

The *mishna* opens: *shloshim v'shesh kritot b'Torah* — there are 36 instances of *karet* in the Torah. The relevance to *Kodashim* is direct: the sins for which one incurs *karet* when committed intentionally are precisely the sins for which one brings a *korban chatat* when they are committed unintentionally. *Karet* is thus the organizing principle for determining which *chatatot* are required.

It is worth clarifying the structure of punishment here. *Karet* is the divine punishment for an intentional violation committed without witnesses and formal warning. But that does not mean *karet* is always the most severe consequence. Many of these same sins, if committed with witnesses and the requisite *hatara*, carry a court-imposed death penalty — *chilul Shabbat*, for example, is *mot yumat*. The death penalty, when applicable, may instead be administered by the court. In the absence of witnesses or warning, God exacts the punishment, and that is *karet*. Some sins carry only *karet* and no court penalty — *Yom Kippur* violations, for instance — while others carry the possibility of *malkot* in lieu of *karet* when witnesses are present. The relationship between *malkot* and *karet* in cases where both might theoretically apply is itself a topic the *Gemara* will address.

### What is Karet

The word *karet* — *venichrat hanefesh hahi me'ameha*, "that soul shall be cut off from its people" — is interpreted differently by various authorities. The *Gemara* most often understands *karet* as a foreshortened life; specifically, the *Gemara* states that one who dies between the ages of 50 and 60 is said to have suffered *mita shel karet*. *Rashi* in several places identifies *karet* with *ariri* — childlessness — and sometimes invokes both: a shortened life and the absence of offspring.

A necessary caution applies here: the inference runs only in one direction. Dying before 60 or living without children are genuine tragedies in their own right, and it would be deeply insensitive to draw reverse inferences from these categories onto people who have experienced such losses. The logical form *if P then Q* does not license *if Q then P*. Indeed, the *Gemara* itself records that a certain *Amora* celebrated upon reaching the relevant age precisely because it demonstrated he had definitively not died in that range — which already acknowledges how dangerous the reverse inference would be.

The *Rambam* reframes these questions in a different key altogether. For the *Rambam*, *Olam Ha-ba* refers to the world of souls after death — not the this-worldly era following the coming of *Mashiach*, as the *Gemara* typically frames it. Accordingly, the *Rambam* understands *karet* primarily as the soul's being cut off from *Olam Ha-ba* at death. This is consistent with the *Rambam*'s broader tendency to understand divine reward and punishment in terms of the soul's natural metaphysical state as shaped by one's religious and intellectual life, rather than in terms of a more transactional scheme of *sachar ve'onesh*.

### Arayot List

The *mishna* begins its enumeration with *arayot* — forbidden sexual relations. The first group listed are those that also carry a court-imposed death penalty: *haba al ha'em* (intercourse with one's mother), *ve'al eshet ha'av* (one's father's wife, even if not one's biological mother), *ve'al hakallah* (one's daughter-in-law, i.e., one's son's wife), *haba al hazachar* (a man who lies with another man), *ve'al habehemah* (bestiality), *ve'ishah hamvi'ah habehemah aleha* (a woman who brings an animal upon herself), *haba al ishah u'vitah* (a man who has relations with a woman and her daughter), and *ve'eshet ish* (a married woman). All of these carry not only *karet* but a court-imposed death sentence; notably, the first three specifically carry *sekilah* — death by stoning.

### Gender in Arayot

The *mishna* — and indeed the *parshiyot* of *arayot* in *Acharei Mot* and *Kedoshim* — addresses these prohibitions from the male perspective throughout. This is not merely a descriptive feature; it also shapes which prohibitions apply to whom. The Torah does not state that an aunt is forbidden to have relations with her nephew — only that a man may not have relations with his father's sister or mother's sister. The *Gemara* in fact discusses uncle-niece marriage as not merely permitted but even particularly appropriate. The *mishna* follows the same framework, so the list as given assumes a male subject except where explicitly stated otherwise — as in the case of *ve'ishah hamvi'ah habehemah aleha*, where by definition there is no male subject to address.

The *Gemara* does address the question of how women are implicated in *arayot* despite the male framing of the Torah's language. The general principle derived is *u'meitu gam sheneihem* — "both of them shall die" — establishing that the woman participating in these acts bears the same culpability as the man.

### Arayot Continued

After the capital cases, the *mishna* lists *arayot* that carry *karet* without a court-imposed death penalty: *haba al achoto* (one's sister), *ve'al achot aviv* (one's father's sister), *ve'al achot imo* (one's mother's sister), *ve'al eshet achi aviv* (one's paternal uncle's wife). Notably, *ve'al eshet achi imo* — one's maternal uncle's wife — appears in parentheses in the text, because that prohibition is rabbinic rather than biblical, and is therefore not counted in the 36.

The *mishna* then adds *ve'al haniddah* — a man who has relations with a woman in a state of *niddah*, which carries *karet* even if she is his wife. This concludes the category of *arayot*.

It is worth pausing over the apparent asymmetry in severity. Relations with a sister carry only *karet*, not the death penalty, while relations with a woman and her daughter carry *mita*. To our intuitions, incest might seem more deeply objectionable than the latter. The *Gemara* will have occasion to address this. One additional observation: ancient Egypt's royal family routinely practiced brother-sister marriage, suggesting that our sense of that particular taboo as self-evidently extreme may reflect more recent cultural formations. And as Freud observed, strong taboos tend to arise around acts for which there exists a corresponding *yetzer hara* — taboos do not generally develop around things people have no temptation to do.

### Non-Sexual Karets

Following the *arayot*, the *mishna* turns to non-sexual transgressions carrying *karet*: *v'hamigadef* (blasphemy — the precise definition of which the *Gemara* will explore), *v'oved avodat kochavim* (idolatry), *v'hanoten mizar'o la'Molech* (passing one's child through the fire in Molech worship — a practice that raises the question of why it is listed separately from *avodah zarah*, though it clearly belongs to that broader category), *u'va'al ov* (one who performs the necromantic practice known as *ba'al ov*), and *v'mechallel Shabbat* (violation of *Shabbat*, which as noted carries *mita* if performed with witnesses and warning but *karet* otherwise).

### Temple Violations

The *mishna* continues: *v'tame she'achal kodesh* — a person who is *tamei* and eats a *korban*. This is distinct from the case where the *korban* itself is *tamei* — that is merely a *lav*. Here the *korban* retains its full *kedusha* and is eaten by a person in a state of *tumah*, representing a violation of that *kedusha* of the gravest sort, hence *karet*. Similarly, *v'haba el hamikdash tamei* — a *tamei* person who enters the *Beit HaMikdash*. These two violations carry no court-imposed death penalty; they are solely *karet*.

The *mishna* also includes *v'hashochet u'ma'aleh bachutz* — one who slaughters an animal intended as a *korban*, or who offers a *korban*, outside the *Beit HaMikdash* at a time when such external offerings are prohibited. This belongs to the same constellation of *Mikdash*-centered concerns.

### Forbidden Foods

The foods carrying *karet* are *chelev* (forbidden fat), *dam* (blood), and *notar u'pigul* — *korbanot* that were left over beyond the permitted time, or that were rendered *pigul* through improper intent at the time of the offering.

This raises the question of why these particular *ma'achalot asurot* carry *karet* when far more familiar prohibitions — pork, *neveilah*, *basar b'chalav* — carry only a *lav*. The common denominator is a *Mikdash* resonance: *chelev* and *dam* are substances that go upon the *mizbeach*. There is also an allusion in the *pesukim* linking *dam* to forms of *avodah zarah* — *lo tochlu al ha-dam lo tenachashu v'lo te'onenu* — and the explicit verse *ki ani netativ lachem al ha-mizbeach lechaper* establishes these as substances dedicated to the altar. That is presumably why *chelev* of a *chaya* carries no such prohibition — animals not fit to be offered as *korbanot* are not subject to this logic. Archaeological evidence offers a striking parallel: ancient Jewish settlements throughout the land of Israel are identifiable precisely by the consistent absence of pig bones, even in periods and contexts where other forms of non-observance are archaeologically evident. The *issur* of pig, though only a *lav*, was apparently the most durably observed prohibition across all social strata.

### Oil, Incense, Chametz

The final group of transgressions enumerated includes *v'ochel chametz b'Pesach* (eating *chametz* on *Pesach*), *v'ochel v'oseh melacha b'Yom HaKippurim* (eating or performing *melacha* on *Yom Kippur* — these are two separate transgressions), *v'hamfatem et hashemen* (compounding the *shemen hamishcha*, the anointing oil, outside its authorized context), *v'hamfatem et haketores* (compounding the incense), and *v'hasach et shemen hamishcha* (anointing oneself with the actual *shemen hamishcha*).

The laws of *shemen hamishcha* and *ketoret* were recently covered in the *parasha*. The Torah in *Ki Tisa* prescribes the formula for the *shemen hamishcha* and then states: *al besar adam lo yisach u'vematkunto lo ta'asu kamohu* — it may not be applied to a human body, and one may not produce oil in the same formulation. Both violations carry *venichrat me'amav*. Similarly, for the *ketoret*, the Torah prohibits making incense with the same composition: *v'haketores asher ta'aseh b'matkuntah lo ta'asu lachem*. One subtle difference between the two: there is no parallel prohibition of *smelling* the actual *ketoret* of the *Mikdash*, because smelling is not halachically considered an act of *hana'ah* at the biblical level, and *me'ilah* does not apply to it. The *issur* of the *ketoret* is specifically in its production for personal use — *lo ta'asu lachem* — which means one who makes *ketoret* for the express purpose of donating it to the *Beit HaMikdash* does not violate the prohibition. That leniency does not apply to *shemen hamishcha*, which may not be produced even with intent to donate.

The question arises whether burning *ketoret* outside the *Mikdash* would constitute a violation of *shochatei chutz*. That prohibition is closely bound to animals, and it is not clear that *ma'aleh ketoret bachutz* would fall within its ambit; *ma'aleh evarim bachutz* or *maktir chelev bachutz* certainly would. This is left as an open question.

Returning to the broader list: why does *chametz* on *Pesach* carry *karet* when the other prominent *ma'achalot asurot* do not? This question connects directly to the final category of the *mishna*.

### Pesach & Milah

The *mishna* concludes its enumeration with *v'hapesach v'hamila* — *Pesach* and *milah*. These are the only two *mitzvot asei* whose non-performance carries *karet*. All the preceding items were prohibitions; these two are affirmative commandments. The Torah is explicit in both cases: by *korban Pesach* it states *v'chadal la'asos hapesach venichrasah hanefesh hahi me'ameha*; by *brit mila* the verse reads *v'arel zachar asher lo yimol et besar orlato venichrasah*.

The underlying reason is that these two *mitzvot* are the most foundational markers of Jewish identity. *Milah* is the physical mark on the body — the seal of personal belonging. *Korban Pesach* is the communal act of participation in the foundational narrative of the Jewish people. It is no accident that those who were unable to bring the *korban Pesach* cried out to *Moshe*, *lamah nigara levilti hikriv et korban Hashem bemo'ado betoch benei Yisrael* — the sense of exclusion from the collective was so profound that a makeup offering, *Pesach Sheni*, was instituted. And this is why *Pesach* remains, by virtually any survey, one of the most universally observed Jewish rituals — something like 95% of those who identify as Jews participate in some form of *seder*. The powerful experiential dimension of the *seder* contributes to this, but so does the deep structure of what *Pesach* means as an expression of communal belonging.

Looking at the plain sense of the *pesukim*, *karet* is always formulated as *venichrat me'amav* or *venichrat hanefesh hahi mitoch benei Yisrael* — the soul is cut off *from the people*. The individualistic conceptions of *karet* as a shortened lifespan or exclusion from *Olam Ha-ba* are real and significant, but they overlay what the Torah itself emphasizes: exclusion from the community. It is precisely because *Pesach* and *milah* are the acts by which one declares and enacts membership in that community that their neglect carries this same punishment of communal severance. This framework also illuminates why *chametz* on *Pesach* carries *karet* among all the *ma'achalot asurot*: the prohibition of *chametz* during *chag hamatzot* is inseparable from the *Pesach* complex of participation in Jewish history. The *issur* of *chametz* is best understood as connected to the *karet* of *korban Pesach* itself.

---

## Intent & Chatat

### Mishna 2 Intro

The *mishna* continues: *al elu chayavin al zedonam karet* — for all of these, if one transgresses willfully, one incurs *karet*, assuming there are no witnesses and warning that would trigger the applicable court-imposed death penalty. *Ve'al shigagatam chatat* — and for an unintentional commission of any of these sins, one brings a *chatat*.

### Shogeg Definition

What does it mean to transgress unintentionally? The pseudo-*Rashi* here, drawing on *Gemaras* throughout *Shas*, identifies two categories of *shogeg*. The first is a mistake of fact: one thought one was sleeping with one's wife and it turned out to be one's sister; one did not realize one was *tamei*; one did not know one was entering the *Beit HaMikdash*; one forgot it was *Shabbat*. The second is a mistake of law — but a specific kind of mistake. Pseudo-*Rashi* describes a case where one knows that a broader category is forbidden and even knows the severe consequence, but did not realize that this specific act fell within that category. For instance: one knows that *avodah zarah* is *chayav mita*, but believed that this particular act was not actually a form of *avodah zarah*. The person is fully aware of the larger prohibition but was mistaken about whether the detail at issue was encompassed by it. These cases of factual or legal mistake render one a *shogeg* and trigger the obligation of a *chatat*.

### Omer Mutar

A harder question is what happens when a person did not know the prohibition existed at all. This is the category the *Gemara* refers to as *omer mutar* — one who claims permissibility, effectively someone who was entirely ignorant of the prohibition. Is such a person a *shogeg* who brings a *chatat*, or are they in a different category?

The *Gemara* in *Makkot* addresses a parallel question with respect to murder: if someone claims killing was permitted, are they a *shogeg* who goes into *galus*, or are they too close to *meizid* to qualify? The framing there is *havei lei lemeida* — is it the person's responsibility to have known? If so, ignorance of the law is no excuse, and the person is *karov l'meizid* rather than a genuine *shogeg*. Pseudo-*Rashi* here takes the position that *omer mutar* in a case like compounding the *ketoret* would constitute *oness* — complete absence of fault. Many *Rishonim*, however, hold that the analysis is case-dependent: by murder, we say *havei lei lemeida*; by *mefatem et haketores*, even though it is an explicit *pasuk*, we might not. The spectrum runs from genuine *meizid* through *karov l'meizid*, through various grades of *shogeg*, to *karov l'oness*, and finally to full *oness*. For the obligation of a *chatat*, one must be somewhere in the middle of that range — neither a true *meizid* nor a true *oness*.

### Asham Talui

The *mishna* continues: *v'lo hoda shelahem asham talui* — if one is uncertain whether one committed such a sin, one brings an *asham talui*, an offering held in suspense pending clarification of whether the sin was actually committed. The classic case is where one slept with a woman but is uncertain whether she was one's wife or one's sister.

However, there is an exception: *chutz m'nitamei mikdash v'kodashav* — the cases of *tum'ah* related to the *Mikdash* and its *korbanot* are excluded. If one is uncertain whether one entered the *Beit HaMikdash* while *tamei* or whether one ate a *korban* while *tamei*, one does not bring a standard *chatat* but an *oleh v'yored* — a variable-cost offering. According to *Rabbi Meir*, the *asham talui* applies only where, if one knew one had sinned, one would bring a fixed *chatat kavua*. A sin whose certain commission would require an *oleh v'yored* has no corresponding *asham talui*; in a case of uncertainty about such a sin, one brings nothing.

### Blasphemer

The *mishna* further records a dispute regarding the *megadef*, the blasphemer. *Chachamim* exclude the blasphemer from the category of *asham talui* — and possibly from *chatat* entirely — citing the verse *torah achas yihyeh lachem l'oseh bishgagah*: one law for one who acts unintentionally. From here the *Chachamim* derive *yatza megadef she'eino oseh ma'aseh* — the blasphemer is excluded because blasphemy requires no physical *ma'aseh*. This raises the question of whether the exclusion from *asham talui* extends to a *chatat* as well: is a *ma'aseh* required for *chatat* liability, or only for *asham talui*? The *Gemara* will clarify the scope of this exclusion. Notably, the transgression that carries *karet* — and potentially the death penalty — requires no physical act at all; *karet* for blasphemy applies to speech alone. But for the purposes of *korban* liability, the *Chachamim* require an action.

---

## Gemara Numerology

### Why 36 Karets

The *Gemara* now opens with its characteristic question: *minyana lama li?* — why does the *mishna* need to state a number? If the *mishna* is going to enumerate the 36 cases of *karet* anyway, what purpose is served by announcing the count in advance?

*Rav Yochanan* answers: *kamashma lan kulam b'helem achat chayav al kol achat v'achat* — the number is stated to teach that if all 36 prohibitions (or rather, their relevant details) were forgotten simultaneously, and all were violated in that single state of forgetfulness, one would be obligated to bring a separate *chatat* for each one of the 34 prohibitions. One cannot reason that because everything was done in one state of forgetfulness only one *chatat* is owed. Each prohibition is a distinct *aveirah*, and each requires its own *chatat* when violated *b'shogeg*. (The two *mitzvot asei* — *Pesach* and *milah* — do not generate *chatat* obligations, so the operative count for purposes of *chatat* is 34, not 36.)

### 39 Melachot

The *Gemara* immediately extends this logic to the *mishna* in *Shabbat*: *avot melachot arba'im chaser achat* — there are 39 *melachot* of *Shabbat*. *Minyana lama li?* The answer is the same: *kulam b'helem achat chayav al kol achat v'achat*. If one forgot that all 39 *melachot* were forbidden on *Shabbat* — while still knowing in some minimal sense that it was *Shabbat*, perhaps retaining awareness that *chutz l'techum* is forbidden — and one performed all 39, one would bring 39 separate *chatatot*. By contrast, if one performed the same *melacha* multiple times in one state of forgetfulness, one brings only a single *chatat*, since it is the same transgression repeated. The point is that 39 *distinct* categories of *melacha* generate 39 distinct *chatatot*, regardless of the unified state of forgetfulness.

### Mechusrei Kapparah

The *Gemara* moves to a later *mishna* in the *masechet*: *arba'ah mechusrei kaparah* — four categories of *mechusrei kapparah*, those who complete a purification process by bringing a *chatat* not because of sin but as the final step in becoming fully *tahor* and permitted to enter the *Mikdash* and eat *korbanot*. *Minyana lama li?* The answer here is different: *l'apokei mi'd'Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov*, to exclude the position of *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov*, who says *chamisha havei* — there are actually five such categories.

What is *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov*'s fifth? *D'tanya*: *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov omer ger mechusar kapparah ad she'yizarek dam alav* — a convert is lacking atonement until blood has been sprinkled on his behalf, meaning a convert must bring a *korban* to complete the conversion process. *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* understands this not as part of the conversion per se, but as the completion of a purification-type process analogous to the other four. By stating *arba'ah* — exactly four — the *mishna* makes clear that it rejects this position.

### Voluntary Offerings

The next *mishna* in the *masechet* states: *arba mevi'in al ha-zadon kishgagah* — there are four types of cases in which one brings a *korban* even for an intentional transgression. Normally a *chatat* is brought only for *shogeg*; these are exceptions, most of them involving the *oleh v'yored* or *asham* category rather than the standard fixed *chatat*. *Minyana lama li?* Here too the number is stated *l'apokei mi'd'Rabbi Shimon*, to exclude *Rabbi Shimon*'s position. *D'tanya: Rabbi Shimon omer shevuat ha-pikadon lo nitan zedonah l'kapparah* — by a false oath regarding a *pikadon*, a deposit entrusted to one's care, *Rabbi Shimon* holds that a willful transgression does not generate a *korban* obligation. According to him there are only three such cases. By stating four, the *mishna* clearly rejects his position.

### Five One Korban

Another *mishna* teaches: *chamishah mevi'im korban echad al aveirot harbeh* — there are five types of people who bring a single *korban* for multiple transgressions. Normally each distinct transgression requires its own *korban*; these are exceptions. *Minyana lama li?* The *Gemara* explains: *mishum d'ka-ba'ei l'mitni seifa nazir she-nitma tumot harbeh* — because the enumeration must include the case of a *nazir* who became *tamei* multiple times. The *nazir* case is not straightforwardly about *aveirot* in the standard sense, since the *korban* brought by a *nazir* after *tumah* is more about restarting the *nezirut* than about atonement for sin. Nevertheless, it is included in this category.

### Nazir Tumah Detail

The *Gemara* presents the case: a *nazir* who becomes *tamei* must undergo a seven-day purification process and then restart his *nezirut*. A dispute between *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi* (Rebbi) governs when exactly the new *nezirut* begins. *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda* holds that the new *nezirut* begins on day seven — upon completing the shaving (*tiglachto*) — even though the *korban* that closes out the old *tumah* is not brought until day eight. *Rabbi* holds that the new *nezirut* begins only on day eight, when the *korban* is actually brought.

This dispute has direct practical implications for the case at hand. Suppose a *nazir* becomes *tamei*, reaches day seven, and — according to *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda* — thereby begins a new *nezirut*, but immediately becomes *tamei* again that same day. He now has accumulated multiple *tumot* attributable to distinct periods of *nezirut*, yet he has never reached day eight and was therefore never obligated in a *korban* for the earlier *tumah* before the new one occurred. When he ultimately brings his *korban*, it covers all these separate *tumah* events together. This is the case of a single *korban* for multiple violations.

According to *Rabbi*, however, the new *nezirut* does not begin until day eight. If the *nazir* becomes *tamei* on day seven and again on day seven, *kulah chada tumah arichta hi* — it all constitutes one extended *tumah* within a single *nezirut*, never generating multiple distinct statuses. And if the new *tumah* occurs on day eight, it arrives after the moment at which the obligation in the first *korban* had already been established — *keivan d'yatza b'sha'a haru'ya l'havi b'korban* — making it a separate *korban* obligation: *chayav al kol achat v'achat*. Thus according to *Rabbi*, the scenario of one *korban* for multiple *nezirut tumot* can never arise. The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *ella shema mina Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda hi* — this *mishna* follows the position of *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda*. The number five is stated to make clear that the *nazir* case is genuinely included, and that the *masechet* is adopting *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda*'s position rather than *Rabbi*'s.

### Oleh V'yored

Another *mishna* in the collection teaches: *chamishah mevi'im korban oleh v'yored* — there are five types of *oleh v'yored*, variable-cost sin offerings. *Minyana lama li?* Because the *mishna* continues to state *nasi k'yotzei bahem* — that a *nasi* is like them — and this requires clarification. The reference is to the principle in *Horayot*: a *nasi* brings his special *korban* — a male goat — only for the same categories of sins for which a *beit din* would bring *par helam davar shel tzibbur* for misleading the public. Both the *beit din*'s special *korban* and the *nasi*'s special *korban* apply only to sins that would generate a fixed *chatat kavua* for an ordinary Israelite. For sins that would generate an *oleh v'yored* for a commoner, the *nasi* brings nothing — neither his special *korban* (since the qualifying condition is not met) nor an *oleh v'yored* (since by definition a *nasi* is wealthy and is not in the *oleh v'yored* category). One opinion holds that a *nasi* brings nothing at all for such a sin and simply has no *kapparah*; another opinion, that of *Rabbi Eliezer*, holds that a *nasi* does bring his *sa'ir* even for an *oleh v'yored* sin. By stating five *oleh v'yored* cases, the *mishna* excludes *Rabbi Eliezer*'s position and makes clear that these sins generate only an *oleh v'yored* and nothing else.

### Avot Nezikin

Finally, the *Gemara* addresses the *mishna* at the opening of *Bava Kamma*: *arba avot nezikin* — four primary categories of property damage. *Minyana lama li?* *L'apokei mid'Rabbi Oshaya*, to exclude *Rabbi Oshaya*, *d'amar telat esrei avot nezikin* — he counts 13, expanding the list well beyond the standard four by including additional forms of damage.
