One of the rationales for stating a precise number in that *mishna* is that the category determines when one must pay with *meitav sadeihu*, the finest of one's land.

The *Gemara* then turns the question around: according to *Rabbi Oshaya*, why does he state 13? *L'apokei mid'Rabbi Chiyya*, to exclude *Rabbi Chiyya*, *d'amar esrin v'arba'ah avot nezikin* — who counts 24. And according to *Rabbi Chiyya*, why state 24? To exclude *moser u'mefagel* — the *moser* who informs on a fellow Jew to an oppressive government, causing the seizure of his property, and the *kohen* who renders a *korban pigul* through improper thought, thereby causing loss to the owner. Both of these are excluded from the *avot nezikin* because the damage is not direct, and the principle of *hezek she'eino nikar* — damage that is not physically manifest — exempts the actor from liability.

With this final exchange, the *Gemara* has completed its enumeration of the numbered *mishnayot* in and adjacent to *Masechet Keritot*, using each as an occasion to introduce the major themes and debates that will occupy the rest of the *masechet*.

---

---

# Keritot 3b

## Multiple Offerings

### Review & Context

Today's shiur opens on the bottom of 2b, where the previous discussion reviewed the various *mishnayot* throughout the *masechet* that give specific numbers, with particular attention to what the number in our *mishnah* is meant to convey. The central point established was that the number in our *mishnah* signals that one may bring multiple *chataot* even within a single state of forgetfulness — though not thirty-six, since two of the cases involve *mitzvot aseh*, and Rashi later specifies the number as thirty-four. The review also covered the other *mishnayot* in the *masechet* that address variations on the themes of *korban chatat*, *asham talui*, *mechusrei kaparah*, and related topics.

### One Forgetfulness

The *gemara* resumes with the phrase *amar mar*, directing attention to the ruling: *hevi'um kulam behe'elam achat chayav al kol achat ve'achat* — if one performed all of these transgressions within a single state of forgetfulness, one is liable for each and every one separately. This represents the clearest case: each act is distinct, each transgression is distinct, and therefore each warrants its own *korban*.

The discussion then turns to the underlying principle. The *gemara* begins by establishing that complete exemption is certainly not an option. The verse states *ki kol asher ya'aseh mikol hato'evot ha'eleh venichretu* — whoever performs any of these abominations shall be cut off. If one transgression incurs *karet*, and *karet* in turn implies a *chatat* when done *beshogeg*, then committing multiple such transgressions in one state of forgetfulness clearly does not render one *patur*. The *gemara* notes this as self-evident.

### Single Offering?

The real question, then, is whether multiple transgressions committed in one state of forgetfulness might nonetheless require only a single *chatat*. As a point of comparison: if one committed the same *aveira* multiple times within one uninterrupted state of forgetfulness — for example, forgetting that cooking on *Shabbat* was prohibited and cooking five separate times without any intervening awareness of the *issur* — one brings only a single *korban*. The question is whether the same logic might extend to different sins: perhaps even distinct transgressions, if performed within one state of forgetfulness, should require only one *chatat*. Where does one find the foundational principle that separate sins committed in a single state of forgetfulness each require their own *korban*?

---

## Sister Prohibition

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan addresses this with a well-known formulation: *lekach yatzat karet ba'achoto lechaleik* — this is why the *Torah* stated *karet* explicitly in connection with the prohibition of sleeping with one's sister, even though a general verse at the end of *Parshat Acharei Mot* or *Kedoshim* already assigns *karet* to all *arayot* collectively. The general verse states *ki kol asher ya'aseh mikol hato'evot ha'eleh venichretu*, which encompasses all prohibited relations. Why, then, did the *Torah* need to reiterate *karet* specifically for one's sister? Rabbi Yochanan's answer is that the *Torah* singled out *achoto* in order *lechaleik* — to treat each case individually. The explicit *karet* by *achoto* signals that each of the *arayot* is to be treated distinctly, and since *karet* is the basis for *chatat* liability when the act is *beshogeg*, each separate transgression will generate its own *chatat*.

### Bibi bar Abaye

Rabbi Bibi bar Abaye challenges this derivation. He argues: *eima achoto deparat kra nitchayev chatat alah* — perhaps the *Torah*'s explicit mention of *karet* by the sister case generates a separate *korban* only for the sister prohibition itself, while all other *arayot* might yield only a single *chatat* regardless of how many are committed in one state of forgetfulness. The *gemara* immediately presses back on this objection: does Rabbi Bibi bar Abaye not accept the hermeneutical principle of *kol davar shehayah bichlal veyatza min haklal lelamed, lo lelamed al atzmo yatza ela lelamed al haklal kulo yatza*? When something that was part of a broader category is singled out with a specific ruling, that ruling is not treated as an exception applying only to that case — rather, it serves as a paradigm for the entire category.

### General Rules

To illustrate this principle, the *gemara* invokes the case of *shelamim*: the verse specifies that eating from a *korban shelamim* while *tamei* incurs *karet*. Yet *shelamim* was already included within the broader category of all *korbanos*. Why was it singled out? *Lehakish aleihem* — to use it as a paradigm. Just as *shelamim* is a *kodshei mizbe'ach* and one incurs *karet* for eating it while *tamei*, so too all *kodshei mizbe'ach* are subject to the same rule. The singling-out of *shelamim* simultaneously excludes *kodshei bedek habayit* from the *karet* prohibition and establishes *korbanos* as the paradigm for the rule's application. In the same way, the singling-out of *achoto* should instruct us about the entire category of *arayot*.

---

## Refining Principle

### Specific Traits

Rabbi Bibi bar Abaye is not satisfied. He accepts the hermeneutical principle — he has no objection to deriving a rule from a paradigm — but he presses on what the specific characteristics of *achoto* actually teach. By the analogy to *shelamim*, what was learned is defined by the relevant features of the paradigm case. Applied here: *mah achoto meyuchedet she'hi ervah* — a sister is *ervah*. One might therefore conclude that only *arayot* generate separate *chataot*, but not other sins that carry *karet*. Furthermore, *ve'ein lah heter bechayei osrah* — a sister can never become permissible during the lifetime of the one who renders her forbidden. This characteristic would exclude a married woman, *eshes ish*, who *can* become permissible if her husband dies. Therefore, Rabbi Bibi argues, the *achoto* derivation might apply only to permanently forbidden *arayot*, not to all *karet* transgressions and perhaps not even to all *arayot*. This leaves open the question of how we know that every separate *karet* offense, regardless of category, generates a distinct *chatat*.

### Explicit Verse

Rabbi Yona — and some say Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua — resolves this by pointing to an explicit verse: *ki kol asher ya'aseh mikol hato'evot ha'eil venichretu*. This verse at the end of the *parasha* expressly groups all the *arayot* together under a single *karet* formulation. The implication is: *hukshu kol ha'arayot kulan l'achoto* — all the *arayot* are explicitly equated with *achoto* with respect to *karet*. Once the verse itself links them all together, one is not required to examine what characteristics of *achoto* define the paradigm. The verse states that they all share the same *karet*, and therefore: *mah achoto chayav aleiha bifnei atzmah af kol chayav aleiha bifnei atzmah* — just as one is liable separately for *achoto*, one is liable separately for each of the *arayot*.

The *gemara* notes, however, that this still leaves a question: how do we extend the principle beyond *arayot* to all other *karet* transgressions? The *gemara* appears to assume that once the derivation is no longer confined to *achoto* alone, generalization follows, though the question could still be raised.

The *gemara* then introduces a further point. There is also a verse concerning *niddah* — *ve'el ishah benidat tumatah lo tikrav* — and the question is raised: why does the verse say *ishah* (woman) when it could simply have said *niddah*? Rashi explains that through the lens of rabbinic usage — where *niddah* names the woman rather than describing the state — the extra word *ishah* comes to teach: *lechaleik al kol ishah ve'ishah*, each woman is treated separately, meaning each *ervah* is a distinct case.

---

## Woman & Sister

### Niddah Woman

The *gemara* draws out a further implication of this word *ishah*. If the Rabbis can derive the principle of *lechalek* — treating each *ervah* separately — from the extra word *ishah* in the *niddah* prohibition, then it would seem one does not need the derivation from *achoto* at all for this purpose. The *gemara* acknowledges as much: *rabbanan nami tipok leh me've'el ishah benidat tumatah* — the Rabbis could have derived the point of separating the cases from this verse. The question then becomes: if the principle can be learned from *ishah*, what additional work does the explicit *karet* by *achoto* perform?

The *gemara* answers: *mibaei leh lechaleik al achoto ve'al achot aviv ve'al achot immo* — it is needed to distinguish between the case of one's own sister, one's father's sister, and one's mother's sister, and to teach that even these closely related prohibitions are treated as distinct for purposes of *chatat*. One might have thought that since these are all variations of the "sister" category, a single act involving one person who happens to be all three simultaneously would incur only one *chatat*. The explicit statement about *achoto* teaches otherwise.

To this the *gemara* objects: *harei shemos mechulakim ve'gufot mechulakim* — these are already distinct prohibitions (*shemos mechulakim*) and, in the ordinary case, distinct persons (*gufot mechulakim*). Where there are separate *lavin* and separate people or objects, no verse is needed to establish separate *chataot*. The *gemara* therefore refines the answer: the verse is needed specifically for a case where *achoto* and *achot aviv* and *achot immo* are all the same individual. While such a scenario requires considerable creative genealogy — best left to a discussion in Yevamos — the case is theoretically possible: a single person who stands in all three of these relationships simultaneously. There one person is involved (*gufot lo mechulakim*), yet the *aveirot* are distinct. The extra word *achoto* teaches that even in that case, the separate *shemot* — the separate prohibitions — are sufficient to generate separate *chataot*.

This articulates a fundamental principle: the criterion for multiple *chataot* does not require multiple persons or multiple objects. A single act, a single person, even a single moment — if multiple distinct prohibitions were violated, each generates its own *chatat*.

### Full vs. Half

The *gemara* introduces yet another view: *leRabbi Yitzchak de'amar chayvei keritot bichlal hayu, velama yatzat karet be'achoto ladun bekaret velo bemalkut*. Rabbi Yitzchak holds that the separate mention of *karet* by *achoto* comes to teach something different entirely — not *lechalek* for *chataot*, but to establish that *karet* for incestuous relations is not displaced by *malkut*. The background question is whether one who received *malkut* for a *karet*-eligible transgression is thereby discharged from *karet*: *kol chayvei keritot shelaku nifteru miyedei keritatan*. Rabbi Yitzchak disputes this and uses the explicit *karet* of *achoto* to demonstrate that *malkut* does not exempt from *karet*. (The *halacha* does not follow Rabbi Yitzchak on this point, but his derivation reorients what *achoto* is teaching.)

Having used *achoto* for this purpose, Rabbi Yitzchak no longer has it available to derive *lechalek*. The *gemara* asks: *lechaleik mena lei?* — from where does Rabbi Yitzchak derive that each *ervah* generates a separate *chatat*? The answer is: *nafka lei me've'el ishah benidat tumatah* — he derives it from the word *ishah* in the *niddah* verse, precisely as discussed above.

In turn, the *gemara* asks: since the Rabbis can also use *ishah* for *lechalek*, what do they do with *karet* at *achoto*? Their answer is that it was needed to address the case of one's full sister — *achoto shehi bat aviv u'vat immo*. The *Torah* explicitly prohibits one's paternal half-sister and one's maternal half-sister. A full sister, being both, might be thought to be covered by either prohibition without requiring a separate verse. Yet conceptually, a full sister is a distinct category from each type of half-sister. One could derive her prohibition through a *kal v'chomer*, but a *kal v'chomer* cannot establish *onesh* — punishment. This is the principle of *ein onshim min hadin*.

### Ein Onshim

The principle of *ein onshim min hadin* — that punishment cannot be derived from logical inference alone — is significant here. The *Torah* assigns *karet* explicitly to the half-sister cases. One might reason by *kal v'chomer* that a full sister, who incorporates both prohibitions, must also incur *karet*. Yet the *gemara* holds that such reasoning is insufficient for imposing a punishment as severe as *karet*. Without a *pasuk*, a *karet* obligation cannot stand. The extra *achoto* in the verse serves therefore to provide that explicit textual basis for the full sister, ensuring that her *karet* rests on the verse rather than on inference alone.

The *gemara* notes, somewhat pointedly, that Rabbi Yitzchak — who believes *onshim min hadin* is valid — does not need *achoto* for this purpose. He holds that the *kal v'chomer* for a full sister's *karet* is legitimate. Alternatively, the *gemara* offers: *yalif ones me'azhara* — since a full sister's prohibition can be derived textually (even if not by an explicit separate verse), Rabbi Yitzchak can link her *karet* to her prohibition by analogy, which is considered more than pure logic and therefore permissible.

A sharp point emerges here: the *nafka minah* of whether a *karet* obligation is textually grounded extends beyond the realm of divine punishment. The practical halakhic consequence is the ability to obligate a *chatat*: without a legitimate basis for *karet*, there is no basis for the *chatat* when done *beshogeg*. The system requires that we can properly establish *karet* status — not merely that we believe God will act in a certain way — for all the downstream halachic implications to follow.

---

## Separate Sins

### Two Lavin

The *gemara* now advances to a more sweeping principle, stated by Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya: *kol makom she'ata motzei shnei lavin ve'karet echad, chilek chataot beineihem* — wherever the *Torah* presents two separate prohibitions with a single *karet* covering both, each prohibition nevertheless generates a distinct *chatat*. The singularity of the *karet* formulation does not collapse the two prohibitions into a single *aveira* for purposes of *chatat* liability. As long as there are separate *lavin*, the transgressions are sufficiently distinct.

### Anointing Oil

The illustrative case is that of the *shemen hamishchah*, the anointing oil. The verse contains two separate prohibitions: *al besar adam lo yisach* — do not apply the anointing oil to a person's skin — and *uvmatkunto lo ta'asu kamohu* — do not compound a private batch of oil according to the same formula. These are two distinct *lavin*. Yet the verse then assigns a single *karet* to both: *ish asher yirkach kamohu v'asher yitein mimenu al zar venichreat me'amav*. One might have thought that this single *karet* covering both prohibitions means that violating both in one state of forgetfulness incurs only one *chatat*. Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya teaches that this is not so. The separation of the *lavin* is what counts; the unity of the *karet* is irrelevant to the question of how many *chataot* are owed.

### Reconciliation

This raises an immediate difficulty: *vachi me'achar delavin mechulakim, karet achoto dechasav Rachamana lama li?* If the principle is that separate *lavin* automatically entail separate *chataot*, why was all the earlier discussion necessary? The entire elaborate derivation from *achoto* — with all its qualifications, the challenge of Rabbi Bibi bar Abaye, the response from *ishah*, and so forth — now appears superfluous.

The *gemara* responds that the earlier verses were in fact needed for other purposes, and the principle of separate *lavin* generating separate *chataot* makes them redundant only with respect to that specific teaching. According to Rabbi Yitzchak, *karet* by *achoto* was needed to establish that *malkut* does not discharge *karet*. According to the Rabbis, it was needed to establish the *karet* obligation for a full sister on textual grounds (*ein onshim min hadin*). Rashi understands the *gemara* to be saying that those verses were genuinely needed for their other purposes; the implication for *lechalek* was incidental and, in hindsight, unnecessary given Rabbi Elazar's principle. This resolution is admittedly somewhat unusual: one is left wondering where Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya himself derived the principle, since it was not stated as a derivation but seemingly as an *a priori* rule. The *gemara* does not address this directly.

The upshot, in any case, is now fully established: separate *chataot* are owed whenever the *aveirot* involve separate *lavin* — regardless of whether the act is singular or multiple, regardless of whether there is one *karet* or separate *karet* formulations, and regardless of whether the same person or object is involved, so long as the prohibitions are distinct.

---

## Mishnah Support

### Non-Sequential

Rav Natan bar Yitzchak offers additional support from the *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah* lists: *hamfatem et hashemen* (one who compounds the anointing oil), *hamfatem et haktoret* (one who compounds the incense), and *vehasach beshemen hamishchah* (one who anoints oneself with the anointing oil). The ordering is notable: the two cases involving the *shemen hamishchah* — compounding it and applying it — are not listed consecutively. Instead, the case of *ktoret* is inserted between them. Why? *Lama li detana hamfatem et haktoret bemetzia* — why did the *tanna* place the *ktoret* case in the middle?

The *gemara* answers: *lav ha kamashma lan* — it must be to convey the following. Just as *ktoret* is a separate *lav* and therefore incurs a separate *chatat*, the same applies to the two *shemen* cases. Since *ktoret* carries its own *lav* and its own *karet*, it generates a distinct *chatat*. The *mishnah*'s insertion of *ktoret* between the two *shemen* cases is a structural signal: even the two *shemen* prohibitions, though they involve the same substance and share a single *karet* verse, are treated as separate *aveirot* generating separate *chataot* — precisely because they are separate *lavin*.

### Not Stylistic

One might object that the *tanna* placed the two *pitum* cases — compounding oil and compounding incense — together for stylistic reasons, grouping the acts of compounding, rather than to signal anything about the *shemen* cases. The *gemara* rejects this. Had the *tanna* intended to group the *pitum* cases, the order could easily have been: compounding incense, compounding oil, and then anointing with oil. That arrangement would have preserved the grouping of the two *pitum* cases while still juxtaposing the two *shemen* cases. Instead, the *tanna* deliberately separated the two *shemen* cases, and this separation carries a message: *deyesh chiluk chataot beineihem* — there is a distinction of *chataot* between them. *Shema mina*.

The *gemara* acknowledges that one might have thought this was already implicit from the *mishnah*'s overall purpose — which is, after all, to enumerate separate cases that each generate a distinct *chatat*. But as the discussion develops, it becomes clear that whether the *mishnah* is claiming a precise count of *chataot* will itself become a matter of inquiry. Rav Natan bar Yitzchak therefore draws on the specific ordering of the *mishnah* as independent structural evidence, beyond any inference from the total count.

---

## Thirty-Four

### One Person?

The question now arises: can a single person actually commit all thirty-six (or thirty-four) transgressions listed in the *mishnah* within a single state of forgetfulness? The entire purpose of listing the number was to establish that one person could potentially bring that many *chataot* in a single state of forgetting. But a closer look reveals a problem.

*Ei b'gavra* — if the *mishnah* is speaking from the perspective of a man, then the case of a woman who allows an animal to be brought upon her (*dal isha venirva*) is unavailable to a man, which reduces the count by one to thirty-three. *Ei b'nashi kachashiv* — if the *mishnah* is speaking from a woman's perspective, then the case of *haba al hazachar* and the case of *dal behema* (a man penetrating an animal) are unavailable, reducing the count by two.

### Homosexual Act

Rabbi Yochanan resolves this by saying *le'olam tana gavrei* — the *mishnah* speaks throughout from the perspective of a man. He then reinterprets the case that had appeared to refer to a woman with an animal: *vetani hava al hazachar vehevi zachar alav* — the *mishnah* is actually listing two separate cases, namely a man who performs the active role in a homosexual act, and a man who performs the passive role.

This raises the question of whether those constitute two distinct sins. The *gemara* identifies the view behind this interpretation as that of Rabbi Yishmael, *de'amar chayav shtayim* — who holds that the two positions in a homosexual act are considered two distinct *aveirot* and therefore incur two separate *chataot*. This follows from the fact that Rabbi Yishmael derives the prohibition from two separate verses.

The first verse is *ve'et zachar lo tishkav mishkevei isha* — with a male you shall not lie as one lies with a woman. This verse addresses the one who performs the act, the active partner, with the phrase *mishkevei isha* emphasizing that the actor is the one taking the role normally associated with lying with a woman. The second source is *velo yihyeh kadesh mibnei Yisrael* — there shall be no *kadesh* among the children of Israel, which Rabbi Yishmael understands as addressing the receptive partner. Since two separate verses generate the two aspects of the prohibition, they are treated as two distinct *aveirot*, each with its own *chatat*.

The *gemara* notes in passing an interesting historical dimension: in the ancient Roman world, and in various societies where such acts were prevalent, a sharp social distinction existed between the active and receptive roles — the receptive role being associated with lower social status, with slaves, servants, or those in a subordinate position. Whether or not this is the conceptual background of the *Torah*'s language in *kadesh*, it helps explain how the Talmud frames these as conceptually distinct acts rather than a single unified transgression.

Rabbi Yishmael's position also entails a consequence for the case of an animal: *haba al habehemah vehevi behemah alav* — even if one argued that a man could play both roles with an animal, Rabbi Yishmael would not separate those into two distinct *aveirot*, because the textual derivation from two verses applies only to the case involving a male human. For the animal case, there is only one verse, and therefore only one *aveira* and one *chatat*.

An additional complication surfaces: the final item in the *mishnah* is *megadef* — blasphemy, a verbal act. The *mishnah* ends with a dissenting voice suggesting that verbal acts without a physical component should not be included, and the *gemara* attributes the view that *megadef* does incur a *chatat* to Rabbi Akiva, based on the principle in Sanhedrin that *akimat sefatav havei ma'aseh* — the movement of one's lips constitutes a physical act.

### Rabbi Akiva

Rabbi Akiva, by contrast, holds *lo chayav ela achat* — one who performs both roles incurs only a single *chatat*, deriving the entire prohibition from a single verse: *et zachar lo tishkav*. Rabbi Akiva reads the same verse in two ways — *lo tishkav* (you shall not lie) and *lo tishachav* (you shall not allow yourself to be lain with) — but treats both readings as aspects of a single prohibition derived from a single textual source. A single source means a single *aveira* and a single *chatat*.

This creates a tension: the *mishnah*'s final line about *megadef* is associated with Rabbi Akiva's position, yet the *reisha* of the *mishnah* — which requires two separate acts for the homosexual case to reach the count of thirty-four — requires Rabbi Yishmael's position. The *gemara* resolves this by saying the *mishnah* is authored by Rabbi Yishmael, who holds the two roles constitute two separate *aveirot* and who, in the case of *megadef*, agrees with Rabbi Akiva that a verbal act incurs a *chatat*.

---

## Pesach & Milah

### 36 Keritot

Rabbi Eliezer in the name of Rava offers an alternative resolution to the question of the *mishnah*'s count: *tani sheloshim veshalosh chataot* — the *mishnah* is in fact enumerating thirty-three *chataot*, not thirty-six. The number thirty-six is the total of *keritot*, not the total of *chataot* a single person can incur. The *mishnah* gives the full tally of thirty-six *karet* offenses in order to complete its enumeration of *keritot*, while the practical *chatat* liability for a single person reaches only thirty-three.

### Exclude Positive

The *gemara* supports this by asking directly: why are *Pesach* and *milah* listed at all? *Pesach u'Milah amai tani lehu?* If the purpose of the list were to enumerate cases where a *korban* is brought, *Pesach* and *milah* should not appear, since one never brings a *chatat* for failing to perform a positive *mitzvah*. A *baraita* confirms the principle: *hukesh kol haTorah kullah le'avodat kochavim* — the entire *Torah*'s *chatat* obligation is modeled on the case of *avodah zarah beshogeg*, as derived from the verse *Torah achat yihyeh lachem la'oseh bishgagah*, juxtaposed with *vehanefesh asher ta'aseh beyad ramah et Hashem hu megadef*. Since *avodah zarah* is a prohibition — a *shev ve'al ta'aseh* — only transgressions of that type generate a *chatat*. Failure to perform a positive commandment never generates a *chatat*. *Pesach* and *milah* are therefore listed solely to complete the tally of *keritot*, not to imply any *chatat* obligation. By the same logic, the debate about the passive role in the homosexual act — whether it generates a *chatat* (Rabbi Yishmael) or not (Rabbi Akiva) — has direct practical implications for the final count.

### 33 Chataot

The *gemara* concludes: *shema mina tana sheloshim veshalosh chataot* — the *mishnah* is enumerating thirty-three *chataot* that a single person can potentially incur. *Ve'hadar tani sheloshim veshesh keritot vesiyumei bekeritot* — it then completes the enumeration of thirty-six *keritot* to provide the full picture of *karet* offenses in the *Torah*. The *masechet* is called *Keritot* because *karet* is the starting point — identifying who is subject to *karet* determines who is obligated in a *chatat*. But the *masechet*'s practical focus is on those *chatat* obligations. The three cases that appear in the list but do not generate a *chatat* — the passive role in the homosexual act (on some views) and the two positive commandments of *Pesach* and *milah* — are present to give the full accounting of *keritot*, not to extend the *chatat* count. One person can bring at most thirty-three *chataot*.

---

## Shabbat Case

### Forgot Shabbat

The *gemara* now turns to *Shabbat* as a case study in how a single state of forgetfulness can interact with multiple possible violations. The *mishnah* lists *hamechallel et haShabbat* as a single entry. Yet one who violates *Shabbat* could potentially incur thirty-nine separate *chataot* — one for each *melacha* — if one knew it was *Shabbat* but forgot that each individual act was forbidden. Rabbi Yochanan explains: *tana shigagat Shabbat vezadon melachot* — the *mishnah* is referring to the case where one forgot it was *Shabbat* entirely, while intentionally performing acts that are in fact *melachot*. Because one's state of forgetfulness was specifically that it was *Shabbat*, all acts of *chillul Shabbat* committed in that state are subsumed under a single *chatat*. They are not thirty-nine distinct *aveirot* because what was forgotten was *Shabbat* itself, not the individual prohibitions.

### Me'achas

The *gemara* grounds this in the verse *asher ya'aseh mei'achas meiheina* — which does not say simply *achas meiheina* (one of these) but *mei'achas meiheina* (from one from these). This phrasing is taken to indicate variability: sometimes multiple actions count as one, and sometimes one category encompasses many. The full *baraita* unpacks both scenarios. The phrase *achas shehi heina* — one that is many — refers to *shigagat Shabbat vezadon melachot*: one forgot it was *Shabbat* and knowingly performed multiple acts. Despite the multiplicity of acts, it is counted as one, because the error was singular. Conversely, *heina shehein achat* — many that are one — refers to *zedon Shabbat veshigagat melachot*: one knew it was *Shabbat* but forgot that specific acts were prohibited. There, each *melacha* constitutes a distinct *aveira*, yielding thirty-nine separate *chataot*.

The *gemara* then asks: given that both scenarios exist, why did the *mishnah* list only the *shigagat Shabbat* case, which yields a single *chatat*? The answer is *demichatas miya lo miftar* — the *mishnah* preferred to cite the case from which one can never be *patur* from at least one *chatat*. In the *shigagat Shabbat* case, a single *chatat* is always incurred regardless of circumstances. In the *zedon Shabbat veshigagat melachot* case, the number of *chataot* is variable — it could collapse to one if one also forgot it was *Shabbat*. The *mishnah* chose the case that guarantees a fixed, certain *chatat* count, even if that count is only one.

---

## Shabbat Case (II)

### Avodah Zarah

A parallel structure applies to *avodah zarah*. Just as *Shabbat* presents two possible scenarios of forgetfulness that yield different *chatat* counts, so too with *avodah zarah*: one may forget that *avodah zarah* is forbidden entirely, or one may remember the general prohibition but fail to recognize that specific acts — *shechitah*, *haktarah*, *hishtachavayah* — constitute *avodah zarah*. The first scenario yields a single *chatat*; the second yields separate *chataot* for each distinct act. The *gemara* proceeds to examine what the first scenario — *shigagat avodah zarah* — actually means in practice, since determining the precise nature of the error is essential to characterizing it as *shogeg*.

---

## Avodah Zarah

### Cases Setup

The *gemara* asks directly: *shigagat avodas kochavim heichi dami* — what exactly does it mean to err about *avodah zarah* itself, as distinct from erring about the specific acts? The question is how one could simultaneously forget that *avodah zarah* is forbidden while still being aware that those acts are in some sense significant or problematic.

### Temple Intent

One proposed scenario: a person was in a temple of idol worship but believed he was in a synagogue, and bowed down. The *gemara* rejects this as a case of *shigagat avodah zarah* with the observation: *harei libo lashamayim* — his heart was directed toward heaven. If he was bowing down intending to pray to God, the fact that he was physically in a pagan temple and facing an idol is irrelevant. His act was directed to God and does not constitute *avodah zarah* at all. There is no *shogeg* because there is no *aveira*.

### Statue Case

A second scenario: one saw a statue — *andrarta*, a royal or decorative statue, not necessarily an object of worship — and bowed down to it. The *gemara* finds this equally unsuitable. *Iy de'kablih le'eloah* — if one treated the statue as a deity, then the worship was fully intentional *avodah zarah* and there is no element of *shogeg*. *Ve'iy de'lo kablih le'eloah* — if one did not treat it as a deity but merely showed obeisance to the king's image, then *lav midy hu* — this is not *avodah zarah* at all. Again, there is no case of *shogeg*.

### Motives

A third and more complex scenario: one worshipped an idol *me'ahavah u'miyirah* — out of love or fear, not out of genuine religious conviction. Rashi offers examples: bowing before an idol to gain social advancement (*me'ahavah*), or performing acts of worship under coercion or threat (*miyirah*). In these cases, one is going through the physical motions of *avodah zarah* but without sincere theological commitment to the idol. One may have believed — incorrectly — that such worship under these circumstances was permissible. That mistaken belief would constitute the *shogeg*.

### Abaye vs Rava

This scenario is the subject of a dispute between Abaye and Rava. Abaye holds *chayav* — even worship performed out of love or fear, without genuine theological belief in the deity, constitutes *avodah zarah*, and one who mistakenly thought such worship was permitted has committed *avodah zarah beshogeg*. Rava holds *patur* — such worship is not *avodah zarah* at all if one does not genuinely accept the object as a deity. Rava's position raises the question of martyrdom: if worship under duress or for ulterior motives is not *avodah zarah*, on what basis is there an obligation to give one's life rather than comply? The *gemara* notes this tension without fully resolving it here. Tosafot addresses it, and the suggestion is that the *kiddush Hashem* dimension operates independently of the technical *aveira* status.

### Thinking Permitted

The *gemara* ultimately settles on a case that works as *shigagat avodah zarah*: *be'omer mutar* — one who knew that *avodah zarah* was an act of idol worship but believed it was permitted. This person was not confused about what the act was; the error was legal — a mistaken belief that the *Torah* permits *avodah zarah*. This constitutes *shogeg*, and in such a case one's single error encompasses all the specific acts performed. All the various acts of *avodah zarah* performed while laboring under this single legal mistake are subsumed under one *chatat*.

The *gemara* closes by noting: *de'ad kan lo ka'ba'ei mineih Rava me'Rav Nachman ela iy echada mechayvei tartei mechayvei* — Rava's question to Rav Nachman was specifically about whether, when both the general prohibition and the specific acts were forgotten simultaneously, one incurs one *chatat* or multiple. The scenario of *be'omer mutar* is the baseline: knowing the acts were *avodah zarah* but thinking them permitted constitutes one clear error, generating one *chatat* for all acts performed in that state. The more complex case — where one forgot both the general prohibition and the particulars — raises the question of whether the two layers of forgetfulness collapse into one or multiply the *chatat* obligation. Importantly, the *gemara* notes that the *patur legamrei* option is not on the table: one minimally brings one *chatat*. This also stands in some tension with a remark attributed to a pseudo-Rashi on 2a, where *be'omer mutar* was characterized as an *ones*. The *gemara* here treats it unambiguously as *shogeg*, at least in the context of *avodah zarah* — though it remains possible that context matters, and *be'omer mutar* for other transgressions may be treated differently.

---

---

# Keritot 4

## Karet vs. Malkus

### Correction: Karet

Before proceeding into the new material, a correction from the previous session is in order. The position discussed there — *karet b'choteh* — was mischaracterized. That opinion, which we do not rule by, holds that for transgressions carrying *karet*, there is no concept of *beis din*-administered *malkus*; the punishment is *karet* alone. The position we do rule by is the opposite: one can receive *malkus*, and if one does, one is exempt from *karet*. These are distinct and should not be conflated.

Returning to the main thread: we were examining how many *chata'ot* one brings for various categories of transgression. For *Shabbos* and *avodah zarah*, one brings a single *chatas* if one erred about the fundamental prohibition, and separate *chata'ot* for each individual violation when one knew the general prohibition but forgot particular details. If one forgot *Shabbos* entirely and violated ten *melachos*, one brings only one *chatas*. If one knew about *Shabbos* but forgot that a particular *melacha* was forbidden, one brings a separate *chatas* for each. Analogously for *avodah zarah*: if one forgot the individual *avodos* — bowing, slaughtering, and so forth — one brings separately for each, but if one made a fundamental error about *avodah zarah* itself and performed multiple *avodos*, only one *chatas* is brought.

The *Gemara* had already asked how someone can make a fundamental error about *avodah zarah* while still performing an act of *avodah zarah*, and answered: *omer mutar* — one who considers it permitted. This renders even a categorical ignorance a *shogeg* sufficient for a *chatas*. The *Gemara* then raised the further question: if one forgot both the category and all the details, do we treat that as multiple errors or one? The ruling is that it constitutes one fundamental mistake, and only one *chatas* is brought.

### Tinok Shenishba

The *Gemara* at the top of 3b continues within this vein. *Rav Pappa* offers an illustration: *mishkachat lah b'tinok shenishba l'vein ha'akum* — the paradigm case is that of an infant taken captive among non-Jews, someone who grew up not knowing he was Jewish. This is where one can genuinely not know the prohibition in the most fundamental sense. It is, in essence, an extreme form of *omer mutar*.

The *Gemara* notes that there is actually a debate elsewhere, in *Shabbos*, whether this constitutes *ones* or *shogeg*. The conclusion is *shogeg* in the sense that one must bring a *korban chatas*. This is striking, because *shogeg* ordinarily implies some degree of fault, and it is difficult to assign fault to someone raised from infancy with no knowledge of his Jewish identity. What this really points to is the principle that a *chatas* is not simply a guilt offering — it atones for the objective fact that a sin was committed. To the degree that one is an *ones* in the sense that a force external to oneself compelled the act entirely, one could argue it was not one's action at all. But when one is choosing and acting — even if entirely blameless — there is a dimension of the sin that requires atonement, and one brings a *chatas*. The case of *tinok shenishba*, by this reasoning, is enough of an act of doing to obligate a *chatas*.

### Omer Mutar

The *Gemara* then qualifies the case and distinguishes it from a straightforward *omer mutar*. The scenario is: *d'yada d'asira avodah zarah* — one knows that *avodah zarah* is forbidden (perhaps through the *sheva mitzvos bnei Noach*, which raises interesting questions if the person turns out to be Jewish), *v'hai avodah zarah lo yada d'asira* — but one did not know that this particular form of *avodah zarah* was forbidden. The *Gemara* imagines one who grew up knowing that worshipping the *Asherah* was forbidden but believing that the *Baal* was permitted, and who therefore worshipped the *Baal* through all its various *avodos*. That is a fundamental mistake even if one performed every possible *avoda*, and thus only one *chatas* is brought.

### Fundamental vs. Detail

The *Gemara* also offers a different scenario not involving someone raised among non-Jews but an ordinary adult Jew who misread the verse: *lo ta'asuni iti elohei chesef ve-elohei zahav lo ta'asu lachem* — do not make gods of gold and silver. One might conclude from this that worship of idols made of other materials is permitted. That constitutes a fundamental mistake about the prohibition — *shegagat karkavan*, as the *Gemara* terms it — even though one performed individual *avodos* knowingly, since one believed those *avodos* directed at a non-gold, non-silver idol were permitted. Again, only one *chatas* is brought.

## Category Consolidation

### Rav Pappa

*Rav Pappa brei de-Rav Ika* then cites a ruling: *tanna shem Shabbos ve-shem avodat kochavim katani* — the *tanna* is listing the categories of *Shabbos* and *avodah zarah*, not trying to enumerate the maximum number of *chata'ot* that can be produced within each category. One should not be troubled by the fact that the *mishna* implies a single *chatas* for *Shabbos* when in reality thirty-nine *chata'ot* are possible, or implies a single *chatas* for *avodah zarah* when four or more are possible. The *mishna* is identifying categories, not maximizing counts.

### Shabbat, Avodah Zarah

This principle is reinforced by a comparison to *arayos*. The *mishna* lists a woman and her daughter and an *eshet ish*, but it does not list every possible *chiyuv karet* within *arayos*. This demonstrates that the *mishna* does not aim to maximize the number of *chata'ot*.

### Arayot Exception

The *Gemara* asks why a man's biological daughter from a woman he assaulted is not listed, given that it carries its own *chiyuv karet*. One reason offered is that the daughter is not made explicit in the *pesukim* in the way that granddaughter is. A further answer: *shem isha u-vita katani* — the *mishna* consolidates everything into the category of a woman and her daughter. Even though there is a halachic distinction between a wife's daughter and a biological daughter from another woman, they belong to the same conceptual category, and the *mishna* consolidates them even at the cost of omitting additional *chata'ot* that could have been listed. Here too: *hacha nami shem Shabbos ve-shem avodah zarah katani* — the point in our *mishna* is likewise one of consolidation by category, not maximization.

## Shechutei Chutz

### Shechita, Ha'ala

*Rav Acha brei de-Rav Ika* points out an apparent contradiction in the positions of *Rav Bibi bar Abaye*. On the one hand, *Rav Bibi bar Abaye* himself said that our *mishna* consolidates categories and is not trying to maximize numbers. Yet there is a *braisa* that teaches: *ha-ma'aleh evarei pnim bachutz chayav, evarei chutz bachutz chayav* — one who brings up on an altar outside the *Beis HaMikdash* the limbs of an animal slaughtered inside is liable, and one who does the same with an animal slaughtered outside is also liable. These are two forms of the prohibition of *shechutei chutz*. *Rav Bibi bar Abaye* understood them to be distinct categories, each producing a separate *chatas*. But if that is so, then since the *mishna* lists 36 *kareisin*, it should have counted both forms — why list only one, given that they are distinct?

### Location Principle

The *Gemara* answers by drawing a distinction based on where these matters are elaborated. *Shabbos* and *avodah zarah* are discussed at length elsewhere — *Shabbos* has its own tractate and *avodah zarah* is elaborated in *Sanhedrin* — and therefore our *mishna* can consolidate without spelling out all the details, since the reader will encounter those details in their proper place. The laws of *shechutei chutz*, however, have no other dedicated place of discussion. If those two forms were genuinely distinct categories producing separate *chata'ot*, one would have expected them to be listed separately here in *Keritot*, which is precisely where that discussion belongs. The fact that the *mishna* does list both *ha-shocheit* and *ha-ma'aleh* separately confirms that this is the appropriate place to articulate any distinctions within that prohibition. The underlying principle is thus that consolidation is appropriate when elaboration will occur elsewhere; when a topic finds its primary home in *Keritot*, the *mishna* does provide separate entries.

## Two Karetin, One Lav

### Ein Onshin

*Rami bar Chama* posed a question to *Rav Chisda*: what is the rule when there are two *kareisin* and one *lav*? The preceding discussion had addressed the case of two *lavin* and one *karet* — the prohibition of preparing the anointing oil and anointing oneself with it, *mefatem ve-sach shemen hamishcha*, where two distinct *lavin* share a single explicit *karet*, and the ruling is that the two *lavin* generate separate *chata'ot*. What if the situation is reversed: a single prohibition but two explicit *kareisin*?

### Gezeirah Shavah

The question is initially deflected: *shocheit* and *ma'aleh* outside the *Beis HaMikdash* would seem to be the relevant example, but the *Gemara* points out that these actually carry two separate *lavin*, not one. The explicit prohibition — *hishamer lecha pen ta'aleh olotecha b'chol hamakom asher tir'eh* — mentions only *ha'ala*, the burning of limbs. How is *shechita* prohibited? One opinion derives it through a *gezeirah shavah*: both *shechita* outside the *Beis HaMikdash* and *ha'ala* outside employ the phrase *lo hevi'o* in the relevant *pesukim*. On the basis of *ein onshin ela im kein mazhirin* — the Torah will not impose a punishment without a prohibition — we must discover a prohibition for *shechita*. The *gezeirah shavah* supplies it: just as there is a prohibition for *ha'ala*, so there is a prohibition for *shechita*.

### Hekkesh

A second opinion derives the prohibition from a *hekkesh* rather than a *gezeirah shavah*. The verse states *sham ta'aleh ve-sham ta'aseh* — "there shall you offer up and there shall you do," with the latter phrase encompassing *shechita* and other acts of the sacrificial service. This comparison (*hekkesh*) between *shechita* and *ha'ala* means that just as there is an explicit prohibition for *ha'ala*, so too for *shechita*. By either derivation — *gezeirah shavah* or *hekkesh* — *shechita* outside the *Beis HaMikdash* carries its own distinct *lav*, and the case of two *kareisin* with only one *lav* remains without a clear example.

## Ov and Yidoni

### One Lav, Separate

The *Gemara* then considers a parallel case involving not *karet* but two separate *mitos*: the prohibitions of *ov* and *yidoni*, two forms of necromancy. The verse *lo yimatze vecha shoel ov ve-yidoni* contains a single prohibition covering both. Yet the verse *ov o yidoni mos yumas* — because it says "A or B shall be put to death" — is understood to impose a separate death penalty on each. So we have one *lav* and two *mitos*. If one performed both in a single state of forgetfulness, does one bring two *chata'ot*? This is the unresolved form of the question: one prohibition, two separate punishments.

## Ov and Yidoni (II)

### Rabbi Yochanan

*Rabbi Yochanan* holds: *hen u-shneihen be-lav echad ne'emru* — both *ov* and *yidoni* were stated within a single prohibition, and therefore even though there are two separate *mitos*, only one *chatas* is brought. The principle as *Rabbi Yochanan* understands it is that it is the *lav* that defines the category for the purpose of *chatas*. Two separate *lavin* with different names generate separate *chata'ot*, as in the case of *mefatem ve-sach*; a single *lav* with two punishments does not.

### Reish Lakish

*Reish Lakish* disagrees. He holds that the fact that each — *ov* and *yidoni* — carries its own distinct death penalty is sufficient to render them separate categories, such that performing both in one state of forgetfulness would in principle require two *chata'ot*. The debate thus crystallizes: according to *Rabbi Yochanan*, the unit of analysis for *chatas* is the *lav*; according to *Reish Lakish*, a separate punishment, even under a shared *lav*, constitutes a separate category.

The *Gemara* also notes that our *mishna* lists only *ov* and not *yidoni*. *Rabbi Yochanan* explains simply: since it is one *lav* and only one *chatas* is brought, the *mishna* lists one entry, and it chose *ov* because that is the first in the *pasuk*. *Reish Lakish* offers a different explanation, which carries a distinct halachic implication.

## Ma'aseh Requirement

### Yidoni Excluded

*Reish Lakish* explains why *yidoni* is absent from the *mishna*: *hoil ve-ein bo ma'aseh* — because it involves no action. The *yidoni* practice involves placing a bone in one's mouth and somehow producing sounds through it; one performs no meaningful physical act. Since there is a requirement of *ma'aseh* — an act — for the obligation of *chatas*, and *yidoni* lacks one, it is excluded from the *mishna* regardless of whether one *lav* or two are involved.

### Akiva Positions

This explanation generates a question for *Rabbi Yochanan*: if *Rabbi Yochanan* holds that no action is required, how can *Reish Lakish's* reasoning hold? *Rabbi Yochanan's* response is: *man tanna Keritot Rabbi Akiva hi de-amar lo ba'inan ma'aseh* — the *tanna* of our *mishna* in *Keritot* is *Rabbi Akiva*, who holds no action is required, as evidenced by the fact that the *mishna* includes *megadef* — blasphemy — which involves no act in the conventional sense. If even *megadef* brings a *chatas*, one cannot exclude *yidoni* on the grounds of lacking an act. According to *Rabbi Yochanan*, therefore, *yidoni* is excluded solely because it is subsumed under one *lav* with *ov*, and only one *chatas* is brought.

## Ma'aseh Requirement (II)

### Minimal Action

*Rav Pappa* notes that regardless of the debate about *chatas*, both *karet* and *misa* can be incurred without an act — there are cases of *chiyuv misa* for which everyone agrees, yet a *chatas* is still not brought. The requirement of *ma'aseh* is specific to *chatas*. It is, as the *Gemara* observes, somewhat counterintuitive that one can receive the most severe punishments without an act, but not bring a *chatas* without one.

*Reish Lakish* responds to the question of why he does not follow *Rabbi Yochanan*: *de-ha chalukin hen be-mitoséihen* — because the two forms carry distinct deaths, he regards them as distinct categories. His response to the *ma'aseh* question is different from *Rabbi Yochanan's*: *Rav Pappa* clarifies that *Reish Lakish* holds *Rabbi Akiva* does require some form of action, but sets the threshold very low — *ma'aseh zuta ba'ei*, a minimal act is needed. Moving the lips constitutes such an act. *Yidoni*, in which nothing of that kind occurs, falls below even *Rabbi Akiva's* minimal threshold, which is why even according to the *tanna* of our *mishna* it produces no *chatas*.

## What Is Action

### Ba'al Ov

The *Gemara* then examines what constitutes a *ma'aseh* in each relevant case. By *ba'al ov*: *hakashat zero'otav havei ma'aseh* — the flapping or tensing of the arms in the conjuring act is considered an action. That is a clear enough physical movement that all opinions can agree it constitutes an act.

By *megadef*: *akimat sefatav havei ma'aseh* — moving one's lips is considered an action. This is *Rabbi Akiva's* position, or, as *Reish Lakish* frames it, the basis on which *Rabbi Akiva* holds that a minimal act suffices.

### Hishtachava'ah

The *Gemara* raises a challenge from a separate discussion in *Sanhedrin*: by *avodah zarah*, one is only liable if one performs an act — *kegon shezivach ve-kiter ve-nisach ve-hishtachavah*. Among these, *hishtachavayah* — bowing down — is listed as an act. But the *Gemara* asks: is bowing down really an act? One is simply moving one's body, not interacting with anything in the physical world. The same conceptual question applies to flapping one's arms and moving one's lips.

*Reish Lakish* answers: *ha mani Rabbi Akiva hi de-amar lo ba'inan ma'aseh* — including *hishtachavayah* as an act reflects *Rabbi Akiva's* position, which accepts minimal action. *Rabbi Yochanan* disagrees and says: *afilu teima Rabanan, kfifas komaso havei ma'aseh* — even the *Rabbanan* would agree that bowing one's entire body is an act, even if they would not accept merely moving the lips. The degree of full-body physical movement crosses a threshold that lip-movement does not.

This generates a further inference. According to *Reish Lakish*, who says bowing is only *Rabbi Akiva's* standard and not the *Rabbanan's*, flapping the arms should also fall below the *Rabbanan's* threshold — and therefore the *Rabbanan* should have explicitly disagreed with the inclusion of *ba'al ov* in the *mishna*, just as they disagree with *megadef*. The *Gemara* answers: they do — *chada mi-tartei katani*, the *Rabbanan* only specified one objection, but their reasoning applies equally to both *megadef* and *ba'al ov*.

## Ba'al Ov Incense

### Ulla Position

*Ulla* offers an entirely different account of the *ba'al ov* act. He says: *ba'al ov de-katni be-makter le-shed* — the *ba'al ov* in the *mishna* refers specifically to one who burns incense to invoke a spirit. This is not the flapping of the arms but a real, concrete action: the burning of incense. If so, the question of whether minimal physical movement constitutes an act becomes irrelevant for *ba'al ov* — it involves a genuine material act.

### Rava Response

*Rava* challenges: if one is burning incense to a spirit, is that not simply *avodah zarah*? *Rava* answers his own question: *mekater le-shed al menat le-chavro* — one is not burning incense to the spirit as an act of worship but as a means of invoking it, of making contact with or exercising control over the spirit world. The intent is not worship but invocation. That distinction takes it outside the category of *avodah zarah*.

### Chover Chaver

*Abaye* presses: if burning incense to invoke a spirit is not *avodah zarah*, then it is *chover chaver* — invoking spirits — which is a separate prohibition, a *lav*, not a capital offense. *Abaye* asks why the *Gemara* treats it as producing *chiyuv misa*. The response is: the Torah treats this particular form of *ba'al ov* — invoking through incense — as carrying *sekila*, not merely a *lav*. The general category of *chover chaver*, which encompasses invoking small spirits, even gathering snakes and scorpions through incantation, carries only a *lav*. But the specific act of the *ba'al ov* in this form is treated more severely.

*Abaye* further elaborates: *hai man de-ba'ei le-mitzmed diburei ve-akraba* — one who seeks to gather bees or scorpions through invocation is forbidden (*chover chaver*). However, if they are coming toward one unprovoked and one uses such means to protect oneself, that may be permitted — either because it falls under *pikuach nefesh* permitting a *lav*, or because the Torah prohibited *chover chaver* in the context of active invocation for one's benefit, not passive self-defense, and the purpose defines the act.

## What Is Action (II)

### Megadef

Returning to *Rabbi Yochanan's* position, the *Gemara* presses: if *Rabbi Yochanan* holds that bowing down is an act that everyone agrees to, why is moving one's lips not equally an act for everyone? Both are purely physical movements without interaction with the external world.

*Rava* answers: *shani megadef ho'il ve-yeshno ba-lev* — *megadef* is fundamentally different because it is in the heart. The curse is not essentially about the physical movement of the lips; it is about the expression of a thought, an attitude toward God. As *Rashi* notes in *Sanhedrin*, if one happens to utter the words of *giduf* without intending them — without understanding what one is saying — it would not constitute an act of *megadef*. The physical utterance is merely the vehicle for an internal expression. Bowing down, by contrast, is inherently about the physical act of prostration; the act itself is what it is, regardless of what passes through one's mind while doing it. The contrast between *megadef* and *hishtachavayah* is therefore not one of magnitude of physical movement, but of what is fundamentally constitutive of each act.

### Eidim Zomemim

The *Gemara* cites a further challenge: we find elsewhere that *eidim zomemim* — false witnesses — are described as an act *she-ein bahem ma'aseh*, lacking an act. Yet they speak. If *Rabbi Yochanan* says moving one's lips is an act, why is testifying falsely not considered an act?

*Rava* answers: *shani eidim zomemim ho'il ve-yeshnam bi-re'iyah* — false testimony is fundamentally about what one saw, about an act of *re'iyah*, of seeing and bearing witness. It is the attestation of an observed fact that constitutes the substance of testimony, not the physical act of speaking. The *Gemara* adds that *Rav Hai Gaon*, according to one reading, understood this line differently, with the *girsa* reading *bi-i'ah* rather than *bi-re'iyah* — and his interpretation was that one witness can fulfill the act of false testimony by merely nodding assent while the other speaks, making no movement of the lips at all. Since testimony can be completed without even moving one's lips, it is categorized as *ein bo ma'aseh*.

The discussion across these sugyas thus coheres around a single conceptual axis: the question of what constitutes an act for the purpose of *chiyuv chatas*, how minimal that act can be, and when an apparently physical movement is rendered legally non-corporeal because the essence of the transgression lies in thought, speech, or attestation rather than in a deed in the world.

## Ochel Chelev

### Multiple Lashes

A *beraisa* is cited: *kol chelev shor ve-chesev ve-ez lo tocheilu* — do not eat any fat of ox, sheep, or goat. The question is whether this verse imposes a single prohibition on eating forbidden fat generically, or whether the separate mention of each animal creates distinct prohibitions. *Rabbi Yishmael* holds: *le-chayev al kol achas ve-achas* — one is liable separately for each animal, producing separate punishments. *Ve-chachamim omrim eino chayav ela achas* — the Sages say there is only one liability.

One might assume the debate turns on the broader principle of *lav she-bichlalos* — whether a prohibition covering multiple items generates separate *malkus* for each. But the *Gemara* clarifies that this is in fact a *malkus* question, not a *chatas* question, and the dispute is more specific.

### Yishmael Argument

*Rabbi Yishmael's* reasoning: had the Torah intended merely to prohibit eating fat with no special significance to the list of animals, it could have written simply *kol chelev lo tocheilu*. Why specify ox, sheep, and goat? *Shema mina le-challek* — the specification must be to tell us that each constitutes a distinct prohibition, and one who eats all three in one state of forgetfulness receives separate punishments for each.

### Sages Argument

The Sages respond: had the Torah written only *kol chelev lo tocheilu*, one might have included the fat of a *chaya* — a non-domesticated animal like a deer — which is in fact permitted. The Torah had to specify *shor, chesev, va-ez* in order to limit the prohibition to these domesticated animals and exclude *chaya* and fowl. The specification is thus necessitated by the need to exclude, not by the desire to multiply. The *Gemara* declares: *shapir ka'amrei* — that is a compelling response.

### Animal Specialties

The discussion then deepens into why no single animal from the three could have served as the representative for all others, which would have made specifying all three redundant. A *beraisa* cited by *Rabbi Chananya* establishes this point in the context of the obligation to offer *imurin* — the internal fats and organs — from a *bechor*: *ach bechor shor o bechor chesev o bechor ez lo sifdeh, es damam tizrok ve-es chelbam taktir*.

Had the Torah written only ox, one might have thought that sheep and goat need not have their *imurin* offered — since ox carries a larger measure of *nesachim*, one might say that is what distinguishes it, and its fat is treated with special sanctity. Had it written only sheep, one might say that sheep alone requires this, given that it alone has the fat tail (*alya*), a distinct element offered on the *mizbeach*. Had it written only goat, one might infer from ox and sheep — but then again, ox has the distinction of larger *nesachim* and sheep has the *alya*, and neither possesses what goat possesses, namely that goat is the only *behemah* brought as a *korban* in the context of *avodah zarah*. Each animal is therefore genuinely distinct and irreplaceable in the context of *kodshim*, and the Torah had no choice but to list all three.

This very same reasoning applies to the prohibition of *chelev*: had only one animal been named, one might either over-generalize or under-specify. The Torah listed all three of necessity.

## Lav from Karet

### Context Mention

The *Gemara* returns to the underlying methodological dispute. The verse containing the *lav* — *kol chelev shor ve-chesev ve-ez lo tocheilu* — appears in proximity to the verse containing the *karet*: *ki kol ochel chelev min ha-behemah asher takrivu mimena korban la-Hashem*. The *karet* verse specifies the prohibition in terms of *behemah asher takrivu* — an animal brought as a *korban* — and makes clear it applies to ox, sheep, and goat. Since the *lav* verse appears in the same context, could one not read the animals listed in the *lav* as already implied by the *karet* verse, making the explicit listing superfluous and therefore interpretively significant?

### Yishmael Learns

*Rabbi Yishmael* applies this logic: *davar ha-lamed me-inyano* — a teaching derived from its context. Since by *karet* the limitation to *shor, chesev, va-ez* is clear, one could have inferred the same for the *lav*. The explicit mention of all three in the *lav* verse is thus not needed to define the scope of the prohibition; it therefore carries additional meaning and signals distinct prohibitions for each animal.

### Sages Restriction

The Sages respond: *lo yalfinan lav mi-karet* — one may not derive the content of a *lav* from what is stated by a *karet*. What appears in the context of *karet* applies to *karet*; one cannot carry it over to establish the scope of a separate *lav*. Therefore, the listing of all three animals in the *lav* verse was necessary to define the prohibition's scope, and it carries no additional meaning. There is accordingly only one *lav* and only one liability for *malkus*.

The debate thus ultimately hinges on whether *Rabbi Yishmael* is correct that one may derive a *lav* from a *karet* — learning the content of a prohibition from the context of a penalty — or whether, as the Sages hold, such cross-derivation is inadmissible.

---

---

# Keritot 7

## Shemen Hamishcha

### Intro to Shemen

The *Tosefta* enumerates the full list of offenses punishable by *karet*, and the *Gemara* — following its characteristic method — focuses on those items that receive less treatment elsewhere in *Shas*. Having addressed the making of *ketores* and the making of *shemen hamishcha* in previous discussions, the *Gemara* now turns to one who anoints himself with the *shemen hamishcha* of the *Beis Hamikdash* — not oil that he himself produced, but the actual consecrated anointing oil.

### Exemptions

A *Tosefta* is cited: *hasach b'shemen hamishcha l'vehema u'v'keilim patur* — if one uses the *shemen hamishcha* on an animal or on vessels, he is exempt from the specific prohibition. (Whether this would constitute *me'ilah* is a separate question, deliberately set aside here.) The prohibition derives from the phrase *al b'sar adam lo yisach* — "it shall not be placed on human flesh" — and since animals and vessels are not *adam*, they fall outside its scope. Similarly, applying it to a corpse (*meis*) incurs no liability, since once a person has died he is called a *meis* and is no longer classified as *adam*. The exemption for non-Jews, however, requires explanation, because non-Jews are in fact referred to as *adam* in Scripture.

### Non-Jews & Adam

This leads into one of the more striking and, as the lecturer notes, deeply unsettling discussions in *Shas* — the question of whether *chazal*, when interpreting a *pasuk* that uses the word *adam*, include or exclude non-Jews. *Tosafos* in several places in *Shas* grapples with the apparent inconsistency: sometimes the *Gemara* derives from *adam* that non-Jews are included, and sometimes it derives that they are excluded.

Here the *Gemara* begins by noting that non-Jews *are* called *adam*, then cites a *pasuk* from Yechezkel: *v'atem tzon mar'isi adam atem* — "you are my flock, the flock of my shepherding, you are *adam*" — from which it derives *atem keruyin adam v'ein ovdei kochavim keruyin adam*, that Israel is called *adam* and non-Jews are not. Two counter-proofs are then raised. First, *v'nefesh adam shisha asar eleph* — the sixteen thousand captives taken from Midyan are described as *adam*. The *Gemara* responds that this usage is merely contrastive with the animals captured alongside them, not a definitive application of the term. Second, *v'ani lo achus al Ninveh ha'ir hagedola asher yesh bah harbe adam* — the book of Yonah refers to the non-Jewish population of Nineveh as *adam*. Again, the *Gemara* responds that this too is contrastive with the *behema raba* mentioned in the same verse. In both cases, the word *adam* appears in proximity to *behema* and is understood only as a contrast to the animal category, not as a full application of the term to non-Jews.

A second, more elegant answer is then offered: *kol sheyeshno b'sicha yeshno b'val yisach* — anyone who is themselves subject to the prohibition of anointing with *shemen hamishcha* is also a prohibited object of that anointing. Since the prohibition of *shemen hamishcha* is part of the *taryag mitzvos* and does not apply to non-Jews through the *sheva mitzvos bnei Noach*, non-Jews are simply not within the framework of the prohibition at all — and therefore placing it on their flesh is also not prohibited.

The broader issue raised by this *Gemara* deserves acknowledgment. While there are real halachic distinctions between Jews and non-Jews, this must be understood in its proper context. Even Rabbi Akiva, who often emphasizes legal distinctions between Jews and non-Jews, is the same tanna who declares *chaviv adam shenivra b'tzelem* — that all human beings are precious by virtue of being created in the image of God — and who then adds *chavivim Yisrael shenikru banim lamakom*, underscoring the unique relationship of *Bnei Yisrael* with God while affirming the universal dignity of all people. The interpretation of *adam* to exclude non-Jews is a technical *derasha* serving a narrow halachic purpose, and should not be read as a broader philosophical statement about the humanity of non-Jews — a position that is both textually and theologically untenable.

---

## Quantity Debate

### Kings & Kohanim

The *Tosefta* continues: *l'melachim u'l'kohanim* — if one anoints kings or *kohanim gedolim* a second time, after the initial anointing has already been performed, *Rabbi Meir mechayev* and *Rabbi Yehuda poter*. This is one debate. A second debate immediately follows: how much oil must be applied in order to transgress? *Rabbi Meir omer kol shehu* — even the smallest quantity — while *Rabbi Yehuda omer kezayit*, requiring an olive's bulk.

The *Gemara* notes an apparent internal contradiction: if Rabbi Yehuda just ruled that one is *patur* when anointing a king or *kohen gadol*, how can he simultaneously require a *kezayit*? The resolution is that these are two distinct debates. The question of whether kings and *kohanim* can transgress at all is one dispute. The question of how much oil is required when anointing an ordinary person who is prohibited (*hedyot*) is a separate dispute — and in that case, Rabbi Yehuda agrees that the person is *chayav*, since the prohibition is clear from the *pasuk*. The quantity debate pertains to that second case.

### Sicha vs. Netina

Rav Yosef identifies the crux of the quantity debate. The *pasuk* uses two different verbs: *al b'sar adam lo yisach* — the prohibition employs the word *yisach*, meaning to anoint (*sicha*) — while the *karet* clause says *va'asher yiten mimenu al zar*, using the word *netina*, meaning placing or giving. These two verbs carry different halachic valences.

### Deriving Kol Shehu

Rabbi Meir holds: *ma sicha kol shehu* — the word *sicha*, anointing, has no established minimum measure elsewhere in *halacha*, so we treat even the smallest amount as actionable. And since *netina* in this context is linked to and derived from *sicha*, *af netina kol shehu* — the act of placing is also governed by the same minimum-free standard.

### Rav Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, holds that we interpret *netina* independently, in accordance with its standard halachic usage: *yalfinan netina de-al zar mi-netina de-alma* — we derive the meaning of "placing on a foreigner" from the general meaning of "placing" elsewhere. And the general meaning of *netina* in *halacha* is a *kezayit*, as derived from the context of *terumah*, where the obligation to return *terumah* to a *kohen* is linked to an act of eating (which requires a *kezayit*), and therefore the associated act of *netina* there also requires a *kezayit*. The same measure applies here.

### Two Debates

Rav Yosef emphasizes that this quantity dispute is specifically confined to the application of *shemen hamishcha* — whether one follows the *sicha*-based reading or the *netina*-based reading. However, *netina de-alma*, the ordinary meaning of *netina* in *halacha*, is agreed upon by all to require a *kezayit*. The two debates — one about kings and *kohanim*, and one about the quantity required for an ordinary prohibited person — are thus clearly delineated, with the quantity debate applying only to the latter category.

---

## Kings & Kohanim Debate

### R. Meir Position

The *Gemara* now returns to the debate about kings and *kohanim* and asks what its underlying logic is. Rabbi Meir holds: *asher yiten mimenu al zar ketiv u-melech v'kohen hashta zar ninhu* — the *pasuk* says one who places it on a *zar*, a foreigner. Once a king or *kohen gadol* has already been anointed and there is no longer any *mitzvah* to anoint him again, he has become, in effect, foreign to the oil — he has no right to receive it a second time. Therefore, anointing him again would constitute a transgression.

### R. Yehuda Position

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *be'inan ad de-ika zarut mi-techilato v'ad sofo* — the term *zar* implies complete foreignness, from beginning to end. Since kings and *kohanim*, as a class, were originally entitled to be anointed with the *shemen hamishcha*, they can never be considered fully foreign to it. The word *zar* does not apply to someone who was ever legitimately within that category.

### Individual vs. Class

This raises an important question: is Rabbi Yehuda speaking about a specific individual who was personally anointed, or about membership in a class that was once anointed? The *Gemara* does not resolve this explicitly. One might wonder whether even a king who was never personally anointed — or a *kohen* who was never personally anointed — would nonetheless be exempt according to Rabbi Yehuda, because his class was once anointed. The case of *malchei Yisrael*, who as a class were generally not anointed with *shemen hamishcha*, would likely remain subject to the prohibition even according to Rabbi Yehuda.

Rav Ika the son of Rav Ami observes that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda are consistent with their respective positions elsewhere: *va'azlu l'ta'amaihu*.

### Kohen's Daughter

A *baraita* is cited to demonstrate this consistency. Consider the case of a *bat kohen* who married a *Yisrael*. While married to a non-*kohen*, she loses her right to eat *terumah*. If she then inadvertently eats *terumah*, she pays back the principal (*keren*) but not the added fifth (*chomesh*) — because the *chomesh* applies only to a *zar*, and she is not considered a *zarah*, given that she once had the status of a *bat kohen* and may return to it if her husband dies childless. Furthermore, if she commits adultery, her execution is by *sreifah*, as befits a *bat kohen*, not *chenek*. This is the ruling in the basic case.

However, if she married someone *pasul* — someone whose marriage disqualifies her permanently from *kohen* status, making her a *chalalah* — Rabbi Meir rules that she pays both the *keren* and the *chomesh*, and her execution would be by *chenek*, not *sreifah*. Rabbi Meir's reasoning is that she retained *bat kohen* status only because of the possibility of returning to it; once that possibility is eliminated, she becomes a full *zarah*. The *chachamim*, whose position aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, rule that even in that case she pays only the *keren* and not the *chomesh*, and her execution is by *sreifah* — because having once been in the category of *bat kohen*, she can never be considered a full *zarah*, regardless of whether she can ever return to that status.

The parallel to the *shemen hamishcha* debate is direct: Rabbi Meir's position is forward-looking (does she still have a path back to the status?), while the *chachamim*/Rabbi Yehuda's position is backward-looking (was she ever in the category?). The same logic governs whether kings and *kohanim* can ever be considered *zarim* with respect to the *shemen hamishcha*.

---

## Shemen Hamishcha (II)

### R. Eliezer's Derasha

Returning to the Tosefta, *tani tanna kamei d'Rabbi Eliezer*: *kol sheyeshno b'sicha yeshno b'val yisach* — whoever is within the framework of the prohibition of *sicha* is also within the framework of the prohibition of *lo yisach*. Rabbi Eliezer responds to the *tanna* with approval: *shapir kamarta* — you have stated it well. The textual basis is the unusual spelling of the word *lo yisach* with a double *yud*, rendering it susceptible to a causative reading: not only is it prohibited to anoint oneself, but it is prohibited to cause it to be placed on the flesh of one who is subject to the prohibition. This reading simultaneously excludes non-Jews, since the prohibition does not fall upon them in the first place.

### Kohen Gadol Case

*Tani Rebbe Chanina kamei d'Rava*: Rebbe Chanina taught before Rava — from where do we know that a *kohen gadol* who takes oil from the *shemen hamishcha* that is on his own head and applies it to his body is liable? The verse states *al b'sar adam lo yisach*. The *Gemara* notes that this is operating within the framework of Rabbi Meir's position — that a *kohen gadol*, once anointed, is considered a *zar* with respect to further applications of the oil.

The more striking point is the specific case: what if the very oil that was just used to anoint the *kohen gadol* is then taken from his head and applied to his abdomen? It is the same oil, in the same moment. Rav Acha the son of Rava asked Rav Ashi: how is this different from the case of a *kohen* who rubs himself with *terumah* oil? In that case, we rule that even a *ben bito Yisrael* — a grandson who is a non-*kohen* — may cuddle against him or have contact with that oil without concern, because the *kohen's* use of the *terumah* oil has already been effected.

### Trumah vs. Shemen

The answer distinguishes the two cases on the basis of separate *pesukim*. By *terumah*, the verse states *umeisu bo ki yechalelu* — "they shall die for it because they have desecrated it." The key word is *yechalelu*: once the *kohen* has used the *terumah* oil on himself, it has been put to use for a human being, and that use desacralizes it — removes it from its *kedusha* status. It is, in effect, no longer *terumah* after the *kohen* has applied it, and so contact with it by a non-*kohen* is no longer a prohibited use of *terumah*.

By contrast, the *pasuk* describing the *kohen gadol* states *ki nezer shemen mishchas Elokav alav* — "because the crown of the anointing oil of his God is upon him." Even after it has been placed on his head, the Torah continues to call it *shemen mishchas Elokav* — the anointing oil of his God. *Shemen mishcha karei Rachmana* — the Torah designates it as *shemen hamishcha* even after it has been applied. *Af al gav d'isa alav lo itchal* — even though it is already upon him, it has not been desacralized. It retains its sacred status and therefore the prohibition remains active. Conceptually, the distinction tracks accordingly: with *terumah*, the sin consists in misusing a sacred object, and once used, the object no longer has that sacred status to misuse; with *shemen hamishcha*, the prohibition is not about misusing the oil's *kedusha* per se but about the specific act identified in the *pasuk*, which the oil retains its identity as *shemen hamishcha* throughout.

---

## Mishnah Conclusion

### Three Categories

The *Mishnah* closes with a general summary statement: *al elu chayavin al zedonam karet, v'al shigagatam chatat, v'al lo hoda shelahem asham talui* — for all the offenses on the list, intentional violation incurs *karet*, unintentional violation requires a *chatat*, and if one is uncertain whether the violation occurred, an *asham talui* is brought.

### Tuma'at Mikdash

The *Mishnah* then states an exception: *chutz mimitamei mikdash vekodashav* — with the exception of one who is *tamei* and enters the *Beis Hamikdash* or eats *kodashim* while *tamei*. For that transgression, a *korban oleh v'yored* is brought — a variable-cost *korban* whose value depends on the sinner's means. The *Gemara* asks: *mimai mapik lei* — from what exactly is this being excluded? The answer is: *chutz mimitamei mikdash vekodashav she'ein mevi asham talui* — this category is excluded specifically from the *asham talui*. The first two categories — *karet* for intentional violation and *chatat* for unintentional violation — still apply. But the *asham talui*, which is brought when one is uncertain whether a transgression occurred at all, applies only where the underlying *chatat* is a fixed-value offering (*chatat kavua*). Where the *chatat* varies in cost, the *asham talui* does not apply.

### Yom Kippur Q

The *Gemara* then raises a further question: given that the *Mishnah* is in the business of excluding categories from the *asham talui*, why does it not also mention the case of one who has passed through *Yom Kippur*? After *Yom Kippur* atones, the underlying sin for which an *asham talui* might have been brought no longer exists — and indeed, as the *Gemara* teaches elsewhere, the *asham talui* is not brought after *Yom Kippur* has intervened. The *Gemara* offers two approaches to this question, which draw the discussion into a much deeper inquiry about the nature and conditions of *Yom Kippur*'s atoning power.

---

## Yom Kippur Debate

### Atone w/o Teshuva?
