Reish Lakish explains why *Yom Kippur* was not listed as an exclusion from *asham talui*: *ki katani heicha de'iteih l'chatat Rachmana patrei* — the *Mishnah* is discussing cases where the sin remains fully present and the person is still obligated in a *chatat*, yet is nonetheless excluded from *asham talui*. In the case of *tuma'at mikdash*, the sin exists but the exemption from *asham talui* is structural (because the *chatat* varies in cost). *Yom Kippur* is different — by *Yom Kippur*, the sin itself has been wiped away: *leiteih lechata'ei dekaper lei*. It is not another way of evading the *asham talui*; it is an erasure of the underlying transgression entirely.

Rabbi Yochanan offers a different explanation. *Bimva'et* — there is a type of person who explicitly declares that he does not want *Yom Kippur* to atone for him: *dekamar ein Yom HaKippurim mechaper li*. For such a person, *Yom Kippur* would not atone, and he would still be obligated in his *asham talui* even after *Yom Kippur*. The *Mishnah* therefore cannot make a blanket exclusion for *Yom Kippur*, since the exclusion does not apply to this case. Rabbi Yochanan adds: *de'ei hadar beih batar Yom HaKippurim ba'ei le'atuyei asham talui* — if, after *Yom Kippur*, that person changes his mind and wants atonement after all, he would then need to bring his *asham talui*.

The implication of Rabbi Yochanan's answer is striking — it presupposes that a person's willingness to be atoned is a condition for *Yom Kippur* to function. Reish Lakish's answer implies no such thing; he simply distinguishes the structural character of the two exclusions. The *Gemara* proceeds to note that Reish Lakish does not adopt Rabbi Yochanan's answer because Reish Lakish holds the more radical position: *miva'et nami mechaper lei Yom HaKippurim* — even a person who says he does not want *Yom Kippur* to atone for him will be atoned for anyway.

### Willingness Question

This brings the *Gemara* to a parallel debate about the *chatat*. What if a person says: *tikarev v'lo titchaper* — bring the offering, but I do not want it to atone for me? Everyone agrees that if a person refuses entirely to have the *korban* brought — *lo tikarev* — it cannot atone, as the verse *yakriv oto* implies the offering must be brought with the consent of the owner (*lirtzono*). The debate concerns one who agrees to have it brought but withholds his consent to the atonement.

### Chatat & Will

Abaye holds: *ein mechaper* — it does not atone, because he has explicitly withheld his willingness. Rava holds: *mechaper* — it does atone, because *keivan de'amar tikarev kaparah mi-meila ati* — once he agrees to have it brought, the atonement follows automatically, regardless of his stated preference.

One way of understanding Rava's position draws on a point discussed earlier in *Keritot* regarding a *tinok she'nishba*, a child raised among non-Jews who violates *Shabbos* unknowingly and must bring a *chatat* despite having no culpability. The *chatat* in such a case is not about personal guilt — it is about the metaphysical fact of a sin having been committed in the world, which requires rectification independent of the sinner's inner state. On this model, even if a person does not want atonement, the bringing of the *korban* addresses the sin itself, not merely the person's guilt. This stands in contrast to an *asham*, which the *Gemara* elsewhere associates with *ashom asham la-Hashem* — it focuses on the person's state of guilt — whereas a *chatat* is a sin offering, addressing the act.

The *Gemara* then notes: *ve-hadar bei Rava* — Rava ultimately reversed his position.

### Baraitot Conflict

The reversal is prompted by a *baraita* from the *Sifra* (and a conflicting one): *yakhol yehei Yom HaKippurim mechaper al shavim v'al she'einam shavim* — perhaps *Yom Kippur* atones even for those who have not done *teshuvah*? A *kal va'chomer* might suggest this: just as a *chatat* and *asham* atone, and *Yom Kippur* atones — and just as a *chatat* and *asham* do not atone for intentional sins but only for unintentional ones, so too *Yom Kippur* should only atone for those who have done *teshuvah*. But one might counter: *chatat* and *asham* are limited in that they do not work for intentional sins; *Yom Kippur*, which does atone even for intentional sins, might be powerful enough to work even without *teshuvah*. The *Gemara* concludes: *talmud lomar ach* — the word *ach* in the *pasuk* *ach be'asor lachodesh hashevi'i* limits its scope. *Ach chalak* — it does not atone for those who have not done *teshuvah*.

A second *baraita* from the same *Sifra* appears to contradict this: *yakhol lo yehei Yom HaKippurim mechaper ela al she'nita'nah bo v'lo asa bo melacha v'kara'o mikra kodesh* — perhaps *Yom Kippur* only atones for one who fasted, refrained from *melacha*, and observed the day properly. What of one who did not fast, performed *melacha*, and failed to treat the day as sacred? *Talmud lomar Yom HaKippurim hu mikol makom* — it atones regardless. This is a striking ruling: one who violates *Yom Kippur* is nonetheless atoned for by it.

Since both *baraitot* are from the anonymous *Sifra* (attributed to Rabbi Yehuda), they cannot simply be assigned to different *tannaim*. The *Gemara* notes they are in tension: *kashya ahadadi*. One might distinguish the cases — perhaps it atones even if one violates it, provided one still wants it to work; but the *Gemara* treats these as part of a single continuum and declines to introduce such a middle position.

### Rabbi's Opinion

Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between two presentations within *Rabbi*'s teaching. One *baraita* records *Rabbi*'s ruling *aliba d'Rabbi Yehuda*, while the other reflects *Rabbi*'s own opinion. *Rabbi* himself holds: *kol aveiros sheba-Torah bein asa teshuvah bein lo asa teshuvah Yom HaKippurim mechaper* — for all transgressions in the Torah, *Yom Kippur* atones regardless of whether one has done *teshuvah*.

### Megaleh Panim

*Rabbi* lists three exceptions: *miforek ol* — one who has thrown off the yoke of Torah entirely; *megaleh panim ba-Torah* — one who acts brazenly against the Torah; and *meifer bris basar* — one who has annulled the covenant of circumcision through physical reversal. The phrase *megaleh panim ba-Torah* appears in *Pirkei Avot* and other *mishnayot* without the appended qualifier *shelo kehalacha* found in some later sources. The *Rambam* in his *Perush Hamishnayot* on *Pirkei Avot*, citing the *Yerushalmi*, interprets *megaleh panim* as a form of *azut panim* — brazenness — directed at the Torah, aligned with the verse *devar Hashem bazah*, which describes one who openly denigrates and attacks the Torah. This fits better with the plain context than the interpretation of making false *drashot*, and the *Rambam*'s reading raises the further question of how it differs from *porek ol* — though the distinction may be one of degree. Even for these extreme categories, *Rabbi* clarifies: *she'im asa teshuvah Yom HaKippurim mechaper* — if they do *teshuvah*, *Yom Kippur* will atone even for them.

### Rava Reversal

Rava offers a different resolution: both *baraitot* reflect *Rabbi*'s own opinion, and they are not in conflict. *U'modeh Rabbi b'aveirot d'Yom HaKippurim gufei d'lo mechaper* — *Rabbi* concedes that for sins involving *Yom Kippur* itself — actual violations of the day — *Yom Kippur* does not atone unless one has done *teshuvah* for those specific transgressions. The *baraita* that requires fasting and observance is speaking about the sins of the day itself; the *baraita* that says it works regardless is speaking about other sins committed during the year.

### Karet Challenge

This resolution prompts an acute question: if *Yom Kippur* atones even for one who violates it, how could one ever incur *karet* for violating *Yom Kippur*? The day itself would immediately atone for any transgression committed upon it. The *Gemara* offers several answers. If the violation occurs at night, the atonement — *itzumo shel yom mechaper* — takes effect only during the day, so one who sins at night and dies before dawn would incur *karet* without atonement. For sins committed during the day itself, the *Gemara* proposes scenarios in which the sinner dies at the moment of the transgression before the atonement can take effect: one who chokes while eating, one who performs *melacha* right up until *shekias hachamah*, or one who is killed mid-act — in each case, *d'lo havi lei sha'os d'yimama d'lechaper lei*, there was no subsequent moment for the day to atone.

The *Gemara*'s broader conclusion is striking: it aligns all the variables — whether *teshuvah* is required, whether observance of the day is required, whether wanting the atonement is required — into a single dichotomy. Either *Yom Kippur* works entirely regardless (*Rabbi*'s position taken to its logical extreme), or all those conditions apply together. What is notably absent from the *Gemara*'s discussion is the most intuitive question: what of a person who is willing to be atoned, who fasts and observes the day, but has not undergone an internal process of *teshuvah*? The *Gemara* does not address this directly, instead reducing the *shavim/she'einam shavim* distinction to a binary of whether the person explicitly accepts or rejects the atonement. The fasting and observance of *Yom Kippur* may perhaps serve as sufficient *teshuvah* in the case of a *shogeg*, but the *Gemara* leaves this largely implicit.

---

## Megadef

### Yidoni Question

Returning to the list, the *Gemara* raises the following question: the *Rabbanan* heard that Rabbi Akiva, in his enumeration, lists *ba'al ov* but not *yidoni*. The *Rabbanan* ask: *mai shna de-lo maisi korban* — why does *yidoni* not bring a *korban*? The answer offered is *mishum de-leis bei ma'aseh* — because there is no significant physical act involved in *yidoni* (which requires only placing a bone in the mouth). The *Rabbanan* then respond: *megadef nami leis bei ma'aseh* — but *megadef* also involves no action. Why does *megadef* bring a *korban* but not *yidoni*? This is the force of the word *af* in the earlier statement — *af megadef* should also be excluded.

Earlier in the *Gemara*, two explanations were offered for why Rabbi Akiva distinguishes between *yidoni* and *megadef*: either he requires some form of action but sets a minimal threshold, and the verbal act of *megadef* satisfies that threshold; or he does not require action at all, and excluded *yidoni* only because it shares a single *lav* with *ov*, such that one would not bring two separate *korbanos* for *ov* and *yidoni* together, though either alone would in principle require one.

### R. Akiva View

A *baraita* is cited: *megadef meivi korban ho'il u-va bo karet divrei Rabbi Akiva* — *megadef* brings a *korban* because *karet* is mentioned in connection with it, in the view of Rabbi Akiva.

### Not All Karet

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this: is it really a general principle that wherever *karet* is written, a *korban* is brought? What of *pesach* and *milah*, where *karet* is stated and yet no *korban* is brought for failing to perform them? The answer is that those are violations of a *mitzvas asei* — a positive commandment — and the general rule linking *karet* to a *chatat* applies only to prohibitions (*lo ta'aseh*).

### Juxtaposition

Rabbi Akiva's position is then more precisely stated: *megadef meivi korban ho'il u-va bo ha-karet bi-mkom korban* — it is not simply that *karet* is mentioned, but that *karet* is specifically mentioned in the same passage (*Bamidbar* 15) that discusses bringing a *korban* for unintentional sin. The structure of the *pesukim* there is as follows: verse 27 states that if one sins unintentionally, he brings a *chatat* (*v'nefesh achas techeta bi-shgagah v'hikrivah ez bas shnasah l'chatat*). Verse 30 then states: *v'ha-nefesh asher ta'aseh be-yad ramah* — one who acts intentionally, *es Hashem hu megadef*, he is blaspheming God, *v'nichresah ha-nefesh ha-hi mi-kerev ammah*, he incurs *karet*. The intentional offender who gets *karet* is juxtaposed directly to the unintentional offender who brings a *chatat*. Since *megadef* and *karet* appear in the same *parasha* as the *korban*, Rabbi Akiva derives that *megadef* brings a *chatat* when done unintentionally.

### Et Hashem

The *Gemara* then asks: *mah hu megadef — mevarech es Hashem*? Is *megadef* in this *pasuk* actually referring to one who curses God? The *chachamim* respond that it is not. The phrase *es Hashem hu megadef* in *Bamidbar* 15 refers rather to a form of *avodah zarah* — not classic *avodah zarah*, which would not require a special verse, but a subsidiary or ritual form: perhaps singing, dancing, or performing some ceremonial act before an idol. This form of service would incur *karet* and, if done unintentionally, requires a *chatat* — but it is not the act of verbally cursing or blaspheming God. How then do we know that verbal blasphemy incurs *karet*? From a *gezeira shava*: the verse by the case of the *mekalel* (*Vayikra* 24, the incident of the *ben ha-Yisraelis*) says *v'nasa chet'o*, and the verse by *Pesach Sheni* also says *chet'o yisa*. Just as the latter carries *karet*, so too the *mekalel* incurs *karet* — but without the *korban* derivation, since that *pasuk* has been reassigned to *avodah zarah*.

### Issi & R. Elazar

Two *tannaim* offer characterizations of what *megadef* means, framing the debate in vivid terms. Issi ben Yehuda says the act of *megadef* is like someone who says to a fellow: *geirasta ha-ke'ara v'chisarta* — you scraped out the bowl and actually took material away from the bowl itself. The *megadef* has, as it were, attacked God directly — a profoundly violent image of verbal assault on the Divine. On this view, *megadef* means one who curses and blasphemes God.

Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah offers a contrasting image: *geirasta ha-ke'ara v'lo chisarta* — you scraped out the bowl but did not actually take material away from the bowl itself. You cleaned it out without damaging it. On his view, *megadef* refers to *oved avodah zarah* — an idolater. The act of *avodah zarah* is, paradoxically, depicted as less of a direct assault on God than cursing. Both *Rashi* and *Rabbeinu Gershom* understand this as saying that *avodah zarah* does not actually harm or diminish God in any direct sense, even though it is a categorical rejection of His sovereignty.

This distinction finds a striking parallel in the *Rambam*'s *Moreh Nevuchim*, where he states explicitly that holding false theological beliefs about God is worse than *avodah zarah*. His reasoning is that *avodah zarah* — whether in the form of worshipping God through images or worshipping other deities — does not necessarily corrupt one's core understanding of the Divine. It is, in his framework, a wrong act. But a false belief about God's nature — such as attributing corporeality to Him — is a fundamental distortion of one's conception of God Himself. The *Gemara* here seems to reflect a similar intuition: cursing God (*mevarech es Hashem*) involves a direct, intimate confrontation with the Divine, whereas *avodah zarah* involves a misdirection of worship, not necessarily an assault on God per se.

### Final Tanya

A final *baraita* crystallizes the dispute: *es Hashem hu megadef* — Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says *be'oved avodah zarah ketiv*, the verse speaks about one who worships idols. *V'chachamim omrim* — the *chachamim* hold that the verse came only to assign *karet* to one who curses God (*l'mevareikh es Hashem*). Whether a *korban* accompanies that *karet*, and what exactly the verse's juxtaposition with the *chatat* passage establishes, is the substance of the debate between Rabbi Akiva and the *chachamim* running throughout this entire discussion.

---

---

# Keritot 8b

## Safek Births/Flows

### Chatas Tahara

The Mishnah at the end of 8a marks a transition in the tractate's overall thematic arc. Up to this point, the discussion has centered on the *chatas* offered as *kaparah* for *kares*-level transgressions. The Mishnah now shifts to a different category of *chatas* — one that forms part of a *tahara* process rather than an atonement for sin. This theme will become fully explicit in the next *perek*, but the current Mishnah already engages its central cases: a woman who must bring a *chatas* at the conclusion of a *leida* process in order to regain her eligibility to eat *kodshim*. This category is known as *mechusrei kaparah* — those who are lacking the completion of their purification — and it will be the explicit subject of the *perek* to come.

### Multiple Safek Births

Within this framework, the preceding Mishnah addressed a woman who had multiple births or miscarriages within certain time intervals, allowing her to combine obligations and bring one *chatas* for several events. The present Mishnah addresses a related but distinct problem: a woman who is uncertain whether her birth or flow generated an obligation at all — for instance, whether a miscarriage occurred before or after forty days, which is the threshold for *leida* status. Even in such a *safek* situation, she must bring at least one *chatas* to enable her to eat *kodshim*. The ruling is that she brings one, but since her obligation is doubtful, she does not eat it and is not liable for the remaining ones. The one she brings serves the *tahara* function, nothing more.

### Price Controls

The Mishnah concludes with the well-known account of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who intervened when the price of birds had risen sharply due to heavy demand. His ruling — that women need not bring their full complement of obligatory *korbanos* — drove down demand and accordingly brought prices back to reasonable levels. This was a form of rabbinic legal activism: it did not render *tamei* women *tahor* without any offering, as they still brought one, but it relieved them of the obligation to bring the full number. Parallel examples of similar interventions exist in other areas of halachic life — pressure on the prices of *lulav* and *esrog*, or communal decisions not to purchase fish for *Shabbos* until prices normalized — though the Gemara itself does not address these parallels.

---

## Vadai & Safek

### Separate Offerings

The Gemara now examines the first portion of the Mishnah, citing a *Tanu Rabbanan*. The best textual reading (*girsa*) of this *braisa* presents the cases in matched pairs: five *vadai* *zivohs* and five *safek* *zivohs*, or five *vadai* births and five *safek* births. In such a scenario, what is the woman's obligation? *Mevia shtei kinim* — she brings two *kinim*, two pairs of birds. *Achas al ha-vadai ve-achas al ha-safek*: one for the definite obligations, one for the doubtful ones. As for the one brought against the *vadai* obligations — *shel vadai ne'echeles ve-ha-shar aleiha chova*: it is eaten by the *kohen* (since it is brought for a definite obligation), but the remaining four *vadai* birds still remain an outstanding obligation, since only one is needed to complete the *tahara* process while the others must still eventually be brought. As for the one brought against the *safek* obligations — *shel safek ein ne'echeles ve-ein ha-shar aleiha chova*: it is not eaten (since a *chatas* brought for a doubtful obligation is not eaten), and the remaining four *safek* birds generate no further liability.

### Separate Scenarios

One might ask: if both the *vadai* and *safek* events occurred simultaneously, why is a second bird needed for the *safek* at all? Surely the one brought for the *vadai* would cover the *safek* as well, since worst case there are ten obligations, and bringing even one suffices for the *tahara* process. The answer is that this *braisa* is in fact not describing a single woman who experienced both categories simultaneously. Rather, it describes four separate scenarios: a woman with only *vadai* events, and a woman with only *safek* events — each subcategory presenting the *ziva* and *leida* variants. If *vadai* and *safek* occurred together, one bird for the *vadai* would indeed suffice. The *braisa* is thus enumerating four distinct halachic situations, not one compound case.

---

## Last vs. Any

### Last Event Only

The *braisa* continues with a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva regarding the designation of the *korban*. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri rules: *ha-vadai tomar al ha'acharona ve-tipater* — in a case of five *vadai* obligations, when she brings the single *korban* that effectuates her *tahara*, she must designate it as being for the *last* event. The logic is sequential: if a woman had one birth in January, February, March, April, and May, and she brings her *korban* in June, designating it for the May birth means it is *metaher* the May birth and thereby everything that preceded it as well. But if she designates it for the January birth, it purifies that first event — while the subsequent births in February through May represent new *tumah* states that arose afterwards and remain unaddressed. The word *ve-tipater* is something of a misnomer here, since the remaining four still remain an obligation; the better term would be *ve-titaher*, since what is being accomplished is the *tahara* process itself rather than a full discharge of all liabilities.

As for the *safek* case: *im yesh vadai beineihem tomar al ha-vadai ve-tipater* — if among the five doubtful events there is one that is *vadai*, she designates the *korban* for that one and is covered. *Ve-im lav* — if all five are *safek*, then *tomar al echad meihem ve-tipater*: she may designate the *korban* for any one of the five and the *tahara* process is satisfied. This leniency for the *safek* case will require explanation, and the Gemara addresses it below.

### Any Designation

Rabbi Akiva disagrees: *bein al ha-vadai bein al ha-safek tomar al echad meihem ve-tipater*. Whether the obligations are *vadai* or *safek*, she may designate the *korban* for any event — earlier, middle, or last — and the *tahara* is accomplished. When she brings the *korban*, it purifies her at that moment regardless of which event she declares it to be for. The *korban* acts as a cleansing act, effective at the time of its offering, whatever its stated designation.

---

## Chatas/Tevilah

### Chatas Model

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak transmits an explanation in the name of Rava: what is the precise point of contention between these two *tanna'im*? *De-Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri medamei lehu le-chatat* — Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri treats this *korban* as analogous to a *chatas* in the sense of an atonement for sin. By that model, *de-man de-chayav chamesh chataos, ad de-mayisei kuleihu besof mechaper lei* — a person who committed five sins requiring five separate *chataos* is not fully atoned until he brings all five. Under this model, the single *korban* must at minimum address the final event so that it "covers" everything that came before it. That is why Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri insists the designation be for the last birth or flow.

### Tevilah Model

Rabbi Akiva, by contrast, *midamei lah le-tevilah* — compares the *korban* to an act of *tevilah*. If a person became *tamei* five different times — touching five *shratzim* or other sources of *tumah* — he need not immerse five times. One immersion in the *mikvah* cleanses all prior *tumah* states regardless of which one he declares he is immersing for. *Keivan de-taval chada zimna itur* — once he has immersed, the act of *tevilah* is fully effective. So too here, once the woman brings her *korban*, it cleanses her *tahara* state entirely, whatever the designated reason. *Hacha nami lo shnai* — here too it makes no difference.

This raises a broader conceptual question about the nature of the *chatas* here, one that connects to discussions earlier in the tractate. The word *chitui* in the Torah — as in *hu yitchata bo ba-yom ha-shlishi u-va-yom ha-shvi'i*, the sprinkling of the *parah adumah* — means cleansing, not moral atonement. The Hebrew root *cheit* and the related noun *chitoi* throughout the Torah carry the primary sense of purification. This is why a *chatas* can be brought in cases where there is no personal guilt whatsoever — as with the *tinok she-nishba*, a child raised without knowledge of Jewish identity who violated *Shabbos*. There is no moral fault, yet there is a metaphysical rupture that requires cleansing. Similarly, the concept expressed in *ha'aretz lo yechupar* — that the land itself is affected by sin — reflects the Torah's understanding that sin creates a metaphysical reality that must be addressed independently of the individual's guilt. The *chatas* is about cleansing that metaphysical reality, not about the personal culpability of the one who brings it. This is not apologetics; it is the *pshat* of the *pesukim*, reinforced by the *pshtanim* and numerous contexts throughout Tanach. The *chatas* of a *yoledet*, a *zav*, and a *zavah* are all cleansing acts with no sin dimension, and that is precisely why the Gemara frames the debate between Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Rabbi Akiva in terms of *tevilah* rather than moral atonement.

---

## Safek Leniency

### Sin Model Problem

Rav Pappa raises a sharp objection against the framework as initially stated. If Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri truly holds that this *korban* is analogous to a *chatas* for sin, why is he lenient in the *safek* case, permitting the woman to designate the *korban* for any one of the five doubtful events rather than insisting it be for the last? The parallel case in the world of sin would be *chamesh ashamot teluyim* — five *asham talui* offerings, each for a separate doubtful transgression. There too, *ki mayisi chad mipater* — one is not discharged when only one is brought. Moreover, the principle *kol she-chalukin be-chatas chalukin be-asham* establishes that the *asham* functions analogously to the *chatas*: if five *chataos* are required for five sins, five *ashamot* would be required for five doubtful sins. If Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri is truly working from the sin model, he should demand all five and should certainly require that the single permissible one be for the last event — even in the *safek* case.

### Cleansing Model

The Gemara's resolution is decisive: *de-chulei alma le-tevilos medamei lehan* — everyone agrees that this *korban* is analogous to *tevilah*. It is a cleansing act, not an act of atonement for sin. The entire framing of the debate in terms of the *chatas* model was only an initial suggestion; the Gemara now establishes that this is not the actual point of disagreement between the *tanna'im*.

### Negligence Concern

What then is the debate? *U-ve-choshshin li-fsheiah ka-mifligi* — the dispute concerns whether we are concerned about negligence (*peshia*). *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri savar chaishinan; Rabbi Akiva savar lo chaishinan.* Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri is concerned about a practical danger: if a woman with five births brings her *korban* in June and designates it for the January birth, she may draw the wrong lesson for the future. She may reason that once she brought a *chatas* for the January birth, the subsequent births were already "covered" — and next time, she might bring a *chatas* right after her first birth and assume she need not worry about future births. By requiring that the designation be for the *last* event, the message is reinforced that the *korban* only covers what preceded it at that moment, not what will follow. Rabbi Akiva is unconcerned by this possibility. In the *safek* case, Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri is lenient because it is rarer and the concern about misapplication is correspondingly lower. But on the underlying principle — that the *korban* functions as a cleansing act analogous to *tevilah* — both agree entirely.

---

## Four Categories

### Mechusrei Kaparah

The Gemara now formally opens the fourth *perek*, whose Mishnah states: *arba mechusrei kaparah ve-arba mevi'in al ha-zadon ki-shgaga* — there are four categories of people whose purification process is incomplete until they bring a *korban* (*mechusrei kaparah*), and there are four categories of people who bring a *chatas* even for willful sin. Normally a *chatas* is brought only for inadvertent transgression, so the latter category is a significant exception. The Mishnah first lists the *mechusrei kaparah*: *ha-zav ve-ha-zavah* — a male or female with an unusual flow; *ha-yoledet* — a woman after childbirth; and *ha-metzora* — a person afflicted with *tzara'as*.

These four individuals share a common status: they complete most of the *tahara* process through immersion, counting of days, and other requirements, but the final step — without which they may not enter the *Beis HaMikdash* or eat *kodshim* — is the bringing of a *korban*. The word *mechusrei kaparah*, while it literally invokes atonement, is used here in the sense of completing a purification process; the connection to sin is absent in all four cases. As already established, the *chatas* here functions as a cleansing of a *tumah* state, not as a response to personal wrongdoing.

It is worth pausing on why these four categories involve *tumah* at all — a broader discussion with significant scholarly literature. Some link *tumah* to the domain of death: illness approaches death, childbirth involves risk of death, and the unusual emissions of a *zav* or *zavah* suggest bodily dysfunction. *Niddah* and *leida* have been explained in terms of unfulfilled potential for life. The general view among those who seek a comprehensive theory of *tumah* centers on proximity to death and its attendant phenomena, tying together the *zav*, *zavah*, *metzora*, and *yoledet* into a coherent framework, though the illness model alone does not account cleanly for *leida* or *niddah*, nor for *tumas meis* from animal carcasses. These are important questions but lie beyond the scope of the present sugya.

### Ger & Nazir

Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov adds two further cases to the list of *mechusrei kaparah*: a *ger* who has converted must bring a *korban* — *ger mechusar kaparah she-yizrok alav ha-dam*, a convert requires the sprinkling of blood — before he may eat *kodshim*. And a *nazir* who completes his term of *nezirus* brings a *korban chatas* as part of the process that ends his *nazirus* and permits him to drink wine, cut his hair, and become susceptible to *tumah* again.

What Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is effectively doing is broadening the category of *mechusrei kaparah* beyond *tumah*-related purification. For the *tana kama*, the category is defined by: a *chatas* that enables the person to eat *kodshim* at the conclusion of a *tahara* process. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov redefines it more broadly: any *korban* that effects a change of status — whether from non-Jew to Jew, or from *nazir* to non-*nazir* — qualifies. Notably, regarding the *ger* specifically, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov also appears to see the *korban* as tied to *tahara* in some sense, connecting conversion to a transition from *tumah* to *tahara* — an interesting framing that perhaps parallels the way immersing vessels in a *mikvah* is understood, though this framing of the non-Jew as *tamei* is obviously theologically fraught and deserves careful attention.

### Zav/Zava Split

The Gemara asks why the Mishnah counts *zav* and *zavah* as two separate categories rather than one. The answer: *de-chaluka tumasam* — their *tumah* is fundamentally different in its mechanics. *De-zav lo metame be-ones* — a *zav* does not become *tamei* if the emission arises through *ones*: that is, if the flow comes as a result of illness or other involuntary external cause and emerges without the characteristic features of *ziva*, it does not generate *tumah*. The Gemara's description indicates that *ziva* for a male involves a discharge that emerges in a manner associated with the sexual organs' activity — the Gemara later in tractates on this subject specifies the nature of the substance and the manner of its emission. A *zavah*'s *tumah*, by contrast, *metamei be-ones* — even if the blood flow is caused by illness or external factors, it is still considered *zivah*. Additionally, *zav metame be-re'iyos ki-yamim* — a male *zav* becomes *tamei* on the basis of three separate sightings, even if they occur on the same day, whereas *de-tana* — as the Baraita teaches — by a female, the Torah uses the language of *yamim rabim*, multiple days, meaning the three sightings must occur on three separate days. These are substantial differences in how *tumah* is acquired and defined, justifying the counting of *zav* and *zavah* as two distinct categories.

### Metzora Gender

The Gemara then asks: should male and female *metzora* also be counted as two categories, since they too differ? The answer is: *ein ikar tumasam chaluka* — their fundamental *tumah* is the same. Both become *tamei* through *nega'im* on the body; the size (*ke-gris*) and appearance of the blemishes are identical for both. The differences that exist are only in the *behaviors* required of the *metzora* after becoming *tamei*: a male *metzora* is required to rend his garments, let his hair grow wild, and is forbidden from *tashmish ha-mita* — the latter derived from *ve-yashav michutz le-oholo*, meaning outside of his tent, understood as separation from his wife. A female *metzora* is exempt from all three: *eina te'una peria u-ferimah*, she does not rend her clothes or let her hair grow wild, *u-muteres be-tashmish ha-mita*, and she is not forbidden from marital relations. The Baraita derives this from the verse *ish ki yihye bo nega* — "a man who has a *nega*" — which specifies the male-specific behaviors without excluding women from *tumah* itself. The general words *ve-ha-tzarua ve-ha-metzora* include women in the *tumah*, while the word *ish* applies specifically to the behavioral restrictions. The *Gemara* notes this asymmetry is worth reflection — why would these particular practices not apply to a woman? One possible consideration involves the framework of *tashmish ha-mita* and the husband's rights; another involves the unseemly appearance that *peria* and *perimah* would create. Neither explanation is fully satisfying on its own, and the connection to the *sotah* procedure (where a woman's hair is uncovered as part of the process) may suggest that such outward displays of physical dishevelment carry a particular gendered valence in halachic discourse.

---

## Ger Conversion

### Ger Kodashim

The Gemara now presents a *Tanu Rabbanan* that forms the core of the discussion of the *ger*'s *korban*. A *ger* is prevented from eating *kodshim* until he brings his *kan* — his pair of birds. This is the *korban* associated with conversion, and it functions as the completion of his transition to full Jewish status with respect to the Temple service and its sanctities.

### Ger Korban Type

The specific nature of the *ger*'s *korban* is established as follows. *Heivi pereidah achas shacharis* — if he brought even one of the two birds in the morning, *ochel be-kodshim le-erev* — he may eat *kodshim* that evening. The parallel to the *yoledet* is explicit: just as a woman who brings one *korban* out of her full obligation completes the *tahara* process even if the rest remain outstanding, so too a *ger* who brings one bird has satisfied the immediate requirement for *tahara* and eligibility for *kodshim*, even though the second bird remains an obligation. Importantly, the *korban* of a *ger* consists not of one *chatas* and one *olah* as would be the case with most *kinim* in the Torah, but of *shtei olos* — two *olos*. *Kol ha-kinim she-ba-Torah achas chatas ve-achas olah; kan shtei olos* — normally when the Torah mandates two birds as an obligatory pair, one is a *chatas* and one is an *olah*; here, both are *olah*.

### Har Sinai Model

The source for why a *ger* brings at all, and why the *korban* is specifically an *olah*, derives from the verse in Bamidbar 15:14: *ve-chi yagur itchem ger o asher be-tochechem le-doroseichem ve-asa ishe rei'ach nichoach la-Hashem ka'asher ta'asu ken ya'aseh* — when a *ger* dwells among you and brings a fire-offering of pleasing aroma to God, he shall do as you do. *Ka'asher ta'asu ken ya'aseh* — as you did, so shall he do. The Gemara understands this not as a directive about what a *ger* must do when he brings voluntary *korbanos*, but as establishing what he must bring upon becoming a *ger*: the same *korban* you brought when you became Jewish. What did the Jewish people bring when they entered the covenant? At the foot of Har Sinai, at the conclusion of Parshas Mishpatim, *va-yishlach es na'arei Bnei Yisrael va-ya'alu olos va-yizbechu zvachim shelamim la-Hashem parim* — Moshe sent the young men of Israel who offered *olos* and *shelamim* to God. Therefore, *ma atem olah u-shelamim af ger olah u-shelamim* — just as Israel brought an *olah* and *shelamim*, so too a *ger* must bring an *olah* and *shelamim*.

### Two Birds Rule

One might then ask: if the obligation is modeled on *olah* and *shelamim* — presumably large animals — why do we permit the *ger* to fulfill the obligation with two birds? The answer involves the principle that one cannot bring a single bird as an independent *korban*. The Baraita states: *she-lo matzinu be-chol ha-Torah kullah* one bird as a standalone *korban* — in the entire Torah, birds are never brought singly as an obligatory offering; they always come in pairs, either two birds or a bird paired with a larger animal. This pairing principle means that if birds are used at all, two are required. But this is a leniency — *ela le-hakel* — a concession allowing the *ger* to fulfill his obligation without bringing large animals. This raises the further question: why then is not even a *minchah* permitted, if we are being lenient? The Gemara's answer is that the verse *ka'asher ta'asu ken ya'aseh* preserves a minimum standard of equivalence — it must be like what the people brought, which involved *damim*, blood. A *minchah*, regardless of how much it costs, lacks blood and therefore does not qualify. Birds, as animal offerings involving blood, satisfy this minimum criterion.

---

## Milah/Tevilah

### Milah Sources

The Gemara now turns to Rebbi's teaching that the Har Sinai model establishes not only the requirement of a *korban* for a *ger*, but all three components of *geirus*: *mah avoseichem lo nichnesu la-bris ela be-milah u-tevilah ve-hartz'as dam* — your ancestors entered the covenant only through *milah*, *tevilah*, and the acceptance of a blood-offering. Rebbi adds the paradigm of *geirus* as a whole, with all three elements sourced from the events at Har Sinai.

Where is *milah* sourced? *Ki mulim hayu kol ha-am ha-yotzim* — the verse in Yehoshua records that all the men who left Egypt had been circumcised, and since bringing the *korban Pesach* requires one to be circumcised, it is evident that *milah* was part of the status of those who entered the covenant. The Gemara also cites the verse from Yechezkel: *va-avor alayich va-erech misboseses be-damayich va-omar lach be-damayich chayi*, referring to the blood of *milah* and the blood of the *korban Pesach* as the dual *damim* through which Israel's covenant was sealed.

A significant halachic discussion emerges here. It is well-attested in *midrashic* tradition that the tribe of Levi did not require a special *milah* before the *korban Pesach* in Egypt — they had maintained the tradition of *bris milah* continuously since Avraham. This means their *milah* was not performed as a formal act of *geirus* or covenant-entry, but simply as the continuation of ancestral practice. From this, many *Rishonim* derive that a *milah* performed as a Jewish *bris milah* — even without specific intent for *geirus* — satisfies the *milah* requirement for a *ger*. The practical application is significant: a baby born to a Jewish father and non-Jewish mother who receives a *bris milah* as a standard Jewish circumcision, and later undergoes conversion, may rely on that original *milah* without requiring a new procedure or even, in some opinions, a ritual drawing of blood (*hatafas dam bris*). The consensus follows that such a *milah* is sufficient. This is not a peripheral leniency; it is a substantive and well-grounded position among the *Rishonim* and has real implications for contemporary conversion practice.

### Tevilah Sources

The source for *tevilah* as a requirement for conversion is derived from the verse describing the events at Har Sinai: *va-yikach Moshe chatzi ha-dam va-yizrok al ha-am* — Moshe took half the blood and sprinkled it on the people. The Gemara reasons: *ein haza'ah belo tevilah* — sprinkling in a *tahara* context, as with the ashes of the *parah adumah*, requires prior immersion. Therefore the sprinkling of blood upon Israel at Har Sinai presupposes that they had first immersed. This derivation does, as one might note, depend on viewing the *dam ha-bris* as operating within a *tahara* framework; if it is primarily a covenantal act rather than a *tahara* ritual, the source for *tevilah* is less direct. The tension between viewing the Har Sinai *korban* as a *tahara* process versus a covenantal ritual is precisely the deeper question underlying the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the *Chachamim*.

### Korban Sources

The source for the *korban* requirement is explicit: *va-yishlach es na'arei Bnei Yisrael* — Moshe sent the young men of Israel and they offered *olos* and *shelamim*. This is the act by which Israel entered the covenant at Har Sinai, and it is the act that a *ger* replicates when he converts.

### Olah/Shlamim

As established earlier, the Gemara derives from *ka'asher ta'asu ken ya'aseh* that the *ger* must bring an *olah* and *shelamim*, mirroring what Israel brought at Har Sinai. The further derivation from *ishe rei'ach nichoach* — "a fire-offering of pleasing aroma" — focuses the essential obligation on the *olah*, understood as *eizehu davar she-kulo la-Hashem*, the component that is entirely consumed before God. This verse licenses any form of *olah*, including a bird *olah*, thereby permitting the use of birds. The *shelamim* component, while modeled on Har Sinai, is subsumed under the broader principle of *kachem ka-ger yihyeh* — he is like you — and *la-chem hukashnu ve-lo le-korbanoseichem*, he is equated to you personally, not to your specific offerings. Therefore the precise composition of an *olah* and *shelamim* is not absolutely mandated; the minimum is an *olah* in any form.

---

## Ola Focus

### Ola Emphasis

The derivation from *ishe rei'ach nichoach* in Bamidbar 15:14 serves to establish the *olah* as the primary and essential component of the *ger*'s *korban*. *Eizehu davar she-kulo la-Hashem* — what is it that is entirely for God? *Hevei omer zeh olas ha-of* or simply *zeh olah* — this must refer to the *olah*, the offering wholly consumed upon the altar. The inclusion of bird *olos* under this rubric is what enables the leniency permitting birds.

### Blood Required

Why can a *minchah* not serve even where leniency might otherwise be applied? *Mah atem minei damim* — as your ancestors entered the covenant through blood-offerings, so too the *ger* must bring something involving blood. The emphasis on blood at Har Sinai is not incidental: it is the *dam ha-bris* that created the binding relationship between Israel and God. A *minchah*, even if fully burned as a kind of substitute *olah*, lacks this blood dimension and therefore cannot fulfill the requirement. *Ka'asher ta'asu ken ya'aseh* sets a minimum standard that cannot be met by a bloodless offering.

### Pairing Principle

If the *ger* fulfills his obligation with a large animal *olah*, one animal suffices. But if he uses birds, two are required. As established earlier, there is no instance in the entire Torah of a single bird brought as a standalone obligatory *korban*. Whether the pairing is with a second bird or with a large animal (as in the case of the *yoledet*, who brings one bird *chatas* paired with a ram *olah*), birds always come paired. This principle thus generates the specific ruling of two bird *olos* for the *ger* when he cannot or does not bring an animal.

---

## Ger Today

### Set Aside Money

The *Tanu Rabbanan* teaches that a *ger* in the present era — after the destruction of the *Beis HaMikdash* — is required to set aside a *rova* (a quarter of a silver *dinar*, the minimum price of two birds at the time) designated for his *korban*, so that when the *Beis HaMikdash* is rebuilt he will be able to fulfill his obligation. Even though the *korban* is not a prerequisite for *geirus* in the absence of the Temple — as derived from *kachem ka-ger yihyeh*, which establishes that there is always the possibility of a *ger* among Israel and therefore conversion cannot be contingent on what is currently impossible — the underlying obligation of bringing the *korban* remains, to be discharged in the future.

### Practice Nullified

Rabbi Shimon records that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai voted to nullify this practice *mipnei ha-takalah* — because of the danger of inadvertent *me'ilah*. If money was set aside as *kodshim* funds, there was a risk that the owner would use it for ordinary purposes, thereby violating the prohibition of *me'ilah*. The Gemara concludes: *Amar Rav Idi bar Gershom amar Rav Adda bar Ahava halacha ke-Rabbi Shimon* — the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon, and no such money is set aside today.

### Korban Replacement

This discussion prompts a fundamental conceptual question: what replaces the *korban* now that the *Beis HaMikdash* is gone? The Gemara's presentation of the Har Sinai model is instructive here. The *korban* at the foot of Har Sinai was not merely a ritual act; it was the tangible expression of the covenant itself. Moshe sprinkled the blood and declared *zeh dam ha-bris asher karat Hashem imachem al kol ha-devarim* — this is the blood of the covenant that God has made with you concerning all of these matters. The *korban* symbolized the *ger*'s acceptance of obligation and entry into a covenantal relationship with God. When a *ger* brought a *korban* to the Temple, this act — in the context of Jewish sacred service — conveyed something analogous: a statement of relationship, obligation, and belonging.

It is notable that several key Talmudic sources on *geirus* enumerate only *milah* and *tevilah*, without explicitly mentioning *kabbalas mitzvos*. Other sources do mention *kabbalas mitzvos*, but do not discuss the *korban*. This may not be coincidental. When the *korban* was available, it served as the covenantal act — the concrete expression of the *ger*'s acceptance of the obligations of Jewish life. Without the *korban*, an explicit verbal declaration of *kabbalas mitzvos* becomes the necessary substitute, filling the same function: expressing the *ger*'s entry into the covenant and acceptance of its demands. The *korban* and *kabbalas mitzvos* may thus be understood as functional equivalents — two forms of the same covenantal act, one ritual and sacrificial, the other verbal and declarative — which is why the sources that have the *korban* do not stress *kabbalas mitzvos*, and why the sources operative today emphasize *kabbalas mitzvos* as the essential third element alongside *milah* and *tevilah*.

---

---

# Keritot 9

## Four Cases: Mezid & Shog…

### Intro: Intentional vs Un…

The ninth daf of *Keritot* opens a new *mishnah* that introduces a distinct category of *chatat*: sin offerings that are brought not only for unintentional violations but for intentional ones as well. Normally, the *chatat* is the exclusive domain of the *shogeg* — the person who transgresses unknowingly or negligently. Here, however, the *mishnah* identifies four cases that blur or override that fundamental distinction entirely: *eilu mevi'in al hazadon kishogeg* — the following bring an offering for even willful sins just as they would for unintentional ones.

It is worth noting at the outset that the *mishnah* is organized numerically rather than thematically. We have just finished discussing the four cases of *mechusrei kapparah* — those who lack atonement and must complete a purification process — and now we move to four cases in which the *mezid/shogeg* distinction is dissolved. These will be followed, as we shall see, by five cases in which one *korban* covers multiple transgressions, and five cases where the *korban* is of variable value based on the offerer's means. The organizing principle is the number, not the underlying legal category.

### Haba al Hashifchah

The first of the four cases is *haba al hashifchah* — one who has sexual relations with a female slave. The *pasuk* in question reads: *ve'ish ki yishkav et ishah shichvat zera, vehi shifchah necheret le'ish* — a man who lies with a woman carnally, and she is a *shifchah* designated to a man — *vehapdeh lo nifdetah o chufshah lo nitan lah* — she has not been fully redeemed nor fully freed. The *mishnah* and *Chazal* understand this to refer to a woman who is half-slave and half-free, quasi-betrothed to a man who is himself half-slave. Because she is not fully free, the betrothal is not fully binding as a proper *kiddushin* would be; yet she is not entirely without status either. It is this liminal state — neither full adultery nor an ordinary relationship — that defines this unique category.

The *pasuk* continues: *vehevi et ashamo l'Adonai el petach ohel moed eil asham, vechiper alav hakohen be'eil ha'asham lifnei Adonai al chatato asher chata venislach lo mechatato asher chata* — he shall bring his guilt offering before God, and the priest shall atone for him, and he shall be forgiven for the sin that he has sinned. The Torah mandates both *malkot* (lashes) and a *korban*, which makes this a striking and unusual case — ordinarily lashes are imposed for *mezid* and a *korban* for *shogeg*, yet here both are applied simultaneously. The important consequence is that both intentional and unintentional acts within this category require the same *korban*.

### Derivation: Redundancy i…

How does the *Gemara* derive that a single *korban* covers multiple acts of this sin, and that the *korban* is brought regardless of whether the act was intentional or unintentional? The *Gemara* cites a *baraita*: *vechiper alav hakohen be'eil ha'asham al chatato asher chata* — "for the sin that he has sinned." The phrase *chatato asher chata* is somewhat redundant; one might have simply written *al chatato*. The *baraita* derives from this redundancy that you bring one *korban* for multiple transgressions: *shemevi korban echad al aveirot harbeh*. And then the *pasuk* continues with a second redundant phrase — *venislach lo mechatato asher chata* — again "the sin that he has sinned." This second repetition teaches *la'asot mezid keshogeg* — to treat intentional sin like unintentional sin.

The *Gemara* raises a subtlety: one might have assumed that the baseline case of the *pasuk* is the *shogeg*, and that the derivation extends it to *mezid*. But the *Gemara* points out, based on *Rashi*'s reading, that the *peshat* of the *psukim* about *shifchah charufa* is actually the *mezid* case — because the *pasuk* of *bikoret tihyeh* is interpreted by *Chazal* as mandating *malkot*, and *malkot* is never administered for an unintentional act. Therefore, the baseline here is *mezid*, and the derivation from *mechatato asher chata* extends the obligation to *shogeg* as well. The *Gemara* reformulates accordingly: *ela eima la'asot shogeg kemezid* — we are extending the rule to treat *shogeg* like *mezid*. Either way, the *halacha* is identical: for *shifchah charufa*, one brings a *korban* across the full spectrum, and if one is a *mezid*, one receives both *malkot* and a *korban* — an altogether unusual combination.

### Nazir Shenitma

The second case is *venazir shenitma* — a *nazir* who became *tamei*. A *nazir* is prohibited from contracting ritual impurity, but if he does, he brings special *korbanot* — and this is so even if he became *tamei bemezid*, intentionally. The *Gemara* asks *minalan* — where do we know this?

The source is the *pasuk*: *vechi yamut met alav befeta pitom* — "and if a corpse should die upon him suddenly." At first glance, this language seems to describe an accident, perhaps even an *ones* — a completely unavoidable circumstance entirely beyond the *nazir*'s control. How, then, does the *Gemara* extract from it a case of *mezid*?

### Pitom: Three-Fold Meaning

The word *peta* — "suddenly" in the simpler sense — is understood to indicate *shogeg*, ordinary unintentional transgression, as in the *pasuk*: *im befeta belo eivah hadafo* — one who pushed another without premeditation or enmity. So *peta* means a normal case of unintended action.

The word *pitom*, however, carries multiple meanings. On one hand, *pitom zeh ones* — *pitom* can indicate something completely beyond one's control, as in *vayomer Hashem pitom el Moshe* — God spoke suddenly to Moshe, and when God addresses someone, it is entirely outside of that person's agency. On the other hand — and this is the striking teaching — *tanya idach*: another *baraita* teaches *pitom zeh mezid*, that *pitom* can mean the exact opposite: an intentional act. The source is the verse in *Mishlei*: *arum ra'ah ra'ah venistar ufetayim avru vena'anashu* — a shrewd person perceives danger and hides, while *petayim* — foolish people — transgress and are punished. The connection between *petayim* and *pitom* teaches that *pitom* can refer to a willful transgression as well.

### Petayim Derivation

The formal derivation relies on the linguistic relationship between *pitom* and *petayim*. The word in *Mishlei* is *petayim* — foolish ones who knowingly transgress — and this connects semantically to *pitom* in the *pasuk* about the *nazir*. Thus *pitom* is shown to encompass the full range from *ones* to *mezid*, with *peta* covering the middle ground of *shogeg*.

### Pitom Range Resolution

The *Gemara* then asks: why does the *pasuk* not simply say *pitom* alone, since as we have established, *pitom* by itself can mean *shogeg*, *mezid*, and *ones* — the entire spectrum? If *pitom* already implies all three, what does *peta* add?

The *Gemara* answers: *ei kasav kra pitom hava amina ki maysei korban be-shogeg* — if it had only said *pitom*, I would have interpreted it in the most natural way for a *korban*, which is *shogeg*. The classic case that obligates a *korban* is the middle ground: not *ones*, where there is no fault and no *korban* is expected, and not *mezid*, where the sin is too grave for a *korban* to serve as atonement. The standard *korban* is for *shogeg*. So I would have read *pitom* as referring to *shogeg*, just as all other cases in the Torah.

Therefore the Torah writes both *peta* — which unambiguously designates *shogeg* — and *pitom*. Since *peta* already covers *shogeg*, the word *pitom* cannot mean *shogeg*, and must therefore teach the other two ends: *ones* and *mezid*. *Ksav Rachmana pesa* — the Torah writes *peta* to signal *shogeg*, *legilluyei alah de-pitom*, to reveal that *pitom* refers specifically to *ones* and *mezid*. And *ve'afilu hachi hiyveih Rachmana* — even so, the Torah obligates the *korban* across that entire range.

The *Gemara* adds that one cannot argue from *ones* to *mezid* or vice versa by a *kal vachomer*, because each can be excluded on its own grounds: one might say *ones* requires no *korban* because the person has no guilt, or that *mezid* requires no *korban* because the sin is too weighty for it to provide *kapparah*. The *pasuk* must explicitly include both.

### Nazir: Metaphysical Fram…

This leads to a deeper conceptual observation. Why would it make sense that a *nazir* brings a *korban* even by *ones* — when he has no fault whatsoever — and even by *mezid* — when his guilt is at the highest level? The answer may lie in how we understand the *nazir*'s *korban* fundamentally. It is not primarily about atoning for the personal guilt of the act of becoming *tamei*. Rather, it is about the process of ending a *nezirut* of *tumah* and initiating a new *nezirut* of *taharah*. The *korban* is part of a transition, a changing of state, not a response to personal culpability.

Another formulation: the sin offering framework can be understood either in terms of personal fault — which is why *shogeg* and *mezid* normally matter — or in terms of a metaphysical reality that has been altered. When a *nezirut* is violated, something real has happened at the level of the *nezirut* itself, independent of the *nazir*'s state of mind. It is that metaphysical reality that the *korban* addresses and rectifies. This is why the categories of *ones*, *shogeg*, and *mezid* collapse here — personal blame is simply not the operative framework.

### Shvuat Eidut

The third case is *shvuat ha'edut* — swearing falsely that one has no testimony to offer. This is addressed explicitly in *Vayikra* 5: *ve-nefesh ki techeta ve-shama kol alah ve-hu eid o ra'ah o yada ve-im lo yagid ve-nasa avono* — a person who hears an oath of testimony, and who saw or knew, and does not testify — shall bear his sin. Critically, this *pasuk* does not contain the phrase *ve-ne'elam mimmennu* — "it was hidden from him" — which appears in adjacent cases involving *tumah* and a forgotten oath (*shvuat bitui*). In those cases, the Torah explicitly conditions the obligation on the transgression having been unintentional. Here, no such condition is stated.

The *Gemara* derives from the absence of *ve-ne'elam* that for *shvuat ha'edut*, intentionality is irrelevant — *lechayyev al hamezid keshogeg*. Since the unintentional criterion is simply not invoked, the obligation spans the full range of intent.

Moreover, this is one of the cases that brings a *korban oleh veyored* — a *korban* of variable value depending on the offerer's financial capacity. The same passage in *Vayikra* 5 covers multiple violations, and the distinction between those that include *ve-ne'elam* and the one that does not is precisely the lesson the *Gemara* draws here.

### Shvuat Hapikadon

The fourth case is *shvuat hapikadon* — taking a false oath to deny that one holds another's object in trust. The *Gemara* derives that this too obligates a *korban* even when intentional. The derivation works by way of a *gezerah shavah*: both *shvuat ha'edut* and *shvuat hapikadon* use the root *tacheta* — "shall sin" — and from that shared language we learn that just as *shvuat ha'edut* obligates across the spectrum of intent, so too does *shvuat hapikadon*: *yalif tach tach mishvuat ha'edut*.

---

## One Korban, Many Sins

### Five Cases Overview

The *mishnah* now moves to a second category of special cases: *chamishah mevi'in korban echad al aveirot harbeh* — five cases in which one *korban* covers multiple transgressions. Ordinarily, one *korban* addresses one sin; here, the rule is suspended. Alongside this, the *mishnah* notes that five cases bring a *korban oleh veyored* — a *korban* whose value varies with one's economic means. As noted, the structure is numerical: the organizing logic is the count, not the shared underlying principle.

The first *mishnah* in this section names only two of the five cases, with the remaining three appearing in subsequent *mishnayot*. The first two — *haba al hashifchah* and *nazir shenitma* — appear on both lists, the list of *mezid keshogeg* and the list of one *korban* for many sins. This overlap is itself instructive.

### Shifchah: One Korban, Ma…

For *haba al hashifchah*, the *mishnah* states: *haba al hashifchah bi'ot harbeh* — one who has sexual relations with a *shifchah charufa* multiple times brings only a single *korban*. The derivation is the same redundancy we saw earlier: *al chatato asher chata* teaches one *korban* for multiple violations, while *mechatato asher chata* teaches that even *mezid* is treated like *shogeg*. So the same textual redundancy in the *pasuk* generates both rules simultaneously.

The *Gemara* discusses the precise framing of the derivation — does the *pasuk* start from *shogeg* and extend to *mezid*, or start from *mezid* (given the presence of *malkot*) and extend to *shogeg*? As we saw earlier, because *bikoret tihyeh* implies *malkot*, the baseline of the *pasuk* is *mezid*, and the extension is to *shogeg*. The *halacha* remains: whether *shogeg* or *mezid*, whether once or many times, it is one *korban*.

### Gufin Mechulakim Distinc…

One might then ask: if the rule is that multiple acts of this sin require only one *korban*, does it matter whether those acts were with the same woman or with different women?

### R. Chanina's Question

This precise question was posed by *Rabi Chanina Tirna'ah* to *Rabi Yochanan*: *haba al chamesh shifchot charufot be'he'elam echad* — if a person had relations with five different *shifchot charufot* in one state of forgetfulness, *mahu*? Does the single-*korban* rule apply, or does he bring five separate *korbanot*? The case is pressed further: normally, five separate acts with the same woman across five states of awareness would require five *korbanot*. Here, the *chiddush* of the *pasuk* is that even five such acts constitute only one *korban*. Why, then, should five different women be treated differently if there is only one state of forgetfulness?

### Different Bodies Princip…

*Rabi Yochanan* responded: *ein shifchah achat gufin mecholakin* — one *shifchah* repeated multiple times does not constitute *gufin mechulakim* — different bodies. Five different *shifchot* are *gufin mechulakim* — they are fundamentally distinct entities. This is a recurring principle throughout *Keritot*: the distinctness of an act is determined far more by whether it involves different objects or persons than by the number of occasions or states of awareness. Multiple acts with the same person are essentially one thing played out through different states of awareness; multiple acts with different people are fundamentally distinct, each requiring its own *korban*.

The *Gemara* then asks: where do we know that the principle of *gufin mechulakim* applies specifically to the *shifchah* case, given the single-*korban* rule? *Rabi Yochanan* answers: just as by *arayot* generally, the word *ve'isha* in the *pasuk* teaches that each distinct woman creates a separate obligation — *lechalek al kol isha ve'isha* — so too by *shifchah*, the phrase *asher yishkav et isha...vehi shifchah* contains a seemingly redundant word that teaches *lechalek al kol shifchah veshifchah* — each *shifchah* constitutes a distinct category. Thus the rule of one *korban* for many acts applies only within a single *shifchah*; different women always require separate *korbanot*.

### Nazir Multiple Impurities

The second case on the list is *nazir shenitma tumot harbeh* — a *nazir* who became *tamei* many times. As with the *shifchah* case, this appears on both lists. The *Gemara* raises an important structural question about what the *chiddush* here actually is. It would be obvious, the *Gemara* implies, that if a *nazir* entered a cemetery five times on the same day — violating a single *nezirut* five times — he would bring only one *korban*. Once the *nezirut* has been violated, subsequent violations of that same *nezirut* add no new *korban* obligation; one *korban* wraps up the violated *nezirut* and initiates the new one. That is not a *chiddush*.

The *Gemara* therefore understands the *mishnah* to be speaking about a more radical case: a *nazir* who violated one *nezirut*, underwent the purification process, began a new *nezirut*, violated that *nezirut* as well, began yet another, and so on — multiple distinct sequential *neziruyot*, each independently violated. In that case, you would expect each violated *nezirut* to generate its own *korban* obligation. Yet the *mishnah* teaches that it is still only one *korban*. The question is: how is that possible?

### Nezirut Beginning: Day 7…

The answer depends on a *tannaitic* dispute about precisely when a new *nezirut detahara* begins. The *pasuk* says *vekidash et rosho bayom hahu* — he shall sanctify his head on that day. What is "that day"? *Rabbi* holds: *biyom havat korbanotav* — on the eighth day, when the *nazir* brings his *korbanot*. That is when his new *nezirut* begins. *Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda* holds: *biyom tiglachto* — on the seventh day, when he shaves; that is when the new *nezirut* commences.

### Day Seven Solution

*Rav Chisda* explains: the *mishnah*'s ruling — one *korban* for multiple violated *neziruyot* — is the opinion of *Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda*. Under his view, the new *nezirut* begins on day seven, before the *korban* is brought on day eight. Therefore, the following scenario is possible: a *nazir* becomes *tamei*, completes his seven-day purification, and on day seven — the moment his new *nezirut* begins — becomes *tamei* again. He has now violated a new *nezirut*, but he has not yet entered the period when he was obligated in a *korban* for the previous one. The cycle repeats: again on the seventh day, a new *nezirut* begins and is immediately violated. Since he never passed through a moment of being obligated in a *korban* before starting the next *nezirut*, all these violations coalesce into a single *korban* obligation at the end.

Under *Rabbi*'s view, this cannot work. *Rabbi* holds that the new *nezirut* begins only on day eight — the same moment the *korban* obligation crystallizes. As soon as day eight begins, he is simultaneously obligated in his previous *korban* and beginning his new *nezirut*. Therefore, if he becomes *tamei* on day eight and violates the new *nezirut*, that is a separate *korban* obligation, because he had already entered the time of obligation for the previous one. If he became *tamei* only on day seven, then under *Rabbi*'s view, he has never yet begun a new *nezirut* at all — it is all still one continuous *nezirut* that has been repeatedly violated. That is not a *chiddush*, and so the *mishnah* adds nothing. The *Gemara* concludes: *shema mina Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda* — this *mishnah* reflects the opinion of *Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda* alone.

This case is a conceptual midpoint between a *korban* brought for sin and a *korban* brought for *taharah*. The *nezirut*'s *korban* is about ending a *nezirut shel tumah* and beginning a *nezirut shel taharah*; it is part of a state-change rather than purely an act of atonement. This is why, as with the *mezid/shogeg* question, the number of violations is not the operative variable: what matters is whether the process has been formally closed and a new obligation has crystallized, not how many times the *nezirut* was transgressed.

---

## Sotah, Metzora, Yoledet

### Hamakane L'Ishto

The *mishnah* continues with additional cases of one *korban* for multiple events. The third case is *hamakane le'ishto al yedei anashim harbeh* — a husband who warned his wife about multiple men, and she was secluded with each of them. The *sotah* process involves the wife being brought to the *Beis HaMikdash* and drinking the *mei hamarim hamarerim*, and she brings a *minchat sotah* as part of that process. The ruling is that even if there were multiple warnings and multiple instances of seclusion, she brings only one *minchah* — not a separate offering for each suspicion.

### Sotah Derivation

The *Gemara* derives this from the verse *zot torat hakenaot* — this is the *Torah* for jealousy. The word *kenaot* is plural — jealousies — yet only one *Torah*, one law, governs all of them: *torah achat lekinuyim harbeh*. This is the source for treating multiple jealousy-episodes as a single case requiring a single *korban*.

The underlying logic, as with the *nazir*, is that the *korban* here is not focused on punishing or atoning for discrete acts of seclusion. It is about addressing the cloud of suspicion and determining the woman's status. Since it is one status question — regardless of how many occasions of suspicion arose — it is one process and one offering.

### Metzora Multiple Lesions

The fourth case is *metzora shenitna benegaim harbeh* — a *metzora* who developed many lesions of *tzara'at*. The *Gemara* derives this from *zot torat hametzora* — this is the law of the *metzora*: *torah achat lemetzoraim harbeh*, one law covering multiple instances. But the application requires clarification: what does it mean to have multiple *tzara'ot*? Simply having additional spots appear while one is already a *metzora* would not constitute distinct cases — that is just one continuous state of being *metzora*.

### Metzora Purification Sta…

The *Gemara* explains by analogy to the *nazir* case. The purification process of a *metzora* is multi-stage. On an early day, the *metzora* brings two birds: one is slaughtered and its blood used in the purification rite, while the other is released. This begins the purification. The *metzora* then waits seven days, shaves on day seven, and on day eight brings the full set of *korbanot* — an *asham*, a *chatat*, and an *olah* — completing the purification process.

The relevant scenario is: a *metzora* completes the birds stage and becomes *tahor* on day seven, but before day eight — before becoming obligated in the *korban* — he contracts *tzara'at* again. The cycle repeats. Since at no point did a *korban* obligation crystallize before the next *tzara'at* began, the *Gemara* holds that the entire accumulated purification process yields only one *korban* at the end. This is structurally identical to the *nazir* case under *Rabbi Yosi bar Rabbi Yehuda*: the new period begins before the *korban* obligation from the previous period is activated.

### Rich vs Poor Status

This leads to a separate legal question about the *metzora*'s *korban*, which is also a *korban oleh veyored* — one whose content varies with the offerer's financial means. If a wealthy *metzora* brings a full sheep as *chatat* and *olah*, while an impoverished *metzora* may substitute birds, at what moment is his status — rich or poor — determined? The *mishnah* addresses this: *ule'akvuei be'aniyut uve'ashirut lo mikva ad sheyavi chatat* — the status is not fixed until the moment of bringing the *chatat*. There is a separate *mishnah* elsewhere (*metzora shehevi ashamo vehe'ashir* — a *metzora* who brought his *asham* and then became wealthy) that confirms: *hakol holech achar chatat* — everything follows the *chatat*. That is the view of *Rabbi Shimon*.

### Three Tahara Views

Three *Tannaim* each interpret the operative phrase *betaharato* — "for his purification" — differently, and that interpretation determines which moment fixes the rich/poor status.

*Rabbi Shimon* holds *davar hamachapro* — *betaharato* means the act that atones for him, which is the *chatat*. Status is therefore determined at the time of the *chatat*. *Rabbi Yehuda* holds *davar hamachshiro* — *betaharato* means the act that renders him fit, that fully cleanses him, and that is the *asham*, which plays the central role in completing the purification ritual itself. Status is determined at the time of the *asham*. *Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov* holds *davar hagotem lo tahara* — it refers to the act that initiates the purification for him, and that is the birds, which begin the entire process seven days earlier. Status is therefore fixed at the time of the birds.

All three base themselves on the same *pasuk* — *asher lo tasig yado betaharato* — and disagree only about which stage the word *betaharato* refers to.

### Sin vs Purification

This three-way debate exemplifies a recurring theme throughout this section of *Keritot*: which of the *metzora*'s *korbanot* is about sin and which is about purification? The *metzora* brings multiple distinct offerings — an *asham* whose blood is used in the physical purification rite, a *chatat* that seems more focused on atonement, and an *olah*. The *asham* is arguably the most distinctive, since its blood is applied to the *metzora*'s ear, thumb, and toe as part of the cleansing ceremony — suggesting it is primarily a purification mechanism rather than an atonement. The *chatat*, by contrast, connotes personal sin.

This ambiguity — between the *korban* as response to personal guilt and the *korban* as part of a metaphysical or ritual cleansing process — is the underlying tension running through all the cases in this *mishnah*. As was noted in the *nazir* context, the *chatat* framework does not map neatly onto personal culpability alone. Here, by the *metzora*, the *halacha* about multiple lesions yielding one *korban* fits naturally when we understand the *korban* as part of the purification process: if the process has not yet concluded, multiple episodes of *tzara'at* are all part of one ongoing purification trajectory, and one *korban* concludes it.

### Yoledet Cases

The fifth and final case is *ha'ishah sheyaldah veladot harbeh* — a woman who gave birth many times. The *Gemara* derives this from *zot torat hayoledet lezachar ule'nekevah* — this is the *Torah* of the woman who gives birth, for male or female: *melamed shemevia korban echad al veladot harbeh*, teaching that she brings one *korban* for multiple births.

The mechanism works as follows. A woman who gives birth to a female is *tamei* for 14 days and has a purification period extending to day 80, at which point — on day 81 — she brings her *korban*. For a male birth, the periods are 7 and 33 days, with the *korban* on day 41. For the rule of one *korban* for multiple births to apply, a subsequent birth must occur before the *korban* obligation from the prior birth has been activated — that is, before day 41 or day 81, as the case may be.

Given the timing, such scenarios require miscarriage: for instance, after a female birth, a woman became pregnant, and the fetus developed at least 40 days — the threshold at which a miscarriage constitutes a *leidah* — before she reached day 81. If this recurred multiple times, all those births occurred within one extended, uninterrupted purification window, obligating only one *korban* at the end. The *Gemara* also mentions the case of *hamapelet te'omim* — a woman whose twins were born days apart. If the second twin emerged before the obligation for a *korban* from the first birth crystallized, it too would be subsumed into a single *korban*.

### Yoledet vs Ziva

The *Gemara* asks whether the single-*korban* rule might extend even further — perhaps a woman who both gave birth and became a *zavah* (exhibiting *zivah*-class discharge) would also bring only one *korban*? The answer is no: *talmud lomar zot* — the word *zot* limits the rule. This is a qualitatively different *tumah* with its own *korban* obligation, and it cannot be collapsed into the *yoledet* process.

The *Gemara* presses the question: is it even meaningful to entertain such a *hava amina*? *Zivah* and *leidah* are entirely distinct categories. The *Gemara* reframes the question more precisely: the real *hava amina* is whether a birth that occurs after day 80 — after the *korban* obligation has crystallized — might nonetheless be subsumed in the single-*korban* rule, as in the *shifchah charufa* case where distinct acts nonetheless generate one *korban*. The answer is no: *talmud lomar zot* — the one-*korban* rule for *yoledet* applies only when the births are genuinely sequential and overlapping, not when they are fully distinct with a completed obligation in between. The *shifchah charufa* case is unique in that respect; the cases of *nazir*, *metzora*, and *yoledet* are grounded in the purification process and require that the new event occur before the prior obligation has closed.

---

## Rabbi Yehuda vs Chachamim

### R. Yehuda: Odd Births On…

Having established the general rule, the *mishnah* now records a dispute. *Rabbi Yehuda* takes a more restrictive position than the *Chachamim*: *mevia al harishon ve'eina mevia al hasheni, mevia al hashlishi ve'eina mevia al harevi'i* — she brings a *korban* for the first birth, not the second; for the third, not the fourth; and so on, alternating through odd and even births. According to *Rabbi Yehuda*, the rule of one *korban* for multiple births applies only to pairs, not to an indefinite chain.

### Incorporation Logic

The logic behind *Rabbi Yehuda*'s position is the concept of incorporation. The second birth, having occurred within the 80-day window of the first, is incorporated into and subsumed by the first — they count as one, requiring one *korban*. But the third birth is not within the 80-day window of the first birth; it may fall within the window of the second. However, once the second birth has been incorporated into the first and they are treated as a unit, the second birth loses its independent identity and cannot serve as an anchor to draw the third into its window. The third is therefore a new, independent event and requires its own *korban*. In turn, the fourth is incorporated into the third, the fifth stands alone, and so forth. *Vlad rishon gorem umivlad rishon moneh* — the first birth is the operative anchor, and counting proceeds from that first birth.

### Chachamim: Endpoint Focus

The *Chachamim* disagree. Their approach is endpoint-focused: *vlad sheni gorem umivlad sheni moneh* — or more precisely, they look to the last event in the chain. The *Chachamim* do not require that everything be incorporated into the first birth; rather, so long as the chain has not yet arrived at a point where a *korban* obligation has crystallized and been completed, all births remain part of one extended, ongoing process. The question is simply: have we reached an endpoint yet? Until a *korban* obligation is formally activated and discharged, the process continues, and all births within it yield only one *korban*. The *Chachamim* thus allow an indefinite extension of the chain, while *Rabbi Yehuda* limits the incorporation strictly to the first birth's 80-day window.

### Twins Clarification

The *Gemara* asks whether *Rabbi Yehuda*'s logic would be modified in the case of twins. One might think that since twins clearly share one pregnancy — one continuous gestational process — *Rabbi Yehuda* would acknowledge that even the second twin is simply a continuation of the first, and therefore that whatever follows the second twin would still be incorporated under the first birth's window, as though the first and second twins were truly one birth. If so, *Rabbi Yehuda* might agree with the *Chachamim* in the twins case, allowing a third birth following the second twin to be incorporated as well.

### Twins Confirm Rule

The *Gemara* answers that *Rabbi Yehuda*'s rule holds even for twins: *ka mashma lan* — the *mishnah* teaches this precisely to exclude that possibility. Even in the case of twins, where the shared gestational origin is obvious, *Rabbi Yehuda* insists that only the first birth is the anchor, and only events within the 80-day window of that first birth are incorporated. The second twin, once incorporated into the first, does not independently extend the window further. A third birth — whether from a subsequent pregnancy or a third triplet emerging separately — cannot be incorporated via the second, because the second has lost its independent standing by being subsumed into the first. *Rabbi Yehuda*'s principle of incorporation is strictly first-birth-focused, and no amount of biological continuity between subsequent births changes that calculus.
