Not all the milk travels into the infant; some remains on the mother. That remainder is not food (it is not going into anyone's belly) and is therefore liquid. This liquid drop touches the milk flowing toward the infant and renders it susceptible. So the milk is *huchshar*, and if it is *tamei*, the infant should become *tamei* too.

### Rabbah Responses

Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha offers a response to this: *she'yanak b'tkifa achat v'lo hiniach tipa m'luchlechet al pi hadad* — the infant nursed in one continuous latch, never detaching, and thus no drop remained on the breast to render the milk susceptible. Rabbah himself then advances two rejoinders to this claim. 

### Wellspring Principle

The first: *d'chazina l'pumei d'yanuka d'malei chalav* — even when an infant nurses without interruption, when he finally detaches, his lips are visibly coated with milk. Milk has not all entered; some always remains outside. That remainder will always function as the liquid that renders the rest susceptible.

The second — and more fundamental — response: *makom chalav ma'ayan* — forget the entire framework of contact with liquid and susceptibility. That framework treats the milk as something external that happened to come into contact with the *tamei* woman. But that is wrong. Fluids produced from within a person's own body have a different status entirely — they are a *ma'ayan*, a wellspring. The principle, as Tosafot explains more clearly: individuals whose *tum'ah* derives from within their own bodies — a *niddah*, a *zavah*, a *zav*, a *yoledes* — transmit *tum'ah* through their own bodily fluids as an *av hatumah*. Their saliva, their blood-flow, their discharge — all are *av hatumah*, not a *rishon*. They do not require *hechsher*; they do not require any contact with external liquid. They are produced by the body itself and carry the body's *tum'ah* inherently.

Applying this to the nursing mother: if she is a *niddah* or *yoledes* (as is commonly the case with a new mother), her milk ought to carry the status of her *ma'ayan* and be *tamei* as an *av hatumah*, not merely a *rishon*. No *hechsher* is needed, and the infant ought to become *tamei* from consuming it. The question of the soiled drop becomes irrelevant.

### Safek Safeka

This makes the infant's *tahara* even more pressing. The *gemara* responds with *rava*'s explanation: *ala amar Rava hainu ta'ama de'tinok tahor — safek yanok she'lo yanok*. The reason the infant is presumed *tahor* is a *safek safeka*, a double doubt. First: perhaps the infant did not drink the full *shiur* — *chatzi pras*, approximately four *kezaysim* — required to make him *tamei* from eating *tamei* food. An infant's nursing session may well not reach that quantity. And even if one grants that he did drink the full *shiur*, the second doubt follows: *safek yanok bichdei achilas pras safek yanok b'yoter mikedei achilas pras* — perhaps he did not consume it within *kdei achilas pras*, which is the required time window. Given this double doubt, the infant is presumed *tahor*.

---

## Tamei Through Food (II)

### Pras Standard

This double doubt also highlights the conclusion discussed earlier regarding the standard of *kdei achilas pras*: it applies uniformly as the measuring window regardless of the quantity of the *shiur* involved. Whether the relevant *shiur* is a single *kezayit* or four *kezaysim* or a *revi'is* of liquid, the time window used for combination is always *kdei achilas pras*. The *revi'is* of liquid, one might expect, should be measured by *kdei shtiyat revi'is*, the time to drink a *revi'is* — yet it too is measured by the eating standard. This unusual feature is noted as something that receives fuller treatment in other places, such as *Nazir*, but for present purposes the rule is clear: *kdei achilas pras* is the universal benchmark.

---

## Nursing Mother (II)

### Nine Fluids

The *gemara* now examines Rabbah's *ma'ayan* principle more closely. *ולרבא מקום חלב מעיין הוא?* — Is it really true, according to Rava, that the source of milk is a *ma'ayan*? If so, does it not require *hechsher*? But the *gemara* notes that this appears to contradict Rabbi Yochanan, who, explaining a *mishnah* about milk from a *niddah* falling into the airspace of an oven, said that the milk became susceptible — *b'tibu v'luchluchis al pi yadeha* — through the soiled drop on the breast. Rabbi Yochanan's entire answer only makes sense if milk is not automatically an *av hatumah* as a *ma'ayan* but requires *hechsher* like any other food. Perhaps Rava simply disagrees with Rabbi Yochanan.

The *gemara* then cites a *baraita* that is more conclusive: *nimtzas atah omer tisha mashkin b'zav* — there are nine fluids associated with a *zav*, and they fall into three categories of three.

### Milk Category Resolved

The three in the lowest category — sweat, putrid liquid, and feces — are *tehorin mikulam*, completely pure, because they are too repugnant to serve any purpose. The three in the highest category — *roko* (saliva), *zovo* (the *zav*'s flow, the *niddah*'s blood), and *mei raglav* (urine) — are *av hatumah b'chol shehu*: they carry the full *tum'ah* of the person, in even the smallest quantity, as a *ma'ayan*. Between these two extremes sit three fluids: tears, blood from a wound, and *chalav isha* — milk of a woman. These *metamin tumas mashkin b'revi'is*: they have the *tum'ah* of ordinary liquids, requiring a *revi'is* in quantity, and do not carry the elevated status of a *ma'ayan*.

*Ve'im amarta d'makom chalav ma'ayan — chalav nami nitma tumah chamurah b'chol shehu k'zovo v'roko* — if milk were truly a *ma'ayan*, it should have the same stringent status as saliva and the flow, *tumah chamurah b'chol shehu*. Since it does not, and instead occupies this middle category, the conclusion is *shema mina makom chalav ishah lav ma'ayan hu* — the source of a woman's milk is not a *ma'ayan*. Rava's earlier argument is thereby refuted: the infant is *tahor* not because of the *ma'ayan* principle, but because of the *safek safeka* — doubt about quantity and time.

The *gemara* also revisits the *baraita* that stated milk is *tamei* whether the woman desired it or not — *bein leratzon bein shelo leratzon* — which Rava had cited to support the *ma'ayan* principle. The *gemara* reinterprets *shelo leratzon*: it does not mean the woman actively did not want the milk; it means she had no active intent either way — *bistama*. If the infant wants the milk, *daiteih d'tinok krevah legabei chalav*, that suffices as the desired contact. Only if the woman actively declared she did not want the milk — *aval amar lo nicha lei* — would it be *tahor*. The requirement of *ratzon* is thus preserved, and the *baraita* does not require treating milk as a *ma'ayan*.

---

## Wine/Intoxication

### Yayin V'Shechar

The *gemara* turns to the prohibition against entering the *Beit HaMikdash* while intoxicated, rooted in the verse *yayin veshichar al tesht atah uvaneykha itakh bevochem el ohel moed velo tamutu* — spoken immediately following the deaths of *Nadav va'Avihu*, which *Chazal* understand to imply that intoxication while performing *avodah* in the *Beit HaMikdash* was among their sins. *Moshe* commands: do not drink wine or intoxicating drink when entering, or you will die — a punishment at the hands of Heaven, *bidei shamayim*.

### Revi'is Shiur

The *tanna kamma* reads *yayin veshichar* not as two separate objects but as a single compound: intoxicating wine. *Yachol afilu kol shehu* — one might think even the smallest amount triggers liability, and even freshly pressed grape juice — *yayin migito*, which has not yet fermented. The response: *talmud lomar veshichar* — *sheichar* qualifies the wine. *Ein assur ela kedei leshaker* — only wine that can intoxicate, meaning it must be fermented (at least forty days old) and must be a *revi'is*, roughly three and a half ounces. However, *yayin* adds a separate level: even the smallest amount of wine, even *migito* before fermentation, constitutes a transgression — just not liability for *mita*. Thus two tiers: transgression for any wine, liability for death only for a full intoxicating *revi'is*.

### Rabbi Yehuda View

Rabbi Yehuda reads the verse differently: *yayin* and *sheichar* are two independent terms. *Ein li ela yayin* — wine I know; *she'ar mashkin meshakrin minayin* — what about other intoxicating drinks? *Talmud lomar veshichar* — the second term includes all other intoxicants. His two tiers are not about quantity and fermentation but about category: wine triggers liability for *mita*; other intoxicating beverages trigger only the prohibition. He derives *sheichar* independently rather than learning it from the *gezeira shava* with *nazir*, which the *tanna kamma* uses to confine *sheichar* to wine.

### Rabbi Eliezer View

Rabbi Eliezer takes yet another reading: *yayin al tesht veshichar al tesht kederekh shichruto* — do not drink wine in the manner of intoxication. The addition of *sheichar* qualifies not what is drunk but how it is drunk. *Ha im hifsik bo o shenatan letocho mayim kol shehu patur* — if one took a break in drinking, or added even the smallest amount of water to the wine, one is exempt. The prohibition attaches not to the wine as such but to drinking wine in a way that produces intoxication. Interruption or dilution changes the character of the act.

### Ruling Applied

The *gemara* then asks which *tanna* the following *baraita* follows: one who eats pressed dates from *Ke'ilit*, or drinks honey, or milk, and enters the *Beit HaMikdash* and performs the *avodah* — this goes like Rabbi Yehuda, who extends the prohibition beyond wine to any intoxicating substance. Note the peculiarity of milk as an intoxicant — one commentator suggests a connection to the episode of Yael and Sisera, where milk produced drowsiness. Whatever the association, Rabbi Yehuda's position encompasses non-wine intoxicants, though without carrying the *mita* penalty.

Rav Yehuda bar Chusai rules: *halacha k'Rabbi Eliezer* — the law follows Rabbi Eliezer. If one drank only a *revi'is* and added a small amount of water or took a break, one is exempt. Rav, upon hearing this ruling about Rabbi Eliezer, called him *tuvina de'chakimei* — among the finest of the sages.

### Rav Acha Case

Rav Acha mi-Hutza had a *neder* involving his wife that required annulment. He went before Rav Ashi to have it dissolved. Rav Ashi told him: go today and return tomorrow — *zil idna ve'ta le'machar*. The reason: *Rav lo moki amora aleih mi'yoma tava le'chavreih* — Rav would not appoint an *amora* to project his teaching from one *Yom Tov* to the next, meaning on consecutive days of *Yom Tov*. Why? Because after the festive meal with wine, he feared he might be mildly intoxicated, and the prohibition extends not only to entering the *Beit HaMikdash* but also, as the verse continues, *u'le'horot et benei Yisrael* — to giving *hora'ah*, halakhic instruction. Thus Rav Ashi declined to rule on the *neder*, citing that same concern.

The one raising the question pointed out: but Rav himself ruled that the *halacha* is like Rabbi Eliezer — and in Rav Ashi's case water had been added to the wine, so it should not be an issue. Rav Ashi replied: *ha lo kashya — ha birevi'is ha b'yoter mi'revi'is*. There is a distinction. If one drank only a *revi'is*, adding water or taking a break is sufficient. But if one drank considerably more than a *revi'is*, this leniency no longer applies — and Rav Ashi, having drunk more at the Yom Tov meal, could not rely on it. The irony is not lost: the very discussion of why halakhic rulings cannot be given while intoxicated is itself a halakhic discussion — though one could argue that insofar as the explanation is informational rather than active *hora'ah*, it falls in a different category.

---

## Drunk Prohibitions

### Kodesh/Chol

The *gemara* now elaborates the full scope of what is prohibited to an intoxicated person. The verse *u'lehavdil bein hakodesh u'vein hachol* — to distinguish between the holy and the profane — identifies one category of forbidden activity. What constitutes *kodesh v'chol* for these purposes? *Elu damim v'erchin charamim v'hekdeshos* — these are assessments of *damim* (monetary values for redemption), *erchin* (bodily assessments vowed to the Temple), *charamim* (consecrated items), and general *hekdesh*. Among the duties of the *kohen* was assessing the value of consecrated items to permit their redemption. Even this kind of monetary determination, requiring a clear head, may not be performed while intoxicated.

### Tamei/Tahor

*Bein hatamei u'vein hatahor — elu tumos v'taharos* — similarly, one may not render rulings on *tum'ah* and *tahara* while intoxicated.

### Hora'ah

*U'lehoros — zu hora'ah*: and to give instruction — this is *hora'ah*, normative halakhic ruling. *Es kol hachukim — elu midrashos*: "all the statutes" refers to *midrashos*, expository teachings. Rashi explains this as referring to what is taught publicly in a *pirkah*, a formal lecture. That *midrash* — seemingly non-binding exposition — is included here as prohibited is somewhat surprising, but the verse subsumes it. *Asher diber Hashem — zu halacha*: the phrase "which God spoke" refers to received *halacha*. The implication is that even transmitting plain, established *halacha* without creative analysis is prohibited, not only *hora'ah* in the sense of novel judgment.

### Mishnah/Talmud

*B'yad Moshe — zeh Talmud*: "through the hand of Moshe" refers to *Talmud*, meaning analytic study and reasoning. Could even *mishnah* be prohibited? *Talmud lomar u'lehoros* — the word *horaah* limits the prohibition to activities requiring judgment and application. Pure *mishnah* — the repetition of tannaitic statements with no ruling function — does not constitute *hora'ah* and is not prohibited.

### Rabbi Yose View

Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda goes further: could even *Talmud* be prohibited? *Talmud lomar u'lehoros* — no, only things that carry actual *hora'ah*, halakhic application, are prohibited. Analytical learning that does not yet reach the level of practical ruling is permitted.

### Rav Permits

The *gemara* notes that this ruling aligns with what is taught in a *baraita*: to say, for example, that a *sheretz* is *tamei* and a *tzfardea* is *tahor* — even intoxicated people can give rulings on such blatantly obvious matters. Who is this like? Perhaps Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda, who permits *Talmud* and restricts only actual *hora'ah*. But even according to the Rabbis, one could say that questions of that kind — *d'zil krei bei rav*, which any schoolchild knows — are so self-evident they do not even rise to the level of making a meaningful statement, let alone *hora'ah*. Rav rules: *halacha k'Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda* — one may engage in *Talmud* study even while intoxicated.

### Rav Exception

But this creates an obvious tension. We just established that Rav refused to give his *shiur* between one *Yom Tov* and the next because of concern about intoxication — yet Rav himself ruled that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda, permitting analytic study while intoxicated. Why, then, could Rav not simply give his *shiur* while making clear he would not render practical rulings?

The *gemara* resolves this: *shani Rav d'orei morei* — Rav is different, because *kol heicha deyativ Rav, lo sagi lei belo hora'ah* — wherever Rav sits, it is impossible for him to avoid *hora'ah*. Either his natural inclination draws him toward rendering rulings, or those in attendance will inevitably press him for answers. A shiur given by Rav cannot remain purely theoretical; it will inescapably produce practical *psak halacha*. For that reason alone, Rav would not give his *shiur* when he had reason to fear he was not fully sober. The ultimate concern throughout all of these prohibitions, as the sugya makes clear, is *psak halacha* — the practical ruling — and it is that which Rav was careful to avoid.

---

---

# Keritot 14

## Multiple Chataos

### Four + One Overview

The *mishnah* at the bottom of 13b continues the broader discussion of how multiple *chatosos* arise from a single act of eating. Earlier in the tractate we considered cases where eating multiple *kezaysim* over time, or eating different types of forbidden food, generates multiple *chatosos*. Now the *mishnah* presents the reverse scenario: a single *kezayis* that carries within it four distinct sin offerings and one *asham*.

The *mishnah* closely parallels the discussion in Makkos, where the question is how many sets of lashes one can incur from a single forbidden act. Here, in *Kerisot*, the parallel question concerns *chatosos* brought *beshogeg* — unintentionally.

### Fat/Impure/Leftover/Kods…

The *mishnah* states: *yesh ochel achilah achas vechayav aleha arba chatos ve'asham echad* — there is one who eats one eating and is liable for four sin offerings and one guilt offering. The case is constructed as follows. A *tamei* person eats *cheilev* — forbidden fat. The fat is simultaneously *nosar* — leftover sacrifice — which itself carries *kares*, adding a second sin offering. The food is *min hamukdashin*, sanctified sacrificial meat, and since a *tamei* person who eats *kodshim* is liable for an *oleh veyored* offering, that is a third. The eating takes place on *Yom Kippur*, generating a fourth *kares* obligation and thus a fourth *chatas*. The *asham* arises from *me'ilah*: since the fat always goes upon the *mizbe'ach* and no person is permitted to eat it, there is a transgression of deriving benefit from sanctified property, which carries an *asham me'ilah*.

### Rabbi Meir's Sixth

*Rabbi Meir* adds: if it happened to be *Shabbos* and the person carried the food out into the public domain while eating, he is liable for yet another offering. The Sages respond that this additional liability stems not from the act of eating but from carrying — it is a separate act, not the eating itself. The respondents' point is that the *mishnah* is specifically enumerating how many obligations can flow from the act of eating alone; a simultaneous but distinct act, such as carrying or lighting a fire, is not part of that count.

---

## Issur Chal Issur

### Can Forbiddance Stack

The *gemara* frames the entire *mishnah* around the question of *issur chal al issur* — the principle that once an object is forbidden in one way, a second prohibition generally cannot take effect upon it. The object's forbidden status is already defined, and it cannot be multiply defined. This is fundamentally an object-based principle: it does not apply when one is simultaneously performing two separate forbidden acts, but rather when a single object already carries a prohibition and a new prohibition seeks to attach to it.

The *gemara* notes that *Rabbi Meir* is the named *Tanna* in the *mishnah*, and asks: does this *mishnah* reflect *Rabbi Meir*'s view that *issur chal al issur* does apply — that prohibitions can stack upon a single object? The *gemara* answers: no. In general, *Rabbi Meir* does not hold of *issur chal al issur*. However, he does accept the principles of *issur kolel* and *issur mosif*, which are recognized exceptions to the rule.

### Three Exceptions

There are three concepts that permit a second prohibition to take effect upon an already-forbidden object.

The first is *issur kolel* — the new prohibition encompasses a broader set of objects. When the new *issur* comes into being, it simultaneously forbids many other things; and because it affects a wider range of objects, it also attaches to this one. A classic example is becoming *tamei*: when a person becomes *tamei*, all *kodshim* become forbidden to him. Since more objects have now become forbidden through this new status, that new status also attaches to an object that was already forbidden on other grounds.

The second is *issur mosif* — the new prohibition affects a broader population. The same object that was forbidden to one person, or one group, now becomes forbidden to more people. When the forbidden circle expands, the new prohibition takes effect even upon those who were already forbidden from this object on other grounds.

The third is *issur chamur* — a weightier prohibition. Here the same object becomes forbidden to the same population, but the nature of the prohibition is more severe. This category is less universally accepted, and the *gemara* notes some skepticism about whether it suffices to generate a second liable status; nonetheless, in our *sugya* the *gemara* proceeds on the assumption that it does.

### Fat Becomes Kodshim

The *gemara* now works through each element of the *mishnah*. Regarding *cheilev*: originally, when one was *tahor*, the fat was forbidden only in eating. *Tahor mi-kara lo assar ela be-achilah*. Then the person sanctified it — *akdeshei*. Since sanctification adds *issur hana'ah* — the fat is now forbidden not merely to eat but to derive any benefit from — the prohibition has become weightier. *Migo de-itosef bei issur hana'ah*, since an additional prohibition of benefit-derivation has been added, *itosef bei legabei cheilev*, that additional status attaches to the fat as well. This is the case of *issur chamur*.

One might ask: since sanctifying a piece of fat necessarily involves sanctifying the entire animal of which it is part, should we not consider this *issur kolel* — a broader set of objects now becoming forbidden? This is a genuine question, but the *gemara* proceeds on the assumption that the relevant category here is *issur chamur*, treating the sanctification as primarily creating a weightier prohibition rather than one that sweeps in new objects.

### Notar Case

The *gemara* then turns to *nosar*. The fat — now *kodshim* — was originally forbidden to human beings but permitted for placement on the *mizbe'ach*: *legabei hedyot hu de-assur aval le-gavoha shari*. Then it is left overnight and becomes *nosar*. Now it is *assur legabei gavoha* as well — forbidden even to God, forbidden for the altar. *Migo de-itosaf issura legabei gavoha*, since the circle of those to whom it is forbidden has expanded to include, so to speak, the divine domain, *itosaf bei legabei hedyot* — an additional prohibition attaches to the ordinary person as well. This is *issur mosif*: a larger population is now subject to the prohibition.

### Yom Kippur Addition

The final layer is *Yom Kippur*. It must be acknowledged that *Yom Kippur* sits oddly in this framework of *issur chal al issur*, since *Yom Kippur* is not a status of the object but rather an obligation upon the person — the food is merely the vehicle through which the fast is broken. The framework of *issur chal al issur* is fundamentally object-oriented, so introducing *Yom Kippur* here is somewhat anomalous and difficult to fully explain. Nevertheless, the *gemara* proceeds: *chal aleih Yom HaKippurim* — *Yom Kippur* arrives. *Migo de-itosaf bei issura legabei chullin* — on *Yom Kippur* all foods become forbidden, not just this one. Since more objects become forbidden, that is *issur kolel*, and therefore *itosaf bei legabei gavoha* — yet another dimension of prohibition is added. The object accumulates yet another forbidden status.

In summary: *issur kolel* (more objects forbidden — e.g., becoming *tamei*, or *Yom Kippur*), *issur mosif* (a broader population is forbidden — e.g., when the fat becomes *nosar*), and *issur chamur* (a weightier prohibition — e.g., the fat becoming *kodshim*) are the recognized exceptions to *issur chal al issur*. These are what allow the multiple *chatosos* of the *mishnah* to be intelligible.

---

## Same Object Question

### Five Chataos Challenge

The *gemara* poses a challenge: rather than four *chatosos* and one *asham*, why not enumerate five *chatosos*? If in the same eating one also consumed a *kezayis* of *piggul* — sacrificial meat slaughtered with the wrong intention regarding the time of eating, which also carries *kares* — that would add a fifth. The proposed formulation is: *v'nisni hei chatos, v'nukma kegon d'achal kezayis piggul b'chada kezayis piggul*.

This question is immediately striking, because *piggul* and *nosar* cannot coexist in the same piece of meat. *Nosar* is meat that was fit for the altar but was left over; *piggul* is meat that was rendered unfit through improper intent at slaughter. Since *piggul* renders the sacrifice unfit, it cannot subsequently become *nosar*. Therefore the *gemara* acknowledges that the *piggul* would have to be a separate *kezayis* from a separate animal. But once we allow separate objects into the same act of eating, one could equally ask: why not also include a *kezayis* of blood, or *chametz on Pesach*, and so on indefinitely? The point the *gemara* is pressing toward is that the *mishnah* is discussing a single object, not multiple objects.

### One Limb/One Kezayit

The *gemara* establishes a series of narrowing constraints. First: *b'chada beheima ka'amri* — we are speaking of one animal. Since *piggul* and *nosar* cannot coexist in the same animal, that rules out combining them across two animals. The *gemara* then asks: perhaps one limb of a single animal was placed on the altar — the altar contact causes the limb to lose its *piggul* status, as stated by *Ulla*: *kometz piggul she'he'ela legabei mizbeiach, paka piggulei mimenu v'havei lei nosar* — a *piggul kometz* placed on the altar loses its *piggul* status and becomes *nosar* if not consumed in time. If such a limb then fell off the altar, it would be *nosar*, while the remainder of the animal that was never placed on the altar would remain *piggul*. Eating one *kezayis* from each would, it seems, yield both prohibitions from one animal.

The *gemara* closes this gap: *b'eiver echad ka'amri b'shnei evarim lo ka'amri* — we are speaking of one limb, not two. Could half a limb rest on the altar while the other half hangs outside, yielding *nosar* in one half and *piggul* in the other? The *gemara* rejects this: one follows the majority of the limb. If the majority is on the altar, the entire limb is treated as on the altar; if the majority is outside, the entire limb is treated as outside. The *gemara* adds that this resolution would in fact settle an open question of *Rami bar Chama* — whether a limb is defined by the majority of its placement — though since *Rami bar Chama* left this as an unresolved inquiry, one cannot simply invoke it as settled.

The narrowing continues to its final form: *bekezayis echad kama'iri bishnei zeitim lo kama'iri* — we are speaking of a single *kezayis*, the minimum unit of forbidden food. If one wishes to incorporate additional prohibitions, that requires an additional *kezayis*, which is a separate act.

A complication is then raised: *Yom Kippur* is not actually violated by eating a *kezayis*. The minimum measure for *Yom Kippur* is a *kosevet* — approximately the volume of a pressed date — which is larger than a *kezayis* and contains at least two *kezaysim*. If the *mishnah*'s case inherently involves two *kezaysim* for the *Yom Kippur* prohibition to apply, should we not be able to assign one of those *kezaysim* to an additional prohibition such as *piggul*?

Three answers are offered. *Rav Zevira* says: *kegon de'achal kulya bechelva* — we are speaking of eating a kidney together with its surrounding fat. The *cheilev* is one *kezayis* and carries all the listed prohibitions; the kidney brings the total volume to that of a *kosevet* for *Yom Kippur*, but the kidney is not itself a separate forbidden item that generates a new *chatas*.

*Rav Pappa* offers a different resolution: *kegon d'maliye b'tamrei* — perhaps the person had already eaten a *kezayis* of dates beforehand. The current single *kezayis* of fat is sufficient to complete the *Yom Kippur* prohibition in combination with what was eaten moments earlier, yet the current act consists of only one *kezayis*.

*Rav Adda bar Ahava* actually preserves a different version of the *mishnah* that reads five *chatosos*, incorporating both a *kezayis* of *piggul* and a *kezayis* of *nosar* through the mechanism of a limb partially placed on the altar (as described above), without recourse to the previous explanations.

### Beth Habliah Limit

The *gemara* then asks why the count stops where it does. If we are willing to incorporate a second *kezayis* in the mouth alongside the first, why not also add a *kezayis* of blood, yielding six? The *gemara* answers: *v'shi'uru chachamim d'ein beit habli'ah machazik yoter mishnei zeisim* — the Sages measured that the *beit habli'ah*, the capacity of the throat for a single swallow, cannot accommodate more than two *kezaysim*. Since eating requires swallowing, a single act of eating is bounded by this anatomical limit. No matter how much one chews simultaneously, the maximum that can constitute one *achilah* is two *kezaysim*.

---

## Shabbat Carrying Debate

### Meir's Shabbat Idea

The *gemara* returns to *Rabbi Meir*'s addition: if the person was carrying the food out on *Shabbos*, he incurs an additional *chatas* for *hotza'ah*. The *gemara* seeks to understand the precise formulation — why *Rabbi Meir* specifies *Shabbos* rather than simply stating that carrying in the course of the event adds another obligation.

### Why Specify Shabbat

The *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama d'katani hayta Shabbos* — what is the reason the *mishnah* qualifies the case specifically as *Shabbos*? The scenario already involves *Yom Kippur*, and *Yom Kippur* presumably also prohibits carrying. If so, *Rabbi Meir* could have simply said: if he also carried, he is liable. Why add the specification that it was *Shabbos*? If carrying on *Yom Kippur* is already forbidden, the *Shabbos* element is redundant.

### Carrying Weakness

To understand the *gemara*'s analysis, some background is necessary. The *melachah* of *hotza'ah* — carrying from one domain to another — is traditionally described by the *Rishonim* as a *melachah geru'ah*, a deficient or weak *melachah*. Its distinguishing feature is that it is non-productive and non-creative; it merely transfers an object from one place to another. This is in contrast to every other *melachah* on *Shabbos*, each of which involves some form of creative or transformative act.

This weakness of *hotza'ah* may explain why carrying is treated so permissively on *Yom Tov*. We instinctively think of carrying as simply permitted on *Yom Tov*, not merely permitted for the sake of food preparation. One could argue that carrying's permission on *Yom Tov* is not rooted in *ochel nefesh* — the license to perform *melachos* necessary for food — but rather reflects a categorical permissibility arising from its status as the weakest of all *melachos*: where *Shabbos* restrictions do not fully apply, *hotza'ah* is the first to fall away.

### Carrying Permitted

*Rafram* draws an audacious conclusion from *Rabbi Meir*'s choice of language. He says: *zos omeres eiruv v'hotza'ah l'Shabbos v'ein eiruv v'hotza'ah l'Yom HaKippurim* — the reason *Rabbi Meir* had to specify *Shabbos* rather than simply invoking *Yom Kippur* is that there is in fact no biblical prohibition of *hotza'ah* on *Yom Kippur*. Carrying is not forbidden on *Yom Kippur* at the *d'Oraisa* level, only on *Shabbos*. Hence *Rabbi Meir* needed to specify that it was *Shabbos* — because only then does carrying generate a biblical *chatas*.

*Rafram* finds support for this position in a *beraisa* discussing the *se'ir l'Azazel* — the scapegoat sent out on *Yom Kippur*. The verse states *v'shilach b'yad ish iti* — the goat shall be sent by a ready man. The *beraisa* derives from this that any man may lead it out, even a *zar*, even someone who is *tamei*, and — crucially — even on *Shabbos*. *Rafram* asks: why does the *beraisa* need to tell us it may be done even on *Shabbos*? If carrying were already prohibited on *Yom Kippur*, the *beraisa* need only say it overrides *Yom Kippur* restrictions. The fact that the *beraisa* adds *afilu b'Shabbos* implies that *Yom Kippur* itself does not prohibit carrying; only *Shabbos* does. Therefore the novelty of *afilu b'Shabbos* is real: it tells us the *Shabbos* prohibition of *hotza'ah* is overridden.

### Rejection of Rafram

The *gemara* rejects *Rafram*'s argument. *Shabbos shani se'ir mishtale'ach d'achshar b'Yom HaKippurim bekach* — the *se'ir l'Azazel* is different, because it is part of the *avodah* of *Yom Kippur* itself. It is natural that *Yom Kippur* restrictions would be overridden for the sake of the *Yom Kippur* service; it is not at all obvious that *Shabbos* restrictions would similarly yield. The *beraisa*'s inclusion of *afilu b'Shabbos* is therefore significant precisely because it is not self-evident — *Yom Kippur* and *Shabbos* are independent systems of prohibition, and the license for the *Yom Kippur avodah* does not automatically extend to *Shabbos* prohibitions. This does not prove that carrying is permitted on *Yom Kippur* absent the *avodah*; it proves only that the *beraisa* needed to explicitly authorize overriding *Shabbos* prohibitions for the sake of the *mitzvas hayom*.

The *gemara* concludes bluntly: *ella d'Rafram brusi* — *Rafram*'s statement is dismissed as unfounded. Carrying is indeed forbidden on *Yom Kippur*. The more interesting observation, however, is what the *gemara*'s *hava amina* reveals: that the permissibility of carrying on *Yom Tov* may be grounded not in *ochel nefesh* but in the categorical weakness of *hotza'ah* as a *melachah*. On that basis, one could imagine a world in which *Yom Kippur* — despite sharing many *Shabbos*-like characteristics — might not prohibit carrying, since *Yom Kippur* is not *Shabbos* per se. The *gemara* completely rejects this, noting that *Yom Kippur* is called *Shabbos Shabbason*, but the *hava amina* itself is not entirely without conceptual foundation.

---

## Sex Prohibitions

### Six from One Act

The *mishnah* now transitions from eating to the domain of prohibited sexual relations. Just as a single act of eating can generate multiple *chatosos*, so too a single act of intercourse can generate six sin offerings: *yesh biah achas vechayav aleha shesh chatos*.

### Daughter/Sister Case

The first case: *haba al bito* — a man who had intercourse with his daughter. The *mishnah* enumerates the prohibitions: *mishum bito*, as his daughter; *ve'achot ishto*, his wife's sister; *ve'achoto*, his sister; *eshet achiv*, his brother's wife; *ve'eshet achi aviv*, his uncle's wife; *ve'eshet ish*, a married woman; and *veniddah*, a menstruant.

How can a single woman be simultaneously his daughter and his sister? The scenario requires that this man previously had intercourse with his mother and the result was a daughter. That girl is therefore both his daughter and the daughter of his mother — his sister. The act with the mother is not counted here because it was a prior, separate act.

The *gemara* addresses *Rabbi Meir*'s implicit agreement with this *mishnah* in light of the principle of *issur chal al issur*. The fact that the woman is forbidden both as daughter and as sister does not raise an *issur chal al issur* problem because both prohibitions took effect simultaneously at her birth — and the principle applies only when prohibitions are sequential, not when they arise at the same moment.

Subsequent prohibitions are explained through *issur mosif*. When she married his brother, she became forbidden not only to him but to all of his brothers — *niset le-achiv, migo de-itosaf issur legabei achiv, itosaf issura legabei didei*. The expanded circle of those who became forbidden is *issur mosif*. When she then married his uncle (*niset le-achi aviv*), she became forbidden to all of his uncle's brothers as well — again, a larger population. *Migo de-itosaf issura legabei she'ar achi aviv, itosaf legabei didei*. When she became a married woman, she became forbidden to all men in the world who are not her husband — the maximum possible expansion of the forbidden population. When she became a *niddah*, she became forbidden even to her husband, the one person who had been permitted to her — *migo de-itosaf issur legabei ba'alah, itosaf nami legabei didei*. Each stage represents a genuine *issur mosif*, permitting the additional prohibition to take effect.

### Granddaughter Case

The next *mishnah*: *haba al bat bito* — a man who had intercourse with his granddaughter. The prohibitions enumerated are: *mishum bat bito*, his granddaughter; *ve-chalato*, his daughter-in-law; *ve-eshet achiv*, his brother's wife; *ve-eshet achi aviv*, his uncle's wife; *ve-achot ishto* (noted as a more complex case); and *ve-eshet ish* and *veniddah*.

How can his granddaughter also be his daughter-in-law? If the granddaughter is through his daughter, then she is the daughter's daughter — his son's niece. His son is permitted to marry his own niece. If the son did marry her, she is simultaneously the man's granddaughter and his daughter-in-law.

How can she be his brother's wife? After the son divorced her, she remained forbidden as a daughter-in-law; nevertheless, his brother (her grand-uncle by marriage) can marry her since she is his niece. The brother then divorced her or died, leaving the prohibition of his brother's wife.

How can she also be his uncle's wife? After the brother, his uncle can marry her — she is his uncle's grand-niece — and the uncle's death or divorce adds *eshet achi aviv* to the list.

The *achot ishto* case — that she is also his wife's sister — involves a more involved generational construction that requires a detailed chart to trace clearly, which we set aside here.

### Father Marriage Case

*Rabbi Yossi* adds: *im avar zaken venasa chayav aleha mishum eshet av* — if this man's father went ahead and married the granddaughter, then she is also forbidden as *eshet av* — his father's wife.

The immediate question is how this can be a binding marriage. The granddaughter is the father's great-granddaughter. Marrying one's great-granddaughter would seem to be a prohibited union (*arayos*), which would render the *kiddushin* void. *Rabbi Yochanan* resolves this: *kegon shenafelu lo leyibbum* — the situation is that this woman came before the father for *yibbum*. One of the scenarios in the *mishnah* was that she had married the father's brother — the man's uncle — and the uncle died childless. The father is therefore obligated in *yibbum*. The *gemara* then asks: but the father would still be transgressing in marrying his great-granddaughter, even through *yibbum*. Why does the *mishnah* say he transgressed (*avar*)?

The answer lies in a *beraisa*: *kallato ervah, kallat bno shniyah* — his own daughter-in-law is a full *ervah*, but his son's daughter-in-law is only a secondary *ervah*, a *shniyah* — a rabbinic prohibition. Similarly, the *beraisa* extends: *v'chen atah motzei b'vat b'no u'vat bat b'no ad sof kol hadorot* — a granddaughter and any further descendant is forbidden only rabbinically, not biblically. This great-granddaughter is thus only rabbinically prohibited to the father. Similarly, the marriage was possible because the uncle who died was the father's brother, making this woman related to the father as *kallat bno* (his son's daughter-in-law, in the generational sense) — also only a rabbinic prohibition. Since both the prohibition of *bat bno* at this generational remove and the prohibition of *kallat bno* at this generational remove are rabbinic, the marriage was binding at the biblical level, even though the father transgressed rabbinic prohibitions in contracting it. Thus the marriage is valid, and she becomes forbidden to the man as *eshet av*.

---

## Rabbi Yossi Position

### Multiple Penalties

A different *mishnah* teaches: *avar aveirah sheyesh bah shtei mitot nidon b'chamurah* — if someone committed an offense carrying two death penalties, he is judged by the more severe one. The four forms of capital punishment — *skilah*, *sreifah*, *hereg*, *chenek* — are graded in severity, and when a single act generates two of them, the more severe is applied.

### Yossi Rejects Stacking

*Rabbi Yossi* disagrees: *nidon b'zikah rishonah sheba'ah lo* — he is judged by the first prohibition that attached to this person. The underlying logic is that *Rabbi Yossi* holds *ein issur chal al issur* — the second prohibition never took effect, and therefore only the first remains operative.

The *beraisa* illustrates: *chamoto v'na'asit eshet ish* — his mother-in-law who subsequently became a married woman. Initially she was forbidden only as his mother-in-law. Then she remarried and became forbidden also as a *married woman*. The Sages say the *issur* of *eshet ish* takes effect — it is *issur mosif*, since she is now forbidden to the broader world — and since *eshet ish* is punished with *chenek* while *chamoto* receives *sreifah*, one gives the more severe, *sreifah*. *Rabbi Yossi* says: the *issur* of *eshet ish* never took effect. She is forbidden only as *chamoto*, and the punishment is *sreifah*.

### Yossi Agrees Mosif

This appears to establish that *Rabbi Yossi* categorically rejects *issur chal al issur* even in cases of *issur mosif*. Yet the *gemara* records that *Rabbi Abbahu* teaches: *modeh Rabbi Yossi be-issur mosif* — *Rabbi Yossi* actually does agree when the new *issur* is an *issur mosif*. Similarly, *Ravin* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan*: *modeh Rabbi Yossi be-issur mosif*.

This is a striking *gemara*. If *Rabbi Yossi* agrees to *issur mosif*, how does it follow that in the mother-in-law case he says the second prohibition does not take effect? The mother-in-law becoming a married woman is precisely *issur mosif* — a broader population becomes forbidden to her.

### First Prohibition Wins

The resolution is elegant. *Rabbi Yossi* agrees that when an *issur mosif* occurs, the second prohibition does take effect. But the practical outcome will always be that the first prohibition's penalty is what is applied. Why? Consider the two possible sequences.

If the first prohibition was *chamoto* (*sreifah*) and then she became *eshet ish* (*chenek*): *eshet ish* is not *issur mosif* — she was already forbidden to everyone as *chamoto*, and becoming *eshet ish* does not expand the circle of those for whom she is forbidden. The second prohibition does not take effect. One is judged by *chamoto*, the first — and it is also the more severe.

If the first prohibition was *eshet ish* (*chenek*) and then she became *chamoto* (*sreifah*): here *sreifah* would be *issur mosif* — becoming forbidden as a mother-in-law forbids her to a new class of people (the son-in-law). *Rabbi Yossi* agrees this takes effect. But the first prohibition was *eshet ish*, and *Rabbi Yossi* says one is judged by the first prohibition. So one applies *chenek*, the lighter penalty.

In all scenarios, it works out that the first prohibition is the operative one. *Rabbi Yossi*'s rule — *nidon b'zikah rishonah* — always yields the first prohibition, and it is internally consistent with his agreement to *issur mosif*, because when *issur mosif* applies, the second prohibition is in fact weaker (having the lighter penalty), and the first still prevails.

### Father Example

The *gemara* asks: what is the concrete example of *issur mosif* in the *mishnah*'s case where *Rabbi Yossi* adds the prohibition of *eshet av* when the grandfather marries the granddaughter?

The answer is: *de-ika bra le-saba* — the man in question also has a son. When the grandfather marries the granddaughter, she becomes forbidden as *eshet av* not only to this man but also to his son, to whom she is now his grandfather's wife (which falls under the broad *issur* of *eshet av* extending to all preceding generations). Since there is now a new person — the son — to whom she has become forbidden, this constitutes *issur mosif*. *Migo de-itosaf issura legabei brei, itosaf issura legabei didei* — since the prohibition expanded to include the son as well, the prohibition also attaches in a new dimension to the man himself.

Specifically: for this man, the two *issurim* now operative are *bat bno* (his granddaughter) and *eshet av* (his father's wife). For his son, the two *issurim* are *bat ach* (his brother's daughter, since she is the son's niece through the other branch) and *eshet av* (his grandfather's wife). The *issur* of *eshet av* extends through all generations in both directions, so the grandfather marrying the granddaughter creates precisely this web of interlocking prohibitions — and it is the expansion of the prohibition to the son that provides the *issur mosif* allowing the new *issur* to attach.

---

---

# Keritot 15

## Mother-in-Law Case

### Case Setup

The *mishna* at the bottom of 14b presents one further case of multiple sins arising from a single act of sex, before the discussion broadens considerably. The case opens: *haba al chamoto* — a man has sex with his mother-in-law — and the *mishna* states that it is possible, though not in every case, for that one act to carry obligations under multiple designations simultaneously.

### Genealogy Explained

How could a man's mother-in-law also be his daughter-in-law? The construction is less complicated than it first appears. Suppose the man is married to a woman — call her Rachel — and Rachel's mother is Sarah. Sarah is his mother-in-law. Now, suppose the man had previously had a son, and that son married Sarah, and they later divorced. Sarah was therefore once his daughter-in-law. After the divorce, she remarried, had a child, and eventually — through the family tree — Rachel was born from that line. The man then marries Rachel, making her former mother-in-law Sarah simultaneously his current mother-in-law and his former daughter-in-law. The *mishna* then layers on further designations: *v'eshet achiv* — this same woman was then married to his brother; *v'eshet achi aviv* — and then to his uncle; *v'achot ishto* — and she is somehow also his wife's sister, which requires their having the same father; *v'eshet ish* — she is a married woman; *v'niddah* — and she is a *niddah*.

### Multiple Relations

The *mishna* continues: *v'chen haba al em chamiv v'al em chamoto* — the same construction applies if one replaces "mother-in-law" with "grandmother-in-law." The prohibition of a man marrying a woman extends not only to her mother but to her granddaughter as well, so an analogous list of overlapping designations can be generated with the grandmother-in-law as its center.

### R. Yochanan b. Nuri

*Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri omer*: a man who has sex with his mother-in-law can be *chayav* for three violations in that single act — *mishum chamoto*, *v'em chamoto*, *v'em chamiv* — mother-in-law, mother-in-law's mother, and father-in-law's mother. The scenario: the man is married to three women — call them Rachel, Rivka, and Sarah — and this one woman is the mother of one, the paternal grandmother of another, and the maternal grandmother of the third. She had one daughter and two granddaughters, one through a son and one through a daughter, and the man married all three. In having sex with this one woman, he has committed three sins: *isha u'bitah*, a woman and her daughter; *bat bitah*, a woman and her granddaughter on the mother's side; and *bat beno*, a woman and her granddaughter on the father's side. The sages respond: *shlosha shemot echad* — although there are three labels, these are all expressions of the single sin of mother and daughter, and therefore only one *chatat* is incurred. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says three *chatatot*; the rabbis say one.

---

## Sex vs. Slaughter

### Sumchus Parallel

*Amar Rabbi Elazar amar Rabbi Oshaya*: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and Sumchus said the same thing — *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri veSumchus amru davar echad*.

### Slaughter Case

What did Sumchus say? A *mishna* on 17a records the following case of *oto v'et beno*, the prohibition against slaughtering a mother animal and its offspring on the same day. Suppose someone slaughtered the grandmother sheep, then the granddaughter, and then the middle generation — the daughter of the grandmother and the mother of the granddaughter. When the middle animal was slaughtered, two violations of *oto v'et beno* were committed simultaneously: she was the daughter of the first and the mother of the third, so slaughtering her was at once *oto v'et beno* in relation to the animal above her and *oto v'et beno* in relation to the animal below her. The question is how many sets of lashes this incurs. The first view is *sofeg arba'im* — only forty lashes, a single transgression committed in two directions. *Sumchus omer mishum Rabbi Meir sofeg shemonim* — no, two sets of forty. One act, two variations of the same prohibition. The parallel to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri is evident: in both cases it is one act with multiple instances of what appears to be the same underlying sin, and in both cases the question is whether this generates multiple obligations.

### Distinct Labels

Rava intervenes to argue that perhaps the two cases are not as parallel as they appear. *Amar Rava dilma lo hi* — maybe they are not the same. When did Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri say that sleeping with this one woman incurs three *chatatot*? *Ela mishum shemot muchlakim* — because the designations are conceptually distinct. The woman carries three different labels vis-à-vis the man: *chamoso*, *em chamoso*, *em chamiv* — mother-in-law, mother-in-law's mother, father-in-law's mother. Although the underlying prohibition in each case is that of a woman and her daughter or granddaughter — articulated in a single *pasuk* — the Torah gives each relationship a different name. One is *isha u'vitah*, another *bat bitah*, another *bat beno*. The labels are *shemot muchlakim*, distinct designations. *Aval gabei oto v'et beno*, by contrast, *d'khulhu oto v'et beno mikayim* — the Torah never distinguishes between slaughtering a mother-and-child versus a child-and-mother. There is only one label: *oto v'et beno*. So he may well say multiple obligations where the Torah provides distinct labels, but not where the Torah uses only a single designation throughout.

### Zimah Argument

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak presses the distinction further in the other direction. Perhaps Sumchus would not agree with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri either. When does Sumchus say the sheep case yields two sets of lashes? *Ela gabei oto v'et beno d'gufin m'chulakin* — because there the animals are different bodies: the grandmother and the granddaughter are two distinct animals, and each one provides the middle animal with a different identity. *Aval hacha d'ein gufin m'chulakin* — here in the case of the mother-in-law there is only one body, one woman. Perhaps Sumchus would say it is all one. The Gemara then resolves the matter through Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the *pasuk* discussing sex with a mother and her daughters or granddaughters closes with the phrase *she'erah henah zimah hi* — "it is the same flesh, it is *zimah*" — using *zimah hi* in the singular. *Hakatuv asan l'khulan zimah achat* — the Torah itself declares all of these acts to be a single *zimah*. That verse is precisely why even Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's case, where the labels are distinct, might ultimately collapse into one sin — yet it is equally the verse that distinguishes this case from *oto v'et beno*, where no such unifying declaration exists. The Gemara does note, though, that the case with the mother-in-law is arguably the stronger candidate for multiple obligations, since not only do different people give her each designation — just as two different sheep give the middle one its identity — but additionally the Torah provides distinct labels for each relationship.

---

## R. Akiva's Questions

### Market Setting

*Amar Rabbi Akiva*: Rabbi Akiva relates that he posed a question to Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua *b'itliz shel Amos* — in the meat market of Emmaus — while they were going to purchase an animal for Rabban Gamliel's son's wedding feast. The detail is noted by Tosafot: *l'hodia shivchan* — to convey the greatness of these sages, who *af al pi shehayu trudim*, even though they were occupied with a practical errand, *hayu oskim b'divrei Torah*, were engaged in Torah discussion throughout.

### The Question

The question Rabbi Akiva posed: *haba al achoto v'al achot aviv v'al achot imo* — a man who has sex with a woman who is simultaneously his sister, his father's sister, and his mother's sister. *Mahu* — is it one *chatat* for all, *chayav achat al kulan*, or is he obligated for each designation separately, *o chayav al kol achat v'achat*? This question is the conceptual foundation of all the previous *mishnayot*, which had assumed without explicit derivation that multiple designations in a single act generate multiple *chatatot*. Here Rabbi Akiva is trying to establish that principle with the sages.

### Sages' Response

*Amru lo lo shamanu* — they had no tradition about this. What they did have a tradition about was the following: *haba al chamesh nashim niddot uvehelem achat shehu chayav al kol achat v'achat* — a man who slept with five wives who were all *niddot* in a single state of forgetfulness brings a separate *chatat* for each one. That is, the same sin — *niddah* — with multiple different women, generates multiple sin offerings.

### Kal Vachomer

*V'ro'im anu shehadvarim kal vachomer* — it seems to us, they said, that a *kal vachomer* follows. If the same sin committed with multiple different people requires multiple sin offerings, then surely different sins — distinct designations — committed against one person in a single act should require multiple sin offerings, since the sins are even more fundamentally distinct. The hidden premise of this *kal vachomer*, however, is precisely what is at stake: it assumes that distinct designations — *shemot mechulakot* — are a stronger ground for multiple obligations than distinct bodies — *gufim mechulakot*. That assumption is exactly what can be challenged.

---

## Names & Bodies

### One Person

The Gemara clarifies the structure of the *mishna*. One might initially read the case as involving three different women — a sister, a father's sister, and a mother's sister — in which case the question would be trivial. *Eileima kidekatani, mai tibei lei* — if it were three different women, what is the question? *Harei shemot mecholakim harei gufi mecholakim* — it would be both different sins and different bodies. *Ela hachi katani* — no, the case is one woman who is simultaneously *achoto shehi achot aviv shehi achot imo* — his sister, who is also his father's sister, who is also his mother's sister. One person, three designations, one act.

### Core Question

The Gemara then formulates the question precisely: *mi amrinan harei shemot mecholakim* — do we say it is distinct sins, distinct labels, and therefore three *chatatot*? *O dilma harei ein gufin mecholakim* — or, since there is only one body involved, is that sufficient reason to say it is one *chatat*? As all the previous *mishnayot* have established, the answer is that distinct designations are indeed sufficient. But here the question is being asked explicitly for the first time.

### Challenge

The *kal vachomer* can be challenged: *mah l'hanei niddot she'kein gufim m'chulakin* — what makes the case of five *niddot* yield multiple obligations is that it is five different bodies, five distinct acts with five distinct people. One cannot straightforwardly infer from there to the case of one person with multiple designations, because perhaps *gufim mechulakot* — different bodies, different acts — is the operative principle, and without different bodies there is no ground for multiple obligations.

### Verse Resolution

The Gemara therefore resolves the matter not by *kal vachomer* but by verse. *Ela amar kra ervas achoto gilah* — the Torah in describing the prohibition of a sister uses what was already noted as a seemingly redundant formulation, specifying *ervas achoto* with the word *gilah*. The reason for this apparent redundancy is precisely *l'chaiv al kol achat v'achat* — to teach that for every distinct designation, even with a single body in a single act, a separate *chatat* is incurred. The *pasuk* teaches the case of *l'chaiv al achoso she'hi achos aviv she'hi achos imo* — a sister who is also the father's sister and the mother's sister — that one is obligated for each designation separately. The principle is thus established not by inference but by explicit *drashah*: both *gufim mechulakot* and *shemot mechulakot* independently require multiple sin offerings.

---

## Genealogy of Evil

### Rasha Bar Rasha

The Gemara now addresses how the scenario of a sister who is simultaneously a father's sister and a mother's sister can actually arise. *Amar Rav Adda bar Ahava*: *mashkachas lah b'rashia bar rashia* — one finds this case in a wicked person who is the son of a wicked person.

### Genealogy Built

The construction proceeds as follows. A man — call him X — has sex with his mother and fathers two daughters, Rachel and Leah. These two daughters are therefore both his daughters and his sisters, since they share his mother. He then has sex with Rachel, and from her a son is born — call him Reuven. Reuven is thus X's son, though also his grandson through the maternal line. The *gemara* then states: *v'chazar ba'al achman v'holid ben uva beno al achot imo she'hi achoto she'hi achot aviv* — the son Reuven then has sex with Leah, who is: his father's sister, because she is the daughter of X and X's mother; his mother's sister, because she is the daughter of X and X's mother who is also Reuven's grandmother through Rachel; and his sister, because she is the daughter of his father X. She is simultaneously *achoto*, *achot aviv*, and *achot imo* — his sister, his father's sister, and his mother's sister. This is the *rasha bar rasha* construction: a wicked person who had relations with his mother, followed by a wicked son who compounded the genealogical violations.

---

## Multiple Acts

### Niddah Case

The Gemara now turns to a *baraita* that directly addresses the question of the same sin with the same person committed multiple times. The case: a husband and wife have sex multiple times while she is a *niddah*, without either of them remembering between acts — *ba'al v'chazar ba'al v'chazar ba'al*.

### R. Eliezer

*Chayav al kol achat v'achat divrei Rabbi Eliezer* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that each distinct act requires its own *chatat*, even when the sin and the person are identical throughout.

### Sages' View

*V'chachamim omrim eino chayav ela achat* — the sages hold that the same sin with the same person, however many times repeated without intervening awareness, generates only a single *chatat*. This is the normative ruling.

### Agreement

Nevertheless, *umodim l'Rabbi Eliezer b'ba al chamesh niddot b'vat achat shehu chayav al kol achat v'achat* — the sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer that if there are five different women, each a *niddah*, and he had sex with all of them in a single state of forgetfulness, he brings a *chatat* for each one. The sin is the same — *niddah* — but the persons are different.

### Causation

The *baraita* explains this with the phrase *ho'il v'hu garam lahem* — since he caused them to bring sin offerings. The reasoning: each of his five wives will herself be obligated to bring a *chatat* for this act. Since each woman brings a separate sin offering, he cannot be treated as having committed a single undivided act when the women's obligations are five distinct ones. Therefore he too brings separately for each.

---

## Causation Challenged

### Hypothetical

Rava challenges this causation principle before Rav Nachman. *Mi amrinan hov hu garam lahem?* — is that truly the operative reason? Consider the following case: *hu b'he'elam achat v'hi b'he'elamot* — he had sex with his wife five times and his state of forgetfulness was continuous throughout, but she remembered between each act and then forgot again. Each time she remembered and then forgot, a new state of forgetfulness began for her.

### Independent Judgment

How many sin offerings does each party bring? She brings five — one for each interval of forgetfulness. He brings one — his forgetfulness was never interrupted. *Hu eino chayav ela achat v'hi chayavet al kol achat v'achat*. Now if the principle were truly that his obligation is determined by her obligations — that because she brings five, he must bring five — then in this case he should also bring five. But he does not. You judge each party independently; the number of *korbanot* one party brings does not determine the other's obligation.

### Real Principle

*Ella eima hovei gufim mocholakim* — the correct principle is simply that different bodies, different people involved in distinct acts, is what creates distinct obligations. The causation language of the *baraita* is not the true underlying reason; the true reason is *gufim muchlakim*. When a man has sex with five different women, there are five distinct acts involving five distinct people, and that alone is sufficient to require five sin offerings regardless of what the women bring.

---

## Shabbat Question

### Picking Apples

The Gemara now raises a new question by analogy. *Iba'ya lehu: katzar v'katzar mai l'amar Rabbi Eliezer?* — what would Rabbi Eliezer say if someone forgot it was *Shabbat* and harvested an apple, and then an hour later harvested another apple? Same sin, same type of act, multiple times — would Rabbi Eliezer require two *chatatot* here as he did for multiple acts of sex?

### First View

One possibility: Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is simply that he did two acts — *de'avid tartei* — and therefore two *chatatot* are incurred. On this reading, multiple distinct acts always require multiple sin offerings regardless of what the act involves, and by *Shabbat* harvesting twice would yield two obligations.

### Second View

*Dilma ta'ama d'Rabbi Eliezer hatam mishum d'i efshar lo l'arvan bi'ah zo b'zo* — alternatively, the reason Rabbi Eliezer requires multiple *chatatot* for sex is specifically that it is impossible to perform two acts of sex simultaneously. There is no conceptual way to combine them into a single act. *Amtu l'hachi amar Rabbi Eliezer chayav al kol achat v'achat* — it is precisely because simultaneity is impossible that each act is irreducibly distinct.

### Why Different?

The contrast then becomes clear. *Aval katzar ke-grogoret v'katzar ke-grogoret*, if one harvested the minimum quantity — a *grogoret* — and then harvested another *grogoret*, *kivan d'efshar lo l'arvei shtei grogorot b'vat achat* — since it would in theory have been possible to harvest both quantities in a single act, perhaps even sequential acts of the same type are considered one act when they could in principle have been combined. The *grogoret* is merely a minimum measure; eating a large loaf of bread is not multiple acts of eating just because it contains multiple *kezayitim*. Similarly, harvesting several apples at once is one act of harvesting that met the minimum size, not multiple acts. On Rav Yosef's reading, then, Rabbi Eliezer would not require multiple *chatatot* for harvesting twice, since the acts could have been combined.

---

## Shiurim Logic

### Minimum Size

The underlying principle being clarified here is that a *shiur* — a minimum measure — defines the threshold of an act; it does not define the unit of repetition. If one harvests a *grogoret*-sized quantity, that is one act of harvesting that has reached the minimum size for liability. The question of whether two such acts are really two acts or one depends not on the *shiur* but on whether the actions were genuinely distinct.

### Simultaneous Acts

The illustration: if one picks three apples in a single motion — hand closes around all three at once — that is one act of picking. The fact that three apples were taken does not multiply the act into three, any more than eating a large piece of bread constitutes multiple acts of eating. The *grogoret* is the standard for what counts, not the dividing line between acts.

### Distinction

Sex acts, however, cannot be performed simultaneously by their very nature. Each act of sex is necessarily sequential, and no act of sex can be subsumed into another. Therefore, for Rabbi Eliezer, each act of sex is irreducibly distinct, and multiple acts require multiple sin offerings. For acts like harvesting, where simultaneity is physically possible, Rabbi Eliezer on Rav Yosef's reading would not impose the same multiplication — because if it could have all been done at once, the sequential version may still be viewed as one act in different moments.

---

## Rava vs. Yosef

### Rava's View

*Amar Rava ta'ama d'Rabbi Eliezer hatam mishum d'avid tartei hacha nami d'avid tartei* — Rava holds that the reason Rabbi Eliezer requires multiple *chatatot* is simply that two distinct acts were committed. This applies everywhere. Whether it is sex or harvesting or any other category, if the acts were distinct, Rabbi Eliezer would require separate sin offerings for each.

### Yosef's View

*Rav Yosef amar: ta'ama d'Rabbi Eliezer hatam d'i efshar l'arvan* — Rav Yosef holds that the reason is specifically the impossibility of simultaneity. Where acts cannot be combined — as with sex — Rabbi Eliezer requires multiple *chatatot*. Where they can be combined, *aval efshar l'arvan eino chayav ela achat* — even Rabbi Eliezer would say one.

### Shabbat Proof

Abaye challenges Rava from Rabbi Eliezer's known position on *Shabbat*: *Rabbi Eliezer mechayev al toldot melachot bimkom avot melachot* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that performing an *av melachah* and its *toldah* in one act still yields two *chatatot*, because they carry distinct labels. This is a *chiddush*. But it implies the converse: if two instances of the *same* *av melachah* were performed, *patur* — meaning one *chatat* only, not two. *Mar berei d'Ravina* and Rav Nachman bar Zechariah explain: the case of the same *av* twice incurring only one *chatat* refers to a specific scenario — *b'dalit ha-mudelet al gabi te'enah* — a vine wrapped around a fig tree, where both were cut in a single act. There it is literally one motion. The case of *av* and *toldah* incurring two *chatatot* is where it is a conceptually distinct type of action — such as cutting a fig (*kotzer*, to take its produce) while simultaneously pruning a vine for growth (*zeriah*, a derivative of planting). Those are different labels and different objects. But two instances of harvesting performed at the exact same moment remain one act.

---

## Vine & Fig

### Scenario

The case of *dalit ha-mudelet al gabi te'enah*: a vine is growing on a trellis around a fig tree, and one wishes to cut a fig to eat it while simultaneously pruning the vine to encourage growth. A single cut of the shears accomplishes both.

### Analysis

*Mishum hachi mechayev Rabbi Eliezer ho'il u-shemot muchlakin v'gufin muchlakin* — Rabbi Eliezer requires two *chatatot* here because two conditions are met: the *melachot* have distinct labels — *kotzer* for the harvest action and *zeriah* for the pruning action — and they are performed on distinct objects — the fig and the vine. Both *shemot muchlakin* and *gufin muchlakin* are present.

### Counter

The contrasting scenario: one cuts two apples from adjacent trees in a single motion. This is *kotzer v'kotzer* — the same *melachah* on different but similar objects. *Heichi mashkachat lah d'chavateih katzar v'katzar d'miptar* — the case of the same *melachah* twice where one would be exempt from multiple obligations is *katzar shtei grogerot b'vat achat* — harvesting two *grogoret*-sized quantities at the exact same moment. That is one act.

### Conclusion

*Aval katzar ke-grogeret v'chazar v'katzar ke-grogeret chayav* — but if one harvested one quantity and then harvested again separately, that is two distinct sequential acts and one is obligated for each. The conclusion: literal simultaneity — one motion, one instant — makes multiple objects part of one act. Sequential acts, even of the same type, remain distinct. For Rava, sequential distinct acts always matter and Rabbi Eliezer would require multiple *chatatot*. For Rav Yosef, Rabbi Eliezer's principle applies only to sex, where simultaneity is inherently impossible; by other *melachot*, acts that could theoretically have been simultaneous are treated as one even if they were not.

---

## Dangling Limb

### Limb Status

The Gemara records a further question Rabbi Akiva posed, perhaps in the same context of the meat market. *Eiver hameduldal biveheimah mahu* — what is the status of a limb dangling from a living animal? Once a limb detaches from a living being, it is *eiver min hachai* and causes *tumah*. But if it has not yet fully detached — if it is still hanging by some connection — does it already carry the status of a detached limb for purposes of *tumah*?

### Human Case

*Amru lo lo shamanu* — no tradition about animals. *Aval shamanu: eiver hameduldal b'adam shehu tahor* — they did have a tradition that a limb dangling from a living person is *tahor*, even though once it fully detaches it would be *eiver min hachai* and *tamei*.

### Pesach Story

*V'kach hayu mokei shechin osim biYerushalayim* — and this is what people with leprosy would do in Jerusalem. The scenario is specifically tied to *erev Pesach*. Such a person had a limb dangling. He wished to bring the *korban Pesach*, and he wanted to deal with his limb before *Pesach* without incurring *tumah*. So he would go *erev Pesach* to the doctor.

### Technique

*V'chotcho ad shemaniyach bo kisa'arah* — the doctor would cut nearly through the limb, leaving it attached by only a thread of skin. The doctor himself does not become *tamei* because the limb is not yet fully detached. Now the patient must sever that last thread without touching the limb — because if he holds it while pulling, he contacts the detached limb at the moment of separation. So *v'tochvo besirah* — he fixes the dangling limb to a wall with a nail or peg while it is still attached by its thread, and then *v'nimshach mimenu* — he pulls away from it, so that the limb is yanked off while he is not holding it. *Venimshach mimenu v'hala oseh pischo v'harofeh oseh pischo* — both the patient and the doctor can then go and bring their *korban Pesach*.

### Kal Vachomer

*V'ro'im anu shehadvarim kal vachomer* — the sages offer a *kal vachomer*. A human being is a greater source of *tumah* than an animal. If a dangling limb from a human is *tahor*, how much more so must a dangling limb from an animal be *tahor*.

---

## Separation Tumah

### Leek Case

*Tnan hatam*: the *mishna* elsewhere discusses a case of *hamochek et hakrisha* — one who squeezes a leek that has absorbed rainwater. Rainwater that has merely been absorbed — and not actively desired — does not yet have the status of a liquid that makes food susceptible to *tumah* (*be-ki yutan*). The liquid inside the leek is *mah shebetocho einah be-ki yutan* — it does not count. *V'yotzei mimenu harei hein be-ki yutan* — but as it is being squeezed out, it acquires liquid status. *Amar Shmuel: d'kalcha atzmah hukhsharah* — Shmuel adds that as the liquid comes out, it makes the leek itself susceptible to *tumah*, because at the moment of separation, while still in contact with the leek, it has already acquired its liquid status.

### Question

*B'sha'as perishah mimena hukhsharah* — the principle is that at the moment of separation the liquid activates and affects the object it is leaving. But how does that square with the *mishna*'s ruling about the dangling limb? If at the moment of separation there is a contact that transmits status — as with the liquid and the leek — then at the moment the dangling limb finally detaches from the person, should it not transmit *tumah* to him at that exact instant of separation?

### Force Factor

*Ki d'amar Rav Yosef b'nitzin b'khol kokhan* — Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by distinguishing on the basis of force. When liquid is *nitzin b'khol kokhan* — squirted out powerfully — it separates cleanly without lingering. There is no moment of extended contact at the boundary. When it is squeezed out slowly, the liquid adheres momentarily before falling away, and it is in that moment of adherence that it touches and activates.

### Application

The same principle applies to the limb. *Hacha nami b'nitzin b'khol kokhan* — the reason the yanking technique works is precisely because it is done forcefully. When the limb is yanked off sharply and quickly, the separation is clean, and there is no moment of lingering contact at the point of detachment. Therefore no *tumah* is transmitted at the moment of separation. Had the limb been removed slowly, the contact at the moment of detachment might well have transmitted *tumah*. This is why the technique prescribed is a forceful, sharp pull away from the wall.

---

## Zav Meis Case

### Rain Water

*Rav Yosef*'s statement about forceful separation was originally made in connection with a different *mishna*: the case of a *zav* or *tamei meis* — both primary sources of *tumah* — walking in the rain. Rain falls on their clothes, and the water becomes absorbed. The question is whether the absorbed water, once on their body, becomes *tamei* or gains liquid status to make other things susceptible. *Af al pi she-sokhtin mitzad ha-elyon l'tzad ha-tachton, tehorin* — even if they squeeze the water along their garment from top to bottom, the water running along the garment remains *tahor*.

### Full Separation

*She-ein machshavin ela ad she-yeitzu mikulan* — the water only attains liquid status once it has completely separated from them — from their hair, their clothing, their body entirely. As long as it is running along their garments, it remains absorbed and has no status.

### Proof

*Yeitzu mikulan harei makhshirin* — only upon full departure does it become a liquid that can make other things susceptible or itself become *tamei*. This is the source for Rav Yosef's principle: complete separation is what activates status, not the boundary moment. *She-ein hukhshar ela l'achar she-yeitzu migufo* — only after full separation from the body. The apparent tension with the leek case, where status activates at the moment of separation, is what Rav Yosef resolves by distinguishing between forceful and gradual separation.

---

## Five Pots Case

### Question

*V'od sha'alan Rabbi Akiva* — Rabbi Akiva posed a further question. *Ha-shocheit chamishah zevachim bachutz b'he'elam achat* — someone slaughtered five different sacrificial animals outside the *Beit HaMikdash* in a single state of forgetfulness. *Mahu* — is it one *chatat* for all five, or a separate *chatat* for each? This is, in a sense, the mirror image of the previous question: where the earlier question was one person carrying multiple designations, here it is multiple animals but the same sin. The presumptive answer based on *gufim mechulakot* would be multiple *chatatot*. *Amru lo lo shamanu* — no tradition. *Amar Rabbi Yehoshua: shama'ti* — but Rabbi Yehoshua said he did have a tradition about an analogous eating case. *Be'ocheil mizevach echad meichamesh tanchuyin be'helem echad* — one who ate from a single sacrifice that had been prepared in five different ways — five different pots — in one state of forgetfulness, and since the blood had not yet been sprinkled this would be *me'ilah*, is *chayav al kol achat v'achat mishum me'ilah*. One sacrifice, five preparations, five separate *me'ilah* obligations. What is striking is that this is the same animal, the same sin, and the only distinction is that it was prepared in different ways. If that suffices for multiple *me'ilah* obligations, *ro'eh ani shehadvarim kal vachomer* — then surely five entirely distinct animals slaughtered outside should generate five obligations.

---

## Me'ilah Notar

### R. Shimon

*Amar Rabbi Shimon: lo kasha'al Rabbi Akiva* — Rabbi Shimon clarifies that this was not actually the structure of Rabbi Akiva's question. Rabbi Akiva was not comparing slaughtering to eating; he was comparing eating to eating, and specifically asking about *notar* — the leftovers of a sacrifice that become forbidden once the time for consumption has passed.

### Refined Q

The refined question: *ela b'ocheil notar mechamesh zevachim b'helem echad* — one who ate *notar* from five different sacrifices in a single state of forgetfulness. *Mahu* — is it one *chatat* or five? This is precisely the question of how *gufim mechulakot* applies to sacrificial meat: are five sacrifices five distinct bodies the way five women are five distinct bodies, or is it all the same type of object and therefore one undivided act?

---

## Five Pots Case (II)

### R. Yehoshua

*Amar Rabbi Yehoshua: shama'ti* — Rabbi Yehoshua's tradition now becomes relevant on the correct comparison. He knew that *be'ocheil mizevach echad meichamesh tanchuyin be'helem echad shehu chayav al kol achat v'achat mishum me'ilah* — one who ate *me'ilah* from one sacrifice prepared in five pots in one forgetfulness brings five separate offerings.

### Kal Vachomer

*V'ro'eh ani shehadvarim kal vachomer* — if one sacrifice prepared five ways generates five obligations, then certainly five distinct sacrifices should generate five obligations, since they are even more physically distinct. The *kal vachomer* now operates within the same category of eating, not across categories.

---

## Me'ilah Notar (II)

### R. Akiva

*Amar lo Rabbi Akiva: im halacha nekabel* — Rabbi Akiva responds: if you have a tradition that eating *me'ilah* from one sacrifice five ways is five *chatatot*, I will accept it on its own terms. *Im ledin yesh teshuvah* — but if you want to reason logically, I have a response. The *kal vachomer* does not work, because *me'ilah* and *notar* are fundamentally different in their stringencies.

### Me'ilah Features

Three stringencies of *me'ilah* distinguish it from *notar*. First, *oseh ham'achal k'ochel* — the one who causes another to eat sanctified food is treated as if he himself ate it; even the feeder incurs *me'ilah*. Second, *v'hamahane k'nehane* — one who causes another to benefit from *hekdesh* is treated as if he himself benefited, even without eating. Third, *tziruf etzel me'ilah lizman merubeh* — by *me'ilah*, benefit that accrues over an extended period of time can combine toward the minimum measure for liability. This is unlike eating prohibitions, where the act must occur within the time of *khdei achilat pras*.

### Conclusion

Because of these stringencies, one could argue that *me'ilah* treats one sacrifice prepared five ways as five distinct acts of misuse, each with its own character. The law may be more stringent and more finely parsed with *me'ilah* than with other prohibitions. *Tomar b'notar she'ein bo achat me'elu* — but *notar* has none of these stringencies. Therefore one cannot infer from the *me'ilah* ruling that five sacrifices of *notar* yield five obligations. Perhaps five sacrifices of *notar* is still one act repeated five times with respect to one undivided prohibition.

---

## Summary

### Central Issue

The concluding discussion highlights the central conceptual problem of this entire sugya: how do we define *gufim mechulakot* as we move from the domain of people to the domain of animals to the domain of meat and sacrifices? When a man has sex with five different women, the distinctness of the acts is obvious — five people, five acts.
