One might have thought that *ikvei assur* simply means there must be an actual *issur* before you at the moment of your act. But the *Gemara's* scenario — in which the non-Jew ate the first piece before the Jew acted — suggests that what matters is whether an *issur* was ever objectively part of the situation, even if it is gone by the time of the act. Tosafot discusses this point at length in relation to other cases, including *bein ha-shmashot* of *Shabbos* — where the *issur* had already been established (it was *Shabbos*) and the only question is whether it has ended yet — which might also satisfy *ikvei assur*, though there are distinctions to be drawn.

### Rava's Challenges

Rava now challenges Rav Nachman with the same three cases that Rabbi Yirmiya raised against Rabbi Zeira — the *koy*, the *yibum*, and the *niddah* — each of which involves an *asham talui* obligation without *ikvei assur*. In each case, Rav Nachman gives the same answer: *ha mani Rabbi Eliezer hi*. These represent Rabbi Eliezer's view that does not require *ikvei assur*.

The *koy* case is straightforward: the *koy* by its very nature never had an established status, so there is no *ikvei assur* at all. The *yibum* case is more complex. One might try to argue that the *ikvei assur* was established here as well — after all, the woman was forbidden to her brother-in-law while her husband was alive, so her *issur* status was in some sense already established and the question is merely whether it changed. But the *Gemara* does not make that argument, and the *yibum* case is treated as lacking *ikvei assur*. The *niddah* case is even clearer in the opposite direction: the woman began as a *non-niddah* and the question is whether she became *tamei* during the act. Since she started in a state of *heter*, the *issur* was never established beforehand, and thus there is no *ikvei assur*.

After Rav Nachman gave his responses and left, Rava reflected: *mai ta'ama lo amarei lei d'ha mani Rabbi Meir hi* — why did I not also say that this could reflect Rabbi Meir's position? For Rabbi Eliezer is not the only *tanna* who does not require *ikvei assur*.

### Rabbi Meir Position

The *Gemara* introduces a *baraita*: one who slaughters an *asham talui* outside the *Beit HaMikdash* (*shechutei chutz*) — is he *chayav* for the prohibition of *shechutei chutz*? Rabbi Meir holds he is *chayav*; the *Chachamim* hold he is exempt.

Rashi explains this debate as being about a case where the *asham talui* was brought for a situation that lacked *ikvei assur* — such as the *koy* case — and the question is whether such an offering still carries the legal status of a *korban*. Rabbi Meir holds it does; the *Chachamim* hold that without *ikvei assur*, the obligation was never established and therefore the animal lacks the full status of a *kodesh* that would trigger *shechutei chutz*.

Rabbeinu Gershom offers a more creative and elegant reading. He suggests that the debate concerns the situation of one who slaughtered his *asham talui* outside — which creates its own *safeik*: if the underlying sin was real, the animal was a genuine *korban* and slaughtering it outside was *shechutei chutz*; if the underlying sin did not occur, the animal was perhaps not a genuine *korban*. The question of whether one sinned with *shechutei chutz* is thus itself a *safeik*. Rabbi Meir holds that for this *safeik* one brings — notably — an *asham talui*, since one might have done *shechutei chutz*. The *Chachamim* say *patur*, because this is not a case of *ikvei assur*. According to Rabbeinu Gershom, therefore, Rabbi Meir's position demonstrates that he does not require *ikvei assur* to be *chayav* in an *asham talui*.

Rava reflects that he could have made this point to Rav Nachman — not merely attributing the dissenting view to Rabbi Eliezer, but noting that Rabbi Meir independently holds the same position. The question of why he did not say so in the moment is left unresolved.

The *Gemara* then asks: why not simply say, as he had been doing, that it is Rabbi Eliezer? The answer is: *ha kamashma lan d'Rabbi Meir b'shitat Rabbi Eliezer kai* — the point is that even Rabbi Meir, a separate *tanna*, stands in the same approach as Rabbi Eliezer. This expands the scope of the dissenting view.

To summarize where we have arrived: there are now three rationales for the requirement of *shtei chatichot* — the *psuk* (formal textual requirement), *efshar levarer* (ability to clarify), and *ikvei assur* (establishment of a concrete prohibition) — and a minority view, held by Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Meir, that requires none of these.

## One vs. Two Pieces Debate

### Two Pieces Required

The *Gemara* now moves to a new statement: *chaticha safeik shel chelev safeik shel shuman, achalah, plugta de-Rabbi Eliezer ve-Chachamim* — a single piece of uncertain status, if eaten, is the subject of the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the *Chachamim*. This seems to simply restate what has been discussed. Tosafot raises a subtlety here: the *Rabbi Eliezer* of this passage may not be the same *Rabbi Eliezer* as the one cited earlier; the earlier cases involved *Rabbi Elazar* (a different figure), while here it is *Rabbi Eliezer*. The distinction matters for understanding whose position is being represented.

### Rabbi Eliezer Alternative

The *Gemara* then asks: *mai irya ki achalah* — why specifically say if you ate it? According to Rabbi Eliezer, *afilu lo achalah nami* — even if you did not eat anything at all, you could bring an *asham talui*. Why? Because of a *mishnah* that records Rabbi Eliezer's remarkable ruling: *misnadeiv adam asham talui bechol yom* — a person may voluntarily bring an *asham talui* every single day. Since every day one might have inadvertently committed some sin, and every day the verse applies — *ve-hu rachum yechaper avon* — one may bring an *asham talui* simply out of general spiritual concern, without any specific concrete basis for suspecting that a sin occurred. This is, in its own way, a striking *halacha* — it gives institutional sanction to a kind of conscientious self-examination and preemptive atonement.

The consequence for the current discussion is: if Rabbi Eliezer allows an *asham talui* even for a wholly abstract, generic doubt, he clearly does not require *shtei chatichot*. But by the same token, the inference about what *obligates* him is complicated: the *nedava* (voluntary) dimension of Rabbi Eliezer's position tells us what one may do, not necessarily what one is required to do. So attributing to Rabbi Eliezer an *obligatory* *asham talui* for *chaticha achat* based solely on this *mishnah* is uncertain.

### Bava ben Buta Reference

Rav Ashi explains that this passage concerns Rabbi Eliezer *aliba de-Bava ben Buta* — in accordance with Bava ben Buta's approach. A *mishnah* records that Bava ben Buta would say he would have brought an *asham talui* even the morning after *Yom Kippur*, so eager was he to have ongoing atonement. His colleagues, however, told him: wait until you have actually entered a realm of doubt. Do not bring an *asham talui* the morning after *Yom Kippur* when everything has just been atoned for. The point is that even within Rabbi Eliezer's broader view, there must be at least some minimal basis — some *smidgen* of doubt — to justify bringing the *asham talui*, even as a *nedava*.

### Obligation vs. Optional

The question thus becomes: when Rabbi Eliezer says you may bring an *asham talui* even for a generic, unspecified doubt, does that also mean you are *obligated* when there is something more concretely problematic but still only *chaticha achat*? Logically, these positions should travel together — if *asham talui* does not require *shtei chatichot* even to do it *as a nedava*, then it seems unlikely that the formal *chiyuv* would require the stricter threshold of *shtei chatichot*. The *Gemara's* resolution is not entirely clear-cut, but the most comfortable reading of the conclusion appears to be: if something concretely problematic occurred, one is *chayav*; for purely abstract, unspecified general doubt — like the morning after *Yom Kippur* — one may bring it optionally as a *nedava*. This framework allows for a hybrid: one can simultaneously hold that *shtei chatichot* is required for a formal *chiyuv* (the position of the *Mishnah*) while still preserving Rabbi Eliezer's category of an optional *asham talui* for lesser degrees of doubt.

## Practical Scenarios

### Two Present Scenario

The *Gemara* now presents a *Tanna de-vei Rebbi* with a series of concrete scenarios, all built around the case of two pieces — one *chelev* and one *shuman* — in front of a person. The first case is the standard one: a Jew ate the first piece, and the standard *asham talui* obligation applies because there were two pieces at the time of his act.

### Non-Jew First, Jew Second

The reverse scenario: a non-Jew ate the first piece, and then a Jew ate the second. In this case, *patur* — the Jew is exempt. Why? Because at the time the Jew performed his act, only one piece remained. There was no *shtei chatichot* at the moment of his action, no *efshar levarer*, and — according to the standard view — no *ikvei assur* properly operative at that moment (even though it had existed earlier). This scenario, notably, appears to contradict the *ikvei assur* framework as discussed earlier, since the *issur* was in principle already present at some point. The *Gemara* does not revisit that tension here, apparently treating this *baraita* as following a different tannaic opinion. *Rabbi* (Rebbi), however, holds that the Jew in this scenario is *chayav*, because according to his view, even *chaticha achat* suffices.

### Mixed Willful/Unwitting

If the person ate the first piece *be-shogeg* (inadvertently) and then the second *be-mezid* (deliberately, knowing it was a *safeik*): for the first piece — when there were two and he ate *be-shogeg* — he is *chayav* an *asham talui*. For the second piece — when there was only one remaining and he ate knowing it was a *safeik* — he is exempt on both counts: both because there was only one piece, and because eating with knowledge of the doubt (*mezid*) disqualifies from *asham talui*. *Rabbi* again holds the Jew is *chayav* because of his lenient position on *chaticha achat*.

If the order is reversed — the first piece *be-mezid* and the second *be-shogeg*: for the first piece, though there were two, the *mezid* quality disqualifies. For the second piece, though it was *be-shogeg*, there was only one piece left. *Patur* in this case. *Rabbi* says *chayav* for the second.

### Both Unwitting

If both pieces were eaten *be-shogeg* — and this now introduces a second person — *sheneihem chayavin*, both are *chayav*. When the first person ate, there were two pieces and he was *shogeg*: clearly *chayav* an *asham talui*. But when the second person ate, there was only one piece. He should logically be *patur*. Why then is he also *chayav*?

### Secondary Eater Issue

The *Gemara* explains: *ha-sheni lo min ha-din* — the second person is not obligated in the strict legal sense. But if we say the second person is *patur*, the implication is that he did not eat the *chelev*, which means the first person did — and that in turn would make the first person *chayav* in a *chatat*, not merely an *asham talui*. One does not wish to create a situation where the second person's exemption functions as an implicit verdict that the first person must bring a *chatat*.

### Stipulation Solution

Rav Ashi resolves this: we instruct the second person to bring an *asham talui* and make a *tenai* — a stipulation. He declares: if the first person ate the *shuman*, then I ate the *chelev*, and this *asham talui* should serve as atonement for my having eaten it. And if not — if the first person ate the *chelev* — then let this offering function as a generic voluntary *asham talui* in the spirit of Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that one may bring it as a *nedava* at any time. This elegant solution draws on the *nedava* dimension of Rabbi Eliezer's position while operating within the framework of *shtei chatichot* for obligatory offerings. The two positions — requiring *shtei chatichot* for a *chiyuv* and allowing *asham talui* as a *nedava* without it — are thus compatible and can coexist within a single legal strategy.

## Multiple Asamim Question

### Rabbi's Position

The *Gemara* now turns to a *Tanna de-vei Rebbi* addressing how many *asham taluim* one must bring when acts of possible sin are separated by intervening awareness. The scenario: a person ate doubtful *chelev*, then became aware he might have sinned, then forgot and ate again, then became aware again, and so on repeatedly. Rebbi (Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi) rules: just as with a *chatat* — where becoming definitively aware that one sinned between acts obligates separate *chataot* for each — so too with *asham talui*, becoming aware in between that one might have sinned obligates a separate *asham talui* for each act. The same *yedi'ah* that divides for *chatat* divides for *asham talui*.

### One Asham View

Against this, Rabbi Yossi, Rabbi Yehudah, Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Shimon hold: *ein meivi ela asham talui echad* — even if there were multiple acts of possible sin separated by awareness, only one *asham talui* is brought. Their proof-text is the redundant phrasing *al shigagato asher shagag* — for the error that he erred — which the *Gemara* reads as teaching that even many *shigagot* of the same type require only one *korban*.

### Guilt vs. Objective Sin

This position reflects a profound conceptual distinction. A *chatat* addresses the objective reality of sin: something must be cleansed, and each separate sinful act requires its own cleansing. This is why a *tinok she-nishba* — a child raised in captivity who violated *Shabbos* without any awareness — still brings a *chatat*. The obligation is not about personal guilt; it is about the objective fact that a sin occurred. An *asham*, by contrast — and an *asham talui* in particular — is rooted in the person's own guilt. The very language of the *pasuk* speaks to this: *asham hu, ashom asham la-Hashem* — the vocabulary of *ashmah*, of personal culpability and guilt. And because the *asham talui* focuses on the person rather than on the objective sin-event, multiple instances of the same category of possible sin constitute a single undivided condition of guilt, not multiple discrete events each requiring separate atonement.

This is a conceptually elegant position: if I repeatedly ate something that might have been *chelev*, my being at fault is a unified personal state, not a series of discrete sinful acts. The minority view here thus isolates the *asham talui* as an expression of personal moral accountability rather than objective sin-reality. The *halacha*, however, follows Rebbi and the *Mishnah*: an *asham talui* is treated like a *chatat*, and when awareness intervenes between acts, multiple *ashamot* are required.

## Asham vs. Chatat Awa (II)

### Learning Chatat from Ash…

Rabbi Zeira now offers a striking reinterpretation of Rebbi's ruling. When Rebbi said that just as definite awareness divides for *chatat* so does doubtful awareness divide for *asham talui*, Rabbi Zeira reads the comparison in the opposite direction: *kan shana Rabbi yedi'ot safeik mechalekot le-chataot* — here Rebbi was not drawing on *chatat* to explain *asham talui*, but rather teaching us something about *chatat* itself by way of *asham talui*. That is: just as doubtful awareness (*yedi'at safeik*) suffices to divide for *asham talui*, so too does *yedi'at safeik* divide for *chatat* — even if a person becomes aware only that he might have sinned, and subsequently continues sinning, then later discovers he definitely did, the acts are divided and he must bring multiple *chataot*.

### Rava's Counterargument

Rava disagrees: *ein yedi'at safeik mechaleket le-chataot* — doubtful awareness does not divide for *chatat*. Only definite awareness does. He reads Rebbi's comparison as an analogy, not a direct application: just as definite awareness creates multiple *chataot*, by analogy doubtful awareness creates multiple *ashamot* — but the *type* of awareness required differs between the two *korbanot*.

### Abaye's Response

Abaye challenges Rava: do you really maintain that doubtful awareness does not divide for *chatat*? If so, a person who experienced only *yedi'at safeik* between acts and later discovered he had definitely sinned would bring only one *chatat*. But then why would he bring multiple *asham taluim*? Abaye's logic is that the comparison between *asham talui* and *chatat* cannot work by analogy — it must be a direct application of the same rule. If the rule for *chatat* is that only definite awareness divides, then you cannot analogically apply it to *asham talui*, because *asham talui* never involves definite awareness. Therefore, the rule must operate identically: *yedi'at safeik* must be sufficient to divide — for both.

### Baraita Evidence

In support, Abaye cites a general principle from a *baraita*: *kol she-challukin be-chatat, challukin be-ashamos* — whatever divides for *sin offerings* divides for *asamot* as well. This demonstrates that the dividing mechanism must be the same for both, and therefore whatever divides for *asham talui* — namely *yedi'at safeik* — must also divide for *chatat*.

## Yom Kippur Mechanism

### Yom Kippur Atonement

The discussion now incorporates *Yom Kippur*. There is a principle that *Yom Kippur* atones for doubtful sins and thereby relieves a person of the obligation to bring an *asham talui* — *Yom Kippur* functions in place of an *asham talui*. At the same time, for a person who is definitively *chayav* a *chatat*, the mere passage of *Yom Kippur* does not cancel the *chatat* obligation. With this in mind, the *Gemara* explores whether *Yom Kippur* can serve as a dividing force analogous to *yedi'at safeik*.

### Pre/Post Yom Kippur Acts

Two background principles are important here. First, when we say awareness divides acts for *chatat* or *asham talui*, one interpretation is psychological — the person consciously recalled the possible sin, which restarts the process. Another interpretation is objective: at the moment of awareness, a *chiyuv* of *asham talui* is created for what came before; subsequent acts are therefore separate from the prior obligation. The *Gemara* elsewhere notes that even the passage of days (*yamim she-beinataim*) can constitute a form of *yedi'ah*, which is difficult to explain psychologically but makes sense if it is about objective *chiyuv*. Second, if *Yom Kippur* functions structurally like an *asham talui*, dissolving the doubtful-sin obligation for what preceded it, then on the objective-*chiyuv* view, it should divide acts — acts before *Yom Kippur* were addressed by one *chiyuv*, acts after begin a new chapter.

## Asham vs. Chatat Awa (II)

### Yom Kippur Challenge

Rava bar Chanan challenges Abaye directly: according to you, who holds that *yedi'at safeik* divides for *chataot*, consider the following — one ate a *kezayis* of *chelev* before *Yom Kippur* and a *kezayis* of *chelev* after *Yom Kippur*, all in a single *he'elem* (uninterrupted state of forgetfulness), without any awareness in between. Since *Yom Kippur* functions structurally like an *asham talui* — and if *yedi'at safeik* divides for *chataot* — should he then bring two *chataot* because *Yom Kippur* intervened? This seems deeply counterintuitive and perhaps absurd. The person never had any awareness at all; he ate in a single continuous state of forgetting. Are we really going to say that the calendar fact of *Yom Kippur* passing divides his undifferentiated forgetful eating into two separate *chatat* obligations?

## Yom Kippur Mechanism (II)

### Awareness Requirement

Abaye defends his position by challenging the premise. He asks: *u-man leima lan de-Yom HaKippurim mechaper al d'lo mityada lei* — who says *Yom Kippur* atones for someone who does not even know he is obligated? Perhaps when the principle states that *Yom Kippur* functions like an *asham talui*, it is limited to someone who is aware of his possible obligation. In the scenario under discussion, the person is in a continuous state of *he'elem* — he has no awareness — and perhaps *Yom Kippur* does not operate as an *asham talui* for such a person at all.

### Yoma Mishna

Rava rejects this defense. The *Mishnah* in Yoma that enumerates what *Yom Kippur* atones for explicitly states *hoda ve-lo hoda* — whether the matter is known to him or not. *Yom Kippur* atones for sins the person does not even know about. One cannot therefore restrict *Yom Kippur's* atoning function to cases of awareness.

### Eating/Drinking Same Day

Rava bar Chanan sharpens the challenge further with a different formulation. A *mishnah* rules: if one ate and drank on *Yom Kippur* in a single state of forgetfulness, he brings only one *chatat*, because eating and drinking both violate the same prohibition of affliction. Now between eating and drinking there must necessarily have been some brief interval of time — and since every moment of *Yom Kippur* functions as an *asham talui* for whatever doubt existed in that moment, if *yedi'at safeik* divides for *chataot*, then that brief interval of *Yom Kippur* should divide the eating and the drinking into two separate *chatat* obligations. Yet the *Mishnah* says only one. This is a powerful concrete challenge from an authoritative *mishnaic* source.

### Unresolved Tension

Abaye attempts a further defense: *u-man leima lan de-chol sha'ata ve-sha'ata mechaper* — who says every individual moment of *Yom Kippur* functions as a separate *asham talui*? Perhaps the entire day constitutes a single act of atonement, operative as a whole from the previous evening through nightfall, not moment by moment. Therefore that brief interval between the eating and the drinking does not constitute an intervening *asham talui*-equivalent that would divide the acts.

Rava bar Chanan responds sharply — the *Gemara* records the phrase *tarda*, which Rashi glosses as something close to *shote*, meaning a naive or obtuse claim — and cites a *baraita*: if on *Yom Kippur* itself a person committed a possible sin, even if it occurred at *im chasheicha*, right at the moment before nightfall, he is *patur* — because *kol ha-yom mechaper*, every part of the day atones. This *baraita* explicitly states that every moment of *Yom Kippur* functions as an atonement mechanism. The defense is therefore untenable.

### Position Attribution

The *Gemara* arrives at an unresolved position on whether *yedi'at safeik* divides for *chataot*. The final suggestion offered is: *teimar Rabbi Zeira le-Rabbi* — attribute Rabbi Zeira's reading to Rebbi; it is Rebbi who holds that *yedi'at safeik* divides for *chataot*, as an extension of his ruling that multiple *asham taluim* are required when *yedi'at safeik* intervenes. The challenges from the *Mishnah* about eating and drinking on *Yom Kippur* and the broader questions raised — these all apply to *Rebbi's* view. *Ha Rabbanan hi* — the rabbis who dispute Rebbi, who hold that only one *asham talui* is required regardless of intervening doubtful awareness, do not face these difficulties, because their entire framework does not treat *yedi'at safeik* as a dividing force.

The sugya thus closes with the tension unresolved and the debate formally assigned to the positions of Rebbi and the *Rabbanan*. The discussion will continue after *Yom Tov*.

---

---

# Keritot 20

## Mit'asek vs. Shogeg

### Mit'asek Definition

We begin at the top of 20a with the concept of *mit'asek*. The word itself reflects a kind of self-involvement or reflexive absorption — one is occupied with a particular act when, incidentally, something else occurs. This distinguishes *mit'asek* from *shogeg*: in the case of *shogeg*, one performs the exact act intended but is unaware of some relevant fact — the nature of the object, or that the act is forbidden. *Mit'asek*, by contrast, involves doing a different physical act than the one intended. A useful illustration is gesticulating and accidentally hitting a light switch; the classic Shabbat case is reaching for one thing and inadvertently touching another.

### Chalavim v'Arayos

The halachic consequences follow from this distinction. A *shogeg* is liable to bring a *korban* if the act is subject to *chayav kares*. A *mit'asek*, because the act is not genuinely attributable to him, is exempt from a *korban* entirely — it is as though the act is not his at all. However, this exemption carries an important qualification: in cases of *chalavim v'arayos* — forbidden fats and illicit sexual relations — because the person derives pleasure from the act, the act cannot be fully divorced from him, and he is treated like a *shogeg* and must bring a *korban*. With that exception, the exemption for *mit'asek* applies *b'chol haTorah kulah* when one is attempting a *heter* and accidentally performs an *issur*.

### Shabbat Mit'asek

On Shabbat, however, a distinct and broader principle applies. Rav Nachman citing Shmuel teaches that *mit'asek* on Shabbat carries its own exemption — not merely the general principle that an unintended act is not attributed to a person, but a specific *pasuk*: *meleches machsheves*, which requires that a Shabbat violation be an intentional, purposeful act. Because of this textual basis, the Shabbat exemption for *mit'asek* applies even when the person was attempting to perform an *issur*. One who is reaching for a cluster of black grapes and instead picks a cluster of green grapes — even though the person was trying to violate Shabbat through the act of picking — is exempt, because the precise act intended was not performed. This is a distinctive *halacha* of Shabbat grounded in *meleches machsheves*.

### Fundamental vs. Technical

This distinction invites a philosophical observation. The first category of *mit'asek* — attempting a *heter* and accidentally performing an *issur* — represents a more fundamental exemption: the act is entirely divorced from the person, as though it never happened. The Shabbat variety is more of a technicality. After all, the person intended to pick grapes and picked grapes; he intended to violate Shabbat and, in a meaningful sense, violated Shabbat. The exemption from a *korban* follows from the technical requirement of *meleches machsheves*, but it does not mean the act is fundamentally unattributable. The practical ramification of this distinction is, for example, the question of *teshuvah*: if one was reaching for a permissible object and accidentally flipped a light switch, there is arguably no need for *teshuvah* whatsoever — the act is not his. But if one was reaching for red grapes and inadvertently picked green grapes on Shabbat, *teshuvah* would still seem to be in order, even if there is no *korban* liability.

---

## Mishna Debate

### Rabbi Shimon's View

The *Mishnah* at the top of 20a presents positions from Rabbi Shimon Shezuri and Rabbi Shimon regarding the parameters of the *mit'asek* debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua. Rabbi Shimon Shezuri states: *lo nechelku al davar shehu mishum shem echad shehu chayav* — there is no debate when the act falls under the same essential category (*shem echad*); in that case, everyone agrees one is liable. The debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua — where Rabbi Eliezer obligates a *chatas* and Rabbi Yehoshua exempts — applies only when the act involves *shnei shemos*, two different categories. What precisely constitutes *shnei shemos* is not immediately clear: does it mean red grapes and green grapes, grapes and figs, or two fundamentally different prohibitions?

Rabbi Yehuda then intervenes and says the debate applies even to a case as similar as black grapes and white grapes. This implies that what Rabbi Shimon Shezuri means by *shnei shemos* involves something more radically different than black and white grapes.

### True Mit'asek

The *Gemara* now turns to its central analytical task: how to reconcile this *Mishnah* — which seems to debate the liability of *mit'asek* in various cases — with the position that by Shabbat, even black grapes and black grapes constitutes *mit'asek* and everyone would agree one is exempt. The answer offered previously was that the *Mishnah* is discussing a special case called *avad melaket milibo*: the picker forgot what he was doing. The scenario is this — the person wanted green grapes, but at the moment of picking he forgot his goal and thought he wanted black grapes, then inadvertently picked the green grapes. At the end, he got what he originally wanted, but not what he was intending at the moment of the act. This is a distinction between *desire* and *intent*: he desired the green grapes but was intending for the black ones. That special case is where the debate applies. But in a true *mit'asek* — reaching for black grapes and getting different black grapes — there is no debate; everyone agrees one is exempt on Shabbat.

### Rabbi Yehuda

The *Gemara* now challenges this reading. Rabbi Yehuda's case of black grapes and white grapes, when set alongside Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's language of *shnei shemos*, seems to be saying the same thing — unless we understand what distinguishes their positions. The *Gemara* proposes: *ela lav mit'asek ika beinaihu* — perhaps the real debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri is whether *mit'asek* itself carries liability. Rabbi Yehuda holds *mit'asek chayav*; Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Shimon Shezuri hold *mit'asek patur*. Under this reading, Rabbi Yehuda's case of black and white grapes is a genuine *mit'asek*, and he is telling us that even real *mit'asek* is sometimes debated. Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's cases of *shnei shemos*, on the other hand, reflect the special *avad melaket milibo* scenario — not true *mit'asek* — and that is where he locates the debate.

### Shem Echad Resolution

The *Gemara* ultimately rejects this approach and reasserts the earlier framework: *mit'asek dekulei alma patur* — in a genuine *mit'asek*, everyone agrees one is exempt on Shabbat. The entire *Mishnah* discussion, including Rabbi Yehuda's case of black and white grapes, pertains exclusively to *avad melaket milibo*. The resolution proceeds as follows. Rabbi Shimon Shezuri holds that in *avad melaket milibo*, when the two items belong to *shem echad* — even black and white grapes, which the *Gemara* now treats as *shem echad* — everyone agrees one is liable, because the similarity is too close. The debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua applies only when it is *shnei shemos* — something like grapes and figs. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees and says the debate applies even in *shem echad*: even something as similar as black and white grapes is subject to dispute, with some holding you may be exempt even there.

What the *Gemara* is effectively doing is reclaiming the principle that true *mit'asek* on Shabbat is universally exempt — even black grapes for black grapes, even candle A for candle B — and consigning the entire *Mishnah* debate to the narrow and unusual case of *avad melaket milibo*, where the person ultimately obtained what he originally wanted but not what he was intending at the moment of action.

---

## Rava on Order

### Candle Baraisa

Rava offers a different reading of the debate between Rabbi Shimon Shezuri and Rabbi Yehuda. He proposes that the *Mishnah* is not about *avad melaket milibo* at all, but rather about a distinct type of case: one in which the person did exactly what he intended to do, but in a different order than planned. The proof is from a *Baraisa*: if one had two candles before him — one lit, one extinguished — and intended to extinguish this one but instead extinguished that one, or intended to light this one and instead lit that one, he is exempt. This illustrates the *mit'asek* principle: even performing the exact type of act intended, on an almost identical object, is sufficient grounds for exemption on Shabbat, because it was not the precise object intended.

### One vs. Two Breaths

The *Baraisa* continues with a more complex scenario: one intended to light one candle and extinguish another, but reversed the order — he extinguished first and then lit. If this happened *binshima achat*, in a single breath — one candle was blown out and the flame simultaneously caught on the neighboring candle — he is liable. If it happened *bishtei nishimot*, in two separate breaths, such that the actions were truly sequential, he is exempt, because he genuinely reversed the intended order.

The *Gemara* notes that this ruling regarding a single breath is not self-evident. One might have said: even in the case of a single breath, the person should be exempt, because *his intention was not fulfilled* — he wanted to light first and then extinguish, and instead he extinguished and then lit. The *Baraisa* therefore teaches: *nehi deakdumumi lo makdim, achurumi nami lo maacher* — granted, he did not do what he wanted to do first; but on the other hand, it was not fully the reverse of what he wanted, because he did not want the extinguishing to come last, and indeed it did not come last — since both actions occurred simultaneously. It was not exactly what he wanted, but neither was it exactly the reverse. That is close enough to his intent to render him liable.

### Machshavto

The *Gemara* clarifies the significance of this *Baraisa* within Rava's framework. The case of two separate breaths — where one truly reverses the intended order — is sufficient to exempt, even when the acts themselves (*shnei shemos*: lighting and extinguishing) are exactly what one intended. This shows how exacting the criterion of intent is on Shabbat: even a reversal of order is enough of a departure from *machshavto*, his intention, to be treated as *mit'asek*. The area of potential debate, in Rava's reading of the *Mishnah*, is when the order issue arises in the context of *shem echad* — for example, two acts of lighting in reversed sequence. There, the difference is so subtle that some authorities may still hold one liable. But when there is a genuine reversal of order in *shnei shemos*, or a genuine *mit'asek* even in *shem echad*, everyone would agree one is exempt on Shabbat.

---

## Shoveling Coals

### Coal Case Setup

The *Gemara* now introduces a *Baraisa* describing a different type of case. One who shovels burning coals on Shabbat — *ha-choteh gechalim b'Shabbat* — is liable to bring a *chatas*. The act of shoveling produces two simultaneous effects: the top coals, which are being moved, are thereby extinguished; and the bottom coals, now exposed, are caused to burn more intensely. The *Tanna Kamma* rules one is liable once; Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar citing Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok rules one is liable twice — once for extinguishing the top coals (*mechabeh*) and once for causing the bottom coals to ignite (*mavir*).

### Havara Dispute

The *Gemara* asks: what exactly is the scenario? If the person intended to do both — to extinguish the top coals and ignite the bottom ones — then why would anyone say he is liable only once? He did precisely what he intended. Conversely, if he did not intend to cause the bottom coals to ignite, then the igniting of the lower coals is a case of *eino mitkavein* — he performed act A (shoveling) and incidentally, as a byproduct, act B (igniting) occurred. On Shabbat, we know that *eino mitkavein* which is a *psik reisha*, a necessary consequence, renders one liable. But the *Gemara* now operates under the assumption that this is *not* a *psik reisha* — it was not necessarily going to happen. In that case, why would anyone say one is liable for the incidental igniting?

The answer, proposed by Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Chanina speaking together, is: the case involves a smelter who explicitly does not want the bottom coals to ignite. He is trying to extinguish the top coals precisely because he wants glowing embers rather than open flames — the flame actually damages the coals he needs for his craft. Rashi reads the word *k'dei* in the text not as "in order to cause the bottom ones to burn," but rather as "in spite of the fact that the bottom ones will burn." The person's focus is entirely on extinguishing; the igniting of the lower coals is not only unintended but genuinely unwanted — *lo nicha lei*.

This transforms the question: what we have is *eino mitkavein*, *lo nicha lei* — an unintended, unwanted consequence. The *Tanna Kamma* exempts because of a further principle: *mekalkel b'hav'arah patur*. For this smelter, the igniting of the coals is destructive to his purpose — it burns away coals he wants to keep as embers. A destructive act (*mekalkel*) is generally exempt on Shabbat, and so even when it comes to fire, the *Tanna Kamma* maintains the exemption. Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok holds *mechayev* because he maintains that *mekalkel b'hav'arah chayav* — when the *melachah* is fire, even a destructive act carries liability.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan confirms that we are speaking of a smelter (*benofeach*) who genuinely has no interest in the flame. Yet even after establishing this, he adds a striking remark: *ad kan lo niskalsah ta'amah shel halachah zu* — the reasoning of this *halachah* has not yet been fully explicated. The explanation given so far is not fully satisfying, and the *Gemara* continues to seek a more adequate account.

### Ami and Chanina

Ami bar Abbin and Chanina bar Abbin both offer a different reading of the case. They suggest that the scenario involves someone who intended to do *both* — to extinguish and to ignite — *kegon sheniskaven lechabos u'lehavir*. If so, why would anyone say he is liable only once rather than twice? The answer lies in a fundamental dispute about the status of *hav'arah*: the *Tanna Kamma* follows Rabbi Yossi's view that the explicit Torah prohibition against kindling fire on Shabbat — *lo tiv'aru esh b'chol moshvoteichem b'yom HaShabbos* — is intended merely as a *lav*, a negative commandment, but not a *melachah* that incurs *karet* or *chatas*. Therefore, one who kindles fire on Shabbat in a case of *shogeg* does not bring a *korban*. Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok follows Rabbi Natan's view that *hav'arah le-chalek yatza'as* — the verse was stated to teach that one is liable separately for each distinct *melachah*, and fire is indeed a full *melachah* carrying *chatas* liability. Under this reading, the debate between the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Tzadok is not about the special circumstances of the smelter or questions of *eino mitkavein* at all; it reduces simply to the dispute whether one incurs a *korban chatas* for *hav'arah*.

Rava then reintegrates this *Baraisa* into his earlier framework about order. He notes that the language of the *Baraisa* — extinguishing and igniting — parallels the candle case discussed earlier. According to Rava, the dispute here is about reversed order: the person intended to first perform one act and then the other, but the two acts happened in the opposite sequence or simultaneously. The second opinion holds one liable twice because order does not matter — both intended acts were accomplished. The *Tanna Kamma* holds one liable only once because there is some departure from the precise intention; the *Shita Mekubetzet* attempts to explain this by arguing that when acts occur simultaneously rather than sequentially, something of the intended structure is preserved — the person cannot be said to have truly reversed his intention — and yet the full doubling of liability is also not warranted. The result is liability once. The precise mechanism remains somewhat difficult to articulate, and the *Gemara* itself does not fully resolve it.

### Rav Ashi

Rav Ashi offers yet a further reading. He frames the case as follows: *kegon deniskaven lechabos vehuvru me'aleihem* — the person intended only to extinguish, and the other coals ignited on their own, without it being a necessary consequence. This returns the case squarely to the domain of *eino mitkavein* without *psik reisha*. The emphasis of *me'aleihem* — "on their own" — signals that the igniting was unexpected and not inevitable.

The *Tanna Kamma* follows Rabbi Shimon's principle that *davar she'eino mitkavein patur* — an unintended consequence does not carry liability. Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi Tzadok follows Rabbi Yehuda's position that an unintended consequence is nonetheless *chayav* — or at minimum *assur*. This is distinct from the *psik reisha* analysis discussed earlier: there, one would need to invoke the special factors of *lo nicha lei* and *mekalkel b'hav'arah*. Here, the scenario is not a *psik reisha* at all — the outcome was not inevitable. The dispute is therefore simply whether Rabbi Shimon or Rabbi Yehuda governs: Rabbi Shimon exempts *eino mitkavein* that is not *psik reisha* entirely; Rabbi Yehuda holds that even when the outcome was not inevitable, once it actually occurred, one is retroactively liable for a *chatas*. One of the *Ba'alei HaTosafot*, the *Ri*, suggests elsewhere that Rabbi Yehuda's position may mean only that such an act is *assur d'rabanan* before the fact, and that even Rabbi Yehuda would agree to exemption from a biblical *chatas*. This *Gemara*, however, seems to read Rabbi Yehuda as imposing genuine biblical liability once the outcome materialized. This same dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon runs throughout Masechet Shabbat and is central to the entire *inyan* of *mitkavein* on Shabbat — making this *sugya*, buried here in the middle of Keritot, a crucial locus for the topic.

---

## Warming with Coals

### Warming Case

A new *Baraisa* is introduced: one who shovels burning coals on Shabbat *lehitchamem bahem* — in order to warm himself with them. This is no longer the case of the smelter who wants embers and dreads flame; here the person genuinely wants the warmth, and a flame happens to arise. One *Baraisa* rules he is liable; another rules he is exempt. The *Gemara* undertakes to resolve the contradiction.

### Obligation Debate

The *Baraisa* that rules liable and the one that rules exempt are addressing different conceptual frameworks. Understanding their disagreement requires introducing a principle that is, in the *Gemara*'s words, one of the most conceptually demanding in all of Hilchot Shabbat.

### Melacha Framework

The concept at stake is *melacha she'eina tzricha legufa* — performing a *melachah* but not for the purpose for which that *melachah* is defined. The classic illustration: a person wants dirt. He digs a hole to get the dirt. On Shabbat, the *melachah* is digging a hole — a form of *binyan*. The person is performing the act of digging, and he knows he is digging a hole; yet he does not want the hole for its own sake. He wants the dirt. Does performing the prescribed *melachah* for a purpose other than its defined purpose exempt him? This is the debate of *melacha she'eina tzricha legufa*, which is itself the subject of dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon.

In our case, one is moving coals. Moving the coals will inevitably produce a flame — Rashi reads it as a *psik reisha*, a necessary consequence. The person knows this will happen and may even welcome the warmth from the flame. Yet what he is doing, properly described, is moving coals, not making a flame. Just as the digger is getting dirt and not making a hole, the coal-shoveler is moving coals and not kindling fire. The *melachah* of fire (*hav'arah*) is technically being performed, but not for the sake of fire as such. One opinion holds *melacha she'eina tzricha legufa chayav aleha*; the other holds *patur aleha*.

### vs. Eino Mitkavein

One might wonder whether *melacha she'eina tzricha legufa* is simply a form of *eino mitkavein*. The *Gemara*'s discussion suggests they are distinct, though the precise boundary is not always explicit. The difference seems to lie in the following: *eino mitkavein* applies when one is not cognizant of the secondary consequence at all — one is dragging an object and may or may not be making a furrow, and one has not even registered the secondary effect as part of what one is doing. *Melacha she'eina tzricha legufa*, by contrast, applies when the person is fully aware that he is performing the prohibited act — he knows he is digging a hole, he knows a flame will arise — but he redefines the purpose of his action. He says: what I am doing is not making a hole, it is getting dirt; what I am doing is not kindling a flame, it is moving coals. That purposive redefinition is what renders the act *she'eina tzricha legufa*.

There is something somewhat counterintuitive here: one might expect that being aware of the prohibited consequence would make a person *more* liable, not less. But the argument runs in the other direction: precisely because he has consciously reidentified what he is doing — I am a digger of dirt, not a maker of holes — he has placed the act outside the defined purpose of the *melachah*. Whether that redefinition is sufficient for exemption is the debate. In the case of *eino mitkavein* that is not *psik reisha*, by contrast, there has been no purposive redefinition at all — the act simply happened as an unregistered byproduct — and the debate there is whether that unregistered, non-necessary consequence still generates liability retroactively.

---

## Blood Laws

### Blood Categories

The *Gemara* now turns to an entirely different subject, opening a new *perek* dedicated to the specific details of prohibitions carrying *karet* and *korban chatas*. The first topic is *dam* — blood. The *Mishnah* identifies which blood carries liability for *karet* and which does not, anchored in the principle *ki hadam hu hanefesh*: blood is identified with the life-force of the creature. Accordingly, liability attaches specifically to *dam shehaneshama yotze bo* — the blood with which the soul of the animal departs, that is, life-blood. Other blood from an animal may carry a *lav* but not *karet* or a *korban chatas*, and the *perek*'s focus is precisely the latter.

The *Mishnah* enumerates cases that carry full *chayav karet* liability: blood from *shechita* — blood that flows at the act of slaughter — whether from a *behema*, *chaya*, or bird, whether kosher or non-kosher species. The inclusion of non-kosher animals is itself noteworthy from the perspective of *issur chal al issur* questions. *Dam nechira* and *dam ikur* — blood resulting from other methods of killing, even without valid *shechita* — are also included. *Dam hakaza* — blood that emerges through bloodletting — is included but with a qualification: only *sheneshama yotze bo*, blood that the soul departs with, renders one liable. Not every drop of blood drawn through bloodletting qualifies as life-blood.

### Blood Types

The *Mishnah* then identifies several categories of blood that do *not* carry liability: *dam hatichel* (blood of the spleen), *dam halev* (blood of the heart), *dam beitzim* (blood in eggs, specifically a blood spot forming within a developing egg, as Rashi's second explanation makes clear from the later *Gemara*), *dam chagavim* (blood of grasshoppers), and *dam tamtzit* — residual blood that is not life-blood. For none of these is one liable for *karet* or obligated in a *chatas*.

The conceptual categories underlying these exclusions are instructive. The blood of the spleen and the heart represents *dam evarim* — blood absorbed within the walls of organs, as distinct from blood coursing through the veins. Experientially, before the microscopic understanding of capillaries, this blood was understood as categorically different from circulatory blood, and it is treated accordingly. Regarding the heart specifically, the *Rishonim* generally hold that the blood in the walls of the heart is what is excluded; blood in the cavity of the heart, which is full arterial blood, may well be life-blood and carry *karet* liability. *Dam tamtzit* is blood of the animal that is nonetheless not life-blood — it may carry a *lav* but not *karet*. The eggs and grasshoppers raise different considerations, addressed in the *Gemara* below.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda takes a stricter position: *Rabbi Yehuda mechayev b'dam hatamtzit* — he holds that even non-life blood of an animal carries full liability. The point of contention, as throughout this *perek*, is whether the liability in question is *karet* and *korban chatas*, not whether there is any prohibition at all; the *lav* may not be disputed.

### Tuma Exclusions

A *Baraisa* is cited that derives the exclusions from a different angle — through the framework of *tuma*. The verse states: *kol dam lo tochalu — l'of ul'vehema* — do not eat any blood, specifying birds and animals. From the juxtaposition of a universal prohibition ("any blood") and a particular specification ("of birds and of animals"), the *Baraisa* derives that the prohibition is calibrated to the specific characteristics that birds and animals share.

### No Prohibition

Those distinguishing characteristics are enumerated: birds and animals have *tuma kala* — a light form of impurity, meaning they can function as food and receive *tuma* from an external source — and *tuma chamura* — a heavy form, meaning they can themselves be a primary source of *tuma* (as a *neveila*). They have both a state of *issur* (when not slaughtered properly) and a state of *heter* (when slaughtered correctly). And they are *min basar* — a type of flesh.

From these characteristics, several exclusions follow. *Dam ha-holech al shtayim* — human blood — is excluded because human beings have *tuma chamura* but not *tuma kala*: a human corpse is among the heaviest sources of *tuma*, but human flesh is never classified as food that receives *tuma* from elsewhere (*tumat ochlin*). Accordingly, human blood falls outside the prohibition entirely. This is why, for instance, one who sucks blood from a cut finger has not violated any biblical prohibition.

The blood of *sheratzim* — certain small creatures — is excluded because even those eight *sheratzim* that are an *av ha-tuma* do not possess the full weight of *tuma chamura* that characterizes *neveila*: they produce *tuma* only through contact, not through carrying, and they render the person *tamei* but not his garments. *Dam beitzim* is excluded because an egg is *ein min basar* — not a type of flesh. Fish and grasshoppers are excluded because *she-kulo heter* — they are entirely in a state of permissibility; they require no *shechita* and may even be consumed alive. For these categories, there is no prohibition against consuming their blood whatsoever, which is why fish blood requires no removal, and the only concern with human blood would be at the rabbinic level. These are categorically different from *dam tamtzit*, which is blood of a *behema* that may carry a *lav* but simply not *karet*.

---

---

# Keritot 21

## Blood Categories

### Overview

Daf 21 continues the discussion of the *issur dam* — the prohibition against consuming blood — and the question of which categories of creatures fall within its scope. The broader agenda of the daf also includes a distinction between *dam hanefesh*, lifeblood, and other types of blood, which bears on whether one incurs *karet* or merely violates a negative commandment. For now, however, the *gemara* is focused on the foundational question: which categories are included in the prohibition and which are entirely excluded? The Torah mentions *oph u-vehemah* — bird and animal — and from that phrase several distinguishing characteristics emerge. These characteristics serve to exclude fish, grasshoppers, humans, and other creatures. The relevant distinguishing features involve whether a species has both a light and a heavy *tumah*, whether there is a distinction between *issur* and *heter* in consuming it, and whether it has flesh classified as meat. Each of these criteria will be developed in turn.

### לעוף ולבהמה

The *gemara* examines why the *pasuk* needed to state both *l'oph* and *l'vehemah* rather than either term alone. Had the *pasuk* stated only *l'oph*, one might have reasoned: birds have no *kilayim* — meaning no fabric material derived from birds can create a *shatnez* problem — and therefore the prohibition should apply only to animals that similarly lack *kilayim*, which would exclude sheep, whose wool is subject to *shatnez*. Hence it was necessary to also say *l'vehemah*. Conversely, had the *pasuk* stated only *l'vehemah*, one might have limited the prohibition to animals that do not carry the prohibition of *eima la-banim* — the commandment against taking the mother together with her young — which would have excluded kosher birds that are subject to that prohibition. Hence it was also necessary to say *l'oph*. Both terms together ensure the full range of birds and animals is covered.

### Klal u-Frat u-Klal

At this point the *gemara* raises a challenge: why not read *kol dam* as a *klal*, *l'oph v'l'vehemah* as a *prat*, and apply the rule of *klal u-frat* — in which case nothing beyond *oph u-vehemah* would be included? The *gemara* answers that there is a second *klal*: *nefesh asher tochal kol dam ve-nichresah ha-nefesh ha-hi me-ameha* — whoever eats any blood shall be cut off — which constitutes a general statement following the *prat*, giving us a *klal u-frat u-klal*. Under that rule the prohibition extends to things similar to *oph u-vehemah* but is not limited exclusively to them.

An objection is raised, however: the first *klal* concerns the prohibition of eating blood, while the second *klal* concerns the punishment of *karet*. Since they address different matters, perhaps they cannot be combined into a single *klal u-frat u-klal*. The *gemara* responds that this is the method of the school of *Rabbi Yishmael*, who does apply *klal u-frat u-klal* even when the concluding *klal* and the opening *klal* address different topics — one the prohibition and one the punishment — and even though the two *klalim* are not perfectly parallel.

### Defining Features

With the *klal u-frat u-klal* established, the *gemara* articulates the principle: whatever shares the defining features of *oph u-vehemah* is included, and whatever does not is excluded. The *gemara* enumerates these features: *oph* and *vehemah* possess both a light *tumah* — the capacity to receive *tumah* as food — and a heavy *tumah* — the capacity to be a source of *tumah* as *neveilah* or *nevelat oph*. They also have *issur ve-heter*, meaning they are forbidden unless properly slaughtered, which distinguishes them from fish and grasshoppers. And they have the quality of being flesh, *min basar*, which excludes things like eggs. Anything sharing these features falls within the prohibition; anything lacking them does not.

---

## Koy Category

### Koy Independence

Having established the abstract criteria for inclusion, the *gemara* asks what, at the end of the day, is actually being included beyond *oph u-vehemah* themselves. *Chayah* is assumed to be subsumed within *behemah*. So what additional creature requires this elaborate *klal u-frat u-klal* framework in order to be included? *Abba bar Avin* answers: *le-atuyei damo shel koy* — to include the blood of the *koy*, an animal whose status as either *chayah* or *behemah* is uncertain, or perhaps — as the *gemara* here maintains — is neither.

The *gemara* then asks: if the *koy* is merely a creature of uncertain status, either a *chayah* or a *behemah* but we cannot determine which, why would a *pasuk* be needed to prohibit its blood? Since its blood would be forbidden under either classification, the question is moot. The *gemara* therefore concludes that the *tanna* who required the *klal u-frat u-klal* held that a *koy* is *biryah bifnei atzmah* — a species entirely unto itself, neither *chayah* nor *behemah*. Because it falls into no existing category, an explicit derivation is necessary to include it. This also carries a practical consequence: according to this position, eating the fat of a *koy* is not merely a *safek issur* for which one might bring an *asham talui*; it is a *vadai issur* with direct biblical prohibition, and a definite *chatat* would apply.

### Koy Laws

Granting that the *koy* is its own category, the *gemara* proceeds to establish each prohibition that applies to it, since it cannot simply be treated as a *chayah* or *behemah*. The prohibition of *chelev*: derived from *mikol chelev* — from *any* fat — which includes even the fat of a *koy*. The prohibition of *neveilah*: derived from *mikol neveilah* — from *any neveilah* — which includes a creature that is neither *chayah* nor *behemah*. The prohibition of *gid hanasheh*: since the *pasuk* forbids eating the sinew that is on the *kaf ha-yarech* — the mound of the thigh — and the *koy* anatomically possesses such a thigh, the prohibition applies to it by virtue of having that body part, regardless of categorical classification.

### Koy Rulings

With *chelev*, *dam*, *neveilah*, and *gid hanasheh* all derived, the *gemara* turns to the related questions of *tumah* and *shechitah*. No independent *pasuk* is required for these, the *gemara* reasons: *midechol mili rabyei rachmana ke-vehemah* — since the Torah has assimilated the *koy* to a *behemah* in all other matters, its *tumah* and *shechitah* requirements follow by the same logic. One subtle but important point emerges from this discussion: the *koy* is treated like a *behemah* for purposes of *chelev*, not like a *chayah*. A *chayah*'s fat is permitted; a *koy*'s fat is forbidden as a *vadai issur*. This distinguishes the *koy*-as-independent-species view from the *koy*-as-doubt view in a concrete and practically significant way. The *gemara* notes a certain parallel between the *koy* and the *androginos* — the *androginos* likewise potentially constitutes a *min bifnei atzmo* — and the discussion of the *koy* here illustrates just how far-reaching that premise can be once it is accepted.

---

## Human Flesh

### Live Human Meat

The *gemara* addresses flesh cut from a living human. Such flesh is not subject to the prohibition of *basar min ha-chai*, which applies to animals, nor does it inherently carry *tumah* in the way *neveilah* does. However, the *gemara* establishes that human flesh from a living person *can* be classified as food — and therefore can receive *tumat ochlin* — but only if two conditions are met: *machshavah*, the intent to use it as human food, and *hechsher*, prior contact with liquid.

This is a striking ruling. The principle of *klal amru be-tumah* is that anything designated for human consumption is susceptible to *tumah* and remains so until it becomes unfit even for the consumption of dogs: *kol ha-meyuchad le-ochel adam tamei ad she-yipaseil me-achilat kelev*. The threshold to acquire food status requires designation for human consumption; the threshold to lose that status is more demanding, requiring that the item become completely inedible. This asymmetry — a lower bar to acquire food status, a higher bar to lose it — reflects a general principle that might be described as a kind of halachic stickiness: once a status is acquired, it adheres and is difficult to dislodge.

In the case of human flesh from a living person, however, no automatic food designation exists. One must affirmatively intend to treat it as food. And if the *machshavah* was for dog food rather than human food — *machshavah le-kelev lav machshavah hi* — it does not suffice. Only intent for human consumption counts.

There is an obvious question here: given the extreme abnormality of treating human flesh as food, should the principle of *batla da'ato etzel kol adam* — that one's idiosyncratic intention is overridden when no normal person would act this way — not apply and categorically exclude it? The *gemara* notably does not invoke this principle here for live human flesh, which is striking. The apparent implication is that, however unusual, the possibility is not treated as so categorically beyond the pale that it nullifies the *machshavah*. A separate question arises regarding *hechsher*: whether human blood can serve as the activating liquid for this purpose is itself subject to discussion, since *dam nefesh* and *dam makah* are treated differently regarding whether they function as *machshir* liquids.

### Dead Human Status

Once a person dies, the analysis changes entirely. The *gemara* states: *hanei milei mechayim* — all of the above applies only to flesh from a living human. After death, the corpse transmits only *tumah chamurah* — specifically *tumas meis* — and the category of food *tumah* becomes entirely irrelevant. The reasoning offered is *batla da'ato etzel kol adam*: no normal person, under any circumstances, considers a human corpse as food.

This invites a question, however: the *gemara* had just acknowledged that flesh from a *living* human can, with appropriate *machshavah*, be considered food. Why does *batla da'ato* apply to the corpse but not to live human flesh? This is noted as genuinely difficult. One might have expected the principle to operate with equal force in both cases, or at least to have been applied first to the arguably more disturbing case of live human flesh. The *gemara* does not resolve this tension explicitly here.

---

## Neveilah Food

### Neveilah Types

The preceding discussion of human flesh raises a parallel question about *neveilah* of animals. When an animal dies, its flesh becomes a source of *tumah chamurah* as *neveilat behemah*. Why, then, does it matter whether such flesh is classified as food and can receive *tumat ochlin*? Is not the heavier *tumah* of *neveilah* simply dominant?

To address this, the *gemara* introduces a *mishnah* that distinguishes among different types of *neveilah* with respect to their food status. *Neveilas behemah teme'ah* — the carcass of a non-kosher animal — requires *machshavah* to be considered food, and this applies regardless of whether it is in a city or a village. Similarly, *neveilas oph tahor bikfarim* — the carcass of a kosher bird in a village — also requires *machshavah*. By contrast, *neveilas behemah tehorah* — the carcass of a kosher animal — and *neveilas oph tahor* in a city, along with *chelev* sold in marketplaces, do not require *machshavah*; they are presumed to be food.

Why does a *neveilah* not require *hechsher*? Because anything destined to carry a heavy *tumah* is exempt from the liquid-contact prerequisite, as derived from the school of *Rabbi Yishmael*: just as seeds require *hechsher* because they will not themselves become sources of heavy *tumah*, so too only things that will not become sources of heavy *tumah* require *hechsher*. Since *neveilah* itself will become a source of *tumah*, it needs no prior contact with liquid.

### No Hechsher

The principle is thus: meat of *neveilah* does not require *hechsher* because it will itself be a source of heavy *tumah*. But it may still require *machshavah*, since not every type of *neveilah* is automatically assumed to be desired for consumption. The fact that a human corpse requires neither — because *tumas meis* supersedes all food-status categories — is precisely what the earlier analysis demonstrated. The *neveilah* of an animal, by contrast, does not completely eliminate the relevance of food classification, as will be shown.

### Half-Kezayit

*Rav* poses the challenge directly: if *neveilah* is already *tamei* in its own right, why does it matter whether we call it *tumat ochlin*? *Rabbi Chiya* responds with a concrete scenario. Suppose one has less than a *kebaitza* of food — the minimum amount needed to receive *tumat ochlin* — and augments it with less than a *kezayit* of *neveilah*. Specifically: one has a *kebaitza* minus a half-*kezayit* of ordinary food, and combines it with a half-*kezayit* of *neveilah*. Together they form a *kebaitza*, enough to receive *tumah* as food. But the half-*kezayit* of *neveilah* is insufficient on its own to transmit *tumah* as *neveilah* — a full *kezayit* is required. Therefore in this case it matters enormously to classify the *neveilah* as food: as food, the combined mass can receive *tumah*; as *neveilah* alone, the sub-*kezayit* quantity cannot transmit it.

The *gemara* then asks: in this scenario — where the *neveilah* is only a half-*kezayit* — it will never become a source of heavy *tumah*, so why does it not require *hechsher* after all? The answer given is that the half-*kezayit* of *neveilah* remains fundamentally of the category of *neveilah*. If even half a *kezayit* more were added, it would become a full *kezayit* of *neveilah* and would be a source of *tumah*. Since it is structurally of the *neveilah* category — even if the present quantity falls short — it does not require *hechsher*. Ordinary foods that have no *neveilah* component at all require *hechsher* precisely because they will never become sources of heavy *tumah*; but anything with even a partial *neveilah* component retains the exemption from *hechsher*.

The *mishnah*'s distinction between *neveilas behemah teme'ah* and *neveilas behemah tehorah* with respect to the need for *machshavah* is puzzling. Both involve animals whose carcasses non-Jews might eat. One would expect non-Jews to be as inclined to eat dead non-kosher animals as dead kosher ones — indeed, in the ancient world, pork was an extremely common food source. The *gemara*'s approach may be that the relevant scenario involves animals that died of natural causes rather than those slaughtered without *shechitah*, in which case a natural death by disease might be presumed less appealing even in the non-Jewish market. But the precise basis for the distinction between kosher and non-kosher animals remains unclear.

### Encased Neveilah

*Rabbi Chanina* offers an alternative scenario for the relevance of food classification. Rather than a sub-*kezayit* of *neveilah*, suppose there is a full *kezayit* of *neveilah* enclosed within dough — the classic case of a *kreplach*-like structure — where the combined meat-and-dough is the size of a *kebaitza*. If something *tamei* touches the outside of the dough, it does not come into contact with the *neveilah* inside. Therefore the item cannot receive *tumah* simply by virtue of the *neveilah* it contains — touching the outer dough does not constitute touching the *neveilah*. However, by classifying the whole structure as food, the outer dough can receive *tumat ochlin* when touched by something *tamei*, since together they constitute a *kebaitza* of food.

The *gemara* challenges: if the enclosed *neveilah* is not transmitting *tumah* through touch, why does the structure not require *hechsher*? The answer is that the *neveilah* inside can still transmit *tumah* through *masa* — carrying — even if not through direct contact. Since the *neveilah*, when carried, does transmit *tumah*, the exemption from *hechsher* applies. The relevance of food classification is thus limited to cases of touch on the outer surface, where the carrier does not come into direct contact with the *neveilah* itself.

---

## Human Flesh (II)

### Corpse Tumah

The *gemara* now returns to the contrast between *neveilah* of animals and human corpse flesh, this time in light of the enclosed-dough scenario. One might have thought that even for a human corpse, the food-status question would be relevant in the *neveilah*-in-dough scenario — for there, the corpse flesh would not transmit *tumah* through touch of the outer dough. The *gemara* rejects this: *tumas meis* operates differently from other *tumah*. It is subject to the principle of *tumah boka ve-olah boka ve-yoredet* — the *tumah* of a corpse breaks through upward and downward. Unless there is a *tefach* of open space and a covering constituting a proper *ohel*, the *tumah* of the corpse radiates directly through whatever surrounds it. Therefore even dough encasing corpse flesh does not block the corpse's *tumah*; anyone above or below it is affected regardless of direct contact. Food classification is thus irrelevant for corpse flesh even in the enclosed scenario.

Interestingly, this second treatment of the corpse question does not invoke *batla da'ato etzel kol adam* — the principle used earlier. Here the *gemara* reasons instead from the mechanics of *tumas meis*, which renders food classification structurally moot regardless of whether anyone would conceivably eat such flesh. This framing offers a more internally consistent treatment: from the standpoint of the *tumah* laws, live human flesh and dead human flesh are treated symmetrically as potential foods in principle — it is only the overpowering, penetrating nature of *tumas meis* that makes the designation irrelevant for the corpse, not a categorical exclusion from food status. This is admittedly still somewhat puzzling given the earlier appeal to *batla da'ato*, but at least the second passage does not compound the difficulty.

---

## Blood Sources

### Fish/Locust Blood

With the structural analysis of the *issur dam* complete, the *gemara* turns to a series of specific blood categories and their halachic status. A *baraita* has stated that the blood of fish and grasshoppers is *mutar* because they are *kulo heter* — entirely permissible. The *gemara* interrogates what this phrase means. It cannot mean that all their parts may be eaten, since a *chayah* likewise has no prohibited *chelev* and yet its blood is forbidden. Nor can it mean they have no *gid hanasheh*, since birds also lack a *gid hanasheh* prohibition yet their blood is forbidden. The *gemara* therefore concludes: *d'lo ba'ei shechitah* — they do not require *shechitah*. Fish and grasshoppers have no *issurim* that *shechitah* comes to address; they may be eaten live, and their entire status is one of unqualified permissibility. That is the characteristic that distinguishes them from birds and animals and justifies excluding their blood from the prohibition.

### Rodent Blood

The *gemara* then records a statement of *Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Rav*: *dam sheratzim lokim alav* — one who eats a *kezayit* of rodent blood receives lashes. A *baraita* is cited that appears to contradict this: it lists blood of bipeds, blood of *sheratzim* and *remasim* as forbidden, but specifies *ve-ein chayavin alav* — one does not incur the transgression. The *gemara* attempts to argue that *ein chayavin alav* means only that one does not incur *karet*, but not that there is no *lav*. Two responses are given. First, if there were a *lav* for rodent blood, the *baraita* would have listed it alongside the other categories subject to a *lav* but not *karet*, such as blood of internal organs and limbs — yet it does not. Second, the *baraita* that has occupied the entire daf explicitly excludes *sheratzim* from the prohibition verse, *yatza dam sheratzim she-ein bahem tumah chamurah*, indicating that the exclusion operates at the level of the prohibition itself, not merely at the level of *karet*.

*Rabbi Zeira* resolves the apparent ruling of *Rav*: *hisru bo mishum sheretz lokeh* — if someone was warned that the blood constitutes *sheretz* and then consumed it, he receives lashes, but not on account of the blood prohibition. Rather, blood of a rodent is treated as the meat of the rodent itself, and one transgresses the prohibition of eating *sheretz*, not the prohibition of blood. The principle at work here is that blood is treated as part of the meat of the creature from which it comes, at least for the purposes of applying other prohibitions. This connects to the earlier debate between *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* regarding whether blood of *neveilah* transmits *tumah* like the meat of *neveilah* — the underlying logic is the same: blood is of a piece with the flesh.

### Human Blood

*Rav* states: *dam dagim she-kinso assur* — if one collects fish blood in a vessel, it is forbidden. The *gemara* immediately asks from the *baraita* that explicitly permits fish blood. The *gemara* resolves: the *baraita*'s permission applies when the blood was not deliberately collected; *Rav*'s prohibition applies when it was gathered together. The concern when collected is one of appearance — it resembles animal blood, and consuming it in that form creates a *marit ayin* issue.

### Fish vs. Human

With this distinction in place, the *gemara* raises a further question: the same *baraita* that permitted fish blood stated that human blood carries some prohibition. If fish blood is only problematic when collected, the *baraita*'s statement about human blood must also be referring to the uncollected case — which would mean that even uncollected human blood is forbidden. But this seems too strict. The *gemara* resolves by refining the fish-blood ruling: the *baraita*'s permission for fish blood applies specifically when the fish has its scales — *de-it bei kaskasin* — present together with the blood, even in a cup. The scales serve as an identifying marker, dispelling the appearance of animal blood and removing the *marit ayin* concern. *Rav*'s prohibition applies when the blood is collected and there are no scales present to identify it.

The comparison to human blood follows accordingly. Human blood collected in a cup and without any identifying feature is forbidden by rabbinic enactment. Uncollected human blood — such as blood that incidentally drips onto food — is not technically forbidden but falls under a norm of *mitzvot prosh*, of avoiding unseemly behavior rather than a formal *issur*.

### Gum Blood

The *gemara* cites a *baraita* that illustrates the practical boundary: if one has bleeding gums and blood gets onto a piece of bread, one should scrape it off before eating. But blood that is still between one's teeth may simply be swallowed without concern. *Rashi* explains that the instruction to scrape away the blood on the bread reflects a norm of *mitzvot prosh* — conduct befitting propriety — rather than a formal rabbinic prohibition; the *baraita* conspicuously does not use the word *assur*. Blood that remains in the mouth, still on one's own body, is a fortiori unproblematic. Exactly where the line falls between the clearly permitted — blood still in the mouth — and the unseemly but not forbidden — blood on the bread — and the actually prohibited — collected human blood in a cup — is a question raised by *Tosafot* elsewhere, and one whose full elaboration goes beyond the scope of the present daf.

---

---

# Keritot 22

## Human Blood Status

### Blood Categories Overview

The current *perek* opens with the *parsha* of *dam shechita*, concerned primarily with which categories of blood fall under the *issur* of blood consumption. The *mishnah* at the bottom of 21b establishes that the blood of humans, fish, and grasshoppers is permitted. The discussion of fish blood invoked the concept of *maris ayin*: although the language of the *mishnah* was *assur*, the context indicated a rabbinic concern that fish blood gathered into a cup resembles forbidden animal blood — a concern dispelled if the fish scales are kept nearby. Human blood was similarly characterized as *assur*, though the precise degree of that prohibition requires further analysis. There are essentially two distinct cases: blood pooled into a cup, which genuinely resembles animal blood, and blood that has left the body but is not gathered, such as blood visible on a loaf of bread (*dam al ha-kikar*).

### Rav Sheshes on Human Blood

On this question, Rav Sheshes states that for *dam mehalechei shtayim* — the blood of bipeds — not even a *mitzvas prisha* applies. This is a striking formulation: Rav Sheshes is not merely saying that human blood carries no biblical or even rabbinic prohibition in the technical sense, but that it is not even subject to the kind of religious fastidiousness or unseemly quality that would otherwise attach to it. There is no requirement to distance oneself from it whatsoever.

### Braita on Blood Types

The *gemara* challenges this with the *braita* cited the previous day: the blood of the *tichol*, the heart (*dam ha-lev*), the kidneys (*dam ha-klayos*), and the other organs (*dam ha-eivarim*) — these carry a *lo ta'aseh*, a negative biblical prohibition, even though they are not *dam ha-neshama*, the life blood. Then the *braita* continues: *dam mehalechei shtayim*, the blood of bipeds, as well as *dam shratzim ve-remasim*, the blood of rodents and creeping creatures, is *assur* — but one does not incur *chiyuv* for it. That is, it is not merely that *kares* does not apply (which was the ruling for organ blood); rather, not even a negative biblical prohibition is transgressed. Nevertheless, it is still *assur* — apparently at a rabbinic level. The blood of rodents, it should be noted, may well be biblically forbidden, but as part of the rodent itself rather than as *blood*. Yet human blood appears clearly from this *braita* to carry at minimum a rabbinic prohibition. How, then, can Rav Sheshes say there is no problem whatsoever?

### Separation Requirement

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *ki tanya assur*, when the *braita* says human blood is forbidden, that refers specifically to blood that has separated from the body (*de-peirash*). When Rav Sheshes said there is not even a *mitzvas prisha*, he was speaking of blood that has not yet left the body (*de-lo peirash*). The *gemara* then cites the relevant distinction: *dam she-al gabei ha-kikar*, blood that has gotten onto a loaf of bread, must be scraped off before eating. But *she-bein ha-shinnayim*, blood still caught between the teeth and within the mouth, one may simply suck out and swallow without concern. The principle, then, is that once blood separates from the body it becomes problematic, and the statement of Rav Sheshes applies only to blood still within the body.

This leaves a certain ambiguity in the middle case: blood that has left the body but is not gathered into a vessel — the *kikar* case. Is the *kikar* case categorized as a full *issur de-rabbanan* similar to blood pooled in a cup, or is it merely the level of *mitzvas prisha*, an aesthetic-religious impropriety short of technical prohibition? The *gemara*'s resolution does not fully resolve that question. A related practical question raised by the *poskim* is the case of a bleeding finger: if one sucks or licks one's own finger, the blood is coming from outside the mouth into the mouth, yet it is arguably still connected to the body. The precise definition of *prisha* — separation — in that case is a matter of discussion.

### Milk vs. Blood

Some authorities attach the statement of Rav Sheshes not to our *mishnah* but to a different *braita*, one that appears in the *gemara* of Ketubot and concerns the status of human milk. That *braita* raises a *kal va-chomer*: a non-*kosher* animal, even though its corpse creates less *tumah* than a human corpse, still has its milk forbidden by a negative prohibition. Human beings, whose corpse generates far greater *tumah* than an animal carcass — as *zavim*, *niddos*, and in various other ways — would seemingly have their milk forbidden *a fortiori*, and perhaps even with a *lav*.
