The *braita* rejects this: the verse says *ve-zeh lachem ha-tamei*, "this is impure for you," referring specifically to the animal world. *Zeh tamei* — only these categories of animals generate the prohibitions of forbidden food, and therefore milk of humans is not *tamei* but *tahor* and entirely permitted.

The same verse is then applied to human blood. One might have thought that since blood is uniformly forbidden across all animals, human blood should be no exception. The *braita* teaches otherwise: *zeh tamei* — the prohibition is specifically within the animal world, and human blood is likewise *tahor* by *din Torah*. This is a different *drasha* from the *klal u-frat u-klal* derivation cited elsewhere, but both arrive at the same conclusion: human blood carries no biblical prohibition. It is on this *braita* that Rav Sheshes states his ruling — *afilu mitzvas prisha ein bo*, there is not even a duty of fastidiousness — declaring that even the most minimal concern does not apply to human blood.

The comparison to human milk raises an interesting parallel. The *gemara* in Ketubot discusses whether a child, after being weaned, may return to nurse from his mother, using the language *k'ilu yonek sheketz*, as if one were nursing from something repugnant. This suggests that the concept of *prisha* is not simply *maris ayin* — it does not depend on whether something resembles forbidden blood or milk. There is a separate category of seemliness and religious appropriateness. This same quality applies to human blood in certain contexts, and the *gemara* in Ketubot explores whether it applies to human milk as well.

---

## Life Blood Definition

### Heart Blood Removal

The *gemara* now cites a *mishnah* from Chullin: *ha-lev kor'o u-motzi es damo* — the heart of a slaughtered animal must be cut open and its blood expressed. If one did not do so, one does not transgress a prohibition retroactively, but the requirement is to make an incision and remove the blood from the heart cavity before eating. This *mishnah* provides the entry point for a broader discussion of *dam ha-neshama*, the life blood.

### Heart Blood Source

The *gemara* asks a remarkable physiological question: where did the blood in the heart come from? This question makes more sense in light of the ancient understanding of cardiac anatomy. The *gemara* and *Rashi* reflect a view, common to classical antiquity and maintained well into the early modern period, that the heart is not an organ of blood circulation but rather an organ of breathing. According to this view, breath enters through the lungs, passes to the heart to be warmed, and then is distributed throughout the body. Indeed, the *Chacham Tzvi*, who wrote an extensive *teshuvah* on the significance of the heart in the context of a famous chicken case, speaks consistently of the heart as circulating *breath*, not blood. It was only William Harvey, approximately four hundred years ago, who demonstrated that the heart circulates blood, and even then the halakhic literature was slow to incorporate this understanding.

Within this framework, the phrase *mishas ha-neshama yotze'ah* — from the moment the *neshama* departs — becomes precisely comprehensible. *Neshama* is closely related to *neshima*, breathing. When the animal dies, the breath (*neshama*) that was in the heart exits, creating a vacuum, and blood is thereby drawn into the heart. The *gemara*'s question is therefore not asking how life blood enters the heart as a matter of circulation; it is asking how any blood at all came to be in the heart, given that the heart's function was understood to be respiratory. The answer — that the exit of the breath at death creates a vacuum that draws blood in — is the *gemara*'s own explanation of what *dam ha-neshama* means in the context of the heart.

### Death Definition

This discussion connects naturally to the halakhic definition of death, which throughout the *gemara* and classical authorities is consistently defined in terms of breathing rather than cardiac activity. The relevant texts, from *Rashi* forward, define death by the cessation of spontaneous respiration. Where a *Rashi* mentions the heart in the context of checking for signs of life, even there the heart is conceived as part of the respiratory system, not as an independent circulatory organ. Any mention of the heart in pre-modern halakhic literature must be understood against this background: those authorities were discussing the heart as they understood it — a breathing apparatus — not as modern medicine understands it.

This has direct implications for contemporary discussions of brain death and organ donation. The practical question in organ donation is whether death may be declared upon cessation of breathing even if the heart continues to beat. The heart has an internal pacemaker and will continue to beat independently even after respiration ceases; if one waits for cardiac arrest, the other organs are deprived of oxygen and become unsuitable for donation. If the halakhic definition of death is cessation of spontaneous breathing — as every *gemara* and every classical *posek* states — then the question of brain death as an alternative criterion becomes in many ways beside the point. The real halakhic question is not brain death versus breathing, but whether both breathing *and* circulation are required, or only breathing. And on this point, the *gemara* and all the *rishonim* speak exclusively of breathing.

### Bloodletting Dispute

Having established what *dam ha-neshama* means in the context of an animal dying, the *gemara* turns to the parallel case during bloodletting (*hakazah*). During bloodletting, the animal does not die, so one cannot speak literally of blood "departing with the *neshama*." The relevant formulation therefore shifts to *dam she-ha-neshama teluyah bo* — blood upon which the *neshama* is dependent, i.e., life blood. What exactly is that during the process of bloodletting?

The process of bloodletting, as described by the *gemara* and *Rashi*, proceeds in stages: first a small drip, then a powerful squirting flow (*kilu'ach*), then a dripping tail at the end. There is also mention of an initial black drop (*tipa mashcheret*) at the outset, before the red blood begins.

Rabbi Yochanan holds that only the blood in the squirting stage constitutes *dam ha-neshama*; the initial and final dripping stages are *dam tamtzit*, non-life blood. Resh Lakish holds that from the black drop onward (*mi-tipa mashcheret va-eilach*) — meaning once the red blood begins, even if it is only dripping — it is life blood.

The *gemara* challenges Resh Lakish from a *braita*: *kol zman she-mekale'ach* — only as long as the blood is squirting is it life blood; *yatza dam ha-tamtzit*, excluded is the dripping blood, *mipnei she-hu shotet*, because it only drips. This *braita* appears to support Rabbi Yochanan fully, contradicting Resh Lakish. The *gemara* attempts to reinterpret the *braita* on behalf of Resh Lakish: the *braita* is actually excluding the black blood (*dam ha-mashchir*), while conceding that the initial and final red dripping blood — even though it only drips — is still *dam ha-nefesh*. However, it is acknowledged that this reading is difficult to sustain from the plain language of the *braita*. Resh Lakish is ultimately left responding *tannai* — admitting that his position corresponds to a minority opinion among the *tannaim*, specifically that of Rabbi Shimon, while Rabbi Yochanan's position corresponds to that of Rabbi Elazar (or Rabbi, according to some variants).

A further *braita* is cited from the school of Rabbi Yishmael, deriving from the verse *ve-dam chalalim yishte* — "and they will drink the blood of corpses" — that blood is classified as a liquid capable of rendering produce susceptible to *tumah* (*machshir*). The *gemara* specifies that this applies to post-mortem blood of humans, while the squirting blood (*dam kilu'ach*), which is life blood, is excluded from being *machshir*. Tosafot notes that the rule is the reverse for *behema*: there, the squirting blood is *machshir*, derived from a separate *pasuk* (*al ha-aretz tishpachenu ka-mayim*), while the post-mortem blood is not. One suggested explanation for why the initial drop appears black is that a small drop coagulates and darkens far more rapidly than a larger volume of blood — an interesting observation that fits the *gemara*'s description well.

### Two Vessel Question

Rami bar Chama posed a question to Rabbi Zeira: if one lets blood from an animal and collects it into two vessels — the first filling up and then a second being used — what is the law? Rabbi Zeira replies that this is simply a direct application of the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish. According to Resh Lakish, both vessels contain life blood (since the red blood throughout is *dam ha-neshama*), and therefore if one ate from both, one would be liable for two *chatta'ot*. According to Rabbi Yochanan, only the first vessel — which primarily contains the squirting blood — consists of life blood, while the second vessel contains only the dripping end-blood, which is *dam tamtzit*. Consequently, Rabbi Yochanan holds one is liable only one *chattat*, for consumption of the first vessel.

---

## Rabbi Yehuda's View

### All Blood Kares

Having concluded the discussion of the bloodletting dispute, the *gemara* notes the position of Rabbi Yehuda: *Rabbi Yehuda mechayev be-dam ha-tamtzit*. Rabbi Yehuda holds that one incurs *kares* not only for consuming *dam ha-neshama* but for all blood of animals — including *dam tamtzit*, the non-life blood. The question of exactly how broadly this extends — whether it includes blood absorbed within the walls of organs — is left somewhat open, but any blood that exits through the veins is not subject to the distinction between life blood and non-life blood according to Rabbi Yehuda.

### Atonement Blood

Rabbi Elazar clarifies an important caveat: *modeh Rabbi Yehuda le-inyan kapparah*. Even though Rabbi Yehuda treats all blood equally for purposes of the *kares* prohibition on consumption, he agrees that for purposes of atonement — i.e., blood used in sacrificial service on the *mizbe'ach* — only life blood qualifies. The *pasuk* states *ki ha-dam hu ba-nefesh yechapper*: the blood atones through the *nefesh*, through its life force. Therefore *dam she-ha-nefesh yotze'ah bo mekhapper*, only blood with which the *neshama* departs can effect atonement, *ve-she-eino ha-nefesh yotze'ah bo eino mekhapper*. The two categories are conceptually maintained even in Rabbi Yehuda's system; they differ only in their practical consequence for eating.

### Sifra Drasha

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports this reading from a *braita* that tracks with the *Sifra*, the halakhic *midrash* on Vayikra, which is attributed to Rabbi Yehuda. The *pasuk* states *kol dam lo tochelu* — you shall not eat any blood. The *braita* asks: why does the *pasuk* say *kol dam*, all blood? Since it has already been stated *ki ha-dam hu ba-nefesh yechapper*, one might have thought that only sacrificial life blood incurs *kares* — perhaps the prohibition is specifically calibrated to blood that serves the atonement function. *Kol dam* — the word *kol*, any — comes to teach that even *dam chullin* (non-consecrated blood) and *dam tamtzit* (non-life blood) are included in the prohibition, and one does incur *kares* for them. Yet the very structure of the *drasha* demonstrates that Rabbi Yehuda acknowledges the category of *dam ha-neshama* as the blood used for sacrificial atonement — it is only for the eating prohibition that he extends *kares* to all blood. And as the *gemara* notes: *stam Sifra mani Rabbi Yehuda hi* — the unattributed position of the *Sifra* reflects the view of Rabbi Yehuda.

---

## Asham Talui Scope

### Me'ilah Dispute

The *gemara* returns to the main topic of the *perek*: the scope of *asham talui*. It is established that one brings an *asham talui* for doubtful violation of a sin that would otherwise carry a *chatat*. The question here is whether an *asham talui* is also brought when one is uncertain whether one committed *me'ilah* — misappropriation of consecrated property. A definite *me'ilah* requires an *asham me'ilos*. Does a doubtful *me'ilah* require an *asham talui*? Rabbi Akiva says yes; the *chachamim* exempt.

*Me'ilah* differs from the standard *chatat* case in two ways. First, the definite violation calls for an *asham*, not a *chatat*. Second, willful *me'ilah* does not carry *kares*: according to Rabbi it carries *misah bidei shamayim*, and according to the *chachamim* it is a negative prohibition — but no one holds it carries *kares*.

Rabbi Akiva further concedes: *umodeh Rabbi Akiva she-eino meivi es me'ilaso ad she-yivada lo* — even according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds one brings an *asham talui* for doubtful *me'ilah*, the actual principal payment (*me'ilaso*, the money owed to *hekdesh*) together with the added fifth (*chomesh*) is not brought until one knows for certain that one actually misappropriated. The *asham talui* itself is not conditioned on payment; the financial obligation awaits certainty. When one does become certain, one then brings the *asham vadai* and pays.

### Tarfon's Strategy

Rabbi Tarfon, who agrees in principle with Rabbi Akiva that an *asham talui* is appropriate for doubtful *me'ilah*, offers a pragmatic alternative: why force someone to bring two *ashamos* — an *asham talui* now and, upon becoming aware, an *asham vadai* later? Since both the *asham talui* and the *asham vadai* are the same species of animal, bring one now and stipulate (*al tnai*). The stipulation runs as follows: bring the *me'ilah* money and the additional fifth, bring an *asham* worth two *sela'im*, and declare: *im vadai ma'alti*, if it turns out I definitely sinned, then the money is my repayment and this is my *asham vadai*; *ve-im safek ma'alti*, if it turns out I only doubtfully sinned and no *asham vadai* is ever required, then the money becomes a gift (*nedavah*) and this *asham* is my *asham talui*. The advantage is clear: one animal, one payment, one act, covering both contingencies. *She-min she-hu meivi al hoda meivi al lo hoda* — it is the same animal whether brought for a certain sin or a doubtful one.

### Akiva Objection

Rabbi Akiva accepts this strategy in principle but objects in the case of a large *me'ilah*. If the amount potentially misappropriated is small — a *prutah* or a trivial sum — fine, the strategy is reasonable. But *sheyavo le-safek me'ilah be-me'ah maneh*: what if one might have misappropriated a hundred *maneh* from *hekdesh*? Rabbi Tarfon's strategy requires paying back the full principal plus the fifth right now, up front, even though one may never have had any obligation to pay. One may never discover whether one sinned at all. To save the cost of one animal, Rabbi Tarfon is forcing the person to pay out an enormous sum of money that may never have been owed. In that case, *lo yafeh lo sheyavi asham bishnei sela'im* — it is better for him to bring the *asham talui* for two *sela'im* now and not pay the money, and perhaps it will never become clear that he sinned, and he will never owe a cent. Rabbi Akiva therefore agrees with Rabbi Tarfon only in the case of *me'ilah mu'etes*, a small amount. The entire exchange here is, at one level, pragmatic advice; yet as the *gemara* will show, substantive halakhic principles are derived from it.

### Gezeirah Shavah

The *gemara* now turns to the question of how the *chachamim* know to exempt doubtful *me'ilah* from *asham talui*. The *pasuk* concerning *asham talui* reads: *ve-im nefesh ki techeta ve-asatah achat mi-kol mitzvot Hashem asher lo tease'inah ve-lo yada ve-ashem*. The word *mitzvot* appears here and also by the *chatat*, linking the two contexts through a *gezeirah shavah* of *mitzvot-mitzvot*. The *gezeirah shavah* teaches: just as the *chatat* applies only to a sin that carries *kares* when done willfully and a *chatat* when done unwittingly, so too the *asham talui* applies only to such a sin. *Me'ilah* fails on both counts: it does not carry *kares* for willful violation, and the definite violation does not call for a *chatat* but an *asham*. The *gezeirah shavah* therefore excludes *me'ilah* from the scope of *asham talui*.

### Vav vs. Gezeirah

Rabbi Akiva's position appears initially to rest on the juxtaposition of the *parsha* of *asham me'ilos* and the *parsha* of *asham talui* — one might think he simply learns the upper *parsha* from the lower. But the *gemara* establishes that all opinions agree to the principle of *lamedim elyon mi-tachton*, learning the first passage from the second, for otherwise one could never derive that cattle offerings for an *olah* must be slaughtered in the north (since that detail appears only in the second *parsha*). The real dispute must be elsewhere.

The *gemara* therefore identifies a specific letter that carries the argument for Rabbi Akiva: the word *ve-im nefesh* opens with a *vav* — *vav mosif al inyan rishon*, the *vav* adds to the preceding subject and teaches that one learns the *asham me'ilos* context from what follows. This is not mere juxtaposition but a formal derivation. Rabbi Akiva holds that this *vav* overrides the limitation imposed by the *gezeirah shavah*: the *vav* specifically introduces *asham talui* as applicable to *me'ilah*.

The *chachamim* respond: they accept the *vav* as operative, but they hold that what it teaches is not that one brings an *asham talui* for doubtful *me'ilah*, but rather the converse — *tachton hu de-gamar me-elyon* — the lower *parsha* of *asham talui* learns from the *parsha* of *asham me'ilos* the rule of *kesef shekalim*, the minimum cost of two *shekalim*. The *vav* links them in that direction: it teaches that an *asham talui* costs at minimum two *sela'im*, just as *asham me'ilos* specifies *kesef shekalim*. The *gezeirah shavah* of *mitzvot-mitzvot*, in their view, overrides the *vav* and precludes bringing an *asham talui* for *me'ilah*; the *vav*'s sole remaining function is to transmit the minimum cost in the other direction.

### Akiva Vav View

Rabbi Akiva's rejoinder is that he does not need the *vav* to derive the minimum cost of an *asham talui*. He derives that from elsewhere: the *pasuk* *zos toras ha-asham*, "this is the *torah* of the *asham*" — *torah achas le-chol ha-ashamos*, one law applies to all *ashamos*, including the minimum cost of two *shekalim*. Since he has an independent source for minimum cost, the *vav* must be fulfilling a different function — namely, teaching that one brings an *asham talui* for doubtful *me'ilah*. The *vav* overrides the limiting implication of the *gezeirah shavah*, establishing an exception specific to *asham me'ilos*.

### Chachamim Response

The *chachamim* reject this by pointing out that even according to those who accept *zos toras ha-asham* as a general equalization, one would not automatically apply the minimum cost to *asham talui*. Here is the logic: if I definitely sinned and bring a *chatat*, there is no minimum cost — a *chatat* can cost as little as a *danka*, a sixth of a *sela*. One might reason *kal va-chomer* that an *asham talui*, brought for a doubtful sin, should be no more costly than what one brings for a definite sin. Therefore even with *zos toras ha-asham*, I might have assumed *asham talui* also carries no minimum cost, like a *chatat*. The *vav* is therefore needed specifically to teach that the minimum cost of *asham me'ilos* — two *shekalim* — applies to *asham talui* as well, overriding what one might have assumed from comparing it to a *chatat*. With the *vav* doing that work, there is nothing left to derive regarding bringing an *asham talui* for *me'ilah*, and the *gezeirah shavah* stands in full force.

The underlying structure of the debate is therefore clear: Rabbi Akiva and the *chachamim* both accept that *ein gezeirah shavah le-mechetzah* and *ein hekesh le-mechetzah* — one cannot apply a *gezeirah shavah* or a *hekesh* halfway. They both accept the force of the *vav*. The dispute is which hermeneutical principle controls: does the *vav* override the *gezeirah shavah* so that *asham talui* applies to *me'ilah*, or does the *gezeirah shavah* override the *vav* so that the *vav*'s sole function is to transmit minimum cost? Rabbi Akiva says the *vav* wins because minimum cost is derivable elsewhere; the *chachamim* say the *gezeirah shavah* wins and the *vav* is needed for minimum cost regardless.

---

## Stipulated Asham

### Akiva Concession

The *mishnah* concludes with Rabbi Akiva conceding that Rabbi Tarfon's strategy of bringing a single stipulated *asham* is sound when the amount potentially misappropriated is small (*me'ilah mu'etes*), while objecting when the amount is large. This establishes the practical contours of the debate.

### Stipulation Language

The *gemara* scrutinizes the exact language of the stipulation proposed by Rabbi Tarfon. The formulation *ve-im safek ma'alti* — "if I doubtfully sinned" — is problematic: the person has already doubtfully sinned. One cannot use this as the conditional arm of a stipulation, since the condition has already been met (or not met) in the past. The stipulation has to be formulated in terms of what will become known in the future, not in terms of what has already transpired.

### Rav Huna Formula

Rav Huna therefore reformulates the stipulation: *im be-sefeko omed le-olam yehei asham talui* — if this matter remains in doubt forever, if I never in my life discover whether I sinned, let this be an *asham talui*; but if it does become clear (*hoda'ah*), let the earlier *asham* retroactively serve as the *asham vadai*. The animal is the same whether brought for a certain sin or a doubtful one (*she-min she-hu meivi al hoda meivi al lo hoda*), so this stipulation is structurally coherent.

### Awareness Objection

The *gemara* raises a deeper objection: even under Rav Huna's reformulation, once the person does eventually discover that he sinned, he is still obligated to bring an *asham vadai*. And we have established throughout this *masechta* that a *chatat* — and by extension an *asham* — cannot be brought until one is aware of the sin (*o hoda eilav chatato*). If awareness is the trigger for obligation, how can one bring an *asham vadai* now, before that awareness exists? The earlier *korban* cannot fulfill an obligation whose precondition has not yet been met.

### Rava Resolution

Rava resolves this from the combined testimony of Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva, who agree in principle on the mechanism even as they disagree on its prudence. From both of them one may derive: *asham vadai lo ba'ei yedi'ah be-techilah* — an *asham vadai* does not require that awareness precede the bringing of the *korban*. This is precisely how an *asham vadai* differs from a *chatat*: by a *chatat*, the verse *o hoda eilav chatato* makes prior awareness a precondition for the *chiyuv*. For an *asham vadai*, awareness is still required — it is not enough that God knows one sinned if the person never discovers it — but the requirement can be satisfied retroactively. If one brings the *korban* now and becomes aware of the sin afterward, that subsequent awareness is sufficient to have the *korban* function as an *asham vadai*. The *korban* need not wait for awareness; rather, awareness, when it comes, reaches back and validates the *korban* already brought.

The practical implication of the entire discussion is therefore this: Rabbi Tarfon's strategy of a stipulated *asham* is halakhically valid precisely because of this principle. Contingent on future awareness, the same *korban* can serve either as an *asham talui* (if awareness never comes) or as an *asham vadai* (if it does). The only remaining debate is the practical one flagged by Rabbi Akiva: whether it is wise to pay the full principal now, when the amount in question may be substantial and one may never incur the obligation at all.

---

---

# Keritot 23

## Woman's Doubtful Birth

### Mishnah Setup

The daf begins with a *mishnah* whose opening case concerns a woman who has brought a *chatas ha'of* under conditions of doubt. In the context of childbirth, a woman is required to bring both an *olas ha'of* and a *chatas ha'of* at the conclusion of her period of *tuma*. Where there is uncertainty whether what she gave birth to constitutes a halachically recognized birth — for instance, whether the fetus had been conceived for forty days or whether other qualifying conditions were met — she faces a difficulty. Bringing an *olas ha'of* under conditions of doubt poses no real problem: one simply declares it either an *olas chiyuv* if obligated, or an *olas nedava* if not. A *chatas*, however, cannot be brought as a *nedava*, so the ordinary solution is unavailable.

Nevertheless, there is a tradition that in this particular case a woman may bring a *chatas ha'of misafek* — a bird sin-offering conditioned on doubt — in order to become *tehora*. Because of the manner in which a bird offering is slaughtered (from the back of the neck), the meat would be considered *neveila* if the offering turns out not to have been obligatory, and therefore it is not eaten. The *mishnah* does not address a possible *chulin ba'azara* concern head-on; the resolution is either that the need to restore the woman's *tahara* overrides that concern, or that there exists a *masora* — perhaps a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* — that specifically permits this practice.

### Safek Chatas Ha'of

The case of the *chatas ha'of misafek* generates its own internal question, which the *mishnah* passes over somewhat quickly: what happens if she becomes certain of her obligation *after* the bird has already been slaughtered? It would seem logical that once certainty is established she ought to be able to eat the offering even if *shechita* has already taken place. Surprisingly, neither the *mishnah* nor the *gemara* explores this scenario directly, leaving the question effectively open.

### Certainty Before Melikah

What the *mishnah* does address explicitly is the case where she becomes certain *before* the *melikah* is performed. The *mishnah* states: *Im ad shelo nimlok noda lah sheyalda vaday, ta'aseh vaday* — if before the *melikah* she learns that she definitely gave birth in the halachically relevant sense, then the offering proceeds as a certain *chatas*, and it may be eaten. The reasoning is that the very same type of offering she would bring for a doubt she now brings for a certainty — *shemin hamin shehevia al hodam mevia al lo hodam* — and therefore nothing prevents the offering from being treated as fully valid and consumed.

---

## Chaticha Mixtures

### Chalal & Kodesh

The *mishnah* now transitions to the central cases of this section, which revolve around the classic *asham taluy* scenario and its more complex variations. The paradigmatic case: there are two pieces of meat before you, one of *chulin* and one of *kodesh* (sanctified property). You ate one but do not know which. This creates a situation of *safek me'ila* — a doubtful violation of the prohibition against deriving personal benefit from sanctified property. *Rabbi Akiva mechayev asham taluy*: Rabbi Akiva holds that one brings an *asham taluy* even for *safek me'ila*, consistent with his position elaborated in earlier discussions.

### Eating the Second

If the same person then ate the second piece as well, certainty is established: one of the two pieces was definitely *kodesh*, so *me'ila* was definitely committed. All opinions agree that one now brings an *asham vadai*. It is worth noting that a residual doubt remains — over *which* piece the *me'ila* was performed — but this does not constitute a sufficient *safek* to interfere with the obligation. The analogy is to one who knows he performed a *melacha* on *Shabbos* but cannot recall which *av melacha* it was: since the identity of the sin is certain, the uncertainty about which specific object it was performed on does not affect the *korban* obligation. One similarly brings an *asham vadai* here, and the question of which piece was *kodesh* — which bears on the repayment obligation — does not affect the *korban*.

### Reuven & Shimon

The *mishnah* then introduces the scenario where two different individuals eat the two pieces: Reuven ate the first piece and Shimon ate the second. Each one is now in a state of *safek me'ila* individually.

### R. Akiva: Two Asham

Rabbi Akiva rules: *zeh mevi asham taluy ve-zeh mevi asham taluy* — each brings an *asham taluy* independently. Two further implications are embedded in this ruling. First, Rabbi Akiva holds that an *asham taluy* is brought for *safek me'ila* at all. Second — and this connects back to a debate from the opening of the *masechet* — by ruling that Shimon also brings an *asham taluy*, Rabbi Akiva implicitly holds that one need not have eaten from two pieces simultaneously in order to incur the obligation of *asham taluy*. When Shimon ate the second piece, only one piece remained before him; there was no longer a pair of pieces from which the doubt arose in the moment of eating. Yet Rabbi Akiva requires him to bring nonetheless.

### R. Shimon: Joint

Rabbi Shimon proposes an alternative: *sheneihem mevi'im asham echad* — let both bring a single *asham* jointly, with stipulation. Reuven declares: if I sinned, this is my *asham vadai*; if I did not, I relinquish my portion to Shimon. Shimon makes the reverse declaration. The *korban* is thus brought without a definitively identified owner, which raises questions about *shechita lishmo ba'alim*, though a *shetam* slaughter would suffice. The technical issue of sanctification and ownership can in principle be resolved through appropriate *kinyan* and conditional *hakdasha*. Rabbi Shimon's real innovation is the claim that stipulated joint ownership is a viable mechanism even for an *asham*.

### R. Yosi: No Joint

Rabbi Yosi rejects Rabbi Shimon's solution: *ein shenayim mevi'im asham echad*. Two people cannot jointly bring one *asham* — or, as becomes explicit later, one *chatas* brought for sin. This is not merely a technical objection about the mechanics of sanctification, but a principled position: a *chatas* or *asham* that comes to atone for sin must be specifically identified with a known owner. One might distinguish this from cases where animals have become physically mixed up — where the *kohen* simply brings the offering for whoever owns it — because in that scenario the uncertainty is about which animal is whose, not about whether a given person is the owner at all. Here the very identity of the obligated party is indeterminate from the outset, and that, for Rabbi Yosi, is disqualifying.

One might wonder whether the same concern applies to a *chatas* brought for *tahara* purposes rather than for sin — for instance, the *chatas* of a *yoledes*. Rabbi Yosi's formulation, elaborated most explicitly later in the *mishnah*, is *kol chatas sheba'ah al cheit ein shenayim mevi'im osah* — any *chatas* that comes on account of sin cannot be brought by two people jointly. This language suggests his objection is limited to sin-atoning offerings, leaving open the theoretical possibility that a *chatas* for *tahara* might be different.

An interesting related question is raised regarding *smicha* and *viduy*: if one does not know whether one sinned, how can one perform *smicha* and make a proper *viduy*? Although *smicha* is generally not *me'akeiv*, there is a *Tosafos* that addresses the case of *tme'im* who are *meshalei'ach* their *korbanos* when they cannot perform *smicha* themselves, since a *shaliach* cannot perform *smicha* on one's behalf — a topic worth studying further, but one the *gemara* does not raise in this context.

---

## Chelev Combinations

### Chelev & Chulin

Having established the framework, the *mishnah* now presents a series of cases that vary the nature of the prohibition involved. The first is the standard *asham taluy* scenario: two pieces before you, one *cheilev* (forbidden fat) and one *chulin*. You ate one and do not know which. This is the classic case — *mevi asham taluy*. If you then eat the second piece as well, you have certainly eaten *cheilev* — *mevi chatas*. Here we have moved entirely away from the *safek me'ila* context and into the paradigmatic case of doubtful consumption of a forbidden substance.

When Reuven eats the first piece and Shimon the second, each brings an *asham taluy*. The *mishnah* is implicitly relying on the assumption that one need not have two pieces in front of oneself at the moment of eating — *chatichah mishtei chatichot* is not required — since Shimon ate when only one piece remained.

Rabbi Shimon again applies his principle: *sheneihem mevi'im chatas achas* — they bring one *chatas* jointly with stipulation. Rabbi Yosi again objects: *ein sheneihem mevi'im chatas achas*.

### Chelev & Nosar

The *mishnah* then considers: one piece is *cheilev* (one *aveira*, one *chatas*) and the other is *cheilev venotar* (forbidden fat that is also leftover sacrifice — two violations, two *chataos*, with *me'ila* bracketed as we shall explain). You ate one and do not know which — *mevi chatas ve'asham taluy*: you certainly ate *cheilev*, and you may have also committed the violation of *nosar*, so you bring a *chatas* and an *asham taluy*.

If you eat the second piece as well: *mevi gimel chatasos* — three sin-offerings — one for each of the two *cheilev* violations and one for *nosar*, assuming a *yedi'ah* separated the two acts of eating. The question of why no *asham* for *me'ila* is brought in the *nosar* case is addressed by the *gemara* directly: the *nosar* piece is generally not worth a *shaveh perutah*, the minimum value required for *me'ila* liability to apply. The reasoning is that once meat becomes *nosar* it loses nearly all its practical value — though it is not categorically excluded from *me'ila*, as Rashi notes that so long as it could theoretically be left on the *mizbe'ach* it retains some residual value to *hekdesh*.

### Chelev & Kodesh

The next variation: one piece is *cheilev chullin* (ordinary forbidden fat) and the other is *cheilev kodesh* (forbidden fat of a sanctified animal). Both pieces are forbidden, but for different reasons: the first gives rise to a *chatas*, and the second gives rise to a *chatas* for *cheilev* plus, potentially, an *asham* for *me'ila*. You ate one and do not know which: *mevi chatas* — you certainly ate *cheilev* — and now the question of *me'ila* is in doubt. *Rabbi Akiva omer af asham taluy*: Rabbi Akiva says you additionally bring an *asham taluy* for the doubtful *me'ila*. The other *tanna'im* do not require this.

If you eat the second piece: *mevi shtei chataos ve'asham vadai* — two *chataos* for the two *cheilev* violations, and an *asham vadai* for the certain *me'ila*.

Where Reuven and Shimon each eat one piece: each brings a *chatas* for the certain *cheilev*, and *Rabbi Akiva omer ze veze mevi'im asham taluy* — Rabbi Akiva says each also brings an *asham taluy* for the doubtful *me'ila*.

Rabbi Shimon: each brings his own *chatas* individually, and for the *asham* — since between them they are certainly liable for one — *ushneihem mevi'im asham echad*, they bring one joint *asham* with stipulation. Rabbi Yosi: *ein sheneihem mevi'im asham echad* — you cannot do this.

### Chelev Kodesh Mix

The most complex case: both pieces are *cheilev*, but both are also *kodesh* — one is simply *cheilev kodesh*, while the other is *cheilev kodesh venotar* (sanctified forbidden fat that is also leftover). Here the full complexity of overlapping prohibitions comes into view. One piece carries two violations (*cheilev* and *me'ila*), while the other carries three (*cheilev*, *me'ila*, and *nosar*). The *me'ila* from the *nosar* piece is again potentially excluded on the grounds of insufficient value.

When Reuven and Shimon each eat one piece, each certainly ate *cheilev*, each is in *safek* regarding *me'ila*, and each is in *safek* regarding *nosar*. Each brings a *chatas* for *cheilev*, and each brings an *asham taluy* for the doubtful *nosar* — assuming, again, that one need not have had two pieces before oneself. Rabbi Shimon: each brings a *chatas* individually, and *sheneihem mevi'im chatas achas* jointly for the *nosar* with stipulation. Rabbi Yosi: *kol chatas sheba'ah al cheit ein shenayim mevi'im osah* — the most fully articulated statement of his position. Any sin-atoning *chatas* requires a specific, identified owner; it cannot be brought as a joint stipulated offering.

The two assumptions running through this entire *mishnah* — beyond Rabbi Akiva's *asham taluy* for *safek me'ila* — are worth highlighting. First, the *mishnah* consistently treats the second person in the Reuven-Shimon scenarios as bringing an *asham taluy* even though he ate from only one piece, not two: *chatichah mishtei chatichot* is not required. Second, an *asham taluy* is brought even in cases where *both* options involved a sin — one just does not know which sin. This is somewhat surprising, since an earlier *mishnah* seemed to endorse the view that *asham taluy* is limited to cases where one *might not have sinned at all*. The present *mishnah* qualifies this: if the two possible violations would have given rise to *different* kinds of *korban* (a *chatas* on one hand, an *asham* on the other), the uncertainty is sufficient to warrant an *asham taluy* for the doubtful *chatas*-type violation.

---

## Issur Chal Al Issur

### Nosar's Value

The *gemara* (Rava's question to Rav Nachman) focuses on several of the surprising features of the preceding *mishnah*. The first issue concerns the *nosar* case: when both pieces have been eaten and we say *mevi gimel chatasos*, why is no *asham vadai* brought for *me'ila* on the *nosar* piece? Rava raises this question explicitly, and Rav Nachman answers: *de-leika shaveh perutah* — the *nosar* piece is not worth a *shaveh perutah*. Since *me'ila* liability requires that the benefit derived be worth at least a *perutah*, and *nosar* has so little practical value, no *me'ila* obligation arises.

This answer does not reflect a categorical exclusion of *nosar* from *me'ila*. Rashi notes that meat which has become *nosar* retains some minimal connection to *kodesh* value because it could theoretically remain on the *mizbe'ach*. Rather, the claim is that its value in practice is so diminished — since you cannot use it for anything permitted — that a typical piece of *nosar* would not reach the *shaveh perutah* threshold.

The *gemara* then challenges this: but earlier cases in the *mishnah* (involving *cheilev kodesh* that was not *nosar*) assumed the piece *was* worth a *perutah*, as evidenced by the fact that an *asham vadai* for *me'ila* was required. Can the same piece be worth a *perutah* in one case and not in another? The answer is that the two cases involve structurally different objects: a piece of sanctified *cheilev* that has not become *nosar* is worth a *perutah* — *kohanim* could eat the non-fat portions of the animal, and the fat itself has value to be placed on the *mizbe'ach* — whereas *nosar* of the same physical size is worth so little in its degraded state that it falls below the *shaveh perutah* threshold.

The *gemara* then raises a further challenge: but we have a *mishnah* that describes a single piece of meat combining multiple violations — among them *nosar* and *me'ila* together — where four *chataos* and one *asham* are brought. That case demonstrates that *nosar* is not categorically excluded from *me'ila*. The resolution: it depends on size — *hahi begassah, v'hacha bedakkah* — or, alternatively, on the season: in summer, when meat spoils quickly, the already-minimal value of *nosar* drops below a *perutah*, while in winter it might retain marginal value. The upshot is that *nosar* is not inherently outside the category of *me'ila*, but in most practical cases its value will not meet the *shaveh perutah* minimum.

This discussion is also notable for a broader reason: the question of *me'ila*'s *shiur* — whether it is measured by *kezayit* (as for eating violations) or *perutah* (as for theft-like violations) — is implicitly touched upon here. By defining *me'ila* liability in terms of *perutah* even in the context of eating, the *gemara* signals that *me'ila* carries a distinctive monetary dimension alongside its character as a prohibition against personal benefit.

### R. Shimon's View

The *gemara* now turns to a deeper structural question. Several cases in the *mishnah* involve a single piece of meat that is subject to multiple prohibitions simultaneously — for example, *cheilev* that is also *kodesh*, or *cheilev* that is also *nosar*. Rabbi Shimon agrees to these cases (he counts the multiple violations), yet Rabbi Shimon is famously the *tanna* who holds *ein issur chal al issur* — that a second prohibition cannot take effect upon an object already subject to a prior prohibition. The question Rava poses to Rav Nachman is: does Rabbi Shimon really hold *issur chal al issur* in cases of *issur kolel* and *issur mosif*?

### Fat & Me'ilah

The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: *Rabbi Shimon omer, ha'ochel neveilah b'Yom HaKippurim — patur*. One who eats *neveilah* on Yom Kippur is exempt (from the Yom Kippur prohibition). Yom Kippur is clearly an *issur kolel* — it applies to all foods, not just *neveilah* — and yet Rabbi Shimon says its prohibition cannot take effect on something already forbidden as *neveilah*. By the same logic, Rabbi Shimon would seemingly reject *issur mosif* as well. And even more strikingly, the *gemara* notes that even *issur chamur* — a weightier prohibition — does not, in Rabbi Shimon's view, overcome *ein issur chal al issur*: Yom Kippur carries *kares* (weightier) while *neveilah* does not, yet Rabbi Shimon still says *patur*. So the question sharpens: how does Rabbi Shimon agree that *cheilev* of *kodesh* meat also carries *me'ila*, since the *issur me'ila* would be taking effect on top of the already-established *issur cheilev*?

### Simultaneous Effect

The resolution: *ella b'kodshim gali rachmana d'ati issur chal al issur* — by sanctified property, the Torah itself has revealed that a second prohibition *can* take effect on top of a prior one. A *baraita* derives from the phrase *asher l'Hashem* that even one who eats the *imurim* (the fats designated for the *mizbe'ach*) while *tamei* — already subject to *me'ila* and *cheilev* — also incurs an obligation for the *tumah* violation. Three prohibitions thus simultaneously govern one piece of fat: *cheilev*, *me'ila*, and *tumah*. By *kodashim*, the Torah has created a special exception to *ein issur chal al issur*.

Rebbi (Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi), who generally holds that *issur chal al issur* does apply — but only when the second prohibition is weightier (*issur chamur al issur kal*) — is shown to hold an even broader principle within the domain of *kodashim*: even a lighter prohibition can take effect on a weightier one. The proof is the *issur me'ila*, which carries only *mita b'yedei shamayim* and is thus lighter than *issur cheilev* (which carries *kares*), yet the Torah explicitly states that *me'ila* takes effect on the fat. From this Rebbi derives — and the *gemara* confirms — that by *kodashim* even a lighter prohibition can take effect on a heavier one.

(Why is *mita b'yedei shamayim* considered lighter than *kares*? Various explanations are offered. Some suggest that *kares* involves premature death *plus* dying childless — *kares ariri* — making it more severe. Rashi here argues that the fact that *kares* leads to an obligation to bring a *chatas* gives it greater halachic weight, whereas *me'ila* leads to an *asham*, which is seen as less weighty — though this reasoning has its difficulties, as Rabbi Akiva would apply *me'ila* to *asham taluy* as well.)

Yet despite Rebbi's expansive view within *kodashim*, Rabbi Shimon explicitly disagrees even with the limited *kodashim* exception: *Rabbi Shimon omer, ein pigul be-olim ve-ein nosar be-olim* — the portions that go on the *mizbe'ach* cannot become *pigul* or *nosar*, since they are already under the prohibition of *me'ila* and, in Rabbi Shimon's view, no additional prohibition can take effect on them even in the *kodashim* context. The *gemara* therefore concludes: *ela tanna'i hi* — it is a dispute among *tanna'im* whether the *kodashim* exception to *ein issur chal al issur* applies. According to the position that it does (represented by our *mishnah* insofar as Rabbi Shimon agrees to the multiple-violation cases there), Rabbi Shimon holds the exception. According to the stricter position — Rabbi Shimon's ruling about *olim* — he does not.

For the view that even by *kodashim* there is no *issur chal al issur*, the verse *kol chelev l'Hashem* establishing *me'ila* on the fat must be explained differently: it refers specifically to an animal born to a sanctified mother (*yaldei kodashim*), where the *issur cheilev* and the *issur me'ila* take effect simultaneously at the moment of birth — *b'havayatan hen kedoshim* — so there is no sequence of one prohibition following another, and the question of *issur chal al issur* does not arise at all.

To summarize the conclusions of this extended analysis: *nosar* is not categorically excluded from *me'ila*, but in many practical cases will not meet the *shaveh perutah* threshold. The principle of *ein issur chal al issur* has a special *kodashim* exception according to one view among the *tanna'im*, explaining how a single piece of meat can simultaneously carry violations of *cheilev*, *me'ila*, and *nosar*. Rabbi Shimon's position is internally complex: in the *mishnah* regarding Reuven and Shimon's stipulation he appears to accept the *kodashim* exception, but his explicit ruling about *olim* suggests he does not — and the *gemara* resolves this as a genuine *machlokes tanna'im*.

---

## Asham Taluy Resolved

### Didn't Sin Case

A new *perek* begins, building directly on a hint from the previous *mishnah*: the case of the *yoledes* who brought her *chatas ha'of* under conditions of doubt and then discovered she was definitively obligated. The new chapter systematically addresses the parallel scenario for an *asham taluy*: one brings an *asham taluy* and subsequently discovers either that one definitely did not sin, or that one definitely did. What is the status of the *asham* at various stages of its processing?

### Before Shechita

The *mishnah* opens: one who brought an *asham taluy* and then discovered that he had not sinned — *Im ad shelo nishchat* — if this is discovered before *shechita*, *yetzei v'yirei ba'eder*, the animal is released back to the flock. This is the ruling of Rabbi Meir. The *gemara* will explain: Rabbi Meir holds that sanctification requires actual knowledge of need — *keivan delo tzarich lei lo makdish lei* — so if it turns out there was no obligation, the original *hakdasha* is retroactively void.

### After Shechita

If the discovery comes *after shechita*, Rabbi Meir rules *yishapeich hadam vehabasar yeitzei l'veit hasreifa* — the blood is spilled and the meat goes to be burned. Since the *hakdasha* was invalid according to Rabbi Meir, the slaughter was that of *chulin ba'azara*. One might ask whether this should require burial (*kevura*) rather than burning (*sreifa*), since burning is typically reserved for *kodshim she'nifsalu* while *chulin ba'azara* are buried. The distinction is that in the *asham taluy* case the doubt was genuine at the time — the offering has more of the character of *kodshim* — so the *chumra* of *sreifa* is applied. We will see below that the comparable case of an *asham vadai* where one discovers no sin was committed is treated differently, calling for *kevura*.

The *chachamim* disagree with Rabbi Meir. Their position — *mitoch libo nokfo, gamar umakdish* — is that because one's heart troubled one, because the psychological reality of doubt was present at the moment of sanctification, the *hakdasha* was valid and complete. The fact that the doubt resolves in either direction afterward does not undo a valid act of sanctification made under genuine uncertainty. This is the key conceptual divide of the chapter.

### Blood Sprinkled

If the blood has already been sprinkled on the altar and one then discovers one had not sinned, *yei'acheil* — even Rabbi Meir agrees the meat may be eaten. At the moment of *zerikat hadam* the doubt was fully present, the offering was validly processed, and the *korban* reached completion in a state of *kashrut*. The subsequent discovery of innocence cannot retroactively invalidate what was done under legitimate doubt.

### R. Yosi: Blood OK

Rabbi Yosi extends this principle one step further: *afilu hadam bekos yizarek vehabasar yei'acheil* — even if the discovery comes while the blood is already collected in the vessel and has not yet been sprinkled, one may still go ahead and sprinkle the blood, and the meat may be eaten afterward. Rabbi Yosi holds *kol ha'omeid lizarek kezaruak dami* — whatever stands ready to be thrown is halachically considered as if already thrown. Since the blood is in the vessel and about to be sprinkled, it is treated as if *zerikat hadam* has already occurred, and the same rule applies as in the post-sprinkling case.

---

## Other Conditional Cases

### Asham Vadai

The *mishnah* draws a contrast with the *asham vadai* — the definite guilt-offering. If one sanctified an animal for an *asham vadai* or a *chatas* and then discovered one had not sinned, this is an instance of *hekdesh b'ta'ut* — a mistaken sanctification. The assumptions of fact that prompted the *hakdasha* were simply wrong, not merely uncertain. Accordingly, *ad shelo nishchat — yetzei v'yirei ba'eder*: before *shechita*, it goes back to the flock, with *universal* agreement (not just Rabbi Meir). If *shechita* has already occurred: *harei ze yikaver* — it is buried, not burned. This is because it never had valid *kedusha* — it was *chulin ba'azara* from the start — and *chulin ba'azara* is buried. After blood sprinkling: *habasar yeitzei l'veit hasreifa* — the meat is burned, because the sprinkling of the blood of something that was never a valid *korban* renders the meat akin to *kodshim she'nifsalu*.

### Shor Haniskal

The *shor haniskal* — the ox sentenced to be stoned — follows the same general pattern as the *asham vadai*, not the *asham taluy*. If the witnesses are found to be lying before the ox is executed (*ad shelo niska*), it is released: *yetzei v'yirei ba'eder*. The entire *gmar din* was a mistake, and the ox never had the status of *shor haniskal*. If it was already stoned and the deception is then discovered: *mutar behana'ah* — it is permitted for use, since it no longer bears the status of *shor haniskal* once the mistaken judgment is exposed. It has the status of *neveilah* but can be used for benefit.

### Egla Arufa

The *egla arufa* — the heifer whose neck is broken in the valley when a murder victim is found and the killer is unknown — is the case most structurally similar to the *asham taluy*, since it too is brought because of an unresolved doubt (the identity of the murderer). Yet the *mishnah* groups it with the *asham vadai* and *shor haniskal*, not with the *asham taluy*, for the pre-breaking stage.

*Ad shelo ne'erfah* — before the neck is broken — if the murderer is identified, *teitzei v'teira'eh ba'eder*: she goes back to the flock. Even the *chachamim* agree to this. This is initially puzzling: is the *egla arufa* not brought because of genuine *safek*, just like the *asham taluy*? The *gemara* will explore this. One possible distinction is that the *egla arufa* does not have *kedusha* in the same way an *asham taluy* does, so the question of sanctification under doubt does not arise in the same manner.

*Mishene'erfah* — after the neck is broken — if the murderer is then identified, *tikaver bimkomah*: she is buried where the neck was broken. The reason given: *she'safek ba mitechilah, kaperas sefeikah vehalchah lah* — it was brought originally for a doubt, it atoned for that doubt at the moment the neck was broken, and it has fulfilled its purpose. The discovery of the murderer afterward does not undo what was done under valid *safek*. In this respect the *egla arufa* post-breaking closely parallels the *asham taluy* after *zerikat hadam*: once the act of atonement was performed at a moment when the doubt was genuinely present, the subsequent resolution of the doubt is irrelevant.

The precise question of why the *chachamim* agree to Rabbi Meir on the pre-breaking stage for *egla arufa* but disagree on the pre-*shechita* stage for *asham taluy* is left for the *gemara* to address — whether it turns on the presence or absence of *kedusha*, or on some deeper difference in the nature of the two atonements.

---

## Sanctification Theory

### R. Meir: Knowledge

The *gemara* articulates the theoretical basis of the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the *chachamim* in precise terms. Rabbi Meir's position: *keivan delo tzarich lei lo makdish lei* — since it turns out he did not need it, he did not truly sanctify it. Rabbi Meir locates the validity of *hakdasha* in the knowledge of actual need. If the need is retrospectively absent, the intention to sanctify was, in his view, never sufficiently grounded to create valid *kedusha*.

### Sages: Intent

The *chachamim* counter with a principle that is almost psychological in character: *mitoch libo nokfo, gamar umakdish* — because his heart troubled him, because the subjective experience of doubt was genuinely present, he made up his mind and fully sanctified the animal. The *kedusha* was real at the moment it was declared, because the doubt that motivated it was real. The resolution of that doubt in either direction thereafter cannot unravel what was validly done.

### When Sin Confirmed

The *gemara* notes that the *baraita* extends the dispute of Rabbi Meir and the *chachamim* to both directions: *bein shenoda shelo chata uvein shenoda shechata pligi* — they disagree whether one discovers one did not sin *and* whether one discovers one did sin. In either case, once certainty is established, the *asham taluy* has become superfluous, and the question of whether its *hakdasha* was valid arises equally.

Why state both cases? *L'hodia kocho d'Rabbi Meir*: to demonstrate the full force of Rabbi Meir's position. Even if one discovers one *did* sin — meaning the worst-case scenario has been confirmed and one will need to bring a *chatas* — Rabbi Meir still rules that the *asham taluy* animal is released (*tetzei v'tireh ba'eder*), because at the moment of sanctification the person did not know this, and therefore *keivan d'be'idna d'afrasha lo yada* — since at the time of setting it apart one did not know — the *hakdasha* is retroactively void.

Conversely, *l'hodia kocho d'Rabbanan*: to demonstrate the full force of the *chachamim*'s position. Even if one discovers one did *not* sin — even though one is entirely off the hook — the *chachamim* hold the *asham taluy* retains its *kedusha*, because *keivan d'be'idna d'afrasha lo yada, libo nokfo, hilkach gamar umakdish* — since at the time of setting it apart one did not know and one's heart was troubled, one fully and validly sanctified it. That psychological reality at the moment of *hakdasha* is what gives the *kedusha* its force, and no subsequent discovery can dissolve it.

---

---

# Keritot 25b

## YK & Chatat/Asham

### Mishna: YK & Obligations

The *mishna* with which our *daf* opens establishes a fundamental principle about the atoning power of Yom Kippur and its relationship to outstanding *korban* obligations. The *mishna* states: *chayvei chataot ve'ashamot vadai she'avar aleihem Yom HaKippurim chayavin lehavi achar Yom HaKippurim* — those who are obligated in *chataot* and *ashamot vadai* and over whom Yom Kippur has passed are still required to bring those offerings after Yom Kippur. By contrast, *chayvei asham talui peturin* — those obligated in an *asham talui* are exempt once Yom Kippur has passed.

The *gemara* immediately asks *mina hani milei* — from where do we derive these rules? The first question is how we know that Yom Kippur does not extinguish one's *chiyuv* in a *korban*.

### Rav Dimi's Drasha

When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he transmitted in the name of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Chanina a *drasha* anchored in the *pasuk* concerning the *se'ir hanasa bifnim* — the goat whose blood is brought inside the sanctuary on Yom Kippur: *vechiper al hakodesh mitumot bnei Yisrael umipisheihem lechol chatatam* — "he shall atone for the sanctuary from the impurities of the children of Israel and from their *pishaim* and all of their *chataim*." The key distinction embedded in this verse is that *pesha* denotes a willful sin while *cheit* denotes an unintentional sin.

The *drasha* proceeds as follows: *chataim dumya depishaim* — the *chataim* that are atoned for are analogous to the *pishaim*. Just as *pishaim* are *delav bnei korban* — not the type of sin for which one brings a *korban*, since willful sins do not generate a *korban* obligation — so too the *chataim* that Yom Kippur atones for are those that are *delav bnei korban*. But *chataim* that are *bnei korban* — those obligated in a *korban* because they involve *kares* and will eventually be accompanied by *yedia* — Yom Kippur is not *mechaper* for.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenged Rav Dimi's *drasha* on structural grounds. This *pasuk*, he pointed out, is written specifically about the *se'ir hanasa bifnim* — not the goat sent to *la'azazel*, but the goat whose blood is offered inside the *Beit HaMikdash*. And that *se'ir* is categorically limited in its atoning scope: it only atones for the sins of *tumot mikdash vekodashav* — the *tumah* of the sanctuary and its sacred objects. It does not atone for a broad array of other sins.

Abaye's objection is therefore this: since the *se'ir hanasa bifnim* already operates in such a narrow domain, perhaps one could say that even within those *chataim* it does atone for, it works even for *chataim d'vnei korban* — sins obligated in a *korban*. The limitation to *delav bnei korban* might be an artifact of the *se'ir*'s restricted scope rather than a universal principle. You cannot prove from this *se'ir* that Yom Kippur generally fails to atone for *korban*-obligated sins.

### Se'ir Types

It is worth pausing to clarify the landscape of the Yom Kippur *se'irim*. The *se'ir hanasa bifnim* — whose blood is sprinkled inside the sanctuary — atones exclusively for *tumot mikdash vekodashav*. All other sins fall under the purview of the *se'ir hanasa bachutz*, namely the *se'ir hamishtaleach*, the goat sent to *azazel*. That latter goat has a far broader, across-the-board atoning effect. Abaye's point is thus that even granting Rav Dimi's *drasha*, one cannot generalize from the inside *se'ir* — which is limited to a very narrow category of sins — to the wide-ranging atonement of the *se'ir hamishtaleach*. The *se'ir hamishtaleach* might well atone even for *chataim d'vnei korban*.

## Se'ir Hamishtaleach

### Abaye's Se'ir Source

The *gemara* therefore asks: given that the *se'ir hanasa bachutz* — the *se'ir hamishtaleach* — is the more sweeping vehicle of atonement, what does one do with it? Rather, says Abaye, the source must come from the *pasuk* about the *se'ir hamishtaleach* itself: *v'hisvada alav es kol avonos bnei Yisrael v'es kol pish'eihem l'chol chatosam* — "he shall confess over it all the iniquities of the children of Israel and all their *pish'aim* and all their *chatosam*."

Here again the *drasha* is *chataim dumya d'pish'aim*: the *chataim* atoned for are analogous to *pish'aim*. Just as *pish'aim* — willful sins — are *delav bnei korban*, so the *chataim* this verse speaks of are those *delav bnei korban*. But *chataim d'vnei korban* — those obligated in a *korban* — *lo mechaper*. The verse thus excludes, and the *gemara* notes that the *pasuk* has effectively limited things: *u'mi'ateih kra b'se'ir hamishtaleach* — the verse limits the *se'ir hamishtaleach* as well, teaching that even it does not atone for *chataim d'vnei korban*.

### Ravin's Version

Independently, when Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, he transmitted the same teaching in the name of Reish Lakish, likewise grounding the *drasha* in the *pasuk* of the *se'ir hamishtaleach*: *v'hisvada alav es kol avonos bnei Yisrael v'es kol pish'eihem l'chol chatosam*. The formulation was identical — *chataim dumya d'pish'aim*, and just as *pish'aim* are *delav bnei korban mechaper*, so too only *chataim delav bnei korban mechaper*, but *chataim d'vnei korban lo mechaper*.

### Ravina's Challenge

Abaye, upon hearing Ravin's version, noted that he himself had tried to use that same *pasuk* — but that Ravina bar Rav Dimi had challenged him. The challenge: *mi yeimar d'hanei pish'aim lav bnei korban ninhu?* Who says that the *pish'aim* referenced in the verse are paradigmatically sins that carry no *korban* obligation? *Dilma hanei bnei korban ninhu* — perhaps these very *pish'aim* are precisely sins for which one does bring a *korban*. As the earlier *mishna* in our *masechet* taught, there are four categories that bring a *korban* even for a willful act — *arba'ah mevi'im al hazadon kish'gagah*. Thus the *pish'aim* cited in the verse might well include *korban*-obligated sins, and therefore the *chataim* linked to them would likewise include *korban*-obligated sins — undercutting the entire *drasha*.

### Abaye's Resolution

Ravin responded to this challenge with the argument of *rov pish'aim lav bnei korban* — the majority of *pish'aim* as a class are sins that carry no *korban* obligation, since the overwhelming majority of willful transgressions do not generate a *korban*. The verse, he argued, must be referring to the typical case.

Abaye, however, was not satisfied. *Midi rov ksiv?* — does the verse say "most *pish'aim*"? The verse speaks of *pish'aim* without qualification, and since some *pish'aim* are indeed *bnei korban*, the argument from majority does not definitively establish the *drasha*.

Abaye therefore proposed a different resolution, drawn from the *reisha* — the opening of the same *pasuk*. A *baraita* teaches: *avonos elu hazdonos* — *avon* means willful sin, as evidenced by the usage *avonah bah*, "her sin is upon her," which refers to a willful act. Since the verse already uses *avonos* to indicate willful sins, the subsequent mention of *pish'aim* — which also denotes willful sins — is redundant. The *pish'aim* are therefore an extra word, and its extra status allows us to interpret it precisely: *pish'aim* here represents sins that are paradigmatically *delav bnei korban*, which is the core characteristic of willful sins as a class. The redundancy eliminates the ambiguity that Ravina bar Rav Dimi had raised, because we are no longer relying on the *rov* of *pish'aim* but on the exegetical force of a repeated term that must be teaching something new. The result: *chataim d'vnei korban eino mechaper* — Yom Kippur does not atone for sins obligated in a *korban*.

It is worth pausing over the underlying logic here, because it is somewhat counterintuitive. There are three categories of sin in relation to Yom Kippur's atoning power: sins so minor or ambiguous that no *korban* is generated — those Yom Kippur atones for; sins that are fully willful and serious — those Yom Kippur also atones for; but sins in the middle, where the transgressor is obligated in a *korban* — those Yom Kippur does not atone for. The reason, presumably, is not that these middle sins are worse. Rather, the principle seems to be that Yom Kippur does not override obligations and rectifications that the *Torah* has already assigned. If the *Torah* prescribes a specific atonement, Yom Kippur is not going to substitute for it. This guiding principle will resurface throughout the subsequent discussion.

## Asham Talui & YK

### Asham Talui Exempted

Having established why Yom Kippur does not extinguish *chatat* and *asham vadai* obligations, the *gemara* turns to the second part of the *mishna*: why does Yom Kippur wipe away the obligation of an *asham talui*? An *asham talui*, after all, is itself a *bnei korban* — one is obligated to bring it. Why should Yom Kippur cancel it when it does not cancel a *chatat*?

### God-Known Sins

The source is derived from the *pasuk*: *mikol chatoseichem lifnei Hashem titharu* — "from all your sins before God you shall be cleansed." From this Rabbi Elazar derives: *cheit she'ein makir bo ela HaMakom Yom HaKippurim mechaper* — a sin that only God knows about, Yom Kippur atones for. The *asham talui* is brought precisely when one is not certain that one has sinned — one suspects it but does not know definitively. Since the person himself does not have definite knowledge of the sin, it is categorically a *cheit she'ein makir bo ela HaMakom*, and Yom Kippur therefore works for it.

### Unknown Sins Rule

Rav Tachlifa, the father of Rav Huna, said in the name of Rava: one need not derive the two halves of the ruling from separate *drashot* as the earlier Amoraim did. Rather, this single *pasuk* — *cheit she'ein makir bo ela HaMakom Yom HaKippurim mechaper* — can do double duty. It tells you that Yom Kippur works for the *asham talui* case, and it simultaneously implies that Yom Kippur does not work for a *chatat* and an *asham*, because those involve sins that the sinner himself knows about.

The *gemara* however immediately notes a problem with making "known versus unknown" the operative criterion. Yom Kippur does atone for known sins — including willful sins that one is fully aware of but for which no *korban* is brought, and ordinary inadvertent sins that do not generate a *korban* obligation. So the rule cannot simply be that known sins are excluded from Yom Kippur's atonement.

## Obligation Framework

### Shvuos Precedent

The *gemara* presses further. Rav Tachlifa also said in the name of Rava: *chayavei malkiyos she'avar aleihen Yom HaKippurim chayav* — one who is obligated in *malkos* and over whom Yom Kippur passes remains obligated. The *gemara* asks *peshita* — this is obvious. Why should it be any different from one obligated in a *chatat* or *asham vadai*?

The *gemara* responds that one might have thought there is a distinction: a *korban* obligation is analogous to a monetary debt — just as Yom Kippur does not wipe away financial obligations and the need to make restitution, it does not wipe away *korban* obligations either. *Malkos*, by contrast, is a punishment imposed on one's body, and perhaps one might reason that since Yom Kippur atones for the sin, the punishment associated with it should also fall away. Therefore the ruling is needed: no, *malkos* obligations remain as well.

This framing is itself striking. One would have expected the *korban* — as an act of atonement — to be more directly comparable to what Yom Kippur accomplishes, while *malkos* as a bodily punishment would seem more readily dissolved by atonement. Yet the *gemara* frames the *korban* as a debt and the *malkos* as a punishment, making the *korban* the more obvious case of persistence and the *malkos* the case requiring explicit ruling.

### Core Principle

The *gemara* then raises a difficulty from the *mishna* in *Shvuos*: *hoda v'lo hoda, asei v'lo ta'asei* — Yom Kippur atones for positive and negative commandments, known and unknown. Explicitly, then, Yom Kippur does work for known sins. If so, how can Rav Tachlifa's formulation — that Yom Kippur only works for what only God knows about — exclude *chatat* and *asham vadai* on the basis that the sinner knows of his sin?

### Hasra'ah Distinction

The *gemara* resolves this: *lo kashya — ha de'asru bei, ha de'lo asru bei*. There is no contradiction. When the sin involved a *hasra'ah* — a formal warning — and the transgressor is truly obligated in *malkos*, Yom Kippur does not wipe it away. When no *hasra'ah* was given and the person has merely sinned without incurring a formal legal obligation of punishment, Yom Kippur does atone.

At the end of the day, the operative principle is not really "known versus unknown" at all. The rule is whether or not the *Torah* has assigned a specific obligation or rectification. *Malkos* and *chatat* — these are assigned obligations that Yom Kippur does not override. Everything else — regardless of whether the sin was known or unknown, willful or inadvertent — Yom Kippur does atone for, so long as it does not carry a specific assigned obligation.

The one genuine exception where "unknown" remains relevant is the *asham talui*. There, although an obligation technically exists, it is an obligation generated by doubt — by not knowing. In that particular case, Yom Kippur does dissolve the obligation. One way to understand this is that while Yom Kippur in the normative sense atones for the person — addressing guilt — when there is an objective, known sin, the *Torah* requires the *korban* to address that objective dimension of sin as well. The *asham talui*, rooted in uncertainty, has no such objective dimension to address, and so Yom Kippur can handle it entirely.

## Safek Korbanos

### Safek Yoledet

The *gemara* now turns to a series of cases involving *safek korbanos* — offerings brought in situations of doubt — and asks why Yom Kippur does not dissolve those obligations just as it dissolves the *asham talui*. The first case: *safek yoledet* — a woman who may or may not have given birth. A *mishna* states explicitly that even if Yom Kippur passes over her, she remains obligated to bring her *korban*. Why? By analogy to the *asham talui*, this is a doubt-based *korban* obligation, and the sinner is unaware of any definite sin. Should Yom Kippur not clear this away?

### Sin vs. Impurity

Rav Oshaya answers with a textual distinction: the verse says *l'chol chatosam* — for all their *sins* — *v'lo l'chol tumasam*, not for all their *tumah*. While the Yom Kippur *psukim* do mention *tumah*, that is *tumah* that flows from sin. Yom Kippur provides *taharah* for sin, but it does not substitute for the *taharah* process that rectifies issues of ritual impurity. The *yoledet*'s *korban* is part of her *taharah* process, not primarily an act of atonement.

### RSBY Yoledet

One might ask: what about the view of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who holds that a *yoledet* is a *chotei* — a sinner? He famously derives from the *yoledet*'s *chatat* that she sinned by swearing during childbirth never to be intimate with her husband again, and she requires atonement for that rash oath. According to this view, there is an element of genuine sin underlying the *yoledet*'s *korban*. Why does Yom Kippur not address it?

### Yoledet Purity

Rav Ashi responds: even according to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the *korban* of a *yoledet* functions *l'ishtruyei b'achilas kodashim* — to render her fit to eat *kodshim* again. Whatever sin element may be present, the fundamental purpose of the *korban* is to complete her *taharah* and restore her status, not to achieve atonement in the primary sense. This is a striking concession: even the view that identifies a sin element in the *yoledet*'s situation acknowledges that the atoning function is not what drives the obligation. Yom Kippur, which addresses atonement, therefore cannot substitute for a *korban* whose essential role is *taharah*.

Rav Ashi further notes that this is effectively demonstrated by our own *mishna*, which states explicitly: *ha'isha sheyesh aleiha chatas ha'of safek v'avar aleiha Yom HaKippurim chayaves l'havi l'achar Yom HaKippurim* — a woman with a doubtful *korban* obligation from a possible childbirth must still bring after Yom Kippur. The reason the *mishna* gives is *mipnei shemachshartah l'echol b'zvachim* — because the *korban* makes her fit to eat sacrificial food. The *taharah* function is explicit.

### Safek Metzora

The *gemara* continues: what about a *safek metzora* — someone whose *tzara'as* status is uncertain — who must bring *korbanos* as part of the *taharah* process at the conclusion of *tzara'as*? Why does Yom Kippur not dissolve that obligation? The answer is the same: Rav Oshaya invokes *l'chol chatosam v'lo l'chol tumasam*. The *korbanos* of a *metzora* are part of the *taharah* process, not an atonement for sin — even though Rabbi Yochanan taught in the name of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani that *negaim* come as a result of seven specific sins. Even when sin is an underlying cause, the *korbanos* serve *taharah*, not *kaparah*, and *ki maysei lav l'chapara maysei* — the *metzora* does not bring these offerings for atonement. Their purpose is *l'ishtruyei b'achilas kodshim* — to allow him to eat *kodshim* again.

### Safek Nazir

The *gemara* moves to the case of *safek nazir* — which in context means a *nazir* who became *tamei* under uncertain circumstances, and must bring a *korban* at the conclusion of the *tumah* period. Why does Yom Kippur not dissolve this doubt-based obligation?

Again: *l'chol chatosam v'lo l'chol tumasam*. The *tumah* dimension places this outside Yom Kippur's atoning reach.

But what about the view of Rabbi Elazar Ben Hakapar, who holds that a *nazir* is a *chotei* — a sinner — precisely because he denied himself wine? Here too the question arises: given a sin element, why doesn't Yom Kippur work? The *gemara* clarifies that Rabbi Elazar Ben Hakapar's *drasha* is specifically directed at the *chatat* brought by the *nazir tamei*, and his point may be that a *nazir* who was so careless as to allow himself to become *tamei* demonstrates that his *nezirus* was not sincerely motivated — which is precisely why this *nazir* in particular is called a *chotei*.

Nevertheless, the *gemara* answers: *nazir ki mayisi korban lav l'kapara mayisi*. The *korban* of the *nazir tamei* is not primarily for atonement. Notably, the usual *taharah*-completion formula — *l'ishtruyei b'achilas kodshim* — does not quite apply here either, since the *nazir* actually achieves *taharah* on the seventh day, and the *chatat* he brings is on the eighth day. Instead, the *gemara* gives a different functional explanation: *l'meichal alei nezirus tahara hu* — the *korban* serves to initiate the next stage of *nezirus*, the *nezirus* of *taharah*. It is not closing out *tumah*; it is opening a new period. This remains fundamentally a procedural and structural function rather than an atoning one, and Yom Kippur therefore does not displace it.

### Safek Sotah

The *gemara* turns to *safek sotah* — a woman who is a *sotah*, whose very status is defined by doubt, since she may or may not have committed adultery. Her *korban* is brought under conditions of uncertainty. Why does Yom Kippur not dissolve this obligation?

One might have argued the case for Yom Kippur applying: this involves a possible trespass against God and against her husband, and the sin — if it occurred — is something only God truly knows about (*cheit she'ein makir bo ela HaMakom*). Should that not bring it within Yom Kippur's purview?

The *gemara* offers several answers. Rav Oshaya's standard formula of *l'chol chatosam v'lo l'chol tumasam* is brought, though many textual variants strike it from this case since the *sotah*'s situation is not fundamentally about *tumah* in the ritual sense, even though she is called *tamei'ah*.

Abaye responds instead: *bo'el makir bo* — the adulterer, if one exists, knows about it. This undercuts the argument that it is a sin known only to God.

Rava gives the definitive answer: *sotah ki matya levar avon ka'ati* — the *sotah*'s *korban* does not come to atone for sin. It comes to clarify — to determine through the *sotah* ritual whether she sinned or not. Since its function is clarification rather than atonement, Yom Kippur, which addresses atonement, cannot substitute for it. The process of clarification must still take place even after Yom Kippur passes.

### Eglah Arufah

The *gemara* takes up the most challenging case: *eglah arufah* — the heifer brought when a murder victim is found between cities and the perpetrator is unknown. This too rests on a foundation of doubt regarding who is responsible. Why does Yom Kippur not dissolve the community's obligation?

Abaye answers: *horeg makir* — the murderer knows. It is therefore not a *cheit she'ein makir bo ela HaMakom*. Someone does have knowledge of the sin, even if the court does not.

Rava's answer draws on a *pasuk*: *vela'aretz lo yekhuppar ladam asher shuppakh bah* — the land cannot be atoned for the blood that was shed upon it except through the prescribed process. There is something categorically unique about murder that places it outside the ordinary reach of Yom Kippur's atonement. The verse signals that no other mechanism — including Yom Kippur — will suffice. The *eglah arufah* ritual holds the situation in abeyance until the murderer is found; only the murderer's death or the performance of this particular ceremony addresses the blood-guilt. This raises the broader implication that Yom Kippur may not atone for *retzicha* at all — a question the *gemara* leaves hovering.

Rav Papa adds yet another source: *kapper le'ammekha Yisrael asher padita* — "atone for Your people Israel whom You redeemed." From this the *gemara* derives that this atonement is fit to atone for those who left Egypt, implying that this particular form of atonement is perpetually required regardless of how many Yom Kippurs have intervened.

## Yedia Criterion

### Unknown During YK

Having established that Yom Kippur does dissolve an *asham talui* obligation on the grounds that it is a *cheit she'ein makir bo ela HaMakom*, the *gemara* now raises a further question. Since during Yom Kippur the sin was unknown — and we said Yom Kippur works for what only God knows — should we not go further and say that if the person later discovers he definitely did sin, he still need not bring a *chatat*? Perhaps Yom Kippur fully resolved the matter at the time, and any subsequent discovery changes nothing. The *gemara* asks: *eima ki mishtakhach leh batar Yom HaKippurim nami lo mayti chatat* — perhaps when one finds out after Yom Kippur, one still need not bring a *chatat*.

### Triple Yedia

Rabbi Zeira rejects this emphatically: *lo matzit amart* — this cannot be said. The reason is that the *pasuk* mentions *yedia* — the becoming-aware criterion for obligating a *korban* — three times: once by the *chatat* of the ordinary *yachid*, once by the *nasi*, and once by the *tzibur* (when the *beis din* issues an erroneous ruling and the community acts upon it). The verse says *o hoda elav chattato asher chata bah* — "or his sin became known to him." Since this appears three times, at least one mention is extra. That extra mention teaches that whenever one becomes aware of the sin — even after Yom Kippur, even if during Yom Kippur one had no knowledge — the *chatat* obligation is triggered.

The logic follows: Yom Kippur, in the context of an *asham talui*, provides protection from liability for the period of doubt. But it does not erase the underlying sin. When knowledge later arrives, the obligation crystallizes. The *asham talui* itself never claimed to wipe away the sin — only to protect the person pending clarification. So too Yom Kippur in this context protects but does not permanently resolve.

### One Case Insufficient
