The *gemara* then examines why all three mentions of *yedia* are necessary — and which one is the "extra." A single mention would not suffice to establish *yedia* as a universal criterion applicable across all three cases, because each case has a particular leniency that would allow one to argue the rule is local rather than universal.

### Yachid & Nasi

If the *Torah* wrote *yedia* only by the *yachid*, one could not derive the *nasi* and *tzibur* from it: *mah leyachid shekein kol korbano nekeivah* — since the *yachid* always brings a female *korban*, which is considered a lighter obligation, one might say the *Torah* goes easy on him and therefore requires *yedia* before obligating him. But the *nasi* and *tzibur*, who bring male *korbanos* — heavier obligations — one might say there the *Torah* is strict, and they would be obligated even without definite *yedia*.

Conversely, if the *Torah* wrote it only by the *nasi*, one could not derive the *yachid*: *mah lenasi shekein ein bishmias kol* — the *nasi* is exempt from the *korban* for failing to testify under oath, since a king cannot be compelled to testify. That leniency regarding the *nasi* might explain why *yedia* is required for him, while the *yachid*, who does bear that oath-testimony obligation, might be held to a stricter standard and obligated even without definite *yedia*.

### Tzibur Uniqueness

If the *Torah* wrote it only by the *tzibur*, one could not derive the others: *mah letzibur shekein ein chayav ela al he'elam davar im shigegas ma'aseh* — the *tzibur beis din* only becomes obligated when there is an erroneous *psak* followed by action in accordance with it. This more limited mechanism for incurring obligation might explain why *yedia* is required, while the *yachid* and *nasi*, who incur obligation through the sin directly without this two-stage process, might not require *yedia*.

### Two-Case Logic

Since no single case can establish the rule, the *gemara* considers whether two cases together could yield the third by common denominator — *tzad hashaveh*. The *gemara* examines all three pairings.

Writing *yedia* by *nasi* and *tzibur* but not by *yachid*: the common leniency of *nasi* and *tzibur* — that neither is subject to the oath-of-testimony *korban* (*bishmias kol*) — does not exist by *yachid*, so one might argue the *yachid* is more strict and does not require *yedia*.

Writing *yedia* by *yachid* and *nasi* but not by *tzibur*: the common feature of *yachid* and *nasi* is that both have at least some *korban* that is female (*nekeivah*) — the *yachid* generally and the *nasi* in the case of *avodah zarah* — which represents a leniency. The *tzibur* has no female *korban*, making it stricter; perhaps the *Torah* is therefore more stringent with *tzibur* and does not require *yedia*.

### Nasi Extra

The third combination — writing *yedia* by *yachid* and *tzibur* but not by *nasi* — succeeds. Any challenge based on the *yachid*'s leniency (*korbano nekeivah*) is answered by *tzibur*, which has no female *korban* and yet is included. Any challenge based on the *tzibur*'s leniency (*he'elam davar im shigegas ma'aseh*) is answered by *yachid*, who has no such requirement and yet is included. The leniency unique to each is not shared by the other, demonstrating that neither leniency is the operative reason for the *yedia* criterion. From *yachid* and *tzibur* together, therefore, one could have derived the rule for *nasi* as well.

The mention of *yedia* by *nasi* is therefore the extra mention. *Im eino inyan legufo* — if it is not needed to teach *yedia* for the *nasi* himself, since that can be derived from *yachid* and *tzibur* — *tanihu inyan leheicha demistayda leh batar Yom HaKippurim* — apply it to teach the case of one who discovers the sin after Yom Kippur: *demayti chatat asher chata'o* — he must bring a *chatat*. Post-Yom Kippur discovery of a sin fully obligates one in bringing a *chatat*, even though during Yom Kippur itself only God knew of the sin.

### Post-YK Discovery

This is the conclusion of the present stage of the discussion. The *yedia* principle operates independently of when awareness arrives. Yom Kippur's capacity to work for a *cheit she'ein makir bo ela HaMakom* does not permanently foreclose the *chatat* obligation — it merely holds it in suspension during the period of unknowing. Once *yedia* arrives, even if Yom Kippur has already passed, the obligation crystallizes in full. We know this specifically from the extra mention of *yedia* by *nasi*, which, having been rendered superfluous by the *tzad hashaveh* of *yachid* and *tzibur*, must be redirected to teach this law of post-Yom Kippur discovery. The discussion of further approaches to this principle will continue in the next session.

---

---

# Keritot 26b

## Yediah & Nasi

### Abaye's Challenge

The discussion opens at the final line of 26a, where the question is how we know that if *yom kippur* atones for an *asham talui* and one subsequently becomes aware of the *chet*, a *chatas* must still be brought. The answer proposed until now is that the extra *yediah* mentioned by the *nasi* was unnecessary and therefore serves to teach this rule. Abaye, however, disagrees. He argues from the bottom of 26a: *idei lo ksiv yediah gabi Nasi, meyachid vetzibur lo asi* — had the Torah not written *yediah* by the *nasi*, one could not have derived it from the *yachid* and *tzibur* alone. Why? *Mishum de'ika lemifrach*: there is a refutation available. *Mah leyachid vetzibur sheken einan asuyin lehishtanos* — the *yachid* and *tzibur* cannot change their status; would you say the same of the *nasi*, who can be deposed? Rashi notes that for a *tzad hashaveh* argument, any point of difference is sufficient to invalidate it. Accordingly, Abaye maintains that the *yediah* written by the *nasi* was indeed necessary, and we therefore cannot extract a free derivation from it.

### Gzerah Shavah

How, then, does Abaye know the rule? *Ela amar Abaye mehacha*: since all three categories — *nasi*, *yachid*, and *tzibur* — are linked by a *gzeirah shavah* through the word *mitzvos*, they share the same rules. Once they are all learned from one another, the fact that each writes *yediah* is entirely redundant — *keivan deyalfei mehadadi, lamah li deksav shalosh yedi'os*? The Torah need only have written it once. Therefore, *im eino inyan legufan*, since you do not need the extra mentions for their primary purpose, *tenahu inyan heicha demisyada leh basar Yom HaKippurim* — apply them to the case where one becomes aware after *yom kippur*, teaching that *hoda demaysi Chatas*, one must still bring a *chatas*.

### YK vs Asham Talui

At this point the Gemara raises a further question. Perhaps what we have demonstrated is only that awareness after *yom kippur* obligates a *chatas* — because *yom kippur* did not come specifically for this sin, its *kapparah* is generic, and when one later becomes aware, one must bring. But by an *asham talui*, which *de'al da'ata decheit asi* — which was brought specifically for this doubtful sin — perhaps it atones completely, such that if one becomes aware afterward, *lo maysi Chatas*? This is a striking point, because the rule that an *asham talui* does not wipe away the underlying sin has been assumed throughout the tractate; here the Gemara is pressing on the basis for that assumption.

### Asham Talui Function

*Amar Rava amar kra o hodah elav mikol makom* — Rava derives from the phrase *o hodah*, with its emphatic *o*, that in whatever circumstance one becomes aware, even after an *asham talui*, a *chatas* is still required. One might add, based on Abaye's reading, that two of the three extra *hodas* are available and one could have served this function — yet for some reason the Gemara does not take that approach and instead follows Rava's derivation from *o hodah*.

This then reopens the question already visited in the previous discussion: *Asham Talui lamah ba?* If it neither atones for the sin nor discharges the obligation, what does it accomplish? Rabbi Zeira answers: *she'im meis meis belo avon* — it provides atonement in the event that one dies having never become aware and therefore never brought a *chatas*. Rava objects: *meis? Misah memarekes* — death itself atones, so why is the *asham talui* needed for that purpose? *Ella amar Rava: lehagin alav min hayissurin* — it protects from punishment. It does not address the sin itself; it addresses one's state of guilt that would otherwise draw punishment. *Yom kippur*, when it arrives, similarly serves *magen mishum hayissurin*. The emphasis throughout is that the *asham talui* operates not by wiping away the sin but by something else entirely — addressing guilt or protecting from punishment — which is precisely why subsequent awareness still requires a *chatas*.

---

## Woman's Chatas

### Rav's Position

The Mishnah now turns — though in fact it doubles back to reunite two scenarios that were split across distant *mishnayos* — to the case of a woman who brought a *chatas ha'of* on doubt, uncertain whether she had given birth. A prior *mishnah* had addressed the case where she became aware before the *melikah* that she had definitely given birth: the offering proceeds as a *chatas vadai*, since *mi she-meivi al lo hoda meivi al hoda* — the same bird brought for doubt serves equally for certainty.

What was not discussed in that earlier *mishnah* is what happens if she becomes aware after the *melikah*. Unlike *asham talui* and *asham vadai*, which are distinct legal categories in the Torah, there is only one category of *chatas* — she simply did not know at the time whether she was obligated. Now that she knows she is obligated, why should she not be *yotzei* with what was already brought? *Amar Rav*: *mazzeh damah u-motzeh damah, v'kipprah u-muteres ba'achilah* — proceed, apply the blood, and it atones; you may eat it.

The text of our *mishnah* then requires clarification. The Gemara interprets Rav as addressing the scenario where *noda* that she was indeed obligated — found out she had given birth — and therefore the offering functions as a valid *chatas*. The reason the *mishnah* says to bury it would then be, on his reading, that no one was guarding it against *tumah* during the interval of uncertainty. The Gemara presses this: *eimas lo mishtameres?* When was it unguarded? Before the *shechitah* it was alive and cannot contract *tumah*; after the *melikah*, *ka minatar lah* — it is being guarded. The Gemara therefore concludes: *ella masnisin benoda lah delo yaldah* — our *mishnah* is in fact the case where she discovers she had not given birth. The offering is *chullin ba'azarah* and is buried. The note that this is *miderabbanan* reflects the position, cited by Rashi, that the *issur achilah* of *chullin ba'azarah* may not be fully *de'oraisa*, though the practical consequence — burial rather than feeding to a dog — follows from its being treated as *chullin ba'azarah*. Rashi raises the strange suggestion that *melikah* might not constitute *chullin ba'azarah*, though the *Shita Mekubetzes* understands the passage as simply reflecting the view that the *issur hana'ah* in this case is at least rabbinic.

### Maris Ha'ayin

Rabbi Yochanan's position differs from Rav's. While he agrees that if she learns after *melikah* that she was indeed obligated she would be *yotzei*, he rules *asurah ba'achilah* — it may not be eaten. The reason: *gezeirah shema yomru chatas ha'of haba'ah al hasafek ne'echeles* — onlookers who see the *kohen* eating will not know that she learned mid-process of her obligation, and will conclude that a *chatas ha'of* brought on doubt may be eaten. One might ask how this concern is realistic when it is only *kohanim* eating at the end of the day, all partaking of the same birds — it is indeed a good question, and the concern about misleading appearances is nevertheless maintained.

### Before/After Melikah

A *baraisa* of Levi is cited in support of Rav: if after *melikah* she learns she had given birth, one applies the blood and it atones, and it may be eaten. A separate *baraisa* aligns with Rabbi Yochanan. That *baraisa* systematically covers both scenarios — before and after *melikah*. Before *melikah*, if she learns she did not give birth: *teitzei l'chullin* — it returns to non-sacred status, or it may be sold to someone who needs to bring a bird *korban*. If before *melikah* she learns she did give birth: *vadai te'aseh vadai* — proceed as a definite *chatas*, since whether she did not know or does know, it is the same *korban*.

### Safek Status Sealed

After *melikah*, if she learns she gave birth: *asurah afilu b'hana'ah*. The language here is striking — *she-al hasafek ba'ah mit'chila kipper sefeika v'halcha lah*. This is the same formula used in the contexts of *egla arufa* and *asham talui*, where those offerings address the state of doubt at the time and their status is sealed accordingly. In truth, those contexts involve atoning for a doubtful sin; here the purpose was to allow her to become *tehora*. The formula is borrowed and does not map perfectly. The basic point, though, is that the offering fulfilled its function, and we will not permit eating it even after the fact, both because of concerns about misleading appearances and — as Rashi reads the language — perhaps because it retains its *safek* status in a more fundamental way, possibly *me-ikar ha-din* rather than merely *miderabbanan*.

---

## Two Rams for Asham

### Sufficient Ram

The *mishnah* establishes that one who sets aside two *sela'im* for an *asham* and purchases two rams at one *sela* each — so that initially neither appears to meet the minimum — may nonetheless bring the one that is worth two *sela'im* for his *asham*. The Torah does not specify how much one must spend; it specifies how much the animal must be worth, as Tosafos observes: even a gifted ram could in principle qualify, since the requirement speaks to value, not expenditure. The second ram, which carries *kedushat asham* but is not needed, is left to graze until it acquires a *mum*, is then redeemed, and the proceeds go toward a *nedava* — specifically an *olah*, since *mosar asham* is brought as an *olah*. One might ask whether this second ram could be saved until it is worth two *sela'im* and used for a future *asham* or transferred to another person's obligation, but the general principle — analogous to the rule that a *chatas* designated for one sin cannot be applied to another — would seem to preclude that.

### Misuse & Meilah

The *mishnah* then turns to the scenario where the person took the sanctified money and used it to buy two rams for his own secular use — *chullin*. This constitutes *meilah*, misuse of consecrated property. The discussion of *meilah* here serves as a transition toward the next *masechet*: the obligation of *meilah* requires repayment of the principal plus a *chomesh* — a fifth added to the base, which is in practice a quarter of the total repaid — as well as the bringing of an *asham me'ilos*, which likewise requires an animal worth two *shekel*.

The scenario constructed is: one *sela* was stolen from the consecrated money (worth four *zuz*), and the ram purchased with that and related funds turns out to be worth ten *zuz*. The arithmetic is deliberate: two *shekel* (eight *zuz*) plus a *chomesh* (twenty percent of eight, which is the extra two, bringing the total repayment to ten) equals ten *zuz*. The ten-*zuz* ram is brought as repayment toward the original *asham* obligation — the money goes back to the purpose from which it was taken. The eight-*zuz* ram — the one worth exactly two *shekel* — goes toward the *asham me'ilos*, since by committing *meilah* one has incurred a fresh obligation requiring an *asham* of minimum two *shekel*. The logic is that the two obligations happen to be satisfiable with the very animals purchased through the stolen money.

### One Sufficient, One Not

When one of the two rams is worth two *sela'im* and the other is worth ten *zuz*, the *mishnah* directs: *hayafeh shenei sela'im yikarev le'ashamo* — the one of sufficient value is brought for the *asham me'ilos*, and the one worth ten *zuz* — which represents the principal plus twenty percent — goes toward *leme'ilato*, the payback for the original misappropriation. The key principle, derived from *ve'et asher chata min hakodesh yeshalem ve'et chamishito yosef alav*, is that the principal and the *chomesh* are paid back together to the same source from which they were taken. The extra fifth does not get redirected toward one's own *asham* obligation; it belongs to whatever *hekdesh* account was drawn upon.

### Divided Usage

The final scenario in the *mishnah* envisions a case where one ram was legitimately designated as the *asham* and one was taken for secular use — *echad le'asham ve'echad lechullin*. One can imagine a concrete case: the man finds a ram worth two *shekel* selling for one, buys it for his *asham*, and then uses his spare *shekel* to buy something for his flock. If *shel asham yafeh shtei sela'im* — the *asham* ram is worth two *sela'im* — it is brought for the original obligation. The second ram, which represents the *meilah*, serves as the *asham me'ilos* assuming it too is worth two *shekel*. Additionally, *veyavi imah sela vechumshah* — he must separately repay the *shekel* he misappropriated plus its *chomesh*. Since the original *asham* was already brought, the repaid money cannot be used for another *asham* designated for the same sin; instead, as the *halacha* of *mosar asham* dictates, it would be used toward an *olah*.

---

## Meilah Terminology

### Reisha vs Seifa

The Gemara notices a terminological inconsistency within the *mishnah*. In the first case (*reisha*), the ten-*zuz* ram is described as going *leme'ilato* — for his *meilah* — meaning it represents the repayment of what was stolen. Yet in the final case (*seifa*), *hasheini limeilato* refers to bringing the second ram as an *asham me'ilos* — the obligatory *korban* for having committed *meilah*. The same word *meilah* thus designates two opposite things: in the *reisha*, the payback; in the *seifa*, the *korban* obligation.

### Chomesh Returns

The Gemara resolves this by articulating the underlying principle: *ve'et asher chata min hakodesh yeshalem ve'et chamishito yosef alav* — the *chomesh* is restored together with the principal, both returning to the original source. The extra fifth does not constitute an independent resource for satisfying other *korban* obligations; it is part of the restitution package. In the *reisha*, where the ten-*zuz* ram physically embodies both the principal and the *chomesh* in animal form, it is natural to call that ram *meilato* — the thing by which the *meilah* is paid back. *Keren v'chomesh* — principal and fifth — are brought together, and the animal therefore represents the *gezeilah*, the stolen amount. In the *seifa*, since the repayment is handled separately in coin form rather than through an animal, the word *meilato* shifts to refer to the *korban* obligation that arose from the act of *meilah*.

### Language Shifts

The Gemara formalizes the distinction: *reisha kari lei l'meiloso gezeilo* — in the first case, the word *meilato* means the stolen item being paid back; *seifa kari lei l'meiloso el asham* — at the end, it means the *asham me'ilos* itself. The principle organizing these usages is that *meilato* attaches to whichever obligation is being discharged in animal form. In the *reisha*, the ram *is* the repayment; in the *seifa*, the repayment is in coin and the ram *is* the *asham*. The usage shifts accordingly, and the twenty percent, in every instance, flows back to the function from which it was taken — if the original *korban* had already been brought, the funds become an *olah* as *mosar asham*.

---

## Shevach Hekdesh

### Rav Menashya's Q

Rav Menashya bar Gada poses a question: *bekinnus chumshin mahu?* — if one has accumulated multiple *chomeshim* from repeated acts of *meilah* against the same sanctified fund, may one use those collected fifths to satisfy the minimum value requirement of a *korban*? The scenario, following the *Shita Mekubetzes*, is where the accumulated fifths reach a full *shekel* — through multiple cycles of misappropriation and repayment — and the question is whether that *shekel*, now being paid back as it were to the fund from which it came, can also serve to satisfy the base cost of a *korban* obligation.

The question is framed against the backdrop of *shevach hekdesh* — the concept of natural appreciation of sanctified property. Normally, *shevach hekdesh* would arise when an animal sanctified as a *korban* gains weight and value after sanctification. Here, the "appreciation" of the *hekdesh* fund comes not from organic growth but from the obligation to pay back more than what was taken, by operation of the *halacha* of *meilah*. The question has two faces. One might say: even if *shevach hekdesh* generally works, here the increase did not come from investment or natural growth — *d'lo tara*, one did not make an effort — and therefore it cannot be used to gain *kapparah*, only the original *kedusha* can. Or one might say: even if natural growth does not work, here the money was directly sanctified for this purpose — *d'afrishei* — and therefore it should work.

### General Question

This frames the general question posed to the *beis medrash*: *mitkaper adam b'shevach hekdesh o lo?* Can a person achieve *kapparah* through the natural appreciation of a sanctified animal — that is, if an animal was sanctified when it was worth less than the required minimum, and it subsequently grew in value to meet the minimum, may it be brought as a valid *korban*?

### Mishnah Support

The Gemara first attempts to answer from our *mishnah* itself. If one of the rams purchased at one *sela* turns out to be worth two — *yikarev l'ashamo*, it is brought for the *asham* — perhaps this is a case of *shevach hekdesh*: the animal was bought for four *zuz* and appreciated to eight? This would demonstrate *mitkaper b'shevach hekdesh*. The Gemara rejects this reading: *d'ozil ro'eh gabei* — the shepherd gave a discount. At the moment of sanctification the animal was already worth two *shekel*, even though only one was paid. It is therefore not a case of post-sanctification appreciation at all — the requirement has always been about worth, not price.

### Fattening Tosefta

The Gemara turns to an explicit *Tosefta*: *lakach ayil b'sela u-pitmo v'he'emido al shtayim* — he bought a ram for one *shekel*, fattened it, and brought it to a value of two *shekel*. *Kasher* — it is valid. This appears to confirm *mitkaper b'shevach hekdesh*. The Gemara immediately qualifies: *pitmo shani* — fattening is different, because one invested one's own money into the animal. If the ram cost four *zuz* and the investment of fattening cost another four *zuz*, one has effectively spent eight *zuz* out of pocket; it is not *shevach hekdesh* in the sense of free appreciation, it is a direct investment. The Gemara then considers the *seifa* of that same *Tosefta*: *lakach ayil b'arba'ah v'ashkachei b'tlata v'shavei tamnya* — one bought it for four, invested only three more, yet it is worth eight. Here the single extra *zuz* of appreciation beyond investment is genuine *shevach hekdesh*. The Gemara will eventually come around to acknowledging this constitutes *shevach hekdesh*, but at this stage it maintains that the case is still one of investment.

### Payment Difference

The *Tosefta* continues: *v'yashlim sela* — even though the *korban* works, one must pay back a *sela* (or, as the Gemara clarifies, *tashlumei d'sela* — the remainder of the *sela*, meaning whatever portion was not invested, as little as one *zuz*). This halacha appears strange: if the animal now genuinely meets the minimum value requirement, why must any additional payment be made? The Gemara's answer is: *gezeirah shema yomru haya pachot mishtei sela'im mechaper* — people will see that someone spent less than two *shekel* and conclude that an *asham* of insufficient value can achieve *kapparah*. The requirement to pay the difference is therefore not a function of the *korban* being invalid — it is fully valid; one is indeed *mitkaper* — but a rabbinic *gezeirah* against creating misleading impressions.

One might press: how would anyone know how much was spent? The answer is that people always talk about bargains. In any case, the practical *halacha* is that even if the animal improved entirely by itself without any investment, *me-ikar ha-din* it achieves *kapparah*, and one must nonetheless pay the difference out of pocket to avoid the misleading appearance that a subminimum *asham* was sufficient.

### Elazar & Yochanan

A *tanna'im*-framed *baraisa* then states directly: *de'ein adam miskaper beshevach Hekdesh*. The Gemara immediately resolves the difficulty: this does not render the *korban* invalid, as the prior analysis demonstrated. Rather, as already established, one must pay the shortfall separately. *Le'olam kasavar adam mitkaper beshevach Hekdesh*, and the payment is purely a rabbinic requirement to forestall misleading impressions — the fundamental *din* is that *shevach hekdesh* functions for *kapparah*.

When Rabbi Elazar asks Rabbi Yochanan this very question — *adam mitkaper b'shevach hekdesh o lo?* — Rabbi Yochanan responds with characteristic astonishment: *kamma shanim gadal zeh beineinu velo shama halakha zu mimeni?* — how many years have you been with us and you never heard me teach this *halacha*? The implication, *mikhlal de'amar Rabbi Yochanan in*, is that Rabbi Yochanan rules yes, one is *mitkaper b'shevach hekdesh*.

### Todah Child

The source Rabbi Yochanan relies upon is: *vlad todah u-tmuratah* — the offspring of a *todah* or a *temurah*, which by themselves do not require bread, but *la-achar kapara* — after the mother has been brought for the obligation — are brought without bread; whereas *lifnei kapara* — before the mother has been brought — the child may serve as the *todah* itself and is brought *taun lechem*, with the full bread complement. This is the ruling sent by Rabbi Chanina in the name of Rabbi Yochanan. What one sees is that the offspring of the sanctified animal — a natural increase after sanctification — can be used to fulfill the *todah* obligation. The birth is a form of *shevach hekdesh*, and it clearly functions to discharge the obligation. *Alma kasavar: miskaper b'shevach hekdesh.*

---

## Living Animals Q's

### Nidachim Question

Following the pattern established in the prior exchange, Rabbi Elazar now poses a further question to Rabbi Yochanan: *ba'alei chayim nidachim o lo?* — can a living animal be rendered *nidach*, stigmatized and permanently disqualified, or does *dichui* apply only after death? Rabbi Yochanan again responds: *harei kamma shanim gadal zeh beineinu velo shamata halacha zu mimeni?* — you have been with us all these years and never heard me teach this? *Miklal d'Rabbi Yochanan amar in* — Rabbi Yochanan holds that even a living animal can be rendered *nidach*.

### Half-Ownership Case

Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on *ba'alei chayim nidachim* derives from the following case: *behema shel shnei shutfin hikdish chetzyo* — an animal owned by two partners, where one sanctified his half. Since half an animal cannot be brought as a *korban*, the *kedusha* cannot function at the *mizbe'ach* level; it is merely *kedushat damim*, a monetary *kedusha*. The partner then buys back the other half and sanctifies that half as well. The result: *kedusha ve-eina kreiva* — it has sanctity but may not be brought, because the initial sanctification already stigmatized it.

### Three Conclusions

*Shma mina tlat* — three conclusions are drawn. First, *ba'alei chayim nidachim* — even a living animal can be *nidach*: the animal here is alive, yet it is permanently disqualified. Second, *kedushat damim madcha* — even a *kedusha* that was never *kedushat mizbe'ach* from its inception can create *dichui*: the initial sanctification was only *kedushat damim* at the time, yet it stigmatized the animal. Third, *yesh dichui be-damim* — *dichui* can exist even at the level of *kedushat damim* alone. Rashi observes, and notes that Tosafos typically wrestles with distinguishing the second and third conclusions in cases of this recurring *sugyah*, that the two are in essence the same point: the novelty is that *dichui* operates even when the animal was never actually fit to be brought as a *korban mizbe'ach*.

---

## Minimum Value Q

### Unavailable Value

Rabbi Elazar poses yet another question, this one connecting directly back to the *mishnah*'s framework: *huzlu tlayim ba-olam mahu?* — if rams become so cheap that none are available at a value of two *shekel*, what is one to do? The *asham* requires an animal worth two *shekel*, but we have established that the requirement is about worth, not price. If no animal of the right age meets the minimum value, can one bring the best available and satisfy the requirement on the grounds of *mivchar nidreichem ba'inan* — we require one's best, and this is the best there is? Or does the Torah's formulation of *kesef shekalim ba'inan* — a specific monetary minimum is required — constitute an absolute threshold that cannot be bypassed?

### Absolute Minimum

Rabbi Yochanan responds — though notably, he says *lo limadnu halacha zu*, we have never taught this *halacha* in the *beis medrash* — with a teaching in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: *mipnei ma lo nitna kitzva be-mechusrei kapara?* Why did the Torah not specify a minimum value for the *korban* brought by those requiring *kapparah* to permit eating *kodashim* — the *mechasrei kapara* category? Because *shema yuzlu telaim ve-ein lahem takana le-echol be-kodashim* — if rams became cheap and one could not satisfy a minimum, they would be permanently barred from *kodashim*. The Torah therefore intentionally omitted a minimum for that category precisely to avoid that outcome. By implication, in the categories *where* the Torah did specify a minimum — such as *asham* — even if animals become so cheap that the minimum cannot be met, one is simply stuck. The minimum is absolute.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenges this reasoning: *ela me-ata chatas chelev tinasen bah kitzva* — if the concern about *mechasrei kapara* is that a minimum would strand people from *kodashim*, the same logic would suggest a minimum for a *chatas chelev* should also be absent. After all, a *chatas* is also purely about *kapparah*, not about restoring eligibility to eat *kodashim*. And yet there is no minimum for a *chatas* either — *ve-lav le-ishtruyei be-achilas kodashim hu*. The argument from *mechasrei kapara* does not cleanly explain why *asham* has a minimum while *chatas* does not.

### Rava's Challenge

Rava presses further: *ela me-ata asham nazir le-havei bei kitzva* — among the various *ashamos*, why does an *asham nazir* not have a minimum? *De-levatala hu de-asi* — an *asham nazir* is unique in that nothing depends on it: it is a *chiyuv*, but it does not unlock *tahara*, does not initiate or conclude the *nezirus*, nothing pivots on it. Rabbi Yochanan himself states in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: *ein lach davar she-ba le-vatala ela asham nazir bilvad* — the only *korban* that functions purely as an obligation without anything depending on it is the *asham nazir*. If the logic is that a minimum is tolerable when delay causes no irreversible harm, then by *asham nazir* — where nothing at all depends on it — a minimum should have been imposed. Yet it was not.

### Why Asham Minimum

*Kashya.* The Gemara leaves the question unresolved. The reasoning advanced — that the Torah omitted minimums where they would cause permanent harm, implying that where a minimum exists it is absolute — does not coherently explain the distribution of minimums across the various *korban* categories. Virtually nothing except certain *ashamos* has a minimum value requirement; the exceptional case is not the absence of a minimum but its presence. The more pointed question, as the Gemara's trajectory reveals, is not why *mechasrei kapara* has no minimum, but why the *asham* specifically was singled out to have one at all. That question remains open.

---

---

# Keritot 27b

## Korban Designation

### Son & Father's Chattat

The *mishnah* opens with a seemingly straightforward case: if a person sets aside a *chattat* and then dies, his son cannot bring that *chattat* in his father's place. This ruling launches an extended discussion about the specificity with which a *korban* is designated—not merely for a particular person, but for a particular sin.

### No Kapara for Dead

Two distinct reasons underlie this prohibition. First, there is no formal halachic *kapara* for the dead—whatever other traditions exist regarding *kaddish* or learning *mishnayot* on behalf of the deceased, no *korban* can achieve atonement for someone who has already died. Second, and more fundamentally, a *chattat* cannot be used for a person other than the one it was designated for, nor can it be used for a sin other than the one it was designated to atone for. The *mishnah* presses this point to its logical extreme: even the person himself cannot bring a *chattat* designated for one act of eating *chelev* to atone for a different act of eating *chelev* on a different day. The specificity is absolute—the *chattat* is tied to the person and to the precise sin.

### Peshat from Vayikra

The biblical source for this principle is the phrase *korbano al chataso*—his *korban* for his sin. The word *korbano* indicates that it must be his own *korban*, not his father's; *chataso* indicates that it must be for his specific sin, not a different one.

### Father's Money Question

The *gemara* then probes further. If an animal is too specifically designated to be transferred, what about money? After all, unlike an animal, money is more abstract—perhaps money sanctified by a father for a *chattat* could be used by the son. The *tana rabbanan* works through several hypothetical cases: perhaps a son cannot use his father's sanctified animal, but could he use his father's sanctified money? And could he perhaps use it even across different categories of sin—light to light, or heavy to heavy?

### Animal vs. Money Kedusha

The *gemara* explains why there is a conceptual distinction between an animal and money, and why that distinction ultimately does not permit reassignment in either case. The key concept is the nature of *kedusha*. When an animal is designated as a *chattat*, its *kedusha* is fixed absolutely—even if one were to commit *me'ila* with that animal, it would not lose its sanctity and exit to *chullin*. This immovability is evidence that its identity is wholly fixed and cannot be switched. Money, by contrast, has a more transferable *kedusha*: if one commits *me'ila* with designated money, that money does become desanctified and exit to *chullin*. One might therefore think that because money's *kedusha* is less fixed, the designation could be reassigned. Similarly, an unblemished animal cannot be redeemed to transfer its *kedusha*, whereas money can be transferred—another indication that the animal's *kedusha* is categorically more rigid.

### Me'ila & Fixed Identity

The *gemara* pursues this logic carefully. For an animal, the reasoning is: *lo ma'al velo kiper*—since *me'ila* would not dislodge the animal's *kedusha*, there is no avenue by which its identity could ever shift, and therefore reassignment is impossible. For money, the argument is more nuanced. Since if one *were* to commit *me'ila* with the money it would become desanctified and one could then use it for a different *korban*—even if illicitly—this shows in principle that the money's designation is not entirely immovable. One might therefore conclude that even *lechatchila* the money could be reassigned. The *gemara* rejects this: the *pasuk* says *korbano al chataso*, establishing that even money designated for a *chattat* cannot be reassigned to a different sin. The identity is fixed regardless.

Rav Pappa clarifies the precise meaning of *lo ma'al velo kiper* in the animal case: since there is no way, even through transgression, to dislodge the animal's *kedusha*, the animal can never serve another purpose—and therefore its designation is absolutely immovable. With money, since transgression *would* in theory result in the money becoming *chullin* and then being used for a different *korban*, one might have thought reassignment should be permitted. The *pasuk* teaches otherwise.

The discussion closes with a note that the same rule governs an *asham talui*: the final ruling follows the *chattat*—it too is specific to person and sin, and cannot be reassigned.

---

## Ola VeYored Switches

### Sheep to Goat Switch

The *mishnah* proceeds to a separate category of cases involving flexibility within the same *korban*. If a person sanctified money to purchase a sheep for a *chattat*, he may change his mind and use the money instead for a goat—and vice versa. This is not considered reassigning the *korban* to a different sin; the money remains *chattat* money. It simply was not specifically sheep money, and the shift from one animal to another of the same halachic category is permitted.

### Up & Down Scale

The more dramatic flexibility concerns the *olah veyored*—the small set of sins for which the Torah mandates a korban scaled to the sinner's economic standing. The *olah veyored* obligates a wealthy person to bring a sheep or goat, a person of middle means to bring two birds (one *chattat*, one *olah*), and a very poor person to bring a *minchah*. The *mishnah* rules that if one's financial standing shifts after setting aside money, one may move along this scale accordingly. If you set aside money for a sheep and became poorer, you may redirect the money to birds. If you became poorer still, you may redirect it to a *minchah*, pocketing any surplus. Conversely, if you set aside money for a *minchah* and became richer, you must add to it and bring a bird; richer still, a sheep or goat.

The *Rambam*'s explanation of the mechanics is instructive: you purchase the birds with your own money and then declare that the *kedusha* of the original sum is transferred onto the birds. While ordinarily one may not transfer *kedusha* from a more valuable item to a lesser one, if one does so it nonetheless takes effect—and here, because the *korban* obligation has itself shifted, this transfer is permitted even *lechatchila*. The remainder of the original sanctified money becomes *chullin* and may be used for personal needs.

It is worth emphasizing that the critical moment for determining one's financial standing is *not* the moment of sanctification. As the *mishnah* makes plain, if you sanctified money for a sheep and later became richer, you are obligated to bring a sheep—you cannot avail yourself of the more lenient category simply because you happened to sanctify the money when you were poorer.

### Mem vs. Alef Derasha

The *gemara* derives the rules of the *olah veyored* scale from two phrases in the *pasuk*. When the Torah speaks of bringing a sheep or goat it uses the term *mechataso*—with a *mem*, meaning "from his sin," indicating a subset of the larger amount. When speaking of the *minchah* it uses the term *al chataso*—with an *alef lamed*, meaning "upon his sin," indicating addition. The *mem* teaches that one may draw *down* from what was designated—i.e., use part of the sheep-money for a bird or part of the bird-money for a *minchah*. The *al* teaches that one may add *up*—supplementing the *minchah* money to bring a bird, or supplementing the bird money to bring a sheep.

### Repetition Defense

One might ask: why does the Torah need to say *mechataso* both by the sheep-or-goat case and again by the bird case? Would it not suffice to state it once and let us infer the rest? The *gemara* explains that without the second statement, one would have thought that moving down from sheep to birds is permitted—since both are blood offerings placed on the altar—but moving down from birds to a *minchah* is not, since a *minchah* is a fundamentally different type of *korban* that involves no blood at all. Therefore the Torah had to state *mechataso* explicitly by the bird case as well, to teach that one may move down even from birds to a *minchah*.

Symmetrically, why state *al chataso* by the *minchah* rather than by the bird? Had the Torah stated it by the bird, one might have inferred that moving up from birds to sheep-or-goat is permitted—since both are blood offerings—but moving up from a *minchah* to a bird might not be, since they are categorically different. By stating *al chataso* at the *minchah* level, the Torah teaches that even from a *minchah* one may move upward to a bird and from a bird to a sheep. Both phrases are thus indispensable.

### Bird Redemption Limit

There is one important limitation in moving down the scale: if one has sanctified the birds themselves—not merely money for birds—and they acquire a blemish, one cannot redeem them and redirect the proceeds to a *minchah*. The reason is that birds have no *pidyon*—there is no halachic mechanism to redeem a sanctified bird. This means that if one has sanctified actual birds rather than money, one is in a very constrained position. The birds cannot be redeemed, they cannot move down to a *minchah*, and one is essentially stuck with them.

---

## Dichuy Principle

### Rich Sets Aside Birds

Rav Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya addresses the following case: a wealthy person who contracted *tum'at mikdash* (entering the Temple while impure or eating *kodashim* while impure)—one of the classic *olah veyored* categories—is obligated to bring a sheep. Instead, this person sets aside birds. Subsequently, the person becomes poor, and birds are now their proper *korban*. Can they now use those birds?

The ruling is *hova'il venidcha yidacheh*—since those birds were pushed away and unacceptable at the moment they were designated, they remain pushed away permanently. When the person was rich, those birds were not their proper *korban*. They were labeled unacceptable at that moment, and that rejection is permanent even though they have now become the proper *korban*. This is the principle of *dichuy*: once a *korban* is stamped as rejected, that stigma does not lift.

Note that this case involves the actual birds, not money. The question of whether the same principle would apply to sanctified money—which is conceptually more fungible—is left open. But once the birds themselves are sanctified, they carry *kedusha* (specifically *kedushat damim*), and the *dichuy* attaches to them with full force. One cannot even redeem them, since birds have no *pidyon*, leaving the birds in an essentially irresolvable state.

### Shema Mina Telat

Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua draws three conclusions from this ruling—a *shema mina telat*. First, *ba'alei chayim nidchin*: live animals can be subject to *dichuy*. Some hold that this is impossible—that a living creature cannot be permanently rejected—but this case implies they can. Second, *kedushat damim nidchah*: even when the *kedusha* was only *kedushat damim* (monetary sanctity) from the outset—since the birds were never fit as this person's proper *korban* from the moment of their designation—this form of *kedusha* is nonetheless subject to *dichuy*. Third, *dichuy mei'ikara havei dichuy*: even rejection from the very beginning, where the object was never once fit, constitutes valid *dichuy*. It is worth noting that these latter two conclusions overlap considerably, and the *gemara* itself acknowledges that the last two tend to collapse into each other when discussing *ba'alei chayim nidchin*—the *gemara* notes that it always seeks three and that the final two tend to be closely related.

### Rabbi Shimon Dispute

Rav Ukva bar Chama challenges from a *braita*: if someone designates a female animal for the *Pesach* offering before Passover (a *Pesach* requires a male), the animal must wait to acquire a blemish, be redeemed, and the proceeds used to purchase a proper *Pesach*. If before that redemption the female gives birth to a male, that male must likewise wait to acquire a blemish and be redeemed—it cannot simply be brought as a *Pesach* directly. But Rabbi Shimon disagrees and says the male offspring *can* be brought as a *Pesach*. 

From Rabbi Shimon's ruling, we see that he holds *ba'alei chayim einan nidchin*—live animals are not subject to *dichuy*. The mother's unacceptability does not invalidate the male offspring; the offspring carries *kedushat Pesach* and, being male, is fit to be brought. This directly contradicts the three-fold conclusion drawn above. The *gemara* resolves the tension by noting that the ruling of Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua was stated in accordance with the majority view that disputes Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Shimon's view—that *ba'alei chayim einan nidchin*—is a known minority position.

### Hagralah Case

Rav Shimi bar Ashi adds a further nuance regarding Rabbi Shimon's position. Rabbi Shimon also holds that the *hagralah*—the drawing of lots over the two Yom Kippur goats—is not indispensable (*einah me'akevet*). These two positions of Rabbi Shimon are linked. In the case where one of the pair of Yom Kippur goats dies after the lots are drawn, the surviving goat was temporarily unfit—it had no pair. Rabbi Shimon says that the surviving goat is not thereby rendered *nidcheh*, since *ba'alei chayim einan nidchin*, and furthermore that when a replacement is found the lots need not be redrawn. For the majority, who hold that *ba'alei chayim nidchin*, the remaining goat is stigmatized by its period of unfitness and cannot simply be reused with a replacement.

---

## Bird Designation Timing

### Rav Chisda Rule

Rav Chisda establishes a foundational principle for the tractate of *Kinnim*: the birds of a *kan* (a pair of birds obligated as one *chattat* and one *olah*) cannot acquire their individual designations—which is the *chattat* and which is the *olah*—except at one of two specific moments. Either the owner designates them at the time of *lekichah*, purchase, or the *kohen* designates them at the time of performing the service. Any designation attempted in between these two moments is halachically inoperative.

### Vayikra Designation

Rav Shimi bar Ashi provides the textual basis for this principle. One *pasuk* says *ve-lakcha shtei torim*—"and she shall take two birds"—and then *echad le-chatas ve-echad le-olah*, "one for a *chattat* and one for an *olah*." The phrase "one for a *chattat* and one for an *olah*" appears at the moment of *ve-lakcha*, the taking or purchase. A second *pasuk* says *ve-asah ha-kohen*—"and the *kohen* shall perform"—followed again by *echad le-chatas ve-echad le-olah*. The designation phrase thus appears exclusively at the moment of purchase and at the moment of the *kohen*'s action, nowhere between.

### Hagralah Challenge

The *gemara* challenges this from the *hagralah* of Yom Kippur. By the two Yom Kippur goats, both goats have already been sanctified, and the question of which is the *chattat* and which is the *la-Azazel* goat is resolved only by drawing lots—which occurs at a middle stage, neither at the time the goats were purchased nor at the time the *kohen* performs the service. This is a form of designation occurring at an intermediate time, seemingly contradicting Rav Chisda's rule.

### Kal VaChomer Analysis

The *gemara* considers a *kal vachomer*. For a normal *korban*, a lot would not sanctify an animal—verbal designation (*shem*) is what creates *kedusha* and identity. By the Yom Kippur goats, the lot *does* create the designation. One might therefore argue: just as lots work at their appointed time for the Yom Kippur goats—a time that is neither purchase nor service—so too should verbal designation work at some intermediate time for birds, and at an even greater degree since verbal designation is the more standard form.

### Verse Override

The *gemara* resolves the challenge by clarifying that the comparison to the Yom Kippur goats is an analogy, not an identity. The *pasuk* states *ve-asahu chatas*—"and it shall make it a *chattat*"—from which the *drashah* derives that only the lot makes it a *chattat*, not verbal designation, and not any action of the *kohen* alone in a non-standard way. The *kal vachomer* would have been persuasive, but the *pasuk* overrides it explicitly. Moreover, the analogy is more subtle: for birds, wherever the right time is—purchase or the *kohen*'s action—verbal designation works at that right time; lots do not. For the Yom Kippur goats, the designated time is the drawing of lots, and verbal designation does not work even then. The two cases operate by different rules, and the *pasuk* for the Yom Kippur goats is explicit that only the lot governs.

---

## Bird Money Subdivision

### Poor to Rich Case

The *gemara* now examines a *braita* related to the *mishnah*'s teaching about moving up the scale. A poor person who incurred *tum'at mikdash* sets aside money for a *kan*—a pair of birds. Subsequently, the person becomes rich, so the bird offering is no longer the correct *korban*; a sheep or goat is required. The person then declares: this portion of the money is for my *chattat* and this portion for my *olah*. He then adds funds to the *chattat* portion and brings a sheep or goat *chattat*. The *braita* permits this addition for the *chattat* portion. However, he cannot add to the *olah* portion and bring a separate *olah* from it, since the obligation of a *chattat-olah* pair applies specifically when bringing birds—when bringing a sheep or goat, only a *chattat* is required, not an *olah*. The *olah* bird money therefore remains designated as *olah* and goes toward a *nedavah*.

This *braita* clarifies the *mishnah*: the permission to add to bird money and redirect it to a sheep or goat applies only when the bird money is undivided and generic. Once it has been subdivided—with specific amounts assigned to the *chattat* and the *olah*—only the *chattat* portion may be supplemented and redirected. The *olah* portion is fixed in its designation.

### Rav Sheshes Challenge

Rav Sheshes objects to the *braita* as it appears to read. The *braita* states that after becoming rich, the person declares which portion is for what. But once a person is rich, birds are categorically not their *korban*. How can such a person, now firmly in the sheep-or-goat category, validly declare which portion of the bird money is for a *chattat* and which for an *olah*? This subdivision is irrelevant to a rich person's obligation.

### Rich Cannot Use Bird

This objection is reinforced by the ruling of Rav Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya stated earlier: if a rich person who incurred *tum'at mikdash* brought a bird offering, he would not be *yotzei* even *bedi'eved*. If a rich person cannot fulfill the obligation with birds even after the fact, then any subdivision of bird money by a rich person is legally meaningless—the designation of which birds would serve as *chattat* and which as *olah* has no operative effect on someone for whom birds are entirely outside the applicable *korban* category.

### Original Designation

The resolution is that the *braita* does not mean the person declared the subdivision *after* becoming rich. Rather, the *braita* must be read as saying the person had already declared which portion was for the *chattat* and which for the *olah* back when he was still poor and originally set aside the money. The subdivision was established at the original moment of sanctification. This also resolves the earlier question about timing: just as one may designate which bird is the *chattat* and which is the *olah* at the moment of purchase, so too may one designate which portion of money serves which purpose at the moment of original sanctification.

### Post-Facto Option

Rav Chaga in the name of Rav Oshaya, however, holds a different position: *bedi'eved*, a rich person who brought a bird offering is *yotzei*. If that is so, then even after becoming rich the person is still in principle within the purview of the bird *korban*, and a declaration of which portion serves as *chattat* and which as *olah* would have legal force. According to this view, the *braita* can indeed be read literally—the person designated after becoming rich—because even a rich person retains a residual connection to the bird *korban bedi'eved*. The *gemara* suggests reading the *braita* accordingly: when it says the person "declared" which is which, it may mean the person *purchased* the birds at that point (the moment of *lekichah*), which is one of the two valid moments of designation identified by Rav Chisda.

---

## Scale Movement Post-Facto

### Metzora Scale

The *gemara* now turns to the question of scale movement in the *olah veyored* after the fact, focusing on the *metzora* as a test case. A *braita* states: a poor *metzora* who brought the richer offering—the more expensive *korban*—is *yotzei*. But a rich *metzora* who brought the poorer offering is not *yotzei*. This establishes that for a *metzora*, going up on the scale is valid even *bedi'eved*, but going down is not.

### Zos vs. Toras

The textual basis for this ruling lies in the language the Torah uses by the *metzora*. The word *zos*—"this is"—implies exactitude: the law is precisely as stated, neither more lenient nor more stringent. By itself, *zos* would prohibit both going up and going down. However, the Torah also uses the word *toras*—"the teaching of"—which is inclusive and broadens the category. The *braita* derives from *toras* that a poor person who brings a richer offering is *yotzei*, but derives from *zos* that a rich person who brings a poorer offering is not.

### Metzora Unique

One might ask: why not derive from the *metzora* case that going down on the scale is forbidden for all *olah veyored* situations? The *gemara* explains that the limitation on going down is unique to the *metzora*, because the Torah uses a limiting word there—*hu*, "he," applied to the poor person—which confines the leniency of the lower-tier offering specifically to a poor person. By contrast, by other *olah veyored* cases (such as *tum'at mikdash*), no such limiting language appears, leaving open the debate whether going down *bedi'eved* is valid.

### Up Down Summary

The conclusion of this discussion is that going up the scale—a poorer person bringing a more expensive offering—is apparently universally valid *bedi'eved* across all *olah veyored* categories. Going down—a richer person bringing a cheaper offering—is explicitly forbidden for the *metzora* by the word *zos*, and is the subject of debate for other *olah veyored* cases. According to the view of Rav Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya, going down does not fulfill the obligation even *bedi'eved*; according to Rav Chaga in the name of Rav Oshaya, going down is valid *bedi'eved* in cases other than *metzora*.

---

## Hierarchies & Rankings

### Sheep vs. Goat

The final *mishnah* of the tractate is taught by Rabbi Shimon. He observes that everywhere in the Torah, sheep (*kevasim*) are mentioned before goats (*izim*). One might therefore conclude that sheep are superior and preferable for *korbanot*. Rabbi Shimon shows that this cannot be the correct reading: in one place the Torah says *ve-im keves yavi korbano le-chatat*—"and if he brings a sheep as his sin offering"—reversing the usual order and mentioning a sheep in a context where a goat had just been discussed. This reversal teaches that the two are entirely equal—the standard ordering is a stylistic convention, not an expression of hierarchy.

### Other Reversals

Rabbi Shimon applies the same reasoning to two other standard pairings. The Torah consistently mentions *torim* (turtledoves) before *bnei yonah* (pigeons), but in one place reverses the order—*ven yonah o tor le-chatat*—teaching that turtledoves and pigeons are equal. Similarly, the Torah consistently mentions the father before the mother, as in *kabed et avicha ve-et imecha*, but in another verse reverses it: *ish imo ve-aviv tira'u*—teaching that both parents are equal in the obligations of honor and reverence.

### Father Precedence

Despite the equivalence established by Rabbi Shimon, the Sages add a practical qualification: in all places, the father takes precedence over the mother. The reasoning given is not that the father is categorically superior, but that the son's mother herself is obligated in honoring her husband. When there is a conflict and a choice must be made, the father takes precedence because the mother too stands in a position of deference to him. This applies, it should be noted, specifically within the context of a marriage; if the parents are divorced or otherwise not in that relationship, no such hierarchy between them would apply.

### Rav Priority

The *mishnah* adds a parallel ruling regarding the primacy of a *rav* over a father in the context of Torah study. If a son has merited to study Torah before a *rav*, that *rav* takes precedence over the father in matters of honor. The *mishnah*'s stated reason is that both the son *and the father* are obligated in honoring the *rav*—meaning the *rav*'s claim on honor supersedes even the father's claim, since the father himself owes honor to the *rav*. Elsewhere in the *gemara* (developed more fully in *Kiddushin*) a deeper reason is given—the father brings a child into this world while the *rav* brings a student into the life of the World to Come—but here the *mishnah* grounds the ruling in the fact that the father himself participates in the obligation of *kavod* toward the *rav*.

---

## Temple Cryings

### First & Second

The tractate concludes with an *aggadic* passage. The *gemara* records that the Temple courtyard cried out four times—personifying the *azarah* as expressing either revulsion or welcome. The first crying was an expulsion: "Remove from here the sons of Eli, Hofni and Phinehas, who defiled the *Heichal*." Their misdeeds are well known from *Tanakh*. The second was a welcome: "Open the gates and let Yochanan ben Nidbai, student of Pinkai, enter and fill his belly from the sacrifices of heaven." Far from being a compliment to his character, this is a tribute to his utility: he was said to eat four *se'ah* of birds as a dessert course, and as long as he was present, there was never meat left over in the *azarah*—the prohibition of *notar* was never violated on his watch.

### Third & Fourth

The third crying was another welcome: "Lift your heads, O gates, and let Elishama ben Phikai, student of Pinchas, enter and serve in the *kehuna gedolah*." The fourth was an expulsion: "Open the gates and remove Issachar ish Kfar Barkai, who honors himself while dishonoring the sacrifices of Heaven."

### Silk Gloves Sin

What was Issachar's offense? He would wrap his hands in silk before performing the *avodah*—he wore what amounted to silk gloves in order to protect his hands. The concern was clearly for his own dignity and comfort rather than for the integrity of the service. This not only expressed contempt for the *korbanot* but also technically invalidated the *avodah*, since contact through an intervening material is *pasul*.

### Hands Cut Off

The story of Issachar's end is told with stark irony. King Yannai and his queen were debating whether goats or sheep are superior meat. They sent the question to Issachar ish Kfar Barkai—he was always at the *korbanot*, they said, so he would know. Issachar replied: if goats were superior, they would have been brought as the *korban tamid*; clearly since sheep are brought daily, sheep are better. Not only did this side him with the queen against the king, but as he made his argument, he accompanied it with a dismissive wave of his hand toward the king. The king ordered that his right hand be cut off—the very hand he had wrapped in silk to protect it. Issachar bribed the executioner, who cut off only his left hand. When the king discovered this, he ordered the right hand cut off as well. Issachar lost both hands. Rav Yosef declares: blessed is God who brought Issachar ish Kfar Barkai his *metafsarei*—his comeuppance.

### Ignorance Added

Rav Ashi adds a final dimension to Issachar's disgrace. The man apparently never even learned the *mishnayot*—specifically the very *mishnah* taught at the end of this tractate. Had he learned it, he would have known that sheep and goats are declared equal by the Torah itself. He could have answered the king's question without siding with anyone: both are the same. Instead, his ignorance compounded his arrogance. Ravina adds: he did not even know the basic *pesukim*, since the Torah's phrasing—*im keves im ez*, "if a sheep, if a goat"—in perfectly parallel construction already signals their equivalence to anyone who has read *Chumash*. The dismissive gesture with the silken hands was the visible expression of a deeper contempt rooted in ignorance.

---

## Peace Through Torah

### Talmidei Chacham

The tractate ends, as is fitting, on a note of reconciliation. After a story about arrogance, contempt, and violence, the *gemara* closes with Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Chanina: *talmidei chachamim marbim shalom ba-olam*—students of the wise increase peace in the world—as it says, *ve-chol banayich limudei Hashem ve-rav shalom banayich*, "and all your children shall be students of God, and great will be the peace of your children," on which the *drashah* is applied: *al tikrei banayich ela bonayich*—do not read "your children" but "your builders." The connection to what precedes it is two-fold: it balances the destructive tendencies on display in the story of Issachar, and it ties into the final *mishnah*'s teaching about the precedence of the *rav* and the centrality of *talmud torah*, suggesting that genuine Torah learning—far from producing the arrogance of Issachar ish Kfar Barkai—is the source of *shalom*.

*Hadran alach masechet Keritot ve-silka lach masechet Keritot.*

---

---

# Meilah 3

## Intro to Me'ilah

### Me'ilah Overview

*Masechet Me'ilah* is distinctive in several respects. Like a number of other tractates, its language departs from the standard diction and grammatical patterns one expects from the Bavli, which has led to the longstanding discussion of whether its final editing was carried out in a different Babylonian academy — whether *Nehardea*, *Sura*, or *Pumbedita*. The *Rashi* on this tractate is standard *Rashi*, and the *Tosafot* here is a mix: some sections are more in the nature of commentary, others involve genuine critical analysis. It is also worth noting — though it pertains to a different tractate — that while the *Rashi* on the opening *daf* of *Kereisos* appeared unusual, as one continued through the tractate it read as authentically Rashi's hand, and the notion that *Rashi* on *Kereisos* is not genuinely his seems to be an overstatement.

As for the substance of the *masechet*, its subject is the Torah prohibition of *me'ilah*: the misappropriation of consecrated property. When one derives benefit from *hekdesh* unintentionally — *beshogeg* — the offender brings a *korban* of *asham me'ilah*, repays the principal, and adds a *chomesh*, an extra fifth (which is in actuality a quarter of the new total). When the violation is intentional — *bemezid* — there is no *korban* and no *chomesh*; there is only repayment of the principal. It is worth pausing over this asymmetry: the *shogeg* case carries more formal consequences. This parallels what was discussed throughout *Kereisos*, where the requirement of *kappara* and atonement can sometimes produce weightier obligations than a deliberate transgression.

### Intentional/Unintentional

This distinction has an important terminological implication throughout the *mishnah* and *gemara*. When the text declares *ma'al* or *lo ma'al* regarding a given case, one must not read *lo ma'al* as meaning that the act was *mutar*. If someone acted *bemezid*, we say *lo ma'al* — meaning the formal category of *me'ilah*, with its obligation of *asham me'ilah* and additional *chomesh*, does not apply — but that is far from saying the act had no consequences. Repayment is still required, and there may well be other *issurim* that apply. *Lo ma'al* has a narrow, technical definition: it means only that the specific obligations of *korban* and *chomesh* are not triggered.

### Me'ilah De'rabbanan

Similarly, there is the concept of *me'ilah de'rabbanan*, which requires careful definition. One must distinguish it from a simple *issur hana'ah de'rabbanan*. In a case where the *gemara* says *lo nehenin velo mo'alin*, the first clause — *lo nehenin* — is a rabbinic prohibition on deriving benefit; nothing more is implied. *Me'ilah de'rabbanan*, by contrast, is a rabbinic extension and expansion of the *de'oraisa* category, carrying substantially greater halachic weight. As the *gemara* established in the previous *daf*, in a case of *me'ilah de'rabbanan* there is no *korban* and no *chomesh* — those belong exclusively to *me'ilah de'oraisa* — but there remains an obligation to repay the principal. The rabbis clearly understood this as a distinct category, and they deliberately refrained from adding the *chomesh* in order to mark the difference from *de'oraisa* liability.

### Theft vs. Benefit

On a conceptual level, a fundamental question runs through the entire *masechet*: how does one understand the essential character of the *aveirah* of *me'ilah*? Is it a form of theft from *hekdesh* — an act defined by taking something that belongs to the divine treasury? Or is it better understood as deriving benefit from something to which one had no entitlement, without necessarily causing a loss? The two framings are not interchangeable, and the tension between them will resurface throughout the tractate.

### Shiur & Kedushah

The *shiur* of *me'ilah* is a *prutah*, which monetizes the prohibition — unlike, say, an *issur achila* measured in *kezayis*. But one must ask: does the *prutah* measure what was taken from *hekdesh*, or what the person benefited? The difference is not merely theoretical. Consider a case where one drinks from a *kos* belonging to *hekdesh*: the person derived benefit, yet *hekdesh* suffered no loss. Yet *me'ilah* applies nonetheless. Conversely, one might transfer an object of *hekdesh* as a gift — causing *hekdesh* a loss — without personally benefiting. These cases pull in different directions depending on which model one adopts.

This question was explored in *Kereisos* as well, where the *gemara* raised the matter of market value versus actual benefit. For most purposes, the operative question is not what the object is worth on the market but whether the person derived *hana'at shaveh prutah* — benefit worth a *prutah*. If the object is *assur behana'ah* and has no market value but was consumed and the person genuinely benefited, *me'ilah* applies. The market-value framing is more relevant when the conception of *me'ilah* skews toward theft rather than unauthorized benefit.

### Kodshei HaShem

A central prerequisite for *me'ilah de'oraisa* is that the object be *kodshei Hashem* — fully consecrated to God in a direct and exclusive sense. This is why there is no *me'ilah* on the meat of *kodashim kalim* that may be eaten, nor on the meat of a *chatat* or *asham* after *zerikat hadam*, when it becomes *mutar* to the *kohanim*. Let us trace the spectrum:

At one end stands the *olah*: from the moment of sanctification through its complete burning, no person has any legitimate right to it (with the narrow exception of the skin), and *me'ilah* applies throughout. At the other end, *shlamim*: as *kodashim kalim*, the offering is conceptually associated with the owner — some even hold *mamon be'alim*, that it remains in a meaningful sense the owner's property — and *me'ilah* does not apply to the meat. The sole exception within *shlamim* is the *imurin*, the portions designated for the *mizbe'ach*, and even those acquire their consecrated status only after *shechita* and *zerikah* render them fit for the altar.

The middle cases — *chatat* and *asham* — are *kodshei kodashim*, fully God's in their fundamental conception. The *kohanim*'s right to eat the meat is a *heter* that comes only after *zerikat hadam*; until that point, even the meat is subject to *me'ilah*. Once the blood has been sprinkled validly, the meat becomes *mutar la'kohanim* and loses its *me'ilah* status.

### Masechet Structure

With this in mind, one should understand what to expect from the tractate as a whole. A striking feature of *Me'ilah* is that the act of *me'ilah* itself — the scenarios in which one actually becomes *mo'el* — appears only toward the very end of the *masechet*. The opening portions are largely devoted to defining whether various objects carry *kedushah* and, if so, what level of *kedushah* they possess. These are prerequisites for *me'ilah*, not *me'ilah* itself. Questions abound: if one consecrates a tree and fruit grows from it, is the fruit subject to *me'ilah*? If one consecrates a well and rainwater collects, does *me'ilah* apply to the water? These involve derivative and indirect *kedushah*. The first two-thirds of the *masechet*, broadly speaking, engages the objects and their *kedushah*; the actual law of *me'ilah* arrives at the end.

---

## Psulo BaKodesh

### Psulo Definition

With this background in place, we turn to the concept that dominated the first *daf* and continues into the present discussion: *psulo bakodesh*. This phrase refers to a category of ritual disqualification — *pesul* — that arises from a technical fault in the performance of the *avodah* within the *Mikdash* itself. It is distinguished sharply from a *pesul* that removes the offering entirely from the realm of *kodesh* — such as slaughtering it outside the *Beit HaMikdash* entirely, or the animal dying on its own. In *psulo bakodesh*, the error occurs within the framework of the temple service; the offering remains, as it were, within the ballpark.

This distinction has direct consequences for *me'ilah*. Even a *korban* that is *pasul* — that cannot be offered — retains *me'ilah* status so long as it qualifies as *psulo bakodesh*. And the operative test for whether something qualifies is the principle of *im alu lo yerdu*: if an item was placed on the *mizbe'ach*, it is not removed. If the halacha dictates that it may remain on the *mizbe'ach* once placed there, this demonstrates that it is still sufficiently within the domain of *kodshei Hashem* to carry *me'ilah*. Conversely, if it must be removed, that indicates it has moved outside the relevant category.

An additional dimension of this principle bears emphasizing: for *kodshei kodashim* such as a *chatat* or *asham*, the *pesul* also has a further implication. In a valid offering, *zerikat hadam* would render the meat *mutar la'kohanim* and remove its *me'ilah* status. But when the *korban* was performed under *pesul* — wrong location, *pigul*, and the like — the meat is never rendered permitted. It was never made *mutar* through a valid *zerikah*, and therefore it remains *me'ilah* indefinitely. This is itself part of the *chiddush* of the *mishnah*: not merely that *me'ilah* continues to apply despite the *pesul*, but that it applies permanently to the meat.

There is also the corresponding point for *kodashim kalim*: in a valid offering, *zerikat hadam* would bring the *imurin* into *me'ilah* status by rendering them fit for the *mizbe'ach*. A flawed *zerikah* cannot accomplish this transformation.

### Mishnah Chain

Against this background, Rav Yosef challenged Rabbah — who had maintained that if one slaughtered a *korban* in the wrong location, it would need to be removed from the *mizbe'ach* — through a tightly constructed chain of three *mishnayot* linked together by the principle of *chada migo chada*: one is learned from the other in sequence, so that Mishnah A illuminates Mishnah B and Mishnah B illuminates Mishnah C.

The first *mishnah* in the chain addresses the case of a bird offering whose *melikah* was performed in the wrong location — whether an *olat ha'of* that should have been performed above but was done below, or vice versa. The *mishnah* rules *bekhulan ein metamei begadim beveit habli'ah*: in all such cases, consuming the bird does not render one's garments *tamei* upon swallowing. This is the halacha associated with *neveilah* — a strangled bird. The ruling thus implies that despite the invalid *melikah*, the bird is not classified as *neveilah*. Because the error was a technical ritual fault committed within the *Mikdash* — *psulo bakodesh* — the identity of the offering is not fundamentally altered. Additionally, *umo'alin bahen*: *me'ilah* still applies, with one exception. A *chatat ha'of* performed correctly — below on the *mizbe'ach*, for the sake of a *chatat* — whose meat is eaten by the *kohanim* does not carry *me'ilah* once that *heter achilah* takes effect.

The second *mishnah* in the chain contributes the conceptual vocabulary: *kol she'psulah bakodesh*, any case that falls within the category of *psulah bakodesh*, does not cause *tum'at begadim* — it is not treated as *neveilah*. This second *mishnah* does not merely repeat the fact pattern; it provides the conceptual label. Where the first *mishnah* described specific actions (wrong location, etc.), the second *mishnah* names the principle: *psulah bakodesh*.

The third *mishnah* then delivers the clinching rule: *kol she'hayah psulah bakodesh im alu lo yerdu* — anything classified as *psulah bakodesh*, if it ascended the *mizbe'ach*, does not come down. Stringing all three together: *psulah bakodesh* → no *tum'at neveilah* → remains *me'ilah* → stays on the *mizbe'ach im alu*.

### Mizbe'ach Test

These three principles — *psulah bakodesh*, *im alu lo yerdu*, and *me'ilah* — are thus shown to be logically intertwined. The *mizbe'ach* functions as a kind of test. If the principle of *im alu lo yerdu* applies — if the item, once placed on the *mizbe'ach*, may remain there — this demonstrates its continued status as *kodshei Hashem* for purposes of *me'ilah*. The *mizbe'ach* absorbing and retaining the offering is evidence of its minimal, residual qualification within the sacred domain, even in a state of *pesul*. The converse is equally true: if the item must come down from the *mizbe'ach*, this shows it has fallen outside even the minimal threshold, and *me'ilah* would not apply.

### Rabbah v. Rav Yosef

Rabbah had maintained that when a *korban* is slaughtered in the wrong place (*shachata badarom*), the item must be removed from the *mizbe'ach* if placed there. In Rabbah's understanding, that case does not qualify as *psulo bakodesh* in the relevant sense. The syllogism assembled by Rav Yosef through the three *mishnayot* now bears directly on this position. If the item must come down, Rabbah is implicitly saying it is *not psulo bakodesh*. But the second *mishnah* established that what is *not psulo bakodesh* causes *tum'at neveilah* — meaning it has lost its sacred identity entirely. And the first *mishnah* established that in such cases there is no *me'ilah*. Therefore, on Rabbah's own logic, there should be no *me'ilah* in the case of *shechita badarom* — yet the *mishnah* treats *me'ilah* as applying. Furthermore, the *mishnah*'s declaration of no *me'ilah* appears categorical, encompassing both *de'oraisa* and *de'rabbanan* dimensions. Rabbah's attempt to preserve *me'ilah de'oraisa* while conceding removal from the *mizbe'ach* cannot be sustained.

---

## Bamat Yachid Case

### Rabbi Elazar Q.

Following the resolution of the Rabbah–Rav Yosef debate, the *gemara* introduces a related question posed by Rabbi Elazar. Rabbi Elazar addresses the case of an *olat bamat yachid* — an *olah* that was consecrated for a private *bamah* (*bamat yachid*). This was permitted during the period when *bamot* were allowed, such as when the central *mishkan* was at *Nov* or *Givon*. During that era, a person could sanctify an offering for his own private *bamah*, with considerably fewer formal requirements: no need for a *kohen*, no *klei shareit*, no obligation to slaughter in the north even for an *olah*. A great deal of latitude was permitted.

Now suppose such a person — having sanctified his *olah* for his private *bamah* — decided to bring it instead to the central *mishkan* at *Nov* or *Givon*. The *halacha* is *kaltuhu mechitzot le'kol davar*: the environs of the central sanctuary absorb the offering in every respect, meaning it is now fully subject to all the requirements of that place. The question posed by Rabbi Elazar is: *olat bamat yachid she'hichnisuha she'nifselah alu mahu she'yerdu*? — if the offering was brought inside and was then disqualified in a way that would *not* have constituted a *pesul* had it been offered on the private *bamah* — for instance, it was slaughtered in the south, which at a *bamat yachid* would have been entirely permissible — and it was then placed on the *mizbe'ach*, does it come down or not?

The *gemara* observes: *midhekam'i ba'ei lei* — from the very fact that Rabbi Elazar poses this more complex question, it appears he takes for granted the answer to the simpler, baseline case of *shachata badarom* by an ordinary *korban*. He finds that simple case obvious — though we do not know whether he holds like Rabbah or like Rav Yosef — and moves directly to ask about the harder case.

The *gemara* then suggests: perhaps Rabbi Elazar does not take the baseline case for granted at all. Perhaps he is asking a *chada migo chada* question — first asking what the halacha is in the base case, and then on the basis of that answer asking what happens with *bamat yachid*. Just because he phrases the question as the harder case does not necessarily mean the easier case is settled.

---

## Psulo BaKodesh (II)

### Tiyuvta de'Rabbah

The *tiyuvta* against Rabbah having been established through the chain of three *mishnayot*, the *gemara* declares *tiyuvta de'Rava tiyuvta* — a definitive refutation. This closes the debate cleanly, and the result sharpens the general principle considerably. The concept of *kodshei Hashem* is now defined with greater precision: beyond the basic *korban*, what constitutes *kodshei Hashem* for *me'ilah* purposes is determined by the *mizbe'ach*. If a *pesul* is of the *psulo bakodesh* variety — technical enough that the item may remain on the *mizbe'ach* if placed there — it retains its status as *kodshei Hashem* and carries *me'ilah*. Once the *pesul* is so severe that the item must come down from the *mizbe'ach*, it can no longer qualify as *kodshei Hashem* for *me'ilah* purposes, even though it retains some degree of *kedushah* in other respects.

---

## Bamat Yachid Case (II)

### Absorption Doctrine

Returning to Rabbi Elazar's question about the *olat bamat yachid*, the *gemara* articulates two competing frameworks for thinking about why the case might go either way.

The first framework explains why Rabbah might rule more leniently in this case than in the standard case.
