In the baseline case of *shachata badarom*, the offering was fully subject to the requirements of the *Mikdash* from the outset: *mechitza ketikna paslah* — the walls of the sanctuary, functioning properly, impose all the relevant requirements, and a violation of those requirements is a real *pesul*. But here the offering was originally consecrated as *kodushat bamat yachid*, where slaughtering in the south would have been entirely acceptable. One might therefore argue that this *pesul* is weaker — that the original *kedushah* of the *bamat yachid* extends greater latitude, and it should stay on the *mizbe'ach*.

The second framework explains why even Rav Yosef — who holds *im ala lo yered* in the standard case — might say this case is *worse* and that the offering must come down. The logic runs as follows: *mechitza ketikna kaltah, shelo ketikna lo kaltah* — the walls of the central sanctuary "absorb" an offering that was sanctified for that place from the beginning, giving it a right, as it were, to remain on the *mizbe'ach* once placed there. But an offering originally sanctified for a *bamat yachid*, which was never fundamentally a *Mikdash korban*, was never absorbed by the *mechitzot* in the relevant sense. It lacks the entitlement to remain, because it did not start as a *Mikdash korban* in the first place.

The result is that the case can legitimately be asked either way, and both directions carry genuine halachic logic. Asking the harder question does not, therefore, signal that the easier question has already been resolved.

One might ask: when a person consecrates an offering for a *bamat yachid*, does he necessarily intend to confine it to that context? Perhaps a person who consecrates *stam* intends simply to sanctify the animal generally, retaining the freedom to bring it wherever he wishes — and the *bamat yachid* designation is therefore not a constraining framework. This is a genuine conceptual difficulty, and the *gemara* does not resolve it.

### Teiqu

The *gemara* concludes: *teiqu* — the question remains unresolved. Whether an *olat bamat yachid* brought into the *Mikdash* and disqualified in a way that would have been permissible on a private *bamah* must be removed from the *mizbe'ach* or may remain there is left as an open question.

---

## Zrikat Pigul

### Rav Giddal Statement

With the *psulo bakodesh* discussion concluded, the *gemara* transitions to a new statement. Rav Giddal said in the name of Rav: *zerikat pigul eina motzi midei me'ilah be'kodshei kodashim* — a *zerikah* performed with *machshevet pigul* (intent to eat the offering *chutz lizmano* or *chutz limkomo*) is not a valid *zerikah* and does not remove *me'ilah* status from the meat of *kodshei kodashim*. Since the *zerikah* is *pigul* and therefore invalid, it does not render the meat *mutar la'kohanim*, and so the meat remains perpetually under *me'ilah*. Similarly, such a *zerikah* does not bring the *imurin* of *kodashim kalim* into *me'ilah* status: *ve'eino mevi lidei me'ilah bekodashim kalim*. A valid *zerikah* is what normally renders the *imurin* fit for the *mizbe'ach* and thereby subject to *me'ilah*; a *zerikat pigul* accomplishes none of this.

At first glance this seems merely to restate what the *mishnah* already established. What is the *chiddush*?

### Tosafot Chiddush

*Tosafot* explains the *chiddush* as follows. There is a well-established principle in the laws of *pigul*: an offering cannot acquire *pigul* status unless it was, apart from the *pigul* intention itself, otherwise fit — *meratzeh le'pigulo*. The *zerikah* must have been performed correctly in all other respects; a *zerikah* accompanied by an additional *pesul*, such as *chutz limkomo*, would not create *pigul* at all. The *zerikah* of *pigul* is thus, by definition, a *zerikah* that was performed correctly in all respects other than the disqualifying intention. The *hava amina* would therefore be: since *zerikat pigul* is a *zerikah* that is, in every formal sense, *meratzeh le'pigulo* — considered fit enough to generate *pigul* status — perhaps we should extend that significance and say that *zerikat pigul* is meaningful enough to affect *me'ilah* status as well. Rav Giddal in the name of Rav rules that this is not the case. *Zerikat pigul* may suffice to create *pigul*, but it does not suffice to change the *me'ilah* status of the meat or of the *imurin*.

### Rav Pappa Challenge

Abaye was transmitting this tradition of Rav Giddal in the name of Rav when Rav Pappa challenged him from the following *mishnah*: *hashochet et hatoda bifnim velachmah bachutz* — if one slaughters a *toda* inside the *Mikdash* while its accompanying bread is outside, *lo kiddesh halachem* — the *shechita* does not sanctify the bread. The *toda* is accompanied by bread, and the *shechita* of the *toda* is what elevates the bread from *kedushat damim* to *kedushat haguf*. But if the bread is outside, it is disconnected from the *korban* and the *shechita* does not affect it. Similarly, if the bread was not yet fully baked — if the crust had not yet formed (*ad shelo karmu paneha batannur*), or if even one loaf among them lacked its crust (*afillu karmu kullan chutz me'achas mehen*) — the bread is not sanctified. The requirement is all-or-nothing.

Critically for our discussion, the *mishnah* continues: *shachat chutz lizmano ve'chutz limkomo* — if one slaughtered the *toda* with a *machshevet pigul* of *chutz lizmano* or *chutz limkomo* — *kiddesh halachem*, the bread is sanctified. So a *shechitat pigul* is sufficient to generate *kedushat haguf* in the bread. The implication appears to be that *pigul* acts are still halachically significant for purposes of *kedushah* — and if for *kedushah*, why not for *me'ilah*?

Abaye was silenced. He went before Rabbi Abba, who then reformulated the response.

It should be noted, as *Tosafot* emphasizes, that the bread was never subject to *me'ilah* to begin with — it is always *mutar ba'achila*, either to the *be'alim* or to the *kohanim*, and is therefore never *kodshei Hashem* in the *me'ilah* sense. The argument from the bread case is therefore analogical in nature, not direct, and the *gemara* will ultimately reject the analogy.

### Shechita v. Zrika

Rav Ashi offered the following response: *amar lei, b'zerikah* — the distinction lies in the *zerikah*. Following *Tosafot*'s reading, the argument runs as follows. The *hava amina* in the original statement of Rav Giddal in the name of Rav was specifically about *zerikat pigul* — that since *zerikat pigul* is *meratzeh le'pigulo*, perhaps it should affect *me'ilah* status. The answer is that it does not. *Zerikat pigul* and *shechitat pigul* are not the same for these purposes.

The key lies in the moment at which *me'ilah* status changes. In the *avoda* of *kodashim*, what changes the *me'ilah* status? For *kodshei kodashim*, a valid *zerikah* causes the meat to become *mutar la'kohanim* and thereby exit *me'ilah*. For *kodashim kalim*, a valid *zerikah* renders the *imurin* fit for the *mizbe'ach* and thereby enters *me'ilah*. In both directions, it is *zerikah* that is the operative moment of change. At that moment — when the *zerikah* is performed — if it is a *zerikat pigul*, the *pigul* is fully operative, and therefore the *zerikah* is entirely ineffective at changing the *me'ilah* status. This is not so for *shechita*: *shechita* is not ordinarily the moment at which *me'ilah* status changes, and a *shechitat pigul*, as will be explained shortly, does not carry the fully operative force of *pigul* at that stage.

---

## Pigul Labeling

### Ula's Kometz Case

The question of when *pigul* status is operative — at *shechita* or only at *zerikah* — is developed through a separate principle. Rav Ashi invoked the teaching of Ulla: *kometz pigul she'he'elah legavei mizbe'ach paka pigulo mimenu* — a *kometz* that was designated as *pigul* and then placed upon the *mizbe'ach*, once burned on the *mizbe'ach*, loses its *pigul* designation. The significance here is the term *kometz pigul* — a *kometz* that has already been *labeled as pigul*, even before the offering's *avodah* is complete. The *kometz* corresponds to *shechita* in the process of a *mincha* — it is the initial act, analogous to *shechita*, prior to the *haktara* on the *mizbe'ach* (analogous to *zerikah*). Yet we call it *kometz pigul* already, before the *avodah* is finished.

The force of this observation is that we label an act as *pigul* before the *zerikah* is complete, which would seem to undercut the reasoning that *shechitat pigul* cannot be called *pigul* at that moment. If we call the *kometz pigul*, we are calling *shechita*-stage acts *pigul* already.

The response is: *isurei d'mati le'pigul* — when we use the term *kometz pigul* or similar formulations before the *avodah* is finished, we do not mean the offering has actually achieved *pigul* status in a legally binding sense. We mean it is a *kometz* that is on track to become *pigul*. The terminology is anticipatory, not constitutive.

### Ilfa Two Avodot

Ravina pressed further. He invoked a ruling associated with Ilfa regarding cases where there are two distinct *avoda* acts, each carrying a different *machshava*: for instance, one performed *shechita* with a thought of *chutz lizmano* (a *pigul* intent) and then performed *zerikah* with a thought of *chutz limkomo* (a *pesul* intent, but not *pigul*). The question is whether the *chutz limkomo* thought at *zerikah* prevents the offering from acquiring *pigul* status. Ilfa rules that this is a genuine dispute — *machlokes bishtei avodos*. The two acts are treated as distinct, and the *machshavot* at each stage interact in a complex way.

Crucially, Ilfa gives a concrete example of *shtei avodos* even within a single *shechita*: if one declared, *hareini shochet siman rishon chutz lizmano, siman sheni chutz limkomo* — the first *siman* of the *shechita* with *chutz lizmano*, the second *siman* with *chutz limkomo* — this counts as *shtei avodos*. The two *simanim* are treated as distinct acts. This matters because it implies that even at the stage of *shechita*, the precise content and sequence of *machshavot* is tracked in a way that affects *pigul* status — which in turn suggests we are already treating the *shechita* acts as relevant to *pigul* determination at the time they occur.

### Ravina Objection

Ravina's objection is pointed: if one maintains that *pigul* status is not fully determined until *zerikah*, and that prior language is merely anticipatory, why would the order of *machshavot* at *shechita* matter? If *pigul* status is only determined at the moment of *zerikah*, then what was thought at *shechita* versus what was thought at *zerikah* should be assessed from the perspective of that later moment. It should always be a case of *shtei avodos*, since the *machshavot* at *zerikah* are always distinct from those at *shechita*. The very fact that the dispute is framed around what happened at *shechita* implies that *pigul* identity is being tracked and attributed from the moment of *shechita* — not merely anticipated, but substantially established.

### Retroactive Status

The resolution is as follows: *lechi zarik igla'ei milsa ei be'avodah achas ei bishtei avodos* — when the *zerikah* is finally performed, it retroactively reveals what occurred: whether it was a case of *avodah achas* (a single act) or *shtei avodos* (two distinct acts). The *zerikah* is still required to complete and vest the *pigul* status, and one is not *chayav karet* for eating the offering until the *zerikah* is done. But critically, the *label* of *pigul* does not affix at the moment of *zerikah* going forward — it applies retroactively to the moment of *shechita*. This is why order matters: the question of which *machshava* came first is assessed at the time the *machshavot* occurred, not at the time of *zerikah*.

This retroactive model has direct implications for the bread case. The claim was that *shechitat pigul* could sanctify the bread because at the moment of *shechita* the *pigul* was not yet fully operative. The objection was: but once *zerikah* is done, retroactively it was *pigul* from *shechita* — so how did the bread get sanctified? The *gemara* now has to address this directly.

---

## Zrikat Pigul (II)

### Toda-Bread Refutation

The challenge from the *toda*-bread case now returns for its final resolution. If *pigul* status retroactively dates to the moment of *shechita*, one might ask: does this mean that the *shechita* retroactively fails to sanctify the bread? Rav Ashi's answer is: *mai kiddesh lifaseil ulvei sreifa* — the *shechita* did sanctify the bread, but only to the degree of making it *pasul* and subject to burning. The *shechitat pigul* is halachically significant — it achieves *kedushat haguf* in the sense that the bread can now become *pasul belina* and must be destroyed — but it does not achieve the level of sanctification that would be relevant to *me'ilah*.

This is the critical distinction. *Me'ilah* requires that an offering be genuinely *kodshei Hashem* in the operative sense — that the *avodah* be fully valid and capable of producing the relevant status changes: meat becoming *mutar la'kohanim*, or *imurin* becoming fit for the *mizbe'ach*. A *shechitat pigul* or *zerikat pigul* can produce partial halachic effects — it can produce *kedushat haguf* in the sense of *pesul* and *sreifa* — but it cannot produce the full, valid transformation of status that *me'ilah* law requires. The analogy from the bread case ultimately fails precisely because the bread never carried *me'ilah* to begin with; its sanctification through *shechitat pigul* is a question of *kedushah* in a narrower sense, not of *me'ilah*. For *me'ilah*, the standard remains a completely valid *avodah*.

---

---

# Meilah 4

## Rav Giddel: Psul Zerika

### Im lo alos tayreidu

We pick up in the middle of daf 4a, approximately four or five lines from the bottom, still engaged with the position of Rav Giddel amar Rav. By way of context: the *mishna* had already established that when *avodos* are performed *b'psul* — whether through *shechita* done with *machshaves pigul*, in the wrong place, or under similar disqualifying conditions — two consequences follow. First, the *korban* retains its consecrated status as *kodshei Hashem* by virtue of the principle of *im lo alos tayreidu*: what has ascended to the *mizbe'ach* is not removed. Second, the meat of *kodshei kodashim* does not exit the category of *me'ila*, as it ordinarily would if the *zerika* had been performed correctly — for a proper *zerika* renders the meat *mutar l'kohanim*, thereby removing it from *me'ila*. When the *avodah* is performed *b'psul*, however, the meat never becomes *mutar l'kohanim* and therefore remains subject to *me'ila*.

### Zerika with Pigul Intent

Rav Giddel amar Rav extended this principle to the case where the *zerika* itself was performed with *machshaves pigul*: since the *zerika* is not considered legitimate, the meat remains in *me'ila*. The same applies to *kodshim kalim* — the *emurim* do not attain the status that would make them subject to *me'ila* (i.e., fit for the *mizbe'ach*) when the *zerika* was invalid.

### Kodshim Kalim & Emurim

The *Gemara* undertakes an extended discussion of why this requires any special derivation at all, given that the *mishna* already seems to establish the principle. Why is Rav Giddel amar Rav's ruling not simply obvious from the *mishna*?

### Mertzeh l'Pigulo

Tosafot addresses this directly. The ruling is not obvious, because in the context of *zerika* there exists a principle of *mertzeh l'pigulo*: for a *korban* to achieve the status of *pigul*, the *avodah* must have been performed in a formally complete manner, such that the *korban* is considered, in a theoretical sense, as though it were a legitimate offering — but one that is disqualified specifically as *pigul*. There is thus a kind of theoretical legitimacy to the *korban*, and one might therefore have supposed that the *zerika* with *machshaves pigul* should count as a legitimate *zerika* for the purposes of *me'ila* status change. Rav Giddel amar Rav tells us this is not the case.

### Pigul Before Zerika

The discussion acknowledges that *pigul* status can exist even at earlier stages, before the *zerika* takes place — the *korban* is already called *pigul* from the moment of *shechita* with the disqualifying intent. This was admitted in the course of the analysis. Yet despite this concession, the status of *me'ila* does not change.

### Shechitas Pigul & Toda

While it was acknowledged that a *shechitas pigul* can accomplish something — for instance, it can sanctify the bread of a *toda* — it will nonetheless not have the effect of altering the *me'ila* status of the *korban*. That requires a *zerika* performed *b'hechsher*, a fully valid sprinkling, which alone renders either the meat fit for *kohanim* (in the case of *kodshei kodashim*) or the *emurim* fit for the *mizbe'ach* (in the case of *kodshim kalim*). Only when this is done properly does the *me'ila* status change.

---

## Braisa on Pigul & Me'ila

### Hapigul l'olam

The *Gemara* now turns to a *braisa* in an attempt to bring a proof: *hapigul l'olam mo'ilin bo* — there is always *me'ila* in the case of *pigul*. This statement would seem to mean that when *pigul* is involved in *kodshei kodashim*, the meat never exits the *me'ila* category, presumably because the *zerika* with *pigul* intent is not a valid *zerika* and the meat therefore never becomes *mutar l'kohanim*. This appears to support Rav Giddel amar Rav directly.

### Zerika vs. No Zerika

The *Gemara* asks: does this *braisa* not mean that even when *zerikas hadam* was performed — albeit with *machshaves pigul* — it is still not considered a legitimate *zerika*, and thus *me'ila* remains? *Umesayei lei* — this would be a support for Rav Giddel amar Rav. But the *Gemara* deflects: *lo, d'lo zarak dam* — perhaps the *braisa* is discussing a case where the blood was never sprinkled at all, meaning the *pigul* occurred at an earlier stage before any *zerika* took place.

### Novelty Question

If that is the reading, the *Gemara* asks, what is the *olam* — the word "always" — adding? And more fundamentally, what is the *chiddush*? Even without *pigul*, if no *zerika hadam* occurred, obviously nothing changes — neither for *kodshim kalim* becoming *mutar* nor for the *emurim* of *kodshei kodashim* becoming fit for the *mizbe'ach*.

### Why Pigul Without Zerika

The *Gemara* presses further: *iy d'lo zarak dam mai l'meimra* — if no *zerika hadam* occurred at all, why mention *pigul*? The status would not change regardless of any *pigul* thought. One does not need the language of *pigul* to teach something that applies universally to any case without *zerika*.

### Olah Me'ila Analysis

The *Gemara* then proposes that the *braisa* may be discussing an *olah*, where there is no status change under any circumstances — before *zerika hadam* all parts belong to the *mizbe'ach*, and after *zerika hadam* they equally belong to the *mizbe'ach*. (The *or*, the hide, is a separate discussion we bracket here.) For an *olah*, then, there is always *me'ila*, and neither *pigul* nor the absence of *pigul* changes anything. *Iy b'olah peshita d'gavoa ihi kulla* — if it is an *olah*, of course there will always be *me'ila*: the entire offering belongs to God both before and after *zerika*, and *machshaves pigul* has no bearing on that.

### Dam Linah & Me'ila

The *seifa* of that *braisa*, however, states: *lan dama* — if the blood was left overnight (*linah*), even if one subsequently performed the *zerika*, *me'ilin bah* — *me'ila* still applies. The reason is clear: overnight blood is disqualified, and therefore no valid *zerika hadam* can be performed, so the meat cannot become *mutar ba'achilah*.

### Zerika Timing Proof

Crucially, this *seifa* implies that had the blood been sprinkled at the correct time it *would* have changed the *me'ila* status. Therefore we cannot be discussing an *olah*, where there is never any change. *Ei amart b'chatas, shapir* — if we are dealing with a *chatas*, it makes perfect sense: a timely and valid *zerika* would remove the meat from *me'ila* status, whereas *dam linah* prevents that change.

### Reisha-Seifa Parallel

Since the *seifa* is clearly discussing a *chatas*, the *Gemara* concludes that the *reisha* should likewise be understood as discussing a *chatas*. *Ho'il umesayei lei seifa, mesayei lei nami reisha* — since the end of the *braisa* supports Rav Giddel amar Rav (inasmuch as it is clearly about a *chatas* and addresses a case of invalid *zerika*), the beginning of the *braisa* should also be read as discussing a *chatas*, where *pigul* at the *zerika* stage fails to change the *me'ila* status. Thus the *braisa* in its entirety provides a proof.

---

## Linah vs. Pigul Intent

### Active vs. Passive Psul

The *Gemara* does not rest with this conclusion, however. Rav Yosef challenges the analogy between *dam linah* and *machshaves pigul* as causes of *psul*. The argument from *dam linah* to the *zerika* of *pigul* is that in both cases the *zerika* is invalid and therefore ought not to change *me'ila* status. But Rav Yosef presses: *mai shna halinah dekavid bayadayim?* — what is the distinction of *linah* that it was, in a sense, committed through active deed?

### Physical Action Element

The subtlety here is the following. With *dam linah*, the blood is physically old blood, left overnight and then sprinkled — there is a concrete, objective defect in the blood itself. With *machshaves pigul*, by contrast, the only problem lies in one's intention. Physically, everything is performed correctly; the only disqualifying element is a thought in the mind of the *kohen*. *Machshava lo ka'avid bayadayim* — thought does not constitute physical action in the manner that leaving blood overnight does. Therefore, *mahni lei zerika le'afokei midei me'ila* — perhaps the *zerika* itself is sufficient to change the *me'ila* status, and the mental *psul* of *pigul* should not block it.

### Concrete vs. Mental

This distinction is, as noted, somewhat counterintuitive. One might have supposed that actively thinking something is more "active" than passively allowing blood to remain overnight. Yet the *Gemara*'s reasoning appears to be that when something must be done and one fails to do it correctly, one is operating within the domain of physical action — even if the action itself is incorrect. The blood was supposed to be sprinkled that day; by leaving it overnight and sprinkling it the next day, one has engaged in the domain of physical action and done it wrong. Whereas if everything physical was done correctly and only the mind went astray, this may be a less objectively concrete form of *psul*. Understood in this light: precisely because the *psul* of *pigul* is less tangible — it resides entirely in the mental realm, while the physical world remained undisturbed — one might argue that the *zerika* is valid enough in the physical dimension to change the *me'ila* status.

### Zerika Pigul Validity

This is the crux of why the *Gemara* cannot simply infer from *dam linah* to *machshaves pigul*. In the case of *linah*, there is an actual, objective disqualification of the blood itself; clearly the status does not change. When only a thought is involved and physically everything is in order, perhaps the *zerika* is considered sufficiently real to effect a change in status. Therefore the *braisa*'s ruling about *dam linah* cannot automatically be extended to the case of *pigul* at the moment of *zerika*.

The *Gemara* nonetheless notes that while this argument prevents a direct proof by analogy, the text of the *braisa* itself still seems to support Rav Giddel amar Rav. Since the *seifa* is clearly discussing a *chatas*, the *reisha* — which states that with *pigul* there is always *me'ila* — should also be understood as discussing a *chatas*, and as addressing the case where *zerika* was performed with *pigul* intent and the status did not change. The *Gemara* therefore does not fully surrender this *braisa* as a support; rather, it brackets the limitation on analogical inference and notes that the simple reading of the *braisa* still points to Rav Giddel amar Rav's conclusion.

---

## Kadashim Braisa & Pigul

### Pigul Kodshei Kodashim

The *Gemara* attempts once more to bring a proof: *hapigul bekadshei kodashim mo'alin bo* — *pigul* in *kodshei kodashim* is subject to *me'ila*. This is a parallel formulation to the one discussed above, apparently stating that even with *pigul*, the meat of *kodshei kodashim* retains its *me'ila* status — which seems to support the view that *zerika* with *machshaves pigul* does not change the status.

### Zerika Pigul Status Chan…

The *Gemara* asks: *lav af al gav dezarak* — does this not mean that even when *zerikas hadam* was performed (albeit with *machshaves pigul*), the status does not change? *Umesayei lei* — and that would support Rav Giddel amar Rav. The *Gemara* answers: *lo, d'lo zarak* — perhaps it refers to a case where no *zerika hadam* occurred at all. And if so, *aval zarak mai?* — if one did perform *zerika*, what would the rule be? Perhaps even with *pigul* intent the *zerika* would change the status.

### Kodshim Kalim No Me'ila

The *seifa* of this *braisa* states: *bekodashim kalim ein mo'alin bo* — in *kodshim kalim*, when there is *pigul*, there is no *me'ila*. The *Gemara* seizes on this. *Amai katani seifa bekodashim kalim ein mo'alin bo?* — why does the *braisa* need to go to *kodshim kalim* to find a case of no *me'ila*?

### Kodshim Kalim Examples

If one genuinely held that *zerika* with *pigul* intent is meaningless and therefore does not change status, then even within *kodshei kodashim* there should be a case of no *me'ila* — namely, after a valid *zerika* is performed. The *braisa* could have stayed within the domain of *kodshei kodashim* and noted that after *zerika* the *me'ila* status changes. The fact that it sought out *kodshim kalim* as its example of no *me'ila* demands explanation.

### Seifa Proof

*Liplug b'reisha v'lisni* — why not subdivide the *reisha* itself and teach: before *zerika* there is *me'ila*, and after *zerika* even with *pigul* intent there is no *me'ila*? The very fact that the *braisa* did not do so implies that after *zerika* with *pigul* intent, *me'ila* still applies. The *braisa* therefore went to *kodshim kalim* to find a categorical example of no *me'ila*, because it could not find that category in *kodshei kodashim* after a *zerika* of *pigul*. *Hahu vadai mesayei lei* — the *seifa* is definitely a proof for Rav Giddel amar Rav.

### Kodshim Kalim Categorical

The reason the *braisa* chose *kodshim kalim* as its example is now explained: by *kodshim kalim* with a *pigul* thought, there is categorically never *me'ila* from beginning to end. Before *zerika* there is no *me'ila* because these are *kodshim kalim*. After *zerika* — even a *zerika* with *pigul* intent — there is still no *me'ila* because the *zerika* does not elevate the *emurim*. The category is thus *pesika* — settled and complete — without any internal exceptions. This makes *kodshim kalim* an ideal vehicle for stating a universal negative.

The *Gemara* then turns to the parallel structural question: since the *seifa* is a clear proof, does it also prove what the *reisha* is discussing? The answer distinguishes between using the *seifa* as an analogy and using it to clarify the *reisha*. As for the analogy: the *seifa*'s ruling that *zerika* of *pigul* does not elevate the *emurim* of *kodshim kalim* strongly implies by analogy that *zerika* of *pigul* similarly does not lower the *me'ila* status of *kodshei kodashim* meat. As for the structural question of whether the *reisha* is necessarily discussing *zerika* and not an earlier stage: the *Gemara* notes that by *kodshim kalim* the categorical absence of *me'ila* covers the entire spectrum, so the *braisa* needed no internal subdivision; but it cannot be inferred from this that the *reisha* about *kodshei kodashim* is necessarily discussing the stage of *zerika*. These are distinguished but ultimately very strained (*dachuk*) responses. The fundamental point is clear from both *beraisot*: with a *pigul* thought, the status does not change in either direction.

---

## Psul & Me'ila Conclusion

### Status Change Required

The *Gemara* arrives at a conclusion. For *me'ila* status to change, an actual change in the *halachic* standing of the meat or *emurim* must occur. The *zerika* that accomplishes this must be a *kasher zerika*, one that genuinely renders either the meat *mutar l'kohanim* or the *emurim* fit for the *mizbe'ach*.

### Pigul Distinction

*Zerika* performed with *pigul* intent occupies a peculiar position: it is, in one sense, "good for *pigul*" — it is the *zerika* that completes the *pigul* disqualification and establishes the transgression of eating *pigul*. In that dimension, the *zerika* is meaningful. But it is not good for *me'ila*: it does not change the *halachic* status of the meat, it does not make the meat *mutar* to *kohanim*, and it does not make the *emurim* fit for the *mizbe'ach*. So the two dimensions are severed: the *mertzeh l'pigulo* dimension is operative for the *din* of *pigul*, but carries no weight for the *din* of *me'ila*.

### Real Criterion

The real criterion for a change in *me'ila* status is physical fitness — either fitness of the meat for the *kohanim*, or fitness of the *emurim* for the *mizbe'ach*. When that actual change in physical *halachic* standing has not occurred, *me'ila* is not affected. A mental *psul* that masquerades as a quasi-valid *zerika* does not meet this threshold.

---

## Mishna: Status Change

### Sha'at Heter Kohanim

The *Gemara* now moves to the next passage of the *mishna*, which addresses precisely this issue of when status change occurs. Rabbi Yehoshua stated a general principle: *kol shena'asa lo sha'at heter lakohanim, ein mo'alin bo* — any time there was a moment when the meat became *mutar l'kohanim*, there is no longer *me'ila* on the meat of *kodshei kodashim*. Conversely, *vekol shelo na'asa lo sha'at heter lakohanim, mo'alin bo* — if it never became *mutar*, it retains its *me'ila* status.

### Status Change Examples

The *mishna* then provides examples of cases where the meat *did* pass through a moment of *heter*: *she'lanah* — the meat stayed overnight (it had been *mutar* but became *notar*); *she'nitme'is* — it became *tamei* after being fit; *she'yatza'as* — it exited the *Beis Hamikdash* and became a *psul yotzei*. In all these cases there was a moment when the meat could have been eaten, and therefore it is no longer subject to *me'ila*.

### No Status Change

Conversely, the *mishna* gives examples where the meat never passed through such a moment: *she'nishchetah chutz lizmano ve'chutz limkomo* — it was slaughtered with a *machshavah* of the wrong time or wrong place, a *pigul*-type disqualification; *she'kiblu psulim ve'zarku es damah* — *pasul* individuals caught the blood or sprinkled it. In all such cases the meat never became *mutar*, and *me'ila* applies throughout.

---

## Bar Kappara Question

### Three Heter Options

Bar Kappara said to Bar Padda — his nephew — the following: *re'ei mah ani sho'alcha lemachar beveis hamedrash* — "See what I want you to ask me tomorrow in the *Beis Hamedrash*." He was, in effect, either prepping his nephew to pose the right question publicly, or setting up the discussion that was to follow. The question he wished to have posed was this: when the *mishna* says that there was a *sha'at heter lakohanim*, what precise moment does that refer to? Three possibilities present themselves: *heter shechitah* — that the *shechitah* was performed correctly; *heter zerikah* — that it was fit for *zerikah*; or *heter achilah* — that it was actually fit to be eaten.

### Definitions of Heter

The terminology here requires precision. *Heter shechitah* means the *shechitah* itself was done correctly. *Heter zerikah* — which is the somewhat confusing formulation — does not mean the *zerika* was performed, but rather that the *korban* was at a stage where it *could* have been sprinkled, which in practice means the *kabalah* was done correctly. So the question is: is the determinative moment the *shechitah*, the *kabalah*, or the actual *zerika* and its making the meat fit for eating?

### Omed Lizrok Principle

The *heter zerikah* option is connected to the principle of *kol ha'omed lizrok kezarak dami* — whatever stands ready to be sprinkled is considered as though it were already sprinkled. If the *kabalah* was done properly, one might argue that the blood is already deemed *k'ilu nizrak*, and at that point the status change has effectively occurred, rendering actual *zerika* unnecessary as the determinative moment.

---

## Chizkiyahu vs. Yochanan

### Chizkiyahu Position

The next day, when the question was posed in the *Beis Hamedrash*, Bar Kappara responded by presenting a *tannaitic*-era debate, or perhaps a debate among *Amoraim*. Chizkiyahu said: *heter shechitah shaninu* — the *mishna* is speaking of the moment of *shechitah*. As long as the *shechitah* was performed correctly, even if a *psul* occurred thereafter, that suffices to establish a *sha'at heter* and remove the meat from *me'ila*.

### Yochanan Position

Rabbi Yochanan disagreed: *heter achilah shaninu* — the *mishna* means the moment at which the meat was actually fit to be eaten. Only when it reached that stage, having passed through a valid *zerika*, is there a true *sha'at heter lakohanim*. Notably, no opinion is recorded for *heter zerikah* in the sense of *kabalah* being the key moment — though that option will resurface shortly.

### Zeira Assessment

Rabbi Zeira then made a striking observation: *lo daka matnisin, delo k'Chizkiyahu, vedelo k'Rabbi Yochanan* — the *mishna* does not read precisely according to either position. This is a significant claim: the *mishna*'s language, if analyzed carefully, does not straightforwardly support either *heter shechitah* or *heter achilah*.

---

## Meat vs. Blood Analysis

### Lanah: Meat or Blood

To demonstrate this, the *Gemara* turns to the specific examples in the *mishna*. The *mishna* says *she'lanah* — it stayed overnight. But what is the "it" that stayed overnight? The *Gemara* initially assumes, given the thrust of the discussion about *sha'at heter*, that the "it" refers to the meat: the meat was *mutar*, remained overnight, became *notar*. But one could alternatively read *lan dam* — the blood stayed overnight.

### Blood Linah Question

If the blood stayed overnight — meaning the *kabalah* was done correctly but the blood became disqualified through *linah* before any *zerika* — does the *mishna* then say the status has changed? If so, it would suggest that *heter zerikah*, the moment of valid *kabalah*, is sufficient to establish a *sha'at heter*, even without actual *zerika* having occurred. The reading of *lan dam* would then be: the blood that was properly caught stayed overnight, and even though *zerika* never happened (and cannot happen with this blood), the status is already considered as having changed.

### Meat Linah Implication

If, on the other hand, we read *lan basar* — the meat stayed overnight — then clearly the *zerika* must have already occurred, because only after a valid *zerika* does the meat attain its *mutar* status and become susceptible to becoming *notar*. Under this reading, the *mishna* is saying: the meat was once *mutar* (implying a valid *zerika* had taken place), subsequently became *notar* through *linah*, and therefore there is no *me'ila* — because there was indeed a *sha'at heter*.

### Zerika Needed

Thus if we read *lan basar*, the *mishna* implicitly requires *zerika hadam* as a precondition for any status change — which aligns with Rabbi Yochanan's *heter achilah* position (or at least is consistent with it), since only after *zerika* does the meat become *mutar ba'achilah*. The *Gemara* concludes that this second reading is the correct one: it is the meat, not the blood, that stayed overnight, and therefore *zerika hadam* was necessarily a precondition. The *mishna*'s example thus does not support the *heter zerikah* / *kabalah* reading.

---

## Kiblu & Zarku Phrase

### One or Two Scenarios

The *Gemara* then examines the second example in the *mishna* of where there was *no sha'at heter*: *she'kiblu psulim ve'zarku es damah* — *pasul* people received and sprinkled the blood. The critical question is how to parse this phrase: are *kiblu* and *zarku* describing one single scenario, or two independent scenarios connected by an implied "or"?

### One Scenario = Kabala

If it is one scenario — *pasulim* both caught and then sprinkled the blood — the *Gemara* asks why both stages need to be mentioned. The natural inference from combining them into a single scenario would be to focus on the *kabalah* as the critical moment of disqualification: the *psul* at *kabalah* is what poisoned the process from the start, and the subsequent *zerika* is included merely because that is how the case proceeded.

### Two Scenarios = Zerika

Alternatively, one could read the *vav* as a disjunction: either *psulim* caught the blood, *or* they sprinkled it. Under this reading, the *mishna* is giving two independent examples of disqualification, one involving *kabalah* alone and one involving *zerika* alone. This would imply that the *zerika* stage is independently significant — a *pasul zerika*, even with a proper *kabalah*, is itself sufficient to prevent the status change. This reading would align the *mishna* with the view that *zerika* is the key moment.

---

## Zevachim Comparison

### Psul Blood No Kibus

The *Gemara* now introduces a comparison to a *halacha* from *Zevachim* in order to evaluate these competing readings of the phrase *kiblu psulim ve'zarku es damah*. That *halacha* concerns the *mitzvas ha-Torah* that blood of a *chatas* which splatters on a garment must be laundered (*kibus*) in a holy place. The *halacha* is that this applies only to the blood of a *chatas kesherah* — a valid *chatas*. A *chatas pesulah* whose blood splatters on a garment does not require *kibus*.

### Timing Irrelevant

In this context of *Zevachim*, the timing of the *psul* is irrelevant. It does not matter whether the *chatas* was once fit and subsequently became disqualified, or whether it was never fit from the beginning. All that matters is its present status at the time of the spattering: if it is *pasul* now, the blood does not have the potency to require *kibus*.

### Zevachim Categories

Nevertheless, the *Gemara* there in *Zevachim* does describe both categories: *she'hayesa la sha'as ha'kosher ve'nifselah* — it was once fit and then became disqualified; and *she'lo hayesa la sha'as ha'kosher* — it was never fit. Although the legal outcome is identical in both cases, the *braisa* describes them separately.

### No Distinction in Zevach…

In the *Zevachim* passage, the same phrase appears: *she'kiblu psulim ve'zarku es damah* — as an example of a *chatas* that was never fit. Rav Yosef raises this parallel as a challenge to the reading proposed earlier in the context of *me'ila*, where one wished to be very precise about the phrase and infer from it that the *kabalah* is the key moment. Rav Yosef points out: if you read this phrase with such precision in *me'ila*, then in *Zevachim* — where the identical phrase appears — you would be claiming that only *kiblu psulim ve'zarku* (both together in one scenario) constitutes a *chatas pesulah*, and that if only *psulim* caught the blood but *kesherim* subsequently sprinkled it, the garment *would* require *kibus*. But that cannot be correct, for reasons the *Gemara* now develops.

---

## Torah Requirement Drasha

### Kri Kan Drasha

The *Torah* states: *va'asher yizeh mi-damah* — "whichever [garment] its blood spatters upon." The *Gemara* derives through a *drasha*: *kri kan asher yizeh mi-damah velo she-kevar huzah* — the verse refers to blood that is *about to be* sprinkled, not blood after it has already been sprinkled on the *mizbe'ach*. Once blood has been properly placed on the *mizbe'ach*, all remaining blood — including blood that was legitimately caught by a *kasher kohen* — loses its potency for the purpose of *kibus*. The remainder becomes *shirayim*, blood that is poured at the base of the *mizbe'ach* but no longer has the active status that would require *kibus*.

### After Zerika No Potency

This means that the case of *kiblu psulim ve'zarku es damah* in *Zevachim* cannot be read as a scenario in which the *psulim* sprinkled the blood in the normal sense of *zerika* on the *mizbe'ach*, because once *zerika* has occurred — even a valid one — the rest of the blood is already *shirayim* and its spattering on a garment is irrelevant. The mention of *zarku* in that context would therefore be superfluous if it meant a literal valid *zerika*.

### Stock Phrase Proof

The *Gemara* therefore proposes: *ela lav davka* — the phrase *kiblu psulim ve'zarku es damah* is not precise; it is a stock phrase (*stam nuscha*) employed generically. In *Zevachim*, the relevant moment is the *kabalah* — whether the blood was caught by a *pasul* person — and the mention of *zerika* is carried along as part of a formulaic phrase without intending to add a separate legal element. Therefore, one should not attempt to derive precision from the phrase in the context of *me'ila* either.

---

## Rav Assi Challenge

### Stock Phrase Origin

Rav Assi is not satisfied with this resolution. *Im ken lama li lemitni tarti?* — if the phrase is a stock phrase, why would it be taught in two places? If it is inexact in both places, then there was no point at which the phrase was used with genuine precision, and one must wonder how such an imprecise formula came into circulation at all. A stock phrase borrowed imprecisely must have had its origin in a place where it was precise. One location must have meant the phrase exactly as stated, and then it was borrowed elsewhere with some looseness.

### Meilah is Precise

Rav Assi therefore argues: *ela le'olam b'me'ila davka* — in *me'ila*, the phrase is precise and means exactly what it says: *psulim* caught *and* sprinkled the blood. In *me'ila*, the phrase was coined with full intentionality and then borrowed for the *Zevachim* context in a somewhat looser manner.

### Psul Oseh Shirayim

But Rav Assi goes further. He argues that in the *Zevachim* passage, the phrase is not merely a stock phrase imported carelessly — there is a genuine reason to discuss *zarku* even in that context. *Depasul oseh shirayim* — even when a *pasul* person performs *zerika*, it renders the other blood *shirayim*.

### Psul Zerika Effect

Here is the scenario: two people caught blood from the same *korban* — one *pasul*, one *kasher*. The *pasul* person goes first and performs *zerika* on the *mizbe'ach*. Then the *kasher* person attempts to perform *zerika* with his blood. What is the status of the *kasher* person's blood? Is it still valid blood whose spattering would require *kibus*, or is it now *shirayim* — remnant blood rendered irrelevant by the prior act of *zerika*? Rav Assi asserts that even the *zerika* of a *pasul* person is sufficient to make the other blood *shirayim*, rendering it no longer "active" blood. The *kasher* person's subsequent *zerika* would be meaningless — *lav klum* — and if that blood splatters on a garment, *kibus* would not be required.

---

## Shirayim Debate

### Shirayim Question

Reish Lakish had in fact posed precisely this question to Rabbi Yochanan: *pasul mahu sheyaaseh shirayim?* — if a *pasul* person performs *zerika* and there is other blood that was caught by a *kasher kohen*, does the *pasul* person's *zerika* make the *kasher* blood *shirayim*?

### Yochanan: Only Pigul

Rabbi Yochanan's answer was striking: *ein lecha davar sheyaaseh shirayim ela chutz lizmano ve'chutz limkomo, ho'il umeratzin lepigulan* — nothing has the capacity to create *shirayim* except *chutz lizmano* and *chutz limkomo*, i.e., a *zerika* performed with *machshaves pigul*. The reason: *pigul* only takes effect when the *avodah* was performed in such a way that the *korban* is considered, in a sense, as though it were accepted — *meratzeh l'pigulo*. Because the *zerika* with *pigul* intent is "as if" it were a valid *zerika*, it is sufficient to make the rest of the blood *shirayim*.

### Mertzeh Concept

This brings us full circle to the central principle discussed throughout the beginning of today's *daf*. The *mertzeh* concept — that a *zerika* with *pigul* intent is in some dimension "as if" valid — does not serve to change the *me'ila* status of the meat, as we concluded at length earlier. But Rabbi Yochanan now establishes that it *does* serve to affect the status of the remaining blood, rendering it *shirayim*.

### Other Psulim Irrelevant

Any other form of *psul*, however, is completely ineffective for this purpose. A *zerika* by a *ba'al mum*, an *onen*, or any other *pasul kohen* who does not fall within the *chutz lizmano/chutz limkomo* category leaves the rest of the blood entirely unaffected. The other blood remains valid, a *kasher kohen* can use it, and if it splatters on a garment it would require *kibus*. The key dividing line is precisely the *mertzeh l'pigulo* concept: only those *psulim* that carry with them some dimension of quasi-validity can affect the rest of the blood.

---

## Pigul & Tuma Validity

### Only Pigul-Type

The *Gemara* then refines Rabbi Yochanan's statement. The formulation *ein lecha davar sheyaaseh shirayim ela chutz lizmano ve'chutz limkomo* — nothing creates *shirayim* except *pigul*-type intent — appears at first to be absolute. Yet this raises an obvious difficulty: what about *tuma*?

### B'Tzibur Overwritten

The *Gemara* therefore clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan's statement was not meant absolutely. The real formulation is: *ein lecha davar she'eino mirtzeh b'tzibur ve'oseh shirayim ela chutz lizmano ve'chutz limkomo* — there is no *psul* that is never overwritten *b'tzibur* yet still has the capacity to create *shirayim*, except for *chutz lizmano ve'chutz limkomo*. The operative category is: is this *psul* one that can ever be overridden by congregational necessity (*b'tzibur*)? If a *psul* is sometimes permitted or overridden *b'tzibur*, then an *avodah* performed with that *psul* retains some quasi-validity, and its *zerika* can create *shirayim*.

### Tuma Overwritten

*Tuma* is precisely such a *psul*. There is a principle that *tuma* is *dchuya* or *hutrah b'tzibur* — either pushed aside or entirely permitted when the *tzibur* (community) is *tamei*. Because *kabalas tamei* and *zerikas tamei* can be *kasher* in certain circumstances (when the entire *tzibur* is *tamei*), an *avodah* performed by a *tamei kohen* is not a completely meaningless act. It carries some dimension of quasi-validity.

### Tuma Zerika Validity

Therefore, a *zerika* performed by a *tamei kohen* can also make the other blood *shirayim*. The same logical structure applies as with *pigul*: since *tuma* can be overridden *b'tzibur*, the *avodah* of a *tamei kohen* is not purely void, and therefore it affects the status of the remaining blood.

### Other Psulim Not

Other *psulim* — those that are never overridden *b'tzibur*, such as the *psul* of a *ba'al mum* — share none of this quasi-validity. Their *zerika* is entirely ineffective, the remaining blood is not *shirayim*, and the law of *kibus* would apply to the other blood if it splatters. The category of *psulim* that create *shirayim* is thus limited to two: *chutz lizmano/chutz limkomo* (*pigul*) by virtue of *mertzeh l'pigulo*, and *tuma* by virtue of *b'tzibur* override.

This clarification, while initially appearing as a digression, in fact crystallizes the conceptual landscape of the entire discussion. We now have two categories of *avodah* that, though *pasul*, carry some residual significance: *pigul* because of *mertzeh l'pigulo*, and *tuma* because of *b'tzibur*. Neither creates a *kasher korban*, and — as we established at the outset — neither is sufficient to change *me'ila* status. But both carry enough quasi-validity to affect the status of remaining blood by rendering it *shirayim*.

---

## Back to Main Question

### Hapigul Revisited

The *Gemara* returns to its main inquiry — the question of which moment determines the status change in *me'ila* — and revisits the first *braisa*: *hapigul l'olam mo'ilin bo*. This is the same formulation examined at the beginning of the *daf*.

### L'olam Inference

The *Gemara* attempts to use this *braisa* as evidence for the *kabalah* position. The argument runs as follows: the phrase *l'olam mo'ilin bo* — "always there is *me'ila*" — implies a universality. Perhaps the emphasis of *l'olam* is to convey that even when *pigul* occurred at an earlier stage, before *zerika*, the *me'ila* status never changes. This would suggest that the key moment is *kabalah* — since if *pigul* attached at *kabalah*, the *zerika* cannot remedy it. The *l'olam* underscores that no subsequent act repairs the problem.

### Lav Delo Zarak

The *Gemara* resists this reading: *lav delo zarak* — this does not mean the blood was not sprinkled at all. We are, in fact, discussing a case where *zerika* did occur. The *braisa* is addressing *zerika* performed with *pigul* intent.

### L'olam Emphasis

What, then, is the significance of *l'olam*? The *Gemara* explains that the emphasis of *l'olam* is directed at precisely the case of *zerika* with *pigul* intent — the very case where one might have thought the *zerika* should count for purposes of *me'ila* because of *mertzeh l'pigulo*. The *l'olam* conveys that *pigul* is always a problem, even at the stage of *zerika*, and that even a *zerika* which operates through *mertzeh l'pigulo* will not change the *me'ila* status. It is specifically the *zerika*-stage *pigul* that the *braisa* is ruling on.

### Zerika Key Moment

The *Gemara* concludes that this emphasis itself points to *zerika* as the key moment. The entire discussion has been centered on whether a *zerika* with *pigul* intent — which is, in one dimension, "as if" valid — should count to change *me'ila* status. The *l'olam* is the *braisa*'s way of unequivocally ruling that it does not. This confirms that it is the *zerika* — and specifically a *kasher zerika* — that is the operative moment for any change in *me'ila* status. The question of whether the key moment is *kabalah* or *zerika* therefore remains technically unresolved in its full formal sense, as the *Gemara* acknowledges that the *mishna*'s language can be read in support of either position, and we will continue with this discussion on the next *daf*.

---

---

# Meilah 6

## Kodshei Kodashim Status

### Basic Me'ilah Rule

The subject under discussion is the way in which a *korban*'s status with respect to *me'ilah* can change once the offering has been brought. *Kodshei kodashim* are entirely subject to *me'ilah* — they belong, as it were, entirely to God. Once the blood is sprinkled on the *mizbe'ach*, however, the meat of a *chatas* or *asham* becomes permissible to the *kohanim*, and therefore *me'ilah* no longer applies to that meat. *Me'ilah* still governs the remaining portions of the *korban*, but the meat itself is released. The reverse dynamic operates for *kodshim kalim*: since those offerings are fundamentally considered the owner's property and will be eaten by the owners, they do not initially carry *me'ilah*. Only the *emurim* — the portions designated for the *mizbe'ach* — become subject to *me'ilah*, and only after *zrikas ha-dam*. Thus, *zrikas ha-dam* operates in two directions: for *kodshei kodashim*, it releases the meat from *me'ilah*; for *kodshim kalim*, it brings the *emurim* into the *me'ilah* category.

### Zrikat Pigul

The *gemara* has been examining what happens when the *zrika* is not a fully valid one, but rather a quasi-valid act. One such case is *zrikas pigul* — a sprinkling performed with improper intent. There is a question whether such a *zrika* is considered meaningful enough to effect the status change. That position appears to be rejected, though the *gemara* will return to it. A second question — which occupies the bulk of this *amud* — is whether the critical moment is the actual *zrika* itself or an earlier moment, namely *kabbalas ha-dam*, the catching of the blood. Once *kabbala* has been performed, the blood is *ra'ui l'zrika* — fit for sprinkling — and one might argue that this earlier moment should be sufficient to effect the status change even before the actual *zrika* takes place. The *gemara* refers to the act of *kabbala* as *heter zrika* — the fitting of the blood for sprinkling — while the actual *zrika* constitutes *heter achila*, the moment when the meat actually becomes permitted for consumption.

---

## Nosar: Before/After Zrika

### Rabbi Shimon: Nosar

The *gemara* opens this section with a citation: *ta shema* — come and hear. Rabbi Shimon teaches that there are cases of *nosar* in which *me'ilah* applies and cases in which it does not. The question is how to understand this distinction. The term *nosar* refers to meat left over beyond its permitted time for consumption, which thereby becomes disqualified.

### Peshat: Nosar Timeline

Reading this at what appears to be the straightforward *peshat* level: Rabbi Shimon's cases are as follows. If the meat stayed overnight — becoming *nosar* — before the blood was sprinkled, and the blood was then sprinkled, the *zrika* at that point was not valid, since the blood itself had also remained overnight; the meat was therefore never rendered *mutar*, and *me'ilah* continues to apply. Conversely, if the blood was sprinkled at the proper time and the meat stayed overnight only afterward, there was a moment when the meat became *mutar*, and consequently *me'ilah* does not apply. The dividing line is simply whether the problem occurred before or after the *zrika*.

The *gemara* then attempts to draw a conclusion from Rabbi Shimon's statement: if he says that when *linah* occurred before *zrika* there is *me'ilah*, that implies that even if the blood had been caught — making it *ra'ui l'zrok* — but the *zrika* was delayed until the next day, the status would still not have changed. From this one might infer that the critical moment is the actual *zrika*, not the *kabbala*. The *gemara*, however, deflects: perhaps the case involves a situation where the blood was caught just before sunset, leaving no time for *zrika* at all — so that there was never a moment when the blood was fit for sprinkling. If that is the case, one cannot derive anything about whether *kabbala* alone, when there was time to sprinkle, would suffice.

### Gemara Challenge

The *gemara* then raises the obvious objection. Granting that interpretation, what of the meat that did stay overnight under those circumstances — when the blood was caught just before sunset? If the key moment is not the *zrika* but rather whether there was time and opportunity for *zrika*, then why does Rabbi Shimon frame the distinction around *zrika* at all? He should have framed the distinction around *sheki'as ha-chamah*: before *sheki'ah* versus after *sheki'ah* — that is, whether the blood was caught when there was still time to sprinkle or not.

### Ra'ui L'zrika

The *gemara* resolves this by saying: indeed, that is precisely what Rabbi Shimon means. When he says "before *zrika*" and "after *zrika*," he does not mean the literal act of sprinkling. He means before or after the point at which the blood was *ra'ui l'zrika* — fit to be sprinkled. If *linah* occurred before there was any opportunity to perform *zrika*, there is *me'ilah*; if it occurred after *kabbala* had been performed and the blood was fit for *zrika*, the status has already changed and there is no *me'ilah*. On this reading, *zrika* throughout Rabbi Shimon's statement is a shorthand for *ra'ui l'zrika*, and the critical moment is the *kabbala*, not the *zrika* itself. The straightforward sense of the *braita*, however, does indicate that the literal act of *zrikas ha-dam* is the critical moment.

### Rashi: Nosar Reading

Rashi reads the entire passage differently, and he is driven to do so by what follows in the *gemara*. In Rashi's reading, the discussion is not about when the problem of *linah* arose but about when the *hana'ah* — the benefit derived — from the meat took place. If one benefited from the meat before the *zrika* of the *nosar* blood, there is *me'ilah*. If one benefited after the *zrika* of the *nosar* blood — even though that blood was *nosar* — Rashi understands that such a *zrika* nevertheless removes the meat from *me'ilah*, analogously to the way we will discuss *pigul*. This is admittedly a difficult reading, since the blood would also be *nosar* if the meat is *nosar*, and it is not clear why such a *zrika* should be effective. Rashi's reading will become more intelligible in light of the next section of the *gemara*, which is why he adopts it here.

---

## Pigul: Before/After (II)

### Rabbi Shimon: Pigul

A parallel teaching follows: Rabbi Shimon states that there are cases of *pigul* in which *me'ilah* applies and cases in which it does not. *Pigul* is the disqualification arising from improper intent at the time of the sacrificial service — intention to eat the meat or burn the *emurim* beyond the permitted time. Again, the dividing line is stated as before or after *zrika*.

### Pigul After Kabbalah

Reading this at the straightforward *peshat* level: if the *pigul* intent arose before *zrika*, the *zrika* was never a valid *matir*, and *me'ilah* remains in effect. If the *pigul* intent arose after *zrika*, the *zrika* had already been a valid *matir*, and therefore there is no *me'ilah*. This is clearly analogous to the *nosar* case.

The problem, however, is immediately apparent, and this is precisely what troubled Rashi. *Pigul* can only arise during specific moments of the *avodah*: *shechita*, *kabbala*, *holacha*, or *zrika*. There is no way for *pigul* to arise after *zrika* — by the time *zrika* is complete, all the relevant moments of the service have passed. One cannot therefore simply say "the *pigul* arose after *zrika*," because that is not a possible scenario. Rashi was thus compelled to read the entire passage — both the *nosar* and *pigul* cases — as being about when the *hana'ah* was derived, not about when the disqualifying event arose. On that reading, even a *zrika* of *nosar* blood or *pigul* blood can change the status and take the meat out of *me'ilah* — which directly addresses, and disputes, the ruling of Rav Gidal in the name of Rav.

An alternative reading at the *peshat* level is to take "*achar zrika*" as not strictly meaning after *zrika* but rather *b'sha'at zrika* — at the moment of *zrika* itself. On this reading, if the *pigul* intent arose earlier, the *zrika* was never a valid *matir*; if it arose during the *zrika*, then it argues with Rav Gidal's position, which holds that *zrikas pigul* does not constitute a valid *zrika*. This makes the *gemara* somewhat less strained, even if the problem is not entirely resolved.

### Gemara: Why Zrika Not Ka…

The *gemara* now presses the same challenge it pressed in the *nosar* case. The statement says that if *pigul* arose before *zrika*, there is *me'ilah* — implying that even in a case where the blood had already been caught and was *ra'ui l'zrik*, but the *pigul* arose afterward, there is still *me'ilah*. This would suggest that the critical moment is the literal *zrika*, not the *kabbala*. From this the *gemara* attempts to conclude that *heter achila* — actual permissibility through *zrika* — is what matters, not mere fitness for *zrika* through *kabbala*.

The *gemara* deflects: the case is one where the blood was caught immediately before *sheki'ah*, leaving no time for *zrika*, so that it was never *ra'ui l'zrika* at all. But this invites the same challenge as before: if the key distinction is whether the blood was *ra'ui l'zrika* or not, why not frame the ruling around *sheki'as ha-chamah* rather than around *zrika*?

---

## Pigul: Before/After (II)

### Zrika = Ra'ui L'zrika

The *gemara* resolves the challenge in the same manner as before: when Rabbi Shimon speaks of "before *zrika*" and "after *zrika*," he means before or after the point at which the blood was fit for *zrika* — that is, before or after *kabbala*. *Zrika* is throughout a shorthand for *ra'ui l'zrika*. The *pigul* case is acknowledged to be more strained in its application of this reading, given the inherent difficulty of locating a moment when *pigul* could arise after *kabbala* but before *zrika* — the only candidate would be the end of *kabbala* itself, as Tosafot suggests. The difficulties notwithstanding, the overarching conclusion from both the *nosar* and *pigul* discussions is that the critical moment according to Rabbi Shimon is the *kabbala*, reframed as *ra'ui l'zrika*, rather than the literal act of *zrika*.

### Braita: Pigul Me'ilah

The *gemara* then cites a *braita* that was encountered in the preceding discussion: *pigul* in *kodshei kodashim* is subject to *me'ilah*. On a first reading, this might seem to mean that *pigul* occurring at the time of *shechita* is what is described — the problem precedes the *kabbala*, and the *zrika* is therefore never a valid *matir*, so *me'ilah* persists. The *gemara*, however, now assumes the opposite: it assumes the *braita* is speaking of *pigul* that occurred even after *kabbala*, at the time of *zrika*, and that the *braita* is telling us that even then *me'ilah* applies — which would imply that the critical moment is not the *kabbala* but the actual *zrika*. This would argue against the conclusion that *zrika* means *ra'ui l'zrika*. The *gemara* deflects: the *braita* is not speaking of a case where the *zrika* took place; it speaks of *pigul* that arose before *zrika*, with no *zrika* having occurred. And if one then asks what happens when a *zrika* did occur under these conditions, the *gemara* replies that the *braita* must be providing the prior case, and the later case would need to be inferred separately.

---

## In vs. Out of Me'ilah

### Why Kodshim Kalim

The *gemara* raises a pointed question. The *braita* states: *pigul* in *kodshei kodashim* — there is *me'ilah*; *pigul* in *kodshim kalim* — there is no *me'ilah*. The *braita* is evidently seeking to illustrate a case in which there is no *me'ilah*. But if, as the *gemara* has been arguing, the key moment is *ra'ui l'zrika*, then there exists a case even within *kodshei kodashim* where there would be no *me'ilah* — namely, where *pigul* arose after *kabbala*. Why, then, did the *braita* run to the case of *kodshim kalim* to furnish an example of no *me'ilah*? It could simply have distinguished within *kodshei kodashim* itself: if the problem arose before *zrika* there is *me'ilah*, and if after *zrika* there is not.

### Two Standards

The *gemara* answers that the *braita* deliberately chose the *kodshim kalim* case because it wishes to convey an additional principle — a distinction in standards depending on the direction of the status change. The principle is stated as follows:

*Kol ha-asui lidei me'ilah* — for something that is meant to be brought into the *me'ilah* category — *zrika ke-tiknah mavia lidei me'ilah*: a fully proper *zrika* is required to effect that transition. *Kol ha-apokei midei me'ilah* — for something that is meant to be removed from the *me'ilah* category — *afilu she-lo ke-tiknah nami mapik midei me'ilah*: even an imperfect *zrika* can effect that removal.

There are two ways to understand the underlying logic of this distinction. One approach is that *me'ilah* designates the status of *kodshei Hashem* — belonging to God — which is a tenuous and rarefied category. Because it is such a narrow category, any ambiguity in status means the item is no longer clearly within it. A questionable *zrika* — whether *zrikas pigul*, or merely *ra'ui l'zrika* — is sufficient to remove an item from that category, since doubt dissolves the certainty required to remain in it. To bring something *into* that category, however, requires certainty; the item must be unambiguously designated as *kodshei Hashem*. The other approach frames the question in terms of *chumra* and *kula*: when we wish to be *machmir* — to prohibit — any doubt suffices; but when we seek to be *meikel* — to permit — a clear, unambiguous act is required.

The *braita* therefore goes to *kodshim kalim* not merely for a case of no *me'ilah*, but to underscore this principle: in *kodshim kalim*, where the *emurim* are seeking to enter the *me'ilah* category, any imperfection in the *zrika* — any questionable element — will prevent that transition entirely. The *braita* thus carries a dual message: *kodshei kodashim* with *pigul* retains *me'ilah* because the imperfect *zrika* suffices to keep it from falling out; *kodshim kalim* with *pigul* never acquires *me'ilah* because the imperfect *zrika* does not meet the threshold needed to bring it in.

### Kol Ha-Apokei

The *gemara*'s analysis here is a significant conceptual statement about the asymmetry between entering and exiting the *me'ilah* category. Across the discussions of this *amud* — *zrikas pigul*, *ra'ui l'zrika*, and now this general principle — the *gemara* is consistently examining whether various categories of imperfect or quasi-valid *zrika* are sufficient to effect a status change. The answer, articulated here, is that the standard differs by direction: a lesser *zrika* may suffice to remove something from *me'ilah*, while a fully valid *zrika* is required to bring something into it.

With these observations, the first *amud* concludes. The essential conclusions are: (1) *zrika* is the critical moment, though there is sustained discussion about whether *ra'ui l'zrika* through *kabbala* may serve the same function; (2) *zrikas pigul* does not constitute a valid *zrika* for purposes of changing status; and (3) the standard for what counts as a sufficient *zrika* may depend on whether the question is one of entering or exiting the *me'ilah* category.

---

## Psul Yotzei: Kodshei

### Mishna: Yotzei

The *gemara* now turns to the *mishna* on 6b, which introduces a new category of *psul*: *psul yotzei*, the disqualification arising when sacrificial meat or *emurim* are removed from the permitted area of the *Beis Hamikdash*. The case discussed is *basar kodshei kodashim she-yatza lifnei zrikat damim* — meat of *kodshei kodashim* that was taken outside the permitted bounds before the blood was sprinkled. The dispute is between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva.

### R. Eliezer: No Change

Rabbi Eliezer rules: *mo'alin bo* — *me'ilah* applies to this meat. Even if a valid *zrika* was subsequently performed for the rest of the *korban*, the meat that went out was already *pasul*. It was never *ra'ui l'achilah* — fit for consumption — and therefore the *zrika* does not change its status. The meat remains in the *me'ilah* category, and moreover, since the meat is already *pasul*, there is no liability of *kares* for the other *pesulim* that might otherwise apply: *ein chayavin alav mishum pigul, notar, v'tamei*. The liability for *pigul*, *nosar*, and *tum'ah* applies only to meat that would otherwise have been *kasher*; this meat was already disqualified, so those categories do not obtain. One who derives benefit from it is liable for *me'ilah* and for eating *psulei mukdashim*, but not for *pigul*, *nosar*, or *tum'ah*.

### R. Akiva: Status Changes

Rabbi Akiva rules: *ein mo'alin bo* — *me'ilah* does not apply. Although the meat has the *psul* of *yotzei*, the *zrika* was nonetheless effective to change its status. The meat is technically not *mutar* for consumption — the *psul yotzei* remains — but the *zrika* creates a virtual permissibility: it is as if the meat were *ra'ui l'achilah*. Because of that virtual status, *me'ilah* does not apply. Conversely, because the meat is treated as though it were otherwise fit, the liabilities of *pigul*, *nosar*, and *tum'ah* do apply: *chayavin alav mishum pigul, nosar, v'tamei*.

Rabbi Akiva offers a proof from a different case. If one sets aside a *chatas*, loses it, and then sets aside a second animal as a replacement, only to find the first animal thereafter — both animals stand before him. Only one can be brought; the other is in the status of *chatas she-kipru ba'aleha b'acheres*, and Rashi understands the case as one where both were slaughtered and their blood caught before the decision as to which would be offered was finalized. Rabbi Akiva argues: *lo k'shem she-dama poter es besara kach hu poter es besar chavertah* — just as the blood of the one sprinkled renders its own meat released from *me'ilah*, so too does it release the meat of its counterpart. His argument is that since at the moment of *kabbala* either animal could have been chosen, they are conceptually unified, and the *zrikas ha-dam* of one therefore operates on the other. He does not go so far as to say the meat of the second animal is *mutar l'achilah* — he says only *poter*, releases, not *matir*. His claim is the narrower one: conceptually they constitute a single *zevach*, and therefore the *zrika* of one removes the other's meat from the *me'ilah* category.

If that is accepted, he argues *kal va-chomer*: if the blood of one *chatas* can release the meat of a different *chatas* from *me'ilah*, surely the blood of a *korban* sprinkled in proper fashion can release its own meat from *me'ilah*, notwithstanding the *psul yotzei* that attaches to that meat. The logic is that *yotzei* is a lesser *psul* — a matter of physical distance rather than intrinsic invalidity — and should not be treated as a more formidable barrier than the separation between two distinct animals. The scope of Rabbi Akiva's leniency is circumscribed, however, to *yotzei*; he does not extend this reasoning to other *pesulim* such as *tum'ah*, presumably because *yotzei* is a less severe disqualification.

---

## Psul Yotzei: Kodshim

### Parallel Case

The *mishna* then presents the parallel case with *kodshim kalim*: *eimurai kodshim kalim she-yatzu lifnei zrikat ha-dam* — the *emurim* of a *shelamim* that were removed outside the permitted area before the blood was sprinkled. For *kodshim kalim*, recall, a valid *zrika* would normally bring the *emurim* into the *me'ilah* category, since they are designated for the *mizbe'ach*. The question is whether a *zrika* performed after *yotzei* has occurred accomplishes that transition.

### Same Machloket

Rabbi Eliezer rules: *ein mo'alin bahen* — *me'ilah* does not apply. These *emurim* are *pasul*; the *zrika* was therefore ineffective in bringing them into the *me'ilah* category. Correspondingly, *ein chayavin aleihem mishum pigul, nosar, v'tamei* — since the *emurim* are not *ra'ui* for the *mizbe'ach*, the other *pesulim* do not apply. Rabbi Akiva rules: *mo'alin bahen* — *me'ilah* does apply. The *zrika* is effective even with *psul yotzei*, and the *emurim* are treated as if they were *ra'ui* for the *mizbe'ach*. Accordingly, *chayavin aleihem mishum pigul, nosar, v'tamei* as well.

The fundamental *machloket* is thus the same in both cases: Rabbi Eliezer holds that *psul yotzei* is like any other *psul* and prevents the *zrika* from being effective, while Rabbi Akiva holds that *psul yotzei* is sui generis and the *zrika* effects the status change regardless.

### Why Both Cases

The *gemara* asks: *ve-hani tartei lama li* — why were both cases necessary? The debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva is substantively identical in both. The *gemara* answers: *tzricha* — both are needed. Had the dispute been stated only for *kodshei kodashim*, one might have understood Rabbi Eliezer's position as follows: he requires a fully valid *zrika* to remove something from *me'ilah* — *zrika ke-tiknah mapka midei me'ilah, she-lo ke-tiknah lo mapka midei me'ilah* — because removal from *me'ilah* requires an unambiguously effective *zrika*. But one might then have thought that in the opposite direction — bringing something *into* the *me'ilah* category — Rabbi Eliezer would agree with Rabbi Akiva. After all, it is always easier to impose a stringency; if the standard for imposing *me'ilah* is lower, then even with the deficiency of *yotzei*, the *emurim* might enter the *me'ilah* category. Stating the dispute in *kodshim kalim* teaches that Rabbi Eliezer maintains his position even there: even when all that is at stake is bringing the *emurim* into *me'ilah*, he requires a fully valid *zrika*, and a *zrika* performed when *yotzei* has occurred is insufficient.

Conversely, had the dispute been stated only for *kodshim kalim*, one might have understood Rabbi Akiva's leniency differently. There, Rabbi Akiva says *me'ilah* applies — that is, he is being *machmir*. One might have thought he is lenient in the sense that even an imperfect *zrika* can impose *me'ilah*, since imposing *me'ilah* is a stringency. But one might then have supposed that when it comes to *kodshei kodashim* — where applying Rabbi Akiva's ruling means saying *me'ilah does not apply*, a leniency — Rabbi Akiva would concede to Rabbi Eliezer. Stating the dispute in *kodshei kodashim* teaches that Rabbi Akiva holds his position in both directions: he is consistently of the view that *psul yotzei* does not prevent *zrika* from effecting the status change, regardless of which direction the change runs. Both cases are therefore necessary to establish the full scope of the *machloket*.

---

## Miktzato vs. Kulo

### R. Yochanan Clarifies

The *gemara* cites Rabbi Yochanan's qualification of Rabbi Akiva's position. Rabbi Yochanan states: *ad kan amar Rabbi Akiva zrika mo'elet l'yotzei* — Rabbi Akiva only says that *zrika* is effective for *yotzei* in a particular circumstance: *she-yatza miktzato* — when only part of the meat (or *emurim*) went outside the permitted area, while the rest remained within.

### Miktzato vs. Kulo

The parallel to the *chatas* proof now becomes clearer. When Rabbi Akiva argued from the case of two *chatos* — that the blood of one released the meat of the other — the conceptual basis was that they could be seen as unified, since both were present in the *azarah* simultaneously and either could have been chosen. Similarly, when only *part* of the *korban*'s meat or *emurim* went out, the *zrika* that worked for the portion that remained can be said to work for the portion that went out, on the theory that they are all part of one *korban*. But *aval yatza kulo* — if the entirety of the meat or *emurim* went outside before the *zrika* — Rabbi Akiva would not apply his ruling. There, Rabbi Yochanan clarifies, Rabbi Akiva would agree with Rabbi Eliezer that the *zrika* is not effective. When nothing remained within the permitted area, there is no basis for treating the *zrika* as having any purchase on those portions.

---

## Pigul on Avud/Saruf

### Avud v'Saruf

Following Rabbi Yochanan's qualification, Rav Assi addresses him and reports a teaching from his colleagues in the Diaspora — *chavray she-ba-golah*: *m'chashvin al ha-avud v'al ha-saruf* — one can form the requisite *machsheves pigul* with respect to objects that have been lost or burned. The case is this: during the performance of the sacrificial service, one forms the intent to consume the meat or burn the *emurim* beyond the permitted time — the classic *machsheves pigul*. The novelty is that at the moment this intent is formed, the meat or *emurim* in question have already been destroyed — they no longer exist. One might have thought that such intent is meaningless, since it is directed at an object that is no longer present. Yet the ruling is that *m'chashvin* — such intent does constitute *pigul*, and the *korban* is disqualified. The reason is that *pigul* does not operate narrowly on the specific object contemplated; it disqualifies the entire *korban*. As long as other portions of the *korban* remain, the invalid intent — even when directed at something no longer extant — is sufficient to render the whole *korban pigul*: *v'ha-avud v'ha-saruf lo hayu ba-olam, v'afilu hachi tani m'chashvin*.

### Implication Teased

Rav Assi is raising this teaching in order to press on Rabbi Yochanan's qualification of Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yochanan had limited Rabbi Akiva's ruling to *miktzato* — where only part went out — implying that something must remain within the permitted bounds for the *zrika* to be effective for the portion that left. But the ruling about *avud v'saruf* suggests that even when the object in question has been entirely destroyed — not merely removed but gone altogether — certain *halachic* mechanisms can still operate in relation to it, so long as something else in the *korban* remains. Rav Assi is teasing out whether the same logic might extend Rabbi Akiva's position beyond the *miktzato* limitation, perhaps even to *kulo*. The discussion will continue on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Meilah 8

## Intro & Rashi Auth.

### Opening

Daf 8 marks the beginning of the second chapter of Maseches *Me'ilah*. One reason this *daf* is notably short is that *Tosafot* addresses all of the *mishnayos* of the chapter together at the outset, providing a unified explanation at the opening of the *perek*.

### Rashi Auth.

This occasion also calls for a clarification about the *rishonim* on *Me'ilah*. An earlier suggestion that the *Rashi* in Maseches *Kerisos* was not authentic *Rashi* turns out to be mistaken. Although Zunz advanced that claim, contemporary scholarship appears to have largely rejected it, and the *Rashi* in *Kerisos* is generally accepted as genuine — even if one particularly lengthy *Rashi* there may be a later gloss. The situation is quite the reverse in *Me'ilah*: there is substantial scholarly opinion holding that the *Rashi* commentary on *Me'ilah* is not actually *Rashi*'s work. Supporting this, *Tosafot* in *Kerisos* frequently cites *Pirush Hakontres* or *Pirush Rashi*, whereas *Tosafot* in *Me'ilah* appears never to do so. This may explain why *Tosafot* in *Me'ilah* so often performs the explanatory function normally associated with *Rashi* — because, in all likelihood, the *rishonim* composing *Tosafot* here did not have an authoritative *Rashi* commentary on which to rely.

## Tumah & Pesul

### Ch. 2 Transition

The first chapter of *Me'ilah* devoted considerable attention to *pesulim* — cases of disqualification and how they affect status changes — and concluded with the fundamental rule: that *zerikas hadam* by *kodshei kodashim* removes the meat from *me'ilah*, while *zerikas hadam* of *kodshim kalim* brings the animal more fully into the domain of *me'ilah*. The second chapter now proceeds in a more apodictic mode, setting out the straightforward law — without special cases — of when and how the status of *me'ilah* changes across the full range of *korbanos*. Interestingly, *Tosafot* chooses to open not with the most standard type of *korban* but with the *chatas ha'of*, the bird sin-offering. The *mishnah* states: *chatas ha'of mo'alin bah* — there is *me'ilah* on a bird *chatas* — *mishehukdeshah*, from the moment it is sanctified. It is *kodshei kodashim*, and therefore subject to *me'ilah* from the outset.
