### Av Hatumah

To follow the *Gemara*'s analysis, it is necessary to understand the basic framework of *tumah* transmission. A source of *tumah* — a corpse, a *zav*, and the like — is called an *av hatumah*. The exception is a *meis*, which stands at the highest level, *avi avos hatumah*. When an *av hatumah* comes into contact with a person or object, that person or object becomes a *rishon*, a first-degree derivative of *tumah*. When the *rishon* then contacts something else, that becomes a *sheni*. In principle, only food can become a *sheni*; people and vessels do not become *sheni* from contact with a *rishon*. Most categories stop at *sheni* — food touching food does not produce a further degree of *tumah*. However, when one deals with items of higher *kedushah*, the capacity to receive *tumah* extends further. *Terumah* can become a *shlishi*, and *kodshim* can reach a *revi'i*.

### Pesul vs. Tamei

When something has contracted *tumah* but is no longer capable of transmitting it further, it is described not as *tamei* but as *nifsul* — invalidated. A *shlishi* of *terumah* is called *nifsul*, not *tamei*, because although it may not be eaten, it cannot pass the *tumah* on. Similarly, a *revi'i* of *kodshim* is *nifsul* rather than *tamei*. The distinction is significant: calling something *tamei* implies it retains the capacity to convey *tumah* to another object; calling it *pasul* means it is disqualified for use but cannot propagate the *tumah* further.

### Tevul Yom

Two special categories require attention here. A person who has immersed in a *mikveh* but is awaiting nightfall to complete the purification process is called a *tvul yom*. A person who has immersed but still needs to bring a *korban* — applicable to a *zav*, *zavah*, *yoledes*, or *metzora* — is called a *mechusar kippurim*, one lacking the *korban* that will complete their purification. Both of these individuals carry an extremely residual form of *tumah*. A *tvul yom* functions at roughly the level of a *sheni*, meaning that in ordinary circumstances contact with *chullin* would have no effect, since a *sheni* cannot transmit *tumah* to non-sacred food. However, because *terumah* and *kodshim* possess elevated *kedushah*, even this residual *tumah* has an effect on them — though only a disqualifying one, not a full *tumah*. The *mishnah*'s statement that the animal is *huchshara l'hipasel bitvul yom uvimechusar kippurim* — rendered susceptible to disqualification through a *tvul yom* or *mechusar kippurim* — means it becomes *pasul*, not *tamei*. The *tumah* of a *tvul yom* is so attenuated that it can disqualify, but it cannot pass the disqualification further.

### Shechita Process

Before the animal is slaughtered it remains a living creature; it is not yet considered food and has not achieved the status of something fit to be brought or eaten. Therefore, even if something *tamei* comes into contact with it, nothing happens. Once *melikah* is performed on the bird — the *kohen* cuts the nape of the neck, rendering the bird dead — it now becomes fit to be placed on the *mizbe'ach* and, in principle, to be eaten, and the word *huchshara* applies: it has become *hechsher*, susceptible to *tumah*. The same word *hechsher* is used when liquids touch food and render it susceptible, as derived from the verse *ve-chi yitten mayim al zera* (Vayikra 11). Once the bird is dead and in the category of food or of something fit for the *mizbe'ach*, it has the *hechsher* needed to become *pasul* through contact with a *tvul yom* or *mechusar kippurim*.

The *mishnah* adds *u-ve-linah* — there can also be *linah*, the disqualification that results from the blood or the meat being left overnight. *Tosafot* emphasizes that the *linah* mentioned at this stage refers specifically to *linat ha-dam*, leaving the blood overnight. *Linat ha-basar*, the *linah* of the meat, presents a problem: the clock for *linat ha-basar* ordinarily starts only after *zerikas hadam*, since it is only then that the meat becomes fit to be eaten. This is confirmed by the final *mishnayos* of the previous chapter, which state *le-achar zerikah chayav alav mishum piggul nosar ve-tamei* — that it is only after *zerikah* that the statuses of *piggul*, *nosar*, and *tamei* apply, and only then is one *chayav kares* for eating the meat. Thus the *linah* here is *linat ha-dam*: if the blood was caught but left until the next morning, it is *pasul* and cannot be used.

Once the blood is squirted — *huzah damah* — the statuses of *piggul*, *nosar*, and *tamei* all take effect: *chayavin alav mishum piggul nosar ve-tamei*. After *zerikas hadam*, when the *korban* is valid and the meat is fit to be eaten, these three statuses are established, and one is *chayav kares* if one eats the meat in a state of *piggul*, *nosar*, or *tamei*. And: *ve-ein bo me'ilah* — there is no *me'ilah*. By a bird *chatas*, there are no *emurim*; the *kohanim* eat all of the meat. So once *zerikah* renders the meat permissible to the *kohanim*, *me'ilah* ceases entirely.

## Chatas Ha'Of

### Chatas Intro

With this framework in place, the *Gemara* returns to examine what the *mishnah* teaches. The general picture is now familiar: *zerikas hadam* changes the status for *me'ilah* with respect to the meat, and *kabalas hadam* — the catching of the blood — is the moment that renders the bird *kodshim* susceptible to *tumah* and *linah*.

### Pesul/Tamei Q.

The *Gemara* homes in on a conceptual difficulty. The *mishnah* states that after *melikah*, the bird is rendered susceptible to *hipasel bitvul yom* — disqualification through a *tvul yom*. The language is precise: *yipasel*, it becomes *pasul*, but not *yitamei*, it does not become *tamei* in the full sense. Now, given that a *tvul yom* functions as a *sheni*, touching *kodshim* should produce a *shlishi*, which in the domain of *kodshim* would be called *tamei* — because *kodshim* can reach a *revi'i*. Why then does the *mishnah* use only the language of *pesul* and not *tumah*? This is precisely the tension the *Gemara* addresses: the *mishnah* implies the *tvul yom* only *posels* — disqualifies — the *kodshim*, but does not render it *tamei* in the sense of a *tumah* that can be transmitted further.

### Tannaim Dispute

The *Gemara* asks: *matnisin mani?* — whose view does our *mishnah* reflect? It concludes: *Rabanan hi* — the position of the *Rabbanan* in a *braisa* cited from the *Tosefta Teharos*, where there is a three-way dispute.

*Abba Shaul* holds that when a *tvul yom* touches *kodshim*, he is treated stringently — as a *rishon*, not a *sheni*. This means whatever he touches becomes a *sheni*, and the *korban* is in that way *tamei* at the level of *sheni*.

*Rabbi Meir* holds that a *tvul yom* is a *sheni*. When he touches *terumah*, it becomes a *shlishi* — which is called *pasul* for *terumah*, since *terumah* goes no further than *shlishi*. When he touches *kodshim*, it becomes a *shlishi* as well, but since *kodshim* can reach *revi'i*, a *shlishi* of *kodshim* is called *tamei* — it can still transmit the *tumah* one more step to a *revi'i*. So *Rabbi Meir* says *metamei es hakodesh ufosel es haterumah* — he renders *kodshim* *tamei* and *terumah* *pasul*.

The *Rabbanan* of the *braisa* take a third position: *keshem shehu posel mashkeh trumah ve-ochlei trumah, kach hu posel mashkeh kodesh ve-ochlei kodesh* — just as he *posels* the food and drink of *terumah*, so too he only *posels* the food and drink of *kodshim*, without making it *tamei* in a transmissible sense. This is puzzling at first glance: if he is a *sheni*, he should render *kodshim* a *shlishi*, which is *tamei*. But the *Rabbanan*'s position is that whatever one calls the formal level of the *tvul yom*, his *tumah* is so residual — so attenuated after the *mikveh* immersion — that it can only go one step further and then stops, regardless of whether that one step is into *terumah* or *kodshim*.

### Rava's Resol.

*Rava* resolves the apparent tension between the tannaitic positions and our *mishnah* by distinguishing between the *d'Oraisa* level and the *d'rabbanan* level. *D'Oraisa*, it is clear from the Torah — *uva ha-shemesh ve-taher* and *ve-achar yochal min ha-kodashim* — that a *tvul yom* may not eat *kodshim* and has some effect on their status. At the *d'Oraisa* level, everybody agrees that a *tvul yom* is *posel* *terumah* and *kodshim*: he renders them unusable, disqualified, but the *tumah* does not propagate further. This is precisely what our *mishnah* says, and it reflects the agreed-upon *d'Oraisa* position.

The debate among *Abba Shaul*, *Rabbi Meir*, and the *Rabbanan* is entirely at the *d'rabbanan* level — a rabbinic stringency regarding how to characterize the *tvul yom*'s status more precisely. *Abba Shaul* holds that *d'rabbanan* the Rabbis treated him like a *rishon*, so that he makes things into a *sheni*. *Rabbi Meir* holds that *d'rabbanan* he functions as a *sheni*, making *kodshim* into a *shlishi* that is *tamei*. But all of this is *d'rabbanan*. Our *mishnah*, which speaks only of *pesul*, represents the *d'Oraisa* baseline on which everyone agrees. The conceptual explanation for why the *d'Oraisa* effect is only *pesul* and not transmissible *tumah* is that the *tvul yom*'s *tumah* after immersion is so residual that it can act on one further object but cannot propagate beyond it — not because of the number of degrees removed, but because the intrinsic weakness of this *tumah* limits its reach. The same *din* applies equally to *mechusar kippurim*, as the *braisa* concludes: *ve-hu ha-din bi-mechusar kippurim*.

### Me'ilah Change

Having established the *tumah* framework, the *Gemara* turns to the *me'ilah* dimension. The *mishnah* states *ve-ein bo me'ilah* — after *zerikas hadam* there is no *me'ilah* — which implies, by its very formulation, that there is nevertheless still some prohibition (*issura ika*). The *Gemara* asks: why should there be any remaining prohibition? After you sprinkle the blood, the *kohanim* are supposed to eat the meat — it belongs to them. What problem remains?

The *Gemara* answers with *Rabbi Chanina*'s explanation, the same answer given on the preceding *daf*: this follows the position of *Rabbi Akiva*, who holds that *zerikah* takes meat that left the *Beis Hamikdash* — *yotzei* — out of the category of *me'ilah*, and yet such meat remains forbidden for consumption (*de-lav l'achilah hi*). So even after *zerikah*, meat that had exited the *Beis Hamikdash* is no longer subject to *me'ilah* but is still *assur* to eat. The *mishnah*'s implication that some prohibition remains is thus accounted for by this specific case of *yotzei* according to *Rabbi Akiva*.

## Mitzuy Debate

### Rav Positions

With the *me'ilah* analysis of the *chatas ha'of* concluded, the *Gemara* transitions to a related and fundamental question: is *mitzuy* — the squeezing out of the blood after the initial squirt — an indispensable act for the *korban*? The Torah describes two distinct actions by the bird *chatas*: first the blood squirts from the severed neck against the wall of the *mizbe'ach*, and then the neck is pressed against the wall and the remaining blood is squeezed out. The question is whether this squeezing is part of *zerikas hadam* proper — and therefore *me'akev*, indispensable — or whether it functions analogously to *shfichas shirayim* in an animal *korban*, namely the pouring of the remaining blood at the base of the *mizbe'ach* after the main *zerikah*, which is not *me'akev*.

*Rav Huna* in the name of *Rav* states: *mitzuy chatas ha'of eino me'akev* — the squeezing out is not indispensable. In support he notes that our *mishnah* uses the language *huzah damah* — the blood was squirted — as the critical moment after which all the status changes occur. If the *mishnah* marks the squirting as the pivotal act, the squeezing that follows cannot be what is *me'akev*.

*Rav Ada bar Ahava*, also in the name of *Rav*, takes the opposite position: *mitzuy chatas ha'of me'akev* — the squeezing is indispensable. He argues that our *mishnah* should be read differently — *mitzah damah*, the blood was squeezed out — so that the pivotal moment is the completed *mitzuy*, not merely the initial squirt.

### Mishna Proof

The two *Amoraim* thus differ over the precise language of the *mishnah*. According to *Rav Huna*, the *mishnah* says *huzah damah*, the blood was squirted, and this is the critical moment. According to *Rav Ada bar Ahava*, the *mishnah* reads *mitzah damah*, the blood was squeezed, making the full *mitzuy* the determinative act.

### Baraita Cite

The *Gemara* now attempts to resolve the dispute from a *baraisa*. The Torah states regarding the bird *chatas* (Vayikra 5): *u-malak et rosho mi-mul orpo ve-lo yavdil ve-hizah mi-dam ha-chatas al kir ha-mizbe'ach ve-ha-nishar ba-dam yimatze el yesod ha-mizbe'ach chatas hi*. The language *chatas hi* — it is a *chatas* — appears at the end of the verse, after the instruction to squeeze the remaining blood to the base. The *Gemara* considers whether this formulation means that only after the squeezing is performed does the offering attain the status of a valid *chatas*, which would make the *mitzuy* indispensable.

*Bishlama l'Rav Ada bar Ahava haynu d'chtiv ve-ha-nishar ba-dam yimatze chatas hi* — according to *Rav Ada bar Ahava* this reads naturally: the verse tells you that only after squeezing the blood is it a *chatas*, confirming that *mitzuy* is *me'akev*. But according to *Rav Huna*, what is the significance of *ve-ha-nishar* and *chatas hi*? The answer given, following the school of *Rabbi Yishmael*, is that *she-im nish'ar* — the verse speaks conditionally: *if* there is remaining blood, you should squeeze it out. It does not mandate that there must be remaining blood; it only instructs what to do when there happens to be some. As for *chatas hi*, the *Gemara* explains that this refers back to the beginning of the verse — *ve-hizah mi-dam ha-chatas al kir ha-mizbe'ach* — and it is after the *hazaah*, the initial squirting, that the offering is declared a *chatas*. The concluding *chatas hi* thus confirms the status established by the squirting, not by the squeezing.

### Repetition Rule

This invokes a broader principle of *kodshim* interpretation. Normally, whenever the Torah mentions a requirement, one might assume it is *me'akev* — that failure to fulfill it invalidates the *korban*. But in the domain of *kodshim*, the general assumption is that a detail mentioned once is a *mitzvah* but not *me'akev*, and only when the Torah repeats the requirement — *shana alav ha-katuv le-akev* — do we conclude that it is indispensable.

*Rav Acha brei de-Rava* raised a challenge to *Rav Ashi*: apply the same logic to the *mincha*. The Torah says *ve-ha-noteret min ha-mincha yochlu Aharon u-vanav* — the remainder of the *mincha* shall be eaten by *Aharon* and his sons. By the same reasoning, should we say that if nothing remains — say, all the *shirayim* spilled — there is no problem? A *baraisa* on 17a explicitly rejects this: *mi-soltah u-mi-shamnah al kol levonatah* — if some of the flour, oil, or *levonah* was missing when the *komatz* was offered, it is invalid. There must be a proper *noteret*, a remainder. The *Gemara* responds by distinguishing the two cases. By the *mincha*, the Torah uses the word *ve-ha-noteret* twice, and the repetition is what makes the requirement *me'akev*. By the *chatas ha'of*, the Torah uses the formulation *ve-ha-nishar* only once, and therefore it is not *me'akev* — it is a *mitzvah* to perform the *mitzuy* if there is remaining blood, but the *korban* is nevertheless valid if the *mitzuy* is not performed.

### Menachos Par.

The challenge from *Rav Acha bar Rava* using the case of *menachos* thus serves to sharpen the principle: the *me'akev* status of a repeated requirement is demonstrated by the *mincha*, where the double mention of *ha-noteret* establishes indispensability, whereas the single mention of *ve-ha-nishar* by the bird *chatas* is not sufficient to establish the same.

### Mitzuy Concl.

The *Gemara* also presents a *baraisa* in the name of *Rabbi Yishmael*'s school: the squeezing is required only if blood remains — *she-nishtayyer ba-dam*. Even then, according to one version, it is not *me'akev*. The *Gemara* also notes a parallel dispute in *Zevachim*, where *Rav Pappa* identifies the question of whether *mitzuy chatas ha'of* is *me'akev* as the subject of a disagreement attributed to *Rabbi Yishmael* himself — with one tradition saying it is not *me'akev* and another saying it is. The *Gemara* concludes: *trei tannaei aliba d'Rabbi Yishmael* — there are two tannaitic traditions in the name of *Rabbi Yishmael* on this point, just as there are two *Amoraic* traditions in the name of *Rav*. The final determination is thus: *mitzuy* is not *me'akev* if there is no remaining blood, and even when blood does remain, the dominant view is that failure to perform *mitzuy* does not invalidate the *korban*.

## Olat Ha'Of

### Olat Ha'Of

The *mishnah* now proceeds to the *olat ha'of*, the bird *olah*. The structure of status changes parallels that of the *chatas ha'of*: *mo'alin bah mishehikdshah* — *me'ilah* applies from the moment of sanctification. Once *melikah* is performed — the bird is killed — *huchshera l'hipasel bitvul yom uvimechusar kippurim* — it becomes susceptible to disqualification through a *tvul yom* or *mechusar kippurim*, and *linah* applies to the blood. Note that by the *olah*, the Torah speaks only of *mitzuy* — the squeezing out of the blood — rather than of an initial squirting. Therefore the *mishnah* states: *mitzat damah* — once you squeeze out the blood — *chayavin aleha mishum piggul nosar ve-tamei*. At that point the statuses of *piggul*, *nosar*, and *tamei* all take effect, and one is *chayav* for those if applicable.

Crucially, unlike the *chatas ha'of*, *me'ilah* does not end here. Since a bird *olah* is entirely consumed on the *mizbe'ach* and nobody — not even the *kohanim* — benefits from its meat, *zerikah* does not change the *me'ilah* status. *Me'ilah* continues — *u-mo'alin bah* — *ad she-tetzei l'veit ha-deshen*, until the ash and the remains are taken out to the place of ashes outside the camp. The underlying principle is that *me'ilah* persists as long as the *mitzvah* of the *korban* has not been fully completed — *na'aseis mitzvato*. This is actually the source for the broader rule applied to *issurei hana'ah*: something remains in the domain of *Kodshei Hashem* as long as its appointed purpose has not yet been fulfilled. By a bird *olah*, the final *mitzvah* is the removal of the ashes to the *beis ha-deshen*, and only then does *me'ilah* cease.

### Olah Me'ilah

The *mishnah* turns to the ordinary animal *olah* — a sheep or cow. *Me'ilah* begins from sanctification: *mo'alin bah mishehikdshah*. After *shechitah*, the animal is dead, no longer alive, and *huchshera l'hipasel bitvul yom uvimechusar kippurim uvlinah* — susceptible to disqualification from a *tvul yom*, *mechusar kippurim*, and *linah* of the blood. After *zerikas hadam* — *mishezarak damah* — the *korban* is valid and the statuses of *piggul*, *nosar*, and *tamei* take hold: *chayavin alav mishum piggul nosar ve-tamei*. These statuses apply even though the meat of an *olah* may not be eaten; the *korban* is fit for the *mizbe'ach*, and that suffices.

Regarding *me'ilah*, there is one significant change after *zerikah*: *ve-ein mo'alin ba-oros* — there is no *me'ilah* on the hide. The *kohanim* receive the hide of the *olah*, as it does not get burned. Thus *zerikah* removes the hide from *me'ilah*. But the meat — *aval mo'alin ba-basar* — remains under *me'ilah* because even after *zerikah*, the meat of an *olah* is destined for the *mizbe'ach* and may not be used by anyone. *Me'ilah* on the meat continues *ad she-yetzei l'veit ha-deshen* — until the ashes are carried outside the camp. The hide is the sole dimension of an *olah* where *zerikah* produces a *me'ilah* status change.

### Burned Offerings

*Parim hanisrafim* and *se'irim hanisrafim* — the bulls and goats that are burned — are those special *korbanos* whose blood is brought inside the *Heichal*, into the innermost sanctuary, and whose carcasses are burned outside the camp entirely. The paradigmatic example is *Yom Kippur*; another case is *par he-elem davar shel tzibbur*. Since nobody ever benefits from these offerings — they are never eaten and not burned on the *mizbe'ach* itself — they resemble an *olah* in that *me'ilah* never diminishes. *Me'ilah* begins from sanctification. After *shechitah*, the animals are *huchsharu l'hipasel bitvul yom uvimechusar kippurim uvlinah*. After *zerikas hadam*, *chayavin aleihem mishum piggul nosar ve-tamei* — the statuses of *piggul*, *nosar*, and *tamei* all apply. This is striking: even for offerings that are never eaten and are burned outside the camp, one can only be *chayav* for *piggul*, *nosar*, and *tamei* once *zerikas hadam* has rendered the *korban* valid. The onset of these statuses is always tied to the *kashrut* of the *korban*, not to the edibility of the meat.

*Mo'alin bahem be-veit ha-deshen* — even in the *beis ha-deshen*, the place outside the camp where they are burned, there remains *me'ilah*. This is because these *korbanos* begin their process outside the camp — they are burned there, not on the *mizbe'ach*. The *mitzvah* is not complete until the meat has fully dissolved: *ad she-yitach ha-basar*, which *Rashi* explains means until it becomes ash — *she-na'aseh eifer*. In a sense this is the symmetrical counterpart of the regular *olah*: the *olah* is burned on the *mizbe'ach* and its *me'ilah* ends when the ashes are taken outside; the *parim hanisrafim* begin outside and their *me'ilah* ends when they turn to ash there. Both conditions — ashes and the appropriate location — are required for *me'ilah* to cease, though the logical structure is inverse.

### Chatas & Asham

The *mishnah* now addresses *chatas*, *asham*, and *zivchei shalmei tzibbur* — all *kodshei kodashim* that are eaten rather than entirely burned. *Zivchei shalmei tzibbur* refers primarily to the communal *shelamim* brought on *Shavuos*. These are like the *olah* in being *kodshei kodashim*, but unlike the *olah* their meat is eaten by the *kohanim*. *Me'ilah* begins from sanctification. After *shechitah*, *huchsharu l'hipasel bitvul yom uvimechusar kippurim uvlinah*. After *nizrak daman* — *zerikas hadam* — the *korban* is valid: *chayavin alav mishum piggul nosar ve-tamei*. And now, *ve-ein mo'alin ba-basar* — there is no *me'ilah* on the meat, because *zerikah* renders the meat permissible to the *kohanim*. However, *aval mo'alin be-eimureihem* — there remains *me'ilah* on the *emurim*, the portions designated for the *mizbe'ach*, such as the fats and specified organs. These retain *me'ilah* status *ad she-yeitzu l'veit ha-deshen* — until the ashes of those portions are taken outside. The pattern is now established: *zerikah* removes *me'ilah* from the meat of *kodshei kodashim* that may be eaten, but the *emurim* that go onto the *mizbe'ach* remain subject to *me'ilah* until they are burnt and their ashes removed.

## Bread & Menachos

### Shtei Halechem

The *mishnah* now turns to offerings that are not animal *korbanos*: *shtei halechem*, the two loaves of bread brought on *Shavuos* together with the communal *shelamim*. *Mo'alin bahen mishehukdeshu* — *me'ilah* applies from the moment the dough or flour is sanctified. The parallel to *shechitah* — the moment that renders the animal susceptible to *tumah* — is the baking. Specifically: *kadshu ba-tanur huchsharu l'hipasel bitvul yom uvimechusar kippurim* — once the loaves achieve a crust in the oven, they become susceptible to disqualification through a *tvul yom* or *mechusar kippurim*.

Note that *linah* is not mentioned here, since *linah* pertains to blood, which is irrelevant for bread. Equally notable is the absence of *linah* as a concern intrinsic to these loaves themselves: the *shtei halechem* was eaten two to three days after it was made, and the *lechem hapanim* was made on *Erev Shabbos* and eaten the following *Shabbos* — a span of nine days. The concept of *linah* would be quite foreign to these *korbanos*, since they are naturally expected to remain for extended periods from baking until consumption.

The reason susceptibility to *tumah* requires the crust stage is conceptually significant. Although the dough is sanctified from the outset, the *kedushah* at that stage is more in the nature of *kedushas damim* — a sanctity of monetary value — rather than *kedushas haguf*, the intrinsic sanctity of the object that will serve as the actual *korban*. Until the dough achieves a crust and becomes bread — *ad she-kramu paneha ba-tanur* — it is not yet the thing that will be the *shtei halechem*. *Kedushas haguf* is only achieved once it is actual bread fit to serve as the offering, and it is that elevated *kedushah* that enables susceptibility to even the residual *tumah* of a *tvul yom*.

Once the loaves have a crust and have reached the status of actual bread, *lishchoto aleiha et ha-zevach* — it is now possible to slaughter the *korban* for the sake of the bread. The lambs brought with the *shtei halechem* on *Shavuos* must be slaughtered in conjunction with the bread; if the bread is not yet bread, the *shechitah* cannot be performed in relation to it. Once *nizrak daman shel kvasim* — the blood of the lambs is thrown — the bread's status is linked to the *korban* and changes accordingly: *chayavin aleihem mishum piggul nosar ve-tamei*. One is *chayav* for *piggul* if the *korban* was *piggul*, for *nosar* if the bread was left beyond the allotted time, and for *tamei* if one ate it in a state of *tumah*. *Ve-ein bahem meila* — there is no *me'ilah* on the bread, because after *zerikas hadam* it is fit to be eaten by the *kohanim*.

### Lechem Hapanim

*Lechem hapanim* — the showbread — follows a parallel structure. *Mo'alin bo mishehukdshah* — *me'ilah* from the time of sanctification. *Kramu ba-tanur* — once the loaves have a crust in the oven, *huchsharu l'hipasel bitvul yom uvimechusar kippurim* — susceptibility to disqualification follows. The absence of *linah* in this *mishnah* is even more pronounced: the *lechem hapanim* was placed on the *shulchan* on *Shabbos* and eaten the following *Shabbos*, nine days later. Once the loaves have achieved the crust stage, they are now fit to be arranged on the *shulchan* — *u-le-hasdir al gabei ha-shulchan*. The parallel to the *shtei halechem*'s *shechitah* is here the offering of the *bazichim* — the small ladles of *levonah*, the frankincense. *Karvu ha-bazichim* — when the *bazichim* are offered on the *mizbe'ach*, that is the act which renders the *lechem hapanim* fit to be eaten. After the *bazichim*: *chayavin alav mishum piggul nosar ve-tamei*, and *ve-ein bo meila* — there is no *me'ilah*, since the bread is now permissible for the *kohanim* to eat.

### Menachos

A standard *mincha* follows a similar but distinct structure. *Mo'alin bah mishehukdshah* — *me'ilah* from sanctification. The pivotal moment for susceptibility to *tumah* is not baking but rather placement in the *kli shares*: *kidshu be-kli, huchsharu l'hipasel bitvul yom uvimechusar kippurim uvlinah*. Here *linah* is reintroduced, because once the *mincha* has been placed in the *kli shares*, it must be offered that same day; if left until the next morning, it is *pasul be-linah*. This is the operative *linah* clock for the *mincha* — the *kli shares* placement starts it.

The *kedushah* dimension here is likewise conceptually layered. A *mincha* is dough, which can contract *tumah* in ordinary circumstances. But *kedushas haguf* — the intrinsic *kedushah* that enables susceptibility to the residual *tumah* of a *tvul yom* and *mechusar kippurim* — is not achieved merely by sanctification. By an animal *korban*, *kedushas haguf* was present from sanctification but the animal still required *shechitah* to become susceptible. By the bread offerings, *kedushas haguf* for purposes of *tumah* required the crust stage. By the *mincha*, *kedushas haguf* is achieved through placement in the *kli shares*, which is when the *mincha* is formally designated as the thing that will be offered.

Once the *komatz* is offered — *karav ha-komatz* — the *korban* is valid: *chayavin lo mishum piggul nosar ve-tamei*. *Ve-ein mo'alin ba-shirayim* — there is no *me'ilah* on the remainder, the *shirayim*, which is eaten by the *kohanim*. *Aval mo'alin ba-komatz* — the *komatz* which is burned on the *mizbe'ach* retains *me'ilah ad she-tetzei l'veit ha-deshen*, until the ashes are taken outside, following the same principle as all things burned on the *mizbe'ach*.

## Me'ilah Ending

### Trumat Hadeshen

The *Gemara* now opens an explicit discussion about when exactly *me'ilah* ceases for ashes on the *mizbe'ach*. On the *mizbe'ach* there would accumulate over time a large mound of ashes, called the *tapuach* — literally "apple," referring to the dome-like shape of the mound. Each morning the *kohen* would perform *trumat ha-deshen*, the symbolic removal of a small portion of ashes, placing them at the side of the *mizbe'ach*. Only periodically, when the mound grew large enough to require actual cleaning, would the ashes be fully removed and carried outside the camp to the *beis ha-deshen*. The *Gemara* asks: *hanehene mi-eifer tapuach she-al gabei ha-mizbe'ach* — one who derived benefit from the ashes in the mound — is there *me'ilah*?

*Lifnei trumat ha-deshen* — before the morning *trumat ha-deshen* is performed — *kulei alma lo peligi de-mo'alin bo* — everyone agrees there is *me'ilah*. The ashes have not yet had *trumat ha-deshen* performed to them; *na'aseis mitzvato* has not occurred, and the *mitzvah* of *trumat ha-deshen* conceptually applies to the ashes every morning. So before that morning *mitzvah* is discharged, the ashes remain fully within *me'ilah*.

### Rav Position

The dispute concerns the period *le-achar trumat ha-deshen* — after the morning *trumat ha-deshen* has been performed. *Rav amar ein mo'alin bo* — *Rav* holds that once *trumat ha-deshen* is done, there is no longer *me'ilah*. The reasoning: *harei na'aseis mitzvato* — the last *mitzvah* that pertains to these ashes has been completed. The subsequent removal of the ash mound to the *beis ha-deshen* is merely maintenance and cleanup, not a *mitzvah* in the halachic sense. Once the *mitzvah* is done, *me'ilah* ceases.

### R. Yochanan

*Rabbi Yochanan amar mo'alin bo* — *Rabbi Yochanan* holds that *me'ilah* continues even after *trumat ha-deshen*. He derives this from the verse (Vayikra 6): *ve-lavash ha-kohen mido vad u-michnesei vad yilbash al besaro ve-herim et ha-deshen... ve-lavash begadim acherim ve-hotzi et ha-deshen el mi-chutz la-machaneh*. The verse indicates that the *kohen* changes into different garments (*begadim acherim*) to carry the ashes outside. *Rabbi Yochanan* understands *begadim acherim* to mean a different set of *bigdei kehunah* — priestly vestments of lesser expense but still formal priestly garb. *Keivan d'tzarich bigdei kehunah bi-kdusheih kai* — since the act of removing the ashes requires *bigdei kehunah*, it constitutes an *avodah*, a formal Temple service, not mere cleanup. So long as this *avodah* remains uncompleted — so long as the ashes have not actually been brought outside — the ash retains its *kedushah* and *me'ilah* continues.

### Mishna Support

The *Gemara* notes that our *mishnah* appears to support *Rabbi Yochanan* clearly: *mo'alin bahen ad she-tetzei l'veit ha-deshen* — *me'ilah* continues until the ashes go out to the *beis ha-deshen*. This is a direct challenge to *Rav*. The *Gemara* resolves: *amar lach Rav* — *Rav* would explain the *mishnah* as: *ad she-tehei re'uyah l'veit ha-deshen* — until the ashes are *fit* to be taken out to the *beis ha-deshen*. That fitness is achieved once *trumat ha-deshen* is performed, because after *trumat ha-deshen* the ashes are now in a state where they may be removed. The *mishnah*'s language of *going out* is thus read not as requiring actual removal, but as requiring that the ashes have reached the stage at which removal is halachically appropriate. This is analogous to the principle sometimes applied in *zerikah*: *ad she-tehei re'uyah li-zerikah* — until it is *fit for zerikah* — rather than until *zerikah* is actually performed. On this reading, *Rav* maintains that *me'ilah* ends once the ashes are *eligible* for removal following *trumat ha-deshen*, while *Rabbi Yochanan* holds that *me'ilah* continues until the ashes are actually removed and carried outside the camp. The *shiur* will continue with this dispute and the fuller analysis of when *me'ilah* concludes in the case of ashes and the *beis ha-deshen*.

---

---

# Meilah 9

## Rav vs. R. Yochanan

### Machlokes Overview

The daf opens with a fundamental *machlokes* between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan concerning the law of *me'ilah* — the prohibition against deriving benefit from consecrated property — as it applies to the ashes of burnt offerings. The simple reading of the Mishnah is that *me'ilah* applies to things burnt on the *mizbeiach* until they are taken out to the *beis hadeshen*, since until that point the *mitzvah* has not yet been fully completed. However, Rav holds that once *terumas hadeshen* — the symbolic morning scooping of ash — has been performed, *me'ilah* no longer applies. Rabbi Yochanan emphasizes the importance not only of the original *terumas hadeshen* but also of the *hotza'at hadeshen*, the full removal of ashes to the area outside the *mikdash*, which is itself an *avodah* performed in *bigdei kehunah*. According to Rabbi Yochanan, until that final stage is completed, the *mitzvah* is not yet finished and *me'ilah* therefore remains in force.

### Zevachim Mishnah

The Gemara opens with a *meiseiv* — a challenge — from a Mishnah in Zevachim. The Mishnah states: *vechulan shepaku mei'agabi hamizbeiach lo yachazir* — if various items fell off the *mizbeiach*, they are not returned. This general rule extends to the case of a *gachelet*, a burning coal: *vechan gacheles shepaku mei'agabi hamizbeiach lo yachazir* — a coal that fell off the *mizbeiach* is not put back. As Rashi notes, this refers not to the burnt innards of a *korban* but to ordinary firewood that has turned into charcoal.

The Mishnah continues: *ha'agabi mizbeiach yachazir* — if, however, the coal was still on the *mizbeiach* and merely moved from the fire to another spot on the *mizbeiach* where there was no fire, it is returned to the fire. The question this raises is: why would one bother returning a coal that has already turned to ash and over which *terumas hadeshen* has presumably already been performed? The very act of returning it suggests that the *mitzvah* has not yet been completed.

The layout of the *mizbeiach* is relevant here. There was a large *ma'aracha gedola* — the main fire — along with a secondary fire (*ma'aracha sheniya*) for the *ketoret*, and a central pile of ashes. Rashi's approach to establishing that we are dealing with a situation after *terumas hadeshen* is somewhat complicated, and his reading depends on identifying the ash in question as coming from the central mound. This is because items actively turning to coal on the main fire would be obviously subject to *me'ilah*, as *terumas hadeshen* would not yet have been done. Rashi therefore establishes that we are dealing with a coal drawn from the central ashes — material over which *terumas hadeshen* has already been performed.

### Coal vs. Ash

The Gemara now applies this Mishnah to the debate. According to Rabbi Yochanan, the ruling is straightforward: even after *terumas hadeshen*, there are still specific *mitzvot* to be performed — namely, *hotza'at hadeshen* — and therefore one would naturally ensure that items are properly situated. However, for Rav, who holds that *me'ilah* ends at *terumas hadeshen*, the question becomes sharp: *ela leRav kashya* — why should it matter at all whether the coal is returned to the fire? Once *terumas hadeshen* has been done, Rav holds the *mitzvah* is complete; the coal's location would seem irrelevant.

The Gemara answers on Rav's behalf: *lo, shani gachelet d'it bah mashasha* — a coal is different because it still has substance. Rav's position is that *me'ilah* ends when the material has fully become ash. A *gachelet* — a burning coal — still has burning left to do; it has not yet become pure ash. Therefore, even according to Rav, it has not yet reached the stage of *na'aseh mitzvaso* and must be returned to the fire so that it can complete its combustion and become ash.

An alternative version of the argument presents the inference in the opposite direction: the only reason the ruling mentions returning the coal at all is precisely because it still has substance — *ta'ama mishum gachelet d'it bah mashasha* — but pure ash that has no further substance would not be returned even if it remained on the *mizbeiach*. This formulation presents the ruling as evidence for Rav's position: only a *gachelet* matters, not already-complete ash.

### R. Yochanan's Reply

Rabbi Yochanan, faced with the inference that favors Rav, responds: *hu hadin d'afilu efer* — the same rule would apply even to ash; the Mishnah chose to speak of a coal not to exclude ash but to teach that even something still possessing substance and still capable of further burning — a *gachelet* — does not need to be returned once it has fallen off the *mizbeiach*. The coal case thus represents the stringent end of the spectrum: if even a coal need not be returned once it has fallen off, certainly ash need not be. This formulation resolves the challenge by interpreting the Mishnah's case as extending, rather than limiting, the category of what is left off the *mizbeiach*. It remains somewhat unclear why falling off the *mizbeiach* should categorically remove the obligation to return an otherwise valid item, but the Gemara does not press this point further, accepting it as a given.

### Tosafot on Terumas

A deeper conceptual question underlies the entire discussion: what exactly does it mean that there is still a *mitzvah* of *terumas hadeshen* to be performed on these ashes? Since *terumas hadeshen* can be performed using any of the ashes and does not require these particular ashes specifically, in what sense is the *mitzvah* "their" *mitzvah*?

The approach offered previously was that these ashes must at minimum be part of the pile from which *terumas hadeshen* is taken, and therefore retain a connection to the *mitzvah* so long as they remain in that pile. Tosafot, however, frames it differently. According to Tosafot, the relevant criterion is not whether *terumas hadeshen* has been performed, but whether the ashes are in a position where they have the *potential* to be used for *terumas hadeshen*. When the coal or ash moves to some part of the *mizbeiach* where the ashes are not normally gathered for *terumas hadeshen*, it is no longer in a position where that *mitzvah* can be applied to it. Therefore, it is not in a state of *na'aseh mitzvaso* — but paradoxically, because the *mitzvah* can no longer be performed on it in its current location, one must move it back. According to Rav, this reasoning applies as long as the item is still a *gachelet* with substance; once it is pure ash it is considered complete. According to Rabbi Yochanan, the *mitzvah* of *hotza'at hadeshen* remains to be done regardless, so the coal or ash retains its significance until that final stage.

---

## Me'ilah Restitution

### Benefit Before/After

The Gemara now pivots to a different but related question: when one has committed *me'ilah* from a *korban*, not by stealing its monetary value but by deriving personal *hana'ah* from the animal itself — what does restitution look like? If I took money set aside for a *korban*, I simply return the money plus the added fifth. But if the *korban* was already an animal and I rode on it, or benefited from the part designated for the *mizbeiach*, to what do I owe restitution and how do I make it?

The Gemara introduces two categories: one who derived benefit from the meat of *kodshei kodashim* before *zerikat dam*, and one who derived benefit from the *imurin* — the designated altar portions — of *kodshim kalim* after *zerikat dam*. In both cases, the person has benefited from something that was wholly destined for the *mizbeiach* or otherwise unavailable for human use, and the question is how to restore it.

### Rav: Olat Nedavah

Rav rules: *mah she'neheneh yipelu lindavah* — the monetary value of what one benefited from is contributed toward a communal *nedavah*, that is, an *olat tzibur*, a communal burnt offering. This is an approximation: the *olah* goes entirely on the *mizbeiach*, and so it serves as the closest substitute for what was taken, which was also destined for the altar.

### Levi: Ketoret

Levi goes further. He holds: *yavi davar shekulo lamizbeach* — one should bring something that goes *entirely* onto the *mizbeiach*. An *olah* does not fully qualify, because the skin (*or*) remains and is not consumed on the altar. What is entirely consumed? The *ketoret* — the incense offering. A *baraita* cited in support of Levi states: *yavi davar shekulo lamizbeach* — bring something that is entirely for the altar — and identifies this as the *minchat kohanim*, which is fully burnt. The *halomedin lifnei chachamim*, identified in a Gemara in Sanhedrin as Levi who would study before Rebbe, said: bring *ketoret*, since the incense is entirely consumed. Since the *kohanim* must actually perform the bringing of *ketoret*, one does not bring it personally but rather contributes the funds to the *tzibur* for that purpose.

Tosafot notes a difficulty: if this phrase (*halomedin lifnei chachamim*) refers to Levi, it is unusual that this appears as a *tanya kevasai d'Levi* — as though a *baraita* is confirming Levi's view — when it would simply be Levi himself speaking. Moreover, Levi is a post-Tannaitic figure and never appears in the Mishnah or standard *beraitot*. Tosafot therefore concludes that the phrase refers to someone else, though his precise identity remains uncertain.

An important conceptual point: while the idea of substituting an entirely-altar offering makes obvious sense for the case of the *imurei kodshim kalim* — which were themselves destined entirely for the altar — it is a significant *chiddush* that the same restitution applies to *basar kodshei kodashim*, the meat of *kodshei kodashim*, which would never have gone onto the *mizbeiach* at all but would have been eaten by *kohanim*. Nevertheless, since it cannot be restored in kind, the best available substitute is an offering that is entirely consumed.

### Money Restitution

The Gemara now takes up the case where what was misappropriated was not the animal itself but money designated for a *korban*. The cases of *chatat* and *asham* money are addressed. If one benefited from money designated for a *chatat* and the *chatat* has not yet been purchased, one simply adds the fifth and uses the combined sum to purchase the *chatat*: *yosif veyavi chatato*. Similarly for *asham* money: *yosif veyavi ashamo*.

The more complex case arises when the *chatat* has already been brought. If one became aware of the misappropriation before the *chatat* was offered, then at that moment an obligation to set aside restitution funds crystallized. Subsequently, a *chatat* was brought — but not from this person's funds. The restitution money now resembles a *chatat she'niskapru ba'aleha be'acher* — a *chatat* whose owners were atoned for by means of another offering. The *halacha* for such a *chatat* is that it must die. By analogy, the money goes to *yam hamelach*: *yolich l'yam hamelach* — it is cast into the Dead Sea.

If, however, the *asham* was brought and a second one exists, the second becomes an *olah*. Therefore, if benefit was derived from *asham* money and the *asham* was subsequently brought: *yipelu lindavah* — the money goes toward a communal *olah*.

### Restitution Principles

The Mishnah then articulates the overarching principles: *kol korbonos hamizbeach l'mizbeach* — whatever was taken from something destined for the altar goes back to the altar; *korbonos bedek habayis l'bedek habayis* — what was taken from Temple treasury funds is restored to the Temple treasury; *korbonos tzibur lindvas tzibur* — what was taken from a communal offering is restored as a communal *nedavah*, that is, as a burnt offering.

This last principle overlaps with Rav's ruling from earlier. The Mishnah states that whatever one derived benefit from a *korban* — including *basar kodshei kodashim* which would never have gone on the altar — is restored through an *olat nedavah*. This is stated without qualification: *lo shena d'ikaper ba'aleha v'lo shena d'lo ikaper* — it does not matter whether the original *korban* was brought or not.

### Contradiction

This creates an apparent internal contradiction in the sources. The earlier ruling said that if the *chatat* was brought before the person became aware, the money is thrown into the Dead Sea. The Mishnah's general principle says that whenever one derives benefit from a *korban*, the money goes to a *nedavah* — with no qualification regarding whether the original *korban* was brought. Why then, in the *chatat* case, do we throw the money into the Dead Sea?

### Rav Gbiha: Reisha/Seifa

The Gemara resolves this by noting that the *reisha* and *seifa* represent two different opinions. The *reisha* — which prescribes casting the money into the Dead Sea — follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that any *chatat* whose owners have been atoned for by means of another offering must die. Applied to the money, this means the funds take on the character of such a *chatat* and must be disposed of accordingly. The *seifa* — which directs that the money go toward a communal *olah* — follows the Rabbis, who hold that a *chatat* in such circumstances is brought as an *olah* rather than destroyed. Thus, the two rulings do not contradict each other; they represent the positions of Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis respectively.

Rav Gbiha from Bei Katil reports to Rav Ashi that Abaye said the same: *reisha* Rabbi Shimon, *seifa* Rabbanan.

---

## Status Changes

### Tamei After Zerikat

Rava now makes a broad statement: everyone agrees that if one derived benefit from the meat of *kodshei kodashim* that became *tamei*, or from *imurei kodshim kalim* after they were placed on the fire (*she'he'elam*), one is exempt from *me'ilah*. The Gemara responds: *peshita* — this is obvious. But this response is surprising, because at least one of these cases is far from obvious.

Consider the meat of *kodshei kodashim* that became *tamei*. If *zerikah* was performed while the meat was already *tamei*, our very first Mishnah in this tractate established that *me'ilah* still applies — the *zerikah* was not *matir* because the meat was *pasul*. So why does Rava say everyone agrees there is no *me'ilah*? And for the *imurei kodshim kalim* that are already burning on the *mizbeiach* but have not yet turned to ash, the discussion about *na'aseh mitzvaso* would suggest the *mitzvah* is not yet complete. Why would everyone agree there is no *me'ilah*?

### Tosafot on Status

Rashi (or Pseudo-Rashi) reads Rava's statement as discussing the case of *basar kodshei kodashim* that became *tamei* before *zerikah* — and understands it as a variant of Rabbi Akiva's principle that once *zerikah* has occurred, even with a *pasul* situation, there is no *me'ilah* on the meat. However, Tosafot strongly disputes this reading. Tosafot argues that Rabbi Akiva's ruling was stated specifically for the case of *yotzei* — an animal that left the *azarah* — and was never extended to other *pesulim*. Moreover, the Gemara would never have said *peshita* with respect to such a reading of Rava.

Tosafot therefore understands Rava as discussing the case where the meat became *tamei* after *zerikat hadam*. Here the reasoning is cleaner: once *zerikah* is performed validly, the meat is released to the *kohanim* for eating, at which point it exits the category of *kodshei Hashem*. If it then becomes *tamei*, there is indeed a *mitzvah* of *srefah* — it must be burned — but that obligation does not draw the meat back into the realm of *me'ilah*. Something can be *assur* without being subject to *me'ilah*: *kodshim kalim* meat, for instance, is forbidden before *zerikah* yet carries no *me'ilah*.

The *chiddush* then lies in the second case: *imurei kodshim kalim* that were placed on the altar fire. One might have thought that since the *mitzvah* requires the *imurim* to be fully consumed — there is a *mitzvah lehapuchei betzinora*, to turn them over and ensure they burn completely — the *mitzvah* is not yet *na'aseh* until they become ash, and therefore *me'ilah* still applies. Rava teaches that this is not so — once placed on the fire and burning, both Rav and Rabbi Yochanan agree that *me'ilah* is gone.

### Gemara Consensus

The Gemara explains: *mahu de-teima*, one might have thought that since *basar kodshei kodashim she'nitma ais lei mitzvat srefah l'kohanim* — there is still a *mitzvah* of burning — and *emurei kodshim kalim ika mitzvah le'hapuchei betzinora* — there is still a *mitzvah* to turn them over on the fire — one would say the *mitzvah* is not complete and *me'ilah* remains. Rava therefore teaches that in both cases, everyone agrees there is no *me'ilah*. The Gemara's *peshita* is directed at the idea that once the meat has exited *kedushat Hashem*, even residual obligations do not bring it back into *me'ilah*; the *chiddush* is that the same applies to *imurei kodshim kalim* on the altar fire.

### Kedusha Levels

This leads to a broader conceptual question: why is it that *kodshim kalim* carry no *me'ilah* on their meat at all, even before *zerikah*, when the meat is clearly forbidden? The answer lies in the nature of the consecration. *Kodshei kodashim* are conceived as *kulo la-Hashem* — entirely for Heaven — so that even the portions eaten by *kohanim* are, as it were, *mishulchan gavoah*, from the table of the Most High. The entire animal, conceptually, belongs to Heaven, and therefore *me'ilah* applies throughout. *Kodshim kalim*, by contrast, are not conceived as *kulo la-Hashem* from the outset. The animal itself is partially the owner's, and only after *zerikah* do the *imurim* crystallize as belonging wholly to the *mizbeiach*, triggering *me'ilah* on them.

This difference in the underlying level of *kedushah* explains a further point: why, once *imurei kodshim kalim* begin burning on the *mizbeiach*, do both Rav and Rabbi Yochanan agree there is no *me'ilah*, even though they dispute whether *na'aseh mitzvaso* requires the ashes to be removed for the case of the burnt *olah*? Tosafot suggests an additional explanation: the *mitzvah* of *terumas hadeshen* and *hotza'at hadeshen* — with their attendant *na'aseh mitzvaso* implications — may be derived from *pesukim* that speak specifically about the *olah*, and therefore may not apply at all to *kodshim kalim*. If so, once the *imurim* of *kodshim kalim* begin burning, there is no remaining *mitzvah* whose non-completion would keep *me'ilah* in force.

---

## Me'ilah Restitution (II)

### Rava: Timing of Awareness

Returning to the contradiction between throwing money into the Dead Sea and bringing an *olah*, Rava offers a precise resolution. The rule of *yolich l'yam hamelach* — casting the money into the Dead Sea — applies only when the person became aware of the misappropriation before the *chatat* was brought (*d'ishtemoda lei kammai kapara*). In that case, at the moment of awareness, the obligation to set aside *chatat* funds crystallized. Since that virtual *chatat* existed, when a different *chatat* was subsequently brought, the money took on the status of *chatat she'niskapru ba'aleha be'acher*, and must be disposed of accordingly.

However, if the person became aware only after the *chatat* was already brought (*l'achar kapara*), then there is no *me'ilah* obligation of the ים המלח variety. The Gemara states: *ein mafrishin l'chatchilah l'ibud* — one does not set aside funds with the aim of throwing them away. Since at the moment of awareness there was already no *chatat* that could be brought — the atonement had already been accomplished by other means — the money never assumed the character of a *chatat* awaiting a parallel. Therefore the funds go toward a communal *olah* rather than being cast into the Dead Sea.

The deeper principle is that the status of *chatat she'niskapru ba'aleha be'acher* requires that the displaced *chatat* virtually existed in advance of the original offering. If the obligation only came into being after the original offering, no such status can be created retroactively.

This resolution also illuminates the broader contradiction between the two models of restitution — give back an *olah* versus give back what you took. When what was misappropriated was money, there is scope for saying "restore what you took" — meaning replace the *chatat* money with *chatat* money — and then, if circumstances change, apply the rules that govern *chatat* funds. But when one derived *hana'ah* directly from the *korban* itself, the animal is still there; there is no concept of "giving back a *chatat*" because the *chatat* exists as a physical reality. In that case, both opinions agree the restitution takes the form of an *olah* — or, according to Levi, something even more fully consumed — which is *kulo lamizbeach*. The principle of giving back what was taken ultimately resolves, in almost every scenario, to bringing an *olah*, since that is the only substitute that adequately replaces what was designated for the altar.

---

## Matirin Rule

### Fully Burned Items

The Mishnah now opens a new chapter and introduces a distinct set of cases: the *kometz* and *levonah* separated from a *minchah*, the *ketoret* brought daily, the *minchat kohanim*, and the *minchat kohen mashiach*, as well as *minchat nesachim* — the flour component accompanying animal offerings. All of these share a common feature: they are entirely consumed on the *mizbeiach*, with nothing remaining for human consumption. The Mishnah states that *me'ilah* applies to these items from the moment of their consecration.

### Three Stages

The Mishnah then identifies a second stage of *kedushah* for these items: *kiddeshan bikli* — once they are sanctified through placement in a sacred vessel, they achieve *kedushat haguf*. From this point, they are susceptible to *tumah* in even its more subtle forms (*tevel yom*, *mechusar kippurim*), and the prohibition of *linah* — overnight invalidation — begins to apply.

The standard structure of a *korban* has three stages: consecration, at which point *me'ilah* applies; the moment of *kedushat haguf* when *tumah* susceptibility and *linah* begin; and the moment the *matir* — the permitting act, typically *zerikat hadam* — is performed, after which *piggul*, *notar*, and *tumah* of eating apply to whatever remains. For items that are entirely consumed on the *mizbeiach*, there is no third stage distinct from the second, because there is no portion that is released for eating or other use after a *matir* is performed. Therefore the Mishnah states: *ve'chayavin aleihen mishum notar u'mishum tamei* — one is liable for *notar* and *tamei* — but *piggul ein bah* — there is no *piggul*.

### Matirin Principle

The Mishnah articulates the underlying rule that governs all of these cases: *kol she'yesh lo matirin* — anything that has a *matir*, meaning an act performed on the *mizbeiach* that releases the remainder of the *korban* for its intended use (such as *zerikat hadam* for most *korbanot*, or the burning of the *kometz* for a *minchah*) — *ein chayavin mishum piggul lo zeh velo zeh ad sheyikrev hamatir* — neither the offering nor the released portion becomes subject to *piggul* until the *matir* has been offered.

Conversely, *kol she'ein lo matirin* — anything that has no *matir*, meaning it goes directly onto the *mizbeiach* without a separate act releasing another portion — *kivan shekidesh bikli* — from the moment it is sanctified in the vessel — one is liable for *notar* and *tamei*, but *piggul ein bo* — there is no *piggul*. The reason there is no *piggul* in this class of cases is that *piggul* requires an act of *ritzuy* — an act that makes the offering valid and releases the remainder. Without a *matir*, there is no such act, no moment at which one could form an invalid intent that would render the offering *piggul*. Since *piggul* is defined by the concept of *lo yeratze* — the offering is not accepted because of a disqualifying intention during one of the service acts — it cannot apply where there are no such service acts that release a remainder.

### Asher Yikrav

The Gemara seeks to ground these principles in *pesukim*. The question arises: perhaps the prohibition of *tumah* — eating *kodashim* while *tamei* — applies only to things that have a *matir*, that is, normal *korbanot* with *zerikat hadam*? A *kal vachomer* supports this: *piggul*, which is the more severe prohibition (applying with only a single moment of awareness, carrying a fixed *korban*, and admitting no exceptions), applies only to things with a *matir*. Should not *tumah*, which is the lesser prohibition (requiring two moments of awareness, carrying an *olah v'yored*, and overridden for *tzibur*), certainly be restricted to the same class?

The Gemara responds by citing a *pasuk*: *emor aleihem ledoroteichem kol ish asher yikrav mikol zarechem* — you shall tell them for their generations that any person who approaches from all your offspring [who is *tamei* shall not approach the sacred things]. The phrase *kol asher yikrav* — all who approach — is understood as *bekhol hakodashim hakatuv medaber* — the *pasuk* speaks of all *kodashim*, even those without a *matir*. Therefore the prohibition of *tumah* applies across the board.

### Rabbi Eliezer

The Gemara then raises the converse question: perhaps *tumah* applies even before the *matir* is performed, for items that do have a *matir*? That is, if one eats the meat of a *korban* while *tamei* before *zerikat hadam*, perhaps one is liable? The Gemara cites *talmud lomar asher yikrav* — the same phrase *asher yikrav* — to teach that liability only begins after the act of *hakravah*, after the *matir* has been brought.

Rabbi Eliezer sharpens this derivation. He notes that the straightforward reading of the *pasuk* — "anyone who approaches the sacred things" — would seem to apply to one who merely *touches* the sacred item while *tamei*. But one is not liable for *kares* by touching *kodashim* while *tamei*; the *kares* applies to eating. Why then does the Torah use the language of *yikrav* — approaching — when speaking about the prohibition of eating *kodashim betumah*? To derive the following rule: *kol davar she'yesh lo matirin eino chayav ad sheyikrevu matirin* — for anything that has a *matir*, one is not liable unless and until the *matir* has been offered. And *kol davar she'ein lo matirin* — for anything without a *matir* — *eino chayav ad sheyikadesh bikli* — liability begins when it is sanctified in the vessel.

This is the organizing principle of the Mishnah. At sanctification, *me'ilah* begins. At *kedushat haguf* — for most *korbanot* this is *shechitah*, for these entirely-consumed items it is sanctification in the vessel — *tumah* susceptibility, *linah*, and related disqualifications begin. And when the *matir* is performed, *piggul*, *notar*, and the prohibition of eating *betumah* fully crystallize. For items without a *matir*, that final stage collapses into the second, and *piggul* never applies at all.

*Hadran lach Chatat Ha'of.*

---

---

# Meilah 11

## Intro: Kedusha & Meilah

### Prev. Perek Review

The previous *perek* dealt extensively with questions about the stages of *kedusha*: once something is sanctified, *me'ilah* applies, and different stages — such as placement into a *keli* or *zerikat hadam* — affect what additional statuses become relevant. The new *perek* turns to examine cases where there is no *me'ilah*, because the sanctified item is no longer fit for the *mizbeach*.

### Pigul & Status

Before proceeding to these cases, it is worth recalling a foundational principle established at the very opening of the *masekhet*: once something is sanctified, even if it subsequently becomes unfit — for instance, through a thought of *pigul* or because the meat becomes *tamei* — *me'ilah* still applies. Indeed, it may apply for a longer duration than usual, since a *korban* that has become *pasul* never becomes *muttar lakohanim* the way normal meat does — at least regarding *kodshei kodashim*. The fact that it is *pasul* does not remove it from the category of *me'ilah*. Until something becomes *muttar* for *achila*, it remains subject to *me'ilah*. With this in mind, one can appreciate the significance of the cases to follow, where the Mishnah teaches that *me'ilah* does *not* apply.

---

## Chatat Shemetah

### Three Cases

The Mishnah at the bottom of 10b, which opens the new *perek*, presents the classic cases of a *chatat* that must be left to die — *chatat shemetah* — because it can no longer fulfill its function of *kapara*. Three standard examples are given: *vlad chatat* (the offspring of a *chatat*, since a *chatat* was a female animal and its offspring cannot serve the function of *kapara*); *tmurat chatat* (the *tmurah* of a *chatat*, since only the original animal can function for *kapara*, not its substitute); and *chatat she'metu be'aleha* (a *chatat* whose owners have died, so there is no longer any relevant *kapara* to be achieved). In all three cases, the ruling is *yamutu* — the animal must be allowed to die.

### Avra Shnata

Two additional cases of *chatat shemetah* depend more on circumstances. The first is *she'avar shnata ve'avda* — the animal became more than a year old, or it was lost and subsequently found to have a *mum*. The second scenario specifies that if *mishekippru haba'alim tamut* — if the owners have already achieved atonement through another offering — then the animal must also die, falling into the category of *chatat shemetah*.

### Unconditional vs. Condit…

One might ask: what distinguishes *avar shnata* from *nitkapper be'acher*? The critical difference is that the first two categories — *vlad chatat* and *tmurat chatat* — are inherently and permanently unfit for *kapara*, and the death of the owners likewise forecloses any possibility of *kapara* entirely. These are unconditional cases. *Avar shnata*, by contrast, is more like a *mum*: there is simply a problem that prevents bringing the animal in its current state, but one could wait until the animal actually develops a *mum* and then be *podeh* — redeem it. Similarly, if the animal was lost and then found with a *mum*, one could have been *podeh* it if the owners had not yet brought another *korban*. These later cases, therefore, represent scenarios where there was a genuine possibility of eventual use that was foreclosed by the owners having gone ahead and brought another offering. In both instances — the one that aged past its year, and the one that was lost — the operative factor is that the owners subsequently achieved *kapara* elsewhere, *nitkapper be'acher*, and only then does the animal fall into the *shemetah* category.

### Tmurah & Meilah Remain

The Mishnah at the top of 11a specifies the converse: if the owners have not yet achieved *kapara* — *ad shelo kipperu haba'alim* — the advice is *teira'eh ad shetistave ve'timacher*: wait for the animal to develop a *mum*, sell it, and use the proceeds to purchase another *korban*. In those cases, since the *kedusha* could eventually transfer to another viable *korban*, the animal *osa tmurah u'mo'alin bah* — it retains the capacity to make a *tmurah*, and *me'ilah* continues to apply. It should be noted that *me'ilah* does not require *kedushat korban* specifically; *kedushat damim* — where the value will ultimately be transferred into a *korban* — also falls within *me'ilah*. What *me'ilah* cannot tolerate is an animal that is entirely and definitively headed for destruction.

### Kodshei Hashem Removal

This brings us to the fundamental reason underlying the entire discussion. By contrast, in the cases where *yamutu* applies unconditionally, the ruling is *ve'lo nehenin ve'lo mo'alin* — one may not derive benefit from the animal even rabbinically, and there is no *me'ilah*. Even a *korban* that has become *pasul* retains *me'ilah*; even *psulei hamukdashim* are treated with a certain sanctity within the framework of the *Beit HaMikdash*. But something that has been completely removed from the category of *kodshei Hashem* — condemned definitively to death with no possible redemptive use — exits the *me'ilah* framework entirely. As *Tosafot* on 12b puts it explicitly: *dekeivan de'azlei le'ibud lo shaikh behu me'ilah velo karinan behu kodshei Hashem* — since they are going to destruction, *me'ilah* is inapplicable and they are no longer called *kodshei Hashem*. The *mefareish* here notes that there may nevertheless be *me'ilah derabbanan* in such cases — but that question remains open for now. The principle is clear in either case: it is still rabbinically forbidden to derive benefit from such animals, even without *me'ilah*. One might ask what practical difference there is between a mere *issur derabbanan* of *hana'ah* and *me'ilah derabbanan*. Among the *nafka minot*: under *me'ilah*, even if there is no *korban* and no *chomesh*, one is at minimum required to restore the monetary value. Under a simple *issur hana'ah*, there is no such obligation.

### Gemara: Reisha vs. Seifa

The *Gemara*'s analysis of this *Mishnah* is brief and self-evident. It asks: *mai shna reisha de'lo kamaplig u'mai shna seifa de'kamaplig* — why does the first part list three cases without qualification, while the second part distinguishes based on whether *nitkapper be'acher* has occurred? The answer is that *reisha psika lei* — in the first three cases, there is simply no scenario where the circumstances could differ. *Vlad chatat* and *tmurat chatat* are never fit for *kapara* under any conditions; if the owners died, *nitkapper be'acher* becomes impossible. There is nothing to qualify. In the *seifa*, *lo psika lei* — the circumstances genuinely matter, and so the distinction must be spelled out.

### Meilah & Tmura Purposes

The *Gemara* then raises one further question: this same *Mishnah* appears in *Tmura* as well — why is it taught in both *masekhtot*? The answer is equally straightforward. The category of a *chatat* condemned to death carries two distinct *halachic* consequences: it cannot make a *tmurah*, and there is no *me'ilah*. *Tana hatam mishum tmurah* — it is taught there for the laws of *tmurah*; *tana hacha mishum me'ilah* — it is taught here for the laws of *me'ilah*.

One might wonder, as a practical matter, whether when the Mishnah advises waiting for the animal to develop a *mum* and then redeeming it, that represents the preferable course of action — since in the meantime the owners remain without *kapara*. The Mishnah does seem to present *teira'eh ad shetistave ve'timacher* as the prescribed path, implying that yes, waiting for the *mum* is indeed what one should do rather than immediately bringing another *korban*. This would mean the owner must continue without *kapara* while the animal waits, which is striking. It is a real tension the sources present without fully resolving.

---

## Nazirite Money

### Undetermined Money

The next *Mishnah* deals with a different category: *hamafrish ma'ot lineziruto* — one who sets aside a sum of money for his *nazir* offerings, without specifying which portion is designated for which of the three required *korbanot* (a *chatat*, an *olah*, and a *shelamim*). The ruling is *lo nehenin velo mo'alin* — one may not derive benefit, and if one does, there is no *me'ilah*.

### Shelamim Default Reason

Why is there no *me'ilah*? Because *mipnei she'hen re'uyin lavo kullan shelamim* — in principle, the entire sum could have been used for a *shelamim*. One might initially have expected that since some portion of the money would necessarily have been designated for an *olah* or a *chatat* — offerings for which there is *me'ilah* — there ought to be at least partial *me'ilah* on that money. But since the owner never specified the allocation, one cannot say that any particular portion was certainly designated for an *olah* or *chatat*. He could theoretically have used the entire sum for a *shelamim* and then separately obtained funds for the other offerings. And since by a *shelamim* there is no *me'ilah* until after *zerikat hadam* — specifically on the *imurin* — undesignated *shelamim* money also carries no *me'ilah*.

This reflects a larger conceptual principle, already developed in the earlier *perek*, that the category of *kodshei kalim* is fundamentally different from *kodshei kodashim*. The distinction is not merely practical — it is not simply about what you are permitted to use. It is conceptual: *kodshei kodashim* is fully *kodshei Hashem*; *kodshei kalim*, by contrast, is characterized by *kodashim kalim mammon ba'alim* — in some sense it remains the property of its owners. This is why, for example, *me'ilah* does not apply to the meat of a *shelamim* before *zerikat hadam* even though that meat is *assur* to eat before that point — just as it is *assur* to eat the meat of *kodshei kodashim* before *zerikat hadam*, yet *me'ilah* applies in the latter case even before *zerikat hadam*. The meat of *kodshei kodashim* is fully *kodshei Hashem* and therefore falls under *me'ilah* until it becomes *muttar*; the meat of *kodshei kalim* is not fully *kodshei Hashem* and therefore only the *imurin*, after they have been designated, fall under *me'ilah*. This same conceptual framework explains why money set aside for a *shelamim* — or money that could be applied to a *shelamim* — carries no *me'ilah*.

### Death Becomes Olah

If the *nazir* dies before completing his *nezirut*, and he had left behind a pile of undesignated money (*ma'ot stumin*) set aside for his *nazir* offerings, the ruling is *yipelu linedavah* — the entire sum is applied to an *olah*. The reasoning, one might understand conceptually, is that a *chatat* cannot be brought because the owner is deceased; the *shelamim* of a *nazir* is somewhat distinctive to the ritual conclusion of *nezirut* itself; whereas an *olah* is simply a generic *stam olah*, with nothing that uniquely ties it to the living *nazir*'s ritual. The money therefore defaults to an *olah*.

### Explicit Money Allocation

If, however, the *nazir* had designated his money explicitly — separate piles for his *chatat*, his *olah*, and his *shelamim* — and then died, each pile is treated according to its designation.

### Chatat Money Status

The money designated for the *chatat* — *demei chatat yolichu l'Yam HaMelach* — is destroyed, effectively analogous to a *chatat she'metu be'aleha*. The same ruling follows: *lo nehenin velo mo'alin* — no benefit, and no *me'ilah* — just as with the *chatat shemetah* discussed above.

### Olah Money Meilah

The money designated for the *olah* — *demei olah yavi'u olah* — is used to bring an *olah*. Unlike the *chatat* and *asham*, an *olah* does not require the specific atonement of its owner; sanctified property designated for an *olah* can be brought even after the owner's death. Consequently, *u'mo'alin bahen* — *me'ilah* applies to this money.

### Shelamim Post-Death

The most complex case is the money designated for the *shelamim*. In principle, a *shelamim* can be brought after its owner's death — unlike a *chatat* or *asham*, it does not require the owner to be present for *kapara*. So the ruling is *yavi'u shelamim* — a *shelamim* is brought. However, because this money was originally sanctified as the *shelamim* of a *nazir*, it retains a quasi-*shalmei nazir* character, resulting in a split *halakha*. On the one hand, *ne'echalin l'yom echad* — it is eaten only for one day, as befits *shalmei nazir*, rather than two days like an ordinary *shelamim*. On the other hand, *ve'ein te'unim lechem* — the bread accompanying *shalmei nazir* is not brought. The reason for this distinction is that the Torah specifies the bread is brought *al kapei hanazir* — on the hands of the *nazir* himself — making the bread intrinsically bound to the *nezirut* ritual and the living presence of the *nazir*. Without the *nazir*, and without the concluding rite of *nezirut*, there is no bread. Yet the *kedusha* of the *korban* itself is sufficient to impose the one-day eating restriction of *shalmei nazir*. It is a genuine split: quasi-*shalmei nazir* in some respects but not others.

### Reish Lakish Challenge

*Reish Lakish* challenges the earlier ruling regarding undesignated *nazir* money by asking: why does the *Mishnah* not teach similarly that one who designates money for *kinim* — bird offerings — incurs *lo nehenin velo mo'alin*, since the money could potentially be applied in a way that would involve a bird not presently fit for the *mizbeach*? This question leads directly into the next *Mishnah*'s discussion of birds.

---

## Bird Age Requirement (II)

### Tosafot: Young Bird Use

*Tosafot* reframes *Reish Lakish*'s challenge in a way that makes it more compelling. *Reish Lakish*'s question cannot simply mean that the money is unsubject to *me'ilah* because one could use it to buy an incorrectly aged bird — that would be an absurd argument, since one obviously should use the money correctly. Rather, *Tosafot* clarifies, *Reish Lakish* is asking specifically about the case of a *tor* that is too young. If one uses the money to buy a *tor she'lo higia zemano* — a dove that has not yet reached its proper age — one has not done anything wrong, because one could simply wait until the bird matures and then bring it. But at the moment of purchase, there would be no *me'ilah*, since a too-young *tor* itself has no *me'ilah*. So the question becomes: why not say that the undetermined *nazir* money also has no *me'ilah*, since it is at least possible that the money will be used to purchase a currently immature *tor* that will later become fit?

---

## Nazirite Money (II)

### Rava's Response

*Rava* responds: *amrah Torah bimostumin havei shelamim* — the Torah is entirely comfortable with all of the undesignated *nazir* money being used for a *shelamim*, but *amrah Torah hada* — does one really think the Torah intends for one to purchase birds that are *she'einam re'uyin lamizbeach*, not presently fit for the *mizbeach*? The point is that when one designates money for a *korban*, we assume that the money's status corresponds to its proper and immediate use. The money is designated to purchase something that can be offered right away, and consequently *me'ilah* applies to that money. There is an implicit assumption of immediate fitness, which forecloses the theoretical argument that the money might be used for an as-yet-immature bird.

---

## Bird Age Requirement (II)

### Tor vs. Benei Yonah

With that background, the *Mishnah* governing bird offerings can be appreciated. There are two types of bird *korbanot*: *torim* (doves), which must be adult, and *benei yonah* (young pigeons), which must be young. If one sanctified a *tor* that has not yet reached its proper age, or *benei yonah* that have passed their proper age, the ruling is *lo nehenin velo mo'alin* — no benefit and no *me'ilah*. One might have expected that, as with an animal that has a *mum*, there should still be *me'ilah* even if the bird cannot presently be used. Why do birds differ?

### No Pidyon for Birds

The answer is that there is no *pidyon* for birds — no possibility of redeeming them and transferring their *kedusha* to another animal or sum of money, even if the bird has a disqualifying defect or is a *mechusar zman*. Since there is no mechanism by which the *kedusha* can ever be realized or transferred, the situation of a wrong-aged bird is structurally identical to the *chatat shemetah*: it is *holekh le'ibud*, heading toward inevitable destruction, completely removed from the category of *kodshei Hashem*. Therefore *lo nehenin velo mo'alin*.

---

## Blood (Dam) Paradox

### Dam Initially No Meilah

*Rabbi Shimon* introduces a striking principle: *hadam kal bitchila ve'chamur besofo* — blood is more lenient at the outset and more strict at the end. Conversely, *nesachim chomer bitchilatan ve'kal besofo* — the wine libations are more strict at the outset and more lenient at the end. The case of the blood is genuinely startling. *Dam bitchilato ein mo'alin bo* — initially, before the blood has served its function on the *mizbeach*, there is no *me'ilah* by the blood. This is counterintuitive to the point of paradox: if anything seems to be *kulo laHashem*, it is the blood of the *korban*. How can there be no *me'ilah*?

### Dam Flow & Sale

After the blood is applied to the *mizbeach*, the excess blood on the floor was washed through drainage channels in the *Beit HaMikdash*, flowing out into the Kidron Valley. The Temple administration would then sell this blood to farmers for use as fertilizer — a practical arrangement for dealing with the large quantities of blood produced daily. The ruling in the *Mishnah* is that once this blood reaches the Kidron and is subject to sale, if one uses it without purchasing it from the Temple, *mo'alin bo* — there is *me'ilah*. This is paradoxical: before the blood served its purpose, there is no *me'ilah*; after it has done its job and flowed out to the Kidron, there is.

### Dam Derabbanan Meilah

One critical qualification, not made explicit in the *Gemara* here but clear from other sources, is that even when the *Mishnah* says *mo'alin bo* regarding blood in the Kidron, this *me'ilah* is only *derabbanan*. The reason is the principle of *na'aseit mitzvato* — once the blood fulfilled its function on the *mizbeach*, the mitzvah was completed, and it is a foundational rule that *ein lecha davar she'na'aseit mitzvato she'mo'alin bo*: nothing for which the mitzvah has been performed remains subject to *me'ilah*. Therefore the *me'ilah* in the Kidron can only be rabbinic. What makes the case of *dam* so extraordinary, then, is that before *zrikat hadam* — when the blood is at its most powerful ritual moment, about to achieve *kapara* — there is no *me'ilah* at all, not even *derabbanan*. After *na'aseit mitzvato*, there is rabbinic *me'ilah*. The pattern is the inverse of everything one would expect.

### Rabbi Meir vs. Chachamim

A *baraita* records a dispute directly on this point. *Rabbi Meir* holds *mo'alin bedamim* — there is *me'ilah* by blood. The *Chachamim* hold *ein mo'alin* — there is no *me'ilah*. The *Gemara* then presents three distinct explanations for the position of those who exempt blood from *me'ilah*.

### Ula: Service to Owner

*Ula* derives the exemption from a verse: the blood was given to you upon the *mizbeach* to atone — *lachem*, for you, meaning it is performing a service on your behalf.
