This somehow removes it from the category of *kodshei Hashem*, and consequently there is no *me'ilah*. This rationale is difficult to internalize. The entire concept of blood as *korban* seems to be the paradigm of something given wholly to God — the soul of the animal, as it were, offered entirely to the divine. Yet here the *pasuk* is read to say that its service is rendered to the benefit of the owner, and that very fact removes it from full *kodshei Hashem* status. The irony is difficult to fully resolve.

### R. Yishmael: Atonement P…

The school of *Rabbi Yishmael* offers a formulation that is conceptually somewhat clearer: *l'chaparah netativo velo lime'ilah* — I gave it for atonement, not for *me'ilah*. The *pasuk* is read as the Torah explicitly exempting blood from *me'ilah* because its entire purpose is to help the person achieve atonement. It is there to assist, not to cause additional stumbling through the prohibition of *me'ilah*. One might immediately ask: why not say the same about the entire *korban*? If the blood is exempt from *me'ilah* because it serves the owner's atonement, surely the meat and the *imurin* also serve the *kapara* process? The question does not receive a direct answer, and the tension remains unresolved.

### R. Yochanan: Blood Soul

*Rabbi Yochanan* derives the rule from a different verse: *ki hadam hu banefesh yichaper* — because the blood is the soul, and through it atonement is achieved. He reads *hadam hu* as establishing a single, unchanging status for blood: *lefnei kaparah k'le'achar kaparah* — blood has the same status before *kapara* as after *kapara*. Since after *kapara* there is clearly no *me'ilah* — because of *na'aseit mitzvato* — the same must apply before *kapara*. The *Gemara* considers the reverse: perhaps one should read *hu* in the other direction, establishing that just as before *kapara* there is *me'ilah* (as one might expect from any sanctified item), so too after *kapara* there should be *me'ilah*? The *Gemara* dismisses this: *veki yesh lecha davar she'na'aseit mitzvato veyesh bo me'ilah*? Is there anything for which the mitzvah has been completed and *me'ilah* still applies? This violates a clear and established principle, and so the *pasuk* must be read as exempting *me'ilah* before rather than imposing it after.

### Exceptions to Na'aseh

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this confident assertion that nothing once its mitzvah is completed retains *me'ilah*. *Harei trumat hadeshen* — the ashes removed in the daily *trumat hadeshen* ritual. The *kohen* takes a scoop of ashes from the *mizbeach*, carries them down the ramp, and places them at the side of the ramp — and yet *me'ilah* continues to apply to those ashes even after the ritual is complete. This is distinct from the question debated in the preceding days regarding whether ashes left on the *mizbeach* still have outstanding *mitzvot*. Here the question is about the specific ashes to which the *trumat hadeshen* act was performed: once the *kohen* has placed them by the *mizbeach*, the mitzvah is done — and yet *me'ilah* continues. The derivation is from the verse *ve'samo eitzel hamizbeach*: the word *samo* implies the ashes must remain there and preserve their state, from which we learn that their *kedusha* — and *me'ilah* — persists. So here is a genuine exception to the principle that *na'aseit mitzvato* eliminates *me'ilah*.

A second exception: the *se'ir hamishtalach* — the scapegoat sent over the cliff on *Yom Kippur*. Even after the goat has been hurled over and its body shattered, the limbs remain *assur behana'ah*, retaining their *kedusha* and *me'ilah* status despite the fact that *na'aseit mitzvato*.

### Two Exceptions Principle

The *Gemara* resolves the tension by invoking the principle of *shnei ketuvim haba'im ke'echad ein melamdim*: when two verses create exceptions to a general rule, those exceptions do not become the rule — they remain limited to the specific cases from which they are derived. *Trumat hadeshen* and *se'ir hamishtalach* are two exceptions; from two exceptions one does not generalize, and therefore *dam* cannot claim to be a third exception.

The *Gemara* further considers: what if one holds that the limbs of the *se'ir hamishtalach* are in fact *muttar* after it goes over the cliff — i.e., that *na'aseit mitzvato* does apply and there is no continued *issur*? In that case, there would be only one exception (*trumat hadeshen*), and one exception normally does become the rule. The *Gemara* responds that in that case, the *bigdei kehuna* of the *Kohen Gadol* after *Yom Kippur* supply the second exception: those garments, by virtue of *ve'hinicham sham* — "he shall place them there" — may never be used again (though *Rabbi Dosa* holds that an ordinary *kohen* may use them during the year). And if *Rabbi Dosa*'s view eliminates the *bigdei kehuna* example as well, the *Gemara* supplies yet another: the *egla arufa*, whose neck is broken in the ritual and which thereafter remains *assur behana'ah* despite *na'aseit mitzvato*. The *egla arufa* is technically not a *kodshim* case and carries no *me'ilah*, but it demonstrates the broader principle — applicable beyond *me'ilah* — that *na'aseit mitzvato* does not always produce a status change. This broader concept encompasses *issur hana'ah* generally, as seen for instance in *chametz* after *sereifah*, where once burned it becomes *muttar behana'ah*: *na'aseit mitzvato* changes the status, even outside the *me'ilah* framework.

It is worth pausing to note that the *Gemara* has not provided a fully direct answer to the original question. The question was how we know that *dam* is exempt from *me'ilah* before *kapara*, given that we compare before and after via *Rabbi Yochanan*'s reading of *hu*. The *Gemara* responded by establishing that *na'aseit mitzvato* always removes *me'ilah*, and that while there are exceptions, they cannot be generalized. But the underlying challenge remains: we are not asking to generalize the exceptions into a rule — we are asking merely why *dam* cannot be one additional exception. Saying there are no exceptions proves too much, and saying the exceptions cannot be generalized merely prevents *dam* from being treated as the norm. The *Gemara* proceeds on the working assumption that unless there is a specific derivation establishing a given item as an exception, it follows the general rule — and for *dam*, the general rule derived from *hu* is no *me'ilah* before *kapara*, while the anomalous rabbinic *me'ilah* after the blood flows to the Kidron is left without extended discussion, presumably because it was a well-known and practically common rabbinic enactment given the daily scale of the *Beit HaMikdash*'s operations.

---

## Nesachim (Wine)

### Wine: Start & End

The counterpart to *dam* is the *nesachim* — the wine libations. Here the pattern is the inverse: *nesachim bitchilatan mo'alin bahen* — initially there is *me'ilah* by the wine, since it is sanctified to be poured as a *korban*. *Yardu lashitin ein mo'alin bahen* — once the wine is poured down into the *shitin* (the channels and caverns within the *mizbeach*), there is no *me'ilah*. This is the standard application of *na'aseit mitzvato* — the mitzvah has been performed, and *me'ilah* ceases. There may still remain a question of *lo nehenin*, but there is certainly no *me'ilah*. The *nesachim* thus exemplify the normal *halachic* trajectory — *me'ilah* before, none after — while the *dam* exemplifies the paradoxical inverse.

### Lul & Wine Residue

The *Gemara* initially considers whether our *Mishnah* (which holds that there is no *me'ilah* after the wine is poured) is inconsistent with the opinion of *Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok*. The *baraita* records that *Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok* described a *lul katan* — a small duct or passage — situated between the ramp (*keves*) and the *mizbeach*, at the western end of the ramp. Once every seventy years, *pirchei kehuna* — young *kohanim*, small enough to fit into this narrow passage — would enter and extract *yayin karush*, congealed wine that had accumulated inside the hollow of the *mizbeach*, which he describes as resembling rounds of pressed figs. They would then burn this congealed wine *bikdusha* — in a sacred manner, in a designated place — just as *psulei hamukdashim* are burned. The apparent implication is that this wine retains its *kedusha* even after having been poured, which would make it an exception to *na'aseit mitzvato* and seemingly at odds with the *Mishnah*'s ruling that there is no *me'ilah* after the wine descends.

### Burning Congealed Wine

The source for burning the congealed wine *bikdusha* is derived from the verse concerning *nesachim* — *bakodesh hasech nesech shechar laHashem* — which, through double language, is taken to indicate that the wine retains a sacred character throughout. *Ravina* derives it through a *gezeira shava* of *kodesh-kodesh*: the word *kodesh* here is linked to the verse *vesarafta et hanotar ba'esh lo ye'achel ki kodesh hu*, which discusses the burning of *notar*. Just as *notar* must be burned because of its *kedusha*, so too this wine must be burned because of its *kedusha*.

### Gemara Initial Assumption

The *Gemara*'s initial reading is that *Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok*'s position — that the wine is burned *bikdusha* — is inconsistent with the *Mishnah*'s position that there is no *me'ilah* after pouring, since the requirement to burn implies continued *kedusha*, which would imply continued *me'ilah*.

### Tosafot: Before Floor

*Tosafot* proposes a resolution: the wine that *Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok* says must be burned *bikdusha* is wine that hit the floor of the *mizbeach*'s hollow. The floor of the *Beit HaMikdash* has its own sanctifying power, which imparts a renewed level of *kedusha* to the wine — at least *derabbanan*. Consequently, the *Mishnah*'s ruling of no *me'ilah* after pouring would apply specifically to wine caught *before* it strikes the floor. If the wine hits the floor of the *mizbeach*'s interior, it is re-sanctified and must be burned. This creates a somewhat unusual scenario in which *na'aseit mitzvato* first removes *me'ilah*, but contact with the *mizbeach* floor then re-ignites *kedusha* — an admittedly strange sequence.

### Burning Derabbanan Only

The *Gemara* ultimately offers an alternative resolution: *afilu tema Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok* — even the *Mishnah* could accord with *Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok*. The answer is *mi-d'rabbanan ve-kra asmakhta* — when *Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok* says to burn the wine *bikdusha*, he means only *derabbanan*. The verse he cites is merely an *asmakhta*, a rabbinic support. In truth, *na'aseit mitzvato* fully applies, and there is no Torah-level *kedusha* or *me'ilah* remaining. The rabbinic enactment to burn the wine — rather than use it or discard it informally — reflects appropriate reverence, and the *Gemara* is comfortable reading *Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok* as not actually claiming continued *me'ilah* but only a rabbinic requirement of proper disposal. Under this reading, there is no conflict with the *Mishnah*'s ruling, since the *Mishnah* speaks of *me'ilah* and *Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok* speaks only of rabbinic practice.

---

---

# Meilah 12

## Ashes: Inner Mizbe'ach

### Deshen Intro

The *mishna* at the bottom of 11b introduces a new subject: *deshen mizbe'ach hapnimi vehammenorah* — the ashes of the inner altar and the *menorah*. The ruling is *lo nehenin velo mo'alin*: one may not derive benefit from these ashes, yet there is no Torah-level *me'ila* for them. To properly situate this ruling, it helps to recall what the *gemara* had been exploring regarding the ashes of the outer *mizbe'ach*, where the question concerned at which stage the ashes are no longer subject to *me'ila* — whether after *terumas hadeshen* or only after they are carried outside. Here, in contrast, we are dealing with ashes generated inside the *heichal*: from the golden inner altar upon which the *ketoret* was burned, and from the *menorah* whose lights were kindled daily.

### Na'asa Mitzvato

The reason there is no *me'ila* for these ashes is grounded in the principle of *na'asa mitzvaso* — once the *mitzvah* of the object has been fulfilled, its sanctity for the purpose of *me'ila* is considered concluded. When the incense has burned or the *menorah*'s lights have been consumed, the *mitzvah* has already been accomplished, and the residual ashes carry no further *me'ila* liability. Notably, the *gemara* does not explore at precisely what stage *na'asa mitzvaso* occurs for the inner altar. However, Tosafot cites another *gemara* that clarifies the matter: for the *ketoret*, the *mitzvah* is complete as soon as the column of fragrant smoke begins to rise — analogous to what the *gemara* states regarding the *emurim* of *kodshim kalim*, where *me'ila* ends essentially at the moment combustion begins.

### Tosafot Distinction

Tosafot draws an important distinction to explain why the inner and outer altars are treated differently. The *mitzvah* of *terumas hadeshen* — the priestly removal of ashes described at the opening of *Parashas Tzav* — applies exclusively to the outer *mizbe'ach*, and even there, according to Tosafot, only in connection with the *olah* or perhaps *kodshei kodshim*. For objects where no specific *mitzvah* of ash-removal exists, the operative *mitzvah* attaches not to the ashes but to the object that is being burned. Consequently, that *mitzvah* is fulfilled as soon as the object begins to combust. Once the *mitzvah* has been performed on the burning object, the resulting ashes are already in a state of *na'asa mitzvaso*, and *me'ila* ceases at that early stage — or perhaps even before the ashes form at all.

### Outer vs Inner

This creates a meaningful structural difference between the two altars. For the outer *mizbe'ach* — specifically by *kodshei kodshim* — the existence of a *mitzvah* of *terumas hadeshen*, or more broadly of ash-removal, postpones the moment of *na'asa mitzvaso*: the ashes retain *me'ila* until that ritual act has been performed or until they are removed entirely from the *beis hamikdash*. For the inner *mizbe'ach* and the *menorah*, where no such *mitzvah* exists, the *mitzvah* completes at the earlier stage of combustion, and *me'ila* ends there as well.

The *gemara* itself, however, does not address this analysis directly. Instead, it pivots to a seemingly unrelated question: since the *mishna* mentions the removal of ashes, and it is elsewhere assumed that ashes from the inner *mizbe'ach* and *menorah* are deposited at the same location as the outer altar's ashes — near the ramp — the *gemara* asks for the biblical source of this practice. The *gemara* traces it through a *gezeira shava* and an exegetical reading of *el mekom hadeshen*, concluding that the ashes of the inner *mizbe'ach* and *menorah* are indeed placed at that designated ash-pile. This is conceptually interesting: although there is no *mitzvah* of *terumas hadeshen* for the inner *mizbe'ach* or *menorah*, the physical destination of the ashes is nonetheless the same location used for the outer altar's ash-ritual.

### Sanctifying Ashes

The *mishna* adds a further ruling: *hamakdish deshen batichla mo'alin bo* — if someone consecrates ashes from the outset, there is *me'ila* on them. Rashi and Tosafot read this in the context of the ash-removal process, suggesting it concerns re-sanctification after the ashes have been burned. The Rambam, by contrast, reads the statement simply and straightforwardly: no matter how trivial the sanctified object may seem — even a pile of ash or dung — if one formally consecrates it, *me'ila* applies. The ruling is thus a general principle about the power of *hekdesh* even over seemingly worthless material.

---

## Birds Unfit by Age

### Mishna: Birds

The *mishna* continues with the case of *torin shelo higia zmanan uvnei yona she'avar zmanan* — turtle-doves that have not yet reached the age at which they are fit for offering, and young pigeons (*bnei yona*) that have passed the age at which they are fit. In both cases, the ruling is *lo nehenin velo mo'alin*: benefit is rabbinically forbidden, yet there is no *me'ila*. This immediately calls for explanation, because as a general principle, a *korban* that becomes *pasul* still retains *me'ila*. Why should these birds be different?

The *gemara* first takes up the question in terms of the passage's structure: *bishlama mizbe'ach hachitzon* — the derivation regarding the outer *mizbe'ach*'s ash-placement is understood, since the verse in *Tzav* states *vesamo etzel hamizbe'ach*. But the source for the inner *mizbe'ach* is not immediately apparent. The *gemara* turns to Rabbi Elazar, who derives the ruling from the verse concerning the *olas ha'of*: *vehishlicho etzel hamizbe'ach kedma el mekom hadeshen* — the offal of the bird is thrown to the east of the altar, to the place of the ashes. The *gemara* reasons that since the phrase *el mekom hadeshen* was not strictly necessary — one could have derived the location for the bird's offal through a *gezeira shava* from the *terumas hadeshen* verse, where *etzel hamizbe'ach* already appears — the additional specification of *el mekom hadeshen* must be teaching something beyond what was already known. What is it teaching? *De'afilu mizbe'ach hapnimi* — that this designated place of ashes serves as the repository even for the ashes of the inner *mizbe'ach*. A further derivation — *deshen hadeshen*, the emphatic doubling of the word — extends the same rule to the ashes of the *menorah*.

The *gemara* thus focuses not on the central *me'ila* question of the *mishna* but on this ancillary issue of the ash-deposit's location, leaving the substantive analysis of *na'asa mitzvaso* to Tosafot's broader framing.

### R. Shimon: Young

Rabbi Shimon's position is presented in the following *mishna*: he holds that *torin shelo higia zmanan* — turtle-doves that are too young — do carry *me'ila*, even though the rabbis disagree. His reasoning is clear: since these birds will eventually become fit for a *korban*, their current unfitness is only temporary. Why, then, should their consecrated status not carry *me'ila*?

The *gemara* notes that Rabbi Shimon's position here is consistent with a principle he articulates elsewhere. In the laws of *oso ve'es beno* — the prohibition against slaughtering a mother animal and its offspring on the same day — Rabbi Shimon rules that *kol hara'uy le'achar zman*, anything that will be fit at a later time but that was consecrated while still temporarily unfit, carries sufficient significance that if one slaughters it outside the *beis hamikdash*, one transgresses the *lav* of *shechutei chutz*, even if no *kares* is incurred. The logic is that future fitness endows the object with present significance. Applied to the birds, Rabbi Shimon reasons that the young turtle-dove, which will become fit in due course, carries enough present sanctity to bear *me'ila*.

### Comparison: Pidyon

The *gemara* then asks the more basic question: why do the rabbis disagree? Even if they reject Rabbi Shimon's position regarding *shechutei chutz*, consider a standard animal that is less than eight days old — *mechusar zman* — and is consecrated. There is no dispute that *me'ila* applies. It will simply become fit when sufficient time has passed, just as the young turtle-dove will become fit. Why should the birds be different?

The *gemara* answers: *mechusar zman midi dehavai aba'al mum* — the case of an animal unfit by reason of age is comparable to an animal with a blemish. The reason *me'ila* applies to a blemished animal is *d'var pidyon hu* — it is something that can be redeemed. Even though a blemished animal cannot presently be offered, the *kedusha* is not purposeless: it can be transferred through *pidyon* to money, which in turn funds another *korban*. The *kedusha* has somewhere to go. The same logic applies to the underage animal: were some complication to arise, *pidyon* would remain an option.

### No Pidyon: Birds

For birds, however, this logic does not apply. As Tosafot clarifies, the claim is not strictly that there is no concept of *mum* by birds — there is, in the form of *mechusar eiver*, a missing limb. The real point is that there is no *pidyon* available for birds under any circumstances: *ein l'ofos pidyon*. Nothing can ever be done to transfer the *kedusha* of an unfit bird; it is not redeemable. Consequently, if a bird cannot presently be used as a *korban*, the *kedusha* has nowhere to go, and the ruling follows accordingly — no *me'ila*.

### Conceptual Issue

This answer, while formally satisfying, leaves a conceptual difficulty. When the bird is too young, the *kedusha* is not actually stuck — one simply waits, and in a matter of days or weeks the bird will be fit for a *korban*. The absence of a *pidyon* mechanism seems like a concern for a hypothetical scenario, not the current reality. One might argue that the availability of *pidyon* for animals simply means that even when complications arise, the *kedusha* is never truly stranded — and that this is what distinguishes animals from birds. Even if the bird is not stuck right now, because there are circumstances under which a bird's *kedusha* would become entirely unresolvable, the absence of *pidyon* in principle is enough to problematize the *kedusha* from the outset. Yet the argument is not entirely satisfying, and Rabbi Shimon's position retains considerable logical force.

---

## Dead/Unfit Animals

### Kodashim Shemeisu

The *gemara* now moves to a statement by Ulla in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kodashim shemeisu yatz'u midei me'ila d'var Torah* — consecrated animals that have died exit the category of Torah-level *me'ila*. This requires contextualizing against what has already been established. A *korban* that becomes *pasul* — disqualified in the context of the *avodah* — retains *me'ila*; there is still a *mitzvas sreifah*, an obligation to burn it, and the object remains within the orbit of *kedusha*. What removes something from *me'ila* is when it becomes *holech le'ibud* — headed toward destruction with no ritual purpose remaining — as with a *chatas hamesa* or the overage birds.

The current case concerns a different end-point: the animal was not *pasul* in any problematic sense, yet it simply died before it could be offered. Without a *mitzvas sreifah* — since it was not *shechted* in a disqualified manner — and without any remaining avenue for use, Ulla holds that the *kedusha* is no longer purposeful, and *me'ila* d'Oraisa no longer applies.

### Rav Chisda Object

Rav Chisda challenges this forcefully: *v'harei kedusha shebahen heichan halcha* — where did the *kedusha* go? The animal was fully consecrated, there was nothing wrong with the *kedusha*, and then it simply died. How can a perfectly valid *kedusha* simply evaporate? Ulla responds by pointing to the *mishna*'s own cases: *torin shelo higia zmanan uvnei yona she'avar zmanan* — birds where the *kedusha* may have started valid (for example, birds consecrated at the appropriate age that subsequently aged out of fitness) and now carries no *me'ila*. The *gemara* could equally have raised the *chatas hamesa* from the very first *mishna* of the *perek*, which may also have begun as a perfectly valid *kedusha* before circumstances — such as *niskafru ba'aleha b'acheres*, atonement being achieved through another offering — rendered it a *chatas hamesa*. Our *perek* is replete with cases in which a *kedusha* that began well becomes purposeless and loses its *me'ila* status. Rav Chisda's objection, while emotionally resonant, cannot be sustained against the weight of these precedents.

### D'Oraisa vs Rabbanan

Ulla concedes the conceptual force of Rav Chisda's point. His concession, as Tosafot reads the somewhat difficult language, is that he agrees: *d'ika me'ila miderabbanan* — there ought to be at least rabbinic *me'ila* in such cases. His original statement — *yatzu midei me'ila d'var Torah* — meant to deny only Torah-level *me'ila*; some form of rabbinic *me'ila* may still apply. The critical distinction between *issur hana'ah* — which is what *lo nehenin velo mo'alin* typically denotes — and *me'ila derabbanan* is not merely one of stringency. The operative difference is that *me'ila derabbanan* involves a notion of taking from the domain of the *beis hamikdash*, such that payment and restitution are required. *Issur hana'ah*, by contrast, like the prohibition against deriving benefit from *chametz* on *Pesach*, carries no mechanism of payment — it is simply a prohibition, transgression of which yields no obligation of repayment.

### Me'ila D'Rabbanan

A further difficulty then arises: *mi ika midi d'meikara lo is bei me'ila u'lesof is bei me'ila* — is there any case where something begins without *me'ila* and subsequently acquires *me'ila*? The question is pointed, because if *kodashim shemeisu* — including *kodshim kalim*, whose meat carries no *me'ila* while the animal lives — die, and Ulla's position implies they would then carry *me'ila derabbanan*, the situation becomes paradoxical: by dying, the animal's status has become worse in practice, yet more *me'ila* now applies than did before. Something that moved further from the *mizbe'ach*, as it were, now attracts a stricter treatment than it had in life.

### Blood Exception

The *gemara* raises the case of *dam* as a potential precedent. The *mishna* teaches that blood, *b'techila*, initially carries no *me'ila* — yet once it flows to the *nachal kidron*, the wadi outside the *beis hamikdash*, rabbinic *me'ila* applies. Here too, something begins without *me'ila* and ends with it. The *gemara* responds: *hasam nami ika me'ila meikara* — the blood case is not truly a counterexample, because there is a way blood could carry *me'ila* even from the outset. This is the teaching cited earlier in the name of Rav: *hamakiz dam l'behemas kodshim assur b'hana'ah umo'alin bo* — blood let from a consecrated animal for therapeutic purposes is fully subject to *me'ila*. Since *me'ila* is not conceptually foreign to blood, its rabbinic application in the *nachal kidron* case is not as startling as applying *me'ila derabbanan* to *kodshim kalim* that die, where *me'ila* was never a relevant concept at all. The *gemara* leaves the difficulty unresolved. The upshot of the entire sugya, however, is clear: *holech le'ibud* and *ibud* itself — actual death without a *mitzvas sreifah* — remove an animal from *me'ila d'Oraisa*, with the possibility of *me'ila derabbanan* remaining a live question.

---

## Blood: Part Animal

### Hematziz Dam

Rav Huna states in the name of Rav: *hamakiz dam b'vehemat kodshim assur b'hana'ah* — one who lets blood from a consecrated animal may not derive benefit from that blood, and moreover *mo'alin bo* — it is subject to full *me'ila*. The reasoning is straightforward: this blood was never designated for *kaparah* on the *mizbe'ach*, so the biblical exclusion of blood from *me'ila* — derived from the verse's language of *lachem*, given over to you, and *lechaper*, for the purpose of atonement — does not apply. That exclusion covers only blood being used for its ritual purpose. Blood extracted therapeutically from a consecrated animal is simply part of the animal's body, and since there is *me'ila* on the animal, there is *me'ila* on this blood as well.

### Blood vs Byproducts

Rav Hamnuna raises an objection from the *mishna* that follows: *kol hamukdashim uveitzei torin* — the milk of consecrated female animals and the eggs of turtle-doves are *lo nehenin velo mo'alin*. Benefit is forbidden, yet *me'ila* does not apply. If blood is treated as part of the animal itself, why are milk and eggs not treated similarly?

The answer given is: *delo miskayem belo dam* — an animal cannot survive without blood; blood is intrinsic to life itself and therefore intrinsic to the animal. *Aval chalav*, milk, by contrast — *deka mikayem belo chalav* — an animal can exist without producing milk. These are products generated by the animal, but they are not constitutive of the animal. They are byproducts, not the thing itself, and therefore *me'ila* does not extend to them.

### Dung Question

Rav Mesharshaya presses the point further: *ha-zevel veha-peresh shebe-chatzer* — dung and the undigested stomach contents found in the yard of a *kodshim* animal are also *lo nehenin velo mo'alin*. Yet, argues Rav Mesharshaya, *lo mikayem belo peresh* — an animal cannot subsist without having some food in its stomach at any moment. By the same logic used to include blood, should undigested food not also be included as intrinsic to the animal?

### Blood Intrinsic

The *gemara* responds: *mah irya* — there is a fundamental difference. Undigested food in the stomach is always food that came from the outside — *de-me'alma ka'asi lah* — and it is constantly being processed through the system, one portion replaced by another: *azil hai ve'asi achrina*. It is never truly the animal itself; it is always outside matter passing through. Blood, by contrast — *la'appokei dam di-gufeih hu* — is intrinsically produced by the body itself and is the body itself; as the commentators add, we are born already filled with blood. The body does not merely receive blood from outside and process it through; it generates blood as an expression of its own life-force. Therefore blood, even when it exits the body, retains the status of the animal itself, and *me'ila* applies accordingly.

---

## Milk & Eggs

### Mishna: Milk/Eggs

The *mishna* states: *chalvan ubeitzaihen lo nehenin velo mo'alin* — the milk of consecrated animals and the eggs of consecrated birds may not be used for benefit, and yet there is no *me'ila* on them. As established, this flows from the principle that byproducts are not the animal itself, and since the *korban* is defined by the identity of the thing going to the *mizbe'ach*, products that are not themselves going to the *mizbe'ach* carry no *me'ila*.

### Bedek HaBayis

The *mishna* then specifies an exception: *uvameh devarim amurim b'kodshei mizbe'ach — aval b'kodshei bedek habayis* — when is it that milk and eggs carry no *me'ila*? Only when we speak of things consecrated for the *mizbe'ach* as a *korban*. But if one consecrates a chicken or a female donkey for *bedek habayis* — the temple treasury — then *mo'alin bah uveitzatah*, *mo'alin bo uvchalavo*: *me'ila* applies both to the animal and to its eggs or milk. The *mishna* deliberately chose a chicken and a female donkey because animals fit for the altar should not be consecrated to the treasury — they should be offered as *korbanos*. These examples involve animals that cannot be brought on the *mizbe'ach* at all.

### Guf vs Damim

The conceptual key to the difference lies in understanding the two fundamental categories of *kedusha*: *kedushat haguf* and *kedushat damim*. *Kedushat haguf* is a *kedusha* grounded in the identity of the thing itself — what the thing *is* and where it is *going*. *Kedushat damim* is a *kedusha* grounded in ownership and value — it is about what the thing is *worth* and who *owns* it. When I consecrate a sheep to be brought as an *olah*, the *kedusha* is entirely about the identity of that sheep as something directed toward the *mizbe'ach*. When I transfer title of my chickens to the temple treasury, the *kedusha* is about ownership — the *beis hamikdash* now owns these animals. If the chicken lays an egg, who owns it? The *beis hamikdash* does. And therefore *me'ila* applies to the egg.

By contrast, when a sheep is consecrated as a *korban* and it produces milk, that milk is not going to the *mizbe'ach*; it is not the *korban* itself; it shares none of the identity-based *kedusha* that makes the sheep a *korban*. There is accordingly no *me'ila* on it.

### Kedushat Haguf

The *gemara* refines the analysis still further. It asks: why did the *mishna* give its exception specifically in the context of *bedek habayis*? Might there not also be *me'ila* on milk and eggs if one sanctified a donkey for the *mizbe'ach* with a *kedushat damim*? The *gemara* answers through the formulation of Rav Papa: *chisorei michasra*, the *mishna* requires supplementation. The correct reading is: *bameh devarim amurim? Keshehikdish kedushat haguf legabei mizbe'ach* — the ruling that milk and eggs carry no *me'ila* applies specifically to *kedushat haguf* for the *mizbe'ach*, where the thing itself is being directed to the altar and *kedusha* is about identity, not ownership or value.

### Kedushat Damim

*Aval hikdish kedushat damim legabei mizbe'ach* — but if one sanctified a donkey or chicken with a *kedushat damim* directed toward the *mizbe'ach* — meaning the animal will need to be sold and the proceeds used to purchase an *olah* — then *na'aseh kemi shehikdisho lebedek habayis*: for purposes of this *halacha*, it is treated as though it were consecrated to the treasury. The eggs and milk carry *me'ila*. The reason is that when *kedusha* takes the form of *kedushat damim*, even if the ultimate destination is the *mizbe'ach*, the *kedusha* at its current stage is not about the identity of the thing but about its value — its cost, what it can fetch in the market. And if the donkey's value is what matters, then when that value increases — through milk production or egg-laying — the *kedusha* extends to that increased value as well.

It is worth noting, as one might observe, that this is not precisely the same as *beis hamikdash* ownership. When I consecrate my donkey with a *kedushat damim* for an *olah*, the *beis hamikdash* does not come to collect; I remain the one who will sell it and bring the proceeds. Yet the *halacha* treats the situation as if it were *bedek habayis*, because in both cases the governing concept is value rather than identity. The *kedusha* is anchored to what the thing is worth, not to what the thing *is*. And therefore, as that worth grows, the *kedusha* grows with it — whereas a *kedushat haguf lemizbe'ach*, anchored to the identity of the specific sheep going to the altar, does not extend beyond that sheep itself.

---

## Summary: 5 Principles

### P1: Psul Status

The first principle concerns the *psul* of a *korban* and its effect on *me'ila*. A *korban* that becomes *pasul* in the context of the *avodah* — *psul b'kodesh* — retains *me'ila*, because there remains a *mitzvas sreifah* and the object has not left the domain of *kedusha*. However, if the animal becomes permanently unusable without any ritual act to perform upon it — as with a *chatas hamesa*, birds that have aged out of fitness, or a consecrated animal that simply died without being *shechted* — then the *kedusha* is considered to have no further purpose, and *me'ila d'Oraisa* no longer applies.

### P2: Issur Hana'ah

The second principle concerns the distinction between *issur hana'ah* and *me'ila derabbanan*. *Issur hana'ah* — like the prohibition on deriving benefit from *chametz* on *Pesach* — involves no concept of taking from a domain or payment. *Me'ila derabbanan*, by contrast, carries the notion that something has been appropriated from *hekdesh*, and therefore payment and restitution are required. The cases in our chapter described as *lo nehenin velo mo'alin* are typically in the category of *issur hana'ah* rather than *me'ila derabbanan*. The question of whether *me'ila derabbanan* applies to consecrated animals that have died — given that *kedusha* once existed and somewhere ought to reside — is left as an unresolved difficulty in the *gemara*.

### P3: Byproducts

The third principle is that byproducts of a consecrated animal — milk, eggs, and the like — are not subject to *me'ila*, because they are not the animal itself. The exception is blood: blood that is drawn therapeutically from a consecrated animal carries *me'ila*, because blood is intrinsic to the animal's very existence and is produced by the body itself, unlike food passing through the digestive system or milk generated in excess of the animal's survival needs.

### P4: Haguf/Damim

The fourth principle distinguishes *kedushat haguf* from *kedushat damim*. *Kedushat haguf* is a *kedusha* of identity — the thing itself, in its specific form, is directed toward the *mizbe'ach* or temple use. *Kedushat damim* is a *kedusha* of value and ownership — what matters is what the thing is worth and who now owns it. These categories cross-cut the distinction between *mizbe'ach* and *bedek habayis*: one can have *kedushat haguf* for *bedek habayis* (a beam consecrated for use in the temple ceiling) or *kedushat damim* for the *mizbe'ach* (money or a blemished animal consecrated so that its proceeds will fund an *olah*).

### P5: Extended Value

The fifth principle concerns the extension of *kedusha* to increased value. When the governing *kedusha* is *kedushat damim* — whether directed toward *bedek habayis* or toward the *mizbe'ach* — the *kedusha* tracks value. As the value of the consecrated asset grows (through milk production, egg-laying, or any other increment), the *kedusha* extends to that growth and *me'ila* applies accordingly. When, however, the *kedusha* is *kedushat haguf lemizbe'ach* — where the *kedusha* is defined by the identity of the specific thing being directed to the altar — the *kedusha* does not extend beyond that thing itself. Byproducts are simply outside its scope, and no *me'ila* attaches to them.

---

---

# Meilah 14

## Idol Breaking

### Idol Status Debate

The daf begins with a discussion that emerges from the previous mishna, which had addressed the case of a bird's nest found in an *asheira* tree — a tree that had been worshipped as *avoda zara*. The mishna established that one may knock the nest down but may not climb the tree, since climbing would constitute deriving benefit from an *avoda zara* object. No problem arises from the nest itself, because the concept of ownership by *avoda zara* does not apply in the same way as *hekdesh* — there is no prohibition of *meila*, and the nest's forbidden status derives only from its association with the tree that was worshipped.

### Yochanan: Assur

Out of this context, the Gemara introduces a formal dispute: *itmar avodat kochavim shenishtabra me'eileiha* — if an idol broke on its own, without any person intentionally destroying it. Rabbi Yochanan rules *asura* — it remains forbidden. An object that was worshipped as an idol retains its prohibited status so long as it was not consciously negated by one of its worshippers. Without a deliberate act of *bitul*, the status persists.

### Lakish: Mutar

Reish Lakish rules *muteres* — it is permitted. His reasoning: any worshipper of that idol would naturally reason, *hee gufa lo matzla ledidi tatzla* — it could not save itself; do I think it is going to save me? Any right-thinking idolater could be expected to render the idol null in his own mind. The question underlying this dispute is whether Reish Lakish intends a subjective assessment — that a particular worshipper would have nullified it — or whether he means something more objective: that the idol's failure to preserve itself defines its status in a way that dissolves the prohibition without requiring any subjective act of *bitul*. The latter reading seems closer to what Reish Lakish is actually arguing, approaching something analogous to the concept of *yeush shelo mida'at*.

---

## Birds' Nests Proof

### Lakish's Challenge

Reish Lakish attempts to bring a proof from our mishna. *Hakan sheberosh ha'ilan* — if there is a bird's nest at the top of a tree of *hekdesh*, the ruling is *ein nehenin ve'ein moalin*: one may not derive benefit from it, but there is no *meila*, because as established, *hekdesh* that acquires something without verbal sanctification — without *kedushat peh* — does not carry *meila*. But if the nest is in an *asheira* tree, one knocks it down with a stick and may derive benefit from it.

The challenge Reish Lakish presses: *mai lav de'itpar migufa* — presumably, the twigs used to build the nest came from the tree itself. Yet the mishna permits benefiting from this nest. If benefit is permitted even though the nest is constructed from the branches of an *asheira* tree, then surely this is evidence that when part of an idolatrous object separates on its own — without conscious human action — it loses its forbidden status. This would support Reish Lakish's position that an idol which breaks by itself becomes *mutar*.

### Twigs from Elsewhere

The Gemara deflects the proof: *lo de'aiti eitzei me'alma* — not necessarily. The case may be that the twigs came from other trees entirely, not from the *asheira* itself. If the nest's material came from elsewhere, there is no evidence that branches naturally falling from an *asheira* become permitted. The counter-pressure in Reish Lakish's argument is that he intends to encompass cases where the twigs could have come from the tree — meaning one should at least be concerned about that possibility unless there is evidence to the contrary. The Gemara's response insists that we know the twigs came from other trees.

This same *sugya* appears in tractate Avoda Zara, where it reads considerably more smoothly. The version here in Meilah is somewhat less polished, as the texts in this tractate are sometimes less carefully edited than those in other masechtot.

### Why Use Stick

The Gemara adds what appears to be a proof in the other direction: *daika nami* — this reading is also supported by analysis of the text itself. If the twigs came from elsewhere, one can understand the ruling of *ein nehenin ve'ein moalin* for the *hekdesh* case — the bird-*hekdesh* connection does not produce *meila* without *kedushat peh*. But if Reish Lakish is correct that the twigs came from the tree itself, then in the *hekdesh* case there should *be* a *meila* obligation, since those twigs are from the very tree that was sanctified. Moreover, in the *avoda zara* case, using them would be prohibited outright. So the absence of *meila* in the mishna proves the twigs came from elsewhere.

Reish Lakish has a response: one can maintain that the twigs did come from the tree, but in the *hekdesh* case, they were branches that grew after the tree was sanctified — *gidulin habaim l'achar mikan* — and the position being assumed is *ein meila b'gidulin*: there is no *meila* for subsequent growth. This reflects an ongoing debate about whether *hekdesh* that bears new growth after the moment of sanctification subjects that growth to *meila*. So Reish Lakish can consistently hold that both the *avoda zara* nest and the *hekdesh* nest are built from branches of the respective trees, that there is no *avoda zara* problem because the branches separated on their own, and that there is no *meila* in the *hekdesh* case because we are dealing with subsequent growth.

Rabbi Yochanan, by contrast, insists the twigs came from elsewhere. On the question of *gidulin*, he would presumably hold that if they *did* come from the sanctified tree itself — not merely subsequent growth — there would be *meila*, reinforcing his view that the twigs must have come from other trees.

The Gemara then raises a further question: *amai yatiz b'kaneh* — if the twigs came from other trees, why does the mishna require knocking the nest down with a stick? Why not simply take it by hand? If the nest material is visually and physically distinct from the tree, and one is not at risk of incidentally grasping branches of the *asheira* itself, what is the concern?

### Tosafot: Accidental Conf…

Tosafot explains the *hava amina* as follows. The concern is not that one will climb the tree — presumably, if the mishna says one could take it directly, the nest is low enough to reach. Rather, the concern is that in the act of reaching in and grabbing the nest, one might inadvertently dislodge and take along some branches of the tree itself, thereby incidentally benefiting from the *avoda zara*. Using a stick, rather than one's hands, reduces the risk of ripping branches loose and confusing them with the nest material. The underlying assumption — which the Gemara accepts as its working premise — is that if the nest came from the tree itself, the material of the nest and the branches of the tree would be visually similar and could be confused; whereas if the twigs came from elsewhere, they might be a different type of wood and visually distinguishable. This is a difficult *Gemara*, and the parallel passage in Avoda Zara presents the same argument far more clearly.

---

## Yochanan Concedes

### Chicks vs. Nest

Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan now introduces an important concession. Reading with the emendation supported by the *Bach* — who crosses out the words *le'olam de'asai me'alma* in order to align this passage with the parallel in Avoda Zara — Rabbi Yochanan in effect concedes to Reish Lakish that the nest material did come from the tree itself. He then offers a different resolution of the mishna entirely.

*Umai yatiz efrochim* — what does it mean to knock down the nest? It means knocking the chicks out of the nest, so that they fall or fly free and one can benefit from them. The wood of the nest, if it came from an *asheira* tree, would indeed carry a forbidden status; similarly, it would be subject to *meila* in the *hekdesh* case. But the interest here is not in the wood at all. The mishna is talking about benefit from the birds themselves. The question of where the twigs came from is simply irrelevant to that, which also explains why a stick is needed — not to avoid touching the wood per se, but to avoid incidentally taking hold of branches of the tree while maneuvering to dislodge the chicks.

### Eggs and Chicks

Rabbi Yaakov then says to Rabbi Yirmiyah: *efrochim kan ve-kan mutarim* — the chicks themselves are permitted in both the *avoda zara* case and the *hekdesh* case. The reason, at least in the *hekdesh* case, is that *hekdesh* cannot truly acquire ownership over birds that fly freely. They are fundamentally unconfined, not subject to proprietary control, and so the tree's status as *hekdesh* does not extend to the birds nesting in it. In the *avoda zara* case as well, the chicks are not considered part of the worshipped object.

The eggs, however, are another matter: *beitzim kan ve-kan asurim* — eggs are forbidden in both cases. In the *hekdesh* case, there is a meaningful sense of *kinyan* — the tree, as *hekdesh*, has a degree of ownership over the eggs it produces, in a way it does not over birds that choose to nest there. In the *avoda zara* case, the reasoning follows Rabbi Yochanan's position: just as the nest itself is forbidden because it is made from the wood of the *asheira*, objects closely connected to and contained within the nest are rabbinically treated as an extension of the nest's forbidden status. The eggs, lying in the nest, share that status.

### Rav Ashi: Young Chicks

Rav Ashi adds a qualification. *Im efrochim tzrichin le'iman kebeitzim damu* — if the chicks still need their mother and cannot survive independently, they are treated like the eggs and are considered part of the nest. Since they are bound to the nest in a functional sense — unable to fly, unable to fend for themselves — they share the nest's status and are likewise forbidden.

The result is a coherent dual reading of the mishna. Reish Lakish reads it as evidence that branches naturally detached from an *avoda zara* tree become permitted, since otherwise one could not benefit from a nest built from such wood. Rabbi Yochanan, after his concession, reads the mishna as being entirely about the chicks: the physical nest, if built from *asheira* wood, is itself forbidden; the chicks are what one benefits from; and the eggs and nest-dependent chicks share the nest's forbidden status. One knocks the nest down with a stick in order to dislodge the permitted chicks without incidentally taking hold of the forbidden wood.

---

## Wood Purchase

### Mishna: Wood Meila

The Gemara moves to the next mishna. *HaGizbarin shelakechu eitzim* — if the temple treasurers purchased wood, *mo'alin ba'etzim* — there is *meila* with respect to the wood itself. However, *ein mo'alin lo b'shipuya v'lo b'nivya* — there is no *meila* with respect to the sawdust or the shavings and cuttings removed in the process of fashioning logs into beams.

### Haguf vs. Damim

This ruling contrasts with the final clause of the previous mishna, which held that one who donates a forest to *hekdesh* — *hamakdish es hachoresh* — is *mo'el* with every part of the forest, down to every piece. What accounts for the difference?

The distinction turns on the difference between *kedushat haguf* and *kedushat damim*. When someone donates an entire forest, the purpose is not to build the forest directly into the temple structure. The forest's value far exceeds whatever timber might be directly used; the intent is that *hekdesh* should own the forest as property and derive benefit — through sale and other means — from the entire thing. This is analogous to *kedushat damim*: the sanctity is one of ownership and monetary value, and every last part of the object participates in that value. Hence, *meila* applies to every component of the forest.

By contrast, when the *gizbar* purchases a log with the intention of fashioning it into a beam for the temple structure, the sanctity is of the nature of *kedushat haguf*: what is being sanctified is the beam that will be built in, not the peripheral byproducts. The sawdust and shavings are analogous to the eggs and milk of a *korban*. Just as the eggs and milk of an animal sanctified as a *korban* — say an *olah* or *chatas* — are not the *ikar* of the *korban* and therefore carry no *meila*, so too the sawdust is not the *ikar* of the beam being sanctified for construction, and there is no *meila* for those byproducts.

This analogy highlights an interesting conceptual tension. With a *korban*, the animal clearly has *kedushat haguf* — one declares *harei zo olah* and the animal's bodily sanctity is unambiguous. With building materials, the line is considerably more fungible: the *gizbar* might start with a log and change his mind about how to use it, or might know in advance that the sawdust will itself have commercial value. Why should we assume the initial purchase carries *kedushat haguf* for the log and only *kedushat damim* for the rest, rather than treating the whole purchase as *kedushat damim* with the *kedushat haguf* only attaching when the beam is ready to be installed? This is a genuine difficulty. The commentators resolve it by focusing on the *gizbar*'s intent at the moment of purchase: he sanctified only what he intended to use as a beam — everything else was simply never within the scope of his sanctification.

---

## Bonin BeChol

### Shmuel's Rule

The Gemara records the principle of Shmuel: *bonin bechol ve'achar kach makdishin* — one builds with non-sanctified materials and only sanctifies afterward, once construction is complete. This principle applies to the general practice of temple construction and renovation. The reason might initially seem obvious — avoiding *meila* during the construction process — but the Gemara first offers a different rationale before reaching that explanation.

### Sanctity Transfer

*Mai ta'ama?* — what is the reason? The Gemara explains: when someone donates money to the temple, he sanctifies the money. The problem is that one must then pay the workers, and paying them with sanctified money would transfer the sanctity to them — leaving them holding *hekdesh* funds. The solution lies in a precise mechanism of *chilul*: transferring the *kedusha* from the money onto the completed structure, and then paying the workers with the now-desanctified money.

The underlying logic: workers improve an object through their labor. If one begins with raw materials worth, say, ten *drachma*, and after all the work the completed structure is worth fifty *drachma*, the improvement in value represents the workers' contribution. By transferring the *kedusha* of the donated money onto the improved structure — *teichol kedushat ma'os abinyan* — one moves the sanctity from the money to a concrete, physical object of increased value. The money is then freed of its *kedusha* and can be handed to the workers as their fee. This is why the sequence matters: you must wait until the structure is complete, so that there is a concrete, improved object onto which the *kedusha* can be transferred.

### Payment Mechanism

The Gemara illustrates this mechanism with the case of *mosar haktoret* — leftover *ketores* from one year that cannot be carried over for use in the next, since *korbanos tzibur* must be purchased from new communal funds collected fresh each year. Yet it would be wasteful to simply discard the leftover *ketores*, which is worth considerable money. The solution: *hayu mafrishin himenah sechar ha'umnin* — one sets aside from the *ketores* an amount equivalent to what one owes the workers. *Umachalelin osah al ma'os ha'umnin* — one transfers the *kedusha* of the *ketores* onto the workers' fund (the money designated to pay the workers, which is itself not yet sanctified). Now the *ketores* is no longer sanctified. *Venosnin osah le'umnin* — you give the now-desanctified *ketores* to the workers as their payment. *Vechozrim venotlin osah mitrumah chadashah* — and then you repurchase it from them using the new communal funds. The *ketores* is now purchased with fresh *teruma chadasha* and can be used as a *korban tzibur* for the new year.

To trace the mechanism step by step: the old *ketores* carries last year's *kedusha*. One transfers that *kedusha* onto the designated workers' money. The *ketores* is now in the workers' hands without *kedusha*. The temple then buys it back from them using this year's communal funds. The *ketores* now carries the new *kedusha* and can be offered. The old money — now bearing the transferred old *kedusha* — can in turn be redirected: next time something is built into the temple wall, that *kedusha* is transferred there and the money is freed. The old *kedusha* presents no problem for *bedek habayit* or construction purposes; the restriction to new funds applies only to *korbanos tzibur* brought in the current year.

What is striking is that *ketores* — which has a form of *kedusha* that has not yet been fully actualized into *kedushat haguf* (it has not yet been placed in a *kli shareis*) — can nevertheless be redirected in this way toward purposes associated with the *binyan* of the *mikdash*. This reveals that the categories of *kedusha* are not always rigidly sealed from one another.

### Direct Transfer

One might ask: if one can transfer *kedusha* from money or from *ketores* to an improved structure, why go through the elaborate mechanism involving the workers' fund at all? Why not transfer the *kedusha* of the *ketores* directly to the completed structure and save the intermediate steps?

The Gemara's answer: *d'leika binyan* — there is no completed construction to which one can transfer it. And even where there is some construction, *d'leika binyan keshurmos* — the value of the improvement is not equivalent to the amount of *kedusha* one needs to transfer. The workers' fee may be two hundred, while the capital improvement to the structure is only one hundred — just as anyone who has renovated a kitchen or bathroom knows that the cost of labor and materials often substantially exceeds the increase in property value. Since the *ketores* is worth two hundred, one cannot transfer its *kedusha* to an improvement worth only one hundred; hence the mechanism runs through the workers' money instead.

This prompts a further question: Shmuel himself rules that *hekdesh shaveh maneh shechilelo al shaveh perutah mechulal* — if one transfers *kedusha* worth a *maneh* onto an object worth only a *perutah*, the transfer is valid, even though it is disproportionate. So why not transfer the *kedusha* of the *ketores* directly to whatever improvement exists in the structure, even if the values do not match?

The Gemara responds: *hani mili dievad* — that rule applies only after the fact. If one already performed such a disproportionate transfer, it works. But *lechatchila lo* — one should not do so initially. Even though in this case *hekdesh* is not losing anything by the disproportionate transfer — it is *hekdesh* itself orchestrating the entire arrangement — the rule is that one should not manipulate transfers of *kedusha* between objects of unequal value, even when no loss results. As Tosafot notes, normally the concern is that *hekdesh* loses out in such a transaction; here that concern does not apply, but the formal rule is still not to engineer such transfers *lechatchila*.

### Pappa: Accidental Meila

Rav Pappa offers a simpler and more direct rationale for the principle of *bonin bechol*. *De-lo nittena Torah le-mal'achei ha-shareit* — the Torah was not given to angels; it was given to human beings, who are fallible. Workers will inevitably sit on the stones, lean against the lumber, or otherwise incidentally use the materials they are working with. *I bana be-kudsha, ishtakach de-ka ma'el be-kodshim* — if the materials were sanctified, they would inadvertently be committing *meila*. Therefore, the materials must remain *chol* — unsanctified — throughout the construction process, and only sanctified upon completion.

This rationale differs in emphasis from the previous one. Where the earlier explanation focused on the need for a concrete, improved object onto which to transfer *kedusha* when paying the workers, Rav Pappa's explanation focuses entirely on preventing inadvertent *meila* during construction. The practical implication may differ as well: according to Rav Pappa's reasoning, one might be able to pay the workers with sanctified funds and allow the *kedusha* to transfer to whatever abstract or concrete improvement exists, since his concern is specifically about the raw materials being *kodesh* during construction — not about the mechanism of transferring *kedusha* through the workers' payment.

---

## Mishna Question

### Contradiction

Having established Rav Pappa's principle, the Gemara raises an immediate difficulty from our mishna. *Ve'amai mo'alin ba'hen* — if the rule is to build with unsanctified materials, why does the mishna say there is *meila* with respect to the wood the *gizbar* purchased? According to Rav Pappa, the *gizbar* should have purchased the beams without sanctifying them — and if he had not sanctified them, there would be no *meila*. Why, then, does the mishna presuppose that the beams are subject to *meila*?

### Pappa: Immediate Use

Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction himself: *ella ki tnan be-matnisin be-eitzim de-yomei* — the mishna is discussing wood purchased for immediate use that same day. The concern behind *bonin bechol* is that raw materials lying around a construction site will be casually used by workers who forget or are unaware of the *kedusha*. But when the *gizbar* purchases a beam that is going directly into the structure today, there is no period of sitting around on a construction site, no risk of someone inadvertently leaning on it or sitting down on it. In that narrow case, the *gizbar* may sanctify it immediately, and *meila* applies. For long-term building stock that will remain on site, the principle of *bonin bechol* holds — but for materials destined for immediate installation, it does not apply.

---

## Wool & Horns

### Korban Parts

By way of a supplementary note, and in connection with the earlier discussion of eggs and milk of *korbanos*, a brief clarification: the Gemara in Rosh Hashanah discusses the horns of a *shelamim* in the context of using them for a *shofar* — involving questions of *mitzvos lav leihanot nitnu* and related issues — and it is clear from that discussion that *meila* applies to the horns. The horns might seem like a borderline case: on the one hand they grow, like milk or eggs; on the other hand they are a permanent, structural feature of the animal. Nevertheless, *meila* does apply.

As for wool: there is a Gemara in Pesachim on 33a that rules that one who warms himself with the shearings of an *olah* — *mischamem b'gizei olah* — is *mo'el*. So *meila* clearly applies to the wool as well. The open question — which that Gemara does not resolve — is whether this refers to wool that was on the animal at the moment of sanctification, or whether it would also apply to wool that grew afterward. The real analogue to the milk-and-eggs debate is *gidulin*: what is the status of wool that grew after the animal was sanctified? The Gemara in Pesachim cannot serve as proof either way on that question, since it may well be referring only to wool present at the time of *hekdesh*. The matter remains unresolved, but it is now established that both horns and wool are subject to *meila*, whatever the further details of their status with respect to subsequent growth may be.

---

---

# Meilah 16

## Core Me'ilah Principle

### Me'ilah Combination

We open on 16b, at the top of the *daf*, in the middle of the chapter of *Kodshei Mizbe'ach*. Before proceeding into the material that occupies the rest of this chapter — which deals not with *me'ilah* per se but with the broader laws of combination (*tziruf*) — it is worth briefly restating the core *me'ilah* principle established at the chapter's outset.

### Kodshei/Bedek Combine

The *mishnah* at the beginning of the chapter taught that one can combine *me'ilah* even across different *korbanot*, or from half a *perutah*'s worth of a *korban* and half a *perutah*'s worth of something belonging to the Temple treasury. This is the rule of *Kodshei Mizbe'ach u-Bedek HaBayis mistarfin ze im ze le-me'ilah* — *kodshei mizbe'ach* and *bedek ha-bayis* combine with one another for *me'ilah*.

### Hana'ah vs. Gezilah

This principle carries significant conceptual weight. The very use of the *perutah* as the operative measure directs us away from understanding *me'ilah* through the lens of *achilah* — forbidden eating — though the prohibition could still be grounded in either *hana'ah* (illicit benefit) or *gezilah* (misappropriation, theft from the sacred). One might have assumed that *gezilah* is more naturally associated with *bedek ha-bayis*, the Temple maintenance fund — where the violation consists in diverting funds from the Temple's coffers — while *hana'ah* is more naturally associated with *kodshei mizbe'ach*, the altar sacrifices, where deriving personal benefit from sacred objects is the offense. If that were so, one might argue that the two categories are fundamentally distinct in character and should not be combinable. The *mishnah* rules otherwise: there is one unified concept of *me'ilah* spanning both categories, and they do combine.

### Rebbi Yanai Position

Importantly, the *mishnah* does not specify which underlying concept is primary. We did have, however, the dissenting position of *Rebbi Yanai*, who held that the paradigmatic case of *me'ilah* is *bedek ha-bayis* — which, if anything, would lend further weight to the *gezilah* model. Yet regardless of which conception is primary, the operative conclusion remains: *me'ilah* is not fragmented by the type of *kedushah* involved, because *korbanot* and *bedek ha-bayis* combine. This tension between *hana'ah* and *gezilah* as the organizing principle of *me'ilah* remains an open question animating the chapter.

---

## Neveilot/Sheratzim

### Mishnah: Combination

The chapter continues to discuss categories of prohibited substances that combine with one another for purposes of their respective prohibitions. The *mishnah* had stated that all *neveilot* combine and all *sheratzim* combine. Two questions must be kept in mind for each: does the combination operate for purposes of *tumah*, or also for purposes of *issur achilah*?

### Neveilah Status

Regarding *neveilot*, the *mishnah* at minimum means that half a *kezayit* from one *neveilah* and half a *kezayit* from another combine for *tumah*. But a further question was raised: might the *mishnah* even mean that they combine for the *issur achilah* itself? This depends on whether a dead non-kosher animal — say, a dead pig — carries the status of *neveilah* in addition to its existing *issur* as a non-kosher species. This is the question of *issur chal al issur*: does the prohibition of *neveilah* take hold on top of the pre-existing prohibition of pig? If it does, then half a *kezayit* of pig and half a *kezayit* of a dead cow would combine for the *issur* of *neveilah*. The *mishnah*'s intent on this point remained an open question, with the combination for *tumah* being the minimum certain meaning.

### Sheratzim Tumah

The *mishnah*'s second clause — that *sheratzim* combine — similarly invites the question: do they combine for *tumah*, for *achilah*, or for both? This question drives the *sugya* on 16b.

---

## Eating Sheratzim

### Rav: Kezayit Amount

At the top of 16b, Rav Yehuda states in the name of Rav: *achilat sheratzim lokeh alav be-kezayit* — one who eats *sheratzim* incurs lashes for eating a *kezayit*. On its face, this seems unremarkable: the standard measure for forbidden foods is a *kezayit*, so of course that would apply here as well.

### Beyah Question

One might raise the question of *beryah* — the rule that eating a complete creature, even one smaller than a *kezayit*, can entail liability. *Rebbi Eliezer* holds that one is liable for a *beryah* even without the standard *shiur*. Whether this is accepted as *halacha* or represents only a minority view requires further investigation, and that matter is set aside here. In any case, Rav's statement is evidently addressing the case of partial *sheratzim* — or more precisely, what *shiur* of *sheratzim* is needed when combining. Thus, bracketing the *beryah* question: if one eats an incomplete *sheretz*, or if the *beryah* rule does not apply in this context, the operative *shiur* for liability is a *kezayit*.

### Braita Linking

The *Gemara* then introduces a *braita*: *ve-hasani Rav Yosef bar Chanina kamei d'Rabbi Yochanan* — Rav Yosef bar Chanina taught the following *braita* before Rabbi Yochanan.

### Parshas Shemini

The *braita* draws from the end of *Parshas Shemini*. The verse there reads: *ve-hivdaltem bein ha-behemah ha-tehorah la-tme'ah, u-vein ha-of ha-tamei la-tahor, ve-lo teshaketzu et nafshoseichem ba-behemah uva-of uv-chol asher tirmos ha-adamah asher hivdalti lachem le-tamei* — "And you shall distinguish between the pure and impure animal, between the impure and pure bird, and you shall not make your souls abominable through animal, bird, and all that creeps on the ground, which I have set apart for you as *tamei*." The *braita* observes: *pasach ha-katuv ba-achilah ve-siyem ba-tumah* — the verse opens with the prohibition of eating (*achilah*) and closes with the concept of *tumah*.

### Opening with Achilah

How do we know the verse opens with *achilah*? Because the first part of the verse — distinguishing between pure and impure animals and birds — concerns what is kosher and non-kosher for eating, not *tumah ve-tahara* in the ritual purity sense. This is the reading of Rashi and Tosafos: the phrase *ve-lo teshaketzu et nafshoseichem*, "do not make your souls abominable," speaks to what one ingests and concerns sin rather than ritual impurity. The closing phrase, *asher hivdalti lachem le-tamei*, "which I have set apart for you as *tamei*," does refer to the transmission of ritual *tumah* — Tosafos explains that *le-tamei* means things that render others *tamei*, the metaphysical *tumah* in the technical halakhic sense. So the verse moves from the realm of *achilah* to the realm of *tumah*, treating them in a single continuum.

---

## Ke'adasha Measure

### Tumah/Achilah Parallel

The purpose of this juxtaposition, the *braita* concludes, is to teach: *ma tumah be-che'adasha af achilah be-che'adasha* — just as the *shiur* for *tumah* is a *ke'adasha* (the size of a lentil bean), so too the *shiur* for forbidden *achilah* is a *ke'adasha*. This is no *chiddush* when it comes to non-kosher mammals or birds, since in those cases both *tumah* and *achilah* require a *kezayit* — so the equation is trivially true and teaches nothing new. But for *sheratzim*, the equation is a genuine *chiddush*: the *shiur* for *tumah* caused by a *sheretz* is a *ke'adasha*, considerably smaller than a *kezayit*. If the verse equates *tumah* and *achilah* for *sheratzim*, then eating a *ke'adasha* of *sheratzim* would also incur lashes — a significant departure from the standard *kezayit* rule.

### Size Distinction

This raises the question of why *tumah* for *sheratzim* is measured in *ke'adasha* in the first place. There is a specific *drasha* for this: Tosafos cites the derivation from the words *meihem* and *bahem*, understood to indicate that some of these rodents begin life at the size of a lentil bean, and the word *bahem* implies them in their entirety — so the smallest complete specimen serves as the paradigm. The smallest one of the eight *sheratzim* that transmit *tumah* begins its existence at the size of a *ke'adasha*, and therefore that becomes the *shiur* for *tumah*. The source for *kezayit* as the *shiur* for *tumah* by non-kosher mammals and birds would require separate examination — much of this may rest on *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* — but the point here is that by *sheratzim*, there is a distinct and specific *drasha* establishing the *ke'adasha* as the minimum.

### Braita Approval

Rabbi Yochanan praised Rav Yosef bar Chanina for this *braita*. The *Gemara* is therefore not prepared to assume that Rav and Rabbi Yochanan are simply in dispute. Rav states a *kezayit*; the *braita* endorsed by Rabbi Yochanan implies a *ke'adasha*. How can both be right?

### Alive/Dead Distinction

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya — chad be-mitatan ve-chad be-chayeihen*. There is no difficulty; the two statements address different cases. One refers to dead *sheratzim* and the other to living ones. The eight *sheratzim* enumerated in the Torah cause *tumah* when they are dead — *be-mitatan*. When a dead *sheretz* causes *tumah* at a *ke'adasha*, eating it is likewise governed by the *ke'adasha shiur*, per the equation in the *braita*. Rav's statement that the *shiur* is a *kezayit*, then, refers to *sheratzim* that are alive — *be-chayeihen*. When one eats a live *sheretz*, it does not currently transmit *tumah*, so the *tumah-achilah* equation does not apply, and the standard *kezayit* governs the eating prohibition.

One might wonder whether concepts such as *ever min ha-chai* or *neveilah* are relevant to *sheratzim*. The answer is clearly no: *neveilah* and *ever min ha-chai* apply only to species subject to *shechita* — mammals and birds — for which the Torah establishes the framework of proper slaughter. The Torah nowhere speaks of *shechita* for *sheratzim*, and tellingly, only the eight specific *sheratzim* named in the Torah transmit *tumah* when dead — other rodents or amphibians that die do not transmit *tumah* at all. This proves that no concept of *neveilah* applies to them, and correspondingly, there is no concept of *ever min ha-chai* either. The only applicable prohibition is *issur sheratzim* itself. Thus when a live *sheretz* is eaten, it is forbidden as *sheratzim* but transmits no *tumah*, and the *shiur* remains the standard *kezayit*.

---

## Rav's Intent Debate

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye raises a challenge. Rav's statement, he argues, is a commentary on the *mishnah* before us, which states that all *sheratzim* combine. Rav had similarly commented on the *mishnah*'s earlier clause regarding *neveilah* — the statement that *lo shanu ela le-inyan tumah aval le-inyan achilah tehorim*, that the *mishnah* about *neveilah* speaks only of *tumah*, not *achilah*. Following that pattern, Rav is here explaining how *sheratzim* combine for *achilah*: they combine for a *kezayit*. Since the *mishnah* speaks categorically about all *sheratzim* combining without distinction, Rav's statement presumably covers both alive and dead *sheratzim*, and one cannot restrict it to the living.

### Rav Yosef Response

Rav Yosef pushes back: *ha hi diyuka dilach* — that connection to the *mishnah* is your own interpretive imposition. *Rav shema'ata be-alma ka-amar* — Rav was simply making an independent statement, not commenting on the *mishnah*. Some versions read *dufka didach* — that is merely your way of gluing things together. Since Rav's statement stands independently, it is open to us to say that it referred specifically to live *sheratzim*, not dead ones.

### Dead Sheratzim Conclusion

The *Gemara*'s conclusion, then, is that for dead *sheratzim* — specifically, the eight *sheratzim* that transmit *tumah* — the *shiur* for *achilah* is a *ke'adasha*, in keeping with the *braita* endorsed by Rabbi Yochanan. For live *sheratzim*, where no *tumah* applies, the *shiur* for eating liability remains a *kezayit*.

---

## Limbs and Tumah

### Limbs No Minimum

Having established that dead *sheratzim* go by *ke'adasha* for both *tumah* and *achilah*, the *Gemara* raises a *meitivei*: *eivarim ein lahem shiur — afilu pachos mi-kezayit neveilah, pachos mi-ke'adasha min ha-sheretz, metamei*. Limbs have no minimum size for *tumah*. Even less than a *kezayit* of a *neveilah*, or less than a *ke'adasha* of a *sheretz*, causes *tumah* if it constitutes a complete limb. So a detached limb — even if it is smaller than the standard *shiur* — is itself a source of *tumah*. One might visualize something like a leg of an insect-like creature: whatever constitutes a discrete limb of the creature, even if minuscule, causes *tumah* independently of the *ke'adasha* threshold. This is, of course, not related to *ever min ha-chai* or *basar min ha-chai*, since as established, those concepts do not apply to *sheratzim*; the limb here comes off a dead animal.

### Lashes/Kezayit

The *braita* then continues with Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: *ein lokin aleihem ela be-kezayit* — despite the fact that a limb smaller than a *ke'adasha* causes *tumah*, one does not receive *malkus* for eating it unless one has consumed a *kezayit*. This appears to contradict what was established earlier — that Rabbi Yochanan endorsed the *ke'adasha* as the *shiur* for eating *sheratzim*.

### Muvdalim/Sheratzim

Rava resolves the contradiction: *be-muvdalim diber ha-katuv* — the verse speaks about the *muvdalim*, the "distinguished" or "separated" ones. This is derived from the closing phrase of the verse: *asher hivdalti lachem le-tamei* — "which I have separated for you as *tamei*." Tosafos explains the resolution as follows: the *ke'adasha* rule for *achilah* applies only to *sheratzim*, specifically because among *sheratzim* there is a distinction — some cause *tumah* and some do not. The end of the verse, *asher hivdalti lachem le-tamei*, is therefore addressing *sheratzim* specifically, where this differentiation exists. Precisely because the Torah links *achilah* and *tumah* via this verse, and that linkage applies only where the verse's closing phrase operates — i.e., among *sheratzim* — only for *sheratzim* does the *ke'adasha shiur* of *tumah* carry over into the *achilah* prohibition.

Rabbi Yochanan's statement that lashes require a *kezayit* is therefore not a contradiction to the *ke'adasha* rule for *sheratzim*. Rather, it is a ruling about *behemah*: although a whole limb of a non-kosher *behemah* causes *tumah* even below a *kezayit*, that does not translate into a reduced *shiur* for eating liability. For *behemah*, the equation between *tumah* and *achilah* does not apply, and *malkus* for eating a non-kosher *behemah* always requires a *kezayit*, regardless of the *tumah shiur* of its limbs.

---

## Extending to Behemot

### Adda's Objection

Adda bar Ahava challenges Rava. If the verse brings together *behemah* and *sheratzim* in the same *pasuk* — *ve-hivdaltem bein ha-behemah ha-tehorah la-tme'ah, u-vein ha-of ha-tamei la-tahor... asher hivdalti lachem le-tamei* — why should the rule linking *tumah* and *achilah* not extend to *behemah* as well? The entire *pasuk* encompasses both, and the *halacha* derived for *sheratzim* — that the *tumah shiur* sets the *achilah shiur* — ought by extension to apply to *behemah* too. In practical terms, since a whole limb of a *behemah* causes *tumah* even below a *kezayit*, perhaps eating such a limb should also incur *malkus*. As Tosafos explains the question: even if the primary focus of *asher hivdalti lachem le-tamei* is *sheratzim*, the *pasuk* as a whole addresses *behemah* and *of* as well; one might therefore apply the *sheratzim* principle of linking *tumah* to *achilah* across the board.

### Hivdalti Response

Rava responds: *ki kamakish rachmana le-val teshaktzu, aval le-shiuram lo* — the Torah's equation, when it links everything to *lo teshaktzu et nafshoseichem*, creates a shared *lav* of abomination, but it does not equate their *shiurim*. The operative phrase *asher hivdalti lachem le-tamei* speaks exclusively to *sheratzim*, among whom there is a genuine internal distinction: some *sheratzim* cause *tumah* when dead and some do not. It is this internal differentiation — *muvdalim* — that makes *sheratzim* uniquely subject to the linkage between *tumah* and *achilah shiurim*. *Behemot*, by contrast, are not subject to this internal differentiation in the same way: all dead *behemot* that are non-kosher are *tamei*, without the kind of internal distinction that the phrase *asher hivdalti lachem* captures. Therefore the equation between *tumah shiur* and *achilah shiur* does not extend to *behemah*.

### Final Halacha

The *Gemara* thus arrives at the following conclusion. Among the eight *sheratzim* that cause *tumah* when dead — these and only these are the *muvdalim* referred to by the verse — eating them while dead carries a *shiur* of *ke'adasha*, because *tumah* and *achilah* are linked by the verse. Other *sheratzim* that are *assur* to eat but do not cause *tumah*, and *behemot* that are non-kosher, are not subject to this linkage — their eating prohibition always requires the standard *kezayit*. Furthermore, even where the *tumah shiur* for *behemah* is less than a *kezayit* (as in the case of a whole limb), this does not reduce the *kezayit* requirement for *malkus*, since the equation between *tumah* and *achilah* operates only for the *muvdalim sheratzim*.

As a corollary to the earlier discussion, the *Gemara* notes in passing that a dead non-kosher *behemah* does not acquire the status of *neveilah* — it retains only its status as a non-kosher *behemah*. The concept of *neveilah*, with its associated *shiurim* and rules of combination, is restricted to species for which *shechita* is halakhically relevant.

---

---

# Meilah 16b

## Me'ilah Principles

### Kodshei Mizbe'ach Combo

We pick up at 16b, in the middle of the perek of *kodshei mizbe'ach*. Before continuing, it is worth briefly reviewing the primary *me'ilah* principle established at the opening of this perek, since the remainder of the chapter deals not with *me'ilah* proper but with questions of combining various prohibited items more generally.
