This is the moment, according to Rabbi Shimon, at which *me'ilah* has occurred — *keivan shehotzi, mo'al* — because that is when the benefit is derived.

The Gemara notes that the literal words *keivan shehotzi* suggest something like "when he takes it out of the treasury," which is indeed the most natural reading, and this is the position of the Nimukei Yosef, who understands *hotzi* to mean the moment one removes the funds from the temple treasury. Rashi and Tosafot, however, understand it to align with Rabbi Shimon's classic position that the moment of benefit is when one brings the animal into the *azarah*.

The Gemara does not fully unpack why the examples are specifically limited to obligatory *korbanot* such as *zavim*, *zavot*, *yoldot*, *chatat*, and *asham*, rather than including cases where the diversion serves another sacred purpose without satisfying a personal obligation. The *Acharonim* may address this, though no resolution is cited here.

### Timoal Ma'al Teaching

Whatever the force of the argument that diverting *hekdesh* to another sacred purpose should not be *me'ilah*, the *braisa* closes with a definitive ruling: *timal ma'al mikol makom*. The word *timoal ma'al* teaches that under all circumstances, even when one is not using the funds for personal gain, even when the diversion serves another *hekdesh* purpose, *me'ilah* is nonetheless transgressed. The crucial qualification, however, is that in all the cited cases the person does gain something — they satisfy a personal obligation by means of *hekdesh* resources. It is worth noting that the teaching *timoal ma'al mikol makom* does not sweep away the requirement of *hana'ah*; it teaches that even *hana'ah* of this indirect kind, the relief from an obligation, is sufficient to constitute *me'ilah*.

---

## Braisa Unpacked

### Nefesh Inclusivity

The Gemara now proceeds to unpack the *braisa* element by element. The *braisa* opens from the *pasuk*: *nefesh ki timoal ma'al* — "if a soul commits an act of trespass." The word *nefesh* signals universality: *echad yachid ve'echad nasi ve'echad mashuach* — whether a lay individual, a king (*nasi*), or a *Kohen Gadol*, all are included in the laws of *me'ilah*.

The Gemara asks why this requires a derivation at all — is it not obvious? The word *nefesh* is written; surely everyone is included. The answer is that one might have thought to exclude the king and the *Kohen Gadol* based on a different *pasuk* concerning the *shemen hamishchah*: *va'asher yiten mimenu al zar* — whoever places the anointing oil upon a *zar*, a stranger, violates. Since a king and *Kohen Gadol* are not *zarim* in relation to the *shemen hamishchah* — the *Kohen Gadol* is anointed with it, and kings are sometimes anointed with it in cases of disputed succession — one might have thought they are similarly not *zarim* with respect to *me'ilah* involving *hekdesh*. There is indeed a parallel discussion in Maseches Kerisos about whether a *Kohen Gadol* who is anointed with *shemen hamishchah* is regarded as a *zar* in relation to subsequent applications of that oil. The *braisa*'s derivation from the word *nefesh* closes off this possibility: the king and *Kohen Gadol* are fully subject to *me'ilah* just as any other person.

One might argue that the more natural basis for the *havah amina* would have been the structural distinctions drawn in the *parsha* of *korbanot* — *asher nasi yecheta* and so on — where the Torah treats different types of individuals differently. The Gemara here, however, focuses specifically on the *shemen hamishchah* connection.

Regarding the term *nasi*: while in the context of the Torah it refers to the head of a tribe, the Gemara's context here translates it into the post-tribal political reality of kingship, since the *pasuk* being leveraged concerns the *shemen hamishchah* and its connection to anointing. There are broader discussions elsewhere of whether *nasi* extends to other forms of political leadership, but here the focus is specifically on the king as the figure who might have been anointed with *shemen hamishchah*.

### Sotah Model

The Gemara turns to the first of the three biblical models. *Va'akish rachmana lesota avodas kochavim uteruma* — the Torah connects *me'ilah* to *sotah*, to *avodah zarah*, and to *terumah*. What is learned from *sotah*? *De'af al gav delo pagim* — even though the object of the benefit (understood in the *sotah* model as the woman herself) is not injured or depreciated. The *sotah* model teaches that *me'ilah* can be constituted by *hana'ah* alone, even without any *pagam* to the object.

This connects to a distinction already implicit in the *Mishnah* between two categories of objects. Some objects, when used, are not normally accompanied by any depreciation or loss — a golden necklace, a golden goblet. There, the mere act of deriving benefit is itself the act of *me'ilah*. Other objects, when used, normally are accompanied by wear and tear — clothing, tools. For those objects, the *me'ilah* requires that the benefit actually be accompanied by the *pagam*, the wear and tear. The *sotah* model establishes the principle governing the first category: *hana'ah* by itself, without *pagam*, can constitute *me'ilah*.

One might ask why the *pasuk* of *sotah* is used rather than simply *eishet ish*. The answer is that the specific language of *me'ilah* — *ki timoal ma'al* — appears only in the *parsha* of *sotah*. Grammatically, the Torah in that *parsha* begins by describing the act of adultery as if it has already occurred: *ish ish ki tisteh ishto umala vo ma'al veshachav ish ota shichvat zera*, and then shifts to the husband's suspicion. So while the *parsha* is technically that of *sotah*, the *me'ilah* language is applied to the act of adultery itself.

The practical application follows: *natan taba'at beyada* — placing a ring on someone's finger is an act of *me'ilah* even without any loss occurring to *hekdesh*, because benefit has been derived from what belongs to the sacred domain.

### Avodah Zarah Model

From *avodah zarah* the Gemara learns a different dimension: *de'ad de'ika shinui* — until there is some kind of *shinui*, a change. As Tosafot understands this, the relevant change is *shinui reshus* — a change of dominion. The worshippers of *avodah zarah* effectively removed themselves from under God's ownership and placed themselves under the control of another power. Applied to *me'ilah*, this is the model for taking possession: removing *hekdesh*'s object from *hekdesh*'s control and bringing it into one's own.

The hatchet case is cited here. If one takes a *hekdesh* hatchet and chops wood with it — *ad de'ika shinui*, until one actually uses it — that constitutes *me'ilah*. Now, reading the text as it stands — with the words *veyifchat ufagum* — the case could be understood as deriving benefit accompanied by *pagam*, since a hatchet does suffer some depreciation through use. That reading would align the hatchet case with the *sotah* model of benefit with accompanying loss. Tosafot, however, prefers to remove those words and read the hatchet case instead as an illustration of taking possession, consistent with the *avodah zarah* model. The difficulty with Tosafot's reading is that the *avodah zarah* comparison then needs to explain what the "change" is — where in the *avodah zarah* context is there a parallel to benefit with loss? The answer, rough as it is, is that the people's shift of allegiance constitutes the relevant *shinui*.

What makes the hatchet case particularly useful is that it forces clarity about what constitutes the act of "stealing" from *hekdesh*. If one declares a hatchet *hekdesh* and then picks it up and carries it into another room, has one stolen it? *Hekdesh* belongs to God everywhere; moving it does not obviously change its ownership. The act of actually using it — chopping wood with it — is the clearest demonstration of taking possession for oneself. This question of when exactly an act of stealing from *hekdesh* crystallizes is treated more fully in the next *Mishnah*.

### Hatchet Case

The hatchet case sits at the intersection of the two models. On one reading — maintaining the words *veyifchat ufagum* — it is a case of benefit with accompanying loss: the hatchet depreciates through use, and so both *hana'ah* and *pagam* are present in the same object, which is the paradigm of *me'ilah* by objects that normally depreciate. On Tosafot's reading — understanding the hatchet case through the *avodah zarah* model — it is a case of taking possession, with the act of chopping serving as the demonstrable assertion of ownership over what belongs to *hekdesh*.

The two readings are not as far apart as they initially appear. Both identify the act of use as the moment of *me'ilah*. The question is whether that use is primarily characterized as deriving benefit (possibly with loss) or as claiming dominion. As we will see, these two tracks are not fully separable, and indeed they must ultimately be unified conceptually because they combine toward the *shiur* of a *perutah*.

### Terumah Model

From *terumah* the Gemara learns: *mah terumah ki yochal prat l'mazik* — just as eating *terumah* incurs an obligation while merely damaging it does not fall under that *parsha*, so too with *hekdesh*. Rashi and Tosafot clarify that this principle is not limited to things that are edible; the point is a structural one. *Me'ilah* is not constituted by damage. Deliberately destroying *hekdesh* is a separate discussion and may be a separate prohibition, but it is not *me'ilah*. *Me'ilah* is fundamentally about taking — taking benefit, taking possession — for oneself. The *pagam* may sometimes be a necessary accompaniment to the *hana'ah* that defines *me'ilah*, but *pagam* alone, without benefit, is simply not in the category.

---

## Unifying Me'ilah

### Both Tracks Combine

The discussion now turns to the relationship between the two tracks. One might suppose that the *hana'ah* model and the taking-possession model are simply two parallel definitions of *me'ilah* that operate independently. But a closer look reveals that this cannot be quite right. We know that half a *perutah* of benefit and half a *perutah* of taking-possession combine to constitute the *shiur* of *me'ilah*. If one derives *hana'ah* worth half a *perutah* — say, by wearing a *me'ilah* ring — and separately takes possession of a *hekdesh* object worth half a *perutah*, the two combine. This means the two tracks cannot be conceptually sealed off from each other; they must share some common underlying definition, because halakhically they are treated as portions of the same act.

### Conceptual Definition

How then to unify them? The *Acharonim* have proposed different framings. One approach is to define everything as a form of stealing: one can steal by adding an object to one's possessions, or one can "steal" the benefit by using it. Another approach is to define everything through the lens of *hana'ah*: one derives benefit by wearing something or using something, and one derives benefit by adding *hekdesh*'s property to one's own assets. Both framings attempt to find a single conceptual core from which both tracks flow, recognizing that the two are two faces of the same underlying *me'ilah* — the diversion of *hekdesh*'s value or identity for oneself. The force of the point is that even half of each is enough, which makes the unification not merely academic but *halakhically* operative.

---

## Benefit & Loss

### Golden Necklace

The *Mishnah* presents a paradigm case for *me'ilah* without *pagam*: wearing a golden necklace. Gold, when worn as jewelry, does not depreciate; there is no wear and tear accompanying the use. Therefore the *hana'ah* alone — without any *pagam* — constitutes *me'ilah*. This is the category governed by the *sotah* model.

### Gold Depreciation

Rav Kahana raises a challenge to Rav Zvid: *ve-dahava lav bar ifkumei hu*? Is gold truly immune from depreciation? He invokes a vivid real-world example: the gold jewelry of the daughter-in-law of a certain Nun — he gave them a great deal of gold, and over time it seems to have worn away considerably. Clearly gold does suffer loss over time.

Rav Zvid's response is instructive: *dilma de-hava de-ramya a-khalsaiya* — perhaps what we are speaking of is gold that is simply left strewn about and exposed, not treated properly. Under normal conditions of careful use, gold jewelry does not visibly or appreciably depreciate.

### Depreciation Timeframe

The Gemara adds a further and more halakhically pointed clarification: *ve-od nehi de-lo it-hazya pegima le-alter* — even granting that gold may eventually depreciate over decades, the critical principle is that the loss must occur within the timeframe of normal usage in order to create a *pagam* requirement. If gold depreciates only over twenty years of wear, then within the period during which one actually wears the piece of jewelry — the minutes or hours in question — there is no depreciation. The *me'ilah* requires *pagam* only for objects where the normal act of benefit is routinely accompanied by visible, measurable depreciation within a reasonable period of use. An object that depreciates only imperceptibly over very long periods does not fall into the category where *pagam* is required alongside *hana'ah*; there, *hana'ah* alone suffices.

This stands in contrast to, say, a garment. The assumption is that every wearing of a garment diminishes its value by some increment, even if the individual decrement is so small as to be almost unmeasurable in practice. The point is not that one can produce an invoice showing precisely how much value was lost per wearing; the point is that the assumption of depreciation attaches to garments as a category. Gold jewelry, under normal conditions, does not carry that assumption.

---

## Live vs Dead Korban

### Unblemished Korban

The last case of the *Mishnah* discusses *me'ilah* from a live *chatat*. The *Mishnah*'s rule is that when one derives benefit from a live *chatat*, the *me'ilah* requires accompanying *pagam*. But this requires explanation. The Gemara asks: *nichze* — let us examine this. If the animal is unblemished (*temimah*), then, says the Gemara, it is equivalent to the golden cup — a paradigm of benefit without loss. And what does that mean? After all, the physical reality is that using an animal — riding it, for instance — does cause it to depreciate in value whether it is *tamim* or a *ba'al mum*.

The answer lies in understanding what *me'ilah* is conceptually tracking. If the animal is *tamim* — unblemished, destined to serve as a *korban* on the *mizbeach* — then *hekdesh* suffers no loss from its diminished market value. Whether the animal is worth a thousand dollars or nine hundred and ninety-nine, the *mizbeach* still gets its *korban*. The Ravad raises the point that perhaps the *kohanim*'s portion (e.g., the hide) might be slightly affected, but the fundamental principle holds: the *mizbeach* gets what it needs regardless. *Hekdesh*, conceptually, is not losing anything when one uses an unblemished *korban* in a way that slightly reduces its monetary value.

This is a crucial conceptual point: the requirement of *pagam* in *me'ilah* is not simply tracking the physical reality of depreciation in the world. It is tracking whether *hekdesh* conceptually suffers a loss. When that concept has no purchase — when there is no way in which we think of *hekdesh* as losing — then *pagam* is not required, and *hana'ah* alone suffices.

### Blemished Korban

Rav Papa provides the answer: the *Mishnah* is speaking of an animal with a *mum*. An animal with a blemish must be redeemed — its sacred status is converted into monetary value through the process of *pidyon*, and those funds are then used for another *korban*. When an animal with a *mum* is used and thereby diminished in value, *hekdesh* does concretely lose something measurable: instead of selling the animal for a thousand dollars, it will sell it for nine hundred and ninety-nine. We are now dealing with dollar signs, with fungible value, and *hekdesh*'s account, so to speak, will reflect the lower figure.

One might object: in the end, that money still goes toward another *korban* and eventually to the *mizbeach*, so how is *hekdesh* truly losing? The answer is subtle and important. It is not even necessarily about *hekdesh*'s ultimate financial outcome; it is about the conceptual register in which we view the object. When an animal has a *mum* and will be redeemed, we look at it and see dollar signs — a monetary value, a market price. In that register, depreciation of value is a real loss, even if in the long run those dollars remain within the sacred system. When an animal is *tamim* and will be offered as-is on the *mizbeach*, we do not look at it through a monetary lens; we look at it as a *korban*. In that register, the concept of loss through depreciation simply does not apply.

This framework implies something important about *kelei sharet* and similar objects. Since a *kli sharet* is always viewed as the thing it is — a sacred vessel — rather than as a monetary asset, loss should arguably be irrelevant to it, and *hana'ah* alone should suffice to constitute *me'ilah*. That case may be distinguishable, though the logic points in that direction.

### Dead Korban

A dead *korban* likewise requires only *hana'ah* without *pagam*, and here the reasoning is clear in a different direction. When one derives benefit from a dead *korban*, the physical reality is that using a dead animal is normally accompanied by depreciation — dog food, leather, whatever one extracts from it does diminish the carcass. But from *hekdesh*'s perspective, a dead *korban* has absolutely no value. Once a *korban* dies, it has zero value in *hekdesh*'s ledger. Therefore, the very concept of *hekdesh* suffering a loss is inapplicable, and *me'ilah* reverts to the model of *hana'ah* alone.

What the combination of these three cases — unblemished live animal, blemished live animal, dead animal — demonstrates is that the *pagam* requirement in *me'ilah* is not merely a formal observation about what normally accompanies benefit in the physical world. It is a conceptually sensitive criterion: *pagam* is required when and only when the type of object is one in which *hekdesh*'s loss can be meaningfully conceptualized. Where that conceptualization is impossible or irrelevant, *me'ilah* is defined purely by *hana'ah*.

---

## Shiur Me'ilah

### Half Perutah Rule

The next *Mishnah* (top of 19b) addresses the minimum threshold. *Neheneh k'chezi prutah, pagam k'chezi prutah* — if one derived benefit of half a *perutah* and caused a loss of half a *perutah*, that is not *me'ilah*. *Me'ilah* requires a full *perutah*'s worth of *hana'ah*. Neither half alone, nor both halves together if they occur in different objects, is sufficient.

### Same Object Rule

The *Mishnah* states: *ad sheyeheh neheneh bishveh prutah v'yifgom bishveh prutah bidavar echad* — one is not *mo'el* until one derives benefit of a *perutah* and causes a loss of a *perutah* in the same object. The requirement that benefit and loss occur in the same object is intuitive: if I am wearing a *hekdesh* garment and simultaneously damaging some other *hekdesh* object with my other hand, those are two unrelated acts involving different objects and cannot be combined to constitute a single act of *me'ilah*.

The requirement that the *pagam* itself be worth a *perutah* is more conceptually challenging. On the one hand, *me'ilah* is fundamentally about *hana'ah*, not *pagam*; we have established that *pagam* can be entirely absent in certain categories. Requiring that *pagam* reach the *shiur* of a *perutah* would seem to elevate it to an independent threshold, which sits uneasily with the framework. On the other hand, one might argue that below a *perutah* of loss, we simply have no halakhic means of measuring and therefore cannot say it has truly occurred in any cognizable way.

A practical difficulty also presents itself: in many of the standard cases of *me'ilah*, it is far from obvious that the benefit derived and the depreciation caused are always commensurate and always each reach a *perutah*. A shirt worn briefly may depreciate by a fraction of a fraction of a *perutah*. Must there always be a *perutah* of *pagam* in each case?

### Textual Variants

There is also a significant textual variant in the *Mishnah* itself. Our standard text reads *bishveh prutah* in both phrases: *neheneh bishveh prutah* and *yifgom bishveh prutah*. But many other textual traditions (*girsaot*) read the *Mishnah* with a *bet* only in the second phrase: *neheneh shveh prutah* (without *bet*) and *yifgom bishveh prutah* (with *bet*). On that reading, the first phrase might be understood to say that the *hana'ah* must be worth a *perutah*, while the second phrase — *bishveh prutah* — means "in that *perutah*'s worth of object," describing the locus of the *pagam* rather than its independent monetary threshold. This reading would mean that the requirement is: the benefit must be a *perutah*'s worth, and the *pagam* must occur in that same object — with no independent *perutah* threshold on the *pagam* side. The word *bet* in the second phrase would indicate location, not valuation. It is admittedly a somewhat forced reading, but it has the advantage of keeping *pagam* in its proper conceptual role as an accompaniment to *hana'ah* rather than as an independent threshold. The plain sense of the *Mishnah*, however, does seem to require a *perutah* of each.

---

## No Double Me'ilah

### Kedushah Disappears

A new *Mishnah* introduces the principle: *ein mo'el achar mo'el b'mukdashin ela b'behema v'khli shareis bilvad* — there is no *me'ilah* after *me'ilah* in consecrated objects, except in the case of a *korban* animal or a *kli sharet*. The principle is that the act of *me'ilah* itself de-sanctifies the object. Once one has been *mo'el* in a *hekdesh* object, the object loses its *kedushah*, and subsequent use of that object — even by another person, even immediately afterward — does not constitute another act of *me'ilah*. The *kedushah* has been violated and, in a sense, displaced.

This makes conceptual sense. *Me'ilah* is about trespass, about diverting. If the *kedushah* is understood, at least for most *hekdesh* objects, as a function of *hekdesh*'s ownership, then once that ownership-identity has been violated through *me'ilah*, it naturally dissipates. Such objects — things that *hekdesh* simply owns, things designated for *bedek habayis* or general temple maintenance — are, in their normal existence, candidates for being sold: their *kedushah* is easily transferable and easily removed through the ordinary mechanics of *hekdesh* transactions. Given that their *kedushah* identity is not deeply fixed, a violation through *me'ilah* dislodges it.

### Kedushat Haguf

The exception is *behemah* and *kli sharet* because these possess *kedushat haguf* — intrinsic sanctity. An unblemished *korban* animal is not simply owned by *hekdesh*; it *is* a *korban*. Its identity is sacred. A *kli sharet* is not simply an asset of the temple treasury; it is a sacred vessel, identified as such by its very nature and function. These objects cannot normally be redeemed or transferred out of the sacred domain (absent a *mum* in the case of an animal). Because their *kedushah* is so bound up with their identity, it does not dissolve even when violated. The trespass of *me'ilah* cannot dislodge a *kedushah* that is structural and intrinsic.

The contrast is with *kedushat bizyan*, a kind of proprietary or monetary *kedushah* that attaches to objects by virtue of their being owned by or designated for *hekdesh*. Objects with only *kedushat bizyan* lose their *kedushah* upon *me'ilah*. Objects with *kedushat haguf* retain it.

Tosafot raises a fascinating question about *kelei sharet* specifically: can a *kli sharet* be sold? Can the *Beit HaMikdash* "deaccession" a sacred vessel — remove it from use and sell it? If so, its *kedushah* is in principle transferable and removable, which might suggest it shares more in common with ordinary *hekdesh* property than with *korban* animals, and therefore might lose its *kedushah* through *me'ilah*. The first opinion in the *braisa* takes precisely this position.

Rabbi Nechemiah's response, however, does not dispute that *kelei sharet* might in principle be redeemable. He argues instead from a *kal v'chomer*: since *kelei sharet* have the power to bestow *kedushat haguf* upon their contents — water poured into a temple vessel for the water libation on *Sukkot* acquires *kedushat haguf* — it follows *kal v'chomer* that *kelei sharet* should have at least enough sanctity to retain their own *kedushah* even after *me'ilah*. If it can sanctify others, surely it can preserve itself.

### Multiple Me'ilah Examples

The *Mishnah* provides examples: *rachav agabei behema, uva chaveiro v'rachav* — one rode on a *korban* animal, then another came and rode on it, then another — *kulan ma'alu*, they all committed *me'ilah*, because the animal's *kedushah* persists through each violation. Similarly, *shasa b'khos shel zahav, uva chaveiro v'shasa* — drinking from a golden *kli sharet*, followed by others doing the same — *kulan ma'alu*. And: *talash min hachatas, uva chaveiro v'talash* — one pulled wool from a *chatat*, then another did the same — *kulan ma'alu*, all committed *me'ilah*.

---

## Rabbi's View

### No Pidyon Rule

Rabbi's formulation of the same principle reads: *kol davar she'ein lo pidyon* — anything that cannot be redeemed — *yeish me'ilah achar me'ilah*, is subject to repeated *me'ilah*. Rather than specifying *behemah* and *kelei sharet* by name, Rabbi identifies the structural characteristic: objects that cannot be redeemed retain their *kedushah* through *me'ilah*. Objects that can be redeemed — ordinary *hekdesh* property — do not.

This formulation raises the question of *kelei sharet* once again, and whether they can be redeemed. If they can, Rabbi's formulation would seem to exclude them from *me'ilah achar me'ilah*, which might align with the first *tanna*'s position that only *behemah* is subject to repeated *me'ilah*.

One might also ask whether this principle would extend to birds offered as *korbanot*. A bird with a missing limb (*mechussar eiver*) that cannot be offered as a *korban* might nonetheless have no process of *pidyon* available to it. If so, Rabbi's formulation would seem to include it in the category of *me'ilah achar me'ilah*, even though it falls outside the category of an ordinary *behemah*. That conclusion appears correct under Rabbi's logic.

It is also worth noting the connection between this discussion and the two conceptual tracks of *me'ilah*. The principle that *kedushah* can be dislodged through *me'ilah* makes intuitive sense if one thinks of *me'ilah* primarily as an act of stealing — of asserting rival ownership over *hekdesh* property. When the *kedushah* is primarily about ownership, a direct challenge to that ownership through theft or diversion can unseat it. It is less obvious why deriving *hana'ah* — merely enjoying the object without asserting ownership — should dislodge the *kedushah*. The *Mishnah* does not distinguish; it treats all forms of *me'ilah* as capable of dislodging *kedushah* unless we are dealing with *behemah* or *kelei sharet*.

Tosafot cites a *Tosefta* that does in fact draw this distinction: it suggests that the *me'ilah* of *hana'ah* alone — benefit without an assertion of ownership — does not dislodge *kedushah* from any object, and only the *me'ilah* of taking possession does so. This is conceptually compelling. Our *Mishnah*, however, does not appear to draw that line, and the examples of riding an animal and drinking from a cup, which are clearly cases of *hana'ah*, are stated to cause *kedushah* to persist — not because *hana'ah* failed to dislodge it, but because *behemah* and *kelei sharet* are structurally resistant to dislodgment regardless of the type of *me'ilah*.

---

## Gemara Challenges

### Wood as Korban

The Gemara asks: is not Rabbi's formulation (*kol davar she'ein lo pidyon*) simply the same as the *Mishnah*'s rule (*behemah v'kelei sharet*)? What new case would they actually disagree about? *Amar Rava: ika beinaihu etzim* — the case of wood separates them.

A *braisa* is cited: if one declares "I am obligating myself to provide wood" to the *Beit HaMikdash*, the *tanna kamma* holds that one must provide no fewer than two logs, which are treated as a contribution to *bedek habayis* — regular temple maintenance. Rabbi, however, holds that donated wood constitutes a *korban* — *etzim korban hen* — and as such requires salt (as all *korbanot* require salt) and *hagasha* (touching to the *mizbeach*), analogous to a *mincha* offering. The implication is that Rabbi understands wood offerings as a type of *mincha*, an inanimate offering, and the category of *mincha* is not limited to grain — a remarkable ruling that the *mizbeach* can receive a wood offering as an actual *korban*.

Rava further draws out the implication: *ledivrei Rebbe etzim te'unin etzim* — if you offer wood as a *korban*, it must be burned on wood, raising the question of who provides that wood, and so on. Rav Papa adds: *ledivrei Rebbe etzim t'richin kemitza* — the wood must be processed to allow *kemitza* (the handful-measure used in *mincha* offerings) to be performed on it.

The halakhic relevance to the *me'ilah* debate is this: the *tanna kamma* regards donated wood as *bedek habayis*, which has *pidyon* — it can be redeemed or sold — and therefore *ein me'ilah achar me'ilah* applies to it. Rabbi regards it as a *korban*, which has no *pidyon* while *tamim*, and therefore *yesh me'ilah achar me'ilah* applies. The debate between Rabbi and the *tanna kamma* in the *me'ilah* *Mishnah* is thus not a debate about the parameters of *me'ilah* itself, but about the classification of this specific type of donation. Rav Ashi's resolution: their debate concerns the category of wood, not the structure of *me'ilah*.

### Dead Animal Redemption

Rav Papa offers an alternative resolution. The practical case that distinguishes Rabbi from the *tanna kamma* involves *kodshei mizbeach* animals that began as *temimim*, subsequently acquired a *mum*, and then were slaughtered (or died) before being redeemed. A *braisa* records the debate: Rabbi holds *yikaveru* — they must be buried — while the *chachamim* hold *yifdu* — they can be redeemed.

The underlying question is whether the process of redemption (*pidyon*) for a *korban* with a *mum* requires the animal to be alive — *ha'amada v'ha'aracha* — or whether a dead animal with a *mum* can nonetheless be redeemed. Rabbi holds that redemption requires the animal to be alive; once it has died, it can no longer undergo *pidyon*, and therefore it falls into the category of *davar she'ein lo pidyon*. Consequently, according to Rabbi, even this dead animal is subject to *me'ilah achar me'ilah*. The *chachamim* hold that a dead animal with a *mum* can still be redeemed — its monetary value can be assessed and the funds transferred to *hekdesh* — and therefore it belongs to the category of things that do have *pidyon*, its *kedushah* dissipates upon *me'ilah*, and *me'ilah achar me'ilah* does not apply.

On this reading, the debate between Rabbi and the *tanna kamma* in the *Mishnah* is once again not a dispute about the abstract principles of *me'ilah*, but about a specific question of *pidyon*: can a dead animal that bore a *mum* be redeemed? That question determines whether such an animal's *kedushah* is sticky enough to permit repeated *me'ilah* or not.

---

---

# Meilah 20

## Overview & Setup

### Daf 20 Setup

Daf 20 of *Meilah* marks the culmination of the tractate, with only two dapim remaining. Despite the sense that we have barely gotten started, this daf brings us to the conceptual heart of the material: what precisely constitutes an act of *me'ilah*, and how does the law of *shlichut* operate within that framework.

### Previous Concepts

In the preceding material, we have examined various forms of *me'ilah* — acts through which one derives benefit (*hana'ah*) from consecrated property (*hekdesh*), particularly where such benefit involves a *pegam*, a diminishment of the object. We have also established the principle of *ein me'ilah achar me'ilah*: once an act of *me'ilah* has been committed, the sanctity (*kedushah*) of the object is discharged, and no subsequent act can constitute a second *me'ilah* — with the exception of items possessing *kedushat haguf*, intrinsic sanctity, such as korbanot. With those foundations in place, the Mishnah on 19b turns to a form of *me'ilah* we have not yet fully examined: that of appropriation.

---

## Appropriation & Taking

### Beam Case

The Mishnah on the bottom of 19b introduces the *me'ilah* of appropriation — the act of stealing or taking possession of consecrated property. The Mishnah states: *natal even o karah shel hekdesh, harei zeh lo ma'al* — if one takes a stone or a beam belonging to *hekdesh*, one has not yet committed *me'ilah* — *ad she'nisnah le'chaveiro, hu ma'al ve'chaveiro lo ma'al* — until one gives it to another person. It is the giver who has committed *me'ilah*, not the recipient.

This immediately raises the question: why is the very act of taking not itself *me'ilah*? After all, if one sneaks into *hekdesh*'s warehouse and removes an object, that would seem to be a paradigmatic act of theft. The Gemara will address this as a special case, but even before that discussion, one can appreciate the conceptual difficulty. If one sanctifies a beam — that is, dedicates it to *hekdesh* — and then takes it back, the act of "taking" is not entirely self-evident. Merely having intent to retain the object may not suffice. The Mishnah resolves this by anchoring the act of appropriation in the moment of giving: once the item is handed to another person, one has clearly removed it from *hekdesh*'s domain, and *me'ilah* is established.

The reason the recipient (*chaveiro*) does not commit *me'ilah* is precisely because *ein me'ilah achar me'ilah*: the original actor has already discharged the *kedushah* through the act of giving, and therefore the object is no longer in a state that can generate a second *me'ilah*.

A further conceptual question presents itself: is this form of *me'ilah* — appropriation — categorically distinct from the *hana'ah*-based *me'ilah* we have been studying, or are the two ultimately unified? The Mishnah itself seems to invite a unifying reading: when one gives the beam to a friend, one could characterize that act as deriving *hana'ah* through the disposition of the object — using it to benefit another person, just as one who takes *hekdesh* oil and applies it to a friend's skin commits *me'ilah* through the *hana'ah* of the recipient. Yet the simpler reading is that this is a genuinely distinct category, rooted in the act of taking rather than the act of benefiting. The two modes of *me'ilah* are not entirely separate — we have seen that half a *perutah* of appropriation and half a *perutah* of *hana'ah* combine — but they remain conceptually distinguishable.

### Building in House

The Mishnah continues: *bana'ah betoch beito, harei zeh lo ma'al ad she'yehaneh tachteha be'shveh perutah* — if one built the beam into one's own house, one has not committed *me'ilah* until one derives a *perutah*'s worth of benefit from dwelling beneath it. This seems counterintuitive. Surely building a consecrated beam into one's house is itself an act of possession? The Gemara will ask precisely this question, along with a second objection: even before one dwells beneath the beam, the mere improvement of the house would seem to constitute *hana'ah*. Both of these challenges will be taken up shortly.

### Bathhouse Case

The Mishnah then presents the bathhouse case: *nasno labalan, af al pi shelo rachatz, ma'al* — if one gave *hekdesh* money to the bathhouse attendant (*balan*), even if one did not yet bathe, one has committed *me'ilah*. Why might one have thought otherwise? Because one might reason that until the transaction is complete — that is, until the service is actually rendered — the money has not truly been transferred. In a commercial exchange, handing over money before receiving goods does not finalize the transaction. So perhaps one has not yet fully divested *hekdesh*'s property.

The Mishnah rejects this reasoning. The bathhouse attendant says: *harei ha'merchatz patuach lefanecha, hacheins u'rechotz* — the bathhouse is open before you, enter and bathe. By accepting payment and extending this invitation, the attendant has completed the transaction. The right to enter and bathe is now in the hands of the one who paid, regardless of whether bathing has actually occurred. The transaction is legally binding from the moment of payment, and therefore *me'ilah* is established at that point.

### Combined Benefit

The final passage of the Mishnah in this section — which the Gemara will not extensively analyze — establishes a general principle of combination in *me'ilah*: *achilato ve'achilat chaveiro, hana'ato ve'hana'at chaveiro, achilato ve'hana'at chaveiro, hana'ato ve'achilat chaveiro, mitztarpin zeh im zeh, va'afilu le'zman merubeh* — one's own eating and another's eating, one's own benefit and another's benefit, one's eating and another's benefit, one's benefit and another's eating — all of these combine with one another, even over an extended period of time.

Unlike the *me'ilah* of eating (*achilah*), which is bound by the constraints of a *kezayit* within the time of *toch kedei achilat pras*, the *me'ilah* of *hana'ah* is measured in monetary value — a *perutah* — and can accumulate over time and across multiple recipients. Significantly, this principle applies even when the *hana'ah* accrues to a friend: if one takes *hekdesh* oil and applies it to another person's skin, it is one's own *me'ilah*, even though it is the friend who receives the physical benefit. This brings us back to the conceptual question: is the appropriation-based *me'ilah* of the earlier cases simply a species of *hana'ah*, where handing over the beam to a friend constitutes deriving *hana'ah* through the recipient? That reading would collapse the distinction between the two modes. The alternative — and perhaps more accurate — reading maintains that appropriation is its own form of *me'ilah*, even if the two share certain structural features.

---

## Treasurer Exception

### Shmuel's Answer

The Gemara opens by asking the obvious question: *mai shna hu mai shna chaveiro* — what is the difference between the taker and the recipient? Why must one wait until giving the beam to another person in order to have committed *me'ilah*? Shmuel answers: *be'gizbar ha'mesuros lo askinan* — we are speaking of the temple treasurer (*gizbar*), a functionary who has legitimate authority to handle all of *hekdesh*'s materials.

For the temple treasurer, the very act of picking up an item — even with some personal intent — does not constitute theft, because he is authorized to handle these objects in the ordinary course of his duties. One could imagine that stealing would begin the moment he removes an item from the temple precinct and brings it home; even a warehouse manager who pockets an item from the stockroom has stolen. Yet the Gemara frames it more broadly: since the treasurer maintains ongoing authority over these materials, his possession of them does not constitute a meaningful act of taking. The act of taking only crystallizes when he transfers the item to another party, at which point it is unambiguously removed from *hekdesh*'s sphere.

This also illuminates the case of one who sanctifies an object already in one's own home and then "takes" it back — a scenario in some ways even more conceptually challenging than the treasurer case, since the item was never in the physical possession of *hekdesh* to begin with. The Gemara's framework consistently locates the act of stealing in the transfer to another, rather than in the initial assertion of personal possession.

### Building Question

This leads to the hard middle case: why is building the beam into one's house not itself an act of misappropriation? The Gemara asks, *lama li ad d'dar tachtei* — why must one wait until actually dwelling beneath it? The Gemara offers what appears to be a textual variant: *keivan de'shani, ma'al* — once one has altered the item, one has committed *me'ilah*. Some versions read *de'vana'ah* — once one has built it in. The underlying logic, on either reading, is that a genuine physical act of taking possession — hammering the beam in, plastering it — should constitute *me'ilah* without requiring the additional step of deriving benefit from dwelling beneath it.

---

## Mechubar Lekarka

### Rav's Position

Rav responds: *kegon she'henichah al pi arubah* — the Mishnah is speaking of a case where one merely placed the beam atop a skylight opening, without actually building it into the structure. One has not altered or embedded the beam; it simply sits there. In that case, placing the beam does not yet constitute an act of taking. One is using the beam — deriving some incidental benefit — but one has not yet taken possession of it in the full sense. The act of appropriation requires something more final, and therefore *me'ilah* is not established until one derives measurable *hana'ah*.

This reading is admittedly difficult with respect to the simple meaning (*peshat*) of the word *bana* in the Mishnah, which implies actual building. The Gemara is pulling back from the Mishnah's apparent implication, arguing that even the act of building does not constitute *me'ilah* in the full appropriative sense unless it involves genuine physical integration — and that the Mishnah's case of "building" is actually the intermediate scenario of mere placement.

### Roof Case

The upshot of Rav's position is a conceptual distinction between using and taking. If the treasurer places a *hekdesh* beam on his roof without affixing it, he is using something that does not belong to him — and that use generates *hana'ah* — but he has not yet taken it. Taking requires either giving it to another, or actually integrating it into his property through genuine construction. This is the framework within which the Mishnah's middle case is resolved.

### Visible Benefit

The Gemara now pivots to what it presents as a side question, though it touches on a fundamental issue in the law of *me'ilah*: the distinction between *metaltelin* (chattel) and *mechubar lekarka* (that which is attached to the ground). There is no *me'ilah* with respect to *mechubar lekarka* — items fixed to the earth. This creates an obvious tension: once a beam is built into a house, it becomes attached to the structure, which is in turn attached to the ground. So why would *me'ilah* apply at all once the beam has been integrated?

The Gemara raises the case of one who worships a house (*hamishtachaveh le'vayit asaro*) and notes that Rav holds such a house is considered *metaltelin*, not *karka*. The reasoning draws on a distinction that *mechubar lekarka* may render something immune to certain halachic consequences — just as worshipping a mountain does not make the mountain forbidden, since the Torah says *eloheihem al he'harim ve'lo he'harim eloheihem* — their gods are on the mountains, but the mountains themselves do not become their gods. Things that are genuine *karka* cannot be rendered forbidden by idolatrous worship. But a house, according to Rav, occupies a different status: it is either not truly *mechubar lekarka*, or it is *mechubar lekarka* but not *karka* in the fullest sense, and therefore it retains the status of *metaltelin* and can be affected by such prohibitions.

The relevance to *me'ilah* is direct: if *me'ilah* applies to a consecrated beam built into a house, that implicitly assumes the beam retains *metaltelin* status even after construction. This would support Rav's position.

Rav Acha the son of Rav Ika offers a different answer: *hana'ah hanir'et la'einayim asra Torah* — the Torah prohibits *hana'ah* that is visible and evident to the eye. This is a difficult and somewhat puzzling response. The laws of *mechubar lekarka* are generally formalistic and categorical; it is hard to see how the visibility or obviousness of the benefit should override a categorical determination of attachment. The *mefaresh* essentially accepts the formulation at face value. *Tosafot* integrates it with additional considerations. But on its own, the claim that visible *hana'ah* cuts through the *mechubar lekarka* exemption seems to lack a clear principled basis. After all, dwelling in a cave belonging to *hekdesh* is equally visible a form of benefit, yet a cave is clearly *mechubar lekarka* and produces no *me'ilah*. The Rambam, notably, ignores this answer entirely.

### Sanctified Chattel

The Gemara then cites a *beraita*: *hadar be'vayit shel hekdesh, keivan she'neheneh mimena, ma'al* — one who dwells in a house belonging to *hekdesh*, once one has derived a *perutah*'s worth of benefit, has committed *me'ilah*. This appears to support the position that a house retains *metaltelin* status and is therefore subject to *me'ilah*.

Reish Lakish, however, offers a key qualification: *hatam be'she'hikdisho u'le'vasof bena'o* — that case speaks specifically of a situation where the materials were sanctified first and then the house was built from them. When the stones and beams were consecrated, they were consecrated while still *metaltelin*. That original status — sanctified as chattel, fit for *me'ilah* as chattel — persists even after they are built into a structure.

The Gemara then asks: if that is Reish Lakish's reason, why does the *beraita* use the case of dwelling in a house to demonstrate that there is *no* *me'ilah* when things are *mechubar lekarka*, rather than using the case of a stone house that was built and only subsequently sanctified? The Gemara answers: the *beraita* prefers a categorical case. A cave is categorically and unambiguously *mechubar lekarka* — there is never *me'ilah* for dwelling in a cave. A stone house presents a more complex picture: sometimes there is *me'ilah*, sometimes there is not, depending on the sequence of sanctification and construction. The *beraita* prefers the clean case.

The resolution, then, is twofold. Either one follows Rav's position that anything beginning as *metaltelin* retains that status even when built into the ground, in which case there is no difficulty at all. Or, setting aside Rav's general position, the more specific answer is that when an item is sanctified while still in *metaltelin* form, it retains its candidacy for *me'ilah* even after it is integrated into a permanent structure. The *nir'eh la'einayim* answer, by contrast, appears strained and is not accepted by the Rambam.

---

## Shlichut & Agency

### Shlichut Intro

With the basic acts of *me'ilah* established, the Mishnah introduces the final *perek* of the tractate: the law of *shlichut* in *me'ilah*. Normally, *ein shaliach le'dvar aveirah* — an agent cannot be appointed to perform a transgression; if one instructs another to commit a sin, it is the agent's sin, not the sender's. *Me'ilah*, however, is an exception: the act of an agent can be attributed to the sender. This exception has a structural parallel to the *hana'ah*-based *me'ilah* we have already seen — just as one who takes *hekdesh* oil and applies it to another person's skin commits *me'ilah* through the recipient's benefit, so too when one sends an agent and the agent acts, the sender remains the causal factor. The agent's act can suffice to generate the sender's liability.

It should be noted that the standard case of *me'ilah* throughout this discussion is *be'shogeg* — an act of inadvertence, where the person genuinely believed the object was permitted. That is the case in which one brings a *korban* and adds a fifth. The cases of *shlichut* we are about to examine likewise envision inadvertent misappropriation.

### Liver vs Meat

The Mishnah states: *ha'shaliach she'asah shlichuto, ba'al ha'bayit ma'al* — if the agent fulfilled his agency, it is the sender who has committed *me'ilah*. *Lo asah shlichuto, ha'shaliach ma'al* — if he violated his agency, it is the agent who has committed *me'ilah*.

The Mishnah provides an illustration: *amar lo ten basar le'orchin* — the homeowner instructs his servant to give meat to the guests, and that meat happens to be *korban* meat — perhaps *basar kodshei kodashim lifnei zerikat damim*, or *olah* meat — which the homeowner did not realize. The agent, however, gives them liver (*kaved*) instead, or conversely, the owner said liver and the agent gave meat. In either case, *ha'shaliach ma'al* — the agent has committed *me'ilah*. Liver is not meat; when one says "give them meat," one intends the standard cut of flesh, not internal organs. The agent has therefore acted on his own initiative, beyond the scope of his instructions, and the *me'ilah* is his.

### Portions Case

The Mishnah then presents a more complex case: the homeowner instructs his servant to give each guest one piece of meat (*ten lahem chatichah chatichah*). The servant tells the guests to each take two (*telu shtayim shtayim*), and the guests themselves take three (*ve'hem natlu shalosh shalosh*). The Mishnah rules that *kulam ma'alu* — all three parties have committed *me'ilah*: the homeowner for the first piece, which was distributed according to his instructions; the agent for the second piece, which he offered on his own authority; and the guests for the third piece, which they took on their own initiative.

As with the beam case, the *me'ilah* here appears to be established at the moment of taking, before anyone has necessarily consumed anything. This reinforces the understanding that appropriation — the act of taking possession and removing from *hekdesh*'s domain — is itself a valid form of *me'ilah*.

---

## Shlichut vs Category

### Rav Chisda

The Gemara opens by identifying the underlying principle of the liver-versus-meat case and asking whose opinion it reflects. The question is: *man tanna de'chol milsa de'mimlach alei shaliach tartei milei havyan* — who is the *tanna* who holds that anything about which an agent would need to consult with his sender (*mimlach aleh shaliach*) is considered a categorically different item?

The assumption is that liver and meat share this character: if sent to procure meat and only liver is available, the agent would return and ask — do you want liver instead? This is not the same as asking whether to bring a completely unrelated item; it is a gray-zone substitute, close enough to require inquiry, but not so close as to be automatically included. The Gemara posits that our Mishnah — which treats the agent's substitution of liver for meat as a violation of his *shlichut* — reflects the view of the *chachamim* who dispute Rabbi Akiva, and not Rabbi Akiva himself.

Rav Chisda articulates this: *amr Rav Chisda de'la ke'Rabbi Akiva* — our Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Akiva. The relevant dispute concerns one who vows to abstain from vegetables (*hanoder min ha'yerek*): the *chachamim* rule that gourds (*diluim*) are not included in such a vow, while Rabbi Akiva rules that they are forbidden. The *chachamim*'s reasoning, as spelled out in that Mishnah, is precisely the *mimlach* principle: if you send your agent to the market to buy vegetables and there are no vegetables, he will return and ask, "there were no vegetables — shall I bring gourds?" That question indicates that gourds are not simply "vegetables," even if they share a family resemblance. Rabbi Akiva disagrees: the fact that the agent asks about gourds rather than about, say, meat, shows that gourds are close enough to vegetables to fall within the category. Similarly, liver and meat occupy this gray zone.

### Abaye's Refinement

Abaye offers a striking refinement: *afilu teima Rabbi Akiva* — one could say our Mishnah reflects even Rabbi Akiva's view. The key is to distinguish between two different questions that the *mimlach* principle answers. In the context of *nedarim*, the question is categorical: does the gray-zone item fall within the defined category of the vow? Rabbi Akiva says yes — gourds are vegetables, liver is meat. The *chachamim* say no. That debate is about classification.

In the context of *shlichut*, the question is different: it is not about category, but about the proper conduct of an agent. Even Rabbi Akiva would agree that when an item falls into the gray zone, the agent is *expected to ask* before substituting. The agent's failure to ask — his decision to go ahead and give liver when instructed to give meat — is what constitutes a violation of his agency. The *mimlach* principle in *shlichut* is not about whether liver counts as meat; it is about whether the agent acted within the reasonable scope of his commission. He should have checked in. Since he did not, he acted on his own, and the *me'ilah* is his.

### Rava Approves

When the Rabbis (here meaning Rava's students) reported Abaye's reasoning to Rava, Rava responded: *shapir ka'amar Nachmani* — Nachmani spoke well. (*Nachmani* being Abaye's name, or at least one of the names by which he was known — whether it was his proper name or a later appellation is a matter of discussion.) Rava's endorsement of Abaye's distinction is notable; Rava does not frequently align himself with Abaye's positions.

The upshot is a clean analytical distinction: the question of whether an agent violates his *shlichut* is independent of the question of how to classify items for purposes of a vow. Even if Rabbi Akiva categorizes liver as falling within "meat," he would still agree that an agent who substitutes liver for meat without asking has stepped outside his commission. The *shlichut* bounds are violated not by category error, but by failure to consult.

---

## Meat Classification

### Rabbi Akiva

The Gemara now turns to identify who among the *tannaim* disputes Rabbi Akiva in the classification debate, associating that position with a specific named authority. The *beraita* cited is as follows: *ha'noder min ha'basar assur be'chol minei basar* — one who vows to abstain from meat is forbidden all types of meat. This includes: the head (*rosh*), feet (*raglayim*), trachea (*kaneh*), liver (*kaved*), heart (*lev*), all internal organs, and the meat of fowl (*basar of*). The one thing excluded is fish flesh and grasshoppers (*basar dagim ve'chagavim*). This first position — which implicitly is that of Rabbi Akiva — takes an expansive view: even items that require inquiry fall within the category of "meat," with only the most obviously distinct items (fish and grasshoppers) excluded.

### R. Shimon b. Gamliel

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel takes a far more restrictive view: *mattir be'rosh u've'raglayim u've'kaneh u've'kaved u've'of u've'dagim ve'chagavim* — the head, feet, trachea, liver, fowl, fish, and grasshoppers are all excluded from the vow. Why? Because all of these are items about which the agent would need to ask. They fall in the gray zone, and the gray zone is, for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, outside the category. He reinforces this position with a characteristically sharp remark: *kerevayim lav basar hen ve'ochleihem lav bar inash* — internal organs are not real meat, and those who eat them are not really human. They belong to dog food, not to the human table. While this strengthens his specific claim about internal organs, it sits somewhat uneasily with his broader theoretical principle, since the most extreme examples are not what drives his general rule.

### Fish Challenge

The Gemara raises a challenge to the first opinion (Rabbi Akiva): *mai shna de'vasar of mishum de'ragil inish de'amar lo ashkach bisra de'chayusa va'asai bisra de'tzipra* — why is fowl included within "meat"? The reason offered is that an agent would plausibly say, "I could not find red meat (*bisra de'chayusa*), but I brought chicken." That substitution makes sense; chicken is a recognizable substitute for meat. But if that is the logic, the Gemara continues, someone might equally say, "I could not find red meat, but I brought fish." By the same reasoning, fish should also be included in the category — yet even Rabbi Akiva excludes fish.

### Rav Papa

Rav Papa resolves this by relocating the entire question into specific contextual settings. The cases under discussion are not generic meals, but medically defined situations. When one has undergone bloodletting (*hakkazat dam*), the dietary expectations are sharply constrained. On a day of bloodletting, one would eat only serious red meat — not fish, because fish is simply not what one eats on such a day. And therefore, in the context of a vow made on such a day, the word "meat" clearly encompasses chicken (since one might reasonably substitute chicken for red meat even on a bloodletting day) but not fish.

The Gemara challenges even this: if one would not eat fish on a bloodletting day, one would also not eat fowl on such a day. Shmuel himself states that *damsuchar*, one who has had blood drawn from the shoulders, and then eats fowl, *parach libei ke'tzipra* — his heart will fly away like a bird — meaning it is medically inadvisable. A *beraita* likewise rules that one should not let blood in preparation for eating fish or fowl. Therefore, on a bloodletting day, both fish and fowl would be excluded from one's intended "meat."

Rav Papa then shifts to a second setting: *biyoma de'cha'ivei lei einei* — on a day that one's eyes are hurting. On such a day, people would not eat fish (fish was considered harmful for eye ailments), and therefore "meat" on that day would encompass fowl but not fish. This contextual resolution, while specific, provides a principled basis for treating fowl and fish differently within the vow's scope.

The entire digression, it should be noted, is subsidiary to the main point established by Abaye and endorsed by Rava: that regardless of these classification disputes, the *shlichut* question is separate. Even Rabbi Akiva, even Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — all would agree that when an agent substitutes one item for another in a gray-zone situation without inquiring, he has violated his *shlichut*, and the *me'ilah* falls on him rather than on the sender.

---

## Partial Violation

### Agency Validity

The Gemara returns to the case of the escalating portions — one piece ordered, two offered by the agent, three taken by the guests — and presses the conceptual question more sharply. If the agent gives more than was ordered, should that not completely negate the *shlichut* altogether? Perhaps one ought to say: two is categorically different from one. The agent who hands out two pieces is not doing the homeowner's bidding at all; he is doing his own thing entirely. In that case, not only is the second piece the agent's *me'ilah*, but the first piece should also be his — the homeowner would never be *mo'el* at all.

### Rav Sheshet

Rav Sheshet answers by limiting the scope of the case: *de'amar shliach tol achas mi'da'ato ve'achas mi'da'ati* — the case is where the agent explicitly tells the guests: one piece is from the homeowner, one piece is from me. When the agent makes this delineation explicit — one steak he hands out on behalf of the *ba'al ha'bayit*, one steak he adds from his own initiative — there is no question of the two being conflated. The first piece is the homeowner's transaction, carried out faithfully. The second piece is the agent's own action. The *me'ilah* for the first falls on the homeowner, and the *me'ilah* for the second falls on the agent.

This parallels a broader halachic question, discussed in *Kesuvot*, about agency in purchases: if one sends an agent to purchase one *amah* of land and the agent purchases two, is the sale binding for the first *amah*? The clean answer is yes — where the agent clearly separates the two transactions — but the question itself indicates that under ambiguous circumstances, one might argue that the agent's overreach undermines even the portion he was authorized to perform.

### Agency Preserved

The *mashmah lan* — the novelty of the Mishnah's ruling — is that even when the agent goes beyond his instructions, the *shlichut* is not entirely negated. Provided the agent delineates clearly — "this one is on the homeowner, this one is on me" — the original commission remains intact. The homeowner's *me'ilah* for the first piece is not undermined by the agent's independent action regarding the second. And *kol she'ken* — all the more so — if the agent had not explicitly said anything but simply handed out an extra piece, the presumption would be that the first piece was still carried out on behalf of the homeowner. The Gemara casts this as the primary *chiddush* of the Mishnah: overreach does not collapse the underlying *shlichut*, as long as the authorized portion remains separable. This discussion sets the stage for the concluding material of the tractate, which will continue to develop the relationship between *shlichut* and *me'ilah* in this framework of taking and appropriation.

---

---

# Meilah 21

## Opening & Ravad

### Intro to Daf 21

We begin at the final *daf* of Masechet Meilah, daf 21a, completing our study of the laws of *me'ilah* — the misappropriation of consecrated property. Before turning to the new *mishnah*, two observations from the previous session deserve elaboration, as both bear directly on what follows.

### Ravad's Expansion

The first concerns the Ravad's understanding of the principle governing when an act of removal from *hekdesh* constitutes *me'ilah*. The point discussed earlier — that merely moving consecrated property from one location to another does not constitute the act of stealing from *hekdesh*, and that *me'ilah* requires transferring the object to a third party — is not limited to the *gizbar* (the Temple treasurer). The Ravad states explicitly that this principle applies to anyone who has an established right to handle the property. So long as such a person is moving it within the scope of his authority, that act alone is not *me'ilah*. The *me'ilah* occurs only when the item is transferred out of his control entirely. The Ravad makes the obvious qualification that if someone enters a Temple storehouse without any right to be there and removes an item, the act of taking itself is *me'ilah* — no transfer to a third party is needed. But within the domain of one who has the right to handle the property, the principle stands.

### Shlichus Yad vs Rights

This is significant for the cases we are about to read, which do not appear to involve a *gizbar* specifically yet operate under the same principle: that mere handling is not *me'ilah* for those with a right to the property. It is worth noting the contrast with the concept of *shlichus yad* — where a *shomer* (guardian) who takes an object under his care for personal use commits an act of misappropriation through that very act of intention and movement. In the laws of *me'ilah*, however, for one who has a genuine right to access the property, that threshold is insufficient. An overt act of transferring the object out of one's control — giving it to someone else — is required.

### Rambam on Kedusha Loss

The second preliminary point concerns a ruling of the Rambam based on the *Tosefta*, which was mentioned earlier and now can be stated more precisely. The principle that an object loses its *kedushah* after *me'ilah* has occurred — and thereby passes into *chullin* — applies, the Rambam rules, only to the *me'ilah* of stealing, not to the *me'ilah* of mere benefit. If one merely warms himself with consecrated wool, for example, that act of benefit constitutes *me'ilah* and requires atonement, but it does not strip the object of its *kedushah*. The *kedushah* is removed only when the object is taken and given to another — an act of dispossession. This makes conceptual sense: since the *kedushah* of *bedek habayis* is fundamentally a matter of ownership, the act most capable of severing that ownership relation is giving the object away. Passive benefit, though prohibited, lacks the power to effect that severance.

The Ravad disagrees with this ruling, maintaining that the Rambam has derived it from the *Tosefta* against the weight of normative *halachah*. Nonetheless, the conceptual framework the Rambam articulates is striking and illuminating. An act of *shinui* — transformation, such as building a beam into a wall — could also constitute a form of "stealing" in this sense, which connects to the earlier *gemara*'s discussion of the beam. Whether a full *perutah* of *pagam* and a full *perutah* of *hana'ah* are each independently required remains, for now, an open question.

---

## Shaliach & Window/Box

### Intro to Shaliach

We now turn to the *mishnah* at the top of daf 21a, which belongs to the chapter known as *HaShaliach She'asah* — the *shaliach* who fulfilled his agency. The entire chapter is built around the question of when agency in *me'ilah* is operative. This is not the ordinary case of agency for benefit — if one simply instructs another to eat some consecrated meat and he does so, that is the agent's benefit and the agent's *me'ilah*. The *me'ilah* framework of this chapter is specifically about acts of dispossession — taking *hekdesh* property and transferring it elsewhere. Since the agent performs that act on behalf of the one who sent him, it is attributed to the sender. This is the conceptual foundation for why *shlichus* functions here at all, and the chapter probes its limits case by case.

### Window/Box Case

*Amar lo* — he said to him: bring me from the window or from the *dluskema* (a box or cabinet), and the agent did as instructed. Even if the *ba'al habayis* later says, "I only meant the other window" or "the other box," the rule is *devarim shebelev einam devarim* — one's unexpressed intentions are legally irrelevant. Since the agent did exactly what was said, the act is attributed to the sender and the *ba'al habayis* is *mo'el*.

A question arises: if the agent merely moved the object from one location to another and delivered it to the sender, where precisely is the act of *me'ilah*? The most natural answer is that unlike a *gizbar*, an ordinary person has no right to be handling consecrated property at all, and therefore the very act of taking it is *me'ilah*. However, the context of the case — which seems to imply the sender does have some relationship to the property — creates hesitation about reducing *me'ilah* to a bare act of moving. Tosafos ultimately suggests that the *me'ilah* is located in the subsequent act of transferring the item to a third party. That resolution, while technically coherent, sidesteps the question of how the intermediate act is characterized.

### Act of Meilah Location

The general principle that emerges is that there is a strong reluctance throughout this chapter to identify the act of *me'ilah* with mere movement or taking. Even in cases where one who does not have a right to the property is involved, the *gemara* gravitates toward requiring some more definitive act of dispossession. This tension runs through all the subsequent cases as well.

### Shaliach Deviation

The *mishnah* then presents the contrasting case: *aval im amar lo* — but if he said to him, bring from the window, and he brought from the box; or bring from the box, and he brought from the window — then *hashaliach ma'al*, the agent is the one who committed *me'ilah*. Even if the two locations are functionally equivalent and the items are identical in kind, any deviation from the precise instructions given breaks the chain of agency. The agent is no longer acting on the sender's behalf; he acted on his own initiative, and the act of *me'ilah* is his. The precise location at which the dispossession from *hekdesh* occurs in these cases remains somewhat ambiguous — the same underlying tension applies — but the attribution is clear: the agent, not the sender, bears responsibility.

---

## Cheresh/Shoteh/Katan

### Incompetent Agents

The *mishnah* proceeds to a remarkable case: *shalach beyad cheresh shoteh vekatan* — one sent the *hekdesh* money through a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, or a minor. Ordinarily, these three categories — collectively called *cheresh shoteh vekatan* — are not *bnei da'as*, not legally competent persons, and cannot serve as agents for any purpose. If one appoints such a person as a *shaliach* to separate *terumah*, to deliver a *get*, or to effect *kiddushin*, the act is void. There is no *shlichus*.

Yet here the *mishnah* rules: *im asu shlichuto* — if they carried out what he sent them to do, *ba'al habayis ma'al* — the sender is *mo'el*. Conversely, *lo asu shlichuto* — if they did not follow his instructions, *chanvani ma'al* — the storekeeper is *mo'el* when he subsequently spends the money.

The scenario the *mishnah* envisions is that the sender gave the incompetent person money and instructed him to go to the market and purchase something. If the person did exactly that, the act is attributed to the sender as if he had done it himself. If the person deviated — say, purchasing something other than what was requested — then the sending cannot be attributed to the sender at all. Since the intermediary cannot bear personal responsibility by virtue of his incompetence, and since the act is not attributed to the sender, the *mo'el* becomes the storekeeper at the moment he accepts and spends the money.

### Gemara Question

The *gemara* immediately raises the obvious question: *v'ha lav bnei shlichus ninhu* — these individuals are not legally capable of being agents! How can the *mishnah* treat their actions as the sender's *me'ilah*?

This question has broad ramifications. The particular character of *me'ilah* must be examined to understand how agency here operates at all. The underlying conceptual point is that *me'ilah* in this chapter is not about benefit but about removal — having *hekdesh* property redirected away from its sacred purpose. The question is therefore not whether these individuals can serve as agents in the technical legal sense, but whether their actions, when done according to the sender's instructions, can be causally attributed to him as the one who initiated and directed the removal. The *gemara* will now explore this through analogy.

One important ramification of the framework presented by the *mishnah*: the storekeeper who receives the money from the incompetent intermediary may be completely innocent. He has no way of knowing that the money is *hekdesh*, that the intermediary is incompetent, or that the sender has no idea the transaction is taking place. Yet the *mishnah* holds him *mo'el* when he spends the money. This is a case of virtually pure *ones* — compulsion or blamelessness — and yet *me'ilah* attaches. The *mefaresh* notes this explicitly, as we shall see.

Before reaching the *gemara*'s two proposed analogies, it is worth noting the broader structure of the case when a fully competent *shaliach* is involved. If I send a competent adult and he does what I said, I am *mo'el*. If he does not follow my instructions, he is *mo'el*. This is the standard framework established earlier in the chapter.

### Olives Analogy

Rabbi Elazar offers the first attempt at explaining why the incompetent messenger's act can be attributed to the sender: *asam k'ma'atan shel zeisim* — he made them like a vat of olives. The reference is to the *halachah* regarding when olives become susceptible to *tumah*. Olives become susceptible once liquid has touched them under conditions where the owner desires that liquid contact. The *mishnah* teaches: *misheyaz'u* — from when they sweat in the vat. When olives are collected into a carrying basket, the liquid that seeps out is unwanted; but once placed in the pressing vat, the owner wants the oil to begin flowing. The sweating that occurs in the vat — without any direct human action, simply by virtue of being placed there according to the owner's will — renders the olives susceptible to *tumah*.

Rabbi Elazar's point: sometimes an act is attributed to you not because you did it directly, but because it occurred according to your will, within a situation you deliberately created. Here too, the sender deliberately directed these individuals and they acted according to his will — that is sufficient to attribute the act to him.

Tosafos, however, finds this analogy strained. In the case of the olives, no action was ever conceptually required in the first place. The question from the beginning was simply whether the seeping liquid is desired, and the answer depends entirely on the owner's will. There was never a framework of "action" to be replaced by "causation." The analogy therefore fails to address the core difficulty: how does one's causal initiative substitute for a legally constituted act of agency?

### Monkey/Elephant Proof

Rabbi Yochanan offers a superior proof: *k'hahu de-tanina* — as we learned in *Eruvin*. If one placed his *eiruv techumin* on the back of a monkey and the monkey carried it to the designated spot, or placed it on an elephant and the elephant transported it — *harei zeh eiruv*, it counts as a valid *eiruv*.

This is a compelling parallel. The monkey and elephant are not agents in any legal sense. They cannot be appointed, they have no legal standing, and yet the *eiruv* is valid because the owner's item was transported to the correct location through the owner's initiative. *Alma ka-avid shlichuteih* — we see from here that "acting through your agency" does not require a legally competent agent; it requires only that the act was accomplished through your causal initiative, in accordance with your intent. *Hacha nami avid shlichuteih* — here too, when the incompetent messenger does what he was sent to do, it is as if the sender acted.

### Tosafos Challenge

Tosafos raises a complication: there is another *gemara* in *Eruvin* that appears to rule that placing an *eiruv* on a monkey or elephant does *not* work. How are these two passages reconciled?

Tosafos first suggests that the case in which it works is when another person was stationed at the destination to receive the *eiruv* and take it off the animal — and this is the parenthetical clause in the *gemara*: *ve-amar le-acher lekabbelo mimenu* ("and he told another to receive it from it"). But Tosafos then notes that this resolution undermines Rabbi Yochanan's proof entirely: if the reason it works is that a second person performed a meaningful act at the end, then it is that second person's act — not the monkey's conveyance — that makes the *eiruv* valid. The proof would not demonstrate anything about acting through a non-agent.

Tosafos therefore revises the answer: the distinction between the two *gemaros* in *Eruvin* is that in one case the animal simply wandered off on its own or the *eiruv* fell off without the owner observing, whereas in the other case the owner was watching as the *eiruv* was placed down — so his involvement and awareness at the moment of placement constitute sufficient participation to attribute the act to him. The upshot is that causal involvement must meet some minimum threshold of active engagement; not every attenuated chain of causation suffices. But where that threshold is met — where one sets the process in motion and it unfolds as intended — the act is attributed to him even without the formal apparatus of *shlichus*.

### Causal Involvement

This framework — attribution through causal initiative rather than through formal agency — is what allows *me'ilah* to function here even where *ein shaliach li-dvar aveirah* ("there is no agency for a sinful act") would ordinarily block it. The reason that rule does not apply here is that *me'ilah* in this chapter is not conceptualized primarily as a sin committed by the sender; it is conceptualized as the *effect* of having *hekdesh* property removed or misdirected through the sender's initiative. If that effect came about through his direction and because of his actions — whether through a competent adult, an incompetent messenger, or even a trained animal — he is the one who caused the removal, and the *me'ilah* is his.

A parallel noted in the *gemara*: if one takes consecrated oil and pours it on another person, it is the pourer — not the person who absorbed the benefit — who is *mo'el*, even though the other person received the benefit. The causal act of diverting the *hekdesh* property belongs to the one who set it in motion.

---

## Remembering Cases

### Shav Ve'afikeih

The *mishnah* turns to the case where the *ba'al habayis* remembers mid-process that the money he sent is *hekdesh*. The *gemara* introduces the concept of *shav ve'afikeih* — the master can reclaim the *kedushah* by performing *pidyon* (redemption), transferring the *kedushah* from the coin held by the storekeeper onto another object of value, thereby neutralizing the risk of *me'ilah* for the storekeeper when he eventually spends the money. This is possible because the money belongs to *hekdesh*, not to the storekeeper, and *hekdesh* property can be redeemed regardless of whose physical possession it is in.

### Braisa: One Remembers

The *mishnah* states that when the *ba'al habayis* remembers before the *shaliach* reaches the storekeeper, the *chanvani* becomes *mo'el* when he spends the money. But this formulation prompts a challenge from a *braisa*: *nizkar ba'al habayis velo nizkar shaliach* — if the *ba'al habayis* remembers but the *shaliach* does not, *hashaliach mahu* — the *shaliach* is the *mo'el*. That is: once the *ba'al habayis* is removed from the equation by his awareness, the *shaliach* — who is still acting unknowingly — becomes the relevant party. The *shaliach* is not simply an extension of the *ba'al habayis* such that the *ba'al habayis*'s awareness automatically transfers to him. Once the *ba'al habayis* is aware and thus cannot be *mo'el*, and the *shaliach* is still unaware and acting, the *me'ilah* falls on the *shaliach*. Only then, when the *shaliach* gives the money to the *chanvani*, does the question of the *chanvani*'s *me'ilah* arise.

### Both Remember

Rav Sheshet resolves the apparent tension between the *mishnah* and the *braisa*: *matnitin keshenizkeru sheneihem* — the *mishnah* speaks of a case where both the *ba'al habayis* and the *shaliach* remember. When both are aware that the money is *hekdesh*, neither can be *mo'el* — the *ba'al habayis* because he is aware, the *shaliach* because... and here the case becomes curious. Perhaps the *shaliach*, knowing it is *hekdesh*, continues anyway because he feels bound by the instructions of his master. He is aware but proceeds. Even so, since the *ba'al habayis* has been severed from the chain of agency by his awareness, it is not his *me'ilah*. And since the *shaliach* is now acting with knowledge, the *me'ilah* is also not his in the conventional *shogeg* sense. It therefore falls to the *chanvani* when he spends the money.

### Problem of Ones

The discussion surfaces a profound difficulty. In multiple scenarios across this *mishnah*, parties who are entirely blameless — acting in complete ignorance, under what amounts to *ones* — are held liable for *me'ilah*.
