The *chanvani* who receives money from an incompetent messenger has no way of knowing the money is *hekdesh*. The *shaliach* who forgot that the money was *hekdesh* and is carrying out his master's instructions is acting without fault. Yet *me'ilah* attaches to them.

The question of whether *ones* exempts from *me'ilah* was raised earlier, but the *mishnah*'s cases seem to indicate it does not — at least not in the full sense. *Me'ilah* is an act of *beshogeg*, inadvertence, and the *gemara* elsewhere discusses what the punishment for *meizid* (deliberate) *me'ilah* would be. But the framework of *me'ilah* as a *korban*-and-*chomesh* obligation does not appear to require the level of negligence one might expect.

### Mountains/Hair

The *mefaresh* acknowledges this directly by citing the famous *mishnah* in Masechet Chagigah: certain *halachot* are like mountains suspended by a hair — vast in their practical consequences but resting on exceedingly slender scriptural support. The law here — that a *shaliach* who acted entirely as instructed is *mo'el* simply because the *ba'al habayis* happened to remember — falls into this category. As the *mefaresh* puts it: *deshaliach anya da mai ka'avid* — what did this poor *shaliach* do? He was simply following his master's instructions. Yet he is *mo'el*. This is the reality of the *halachah*, even though it is genuinely difficult to justify intuitively. The *gemara* acknowledges the difficulty and does not resolve it away; it is a *halachah* like mountains suspended by a hair, binding but not easily rationalized.

---

## Partial Fulfillment

### Half/Half Case

The *mishnah* now presents a series of cases involving partial fulfillment of instructions, exploring when the *shaliach*'s deviation from his mandate makes him the *mo'el* and when the *ba'al habayis* retains that status for the portion of the instructions that was followed.

The first case: *natan lo perutah* — he gave him one *perutah*. He said: spend half on oil lamps and half on wicks. The *shaliach* went and spent the entire *perutah* on wicks alone, or the entire *perutah* on lamps alone. Alternatively: he instructed him to spend it all on wicks or all on lamps, and the *shaliach* split it half and half. In both scenarios — *sheneihem lo ma'alu* — neither committed *me'ilah*.

The reasoning: in any of these configurations, for each half-*perutah* unit, either the *ba'al habayis* directed it (so the *me'ilah* would be his) or the *shaliach* acted on his own (so the *me'ilah* would be his). But there is no *me'ilah* on a half-*perutah*. The two halves cannot be combined because they belong to two different parties — one half is the *ba'al habayis*'s action and one half is the *shaliach*'s action. Since neither has a full *perutah* of *me'ilah*, neither is *mo'el*.

### Both Not Moel

This case illustrates the principle that the threshold of a *perutah* applies individually to each party. Even where there is a technical deviation and a technical fulfillment, if neither party's involvement reaches the *perutah* threshold independently, no *me'ilah* has occurred.

### Store Deviation

However: *aval im amar lei* — if he specified the exact stores — bring half for lamps from this store and half for wicks from that store — and the *shaliach* reversed which store he went to for which item, even though everything else was done correctly, *hashaliach ma'al*. Any deviation from the specific instructions severs the agency entirely. Since the *shaliach* deviated for both halves, both half-*perutot* belong to his unauthorized acts, and together they constitute a full *perutah* of *me'ilah* — his *me'ilah*.

### Etrog/Pomegranate

The second case: *nasan lo shtei prutos* — two *perutot* were given, with instructions to buy an *esrog*. The *shaliach* spent one *perutah* on an *esrog* and the other on a pomegranate. *Sheneihem ma'alu* — both are *mo'el*. The *ba'al habayis* is *mo'el* for the *esrog* purchase, because the *shaliach* did at least partially fulfill his instructions — he spent one *perutah* on the item requested. That half is the *ba'al habayis*'s *me'ilah*. The *shaliach* then spent the remaining *perutah* on his own initiative, making that his *me'ilah*.

### Rabbi Yehuda Dispute

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *ba'al habayis lo ma'al* — the sender is not *mo'el* even for the *esrog*. His reasoning: *esrog gadol hayisi mevakesh v'heiveisa li katan vera* — "I wanted a large, fine *esrog*, and you brought me a small, inferior one." Spending only half the allocated money on the requested item does not constitute fulfillment of the agency, because the sender's intent was to acquire a quality specimen with the full sum. A cheap, small *esrog* is not half of what was requested — it is not what was requested at all. Therefore, the *shaliach* did not fulfill the *ba'al habayis*'s *shlichus* even for the *esrog*, and no portion of the *me'ilah* belongs to the sender.

### Shirt/Tallis Case

The third case: *nasan lo dinar zahav* — a golden *dinar* was given with instructions to purchase a fine garment. The *shaliach* spent three *slaim* on a shirt and the other three *slaim* — the remaining half of the *dinar* — on a *tallis* (here meaning a large outer wrap, not a *tallis* with *tzitzis*). *Sheneihem ma'alu* — both are *mo'el*, by the same reasoning as the *esrog* case: the *ba'al habayis* is *mo'el* for the shirt (since the *shaliach* did at least purchase the requested type of garment), and the *shaliach* is *mo'el* for the *tallis*.

### Cheap Shirt

Rabbi Yehuda again: *ba'al habayis lo ma'al* — the sender is not *mo'el*. *Chaluk gadol hayisi mevakesh v'heiveisa li chaluk katan vera* — "I wanted a fine, substantial garment, and you brought me a small, inferior one." Spending only half the sum does not constitute fulfillment of the instruction; it produces a fundamentally different object than what was requested, and therefore the *shaliach* did not act as the *ba'al habayis*'s agent at all.

---

## Half vs Half Price

### Half Purchase Inference

The *gemara* draws an inference from the position of the *Tanna Kamma* (the first, anonymous opinion that disputes Rabbi Yehuda). *Man de-amar lishliacho zil zavin li kura de-ara* — if one sends his agent to purchase an acre of land, and the agent returns having purchased only a half-acre — *kani lokeiach* — the buyer acquires it. This inference follows from the *Tanna Kamma*'s position that purchasing the *esrog* for one *perutah* instead of two still counts as partial fulfillment of the agency. If doing half of the task is still acting as an agent, then purchasing a half-acre when instructed to buy an acre should similarly constitute a binding acquisition for the sender.

### Sale Resolution

The *gemara* rejects this inference: *hacha heichi dami* — what is the actual case in the *mishnah*? *De-aisei lei shaveh sheish bishlosh* — the *shaliach* brought him something worth six for the price of three. The item's actual value matched what was requested; it simply happened to be available at half price. In that case, the *shaliach* fully performed his task — he acquired the item the *ba'al habayis* wanted — and the *shlichus* is intact. One cannot extrapolate from this to a case where the *shaliach* actually did only half of the task.

### Sale vs Half Task

This distinction — between doing the full task at a bargain price versus doing only half the task — is conceptually important. In the bargain case, the *shaliach* obtained exactly what was requested; the question is only about money. In the half-task case, the *shaliach* obtained something qualitatively or quantitatively different from what was requested.

### Full Expenditure Point

Rabbi Yehuda, however, challenges even the bargain case: even if the item obtained is what was requested, part of the *shlichus* was to spend the entire amount. If the full sum had been spent, an even finer item could have been obtained — *ai havas dinar kula, hayisi shaveh shenei dinar* — "if you had spent the full *dinar*, I could have gotten a shirt worth two *dinar*." Therefore, the *shaliach* did not fully execute the agency even in the bargain case, and the *ba'al habayis* is not *mo'el*.

The *gemara* thus reads the dispute between the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda as specifically about this bargain scenario. The *Tanna Kamma* holds that obtaining the requested item — regardless of price paid — constitutes fulfillment of the *shlichus*. Rabbi Yehuda holds that full expenditure of the allocated sum is itself part of the mandate, and failing to spend the full amount means failing to fully execute the agency. On the question of whether doing literally half a task constitutes partial agency, both may actually agree that it does not — that case is simply not what the *mishnah* is debating.

---

## Kitnis Special Case

### Kitnis Concession

A *braisa* is cited: *modeh Rabbi Yehuda be-kitnis she-sheneihem ma'alu* — Rabbi Yehuda concedes that in the case of *kitnis* (legumes or similar uniformly measured commodities), if the *shaliach* spent only half the money on the requested *kitnis*, both the *ba'al habayis* and the *shaliach* are *mo'el*. This is the opposite of Rabbi Yehuda's ruling in the shirt and *esrog* cases. Why does Rabbi Yehuda concede here?

### Why Kitnis Differs

The answer is intuitive upon reflection. When one asks for a shirt or an *esrog* and the *shaliach* returns with a cheaper, smaller version, the sender can legitimately say: this is a fundamentally different object than what I requested. A Kmart shirt is not half an Armani shirt; a small, inferior *esrog* is not half a large, fine *esrog*. They are categorically different things. The *shlichus* was not partially fulfilled — it was entirely missed.

By contrast, *kitnis* is a homogeneous commodity sold by measure. One pound of lentils is simply half of two pounds of lentils. It is not a different object; it is a smaller quantity of the same thing. If the *ba'al habayis* sent for two pounds and the *shaliach* returned with one pound, the *shaliach* did at least half of what was requested. One cannot say that one pound of lentils is entirely different from two pounds — it is precisely half of what was asked. Similarly, land by the half-acre does present a genuine complication (a full acre enables uses a half-acre cannot), but *kitnis* by the half-measure does not. Rabbi Yehuda therefore agrees that the *ba'al habayis* is *mo'el* for the half he received and the *shaliach* is *mo'el* for the half he spent on his own initiative.

### Bargain Principle

The *gemara* challenges this concession, pressing on the internal consistency of Rabbi Yehuda's position. If Rabbi Yehuda's entire argument against the *Tanna Kamma* in the shirt case is that the *shaliach* could have obtained a better bargain had he spent the full amount — *ai yahavta sela, mozli tefei* — then why doesn't the same logic apply to *kitnis*? If you had given the full *sela* for lentils, the merchant would have given you a better price per unit. So even by *kitnis*, Rabbi Yehuda should argue that the *ba'al habayis* could have gotten more for his money.

### Rav Papa's Answer

Rav Papa resolves the difficulty: *beduchta de-mizvni bekanei* — the concession of Rabbi Yehuda in *kitnis* applies specifically to places where the commodity is sold by exact fixed measure. *Kanei kanei, beperuta* — each measure has a set, fixed price; one *perutah* per measure, and so on. In such a market, there are no volume discounts, no bargains, no economy of scale. Every measure costs the same regardless of how much one buys. Therefore, Rabbi Yehuda's argument — "you cheated me of a better bargain" — simply does not apply. There was no better bargain to be had. In that context, Rabbi Yehuda concedes that spending half is a genuine partial fulfillment of the *shlichus*, and both parties are *mo'el*.

The implication the *gemara* draws is clarifying: the entire dispute between the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda is not about whether doing literally half a task counts as agency (on which both would agree it does not), but specifically about the bargain scenario, where the full item was obtained at less than full price. And Rabbi Yehuda's argument — that the *shlichus* includes spending the full amount to maximize value — is neutralized in precisely those markets where fixed pricing makes maximization impossible.

---

## Shulchani Case

### Bound/Unbound

The final *mishnah* of the tractate opens a new category: *hamaphkid ma'os etzel shulchani* — one who deposits *hekdesh* money with a *shulchani* (money changer). The underlying premise of all these cases, as before, is that *me'ilah* does not occur at the moment of taking or holding; the money must actually pass out of control — be spent, transferred, or given to a third party — before *me'ilah* is incurred. This confirms that the principle requiring actual dispossession, not merely handling, extends well beyond the *gizbar* and applies to any case where a party has some relationship to the property.

If the money was placed with the *shulchani* in a bound-up pouch — *bitzrur* — the norm is that the money changer is not permitted to use it. A bound purse signals that the depositor does not consent to the money changer accessing the funds. Therefore, if the *shulchani* uses the money — *im hotzi ma'al* — as soon as he spends it, that is his *me'ilah*. He had no right to use the money, acted entirely on his own, and the dispossession is attributable solely to him.

### Implicit Permission

If the money was not bound up — *im mutarim* — the understanding is different. An unbound deposit with a money changer carries an implicit license: it is well understood that money changers regularly use the funds in their possession and replace them as needed. The *ba'al habayis*, by depositing loose coins with a *shulchani*, is implicitly permitting him to use them. Therefore — *ulephichach im hotzi lo ma'al* — if the *shulchani* spends the money, he is not *mo'el*. He acted with implicit permission, which transforms the character of the act. This is something more than mere inadvertence or *ones*: it is actual, if implicit, permission conferred by the owner.

### Chanvani Liability

If neither the *ba'al habayis* nor the *shulchani* is *mo'el*, who is? The *mo'el* is whoever ultimately receives and spends the money — the *chanvani* (storekeeper) or whoever else accepts the coin in a transaction. At that point, the *hekdesh* money leaves *hekdesh*'s realm through the act of a third party who had no right or permission from *hekdesh* itself.

### Rambam View

The Rambam's position extends this logic: since the *ba'al habayis* never explicitly instructed the *shulchani* to spend the money, and the *shulchani* acted — albeit with implicit permission — on his own initiative, neither is *mo'el*. The Rambam draws a firm line: *me'ilah* of the sender type requires that the sender actually directed the spending. Implicit permission without directive instruction does not create the kind of agency-in-effect that makes the sender *mo'el*. The *me'ilah* thus falls on the end recipient when he uses the money.

This ruling is conceptually interesting and somewhat counterintuitive. The *shulchani*, by spending the money, is taking *hekdesh* property and directing it to secular use. One might have thought that even with implicit permission, the act of spending is an act of *me'ilah* — after all, in other contexts we saw that even a complete *ones* does not exempt from *me'ilah*. Yet the Rambam holds that genuine implicit permission — not merely a mistaken belief that one has permission, but actual permission conferred by the owner — alters the characterization of the act sufficiently to remove *me'ilah* liability from the one who was given that permission.

### Regular Homeowner

The *mishnah* contrasts the *shulchani* with the ordinary homeowner: *bein kach u'vein kach lo yishtamesh bahen* — whether the money is bound or unbound, a regular private individual entrusted with money for safekeeping has no implied permission to use it. Private individuals are not in the business of using deposited funds; no such norm exists. Therefore, if the ordinary *baal habayis* entrusted with money uses it — *lefichach im hotzi ma'al* — he is *mo'el* as soon as he spends it. He acted without any permission, and the act of dispossession is entirely his.

### Chanvani Status

The *mishnah* concludes with a dispute about the *chanvani* (storekeeper). Is a storekeeper more like the *shulchani* or more like the ordinary homeowner? *HaChanvani k'va'al habayis divrei Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir says the storekeeper is like the ordinary homeowner; there is no implicit license for him to use deposited money, even if it is unbound. *Rabbi Yehuda omer k'shulchani* — Rabbi Yehuda says he is like a money changer and does have implicit permission to use unbound funds.

What emerges from this final *mishnah* as a whole: the tractate consistently resists locating *me'ilah* in the act of mere taking or handling. *Me'ilah* requires actual dispossession — money leaving *hekdesh*'s realm through spending or transfer. The concept of permission, whether explicit or implicit, plays a significant role in determining to whom that act of dispossession is attributed. And the Rambam's position introduces an additional nuance: even implicit permission, where genuine, breaks the chain in a way that pure inadvertence does not.

---

## Mixed Coins

### Coin Drop

The *mishnah* now introduces a different scenario: *nafal pruta shel hekdesh betoch kiso* — a *hekdesh* coin accidentally fell into one's purse. Or: one declared *pruta bekisi hekdesh* — one coin in my purse is *hekdesh* — without specifying which one.

### Rabbi Akiva

Rabbi Akiva says: *kivan she-hotzi et harishona ma'al* — as soon as he takes out the first coin, he has committed *me'ilah*.

### Chachamim View

The *Chachamim* say: *ad she-yotzi et kol hakis* — only after he has spent all the coins in the purse has *me'ilah* certainly occurred. The *Chachamim*'s position is intuitive: until all the coins are spent, there is always a *safek* (doubt) as to whether the particular coin spent was the *hekdesh* one. *Me'ilah* with certainty can only be established once all coins have been disbursed.

### Batel BeRov Q

Tosafos raises a searching question: why doesn't the principle of *batel berov* apply? If a *hekdesh* coin falls into a purse containing many other coins, the *hekdesh* coin should be nullified by the majority, rendering the entire purse *chullin*. Tosafos anticipates the standard answers — *davar sheish lo matirin*, or other rabbinic reasons for blocking *bitul* — but notes that those principles are rabbinic in origin, whereas the question of *me'ilah* is a Torah-level concern. Those answers therefore do not resolve the question at the *de-oraita* level.

### Asham Taluy

Tosafos first notes that the *Tosefta* may resolve the difficulty with Rabbi Akiva's position. According to the *Tosefta*, Rabbi Akiva does not mean that spending the first coin constitutes definite *me'ilah*; rather, it creates a *safek me'ilah* for which one brings an *asham taluy*. This connects to a debate in Masechet Kerisos: Rabbi Akiva held that one can bring an *asham taluy* for doubtful *me'ilah*, while the *Chachamim* disagreed. Without the *Tosefta*'s clarification, Rabbi Akiva's ruling in the *mishnah* would be difficult to understand — how can the first coin taken be *vadai me'ilah* when there is manifestly a *safek* as to whether it is the *hekdesh* coin? The *Tosefta* resolves this: Rabbi Akiva means it creates *safek* liability, not *vadai* liability. After all coins are spent, one brings an *asham vadai* for the certain *me'ilah* that has by then occurred.

### Status/Ownership

Returning to Tosafos's question about *batul berov*: the most fundamental answer lies in a distinction between *bitul* as applied to *status* versus *bitul* as applied to *ownership*. The principle of *bitul berov* operates in the domain of *status* — when a forbidden substance is mixed with a permitted majority, the *issur* status is annulled and the mixture is treated as entirely permitted. But ownership is different. If Michael drops a hundred dollars into a box of my bills, I cannot declare his money *batel* in the majority and claim it all as mine. Ownership persists through the mixing; it is not subject to *bitul*. Since the *hekdesh* coin retains *hekdesh* ownership — it belongs to *hekdesh* regardless of where it is found — the concept of *bitul*, which addresses status rather than ownership rights, simply does not apply. One cannot tell *hekdesh*, "I'm sorry, your coin was nullified in the majority." The coin must be found or replaced. This is the conceptual resolution, and it applies at the *de-oraita* level.

### Explicit Exemption

The *mishnah* then notes: *u-modeh Rabbi Akiva le-Chachamim* — Rabbi Akiva agrees with the *Chachamim* in the case where one says *pruta min hakis zeh Hekdesh* ("a coin from this purse is *hekdesh*") rather than *pruta bekis zeh* ("a coin in this purse is *hekdesh*"). In that case — *she-motzi ve-holekh ad she-yotzi et kol hakis* — one must spend through all the coins before *me'ilah* is certain; the last coin taken is the *hekdesh* one. The difference between "in" and "from" seems to indicate whether the first or the last coin is designated as *hekdesh*, but the *gemara* will interrogate this.

---

## Which Coin/Ox

### In vs From

The *gemara* opens by questioning the distinction the *mishnah* draws between saying a coin is *hekdesh* "in" the purse versus "from" the purse.

### Reish Lakish Q

Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan: *mai shna reisha u-mai shna seifa* — what meaningful difference is there between these two formulations? Both describe a single unidentified coin in the same purse. The linguistic variation seems too thin to carry the weight of such a fundamental distinction in *me'ilah* liability.

### Yochanan Answer

Rabbi Yochanan responds: the *seifa* (*u-modeh Rabbi Akiva*) does not actually describe a case where someone said *min hakis zeh* without further specification. Rather, it refers to a case where one explicitly said *lo yipater kis zeh min hahekdesh* — "this purse will not be free of *hekdesh*," meaning there will always remain a *hekdesh* coin in the purse until the very last one is taken. That explicit, unusual formulation designates the last coin. Without such explicit language, one would not naturally read any standard declaration as designating the last coin.

### Oxen Parallel

A parallel case is raised from another *mishnah*: if one says *echad mishorai hekdesh* — one of my oxen is *hekdesh* — and he has two oxen, *hagadol shebahen hekdesh* — the larger one is *hekdesh*, because we assume one sanctifies generously, giving the best of what one has. If that principle applies to oxen, why don't we apply it to coins and say the most valuable coin in the purse is the *hekdesh* one, rather than defaulting to the first or the last? The *gemara* takes note of this challenge.

The answer Rabbi Yochanan gives is the same: in the *seifa* of the *mishnah*, the designation of "last coin" is not derived from any inference or default rule — it is derived from the explicit language *lo yipater kis zeh min hahekdesh*, which directly indicates that the purse will retain a *hekdesh* coin until its very end.

### Wine/Breira

A *braisa* is cited involving a related case: *halokeach yayin miben hakutim* — one who purchased wine from Samaritans, where even *terumah* (not merely *ma'aser*) must be assumed not to have been separated. If it is *erev Shabbat* and one cannot perform the full *hafrasha* now, one may declare: the two *lugin* that I will eventually separate shall be *terumah*, the ten that I will separate shall be *ma'aser rishon*, the nine I will separate shall be *ma'aser sheni*, and the *kedushah* of the *ma'aser sheni* is transferred onto a coin — and then one may drink immediately. This is the principle of *breira*: the portions not yet physically designated are identified retroactively as *terumah* and *ma'aser* by virtue of the declaration made now and the subsequent act of separation.

Rabbi Meir permits this — *yesh breira*, the retroactive designation is valid. Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yossi, and Rabbi Shimon forbid it — *ein breira*, there is no retroactive designation; the portions must be identified in real time.

### Breira Challenge

Tosafos raises the connection to our case: according to Rabbi Meir, does the *breira* framework — which requires explicit declaration for the designated portion to be identified — support or complicate Rabbi Akiva's position regarding the last coin? Tosafos notes that if Rabbi Meir requires explicit stipulation to make the last portion effective as *terumah*, then Rabbi Akiva's position — that in the *seifa* the last coin is *hekdesh* without explicit language — appears inconsistent. How does designating the last coin work without such specification?

### Final Resolution

The *gemara* gives the same answer throughout this section: the *seifa* of the *mishnah* is not a case without explicit language. It is specifically the case of *lo yipater kis zeh min hahekdesh* — an explicit declaration that the purse will not be free of *hekdesh*, which directly and unambiguously designates the last remaining coin. Rabbi Akiva would not derive "last coin" from any default rule or *breira* principle; the explicit language of the declaration creates the designation. Without that language, no such designation would operate retroactively, and the case would not differ from the *reisha*.

---

## Conclusion

### End of Meilah

*Hadran alach Shaliach She'asa Shlichuto u-slika lah Masechet Me'ilah.* With this, we complete Masechet Meilah.

---

---

# Kinnim 23

## Kan Stuma Intro

### Chova Structure

The second *perek* of Kinnim opens with the concept of a *kan stuma* — an undifferentiated nest — which corresponds to what the first *perek* called a *chova*, an obligatory nest. In such a nest, one bird is a *chatas* and the other is an *olah*. When a woman has multiple obligations bundled together, half the birds function as *chataot* and half as *olot*, though their individual identities remain undetermined until the moment of offering. The previous *perek* addressed scenarios in which two such groups become mixed, establishing that one may bring only up to half from a combined pool, since bringing more risks exceeding the correct proportion of *chataot* or *olot* from any one original group. It also treated the case of a designated *olah* that flew into an undifferentiated group, which restricts subsequent offerings to only the *olot* and only in the number with which that group began.

### One Bird Flies

The first *mishna* of this *perek* presents a straightforward case: *kan stuma sheparach mimena gozal la-avir o sheparach levein hametot o shemet echad mehen* — a bird from an undifferentiated pair flew away into the open air, flew among birds that must die (for reasons discussed in the previous *perek*), or died outright. In any of these situations the remaining bird cannot be paired with its lost companion, since it is impossible to know which role each bird was destined to fulfill.

### Pairing Solution

The resolution is simple: *yikach zug lesheni* — one acquires a replacement to pair with the survivor. The comparison to the two goats of *Yom Kippur* is apt: if one of the pair is lost, one simply replaces it. One might have thought that if the pair had already been notionally differentiated — this one a *chatas*, that one an *olah* — the fate of one would determine a fixed obligation for the other. But even if they had not yet been differentiated, the *mishna* teaches that the intertwining of their fates does not prevent replacement. One simply purchases a new bird and reconstitutes the undifferentiated pair as it was before. This is the easy case.

## Two Groups Mixing

### 4+4 Mixing

The *mishna* now introduces the principle that will drive the more complex discussion to follow: *parach levein hachrevot* — a bird flew into another group that was itself destined to be offered. Consider two groups, each containing four birds — that is, two *kanim*, two pairs — each group undifferentiated, with two *chataot* and two *olot* among them. One bird departs from one group and enters the other. We now have three in the first group and five in the second. The rule stated is: *shehagozel haporeach pasul uposel echad kenegdo* — a bird that flies is itself invalid and invalidates one opposite it.

### Fixing Identity Problem

Why can one not simply bring all three remaining birds from the smaller group? Suppose one were to bring two *chataot* and one *olah* from those three. By doing so, the bird that flew away would by definition be fixed as an *olah* — since the remaining birds in its original group were used as two *chataot* and one *olah*, the only identity left for it is *olah*. Now that bird, with a fixed identity as an *olah*, has entered the second group. The rule established in the previous *perek* is that when a designated *olah* flies into an undifferentiated group, one may bring only the *olot* from that group and only in the number with which the group began. Fixing the flying bird's identity would thus severely restrict what the owner of the second group could bring.

The critical point is that the bird's identity must remain undetermined, because the identity of an undifferentiated bird should only become fixed when it is clear what it is — and it is not clear. By bringing only two birds from the first group — one *chatas* and one *olah* — the remaining bird retains a flexible, unfixed identity. The identity of the bird that flew away thus also remains open, and the second group's owner is not unduly burdened.

### Pesul Principle

What then may the owner of the second group bring from his five? He cannot bring all five — say, three *olot* and two *chataot*. If he were to designate three as *olot*, he might be taking all three *olot* from his original four, which would exceed the permissible proportion from his own group. Because he cannot distinguish which bird among the five belongs to the first group, bringing more than two of either type risks selecting improperly from his original pool. He therefore brings two of each type, leaving one bird unbrought.

This is the *halacha* of *pasul*: the flying bird is invalid and *posel echad kenegdo* — it invalidates one corresponding bird in the group it left and one in the group it entered. The first group had three but may bring only two; the second group had five but may bring only four. The two unbrought birds remain in a state of unresolved identity and are left to die. The underlying principle is that as long as some birds from each original group remain unbrought, those that were brought retain a flexible identity, and no improper fixation occurs.

## Bidirectional Flying

### First Flight

The next *mishna* makes the scenario more complex: *shtei nashim lezo shtei kanim ulezo shtei kanim* — two women, each with two pairs, four birds apiece. *Parach mizo lezo* — a bird flew from one group to the other. *Posel echad bahalichatah* — it invalidates one in its going. This is precisely the scenario just described: one bird departs, and one bird from the group it left and one bird from the group it entered are invalidated.

### Return Flight

Now a bird flies back: *vechazar, posel echad bachaziratah* — it invalidates another one upon its return. The analysis requires careful attention. After the first flight the groups stand at three and five. When a bird flies back from the five to the three, we are again at four and four — but it is not necessarily the same bird that originally left. In the best case, the exchange is seamless and all eight birds are fully usable. In the worst case, one bird flew from group A to group B, and a different bird flew from group B back to group A, creating an effective exchange: each group now contains three of its original birds and one interloper.

### Worst Case ABAB

In this worst-case scenario, consider what happens when offerings are made. One brings from the first group a *chatat* and an *olah*, and from the second group a *chatat* and an *olah*. Suppose, in the worst arrangement, the two *chataot* brought happen to be from the same original group and the two *olot* from the same original group. Once those birds have been brought with their identities fixed in that manner, one cannot bring another bird of the same original group as a *chatat* — because it may already be that all the birds of that group which are *chataot* have been brought, and any additional bird could only be an *olah*. Since one does not know how the offering was designated, one cannot safely bring more.

The key principle is that the groups cannot be collapsed into one large undifferentiated pool of eight. Each group's identity is determined by its original members. Even after mixing, one must continue to treat these as two groups of four and remain sensitive to the possibility that birds from the original group may have been disproportionately used. Because the worst-case scenario yields an arrangement in which all remaining birds may have fixed identities — the A birds all used as one type, the B birds as the other — one cannot bring any further birds beyond the four already brought. The *halacha* is therefore two from each group, for a total of four.

### Multiple Flyings

*Parach vechazar parach vechazar* — what if birds continue to fly back and forth many times? The answer is *lo hisid klum* — one loses nothing additional beyond what was already lost. The principle is *she'afilu hen me'uravot ein pachot mishnayim* — even if they are completely mixed, there will never be fewer than two pairs that can be brought. The rule established in the previous *perek* is that when two same-sized undifferentiated groups are fully intermixed, one can bring at minimum half of the total. Since these two groups each contain four birds, and half of the combined eight is four, one is already at the minimum by bringing two from each group. No further flying back and forth can reduce that minimum further. Were the groups of different sizes — say, ten each — then additional flights would continue to reduce the number that could be brought, until reaching the absolute minimum dictated by the size of the smallest group.

## Seven Women

### Setup 1-7

*Mishna* 3 presents a far more elaborate case: *lezu achat ulezu shtayim ulezu shalosh ulezu arba ulezu chamesh ulezu shesh ulezu sheva* — seven women, each holding a successive number of pairs: one pair, two pairs, three pairs, four pairs, five pairs, six pairs, and seven pairs respectively. The unit here, as in the previous *mishna*, is pairs, not individual birds. A bird then flies from the first woman's group to the second, from the second to the third, continuing through to the seventh, and then flies back — forming a complete circuit.

### In-Out Rule

The *mishna* states: *parach mechazar posel echad bahalichato ve'echad bachazirato* — it invalidates one in its going and one in its returning. Applying the rule established in the previous *mishna* — that every time a bird enters a group one pair is lost, and every time a bird leaves a group one pair is lost — yields the following result. Groups one and two lose two pairs each and can bring nothing: *harishona vehashniya ein lahem klum*. Group three loses two pairs and can bring one: *shlishit yesh la achat*. Group four can bring two, group five can bring three, group six can bring four. Group seven, being an endpoint of the circuit, had a bird enter and a bird leave — the same as the others — but loses only one pair, not two, because it is the terminal point of the loop. It can therefore bring six: *hashvi'it yesh la shesh*.

### Logic Check

The mathematical rule of the previous *mishna* — every entry or exit costs one pair — generates these results cleanly. But the *meforshim* question whether the underlying logic always supports the rule in this more complex case.

The logic behind the rule is this: when a bird leaves a group, one must leave behind a bird from that group without bringing it, so that the departed bird's identity remains unfixed. If one were to bring the remaining bird, that would define the departed bird's identity by exclusion, and then its entry into another group would unduly restrict offerings there. Similarly, when a bird enters a group from outside, one cannot bring one additional bird from that group, lest one inadvertently fix the identity of the foreign bird. Hence: one pair lost on departure, one pair lost on entry.

The logical difficulty emerges at group three. Group three lost two birds — one flew to group two, one flew to group four. Two birds of group three remain among the larger pool, and bringing one pair should be safe, since the remaining pair of group three birds, left unbrought, keeps those identities open. But consider: group two has already been reduced to zero. If nothing is brought from group two, then the bird of group three that flew into group two is in a pool from which nothing will be brought. This means that bird's identity is not being fixed by any offering in group two. One might therefore argue that group three should be able to bring more than one pair — perhaps all two — without the usual constraint, since the bird that flew out toward group two is effectively stranded in a pool from which nothing is offered. The *meforshim* raise this question. The answer is that the *mishna* operates as a blanket rule — *lo plug* — without making fine distinctions based on the downstream fate of individual birds. The principle is applied consistently: two pairs lost for interior groups, one pair lost for the endpoint.

### Second Round

The *mishna* then considers a second round of flying along the same circuit. Of the birds that remained eligible after the first round — zero, zero, one, two, three, four, six pairs respectively — the same flying pattern now repeats. Applying the same rule, subtracting two pairs from interior groups and one from the endpoint: *hachamishit vehashishit ein lahem klum*, groups five and six can now bring nothing; *hashvi'it yesh la arba*, group seven can bring four.

### Seventh Group

At this stage the *mishna* records a dispute: *veyesh omrim hashvi'it lo hipsida klum* — some say group seven has lost nothing, meaning it retains its full remaining allotment without further reduction. The reasoning is that when all the other groups have been reduced to zero, the constraint that justified reducing group seven no longer applies: there is nothing in those other groups from which an improperly fixed identity could cause harm. Everything in those other groups was left unbrought precisely in order to ensure that the identities of flying birds remain open; once those groups yield zero, all the remaining birds are by definition undetermined, and group seven should be free to bring everything it holds. Whether *lo hipsida klum* means group seven reverts to its original seven pairs or simply retains its position without further loss from the most recent round is itself a point of discussion among the *meforshim*, with some reading it as a return to the maximum and others as merely a stay of further reduction.

## Seven Women (II)

### Metot Mixing

The *mishna* adds: *ve'im parach min hametot vechulan harei kullan yamutu* — if a bird that was designated to die flew among the other groups, all the birds in the affected group must die. This raises the question of what qualifies as a bird "designated to die" in this context. The *meforshim* understand it to include the birds left over from groups one and two, which were brought down to zero. Those birds were not offered precisely to preserve the undetermined status of the flying birds; they were effectively left to die as a consequence of that strategy. If one of those unbrought, effectively condemned birds now flies into another group, it becomes a *parach min hametot*, a bird from the pool of those designated to die, and all birds in the group it enters must die as well.

It should be noted that this characterization is somewhat a *chidush*. Strictly speaking, the birds left at zero in groups one and two were not given a positive legal designation of death — they were simply not chosen for offering as part of an optimization strategy. One could theoretically have chosen to bring those birds and left others unbrought. The status of *metot* is not explicit in the *mishna* and the *meforshim*'s assumption that those birds constitute *min hametot* is an extension of the reasoning rather than an express ruling. Nevertheless, most *meforshim* adopt this understanding.

## Stuma to Meforashet

### Stuma Flies In

The *mishna* turns to a different configuration: *kan stuma vekan meforashet* — an undifferentiated pair and a differentiated pair. *Parach min hastuma limeforashet* — a bird from the undifferentiated pair flies into the differentiated pair. The differentiated pair consists of a clearly designated *chatas* and a clearly designated *olah*. Once the undifferentiated bird enters, the three birds in the differentiated group cannot be distinguished from one another, and since a *chatas* and an *olah* are now mixed together without clear identity, none of the three can be offered. The entire group of three must be left.

## Stuma to Meforashet (II)

### Pairing Remaining

The single bird remaining from the undifferentiated pair is treated just as in the opening *mishna*: *yikach zug lasheni* — one acquires a replacement to pair with it. One cannot take a companion for it from the contaminated group of three, since any bird drawn from there could be the wrong type. If the bird subsequently returns from the differentiated group — or if a bird from that mixed group, where all are now destined to die, flies back — it constitutes a *parach min hametot* entering the surviving good bird's space, and *harei kullan yamutu* — they all must die.

## Chatat-Stuma-Olah

### Setup Trio

The *mishna* now introduces a three-group configuration: *chatat mikan ve'olah mikan ustumah be'emtza* — a defined *chatas* group on one side, a defined *olah* group on the other, and an undifferentiated pair in the middle.

### No Loss First

A bird from the middle flies to the *chatas* side, and another from the middle flies to the *olah* side: *parach min ha'emtza latzdadim echad heilech ve'echad heilech, lo hifsid klum* — one has lost nothing. The undifferentiated birds have flown to clearly designated groups. One simply hands all the birds on the *chatas* side to the *kohen* to be offered as *chataot*, and all on the *olah* side to be offered as *olot*. When the *kohen* reaches the bird of originally undetermined status among the *chataot*, he simply designates it as a *chatas*, not knowing which one it is — and this is entirely valid. The same applies on the *olah* side. *Ze shehalach lechan chatat chatat* — that which went to the *chatas* side is designated as a *chatas*; that which went to the *olah* side is an *olah*. No loss results.

### Middle Dies

Now a bird from the *chatas* side and a bird from the *olah* side each fly back into the middle: *chazar l'emtza*. The middle now contains a mixture of a bird of *chatas* identity and a bird of *olah* identity, but one cannot tell which is which. Since a *chatas* and an *olah* are mixed and indistinguishable, neither can be offered. *Hen yamutu* — these middle birds must die. The birds remaining on each side — the defined *chatas* pile and the defined *olah* pile — are unaffected: *elu yikarvu l'chatas, elu yikarvu l'olah*. If subsequently birds from the dead-designated middle fly out to the sides, everything must die, since those birds carry the contaminating uncertainty wherever they go.

## Chatat-Stuma-Olah (II)

### Continuous Cycle

The *mishna* closes this case with the reading that many *meforshim* prefer: *chazar veparach min ha'emtza latzdadim, harei kulam yamutu* — if birds that were in the middle, now a mixture of *chatat* and *olah* required to die, fly out to the sides, everything dies. Once a bird from a must-die pool is indistinguishably mixed into a valid group, there is no way to safely offer any of them. The principle throughout is consistent: anything contaminated by a bird of fixed, irresolvable mixed identity brings death to all those with which it mingles.

## Species Matching

### Same Species Rule

An entirely distinct rule now enters: *ein mevi'in torin keneged benei yonah velo benei yonah keneged torin* — one may not bring *torim* (one species of bird) paired against *benei yonah* (the other species), or vice versa. The *Torah* permits bringing either species for the pair of *chatas* and *olah*, but the two birds of a single obligation must come from the same species. One may not mix species within a single obligation.

### Pigeon-Dove Case

If a woman brought her *chatas* as a *tor* and her *olah* as a *ben yonah*, a mismatch has occurred. Which offering must be redone? The first opinion in the *mishna* directs her to redo the *olah*: *tichpol vetavi olas tor* — bring an *olah* of the same species as the *chatas*. The rationale is that the *olah* already offered, even if it did not fulfill her obligatory *olas chova*, remains valid as an independent *olas nedavah* — a voluntary burnt offering. It is a valid *korban*, merely not her obligation. Redoing the *olah* resolves the mismatch without invalidating anything already brought. Redoing the *chatas*, by contrast, would implicitly render the first *chatas* invalid, since one does not duplicate a *chatas* offering.

### Dove-Pigeon Case

The symmetric case — *olasah tor vechatasah ben yonah* — she brought her *olah* as a *tor* and her *chatas* as a *ben yonah* — also yields: *tichpol vetavi olah ben yonah* — redo the *olah* as a *ben yonah*. The first opinion consistently resolves the mismatch by redoing the *olah*, preserving the *chatas* in both cases and treating the first *olah* as a valid *olas nedavah* in any event.

## Species Matching (II)

### Ben Azzai View

*Ben Azzai omer: holchin achar harishon* — Ben Azzai says one follows the first offering brought. Whatever species was used first determines the required species for the second. If the *olah* was brought first as a *tor*, the *chatas* must also be a *tor*; if the first offering was a *ben yonah*, the second must match it. This has the consequence that if the first offering was the *chatas* and the second was a different species, Ben Azzai would require redoing the *chatas* — unlike the first opinion, which never redoes the *chatas*. There is a conceptual resonance between Ben Azzai's position and the broader themes of this *masechet*: just as throughout Kinnim the identity and fate of individual birds is determined by their group of origin and the fixed identity of others in relation to them, Ben Azzai reasons that the first bird brought sets the defining frame for what follows.

## After Death

### Olah Required

A final pair of cases involving death of the obligant: *ha'ishah shehevi'ah chatasah umetah* — a woman brought her *chatas* and then died before bringing her *olah*. *Yavi'u yorshim olatah* — her heirs must bring the *olah*. The obligation to bring the *olah* constitutes a lien on the estate; the *olah* does not require the obligant to be alive at the time of offering. Whether the *yorshim* are considered the *be'alim* of the *korban* — a question with implications for whether they perform *semichah* — is itself a subject of a separate *machlokes*, and the answer presumably tracks that dispute.

### Chatas Waived

The converse case: *olatah umetah, lo yavi'u yorshim chatasah* — she brought her *olah* and then died, and the heirs may not bring the *chatas* on her behalf. A *chatas* may only be offered for a living person; there is no *kaparah lamesim*, no atonement for the dead. Unlike the *olah*, the *chatas* is intrinsically tied to the life and atonement of the individual, and once she has died the obligation lapses entirely. The heirs have no standing to offer it and no obligation to do so.

*Hadran alach ken stuma.*

---

---

# Kinnim 24

## Perek 3 Overview

### Perek 3 Introduction

The third *perek* of Kinnim is, in a fundamental sense, a parallel to and commentary upon the first *perek*. The language echoes throughout, and the cases map directly onto those treated earlier. Where the first *perek* governed what a *kohen* should do when he comes to ask guidance, the third *perek* addresses what happens when he acts without asking at all.

### Permission Framework

The *perek* opens with the phrase *bameh devarim amurim* — "when is all of this said?" The answer: *b'chohen hanimlach*, when the *kohen* comes to ask permission. Everything taught in the first *perek* about how many birds may be brought when groups become mixed presupposes that the *kohen* is consulting with authorities beforehand. When he does so, he is told to bring only the number of birds that can be guaranteed not to cause a problem. The rules are strict precisely because the goal is to ensure that not even one bird is brought incorrectly.

### Paradox Setup

The third *perek* then pivots: *aval b'chohen she'eino nimlach* — but what about the *kohen* who did not ask permission and simply went ahead? As counterintuitive as it sounds, this *kohen* may end up with a more favorable outcome. Because he brings everything, some will inevitably be done incorrectly — but some will also be done correctly. The result is that more birds end up *kosher* than would have been permitted had he asked first. This is the governing paradox of the entire *perek*.

---

## Equal-Sized Groups

### Equal Groups Rule

The language of the *perek* directly parallels the first: *achas l'zu v'achas l'zu*, *shtayim l'zu v'shtayim l'zu*, *shalosh l'zu v'shalosh l'zu* — one pair mixed with one pair, two with two, three with three. These are equal-sized, undifferentiated groups. In the first *perek*, the rule was that you may bring only the smallest group's worth — which in the case of equal groups means half, since both groups are the same size. Half can be brought safely because dividing equally between *olos* and *chataos* guarantees that no individual bird is certainly brought incorrectly.

### Three Scenarios

Now the *kohen* did not ask permission. What did he do?

*Asa kulam l'mala* — he did all of them above, treating every bird as an *olah*. The result: *mechtza kasher mechtza pasul*. Half are *kosher*, because only half of the birds were actually *olos* — those are valid; the other half, which were *chataos*, were done incorrectly above.

*Kulam l'mata* — he did all of them below, as *chataos*. Again, *mechtza kasher mechtza pasul*. The *chataos* are now *kosher*, the *olos* are not.

*Mechtza l'malah u'mechtza l'mata* — he split them, half above and half below. The *mishnah* states that the half done above yields *mechtza kasher mechtza pasul*, and the half done below likewise yields *mechtza kasher mechtza pasul*. Each half independently yields fifty percent valid.

### Worst-Case Analysis

Why is the result always half? The analysis proceeds by examining the two extremes. At the best-case extreme, the top half is drawn fifty percent from group A and fifty percent from group B, as is the bottom half — every bird lands exactly where it belongs, and everything is *kosher*. At the worst-case extreme, the top half consists entirely of group A and the bottom half entirely of group B. In that scenario, the top half has all of group A's *olos kosher* — which is fifty percent — and all of group A's *chataos pasul*. The bottom half has group B's *chataos kosher* and group B's *olos pasul*. So even at worst, half is *kosher*. Since we must always assume the worst case, we conclude that half is *kosher*.

Crucially, this means that for equal-sized groups, the post-facto outcome of not asking permission is identical to what would have been permitted had permission been asked. In the first *perek*, you were told to bring half; here, half is what turns out to be *kosher*. The *kohen* who did not ask gained nothing — but lost nothing either. The cases where not asking permission genuinely makes a difference are yet to come.

One might ask whether there is a prohibition involved in knowingly bringing a *pasul korban*. It is indeed assumed that one is not permitted to do so, and the sanctity of the *avodah* makes it implicit that one cannot deliberately offer something invalid. Whether there is a formal biblical prohibition or whether the violation is somehow embedded in the broader prohibition against desecrating sacrificial sanctity is a question worth investigating further. The practical scenario may also involve a *kohen* who simply did not realize there was any problem — perhaps he was under the impression that all the birds belonged to one undifferentiated group and that he had full license to split them half and half.

---

## Unequal Groups

### Permission: Smallest Size

*Achas l'zu v'shtayim l'zu* — one pair mixed with two, and by extension three, five, ten, a hundred. When groups are of unequal size and the *kohen* asks permission, the rule is that he may only bring as many birds as the smallest group. The reasoning is straightforward: the moment he exceeds the smallest group's count, he risks bringing a bird from that smaller group in the wrong mode. For example, if the smallest group was one pair, bringing three birds risks having offered the *olah* of the smaller group and then bringing its *chatat* as though it were an *olah*, or vice versa. So the ceiling is always the smallest group.

### No Permission: Half Kosher

If the *kohen* did not ask, *kulam l'mala* — all above — then *mechtza kasher mechtza pasul*. Consider an extreme case: one group of one hundred pairs mixed with one group of one pair, for a total of one hundred and one pairs. If you asked permission, you would be told: bring only one full group — two birds. But the *kohen* went ahead and brought all one hundred and one pairs above. How many are *kosher*? Half. He has effectively brought one hundred and one *chatat-olah* pairs, all treated as *olos* — so all the actual *olos* are *kosher*, which is half. Similarly, *kulam l'mata* yields half *kosher* as well. In stark contrast to what permission would have allowed — a single pair — the *kohen* who acted without permission ends up with over fifty pairs that are *kosher*.

### Hameruba Kasher

What about the case where the *kohen* splits them — *chetzi l'mala v'chetzi l'mata*, half above and half below? The rule here is *hameruba kasher* — the size of the larger group determines what is *kosher*.

### 116 vs 100 Example

To illustrate this concretely: suppose one group has one hundred pairs and the other has sixteen pairs, for a total of one hundred and sixteen pairs. The *kohen* does one hundred and sixteen birds above and one hundred and sixteen below.

At the best-case extreme, all one hundred and sixteen are distributed perfectly — one hundred of group A and sixteen of group B above, and the same below. In that case everything is *kosher*.

At the worst-case extreme, all sixteen of group B are placed above, accounting for thirty-two birds among the top tier, leaving the remaining eighty-four above from group A. How many *olos* are *kosher* from this top tier? The eighty-four from group A are all valid *olos*, since the entirety of group A spans two hundred birds, some above and some below, and those above are certainly *kosher*. As for the thirty-two from group B — in either extreme scenario, sixteen are *kosher olos*: if they are all from B, then half of B is *kosher*; if they were from A, then certainly sixteen are *kosher*. So even at worst, the top tier yields one hundred *kosher olos*.

By the same analysis flipped, the bottom tier yields one hundred *kosher chataos*. The total is one hundred pairs *kosher* — which is the size of the larger group. This is *hameruba kasher*.

It is worth noting that equal-sized groups are simply a special case of this rule. If both groups are one hundred pairs, then *hameruba kasher* says one hundred pairs are *kosher* — which is exactly half. The *klal* of *hameruba kasher* thus subsumes the earlier equal-groups rule.

### General Rule

*Zeh klal* — this is the encompassing rule. *Kol makom she'atah yachol lachlok et hakinim shelo yehe mi-shel isha achas bein l'mala u-vein l'mata* — wherever it is possible to divide the *kinim* such that one woman's birds need not be both above and below, then *mechtza kasher mechtza pasul*, half is *kosher*. This describes the equal-size scenario: in theory, all of woman A's birds could land above and all of woman B's could land below. Since that configuration is possible, the worst-case is genuinely half-and-half, and so half is *kosher*.

*V'kol makom she'ein atah yachol lachlok et hakinim ad she'yiheyu mi-shel isha achat bein l'mala u-vein l'mata* — wherever it is impossible to divide the *kinim* without one woman's birds appearing both above and below, as in the case of one hundred and sixteen pairs where group A's two hundred birds cannot all be placed on one side, then *hameruba kasher* — the larger group's count determines what is *kosher*.

In truth, these are not two distinct *halachos* but one and the same: the larger group's count is always what is *kosher*, and in an equal-sized case, either group qualifies as "the larger," so the count comes out to half. Whether one says half or says *hameruba kasher*, the underlying principle is identical.

---

## Chatat & Olah

### All Die Rule

*Chatat lazu v'olah lazu* — this is a direct parallel to the corresponding case in the first *perek*. When a designated *chatat* becomes mixed with a designated *olah*, the rule is that all must die. There is no room for maneuver when the birds have been individually specified. Had the *kohen* asked permission, every bird would have to be left to die.

### Without Permission

But this *kohen* did not ask. So *asa kulam l'mala* — he did all of them above — *mechtza kasher u'mechtza pasul*. Say fifty *chataos* were mixed with fifty *olos*; both groups were designated. The *kohen* brings all one hundred birds above. Half — the actual *olos* — are *kosher*. The other half, the *chataos* done above, are *pasul*. Similarly, *asa kulam l'mata* yields the same result: the *chataos* done below are *kosher*, the *olos* are not. In contrast to the requirement that all die had permission been sought, not asking and proceeding yields fifty percent *kosher* in either of these scenarios.

One might wonder what practical use it is to know that half are *kosher* if one cannot identify which half. In monetary terms, the solution would involve pooling the shared obligation, making stipulations, bringing additional birds conditionally, and sanctifying them based on those conditions. This *masechta* does not work through the mechanics of remediation — it simply establishes what is *kosher* and what is *pasul* as a matter of principle.

### Half and Half Result

*Chetzi l'mala v'chetzi l'mata* — now he splits them, half above and half below. The result: *shteihem pesulos* — both are *pasul*, everything is invalid. The reason: *she'ani omer chatat krevah l'mala* — we must assume the worst case, that all the *chataos* were done above and all the *olos* below. Since we can never rely on probability — one must assume the worst-case scenario, rooted in principles like *safek d'oraita* — we conclude that nothing is valid.

This means that for the designated *chatat*-and-*olah* case, splitting half-and-half is the single worst outcome. Doing all above or all below at least yields fifty percent *kosher*; splitting yields nothing. This is the stark contrast with the undifferentiated case, where splitting half and half also yielded half *kosher*. Here, it yields nothing at all — the same result as if permission had been asked and the birds left to die.

---

## Mixed Types

### Three-Type Mix

Now a case not present in the first *perek*: *chatat v'ola stuma u'mefureshet* — a designated *chatat*, a designated *olah*, and one undifferentiated (*stuma*) pair, all mixed together. Concretely: one woman has a designated *chatat*, another has a designated *olah*, and between them they share one undifferentiated *chatat-olah* pair. All get mixed together. In total, there are two *chataos*, two *olos*, and two undifferentiated birds — three pairs in all.

### Only Stuma Good

*Asa kulan l'mala* — all above. *Mechtza kasher u'mechtza pasul*. Likewise, *kulan l'mata* — all below — yields half *kosher*. These results track straightforwardly from the earlier analysis.

*Chetzi l'mala v'chetzi l'mata* — half above, half below. Here the designated birds — the specific *chatat* and the specific *olah* — are not *kosher*, because we must assume the worst case: that they were placed exactly incorrectly. *Ein kasher ella stuma* — only the undifferentiated pair is *kosher*. Moreover, *vehi mitchaleket beneihem* — it is divided between the two women, meaning each receives credit for half.

The underlying structure assumes two women: each brought part of her respective obligation, and the undifferentiated pair belongs to both of them jointly. The designated *chatat* and the designated *olah* each must be assumed to have been done wrong, so they contribute nothing valid. The *stuma*, however, cannot be assumed to have been entirely mishandled.

Why not? Because any attempt to construct a worst-case scenario for the *stuma* is self-defeating. Suppose one tries to move both *stuma* birds above, claiming they were done incorrectly as *olos*. But moving them above forces one of the other birds — an *olah* — to move below to fill the balance, and that *olah* done below is now *kosher* as a *chatat*. The worst-case scenario for the *stuma* automatically creates a best-case scenario for one of the designated birds. By symmetry, the same logic applies in reverse. The result is that no matter how one arranges the worst case, one *chatat* and one *olah* from the total will always be *kosher* — and the count equals the size of the *stuma*.

### Raavad's View

The *Raavad* reads the *mishnah* precisely along these lines. When the *mishnah* says *ein kasher ella stuma*, it does not mean that the *stuma* birds themselves are necessarily the ones that are *kosher*. Rather, it means that the *number* of birds equal to the size of the *stuma* is what is *kosher*. The identity of which specific birds were *kosher* remains unknown — it might have been the *stuma* itself, or one of the designated birds may have ended up in the correct position. This is why the *mishnah* adds that it is divided between the women: neither can claim certainty about whose birds were actually valid. The practical remedy is for both women to bring additional birds with appropriate stipulations, knowing with certainty only that between them, one *chatat* and one *olah* were brought correctly.

---

## Chatat in Chovah

### Permission Rule

*Chatos shenisarvu bechovah* — a designated *chatat* mixed into an undifferentiated group (*chovah*). This is the case from the very first *mishnah* of the tractate. If a single designated *chatat* flies into a *chovah* of, say, one hundred pairs, what is the rule if the *kohen* asks permission? *Ein kasher ella minyan chataos shebechovah* — only the count of *chataos* in the original *chovah* may be brought. No *olos* at all may be offered, because bringing any *olah* risks bringing the counterpart of the designated *chatat*, and no more *chataos* than the original group contained, because exceeding that number risks treating a designated *chatat*'s counterpart *olah* as though it were a *chatat*.

### Chovah 2x Chatat

Now the *kohen* did not ask. *Shnayim bechatas* — the *chovah* is twice the size of the designated *chataos* that flew in. For concreteness: two designated *chatat* birds flew into four undifferentiated birds. If he had asked permission, he would be told to bring only two *chataos*. Instead, he brought everything half above, half below — three birds above and three below.

At best-case, the *chataos* are placed exactly where they belong, and the distribution otherwise falls naturally — everything is as correct as possible. Working through the extremes: even in the worst-case scenario where the *chataos* land entirely in the wrong position, three birds are still *kosher* — one undifferentiated pair plus one additional *stuma* bird. This is half of the total of six birds. So *mechtza kasher mechtza pasul* — half *kosher*, half *pasul*. Notably, the breakdown among those *kosher* birds skews toward *olos*: roughly two-thirds of the valid birds are *olos* and one-third is a *chatat*, though the bottom line is simply that half are *kosher*.

### Chatat 2x Chovah

Now the reverse: *chatas u'shnayim shebechovah* — the designated *chatat* birds that flew in are twice the size of the *chovah*. Four designated *chatat* birds flew into two undifferentiated birds. Half above, half below.

At the best-case extreme, the four *chataos* are placed below where they belong, and the two *stuma* birds are distributed one above and one below — all four *chataos* valid, both *stuma* birds valid, for a total of five *kosher* birds. At the worst-case extreme, all four *chataos* land above where they do not belong, and the two *stuma* birds fill below — only the two *stuma* birds are *kosher*, one pair. That is exactly the count of the original *chovah*. Therefore: *haminyan shebechovah kasher* — the size of the original undifferentiated group is what is *kosher*. When the *chovah* is larger, it is half; when the *chatat* that flew in is larger, the determining count is the size of the original *chovah*.

---

## Olah in Chovah

### Olah Symmetry

*Olah shenisarev bechovah* — when designated *olah* birds become mixed into a *chovah*, the same structure applies in perfect symmetry. *Ein kasher ella minyan olah shebechovah* — if permission were asked, only the count of *olos* in the original *chovah* may be brought.

When the *kohen* does not ask and acts: *chovah shtayim be'olah* — if the *chovah* is twice the size of the designated *olos* that mixed in, then *mechtza kasher mechtza pasul*, half is *kosher*, just as in the corresponding *chatat* case. *Olah shtayim bechovah* — if the designated *olos* that mixed in are twice the size of the *chovah*, then *haminyan shebechovah kasher* — the size of the original *chovah* is *kosher*. The reasoning is entirely parallel, with *olos* and *chataos* reversed throughout.

It is worth noting that in all these cases the *mishnah* describes a *kohen* who divides them half and half — not all above or all below. One might ask: if he knows *chataos* flew in, why not simply do everything below and maximize the number of valid *chataos*? The answer is that this *kohen*, having not asked permission, presumably also did not think carefully about how to optimize. He treated the situation as a routine undifferentiated group and split them half and half, without regard for what was mixed in. A *kohen* who knew what he was doing and was determined to maximize validity could indeed choose all-above or all-below to get a better result. But the *mishnah* is not instructing him to optimize — it is simply analyzing the outcome of the most natural course of action.

---

## Woman's Vow

### Correct Procedure

*Ha'ishah she'amrah harei alai kan kesheyelled zachar* — a woman who says: I accept upon myself to bring a nest of birds when I give birth to a male child. She gives birth to a boy. She now must bring *shtei kinim* — two pairs of birds: one for her vow (*nidrah*), which consists of two *olos* since a voluntary donation of birds is always two *olos*, and one for her obligation as a *yoledet* (*chovatah*), which is one *chatat* and one *olah*. She hands all four birds to the *kohen*. The correct procedure is *gimel pereidin milmala v'achas milmata* — three birds above and one below. The one *chatat* goes below; the three *olos* — two from her vow and one from her obligation — go above.

### Priest's Mistake

*Lo asah ken* — he did not do this. Instead: *bet milmala u'vet milmata* — two above and two below, the intuitive equal split, without consulting anyone (*velo nimlach*). He treated it as a normal undifferentiated pair-and-pair situation and split evenly.

The scenario assumes that the *kohen* was subsequently able to communicate the error to the woman. (This raises its own practical question — in cases where the *yoledet* simply deposited money in a communal fund and the birds were purchased and offered entirely by the *kohanim*, she would have had no way of knowing, and the normal assumption would be that everything was done correctly. The *mishnah* is presumably addressing a case where she brought the birds herself or where the error was otherwise communicated to her.) The question of priestly liability for errors that cause loss to the donor is a separate discussion found in Masechta Gittin.

### Woman's Makeup

*Tzrichah lehavi od preidah achat* — she must bring one additional bird. Since it should have been three above and one below, and instead it was two and two, one bird that belonged above was done below — an *olah* treated as a *chatat*. She must now supply one additional bird to be brought above. *Veyakrivennah milmala* — and it is to be offered above as an *olah*. This is all assuming *mimin echad* — all birds were of the same type, either all *tor* (turtledoves) or all *benei yonah* (young doves). The *mishnah* will now complicate matters by introducing the possibility of mixed types.

---

## Mixed Types Problem

### Type Unknown

*Mishnei minim* — now suppose the woman brought birds of two types, one pair of *tor* and one pair of *benei yonah*, and the *kohen* went ahead and did two above and two below. He subsequently forgot which he did above and which below; she similarly forgot which pair she designated as her vow and which as her obligation.

The structure here depends on an implicit assumption — that the *kohen* handled each pair as a unit, not randomly intermingling birds from different pairs. Given that a pair must be of one type, each pair is treated as distinct. The problem is that the makeup bird she now brings must be of the same type as the *olah* it accompanies from her vow, and since neither party remembers which type fulfilled which role, she cannot know which type she needs.

### Two Types Solution

*Mishnei minim tavi shtayim* — she must bring two birds, one of each type, and offer each above. She cannot simply choose either type and assume it is acceptable, because a kosher pair requires a matched type, and it would be improper to presume she knows what was brought. By bringing one *tor* and one *benei yonah* above, she guarantees that whichever type is the correct makeup bird is covered.

---

## Explicit Vow

### Forgot But Single Type

*Pirshah nidrah* — now suppose the woman made her vow explicit, specifying a particular type. She vowed to bring either specifically *tor* or specifically *benei yonah*. But she forgot what she vowed, and also forgot what was actually brought. The *kohen* likewise forgot what he did.

### Three Bird Makeup

In a scenario where it is known that all four birds were of the same type — even if nobody recalls which type — she can eliminate one bird from her accounting. She knows that at least one of those birds was brought above correctly in some form. Therefore she needs to bring only three additional birds *mimin echad* to complete her obligation with certainty. The one bird she can credit against the total is the one that was undoubtedly among those offered, even if the exact circumstances are unclear.

### Four Bird Solution

If, however, the situation involves genuine uncertainty about the types as well — nobody knows what was brought, whether *tor* or *benei yonah* — then she cannot credit any of the original four birds toward her obligation. She cannot eliminate any from the accounting because she has no way of knowing whether what was done satisfies even part of her commitment. She must therefore bring four birds total, covering all possibilities.

---

## Kava Nidrah

### Togetherness Requirement

*Kava nidrah* — the woman stipulated that her vow is to be brought together with her *korban* as a single unit. Concretely, this means that all three *olos* — the two from her vow and the one from her *yoledet* obligation — must be offered together as a group. (The *chatat* is not subject to this grouping requirement; the togetherness applies specifically to the *olos*.) When the *kohen* errs and the woman must now reconstruct her offering, this togetherness condition adds a layer of complexity: she cannot simply bring each piece independently, because the three *olos* must be brought together. Even if part of what was done originally might have been valid in isolation, the failure to bring all three *olos* as a unified group invalidates the whole for purposes of her *kava nidrah*.

### Five Birds Single Type

*Tzrichah lehavi od chamesh peridin mimin echad* — when all the birds are of a single type but she does not know what was properly accomplished, she must now bring five additional birds. The reasoning: since the togetherness requirement means that none of the original offering can be credited as a valid partial fulfillment, she must reconstruct the entire obligation from scratch. She must bring two birds to reconstitute her vow's *olos*, one bird to serve as the *yoledet* *olah*, and the necessary additional bird alongside the *olah* to meet the *kava nidrah* condition. Working through the counting, this comes to five birds. Although the *chatat* and the *olah* from her *yoledet* obligation do not need to share the same type as one another, the makeup for the *neder* must account for what was originally brought — and since everything must now be done together, the total reaches five.

### Six Birds Two Types

*Mishnei minim tavi shesh* — when two types are involved and all information about what was originally brought has been lost, she must bring six birds. The additional bird beyond five is required because of uncertainty about what type was used for the *chatat*, and since the accompanying *olah* must match the type of the *chatat* that was brought, she must now provide two candidate *olos* — one of each type — to cover both possibilities. This brings the total to six, accounting for every combination of type and role that her original offering may have taken.

---

---

# Kinnim 25

## Mixed Vow & Obligation

### Woman's Forgotten Vow

The final case of *Kinnim* involves a woman who took a *neder* to bring a bird offering together with her obligatory *korban yoledes*. She specified that she would bring the *neder* of a particular type — either *tor* or *bnei yonah* — but subsequently forgot which she had specified. Because she cannot recall what she vowed, she cannot verify that her obligation was discharged, and must therefore repeat the entire sequence. It should be noted that the *rishonim* debate at considerable length how to read this case, since a number of assumptions must be built into the analysis to make it cohere.

### 'Together' Requirement

The operative word in her vow is "together." As this case is understood, the togetherness requirement means that all of her *olos* must be brought simultaneously: the two *olos* of her *neder* and the *olah* of her *chovah* — the obligatory *olah* that accompanies the *korban yoledes*. Since she cannot establish what she vowed and cannot confirm what was previously performed, she must bring everything again. Because her obligatory *olah* was already offered on a prior day and she cannot retroactively join her *neder* offering to it, the only way she can now satisfy the togetherness condition is to bring an additional bird as an *olah*. This extra *olah* need not be of a specific species — she may choose whichever type she wishes.

### Single Species: Five

When everything belongs to a single species — when all the birds involved were of the same *min*, whether all *tor* or all *bnei yonah*, even though she does not remember which — the total comes to five. She must bring two *olos* of *tor* and two *olos* of *bnei yonah* on account of the *neder* she cannot identify, plus one additional *olah* to satisfy the togetherness condition with respect to her obligatory offering. That yields four plus one: five birds in all.

---

## Mixed Species: Six

### Chatas Determines Olah

When the offering she brought previously involved different species — that is, when she does not know what her *chatas* was — the count rises to six. The reason lies in the *halacha* that the *min* of the *chatas* determines the *min* of the matching *olah*: if the *chatas* is a *tor*, the *olah* must likewise be a *tor*; if the *chatas* is *bnei yonah*, the *olah* must be *bnei yonah*. Since the *chatas* determines which *olah* is valid, uncertainty about the *chatas* propagates directly into uncertainty about the obligatory *olah*.

### Two Olos per Species

Because she does not know what species her *chatas* was — whether it was a *tor* or *bnei yonah* — she cannot simply bring a single additional *olah* to discharge the togetherness obligation. She must bring one *olah* of *tor* and one of *bnei yonah*, ensuring that whichever species the prior *chatas* turns out to have been, the matching *olah* has been covered. Combined with the four *olos* already required for the unresolved *neder*, this produces a total of six.

---

## Priest's Uncertainty

### All Above Scenario

The next case introduces a further complication. The *mishna* states: she gave the birds above — to the *kohen* — and it is not known what she gave, and the *kohen* went and performed, and it is not known what he performed. On the surface this resembles everything discussed until now. The critical difference, however — which the text does not spell out explicitly — is that in this scenario the *kohen* may have performed *all* of the offerings above. In prior cases, we assumed the *kohen* performed some above and some below, simply without remembering which went where. Here, the uncertainty extends to whether anything at all was done below.

### Four + Two + One

Given this expanded uncertainty, the *mishna* requires an additional bird: four for her *neder* — two *tor* and two *bnei yonah* as before — two for her obligatory *olah*, covering both species to match whatever the *chatas* may have been, and now one *chatas* as well. That totals seven.

### New Chatas Needed

The reason a *chatas* must now be added is that since the *kohen* may have performed everything above, it is possible that no *chatas* was offered at all. She must therefore bring a *chatas* to cover that possibility. At the same time, the two *olos* remain necessary: if a *chatas* was in fact offered below on the prior day, its species would determine what the *olah* must be, and since she does not know which species that *chatas* was, she must bring an *olah* of each species. She must thus provide both the *chatas* in case nothing was offered below, and the two *olos* in case something was. Seven birds in total.

---

## Ben Azzai: Eight Birds

### First Determines Second

*Ben Azzai* disagrees and requires eight birds. His position, stated earlier in the tractate, is that it is not the *chatas* that categorically determines the *min* of the *olah*.
