Rather, whichever offering was performed *first* determines the species of the second. This principle cuts in both directions.

### Olos & Chatasim

If the *chatas* was performed first, then the *olah* must match it, and since the species of that prior *chatas* is unknown, two *olos* — one of each species — are required. But it is equally possible that the *olah* was performed first. In that case, the *chatas* must match the *olah*, and since it is not known which species the *olah* was, two *chatasim* are required. The scenario in which everything may have been done above means that both possibilities must be covered simultaneously: two *olos* to account for the case where the *chatas* came first, and two *chatasim* to account for the case where the *olah* came first. Combined with the four *olos* required for the unresolved *neder*, *Ben Azzai*'s accounting reaches eight birds. With that, all the permutations of this final case are exhausted.

---

## Aggadic Riddle

### One to Seven

It is characteristic of many *masechtot* that they close with material of an aggadic nature, and *Kinnim*, as the final *masechta* of *Seder Kodshim*, follows this pattern. The *Rambam* likewise closes each of his fourteen *sefarim* with an aggadic passage, not merely his individual *halachot*.

*Rabbi Yehoshua* opens by citing a saying: when something is alive it has one voice, and when it dies it has seven voices. This was evidently a familiar riddle, and *Rabbi Yehoshua* connects it to the case just concluded in our *mishna* — the progression from a single pair of birds to the seven birds required under the final scenario. The fit is admittedly imperfect: the case did not begin with one bird that grew to seven, but with four that grew to seven. Nevertheless, *Rabbi Yehoshua* intends the aphorism as a peg on which to hang the *mishna*'s climactic ruling.

### Seven Instruments

The *mishna* then offers what may be the more straightforward reading of the aphorism — one applying to a ram rather than a cow, as the text will shortly mention wool. When the animal is alive it produces one voice; when it dies its body yields seven. Its two horns become two *chatzotzerot* — whether these are understood as *shofarot* for use on *Rosh Hashanah* or as the animal-horn instruments used by the *levi'im* for musical accompaniment is itself a matter of debate. Its two leg bones become two *chalilim*, flutes fashioned from the hollow of the bone. Its hide becomes a drum. Its stomach or entrails become strings for a *nevel*, some form of lyre or plucked instrument — much as catgut, despite the name, is derived from animal intestines. And the finer intestines serve as strings for the *kinnor*, a harp-like instrument, the difference between the two sets of strings perhaps being one of quality or gauge. That accounts for seven. Some add that the ram's wool can be used to produce *techelet*, and that the *kohen gadol*'s *me'il techelet* bore bells at its hem that produced sound — though this connection is acknowledged to be somewhat strained, since it is the bells rather than the wool itself that make the sound.

### Elders & Wisdom

The *masechta* closes with a final *aggadata* from *Rabbi Shimon Hakashia*. He observes that among *ziknei am ha-aretz* — the elderly of the uneducated class — the older they become, the more their minds become disordered and confused, as the verse states: God removes speech from the trustworthy, and the discernment of elders is taken away. This describes a recognizable reality; the prevalence of dementia in advanced age is well-documented.

But the point of citing this verse is to establish a contrast. *Aval ziknei Torah* — the elders of Torah — are not like this. For them, the very opposite holds: the older they grow, the more settled and clear their thinking becomes. They accumulate wisdom rather than losing it, as the verse declares: *bishishim chochma* — with the aged is wisdom — *v'orech yamim tvunah* — and with length of days, understanding.

One might ask what this *aggadata* has to do with *Kinnim* in particular. One suggestion is that since the *masechta* has been speaking of one thing becoming seven — of something that increases with age, so to speak — the transition to elders who grow in wisdom rather than declining is a natural, if loosely associative, conclusion. A more pointed reading is that the *masechta* of *Kinnim* is itself an exercise in sustained mental acrobatics — the tracking of combinatorial permutations across multiple layers of uncertainty — and the closing passage affirms that precisely this kind of rigorous intellectual engagement is what preserves and sharpens the mind with age. There may also be a subtle wordplay at work: *zkeinim* and *ziknei* bear a resemblance to *Kinnim*, and the word *m'terefet* — meaning disordered or confused — evokes the mixing and confusing of birds that is the tractate's central subject. Whether or not those connections are intended, the thematic resonance is apt.

*Hadran alach masechet Kinnim. Uslika la masechet Kinnim.*

---

---

# Kinnim 25b

## Tamid Overview

### Tamid Scope

With the conclusion of *Kinnim*, we turn to *Masechet Tamid*, which begins on 28b. A brief orientation to the nature of this *masechet* is in order. In principle, *Masechet Tamid* is a discussion of how the *korban tamid* was brought every morning. But before reaching the actual offering of the *tamid*, the *masechet* describes what happened in the *Beit HaMikdash* during the early morning hours — essentially from the time of the night watches through the opening of the gates, the *terumat hadeshen*, and all the early preparations, up through the *korban tamid* itself. For most of us, this is a remarkable opportunity: after nearly seven and a half years through *Shas*, we finally get a direct, detailed account of what actually happened.

### Rambam: Why Last

The Rambam's *Peirush HaMishnah*, in his introduction written at the beginning of *Zeraim*, discusses the ordering of *masechtos* within each *seder*. At the end of that discussion, he explains why *Masechet Tamid* appears where it does. He writes: *ve'achar meilah masechet Tamid* — after *Meilah* comes *Tamid*. Why is *Tamid* placed last? *Lefi she'ein bah dinim velo issur veheter* — because it contains no *halacha* discussion, no analysis of what is forbidden or permitted. *Ella sippur* — it is purely narrative. *Heich hayah tamid karev* — how was the *tamid* brought? And why do we need to know this? *Kedei sheyehei nahug tamid* — so that when the next *Beit HaMikdash* is built, we will know how to bring the *korban tamid* properly.

The Rambam continues: *ve'achar Tamid Middos* — after *Tamid* comes *Middot*. And *ve'ein inyanah ella sippur middas HaMikdash vetzuratah* — its subject matter too is entirely descriptive, describing the dimensions and form of the *Beit HaMikdash* and how it was constructed. The reason for preserving this knowledge? *Shekesheyibaneh nishmor bo osah tzurah veoso hayachas* — so that when the Temple is rebuilt, we will maintain the same form and the same proportions. As the verse says, *ki hakol Hashem alai hiskil*.

One might ask whether the dimensions in *Masechet Middot* are rendered superfluous by the descriptions of the Temple found in *Tanakh* itself. The answer is that the *pesukim* in *Yechezkel* describe a different structure — the *Beit HaMikdash Rishon* and the prophetic vision differ from the *Beit HaMikdash Sheni*. There is even a broader *machlokes* about whether the Third Temple must replicate the Second or will come down from heaven in an entirely different form. These are real questions, and the Rambam's remark that we preserve these proportions *shekesheyibaneh* is not entirely free of ambiguity.

### Descriptive Nature

What emerges clearly, then, is that both *Tamid* and *Middot* are purely descriptive *masechtos*. Some *halachos* are alluded to or implicit within the descriptions, but there is no *halacha* as such — no debates about permissibility, no *machlokes* between *Tannaim* about legal conclusions. One striking consequence of this is the near-total absence of named *Tannaim* in both *masechtos*. It is almost entirely *stam* — anonymous — because there are no disputes to attribute to anyone. One might have expected that even descriptive accounts would generate differing recollections, but the text is remarkably uniform and unattributed throughout.

---

## Guard Stations

### Three Stations

The opening *mishnah* of *Masechet Tamid* states: *bishlosha mekomot hakohanim shomrim beveit hamikdash* — the *kohanim* would stand guard in three places in the *Beit HaMikdash*: *Beit Avtinas*, *Beit HaNitzotz*, and *Beit HaMoked*. Looking at a diagram of the *Beit HaMikdash*, these three locations can be identified. *Beit HaNitzotz* and *Beit HaMoked* appear in the north of the *azarah*, while *Beit Avtinas* — more precisely, *lishkat Beit Avtinas* — appears on the south. There is some question about the precise order and arrangement; some say *Beit HaMoked* was positioned further east. In any event, these were the three priestly guard stations.

### Priestly vs. Levite

The first *mishnah* of *Masechet Middot* opens with an identical formulation — *bishlosha mekomot hakohanim shomrim beveit hamikdash*, in *Beit Avtinas*, *Beit HaNitzotz*, and *Beit HaMoked* — but then adds: *vehaleviyim be'esrim ve'echad*, the *Leviyim* stood guard in twenty-one places. *Chamisha al chamisha shaarei har habayit* — five by the five gates of *Har HaBayit*, the outer wall where the *Kotel* stands today. *Arba'a al arba pinotav mitokho* — four at the corners of that wall, on the inside. *Chamisha al chamisha shaarei ha'azarah* — five by the five gates of the *azarah*, and four at its corners, and so on. So the *Leviyim* were stationed at the gates and outer perimeter of *Har HaBayit* and around the *azarah* itself — a total of twenty-one positions.

The roles of *kohanim* and *Leviyim* were spatially distinct. The *Leviyim* were at the gates and on the outside; the *kohanim* were on the inside, and specifically, as we will see shortly, on the rooftops of these structures. The *Leviyim* guarded below at the gates, while the *kohanim* watched from above.

### Sources: Guarding

The *Gemara* establishes that the *mitzva* to guard the *Mikdash* applies to both *kohanim* and *Leviyim*. The *Torah* says to *Aharon*: I have given you the *Leviyim* to be *shomer mishmeret ohel moed* — to guard the protection of the *Ohel Moed*. And the *Torah* speaks of *Moshe Aharon uvanav shomrim mishmeret hakodesh* — they would guard the *Ohel Moed*. Since *Moshe* was a *Levi* and not a *kohen*, we learn that both *kohanim* and *Leviyim* — in different but complementary roles — share in this obligation of *shemirat haMikdash*.

---

## Guard Purpose

### Mefaresh: Decree

What is the purpose of this *shemira*? The *mefaresh* — the commentator printed alongside the *mishnah*, whom nobody identifies as Rashi, but rather refers to consistently as the *mefaresh* — offers a surprising view. He says the guarding is a *gezeirat hakatuv*, a divine decree, because logically one might have reached the opposite conclusion: God can protect His own Temple, and stationing guards might actually undercut the *kavod* of the *Mikdash*, suggesting that something might be stolen. He writes: *de'ein aniyut bemakom ashirut* — we do not want to look poor in a place of wealth. If something were stolen from the *Mikdash*, a truly wealthy establishment might simply replace it: *ve'i ganvei klei mikdash kanya achrinei*. And perhaps *bechad shomer sagi* — one guard might suffice. The entire elaborate guarding system is therefore justified only by the explicit *pasuk*, since pure reason might have argued against it.

### Rambam: Honor

The *Rambam* takes the diametrically opposite position. In *Perek 8* of *Hilchot Beit HaBechirah*, he writes: *shemirat hamikdash mitzvat aseh* — guarding the Temple is a positive *mitzva*. And the reason? *Ve'af al pi she'ein sham pachad me'oyev velo milistim* — even though there is no fear of enemies or robbers — *she'ein shemirato ella kavod lo* — the guarding is entirely for the sake of honor to God. He explains: *eino domeh paltorin sheyesh alav shomrim lepaltorin she'ein alav shomrim* — a palace with guards is simply not the same as a palace without guards. The entire ceremony of changing guards, of armed sentinels marching about — this is precisely how one expresses majesty and respect. Nobody looks at the guards of a king's palace and says it signals weakness or poverty; they say it signals grandeur. The guarding of the *Mikdash* achieves this same expression of *kavod*.

The *Rambam* continues: *shemirah zu kol halaylah* — this guarding is performed all night. *Vehashomrim hem hakohanim vehaleviyim*, citing *vehachonim lifnei hamishkan lifnei ohel moed kedma* and *ushmartem et mishmeret hamishkan* — *Kehat*, *Moshe*, *Aharon*, and his sons. In *Halacha 3*, the *Rambam* adds that this is not only a positive *mitzva*: if it is not performed, there is also a violation of a negative prohibition. *Shene'emar ushmartem et mishmeret hakodesh — leshon shemirah azharah hi*. This is somewhat surprising, because ordinarily *leshon shemirah* denotes a negative prohibition in the sense of *hishamer lecha* — guard yourself against doing something — whereas here the *shemirah* is the literal act of guarding, not a prohibition against transgression. Nevertheless, the *Rambam* derives both a positive and a negative from the same formulation.

### Roles & Purposes

In *Halacha 4*, the *Rambam* states: *hakohanim shomrim mibifnim vehaleviyim mibachutz* — the *kohanim* guard from the inside, the *Leviyim* from the outside. This confirms what we see from the sources: the *Leviyim* are stationed at the gates and the outer perimeters; the *kohanim* are positioned more inward.

One might wonder: if the *Rambam*'s rationale for *shemirat haMikdash* is *kavod*, should it not apply during the day as well, when people can actually see the guards and appreciate the majesty they represent? The *Rambam* nevertheless limits the obligation to nighttime — *kol halaylah* — while the *mefaresh* and others maintain that the *mitzva* applies both day and night. This remains a genuine *machlokes*. Both the *mefaresh* and the *Rambam* agree, however, on one fundamental point: the *shemira* is not for any pragmatic protective purpose. The *Rambam*'s formulation — guards as an expression of honor, like the ceremonial guards of a royal palace — is the interpretation most widely adopted.

---

## Beit HaNitzotz

### HaNitzotz Role

The name *Beit HaNitzotz* means "the house of the spark." Some hold that there was a fire maintained there, from which one could kindle the fire of the *mizbe'ach* — since although the *mishnah* teaches that a divine fire descended upon the *mizbe'ach*, there is a *mitzva* nonetheless to add human fire, *mitzvah lehavi min hahedyot*. However, most authorities associate the perpetual fire more directly with *Beit HaMoked* — *moked* itself meaning "place of the bonfire." A separate view, cited in the name of *Tosafot*, is that *Beit HaNitzotz* takes its name from the first rays of sunlight that would strike it. The *Tiferet Yisrael*, however, raises an objection: *Beit HaNitzotz* was located in the north, and the sun comes from the other direction entirely, which makes this etymology difficult to sustain. He himself explains the name as referring to the constant sparks of fire there — *tamid hayu bo nitzotzot shel esh, mimenu yakhol lehadlik et esh hamizbe'ach* — from which the fire of the *mizbe'ach* could be kindled. The debate about the precise etymology and function of *Beit HaNitzotz* thus turns on both linguistic and geographical considerations.

### Archers on Roof

The *mishnah* states: *u'vBeit HaNitzotz hayu aliyot harovim shomrim sham* — in *Beit HaNitzotz* there were elevated areas, and the *rovim* would watch there. The word *rovim* almost certainly refers to archers. Anyone familiar with ancient fortifications knows the arrangement: archers would be positioned along the tops of walls, sheltered behind narrow slits, able to shoot downward while remaining protected. This fits precisely with the role described. Whether the *kohanim* stationed there actually carried bows and arrows is an interesting question — but they were at minimum functioning in an archer's capacity, watching from elevated positions on the rooftop.

Some commentators suggest, based on Aramaic, that *rovim* derives from the word *ravya*, meaning children or young men, i.e., the junior *kohanim*. This reading is far less convincing. The word *rovim* fits the context of guarding from an elevated position far more naturally, and Mishnaic Hebrew usage supports the meaning of archers. The *mefarshim* indicate that the same arrangement applied to *Beit Avtinas* as well — while the *mishnah* does not spell it out explicitly, the pattern is consistent: *Leviyim* guarded at the gates below, while *kohanim* watched from the roof above.

---

## Beit HaMoked

### Structure

The *mishnah* describes *Beit HaMoked*: *kipa* — it had a dome on top. This is worth noting architecturally: domed construction was characteristic of the Herodian period, and this is indeed Herod's *Beit HaMikdash*. A dome would also have had the practical benefit of allowing smoke to escape, which is relevant given the large fire maintained there. Looking at the diagram, one can see the dome indicated by a small circle at the center of *Beit HaMoked*. The structure was also *bayit gadol* — a large room — and as the diagram suggests, there were four smaller chambers opening off the main central space. *Mukaf rovadim shel avanim* — it was surrounded by stone steps, though the precise arrangement of these steps is not entirely clear: some understand them as interior steps rising toward a higher level within the room; others connect them to the smaller side-chambers.

### Sleeping Quarters

*Ziknei Beit Av* — the elders, or senior functionaries, of the *beit av* — would sleep there. The *beit av* was the subdivision of the *mishmar* serving on a given day, and the *ziknei beit av* were its senior members. The *mefaresh* explains that they would sleep in small niches in the walls of *Beit HaMoked*, reached by climbing the surrounding steps.

The *mishnah* then adds that *pirchei kehunah* — the young *kohanim* — had their garments on the ground beside them, indicating that they too slept there. It appears that both senior and junior *kohanim* slept in *Beit HaMoked*: presumably the *ziknei beit av* in the upper niches, and the *pirchei kehunah* below. This raises an obvious question: if everyone is sleeping, who is actually doing the guarding? Some suggest the *pirchei kehunah* were the *shomrim* and their sleep refers to rotational shifts. Others propose that the actual guarding was conducted from the top — perhaps from a walkway around the dome — since one cannot meaningfully guard from inside an enclosed room.

### Keys & Authority

The reason the *ziknei beit av* slept in *Beit HaMoked* is now made explicit: *u'maftechot ha'azarah beyadam* — they held the keys to the *azarah*. They needed to be present in order to open the gates at the start of the service each morning, and it was therefore practical and respectful that they sleep close by rather than travel from elsewhere. When the *mishnah* speaks of the keys to the *azarah*, this refers primarily to *Sha'ar Nicanor* and the entrance to *Ezrat Yisrael*.

There is also the structural question of how *kohanim* could sleep in *Beit HaMoked* at all, given that one is forbidden even to sit within the *azarah*. Looking at the diagram again, one can see a faint dotted line running horizontally through the building, indicating a division: the outer half of *Beit HaMoked* did not possess *kedushat azarah*, while the inner half did. The *kohanim* slept in the outer, non-sanctified half, thereby avoiding any violation.

### Garment Protocol

The *mishnah* specifies: *lo hayu yeshenim be'vigdei kodesh* — they did not sleep in the *bigdei kehunah*. Rather, *ella hayu poshtim* — they would remove their priestly garments — *u'manichim otan tachat rasheihem* — and place them beside their heads. This does not mean literally under the head, which would constitute deriving benefit from *bigdei kehunah*, but rather alongside. *U'mitkasim bi'kesut atzman* — they would cover themselves with their own ordinary garments and sleep in those. The *bigdei kehunah* were thus set aside properly for the morning service.

---

## Nocturnal Emission

### Exit Protocol

The *mishnah* now turns to a challenging situation: *ira keri leachad mehem* — if one of the *kohanim* experienced a nocturnal seminal emission during the night. He has now become *tamei* as a *ba'al keri* and is forbidden from remaining in, or passing through, the *azarah*. Fortunately, he is sleeping in the outer half of *Beit HaMoked*, which lacks *kedushat azarah*, so his immediate location is not the problem. The question is how he exits without crossing through the sanctified space.

The *mishnah* answers: *yotzei veholech lo bimsiba haholechet lo tachat habira* — he departs via a passage or tunnel that runs beneath the *bira*. The precise meaning of *bira* is debated — some understand it to refer to the entire *Beit HaMikdash*, others to a particular section or chamber — but in any event, the reference is to some form of underground passage that allowed egress without crossing the sanctified areas. Looking at the diagram of *Beit HaMoked*, one of the four corner chambers is labeled *yeridah lebeit hatvilah* — descent to the immersion chamber — which confirms this route.

### Tunnel System

The passage was not dark: *nerot dolkim mikan umikan* — candles were lit along both sides of the tunnel, illuminating the way. Whether these were maintained by someone who went through daily to relight them, or whether the *kohen* himself lit them as he proceeded, is not stated explicitly. The tunnel led *ad shehu magia lebeit hatvilah* — until he reached the *beit hatvilah*, the immersion house containing the *mikvah*.

### Mikvah & Toilet

*U'medura hayata sham* — there was a fire maintained by the *mikvah* to provide warmth, since a *kohen* might need to immerse in the early morning hours. One would not want practical discomfort to deter anyone from purifying himself promptly, so a fire was kept there for warmth.

*U'beit hakise shel kavod* — and there was an honorable bathroom facility. The rationale for its placement is not merely convenience: if a *kohen* still has residual semen within him and does not urinate before immersing, he risks becoming *tamei* again immediately after his *tevilah*. The bathroom therefore serves a ritual function, ensuring that he is fully purified before immersing. *Ze haya kevodo* — this was the honorable manner in which it operated.

The system of use was also dignified: *matzu naul yodea sheyesh sham adam* — if the door was found locked, one knew someone was inside; *patuach beyadua she'ein sham adam* — if it was open, it was unoccupied. One might think this is simply common sense, but the *mishnah*'s attention to this detail is itself significant. In an era and environment where privacy in personal hygiene was not universal — people often simply stepped outdoors — the *Beit HaMikdash* established a dignified convention, and the *kohanim* were careful to observe it. The locking system protected the privacy and honor of each individual, befitting the sanctity of the surroundings.

---

---

# Tamid 26

## Ba'al Keri & Mikvah

### Ba'al Keri Restrictions

The final topic of the previous session concerned the nocturnal watch in the *beit hamikdash*. The *kohanim* on duty would spend the night in the *beit hamoked*, the large chamber with its warming fire. If one of them experienced a seminal emission during the night and thereby became a *ba'al keri*, the halakhic consequences were significant. A *ba'al keri* is prohibited not only from entering the *mikdash* proper but from being present anywhere on *har habayit* at all.

This point carries considerable practical relevance for the contemporary Temple tours that bring visitors onto *har habayit*. The common justification offered for such tours is that *tumeas meit* — impurity contracted through contact with a corpse — does not disqualify one from *har habayit*. That is correct as far as it goes: a *tmei meit* is indeed permitted on *har habayit*, provided he does not enter the area of the *mikdash* itself. This is the basis on which many groups ascend, having first immersed in a *mikvah*. However, a *ba'al keri* — and likewise a woman who is a *niddah* — is categorically prohibited from *har habayit* entirely. The distinction is between *tumah* that originates externally, through contact with an outside source, versus *tumah yotzeis migufo*, impurity that emanates from within one's own body. The latter category carries a stricter prohibition that extends to all of *har habayit*, not merely the *mikdash* proper.

### Tunnel System

Since the *ba'al keri* cannot traverse *har habayit*, the Temple employed a tunnel system for precisely this situation. The principle underlying the tunnels is the well-established rule that rooftops and underground passages — *lo nitkadshu* — were not sanctified with the *kedusha* of the *mikdash*, and by extension, presumably also not with the *kedusha* of *har habayit* itself. This is certainly what must be said to make the tunnel system coherent. The *kohen* who became a *ba'al keri* could therefore travel underground to reach the *mikvah* without transgressing the prohibition against being on *har habayit* in a state of *tumah yotzeis migufo*.

### Immersion Process

The *mishnah* describes what follows: *yarad v'taval* — he descends into the *mikvah*, which was naturally situated in a pit in the ground. *Alah v'nistafeg* — he emerges and dries himself off. *V'nitchamem kineged hamedurah* — he warms himself by the fire. This presupposes that there was a bonfire near the *mikvah* itself, since emerging from cold water in the middle of the night, unclothed, demands warming. Recall that the *beit hamoked* also had its own fire, which is where the *kohanim* were sleeping.

### Return & Wait

After drying and warming himself, *u'va v'yashav lo eitzel echav hakohanim* — he returns and sits with his fellow *kohanim*. This is the shift of *kohanim* who will be working the following morning, and so he returns to the *beit hamoked* to wait with them. He remains there *ad she-hayu shearim niftachim* — until the gates of the *azara* open at daybreak. At that point, *yotzei v'holech lo* — he departs and goes home, because he cannot perform any *avoda* that day.

### Tvul Yom Status

The reason he cannot work is that despite having immersed in the *mikvah*, he is still a *tvul yom*. Immersion on its own does not restore full *tahara* until nightfall of that same day. The question then arises: why did he not simply go home in the middle of the night rather than waiting until morning? One might suggest that he went through a tunnel to the *mikvah* and could have exited on the other side without needing to re-enter through the gates — and indeed, if the *mikvah* had a separate exit, that point has some force. But the general answer given is that we do not want to embarrass this *kohen* by forcing him to make his way home in the middle of the night.

This raises a sharper question, however. A *tvul yom* who is a *ba'al keri* remains prohibited on *har habayit* until nightfall, even after immersion. So how was he permitted to remain in the *beit hamoked* at all? The distinction between types of *tumah* is again relevant here. *Tumah* contracted from an external source permits one on *har habayit* but not in the *mikdash* proper. But *tumah yotzeis migufo* — like that of a *ba'al keri* — prohibits one from *har habayit* itself, and this prohibition continues even after immersion until nightfall. So the question stands.

### Rabbinic Leniency

Two answers are offered. The first is that the prohibition of a *ba'al keri* on *har habayit* is only *derabanan*, and the Rabbis waived it in this circumstance so as not to subject this *kohen* to embarrassment by compelling him to leave in the middle of the night. The second answer is that he does not technically remain on *har habayit* at all. The *meforshim* suggest that even the space of the *beit hamoked* where he sits may be a rooftop or a subterranean level — somewhere that does not technically carry *kedushat har habayit*. On balance, the simpler explanation is likely the first: it is *derabanan*, and it was waived.

### Kedusha Levels

This discussion of rooftops and tunnels opens a broader topic of considerable practical importance. The principle that rooftops and underground spaces *lo nitkadshu* — were not sanctified — means that *kedushat har habayit* attaches to the surface of *har habayit*, understood as an extension of the floor of the *mikdash* itself. Just as the sanctity of the *mikdash* is conceived as centered on the floor of the *mikdash*, so too *kedushat yerushalayim* and *kedushat har habayit* are understood as extensions of that floor, applying to the surface of those areas.

An interesting parallel arises regarding *yerushalayim* itself. For some *halachot*, *yerushalayim* is treated as an extension of the *mikdash* floor — for example, the question of whether *kodshim kalim* such as the *korban pesach* may be eaten on a second floor, where one might say the elevated space does not share the same status as the ground-level extension of the *mikdash*. For other *halachot*, such as *maaser sheni*, the status of *yerushalayim* is conceived differently and an *aliyah* may be more permissible. These are distinct discussions with their own *rishonim*.

Returning to the tunnels: the question of what lies beneath the present surface of *har habayit* is a genuinely fascinating one. The general rule is that underground spaces were not sanctified. But a sharper question emerges: what if the ground level has shifted? If what was once the surface of *har habayit* is now underground due to accumulation of debris or construction over the centuries, does the original surface retain its *kedusha*? This remains an open question without a clear answer. The simpler case — steps descending from the surface — presumably remains part of *har habayit*, but the exact demarcation of where ground level ends and non-sanctified space begins is not entirely resolved by the sources.

---

## Terumas HaDeshen

### First Service

Having concluded the account of the night watch, the *mishnah* turns to the beginning of the morning's activities. The first *avoda* of the day in the *mikdash* was *terumat hadeshen* — the removal of the ashes from the outer *mizbeach*. This is rooted in the beginning of *Tzav*: *v'herim et hadeshen asher tochal ha'eish et ha'olah al hamizbeach v'samo eitzel hamizbeach* — the fire burns the *olah* throughout the night, and the first act of the morning is removing those ashes. This service was performed before sunrise, approximately at the time of the cockcrowing, which corresponds roughly to *alot hashachar*, about 72 minutes before sunrise.

### Pre-lottery Immersion

Because the right to perform *terumat hadeshen* was assigned by lottery, any *kohen* wishing to participate in the lottery had to be prepared in advance. Even a *kohen* who had not experienced any *tumah* during the night was required to immerse in a *mikvah* before entering the *azara* to perform *avoda*. Thus, *mi shehayah rotzeh litrom et hamizbeach mashkim v'tovel* — whoever wished to perform *terumat hadeshen* arose early and immersed — *ad shelo yavo hamemuneh* — before the appointed official arrived to conduct the lottery.

### Official's Arrival

One might ask at what time the appointed official would arrive, so that the *kohanim* could calibrate their preparation. The *mishnah* answers: *lo kol ha'ittim shavin* — the times were not always the same. *Pe'amim shehu ba mikriat hagever* — sometimes he came at the time of the cockcrowing — *o samuch lo, milefanav umilacharayiv* — or somewhat before or after. The timing was unpredictable, which meant that a *kohen* who wished to participate had to be ready early enough to account for this variability.

### Lottery Process

When the official arrived, he knocked on the door of the *beit hamoked* where the *kohanim* had spent the night. *Vehem patchu lo* — they opened the door for him. He then announced: *mi shetaval yavo veyafis* — whoever has immersed, come and participate in the lottery. *Hefisu* — they conducted the lottery. The method, familiar from the parallel account in *Yoma*, involved all the *kohanim* standing in a circle, one removing his hat to mark the starting point, and then counting outward from a number called out at random. Whoever the count landed upon won the right to perform *terumat hadeshen*: *mi shezacha zacha lo* — he who won, it was his.

### Lottery Location

The first lottery was conducted inside the *beit hamoked* itself, in the room where the *kohanim* had been sleeping and where the fire burned. The *meforshim* note that while there is a general sensibility of *beit elokeinu nehalech beragesh* — performing such proceedings in the sacred space to reflect eagerness — the exposed courtyard of the *azara* was not used for this particular lottery. Two reasons are given. First, the process required a *kohen* to remove his hat, and standing in the *azara* without the proper *bigdei kehuna* is not respectful. Second, having the *kohanim* stand in a circle means some would inevitably have their backs to the *mizbeach* or the *kodesh kodashim*, which is likewise not appropriate. The subsequent lotteries, conducted once the *kohanim* were already at work, took place in the *lishkat hagazit* — the Chamber of Hewn Stone — which was also where the *sanhedrin* sat. This chamber was adjacent to the *azara* but not fully exposed within it, striking the balance between sacred space and dignified procedure.

It should be noted that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, in *Midos*, differs regarding the arrangement for the *ba'al keri* discussed earlier, holding that after immersion the *kohen* exits through a designated tunnel rather than remaining in the *beit hamoked*. This is a minority position and not the view followed in our *mishnah*.

---

## Sources & Zones

### Guard Obligation

The *gemara* now asks: *mena hani mili* — from where do we know that *kohanim* are obligated to guard the *mikdash*? The *rambam* counts this as a *mitzvas aseh*, though there is a dispute as to whether the obligation applies only at night or both day and night. The *gemara* seeks the scriptural basis.

### Abaye's Source

*Amar Abaye amar kra* — Abaye derives it from a *pasuk* in *Bamidbar*: *vehachonim lifnei hamishkan kedmah lifnei ohel moed mizrachah, Moshe v'Aharon uvanav, shomrim mishmeret hamikdash lemishmeret bnei Yisrael* — those who encamp before the *mishkan* to the east, before the *ohel moed* to the east, are Moshe, Aharon, and his sons, who guard the watch of the *mikdash* for the watching of *bnei Yisrael*. This establishes the principle of *shimur* and, since Moshe belonged to the *shevet levi*, it establishes that both *kohanim* and *levi'im* are involved in this obligation.

### Zone Distinction

One might accept that this *pasuk* establishes the requirement of *shimur* and establishes that *kohanim* and *levi'im* are involved — since *Moshe v'Aharon uvanav* encompasses both. However, the *mishnah* in our tractate states that *kohanim* guard in three places, and the *mishnah* in *Midos* states that *levi'im* guard in 21 places. The *pasuk*, by contrast, groups them all together without indicating separate zones. The question is therefore: where do we derive that there are fundamentally different zones for *kohanim* and *levi'im*?

The *gemara* answers by parsing the *pasuk* itself more closely. The verse contains two distinct clauses: *vehachonim lifnei hamishkan* — referring to those who *encamped* before the *mishkan* — and then *Aharon uvanav shomrei mishmeret hamikdash* — Aharon and his sons as *shomrim* of the *mikdash*. The word *chonim* — encamping, dwelling at the perimeter — applies to Moshe, representing the *levi'im*, stationed on the outer perimeter. The word *shomrim* — active guarding — applies to Aharon and his sons, the *kohanim*, stationed in the *mikdash* proper. The use of two distinct verbs, *hachonim* and *shomrim*, signals two separate functions and two separate zones. *Chonim lachud, shomrim lachud* — each term is independent.

### Three Places

The remaining question is how we know the *kohanim* specifically guard in three distinct places, as the *mishnah* requires. One might read *Aharon uvanav* as all being together in a single zone. The *gemara* responds: *lo salka daitach* — this cannot be correct. The *pasuk* groups *Moshe v'Aharon uvanav* together, and just as Moshe — a single individual — occupied his own dedicated space, so too each member of *Aharon uvanav* occupies his own dedicated space. *Aharon bechad makom uvanav bishnei mekomot* — Aharon in one place and his sons in two, yielding three distinct locations.

This derivation is admittedly not without its difficulties. The analogy would seem to imply that all the *levi'im* are in one place in the same way that all the *kohanim* would be in one place, which is not what the *mishnah* in *Midos* says — the *levi'im* guard 21 distinct positions. The *gemara* here is providing a partial answer, and a more satisfying resolution follows.

### Rav Ashi's Answer

Rav Ashi offers an alternative derivation. He notes that this is the first Amoraic statement encountered in tractate *Tamid*, which is otherwise remarkably *stam* in character — something that reflects its narrative, descriptive nature rather than the theoretical *halacha* debate that dominates most *gemaras*. *Rav Ashi amar miseifa dikra* — Rav Ashi derives the three places from the end of the *pasuk* itself. The *pasuk* employs the word *mishmeret* three times: *shomrim mishmeret*, *mishmeret hamikdash*, and *lemishmeret bnei Yisrael*. Three instances of *mishmeret* in a single verse indicate three separate and distinct watch positions. This is the more direct and elegant derivation for the number three.

One might ask whether this entire *sugya* is perhaps an *asmachta* — a rabbinic enactment supported post-hoc by a scriptural verse rather than genuinely derived from it — particularly since the *pasuk* speaks of the *ohel moed* and *mishkan*, institutions quite different in structure from the permanent *beit hamikdash* with its locked gates and chambers. This is a question worth exploring among the *rishonim*, though the *gemara*'s plain presentation treats the derivation as substantive. As with many areas of *Torah sheba'al peh*, the conclusion is one that *pshat hasukim* alone would not have yielded.

---

## Watch Chambers

### Two Chambers

The *gemara* now turns to the physical locations of the three watch chambers. *Beit Abtinas* and *beit hanitzotz* were two of the three places where *kohanim* kept watch. All three chambers opened into the *azara* proper — the *mikdash* in its primary sense — since the obligation is *shomrim mishmeret hamikdash* and the *azara* is the heart of that sanctity. To orient these chambers: the *azara* and *ezrat kohanim* constitute the *mikdash* proper in the biblical sense, with *ezrat nashim* carrying only *derabanan* elevated status. These chambers were accordingly positioned around this space. *Beit hanitzotz* was located to the north, and the gate associated with it — *shaar hanitzotz* — provided access from that direction.

It is worth noting here that for the purposes of Temple tours that are conducted on *har habayit* today, the portions that are avoided are those identified with the *azara* proper. The area of *ezrat nashim* and *ezrat yisrael* are technically distinct: *ezrat yisrael* and *ezrat kohanim* share the same biblical level of *kedushat mikdash*, and women would enter those spaces only for specific purposes such as bringing a *korban* or as a *sotah*. Generally, *ezrat nashim* was accessible to all, including the question of non-Jews — a matter treated in the *mishnah* in *Kelim* regarding access *lifnim me'hacheil* that deserves separate examination.

### Aliyot Question

The *mishnah* had stated that in *beit abtinas* and *beit hanitzotz* there were *aliyot* — upper levels — from which *kohanim* kept watch. The *gemara* raises the question: *aliyot mamash* — were these literal second stories, true upper floors built atop the chambers? Or does the term *aliyot* here mean something more modest — elevated platforms, raised structures that were *gevihim ka'aliyot*, high like *aliyot*, but not actual independent upper stories in the architectural sense?

### Portico Design

A *mishnah* is cited to resolve this question: *ta shema detnan*. In the north of the *azara*, the *shaar hanitzotz* is described as follows: *kemin achsadra haya* — it was like a portico. A portico is an open colonnaded structure: columns supporting a walkway or covered area above, with an open space below. *Ve'aliyah bnuya al gabah* — and an *aliyah* was built upon it — *shehakohanim shomrim milmala* — from which the *kohanim* kept watch above — *vehaleviyim milmata* — while the *levi'im* were below. *Upetach haya lo lachol* — and it opened outward to the non-sanctified area, meaning the opening faced outward toward *har habayit* rather than inward toward the *azara*.

This *mishnah* answers the question. What is called an *aliyah* here is not a full second story of a building in the conventional sense, but rather the walkway atop the columns of the portico structure. The *kohanim* would stand or walk along this elevated walkway above the columns, keeping watch over the area. The *levi'im* would be stationed at the gate level below. This is what is meant by *aliyot* in this context.

Picturing the structure: the *shaar hanitzotz* forms a gate, with columns on either side supporting an elevated platform or walkway above — something architecturally reminiscent of the great colonnaded structures of the Herodian period. Indeed, since this is Herod's Temple, the presence of such architectural elements is not surprising. The *kohanim* patrol above on this walkway, while the *levi'im* guard at the gate below.

### Access & Kedusha

A critically important halakhic point emerges from the detail that *upetach haya lo lachol* — the opening faced outward. The *kedusha* that attaches to a chamber in the *mikdash* complex is determined by the direction of its access. A space that opens inward toward the *azara* takes on *kedushat mikdash*; a space whose access is from the outside — from *har habayit* — is considered to have *kedushat har habayit* rather than *kedushat mikdash*. This is somewhat analogous, though not precisely parallel, to the question of which side a *mezuzah* is placed on based on the direction of entry.

This principle is what creates the famous division within the *beit hamoked* itself. The *beit hamoked* had one gate opening toward the *azara* and one gate opening outward. Because it had both, the *beit hamoked* was divided in its *kedusha* — half the room has *kedushat mikdash* and half has *kedushat har habayit*. It is for this reason that the *kohanim* sleeping in the *beit hamoked* slept only in the outer half. The direction of access, in short, is the determining factor for the level of sanctity the space carries.

### Kohanim/Levi'im

The arrangement at *beit hanitzotz* thus places the *kohanim* above — on the walkway atop the portico — and the *levi'im* below, at the gate. Though they occupy different vertical positions, they are guarding the same location together, each from their respective post. This physical arrangement reflects the broader principle of distinct but complementary zones for *kohanim* and *levi'im* in the *shimur* of the *mikdash*.

The question of what function the chamber behind the gate actually served remains somewhat unclear. If all the openings face outward, how would those working inside the *mikdash* make use of these chambers? Perhaps there was a small interior access point not described explicitly, or perhaps one moved laterally between rooms by passing through an adjacent chamber that did open inward. The name *beit hanitzotz* — the chamber of the spark — is itself unclear. Some suggest it housed a secondary fire used to add flame to the *mizbeach*, others that it simply provided warmth. Both functions would have been equally available in the *beit hamoked*, so the precise purpose of *beit hanitzotz* remains uncertain.

---

## Levi'im Source

### Baraita Posuk

Having established the *kohanim*'s obligation of *shimur* from *Bamidbar*, the *gemara* now seeks the source for including the *levi'im* in the watch alongside *kohanim* in the same space. A *baraita* is cited: *veyilavu alecha veyeshorshucha* — they, the *levi'im*, shall accompany you and serve you. The word *ba'avodatecha* — in your *avoda* — implies that they take a share of the *avoda* performed by the *kohanim*.

### Two Readings

Two interpretations of this verse are possible. The first reading is that the *levi'im* take a direct part in the *avoda* of the *kohanim* — that is, they literally share in the *kohanim*'s work. The second reading is that the *levi'im* accompany the *kohanim* and help them by doing their own work — their own separate duties — which alleviates the burden on the *kohanim*. On this second reading, *veyeshorshucha* does not mean they share in the *kohanim*'s tasks but rather that they serve the *kohanim*'s interests by fulfilling their own independent role, thereby reducing the *kohanim*'s responsibility.

### Resolution

The *baraita* resolves this by noting that another verse already addresses the *levi'im*'s own duties: *veshamru lechol klei hamikdash lechol kelav u'lechol avodato* — they shall guard all the vessels of the *mikdash* and all its work. Since this verse already accounts for the *levi'im*'s independent obligations, the additional verse — *veyilavu alecha veyeshorshucha* — must be teaching something beyond their own work. That extra verse teaches that the *levi'im* share specifically in the *kohanim*'s obligation of *shimur*. Not in the *avoda* of the altar or the inner service, which only *kohanim* perform, but in the one element of the *kohanim*'s responsibility that is accessible to *levi'im*: the guarding of the *mikdash*. *Keitzad? Kohanim shomrim milma'la u'levi'im milmata* — how so? The *kohanim* watch from above, the *levi'im* from below. They occupy distinct positions but share a single act of *shimur*.

---

## Beit HaMoked

### One Guard

The *mishnah* states that the *beit hamoked* — the primary guard chamber, distinguished by its dome and its large size — had one guard. This prompts an immediate difficulty. A *baraita* teaches that there were two gates in the *beit hamoked*: *echad patuach l'chol v'echad patuach l'azara* — one opening outward and one opening into the *azara*. If there were gates in two directions, would one not expect two guards, or at minimum two guard positions?

Abaye resolves this: *keivan degabei hadadi havu kaimei sagi lehu bechad shomer* — since the two doors were positioned close to one another, a single guard sufficed. *Davi lehacha vedavi lehacha* — he could look in one direction and then the other without difficulty. The guard, whether stationed on the rooftop or on an elevated platform of the *beit hamoked*, could scan one gate and then the other with a simple turn. The room was fundamentally one space, and a single guard covering both ends was adequate.

This also corrects an earlier impression: it appears from the *gemara* that each of the three watch locations was staffed by literally one person, not a larger complement of guards. The *mishnah*'s language of *bishlosha mekomot* — three places — speaks of locations, not numbers of personnel, but the *gemara*'s discussion implies a single guard per station.

### Trapdoor

The *baraita* records an additional detail regarding the inner gate, the one opening into the *azara*. Rabbi Yehuda teaches: *pishpash katan haya lo shebo nichnasim livlosh ha'azara* — there was a small trapdoor within the large gate, through which one could pass in order to *livlosh* — to scout or inspect — the *azara*. As the commentators explain, this small door served a supervisory function: those responsible for oversight could slip through the small trapdoor without making a conspicuous entrance through the main gate. By entering quietly through the small door, they could check on the guards unobtrusively to ensure they were attentive and properly performing their duties, without the guards being forewarned by the sound or sight of the large gate being opened.

### Stone Steps

Returning to the *mishnah*, it describes the *beit hamoked* as *mukaf rovdim shel even* — surrounded by stone steps or hewn stone platforms. As the commentators explain, these *rovdim* were the stone steps leading up to the sleeping niches set into the walls at a higher level, where the senior *kohanim* — the elders of the *beit av* — would sleep. The *gemara* asks: *mai nihu rovdim?* — what exactly are these? *Gizizta de-itztaba desaliku lehu le-itztaba* — they are hewn stone structures for a platform, steps by which one ascended to the sleeping platform above.

### Stone Cutting

A significant halakhic question immediately arises. How could these stones have been hewn at all? The *pasuk* states *habayit behibanoto even shleimah umasa nivnah* — the Temple was built of complete, undressed stones — and regarding the *mizbeach* the Torah states explicitly *lo tivneh atehen gazit* — you shall not build it of hewn stones. Moreover, the verse in *Melachim* recording the construction of *Shlomo*'s Temple states that no sound of iron tools was heard within the entire structure. If hewn stones were forbidden in the *mikdash*, how were these *rovdim* constructed?

The *gemara* answers: *amar Abaye demetaknei umayeiti mei'ikara avnei zutrayata v'avnei ravrevata* — Abaye explains that they prepared and brought from the outset both small stones and large stones, as the verse itself references: *avnei eser amot v'avnei shmoneh amot* — stones of ten *amot* and stones of eight *amot*. The *mefaresh* elaborates: the cutting and shaping of the stones was performed *chutz la'azara* — outside the *azara* proper, even if still on *har habayit*. It was only within the *azara* itself that the prohibition against iron tools applied. *Mechutz la'azara mutar lechatchan u'lehashchizan b'barzel* — outside the *azara* it was permitted to cut and smooth them with iron. *Aval mishebau la'azara, assur lehanif aleihem barzel* — but once they entered the *azara*, it was forbidden to apply iron to them. The verse *lo nishma babayit behibanoto* — no sound was heard *babayit* — means specifically within the *azara*, the *bayit* in the narrow sense. Outside the *azara*, even on *har habayit*, the work could proceed with iron tools. The stones were cut and dressed to size before being brought in, and once within the *azara* no further cutting was done.

This pre-fabrication principle — preparing materials to their final dimensions at a site removed from the construction location — is an elegant solution, and it anticipates by two millennia what many modern construction operations employ as standard practice.

### Sleep Arrangements

The *mishnah* records that *ziknei beit av hayyu yeshenim sham* — the elders of the *beit av* slept there, in those niches or elevated platforms of the *beit hamoked*. The *gemara* asks: *amai?* — why niches? Why not bring beds? *Amar Abaye: lav orach ara le'alu'ei mitot l'beit hamikdash* — it is not dignified or appropriate to bring beds into the *beit hamikdash*. Even though the *kohanim* were sleeping in the outer half of the *beit hamoked*, the half that carried *kedushat har habayit* rather than *kedushat mikdash* proper, nevertheless the room is within the *beit hamikdash* complex, and bringing furniture such as beds into that space is not befitting its sanctity.

### Rovim vs Pirchei

The younger *kohanim*, *upirchei kehuna ish ksuto ba'aretz* — the junior *kohanim* slept on the ground, each with his garment beneath him. The *gemara* then raises an interesting terminological question: in the earlier context, those doing the watch were referred to as *rovim*, while here, the younger *kohanim* sleeping on the floor are called *pirchei kehuna*. Why the different terminology?

The *rambam* and the *meiri* had interpreted *rovim* in the *mishnah* to mean archers — *kohanim* stationed with bows and arrows, which is contextually apt for a guard function. The *gemara* here, however, treats *rovim* as derived from the root meaning youth — young ones, *rabya* — those who have not yet reached the age of performing *avoda*. *Pirchei kehuna*, by contrast, from the word *perach* — a blossom — describes those who are already at the threshold of full priestly service, about to flower into their role.

The *gemara* explains: *hatam dela matu lemiavad avodah, kari lehu rovim* — those not yet of age to perform *avoda* are called *rovim*. *Hacha dematu lemiavad avodah, karu lehu pirchei* — those who are already fit to perform *avoda* are called *pirchei kehuna*, for they have already blossomed into readiness. The *pirchei kehuna* sleeping on the ground are the younger *kohanim* who will participate in the morning's lottery and are preparing to perform the day's *avodot*. If *rovim* are understood as those not yet fit for *avoda*, then the guards stationed on the rooftops were remarkably young — a striking conclusion that sits in some tension with the *rambam*'s concern for *derech kavod* in the *mikdash*'s guard arrangements.

---

---

# Tamid 27

## Kohanim & Entry Rules

### One Kohen or Group?

We open on daf 27a of Tamid, picking up in the middle of the first *perek*. A point worth noting from earlier discussion: the *Gemara* had given the impression that there was only one *Kohen* per watching station. The *Rambam*, however, when he discusses the *mishmarot*, describes an *edah shel Kohanim* at each station — a community or collective. A number of *Acharonim* suggest he means ten, deriving the concept of *edah* from the same source we derive the requirement for a *minyan*. In any event, the *Rambam*'s position is clear: it was not a single *Kohen* at each station but a group of *Kohanim*.

### Non-Jewish Access

The question of non-Jewish access to the *Mikdash* was also raised. Non-Jews are not permitted in the *Ezrat Nashim*; they are kept outside of the *cheil*, which is the outer wall surrounding the Temple complex. They do not enter beyond that perimeter.

### Tumah Restrictions

Similarly, while a *tamei meis* is, biblically speaking, permitted on *Har Habayit* — and technically the *Ezrat Nashim* carries the status of *Har Habayit* — nevertheless, the Rabbis accorded the *Ezrat Nashim* an additional level of *kedushah* and decreed that a *tamei meis* was not permitted there. That is the extra rabbinic restriction that applies to a *tamei meis*. A *ba'al keri*, as we will see in today's *Gemara*, is *assur* on *Har Habayit* outright. A *tevul yom* is likewise *assur*. As for non-Jews who brought *korbanos*, according to the understanding of the *Mishnah* and *Gemara*, they would send their offerings without being personally present.

---

## Leviim 24 Watches

### Middot Parallel

The *Gemara* now cites *t'nan hatam* — a parallel *Mishnah* found at the beginning of *Middot*. When we first encountered our *Mishnah* in *Tamid*, it was noted that the *Mishnah* in *Middot* addresses not only the *Kohanim* but also the *Levi'im*. The text of that *Mishnah* runs as follows:

*Bishlosha mekomos haKohanim shomrim b'Veis HaMikdash* — in three places the *Kohanim* guard in the *Beis HaMikdash*: in *Beis Avtinas*, in *Beis HaNitzotz*, and in *Beis HaMoked* — the three chambers embedded within the walls of the *Azarah*. *VehaLevi'im b'esrim v'echad makom* — and the *Levi'im* in twenty-one places.

The *Mishnah* then details those twenty-one locations. *Chamisha al chamisha sha'arei Har Habayit* — five at the five gates of *Har Habayit*. These are the gates entering the outer Temple Mount, such as those visible today in the archaeological excavations along the southern wall. *Arba al arba pinosav* — and four at the four corners. One notes that the *Meforesh* here translates *pinos* as "angles," remarkably close to the English word. Importantly, *mitocham* — all of this watching on *Har Habayit* was performed from the inside of the walls.

This requires some reflection. One would naturally expect guards — particularly at corners and gates — to be stationed on the outside, where they would be more visible and better positioned to monitor approach. Yet the *Mishnah* specifies the inside. Together that gives us nine stations for *Har Habayit*: five gates plus four corners.

Next: *chamisha al chamisha sha'arei azarah* — five at the five gates of the *Azarah*. We will shortly discuss whether there were really five or seven (or even eight) gates; for now the *Mishnah* states five. *Arba al arba pinoteha* — and four at the four corners of the *Azarah*. This time, however, the *Mishnah* specifies *mibachutz* — on the outside. So for the *Azarah* proper we have five plus four on the outside, for another nine, bringing the running total to eighteen.

Finally, the *Mishnah* adds three more locations: *echad beLishkat HaKorban* — one in the *Lishkat HaKorban*, which was a chamber within the large space of the *Beis HaMoked*; *ve'echad beLishkat HaParochet* — one in the *Lishkat HaParochet*, the location of which is not entirely clear; and *ve'echad achorei Beis HaKapporet* — one behind the *Kodesh Kodashim*. These three bring the total to twenty-one.

### Deriving 21 Watches

The *Gemara* now asks: *Mina hani mili*? Where do we derive these twenty-one watching locations? Yesterday we learned that the obligation for *Kohanim* to watch was derived from the *pasuk* of *sha'aru vanu veno*, and that *Levi'im* shared in that watch as well, drawn from the *pasuk* of *veyilavu alecha* — the *Kohanim* above, the *Levi'im* below. But the question of where twenty-one specifically is derived from remains open. The *Gemara*'s working assumption is that this number traces back not merely to convention but to *Torah* — or at least to a substantive source. One might fairly ask: why does it feel the need to derive this from a *pasuk* at all? Even if the derivation will come from *Divrei HaYamim* rather than the *Torah* itself, it does not establish the number as biblically mandated. The best answer seems to be that the *Gemara* is not asking "how do we know this is true" — it accepts the *Mishnah* as factually accurate — but rather "what is it based on?" The goal is to establish continuity, to show that this arrangement traces back to the time of King David and was not invented arbitrarily.

### Divrei Hayamim Source

*Amar Rav Yehuda miSura ve'amri lah bemasnisa tana* — Rav Yehuda from Sura says, and some say it was taught in a *Baraisa*: the source is a *pasuk* in *Divrei HaYamim*. That book, in its listing of Levitical families, describes two functions of *Levi'im*: the *meshorerim* — singers and musicians — and the *meshoarim* — those who guard the gates. At the conclusion of listing all the families, it enumerates their assigned stations.

The *pasuk* reads: *Lemizrach HaLeviyim shisha* — to the east, six *Levi'im*. *Latzafona laLevi'im arba'ah* — to the north, four. *Lanegba laLevi'im arba'ah* — to the south, four. *La'asufim shnayim shnayim* — to the *asufim* (some translate this as antechambers or a similar space), two and two. *LaParbar lama'arav arba'ah lamesilah ushnayim laParbar* — for the *Parbar* to the west: four to the path leading up to it and two to the *Parbar* itself. The *Gemara* will shortly explain what *Parbar* means.

### Math to 21

If one simply totals these figures — six, four, four, four, four, and two — the sum is twenty-four, not twenty-one. The *Gemara* immediately confronts this: *ami hani chaf daled havu* — but that adds up to twenty-four.

*Amar Abaye*: *hachi ka'amar* — here is how to read the *pasuk*. When it says *la'asufim shnayim shnayim*, the doubled expression "two and two" does not mean four. It means simply two. As the *Meforesh* explains, *shnayim shnayim* is a way of concluding the *pasuk*, after which the next *pasuk* begins with *laParbar*. If the intent were four, it would have said four. The doubling is merely emphatic — it really means only two. This reduces the total from twenty-four to twenty-two.

But the *Gemara* presses: *achti esrin utrei havei* — it is still twenty-two, not twenty-one. The *Gemara* answers: *hacha deparbar, chad havei* — regarding the *Parbar*, it said two but only one station was actually required. Why then does the text mention two? *Vachrina betzavta hu de'azil veyatv gabeih* — the second person simply went along to keep the first one company. It was only one *Levi* genuinely on watch; the second was there so he would not be alone. This implies, incidentally, that the *Gemara* reads these numbers quite literally — one means one — though as noted earlier, the *Rambam* uses the term *edah* for each station. Perhaps the *Parbar* was a particularly isolated outpost, the furthest point from the flow of traffic, and therefore a companion was sent along.

Rabba bar Rav Sheila offers an Aramaic gloss on the word *Parbar* itself: *keman de'amar klapei bar* — it means "toward the outside," the most outward and distant station. That accounts for the companion. And the point about *derech kavod* — that no part of the Temple precinct should be left unwatched, unattended — explains why a watch was maintained there at all.

### Kohanim as Leviim

The *Gemara* then offers an alternative resolution: *ve'iba'it eima le'olam chaf daled* — perhaps the total really is twenty-four. *Tlata mineihu deKohanim* — three of those twenty-four stations belonged to the *Kohanim*. If three were for *Kohanim* and twenty-one for *Levi'im*, then the *pasuk* in *Divrei HaYamim*, which totals twenty-four, fits precisely: three *Kohanim* plus twenty-one *Levi'im*.

But this raises an obvious objection: the *pasuk* speaks throughout of *Levi'im*, not *Kohanim*. The *Gemara* invokes Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who taught that in twenty-four places in *Tanach* the *Kohanim* are called *Levi'im*, because *Kohanim* are a subset of *Levi'im*. One particularly clear example: *vehaKohanim haLevi'im b'nei Tzadok* — "the *Kohanim*, the *Levi'im*, the sons of Tzadok." These are unmistakably *Kohanim*, yet they are referred to as *Levi'im*. Thus, even where the *pasuk* in *Divrei HaYamim* says *Levi'im*, it may also encompass the three *Kohen* stations. The *pasuk* derives from the era of King David — before the *Mikdash* was built, when the arrangement was still that of the *Mishkan*. Nevertheless, the *Gemara* treats it as the model for what would later obtain in the *Beis HaMikdash* of Shlomo, and thereafter as well, emphasizing continuity across the generations.

---

## Inside/Outside Watch

### Difference Question

Having established the twenty-one Levitical stations and their locations, the *Gemara* turns to a pointed question: *Mai shna Har Habayit de'avidina mitcha* — why, when it comes to *Har Habayit*, did the *Levi'im* watch from the inside? *U'mai shna Azarah de'avidina mibachutz* — and why, when it came to the *Azarah* proper, did they watch from the outside?

This asymmetry is not self-evident. One might expect the default to be watching from the outside, where an honor guard would be more visible and where those approaching could be monitored. That the inside should be the default — and that the *Azarah* represents a deviation from it — requires explanation.

### Sitting Rule

The *Gemara* answers: *Har Habayit de'itama, ubai l'meysev, yasiv* — on *Har Habayit*, if a *Levi* grew weary and wished to sit and rest, he could do so. Because sitting is permitted on *Har Habayit*, we station them on the inside; no accommodation is needed. But in the *Azarah* — *de'itama, ubai l'meysev, lo matzi yasiv* — if a *Levi* grew weary and wished to sit, he could not. Why? *Ein yeshiva b'Azarah ela l'malchei Beis David bilvad* — sitting in the *Azarah* proper is reserved exclusively for kings of the Davidic line. Therefore, since a *Levi* stationed inside the *Azarah* would have no opportunity to rest, the *Gemara* says we move him to the outside, where he can sit down when he needs to.

This answer, however, leaves one question somewhat open. If the default is the inside, one might have expected the *Azarah* corners — particularly those adjacent to the *Ezrat Nashim*, where sitting would not be prohibited — to also be on the inside. Yet the *Mishnah* says *mibachutz* for all the *Azarah* corners and gates, which suggests that the outer positions of those corners were at the walls of the *Ezrat Nashim*, and thus the "outside" of those corners places the *Levi'im* at points that are not architecturally visible corners at all, but midpoints of the outer wall. The question of precisely where those four corners were located — whether the inner corners of the *Azarah* proper or the outer corners including the *Ezrat Nashim* — remains somewhat open in the discussion.

---

## Gate Count Debate

### Five vs Seven

The *Gemara* now returns to the *Mishnah*'s statement that the *Levi'im* watched at the five gates of the *Azarah*. The *Gemara* objects: *shiva'ah sha'arei hayu ba'Azarah* — were there not seven gates in the *Azarah*? Three in the north, three in the south, and one in the east. Most diagrams of the *Azarah* that have come down to us indeed show seven chambers and gates, and some depictions show even more. How then does the *Mishnah* say five?

### Abaye's Answer

*Amar Abaye*: *trei mineihu lo tzrichi shimur* — two of the seven gates did not require separate watching. The explanation given by Rabbeinu Gershom and the *Rosh* is that if the two outer gates in a row were guarded, the middle gate was effectively covered as well, since a watchman positioned atop an outer gate could observe in both directions and effectively monitor the gate between them. Thus, while there were seven gates, only five required dedicated watchmen. This is Abaye's resolution.

### Officers Debate

*Rava amar*, however: this is a dispute among *Tanna'im*. A *Baraisa* teaches: *ein pochtin mi-yud gimmel gizbarin u-mi-shiva'ah amarkalin* — there were no fewer than thirteen *gizbarin* (officers, at a lower supervisory level) and seven *amarkalin* (senior supervisors) in the *Mikdash* at any given time. Rabbi Natan asks, where does the number thirteen *gizbarin* come from? *Keneged yud gimmel she'arim* — corresponding to thirteen gates in the entire Temple complex. Five belong to *Har Habayit*, leaving eight for the *Azarah*. Thus Rabbi Natan's formulation implicitly presupposes eight gates in the *Azarah*, not five or seven.

### Factual Dispute

The *Gemara* concludes: *alma ika tanna de'amar tamnya havu* — we now see there are those who say eight; *ika tanna de'amar shiv'ah* — those who say seven; *ve'ika tanna de'amar chamishah havu* — and those who say five. This is, as the *Gemara* acknowledges, a dispute. What is notable is that this is not a *halachic* dispute — it is a factual-historical one. These things are generally stated without attribution, as accepted fact, and it is somewhat unusual to frame them as a *machloket*. One possibility: the disagreement may be partly definitional — what exactly counts as a "gate" warranting its own designation may have varied. In any event, the *Gemara* accepts that there were divergent traditions regarding the precise number of gates in the *Azarah*.

---

## Sleep Garments

### Under the Head

The *Gemara* now turns to the *Mishnah*'s description of the *Kohanim* sleeping in the *Beis HaMoked*. They slept in their own garments, not in *Bigdei Kodesh*, and would take off their *Bigdei Kehunah*, fold them, and place them *tachat rosheihem* — under their heads. It is worth noting, following the *Rambam*, that it was specifically the *Kohanim* who were on watch — or at least those watching in that chamber — who slept there, presumably on some rotation system.

### Benefit Question

The *Gemara* infers from the *Mishnah*'s formulation: since it says they did not *sleep* in the *Bigdei Kehunah* — implying that walking around in them would have been permitted — can we derive from this that *Bigdei Kehunah nitnu lhenot bahen*? That is, that one may derive personal benefit from the priestly garments? This is a significant question, given that we have just finished *Meilah*, with its prohibitions on deriving benefit from sanctified objects. During the *Avodah*, a *Kohen*'s wearing of the *Bigdei Kehunah* is not considered personal benefit; it is required. But what about moments outside the *Avodah*?

The *Gemara* deflects this inference: one could say that even walking around in them was not permitted; the reason the *Mishnah* says "they did not sleep in them" is simply to set up what follows — *ela poshtin umikaplin umanichin otan tachat rosheihen* — that they took them off, folded them, and placed them beneath their heads. The *Mishnah* is being descriptive about sleep-time behavior, not drawing a contrast that would imply other uses were permitted.

### Opposite Meaning

But now the *Gemara* turns to that description itself. *Umanichin otan tachat rosheihen* — they placed them under their heads. This sounds as though they used the garments as a pillow. Would that not constitute deriving benefit from *Bigdei Kehunah*? One might answer: *eima keneged rosheihem* — perhaps *tachat* here does not mean literally beneath but merely near, adjacent to. The garments were kept close at hand, not used as actual pillows. The classic use of *tachat* to mean something like "at the foot of" or "in proximity to" — as in *tachat hahar* — supports this reading, even if it is a stretch.

Rav Papa draws a practical ruling from this passage: *shma mina tefillin min hatzad sharyon* — from the fact that even if the garments were only placed near the head, and we are not concerned that a person might roll over onto them in the night, we may infer that *tefillin* placed to the side of one who is napping need not be worried about. *Velo chayshinan dilma mignadar vnafal aleihu* — we are not concerned that one might roll over and come to rest upon them. This inference draws on the well-established parallel between *tefillin* and *Bigdei Kehunah* — including the *tzitz* — as objects that confer a sense of *kedushah* and direct one's thoughts toward God.

### Kilayim Proof

The *Gemara* now offers a stronger proof that *tachat rosheihem* cannot be taken literally. *Hachi nami mistabra* — this interpretation also makes better sense for the following reason: even setting aside the question of benefit from *Bigdei Kehunah*, there is the problem of *kilayim*. The belt (*avnet*) of the *Kohen* was, by the account of many, made from wool and linen together — *shatnez*. During the *Avodah*, wearing *shatnez* is permitted because the *Torah* explicitly requires the *Bigdei Kehunah* in that context. But as soon as the *Kohen* is no longer engaged in the *Avodah*, the prohibition of *kilayim* reasserts itself. To use the belt as a pillow — placing it beneath one's head — would constitute a form of using *shatnez*, even without wearing it.

One might object: the *pasuk* forbids *shatnez lo ya'aleh alecha* — it shall not be placed *upon* you. If it is beneath you, perhaps it is not prohibited? The *Gemara* addresses this: *d'Oraita*, that might be correct. But *amar amru chachamim assur la'asot ken* — the Rabbis nonetheless prohibited it, *shema tichrach nima achat al besaro* — lest even a single thread curl upward onto the skin, providing a trace of warmth. This is a rabbinic *gezeirah*, and the *Gemara* adds that even ten blankets laid atop *kilayim* do not resolve the problem, as taught by the holy congregation in Jerusalem in a tradition transmitted through Rabbi Yosi ben Shaul, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and Rav Shimon: *afilu eser matza'ot zu al gav zu, v'kilayim tachteichem, assur lishon aleihem* — even ten mattresses stacked one upon the other, with *kilayim* beneath them all, are forbidden to sleep upon. This is also structurally reminiscent of the *halacha* of *mishkav u'moshav* of a *zav* or *zavah*, where the object beneath is affected even through many layers.

Accordingly, if even rabbinic restriction prevents using *shatnez* as a pillow — and *ein shvut b'Mikdash* does not apply here since this does not impede the *Avodah* — it is clear that *tachat rosheihem* cannot mean they literally used the *Bigdei Kehunah* as pillows. It must mean near their heads.

### No Belt Theory

The *Gemara* offers a partial counter: *haniha leman de'amar avneto shel Kohen Gadol lo zehu avneto shel Kohen Hedyot* — this reasoning works well if one holds that the belt of the *Kohen Gadol* was not the same as the belt of the ordinary *Kohen*. If the ordinary *Kohen*'s belt did not contain *shatnez*, then the *kilayim* argument collapses and perhaps the *Kohanim* did literally use the garments as pillows. But *ella leman de'amar avneto shel Kohen Hedyot zehu avneto shel Kohen Gadol* — if one holds the opposing view, that the ordinary *Kohen*'s belt was made of the same material as the *Kohen Gadol*'s — wool and linen — then the *kilayim* proof stands.

The *Gemara* also entertains another escape: *de'chi teima kilayim be'ha'alah u'velivishah hu de'assur* — perhaps *kilayim* is only prohibited when worn or placed upon one. If it is beneath one, maybe it is permitted even rabbinically? The *Gemara* rejects this, as noted above, based on the *Baraisa* that even placing it beneath many coverings is rabbinically forbidden. And the suggestion that perhaps the garments were folded beneath something else — so the *shatnez* fibers would never be in contact with the skin — is also rejected by the ruling of the holy congregation in Jerusalem.

However, the *Gemara* notes: *ve'iba'it eima, be'avnet she'ein bo kilayim* — alternatively, perhaps they used the garments as pillows and simply excluded the belt. The belt was the only garment containing *kilayim*; the outer garment, the *mitznefet*, and other items did not. So perhaps they placed everything except the belt beneath their heads, and that was perfectly fine. This leaves the question genuinely unresolved: we cannot definitively prove from the *kilayim* argument alone that *tachat rosheihem* is not literal.

### Hard Fabric Theory

*Rav Ashi amar Bigdei Kehunah kashim hein* — Rav Ashi offers yet another approach: the *Bigdei Kehunah* were hard and stiff. This is developed from a teaching of Rav Huna beray de-Rav Yehoshua: *ha-Namta Gamda de-Narsh sharya* — the hard felt of Narsh (a place name) is permitted, even if it contains *kilayim*. The principle is that if a fabric is extremely stiff and rigid — more like leather than cloth — it is physically incapable of draping over the skin and providing warmth in the manner of a garment. The entire *kilayim* prohibition in the context of *mishkav* is predicated on the possibility that a thread might curl up and touch the skin. If the fabric is so rigid that this is impossible, the rabbinic decree does not apply.

Ironically, this is the inverse of the usual softness concern: a soft fabric is forbidden even beneath ten mattresses because a single fiber might reach the skin; a hard, stiff fabric is permitted even directly beneath one because it is structurally incapable of doing so. If the *Bigdei Kehunah* were of this stiff, hard consistency, then even lying upon the belt directly would pose no *kilayim* concern, and *tachat rosheihem* may well be literal after all.

The *Gemara* thus concludes with multiple positions: the *kilayim* argument cannot definitively prove that the *Kohanim* did not sleep on the garments, because (a) the ordinary *Kohen*'s belt may not have been *shatnez*; (b) even if it was, they may have excluded it from what they placed beneath their heads; (c) even if they included it, the stiffness of the fabric may have resolved the rabbinic concern. Whether *Bigdei Kehunah nitnu lhenot bahen* when in the *Mikdash* — and whether the *Kohanim* literally used their garments as pillows — remains a matter of genuine discussion.

---

## Ba'al Keri Protocol

### Tunnel Route

The *Gemara* now turns to what happened if one of the *Kohanim* sleeping in the *Beis HaMoked* became a *ba'al keri* — experienced a nocturnal emission. He would exit through a tunnel, immerse in a *mikvah*, and wait until morning.

### Unconsecrated Tunnels

*Mesayei lei l'Rebbi Yochanan d'amar mechilos lo niskadshu* — this supports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that the underground tunnels were not consecrated with *kedushat Mikdash*. The very fact that the *ba'al keri* would route himself through the tunnel, rather than walking out openly, demonstrates that the tunnel offered a solution — and it could only offer a solution if the tunnels lacked the sanctified status of the areas above. Had the tunnels shared the *kedushah* of *Har Habayit*, passing through them would not have helped.

### Two Camps Rule

The procedure also establishes a second principle: *u'ba'al keri mishtale'ach chutz l'shnei machanos* — a *ba'al keri* is required to leave two camps. In the *Mishkan* in the wilderness, there were three concentric zones: the *Machaneh Kehunah* (the *Mishkan* itself), the *Machaneh Leviyah* (the *Levi'im* encamped around it), and the *Machaneh Yisrael* (the broader Israelite camp). These translate in *Yerushalayim* as follows: the *Azarah* corresponds to *Machaneh Shechina*; *Har Habayit* (including the *Ezrat Nashim*) corresponds to *Machaneh Leviyah*; and *Yerushalayim* itself corresponds to *Machaneh Yisrael*. The *metzora* — the most severe form of *tumah* — must leave all three camps, as the *Torah* says *badad yeisheiv*, he dwells completely alone outside the camp. The *zav*, *zavah*, *niddah*, and — as *Chazal* understand — the *ba'al keri* as well (*tumah yozei migufo*) are sent out of two camps: they may not be on *Har Habayit* (*Machaneh Leviyah*), though they remain within the city of *Yerushalayim*. The entire tunnel procedure thus demonstrates that even the *ba'al keri*, sleeping in the outer half of the *Beis HaMoked* which carried only *kedushat Har Habayit*, was nonetheless required to leave *Machaneh Leviyah*.

### Tevul Yom Status

After immersing in the *mikvah*, the *ba'al keri* becomes a *tevul yom* — one who has immersed but for whom nightfall has not yet arrived. A *tevul yom* of a *ba'al keri* is also prohibited on *Har Habayit*, just as the *tevul yom* of a *zav*, *zavah*, or *niddah* is prohibited there. The *Gemara* does not enter into the question of whether this prohibition is *d'Oraita* or rabbinic. The simplest explanation for why he was permitted to remain until morning — once the immersion was complete — is that the *tevul yom*'s prohibition on *Har Habayit* is only rabbinic in nature, and therefore it was not enforced in a way that required him to remain outside for the entire night.

### Beit Kisei Setup

The tunnel was lit with candles on both sides as the *Kohen* made his way through it. At the far end was the *beis kisei shel kavod* — the bathroom of dignity.
