Its *kavod* consisted precisely in its having a door. A locked door signaled that someone was present inside, and no one would enter an occupied bathroom. This was the standard of privacy maintained in the *Mikdash* itself.

---

## Rav Safra Story

### Snort Signal

The *Gemara* now applies this last detail to a contemporary episode. *Rav Safra hava yativ b'veit hakeisei* — Rav Safra was sitting in a bathroom. Rav Abba came and snorted — *nachar lei*. This was apparently the accepted signal: since one does not speak in a bathroom, one would snort, and an occupant would snort back to indicate the facility was in use. Rav Safra, however, did not snort back — he spoke. Not only that, but he said *leieil mar* — please come in.

### Rebuke

After Rav Safra emerged, Rav Abba rebuked him: *ad kan lo salikat l'Seir v'gamart milei d'Seir* — you have never been to Seir and yet you act like a Seirite. The reference to Seir — whether to Rome or to some other people known for boorish behavior — was a pointed insult: you have adopted the ways of the immodest without even going there. *Hachi tnan* — did we not learn in our *Mishnah* in *Tamid*: *matzo naul beyadua sheyeish sham adam* — if the door was found locked, it was known that someone was inside. Our very *Mishnah* reflects the principle that one does not intrude upon another in a bathroom. That is the behavior which *Tamid* calls *beis kisei shel kavod* — privacy as a form of dignity.

### Safra's Defense

Rav Safra defended himself: *dilma mesukan hu* — he was afraid the other might be in danger. If someone urgently needed to relieve himself and was forced to wait, Rav Safra was prepared to waive his own *kavod* and dignity rather than allow the other person to suffer potential harm. As the following *Baraisa* makes clear, this concern is medically serious.

---

## Bathroom Etiquette

### Health Consequences

*Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel omer*: *amud hachozer meivi et ha'adam lidei hadrokan* — the pillar that returns (meaning, the feces that is withheld and drawn back) leads a person to a condition of *hadrokan*, a painful abdominal illness, understood to include hemorrhoids. *Silon hachozer meivi et ha'adam lidei yarkon* — withholding urination leads to *yarkon*, jaundice. These medical observations explain why Rav Safra considered the situation potentially dangerous and why he was willing to compromise his modesty.

### Optimal Timing

*Amar lei Rav l'Chiya breih*, and similarly *amar lei Rav Huna l'Rabbah breih*: *chashich takin nafshach, v'kadim takin nafshach* — when it gets dark, take care of yourself; and when you rise early in the morning, take care of yourself. The reasoning: at nightfall, when people have returned home, and in the early morning, before they have gone out to work, one can relieve oneself close to home without embarrassment and without having to venture far into a forest or field. *Ki heichi d'lo tirchak* — so that you do not have to go far. Traveling deep into a forest or isolated area creates its own dangers, both in terms of physical safety and in terms of the discomfort that leads to illness when one avoids going to the bathroom because the journey is too inconvenient. By timing these activities well, *shalom al Yisrael* — one avoids endangering oneself altogether.

### Modesty Rules

When one actually uses the bathroom: *pra v'sheiv* — first sit, then uncover yourself. Do not expose yourself and then sit. *Kasi v'kum* — cover yourself before standing up. One remains covered whenever one is on one's feet. The principle is that exposure occurs only while seated.

### Cup Hygiene

*Shtof u'shetei* — rinse a cup before drinking. *Shtof ve'achit* — and rinse it after putting it down, for the benefit of whoever uses it next. One does not know whether the previous user was as careful about cleanliness; one should likewise not assume the next user will be. General hygienic consideration for others governs these practices.

*Shfoch mehen ve'achar kach ten letalmeidecha* — when sharing a cup of water with students, first pour some out, and then give it to them. The *Rosh* explains: a teacher would naturally share a cup with students as a form of *shirayim*, an honor conferred by passing one's cup. But the students would then be drinking from the part of the rim touched by the teacher's lips. By spilling some water from the edge, one effectively rinses the lip of the cup and spares the students from ingesting what had accumulated there.

### Death Story

*Uma'aseh be'echad sheshata mayim velo shafach mehen venatan letalmido* — there was once a case in which someone drank water and did not pour any out before passing the cup to his student. *Ve'oto talmid istanis haya* — that particular student was extremely fastidious. *Velo ratza lishtot* — he refused to drink. *Umet batzama* — and he died of thirst. This is a striking *Gemara*. The story implies there was no other water available and that the student would not pour out the water himself — presumably because doing so might have appeared disrespectful toward his teacher. The lesson drawn is severe: *be'ota sha'ah amru, lo yishte adam mayim veyiten letalmido ela im ken shafach mehen* — from that moment it was declared that one must pour out first before sharing.

### Respect Clarified

*Rav Ashi amar*: *hilkach hai talmida deshaffich kamey rabbeih, leit beih mishum apikureita* — therefore a student who pours out water before his master should not be considered to have committed *apikureita*. The term *apikureita*, as *Sanhedrin* defines it, refers to disrespect toward Torah scholars. One might worry that spilling water in the presence of one's *Rebbe* looks like an act of contempt. Rav Ashi clarifies: it is nothing of the sort. The student does it for cleanliness, not out of disrespect, and it is an act that saves lives. There is no insult in it, and therefore no concern.

---

---

# Tamid 28

## Cup Lip & Respect

### Cup Cleaning

We pick up at the very bottom of 27b, approximately six lines from the end, at the small *dalet* in parentheses. Rav Ashi rules: *hai talmida d'shafich chamra kammai rabbeh* — a student who pours out some drink in front of his teacher, specifically to clean the lip of the cup, is not guilty of *afkivuta*, disrespect toward a Torah scholar. The context is the preceding discussion about a student who was so fastidious about the lip of a shared cup that he preferred to die of thirst rather than drink from it. Rav Ashi is clarifying that this kind of fastidiousness, pouring out a little liquid to cleanse the rim, does not constitute degradation of a Torah scholar, because the intent is cleanliness, not contempt. The general rule that follows is *kol mili lo tiphut b'apei rabach* — in general, you should not spit or pour things out in front of your master.

### Squash & Porridge

There is, however, an exception beyond the cup of water already discussed: *mi-kra v'daisa* — squash and *daisa*, a type of porridge or oatmeal-like dish. The reason given is *d'kaptila shel avar damu* — they are likened to a strand of molten lead, an allusion to the method of execution by *sreifa*, in which fiery lead would be poured down the throat. The point is that saliva mixed with these particular foods is considered especially dangerous, so there is genuine justification to remove someone else's spit before consuming them. Thus, even in front of one's master, spitting out such food is permitted and appropriate.

---

## Watch Enforcement

### Officer Circulation

The Gemara transitions with *tnan hatam* — we learned in a Mishnah elsewhere. This is a Mishnah from Middot, cited here because, as the Rosh notes, since there is no Gemara on Middot, the Gemara in Tamid takes the opportunity to explicate certain Mishnayos from that tractate. The Mishnah reads: *Ish Har HaBayit hayah mechazer al kol mishmar u-mishmar* — the officer of Har HaBayit would make his rounds among all the watches. The reference to Har HaBayit is significant: recall that half the watches of the *Levi'im* were stationed around Har HaBayit itself rather than inside the *Mikdash* proper. He would go from watch to watch *v'avukas dolkos lefanav* — with torches burning before him, presumably carried by his attendants.

### Sleeping Detection

The Mishnah continues: *v'chol mishmar she'eino omed v'omer lo, Ish Har HaBayit shalom alecha* — any watch that, upon his approach, did not immediately stand and say "Ish Har HaBayit, shalom alecha," demonstrated that they had been asleep. One might ask how he could sneak up on anyone while carrying large torches. The answer is implicit: the test was not surprise but speed of response — the moment he became visible, the watchman was expected to jump to his feet. Failure to do so *nikar shehu yashen* — revealed that he had been sleeping. It is worth noting that sitting appears to have been the accepted norm for the *Levi'im* on watch, at least in certain positions; what was forbidden was sleep, not sitting.

### Burning Garments

*Chovto b'maklo* — the officer would strike the offending watchman with his stick. Beyond that physical punishment, *reshut hayeta lo lisrof et kesuto* — he had explicit permission to burn his garment. The Gemara then describes the reaction of those nearby: *mah kol ba'azara?* — what is that sound in the *azara*? And the answer: *kol ben Levi lokeh ubigadav nisrafim sheyashen lo mimishmaro* — it is the sound of a Levite being struck and his garments burned because he fell asleep at his post.

This passage is genuinely disturbing. It is one thing to impose physical discipline; it is another to set someone's clothing on fire, potentially while it is still on his person. The phrase *kol ba'azara* is also slightly puzzling, since the *Levi'im* were not in the *azara* proper and were presumably sitting — they would certainly not be in the inner courtyard. Perhaps it means the *Kohanim* who were inside the *azara* were hearing sounds emanating from outside, and so the phrase reflects their vantage point. As for the burning of garments on a person's body — one suggestion is that perhaps the watchman, having fallen asleep unintentionally, had not removed his clothing as the *Kohanim* did when they slept intentionally in the *Beis HaMoked* (where they would remove their *bigdei kehuna* and place them beside their heads). Another reading, perhaps more charitable, is that the burning was figurative — a kind of shaming or symbolic defroking — and that *kol ba'azara* reflects how people would gossip about the incident afterward. That said, the story of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's own uncle strongly suggests the account is entirely literal: *pa'am achat matzu es achi imi yashen vesarfu es kesuso* — once they found my mother's brother sleeping and burned his garment. No concern is expressed about danger to his person, which is itself striking.

It is worth remembering that in the ancient world, army discipline was severe and unambiguous. The Romans, for example, were known to execute soldiers summarily for dereliction of duty. The text appears to reflect a similarly uncompromising culture of military-style order in the Temple service.

### Ancient Discipline

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba reports: *ki mati Rabbi Yochanan bahai matnisa* — when Rabbi Yochanan reached this Mishnah, he said: *ashreihem larishonim* — praiseworthy are the earlier generations, who maintained such discipline that they would even punish people for *onesh sheina* — falling asleep — which is not a willful act; sleep overcomes a person involuntarily. *Shelo al onesh sheina al achas kama v'chama* — how much more rigorous must their discipline have been when dealing with fully willful violations. The implicit contrast is with Rabbi Yochanan's own era, where even voluntary transgressions went unchecked. Whether one reads this as sincere admiration or as tinged with irony, it reflects a clear reckoning with the passage of a certain kind of institutional discipline.

---

## Rebuke & Feedback

### Rebbi's Path

The Gemara cites a *braita*: *Rebbi omer, eizehi derech yeshara sheyavor lo ha'adam — ahavat hatochechot* — Rebbi says, what is the proper path a person should choose for himself? Love of remonstration. The *masores ha-Shas* points to Pirkei Avot for a parallel statement by Rebbi. The placement here is deliberate: having just described a regime of strict discipline and physical punishment for failures, the Gemara pivots to the spiritual dimension of correction and rebuke. Rebbi is not speaking of physical punishment but of welcoming critical feedback. The connection is clear — people being disciplined should not react with resentment; rather, a person who genuinely loves *tochachah* understands that it comes from a place of care and serves growth.

### Rebuke Blessing

*Shekol zman shetochachot ba'olam* — as long as people are giving genuine *mussar* to one another, and presumably also willingly receiving it, *nachat ruach ba'ah la'olam* — pleasantness comes to the world — *tovah u'vrachah ba'im la'olam v'ra'ah mistaleket min ha'olam* — goodness and blessing come to the world and evil is removed from it. The proof text cited is *v'lamochichim yinam* — to those who give rebuke it will be pleasant — *va'aleihem tavo birchat tov* — and upon them will come the blessing of good. The *mefaresh* notes that since the context is about loving to *receive* rebuke, he reads the verse as referring to those who accept rebuke — though grammatically, the verse speaks of those who *give* it.

The deeper point is profound. A society in which people earnestly want to hear what they could do better is a society in which everyone is working on self-improvement, and in which honor and pride do not become obstacles to growth. Many people are fundamentally decent, yet so protective of their dignity that when confronted with criticism they dig in their heels and bad behavior perpetuates. Rebbi's teaching is a call to cultivate the desire to hear honest and constructive feedback.

It is worth noting, as the Gemara elsewhere acknowledges, that not only does no one today want to receive *mussar* — no one even knows how to give it properly. Rebuke delivered from anger, wounded pride, or a love of criticizing is not true *tochachah* and will not be received as such. Part of the responsibility lies with the giver as much as the receiver. If the recipient senses that the feedback comes from genuine care, it becomes far easier to hear.

There is a well-known story — attributed either to the Vilna Gaon and the Dubna Maggid, or to another pairing of that era — of a great Torah personality who would invite a *maggid* regularly, whether weekly or monthly, specifically to receive *mussar*. This is the very spirit Rebbi is describing: turning toward someone and deliberately asking to hear what one might do better.

### Emunah Trust

*V'yesh omrim* — some say the proper path is *yachazik b'emunah* — to hold fast to *emunah*. Here *emunah* should be understood not primarily as theological faith but as trustworthiness in one's dealings with others, in the sense of *noseh v'noten b'emunah* — conducting business and human interactions with the greatest rectitude. The *mefaresh* explains it this way, and this reading fits the broader context of Rebbi's statement in Pirkei Avot as well. The proof text cited is *einai b'ne'emnei aretz lashevet imadi* — my eyes are toward the trustworthy of the land, that they may dwell with me — meaning, with God. *Ba'emunah yeteirah* — through an abundant measure of trustworthiness in one's dealings.

### Rebuke Heaven

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: *kol ha-mochiach et chaveiro l'shem shamayim* — whoever rebukes his friend for the sake of heaven alone, not out of personal offense or to feel superior, but out of genuine concern — *zocheh l'chelko shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu* — will merit to be in the portion of the Holy One Blessed Be He in *Olam Haba*, as the verse says, *mochiach adam acharai* — one who gives rebuke will come after me, meaning into God's inner circle.

*V'lo od ela she-moshchin alav chut shel chesed* — not only that, but a thread of *chesed* is drawn over such a person. This phrase, *chut shel chesed*, appears in several places in the Gemara — in connection with one who learns Torah by day and night, and in the *Aggadata* of Esther, where she is described as having this quality. It suggests an aura or halo of divine loving-kindness that surrounds the person. The proof text is *chen yimtza mi-machalik lashon* — favor will be found by one with a smooth tongue — meaning someone who knows how to speak in a way that is heard, that lands well, that is accessible and palatable to the recipient.

This is also a kind of encouragement for those who give *mussar* and face pushback: even if the receiver — or bystanders — reacts with "who are you to tell me what to do?", the one who gave rebuke in the right spirit will find divine favor and will be remembered well. The arc of the discussion moves naturally from the harsh physical discipline of the Temple watch to the verbal, interpersonal, and ultimately spiritual dimensions of correction and feedback — each step refining the previous one.

---

## Trumat HaDeshen Lottery

### Lottery Problem

The Gemara now turns to the actual *avodah* of *trumat hadeshen*. The Mishnah states: *mi she-rotze litrom et ha-mizbe'ach mashkim v'tovel ad she-lo yavo ha-memuneh* — whoever wishes to perform *trumat hadeshen* should rise early and immerse before the appointed officer arrives. Then the Mishnah continues and says *yavo v'yapayes* — the officer arrives and says, let us draw lots. The Gemara identifies a tension: *ha-gufa kashya* — the passage is internally contradictory. The first clause says "whoever wishes to do *trumat hadeshen*" — implying it is not determined by lottery at all, just by desire or perhaps by some other mechanism. Yet the second clause explicitly introduces a lottery. *Alma lav b'payes talya milta* — it sounds like the selection is not lottery-based. And yet: *alma b'payes talya milta* — it sounds exactly like it is.

### Before/After Edict

Abaye resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya — kan kodem takkana, kan l'achar takkana* — the two clauses refer to two different historical periods, before and after a rabbinic enactment. Before the *takkana*, the practice was: *kol mi she-rotze litrom et ha-mizbe'ach, torem* — whoever wished to perform *trumat hadeshen* could simply do so, as perhaps only one person would want to on a given morning. When multiple *Kohanim* sought the privilege, *ratzin v'olin b'keves* — they would race up the ramp of the *mizbe'ach*, and *kol ha-kodem et chaveiro b'toch arba amot zachah* — whoever preceded his fellow within four *amot* of the top won the right. There is something symbolically apt about this: *trumat hadeshen* is the very first act of the day, and *zerizin makdimin l'mitzvot* — those who are eager precede others in the performance of *mitzvot*. A race up the *mizbe'ach* is itself a demonstration of that very eagerness. In the event of a tie, the appointed officer would say *hatzbi'u* — extend your fingers — and they would hold out one or two fingers (but not the thumb; the Mishnah specifies *v'ein motzi'in godel ba-Mikdash*). The most creative explanation offered for excluding the thumb is that two fingers clearly emerge from a single hand and count as one, whereas a thumb extended alongside a finger might be misread as coming from two separate people — a way of preventing a *Kohen* from being counted twice in the count.

### Broken Leg

The reason the system changed is recorded in the Mishnah: *ma'aseh she-hayu shavin, ratzin v'olin b'keves, v'dachaf echad mehen et chaveiro v'nishberah raglo* — there was an incident where two *Kohanim* were neck and neck racing up the ramp, and one pushed the other off, and his leg broke. *U-chesherau Beis Din she-hayu ba'im lidei sakanah* — when the court saw that things were reaching the point of genuine danger, *hitkinu shelo yitramu et ha-mizbe'ach ella b'fayas* — they enacted that *trumat hadeshen* would henceforth be determined only by lottery. The racing was abolished entirely.

### Rava's View

Rava disagrees with Abaye's reading. *Idi v'idi achar takkana* — both clauses of the Mishnah are post-enactment, and there is no contradiction. When the Mishnah says "whoever wishes to do *trumat hadeshen*," it means whoever wishes to *be part of the lottery* for *trumat hadeshen* should immerse early. The word "*litrom*" does not mean he proceeds directly to perform the act; it means he wants a chance at it. This, it should be said, is quite clearly the plain *pshat* of the Mishnah.

---

## Service Order

### Pispas Opening

Having resolved the question of the lottery, the Mishnah now describes the actual sequence of events. The winning *Kohen* takes the key — which, as we learned in an earlier Mishnah, was kept under the custody of the elders of the *Kohanim* in the *Beis HaMoked* — *u'fasach et ha-pispas* — and opens the small door. The *pispas* is a small doorway inset within the large gate, analogous to a dog door set within a full-sized door, or a postern gate within a castle wall. At this pre-dawn hour, opening the massive main gate to the *azara* is premature and inappropriate. Instead, a small door that is built into the gate allows passage. This is the passage from the *Beis HaMoked* into the *azara* proper.

*V'nichnasu ha-Kohanim acharav* — the *Kohanim* entered behind him into the *azara*, *u'shtei avukot shel ur b'yadaim* — with two torches of light in hand among them.

### Group Division

*Necheleku lishtei kitot* — they divided into two groups. *Eilu mehalchim ba'achsadra derech mizrach, v'eilu mehalchim ba'achsadra derech ma'arav* — one group went along the portico to the east, and the other went along the portico to the west. The *achsadra* was a colonnaded walkway with a balcony-like structure above — and the Gemara will later clarify that they were walking beneath it at floor level, not above. *Hayu bodkin v'holchin* — they went checking as they walked. The *meforshim* explain this as an inspection for misplaced *keilim* or anything out of order, a kind of early-morning sweep of the entire *azara*. One might think such a check would be done at the end of the night rather than the beginning of the morning, but perhaps the analogy is a cleaning or inspection crew that arrives in the very early hours precisely because everyone from the previous night's service has long since finished.

Those going to the east had only a short stretch to cover; those going to the west had to traverse nearly three-quarters of the inner perimeter before meeting the eastern group. Both groups converged at the eastern wall — specifically, at the chamber of the *Chavitin*, located near *Sha'ar Nikanor*, the main gate into the *azara* proper.

### Chavitin Start

*Higi'u, higi'u* — having arrived, *eilu v'eilu omrim: shalom, hakol shalom* — both groups would declare to one another: peace, all is well. The parallel to the earlier scene — where the officer of Har HaBayit would receive *shalom alecha* or, failing that, would reach for his stick — is noticeable: both scenes are structured around a greeting that signals all is in order. Here, however, *hakol shalom* is the expected and happy result. *He'emidu osei chavitin la'asot chavitin* — they would then announce: let those who make the *chavitin* arise and begin preparing. The *chavitin* is the *Kohen Gadol*'s morning *mincha*, a meal-offering he would bring after the *Tamid shel shachar*. It would not be the first offering placed on the *mizbe'ach*, but the preparation — heating water, starting the process — had to begin early. The announcement at this moment is formulaic: it signals that the morning has begun and each department should move to its task.

It is worth pausing to note the distinctly military character of the entire sequence: the torches, the two-column march, the password-style greeting, the division of responsibilities, the immediate and ordered response to the announcement. The *Ramban* observes that the system of *mishmarot* in the Temple was modeled on the manner in which royal palaces were guarded and run. Every element of this morning procedure reflects that sensibility: the Temple is the palace of the King, and it is run accordingly.

---

## Kohen Trumat

### Washing First

The Mishnah now addresses the *Kohen* who has won the lottery for *trumat hadeshen*. *Mi she-zacha litrom et ha-mizbe'ach, hu yitrom* — he shall perform it. Before he proceeds, the others instruct him: *hevei zahir she-lo tiga b'kli ad she-tekadesh yadecha v'raglecha min ha-kiyor* — be careful not to touch any *kli sharet* until you have washed your hands and feet from the *kiyor*, the copper laver described in the Torah at the beginning of *Ki Tisa*. The relevant verse: *v'rachatzu yedeihem v'ragleihem v'lo yamutu b'vo'am el ohel mo'ed o b'gishtam el ha-mizbe'ach lesharet* — they shall wash their hands and feet so that they do not die when they come to the *Ohel Mo'ed* or when they approach the *mizbe'ach* to serve. The concern is *linah*: whatever *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim* was performed the previous night is invalidated by the passage of the night. He must wash anew this morning. The walk-around the *azara* that the group just performed does not itself constitute *avodah*, so those *Kohanim* had not yet been obligated to wash; but now, before touching any sacred vessel, the *Kohen* designated for *trumat hadeshen* must first go to the *kiyor*.

They also point out to him: *v'harei ha-machtah netunah b'miktzoa bein ha-kevesh la-mizbe'ach b'ma'aravo shel kevesh* — behold, the silver shovel is placed at the corner between the ramp and the *mizbe'ach*, at the western side of the ramp. This is in the same general zone as the *kiyor*. The instruction is explicit: you will see the *machtah*; do not touch it. First go and wash.

### Alone Walk

*Ein adam nichnas imo, v'lo ner b'yado* — no one accompanies him, and he carries no candle. He goes alone to the *kiyor*, and then alone up to the *mizbe'ach*. *Ella mehalech l'or ha-ma'arachah* — he makes his way by the light of the fire burning on the *mizbe'ach*. The reason he carries no candle is not entirely explained, though practically, one cannot hold a candle while washing hands and then handling the shovel, and there is no obvious place to set it down. As for why no one accompanies him — it is simply the prescribed manner of performing this particular *avodah*; he walks alone.

*V'lo hayu ro'im oto* — the other *Kohanim* could not see him, because the *mizbe'ach* and its ramp were very tall and he was passing between the ramp and the *ulam*, on the side away from where the others stood. *V'lo hayu shom'im et kolo* — they could not even hear him moving.

### Kiyor Machinery

The *Kohanim* outside knew he had reached the *kiyor* when *ad she-hayu shom'im kol ha-etz she-asah Ben Katin muchani la-kiyor* — they heard the sound of the wooden gear-mechanism that Ben Katin had constructed for the *kiyor*. The problem Ben Katin's device solved was this: any water left standing overnight in the *kiyor* — a *kli sharet* — would become *pasul b'linah*, invalidated by overnight exposure. To prevent this, a system of levers and gears was built that lowered the *kiyor* into a pit beneath the *azara* floor each night. Once submerged, the water was considered connected to the ground and did not become *pasul*. Each morning, the first *Kohen* to use the *kiyor* would operate the mechanism to raise it back out. When the other *Kohanim* heard the sound of that machinery — the creaking and turning of the wooden gears — they knew: *higi'a eit kiddush yadayim v'raglayim min ha-kiyor* — the time for washing hands and feet from the *kiyor* has come.

### Altar Ascent

*Natal machtas ha-kesef* — he took the silver shovel that had been left in its designated spot between the ramp and the *mizbe'ach*. *V'alah l'rosh ha-mizbe'ach* — he ascended to the top of the *mizbe'ach*. *Pina et ha-gechalim haylach va'haylach* — he moved the live coals aside, clearing space to access the inner ash deposits. *Choteh me-hachmot ha-pnimiyot* — he scooped from the innermost ashes, those that had been fully consumed, not the coals. He then descended the ramp on the other side, facing away from the *mizbe'ach*. *Hafach panav la-tzafon* — he turned his face to the north, turning back toward the face of the *mizbe'ach*. *Halach b'mizrachah shel keves ke-eser amot* — he walked about ten *amot* down the eastern side of the ramp, roughly a third of its length.

### Ash Piling

*Tzavar et ha-gechalim al gabei ha-ritzpa* — he piled up the ashes and coals on the floor of the *azara*. This is the act of *trumat hadeshen* itself: removing a symbolic scoop of ash from the *ma'aracha gedolah*, the main fire where the *olah* and fats had burned through the night, and depositing it at the designated spot alongside the ramp. *Rachok min ha-keves shlosha tefachim* — about three *tefachim* removed from the ramp. This location is the same spot where the innards of the bird-*olah* were deposited (*morat ha-of*), as well as the ash-cleanings of the inner *mizbe'ach* where the *Ketoret* was burned, and the ash-cleanings of the *Menorah*. Notably, the *mefaresh* here distinguishes between these latter items — which he holds were miraculously absorbed into the ground where they were placed, as Abaye's statement in Yoma implies — and the *trumat hadeshen* itself, which he believes was not absorbed. His proof: the Gemara elsewhere states that one may not derive *hana'ah* from the *trumat hadeshen* even after it has been placed. If it were absorbed, why would such a prohibition be necessary? This is a striking observation, since we generally assume a unified miraculous treatment of all these deposits, yet this *mefaresh* argues the *trumat hadeshen* stood apart.

---

## Architecture & Order

### Balcony Question

The Gemara asks: *umi havu achsadra'ot ba'azara?* — could there really have been balconies or colonnaded structures in the *azara*? A *braita* cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: *minayin she'ein osim achsadra'ot ba'azara?* — how do we know that one may not construct *achsadra'ot* in the *azara*? The verse is *lo tita lecha ashera kol etz etzel mizbe'ach Hashem Elokecha* — you shall not plant any tree beside the altar of Hashem. Read expansively: beyond the prohibition of an *ashera*, there is a prohibition against any wooden structure (*kol etz*) near the *mizbe'ach* — including wooden balconies in the *azara*. The resolution is straightforward: Rav Chisda rules *b'achsadra'ot shel binyan* — the *achsadra'ot* of the *azara* were built of stone, not wood. There is no reason to assume they were made of wood, and therefore no violation.

### Service Sequence

The Mishnah's instruction to get the *chavitin* makers started seems to imply the *chavitin* was among the first things offered after *trumat hadeshen*. The Gemara addresses this: *minayin she'ein davar kodem la-Tamid shel shachar?* — how do we know that nothing precedes the morning *Tamid* in terms of offerings on the *mizbe'ach*? The verse says *v'arach aleha ha-olah* — everything goes up upon the *olah*, meaning the *Tamid* as the *olah* comes first. Rava adds: *ha-olah olah rishona* — the *olah* is placed first before everything. The *chavitin*, though it required early preparation, was not offered before the *Tamid*.

### Water Heating

Rav Yehuda resolves the apparent inconsistency: *le-hachaim chammin l'revicha* — the instruction to get started was not about offering the *chavitin* first, but about heating the water needed to make it. The *chavitin* required boiling water and a process that took time. While the actual offering would come only after the *Tamid shel shachar*, the preparation had to begin much earlier. Thus, the announcement at the chamber — *he'emidu osei chavitin la'asot chavitin* — was a call to begin the preparatory work, not the offering itself.

With this the first *perek* concludes: *Hadran alach bishloshoh mekomot.*

---

## Morning Tending

### Kohanim Rush

The second *perek* opens immediately. *Ra'u echad she-yarad* — the other *Kohanim* saw the *Kohen* designated for *trumat hadeshen* descending the ramp, indicating he was nearly done. *V'hen ratzin u-va'in* — they came running. *Maharu v'kidshu yedeihem v'ragleihem min ha-kiyor* — they hurried and washed their hands and feet from the *kiyor*, because now that the *trumat hadeshen* is complete, the full morning *avodah* is about to begin and they must be prepared to handle the *keilim*.

### Clear Meat

*Natlu et ha-magrefot v'et ha-tzinorot* — they took the various shovels and pitchforks. *V'alu l'rosh ha-mizbe'ach* — they ascended to the top of the *mizbe'ach*. The task before them: *evarim u-fedarim shelo nit'aklu mibe'od erev* — the limbs of the *olah* and the fats that had not been fully consumed overnight. These had been placed on the *ma'aracha gedolah*, the main fire, but may not have burned through entirely by morning. They had to be cleared away so that the ash-tending could proceed. But they could not simply remove this material from the *mizbe'ach*: any *evarim* or *fedarim* from the previous day, if taken off the *mizbe'ach*, would be *pasul b'linah* and could never be returned. So long as they remained on the *mizbe'ach*, they were valid; once removed, they could not be put back.

### Side Placement

*Sokin otan al tzidei ha-mizbe'ach* — they pushed them to the sides of the *mizbe'ach*, getting them out of the way without removing them. *Im ein tzadadim machzikin* — if the sides were too crowded, *sodrin otan ba-sovev* — they arranged them on the *sovev*, the walkway that ran around the mid-level of the *mizbe'ach*. If even that was insufficient, the *evarim* could be placed on the ramp itself. In every case, the material stayed on the *mizbe'ach* or its ramp — never off it.

### Ash Pile

*Hechelu ma'alin ba-eifer al gabei tapuach* — they began transferring the accumulated ashes up to the *tapuach*, the great ash pile in the center of the *mizbe'ach* surface. This is the real and practical tending of the fire, as distinct from the symbolic single-scoop *trumat hadeshen*. The ashes from the *ma'aracha gedolah* would build up; they needed to be moved to the central pile. The *tapuach* stood in the middle of the *mizbe'ach*. *Pe'amim she-haya alav ke-shlosh me'ot kur* — at times there were 300 *kur* of ash on it, an enormous quantity, representing a veritable mountain.

### Festival Ashes

*U-varegalim lo hayu medashnin oto* — on the *Regalim*, the pilgrimage festivals, when all of Israel was present and the volume of sacrifices was extraordinary, they would deliberately not clear out the *tapuach*. *Mipnei she-hu noy la-mizbe'ach* — because the great ash mound was considered beautiful, a dignified aesthetic feature, and a visible testament to the abundance of *korbanos* being offered. To see an enormous ash pile was to understand the scale of the nation's service. Nevertheless, *u-miyamav lo nitatzel ha-kohen milhotzi et ha-deshen* — never in all the days of the Temple did a *Kohen* prove lazy about removing the ashes when the time came to do so. However large the pile, however demanding the task, no one ever said: it is someone else's turn. We will continue with the tending of the fire in the next session.

---

---

# Tamid 30

## Lottery & Service Roles

### Service Roles Overview

The third *perek* opens with the *memuneh* — the appointed supervisor — addressing the assembled *kohanim*: *bo'u vehifisu*, come and take part in the lottery. The *memuneh* then enumerates the roles to be distributed. Who will perform the *shechita* of the *tamid*? Who will do the *zrika* — the throwing of the blood? It is worth noting that *kabalat hadam* and *holachat hadam*, the receiving and conveying of the blood, are not listed separately; those roles belonged to the same *kohen* who also performed the *zrika*. The *mekabel* caught the blood, brought it to the *mizbeach*, and performed the throwing — all as a single assignment.

### Shechita & Zrika

The *mishnah* continues: *mi medashen mizbeach hapnimi*, who will remove the ashes from the inner *mizbeach*? And *mi medashen et hamenorah*, who will remove the ashes from the *menorah*? The verb *medashen* here carries the sense of removal — stripping away — rather than adding anything. Similarly, *shechita* was in principle permissible even by a non-*kohen*, though for the *tamid* specifically this was certainly not the practice. The *payisot*, the lotteries, were conducted in the morning and applied primarily to the communal aspects of the service. Individual *korbanot* were handled differently — there was presumably some form of floor management to keep things moving, and a lottery was not conducted every time a private person arrived with an animal. The *mishnah* in *Shekalim* even names a specific individual as the *memuneh al hapayisot*, suggesting this was a recognized, ongoing appointment rather than a one-time role.

### Dishing Altar & Menorah

After the four roles just described — *shechita*, *zrika*, *dishun mizbeach hapnimi*, and *dishun hamenorah* — the *mishnah* turns to those who will bring the limbs of the *olat tamid* to the ramp. The sequence of roles in the *mishnah* does not reflect the actual order of performance. The *shechita* and *zrika* are listed first because the *tamid* itself is the focus, but as will become clear, the *dishun* — cleaning the inner *mizbeach* and the *menorah* — was actually performed first. The listing prioritizes the *tamid* thematically even while the operational sequence begins elsewhere.

### Payis & Allocation

The lottery itself — *hefisu*, they did the *payis* — resulted in assignments, and *zacha mi she-zacha*, whoever won, won. Beyond the daily morning roles, *payisot* were conducted for communal *musafim* as well. The *mishnah* in *Sukkah*, for instance, describes how the seventy *parei hachag* were distributed among the twenty-four *mishmarot*, three bulls each, accounting for seventy-two of the offerings, with the remaining two allocated by a separate arrangement. Similarly, *Shemini Atzeret*, as a *regel bifnei atzmo*, received its own *payis bifnei atzmo* for its *musafim*. Communal offerings generally required a lottery; private ones did not.

### Ma'aleh Evarim

The *mishnah* now enumerates the full list of *kohanim* involved in *ma'aleh evarim*, bringing the limbs of the *tamid* to the ramp. The first *kohen* brings the *harosh veharegel* — the head and the right rear leg. The second brings *shtei hayadayim* — the two forelegs. The third brings the *uketz veharegel shel smol* — the tail and the left rear leg. The fourth carries the *chazeh vegeirah* — the chest along with the trachea, esophagus, and associated thoracic organs including the heart and liver. The fifth brings *shtei defanot* — the two flanks. The sixth carries the *kirvayim* — the inner organs, meaning the stomach and intestines. That gives us six *kohanim* for the limbs alone.

To these six are added three more: *vehasolet*, the one who brings the flour of the accompanying *mincha*; *veha-chavitin*, the one who brings the *chavitei kohen gadol*, the daily *mincha* of the *kohen gadol* prepared concurrently with the *tamid* — the preparation for which, as noted in the previous *perek*, had already begun during the *terumat hadeshen*; and *vehayayin*, the one who brings the wine of the *minchat nesachim*. Combined with the four roles enumerated earlier — *shochет*, *zoreik*, *dishun mizbeach hapnimi*, and *dishun hamenorah* — the total comes to thirteen *kohanim*. It is worth noting that the one who actually flays and dismembers the animal does not appear explicitly in this count, which is curious given that *nikkur* requires considerable skill; it may be that not every role considered prestigious or specialized was subject to lottery in the same way, or that this was folded into the assignments of those handling the limbs.

The *chavitei kohen gadol*, it should be noted, were brought on the *kohen gadol*'s behalf even in his absence. He was not required to be present each morning, though had he wished to perform any part of the service himself he retained the prerogative — the *kohen gadol* may perform any service he chooses.

---

## Service Order & Timing

### Morning Readiness Check

Once the lottery was complete, the *memuneh* addressed those assembled: *tze'u ure'u im higia zeman shechita* — go out and see whether the time for *shechita* has arrived. They were gathered indoors, so someone had to go and verify. The requirement is not sunrise precisely but *alot hashachar*, the first appearance of the morning star, for *shechita* to be valid.

### Barkai Signal

The one on watch — *haro'eh* — presumably among the *shomrim* stationed on the rooftops — would call out *barkai*, an exclamation derived from the root of *boker*, meaning something like "it has shone forth." *Matya ben Shmuel*, who according to one version of the *mishnah* held the position of *memuneh al hapayisot*, would then add a verification: *he'ir p'nei kol hamizrach* — has the entire eastern sky lit up? *Ad she-be-Chevron* — all the way to *Chevron*? And the watchman would confirm: *hen*, yes.

The question of who is saying what here is itself a point of discussion. According to one reading, *Matya ben Shmuel* is not being cited as a *Tanna* but quoted as a *kohen* who, during his tenure, introduced this more rigorous formulation. Before and after him, the exchange may have been simpler — just the watchman calling *barkai* and the *memuneh* accepting it. But during his time, he would press for the fuller confirmation: has it lit up all the way to *Chevron*?

According to the version in *Yoma*, it was the watchman on the roof who said the entire east has lit up, and the *memuneh* — or *Matya ben Shmuel* — who responded by asking "All the way to *Chevron*?" eliciting the final *hen*. The reason for specifically mentioning *Chevron*, according to another discussion elsewhere, was to evoke *zechut avot* in the context of the *korbanot* — an interesting resonance given the broader theme of *tefillah keneged avot* and *keneged korbanot*.

### Pre-Dawn Error

The reason for this careful double-verification was rooted in a historical incident: on one occasion they mistook an early glow for *alot hashachar*, slaughtered the *tamid*, and the entire service was rendered *pasul* — invalid — because it had been performed before it was actually light.

### Sheep Inspection

Following the check, the *memuneh* instructed the *kohanim*: *tze'u vehavi'u taleh me-lishkat hatla'im* — go and bring a sheep from the chamber of sheep, where animals were held for four days of examination to ensure they were without blemishes. The *lishkat hatla'im* is described as being in the northwest — this refers to the location of the *Beit Hamoked* as a whole, within which the chamber occupied its own position. The sheep kept there were checked each day, with one removed as another was introduced on a rolling basis.

---

## Beit Hamoked Chambers

### Four Chambers

A *Baraita* teaches that the *Beit Hamoked* contained four chambers — *arba lishchot hayu sham*. These were housed within the large structure of the *Beit Hamoked* itself.

### Chamber of Seals

The first chamber was *lishkat hatla'im*, for the sheep. The second was *lishkat hachotamot*, the chamber of seals. This chamber served the needs of those bringing private *korbanot*: if a person needed to provide the *minchat nesachim* — the oil, flour, and wine accompanying his *korban* — he would go to this chamber, pay, and receive a *chotam* or *petek*, a kind of receipt or token. He would then present this token when his offering was being processed, and the *kohanim* would supply the requisite materials on his behalf.

A natural question arises: how could an ordinary Israelite access a chamber that seems to be located deep within the *azarah*, well into the *ezrat kohanim*? The answer is that the chamber was accessible from the outside — through an entrance that did not require the person to enter the sanctified area. The gate associated with this access may well have been *Sha'ar Hakorban* for this very reason. The visitor would remain on the portion of the chamber that was not within the full sanctity of the *azara* and conduct his transaction from there. It is also worth noting, incidentally, that according to the *Gemara* the *Chashmonaim* buried the stones of the defiled *mizbeach* — the *avnei mizbeach* that had been desecrated by the *Yevanim* — beneath the floor of this chamber.

The third chamber was *lishkat beit hamoked* proper, which housed a fire — though since the main structure also had a central fire, the precise function of this subsidiary chamber is not entirely clear. The fourth chamber, situated in the holy interior, was where the *lechem hapanim* was actually baked — *lishka she'osim bah lechem hapanim*. One chamber noted in other sources but not named in this list is the one containing the underground passage down to the *mikvah*, which was discussed in the first *perek*.

### Vessels & Gold

After retrieving the sheep from the *lishkat hatla'im*, the *kohanim* also went to another chamber — the storage room for the *klei shareit* — and brought out ninety-three gold and silver vessels. According to the *Yerushalmi*, the number ninety-three corresponds to the number of times God's name appears in the prophecies of *Chaggai*, *Zechariah*, and *Malachi* — the *nevi'im* of the return from exile who were present at the building of the second *Beit Hamikdash*.

### Final Inspection

They then gave the *tamid* water to drink from a gold goblet — *hishku et hatamid bechos shel zahav* — apparently to make subsequent flaying easier. Although the animal had been checked for blemishes over the preceding four days, the *mishnah* specifies that they would check it one final time: *mevakrim oto l'or avukot*, by the light of torches. The use of torches raises a question as to timing — was it still dark? The *mefaresh* suggests this checking took place before the full light of dawn, since even once the watchman on the roof could detect the first gleam, the chamber itself would still require artificial light. Another possibility raised is that they brought the animal indoors for this examination precisely to avoid having to return it to the *azara* once taken out if a blemish were subsequently discovered.

---

## Heichal Door Opening

### Pesach Ohel Moed

One of the fundamental requirements for the daily service is that the *shechita* of the *tamid* may not take place until the doors of the *heichal* have been opened. This is derived from the *pasuk* of *pesach ohel mo'ed* — the opening of the *ohel mo'ed* in the time of the *mishkan*, which represented the covered sanctuary space. Just as the *mishkan* required its entrance to be opened, so too the doors of the *heichal* must be *pasuach* before the service begins. The opening of those doors was, in effect, the moment the *mikdash* opened for business.

### Small Door & Keys

However, before the main gate was opened, the *kohanim* responsible for the *dishun mizbeach hapnimi* and the *dishun hamenorah* needed access to the interior. For this purpose, a small door — a *pishpash* — was built into the large gate, and entry was possible through it prior to the full opening. This is the purpose of the two keys described earlier: one key that would go into the *beit hashachi* — the underarm-length mechanism — and one that opened *keivan*, directly.

Several interpretations of this mechanism exist. One holds that there were two locks requiring simultaneous operation, one from inside and one from outside, with a small aperture in the wall through which one arm was inserted to turn the inner lock while another person operated the outer one from outside. A simpler interpretation understands *beit shachi* from the root *lishoch*, to bend down — meaning one lock was at a lower position and required the *kohen* to stoop, while the other was at normal height. Either way, two locks were involved.

### North/South Doors

The *mishnah* specifies that there were two *pishpashin* — small doors — built into the main gate of the *heichal*: *achat batzafon ve'achat badarom*, one in the northern portion and one in the southern. The *kohen* who merited the *dishun* would take his key and open the northern *pishpash*, entering first the small inner chamber — the hollow space within the thickness of the gate — and from there passing into the *heichal* proper.

### Ezekiel's Prophecy

As for the southern *pishpash* — *shebadarom lo nichnas bo adam* — no one ever entered through it. The reason is drawn from a *pasuk* in *Yechezkel*, which speaks of the third *Beit Hamikdash* yet was understood to apply to the second as well: *hasha'ar hazeh sagur yihyeh lo yipate'ach ve'ish lo yavo bo ki Hashem elokei Yisrael ba bo* — this gate shall be closed, it shall not be opened, no man shall enter it, for Hashem the God of Israel has entered through it, and it shall remain closed. One of the *mefarshim* explains this not as a straightforward statement of divine entry but as a theological emphasis: God does not require an open door to be present. Humans need doors opened to access a place; this door remains sealed to demonstrate that divine presence operates independently of physical access. The *pasuk*, of course, was said after the *churban* of the first *bayit*, yet the community understood it as binding for the second *Beit Hamikdash* as well.

### Opening Main Gate

The *kohen* who entered through the northern *pishpash* made his way through the interior of the gate and then turned to face the main gate itself. He then *he'evir et hanagar* — removed the great bolt — and *ve'et hapotechos* — undid the locks. Only once this was accomplished, once the sound of the great gate opening was heard, could the *shechita* of the *tamid* proceed: *lo hayah shochet hashochet ad sheshome'a sha'ar hagadol sheniftach* — the slaughterer would not slaughter until he heard the main gate open.

---

## Jericho Sounds

### Gate Heard Far

*MiYericho hayu shomein kol sha'ar hagadol sheniftach* — from *Yericho*, they could hear the sound of the great gate opening. The distance from *Yerushalayim* to *Yericho* is approximately seventeen miles, much of it open desert through which sound could travel and echo through the valleys. The *Gemara* never applies the term *guzma* — exaggeration — to this claim, and treats it as literal.

### Temple Sounds

The *mishnah* continues with an extended catalogue of sounds and even a scent, each heard or detected all the way to *Yericho*. *MiYericho hayu shomein kol magreifa* — they heard the sound of the *magreifa*, one of the musical instruments played by the *Leviyim*. According to some textual variants, they also heard *kol hashir* — the actual singing of the *Leviyim*, though this appears in some *girsaot* and not others. *MiYericho hayu shomein kol Ben Arza makish betziltzal* — they heard the sound of *Ben Arza* striking the *tziltzal*, a percussion instrument. *MiYericho hayu shomein kol hachalil* — they heard the flute, which was played on the twelve occasions of *Hallel* in the year. *MiYericho hayu shomein kol Gevini Karoz* — they heard the voice or sound of *Gevini Karoz*, apparently another musical instrument or trumpeter. *MiYericho hayu shomein kol ha'etz she'asa Ben Katin mechona laki'or* — they heard the sound of the wooden mechanical contraption constructed by *Ben Katin* to lower the *ki'or* into the ground overnight so that the water within it would not become *pasul bilina*, invalidated by remaining stationary overnight. *MiYericho hayu shomein kol shir* — the sound of song. *MiYericho haya shomeia kol hashofar* — they heard the *shofar* blown at the time of the *korbanot*. And *veyesh omrim af kolo shel kohen gadol besha'ah shehu mazkir et HaShem beYom HaKippurim* — some say they could even hear the *kohen gadol* pronouncing the Divine Name on *Yom HaKippurim*, though others understand this not as the *kohen gadol*'s voice itself but the sound of the entire assembled congregation responding *baruch shem kevod malchuto l'olam va'ed*.

The rhythmic repetition of *MiYericho hayu* throughout this passage is striking — one wonders whether this formulation may have had some early liturgical character, similar to other repeated refrains found in early *tefillah* compositions.

### Incense Smell

*MiYericho hayu merichin reiach pitum haktoret* — from *Yericho* they could even smell the burning of the *ketoret*. *Rabbi Elazar ben Diglai* adds: his father had goats in the hills of *Michvar* — a distant location — and those goats would sneeze (*mitatshot*) from the smell of the *pitum haktoret*. This anecdote serves as independent testimony to how far the fragrance of the incense could travel, reinforcing the *mishnah*'s remarkable claim about the reach of the Temple's sights and sounds.

---

## Slaughter House Area

### Slaughter Location

The *mishnah* turns next to the group that merited the *tamid* itself. *Mi shezacha batamid meshacho vehalach leBeit Hamitbachayim* — the one who won the *tamid* took the sheep and went to the *Beit Hamitbachayim*, the slaughter area, together with *umi shezachu ba'evarim holchim imo* — the *kohanim* who would deal with the limbs went along with him. The assumption is that those assigned to bring the limbs were also the ones who retrieved the sheep from the *lishkat hatla'im*.

*Beit Hamitbachayim hayu tzefono shel mizbe'ach* — the slaughter area was to the north of the *mizbeach*. This is consistent with the requirement of *tzafona lifnei Hashem* — that *kodshei kodashim*, including the *tamid*, had to be slaughtered to the north of the *mizbeach*. The area also contained marble tables for flaying, dismembering, and washing out the intestines, all of which took place in this same space.

### Pillars & Hooks

*Ve'alav shemonah amudim nanasim* — over this area stood eight miniature pillars, short columns, each topped with *revi'im shel erez* — square frames of cedar wood. *Ve'onkla'ot shel barzel hayu kevu'im bahem* — iron hooks were fixed into these cedar frames. *Ve'gimmel sedarim lechol echad ve'echad* — three rows of hooks for each pillar. *Uvahem tolim umafshitim* — on these the *korbanot* were suspended and flayed.

The reason for three rows of hooks on each frame is likely practical: different animals — sheep, goats, and cattle — vary considerably in size, and a single fixed height would not serve all of them. An adjustable arrangement, or at least multiple levels, would accommodate the range of animals brought.

### Marble Tables

*Al shulchanot shel shayish shebein ha'amudim* — between the pillars were marble tables. These are where the flaying and dismembering took place, and where the intestines were washed out. The relationship between the pillars and the tables — whether interspersed or simply in proximity — is illustrated by the layout of the area itself.

---

## Altar & Menorah Clean

### Altar Ashes

The *mishnah* now addresses the actual performance of the *dishun mizbeach hapnimi*. *Mi shezacha bidishun mizbeach hapnimi nichnas venatal et hateni* — the one who merited the cleaning of the inner *mizbeach* entered and took his gold basket. *Vehinicho lefanav* — he set it down on the floor before him. *Vechofen venoten letocho* — and then, remarkably, he would scoop the ashes off the top of the inner *mizbeach* with his bare hands, placing them into the basket. The choice to use hands rather than an implement is not explained; it is simply the practice.

*Uva'acharono kibed et hash'ar letocho* — and at the end, having scooped what he could by hand, he would sweep the remainder into the basket. Though the *mishnah* describes him as carrying only four vessels with no explicit mention of a brush, he apparently had some means of sweeping the residue. *Vehinicho veyatza* — and he left the basket where it was and exited. The process was not yet complete; as with the *menorah*, the *dishun* of the inner *mizbeach* was performed in stages.

### Menorah Candles

*Mi shezacha bedishun hamenorah nichnas umatza shtei nerot ma'araviyot dolkot* — the one who merited the cleaning of the *menorah* entered and found the two western candles burning. The question of which candles are designated as the *nerot ma'araviyot* is itself a matter of debate. If the *menorah* was oriented along an east-west axis, then the most natural reading is that the westernmost lamp — the one facing the *kodesh kodashim* — was the *ner ma'aravi*. Others hold that the *menorah* was oriented differently and that the *ner ma'aravi* was the central shaft, which faced west. Still others read the *mishnah* as referring to the easternmost pair, with the *ma'aravi* being the one that was west relative to the outermost candle. The *mishnah*'s own language — two western candles — is at the heart of this discussion.

### Two Stages

The *mishnah* specifies that the *dishun hamenorah* was performed in two stages. The *kohen* would clean out five of the seven lamps, then leave two burning — or make them burning if they had gone out — and depart. The two-stage process is derived from *psukim*: *yaarchenu hakohen*, repeated twice in the Torah, implies that the attending *kohen* would arrange the *menorah* in two separate acts, each involving multiple lamps. *Medashen et hash'ar* — he cleans the remaining five. *Umeniach et elu dolkot bimcoman* — and he leaves these two burning in their place.

If those two had already gone out — *matza shekavu* — then *medashnan umadlikan min hadolkim* — he cleans them and relights them from whatever lamps were still burning, *ve'achar kach medashen et hash'ar* — and only then proceeds to clean the others. The two designated lamps must be lit before the remaining five are extinguished, so that the two-stage sequence is preserved in all circumstances.

### Stone & Steps

*Ve'even hayta lifnei hamenorah* — there was a stone in front of the *menorah*, *uvah shlosha maalot* — with three steps cut into it. *She'aleha kohen omed umetiv et hanerot* — the *kohen* would stand on these steps to service the lamps, since the *menorah* stood at a height that required elevation for proper access, particularly for cleaning and wick replacement.

### Pitcher & Exit

*Umaniach et hakuz al ma'ala shniya* — he placed the pitcher — the vessel he carried for this purpose — on the second step. Into this pitcher went the old wicks and whatever residue had been cleaned from the lamps, in the same way the basket received the ashes from the inner *mizbeach*. *Veyatza* — and he exited. As with the *dishun mizbeach hapnimi*, the process was left in an intermediate state: two lamps burning, five cleaned, and a return visit yet to come. The continuation of these final steps will be addressed at our next session.

---

---

# Tamid 31

## Chapter Four Opening

### Perek Dalet Overview

With this daf we begin the fourth *perek* of Masechet Tamid, which addresses the morning service in the Beit HaMikdash leading up to and through the *korban tamid*. The *masechet* as a whole is named for the *tamid*, and this chapter brings us at last to the actual *shechita* of the morning sacrifice — the culmination of all the preparatory activity described in the preceding chapters.

### Gate Opening Before Shec…

Before reaching the *shechita* itself, the *mishnah* reminds us of the sequencing already established: the gate of the *heichal* had to be opened before the *tamid* could be *shechted*. The two *avodot* performed inside the *heichal* — the cleaning of the ashes of the *menorah* and the cleaning of the ashes of the golden *mizbe'ach* used for the *ketoret* — preceded the *shechita* as well, even though the *shechita* is the central act. Now, at last, we arrive at it.

---

## Binding & Positioning

### Ma'akdin vs. Koftin

The *mishnah* opens: *lo hayu koftin et ha-taleh ella ma'akdin oto* — they would not *kofet* the lamb, but rather they would be *ma'akdin* it. What is the difference? *Kofet* implies binding both hind legs together and both front legs together — or all four together — which is precisely how one would conveniently carry a sheep on one's shoulders. That is what they did *not* do. *Ma'akdin*, by contrast, means binding a front leg together with a hind leg on each side: right-front with right-hind, left-front with left-hind. This is quite different from the standard way of restraining an animal for transport or slaughter.

The *Rambam* has an alternative reading: that they did not bind the animal with a rope at all, but instead placed its legs through the metal *taba'at* — the ring used to hold the animal's neck — so that the ring itself served to restrain the limbs without any binding. However the precise mechanics of *ma'akdin* are understood, the binding method was specifically distinguished from the ordinary way.

### Akedat Yitzchak Link

The connection to *Aqeidat Yitzchak* is immediate: the *gemara* picks up on the word *aqad* — the same root as *aqeidah* — and notes explicitly that this manner of restraining the animal was like *aqeidat Yitzchak ben Avraham*. This linguistic and conceptual link is significant. The *aqeidah* serves in several places as a model for *qorbanot* — in Zevahim and Menahot we learned, for instance, that the *aqeidah* teaches the requirement of a *ma'akhelet* (a knife) and the necessity of a *kli sharet* for the *shechita*. The *aqeidah* thus functions as the primordial *qorban*, the originating template.

This raises a genuine question about how far the model extends. One might argue that the very point of the *aqeidah* was that God never intended it to be completed — that He does not desire human sacrifice — and therefore using it as a normative model is itself surprising. Yet the liturgy in several places treats the *aqeidah* as if it were in fact completed and as if it should be regarded as an actual *qorban*, with its merit standing for Israel. The degree to which *aqeidat Yitzchak* serves as a template for *qorbanot* is a rich question that reaches the heart of what the sacrificial system means and why it was instituted.

It is also worth noting that the binding of Isaac as envisioned in most contemporaneous imagery does not look at all like the *ma'akdin* described here — binding a front leg together with a hind leg in the manner one does with an animal — which would be a very strange thing to do to a person.

### Animal Orientation

The *mishnah* specifies: *rosho la-darom* — its head is to the south — *u-fanav la-ma'arav* — and its face is to the west. The animal is oriented lengthwise along the north-south axis, positioned to the north of the *mizbe'ach* since *kodshei kodashim* must be *shechted* in the north. Its rear faces north — away from the *mizbe'ach* — so that it does not, as it were, turn its back on the sacred precinct (and so that any dung dropped does not fall toward the *mizbe'ach*). The head is thus to the south, and the animal's face is turned to face the *heichal* in the west — toward the *kodesh* and *kodesh kodashim*. Dignity and orientation toward the sacred are maintained throughout.

### Shochet Position

The *shochet* stands to the east of the animal, *panav la-ma'arav* — also facing west. This ensures that neither the *shochet* nor the animal presents its back toward the *heichal*. Both face the *heichal*. The *shochet* stands behind the animal from the animal's perspective, to its east, facing the same direction as the animal — toward the west, toward the sacred center of the Temple.

---

## Shechita Location & Blood

### Morning Tamid Location

*Shacharit hayah nishchat al keren tzevonit ma'aravit al taba'at shniyah* — the morning *tamid* was *shechted* at the northwestern corner, at the second ring.

### Afternoon Tamid Location

The afternoon *tamid* — *shebe'ein ha'arbayim* — was *shechted* at the northeastern corner, also at the second ring.

The twenty-four rings in the *azarah* corresponded to the twenty-four *mishmarot* (priestly watches), each *mishmar* with its own designated ring; the ring of *Bilgah* was famously sealed. For the *tamid*, however, the same ring was always used: the morning one in the northwest, the afternoon one in the northeast.

### Ring Placement Rationale

Three considerations govern this placement. First, the north: the requirement that *kodshei kodashim* be *shechted* in the north is paramount, and the placement as far north as possible emphasizes and maximizes this requirement.

Second, the east-west distinction between morning and afternoon: the *mishnah* in other sources teaches that the *tamid* should be *opposite* the sun. In the morning the sun rises in the east, so the morning *tamid* is placed in the west — as far from the rising sun as possible, specifically to preclude any appearance of sun-worship. In the afternoon the sun sets in the west, so the afternoon *tamid* is in the east. One participant raised a natural objection: perhaps the point is not "opposite the sun" in the sense of facing away from it, but rather that one does it in a direction that specifically *contrasts* with the sun's position — i.e., as a deliberate counter-gesture to avoid any possible association with solar worship. The *gemara* will cite a *pasuk* to this effect.

Third, the second ring rather than the first (northernmost): the shadow cast by the north wall would fall over the first row, meaning that an animal placed there would not actually be in direct sunlight. Moving one ring inward puts the animal in the sun — which is necessary in order for the placement to be meaningfully "opposite" the sun at all.

To summarize: the placement is as far north as possible to emphasize *tzafon*, opposite the sun's position (east-west) to express non-worship of the sun, and specifically the *second* ring rather than the first to avoid the shadow of the north wall.

### Blood Sprinkling Diagona…

After the *shechita*, the one who caught the blood — a separate *kohen* from the *shochet* — proceeded to sprinkle it on diagonal corners of the *mizbe'ach*. The *mishnah* states: *ba lo le-keren mizrachit tzevonit ve-notein ve-notein mizracha tzevona; maaravit deromit ve-notein ve-notein maarava deroma*. He came first to the northeastern corner and threw the blood there; then he came to the southwestern corner and threw it there.

Why diagonal corners specifically? The blood must go *saviv* — all around. By throwing at diagonally opposite corners, each throw covers two walls — the blood spatters in two directions from each corner — and the two throws together reach all four walls. The reason these two specific diagonals are chosen and not others relates to the *yesod*: the foundation ledge of the *mizbe'ach* did not run all the way around. The *yesod* ran only along two sides — the south and the east — meaning that the northwestern and southwestern corners were available for diagonal throws only at southwest and northeast, since those are the only two opposite corners that each have a *yesod*. The northwest corner had no *yesod*, which is why the throw could not be made there.

### Blood Spilling Foundation

The remainder of the blood — *shearei hadam* — was poured out at the southern *yesod*: *haya shofech al yesod dromi*. Since the *yesod* itself ran only partway, the actual area available for this pouring was quite limited — essentially just the small portion of the southern foundation. The *kohen* would finish the blood service at the southwestern corner and then pour out the remaining blood there at the south.

---

## Flaying & Initial Cuts

### Flaying Through Knee

The *mishnah* opens this section: *lo haya shover bo et ha-regel* — they would not break the leg of the animal. In ordinary butchery it was apparently common practice to break a leg as a convenience in hanging or suspending the carcass. Here, instead, they would make a hole — *nokvo* — at the *arkuvo*, the knee joint of the hind leg, and suspend the animal through that hole. The animal thus hangs by its hind legs, and the flaying proceeds from top — the hind — downward toward the head.

### Skin Removal Process

*Haya mafshit veyored* — one flays it going downward — *ad she-magia la-chaze* — until reaching the chest area. At that point most of the skin has been removed from the hind region down through the upper body, leaving the head area — and the very extremities of the lower legs — still unskinned. Flaying the extremities near the bone is far more difficult, analogous to trying to remove skin from a chicken wing versus a breast, and so those areas were left. Once the flaying reached the chest, the head was removed.

### Head Removal

*Chatach et ha-rosh ve-natno le-mi she-zacha bah* — the head was cut off and given to the *kohen* who had won it in the lottery. It is given with the skin still on, since the head area was not flayed. As we will see, the head goes together with the right rear leg and is assigned to the first *kohen* in the procession.

### Lower Legs Cut

*Chatach et ha-kra'ayim ve-natno le-mi she-zacha bahen* — the lower extremities, the *kra'ayim*, were cut off and given to the one who merited them. These are not the primary legs (*yadayim* and *raglayim*) but rather the feet — the joints nearest the hooves. Sheep and cattle have an additional joint in the lower leg (analogous to the distinction between knee and ankle in humans, though positioned somewhat differently), and it is there that the cut was made. Notably, the *mishnah* does not at this point specify who received the feet; we will find out later that they went together with the inner organs.

### Heart Blood Removal

*Vekara et ha-lev ve-hotzi et damo* — and he tore open the heart and extracted its blood. This line appears somewhat out of place at this stage of the *mishnah*'s account. The animal has been flayed and the head and feet have been cut off, but the chest cavity has not yet been opened — so one wonders how the heart is being accessed. Various explanations are given: perhaps a specific incision was made to reach the heart, or perhaps the line is better understood as a prospective note indicating what one does when one eventually reaches the heart. The plain sense seems to be that it is describing what one does at that stage of the process when the heart is eventually exposed, even if the placement of the line here is somewhat surprising.

---

## Limb & Organ Removal

### Front Hands Cut

*Chatach et ha-yadayim ve-natnam le-mi she-zacha bahen* — they cut off the front hands (*yadayim*) and gave them to the one who had won them. The *yadayim* — the front forelegs — are distinct from the *kra'ayim* (the feet removed earlier) and from the *raglayim* (the rear legs). Different *kohanim* received the front hands and the rear legs respectively, since these go to separate people in the lottery. The second *kohen* in the procession receives the *shtei yadayim*.

One might pause to note the order of processing: the animal is suspended by its hind legs; the head, feet, and hands have now been removed; the animal is partially flayed; and the orderly dismemberment is beginning to proceed from head toward the rear.

### Right Leg & Opening

*Ala le-regel ha-yemanit va-chatachah ve-netanah le-mi she-zacha bah* — he went to the right rear leg, cut it off, and gave it to the one who won it. *U-veitzim imah* — the two testicles came together with the right rear leg. The right leg together with the head goes to the *first kohen* (the first in the procession, *alef*). *Kera'o ve-nimtza kulo galui lefanav* — then the animal was cut open lengthwise, and the entire interior was exposed.

*Natal et ha-peder ve-natno al beit shechitat ha-rosh milmala* — he took the fat (*peder*) and placed it over the place where the head had been severed. This served an aesthetic purpose: the severing point was bloody and exposed, and covering it with fat — which was considered the most prized portion of the *qorban* — was regarded as dignified and pleasing. The head would subsequently be carried to the ramp with this fat arranged upon it.

### Fat & Organs Removed

*Natal et ha-kirvayim ve-netanam le-mi she-zacha bahen le-hadichan* — he took the inner organs and gave them to the *kohen* who had won the right to rinse them. In the lottery distribution, the *kirvayim* went to the sixth *kohen* (*vav*). Those organs were now carried to the rinsing tables.

### Rinsing Organs

*Ve-ha-keres madichin oto be-veit ha-madichin* — the stomach (*keres*) was rinsed in the *beit ha-madichin*, a separate rinsing chamber. *Ve-ha-kirvayim madichin otam shalosh pe'amim* — the intestines were rinsed three times minimally — *al shulhanot ha-shayish she-bein ha-amudim* — on the marble tables between the pillars.

The distinction here is significant. The intestines were rinsed right there in the *beit ha-mitbehayim*, on the marble tables adjacent to the pillars used for flaying. The stomach, however, because it contained a particularly large amount of fecal matter and waste, was taken to a separate room — the *beit ha-madichin* — located at the other end of the *azarah*, away from the main slaughtering area. The *meforshim* confirm this separation. The intestines were processed close at hand for efficiency; the stomach, because of the quantity of waste involved, warranted removal to a dedicated rinsing chamber.

### Organ Separation

*Natal et ha-sakin ve-hiprish et ha-re'ah min ha-kaved ve-etzba ha-kaved min ha-kaved* — using a knife, one separated — not fully excised, but separated at their points of attachment — the lung from the liver, and the lobe of the liver from the liver. *Ve-lo haya mezizah mi-mekomah* — he did not actually remove the lobe of the liver from where it was. The reason is that the lung, the liver, and the lobe of the liver were each destined to accompany a *different* section of the animal in the procession. By separating them at their junctions without removing them, one prepared them to go their separate ways while leaving them in place until the appropriate moment.

---

## Chest, Flanks, Throat, T…

### Chest Removal

*Nokev et ha-chaze ve-netanah le-mi she-zacha bah* — he made an opening in the chest area and gave it to the one who had merited it. The chest was assigned to the fourth *kohen* (*dalet*) in the lottery. It is described as *noikev* — making a hole or an incision — which is a somewhat striking phrase, but it refers to cutting out the chest section and conveying it to the appropriate person.

At this stage it is worth noting the interplay between the dismemberment order and the procession order. The animal has now yielded: the head (to *kohen alef*), the two front hands (to *kohen bet*), the inner organs for rinsing (to *kohen vav*), and the chest (to *kohen dalet*). The right rear leg went to *kohen alef* together with the head. The dismemberment does not proceed in a single strict sequence matching the procession order; rather, pieces are given out as they become ready, and each recipient waits with their portion until the entire animal has been processed.

A question arises about the *kirvayim* and the location of rinsing. The *mishnah* mentions the *beit ha-mitbehayim* and the tables *bein ha-amudim*, and one might wonder whether these refer to the same place. They do not. The *beit ha-madichin* for the stomach and the marble tables between the pillars for the intestines are two distinct locations. The marble tables were situated adjacent to the pillars where the flaying took place — the pillars served as suspension points, and the tables immediately beside them served as rinsing surfaces. The *beit ha-madichin* for the stomach was a separate, dedicated chamber at the far end of the *azarah*.

### Right Flank Removal

*Ala la-dofen ha-yemanit — haya choteikh ve-yored ad ha-shidra* — he came to the right flank, cutting downward toward the spinal cord. *Ve-lo haya nogei'a ba-shidra* — he would not actually cut into the spinal cord. *Ad she-magia le-vein shtei tzla'ot dakot* — he cut until reaching the area between the two thin ribs — the small ribs at the very top and bottom of the flank — and left those in place. *Ve-chatacha ve-netana le-mi she-zacha bah* — he cut out the right flank and gave it to the one who won it. *Ve-ha-kaved teluyah bah* — the liver was attached to it and went along with it.

The right flank thus went to the fifth *kohen* (*heh*), who would eventually receive both flanks. The *shidra* — the spinal cord — was left attached to neither flank yet, as it would go with the left flank.

### Throat Area Removal

*Ba lo la-gerah* — he came to the throat area. *Hini'ach bah shtei tzla'ot mi-kan u-shtei tzla'ot mi-kan* — he left in place the two little ribs on each side, which are at the top of the neck near the spinal cord. The ribs at the very bottom of the animal had gone with the rear section, and the ribs here at the top of the neck were left similarly undisturbed. *Ve-chatachah ve-netanah le-mi she-zacha bah* — he cut out the throat area and gave it to the one who had won it. *Ha-kaneh ve-ha-lev ve-ha-rei'ah teluyim bah* — the trachea, the heart, and the lungs were all attached to this section and went with it.

The throat area — *gerah* — went together with the chest, assigned to *kohen dalet* (*he-chazeh ve-ha-gerah*). So *kohen dalet* first received the chest section, and now received the throat with the heart and lungs hanging from it. The heart blood, as noted earlier, was extracted from the heart when the heart was reached — it was opened and its blood removed, though that step appeared somewhat out of sequence in the *mishnah*'s presentation.

### Left Flank Removal

*Ba lo la-dofen ha-smalit* — he came to the left flank. *Hini'ach bah shtei tzla'ot dakot milmala u-shtei tzla'ot dakot milmata* — he left in place the two thin ribs at the top and two at the bottom, just as he had done on the right side. *Ve-khakh hayah maniach be-chaverta* — the same had been done on the other side (the right flank). *Nimtza maniach shtayim shtayim milmala shtayim shtayim milmata* — the result is that two and two were left on top and two and two on the bottom.

*Ve-chatachah ve-netanah le-mi she-zacha bah ve-ha-shidra imah* — he cut out the left flank and gave it to its recipient, with the spinal cord attached. *Ve-ha-techol talui bah* — the spleen was attached to it. *Ve-hi hayetah gedolah* — this section was in fact the larger one, since it included the spinal cord.

*Ela she-ha-yamin korin gedolah* — yet they call the right flank "the big one." *She-ha-kaved teluyah bah* — because the right flank has the liver attached to it, and the liver is a large and significant organ. The *meforshim* note simply that the liver was a substantial additional piece. (The kidneys, it should be noted, are traditionally regarded as the seat of intelligence; the liver is simply very large, which is why having it attached elevates the perceived importance of the right flank.)

### Tail Removal

*Ba lo la-oketz* — he came to the tail. *Chatcho ve-natno le-mi she-zacha bo* — he cut it and gave it to the one who won it. *Ve-ha-alyah ve-etzba ha-kaved* — the fat tail (characteristic of the broad-tailed sheep) and the lobe of the liver went with it. *U-shtei klayot imo* — and the two kidneys as well.

The *oketz* section with the fat tail, lobe of liver, and kidneys thus went to the third *kohen* (*gimel*) in the procession.
