The fat tail was considered especially prized — fat is consistently treated as the finest portion of the *qorban* — and the kidneys, traditionally the seat of understanding and discernment, were also attached to this section.

### Left Leg Final Cut

*Natal et ha-regel ha-smalit ve-chatachah ve-netanah le-mi she-zacha bah* — he took the left leg, cut it, and gave it to the one who won it. *Nimtze'u kulam omdim be-shurah* — they now all stood in a line.

The left leg is cut last because it is the leg from which the animal was suspended throughout the entire process of flaying and dismemberment. One could not remove it earlier without bringing the animal down. Once the left leg is finally severed, every piece has been distributed and every *kohen* is holding his portion. The left leg goes together with the tail section — assigned to the third *kohen* (*gimel*) — whose *kohen* had been waiting since receiving the tail and had to wait until the very end for his full portion.

The ordering throughout is driven entirely by practical efficiency rather than by any ritual prescription. As the *mefaresh* notes: *ve-khol ha-seder ha-zeh ein shum pisuk ki im sevara — lefi mah she-nakhon la'asot osim* — the entire sequence has no specific scriptural derivation, only logic. They did it in whatever way made the most convenient practical sense.

---

## Kohanim Procession

### First Kohen - Head & Leg

*Ha-rishon be-rosh u-ve-regel* — the first *kohen* carried the head and the right rear leg. *Ha-rosh be-yemino ve-chotmo klapei zero'o* — the head was in his right hand, nose oriented inward toward his arm rather than pointing outward. *Ve-karnav bein etzbe'otav* — the horns were held between his fingers for stability. *U-veit shehitato milma'alah* — the severed side — the place of the *shechita* — was facing upward. *Ve-ha-peder netunah aleihem* — and the fat was placed over it, covering the severed site in a dignified and aesthetically fitting manner, presenting the finest portion of the *qorban* outward.

*Ha-regel shel yamin be-smolo* — the right rear leg was in his left hand. *U-veit ha-or mi-bachutz* — the skin-side was facing outward, as this was the cleaner and more presentable side — the exterior of the limb as opposed to the cut surface.

### Second Kohen - Hands

*Ha-sheni bi-shtei yadav* — the second *kohen* held both front hands. *Shel yamin be-yemino ve-shel smol bi-smolo* — right in right, left in left. *U-veit ha-or mi-bachutz* — skin-side facing outward.

### Third Kohen - Tail & Leg

*Ha-shelishi be-oketz u-ve-regel* — the third *kohen* carried the tail section and the left rear leg. *Ha-oketz be-yemino* — the tail in his right hand. *Ve-ha-alyah medudelet bein etzbe'otav* — the fat tail was suspended between his fingers; it was placed in the right hand because the fat is considered the choicest portion of the *qorban*. *Ve-etzba ha-kaved u-shtei klayot imah* — the lobe of the liver and the two kidneys were with it. *Ve-ha-regel shel smol bi-smolo* — the left leg in the left hand. *U-veit ha-or mi-bachutz* — skin-side out.

### Fourth Kohen - Chest & T…

*Ha-revi'i ba-chaze u-va-gerah* — the fourth *kohen* carried the chest and the throat area. *Ha-chaze be-yemino ve-ha-gerah bi-smolo* — chest in the right, throat in the left. *Ve-tzla'otav bein shtei etzbe'otav* — the small ribs of the throat section — the two thin ribs that had been left at the top near the neck — were held between his fingers. Attached to the throat section were the trachea, the heart, and the lungs.

### Fifth Kohen - Flanks

*Ha-chamishi bi-shtei defanot* — the fifth *kohen* held the two flanks. *Shel yamin be-yemino ve-shel smol bi-smolo* — right in the right, left in the left. *U-veit ha-or mi-bachutz* — skin-side outward. The right flank carried the liver; the left flank carried the spinal cord and the spleen. Although the left was physically larger, the right was called "the big one" (*gedolah*) on account of the liver.

### Sixth Kohen - Organs & F…

*Ha-shishi ba-kirvayim* — the sixth *kohen* held the inner organs, *ha-nitunim ba-bazeich* — placed in a vessel. *Ve-ha-kra'ayim al gabeihen* — and the feet (*kra'ayim*) placed on top of them. This answers the question raised earlier as to who carried the feet: the feet went with the inner organs. Both were considered less prestigious portions — the feet were bony and difficult to flay, and the inner organs required extensive rinsing — and they traveled together in a single vessel.

### Flour, Mincha, Wine

The seventh *kohen* (*hashvi'i*) carried the *solet* — the flour offering. The eighth (*hashmini*) carried the *chavitin* — the daily *mincha* of the *kohen gadol*. The ninth (*hatishi*) carried the wine. It is noteworthy that the *solet* and wine, which are components of a single *qorban*, are separated between two people; the flour preparations appear to have been done first, with the wine following.

### Ramp Placement & Salt

*Halchu u-netanum me-chatzi ha-kevesh u-le-matah be-ma'aravo* — they walked and placed all of the pieces on the lower half of the ramp, on the western side. The ramp was ascended on the east, so placing the portions on the western side preserved the open lane for the next procession to travel up unimpeded. When the time came, the *kohanim* would come up the eastern side and retrieve the pieces from the west, bringing them up in a second stage to the top of the *mizbe'ach*. This two-stage process — first to the lower half, then to the top — reflects a broader pattern in the *avodah* of investing multiple steps in actions that could theoretically be done in one, lending greater weight and ceremony to the proceedings.

*U-melachum* — they salted everything, including the *menachot*, since everything placed on the *mizbe'ach* requires salt.

---

## Shema Recitation

### Lishkat Hagazit

*U-va'u lahem le-lishkat ha-gazit* — and they came to the *lishkat ha-gazit*, the Chamber of Hewn Stone, where the *sanhedrin* sat. *Likro et shema* — to recite *shema*.

### Prayer & Sacrifices

The timing of *keriat shema* here is significant on more than one level. From a purely practical standpoint, the early morning light — just as the morning star has risen — is one of the ideal times for *keriat shema*, and so reciting it at this juncture is entirely appropriate. But there is a deeper dimension as well.

The *mefaresh* on this passage emphasizes that the *kohanim* recite *tefillah* at this precise moment — after the *zerikat ha-dam*, which technically completes the *korban*, but before the *ketoret* is burned, and before the limbs and fats are offered. His formulation is striking: *ve-hachi nakhon ha-davar she-yitpallelu kodem she-yaqtir shum haqter* — it is most fitting that they pray before any *haqtarah* (burning) takes place. And the reason: *veya'al qorbanam le-rei'ach nihoach* — so that the sacrifice will ascend as a *rei'ach nihoach*, as a pleasing fragrance. The idea is that the *tefillah* frames the burning of the *qorban*, contextualizing it and investing it with the intention and devotion that causes it to be received favorably. The *tefillah* comes first so that the *qorban* rises in its proper spirit.

This speaks directly to the fundamental relationship between *tefillah* and *qorbanot* — a question that runs through the entire architecture of Jewish prayer. Our *tefillot* are in many respects structured around the *qorbanot* they replaced and complemented. Here, in the Temple itself, the relationship is made explicit: the *tefillah* is not merely personal preparation, but a theological frame for the sacrificial act that follows.

---

## Gemara: Binding & Tables

### Binding Method Dispute

*Lo hayu koftin et ha-taleh* — the *gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama* — what is the reason for avoiding the standard binding? Two *amoraim* dispute the matter. Rav Huna and Rav Hisda disagree: one says *mishum bizui qodashim* — it is a disgrace to sacred offerings; the standard way of binding an animal (all four legs together, or front-to-front and hind-to-hind) is the ordinary, undignified way one moves an animal to the butcher, and it is beneath the dignity of a *qorban*. The other says *mishum de-mahalkhu be-huqqei ha-amim* — because that is how non-Jewish peoples bind their sacrificial animals, and we must do things differently.

It is notably striking that neither opinion gives the reason as *aqeidat Yitzchak ben Avraham* — which suggests that the reference to the *aqeidah* in the *mishnah* was more descriptive than prescriptive. The *aqeidah* language explains *what* was done; these two *amoraim* explain *why*.

*Mai beinaihu* — what practical difference follows from the two reasons? *Ika beinaihu de-kaftei be-shiraei* — a case where one bound it with silk scarves — *o be-shushalta de-dahava* — or with a golden chain. If the reason is *bizayon*, disgrace, then silk and gold are not disgraceful — they are luxurious — and such binding would presumably be permitted. But if the reason is *huqqei ha-amim*, the prohibition on imitating non-Jewish sacrificial practice, then even binding with gold chains would be forbidden, since the manner itself (not the material) is what must be avoided.

### Thirteen Tables

*Tnan hatam* — the *gemara* cites a *mishnah* from elsewhere: *shloshah asar shulhanot hayu ba-miqdash* — there were thirteen tables in the *miqdash*. The *gemara* then proceeds to enumerate them.

### Washing Tables

*Shemonah shel shayish be-veit ha-mitbehayim* — eight tables of marble in the slaughtering area. *She'aleihem madichin et ha-kirvayim* — these were the tables on which the inner organs were rinsed. As discussed in connection with the *mishnah*, these marble tables stood between the pillars used for flaying, and it was on them that the intestines were washed.

### Ramp Tables

*Shnayim be-ma'aravah shel kevesh* — two tables at the west of the ramp. *Ehad shel shayish ve-ehad shel kesef* — one of marble, one of silver. *Al shel shayish notnim et ha-eivarim* — on the marble one, the limbs were placed. This would apply not only to the *tamid* but to other *qorbanot* as well, where the various pieces needed a resting place as they were being carried to the ramp. *Ve-al shel kesef klei sharet* — on the silver one, the sacred vessels were set down.

### Ulam Tables

*U-ve-ulam shnayim mi-bifnim* — in the *ulam* (the hall before the *heichal*), two tables on the inside. *Al petach ha-bayit* — right by the entrance to the *heichal* proper. *Ehad shel kesef ve-ehad shel zahav* — one of silver, one of gold. *Al shel kesef notnim lechem ha-panim be-chnisato* — on the silver table, the *lechem ha-panim* was placed when being brought in. The new loaves of *lechem ha-panim* were baked, carried to the *heichal*, and set down on the silver table as a resting point — a two-stage process similar to what we observed with the ramp. *Ve-al shel zahav be-yetzi'ato* — on the gold table, the *lechem ha-panim* was placed when being taken out — when the old loaves were removed from the golden table inside the *heichal* and brought out.

Why one of silver for the inbound bread and one of gold for the outbound? *She-ma'alin ba-kodesh ve-lo moridin* — one ascends in holiness, one does not descend. The bread is going toward the golden table inside the *heichal*, so it must rest on a table of lesser sanctity — silver — so that its final placement on the golden table inside represents an ascent. On its way out, having rested on the gold table in the *heichal*, it cannot be placed on something lesser — and so the outbound resting table must also be gold. There was no material more prestigious than gold available to go higher, so both the inner table and the outbound table were gold.

### Showbread Table

The thirteenth table is, of course, the golden table inside the *heichal* upon which the *lechem ha-panim* rested continuously. *She'alav lechem ha-panim tamid* — this is the table on which the showbread sat at all times. The enumeration: eight in the slaughtering area, two by the ramp, two in the *ulam*, and one inside the *heichal*, brings the total to thirteen.

### Marble vs. Metal

*Mikh-di ein aniyut bi-meqom ashirut* — surely there is no poverty in a place of wealth. Given the extraordinary resources devoted to the *miqdash*, why were any of the tables made of marble? Why not make all of them of silver or gold?

*Amar Rabbi Chanina be-shem Rabbi Assi, Rabbi Assi be-shem Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak: mipnei she-hu martiach* — because metals conduct heat; they literally "boil" — they warm whatever is placed on them and would cause the meat and inner organs to spoil. Marble is cold and keeps its surface cool, making it suitable wherever food was placed on it. Accordingly, every table used for limbs or intestines — in the slaughtering area and at the ramp — was of marble. Only where vessels or bread were set down — surfaces that did not need to keep food cold — could the tables be of silver and gold as befitted the *miqdash*'s splendor.

---

---

# Tamid 32

## Daily Offering Location

### Binding Legs

The daf begins near the bottom of 31b, continuing into 32a, with the *gemara*'s inquiry into the source for the placement of the *tamid* offering: *shachar haya nishchat al keren mizrachit tzfonit* — the morning offering was slaughtered at the northeastern corner. Before examining the positioning directly, it is worth noting a point raised in the previous session: the Rambam's distinctive understanding of the binding of the animal's legs. Most authorities hold that the front leg and front foot were bound together on the left side, and similarly on the right — that is, each leg bound to its corresponding foot — before the animal was placed on the hooks for *shechita*. The Rambam, however, understands that no binding in the conventional sense took place at all. Rather, the leg and foot were threaded together through the ring itself, which served to hold the animal steady during slaughter. Virtually all other *mefarshim* reject this view, but it is the Rambam's characteristic position.

### Ring Positions

As for the rings themselves: there is some confusion in the sources regarding precisely which rings are meant. The *mishnah* specifies that the morning *tamid* was slaughtered on the northwest corner — *keren tzfonit ma'aravit* — on the second ring, and the afternoon *tamid* on the northeast corner — *keren tzfonit mizrachit* — again on the second ring.

Most *mefarshim* understand "northwest" and "northeast" to refer to the rings near the northwest and northeast corners of the *mizbe'ach* itself, not of the entire Temple precinct. However, the Yachin u'Voaz — that is, the *Tiferet Yisrael*'s classic commentary on the *mishnah* — argues, and suggests that the Rambam concurs, that "northeast" and "northwest" refer to the northeast and northwest of the entire space, not merely of the *mizbe'ach* corners. Under that reading, the rings in question would be the further row. This remains a point of discussion among the commentators.

### Facing the Sun

The *gemara* then asks: *mina hanei mili* — what is the source for this positioning? Rav Chisda cites the verse *shnayim layom kineged hayom* — "two each day, facing the sun" — where *yom* is understood to mean the sun itself. A *baraita* then confirms this reading. The verse already states explicitly that one lamb is brought in the morning and one in the afternoon — *chovat hayom*, the daily obligation, is thus already established. Why then does the Torah again say *shnayim layom*? To teach *kineged hayom* — that the positioning must face the sun. The *baraita* then elaborates: *tamid shel shachar haya nishchat al keren tzfonit ma'aravit* — the morning offering at the northwest corner, *al taba'at shniya* — on the second ring; and the afternoon offering at the northeast corner, again on the second ring.

The reasoning is geometric and practical. In the morning, the sun rises in the east, casting shadows from the eastern wall westward. To have the animal positioned in direct sunlight — *kineged hayom* — one places it at the northwest, away from those shadows. In the afternoon, the sun is in the west, and shadows fall in the opposite direction; accordingly, the afternoon offering is placed at the northeast. One might have thought the Temple service would specifically *avoid* any appearance of solar orientation, but the *gemara* takes the requirement at face value: the positioning is designed to ensure the animal stands fully exposed to sunlight.

---

## Alexander & Ten Sages

### Ten Questions

The *gemara* now introduces a lengthy and remarkable *aggadata*: *asara devarim she'al Alexandros Mokdon et ziknei ha-Negev* — ten things that Alexander the Great, Alexander of Macedon, asked the elders of the South. The connection to the preceding discussion of east, west, and the sun will become apparent as we proceed.

### Heaven/Earth vs East/West

The first question: *min shamayim la-aretz rachok o mi-mizrach le-ma'arav* — which is the greater distance, from earth to the heavens or from east to west?

### Distance Answer

The sages answered: *mi-mizrach le-ma'arav* — from east to west is the greater distance. Their proof: *chama be-mizrach ha-kol mistaklin bah* — when the sun is in the east at sunrise, everyone can look directly at it; *chama be-ma'arav ha-kol mistaklin bah* — when the sun is in the west at sunset, everyone can look at it. But *chama be-emtza raki'a ein ha-kol mistaklin bah* — at noon, when the sun is directly overhead, no one can look at it. The sages inferred from this that the sun must be *closer* to the earth at midday, and its greater intensity at that distance makes it impossible to view directly. If east to west were a shorter distance than the distance from earth to sky, the sun would be further from us at noon than at sunrise or sunset — but the evidence suggests the opposite.

This reasoning is, of course, scientifically incorrect, and the *gemara* itself immediately qualifies it. *Ve-chachamim omrim: zeh va-zeh ke-echad shavin* — the Sages say both distances are actually equal. The proof is from the verse in Psalms, which in a single metaphor compares something to *ki-gevo'ah shamayim al ha-aretz* — the height of the heavens over the earth — and then to *ki-rachok mizrach mi-ma'arav* — the distance from east to west. If one were greater than the other, the verse would have cited only the larger distance for its comparison. The fact that both are used side by side implies they are equal.

### Sun Brightness

If the two distances are equal, however, what is the actual explanation for the sun appearing more intense at midday? The *gemara* answers: *meshum de-kai le-hedya* — because at noon it stands directly overhead, *ve-lo kasi lei midi* — and nothing screens it. The *mefarshim* explain that when the sun is low on the horizon, its rays must travel through the terrain and geography lying between the observer and the sun — mountains, surface features, and the like — which diffract or attenuate the light. When the sun is directly overhead, nothing interposes. The scientific explanation, which is closely related, involves the angle at which sunlight strikes the earth's surface and the atmosphere it must traverse. When the sun is at a low angle, a given unit of solar energy is spread across a larger surface area and passes through a thicker cross-section of atmosphere; when the sun is directly overhead, that same unit strikes a smaller area perpendicularly, concentrating its intensity. This angle-of-incidence effect is also related to the well-known phenomenon of the moon appearing larger near the horizon than it does high in the sky. The sages of the *gemara*, working within a cosmological framework that imagined the sky as a solid dome and the sun as traveling beneath it by day and above it by night, arrived at their answer through a different mode of reasoning — but they were asking the right question.

### Light vs Darkness

The next question: *or nivra techila o choshech* — was light created first, or darkness?

### Strategic Refusal

Here the sages refused to answer — *milta da ein lah petar*, there is no resolution to this matter. The *gemara* challenges this: surely they could have said darkness was created first, since the verse in *Bereishit* describes *tohu vavohu* and *choshech* — formless void and darkness — and only afterward does God say *yehi or*. Why the silence?

The *gemara* explains: *savri dilma asi leshiyuleina* — they were concerned that once they began engaging with cosmological questions, Alexander would proceed to ask *mah lema'ala mah lemata mah lefanim mah leachor* — what exists above, what below, what before creation, what after — precisely the matters enumerated in the famous *mishnah* in Chagigah as subjects not to be expounded in public. After all, when Alexander asked about heaven and earth, they answered readily, thinking it was a one-off question. But when he returned immediately with a question about light and darkness, they recognized a pattern: he was systematically probing the secrets of cosmological origins. So they shut it down.

The question of light and darkness is itself theologically weighty. There is a real dispute among commentators as to whether darkness is an independent created entity or merely the absence of light — a distinction with significant implications for how one understands the origin of evil. The morning liturgy recites *yotzer or u'vorei choshech* — "who creates light and creates darkness" — but the concluding phrase of that verse, *oseh shalom u'vorei ra*, "who makes peace and creates evil," is modified in prayer to *u'vorei et hakol*, "who creates everything," out of discomfort with the plain meaning. The sages' reticence here may thus reflect not only a desire to avoid cosmological disclosure but also the genuine sensitivity of the question itself.

Why would the sages withhold such knowledge even from a sincere questioner? This connects to the broader framework in *Chagigah* around *ma'aseh bereishit* and esoteric learning generally — the sense that certain knowledge carries dangerous power, and that not every questioner, however brilliant or well-intentioned, is a fit recipient.

### Wisdom & Virtue

Alexander then pivots to a series of questions that seem, on the surface, far more straightforward: *idin mitkari chacham* — who is called wise? *Idin mitkari gibor* — who is called mighty? *Idin mitkari ashir* — who is called wealthy?

### Sages' Answers

The sages' answers are drawn directly from *Pirkei Avot*: *eizehu chacham ha-roeh et ha-nolad* — the wise person is one who anticipates the future; *eizehu gibor ha-kovesh et yitzro* — the truly mighty person is one who conquers his own *yetzer*; *eizehu ashir ha-samei'ach be-chelko* — the truly wealthy person is one who is content with his portion.

Alexander then asked: *ma ya'avid inish v'yichyeh* — what should a person do in order to live? *Yamit atzmo*, the sages replied — let him "kill himself." The *mefarshim* offer several interpretations: self-denial of physical pleasures, hard honest labor, or — most evocatively — the formulation from the *midrash* that *ein ha-Torah mitkayemet ela bemi she-meimit atzmo aleha*, Torah endures only with those who sacrifice themselves for it. The counterpart follows immediately: *ma ya'avid inish ve-yamut* — what leads a person to death? *Yechaye et atzmo* — let him "give himself life," meaning: indulge the bodily self, pursue comfort and pleasure, inflate the ego.

### Authority & Favor

The next question: *ma ya'avid inish ve-yitkabel al ha-briyot* — what should a person do to find favor with people? *Yisne malchut ve-shilton*, the sages answered — despise kingship and rule. This is, of course, a pointed remark to make in the presence of a world conqueror. One interpretation takes it personally: avoid positions of authority yourself, since public office earns more resentment than gratitude. Another reading invokes the *Pirkei Avot* counsel of *tisrachak min ha-reshut* — keep your distance from government — not because authority is inherently wrong, but because proximity to power inevitably entangles one in its conflicts and costs.

### Alexander's Counter

Alexander was not persuaded. *Didi tava midichon*, he said — my answer is better than yours. Rather than *yisne malchut*, one should *yerachem malchut ve-shilton* — embrace and love kingship and rule, because power wielded rightly enables one *le-maheni livnei insha*, to benefit others. This is the one moment in the exchange where Alexander pushes back with a substantive counter-argument rather than simply receiving the sages' teaching.

### Ocean vs Land

Another question: *beyama yae lmeida o be-yabeshta yae lmeida* — is it better to live on the sea or on dry land? The sages answered without hesitation: dry land is better, and their proof is behavioral — *de-kol nechutei yamma*, all sailors, *lo mitba daitaihu ad de-salki le-yabeshta*, they have no peace of mind until they are back on solid ground. The very longing of seafarers for land demonstrates that land is the natural and proper home of human beings.

### Who is Smartest

*Idi minnechon chakim yatir* — which among you is the wisest? *Kulanu ke-chada shavinan*, came the reply — we are all equally wise. *De-hachol milta de-amarta lan be-chada patanu lach* — every question you posed to us, we answered as one.

### Opposition & Satan

Alexander then pressed: *mah beini Aristom le-kabli* — why do you oppose me? Many *mefarshim* understand this as a challenge to their refusal to accept his religion or acknowledge his supremacy. The sages replied: *stitna natzach* — the Satan has won. As the Soncino notes, this was a double entendre: framed as a concession — "the evil inclination has gotten the better of us" — it actually carried the sharper meaning that the adversarial force, the *stitna*, is currently in ascendancy. Power does not confer righteousness.

### Threat & Honor

Alexander responded by threatening their lives: *hana maktalina yathkon be-gzeirat malkhin* — I will have you put to death by royal decree. The sages replied with calm precision: *shilton be-yad malka* — the king's authority is in his hands, *ve-lo ya'eh le-malka ke-dav* — but it is unbecoming for a king to lie. They invoked whatever prior assurance he had given them that their answers would not endanger them, and held him to it.

### Royal Reward

Alexander reversed himself entirely. *Miyad albishinhu levushin dargavan* — he immediately clothed them in royal purple garments, *ve-shavi manicha de-dahava al tzavreihon* — and placed gold necklaces around their necks. The scene echoes both the honoring of Mordechai — *Mordechai yatza bi-lvush malchut* — and the elevation of Joseph — *ve-ravid ha-zahav al tzavaro*.

### Thematic Analysis

The overarching theme of the entire exchange becomes clear when one considers who Alexander was and what he represented. His tutor was Aristotle. His life's project was the conquest of the entire world — east and west, land and sea. The very questions he asked — heaven or earth, east or west, light or darkness — are the questions of a man whose imagination spans the cosmos. And against all of that, the sages offer a systematic counter-philosophy.

Who is wise? Not the student of Aristotle — but *ha-roeh et ha-nolad*, the one who sees consequences. Who is mighty? Not the conqueror of nations — but *ha-kovesh et yitzro*, the one who masters himself. Who is wealthy? Not the possessor of gold and armies — but *ha-samei'ach be-chelko*, the one satisfied with what he has. How to live? *Yamit atzmo* — self-denial and sacrifice. How to die? *Yechaye et atzmo* — indulge yourself.

And then the question of the sea versus the land comes into focus. It is not merely a geographical curiosity. A man whose desires are boundless will not be content at home — he will want to sail the ocean and claim what lies beyond. But the sages say: you cannot live on the sea. Settle down. Be content. *Eizehu ashir ha-samei'ach be-chelko.*

### Classical Parallels

This entire episode has a remarkable parallel in classical literature. The *Jewish Encyclopedia*, which has an extensive section on Alexander the Great and Talmudic legends, notes that the account of the ten questions — composed in classical Aramaic, which itself suggests it was borrowed from an earlier written record — is closely analogous to an episode described by Plutarch, in which Alexander posed ten questions to ten *Gymnosophists* who had rebelled against him. Several of the questions are identical or closely parallel to those in our *gemara*.

In Plutarch's account, Alexander threatened to put to death whoever gave the worst answer, and to proceed in order through the rest. The questions included: which are more numerous, the living or the dead (answer: the living, since the dead no longer exist); which was older, day or night (answer: day, by one day — to which the sage added that hard questions require strange answers, a remark closely echoing the strategic refusal in our *gemara* to answer about light and darkness); and how could a man best be loved (answer: if he is most powerful yet does not inspire fear — note the contrast with our *gemara*'s answer of *yisne malchut*, which rejects power altogether). The structural parallel to the conclusion is especially striking: in Plutarch, Alexander asks the judge which of them answered worst, and the judge declares them all equally bad — an echo of *kulanu ke-chada shavinan*. Alexander then threatens to kill the judge for the verdict, and is foiled by an argument that he had promised to punish only wrong answers, not all of them.

One significant structural difference: in Plutarch's version each sage gives a different answer, whereas in the Talmudic narrative they answer as one — a point emphasized at the end by *kulanu ke-chada shavinan*, and which may carry a thematic point about unity. Some versions of the story locate the *Gymnosophists* in India and identify them with Brahmin sages, suggesting a further complex history of transmission. But the *Jewish Encyclopedia* notes plainly that this appears to be a fragment of a non-Jewish narrative that has been reworked and absorbed into the Talmudic tradition.

The implicit message of the Jewish reworking is the same as the explicit message of the sages' answers: against Alexander's vaunting ambition and his Aristotelian model of greatness — wisdom as knowledge, strength as conquest, wealth as acquisition — the sages substitute a wholly different value system. The next story, involving the Amazons and the Garden of Eden, continues and deepens precisely that theme.

---

## Africa & Amazons

### Journey to Africa

At the bottom of 32a, Alexander turns from philosophical debate to exploration. *Ba'ina de-azalna le-medinat Afriki* — I want to go to Africa. The sages immediately warn him: *lo matzyat azlat* — you cannot go. *Di-fsikei harei choshech* — the mountains of darkness lie between you and Africa. The geographical imagination of the *gemara* here evokes something out of epic literature: impenetrable mountains of total darkness separating the known world from a hidden continent.

Alexander is unmoved. *Lo sagi de-lo azalna* — it will not suffice not to go. I am going. He is not asking permission; he is asking for practical guidance.

### Crossing Darkness

*Aisi chamrei liva'ei* — bring Libyan donkeys, the sages advise, *de-farshi be-chavra* — which can navigate through the darkness (some read: which follow your voice). *Ve-aisi kivorei de-masni* — bring coils of rope; *de-katra be-hai gisa* — tie one end here, so that *ki asis le-asrach* — when you return, *nagdis be-gavaihu* — you can follow the rope back. The Libyan donkeys carry one end of the rope through the mountains, and on the return journey Alexander follows the line back through the darkness. Perhaps the Libyan origin of the donkeys was not incidental — if they are homing animals, like homing pigeons, they will find their way through without needing to be guided.

---

## Africa & Amazons (II)

### City of Women

Alexander followed this advice and proceeded. *Ve-azal mato lehu le-machoza de-kulhu neshei* — he arrived at a city entirely populated by women. This is the city of the Amazons. According to various classical myths, the Amazons dwelled in Libya — and the name Libya was used in antiquity to refer to the African continent as a whole, which also accounts for the Libyan donkeys mentioned in the instructions. There are indeed classical myths of Alexander encountering the Amazons.

*Ba'ei le-mevid karva be-hadaihu* — he wanted to wage war against them. The women confronted him with an unanswerable dilemma: *ei katalin lan, yameru neshei katalei* — if you kill us and win, people will say you slaughtered women; *ei katlina lach* — and if we kill you, it is far worse — *yamru malka de-katluhu nashi*, they will say the great king was slain by women. There is no honorable outcome. Alexander recognized the logic and stood down.

### Gold Bread

*Aisu lei nahama de-dahava a-patura de-dahava* — the women brought him bread made of gold, on a golden table. Alexander protested: *mi achli inshi nahama de-dahava* — who eats golden bread? The women's reply is devastating: *ela ei nahama bayat, lo hava lach be-atrach nahama le-meichal* — if it was simply bread you wanted, you could have eaten bread back home. Why did you travel so far? What did you actually come here looking for?

The *Jewish Encyclopedia* notes that this satire on the ambition of conquerors appears frequently in Jewish legends and has a classical parallel: Plutarch's essay on the virtuous deeds of women describes Pytheas, a wealthy Greek of the time of Xerxes, being served by his wife with golden bread to demonstrate the absurdity of his greed. The moral is identical: *eizehu ashir ha-samei'ach be-chelko*. If what you want is bread to sustain you, you had that at home. The relentless pursuit of gold leads not to satisfaction but to the inability to eat.

### Gate Inscription

When Alexander left the city, *ketiv a-bava de-machoza* — he wrote on the city's gates: *ana Alexandrus Mokdon havaeina shatya* — I, Alexander of Macedon, was a fool, *ad de-asisi li-medinat Afriki de-nashi* — until I came to the land of Africa of women, *ve-yalfit eiza min nashi* — and learned wisdom from women.

This is a striking moment. Through the entire encounter with the ten sages, Alexander never concedes. He pushes back, threatens, counter-argues, and ultimately rewards them while remaining unpersuaded in any deep sense. Here, by contrast, he publicly inscribes his own humiliation on the city gates. The women taught him something the sages, for all their wisdom and wit, apparently could not. Perhaps the sages' exchange was more of an intellectual contest — a battle of wits — while the Amazons made the lesson concrete and unavoidable. One cannot argue with golden bread.

---

## Garden of Eden

### Fountain Discovery

*Ki shakil ve-ati* — as Alexander was traveling through Africa on his various journeys — and he did historically venture into Libya and parts of the Sahara — *yatib a-hahu mayina* — he sat by a well. *Ka-akhal nahama* — he was eating bread. *Havei bideih kavrei de-milkha* — he had some salted fish. *Ba-hadi de-makhvrei lehu* — as he rinsed them in the well water, *nafal behu reikha* — a remarkable scent arose from them. Some versions say *rukha* — that they came back to life, revived.

### Stream to Eden

*Shema mina hai eina mi-gan eden ati* — from this, Alexander reasoned, this spring must flow from the Garden of Eden. He had found the *makor*, the source, of Eden's waters. One account says he washed his face with the water. Another says *adli kulei* — he followed the entire stream, *ad de-mata le-pitcha de-gan eden* — until he arrived at the very gate of the Garden.

### Eyeball Gift

*Rama kala: pitchu li bava* — he called out: open the gate for me. The response came immediately: *ze ha-sha'ar la-Hashem, tzadikim yavo'u vo* — this gate is for God, the righteous enter through it. This is the same lesson the ten sages had tried to convey with their answers about wisdom, valor, and wealth. True greatness is righteousness — and Alexander, conqueror of the world, does not qualify.

Alexander did not argue the point of his righteousness. Instead: *ana nami malka ana, chashiv chashivina* — I am at least a king, a person of significance. *Havu li midi* — give me something, anything, from the Garden. *Yahavu leih gulgata chada* — they gave him one eyeball.

### Eyeball Weighs More

*Taklei le-khulei de-hava ve-kaspa dideih* — he placed all of his gold and silver on one side of the scale, and the eyeball on the other. *Lo hava matkala* — the eyeball outweighed everything. All the wealth of Alexander's conquests could not counterbalance a single human eye.

### Never Satisfied

He brought the eyeball to the *rabanan* — understood here as the same Jewish sages he had encountered before — and asked: *mai hai?* What is this? *Gulgata de-eina de-bisra ve-dama, de-lo kasava* — this is the eyeball of flesh and blood, which is never satisfied. The eye's desire always exceeds what one possesses. You can conquer the entire world and it will not be enough, because desire perpetually outruns acquisition. *Ohev kesef lo yisba kesef* — one who loves money will never have enough.

And then the sages demonstrated: *shakli kalili de-afra ve-chasye* — take a little dirt and cover it. He did so. *Le-altar takla* — immediately it balanced. The eye, covered with earth, no longer outweighed anything. The allusion is immediate: when a person dies, dirt covers the eyes. Only death finally satisfies the eye's desire.

### Sheol Verse

*De-chtiv: she'ol va-avaddon lo tisbe'enah* — as the verse says, Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied — and the verse concludes, *ve-einei adam lo tisbe'enah*, nor are the eyes of man. The association with *she'ol*, the underworld, drives home the connection between insatiable desire and death.

The *gemara* appends a tradition from the school of Eliyahu: *gehinnom lema'ala min ha-rakia* — Gehinnom is above the heavens. *Ve-yeish omrim: le-achorei harei choshech* — others say it is behind the mountains of darkness — precisely where Alexander traveled. Whether these represent two distinct physical-theological conceptions or two metaphoric types of transgression — the soaring ambition that exceeds the heavens, and the depravity that dwells in the mountains of darkness — is left open. What is clear is that the narrative has come full circle: the mountains of darkness from which Alexander's journey began are now identified as the location of Gehinnom itself.

The sages, in the end, have the last word — though Alexander only openly admitted defeat to the women.

---

## Torah & Peace

### Night Study

With the conclusion of the Alexander narrative, the *gemara* turns to a brief set of teachings that bring *Seder Kodshim* to a close. *Tana Rabbi Chiyya: kol ha-osek ba-Torah ba-laila, shechinah kenegdo* — whoever engages in Torah study at night, the *shechinah* is opposite him. The connection to what preceded may be the motif of *choshech* — darkness — that has run through the entire aggadic section. The verse cited is *kumi roni ba-laila le-rosh ashmurot, shifchi cha-mayim libbech no-ach pnei Hashem* — rise and sing in the night, at the head of the watches, pour out your heart like water before God's presence.

Night study carried particular weight in the ancient world, where artificial light was minimal and the hours after dark were the domain of sleep. To learn at night was to extend oneself beyond natural rhythms in an act of devotion. And why does the *shechinah* attend one who learns at night specifically? Perhaps because night removes the social and communal dimensions of learning — there is no *beit midrash*, no *chavruta* — and one is left alone with the Torah and with God.

### Increase Peace

*Amar Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah: talmidei chachamim marbim shalom ba-olam* — disciples of the wise increase peace in the world. The connection here is perhaps to the sages in the Alexander narrative, whose wisdom — even when unheeded by the conqueror himself — represents a countervailing force to war and destruction.

### Peace Verse

*Shene'emar: ve-chol banayich limudei Hashem, ve-rav shalom banayich* — as it is written, all your children are taught of God, and great is the peace of your children. It is worth noting that this citation does not include the well-known homiletic reading *al tikrei banayich ela bonayich* — do not read "your children" but "your builders." That addition, while familiar, is absent here. Perhaps it was appended later; the verse as cited already speaks of those who learn from God, and the connection between Torah study and *shalom* is made without needing the wordplay.

### End of Gemara

This is the final *gemara* of *Seder Kodshim*. The tractate of Kinnim, which follows in the standard Vilna *Shas*, consists entirely of *mishnayot* without *gemara*. That means this passage — ending with the value of *talmud Torah* and the peace it brings to the world — is the last piece of *gemara* in the entire order of *Kodshim*. It is characteristic of the *gemara* to conclude a tractate or section with *midrash* and *aggadata* of this kind, and the choice to end here with the pursuit of learning and the increase of peace feels fitting after the long meditation on Alexander's insatiable ambition and the sages' consistent counter-testimony.

*Ha-dran alach hayu kotzim* — with this, the fourth *perek* of Tamid and the *gemara* of *Seder Kodshim* come to a close.

---

## Temple Service

### One Blessing

The *mishnah* continues with the *Avodah* of the morning service. The appointed official — *ha-memuneh*, the overseer of the division of responsibilities — addresses the assembled *kohanim* after the animal has been brought halfway up the ramp: *barchu bracha achat* — make one blessing.

### Shema Recitation

The *kohanim* then proceeded to the *Lishkat ha-Gazit*, the Chamber of Hewn Stone, where they recited *Kriyat Shema*.

### Abbreviated Service

Their *tefillah* was abbreviated, because they needed to return promptly to the *korbanos*. There is extensive discussion in *Berachot* about people whose obligations preclude a full *davvening*, and the *kohanim* exemplify this tension. Specifically, they did not recite the blessing of *Yotzer ha-Me'orot*, because at this point in the morning it was still only *alot ha-shachar* — the first light of dawn — and sunrise (*hanetz ha-chama*) had not yet occurred. The blessing of *Yotzer ha-Me'orot* requires daylight. Accordingly, they said only the blessing of *bocher be-amo Yisrael be-ahava*.

### Ten Commandments

They then read the *aseret ha-dibrot* — the Ten Commandments — before the three *parshiyot* of *Shema*, *Ve-haya im shamoa*, and *Vayomer*. The *gemara* in *Berachot* records that there was initially a movement to incorporate the *aseret ha-dibrot* into the standard daily liturgy for all Jews, precisely because of their centrality and their capacity to encapsulate the *mitzvot*. This was ultimately suppressed out of concern that the *minim* — Jewish sectarians, perhaps including Jewish Christians — would seize upon it as confirmation that the Torah consists solely of the Ten Commandments and nothing more. In the Temple, however, this concern did not apply, and the *aseret ha-dibrot* remained part of the *kohanim*'s service.

### Three Blessings

Following *Shema*, they recited three blessings. The first was *Emet ve-Yatziv* — the blessing after *Shema*, concluding with *Go'el Yisrael*. The second was *ha-Avodah*, the blessing concerning the Temple service — not the exile-era formulation of *Ha-machazir shechinato le-Tziyyon*, but a blessing in keeping with the active sacrificial service, either a prayer that God accept the sacrifices with favor, or the blessing recited in connection with *birkat kohanim*, ending with *she-otcha levadecha be-yira na'avod*. The third was *birkat kohanim* itself — though in a form distinct from the public *nesiat kapayim*: either the blessing *kohanim* recite before raising their hands, a form of blessing their own role, or a recitation of the biblical verses without the actual spreading of hands over the people.

### Shabbat Blessing

On *Shabbat*, an additional element was added: *u-v'Shabbat mosifim bracha achat le-mishmar ha-yotzei* — the departing *mishmar*, the weekly division of priests completing their service, would add one blessing for the incoming *mishmar*. This blessing was not a standard liturgical *berachah* in the technical sense but a personal blessing of farewell and welcome: *mi she-shachan shemo ba-bayit ha-zeh, hu yitein beineichem ahavah ve-achvah shalom ve-rei'ut* — may He whose name dwells in this house place among you love and brotherhood, peace and friendship. That such a blessing of unity was directed specifically toward the incoming *kohanim* may reflect the natural tensions of rotating communal responsibility and the competition inherent in the lottery system for *korbanos*. The blessing addresses that directly: whatever the outcome of the lots, let there be peace between you.

The relationship between *tefillah* and *korbanos* that emerges from this *mishnah* will be taken up further in the sessions ahead — the *tefillah* framing the *korban*, and the *berachah* consecrating the *avodah*, each illuminating the meaning of the other.

---

---

# Tamid 33

## Prayer & Korban

### Review & Context

We resume from the bottom of 32b, picking up at the beginning of the fifth *perek*. To orient ourselves: the *kohanim* have already completed the *terumat hadeshen*, the *dishun* of the *mizbe'ach hapnimi* and the *menorah* — removing ashes and performing the initial cleaning — and then proceeded to the *shechita* of the *tamid*, the sprinkling of the blood, the binding and dismembering of the animal, and finally the bringing of its parts halfway up the ramp. With those stages complete, the *kohanim* gathered in the *lishkat hagazit* for a further lottery — but before that lottery, they first paused to daven.

### Kriat Shema

That brief service is what the first *mishnah* described: *kriat shema*, followed by three *brachot* — *emet ve-yatziv*, which is the blessing of *ga'al yisrael*, and two blessings drawn from the *shemoneh esrei*, one concerning the *avodah* and one concerning *birkat kohanim* (not the actual *birkat kohanim* itself). There was also a special blessing recited on *Shabbat* by the departing priestly division for the entering one.

### Prayer Framing

This interweaving of *tefillah* with *korbanot* is theologically significant and deserves careful attention. The *mefaresh* here — the Pseudo-Rashi — emphasizes at the close of the previous *perek* that the reason they went to the *lishkat hagazit* to recite *shema* was, in his words, *kedei she-yitpallelu kodem she-yaktiru shum haktar ya'alu k'vanam le-rei'ach nicho'ach* — that it is fitting they should pray before any *haktar* ascends, so that their intention should rise up as a pleasing fragrance. The blood of the *tamid* had already been sprinkled, but the smoke had not yet gone up; the *ketoret* had not yet been offered. All of that is still ahead. And they wanted to frame it with *tefillah*.

What does it mean to frame a *korban* with *tefillah*? The simple reading is that the *korban* is the center of gravity, and the words of prayer give it meaning — just as one who brings a *chatat* lays his hands on it and recites a *viduy*, or as the Rambam suggests that one who brings a *shelamim* would lay hands and speak words of praise. Words frame the significance of the act. And the two *brachot* the *kohanim* recited — beyond *ga'al yisrael*, which accompanies the *shema* — were specifically about the *avodat hakorbanot* being accepted and about the *birkat kohanim* they were about to perform. These are not independent spiritual exercises; they are precisely calibrated to the service at hand.

Yet even granting all of this, even if the *tefillah* here is "merely" a frame, its framing role is itself of tremendous consequence. The *korbanot* do not, as it were, speak for themselves. Their meaning, and the manner in which they ascend, is bound up with the words one says and the intention one brings. The recognition that *tefillot* preceded *korbanot* — that almost the first thing that happens is prayer — is a critical point.

### Antiquity of Prayer

This further implies something about the antiquity of *tefillot* themselves. The *nusach* of *emet ve-yatziv* already reflects the classical form of that *bracha*, and the structure mirrors the *shemoneh esrei*. It was only the *kohanim* themselves who were praying here — they were the ones bringing the *korbanot* — but the institution of *tefillah* as something that corresponds to and accompanies the *avodah* is clearly ancient. In *Ta'anit*, the discussion of the *ma'amadot* — the representatives of *yisrael* who traveled to the *mikdash* in rotation, twenty-four groups corresponding to the twenty-four priestly divisions — shows that even the *yisraelim* who remained behind had special Torah readings and forms of communal expression. *Tehillim*, for its part, functioned as an ancient prayer-book of sorts: before *tefillot* were formalized, one would select the appropriate psalm for the moment. Prayer as a profound human spiritual need goes back to *Avraham*, or earlier still to *Noach*. What this *mishnah* implicitly addresses is when it became more statutory, when it acquired a fixed form — and that question is very much alive in these lines.

---

## Ketoret Lottery

### Lottery Call

The *mishnah* continues. The *memuneh* — the appointed officer, the floor manager responsible for distributing and overseeing all of the assignments — now addresses the assembled *kohanim* in the *lishkat hagazit* following their *davening*: *chadashim la-ketoret* — anyone who has not yet had the merit of offering the *ketoret*, come and participate in the lottery. The offering of *ketoret* was regarded as a *segulah* for wealth, and as a result, a *kohen* was permitted to do it only once. Given that most *kohanim* came to the *mikdash* only twice a year outside of the *regalim*, and that there were a very large number of *kohanim*, many would never have had the opportunity even once. So the lottery was called among those who had not yet had their turn, and *zacha mi shezacha* — whoever won it, won it.

### Sequential Lotteries

Then the *memuneh* called for a second lottery: *chadashim im yeshanim* — both those new to the task and those who had done it before — *mi ma'aleh eivarim min hakeves lamizbe'ach?* Who will bring the limbs of the *tamid* from the midpoint of the ramp to the top? The pieces had been laid at the lower half of the ramp; a fresh lottery now determined who would bring them the rest of the way. The *meforshim* explain that this second lottery, layered atop the first, was specifically a matter of *kavod*. By splitting the task into stages and conducting separate lotteries for each, the process drew attention to itself and gave it weight. Had the entire carrying of the limbs up the ramp been done in a single unbroken motion, it would have been over before one realized it. The multiplication of lotteries and participants transforms what might be a brief act into something charged with honor.

### R. Eliezer View

One might naturally wonder whether this arrangement is not rather forced — surely whoever began the task should finish it? Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds precisely this view: *ha-ma'aleh eivarim la-keves hu ma'aleh otam al gabei hamizbe'ach* — whoever brought the limbs to the halfway point of the ramp is the one who brings them the rest of the way. He does acknowledge two distinct stages, but he holds that a separate lottery for the second stage is unnecessary. The principle he invokes is: *hitchil be-mitzva omrim lo gemor* — if one has begun a *mitzva*, we tell him to complete it.

---

## Garment Storage

### Change of Clothes

The next *mishnah* presents what is, frankly, a puzzling arrangement. Now that various *kohanim* have completed their assigned tasks, the *mishnah* says: *masru la-chazzanim* — they were handed over to the *chazzanim*. The precise status of the *chazzanim* is not entirely clear — they may be a position of authority or, given that they are here assisting the *kohanim* in undressing, perhaps more of an attendant role. What is clear is that the *chazzanim* would undress the *kohanim* who were not currently assigned to the next stage, removing their *bigdei kehunah*, and leaving them with only their *michnasayim* — the priestly breeches. Then, in a sequence described by the *gemara*, the *kohen* would put on his non-priestly garment — a cloak or toga — and remove his *michnasayim* from underneath, subsequently changing into his ordinary undergarments. So there would be no moment of actual undress.

This raises an immediate question: why are they changing out of their *bigdei kehunah* at all? They are not done for the day. They will need to return. The most plausible answer is connected to the principle of *bigdei kehunah nitnu li-henot bahem* — whether *kohanim* are permitted to wear their vestments for personal enjoyment or leisure. If they were going to take a break, perhaps walk around *har habayit*, they could not do so in *bigdei kehunah*. It is, nonetheless, a striking arrangement — one would have expected them simply to stand and wait.

### Kevach System

*V'hachalonot hayu sham* — and there were small cubbies, *chalomot*, in that space. *V'chatuv aleihem tashmish ha-keilim* — and written on them was the designation of use: one marked for hats, one for breeches, one for cloaks. So there was an organized storage system for the priestly garments of those not currently serving.

### Cubby Details

A closer look raises interesting practical questions. The *gemara* establishes the principle *mido bad she-hi ke-midato* — that priestly garments had to be fitted to the *kohen's* individual measurements, at least in the case of the tunic and its length. If each garment was custom-fitted, some system of individual assignment would have been necessary. Perhaps the cubbies were organized by size — like, one might imagine, a bowling alley shoe counter where one requests a particular size. The hats may be another matter; whether the principle of individual measurement applied equally to headgear is less clear. In any case, each *kohen* retained his own undergarments — and whatever the precise system, the interval between the change of clothes and the next stage of service was apparently not very long, given that we will soon see the *kohanim* summoned back by the sound of the *magreifa*.

---

## Ketoret Vessels

### Kaf Description

The *mishnah* now turns to the person who won the lottery for the *ketoret*: *mi she-zacha ba-ketoret haya notel et ha-kaf* — he would take the *kaf*, a ladle or deep vessel. *V'ha-kaf domeh le-tarkav gadol* — it resembled a large *tarkav*, which is a two-*kav* carrying container. Imagining it as something between a ladle and a pot — with depth and a handle — captures the idea. *Shel zahav* — it was made of gold. *U-machazeket shloshet kavin* — its capacity was three *kavin* of *ketoret*.

### Bazach Structure

The *ketoret* itself, however, was not placed directly in this larger vessel. *V'ha-bazach haya be-tocho* — the *bazach*, a smaller vessel, was nested inside it. *Malei ve-gadush ketoret* — the *bazach* was filled and overflowing, heaped up with a mound of *ketoret*. The nesting arrangement served a clear purpose: the *bazach* was piled so high that the *ketoret* might spill during transport, and the larger *kaf* caught any overflow. One might ask why the *ketoret* was not simply placed in the larger vessel in the first place. The answer is *kavod*: it is more impressive to display a vessel entirely full and overflowing than to have a modest quantity lying at the bottom of a larger container. The aesthetics of abundance and fullness were themselves a form of honor.

*V'chisuy haya lo* — there was also a cover. Exactly which vessel the cover belonged to is not entirely clear from the text. And one might ask how a cover can fit over a vessel that is overflowing — perhaps it was a flat cover, or perhaps some form of dome.

### Metultelet

*U-che-min metultelet haya alav mi-lma'alah* — and there was something called a *metultelet* on top. What is a *metultelet*? Opinions differ. Some say it was a metal ring handle, analogous to the handle on a pot lid. Others say it was a cloth covering — perhaps what we might call a pot-holder, though the *ketoret* was not itself hot. The Rambam reads the text differently from either of these: he understands the *chisuy* and the *metultelet* as two distinct items — a cover for the inner *bazach*, and then a cloth covering over the larger *kaf*. On the Rambam's reading, the *ketoret* was entirely concealed beneath layers of covering, and no one would have seen the *ketoret* itself during transport.

### Eyewitness Detail

These details are remarkably specific — the exact capacity, the nesting structure, the nature of the handle or covering. One is struck by the observation that these descriptions read like eyewitness accounts. How else would one know these precise particulars about vessels used in the *heichal*? The specificity suggests that those who transmitted these *mishnayot* had direct familiarity with the service, not merely inherited abstractions.

---

## Coal Procedure

### Silver Shovel

*Mi she-zacha ba-machtah natal machtat ha-kesef* — whoever merited the *machtah*, the shovel, took a silver shovel, *ve-alah le-rosh hamizbe'ach* — and ascended to the top of the outer *mizbe'ach*. There he moved aside the coals, *u-finah et ha-gechalim hilech ve-hilech*, to expose the best coals in the center. The outer *mizbe'ach* maintained a special fire specifically for producing coals for the *ketoret* — positioned toward the west, closer to the *heichal*, symbolizing its purpose. He scooped the coals — *chatah* — and then descended, *yarad ve-iram le-toch shel zahav*, pouring them from the silver shovel into a gold shovel.

The reason for using silver first and gold second: gold is precious, and the rough action of scooping coals directly would wear it down. So the initial scooping was done in silver, and the coals were then transferred to gold. One might note in passing that pure gold, being highly malleable, would in practice require some alloy — but in any case, the intention is clear.

One practical question arises: how does a *kohen* handle a shovel full of burning coals without injury? A long handle would provide some insulation, and the contact is brief — the scooping takes only moments. But if there were any kind of cloth handle or intermediate material, one might ask whether that constitutes a *chatzitzah* between the *kohen* and the *kli shareit*. There is a broader discussion of whether something done *le-kavod* avoids this problem, but here the reason is purely practical rather than honorific. The question is left open; a sufficiently long handle may simply be the answer.

### Shovel Transfer

The fire used for the *ketoret* coals had a capacity of roughly five *kavin*. He scooped four *kavin* from it in his silver shovel. The gold shovel, however, had a capacity of only three *kavin*. When he poured the four *kavin* of coals from the silver shovel into the gold one, one *kav* of coals inevitably spilled out. So both vessels are, in a sense, comparable in size to a large soup pot — the three-*kav* gold shovel, and the three-*kav kaf* that holds the nested *bazach* of *ketoret*. Two *kohanim*, each carrying something roughly that size in gold, approach the *heichal* together: one with coals, one with *ketoret*.

### Spilled Coals

*Ve-haya mechabdan la-amah* — the spilled *kav* of coals was swept into the *amah*. The *amah* was a channel through which water flowed, running through the *beit hamikdash* and draining out beyond it. It served as the receptacle for blood from the various *korbanot* as well, swept in by a kind of squeegee action and carried away. The spilled coals were handled similarly.

### Psachtar Vessel

On *Shabbat*, however, sweeping was not permitted — the coals were *muktzah*, and extinguishing them (*kibuy*) was forbidden. So *u-ve-Shabbat haya kofeh aleihen psachtar* — they would place a large cauldron, the *psachtar*, over the spilled coals. The principle that there are no *d'rabananm* in the *mikdash* applies specifically in the context of the *avodah*; but covering coals that have spilled is not itself part of the *avodah*, and so *muktzah* and the prohibition of *kibuy* apply.

The *psachtar* itself was a very large vessel — *machazekes letach*, containing a *letach*, which is half a *kor*, equivalent to fifteen *se'ah* or ninety *kavin*. Compared to the three-*kav* capacity of our "soup pot," the *psachtar* is thirty times as large — not a pot at all, but something more like a massive metal vat or cauldron.

One might ask why so large a vessel was needed merely to cover a *kav* of spilled coals. The answer is likely practical: a small cover could be tripped over and dislodged. A cauldron thirty times the size of the surrounding items cannot be easily tripped over or overturned. And a secondary function on *Shabbat* is noted as well: if a dead rodent were found in the *beit hamikdash* on *Shabbat*, it too was *muktzah* and could not be removed. The *psachtar* would be placed over it as well — both to prevent accidental contact with something *tamei* and to mark clearly that something was there. It is striking that even the symbolically disturbing presence of a dead creature in the *mikdash* was left in place until after *Shabbat*, covered by the cauldron.

### Chains System

*U-shtei sharsheros hayu vah* — the *psachtar* had two chains. *Achat she-hu moshech vah ve-yored* — one for drawing it down, *ve-achat she-hu ochetz mi-lma'alah* — and one for holding it from above, *bishvil she-lo yisgalgel* — so it would not roll.

This explains how the large ash removal was accomplished. When the main ash pile on the outer *mizbe'ach* needed to be cleared — not the symbolic *terumat hadeshen*, which was done daily, but the full removal done less frequently — the *psachtar* would be filled with ashes at the top of the *mizbe'ach* and then needed to be brought down the ramp. With a cauldron of that size, carrying was impossible. One *kohen* would hold the chain from above to keep it stable; another would pull the chain from below, walking down the ramp. The two chains allowed them to lower the cauldron in a controlled descent without it rolling or tipping.

*U-vishlosha devarim hayeta meshamashes* — this large cauldron thus served three functions: covering the spilled coals on *Shabbat*, covering a dead rodent found in the *mikdash* on *Shabbat*, and serving as the vessel for removing the main ash pile from the *mizbe'ach*.

---

## Magreifa Gong

### Throw Action

*Higiu bein ha-ulam ve-la-mizbe'ach* — they arrived at the space between the *ulam* and the *mizbe'ach*. The *ulam* is the vestibule — the entry hall before the *heichal* proper — and the space between it and the *mizbe'ach* is a charged and liminal zone. It is still within the *azara*, yet it stands directly at the threshold of the *heichal*. The *kiyor*, the laver, was located there as well.

Upon reaching this space, *natal echad et ha-magreifa ve-zarka bein ha-ulam ve-la-mizbe'ach* — one of them took the *magreifa* and threw it into that space. The *magreifa* could simply mean a shovel, and there is a known *kli shareit* by that name. But what is being described here is better understood as a large percussive instrument — something that, when thrown, produced an enormous sound, akin to striking a gong.

### Sound Signal

*Ein adam shomeia kol chaveiro bi-Yerushalayim mi-kol ha-magreifa* — no person could hear his fellow's voice in Yerushalayim over the sound of the *magreifa*. We have already heard that the opening of the doors of the *heichal* was audible as far as Yericho; this sound, produced at close range within the *azara*, was of such magnitude that ordinary conversation was impossible throughout the city.

### Three Functions

*U-lishlosha devarim hayeta meshamashes* — and this sound served three purposes.

First: *kohen she-shomea et kolah yodea she-echav ha-kohanim nichnasim le-hishtachavot* — a *kohen* hearing this knew that his fellow *kohanim* were about to enter for the *hishtachavaya*, the prostration, and *ve-hu ratzu va* — he ran to take his place. This raises a question worth pausing over: the *mishnah* has just told us that the *kohanim* who were not currently assigned took off their *bigdei kehunah* and changed into their ordinary garments. Yet now, only minutes later — after the scooping of coals and the brief transit to this space — they are being summoned to run and get ready? The tension between the clothing interlude and the immediacy of the next stage is genuinely puzzling.

Second: *u-ven levi she-shomea et kolah yodea she-echav ha-leviyim nichnasim le-daber be-shir* — a *levi* hearing this knew that his fellow *leviyim* were about to take their positions on the *duchan* to perform their music and song, *ve-hu ratzu va* — and he too ran to prepare.

Third: *ve-rosh ha-maamad haya ma'amid et ha-tameim be-sha'ar mizrach* — the head of the *maamad* would position the *tameim* at the eastern gate.

It is worth pausing here to note what this signal represents in the broader rhythm of the morning. The first audible mark of the day's service was the opening of the *heichal* doors, heard as far as Yericho. That initiated the *kohanim*'s preparatory work — *terumat hadeshen*, *shechita* of the *tamid*, all the steps of dismembering and arrangement. The *azara* gates had not yet been opened to the public; the *beit hamikdash* was not yet "open for business." This second signal — the *magreifa* — indicates that the final preparatory stages are underway, and that very soon the *azara* will be open. It is the equivalent of the store clerk announcing that the doors are about to open, that everything is nearly ready for the public. Interestingly, unlike a fixed-time alarm, this signal is triggered by reaching a particular stage of the *avodah*. The time is marked not by the clock but by the progress of the service itself.

There is also a connection here to the bells of the *kohen gadol*'s robe: *ve-nishma kolo be-vo'o el ha-kodesh ve-lo yamut* — his sound shall be heard when he enters the holy place, so that he does not die. There is something symbolically consistent between the bells that announce the *kohen gadol*'s entry into the *kodesh* and the *magreifa* thrown into the space between the *ulam* and the *mizbe'ach* to announce the imminent entry for *ketoret*. In both cases, the act of entering a sacred inner space is preceded by a sound that announces it.

### Tameim Placement

*Ve-rosh ha-maamad haya ma'amid et ha-tameim be-sha'ar mizrach* — the head of the *maamad* would stand the *tameim* at the eastern gate, which is the gate of the *azara*. The word *tameim* here refers to those — whether *kohanim* or the *yisraelim* of the *maamad* — who were in a state of *tuma* that required them to bring a *korban* before their purification process could be complete.

### Tameim Debate

There is a debate about the purpose of this placement. Most commentators understand it as one of two things. The first reading is that it was a public shaming — placing the *tameim* visibly at the gate so that all could see: look, these *kohanim* were so negligent that they became *tamei* on the very day they were scheduled to serve. This is a harsh reading. The second reading, which appears to be the view the Rambam prefers, is precisely the opposite: this was a kindness. When people saw that certain *kohanim* were absent from the service, they might wonder or be troubled. Positioning the *tameim* visibly at the gate explained their absence without suspicion or complaint.

The Rambam, however, offers a third and quite different explanation. The *tameim* were positioned at the gate so that they could be brought to the front of the line. Certain states of *tuma* end only when the individual brings a *korban*; the *maamad* head, hearing the *magreifa* and knowing that the *azara* would soon open, assembled those who needed to bring their *korbanot* and placed them at the head of the queue — like giving priority boarding to those with special needs. This is by far the most generous interpretation and has an appealing practical logic.

One practical question here: how was the *maamad* head already at the eastern gate of the *azara* before it was opened? To reach the eastern gate of the *azara* one would have had to pass through the *ezrat nashim*. Whether the gates of the *ezrat nashim* had already been opened at this point is not stated explicitly in the *mishnah*, but the question is a fair one and worth examining further.

---

## Ash Removal

### Ascending Ulam

*Hitchilu olim be-ma'alot ha-ulam* — they began ascending the steps leading up to the *ulam*. The *ulam* itself had no gate — it was an open vestibule, a covered space extending before the *heichal* door. One might compare it to the small antechamber that many synagogues place before their main sanctuary: a transitional space that allows one door to close before the next opens. The steps leading to the *ulam* are visible in the architectural reconstructions. This entire structure — the *ulam* together with the main hall — was under one roofed unit, though one still passed through a doorway before entering the *heichal* proper.

### Inner Altar

*Mi she-zacha be-dishun mizbe'ach hapnimi ve-ha-menorah* — the ones who had merited the cleaning of the inner *mizbe'ach* and the *menorah* preceded the others. The first cleaning had been done earlier in the morning; this was the completion of that work. *Mi she-zacha be-dishun hamizbe'ach hapnimi nichnas* — the one assigned to the inner *mizbe'ach* entered, *ve-natal et ha-teni* — and took the basket filled with ashes, *hishtachavah* — he prostrated himself, *ve-yatza* — and left.

Why the prostration? The *heichal* is the inner sanctum, the throne room of the King. When a servant enters and then prepares to leave such a space, he bows in a gesture of reverence and permission to depart. Whether an analogous prostration was performed upon entry is a separate question; what the *mishnah* records is the bow upon leaving.

### Menorah Cleaning

*Mi she-zacha be-dishun ha-menorah* — the one who merited cleaning the *menorah* entered. Earlier, when the *menorah* cleaning had begun, he had left two of the lamps still burning. *Nichnas u-matza shtei nerot maaraviyim dolakim* — he found the two western lamps still burning.

A note on the term "western": there is a broader debate about precisely which lamp is called the *ner ha-maaravi*, whether it is literally the westernmost lamp or refers to a lamp that stands west relative to the next one in sequence. But regardless of the precise identification, the operative point is that two lamps had been left burning, and he now had two lamps remaining to clean.

*Midashen et ha-mizrachim* — he cleaned out the more eastern of the two. *U-maniach et ha-maaravi dolek* — and he left the western one burning. *She-mimmennu haya madlik et ha-menorah she-bein ha-arbayim* — because this was the lamp from which the *menorah* would be lit in the afternoon. Whichever lamp the *ner ha-maaravi* was, it was preserved so it could serve as the source of flame for lighting the other lamps at the evening service. He did clean one lamp — completing part of the *dishun* — but left this one to continue burning for that purpose.

What if the *ner ha-maaravi* was found extinguished? *Matzo she-kava midashno u-madliko mi-mizbe'ach ha-olah* — he would clean it out and relight it from the outer *mizbe'ach*. The *gemara* derives this from a *pasuk*: the *olah* altar is described with the phrase *esh tamid tukad al ha-mizbe'ach*, and the *menorah* is similarly described as burning *tamid* before God — *lifnei Hashem tamid*. One lights the *tamid* from the *tamid*, drawing fire from the outer *mizbe'ach* whose fire never ceases.

### Koz Pitcher

*Natal et ha-koz* — he took the *koz*, a small pitcher that held the oil, wicks, and other materials needed for the *menorah*. *Mi-ma'alah shniyah* — it had been placed on the second step of the *menorah* stand. *Hishtachava ve-yatza* — he prostrated himself and departed.

---

## Ketoret Offering

### Spreading Coals

*Tziber et ha-gechalim al gabei ha-mizbe'ach* — the *kohen* who had won the lottery for the *machtah* now placed the coals on top of the golden inner *mizbe'ach*. This was done after the ashes had been cleared and the prostrations made. *Ve-ridedan be-shulei ha-machtah* — he flattened them with the underside of the shovel, because spreading the coals evenly was essential: one does not want a heaped mound but a distributed layer on which the *ketoret* will be placed. *Hishtachava ve-yatza* — he prostrated himself and left.

### Bazach Transfer

Now the one who had won the *ketoret* lottery entered. *Haya notel et ha-bazach mi-toch ha-kaf* — he took the inner *bazach* from within the larger *kaf*, and *ve-natno le-ohavo o le-krovo* — he gave it to his friend or relative. Now, this seems surprising — he has just won the lottery for the *ketoret*, and he is handing it to someone else? The *meforshim* explain that what he gave away was not the *ketoret* but the larger outer *kaf*: here, you hold this large vessel, I need my hands free for the actual offering. The presence of this third person — a friend or relative who simply holds the larger pot — means that what appeared to be a two-person ceremony actually involves at least three: the one who spread the coals, the one doing the *ketoret*, and this helper.

### Hand Pouring

*Nitpazru mimenu le-tochah* — some of the *ketoret* may have scattered from the *bazach* into the larger outer *kaf* during transit. *Ve-natno lo be-chofnav* — and so the helper would gather this scattered *ketoret* and place it back into the hands of the one performing the offering.

This explains the logic of the arrangement. The *kohen* doing the *ketoret* is trying to pour the contents of the *bazach* into his cupped hands — this was considered one of the most physically demanding *avodot*. He is manipulating a vessel while trying to receive its contents in his palms, without a flat surface to work on. He performs this over the larger *kaf* so that whatever spills is caught. The helper then takes whatever landed in the larger *kaf* and returns it to his hands, enabling him to have the full quantity without loss.

### Burning Warning

*Melamdin oto* — those who had previously performed the *ketoret* would instruct the *kohen* about to do it. The key warning: *hevei zahir she-ma tatchil mi-lefanecha she-lo tik-aveh* — be careful not to begin scattering from close to your body moving outward, for if you do, the rising smoke and heat will burn your hands. Instead, begin from far away and move inward. The *ketoret* placed on hot coals begins to smoke immediately; one must be positioned and moving in the right direction from the very first moment.

### Performance

*Hitchil meradded ve-yatza* — he began to pour it out in a smooth, spread layer — *meradded* carries the sense of flattening or sifting, letting it fall in a distributed, even covering rather than in a lump — and then departed. The mechanics of the pouring are clear: the hands are held open, and the *ketoret* is allowed to fall gradually across the coals.

### Authorization

*Lo haya ha-maktir maktir ad she-ha-memuneh omer lo hakter* — the *maktir*, the one performing the *ketoret*, would not begin until the *memuneh*, the appointed officer, gave the word: *hakter* — do the incense. It is not entirely clear where the *memuneh* was positioned at this moment — was he inside with them, or calling from outside? — but the point is that the performance did not begin at the performer's own discretion.

*Ve-im haya kohen gadol, ha-memuneh omer lo: ishi kohen gadol, hakter* — and if it was the *kohen gadol* performing, the *memuneh* addressed him accordingly, with the honorific *ishi kohen gadol* — "my lord *kohen gadol*" — and only then gave the command. The sudden mention of the *kohen gadol* here is striking; it looks ahead to *Yom Kippur*, when the *kohen gadol* himself performs the *ketoret* in the *kodesh kodashim*.

### People Separate

*Pirshu ha-am* — the people separated and withdrew. *Ha-maktir* performed the *ketoret*, *ve-hishtachaveh ve-yatza* — prostrated himself, and left.

What does *pirshu ha-am* mean, and why was it necessary? The answer lies in a principle derived from the verse *kol adam lo yihyeh be-ohel mo'ed be-vo'o lechaper ba-kodesh ad tzeito* — no person shall be in the *ohel mo'ed* when he enters to effect *kapara* in the *kodesh*, until he goes out. The *ketoret* is understood as a form of *kapara* — recall that when *Aharon* used the *ketoret* to halt the plague, it was *mechaper al benei yisrael*. Whenever a *kapara* is performed inside the *heichal*, no one else may be present — not only on *Yom Kippur*, but anytime: for example, *par helam davar shel tzibur*, when the *beit din* rules erroneously and the community follows, the *zerikat hadam* inside the *heichal* similarly requires the area to be cleared.

Where exactly did they have to withdraw? Other *gemarot* specify that they had to leave not only the *heichal* and the *ulam*, but the space *bein ha-ulam ve-la-mizbe'ach* — the very transitional zone from which the *magreifa* had been thrown. That space, which represents the threshold of entry into the *heichal*, is treated as an extension of the *heichal's* sanctity. When the *kapara* is performed within the *heichal*, the zone of required separation extends outward to include even that liminal corridor. Thus the space *bein ha-ulam ve-la-mizbe'ach* functions on multiple levels: it is the place from which approach to the *heichal* is announced, and it is the boundary that must be cleared before the *heichal*'s most sacred acts are performed.

On *Yom Kippur*, when the *ketoret* is offered in the *kodesh kodashim*, it suffices for people to withdraw from the *heichal*, since the *kapara* is being done one level deeper. But when the *kapara* is done in the *heichal* itself, withdrawal must extend further out — to and including the *bein ha-ulam ve-la-mizbe'ach*. The sequencing — *memuneh* gives the word, all clear, everyone withdraws, he performs, prostrates, and exits — captures this carefully calibrated protocol.

---

## Tamid Opening

### Middot Conclusion

We conclude with the *hadran* for Masechet Middot: *hadran alach Masechet Middot ve-da'atan alach Masechet Middot, lo titnashi minan Masechet Middot ve-lo nitnashi minach, lo be-alma ha-dein ve-lo be-alma de-atei.*

### Guard Stations

With Masechet Middot behind us, we open Masechet Tamid.
