The first *mishnah* of *perek* 1 reads: *bi-shlosha mekomot ha-kohanim shomrim be-veit ha-mikdash* — in three places the *kohanim* stand guard in the *beit hamikdash*: in the *beit avtinas*, the *beit hanitzotz*, and the *beit hamoked*. *Ve-ha-leviyim be-esrim ve-echad makom* — and the *leviyim* in twenty-one places: five at the five gates of the *beit*, four at its four inner corners, five at the five gates of the *azara*, four at its four outer corners, one in the chamber of the sacrifice, one in the chamber of the curtain, and one behind the *beit ha-kapores*.

### Honor Guards

What is the purpose of these guards? There are no thieves to fear in the *beit hamikdash*. The answer is already given in the fifth *perek* of Masechet Middot, at 36a: the *shemira* of the *beit hamikdash* is only *le-kavod* — for honor. A palace with no guards is not an honorable palace. The guards were stationed not out of security necessity but to manifest the greatness and dignity of the place — which is precisely why both *leviyim* and *kohanim* were assigned, in separate roles, to separate stations. *Eino domeh palatin she-yesh aleha shomrim le-palatin she-ein aleha shomrim* — a palace that has guards is simply not comparable to one that does not. The more guards, the greater the honor; and so twenty-four stations were established throughout the *mikdash* complex, three held by *kohanim* and twenty-one by *leviyim*.

---

---

# Tamid 33b

## High Priest & Blessing

### High Priest Retinue

The final section of Masechet Tamid opens at 33b by describing the procedure when the *kohen gadol* himself chose to participate in the morning service. The *mishnah* establishes a baseline: at this stage of the *avodah*, the *kohanim* who had performed the work inside the *heichal* — cleaning the *menorah*, the golden *mizbeiach*, and offering the *ketores* — would enter the *heichal* to perform *hishtachavayah*, prostration, before the next phase began. The *mishnah* specifically highlights what occurred when it was the *kohen gadol* who came to prostrate himself.

The text states: when the *kohen gadol* entered to bow, *shlosha ochezim bo* — three men would hold him, one on his right, one on his left, and one holding the precious stones. This retinue was clearly an expression of *kavod*, befitting the dignity of the office. The precise meaning of "holding the precious stones" invites some discussion. Some understand the reference to be the *avnei shoham* on the shoulders of the *ephod*, or perhaps the *choshen*. One possibility is that the stones were carried separately by an attendant walking before the *kohen gadol*, functioning as a ceremonial display of the jewel-encrusted vestments. Another possibility is that the *ephod* itself, being heavy, may have required physical support. The text does not fully resolve this.

As the *kohen gadol* was completing his prostration and leaving the *heichal*, one could hear him approaching through the *pe'amonim*, the bells of the *me'il*. The *memunneh* — the supervising official — would then lift the curtain at the entrance between the *ulam* and the outside, allowing the *kohen gadol* to exit. The *memunneh* himself would then enter and prostrate, followed by all the other *kohanim*, who entered and performed their *hishtachavayah* in turn.

### Prostration Sequence

This passage confirms what had been left implicit in the preceding *mishnah*: all the *kohanim* who were serving that day, after the *ketores* was completed, went into the *heichal* to perform *hishtachavayah*. The *meforshim* understand that this was the moment — after the *ketores* offering — when the assembled *kohanim* entered the inner sanctuary not to perform any specific *avodah*, but simply to prostrate themselves before the Divine presence.

This is a theologically significant detail. The *heichal* was not ordinarily a place one entered without purpose; entry was restricted to those performing the *avodah*. Yet once the morning *avodot* were complete, this act of *hishtachavayah* was permitted and indeed practiced. It reflects a dimension of the Temple service that is less transactional than the *korbanot* themselves — a moment of direct personal connection to the *Shechinah*, which was understood to rest particularly over the *aron* in the *kodesh kodashim* and by extension to fill the *heichal*. This is the world of *tefillah* as opposed to *korban*, the personal encounter with God's presence.

### Blessing Positions

After completing their *hishtachavayah*, the *kohanim* emerged and took their positions on the steps of the *ulam*. The *mishnah* states: *ba'u ve'amdu al ma'alos ha-ulam* — they came and stood on the steps of the *ulam*. Those who had performed the various *avodot* of the *heichal* — the five *kohanim* who carried the *kelei hamikdash* — stood to the south of the steps, each holding his respective vessel: one held the *teni*, the gold basket with the ashes from the golden *mizbeiach*; one held the *kuz*, the pitcher containing the material cleared from the *menorah*; one held the *machtah*, the gold shovel with the coals; one held the *bazach*, the small gold vessel with the *ketores*; and one held the *kaf* with its cover, the larger container.

The entire assembly of *kohanim* then stood on these steps — the very same steps where, on ordinary occasions, the *leviyim* would stand to sing their *shirah* — and performed *birkat kohanim*, the priestly blessing. There is a striking parallel here to the account in *Shmini*, where *Aharon* exits the *ohel mo'ed* and blesses the people: *vayisa aharon et yadav el ha'am vayivarkhem*. The *chazal* understand that as a reference to *birkat kohanim*, and indeed the structure here mirrors that: the *kohanim* enter the *heichal*, perform their prostration, emerge, and then bless the people. The parallel is not exact — in *Shmini*, *Aharon*'s blessing followed the offering of the *korbanot* before he entered, whereas here it follows the exit from the *heichal* after the *hishtachavayah* — but the resonance is clear and intentional.

By this stage in the service, the *yisraelim* were evidently already gathered in the *azarah*, for the blessing was directed toward them. Precisely when the gates were opened to the public is never stated explicitly in the *mishnah*, a point that will be discussed below.

### Single Blessing Format

The *mishnah* specifies that the *kohanim* recited *birkat kohanim* as *bracha achat* — a single blessing. This requires explanation, since we ordinarily speak of the priestly blessing as three distinct verses. The answer given is that in the *mikdash*, the three verses were recited continuously, without any *amen* response between them. It was said as an uninterrupted unit, and therefore counted as one. Outside the *mikdash*, by contrast, the blessing is divided into three, with the congregation responding *amen* between each verse — making it, in effect, three blessings.

### Divine Name & Hands

Two further distinctions between the *mikdash* practice and that of the *medinah* — outside the Temple — are noted here. First, *bamikdash hayu omrim et hashem kichtavo*: in the *mikdash*, the *kohanim* pronounced God's name as it is written, using the ineffable four-letter name. Outside the *mikdash*, the name is pronounced by its substitute, as is universal practice today.

Second, there is a distinction in the height at which the hands are raised. Outside the *mikdash*, the *kohanim* raise their hands to shoulder height, *keneged kitfeihem*. In the *mikdash*, they raised their hands above their heads. The reason given is that within the *mikdash*, the *Shechinah* was understood to rest upon the hands of the *kohanim* as they blessed. In such a context, one must not have any part of his body higher than the locus of the Divine presence — and therefore the hands had to be elevated above the head.

There is one exception: the *kohen gadol* did not raise his hands above the *tzitz*, the gold headband bearing the inscription *kodesh l'Hashem* that he wore on his forehead. Since the *tzitz* itself represents the presence of holiness at the top of the head, the *kohen gadol* need not raise his hands above it, as that level already satisfies the requirement. *Rabbi Yehuda* disagrees and holds that even the *kohen gadol* must raise his hands above the *tzitz*, deriving this from the verse *vayisa aharon et yadav el ha'am vayivarkhem* — he lifted his hands and blessed them — implying an unrestricted elevation of the hands.

---

## Offering Limbs

### Ascending Ramp

The *mishnah* now describes the final act of the *tamid*: the burning of the limbs that had been placed halfway up the *kevesh*, the ramp of the outer *mizbeiach*, earlier in the morning. When the *kohen gadol* wished to participate in this *haktarah* — the offering of the limbs onto the fire — the procedure was adapted to accommodate him. He would ascend the ramp, and the *sgan*, the deputy *kohen gadol*, would stand at his right. At the midpoint of the ramp, the *sgan* would take hold of the *kohen gadol*'s right hand and assist him the rest of the way up. The text does not shy away from the implication: the *kohen gadol*, often a political appointee unfamiliar with the rigors of the *avodah*, may not have been physically capable of ascending the full length of the ramp unassisted.

### Limb Presentation

Once the *kohen gadol* was positioned at the top, the other *kohanim* — those who had carried the limbs up — would hand them to him one by one. The *mishnah* specifies that the first *kohen* handed him *harosh veharegel*, the head and the foot, and the *kohen gadol* would perform *semikhah* on them — laying his hands upon them — and then throw them onto the fire. This *semikhah* is, as the text itself acknowledges, largely symbolic. Normally, *semikhah* is performed on a living animal prior to slaughter; here it is a gesture of connection and *kavod*, linking the *kohen gadol* to an offering in which he had played no prior role.

### Throwing Limbs

After the first *kohen* handed over the head and foot, the second *kohen* — who had carried the two forearms — would hand them to the first *kohen*, who in turn would hand them to the *kohen gadol*. The *kohen gadol* would again perform *semikhah* and throw them onto the fire. The second *kohen* would then depart, and the process would repeat with each subsequent pair of *kohanim*: each one handing his limbs to the *kohen* stationed permanently beside the *kohen gadol*, who then passed them up. This arrangement preserved a sense of dignity and order, sparing the *kohen gadol* from the somewhat unseemly scene of a constant stream of *kohanim* arriving and departing at his side.

If the *kohen gadol* wished, he could limit his personal participation to the *semikhah* alone and allow the *sgan* or another *kohen* to perform the actual throwing onto the fire.

### Altar Circuit & Wine

Upon completing the offering of the limbs, the *kohen gadol* descended and circumambulated the *mizbeiach*. The general rule *kol pinot she'ata poneh lo yehu ela leyamin* — all turns are made only to the right — means the circuit proceeds counterclockwise as viewed from above. The *kohen gadol* began at the southeast corner, proceeded to the northeast, then to the northwest, and completed the circuit at the southwest corner. It was at the southwest corner that the *nisuch hayayin*, the wine libation, was performed, the wine being poured through the dedicated funnels that channeled it down beneath the *mizbeiach*.

---

## Signals & Song

### Flag Signals

The *sgan* stood at the corner holding *sudarim* — flags or handkerchiefs — to be used for signaling. Two *kohanim* stood by the *shulchan hachalavim*, the fat table in the space between the *ulam* and the *mizbeiach*, each holding a *chatzotzrah*, a trumpet. When the *kohen gadol* (or whoever performed the *nisuch*) was about to pour the wine, they would sound *tekiah teruah tekiah*. They then proceeded to stand beside Ben Arza, who was positioned at the *tzeltzel*, some form of percussion instrument — perhaps resembling a triangle or gong. One trumpet-bearer stood on his right and one on his left.

---

## Signals & Song (II)

### Trumpets & Alert

As the officiant bent down to pour the wine — the moment of *nisuch hayayin* — the *sgan* waved the flags, signaling that the libation was actually beginning. Ben Arza then struck the *tzeltzel*, and the *leviyim* opened into song: *vedibru haLevi'im beshir*.

### Song with Wine

The *leviyim* were stationed on the *duchan*, the steps of the *ulam* — the same location where the *kohanim* had just stood for *birkat kohanim*. The musical performance combined instrumental accompaniment with vocal singing, and the *mishnah*'s phrasing *dibru beshir* — literally "spoke in song" — emphasizes the primacy of the vocal element. This relates to a broader debate as to whether *ikar shirah bepeh* or *ikar shirah bikli* — whether the essential component of the Levitical *shirah* is the singing or the instrumental accompaniment — but the language here favors the vocal dimension.

A fundamental principle underlies the timing of the *shirah*: *ein shirah ela al hayayin* — there is no song except over wine. The *gemara* derives this from various associations between wine and joy, including the verse in *Shoftim* where the vine declares that its wine *mesameiach levav anashim* — gladdens the heart of men. Because of this principle, the *leviyim* did not sing during the *shechitah* of the *tamid*, or during the *zerikas hadam*, or during the burning of the *evarim*. They waited until the very moment of the *nisuch hayayin*. This same principle underlies the institution of *kiddush* over wine, and more broadly the practice of performing many significant ritual acts *al hakos*, over a cup of wine — a practice that, while not found in the *gemara* itself for occasions such as a *bris milah* or a wedding, was introduced relatively early precisely because of wine's established ritual significance.

### Psalm Divisions

Each *psalm* — the *shir shel yom*, as we shall see — was divided into three sections. When the *leviyim* completed the first section and arrived at the break, the *kohanim* sounded another *tekiah teruah tekiah*. At each such *tekiah*, the assembled people bowed — *vayishtachavu ha'am*. This happened three times, corresponding to the three sections of the psalm: *al kol perek tekiah*, and *al kol tekiah hishtachavayah*. The intent was evidently to synchronize the completion of the wine pouring with the completion of the singing, so that both acts concluded together.

### Closing Statement

The *mishnah* concludes with a remarkable closing line: *zeh'u seder hatamid la'avodat beit eloheinu, yehi ratzon sheyibaneh bimeherah beyameinu amen* — "This is the order of the *tamid* for the service of the house of our God; may it be His will that it be rebuilt speedily in our days, amen." The insertion of this prayer indicates that the *mishnah* was composed — or at least this closing was added — after the *churban habayit*. The *gemara* at the beginning of *Middot* will discuss the authorship of these tractates and suggests that the author was someone who had himself witnessed the Temple in his lifetime. This closing line transforms the descriptive *mishnah* into an act of longing and prayer.

---

## Levitical Songs

### Day One Song

The final *mishnah* of the tractate records the *shir shel yom* — the psalm recited by the *leviyim* for each day of the week. On the first day of the week, *bayom harishon hayu omrim: L'Hashem ha'aretz umlo'ah, tevel v'yoshvei vah* — Psalm 24. The connection to the first day is transparent: the first day of creation, when God established dominion over the earth, is directly reflected in the psalm's opening declaration that the earth and its fullness belong to God.

### Day Two Song

On the second day, the *leviyim* recited *Gadol Hashem u'mihullal me'od b'ir Elokeinu har kodsho* — Psalm 48. The connection to the second day — the separation of the upper and lower waters and the formation of the heavens — is less immediately obvious. One approach found in the *Zohar*, cited by *Kehati*, reads the six days of creation as symbolic of six millennia of history, with each thousand-year period corresponding to a day. Under that framework, the second millennium was the age of *Avraham Avinu* — born in the year 1948 from creation — and the pivotal events of *Akeidas Yitzchak* and the choosing of *Har HaMoriah*, the *ir Elokeinu*, the city of God. This renders the mention of *b'ir Elokeinu har kodsho* apt for the second day.

### Days 3-7 Songs

On the third day: *Elokim nitzav ba'adas Eil, b'kerev elokim yishpot* — Psalm 82. The *Zohar* associates the third millennium with *matan Torah*, the settlement of *Eretz Yisrael*, and the eras of the first and second *Beit HaMikdash* — a period when God was fully present and engaged with His people, *Elokim nitzav ba'adas*.

On the fourth day: *Eil nekamot Hashem, Eil nekamot hofi'a* — Psalm 94. The fourth millennium was the period of the *churban habayit* and *galus*, when Divine judgment fell upon the people — hence the theme of retribution and justice.

On the fifth day: *Harninu l'Elokim uzeinu, hari'u l'Elokei Yaakov* — Psalm 81. The *Zohar* connects this to the ongoing *galus*, where in the absence of the *Beit HaMikdash*, the Jewish people's connection to God is maintained through prayer and song — *harninu* — rather than through the *avodah*.

On the sixth day: *Hashem malach ge'us lavesh, lavesh Hashem oz isazar* — Psalm 93. The sixth millennium anticipates the rebuilding of the *Beit HaMikdash* and the ultimate sovereignty of God.

On *Shabbos*: *mizmor shir l'yom hashabas* — Psalm 92. This is both the plain meaning — the song of *Shabbos* — and, according to the *mishnah* itself, something more: *shir l'asid lavo, l'yom shekulo shabbos u'menucha l'chayei ha'olamim* — a song for the era to come, for the day that is entirely *Shabbos* and rest, for eternal life. The *Zohar*'s interpretive framework, which read the six weekday psalms as corresponding to the six millennia of history, here reaches its natural culmination: the seventh psalm is not merely about the seventh day, but about the seventh millennium — the ultimate *menucha*, the era of *olam haba*.

With this, the *mishnah* concludes, and the tractate closes: *hadran alach perek zman shehein gadil, u'selikah masechet Tamid*.

---

---

# Middot 34

## Levite Posts

The *mishnah* opens with a formulation that should sound familiar — it parallels the opening of *Masechet Tamid*: in three places the *kohanim* keep watch over the *Beis HaMikdash* — in *Beis Avtinas*, *Beis HaNitzots*, and *Beis HaMoked*, those three chambers embedded within the walls of the *azarah*. The *mishnah* then turns to the *leviyim*, who guard in twenty-one places.

### Gates of Har HaBayit

The *mishnah* states: *chamisha chamisha shaarei Har HaBayit* — five *leviyim* at the five gates of the *Har HaBayit*. Looking at the full plan of the *Har HaBayit* complex, one can see the five openings in the outer wall: two on the south side and one each in the remaining three directions. Each of these access points to the *Har HaBayit* had a *levi* stationed at it as a guard.

### Corners of Har HaBayit

Beyond the five gates, the *mishnah* assigns *leviyim* to *arba al arba pinosav* — four guards at the four corners of the *Har HaBayit*, stationed on the inside, *mitcho*. The *gemara* in *Tamid* had raised the curious implication that "inside" extended even to the interior of the gate itself; from this *mishnah*, however, one might have read "inside" simply as referring to the inner corners of the compound. In any case, four *leviyim* occupied those corner positions — likely patrolling back and forth along the adjacent walls.

### Gates of Azarah

*Chamisha chamisha shaarei azarah* — five *leviyim* at the gates of the *azarah*. This is worth pausing over. The *kohanim* guarded three of the *azarah*'s gates, and they did so from above, from an elevated position resembling a balcony. The *leviyim*, by contrast, watched from below, and their posts were more numerous — five compared to the *kohanim*'s three. The *mishnah* speaks of five gates of the *azarah*, though most authorities assume there were at least seven. Either this *tanna* holds that there were only five, or — as was suggested in the discussion of *Tamid* — two of the gates required no additional *levi* because they were already covered by the *kohanim* or were otherwise supervised.

### Corners of Azarah

As with the *Har HaBayit*, four *leviyim* were posted at the four corners of the *azarah* — but here the *mishnah* specifies *mibachutz*, from the outside. This distinction is significant: because the *leviyim* were not permitted to sit and rest within the *azarah* itself, all their posts around the *azarah* — at the gates and at the corners alike — were on the exterior.

### Seven Chamber Posts

Beyond the gates and corners, the *mishnah* enumerates seven additional posts. One *levi* was stationed at *lishkat hakorban*. The *Rosh* understands this as the chamber of the sheep within *Beis HaMoked* — the sub-room where the *tamid* offering was kept for inspection — though this is problematic, since that location is inside the *azarah* and, as noted, the *leviyim*' posts were always on the outside. Alternatively, the reference may be to *Shaar HaKorban*, a gate located on the exterior, and *lishkat hakorban* means the chamber associated with that gate. The question remains open.

A second *levi* was at *lishkat haparochet* — the chamber associated with the *parochet*, the curtain — though its precise location is not entirely clear. And a third was stationed *lachorei beis hakapporet*, at the very back of the *Beis HaMikdash*, behind the *Kodesh Kodashim*. This was necessarily on the exterior, in the narrow space between the rear wall of the *Beis HaMikdash* building and the outer wall of the *Har HaBayit*.

---

## Oversight & Discipline

### Overseer's Rounds

The *mishnah* introduces the *Ish Har HaBayit*, the appointed overseer of the *Har HaBayit*: *haya mechazer al kol mishmar umishmar* — he would circulate and check every guard post. It bears emphasizing that *mishmar* here does not refer to the twenty-four-week *mishmar* rotation of *kohanim*, but rather to each individual on guard duty. The overseer would make his rounds to ensure that everyone assigned to a post was alert and attentive. While the watch could apply by day as well, the emphasis throughout this context is on the nighttime watch.

### Punishment Protocol

The *mishnah* describes what happened when the *Ish Har HaBayit* arrived at a post and the guard failed to rise and declare *shalom alecha*: it was self-evident that the man had been sleeping. The protocol was twofold. First, *chovto bemaklo* — he would strike him with his staff. Second, and more dramatically, *urshus haya lo lishrof es kesuso* — he had the authority to burn the guard's garment.

This second punishment raises an obvious question about the physical safety of the offender, and the likely answer is that the guard was first made to remove the garment before it was set alight. What makes this detail especially pointed is the observation that the burning takes place *ba'azarah* — in the *azarah*, the very courtyard where animal offerings are consumed by fire. There is an implicit message: someone who abandoned his sacred duty deserves, in a symbolic sense, to share the fate of the sacrifices burned in that place. Moreover, the fact that the guard had garments to burn indicates he had arranged himself for sleep — he had not merely dozed off inadvertently but had deliberately settled in. That intentionality makes the humiliation and punishment more fitting.

The witnesses to this spectacle would call out: *mah kol ba'azarah* — what is that sound in the *azarah*? — and the answer: *kol ben levi loke uvgadav nisrafim sheyeishen lo al mishmaro* — it is a *ben levi* being beaten and his garments being burned because he fell asleep on his watch. The exclamation is attributed to *ba'azarah* even though the guard was technically posted outside, presumably because the commotion could be heard that far.

### R. Eliezer ben Yaakov

*Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* gives not merely a legal opinion here but a firsthand account: *paam achas matzu es achi imi yashen vesarfu es kesuso* — once they found my mother's brother sleeping, and they burned his garment. This is a remarkable passage. According to both the *Bavli* and the *Yerushalmi*, *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* is identified as the author of *Masechet Middos* — and possibly *Tamid* as well. He lived at the end of the period of the *Beis HaMikdash*, and his name will appear again in the *masechta*. The personal testimony here lends unusual vividness to the law: this was not theoretical but something he witnessed happening to a family member.

One further question left unresolved: the *mishnah* and the punishment described apply clearly to *leviyim*. What of a *kohen* who fell asleep on his watch? Was the *Ish Har HaBayit* authorized to beat *kohanim* and burn their garments? And if so, one would hesitate to burn *bigdei kehunah* — priestly vestments — so perhaps the protocol was different. The *gemara* does not spell out who supervised the *kohanim* on watch, and the matter is not fully resolved.

---

## Five Gates Overview

### Shaarei Chulda South

*Mishnah 3* opens: *chamisha shearim hayu lo leHar HaBayis* — there were five gates to the *Har HaBayit*. In the south: *shnei shaarei Chulda min hadarom* — the two gates of *Chulda*, named for *Chulda HaNeviah*, the prophetess. These were the primary entrances and exits: *meshamshim knisa veyitzia* — they served as the main thoroughfare in and out of the *Har HaBayit*.

### West & North Gates

In the west was *Shaar Kiponos* — the gate of *Kiponos*. One explanation holds that *Kiponos* derives from a Greek word connected to garden work, and that a garden of some kind stood nearby. This gate also functioned as an entrance and exit when needed.

In the north was *Shaar Tedi* — the gate of *Tedi*. The name may be a personal name, or, as some *meforshim* suggest, an Aramaic form of *tari*, meaning private or discreet. This is fitting, because the gate's primary known use was for the *kohen gadol* who experienced a nocturnal seminal emission and had to leave the *Beis HaMoked* quietly before the morning service. The *mishnah* says *lo haya meshamesh klum* — it was not used for anything — but that clearly cannot mean it served no purpose at all, since it was used precisely for that sensitive circumstance.

### Eastern Gate & Parah

The eastern gate bore the image or inscription of *Shushan Habira* — Shushan the capital — apparently carved into the arch or stonework. This commemorates the Persian period, when Cyrus granted permission to rebuild the *Beis HaMikdash*, and *Shushan* was the imperial capital at that time.

The eastern gate's primary function was the ceremony of the *Parah Adumah*: *shebo Kohen Gadol soref es haparah* — through it the *Kohen Gadol* (though it need not necessarily be the *Kohen Gadol*) would lead the entire retinue of the red heifer — the cow, the attendants, and all the associated personnel — *yotzim lehar hamishchah*, out toward *Har HaMishchah*, the Mount of Anointing, which is *Har HaZeisim*, the Mount of Olives.

---

## Topography & Gates

### 3D Temple Structure

Looking at a three-dimensional reconstruction of the *Beis HaMikdash* complex helps clarify what the two-dimensional diagrams can obscure. The *Ezras Nashim* appears as a large courtyard in a cross-like shape when viewed from above, and the *Heichal* building itself was enormous in terms of height relative to everything around it. From the front, one sees the great facade of the *ulam* — the entrance hall — and then beyond it, the *heichal* proper. The *ulam*'s roofline extended slightly beyond the *heichal* when viewed from above, but approaching it directly, one encountered simply the massive frontal section of the structure.

The sight lines of the complex also deserve attention. The general Israelite population, entering through the *Ezras Nashim*, could not see the *kohanim* performing the *avodah*. Only upon passing through *Shaar Nicanor* — the Nicanor gates — and entering *Ezras Yisrael* could one actually observe what was happening in the inner *azarah*. The *leviyim* who sang stood on the *duchan*, the steps inside *Ezras Yisrael* — the straight interior steps, not the rounded steps visible in some reconstructions. The rounded steps and the outer broad stairways served a different function entirely.

A remarkable archaeological find bears mention here: a stone was discovered bearing the inscription *l'veis hatkiya* — "for the house of the *tkiya*," the chamber of the *shofar* blasts. This suggests that a specific location existed where the *tekiyot* were sounded, and archaeological reconstructions have attempted to situate it within the overall complex.

### Geographic Context

The deeper question — why were the main gates in the south rather than the east, which faces the primary axis of the sanctuary? — is answered by geography. The old city, *Ir David*, was built along the southern slope of the mountain. All of ancient Jerusalem was concentrated to the south, climbing up the hillside. Worshippers approaching the *Har HaBayit* were naturally coming from the south, which is precisely why the main gates — *Shaarei Chulda* — were placed there. The south was where the population was.

### Chulda Steps Design

The east presented an entirely different situation. Directly to the east of the *Har HaBayit* lies the Kidron Valley — a dramatic drop-off that makes entry from that direction essentially impossible. That is why there was no functional main gate in the east, even though the *Shaar Mizrachi* opened eastward for the *Parah Adumah* ceremony. When the *Kohen Gadol* and the retinue went out toward *Har HaZeisim*, some kind of passage was navigated, because the *kohen* performing the burning had to stand on *Har HaZeisim* in a position from which he could look back and see *Petach Ohel Moed* — the entrance to the sanctuary. But the main flow of traffic to and from the *Har HaBayit* ran through the south.

What remains from the actual *Shaarei Chulda* steps is illuminating in its own right. The surviving steps — with the lowest two courses being modern reconstructions — are strikingly narrow. Archaeological observation confirms that the narrowness of the steps was not incidental: narrow steps force pedestrians to slow down considerably, functioning as a natural mechanism of traffic control at the primary entrance to the most sacred site in the world.

### Chulda Etymology

This observation connects to one proposed etymology of the name *Chulda*. While the standard identification is with *Chulda HaNeviah*, the prophetess, a secondary suggestion holds that the name reflects the Hebrew word for weasel — *chulda* — and that the weasel-like slowness of movement enforced by the narrow steps gave the gates their name. The etymology is speculative, and the weasel is not obviously a slow-moving creature, but the physical evidence of the steps themselves — designed, it seems, to deliberately moderate the pace of those entering — lends the suggestion a certain plausibility. To be continued.

---

---

# Middot 34b

## Parah Adumah Bridge

### Opening Review

We pick up at the bottom of 34a in *Middot*, having completed our treatment of the gates of *Har HaBayit* proper in the previous session. The mishnah now turns to the gates of the *Azara*, and before proceeding, a brief note from the prior discussion bears revisiting.

### Kidron Valley Bridge

The mishnah had mentioned that the eastern gate of *Har HaBayit* was used to access *Har HaZeitim* — the Mount of Olives — for the *Parah Adumah* ritual. This raises an immediate geographical difficulty: the east opens directly onto the Kidron Valley, which drops away steeply, making regular access essentially impossible. If so, how did they actually get across to *Har HaZeitim*?

The answer, as the *Mishnah* in *Parah* records explicitly, is that they built a bridge — *keves hayu lo* — spanning the Kidron Valley, connecting *Har HaBayit* to *Har HaZeitim*. Whether this was a permanent stone structure or a more temporary construction is not entirely clear from the sources. The description in *Parah* gives the impression of something substantial, perhaps great stone vaults — the kind of feat of engineering the Romans were particularly renowned for, capable of beginning a bridge from one bank alone and extending it across. Whatever its precise form, the bridge was the means by which the *Parah Adumah* procession crossed.

### Tumah & Drainage

The bridge's design was also specifically engineered to avoid *tumah*, a consideration the *Mishnah* in *Parah* addresses in some detail. The concern was not merely practical access but ritual purity: those participating in the *Parah Adumah* ceremony had to be protected from any inadvertent contact with sources of impurity along the route.

One further note about the Kidron Valley: beyond serving as the geographical barrier that necessitated the bridge, it also functioned as the drainage outlet for the *Beit HaMikdash* — the channel into which the blood and other byproducts of the *avodah* would flow out of the *Mikdash* precincts.

---

## Shiva Shearim Azara

### Seven Gates Intro

The mishnah states: *shiva shearim hayu ba-azara* — there were seven gates in the *Azara*. This subject had already been touched upon when learning *Tamid*, in the context of the *Kohanim*'s movements through the complex. The distribution was *shlosha ba-tzafon u-shlosha ba-darom* — three in the north and three in the south — *ve-echad ba-mizrach*, and one in the east.

### Sha'ar HaDelek

The southern gates are enumerated first. The first is *Sha'ar HaDelek* — literally, the Fuel Gate. *Delek* means fuel or combustible material, and the obvious implication is that this gate served as the delivery entrance for firewood and other materials needed for the *mizbe'ach*. One would not transport loads of wood through the main entrance; this was effectively the service entrance at the back.

What is striking, however, is that looking at the diagrams of the *Beit HaMikdash*, this gate appears to have had an opening only to the outside, with no corresponding opening into the *Azara* proper. If so, perhaps the wood was stored here temporarily and then brought in through a different gate — possibly via the *Ezrat Nashim* or some other route — when needed. This raises the broader question about the *lishchot* generally: the *Gemara* elsewhere establishes that the *kedushah* of any chamber was determined by the location of its opening. If these southern chambers opened only outward, they would be *chol*, non-sanctified — yet the presence of *Levi'im* standing guard on the outside seems to imply they were *kodesh*. The *mefarshim* do not appear to address this directly, and it warrants further investigation.

It is also possible that *Sha'ar HaDelek* was used for oil deliveries as well, since oil was required for the *menorah*, though the term *delek* would be an unusual way to describe lamp oil.

### Sha'ar HaBechoros

The second southern gate is given in many textual variants as *Sha'ar HaBechoros* — the Gate of the Firstborns — rather than simply *Sha'ar HaKorban*. This makes good sense functionally: rather than requiring someone who had arrived with their *bechor* to wait in the main lines, this gate served as a kind of drop-off point. Much as one might deposit books at a library return slot, a person could bring his *bechor* here and continue on, with the *Kohanim* collecting them at the appropriate time.

There is an additional reason this gate was placed in the south. *Bechoros* are *kodashim kalim*, which do not require slaughter in the north — they could be brought in the south, near the *mizbe'ach*. One might ask why this distinction was needed to separate *bechoros* from other *shelamim*-class offerings. The answer may be that since the *Kohen* eats the *bechor* — as he does with *kodshei kodashim* — there was concern about confusion, even though *bechoros* may be eaten throughout *Yerushalayim*, and so it was specifically designated to the south.

### Sha'ar HaMayim

The third southern gate was *Sha'ar HaMayim* — the Gate of Water — named for its role in the *Nisuch HaMayim* ritual on *Sukkot*. The water drawn for the libation would be brought in through this gate and then conveyed to the *mizbe'ach*. This implies, as with the other gates, that there must have been an opening on both sides — one facing outward for bringing the water in, and one facing the *Azara* to bring it forward to the *mizbe'ach*. Whether this was a full secondary opening or something more like a small door is not entirely clear; the *Gemara* makes much of where these openings were located, and the precise configuration remains somewhat uncertain.

### Sha'ar Nikanor

Moving to the east, the lone eastern gate was *Sha'ar Nikanor*. This was the primary entrance from the *Ezrat Nashim* into the *Azara* proper — the main door through which all *Yisrael* would pass when approaching the *avodah*. If the *Ezrat Nashim* served as the waiting area or anteroom, *Sha'ar Nikanor* was the threshold into the sacred precincts themselves.

### Nikanor's Doors

The gate was named for the man who brought its doors from Alexandria. The *Gemara* tells that *Nikanor* was transporting these great brass doors by sea when a severe storm arose, threatening to sink the ship. In an effort to lighten the load, one of the doors was thrown overboard. When the storm continued, *Nikanor* declared that they should throw him in along with the remaining door — at which point the sea calmed. When the ship arrived at port, the door that had been cast overboard was found attached to the hull of the ship, having arrived miraculously. The gate was thereafter named in his honor.

### Nikanor Chambers

Off the sides of *Sha'ar Nikanor* were two chambers — *u-shtei lishchot hayu lo*, one on each side. One was called *lishkat Pinchas ha-malbish*, the chamber of *Pinchas* the dresser — the individual who assisted the *Kohanim* in donning and removing their priestly garments. We had noted elsewhere that this function was associated with the *Lishkat HaGazit*, but here *Pinchas* may have used this chamber as a base of operations or storage. The other chamber was *lishkat osei chavitin* — the chamber of those who prepared the *chavitin*, the griddle-offering of the *Kohen Gadol*.

### Sha'ar Nitzotz

The northern gates are enumerated next, beginning from the west side moving eastward. The first is *Sha'ar Nitzotz* — the Gate of the Spark. Its name likely relates to fire: one explanation is that this was the gate through which fire was brought to supplement what was on the *mizbe'ach*, since the requirement is to bring one's own fire and not merely rely on what is already burning. The *mishnah* describes it as being *ke-min achsadra* — like a portico — with two columns supporting a roof or some kind of overhead structure, with a balcony or platform above it. The *Kohanim* would watch from above and the *Levi'im* below.

This description illuminates something worth noting across all the diagrams of the *Beit HaMikdash*: most of them show what appear to be columns at the gate structures. It is plausible that this *achsadra* configuration, highlighted here in connection with *Sha'ar Nitzotz*, was in fact a feature common to many or all of the gates, and those columns in the diagrams represent precisely this kind of portico construction.

### Opening to Chel

The *mishnah* adds a detail about *Sha'ar Nitzotz* that is not mentioned for any of the other gates: *u-pesach hayah lo la-chel* — it had a specific opening into the *chel*. The *chel* was the buffer zone between the *soreg* fence and the *Azara* proper — approximately ten *amot* wide, roughly fifteen feet — a transitional space that was itself restricted. Non-Jews, it should be noted, were forbidden from entering even the *chel*, let alone the *Azara*. The distinction between those permitted in the *chel* and those permitted in the *Ezrat Nashim* may hinge on categories such as *tevul yom* and *temei meit*.

What is puzzling is that this opening into the *chel* is mentioned only here and not for the other gates — yet all of those gates presumably also opened to the outside in some fashion, as that was their functional purpose. The *mefarshim* consulted did not resolve this question satisfactorily, and it remains open.

---

## Beit HaMoked Chambers

### Four Chambers Layout

*Arba lishchot hayu b'Beit HaMoked* — there were four chambers in the *Beit HaMoked*, arranged like small rooms opening off a great hall, *ke-kitonot ha-ptuchot la-traklin*. The *Beit HaMoked* was the central structure where the *Kohanim* would sleep, and it straddled the boundary between the *Azara* proper and the outside space, with two chambers in the sanctified area and two in the non-sanctified.

### Kodesh/Chol Division

The mishnah states: *shtayim be-kodesh u-shtayim be-chol* — two in the *kodesh* and two in the *chol*. This division arose from the fact that the *Beit HaMoked* had openings on both sides — one into the *Azara* and one to the outside — and therefore the line of sanctity passed through the structure itself. What marked that line? *Ve-roshei pispasin mavdil bein kodesh le-chol* — the tops of the *pispasin* distinguished between the *kodesh* and the *chol*.

The identity of the *pispasin* is debated. One view is that they were beams protruding from the walls at the midpoint, creating a visible marker. The Albeck offers a more visually evocative explanation: *pispeis* in modern Hebrew means mosaic, and he proposes that a different mosaic pattern on the floor — or the point at which the mosaic began — served as the dividing line between the sacred and non-sacred portions of the chamber.

### Southwest Chamber

The southwest chamber was in the *kodesh* portion — anything in the south of the structure falling within the *Azara* space. This was *lishkat korban*, or according to some versions *lishkat tela'ei ha-korban* — the chamber of the sacrificial sheep. This is where the lambs designated for the *tamid* offering were inspected for four days prior to their being brought as a *korban*.

### Southeast Chamber

The southeast chamber, also in the *kodesh*, was *lishkat lechem ha-panim* — the chamber where the *lechem ha-panim* was baked. This was a hot space, with a substantial fire maintained for the baking of the showbread.

### Northeast Chamber

Moving clockwise, the northeast chamber was now in the *chol* portion of the *Beit HaMoked*. The *mishnah* records: *bo ganezu Beit Chashmonai et avnei mizbe'ach she-shiktzum malchei Yavan* — it was here that the *Chashmonaim* stored the stones of the *mizbe'ach* that had been defiled by the Greek kings. After the Maccabean victory, those stones that the *Yevanim* had rendered unfit were dismantled and placed in storage here — a question unto itself as to what precisely constituted defilement of the stone *mizbe'ach*, but a separate discussion.

### Chotamot System

Elsewhere this same chamber is identified as *lishkat chotamot* — the chamber of receipts — which we had encountered in *Tamid*. The system worked as follows: if a person brought a *korban* and required *nesachim* — the accompanying libations of wine, oil, and *mincha* — he would go to this chamber, pay, and receive a *chotam*, a receipt or token. When he presented his *korban* to the *Kohanim*, he would hand over this receipt, and the *Kohanim* responsible for oil and libations would know that payment had been made and would provide the appropriate *nesachim*.

One might ask: why a receipt system at all? Why not simply deposit money into a box, as was done for bird offerings? The answer likely lies in the variability of the nesachim requirement. Bird offerings have a fixed price; *nesachim* varied depending on whether the animal was a sheep, goat, or ox — different quantities and therefore different costs. A simple money box would not permit accurate accounting. Beyond that, if a person brought his animal without having paid for *nesachim*, the *Kohanim* who slaughtered it would themselves be implicated in an incomplete service. The receipt system ensured accountability — the *Kohanim* could verify that the *nesachim* had been arranged before proceeding.

One picture examined in the course of this discussion suggested that the transaction may have taken place entirely within this one chamber — a person would enter on one side, pay, and receive the receipt from someone on the other side, something like a clerk's window — rather than requiring the holder to carry the receipt across the complex and present it elsewhere. Either way, the *chotam* was the operative mechanism.

### Northwest Chamber

The northwest chamber, the fourth and final, was *bah yordim le-beit ha-tvilah* — from here one descended to the *mikveh*. This served the *Kohanim* who required purification, as will be discussed momentarily in greater detail.

---

## Beit HaMoked Gates

### Two Gates System

*Shnayim shearim hayu le-Beit HaMoked* — the *Beit HaMoked* itself had two gates: *echad patuach la-chel ve-echad patuach la-Azara* — one opening to the *chel* and one opening into the *Azara*. It is worth noting in passing that the word *chel* may be a deliberate softening of the word *chol* — one cannot quite call *Har HaBayit* profane, but this terminology emphasizes that the space is not the *Azara* proper.

### Pishpash Scouting

*Amar Rabbi Yehuda*: the gate that opened into the *Azara* had inset within it a *pishpash katan* — a small door set into the larger gate — *shebo nichnasim livlosh et ha-Azara*. Through this small door, one could enter the *Azara* to scout it out — to check that all the *keilim* had been put away and that everything was in order before the start of the new day's service. We had encountered this scouting procedure in *Tamid*, though the specific mechanism of the *pishpash* is clarified here.

---

## Guard & Key Storage

### Dome & Steps

*Beit HaMoked*, the *mishnah* now elaborates, was *kippah* — it had a dome. And it was a substantial structure: *mukaf revadim shel even*, surrounded by stone steps on the interior. These steps apparently lined the inside of the domed building, either serving as platforms on which the occupants slept, or leading to small carved-out niches in the wall where one could rest.

### Elders & Keys

*Ve-ziknei beit av yeshenim sham* — the elders of the *beit av* of that day's rotation would sleep there. We had learned in *Tamid* that the *Kohanim* on duty slept in the *Beit HaMoked*, and at least the elders among them — the senior members of that day's *mishmar* — slept up near or on the stone steps. *U-miftechot ha-Azara beyadam* — in their hands they held the keys to the *Azara*, since the *Azara* was locked from the inside at night and could only be opened by someone already within.

### Young Kohanim

*U-pirchei kehunah ish kesuto ba-aretz* — the younger *Kohanim*, by contrast, did not sleep on the elevated steps but on the ground, each man with his garment beneath him. This echoes a discussion from *Tamid* about whether the *bigdei kehunah* could be used for personal comfort — whether one could derive benefit from the priestly vestments by sleeping on them.

### Key Storage Ritual

The *mishnah* now provides one of its more distinctive passages regarding the physical storage of the keys. *U-makom hayah sham amah al amah* — there was a spot measuring one *amah* by one *amah*, roughly a foot and a half square. Upon it rested *tavla shel shayish*, a marble cover, *hayeta kevuah bah* — fixed in place on this low platform. *Ve-shalshelet shel maftechot hayu tluyot bah* — a chain holding the keys was suspended from it.

The precise image is somewhat ambiguous: was this a small chamber sunk into the floor with a marble cover sealing it, beneath which the keys hung on a chain? Or was the chain attached directly to the underside of the marble slab itself, so that lifting the cover revealed the keys hanging from it? The grammar admits either reading. What is clear is that the keys were stored within or beneath this marble platform, with the chain serving as a kind of organized keyring.

Why this elaborate arrangement? One possibility is that the marble platform was not immediately obvious to someone unfamiliar with the location — a kind of concealment by obscurity, though of course the *mishnah* now publishes the secret. Another possibility is that the marble platform and chain gave the entire procedure a ceremonial character befitting the locking and unlocking of the *Azara*.

### Locking Procedure

*Higgia zman ha-neila* — when the time for locking arrived, the appointed *Kohen* would *higbia et ha-tavla* — lift the marble cover. A ring was set into the top of the cover to facilitate lifting it. He then *natal et ha-maftechot min ha-shalshelet* — removed the keys from the chain — *ve-naal* — and proceeded to lock all the doors from the inside.

Immediately there is an apparent tension with what was stated a moment ago: *mishnah 8* said the keys were *be-yadam* — in the hands — of the *ziknei beit av* sleeping on the steps above. But this passage describes keys stored in a marble box on the floor, with someone sleeping on top of it. How do we reconcile the two? One approach is to take *be-yadam* non-literally, meaning that the keys were under their authority and stewardship, rather than physically in their grip. Another is to suggest that the two references describe different sets of keys, or different stages of the same procedure. The descriptions do remain textually distinct, however.

Following the locking, the *mishnah* adds: *he-Kohen mi-bifnim u-vein Levi yashen lo mi-bachutz* — the *Kohen* was on the inside and a *Levi* slept adjacent from the outside. The word *yashen* — slept — has struck some as inappropriate for a guarding function. One variant reading substitutes *yashav*, sat, which would be more consistent with an active watch. But the *girsa* of *yashen* is attested, and may simply reflect that the guard was permitted to rest so long as he remained at his post.

Once the locking was complete: *hechzir et ha-mafteach la-shalshelet ve-et ha-tavla li-mekomah* — the key was replaced on the chain and the marble cover returned to its place. Then *natan kesuto aleha ve-yashan lo* — the one responsible for the keys placed his garment on top of the marble cover and slept upon it. The person guarding the keys thus literally slept on top of them, ensuring that no one could access them without waking him.

---

## Nocturnal Emission

### Nocturnal Event

*Ira keri be-echad me-hem* — should one of the *Kohanim* experience a nocturnal emission, he became *tamei* and was no longer permitted to remain within the *Azara*. We had addressed this situation when learning *Tamid*.

### Underground Route

*Yotze ve-holech lo ba-misila ha-malechet tachat ha-birah* — he would leave by way of the passageway that ran beneath the *birah*, whether that term refers to the *Mikdash* as a whole or to one particular section of the complex. This passageway was lit throughout — *ve-nerot dolkim mi-kan u-mi-kan* — with lights on both sides — *ad she-yagia le-beit ha-tvilah*, until he reached the place where he could immerse in the *mikveh*.

### Sha'ar Tadi Route

*Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* offers an alternative account. In his view, the *Kohen* did not remain underground within the *Mikdash* complex but instead traveled *ba-misila ha-malechet tachat ha-chayil* — through a passageway running beneath the *chel*, effectively exiting the *Azara* precincts entirely — *ve-holech lo be-Tadi*. He would exit via *Sha'ar Tadi*, the northern gate that the *mishnah* had earlier characterized as serving no particular function.

This resolves the earlier puzzle about *Sha'ar Tadi*'s purpose: according to *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov*, it was the private exit for the *Kohen* who needed to leave in the middle of the night. Some have proposed that the name *Tadi* should be read as *tari*, the Aramaic word for private, emphasizing that this was the discreet exit used for such occasions.

It is worth noting that *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* is the *Tanna* cited almost exclusively in *Middot* and *Tamid* not for *halachic* rulings but for descriptive accounts of the *Beit HaMikdash* — which is part of why both the *Bavli* and *Yerushalmi* assume that he was the primary author of tractate *Tamid*.

The divergence between this account and the version learned in *Tamid* is significant: where *Tamid* gave the impression that the *Kohen* would go to the *mikveh* and return to his post by morning, *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* here describes a scenario in which the *Kohen* was actually required to leave *Har HaBayit* immediately — going to the *mikveh* only once outside the complex — and did not remain inside waiting for dawn.

---

## Har HaBayit Dimensions

### Overall Size

*Har HaBayit hayah chamesh me'ot amah al chamesh me'ot amah* — the entire *Har HaBayit* measured five hundred by five hundred *amot*, approximately 750 feet on each side — roughly three city blocks square. When a dimension is stated with such mathematical precision for what is ultimately a natural hilltop, one assumes this refers to the retaining walls constructed around it: the builders determined where to erect the perimeter wall and thus created a defined square of that measurement.

### Space Distribution

*Rubo min ha-darom* — the largest portion of the space was to the south. *Sheni lo min ha-mizrach* — the second largest allocation was to the east. *Shelishi lo min ha-tzafon* — third was the north, each strip progressively narrower. *Mi'uto min ha-maarav* — and the smallest allocation was to the west. *Makom she-hayah rov midato sham hayah rov tashmisho* — greater space was given where there would be greater use.

### Usage Rationale

The rationale for this distribution follows naturally from the patterns of access. The south received the most space because that is where the city of *Yerushalayim* was built and from where the slope permitted approach — the *Shaarei Chulda* were the primary entry points, and so the broad southern plaza served as the arrival and gathering area. The east received the second largest space because, once assembled in the south, the crowds would move toward the eastern section where the *Azara* was accessed through *Sha'ar Nikanor* and the *Ezrat Nashim*. Here too one might purchase *nesachim*, present one's *korban*, and spend time in the complex. The west, by contrast, was deliberately kept minimal: it lay directly behind the *Kodesh Kodashim*, and it would have been inappropriate for large numbers of people to congregate in the area most proximate to that innermost sacred space. The *Kotel* as we know it today stands along precisely this western retaining wall — the wall built closest to where the *Kodesh Kodashim* stood.

---

## Entry/Exit Flow

### Right Enter Left Exit

*Kol ha-nichnasim le-Har HaBayit nichnasim derech yamin* — all who entered *Har HaBayit* turned to the right upon entry. *U-makifin ve-yotzin derech smol* — and they would circle around and exit to the left. The movement was consistently counterclockwise: enter on the right, proceed around the complex, and exit via the opposite direction.

The mechanics of this circulation are worth examining. The straightforward reading is that worshippers entered the complex, moved to the right through the space — past the southern area, through the eastern sections where the *Azara* lay — completed a full circuit, and exited by the other southern gate. *Tosafot* acknowledges that this would require a complete *sivuv*, a full circuit, though this raises questions given the relatively narrow space available on the western side. An alternative reading is that the circular movement was partial — one entered from one gate and exited via another without necessarily traversing the entire perimeter.

### Avel Exception

*Chutz mi-mi she-ira bo davar she-hu makif le-smol* — except for someone to whom something has occurred, who circles to the left instead. The *mishnah* describes how such a person, moving in the reverse direction, would encounter the rest of the worshippers coming the other way. They would notice the anomaly and ask: *mah lecha makif le-smol* — why are you going in the wrong direction?

The person might answer: *she-ani avel* — I am a mourner. At first glance, this seems to describe someone who has just learned of a death and is rushing out. But on reflection — and here a sharper reading is warranted — the phrase *ira bo davar* need not indicate something that just occurred at that moment. The better understanding is that the *avel* had come to *Har HaBayit* in his state of mourning and deliberately walked in the reverse direction in order to prompt exactly this exchange. This also accounts for the parallel case of the *menudeh*, the person under *cherem*, who similarly cannot have just been excommunicated in that instant.

The purpose, in other words, was communicative and social: by moving against the flow, the mourner or excommunicate created a visible signal that invited others to ask about his situation and offer consolation or encouragement.

### Consolation Formula

Upon learning that the person was an *avel*, the response given was: *ha-shochen ba-bayit ha-ze yenachamecha* — may the One who dwells in this house console you.

The case of the *menudeh* — the excommunicated individual — generated a *machloket* between *Rabbi Meir* and *Rabbi Yose*. *Rabbi Meir*'s formula was: *ha-shochen ba-bayit ha-ze yiten be-libam ve-yekarvucha* — may the One who dwells in this house place it in their hearts and bring you close again. *Rabbi Yose* objected: *asitem ke-ilu avru alav et ha-din* — by saying "may God place it in their hearts," you are implying that they were in the wrong for excommunicating him, essentially suggesting that their judgment was unjust. Rather, *Rabbi Yose* said, one should say: *yiten be-libecha ve-tishma le-divrei chaverecha ve-az ve-yekarvucha* — may God place it in your heart to heed the words of your fellows, and then they will draw you close. The consolation formula here points inward to the *menudeh* himself — you should change, and then reconciliation will follow.

---

## Soreg Fence

### Soreg Description

*Lifnim mimenu ha-soreg* — further inward from the general *Har HaBayit* space was the *soreg*, a woven lattice fence. It was *gavo'ah yud tefachim* — ten *tefachim* high — and it created the boundary beyond which non-Jews were forbidden. It defined the outer edge of the *chel*, the buffer zone of ten *amot* width that separated the *soreg* from the *Azara* wall itself.

### Greek Breaks

*U-shlosh esreh pertzot hayu vo* — there were thirteen breaks in this fence. These were not original openings but deliberate breaches: *she-peratzum malchei Yavan* — the Greek kings had broken through in thirteen places. The symbolic intent is clear: the *soreg* was the explicit marker of the boundary beyond which non-Jews could not proceed, and so the *Yevanim*, in their conquest and desecration of the *Mikdash*, deliberately violated that fence in thirteen places as an act of defiance. *Chazru u-gedarum* — subsequently, the *Chashmonaim* repaired all thirteen breaches.

### Thirteen Prostrations

*Ve-gazru kenegdan yud gimmel hishtachavuyot* — and corresponding to those thirteen breaks, the Sages instituted thirteen prostrations. The better understanding of this ordinance is that each time a worshipper passed one of those repaired breaks, he would prostrate himself — in gratitude to God for the restoration of Jewish sovereignty over *Har HaBayit* and the expulsion of the Greeks. The number thirteen, it should be noted, carries its own significance in Jewish tradition, and it is possible that the choice was partly symbolic in that broader sense.

---

## Chel & Steps

### Chel Dimensions

*Ha-chel eser amot* — the *chel* was ten *amot* wide. Beyond it, ascending toward the *Azara*, were *shteim esrei maalot* — twelve steps. Each step was *chatzi amah* high and *chatzi amah* deep — half an *amah* of rise and half an *amah* of tread — roughly nine inches in each direction. Twelve steps of half an *amah* each account for six *amot* of total height — more than half the ten-*amah* width of the *chel* was thus consumed by the staircase, with the remaining four *amot* being level ground before the steps began.

This arrangement meant that even after entering through the *Har HaBayit* perimeter, passing through the *soreg*, crossing the *chel*, one still had to physically ascend twelve steps before reaching the *Azara* itself. There is something deeply intentional about this: one does not walk directly into the sacred space; one climbs toward it. *Maalin ba-kodesh* — we ascend in holiness — embodied quite literally in the architecture.

The mishnah generalizes: all steps throughout the complex were built to these same half-*amah* proportions — *chutz mi-shel ulam*, except for the steps leading into the *Ulam*, which were built differently, as will be discussed in a subsequent mishnah.

### Gates & Openings

All gates and openings throughout the complex were *gevohim esrim amah ve-rochban eser amot* — twenty *amot* high and ten *amot* wide, approximately thirty feet in height and fifteen feet across. These are imposing dimensions that match the towering impression conveyed in every reconstruction of the *Mikdash*. All openings had doors — *hayu lahem delatot* — with the sole exception of the *Ulam*, which was closed not by doors but by a curtain. This is the curtain through which the *Kohen Gadol* would emerge after the *ketoret* service and before which the assembled *Kohanim* would prostrate themselves.

All the gates likewise had *shkofot* — lintels — with one exception: *Sha'ar Tadi*, the gate through which the *Kohen* would exit after a nocturnal emission. The other gates had simple, straight horizontal lintels. *Sha'ar Tadi* had a different structure: *shtei avanim mutot zo al gav zo* — two stones leaning one against the other, forming an arched or angled top, something closer to the triangular or voussoir-style arch of Greek and Roman construction.

### Golden Gates

*Kol ha-shearim she-hayu sham nishtanu lihyot shel zahav* — all the gates were eventually replaced with gold. This was not their original form but came later, when the resources were available. *Chutz mi-Sha'ar Nikanor* — except for *Sha'ar Nikanor*, which remained in its original brass. The reason given by the primary view: *mipnei she-naasah bahem nes* — because of the miracle associated with those doors, they were left as they were, preserved as a testament to what had occurred.

*Ve-yeish omrim* — but some say the reason was different: *mipnei she-nechushtan mazhiv* — because the copper of those doors shone like gold. According to this view, the decision to leave *Sha'ar Nikanor* unchanged was not commemorative but practical: since the brass already gleamed with a golden appearance, there was no need to replace it. While the general principle is *ein ani bi-mekom ashirut* — one does not accept lesser quality where greater quality is available — if the brass looked identical to gold, no aesthetic principle was compromised.

---

---

# Middot 36

## Southwest Corner

### Face of Altar

The mishnah opens with a discussion of the southwest corner of the *mizbe'ach*. To orient ourselves: the ramp (*kevesh*) approached from the south, and the west side of the *mizbe'ach* faced the *Heichal*. This places the southwest corner at the junction of those two sides — and that corner carries a particular significance, for it is *pnei hamizbe'ach*, the face of the altar. It is simultaneously *lifnei Hashem*, before God, because it faces the *Heichal*. This dual quality — facing the direction of approach from the ramp and facing the *Heichal* — made the southwest corner the focal point for many of the *zrikos* of the blood, since certain acts of *zrikat hadam* require this corner specifically in order to achieve both conditions at once.

It bears repeating what was established at the end of the previous session: the *mizbe'ach* did not have a *yesod* (base) running along most of the east side or most of the south side, but it did have a *yesod* at the northeast and southwest corners. This meant that *zrikat hadam* could not be performed at the southeast corner, since *zrikat hadam* requires *keneged hayesod* — it must be performed above a base. For the standard *zrikos* of non-*chatas* offerings, two *zrikos* were performed, each at a corner and each spreading across two walls, so that four sides of the altar were effectively covered. The only diagonally opposite pair of corners that both had a *yesod* beneath them were the northeast and the southwest — and so those were the corners used.

### Blood Holes

The mishnah now tells us that in this southwest corner there were *shnei nekavim*, two holes, described as *k'min shnei chotamim dakim* — like two thin nostrils. Through these holes the bloods that were placed on the *yesod maaravi* and the *yesod dromi* would flow down.

Some bloods were poured on the western base. These were the bloods brought out of the *Heichal* after *zrikat hadam* had been performed inside — the special cases of the *parim hanisrafim*, such as the bull brought when the *Beis Din* issued an erroneous ruling and the community followed it, and similarly the offerings of *Yom Kippur*. When the *kohen* exited the *Heichal* carrying this blood, the first thing he encountered was the western base, and so the blood was poured there — specifically on the western portion of the southwest corner. Other bloods were poured on the southern base: when descending from the *mizbe'ach* after the normal *zrikat hadam* on the outer altar, the *kohen* found himself opposite the southern face of this corner and poured the blood on the southern portion.

The arrangement of the two holes thus reflected these two distinct flows: one hole oriented more toward the west for the blood brought out of the *Heichal*, and one oriented toward the south for the blood from the regular outer-altar *zrika*. Both holes were aligned along a single line rather than being placed at a diagonal; one was simply positioned somewhat more to the west, and the other somewhat less so. The bloods that passed through these holes descended, mixed together in a channel (*amah*), and from there flowed out to the Kidron Valley to the east.

### Underground Chamber

The mishnah continues: *lemata b'ritzpa b'ota keren makom haya sham amah al amah* — lower down on the floor of that corner there was a space of one *amah* by one *amah*, covered by a *tavla shel shayish*, a marble slab serving as a kind of manhole cover. Unlike the round manhole covers familiar from modern infrastructure — chosen precisely because a round cover cannot fall through a round hole at any angle, whereas a square cover could — this one was square. It had a ring affixed to it, *tabaat hayta kvua ba*, by which it could be lifted, and through it one could descend to the underground caverns: *shebo yordim lashit*.

This connects to a discussion in tractate *Sukkah* about the *shis* — the underground hollow, whether understood as deep underground caverns or as a hollow space within the structure of the *mizbe'ach* itself — into which wine and water would flow when poured at the top of the altar during the libations of *Sukkos*. The access point through this manhole cover in the southwest corner served as the entry by which the caverns could be cleaned out. The mishnah states explicitly: *yordim lashit u'menakin oto* — they would descend and clean it out. In context this refers to congealed blood that had somehow accumulated there on its way through to the *amah*, though the *shis* is more commonly discussed in connection with the congealed wine and water of the *Sukkos* libations.

---

## The Ramp

### Ramp Dimensions

The mishnah tells us that the *kevesh* — the ramp — was to the south of the *mizbe'ach*: *vehakevesh haya lidromo*. Its length was 32 *amot* and its width was 16 *amot*. To place this in context: the base of the *mizbe'ach* was 32 *amot* across, and by the level of the *karnaiot* it had narrowed to 28 *amot*. A ramp of 16 *amot* width thus left 6 *amot* of the altar face visible on each side of the ramp at the top. The full width of the base below allowed 8 *amot* of clearance on each side.

### Ramp Angle

With a length of 32 *amot* and a rise of 10 *amot*, the ramp forms a right triangle with legs of 10 and 32. The angle of incline works out to approximately 17.35 degrees — a very gentle, manageable slope, which makes sense given that *kohanim* ascended and descended it constantly throughout the day carrying offerings, vessels, and burning coals.

### Bird Offering Niche

On the western side of the ramp there was a *revuva* — a carved-out section or niche: *ushrevuva hayeta lo bama'aravo*. This is where *psulei chatat ha'of* were stored — disqualified bird *chatas* offerings. They were placed there and left until they became *pasul* through *linah* (overnight), at which point they would be burned.

It is not immediately clear why *psulei chatat ha'of* specifically would require such a storage niche. One possibility, however, is that the phrase here really refers to the *chatat ha'of al hasafek* — the bird *chatas* brought in cases of doubt. There is a well-known *halacha* that one may not ordinarily bring a *chatas* when uncertain of one's obligation, as this would constitute *chullin ba'azarah*. Nevertheless, a special tradition permits the *chatat ha'of al hasafek*, most notably in cases involving a *yoledet* — a woman who has given birth — where a miscarriage may leave genuine uncertainty as to whether she is obligated. In such cases the bird *chatas* is brought conditionally, and since it cannot be eaten and cannot simply be discarded, it must wait until it is rendered *pasul b'linah* and then burned. If the incidence of such offerings was significant, a dedicated storage niche would have been practically necessary. The ramp was constructed entirely of stone, and this niche was simply a hollowed-out section within it.

---

## Altar Stones

### Biblical Sources

The mishnah now addresses the construction materials of both the ramp and the *mizbe'ach* itself. Stones for both were quarried from Beit Kerem, digging below the *betulah* — the virgin earth, ground that had never previously been dug — so as to bring up *avanim shlemot*, whole, uncarved stones. This requirement derives from two distinct *pesukim*: one states *avanim shlemot tivneh et mizbe'ach Hashem Elokecha* — the altar shall be built of whole stones; the other states *lo tivneh atehen gazit ki charbecha hunafta aleha vatachalaleha* — do not build them of hewn stone, for your sword you have waved over it and thereby desecrated it.

### Quarrying Methods

One might ask: if the stones had never to have iron waved over them, how were they extracted from the earth at all? *Rashi* states that they would dig with wooden axes: *v'chofrin b'kardumot etz*. How effective a wood implement would be against virgin earth is not entirely clear. Another possibility is that the prohibition is specific to *barzel* — iron — as the text explicitly says, and so other metals might have been permissible, or alternatively that the metal tools were wrapped in cloth so that the metal never directly contacted the stone. Perhaps the initial breaking of the earth was done with metal and then wood implements were used once the stone was exposed. These remain genuinely open questions.

### Iron Invalidation

The mishnah makes explicit that the concern is not limited to chipping: *shehabarzel posel b'negi'ah* — iron invalidates even by mere contact, even without chipping. And *hapgima b'chol davar* — a chip caused by anything, not only iron, also invalidates. The mishnah thus articulates two distinct disqualifications: a chip from any cause, and mere contact with iron even if the stone remains perfectly intact.

The reason iron is singled out goes beyond the practical concern of chipping. The mishnah concludes with a striking observation: *shehabarzel nivra l'katzer yamav shel adam* — iron was created to shorten human life, being the material of weapons of war; *v'hamizbe'ach nivra l'haarich yamav shel adam* — and the altar was created to extend human life, through atonement; *eino badin sheyanif ham'katzer al ham'aarich* — it is not fitting that the shortener be waved over that which exists to lengthen. This reasoning accounts not only for the prohibition on chipping but for why even contact alone suffices to invalidate.

It should be noted that this strict rule applies specifically to the *mizbe'ach*. For the other stones of the *Beis Hamikdash*, the prohibition appears to derive from a different *pasuk*, specifically regarding Shlomo's Temple, where no *kli barzel* was heard on *Har Habayis*. Some understand that verse to permit carving the stones outside of *Har Habayis* and then bringing them in — an extension that applies only to those other stones. With respect to the *mizbe'ach* itself, no such leniency is stated, and the absolute requirement of *shleimos* and freedom from iron contact remains in force. This explains why the *mizbe'ach* was apparently constructed not from large carved blocks but essentially from an aggregate of many small stones held together by a kind of plaster or cement — the only way to achieve a precise geometric shape using only whole, uncarved stones.

### Maintenance

If one of the stones of the *mizbe'ach* became chipped, only that stone is invalidated; the rest of the *mizbe'ach* remains valid. The damaged stone is removed and replaced, but there is no disqualification of the whole structure. The mishnah then states that the altar was whitewashed — *u'malbinin otan pa'amayim bashana* — twice a year: once before *Pesach* and once before *Chag* (Sukkos), the two major *regalim* that drew the largest pilgrimages. The *Heichal* — or, according to some *mefarshim*, the entire *Beis Hamikdash* — was whitened once a year, before *erev Pesach*, the time of greatest public attendance.

The *mefarshim* understand "whitening" here to mean replastering, applying a fresh coat of plaster. One might wonder whether repeated coats of plaster applied year after year would gradually expand the dimensions of the *mizbe'ach* beyond its prescribed measurements. The likely answer is that the lime plaster used was extremely thin — essentially a whitewash — and moreover that any replastering would have been preceded by scraping off the old coat, much as one prepares a surface before repainting. Lime is also a disinfectant, which would have been practically valuable given the volume of blood involved.

### Weekly Cleaning

*Rebbi* adds a further practice: *kol erev Shabbos malbinoson b'mappa mipnei hadamim* — every *erev Shabbos* they would clean the stones with a rag on account of the blood. This is not the twice-yearly replastering but a more modest weekly wiping, presumably with water, to remove the blood that had accumulated throughout the week.

The mishnah then notes that the plaster was not applied with an iron applicator — *lo haya sado b'chafis shel barzel* — lest the applicator accidentally touch the stone itself and thereby invalidate it. Even though the plaster ordinarily forms a *chatzitza* between the tool and the stone, one cannot always be sufficiently careful, and there is a risk of direct contact.

---

## Slaughtering Station

### Slaughtering Rings

The *taba'os* — the rings — were to the north of the *mizbe'ach*. The *kodshei kodashim* must be slaughtered in the north of the *azarah*, so the entire apparatus for *shechita* and subsequent processing was set up there. The rings were arranged in either six rows of four each or four rows of six each — in any event a six-by-four arrangement, the only question being which dimension ran along which axis. It was upon these rings that the *shechita* of the *kodshim* was performed.

According to most opinions, the rings were half-rings into which the neck of the animal was placed, with the other half then fixed into the ground — somewhat like a handcuff. According to the *Rambam*, however, the rings were used for the *akeidah* of the animals, holding their legs.

### Slaughterhouse Building

Beyond the area of the rings, further to the north, was the *beis hamitbachayim* — the slaughterhouse building — where the flaying, dismemberment, and disemboweling of the animals took place after *shechita*. The *beis hamitbachayim* had eight short pillars, *chet amudim nannasim*, with cedar frames resting on top of them.

### Iron Hooks

Into these cedar frames were fixed iron hooks — *ankleyot shel barzel hayu kevu'im bahem* — arranged in three rows on each frame. It is suggested that the three rows corresponded to the three types of animals offered: cattle, goats, and sheep, each requiring a different hanging height so that the full body of the animal could be properly suspended and extended for flaying.

### Flaying Tables

On these hooks the animals were suspended upside down — *shebahem tolin umafshitin* — and then flayed. The actual work of flaying was performed on marble tables positioned between the pillars: *al shulchanot shel shayish shebein ha'amudim*. Marble was used precisely because it is cold and non-porous, keeping the meat from spoiling. The arrangement seems to have been that the animal was first set up on the frame, hung at the appropriate height, and then transferred to the marble table for the skilled work of flaying and butchering.

---

## The Laver

### Laver Position

Moving inward from the *mizbe'ach* toward the *Ulam*, the mishnah turns to the *kiyor* — the laver, the large vessel of water in which the *kohanim* would sanctify their hands and feet before performing the *avodah*. The *kiyor* stood between the *Ulam* and the *mizbe'ach*: *hakiyor haya bein ha'ulam lamizbe'ach*. It was not centered in that space but was offset toward the south — *umashuch klapei hadarom* — in the direction of the ramp.

---

## Twelve Steps

### Step Space

The space between the *Ulam* and the back of the *mizbe'ach* measured 22 *amot*. The progression of sacred spaces as one moves from east to west is thus: the *Ezrat Nashim*, then the *Ezrat Yisrael* (11 *amot*), then the *Ezrat Kohanim* (another 11 *amot*), then the *mizbe'ach* with its 32-*amah* base, and then this 22-*amah* space before the steps of the *Ulam*.

### Step Dimensions

In ascending from the *azarah* to the *Ulam*, one climbed twelve steps. According to the *Bartenura*'s reading, the steps were configured as follows. The first step was half an *amah* high and one *amah* deep. Steps two and three were each one *amah* high and one *amah* deep. Then there was a *rovad* — a platform — of three *amot*. This pattern then repeated: one *amah*, one *amah*, *rovad* of three *amot*; again one *amah*, one *amah*, *rovad* of three; and finally another *amah*, *amah* sequence leading to the uppermost *rovad*, which measured four *amot* deep (and according to *Rabbi Yehudah*, five *amot*).
