If the tree has already been cut before, however, there is more room to permit certain actions to prevent loss, which would not be considered actual *avoda* (agricultural labor) in the full sense.

### Virgin Qualifier

Returning to the difficulty: since the *Tosefta* enumerates only three things called *besula*, how does our Mishnah introduce *besulas damim* as a fourth? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the question as follows: the *Tosefta* lists things called *besula* without any qualifying word — *shelo ra'asa*, no modifier necessary. But *besulas damim* — a virgin of blood, one who has never menstruated — requires a qualifier (*shem levai*) to convey its meaning. The *Tosefta*'s three are things that carry the meaning of "virgin" in unmodified form. Something that requires modification to communicate its particular sense of virginity is in a different category and was never included in the *Tosefta*'s list.

### Virgin Negation

Rav Sheshes son of Rav Idi offers an alternative answer. The *Tosefta*'s three types of *besula* share a defining feature: their virginity is negated through an act — through sexual intercourse, through working the earth, through cutting the tree. *Besulas damim*, by contrast, is terminated not by any deliberate action but by a natural process: the woman's body simply begins to menstruate. This is a categorically different kind of virginity, not the sort the *Tosefta* intended to enumerate.

### Virgin Irreversible

Rav Chanina son of Rav Ika offers a third answer: the *Tosefta* lists things whose virgin status, once lost, can never be restored. A woman who has had intercourse cannot become a *besulas adam* again. Earth that has been plowed is no longer virgin earth. A tree that has been cut is no longer a virgin sycamore. But a woman who has had her period might, later in life, enter a state where she no longer bleeds — postmenopause. In some sense, one might say she has returned to a condition resembling her original state. Since *besulas damim* can in this way be approximated again later, it is not of the same type as the three irreversible virginities listed by the *Tosefta*.

### Virgin Valued

Ravina offers a fourth answer: the *Tosefta* lists things that buyers and parties to a transaction *want* and *seek*. People desire to marry a virgin woman. People want to purchase virgin earth. People want to buy a virgin sycamore. *Besulas damim*, however — a woman who has never menstruated — is not something that is particularly sought after. Therefore it was not included in the *Tosefta*'s enumeration of desirable virginities.

### Blood & Fertility

The Gemara challenges this last answer. Is it really true that no one cares whether a woman has yet menstruated? A *baraita* is cited: Rabbi Chiya says, just as yeast (*se'or*) is beneficial for dough, so too abundant menstrual blood is beneficial for a woman. And it is taught in a *baraita* in the name of Rabbi Meir: *kol ishah shedameha merubin baneha merubin* — any woman whose menstrual flow is abundant will have many children. The Gemara's underlying medical assumption is that menstrual blood constitutes the "red matter" contributed by the mother to the formation of the embryo — the father's semen provides the white matter (skin, teeth, and so on), while the mother's blood provides the red matter (blood, organs, and so on). On this model, abundant menstrual blood correlates with greater reproductive capacity. If this is a known fact, one might think that men would very much care whether a woman is a *besulas damim* — a woman who has never bled — since that could correlate with a thinner endometrial lining and therefore with fewer or less healthy children.

### Virgin Definition

The Gemara therefore revises Ravina's formulation. The *Tosefta*'s three types of *besula* are not merely things that people care about, but things that people actively *desire* and *seek*: *midi dekafid vesalyi bizvina* — something that people care about and that buyers actually want to acquire. By contrast, *besulas damim* is not something people want. Men do not seek to marry a woman who has never menstruated; quite the contrary, the fact that a woman has a robust menstrual history is considered desirable. A *besulas damim* is a kind of virgin that is not in demand, and therefore she falls outside the *Tosefta*'s enumeration — which covers only those virginities that are valued and sought after.

---

## Pregnant Woman

### Pregnant Bleeds

The Gemara moves to the second category of women who receive *dayah sha'atah*: a pregnant woman. She is considered *mesuleket damim* — removed from menstruation — and therefore, if she sees blood, she is not retroactively *tamei* for the preceding twenty-four hours.

### Three Months

The Mishnah's formulation is *me'uberet misheyivada ubarah* — a pregnant woman from the time her pregnancy is recognizable. The Gemara asks: how far along must the pregnancy be to be considered *hakarat u'bara* — recognized? Sumkhos says in the name of Rabbi Meir: three months.

### Tamar Proof

The Gemara notes that there is no explicit scriptural *proof* for the three-month threshold, only a *zecher la'davar* — a scriptural hint. The verse describes Tamar's situation: *vayehi k'mishlosh chadashim* — and it was after three months that her pregnancy became apparent and she was brought forward to be punished. This indicates that three months is the standard for a pregnancy to become visible and recognized.

### Seven vs Nine

The Gemara immediately questions why this is called merely a *zecher* (hint) rather than a full *rayah* (proof). The answer: since some women carry to term at nine months and some at seven, the relevant stage of visibility might vary. Perhaps for a woman who will give birth at seven months, the one-third point of her pregnancy — approximately two and a third months — is when the pregnancy becomes apparent. It is therefore not a clean universal proof that three months is the threshold for all women, which is why the Gemara calls it only a hint.

### Miscarriage Case

The Gemara now presents a more complex case. A woman was known to be pregnant and she bled. Because she is pregnant, she is considered *mesuleket damim*, so she receives *dayah sha'atah* — retroactive *tumah* is not applied. Afterward, however, the pregnancy was unsuccessful: she gave birth to a *ruach* (literally "wind" — a non-viable fetus or a false pregnancy) or to something that was *she'eino shel kayama*, not viable. The question is: now that we know the pregnancy was unsuccessful, does that retroactively undermine her status? When she bled weeks earlier, she was presumably already pregnant — but since it never produced a viable birth, perhaps we should now consider that the pregnancy did not carry the relevant *halachic* weight, and she should be retroactively *tamei* for the twenty-four hours preceding that earlier bleeding.

The Gemara poses this question by noting a related *halacha* from a prior discussion: a woman who experienced birth pangs (*kashta*) for two days, bled throughout, and on the third day gave birth to something non-viable — the ruling is *harei zo yoledes b'zav*, she is a *zavah*. The reason is that the birth pangs and the labor can only attribute the bleeding to the birth if the birth was ultimately successful (*leida ma'alya*). If the birth was unsuccessful, the bleeding cannot be attributed to the birthing process, and therefore she becomes a *zavah*. This implies that when a pregnancy ends unsuccessfully, the *halachic* reality of pregnancy is retroactively undermined — which would seem to apply equally to our question.

### Negate Status?

The Gemara frames the tension sharply: if you say that even an unsuccessful birth is still considered a *leida* (birth) in the *halachic* sense — *kol she'samuch l'leida rachmana tahara* — then the bleeding surrounding it should not make her a *zavah*. But the ruling is that it does make her a *zavah*, which demonstrates that when a pregnancy ends unsuccessfully, the *halachic* status of pregnancy is not operative. If so, the same logic should apply to *dayah sha'atah*: retroactively, she should be *tamei* for the twenty-four hours before she bled, since her pregnancy turned out not to be halachically meaningful.

### Rabbinic Leniency

Rav Papi answers: *hanei milei miderabanan*. The twenty-four-hour retroactive *tumah* is only rabbinic in origin, not biblical. Since the entire institution of retroactive *tumah* is rabbinic, the Gemara is reluctant to apply it with full rigor, especially in cases where it would result in a kind of double retroactivity. The Tosafot explains that the reason retroactive *tumah* is treated leniently even among rabbinic rules is that it is a category of *tumah* one cannot actively protect against — a woman bleeds and only afterward discovers that the preceding hours are now implicated. Since there was no opportunity for prevention, the Rabbis are more inclined to find leniencies. In our case, once the pregnancy turns out to have been unsuccessful, to then go back further and declare her retroactively *tamei* for the period before the bleeding would be a double retroactive application — and that the Rabbis would not do.

### Pregnancy Reality

Rav Papa offers a sharper answer that dissolves the comparison entirely. The reason a pregnant woman does not bleed — and therefore is considered *mesuleket damim* — is not a formal *halachic* designation that depends on the outcome of the pregnancy. Rather, it reflects a physiological reality: *rosha kaved aleiha ve-eivarim kvedim aleiha* — her head feels heavy, her body feels heavy. The Gemara observed that pregnant women do not menstruate and attributed this to the specific physical symptoms they experience: a heaviness of head and limbs. That physiological reality does not change based on whether the pregnancy will ultimately succeed. The woman's body, while pregnant, is in that state — and that is what causes the absence of menstruation.

The question of whether the bleeding before childbirth makes a woman a *zavah*, by contrast, is a separate *halachic* determination: can the blood be *attributed* to the child? That attribution depends on whether there was actually a viable child. These are two different questions. One asks about the physiological cause of the absence of menstruation during pregnancy (which does not depend on the outcome), and the other asks about the legal attribution of bleeding to a specific birth event (which does depend on outcome). Rav Papa's conclusion: *hacha nami rosha ve-eivarim kvedim aleiha* — even when the pregnancy ends unsuccessfully, the physical reality that governed her body during pregnancy was real and genuine, and her status as *mesuleket damim* while pregnant is therefore unaffected.

### Early Pregnancy

Having resolved the question of unsuccessful pregnancies, the Gemara turns to a different and highly practical question. Rav Yirmiyah asked Rav Zeira: what is the status of a woman who bled and then, shortly thereafter, her pregnancy became visible — meaning she was clearly pregnant when she bled, but the pregnancy had not yet reached the three-month threshold of *hakarat u'bara*? Is she considered *mesuleket damim* even during the early months of pregnancy, before the three-month mark? Or is her *dayah sha'atah* status only operative once the pregnancy is recognizable?

The question has two dimensions. On one hand, she was objectively pregnant — the biological reality of pregnancy was present. On the other hand, the Gemara explicitly ties the status of *mesuleket damim* to a recognizable pregnancy (*misheyivada ubarah*), and the Tosafot emphasizes that the Gemara's question assumes the relevant threshold is indeed near that three-month point. The two possibilities the Gemara raises: perhaps since at the moment she bled the pregnancy was not yet visible, she is *tamei* retroactively (*mitamya*); or perhaps since the pregnancy became visible very shortly thereafter, it is obvious she was already in that state and she is not *tamei* retroactively (*lo mitamya*).

### Three-Month Threshold

Rav Zeira answers the question by referring back to the physiological reasoning already established. The reason a pregnant woman is *mesuleket damim* is *ella mishum deroshya kavid alei ve-eivarya kveidin alei* — because her head feels heavy and her body feels heavy. Before the three-month point, that physiological reality has not yet set in. Women do not generally begin experiencing the characteristic heaviness and physical symptoms of pregnancy until they are further along. Therefore, a woman who bleeds in the first trimester, before her pregnancy has reached the stage where these symptoms appear, is not yet considered *mesuleket damim* — the underlying condition that causes the exemption does not yet exist, even though she is technically pregnant.

### Modern Tests

This ruling has direct implications today. Pregnancy tests can now confirm pregnancy well before the three-month mark. The question arises: does a woman who tests positive and knows she is pregnant immediately acquire the status of *mesuleket damim*, or must she wait until three months? The Gemara's answer, as stated, is explicitly tied to the physiological state of feeling heavy — not merely to the knowledge of being pregnant. Modern medicine understands that the underlying hormonal changes of pregnancy begin immediately at conception, which is precisely what suppresses menstruation — not the feeling of heaviness as such. This raises a genuine *halacha* and science question: should we rule that *mesuleket damim* status begins from the moment a pregnancy is confirmed by test, since we now understand the true mechanism? There is discussion among the *poskim* on this point. Rav Moshe reportedly has a *teshuva* addressing the use of pregnancy tests to establish this status without waiting for three months. It is worth noting that accepting such a ruling would constitute a significant *chiddush*, because the Gemara explicitly grounds the *halacha* in a physiological description — *rosha kaved, eivarim kvedim* — and to rule on the basis of our scientific understanding rather than the Gemara's description is a substantive step in the application of science to *halacha*.

---

## Period Schedule Pregnancy

### Expected Day

The Gemara now introduces a related question from an elder (*saba*) who posed it to Rabbi Yochanan: *higgia vesat bimei iburah* — the time a pregnant woman would normally expect her period has arrived. Must she be concerned? In the laws of *niddah* as they apply today, the day a woman expects her *vesset* (established menstrual cycle) is a day on which the couple must separate, since having relations at the moment the period begins would mean she becomes a *niddah* mid-intercourse. The question is whether pregnancy exempts a woman from this concern — whether the fact that she is pregnant and is *mesuleket damim* overrides the obligation to be concerned about her *vesset* arriving.

To frame the question properly: imagine a woman whose *vesset* is calendar-based rather than interval-based — for example, she always sees on *Rosh Chodesh*. If she becomes pregnant, there will come a *Rosh Chodesh* during the pregnancy when she would normally expect her period. Must she and her husband separate that day? This scenario requires some ingenuity to construct within the Gemara's parameters, since three full periods without bleeding would ordinarily undermine a *vesset* — but one can imagine a *vesset* that occurs every other month, or some other configuration. In any event, the *halachic* question stands independently of the specific scenario: does pregnancy status override *vesset* concern?

### Vesset Biblical

The question is posed *aliba d'man d'amar vestot d'oraita* — according to the view that the obligation to anticipate one's *vesset* is biblical, not merely rabbinic. On this view, not only must a woman separate on the day she expects her period, but if that day passes and she has not checked herself, she is presumed *tamei* unless she can demonstrate otherwise. The *vesset* is so reliable a predictor, according to this position, that its arrival creates a presumption of *tumah* that must be actively rebutted. Given that background, the question is: does the state of being pregnant constitute sufficient counter-evidence to rebut that presumption without checking — or does the biblical-level force of the *vesset* require an actual *bdikah* (examination) even for a pregnant woman?

### Fear Withhold

Rabbi Yochanan answers by citing a proof from a Mishnah. Rabbi Meir rules: if a woman was hiding in a cave — the assumed scenario being flight from Roman persecution — and her *vesset* time arrived and she did not check herself, she is *tehorah*. She need not assume she became *niddah*. The reason: *shecharadah mesaleket et hadamim* — fear causes the blood to be withheld. Although the Gemara (and apparently Rabbi Meir) believed that extreme fear or stress could suppress menstruation, the key *halachic* inference is this: the reason Rabbi Meir permits her to assume *tehorah* is specifically because of the fear. This implies that absent the fear, a woman in whom the *vesset* time has passed without checking would be presumed *tamei*. The *vesset*, in other words, does carry biblical-level presumptive force.

And yet Rabbi Meir rules that fear is sufficient to override that presumption entirely — she does not even need to check. This is striking: even a biblical-level *vesset* prediction can be completely overridden by a counter-condition (fear) that makes it physiologically implausible that she would bleed. The Gemara concludes that pregnancy functions analogously.

### Pregnancy Vesset

The Gemara pauses to consider how this analogy works. One might wonder: since we know a pregnant woman is not going to bleed — or at least the Gemara presumes this — why is the *vesset* concern relevant at all? The answer seems to be that the Gemara did not understand pregnancy as creating an absolute hormonal certainty of no menstruation. Rather, the Gemara understood pregnancy as introducing a set of physiological conditions — heaviness of head and limbs — that tend to suppress bleeding, much as fear does. On this model, pregnancy is not categorically different from fear; both are conditions that interfere with the menstrual process, and the question is how strongly either can override the *vesset* prediction.

### Pregnancy Override

The Gemara concludes: just as the reality of fear is sufficient to completely override even a *vesset* that carries biblical presumptive force, so too the reality of pregnancy — *dameha mesulakin* — is sufficient to override the *vesset* concern. A pregnant woman does not need to check herself on the day she would have expected her period, and she may assume she is *tehorah* without doing so. The practical contemporary application is clear: a pregnant woman whose *vesset* day arrives is not required to separate from her husband on that day, even according to the stringent view that *vestot* are *d'oraita*.

---

## Nursing Woman

### Twenty-Four Months

The Gemara now addresses the third category of *mesuleket damim*: a nursing woman. As established in the Mishnah, she enjoys *dayah sha'atah* status for as long as she nurses, and this extends through the twenty-four-month standard period of nursing after childbirth. If she sees blood during this time, retroactive *tumah* for the preceding twenty-four hours is not applied.

### Child Death

The *baraita* introduced by the Gemara addresses a tragedy: *menika shemeis b'nah* — a nursing woman whose child dies within the twenty-four months. In such a case, *harei hi kechol hanashim* — she reverts to the status of all other women. She is no longer *mesuleket damim*, and if she subsequently bleeds, she is *tamei* for the preceding twenty-four hours or back to the last time she checked. This is because the status of a nursing woman, as the Gemara understands it, derives from the reality of nursing — and when the nursing ceases, so does the status.

### Reality Nursing

The *baraita* continues: *ulifichach im haysa menikaso v'holeches arba v'chamesh shanim* — and conversely, if she continued nursing for four or five years, she retains *dayah sha'atah* status for that entire extended period. This is the view of Rabbi Meir: the *halacha* follows the reality of nursing, not a fixed time period. If nursing stops early, the status stops. If nursing continues beyond twenty-four months, the status continues.

### Twenty-Four Fixed

Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yossi, and Rabbi Shimon disagree. They hold that the status of *mesuleket damim* for a nursing woman is determined by the passage of twenty-four months from birth — *kol esrim v'arba chodesh* — regardless of whether she is actually nursing. If the child died but she is within twenty-four months of birth, she retains *dayah sha'atah* status. If twenty-four months have passed but she continues to nurse, she loses the status. The time period, not the physiological reality of nursing, is the determining factor.

### Blood to Milk

The Gemara then articulates what it takes to be the underlying dispute. It says *kishetimtza lomar* — "when you want to say," a phrase indicating that this is the Gemara's analysis rather than an explicit statement of the *Tannaim*: Rabbi Meir holds *dam ne'ekar vena'aseh chalav* — the blood that would otherwise become menstrual blood is transformed into milk. On this view, lactation is literally the conversion of menstrual blood into another substance. As long as the body is producing milk, the blood is being diverted into that production and will not manifest as menstrual blood. The moment nursing stops — whether because the child has died or been weaned — the blood is no longer being converted and menstruation can resume. This is why Rabbi Meir holds that the reality of nursing, and only the reality of nursing, determines the status.

### Body Recovery

The other *Tannaim* hold a different medical model: *eivareha mitparkin ve'ein nafsha chozeret aleiha ad esrim v'arba chodesh* — after childbirth, a woman's body feels disjointed and weakened, and it does not return to its normal strength for twenty-four months. On this view, the absence of menstruation after childbirth has nothing to do with nursing per se; it is a consequence of the physical trauma of birth and the body's extended recovery process. This recovery takes twenty-four months regardless of whether the woman nurses. Therefore, the relevant measure is the passage of twenty-four months from birth, not the continuation of nursing.

### Extended Case

The Gemara asks: given each view, why did each side need to specify the extended case (*lefichach*)? According to Rabbi Meir, it is obvious that if nursing continues for four or five years, the status continues — that follows directly from his principle. The Gemara answers: Rabbi Meir stated the *lefichach* in order to respond to Rabbi Yossi's position of twenty-four months, making explicit that he disagrees and that any duration of nursing determines the status. Similarly, one might ask why Rabbi Yossi needed to state that if nursing extends beyond twenty-four months the status ends — surely that follows from his principle. The Gemara answers: one might have thought Rabbi Yossi holds that *either* condition is sufficient — either twenty-four months from birth *or* active nursing — and that both together, or either independently, suffice to grant *dayah sha'atah* status. Therefore Rabbi Yossi had to make explicit that he goes solely by twenty-four months, and that extended nursing beyond that period adds nothing.

### Sources Both

A *baraita* is then cited that confirms this reading of the dispute explicitly: *dam ne'ekar vena'aseh chalav divrei Rabbi Meir* — the blood congeals and turns into milk, the words of Rabbi Meir. *Rabbi Yose omer: eivareha mitparkin ve'ein nafsha chozeret aleiha ad esrim v'arba chodesh* — Rabbi Yossi says her body is disjointed and does not recover for twenty-four months.

### Job Verse

Rabbi Ila'a then asks: what is Rabbi Meir's scriptural source for the idea that blood transforms into milk? He cites the verse from Iyov: *mi yiten tahor mitamei lo echad* — "Who will give something pure from something impure? Is it not the One?" — meaning God. Something *tahor* emerges from something *tamei*. Rabbi Meir interprets this as a reference to milk (*tahor*) emerging from menstrual blood (*tamei*).

### Semen Parallel

The Rabbis interpret the same verse differently. Rabbi Yochanan says: *zu shichvat zera shehi tme'ah v'adam notzar mimena tahor* — this refers to semen, which is itself *tamei*, and yet a human being — who is *tahor* — is formed from it. The verse speaks to the broader phenomenon that the generative substances of human reproduction, both the semen and the menstrual blood, are *tamei*, yet they produce something *tahor*. Rabbi Elazar offers a third interpretation: the verse alludes to the waters of *parah adumah*, which are called *mei niddah* in the Torah. These waters present the classic paradox of *parah adumah*: those who are involved in the purification process — the one who sprinkles and the one who is sprinkled upon — become *tahor*, while those who merely touch or carry the waters become *tamei*. *Tahor* emerges from *tamei*.

The Gemara's analysis of this final interpretation involves a careful parsing of the verses. One verse states that *umazzeh mei haniddah yechabbes begadav* — the one who sprinkles must wash his clothes, indicating he is *tamei*. Another verse addresses the one who *touches* the water. The Gemara concludes that both the one who sprinkles and the one who touches are *tamei*, and indeed the sprinkler (*hamazzeh*) is *tamei* to a greater degree than the one who merely touches (*hanogea*), since the sprinkler's clothes are also *tamei* while the one who touches does not have that stringency. How then does one say that something *tahor* emerges from something *tamei*? The Gemara reinterprets *mazzeh* in the verse not as the active sprinkler but as the one who *carries* the water (*noseh*). And one is not *tamei* for merely carrying the water unless one carries at least the minimum amount required for sprinkling. The Tosafot notes the further question: this works well according to the view that there is a minimum measure (*shi'ur*) for *haza'ah* (sprinkling); according to the view that no minimum measure is required for *haza'ah* to be effective, what can be said? The Gemara answers: even according to that view, the requirement of a minimum measure applies not to the amount that strikes the person being purified, but to the amount in the vessel from which the *hyssop* is dipped — *beinah shi'ur* — which is measured as enough to dip the tops of the hyssop branches and successfully sprinkle. The Mishnah elsewhere specifies this minimum: *kedei sheyitbol roshei givolim veyazah* — enough water to dip the hyssop tips and sprinkle. This paradox — that the very substance that causes *tumah* to those outside the purification process causes *tahara* to those within it — is what Shlomo had in mind when he said *amarti echkama vehia rechoka mimenni*: "I thought I would become wise, and realized it is beyond me." *Parah adumah* is the classic *chok*, the paradigmatic law that defies rational comprehension.

---

## Postmenopausal

### Three Cycles

The fourth and final category of *mesuleket damim* is the *zekeinah* — the postmenopausal woman. She is defined as one who has had three regular cycles pass (*shalosh onot*) without bleeding, and this must occur *samuch leziknata* — at a time proximate to her old age.

### Peers Perceive

The Gemara asks what constitutes *samuch leziknata*. Rav Yehuda defines it: *kol shechaveroteha omrot aleiha zekeinah hi* — any woman whom her peers describe as old, as a *zekeinah*.

### Called Imma

Rabbi Shimon offers a different formulation: *kol shekorein lah imma imma ve'eina bosha* — anyone who is called *imma imma* (mother, or in this context, grandmother) and is not embarrassed by it. Some versions of the text have only a single *imma* rather than the double form.

### Embarrassment

The Gemara records a further refinement from Rav Zeira and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak. One of them says the criterion is *kol she'eina makpedes* — she does not object or protest. The other says *kol she'eina bousha* — she is not embarrassed. What distinguishes these two? The Gemara explains: the case of *bousha ve'eina makpedes* — she is inwardly embarrassed but does not verbally object. On one reading, the psychological experience of embarrassment comes later in this sequence than the willingness to register a formal protest; one might feel inward discomfort before she is ready to openly object. Or alternatively, *makpedes* refers to a verbal protest while *bousha* is a deeper, more personal emotional reaction. In either reading, the case of a woman who feels embarrassed but says nothing is the distinguishing scenario between the two opinions.

Tosafot notes that this formulation seems strange: why would a woman's subjective emotional response determine her *halachic* status? Tosafot therefore explains that the criterion is not truly about the individual woman's psychology, but about what a normal woman of her apparent age would or would not be embarrassed about. The perception by others — and the typical emotional response of women at that stage of life — serves as a social indicator of her apparent age.

The absence of a fixed chronological age threshold is also striking. One might have expected the Gemara to say "a woman of fifty" or "a woman of sixty." The Gemara instead anchors the definition to social perception and appearance. This presumably reflects an understanding that the onset of menopause varies significantly among individuals and does not correspond to a single age.

### Estrogen Link

Interestingly, there is a scientific correlation underlying the Gemara's formulation. The question one might ask is: why should the appearance of old age correlate with the cessation of menstruation? The answer is that the depletion of estrogen causes both phenomena simultaneously. It is estrogen that maintains both the menstrual cycle and many of the physical qualities associated with a youthful appearance. As estrogen levels decline, both menopause and the visible signs of aging progress together. The causation runs from estrogen depletion to both consequences — not from one to the other — but the *correlation* between the two is real and well-grounded in physiology. The Gemara, in other words, was entirely correct not to set a fixed chronological age, and instead to point to the appearance of aging as the relevant indicator — since that appearance is driven by the same underlying biological process that causes menopause.

### Cycle Length

How long is three *onot* (cycles)? Resh Lakish says in the name of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia: *ona beinonit shloshim yom* — the average cycle is thirty days. Therefore three cycles constitute ninety days. Rava says in the name of Rav Chisda: twenty days. The Gemara explains that these opinions do not actually dispute one another. One authority is counting the full cycle including the seven days of *tumah* (during which she is a *niddah*) plus the following twenty-three days until the next bleeding — totaling thirty. The other is counting only the twenty-three days of *tahara*, excluding the seven days of *tumah*. Some textual versions have twenty-three rather than twenty, which would correspond exactly to this calculation. In any case, everyone agrees that the standard menstrual cycle in the Gemara's reckoning is thirty days — and therefore a *zekeinah* who has gone three cycles, ninety days, without bleeding, and who appears old enough that her peers would call her a *zekeinah* or call her *imma*, is considered postmenopausal and *mesuleket damim* going forward.

---

---

# Niddah 10

## Elderly Woman & 90 Days

### Mesulakat Damim

The daf begins with a *baraita* — *tanu rabbanan* — that takes up the theme of *mesulakat damim*, the woman who does not ordinarily expect to receive her period. As we have seen in the preceding pages, such a woman, when she discovers she has bled, is not obligated to extend her concern retroactively. The legal category of *mesulakat damim* now comes to bear on a specific case: an elderly woman who is in the process of transitioning to a post-menopausal state.

### First 90 Days

The *baraita* opens: *zekeina she-averu aleha shelosha onot vera'ata* — an elderly woman (a category whose parameters were defined earlier) over whom three *onot* have passed, meaning ninety days have elapsed without any menstrual bleeding. This woman is now classified as *mesulakat damim*. Accordingly, when she does bleed, the rule is *dayah sha'atah*: she is concerned only from the moment of seeing, not retroactively for the preceding twenty-four hours.

### Second 90 Days & Rebleed

The *baraita* continues: *ve'od averu aleha shelosha onot vera'ata* — another ninety days pass and she bleeds again. One might have expected that this second bleeding, coming after the initial ninety-day gap, would constitute counter-evidence against her status as *mesulakat damim* — essentially proving that she is still capable of menstruating. And indeed, had she bled again within thirty days, that subsequent bleeding would have retroactively undermined her *mesulakat damim* status and subjected her to the twenty-four-hour retroactive window. But the crucial point here is that she did not bleed within thirty days. She waited another ninety days before bleeding again. That second ninety-day gap re-establishes her *mesulakat damim* status. Her renewed bleeding is therefore again governed by *dayah sha'atah*. The same dynamic occurs a third time: yet another ninety days passes without bleeding, she bleeds again, and again the rule of *dayah sha'atah* applies.

### Three 90-Day Pattern

Now the *baraita* introduces a twist. After a fourth ninety-day gap — *ve'od averu aleha shelosha onot* — one might expect the familiar conclusion: the gap has again restored her *mesulakat damim* status, so *dayah sha'atah* governs once more. But that is not the ruling. *Harei hi ke-chol ha-nashim* — she is now treated like all other women — *umetamei me-et le-et umipekida li-fekida*: she is concerned retroactively twenty-four hours or since her last bodily examination, whichever is the shorter interval.

Why? Because three cycles of ninety-day gaps followed by bleeding now constitute a recognized pattern. Her bleeding every ninety days — whether exact or approximate — establishes that she is not truly *mesulakat damim*. She is simply a woman with a very long cycle. The ninety-day intervals are no longer evidence of post-menopausal cessation; they have become her *veset*, her regular pattern.

### Exact vs. Inexact

The *baraita* adds: *velo she-kivna ela afilu pichsa ve-hotira* — and not only when the intervals were exactly ninety days, but even when they were inexact, say ninety, ninety-two, ninety-four days. The *gemara* pauses over the phrasing. The *baraita* appears to say that it goes without saying (*lo mibaya*) that when she is exact the concern applies, and that the novelty (*chidush*) lies in the inexact case. But the *gemara* challenges this framing sharply.

### Gemara Analysis

*Adarabba* — the *gemara* says the opposite ought to be true. When the woman's intervals are exact — ninety days, ninety days, ninety days — she has established a *veset kavua*, a fixed cycle. And as our opening *mishnah* taught, a woman with a *veset kavua* is *dayah sha'atah* — she is not concerned retroactively, because she bleeds predictably when her cycle arrives. So an exact pattern would seem to *reduce* her retroactive concern, not establish it. It is the inexact pattern that is the genuine *chidush*, where one might have argued that without a fixed cycle the ninety-day gaps still qualify as *mesulakat damim* status. Accordingly, the *gemara* concludes *tani* — emend the text: read it as *lo shepichsa ve-hotira ela afilu kivna*, not only when she is inexact is she concerned retroactively, but even when she is exact.

This preserves the underlying *halacha* — both exact and inexact patterns generate a retroactive twenty-four-hour concern — while correcting the *baraita*'s formulation to reflect the proper direction of the argument.

The *gemara* then offers an alternative resolution: *ve-iba'it eima hachi ka'amar* — perhaps the *baraita* can be read as stated without emendation. On this reading, the case of exact intervals is excluded from the twenty-four-hour concern precisely because it constitutes a proper *veset kavua*, and the *baraita* is authored according to Rabbi Dosa's position that a woman with a fixed cycle is *dayah sha'atah*. The only case generating a retroactive concern is the inexact one, and this reading attributes the *baraita* to Rabbi Dosa.

The underlying *halacha* bears emphasis: a woman who passes through three cycles of ninety-day gaps punctuated by bleeding has established a pattern. Whether those intervals are exact or approximate, the three repetitions are sufficient to transform what had appeared to be post-menopausal cessation into a recognized, if unusually long, menstrual cycle. There is a genuine *chidush* even in the inexact case, because one might have argued that without a fixed pattern the ninety-day gaps should perpetually restore her *mesulakat damim* status — and the *gemara* rejects that reading.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer 90-Day

### Rabbi Eliezer Ruling

The *gemara* now turns to Rabbi Eliezer's position: *kol isha she-avra aleha shelosha onot* — any woman who has gone ninety days without bleeding is classified as *mesulakat damim*, regardless of age or life stage. Rabbi Eliezer's view is not limited to post-menopausal women; it extends to any woman for any reason. The biological reality acknowledged here is that women may cease menstruating due to causes other than menopause — including, as will become immediately apparent, malnutrition.

### Heitalu Story

To support his position, Rabbi Eliezer cites a precedent: *ma'ase be-riva achas be-Heitalu* — there was an incident involving a young woman in a place called *Heitalu*, who went ninety days without bleeding. When she subsequently bled, the case came before the sages, and they ruled *dayah sha'atah* — she was not concerned retroactively, because her ninety-day gap had conferred upon her the status of *mesulakat damim*, even though she was young.

### Rabbis' Response

The sages' counter-response is direct: *ein sha'at ha-dechak re'ayah* — an emergency ruling is not a proof for general law. The ruling in the *Heitalu* case was issued under extenuating circumstances and cannot be generalized into standard *halacha*.

### Famine & Loss

What were those extenuating circumstances? The *gemara* offers two explanations. The first: *shenei vatzoret havu* — it was a time of famine. Ruling that this woman was *tamei* retroactively for twenty-four hours would have required invalidating *terumah* handled during that period, and during a famine one is exceedingly reluctant to destroy food. It is also worth noting, though the *gemara* itself does not make this connection explicitly, that famine-induced malnutrition is itself a well-known cause of menstrual cessation — which would explain how a young woman came to go ninety days without bleeding in the first place.

The second explanation is more local and arguably more striking: *tahara apisha la-vidah* — in this particular woman's case, she had handled an unusually large quantity of *terumah* in the preceding twenty-four hours. The retroactive *tumah* would therefore have entailed an exceptional loss specific to this individual. This second explanation makes clear that the *sha'at ha-dechak* need not be a national emergency — even a case of extraordinary individual financial loss can qualify.

If anything, the second explanation sharpens the debate: whatever prompted this young woman's ninety-day gap, whether illness, famine, or something else entirely, the rabbis' leniency was grounded entirely in the magnitude of the potential loss of *taharot*, not in any independent assessment of whether her *mesulakat damim* status was genuine. The general principle thus stands: absent a *sha'at ha-dechak*, a young woman who has gone ninety days without bleeding is not thereby classified as *mesulakat damim* according to the majority of the sages.

---

## Rabbi's Reversal

### Rabbi Reconsiders

The *gemara* now records a remarkable episode: *ma'aseh ve-asah Rebbi ke-Rabbi Eliezer* — Rabbi once issued a ruling in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer's position, treating a woman as *mesulakat damim* after ninety days regardless of her age. *Le-achar she-nizkar* — afterward, once he recalled his error, he acknowledged that he should not have ruled that way.

### Formal vs. Practical

Yet even upon recognizing the error, Rabbi did not retract the ruling entirely. Instead, he articulated a principle: *kedai Rabbi Eliezer lismoch alav be-sha'at ha-dechak* — Rabbi Eliezer's opinion is reliable enough to be leaned upon in a case of urgent need. The ruling already given would stand on that basis.

What exactly had Rabbi recalled? *Le-achar she-nizkar de-lav yachid palig alei ela rabim palig alei* — he remembered that it was not a single dissenting opinion that stood against Rabbi Eliezer, but a majority of the sages. There had been no explicit formal ruling that *halacha* does not follow Rabbi Eliezer — *de-lo itmar hilcheta lo ke-mar ve-lo ke-mar* — but the ordinary calculus of *pesak* would have led inescapably to that conclusion. Rabbi had acted on Rabbi Eliezer's position without weighing that calculus carefully enough.

### She'at Ha-Dechak

This episode illuminates a broader principle of fundamental importance. A minority opinion — *da'at yachid* — that has not been formally and explicitly rejected retains a latent viability. In a case of *sha'at ha-dechak*, extenuating circumstances, it may be relied upon even against the weight of the majority. The critical variable is precisely the distinction between an opinion that has been formally overruled and one that has simply been passed over in practice. Rabbi Eliezer's position was squarely in the latter category.

This generates an ongoing and consequential tension in *pesak halacha*: at what point does an opinion become so definitively rejected — whether by explicit ruling or by sufficiently overwhelming consensus — that it may no longer serve as a *sha'at ha-dechak* fallback? The same question arises in later *halachic* literature with respect to the *Shulchan Aruch* and the *Rema*. When the *Shulchan Aruch* quotes a position under *yesh omrim* and then rules against it, does that position remain a viable *da'at yachid* for emergencies? The *gemara*'s treatment of Rabbi Eliezer's ruling here is a foundational moment in thinking through that question.

### Tosafot Explanation

*Tosafot* raises an obvious difficulty: if the larger *sha'at ha-dechak* of a famine was itself sufficient for even the majority sages to be lenient (as the *Heitalu* story implies), then what exactly was Rabbi's error? Why should a case of comparable emergency require reliance on Rabbi Eliezer at all?

*Tosafot*'s answer is striking. The *sha'at ha-dechak* in Rabbi's case was not the recipient's distress but Rabbi's own inconvenience. He had issued the ruling and the person had already left, residing several towns away. Retracting and traveling to reverse himself would have been a considerable burden. That — the practical difficulty of self-correction — was the *sha'at ha-dechak* that Rabbi invoked. This explanation accounts for why a more serious *sha'at ha-dechak* might be handled by the majority sages without recourse to Rabbi Eliezer at all, while a comparatively minor personal inconvenience could still invoke the *da'at yachid* principle. The threshold for *sha'at ha-dechak* is contextual, not absolute.

---

## Young Girl Bleeding

### First Two Sightings

The *gemara* now turns to the opposite end of the life cycle: *tinoket shelo higia zemanah lirot* — a young girl who has not yet reached the age of puberty, who nonetheless bleeds. The rule for such a girl is articulated in stages.

The first time she bleeds: *dayah sha'atah* — no retroactive concern. It is treated as a total fluke. Even after puberty, the first bleeding of a woman who has been *mesulakat damim* is *dayah sha'atah*, and all the more so for a girl who by physiological expectation should not yet be bleeding at all.

The second time: still *dayah sha'atah*. Even having bled once, a girl of ten years old who bleeds a second time has not yet established that she is menstruating. Normally, a woman who has bled once is presumed to have left her *mesulakat damim* status and is subject to greater concern thereafter. But because this girl is below the age of puberty, even the second occurrence is treated as an isolated incident.

### Third Sighting

The third time: *harei hi ke-chol ha-nashim* — she is now treated like all other women — *metamei me-et le-et umipekida li-fekida*. She is concerned retroactively twenty-four hours or since her last examination. Three occurrences, even in a pre-pubescent girl, establish that this is not a fluke. She is bleeding, however anomalously early, and *halacha* responds accordingly.

The structure here reflects a debate elsewhere in the *gemara* between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel over how many repetitions constitute a *chazakah*. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires three; Rabbi holds that two suffice to establish a pattern. The *gemara* will later note that the assumption underlying this *baraita* — that the third bleeding generates a twenty-four-hour retroactive concern — implies that the *pattern* was established already by the second bleeding, and it is that established pattern which causes the third bleeding to be treated as regular. This is consistent with Rabbi's view that two repetitions create a *chazakah*.

### Pattern Recovery

Now the *baraita* continues: *avru aleha shalosh onot* — ninety days pass after those three bleedings without any further bleeding. The same principle we saw with the elderly woman applies here. This ten-year-old girl, having gone ninety days without bleeding — and here the *gemara* will later note this operates according to Rabbi Eliezer's position that ninety days re-establishes *mesulakat damim* status for any woman — is again considered *mesulakat damim*. When she then bleeds, *dayah sha'atah* applies. It is as if there has been a reboot.

Another ninety days elapse: again *mesulakat damim*, again *dayah sha'atah* upon bleeding. Another ninety days — and now, as with the elderly woman, three repetitions of ninety-day gaps followed by bleeding establish a pattern. She is no longer *mesulakat damim*; she is a woman with very long cycles, and the retroactive twenty-four-hour concern resumes: *harei hi ke-chol ha-nashim umetamei me-et le-et umipekida li-fekida*.

The parallel to the post-menopausal woman is exact: three ninety-day gaps prove a pattern, not cessation.

---

## Reboot Status Debate

### Reboot Question

Having established that a ninety-day gap produces a *dayah sha'atah* reboot, the *gemara* now poses a more delicate question. The scenario involves the same young girl who bled three times and is now subject to twenty-four-hour retroactive concern. A ninety-day gap then occurs, resetting her to *mesulakat damim*. Now she bleeds again. We have established that this bleeding is *dayah sha'atah*. But what is her precise status going forward?

Here is the crux of the problem. Before the ninety-day gap, this girl had bled three times and was treated *ke-chol ha-nashim* — like an ordinary menstruating woman. The question is: after the reboot, has her status reverted entirely to that of a pre-pubescent girl (i.e., one who has never yet established that she bleeds), or does she retain some residual status as someone who has already demonstrated that she bleeds?

The practical stakes are significant. A girl who is treated as pre-pubescent requires three bleedings before she is subject to the twenty-four-hour retroactive concern. A girl at the age of puberty — ready to bleed — is subject to that concern already by the second bleeding. After the ninety-day reboot, if the first bleeding is *dayah sha'atah*, what happens when she bleeds again at thirty days? Is that second bleeding already a cause for twenty-four-hour retroactive concern, as it would be for a girl at the age of puberty? Or does she require a third bleeding, as a pre-pubescent girl would?

### Complete Reboot

*Amar Rav Gidel amar Rav*: the reboot is complete. *Pa'am rishonah u-sheniyah dayah sha'atah, shelishit metamei me-et le-et umipekida li-fekida* — after the ninety-day gap, the first and second bleedings are both *dayah sha'atah*; only the third bleeding triggers the twenty-four-hour retroactive concern. In other words, the girl has returned entirely to pre-pubescent status, as if the earlier pattern never existed. Just as she originally required three bleedings to establish regularity, so too after the reboot she requires three.

The logic, as Rav articulates it, is that the ninety-day gap is not merely a temporary interruption. It constitutes genuine counter-evidence that neutralizes the earlier pattern. The earlier three bleedings proved she was bleeding; the ninety-day gap proved she had stopped. The two pieces of evidence balance each other out, and in the resulting equilibrium the formal rule reasserts itself: she is treated as a pre-pubescent girl whose bleeding status is undetermined.

One might object — and the *gemara* acknowledges this implicitly — that this seems biologically artificial. In fact, irregular menstrual patterns in early adolescence are entirely normal, and a ninety-day gap after an initial series of bleedings is not particularly surprising physiologically. Whether the *gemara* was unaware of this biological regularity or was applying a formal legal framework that operates independently of biological expectation is a question worth considering. Both possibilities are live.

### Full vs. Partial

The *gemara* now pushes the question further: *ve-od ra'ata gimmel onot u-firsa* — she has now bled twice more after the reboot (with *dayah sha'atah* for both, as Rav Gidel ruled) and now a second ninety-day gap occurs. She bleeds again. Is *this* reboot also complete — such that she once again requires three bleedings before the twenty-four-hour concern — or has the accumulation of evidence (three initial bleedings, then two more after the first reboot) established something more durable?

### Limited Reboot

*Amar Rav Kahana amar Rav Gidel amar Rav*: the second reboot is limited, not complete. *Pa'am rishonah dayah sha'atah, sheniyah metamei me-et le-et umipekida li-fekida* — after the second ninety-day gap, the first bleeding is *dayah sha'atah*, but the second bleeding already triggers the twenty-four-hour retroactive concern.

After this second reboot, the girl is no longer treated as pre-pubescent. She is treated as a girl who is at the age of puberty and expected to bleed — for whom the second bleeding, not the third, marks the onset of the twenty-four-hour concern. The first ninety-day gap could fully neutralize the initial pattern of three bleedings. But once she has bled again after that first reboot — and then bled again after the second ninety-day gap — the cumulative weight of evidence is too strong to permit a full reversion to pre-pubescent status. The reboot is partial: it restores *dayah sha'atah* for the first bleeding, but not the full three-bleeding threshold of the pre-pubescent category.

---

## Pattern Attribution

### Rabbi Two Sightings

With the substantive *halacha* of the reboot established, the *gemara* turns to a question of attribution. The structure of the ruling — specifically the fact that it is the *third* bleeding (in the full-reboot scenario) that triggers the twenty-four-hour retroactive concern, not the third bleeding itself as a first instance — implies that a pattern was already established by the *second* bleeding. The third is treated as the realization of an established pattern. This presupposes that two bleedings suffice to establish a *chazakah*. As noted, this is the position of Rabbi (*Rebbi*), who holds *be-trei zimnei havei chazakah*.

### Attribution Mix

This raises a difficulty. The end of the same *baraita* states that even a girl who has reached the age of puberty and begun bleeding returns to *dayah sha'atah* status after a ninety-day gap. That ruling — that a ninety-day gap makes any woman *mesulakat damim* — is the position of Rabbi Eliezer, as we established earlier. How can a single *baraita* simultaneously reflect the view of Rabbi (two bleedings establish a pattern) and the view of Rabbi Eliezer (ninety-day gap applies universally)?

### Dual Attribution

The *gemara* resolves this with a precise bifurcation: *ela Rabbi Eliezer hi, u-vi-zmanim savar lah ke-Rebbi* — the author of the *baraita* is Rabbi Eliezer, whose position governs the ninety-day reboot; but when it comes to the number of bleedings required to establish a pattern, Rabbi Eliezer agrees with Rabbi that two suffice. The *baraita* thus represents Rabbi Eliezer's comprehensive position, incorporating Rabbi's principle on pattern establishment. No internal contradiction remains.

---

## Stains & Purity

### Stain 1-2

The *gemara* now shifts to the question of *kesamim* — bloodstains — found on a garment or surface, in the context of the pre-pubescent girl. The principles governing *kesamim* differ from those governing actual sightings of blood, because with a stain there is inherent uncertainty: the blood may have come from the woman, or it may have come from any number of external sources. In the environment the *gemara* presupposes — where women lived in proximity to slaughtered animals, unsanitary conditions, and various other sources of blood — a stain on an inner garment layer did not automatically implicate the woman.

For a stain found between the first and second bleeding of a pre-pubescent girl: *tahor* — unconditionally pure. At this stage, her two bleedings have been treated as flukes, and we attribute no regularity to her at all. The stain is simply not assigned to her.

### Stain 2-3 Debate

The question becomes more interesting when the stain is found between the second and third bleeding. Here, a *machlokes* is recorded between Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan.

### Chizkiyah Impure

Chizkiyah: *tamei*. His reasoning is *keivan de-ilu chazya mitamya* — since were she now to bleed a third time, that bleeding would be treated as *tamei* and subject to the twenty-four-hour retroactive concern (because the pattern is already established by two bleedings, following Rabbi's view), so too her stain should now be treated as *tamei*. The potential for regular status is already present, and it casts its shadow onto the stain.

### Rabbi Yochanan Pure

Rabbi Yochanan: *tahor*. His reasoning: *keivan de-lo itchazka be-dam* — since she has not yet actually had her status treated as that of a regular menstruant through actual bleeding, we do not yet apply that status to the stain. The pattern has been established in potential by two bleedings, but it has not yet been actualized. Until actual blood triggers the full *halachic* status of regular menstruation, the stain remains *tahor*.

*Rashi* notes that this is consistent with Rabbi's two-sighting principle: yes, the pattern is established by two bleedings, but it is only *applied* — given practical *halachic* effect — at the third actual sighting. The stain, found between the second and third sighting, has not yet been swept into that applied pattern.

One might ask: is there not a parallel to the case of a *betulah* — a virgin — whose post-wedding hymenal stains are treated as *tahor*? Rabbi Ila raises precisely this comparison. If Chizkiyah treats the pre-pubescent girl's stain as *tamei* between two and three, how is this different from the virgin's stains, which are treated as *tahor* even though she is certainly bleeding?

### Virgin Distinction

Rav Zeira answers: *zu tzirpa metzuyah ve-zu ein tzirpa metzuyah* — for the virgin, there is an available alternative source of blood (the hymenal flow, metaphorically described as *tzirpa*, the sap-flow), to which the stain can be attributed. Her stains can therefore be rendered *tahor* because we assign them to that alternate source. The pre-pubescent girl who has bled twice has no such alternative attribution available. Her stains must therefore be considered as coming from her, rendering them *tamei* — at least in Chizkiyah's view.

### Marketplace Stain

The *gemara* now cites a further ruling: *amar Ulla amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak* — in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak, a pre-pubescent girl who has bled once and twice and whose spit (*roka*) or surface she sat on (*midrasah*) is found in the marketplace (*ba-shuk*) — those items are *tahor*. The principle of *sefeika de-reshut ha-rabim tahor* — doubt in the public domain is resolved as pure — applies, and since we do not know when she sat or spat, or whether at that moment she was *tamei*, we resolve the doubt leniently.

Rabbi Yochanan connects this ruling back to the question of the *kesem* between two and three: just as the *midras* in the marketplace is *tahor* because of the doubt, so too her *kesem* is *tahor* in that interval.

The *gemara* then notes a question about attribution: when Rabbi Yochanan cites this in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak, is this Rabbi Yochanan transmitting his *rebbe*'s view, or is it Rabbi Yochanan's own view that he attributes to his *rebbe*? The practical difference is whether we have two opinions (*Chizkiyah* vs. *Rabbi Yochanan*) or three (*Chizkiyah* vs. *Rabbi Yochanan* himself vs. *Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak*), which affects the vote count in the *machlokes*.

### Rabin's Report

*Ki ata Ravin be-chol nachetei yama* — when Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael together with those who traveled from there to Bavel, they reported that the ruling of *tahor* for the *kesem* between two and three was indeed that of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak as an independent opinion distinct from Rabbi Yochanan's own. This establishes that two authorities — Rabbi Yochanan and his teacher Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak — both hold the stain to be *tahor*, against Chizkiyah's single contrary opinion of *tamei*. With two against one, the *halacha* is that the *kesem* is *tahor*.

---

## Continuous Bleeding

### Continuous Seven Days

*Amar Rav Hilkiya bar Tuvi*: a pre-pubescent girl who bleeds continuously for seven days — *shofas kol shiva* — this counts as only one sighting (*reia achat*), not as multiple sightings. She has not thereby established a pattern of multiple bleedings that would render her regular.

### Continuous Challenge

The *gemara* challenges this on its own terms: *afilu shofas* — you say even if she flows continuously? It would seem obvious that *continuous* bleeding is one event. The non-obvious case would be *interrupted* bleeding. The *gemara* suggests that the ruling should have been stated about the interrupted case rather than the continuous one, since it is the interrupted case where one might have thought multiple sightings were accumulating.

### Interrupted Multiple

*Adarabba* — in fact, the *gemara* says, interrupted bleeding (*poseskes*) — bleeding that stops and resumes — should be considered *multiple* sightings. If a girl bleeds on day one, stops on day two, bleeds again on day three, stops on day four, and bleeds again on day seven, even though this all occurs within a single week, each separate episode of bleeding counts as a distinct *reia*. Three such episodes within a short period would therefore establish her as regular and subject to the twenty-four-hour retroactive concern.

This is admittedly somewhat counterintuitive from a biological standpoint. The stopping and starting is part of a single menstrual event, and it might seem odd that its episodic character makes it count as multiple separate sightings establishing regularity. Yet the *gemara* applies the rule formally: separate visible episodes of bleeding, with gaps between them, are distinct *re'iyot* for these purposes.

### Dripping Definition

*Amar Rav Shimi bar Hiyya* introduces a further distinction: *medalefet eina ke-shofas* — a woman who is merely dripping (*medalefet*), as opposed to flowing, is not treated as one who is flowing continuously (*shofes*). Rather, *eina ela ke-poseskes* — she is treated as one whose bleeding is interrupted.

The implication is that continuous flow that would constitute a single *reia achat* requires actual sustained flow, not a gradual trickle. If the blood is merely dripping — slowly and intermittently, even if without discrete stops — it is functionally equivalent to interrupted bleeding, and each episode of dripping can count toward establishing a pattern of multiple *re'iyot*.

The *gemara* gently notes the implicit absurdity of the alternative: would a girl have to flow *ke-nahar* — like a river — for it to count as a single continuous sighting? That extreme is obviously not the intent. The clarification is that what counts as *shofas* (continuous flow amounting to one sighting) is actual sustained flow, while dripping or gradual seepage falls into the category of interrupted bleeding that counts as multiple sightings.

---

## General Presumptions

### Pre-Pub Presumed Pure

The daf closes with a broad *baraita* establishing general presumptions: *tanu rabbanan chazakah bnot Yisrael ad shelo higiu le-firkam harei hen be-chezkat tahara* — girls of Israel who have not yet reached the age of puberty are presumed to be in a state of *tahara*. No one needs to check them. They are not expected to bleed, and absent specific evidence to the contrary, *tahara* is assumed.

### Post-Pub Risk Status

Once girls reach puberty — *mi-she-higiu le-firkam harei hen be-chezkat tumah* — they enter a presumptive state of concern. This does not mean they are definitively *tamei*, but it means that menstruation is expected and must be accounted for. Other women assist in checking them — *ve-nashim bodkot osan* — because the onset of menstruation, combined with the obligations of *bedikah* before handling *terumah* or before marital relations, meant that a girl newly arrived at puberty required ongoing monitoring.

### No Manual Check

*Rabbi Yehuda omer ein bodkin osa be-yad* — Rabbi Yehuda prohibits manual internal examination, because *mipnei she-ma'avtos osan* — such examination risks causing physical harm. The concern is twofold: the examination could rupture the hymen, or it could scratch the interior and cause bleeding that would then complicate the assessment of her actual menstrual status.

### Oil Method

Instead, Rabbi Yehuda recommends an alternative method: *sachos osan be-shemen* — they rub her with oil, including internally, *umekanchos osan mi-bachutz* — and wipe externally. Through this approach, *ve-hayn nizakot me-alehen* — if she is ready to bleed, evidence of bleeding will become apparent through the process without the risks associated with a direct manual examination.

---

---

# Niddah 10b

## Post-Menopause 90-Days

### 90-Day Reboot Status

The sugya opens with a *tanu rabbanan* concerning an elderly woman — one who has begun to show signs of age and has gone three *onot*, meaning ninety days, without menstruating. Having established that she is *mesuleket damim*, the *halacha* follows that when she does see blood, she applies the principle of *dayah sha'atah*: she need only be concerned from the moment of the sighting, not the preceding twenty-four hours.

### Pattern from 90-Days

The *baraita* does not end there, however. If another ninety days pass and she sees again, the governing rule of *dayah sha'atah* returns. The logic is as follows: when this woman bled the first time, one might have concluded that this constituted counter-evidence against her status as *mesuleket damim* — had she bled again within thirty days, we would have said she was no longer considered *mesuleket damim* and applied the standard twenty-four-hour retroactive concern. But because she waited another ninety days before bleeding again, that gap itself re-establishes her status as *mesuleket damim*. Each successive ninety-day interval, followed by a sighting, again qualifies for *dayah sha'atah*.

### Three 90-Day Cycles

The critical turning point arrives when this cycle repeats a third time. After a third interval of ninety days she sees blood again — but now the *baraita* rules *harei hi ke-chol ha-nashim*, she is treated like all other women. Why? Because she has now established a pattern. Her *onah* is ninety days. She is no longer classified as *mesuleket damim* but rather as a woman with an unusually long cycle. The consequence is that she is once again subject to the full retroactive concern: *metame'ot me-et le-et u-mi-pekidah li-pekidah*, she renders things impure going back twenty-four hours or to the last time she examined herself, whichever is closer.

### Exact vs. Inexact

The *baraita* then adds that this ruling applies not only when her intervals were precisely ninety days, but even when they were inexact — *afilu pichtah ve-hotirah* — whether the gap shortened somewhat or lengthened somewhat. An irregular pattern of, say, ninety, ninety-two, and ninety-four days would still qualify.

### Gemara Analysis

The *Gemara* takes issue with the phrasing of the *baraita*. The *baraita* as stated implies that even an inexact pattern generates concern — which ostensibly treats the exact case as obvious. But the *Gemara* objects: *adarabba*, the reverse is true. If her intervals were exactly ninety days, she would have a *veset kavua*, a fixed cycle. Our *mishnah* earlier established that a woman with a fixed cycle who bleeds at the expected time need not be concerned retroactively — she need only worry from the moment of sighting, *dayah sha'atah*. So when the pattern is exact, there is actually *less* cause for retroactive concern, not more. It would therefore be a greater *chiddush* to say she is subject to retroactive concern when her pattern is *exact*, not when it is inexact.

The *Gemara* resolves this with two approaches. The first is simply to invert the language of the *baraita*: rather than reading it as "not only in the case of exactness but even in the case of inexactness," we should read it as "not only when she is inexact — even when she is exact." That is, even with a precise ninety-day cycle, she is still subject to the twenty-four-hour retroactive concern. This latter position follows the *rabanan* who disagree with Rabbi Dosa, for Rabbi Dosa holds that a woman with a fixed cycle who bleeds as expected is entirely exempt from retroactive concern, while the *rabanan* hold otherwise.

The second approach (*ve-iba'it eima*) reads the *baraita* as actually following Rabbi Dosa: the *baraita* means to say that only in the inexact case is retroactive concern required, while in the exact case — where she has established a *veset* — she enjoys *dayah sha'atah*. Either way, the *Gemara* confirms that the core *halakha* stands: whether exact or inexact, there is some position that requires retroactive concern. The precise framing determines whose opinion the *baraita* represents.

It is worth noting, as a matter of broader analysis, that even the inexact case involves a genuine *chiddush*. One might have argued that a woman who went ninety days, then ninety-three, then ninety-two, should remain *mesuleket damim* — after all, she went ninety days again without bleeding each time, and without a fixed pattern to replace the earlier status, perhaps she simply keeps returning to that state. The *Gemara* does not adopt this reading, but it is worth recognizing that the ruling that even an inexact pattern of long-interval bleeding renders her no longer *mesuleket damim* is not self-evident.

## Rabbi Eliezer 90-Days

### Rabbi Eliezer Rule

The *baraita* continues with the position of Rabbi Eliezer, which extends the ninety-day rule significantly. Whereas the preceding discussion assumed that the ninety-day interval is most naturally applicable to a post-menopausal woman, Rabbi Eliezer holds that any woman who goes ninety days without bleeding — regardless of the reason and regardless of her age — is classified as *mesuleket damim*. This is not limited to cases of menopause. A woman might stop menstruating due to malnutrition, illness, or other causes, and Rabbi Eliezer would apply the same ruling.

### Heitalu Story

A *baraita* records that Rabbi Eliezer brought a proof from an actual incident: there was a young woman in a place called Heitalu who had gone ninety days without bleeding. The case came before the Sages, who ruled *dayah sha'atah* — she need not be concerned retroactively, as her ninety-day gap established her as *mesuleket damim*.

### Emergency Exception

The *chachamim* rejected this proof. Their response was: *ein sha'at ha-dachak re'ayah* — a ruling made under emergency conditions cannot serve as general legal precedent. The Heitalu case was an exceptional circumstance, and the lenient ruling applied there would not become normative *halacha*.

### Sha'at Dachak

The *Gemara* then asks: what was the *sha'at dachak*, the emergency situation? Two answers are given. The first is that it was a time of famine — *shnei batzoret havu*. This explanation has a double resonance: on one hand, during a famine one would be loath to declare large quantities of *terumah* retroactively impure, since food was desperately scarce. On the other hand — though this is not the *Gemara*'s own point — it is notable that malnutrition itself is a recognized cause of amenorrhea, which would explain why this young woman had stopped menstruating.

The second explanation is more local in character: *taharos nefisha lah avida* — in this particular case, the woman had handled an unusually large quantity of *taharos* in the preceding twenty-four hours. Retroactively declaring her impure would have resulted in a disproportionate loss. This explanation is significant because it removes any necessary connection between *sha'at dachak* and a broader societal crisis. Even a situation involving one woman and one particularly large handling of *terumah* could qualify as *sha'at dachak*. Conversely, the *sha'at dachak* is defined by the magnitude of the potential loss, not by the cause of the woman's cessation of bleeding.

This raises a further question: if virtually any unusual circumstance involving significant loss of *taharos* could qualify as a *sha'at dachak*, is there any meaningful disagreement between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* at all? The answer is yes — the disagreement concerns the standard case, where the potential loss is ordinary. The *chachamim* insist that absent a significant special circumstance, the ninety-day rule does not apply to women generally; Rabbi Eliezer would apply it across the board.

The broader *halakhic* discussion of *sha'at dachak* has significant implications. There is a general principle that one may rely on minority opinions — *da'at yachid* — in times of pressing need. But this raises two distinct questions: first, what qualifies as *sha'at dachak*; and second, at what point does a minority opinion become not merely unaccepted but actively *rejected*, such that it cannot be relied upon even in extremis?

### Rebbe Relies R. Eliezer

The *Gemara* records that Rebbe himself once ruled in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer — applying *dayah sha'atah* to a woman who had gone ninety days without bleeding. Subsequently, upon reflection, he declared: *kedai Rabbi Eliezer lismoach alav bi-sha'at ha-dachak* — Rabbi Eliezer's opinion is weighty enough to be relied upon in a time of pressure.

### Rebbe vs. R. Eliezer

The *Gemara* then examines what precisely Rebbe had "remembered" that prompted this formulation. One reading would be that he recalled a formal ruling that the *halacha* does not follow Rabbi Eliezer. But the *Gemara* rejects this: if Rabbi Eliezer's opinion had been formally and explicitly rejected, how could Rebbe rely on it even in a case of *sha'at dachak*? A truly rejected opinion cannot be invoked at all.

The *Gemara* therefore explains differently: what Rebbe recalled was not a formal ruling against Rabbi Eliezer, but rather the fact that it was not merely one authority who disagreed with him — *rabbim palig alei*, the majority disagreed. In the absence of an explicit ruling, the normal conclusion would have been to rule against Rabbi Eliezer based on the preponderance of opposing opinions, but there had been no formal declaration to that effect. Since the opinion had never been formally rejected, merely generally disfavored, it retained the status of a *da'at yachid* upon which one may rely in a *sha'at dachak*.

This passage is important well beyond this immediate context. It illustrates the difference between an opinion that has been formally overruled and one that has simply not prevailed in practice. A formally ruled-against position cannot be resurrected even under pressing circumstances, whereas a minority position that was never explicitly rejected may still serve as a basis for leniency when needed. This same tension arises in later discussions of the *Shulchan Aruch* and its relationship to dissenting *rishonim*: when a *posek* rules against an opinion — particularly with the formula *yesh omrim* followed by rejection — does the opposing view retain viability as a *da'at yachid*? The *Gemara* here provides the conceptual framework for that debate.

*Tosafot* offers one particularly striking explanation of Rebbe's *sha'at dachak* in this case: it was not the questioner's urgency that prompted leniency, but Rebbe's own practical situation. Having already issued the ruling, the person had departed and was living at some distance. Reversing himself would have required traveling there in person. According to *Tosafot*, it was this inconvenience — Rebbe's own reluctance to travel — that constituted the *sha'at dachak* for maintaining the ruling. This explanation is notable precisely because if the original case had involved a more severe *sha'at dachak*, it seems even the *chachamim* themselves would have agreed to leniency, so the question of relying on Rabbi Eliezer would not have arisen in the same way.

## Pre-Pubescent Girl

### Three Sightings

The *baraita* now shifts from the post-menopausal woman to the opposite end of the spectrum: a *tinoket shelo higia zmanah lir'os*, a young girl who has not yet reached the age at which she would ordinarily expect to begin menstruating, and yet she sees blood.

### First Two Sightings

The first time she bleeds, we apply *dayah sha'atah* — no retroactive twenty-four-hour concern. This follows directly from her status as *mesuleket damim*: since she is not expected to menstruate, the bleeding is presumed a fluke, and we do not project backwards. Remarkably, the second time she bleeds, the same rule applies. Ordinarily, a woman who has already bled once is no longer considered *mesuleket damim* — the first sighting is counter-evidence against that status. But this girl is ten years old. Even after one incident of bleeding, she is not yet presumed to be entering a regular cycle. The second sighting is still treated as anomalous.

### Third Sighting Rule

By the third time, however, even a very young girl who has bled three times is treated *ke-chol ha-nashim* — like all other women. Three sightings establish that she is menstruating, however premature, and she is thereafter subject to retroactive concern: *metame'ot me-et le-et u-mi-pekidah li-pekidah*.

It is worth noting that the age of menarche has shifted considerably over the centuries, as has likely been apparent to many students of this material. While in recent generations the average age has declined — likely due in part to nutritional factors and, as some have noted, hormonal exposure in food — it appears that in the era of the *Gemara*, based on what the sources suggest about standards of living, the onset of menstruation was in some periods earlier than the early modern baseline of around seventeen. These biological shifts do not affect the formal *halakhic* categories, but they illuminate why the *Gemara* takes seriously the possibility of a ten-year-old presenting with what appear to be regular cycles.

The *Gemara* will presuppose here a debate between Rebbe and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel regarding how many repetitions establish a *chazakah*. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds the standard position: three times. Rebbe holds that even twice suffices. The *Gemara* assumes this *baraita* follows Rebbe, since by the third sighting the girl is treated as *ke-chol ha-nashim* — implying that two sightings already established a pattern, and therefore by the third one she is subject to the concern. The question of whether the pattern-establishing sighting is the one that triggers retroactive concern, or whether retroactive concern begins only on the subsequent sighting after the pattern is established, is one the *Gemara* will return to.

### 90-Day Reset

The *baraita* continues: if after three sightings this young girl then goes ninety days without bleeding — *avru aleha shloshah onot* — she reverts to the status of *mesuleket damim*, and when she sees again, *dayah sha'atah* applies. Another ninety-day interval produces the same result. But if this pattern of ninety-day gaps followed by a sighting repeats three times, she is again treated *ke-chol ha-nashim* — she has established a pattern of long-interval bleeding, and the full retroactive concern is restored.

This mirrors the structure we saw for the post-menopausal woman: a single ninety-day gap can reboot *mesuleket damim* status; three such reboots in sequence establish a new *veset* and eliminate that status.

## Reboot Question

### Reboot Status

Having established that a ninety-day gap resets this girl to *mesuleket damim* status, the *Gemara* poses a more refined question. Before the ninety-day gap, this girl had established herself — through three sightings — as someone who bleeds. After the reboot, if she bleeds again and then bleeds once more thirty days later, what is her status? Is she treated like a girl who has never yet reached the age of expected menstruation — in which case the first and second sightings are still flukes and *dayah sha'atah* applies to each — or is she treated like a girl who has reached puberty, in which case the second sighting already triggers retroactive concern?

The question has real *halakhic* stakes. If the reboot is complete, she goes back to needing three sightings before retroactive concern applies. If the reboot is incomplete — if the earlier pattern still resonates — then even after the ninety-day gap, the second sighting post-reboot would immediately trigger retroactive concern. The key variable is which category governs her: a *tinoket shelo higia zmanah*, for whom you need three to establish regularity, or a girl *she-higia zmanah*, for whom two suffice.

### Complete Reboot

Rav Giddel said in the name of Rav: *pa'am rishonah u-shniyah dayah sha'atah, shlishit metame'ah me-et le-et u-mi-pekidah li-pekidah*. The reboot is complete.
