The Gemara now returns to evaluate both proposed resolutions — Rav Chisda's and Rav Ashi's — in light of the explicit *beraisa* from Yavneh, which states unambiguously that the period of getting off the bed is the third period, not the second. For Rav Chisda, this is perfectly consistent: his entire approach rests on the claim that the *mishnah*'s reference to getting off the bed describes the third period, and the Yavneh *beraisa* confirms this exactly. *Bishlama l'Rav Chisda* — this works well: the leniency of the *chachamim* who do not treat the husband as a *boel niddah* is because this is the third, purely rabbinic period.

*Ela l'Rav Ashi* — but according to Rav Ashi, who maintained that getting off the bed and reaching under the pillow for a cloth are descriptions of the same second period, the *beraisa* poses a difficulty. If getting off the bed is the second period, why do the *chachamim* apply their leniency at that point? According to Rav Ashi, that should still be a biblical *safek* with full consequences. The Gemara attempts to rescue Rav Ashi by suggesting that the *beraisa* may be describing a case where she was not holding the cloth, so that getting off the bed combined with retrieving the cloth would push into the third period. But the Gemara rejects this: if the distinction hinged on whether she was *biyada* (cloth in hand) or *einah biyada* (not holding the cloth), the *beraisa* should have said so explicitly. Since it does not, Rav Ashi's equation of the two time-references cannot be sustained. The Gemara concludes: *kashya* — Rav Ashi's approach remains difficult in light of the Yavneh *beraisa*.

The practical upshot is clear regardless of which resolution is accepted for the theoretical *sugya*: by the time it takes to get off the bed, one is definitively in the third, purely rabbinic period. The three periods are: checking immediately with cloth already in hand — definite *chatat*; time elapsed to retrieve a cloth and check — biblical *safek*, possible *asham taluy*; from getting off the bed through twenty-four hours — purely rabbinic, subject to the *machlokes* between Rabbi Akiva and the *chachamim*.

A question arises about the husband's precise level of *tumah* in the rabbinic period. To clarify: a woman who is *niddah* is an *av ha-tumah*, as is the husband who had relations with her when she was definitely a *niddah*, as well as whatever she sits upon. Anything she merely touches is a *rishon*. In the purely rabbinic third period, having had relations before the *niddah* status was known, the husband is *tamei* rabbinically — a *rishon de-rabbanan* — for having been in contact with a woman who was at most rabbinically *niddah*. A further point of texture: in the *Torah*, the word *niddah* functions as a verbal noun — *betumat niddatah*, referring to the flow itself — and it is only in the *mishnah* and *gemara* that the woman herself is called a *niddah*. This observation bears on how we speak about these *halachot* with appropriate care.

---

## Stains on Cloth

### Ketem Stringency

The *mishnah* states: *u-modim chachamim l'Rabbi Akiva be-ro'eh ketem* — the *chachamim* agree with Rabbi Akiva in the case of a *ketem*. A *ketem* is a stain discovered on cloth or bedding, as distinct from blood found directly on the body. On one hand, a *ketem* is more lenient in one respect: because there is a possibility the blood originated from an external source — a louse, for example — one first attempts to attribute it to such a source, and if that is possible, she is *tehorah legamrei*. If one cannot attribute it elsewhere, she is *teme'ah* rabbinically, not biblically.

### Retroactive Tumah

Yet in other respects a *ketem* generates greater stringency. When a woman sees blood from her body, the timing can be limited — the blood probably appeared very recently, allowing the retroactive *tumah* to be bounded. When a stain is discovered on cloth, there is no such natural limitation: the stain may have been there for a day, two days, a week. The retroactive extension of *tumah* is therefore potentially longer and more serious.

Rav rules: *l'mafrei'a* — the *chachamim*'s agreement with Rabbi Akiva by a *ketem* means going backward — if they had relations during the period the stain retroactively renders her *teme'ah*, the husband is as *tamei* as she is. This is the view of Rabbi Meir, who is strict with *ketamim*. Shmuel disagrees: *mikan u-le-haba* — the *mishnah* refers only to relations that occur after the stain is discovered. The rabbis, who dispute Rabbi Meir, hold that during the retroactive period covered by the *ketem*, the husband who had relations is not rendered as *tamei* as his wife. Resh Lakish aligns with Rav's reading, attributing the *mishnah* to Rabbi Meir; Rabbi Yochanan aligns with Shmuel, reading the *mishnah* as referring to the *rabbanan* going forward only.

### Prospective Tumah

According to Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan, the *mishnah*'s statement that the *chachamim* agree with Rabbi Akiva regarding a *ketem* means: if relations occur *after* the stain is discovered, the husband is as *tamei* as the wife. The Gemara asks: *pshita* — is this not obvious? If she is definitely at least rabbinically *teme'ah* and he then has relations with her, of course he is equally *tamei*.

### Stricter Prospective

The Gemara answers that this ruling is not self-evident. One might have thought: since the entire twenty-four-hour retroactive framework is rabbinic, and *ketamim* are themselves rabbinic, perhaps we apply the same leniency prospectively that we apply retroactively. We have already seen that in the third, purely rabbinic twenty-four-hour period, the husband who had relations is not treated as an *av ha-tumah* — he is a *rishon*, not an *av*. One might extend this logic: since *ketamim* are also rabbinic, even going forward the husband should not be rendered as *tamei* as the wife. *Ka mashma lan* — the *mishnah* teaches that this is not so.

The Gemara then presses: why not? Both are rabbinic, so why the asymmetry? The Gemara answers with a vivid image: *ein shor shachut lefanecha* — in the twenty-four-hour retroactive period, there is no slaughtered ox standing before you. During those previous hours, there was no knowledge that she was *teme'ah*; the *tumah* is projected backward into a period when the problem was not apparent. This is why the rabbinic leniency applies — because the problematic status was not manifest at the time. *Hacha* — here, with the *ketem* in front of you, *yesh shor shachut lefanecha* — the problem is staring you in the face. When the problem is manifest and visible, we do not apply the same leniencies, even though the underlying *tumah* category is also rabbinic.

---

## No Taharot Status

### All Women Tahor

The Gemara now turns to a *mishnah* of considerable practical importance. *Kol ha-nashim b'chezkat taharah le-ba'aleihen* — all women are presumed *tehorah* for their husbands. This establishes a *chazakah* that when there is no specific knowledge otherwise, a woman is presumed not to be *niddah* for the purpose of marital relations.

### No Checking Needed

This *mishnah* connects directly to a theme discussed in earlier dapim: the question of whether women must perform *bedikot* before and after relations when they are not engaged in the broader world of *taharot*. The conclusion reached was that when not living in a context of *tumah v'taharah* observance generally, women should not — and need not — check before and after relations, as such checking would only generate anxiety without any halachic purpose. This *mishnah* provides one of the key textual bases for that conclusion.

One possible reading of *le-ba'aleihen* — "for their husbands" — is significant: women are *b'chezkat taharah* not in the general *taharot* sense, but specifically for the purpose of marital relations. A woman who is *asuka be-taharot* — actively engaged in *taharot* observance — checks regularly and has different obligations. The *mishnah* may thus be establishing that even a woman engaged in *taharot* observance retains a *chezkat taharah* specifically for the purpose of *hetter le-ba'alah* — permissibility for her husband — distinct from any separate *taharot* obligations she may have. Put differently: the checking requirement and the question of whether relations are permitted are independent. A woman may have obligations to check as part of *taharot* observance, but failure to check before or after relations does not itself render her forbidden to her husband.

---

## Returning Husband

### Journey Return

The *mishnah* adds: *ha-ba min ha-derech* — one who returns from a journey — *ishto meshulemet lo b'chezkat taharah* — his wife is available to him with a presumption of *taharah*. This is a significant *chiddush*. If a husband has been away for an extended period — a month or more — one might expect that he would need to ask whether she had her period during his absence, or that she would need to check before they resumed relations. The *mishnah* rules otherwise: the *chezkat taharah* established before he left continues to apply upon his return without any requirement to verify.

---

## No Taharot Status (II)

### Check vs. Hetter

Returning to the *mishnah* of *kol ha-nashim*, a second interpretive layer emerges. The phrase *le-ba'aleihen* — specifically "for their husbands" — may be read as a deliberate contrast: in the world of *taharot*, a woman is not necessarily in a state of *chezkat taharah* because she is subject to checking obligations and careful scrutiny. But *le-ba'aleihen* — for the specific question of marital permissibility — the *chezkat taharah* remains intact. This may be the *mishnah*'s way of saying that the *taharot* checking requirement and the *hetter* for marital relations operate on separate tracks.

---

## Returning Husband (II)

### Wife Would Inform

The Gemara asks why the case of the returning husband needs to be stated separately: *lama li lemisni ha-ba min ha-derech*? The Gemara answers: *salka da'atach amina* — one might have thought that when the husband is in the city, the reason she is presumed *tehorah* is that she knows he is coming home and checks in anticipation — *ramya anafshah u-vadkah* — and if she found herself to be *niddah*, she would have informed him. On this reading, the *chezkat taharah* is not an independent presumption but rather rests on the inference that she would have acted and spoken. When the husband was away for a long trip — *leisa b'masa* — she was not expecting him at any particular moment, had no reason to check, and therefore might not have reported her status. On this reading, the *chezkat taharah* would not apply to the returning husband.

The *mishnah* therefore teaches that this is not the correct reading. The case of the returning husband establishes that *ka mashma lan* — the reason she is presumed *tehorah* is not that she would have checked and reported. The *chezkat taharah* is an independent presumption, grounded in the fact that there is simply no need to check.

### No Checking Reason

Resh Lakish citing Rabbi Yehuda Nesia qualifies this: *vehu she-ba u-matz'ah be-toch yemei onasah* — the *chazakah* applies when he returns within the period of her cycle, before her next expected period has arrived. This is the operative condition: if he returns before the time of her expected *veset*, she remains *b'chezkat taharah*. If he returns after the *veset* time has passed, she would be *assurah*.

---

## Veset Status

### Rav Huna View

Rav Huna refines this further: *lo shanu ela she-ein lah veset* — the *chazakah* of *taharah* upon the husband's return applies specifically when she does not have a fixed *veset*. *Aval yesh lah veset, assurah* — if she has a regular cycle, then upon returning the husband may not presume she is *tehorah*. The Gemara immediately objects: *ipcha mist'abra* — the opposite reasoning seems more intuitive. A woman without a fixed *veset* might have seen her period at any point; a woman with a fixed cycle has a predictable schedule, and if the husband returns before that scheduled day, surely she remains *tehorah*. The Gemara corrects the formulation: Rav Huna's statement must be read as follows — *lo shanu ela she-lo higi'a sha'at vestah* — the *chazakah* applies only when the expected time of her *veset* has not yet arrived. *Aval higi'a sha'at vestah, assurah* — if the husband returns after her *veset* time has passed, she is *assurah*.

Tosafos notes that this does not contradict the previous point: for a woman without a fixed *veset*, there is no specific day that serves as a trigger — and therefore she is never necessarily *assurah* upon her husband's return in the same way. For a woman with a regular cycle, the passing of her expected day is significant. The corollary is that a pseudo-threshold of thirty days functions even for a woman without a fixed *veset*, since most women will have seen by that point.

### Veset Dispute

The Gemara now introduces the pivotal question: *kasavar vesasot d'Oraita* — Rav Huna apparently holds that the observance of *veset* is of biblical force. This is the reason why, once her expected day has passed, she is definitely *assurah*: if *veset* is biblical, the expectation of the period is weighty enough to change her prior *chezkat taharah* and presume she has now become *niddah*. This generates a substantial debate.

The rationale for treating *veset* as biblical is its character as a *chazakah*: once a woman establishes a regular pattern, the expectation that she will see again on that day carries the weight of a presumption. The counterargument is that women's periods do not always remain fixed — *chazakah d'asuya l'ishtanos* — and it may therefore not be sufficiently reliable to rise to the level of a biblical presumption.

A deeper analytical distinction must be drawn here. There are two separate questions that the concept of *veset d'Oraita* or *veset de-rabbanan* implicates. The first is whether the couple is forbidden to have relations during the time when her period is expected, out of concern that she may become *niddah* at any moment. This prohibition — refraining during the time of *veset* — may be arguable as biblical according to most opinions. The second, more contested question is whether the mere arrival and passing of the expected day, without any actual checking, is sufficient to overturn her prior *chezkat taharah* and render her presumptively *niddah*. If *veset* is *d'Oraita* in this strong sense, the passing of the day definitively changes her status. If *veset* is only *de-rabbanan*, the prior *chezkat taharah* is not overridden, and she remains presumptively *tehorah* unless she actually found herself to be *niddah*.

### Rabba Opinion

Rabba bar bar Chana takes the lenient position: *afilu higi'a sha'at vestah, nami muteres* — even if the husband returns after her expected period has passed, she remains permitted. *Kasavar vesasot de-rabbanan* — he holds that *veset* is of rabbinic force only, and therefore does not override the prior *chezkat taharah*. On this view, in the most extreme formulation, even if a husband returns long after the expected period, the *chezkat taharah* established before his departure remains in place, since we cannot say with certainty that she saw.

### Gemara Challenge

The Gemara challenges this position: *vechi l'olam lo tireh* — does one forever maintain that she never had her period? There must be a point at which the accumulated time demands a reassessment. The Gemara implies this challenge but notes that in the historical context, women spent much of their reproductive years pregnant, which substantially reduced the frequency of menstrual cycles and gave the presumption of *taharah* greater statistical weight. Nonetheless, the logical difficulty of maintaining the *chazakah* indefinitely remains.

---

## Husband Away

### Veset Calculation

Shmuel in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules: *ishah she-yesh lah veset, ba'alah mechashiv yemei vestah u-va'alah* — if a woman has a fixed cycle and her husband is away, the husband can calculate her *veset* days. If sufficient time has elapsed since her expected period — long enough for the period to have concluded (at least seven days), and for her to have immersed in the *mikvah* — he may assume she is *tehorah* upon his return and resume relations.

A tension is noted in passing: the formulation of the husband calculating and acting upon those calculations, without explicit inquiry to his wife, raises questions about agency and communication in these laws. The assumption embedded in *u-va'alah* — "and [has relations with] her" — upon returning is worth marking, even if it is not directly resolved by the Gemara.

### Mikvah Assumption

The more pressing halachic question is whether the husband can assume not only that she had her period, but that she subsequently immersed in the *mikvah*. The *chezkat taharah* applies when there is no definite *tumah*. But if we know — even rabbinically — that she was *niddah* during the period, can we then assume she went to the *mikvah* without certainty?

### Mikvah Challenge

Rav Shmuel bar Yeva raises the question to Rav Abba: would Rabbi Yochanan apply this even in the case of a young girl — *yaldah d'beziza l'mitvhal*? Rashi understands *yaldah* as referring to a young girl who would be embarrassed to go to the *mikvah* independently, and might only do so if her husband was present and prompting her. If he is away, perhaps one cannot assume she went. Tosafos reads the word differently — not *yaldah* (child) but understanding *beziza* as indicating not embarrassment but fear: a woman who recently gave birth and is afraid to immerse in cold water for health reasons. Would Rabbi Yochanan maintain the assumption of immersion even in such a case?

### Safeik Resolution

The response to this challenge is critical: *atu vadai ra'atah mi amar Rabbi Yochanan* — Rabbi Yochanan never claimed that we can assume she immersed when we know definitively that she was *niddah*. *Eima d'amar Rabbi Yochanan: safeik ra'atah, safeik lo ra'atah* — Rabbi Yochanan's ruling applies only in a case where it is itself uncertain whether she had her period at all. This is the crux: Rabbi Yochanan holds *vesasot de-rabbanan*, and therefore even the passing of the expected day does not create a *vadai* that she saw. There is still a *safeik* whether she menstruated. Given that uncertainty, the husband can add a further *safeik* — perhaps she even went to the *mikvah*. Two layers of uncertainty combine: maybe she saw, and even if she did, maybe she immersed. Together, these permit the husband to maintain the *chezkat taharah*.

This resolution is available only because *veset* is treated as *de-rabbanan*. If *veset* were *d'Oraita* and the passing of the expected day created a definite *niddah* status, the husband could not subsequently assume she immersed — for this would be a case of *safeik motzi midei vadai*.

---

## Safeik Motzi Midei

### Principle Stated

This leads directly to the Gemara's discussion of the principle *ein safeik motzi midei vadai* — a doubt cannot overturn a definite status quo. The scenario under discussion is one where an object or person has a definite problematic status, but there exists the capacity — and indeed the normal expectation — that the problem would have been remedied. Can an almost-certain assumption that the remedy was performed override the definite prior status?

### Chavér Example

The Gemara brings a *beraisa*: *chaveir she-meis v'hinniah megurah male'ah peiros* — a *chaveir*, someone scrupulously observant regarding *terumot u-ma'asrot*, dies and leaves a storage area full of grain. The grain was definitely *tevel* — not yet tithed. Did he tithe it before he died? *Afilu hein b'nei yoman* — even if the grain was harvested that very day, *harei hein b'chezkat metukannim* — it is presumed to have been properly tithed. Here we have a definite prior *tumah* (or more precisely, a definite *tevel* status), and a *safeik* whether the remedy was performed, yet the Gemara seems to allow the *safeik* to override the definite prior status.

### Chavér Reliability

The Gemara resolves this apparent contradiction: *hatam vadai vadai hu* — there, it is not truly a *safeik* at all; it is a *vadai*. *De-amar Rabbi Chanina Chuzah: chazakah al chaveir she-einah motzi mi-tachat yado davar she-eino metukan* — it is a presumption, almost an axiom, that a *chaveir* will not allow untithed produce to leave his possession. This *chazakah* is sufficiently reliable that we elevate the "almost certain" to the level of *vadai*. When human behavioral reliability is so high and so established, the presumption is not a mere *safeik* overriding a *vadai*; it is a *vadai* — a different kind of certainty — overriding the prior status.

### Scheming Option

A final resolution is offered: *v'iba'it eima, safeik b'safeik hu* — alternatively, the case of the *chaveir*'s grain is not even a case of definite *tevel* to begin with. *Ke-d'Rabbi Oshia: ma'arim adam al tvu'ato u-machnisah b'motzlah* — a person may bring grain into storage with its chaff still attached, feeding it to his animals and thereby exempting it from *ma'aser* at the biblical level, since the biblical obligation of *ma'aser* attaches only once the grain is fully processed in the field. If the finishing process occurs inside the house, it is exempt from *d'Oraita* *ma'aser*. We do not know that the *chaveir* did not use this legitimate stratagem. Therefore, the prior status is itself only a *safeik* — perhaps the grain was never definitively *tevel* at the biblical level. When both the prior status and the remedy are each uncertain, combining those uncertainties resolves in favor of permissibility.

The Gemara thus arrives at the following framework as the sugya closes: the principle *ein safeik motzi midei vadai* applies when the original problematic status was a genuine *vadai* and the purported remedy is only a *safeik*. Where the original status can be elevated from *safeik* to *vadai* through the reliable conduct of a *chaveir*, or where the original status itself was never a full *vadai*, the principle does not block a lenient ruling. The unresolved question — to be continued — is what the halacha is when the original status is a true *vadai* and the remedy is a highly probable but not certain *safeik*.

---

---

# Niddah 16

## Vestos Status Review

### Vestos Debate Overview

Yesterday's discussion centered on a fundamental and far-reaching debate: are *vestos* — a woman's established, regular menstrual cycle — *de'oraisa* or *de'rabbanan*? That is, does the anticipation of a woman's period carry biblical weight or only rabbinic weight? The immediate practical concern is well known from *Gemara Shavuos* and related contexts: a husband and wife must be *poresh* — they cannot have relations during the days of an expected period. But the more focused question driving our discussion is what her status is *after* that period passes.

The woman entered that window with a *chezkas tahara* — a presumptive status of *tahara*. Now an expectation has arisen that that status will change. Is that expectation strong enough to override her status quo? The *Gemara* frames this as the question of whether *vestos* are *de'oraisa*. The meaning of "biblical" here is that there exists a general biblical principle of *chazaka* — that we follow established patterns and habits. A woman who habitually sees blood every thirtieth day exhibits a clear pattern. The question is whether that habitual pattern is sufficient to say it has changed her status quo without specific knowledge that the anticipated event has actually occurred.

### Three Status Possibilities

There are in fact three possible positions. First: she remains completely *tehora*, going by her status quo until we know otherwise. Second: she is completely *teme'ah* — the time of her expected period passed, and she is assumed to be definitively *teme'ah* unless there is absolute evidence to the contrary. Third, and intermediate: the expectation was enough to say she is no longer definitively *tehora*, but not enough to declare her definitively *teme'ah* — it places her in a state of *safek*.

### Rabbi Yochanan Position

The discussion from yesterday actually concluded with the position of Rabbi Yochanan, which occupies the intermediate ground. Rabbi Yochanan said it depends on whether sufficient time has passed for her to have gone to the *mikvah*. Consider the case: he left on day 20 and returned on day 40 since her last period. The time of her expected period has passed, but also enough time has elapsed for her to have immersed. Rabbi Yochanan said that in such a case one may assume she is *tehora*. The *Gemara's* explanation is that since there is uncertainty both about whether she bled and about whether she subsequently went to the *mikvah*, and since there is a good chance she did immerse, you combine the two probabilities and conclude she is *tehora*.

This shows that according to Rabbi Yochanan, the passing of the period moves her from definitively *tahor* to *safek* — not definitively *tamei*, but *safek*. Since she is not definitively *tamei* and there is a reasonable likelihood she went to the *mikvah*, the combination suffices to presume *tahara*.

### Rishonim on Yochanan

Which of the three positions Rabbi Yochanan is actually occupying is itself a *machlokes Rishonim*. Tosafos says Rabbi Yochanan sides with *vestos de'rabbanan*: if *vestos de'rabbanan*, she is *safek*; if *vestos de'oraisa*, she is *vadai teme'ah*. Accordingly, even under *vestos de'rabbanan*, the assumption that she is *tehora* after the period passes only holds once enough time has elapsed to presume she went to the *mikvah* — the seven-day waiting period serves as a counterweight to her *safek* status.

The Rashba and other *Rishonim* take the opposite position. Under *vestos de'rabbanan*, she is definitively *tehora* — the husband can return the very next day and assume she is completely *tehora*, as the rabbinic force of the *veset* is insufficient to disturb her status quo at all. It is *vestos de'oraisa* that moves her to *safek* — enough to counterbalance the *chazaka* of *tahara* and place her in doubt. The practical map, then, is: under Tosafos's reading, *de'rabbanan* yields *safek* and *de'oraisa* yields *vadai teme'ah*; under the Rashba's reading, *de'rabbanan* yields *vadai tehora* and *de'oraisa* yields *safek*. According to Rabbi Yochanan she is *safek*, and waiting a week allows the husband to assume she has gone to the *mikvah* and resolve that *safek* in the direction of *tahara*.

### Husband-Wife Authority

One might reasonably ask: why does all of this discussion presuppose that the husband makes assumptions about his wife's status without simply asking her? This question is pointed and the *Gemara* reflects a reality that is genuinely troubling. One answer sometimes assumed in the *Gemara* is that he is having relations while she is asleep — the *Rishonim* tone this down to suggest she is in a half-awake state and cannot give a coherent response, which is not much of an improvement. A somewhat more sympathetic framing is that given the power dynamics of the time — and sometimes still today — a wife may feel unable to freely assert herself and say, "we cannot, I am a *niddah*." Pressures within the relationship may create circumstances where a woman does not feel free to speak. Yet the obvious counterresponse is that by framing the halachic discussion around what the husband may assume without asking, the very literature feeds into that dynamic. There is no fully satisfying answer here; the *Gemara* is reflecting a social reality, and recognizing it as troubling is appropriate.

### With/Without Vestos

Two related clarifications are worth noting. First, a woman who has no established *veset* — *ein la veset* — presents no difficulty for anyone; her *chezkas tahara* holds completely. The question of *vestos de'oraisa* or *de'rabbanan* is only relevant where a regular period exists. As will be seen shortly, there is a separate question about a pseudo-*veset* of thirty days for women without a fixed cycle. Second, and relatedly: before the time of the expected period, there is simply no issue at all. We are not *choshesh* for the mere theoretical possibility that she became a *zavah* or some other status, because she has a *chezkas tahara*, and without an established predictive expectation, we do not disturb that status quo.

---

## Safek Overriding Vadai

### Principle Stated

The *Gemara* now turns to the second part of the discussion: if she was definitively *teme'ah*, one could not assume she went to the *mikvah*. It is only because she is *safek* — whether under the *de'oraisa* or *de'rabbanan* reading — that you can factor in the likelihood she immersed and thereby presume *tahara*. This leads to the underlying principle: *ein safek motzi midei vadai* — doubt cannot displace certainty. The principle is clear enough on its face. But the relevant case here is not just any *safek*: there is a very good chance, a near-expectation, that his wife went to the *mikvah*; he simply does not know for certain. Can such a *safek* — a highly probable one — be *motzi midei vadai* when a prior status of *vadai* existed?

### Masik's Servant Case

The *Gemara* challenges the principle by citing a *baraisa*: there was a story involving the servant of a *Masik* — either an olive presser or a strong, violent man, depending on interpretation — in a place called Rimmon. This servant had a miscarriage and cast the fetus into a pit. A *kohen* went and leaned over the pit to look in, in order to determine whether it was male or female — which would determine whether the maidservant's period of *tumah* was seven or fourteen days. The problem, of course, is that a *kohen* may not contract *tum'as meit*. The *Gemara* offers several suggestions for how this occurred: perhaps the man was violent and compelled the *kohen*; perhaps the *kohen* was a minor, though that is not entirely satisfying since adults are commanded to prevent minors from becoming *tamei*. Rashi's preferred explanation is that the *kohen* was simply an *am ha'aretz* who did not know or care about the *halacha*. In any event, the case came before the *Chachamim*, and they declared the *kohen* to be *tahor* — he apparently saw nothing — because weasels and moles (burrowing, scurrying animals) are commonly found there, and one may assume that they dragged the fetus away.

Now the *Gemara* raises the problem: the fetus was definitely there — *vadai hetilah nefel l'vor*. Whether it was dragged away is a *safek* — perhaps yes, perhaps no. There is some supporting evidence in that the *kohen* saw nothing, but it is still not a *vadai*. Yet this *safek* appears to be *motzi midei vadai*, displacing the *kohen's* definite prior status of having been in proximity to a *meis*.

### Fetus Status Unclear

The *Gemara* responds with its first resolution: do not read the case as one where it was definite that a fetus — a *nefel* — was cast into the pit. Read it rather as *k'mi nefel* — something that may have been a fetus. Depending on the nature of the miscarriage, it may not have had the halachic status of a *meis* at all; it may have been mere discharge. So the problem was never a *vadai* to begin with.

But the *Gemara* objects: the *baraisa* says the *kohen* wanted to determine whether it was male or female — which presupposes it was definitely a fetus. The *Gemara* therefore re-reads the passage: the *kohen* first wished to establish whether it was a real fetus in the embryonic sac at all or not, and only secondarily, *if it was indeed a fetus*, to determine male or female. So it was never a *vadai* problem from the outset.

### Weasels Certainty

The *Gemara* offers a second approach: *ve-iba'is eima* — if you wish, you may say instead that since the weasel and mole are definitely found there, *vadai geraru* — we can be so certain they dragged it away that we treat the likelihood as a *vadai*, especially in combination with the supporting evidence that the *kohen* saw nothing at all.

### High Likelihood Standard

The upshot of the discussion is this: *ein safek motzi midei vadai* holds — unless the likelihood is so overwhelmingly high that we are prepared to treat it functionally as a *vadai*. So the ways in which a *safek* can override an original *vadai* are either: (a) the original situation was not truly a *vadai* to begin with, or (b) the probability of change is so high that it effectively functions as a certainty, and we are prepared to treat it as such.

### Two Types Chazaka

It is worth pausing here to note an important conceptual distinction that this discussion illuminates. The word *chazaka* is used in two very different senses in halachic literature. One sense is *chazaka* as *status quo*: a woman has a *chezkas tahara*, grain has a *chezkas tevel* — whatever the current status is, we presume it remains until something changes it. The second sense is *chazaka* as an established pattern of behavior: it is a *chazaka* that a woman always goes to the *mikvah* as soon as she is permitted; it is a *chazaka* that a *chaver* does not leave his grain without separating *terumos u'masros*. These are well-established human behaviors that we rely upon. The underlying question here is whether the second type of *chazaka* — a behavioral pattern — is strong enough to override the first type, a status quo. The *Gemara* does not frame it in the language of *chazaka*; it speaks in terms of *vadai* and *safek*. In the end, a *safek* can displace a *vadai* only when the likelihood rises so high that we treat it as a functional *vadai*.

---

## Vestos Biblical/Rabbinic

### Question to Rav Nachman

The *Gemara* now returns directly to the question of *vestos de'oraisa* or *de'rabbanan*. Rav Nachman was asked explicitly: *vest de'oraisa o de'rabbanan*? Is the halachic weight of a woman's established cycle biblical or rabbinic? As summarized above, one way to frame the question is whether, after the expected period passes, she is *vadai teme'ah* or *safek teme'ah* — or alternatively, whether she is *safek teme'ah* or remains *tehora*. The three possibilities stand, and the question is which two positions are in play.

### Unchecked Bleeding Case

Rather than answering directly, Rav Nachman responds by citing what Huna, described as "our friend," said in the name of Rav. The case: a woman who has an established *veset* — the time of her period arrives, and she does not perform a *bedikah* during that time. Then, some time later — an hour, a day — she finds she is bleeding.

### Huna's Ruling

Huna in the name of Rav ruled: *chosheshes le-vistah ve-chosheshes le-reiyasah* — she must be concerned both for the time of her *veset* and for the time she actually saw the blood. What does this mean practically? On one hand, anything she handled from the time her *veset* was expected must be treated with concern, because she may have become *teme'ah* at that earlier point. On the other hand, when counting toward her permitted immersion, she cannot count from the day of her *veset* — she counts only from the day she actually confirmed bleeding. Similarly, the day she actually saw blood is crucial for establishing the future pattern of her cycle: whether future bleedings will render her a *niddah* or a *zavah*, and when she becomes eligible to go to the *mikvah*. Both days carry legal weight, and she must be concerned for both.

### Failed Proof

At first glance this *baraisa* seems to prove that *vestos de'oraisa* — for the *Gemara* initially assumes that the case would require concern for the day of the *veset* even had she not subsequently bled; that the retroactive concern for the day of the *veset* is inherent to the *veset* itself, not dependent on the later seeing of blood. If so, *vestos* carry definite biblical weight.

But the *Gemara* quickly rejects this reading, and correctly so. Your observation that the *baraisa* proves nothing is validated by the *Gemara* itself.

### Seeing Is Evidence

The *Gemara* restates the case: *ta'ama de-raata* — the reason we are concerned retroactively about the day of the *veset* is precisely *because* she saw blood afterwards. *Ha lo raata, ein chosheshin* — had she not seen blood at all, we would not treat her as *teme'ah* from the day of her *veset* simply because it passed. The passing of the day alone, without any subsequent confirmation, would not render her *teme'ah*. This suggests *vestos de'rabbanan* — and therefore the *baraisa* is inconclusive. It does not establish whether *vestos* carry definite biblical weight or only rabbinic weight; it only tells us how to handle a case where both the *veset* day and a subsequent sighting are in play.

---

## Rav vs. Shmuel

### Rav's Check Standard

Having established that the *baraisa* is inconclusive, the *Gemara* presents a direct *amoraic* dispute. The case: a woman with an established *veset*, the time of her *veset* arrives, and she did not check during it — but she checked afterward. Rav rules: *badka u-matzas teme'ah, teme'ah; badka u-matzas tehora, tehora*. If she checks after the fact and finds she is bleeding, she is *teme'ah*; if she checks and finds she is *tehora*, she may be presumed *tehora*. The critical and consequential part of Rav's ruling is the second clause — a later *bedikah* finding *tahara* is sufficient to establish that she did not have her period during the time of her *veset*.

### Shmuel's Stringency

Shmuel disagrees sharply: *afilu badka u-matzas tehora nami teme'ah* — even if she performs a *bedikah* afterwards and finds she is *tehora*, she is nonetheless *teme'ah*. Why? *Mipnei she-oreiach bizmano ba* — "the guest comes at its appointed time." The monthly visitor arrives on schedule. This formulation sounds very much like an assertion of *vestos de'oraisa* — the cycle is so definite and expected that even a clean *bedikah* afterwards does not constitute proof that she did not bleed.

### Timing of Check

The *Gemara* initially reads this as a dispute about whether *vestos* are *de'oraisa* or *de'rabbanan*: one holds *de'oraisa* and therefore a later check is insufficient; the other holds *de'rabbanan* and therefore a later check suffices. But Rabbi Zeira offers a different framing.

### Bedikah Window

Rabbi Zeira says: *lo de-chulei alma vestos de'oraisa* — in fact, both Rav and Shmuel could agree that *vestos* are *de'oraisa*. The difference between them is not about the halachic status of *vestos* at all, but about the timing of the *bedikah*. The *Gemara* explains that a woman does not have a *veset* covering an entire day. The *Gemara* envisions a much more precise window — think of a *veset ha-guf*, where bleeding accompanies specific physical sensations such as menstrual cramps. The period in question is a narrow, finite span of time. A *bedikah* performed during that precise window — or immediately after it, even seconds after — constitutes absolute proof that she did not bleed. But a *bedikah* performed meaningfully later, even an hour later, does not prove that she was clean during the relevant window. She may have bled during the *veset* time itself, and the blood may have been absorbed into her clothing or otherwise gone undetected by a check performed later.

This is an important point for understanding the *Gemara's* logic: a check during the *veset* period provides direct proof; a check shortly after — *betoch shiur veset*, immediately within the window's close — is treated like a check during the period itself and is equally probative. But a check performed well after the window is closed provides only supporting evidence, not definitive proof, because one cannot be certain the bleeding did not occur and then abate before the check was performed.

From this emerges the resolution: according to Rav, the *bedikah* in question was performed immediately after the *veset* window — close enough to be treated as a check during the *veset* itself, and thus absolute proof of *tahara*. According to Shmuel, the *bedikah* was performed significantly later, at which point it is no longer probative, and since *vestos de'oraisa*, the presumption of bleeding stands.

### Timing Resolution

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, however, maintains the simpler reading: *bevestos gufaihu kamifligi* — Rav and Shmuel do directly dispute the *vestos* question. Shmuel holds *vestos de'oraisa* — the cycle carries definitive biblical weight, and even a later *bedikah* finding *tahora* cannot override the presumption that the "guest arrived at its appointed time." Rav holds otherwise, and a later check is dispositive.

---

## Eliezer vs. Yehoshua

### Tannaim Dispute

Rav Sheshes then observes: *ki-tannai* — this is actually a dispute among *Tannaim*. Rabbi Eliezer says: *teme'ah niddah*. In the same scenario — a woman who did not check during her *veset* — Rabbi Eliezer rules she is definitively *teme'ah*, a *niddah*. Notably, he does not say *safek*; he says *niddah* — the language of certainty. This sounds like *vestos de'oraisa* yielding definitive *tum'ah*, and a check afterwards cannot undo it.

### Meir vs. Chachamim

Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees: *tibadek* — let her check, and that will determine her status. This sounds like *vestos de'rabbanan*, or at most *safek*, where a check can resolve the question in favor of *tahara*. A parallel *tannaitic* dispute reinforces this: Rabbi Meir says *teme'ah niddah*, reflecting *vestos de'oraisa* and definitive *tum'ah*; the *Chachamim* say *tibadek*, reflecting *vestos de'rabbanan* and the adequacy of a subsequent *bedikah*. The alignment is clear: Rabbi Eliezer corresponds to Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehoshua to the *Chachamim*.

### Cave Mishnah Proof

Abaye then offers a proof from a *mishnah* that Rabbi Meir holds *vestos de'oraisa*. The *mishnah* states: Rabbi Meir says that if a woman was hiding in a cave — concealing herself from bandits — and the time of her *veset* arrived, and she did not perform a *bedikah*, she is *tehora*. The reason: *she-charada mesalekes es ha-damim* — fear causes the suppression of bleeding. This is the principle of *mesulekes damim*, the same concept that applies to pregnant women and those past menopause: certain physiological states prevent menstrual flow.

### Fear Logic

The *Gemara* draws the following inference: *ta'ama de-ika charada* — the reason she is *tehora* is specifically because fear suppressed the bleeding. *Ha leika charada* — if there were no fear present, we would assume she is *teme'ah*. This implies that in an ordinary case, after the *veset* time passes without a *bedikah*, the default assumption is *teme'ah* — that is, *vestos de'oraisa*. Tosafos engages with the precise logic of this proof, noting that it is not entirely obvious, since the case without fear might only require a *bedikah* rather than presuming definitive *tum'ah*. Nonetheless, the *Gemara* seems to take the inference as sufficiently clear that *vestos de'oraisa*, at least according to Rabbi Meir, means definitive *tum'ah* after the period passes — not merely *safek* — and that only absolute evidence (such as a *bedikah* during the window, or the special circumstance of fear suppressing blood) counteracts it.

---

## Wound Blood Debate

### Gamliel Ruling

The *Gemara* now presents a *baraisa* with a case that appears, on the surface, to be directly about the *de'oraisa*/*de'rabbanan* question. The case: a woman is bleeding from an internal wound — *dam makah* — during the time of her expected *niddah* period. Rabban Gamliel rules she is *tehora*. This means that even as her *veset* period passes, since we can attribute the blood to the wound, we do not presume she has had menstrual bleeding.

### Tahora Without Check

This immediately raises a difficulty: how can she be *tehora* after the *veset* passes without a *bedikah*? We have established that at minimum a check is required. Is Rabban Gamliel simply waiving that requirement?

### Ramban Solution

The Ramban addresses this directly. The requirement to perform a *bedikah* during or after the *veset* is a rabbinic requirement. When a *bedikah* is impossible — as when the woman has a wound that makes any check unreliable or unperformable — the *Chachamim* waive their own rabbinic requirement. Since *vestos de'rabbanan*, the underlying principle is that the woman genuinely retains her *chezkas tahara*, and if the one mechanism the rabbis instituted to verify that status is unavailable, she remains *tehora* on the strength of the *chazaka* itself.

### Reading Debate

The *Gemara* initially reads the dispute that follows — in which Rabbi Shim'on ben Elazar and Rabbi appear to differ — as a dispute about whether *vestos de'oraisa* or *de'rabbanan*, with one position holding her *tehora* (because *de'rabbanan* and the *bedikah* requirement is waived when impossible) and the other holding she must be concerned for her *veset* (because *de'oraisa*).

### Ravina Reframe

Ravina, however, offers a striking reinterpretation: *de-chulei alma veses de'rabbanan* — everyone in this dispute actually agrees that *vestos de'rabbanan*, and therefore everyone agrees the woman herself is *tehora*. The dispute is about something else entirely.

### Mekor Taharah

The debate, Ravina explains, concerns the status of the *makor* — the uterus — and specifically whether blood that passes through the uterus but is not menstrual blood is nonetheless *tamei*. The conceptual question: a woman becomes a *niddah* only through menstrual bleeding from the uterus. But what if there is a wound in the uterus and the blood emerging is unambiguously not menstrual blood — does this blood carry *tum'ah* for purposes of *taharos* (such as *terumah*), even though it does not render the woman a *niddah*? The proposition is that the *makor* itself imparts *tum'ah* to any blood that passes through it, independent of whether that blood constitutes *dam niddah*.

### Shim'on Position

Rabbi Shim'on ben Elazar holds: the woman is *tehora* — everyone agrees on this, since *vestos de'rabbanan* — but the blood itself is *tamei*, because *de-ka'asi derech makor* — it comes by way of the uterus. Even if the blood is wound blood and not menstrual blood, its passage through the uterus renders it *tamei* for purposes of the laws of *tum'ah ve-tahara*.

### Rabbi Counter

Rabbi responds: *i chayshas le-veses, isha nami teme'ah* — if you wanted to be concerned about her *veset* period, you should say the woman herself is *teme'ah*. Clearly you are not saying that — you are saying she is *tehora*. So be consistent: *i lo chayshas le-veses, m'kor m'komo tahor hu* — if you are not concerned about her *veset* because *vestos de'rabbanan*, then the blood is also *tahor*. The only basis for treating the blood as *tamei* would be if it were *dam niddah*, not merely because it passed through the uterus. Since we are not treating her as a *niddah*, the blood that emerges is *tahor* as well. The uterus does not independently contaminate blood that is not menstrual blood.

This is admittedly a conceptually challenging idea to contemplate — that the uterus as a location might cause blood to become *tamei* independent of the woman's *niddah* status. The very idea that the *makor* carries some inherent power of *tum'ah* takes the discussion to a different level. The question of how the *Rambam* and later authorities *pasken* this is worth examining, though in practical terms it is relevant primarily to laws of *tum'ah ve-tahara* rather than to the present issur-based context.

### Toleh Limits

One further important practical issue is raised by Tosafos in this context. The principle of *toleh be-makah* — attributing bleeding to a wound rather than to menstruation — has limits. Tosafos rules that *toleh be-makah* is only applicable when there is positive supporting evidence that the blood is wound blood: a physical sensation accompanying the blood, a characteristic appearance or color, or pain associated with the wound. Without such supporting evidence, one cannot simply attribute any bleeding to a wound and thereby exempt the woman from *niddah* status indefinitely. The concern Tosafos raises — *de-hacha le-olam lo tihye niddah* — is real: if any blood could always be attributed to the wound, a woman would in principle never again become a *niddah*, which is clearly untenable. Therefore, when there is supporting evidence of *dam makah*, we do not require concern that *dam niddah* is mixed in. When there is no supporting evidence, the bleeding must be treated as *dam niddah*.

---

## Practical Halakha

### Consensus Ruling

How do we actually *pasken* the question of *vestos de'oraisa* or *de'rabbanan*? The answer is that all authorities rule *vestos de'rabbanan*. One of the most compelling weights toward this conclusion is the *sugya* itself: a discussion that on the surface appeared to be openly debating *de'oraisa* versus *de'rabbanan* was ultimately re-read by Ravina — and the *Gemara* accepted this re-reading — as a dispute in which everyone agrees *vestos de'rabbanan*. When the *Gemara* itself drives toward unanimity on *de'rabbanan*, that shapes the *psak*. Tosafos, on the *sugya* of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, states explicitly: *nireh de-halakhah de-vestos de'rabbanan* — the *halacha* is that *vestos* are *de'rabbanan* — and then marshals the arguments accordingly.

The practical significance of this ruling is substantial. If *vestos de'oraisa*, then even if a woman performs a *bedikah* after her *veset* period and finds herself *tehora*, the couple cannot have relations; the presumption of having had her period would stand, with all associated *halachos* of *niddah*. Since *vestos de'rabbanan*, a later *bedikah* finding *tahara* is effective and the couple may be permitted.

### Practical Requirements

The *halakha lema'aseh* as codified in the *Shulchan Aruch* follows from this: a woman with a regular *veset* should ideally perform a *bedikah* during the time of the *veset* itself. *Le-chatchilah tzrichah livdok bi-shas vesetah* — ideally she checks during the *veset* period. If she did not check during that time and checks later, she may rely on the later *bedikah*. Tosafos articulates the ruling explicitly: *isha she-yesh lah veset ve-lo badkah bi-shas vesetah, ve-acher kach badkah u-matzas tehora, tehora le-baalah* — a woman who has an established *veset* and did not check at the time, and later checked and found herself *tehora*, is *tehora* to her husband, because *vestos de'rabbanan*.

It should be noted that the ideal of checking during the *veset* period presents a practical challenge. The *Gemara* envisions a fairly narrow and precise window — perhaps tied to specific bodily sensations such as cramps, making a definitive check during the exact moment feasible. How this translates to contemporary reality, where a woman's *veset* may span an entire twelve-hour period, is a separate and complex discussion — some opinions suggest an inserted cloth left in place throughout the period, while other approaches address it differently. But the core *halakha* is clear: *le-chatchilah* check during the *veset*; *be-di'eved*, a later check suffices.

### Thirty-Day Default

The final *halakha* point concerns a woman who has no fixed *veset* at all. Rashi — and this is Rashi's own contribution, not explicit in the *Gemara* itself — understands that the *Gemara's* discussion of the thirty-day standard, which appears in the context of establishing when a woman is *mesulekes damim* (having not bled for three *onos*), reflects a default *veset* of thirty days for women without a fixed cycle. Rashi understands the standard *onah* as thirty days, and treats the thirtieth day as a pseudo-*veset kavua* for such a woman. In Rashi's comment to the line *afilu bi-ymei niddasah*, he writes: *klomar bi-yamim she-hee lemudah li-ros, de-hainu she'as onasah o she'as vesetah* — meaning the days she is accustomed to seeing, which is the time of her *onah* or her *veset*. The *onah* here refers to the thirtieth day, which Rashi treats as a default *veset* for women without an established cycle. This has a very significant practical impact in *halacha*: every woman is treated as having either an established *veset* or a default pseudo-*veset* of day thirty.

---

## Sex Checking Rules

### Shammai Rule

We return now to the *mishnah*. Beit Shammai says: *tzrichah shnei edim le-chol tashmish ve-tashmish* — she needs two cloths for each and every act of *tashmish*. The *mishnah* then adds: *o tashmish le-or haner* — or one may have relations by candlelight. The context assumes that a couple may have relations multiple times in a single night. Beit Shammai is concerned that without separate cloths for each act, evidence of earlier bleeding may be masked — semen and other fluids from a second encounter could cover up any blood deposited on the cloth from the first. Therefore, either use separate cloths for each act of relations, or examine the cloth by candlelight between each act before proceeding.

It is worth noting that Beit Shammai does not say "light a candle and check." He says one may have relations by a lit lamp, implying a light burning in the room throughout. Lighting something at night was not trivial. But the principle is: either produce fresh evidence for each act, or maintain the ability to inspect the evidence before proceeding to the next.

### Hillel Rule

Beit Hillel says: *daya bi-shnei edim kol halaila* — two cloths are sufficient for the entire night. No additional cloths, no intermediate inspections between acts of relations. Notably, after the *masechta* opened with Shammai taking the more lenient position on a certain question, here Beit Hillel reverts to their more typical role of providing the more lenient ruling.

### Cloth Interpretation

The question of which "two cloths" Beit Hillel refers to is debated by Tosafos and Rashi. Tosafos's reading — which follows the more straightforward *peshat*, since *shnei edim* throughout the *masechta* consistently refers to the cloths used by husband and wife after relations — holds that we are speaking of the two cloths used by husband and wife following each act of *tashmish*. Under Tosafos's reading, the dispute concerns how many such pairs of cloths are needed, not how often one must examine them.

Rashi, however, reads the "two cloths" as one cloth used before and one used after a given act of relations. On Rashi's reading, the discussion is about the checks bracketing an act of *tashmish*.

### Check Frequency

The dispute about frequency follows from the dispute about the cloths. According to Tosafos, everyone agrees that one must check after each act of relations — because there is a concern that *tashmish* may trigger bleeding — and the only question between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel is whether you need fresh cloths each time, or whether the same cloths may be reused. Beit Shammai requires fresh cloths for each act so that evidence is not masked; Beit Hillel is lenient, noting among other things the considerable expense and impracticality of requiring fresh cloths each time given the fluids involved.

According to Rashi, Beit Hillel is far more lenient in a different dimension: not only does Beit Hillel not require fresh cloths, but Beit Hillel does not require a check before each act at all. One check at the beginning of the night and one check at the end suffice — there is no need to inspect between each interval. Tosafos raises a reasonable objection to Rashi's reading: how would one know when the "last" act of the night is, so as to time the final check appropriately?

---

## Masking Evidence

### Masking Problem

The *Gemara* now presents the *baraisa* that records the actual exchange between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. It opens with the observation that undergirds Beit Shammai's stringency. Even though having relations by lamplight is called *meguneh* — vulgar or unseemly — as we will discuss in the next *sugya*, nevertheless Beit Shammai insists: *tzaricha shnei eidim al kol tashmish ve-tashmish, o tashmish l'or* — either fresh cloths per act or a lamp burning in the room so the cloth can be examined between acts. The core concern Beit Shammai articulates: *shema tira tipat dam ke-chardal be-vi'ah rishona ve-tachapennah shechvat zera be-vi'ah shniyah* — perhaps she will have bled a drop of blood as small as a mustard seed during the first act, and the semen from the second act will cover over and mask that blood on the cloth. So using the same cloth for multiple acts means the second check may produce a false negative, obscuring evidence of bleeding that occurred during the first act.

### Hillel Response

Beit Hillel responds: *af le-divreichem* — even according to your own position, *lechu she-harok she-betoch ha-peh* — while the "spit" is still within, meaning while the semen is still within the woman's body during a single act, other fluids are already present and could already be masking blood. No check, even if performed after a single act, can be guaranteed to be accurate, because blood could have dissolved or been masked even within that single encounter. *Shema nimmok ve-halach lo* — perhaps the blood dissolved and disappeared before the check. If you are concerned about masking, there will always be masking, and no check system will ever be perfectly reliable.

### Shammai Counter

Beit Shammai is unmoved: *lefi she-eino domeh nimmok pa'am achat le-nimmok shtei pe'amim* — it is not comparable to have something masked once versus having it masked multiple times. A single check, even if imperfect, involves one layer of potential masking. Multiple checks on the same cloth multiply the layers of potential masking, and that graduated risk is meaningful. The more opportunities for evidence to be covered over, the worse the evidentiary picture becomes. Therefore Beit Shammai maintains that separate cloths for each act — or examination between acts — is required.

---

## Yehoshua Stringency

### Students' Complaint

A *baraisa* records that Rabbi Yehoshua said: *ro'eh ani et divrei Beit Shammai* — I find Beit Shammai's position compelling. His students reacted: *Rebbi, harachta alainu* — Rabbi, you have placed too great a burden upon us! The demands of Beit Shammai — separate cloths for each act, or examination by lamplight between each interval — are onerous. Is this really what you are requiring of us?

### Yehoshua Response

Rabbi Yehoshua responded: *mutav she-aarich aleichem ba-olam ha-zeh kedei she-ya'arichu yemeichem la-olam ha-ba* — it is better that I place greater demands upon you in this world, so that your days may be lengthened in the world to come. The wordplay on *harachta* — lengthened — is deliberate: I will lengthen the demands on you in *this* world so that your days may be lengthened in the *next*.

It should be noted that this entire discussion of checking before and after *tashmish* takes place in the context of *isuk be-taharos* — a world of *taharot*, in which the couple is engaged in practices that require *tahara*. The students of Rabbi Yehoshua, their complaint about the burden notwithstanding, were apparently living in that world.

---

## Taharot to Issur

### No Double Relations

Rabbi Zeira draws a broader practical lesson from the positions of all the *Tannaim* discussed: *mi-divrei kulam nilmad* — from what all of them say, we may derive that *ba'al nefesh lo yivol ve-yishneh* — a person of genuine piety should not have relations twice in the same night. The reasoning: even if no one explicitly prohibits a second act, the concern that *tashmish* may trigger bleeding — which is why the *Chachamim* instituted checking — means that a second act places the couple in a position of doubt that they could have avoided. Even according to Beit Hillel, who does not demand fresh cloths, there remains an underlying concern that bleeding could have occurred. A *ba'al nefesh*, conscious of these concerns, should therefore not put himself in the situation of a second act, since the concern of bleeding following *tashmish* is real, and why create the doubt?

### Rava Limitation

Rava, however, disagrees sharply: *bo ve-shoneh* — one may go ahead and have relations multiple times. His reasoning: *ki tanya hi le-taharah* — this entire discussion — all of the checking requirements, the debates about cloths, the concern about masking — applies only in the world of *taharos*. When a couple is *asukah be-taharos* and the practices of *tum'ah ve-tahara* are operative, there are heightened concerns across the board, and those concerns translate into requirements of checking. But these requirements and concerns do not translate into a practical prohibition against having relations in the ordinary sense. Accordingly, the halachic discourse around checking does not create an *issur* outside the context of *taharot*.

It is worth noting that other *Gemaros* — in *Pesachim* and elsewhere — actually speak positively of having relations multiple times at night, addressing the wife's sexual needs and gratification and the husband's responsibility to attend to them. There is thus an interesting tension: one *sugya* questions a second act on grounds of piety in the world of *taharos*, while another *sugya* actually encourages it for reasons of *shalom bayis* and the wife's satisfaction. The practical *halacha* follows Rava: outside the context of *taharos*, there is no prohibition.

### Status Quo Principle

From within the *baraisa*, the *Gemara* also articulates a broader principle governing the practical *issur* of *niddah*: *she-hinnicha be-chezkas tahara* — when the husband left his wife in a status of *tahara*, the default assumption in his absence is that she remains *tehora*, and he may proceed on that assumption. *Aval hinnicha be-chezkas teme'ah* — but if he left her in a status of *tum'ah*, she retains that status and is presumed *teme'ah le-olam hi be-chezkatah* — until she explicitly tells him *tehora ani*. This echoes the broader principle established earlier: *chazaka* of status quo holds until actively displaced by new information.

### Lost Cloth Rule

A new case: *badka be-ed ve-avad* — she performed a *bedikah* with a cloth and then the cloth was lost before she could examine it. The ruling: *assurah le-shamesh ad she-tibdok* — she may not have relations until she performs a new *bedikah* and examines the result. The question arises: in a world of *taharos*, where there is a concern that *tashmish* may cause bleeding, the couple cannot proceed without evidence. If the evidence — the cloth — has been lost, what do they do? The ruling is that she must check again.

### Ila Challenge

Rabbi Ila challenges this: if she had checked and the cloth remained in existence — even unexamined until the following morning — she could have relations again that night. The couple does not need to inspect the cloth immediately; they wait until the next morning. So even without knowing the result, they proceed. Why then, if the cloth was lost, should she be forbidden? If the unexamined cloth is no impediment to relations, then the absence of the cloth should be equally no impediment.

### Rava's Logic

Rava responds: *zu mochia'ha ve-zu eina mochia'ha* — in one case there is evidence that can be examined later; in the other, there is no evidence that can be examined later. This distinction is crucial. The reason the couple can proceed without examining the cloth immediately is that the underlying concern is at a low level. It is not a high-level concern that she is actually a *niddah*; it is a concern rooted in the world of *taharos*, where heightened vigilance is appropriate. Because it is a low-level concern, the couple can wait until the morning to examine the evidence. But that leniency depends entirely on the fact that the evidence *exists* and *will* be examined. Once the cloth is lost and there is no evidence to examine, the situation changes: the low-level concern cannot be resolved at all, and in a world of *taharos* where we have said that checking is required and cannot be waived, we now say the couple cannot proceed until a new check is performed. If the concern were high-level — if she were actually in danger of being a *niddah* — we would demand immediate examination. The fact that we allow waiting until morning shows the concern is low-level, but the ability to wait is predicated on the existence of eventual evidence.

Rashi adds an important dimension: the entire checking system is rooted in *taharos*, not in the *issur* of *bi'ah*. The concern is not primarily whether she is a *niddah* in the forbidden-relations sense; it is whether contact will render *taharos* impure. Therefore, in ordinary circumstances — outside a world of *taharos* — the checking requirement does not apply at all. But within that world, the requirement of evidence cannot simply be waived, and its loss triggers a requirement to generate new evidence before proceeding.

---

## Daytime Relations

### Daytime Prohibition

Having concluded the discussion of *taharos*, the *Gemara* turns to a new topic that will be developed further in the next session: the conditions and circumstances under which marital relations are or are not appropriate. Rabbi Yochanan rules: *assur le-adam she-yishamesh mitato ba-yom* — it is forbidden for a man to have relations with his wife in the daytime.

### Conception Verse

Rav Huna is cited as offering a scriptural basis. He quotes from *Iyov*: *Yovad yom ivaled bo, ve-halailah amar horah gaver* — "Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night which said 'a man was conceived.'" Conception is associated with night in this verse. Rav Huna draws the inference: *laila nitan le-herayon, ve-yom lo nitan le-herayon* — conception is given to the night; the day is not given to conception. Daytime relations are thus less conducive to the purpose of *pru u-rvu*. One might note that this framing subtly implies that what makes the act of relations licit is tied to the possibility of conception — though the *Gemara* leaves that implication implicit.

### Vulgarization

Resh Lakish offers a different source: *bozeh drachav yamut* — "one who vulgarizes his ways shall die." The word *drachav* — "his ways" — is interpreted as referring to sexual behavior. One who treats sexual relations in a degraded, exposed manner has committed a form of *bizayon*, and the verse implies dire consequences.

### Rashi Reframe

One might immediately read this as an expression of the view that sex is somehow dirty or shameful, and that the darkness of night serves to conceal what is embarrassing. But Rashi, strikingly, redirects the reading. Rashi cites another *Gemara* that states explicitly why relations should not take place in full daylight: perhaps a husband will see something about his wife in the bright light and find it repulsive. Now, this could be read offensively. But Rashi's framing points in a different direction.

### Mystery View

What Rashi is actually highlighting is not that the act is shameful, but that full physical exposure under bright light is not conducive to the emotional and relational dimensions of intimacy. There is a sense in which mystery, connection, and intimacy are undermined when everything is placed under a spotlight. The concern is not that the body is disgusting, or that the act is dirty — it is that something about the full, unmediated physical exposure in bright light can disrupt the experience of connection and intimacy, causing a reaction that is harmful to the relationship. It is about attending to the emotional and relational quality of the encounter, not about concealing something shameful.

This reading has practical implications, since it immediately raises the question of intermediate lighting — not full daylight, but not complete darkness either. What about candlelight? What about dim light? Rashi's framing opens those questions in a productive direction. Rather than "sex must be hidden in darkness because it is embarrassing," the principle becomes: the conditions of intimacy should be ones that are conducive to connection and not to a reaction of repulsion or disconnectedness. This is a meaningfully different orientation, and Rashi's choice to introduce it here, rather than simply reading *bozeh drachav yamut* as a condemnation of sexual expression, is itself noteworthy.

---

---

# Niddah 17

## Sex & Light

### Beit Shammai/Hillel

The daf opens by returning to a discussion that had been underway: the dispute between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* regarding the practices a woman observes while engaged in questions of *tumah* and *taharah* — handling *terumah*, performing the required checks before and after relations, and whether those checks must be performed by candlelight at night. One position attributed to *Beit Shammai* is that relations should take place by candlelight so that the cloth can be examined before and after each act during the night. This formulation sets the stage for the *Gemara*'s broader discussion about the propriety of relations in the daytime and under light.

### R. Yochanan Daytime

Rabbi Yochanan had stated: *assur l'adam sheyishamesh mitato bayom* — it is forbidden for a man to use his bed by day. Two reasons had been offered. The first was biological: daytime is not as conducive to conception. The second was more general: it constitutes *bozeh drachav*, a denigrating or shaming of one's path. This second rationale raises an important question. Does the *Gemara*'s concern with relations under bright light reflect a sense that intimacy is somehow shameful and must be hidden, or does it reflect something more nuanced — a sense of privacy and of relating to the person rather than merely the body? Rashi ties *bozeh drachav* to precisely the latter concern, which the *Gemara* will develop further: bright light directs attention entirely to the physical, to the body inspected as it were under a spotlight, stripping away the intimacy and mystery that properly attend the marital relationship.

### Reish Lakish/R. Chanina

The *Gemara* now asks what Reish Lakish does with the verse that Rabbi Yochanan had quoted — the verse from Iyov about a man conceived at night, which Rabbi Yochanan had used to show that nighttime is propitious for conception. Reish Lakish, it turns out, needs that verse for a different purpose: *miba'ei lei l'khid'darash Rabbi Chanina bar Papa*. Rabbi Chanina bar Papa taught the famous *midrash* that the angel appointed over conception is named *Layla* — "night." Thus the verse's repeated use of *layla* does not mean only that night is the time for conception, but rather refers to this angel called *Layla* who oversees the act. The *Tosafot* notes that a *Gemara* in Ta'anit distinguishes between conception, overseen by this angel, and actual childbirth, in which God is directly involved.

The rest of the teaching elaborates: this angel takes the drop — the newly conceived union of seed and egg — and brings it before the Holy One, blessed be He, saying: *Ribono Shel Olam, tipa zo mah tehei aleha* — Master of the Universe, what will become of this drop? Will it be mighty or weak? Wise or foolish? Rich or poor? Notably, the angel does not ask whether the person will be wicked or righteous. That question is left conspicuously unasked.

This connects to the teaching of Rabbi Chanina: *hakol biydei shamayim chutz miyirat shamayim* — everything is in the hands of Heaven except for the fear of Heaven, as derived from the verse in Devarim, "And now, Israel, what does Hashem your God ask of you but to fear Him" — meaning that fear of Heaven, and by extension moral choice, is precisely what God asks of you because it lies within your own power. So much of a person's life is determined at the moment of conception: genetic makeup, intellectual capacity, physical constitution, family circumstances, socioeconomic standing. All of this is decreed. But moral choice — whether one will be righteous or wicked — that is not decreed. It remains in the hands of the person. The *Gemara* acknowledges that God, of course, knows the future, and *Tosafot* addresses the tension between divine foreknowledge and free will, but the *Gemara* itself does not resolve the broader philosophical question here. The verse about *layla* thus serves, in Reish Lakish's reading, not as a statement about the biology of conception but as an entry point into this profound teaching about predestination and human agency.

### Bozeh Drachav & Ben Sira

The *Gemara* then asks: and what does Rabbi Yochanan do with the verse of Reish Lakish — the verse about *bozeh drachav* — since Reish Lakish has taken the Iyov verse for himself? Rabbi Yochanan uses it, the *Gemara* says, *ibaye leh lechadechtiv besefer ben sira* — as it is written in the book of Ben Sira.

This is an occasion to note the notably ambivalent relationship *Chazal* have with the book of Ben Sira. Ben Sira was a wisdom book composed during the period of the Second *Beit Hamikdash*, serving a role similar to Mishlei. On the one hand, *Chazal* at times caution against reading it or treating it as canonical. On the other hand, they quote it, and they do so with weight — using the formula *kedihtiv*, "as it is written," signaling a kind of scriptural seriousness. That ambivalence is on full display here.

What does Ben Sira say? *Shlosha saneti ve'arba'ah lo ahavti* — three things I hated and four I do not love. The poetic structure echoes the prophetic formula of *al sheloshah... ve'al arba'ah* but is somewhat less polished. What are these four things? The first: *sar hanagar* — and Rashi reads *sar* here as a *talmid chacham*, a sage who spends too much time in drinking houses. The *Gemara* notes variant readings: *sar hanagan* (one who gossips excessively) or *sar hanagaz* (one given to quick anger). The second: *vehamoshiv shavas bimromei karas* — one who places his house of study at the highest point of the city, which is an act of arrogance. The third: *veha'ochez be'amah umashtin mayim* — a man who holds onto his genitals while urinating. The fourth: *vehanichnas leveish chaveiro pisom* — one who enters suddenly into his friend's house without knocking.

Rabbi Yochanan adds: *ve'afilu leveiso* — one should not even walk into one's own house without first announcing oneself. Rashi explains: *dilma avid midi ditzni'usa* — perhaps the person inside is engaged in something private. This applies to spouse and, it may reasonably be added, to one's children. The respect for privacy, even in one's own home, is considered a basic value. The concept of *bozeh drachav*, then, is not primarily about sex at all — it encompasses this broader category of behaviors that are inappropriate for proper, civilized conduct: rushing into spaces without regard for others, violations of privacy, and failures of self-restraint.

### Four Things God Hates

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai then offers his own parallel formulation: *arba'ah devarim Hakadosh Baruch Hu sanean va'ani eini ohavan* — four things God hates, and I too do not love. The first is entering one's house suddenly, *vechol sheken leveish chaveiro* — and certainly someone else's house. The second is a man who holds onto his genitals while urinating. The third is *umashtin mayim arom lifnei mitaso* — urinating naked in front of one's bed. Even in the privacy of one's bedroom, standing completely naked before a chamber pot was considered improper. The *Tosafot* cites a *Gemara* in Shabbos suggesting this carries health or metaphysical consequences and may lead to poverty.

At this point, a very important *Tosafot* must be noted. Some versions of the text here read not *umashtin mayim lifnei mitaso* but *meshamesh mitato arom* — having marital relations while completely naked. The *Tosafot* cites *Vayikra Rabbah* in support, and the reasoning is that even during *tashmish*, a person should maintain a degree of *tzniut* — perhaps only the relevant area exposed, but not fully unclothed.

This, however, must be read against a competing and, in the view of *Chazal*, far more authoritative position. The *Gemara* in Ketubot states clearly that a husband cannot insist on having relations while clothed; his wife may demand otherwise. The *Rambam* reads the verse *she'era kesuta ve'onata lo yigra* as encompassing not just the act of *onah* but the physical intimacy of husband and wife together — and the assumption is that they are naked. The *Gemara* in Ketubot further notes that the requirement of separate beds when the wife is a *niddah* was considered necessary precisely because without that status they would be sleeping together without clothing — and pajamas alone would not suffice as a barrier. The sense of physical closeness and nakedness between husband and wife is thus given very considerable weight by *Chazal*. The minority voice recorded in *Tosafot* exists, but it is decidedly not the emphasis.

The fourth thing God hates is *ve'hamishamesh mitato bifnei kol chai* — having relations before all living things. The *Gemara* initially understands this to mean in front of other people, which would be self-evident. Rav Yehuda then asks Shmuel: *va'afilu bifnei achbarim* — does this mean even in front of rats? Shmuel replies, addressing him as *shinena* — sharp one — and says no, not rats, but *kigun shel beit ploni*: like the household of such-and-such (whose name the *Gemara* declines to record), who would have relations in the presence of their male and female servants, treating those servants as invisible presences, essentially as animals. Shmuel's willingness to identify actual households engaging in this practice reflects the seriousness of the violation; it was common knowledge and needed to be named as unacceptable.

The *Gemara* then asks what *drasha* those households could possibly have offered in defense of their behavior — the very fact that the *Gemara* entertains this question is itself striking, as it grants even condemned behavior a place in rabbinic discourse. The verse they apparently invoked was Abraham's instruction to his servants: *shvu lachem po im hachamor* — stay here with the donkey. The *Gemara* reads *im hachamor* as *im hadomeh lachamor* — with those who are like a donkey — meaning that in some legal and social frameworks, slaves occupied a category adjacent to property, and therefore their presence was considered of no moral account. The *Gemara* rejects this premise entirely.

Following this discussion, the *Gemara* notes that Raba bar Rav Huna would ring the bells of his bed canopy — though *Tosafot* disputes this reading and argues the word refers not to bells (*zagei*) but to flies (*gazei*), and that he would wave away flies rather than announce himself. Abaye would similarly shoo away flies, and Rava would swat away gnats. The precise nature of the concern about animals being present during relations is not made entirely explicit by the *Gemara*. It may reflect an extreme expression of the value of privacy, or it may relate to a sense that the presence of any other creature — even one incapable of comprehension — alters the nature of the act by introducing a felt sense of being observed. Whatever the precise reasoning, this practice is indeed codified in the *Shulchan Aruch*.

## Health Hazards

### Five Hazards Intro
