This is significant also because the *Mishnah*'s cases of shells and hairs clearly parallel the two stories of Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok — suggesting the *Mishnah* codified these real cases as its paradigm examples.

### Testing Methods

Reish Lakish rules that the water used for the test must be *poshrin* — lukewarm, neither too cold nor too hot, which might produce a false positive or false negative. A *baraita* confirms this requirement. The *Chachamim* offer an alternative procedure: the matter is placed on a fingernail with some saliva and pressed — if it liquefies under pressure, it indicates the presence of blood.

The *Gemara* asks what practical difference exists between these two approaches. Ravina answers: *me'uchah al yedei ha-dechak* — the dispute concerns whether material that liquefies only under manual pressure counts. The first opinion, requiring it to dissolve on its own in water, would hold that material requiring active compression is not confirmed as blood; the second opinion, using the spit-and-fingernail method, might hold that even dissolution under pressure suffices.

A further question arises from a parallel *Mishnah* about dried blood of a *niddah* or flesh of a corpse: in order to determine whether desiccated matter retains its *tum'ah* status, one immerses it in lukewarm water for *me'et la'et* — a full twenty-four-hour period. Must the same twenty-four hours apply here? The *Gemara* notes the cases differ: there, the question is whether matter that began moist has become sufficiently desiccated to lose its *tum'ah* status — one is testing the degree of desiccation of a *sheretz* or *neveilah* that begins hard. Here, the question is simply whether the substance is blood at all, and blood is naturally softer — perhaps less time suffices. The *Gemara* leaves this as *teiku*, unresolved.

---

## Uterus Opening Principle

### Fish-Like Fetus Case

The *Gemara* returns to the central focus of the *perek*: what constitutes a legally significant fetus? The *Mishnah* ruled that if the expelled matter resembles a fish or other non-human creature, she is *tehorah* — it is not treated as a human fetus. The question now is: even if it is not a fetus for purposes of *yoledet* status, something was expelled from the uterus. Why not apply *ee efshar lifteechat hakever b'lo dam* — it is impossible for the uterus to open without blood accompanying the expulsion — and render her *tamei* as a *niddah* on that basis?

Reish Lakish answers: *b'machloket shnuyah, rabbanan hee* — the *Mishnah* reflects the majority view. According to Rabbi Yehuda, however, even the expulsion of a fish-like form would cause the uterus to open and blood to accompany it, rendering her *tamei*.

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees with this analysis. He argues that even Rabbi Yehuda would concede the woman is *tehorah* in this case. The reason Rabbi Yehuda ruled *tamei* in the *chaticha* case — the expelled mass — was not because the opening of the uterus causes blood to flow, but because he understood the mass itself to be dried *niddah* blood: *chaticha d'avid dam d'karish* — a mass that is itself congealed blood. In the case of a fish-like form, however, even Rabbi Yehuda recognizes this is a biological entity, not dried blood, and he would agree she is *tehorah*.

### Rabbi Yehuda Debate

This brings the two interpretations of Rabbi Yehuda's position into sharp relief. When Rabbi Yehuda ruled that a woman who expelled a mass is *tamei*, did he reason that the mass was itself dried *niddah* blood — *chaticha d'avid dam d'karish* — or did he apply the principle of *ee efshar lifteechat hakever b'lo dam*, reasoning that whenever the uterus is opened to expel something, blood necessarily accompanies it?

If the former, then in the case of a fish-like form — which is clearly not dried blood — Rabbi Yehuda would agree with the majority: *tehorah*. If the latter, then Rabbi Yehuda should rule *tamei* whenever the uterus expels anything large enough to open it, regardless of whether the matter is blood.

The *Gemara* notes that Rabbi Yochanan himself is credited elsewhere with the principle of *ee efshar lifteechat hakever b'lo dam* as the basis of the debate. Under that reading — which is one version of his position — Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish would agree: the *Mishnah* is Rabbi Yehuda's opponents, and Rabbi Yehuda himself, applying *ee efshar lifteechat hakever b'lo dam*, would require *tum'ah* even for the fish-like fetus.

### Size Requirements

A closely related question emerges from the earlier case of hairs and shells. If Rabbi Yehuda holds that any expulsion from the uterus necessarily brings blood with it, why did the *Gemara* not challenge those cases — why does not Rabbi Yehuda require *tum'ah* when a woman expels shell-like or hair-like matter?

*Tosafot* address this directly: *a'se'ara u'v'klipa lo parich* — the *Gemara* did not ask about hairs and shells because *d'muatin ninhu v'lo shayach behu petechat hakever* — these are minute, and such tiny matter does not cause the opening of the uterus. The principle of *ee efshar lifteechat hakever b'lo dam* applies only when something of sufficient size is expelled.

This size threshold has immediate practical implications and is foundational to Rav Moshe Feinstein's approach. Even according to the *Noda B'Yehuda*, who extends *ee efshar lifteechat hakever b'lo dam* to instruments inserted from outside the body, Rav Moshe concludes that only an instrument of sufficient diameter — he specifies three-quarters of an inch — would trigger the concern. Since virtually no standard gynecological instrument approaches that circumference, the *Noda B'Yehuda*'s ruling is rendered almost entirely moot in practice. This size limitation is rooted precisely in the *Tosafot*'s observation here: small matter does not open the uterus, and therefore does not bring blood with it.

---

---

# Niddah 23

## Intro: Animal-like Fetus…

### Yoledet Status

The entirety of this *perek* is concerned with the question of when a woman acquires the *tumah* of a *yoledet* — one who has given birth. This *tumah* is of practical relevance even today, since it carries the same prohibition of conjugal relations as *tumah* of *niddah*. The discussion encompasses not only live births but also miscarriages: a child need not be viable to generate this status, but the fetus must meet certain halakhic criteria.

The *perek* has already examined at length whether the expulsion of matter from the uterus necessarily involves blood, and whether the manner in which blood exits the body affects its halakhic character. We now turn to the central question: what constitutes a fetus, *ולד*, in the first place — specifically, whether the *fetus* must bear human appearance in order for the woman to be defined as having given birth.

### Mishna: Animal Appearance

The *mishna* presents the following case: *hamapelet kemin behemah* — a woman who miscarries something that resembles a *behemah*, a domesticated animal. Rabbi Meir holds that even this counts as a *vlad* and renders the woman *tamei* as a *yoledet*. The *chachamim* disagree. Notably, the *mishna* specifies "looks like" a *behemah* — the language of appearance, not of actual nature. For the moment, the most natural reading is that this is a human fetus that, for some reason, failed to take human form. The question is one of *tzurah*, appearance, not of *mahut*, essential nature — analogous to the *gemara*'s treatment of blood: even if something is biologically blood, if it lacks the requisite color, it may not carry the halakhic status of *niddah* blood. The *mishna* may be operating in precisely that vein: this is a human fetus, but its failure to appear human may exempt the woman from the laws of *yoledet*.

---

## R. Meir & Yetzirah

### Yetzira Parallels

The *gemara* opens by asking: *mai ta'ama de-Rabbi Meir* — what is Rabbi Meir's reason? The answer, cited by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, is a *gezerah shavah* based on the verb *yetzira* — divine fashioning. The *gemara* notes that when the Torah describes God's creation of animals, it uses the same verbal root as it uses for the creation of humans. This shared linguistic form, Rabbi Meir contends, places certain animals in a category sufficiently analogous to humanity that a fetus resembling such an animal retains the halakhic status of a human *vlad*. Fish, however, are excluded: the Torah's description of aquatic creation uses the verb *yishretzu* — "let the waters teem" — and never employs the root *yatzar*. Birds are included, as we will see, because the relevant verse in *Bereishit* chapter 2 uses *vayitzer* for them as well.

### Bereishit Verbs

To understand the argument precisely, one must survey the relevant verses across both chapters of *Bereishit*. In chapter 1, the Torah uses different verbs for each category of creation: *yishretzu* for fish, *vaya'as* for land animals, and *vayivra* for humans. These are three distinct verbs for three distinct categories — no basis for linguistic linkage between humans and animals. But chapter 2 introduces a new description: *vayitzer Hashem Elokim min ha'adamah kol chayat hasadeh ve'et kol of hashamayim* — "God fashioned from the ground every animal of the field and every bird of the sky." This same root, *vayitzer*, appears earlier in that chapter in the account of the creation of the human being. Thus, in the second *perek*, the Torah uses *vayitzer* both for the human and for the land animals and birds — the very same verb, which Rabbi Meir reads as a halakhically meaningful link.

---

## Gezerah Shavah Rules

### Sea Monsters Problem

The *gemara* immediately presses: if the argument rests on a shared verb, why not extend the ruling to a case where a woman miscarries something resembling a *tannin*, a great sea creature? The verse in chapter 1 reads *vayivra Elokim et hatanninim hagedolim* — "God created the great sea monsters" — and the same root *bara* appears in the verse describing the creation of the human: *vayivra Elokim et ha'adam*. So there is a shared verb between sea monsters and humans as well. Why should the *gezerah shavah* not extend there?

The *gemara* answers: *danin yetzirah mi-yetzirah ve-ein danin briah mi-yetzirah* — we connect *yetzira* to *yetzira*, and we do not connect *briah* to *yetzira*. In other words, the preferred linkage is between two instances of the same verb in its most precise form. One might object: does it not say *vayivra* by humans as well? Indeed it does. The *gemara* therefore acknowledges that there are actually two verbs associated with humans in the Torah — *vayivra* in chapter 1 and *vayitzer* in chapter 2 — and similarly two verbs associated with sea monsters: *vayivra* in chapter 1 and, as the *gemara* initially suggests, possibly *vayitzer* via the verse mentioning *remes ha'adamah*. But the *gemara* refutes this: the *remes* mentioned in connection with *vayitzer* refers to land creatures, and sea monsters are not land animals. So the sea monsters have only one verb — *vayivra* — and that verb is not free.

### Mufneh Principle

This brings the *gemara* to a general methodological discussion about the limits of *gezerah shavah*. The principle at stake is *mufneh* — whether the word used to establish the *gezerah shavah* is "free," i.e., not already fully occupied by its role in the verse. The *gemara* introduces three tiers:

The strongest form is *mufneh mishnei tzedadim* — the word is free on both sides, meaning the linking term in each of the two source passages can be considered extra, since another word is doing the primary work of each verse. In such a case, one can say the shared word was placed there precisely to create a halakhic link.

The intermediate form is *mufneh mitzad echad* — one of the two instances of the linking term is extra, the other is not.

The weakest form is when neither instance is extra — both words are doing their ordinary work in their respective verses, and they simply happen to be the same word.

The *gemara* applies this framework here. The word *vayitzer* appears twice in connection with the cases under discussion: once by humans in chapter 2, and once by the animals and birds in chapter 2. Is either of those instances free? By humans: the verse in chapter 1 already has *vayivra*, so *vayitzer* in chapter 2 can be argued to be extra. By animals: the verse in chapter 1 already has *vaya'as*, so *vayitzer* in chapter 2 can be argued to be extra there as well. Both instances of *vayitzer* are therefore candidates to be considered free — *mufneh mishnei tzedadim*. By contrast, the word *vayivra* appears by the sea monsters in chapter 1 with no competing verb for that category, so it is not free — *eino mufneh*.

### Yishmael Dispute

The *gemara* then cites a tradition transmitted by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, in the name of Rabbi Yishmael, regarding the practical difference between these tiers. According to Rabbi Yishmael: if neither word is free (*eino mufneh kol ikar*), one cannot make the *gezerah shavah* at all. If one word is free (*mufneh mitzad echad*), one may derive from it and the derivation is not subject to refutation. The *Rabbanan* — presumably Rabbi Akiva's school — take a stricter position: even when one word is free, the *gezerah shavah* may be made but remains vulnerable to logical critique (*meshivin*). Only when both words are free do all opinions agree that the derivation is airtight and no challenge can overturn it.

A parallel tradition, attributed by Rav Acha the son of Rava to Rabbi Eliezer, presents what the *gemara* calls a *lenient* formulation — not lenient in the practical legal sense, but lenient in the sense of setting a lower threshold for making the *gezerah shavah* at all. According to this version: even when neither word is free, one may still make the *gezerah shavah*, but it remains open to refutation. When one word is free, Rabbi Yishmael agrees it is airtight; the *Rabbanan* still permit critique. When both words are free, all agree it is watertight. The difference between the two traditions, then, concerns only the case where neither word is free: the first tradition forbids the *gezerah shavah* entirely; the second permits it, subject to challenge.

It is worth pausing over what this extended discussion reveals. The *gemara* clearly recognizes that *gezerah shavah* is among the most formally arbitrary of the thirteen hermeneutical principles: a word appears in one context, the same word appears in another, and a legal consequence is transferred between them. To restrain this arbitrariness, the *gemara* imposes a hierarchy of legitimacy. The Ramban elsewhere observes that the precise determination of which *gezerah shavah* is operative was never entirely fixed — the tradition was not that specific — and so the *gemara* engages in these comparative evaluations. But the underlying point stands: *gezerah shavah* requires some signal, beyond mere coincidence of vocabulary, that the Torah intended a link.

### Airtight Connection

The *gemara* now concludes: *ve-lahachi afneih Rachmana le-vehema mishnei tzedadim* — the reason the Torah made the word *vayitzer* available at both ends, by the humans and by the animals, is precisely to indicate that the proper linkage is between those two categories, and not between humans and sea monsters via *vayivra*. When both words are free, the *gezerah shavah* is watertight; no logical objection may be raised against it.

What logical objection might otherwise have been raised? The *gemara* suggests: *mah le-adam shekein nitchayev be-mitzvot* — one might distinguish humans from animals on the grounds that humans are subject to *mitzvot*, and consequently to a broader regime of *tumah* — for a living animal cannot become *tamei*, while a living human can. Therefore, the laws of *tumah* associated with childbirth might not transfer to an animal-shaped fetus. But since the *gezerah shavah* is *mufneh mishnei tzedadim*, this critique is not admitted. The verse itself has signaled the link, and the link holds regardless of this potential distinction.

The *gemara* thus establishes Rabbi Meir's position: a woman who miscarries a fetus with the appearance of a mammal or bird is nonetheless a *yoledet* for purposes of *tumah*. Fish are excluded because the Torah never uses the root *yatzar* for them. Sea monsters are excluded because the only available verb for them, *vayivra*, is not free. The connection is built entirely on *vayitzer* — a word the Torah went out of its way to use in two categories, rendering it free in both, and thereby creating an airtight halakhic link.

---

## Facial Features Test

### Eyes Similarity

A parallel tradition, cited by Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, offers a different rationale for Rabbi Meir's position. The reason that a fetus resembling an animal falls under the laws of *yoledet*, according to this account, is not primarily the shared verb in scripture but rather a physical fact: *eineihem domot ke-shel adam* — the eyes of such animals resemble those of a human being. Rashi understands this to mean specifically that the pupil is round, in contrast to fish eyes which have a different configuration.

The *gemara* immediately raises a challenge from another direction. Rav Ami asks: if it resembles a *tannin*, would the mother be *tamei*? We have already dealt with that. The *gemara* then asks a stranger question: what if the fetus resembles a mountain? After all, the verse says *ki hinei yotzeir harim* — God fashions mountains — using the root *yatzar*. Ought we then derive that a mountain-shaped fetus renders the mother a *yoledet*? The response is direct: nothing that emerges from a woman's body would actually resemble a mountain; at best it might be described as a lump of earth. The category simply does not apply.

The *gemara* then asks: what if she aborts *ruach* — wind, or air? In context, this refers to the phenomenon where the embryonic sac appears filled with air rather than substance. The verse *uvorei ruach* — "and He creates wind" — uses the root *bara*, which might arguably be considered extra since the verse could have said *yotzeir harim ve-ruach* without a separate verb. Hence *borei ruach* could be free and available for a *gezerah shavah*. The *gemara* rejects this: *donin divrei Torah mi-divrei Torah ve-ein donin divrei Torah mi-divrei Kabbalah* — one derives *Torah* law from other books of *Torah*, meaning from the *Chumash*, and does not derive it from the later books of *Nevi'im* and *Ketuvim*. The verse about God fashioning mountains and creating wind is from the prophets, and cannot serve as the basis for a *gezerah shavah* in this context.

One might consider whether these questions — the mountain, the wind — were posed as genuine legal inquiries or as *reductio ad absurdum* challenges, designed to press the limits of a purely textual argument. If all that is required is a shared verbal root, the conclusions become strange indeed. The *gemara*, however, treats the objections seriously and answers them on their own terms. Nevertheless, the cumulative weight of these questions suggests that behind Rabbi Meir's position there may be an additional implicit premise: that the physical resemblance between certain animals and humans is not merely coincidental, but reflects a genuine proximity of form that makes the halakhic equation defensible. The verse serves as a peg, but the intuition about appearance does real work.

### Snake Objection

Returning to the physical-appearance rationale of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba: if the critical feature is that the eyes resemble human eyes, one might ask why the *mishna* does not include the case of a fetus resembling a snake. After all, the *gemara* asserts that the pupil of a snake's eye is round, just like that of a human. The *gemara* answers this omission purposefully. Had the *mishna* mentioned snakes, one might have concluded that the *rabbanan* dispute Rabbi Meir's position *specifically* in the case of snakes — precisely because the Torah does not use the root *yatzar* for snakes — and that by *behemah* and *chayah*, where *yetzira* is written, even the *chachamim* might concede. By omitting the snake case, the *mishna* ensures that the reader understands the *rabbanan* dispute Rabbi Meir across the board: whenever the fetus lacks a human appearance, regardless of which animal it resembles, the *chachamim* do not consider it a *vlad*.

### Eye Anatomy

A tension now arises from a source in *Bechorot*: if an animal's eye is round like a human eye, that is considered a *mum*, a blemish, in the animal. This implies that normally an animal's eye does not look like a human eye — which seems to contradict the claim that animal eyes generally resemble human eyes. The *gemara* resolves this: *ha be'uchma, ha be-tziraya* — one statement refers to the pupil (*the black*), the other to the socket or setting of the eye. The pupil of many animals does resemble a human pupil in being round; it is the overall shape and setting of the eye within the face that differs. The *mum* in *Bechorot* refers to an animal whose entire eye — the socket, the shape — looks human, which is abnormal. The claim about resemblance used by Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba concerns only the pupil.

### Eye Position

Rabbi Yannai offers yet another formulation of Rabbi Meir's reasoning: *eineihem holchot le-faneihem ke-shel adam* — their eyes are directed forward, as with humans, rather than positioned on the sides of the head. This forward-facing orientation is characteristic of predators and certain mammals, and it creates a face that resembles the human face in a recognizable way. Fish, by contrast, have eyes on the sides of the head and a correspondingly different facial structure.

### Owls vs. Other Birds

The *gemara* raises a difficulty with this rationale as applied to birds. If the criterion is that the eyes face forward, then most birds — whose eyes are typically set on the sides of their heads — would not qualify. Yet the *mishna* includes birds in the categories that Rabbi Meir subjects to his ruling. How can that be? The *gemara* clarifies: when Rabbi Meir includes *of*, birds, he does not mean all birds. He refers specifically to owls — the *bakiya* and *kipufa* — whose faces are strikingly human-like, with forward-facing eyes and rounded facial structures. Other birds would not qualify even according to Rabbi Meir.

### Compromise View

Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel articulates a middle position. He says: *nirin divrei Rabbi Meir bi-vehemah ve-chayah* — the reasoning of Rabbi Meir appears compelling when it comes to land mammals; *ve-divrei Chachamim be-ofot* — while the position of the *chachamim* seems more persuasive when it comes to birds. The *gemara* asks: what does he mean by birds? If he means owls — creatures with notably human-like faces — why would he concede that case to the *chachamim*? Their faces are as human as those of many mammals. The *gemara* therefore concludes that Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel must be ruling against Rabbi Meir specifically in the case of *other* birds, those whose eyes are on the sides. From this it follows that Rabbi Meir himself must have applied his ruling even to non-owl birds — otherwise there would be no dispute to resolve in that category.

The *gemara* therefore emends the *braita*: *chasuri mechasra* — the text is incomplete. The correct reading is that Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel accepts Rabbi Meir's position for land mammals *and* for owls, and accepts the *chachamim*'s position for all other birds. And this also implies, the *gemara* concludes, that Rabbi Meir himself actually did not extend his ruling to non-owl birds — he agreed with the *chachamim* there — so the only genuine dispute between Rabbi Meir and the *chachamim* was with respect to owls.

What is striking about this section is the way in which the two distinct rationales — the textual *gezerah shavah* based on *vayitzer*, and the physical rationale based on facial resemblance — lead to different practical outcomes. The textual argument groups all birds together with mammals under the shared verb. The physical argument introduces fine-grained distinctions: owls yes, other birds no; perhaps even the position of the eyes matters. The *gemara* does not force a single answer, but its ultimate resolution — that the actual halakhic dispute is limited to owls — reflects a strong pull toward the appearance-based rationale.

---

## Animal or Animal-Like?

### Braita Wording

The *gemara* now introduces a *braita* that generates significant interpretive difficulty. Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok states: *hamapelet min behemah va-chayah* — a woman who miscarries a *behemah* or a *chayah*. The language is troubling. Earlier, the *mishna* consistently said *kemin behemah* — "resembling a *behemah*." Here the *braita* drops the word *kemin* and says simply *min behemah* — a *behemah* itself. According to Rabbi Meir this constitutes a *vlad*; according to the *chachamim* it does not.

The *braita* continues: when it comes to birds, *tibbadek* — one must examine. This implies that Rabbi Meir's ruling applies to some birds and not others, precisely as the *gemara* concluded in the previous section: owls yes, others no. The *gemara* notes that this *tibbadek* is being evaluated according to Rabbi Meir — whether the particular bird-like form triggers his ruling — which aligns with the conclusion that Rabbi Meir distinguishes even within birds, accepting owls and rejecting others.

The more pressing question remains the language of the *braita* itself. Is it using *behemah* as shorthand for "something that looks like a *behemah*," or is it genuinely positing that a *behemah* — an actual animal — might be found in a woman's womb? One might argue that the *gemara* simply abbreviates, replacing the full *mishna* language with the shorter form. Yet the questions the *gemara* proceeds to ask make it increasingly difficult to sustain that reading.

### Kiddushin Question

Rav Yirmiyah poses a question to Rabbi Zeira: according to Rabbi Meir, who says that *behemah bi-mei isha vlad me'alya hu* — an animal in the mother's womb is a full-fledged *vlad* — if the father accepted *kiddushin* on behalf of this fetus, assuming the fetus is a daughter, would the *kiddushin* be valid? This question presupposes the general rule that a father may betroth his daughter before she is born if the fetus is viable. The question is whether this particular fetus — the *behemah*-like thing — qualifies.

The language *behemah bi-mei isha* — an animal in the mother's womb — is no longer easily read as mere shorthand. The *gemara* appears to be genuinely entertaining the possibility that the entity in question has some form of animal status, and the question about *kiddushin* is probing what its human or non-human status implies in practice.

### Viable by Species

The *gemara* responds: *le-meimra de-chayei* — does this imply the thing will actually live? But Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *lo amar Rabbi Meir ela ho'il u-mino mitkayem* — Rabbi Meir only included this in the category of *vlad* because its *species* — the actual animal it resembles — is viable. The fetus itself, however, is never viable. It does not actually live. Therefore, the question of *kiddushin* is moot: betrothal can only apply to a fetus that is itself potentially viable. A fetus that was never capable of living independently cannot be the subject of a valid *kiddushin*, regardless of what it looks like.

Several *Rishonim* press this point further. Even if the thing will not live, are there not other halakhic implications — for instance, does the man who effected the *kiddushin* become forbidden to the mother? They respond: when the *gemara* says it is not viable, it means that *kiddushin* is simply inapplicable from the outset. The entire framework of a father accepting *kiddushin* on behalf of an unborn daughter presupposes a viable fetus. Something that is by nature never viable is categorically outside that framework.

### Absurd Question

Rav Acha the son of Rav Yaakov remarks: *ad kan hivi Rabbi Yirmiyah le-Rabbi Zeira li-yadei gichuch* — Rabbi Yirmiyah almost brought Rabbi Zeira to laughter — *ve-lo gachich* — but he did not laugh. The question was apparently intended to be amusing, or at minimum to be a *reductio* of sorts. But in which direction? Was the absurdity meant to highlight the strangeness of treating this entity as an animal — and thereby deflating that implication — or was the absurdity meant to press the outer edge of treating it as a human subject of *kiddushin*? The *gemara* does not say, and Rabbi Zeira's refusal to laugh suggests he took the question seriously rather than as a joke.

### Tosafot: Bestiality

*Tosafot* make explicit what the *gemara* leaves implicit. They note that the *gemara* could have raised an even sharper version of the question. If at the moment the *gemara* was entertaining the possibility that this creature could be born viable, one could have asked: if someone had sexual intercourse with it, would they be liable for *sekila* — execution — as one is liable for the act of *bi'ah im behemah*, relations with an animal? *Tosafot* thus confirm that the underlying tension in this passage is precisely the question of human versus animal status. On one side of the ledger: is *kiddushin* binding, treating the fetus as a human? On the other side: would sexual contact with it constitute bestiality, treating it as an animal? These two halakhic questions bracket the same conceptual uncertainty.

The *Rosh* engages the question from yet another angle, asking whether the passage could have raised the issue of *tumat met* — corpse impurity. Would this entity, once miscarried, generate the *tumah* of a human corpse? The *Rosh* in his *Tosafot* answers that this was never a real question: since Rabbi Meir considers the mother to be a *yoledet*, the fetus necessarily has the status of a human *vlad* and is *tamei* as a *nefal*, a miscarried human fetus. Its human status for purposes of *tumah* is settled. The uncertainty that generates the *gemara*'s questions lies elsewhere — in those areas of halakha where the animal-like form of the entity creates genuine ambiguity about its classification.

---

## Viability & Inheritance

### Bechorot List

The *gemara* now introduces a *mishna* from *Bechorot* that provides a list of types of miscarriages with the following halakhic consequence: the child born after them is a *bechor* for inheritance — receiving a double portion — but is not a *bechor* for *pidyon haben*. Understanding this requires clarifying the two distinct categories. For *pidyon haben*, the operative criterion is *peter rechem* — literally the first to breach the womb. Whether that first-born will live is irrelevant; it is a question of priority of birth. For the double portion in inheritance, however, the criterion is that the first-born was *viable* — a living child that survived. A miscarriage of something previously viable displaces the next child from receiving the double portion, since technically there was already a first-born. But a fetus that was *never* viable — that could never have lived — does not count as a prior birth for purposes of inheritance, and so the subsequent child receives the double portion.

On this framework, there is a category of birth that simultaneously generates both consequences: the subsequent child is *bechor le-nachalah* — receives the double portion — because the prior fetus was never viable, yet is *not bechor la-Kohen* — does not require *pidyon haben* — because the prior fetus did breach the womb. This is the category described in the *mishna* from *Bechorot*: the *sandal*, the *shilya*, the *shafir merukam*, and the dismembered fetus. These are forms that establish the act of prior birth but were never genuinely viable.

### Never Viable

The *gemara* applies this framework to the case of the animal-like fetus. Rabbi Meir's own position, as stated in this *braita*, is that the animal-shaped fetus falls into exactly this category. It is a *vlad* — a miscarriage that constitutes a birth — and therefore the subsequent child is not *bechor la-Kohen* for *pidyon haben*. Yet Rabbi Meir also holds that it was *never* viable, and therefore the subsequent child *is* the *bechor le-nachalah* and receives the double portion.

Rabbi Yirmiyah raises a challenge from this very ruling. The *gemara* notes: *va-afilu salka deitach de-chayei* — even if one were to entertain the possibility that such a fetus could be viable, the *mishna*'s ruling that the subsequent child receives the double portion would then be wrong. Since it is indeed ruled that the subsequent child receives the double portion, this proves that the animal-like fetus was never considered potentially viable. It is viable in name only — *mino mitkayem*, the species it resembles is viable — but the fetus itself has no potential for life.

The *chachamim* take the opposite position: since they do not consider the animal-shaped fetus a *vlad* at all, they would hold that the subsequent child is *bechor la-Kohen* as well, since no prior birth occurred.

### Father's Pain

Rava attempts to resist the proof. He argues: perhaps one could say the animal-like fetus *is* potentially viable, and yet the subsequent child still receives the double portion — not because the first was never viable, but because of a different *derashah*. The verse says *reishit ono* — "the first of his strength" — which the *gemara* reads as *mi she-libo daveih alav*, the child whose loss causes the father anguish. The implication is that the double portion applies only when the father genuinely mourns the loss of the first child. If the first "child" had an animal-like form, the father would not be pained by its loss — *zeh she-ein libo daveih alav* — and therefore the verse's criterion is not met, and the subsequent child receives the double portion, even if the first was technically viable.

### Miscarriage Status

The conclusion drawn by the *gemara* can now be stated. According to Rabbi Meir, the animal-like fetus carries *torat leida* — the legal character of a birth — and therefore the mother is a *yoledet*, and the subsequent child is not the *bechor* for *pidyon haben*. Yet this same fetus was never considered viable, and therefore the subsequent child receives the double portion in inheritance. The *chachamim* disagree at the foundational level: since the fetus did not have human form, it is not a *vlad* at all, and the woman is not a *yoledet*; the subsequent child is simultaneously the *bechor* for *pidyon haben* and eligible for the double portion.

Throughout this discussion, the *gemara*'s language — speaking of *behemah bi-mei isha* rather than *kemin behemah* — raises profound questions about how the fetus is being conceptualized. Whether the *gemara* ultimately resolves this as a matter of appearance and form alone, or whether it genuinely entertains the possibility of an entity of ambiguous human/animal status, the questions posed by *Tosafot* and the *Rosh* make clear that later authorities understood the passage to carry real halakhic weight along precisely these lines. At minimum, the *gemara* here is working through what it means for something to have human *tzurah* — human form — and whether form, rather than origin or biology, is the determinative criterion for acquiring the full range of halakhic statuses associated with human birth.

---

---

# Niddah 24

## Animal Appearance

### Fetus with Animal Appear…

The discussion on 24b begins slightly earlier, at 23b, and concerns a fetus that has the appearance of an animal (*behemah*). The Mishnah had raised the question of whether such a fetus, emerging from a human mother, confers upon her the status of a *yoledet* — a woman who has given birth — with all attendant laws of *tumah vetaharah*. Before proceeding further, it is worth clarifying a distinction that bears on the broader context of these laws.

### Pidyon HaBen Context

The Mishnah in Bechorot draws a clear line between two different firstborn frameworks. For the purposes of the double inheritance portion, the firstborn must be born alive; a stillbirth or miscarriage, even a fully developed one, does not count, and the next living son retains *bechor* status for inheritance. For *pidyon haben*, however, the Torah speaks of *peter rechem* — the one who breaches the womb — and here the standard is halachic birth rather than live birth. Accordingly, any miscarriage that constitutes a *halachic* birth, even a stillbirth, means the next son is no longer a *peter rechem* and does not require redemption. The standard for what constitutes such a birth is, practically speaking, the same as the standard governing whether the mother becomes a *yoledet* subject to the laws of *tumah vetaharah* — and that is precisely the question our Gemara is exploring.

It is worth noting that the occasions for *pidyon haben* are in practice quite rare. A girl born first, a prior miscarriage that halachically constituted a birth, and a father or mother who is a *kohen*, *bat kohen*, *levi*, or *bat levi* — all of these eliminate the obligation before we even reach the question of fetal appearance.

### Meir's Position

With that context established, the Gemara presents a question posed by Rav Adda bar Ahava to Abaye. The Mishnah had stated that according to Rabbi Meir, a fetus that looks like an animal (*behemah beme'ei imo*) is nonetheless a real fetus (*velad ma'alya*) for the purposes of childbirth law. The question then arises: what about the reverse scenario?

### Human in Animal Womb

*Adam beme'ei behemah mai?* — what is the law if a human form is found in the womb of a cow? The Gemara immediately narrows the question: *lemai nafka mina* — what is the practical difference? And the answer is striking in its narrowness. The question is not whether such a creature has human status in any broad sense — whether it is subject to commandments, whether killing it constitutes homicide. The Gemara frames the question entirely around *le'ishtaru'ei ba'achilah* — whether it may be eaten. Is this creature to be treated as a calf, slaughtered through a kosher *shechitah* and eaten? Or does its human-like appearance disqualify it from the category of *behemah* entirely?

This restraint is itself revealing. Notably, even Rabbi Meir, who had argued that a fetus looking like an animal inside a human mother is still a *velad*, never suggested that such a fetus *is* an animal in any biological sense. Nor does the Gemara here suggest that a human-appearing creature in an animal's womb is actually human. The far-reaching implications of that claim — is it cannibalism to eat it? — would be unavoidable, and the Gemara says nothing of the sort. The question throughout is how appearance shapes *halachic* status, not biological identity.

### Dove-like Fetus

The Gemara attempts to resolve the question from a ruling of Rabbi Yochanan: one who slaughters a *behemah* and finds within it a fetus resembling a dove (*demus yonah*) — it is forbidden to eat that fetus. The use of the word *demus* — appearance — is notable; the Gemara shifts easily between saying something *is* a thing and saying it *looks like* a thing, reinforcing the interpretation that we are always speaking about appearance rather than actual species identity. The fetus resembles a dove and is therefore forbidden, presumably because it cannot be considered part of the *behemah* and was not itself subjected to a proper *shechitah*.

### Hoof Distinction

The Gemara, however, rejects this proof. *Hachi hashta* — how can the cases be compared? There, the dove-like fetus has neither split hooves nor even a single hoof — *lo parsos ika v'lo parsah ika*. Here, a human-appearing fetus does have feet, and the Torah's description of a *behemah* uses the word *parsah*. Since the human form possesses something that at least partially corresponds to the descriptors of a *behemah* found in the verse, perhaps it is still sufficiently categorized as part of the *behemah* and may be eaten. The dove-like fetus matches none of those descriptors at all, and so the two cases cannot be equated.

### Chachamim Requirement

The Mishnah continues with the position of the *chachamim*: anything that lacks *tzuras adam*, a human appearance, does not constitute a fetus for purposes of childbirth law. It is with this foundation that the Gemara proceeds to examine precisely what constitutes human appearance.

---

## Facial Features

### Consensus Hybrids

Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba said in the name of Rav: *hakol modim* — everyone agrees in certain cases. If the body is that of a ram and the face is human, the mother is *temei'ah leidah* — both Rabbi Meir and the *chachamim* agree. This is a striking point about the centrality of the face: even the *chachamim*, who demand *tzuras adam*, are satisfied when the face appears human, regardless of the body. The face carries the whole determination.

Conversely, if the body is human but the face resembles a ram, *v'lo klum* — everyone agrees there is no fetal status, even according to Rabbi Meir. This might seem surprising. Rabbi Meir had just argued that even a fully animal-appearing fetus can count. Why would a hybrid case fare worse? Tosafot addresses this, noting a distinction between something that wholly resembles an animal and something so thoroughly mixed that it resists categorization in any direction. The hybrid is, in some sense, a harder case than the uniform animal appearance, though the precise logic is not entirely transparent.

The point about the *talya* — a ram — being the chosen example is itself curious. One possibility raised is that it was selected because of its semi-mythological or exotic resonance, much like the *tachash*, serving to highlight the theoretical and classificatory nature of the discussion.

### Mixed Eye Debate

The actual dispute between Rabbi Meir and the *chachamim* is now defined more precisely. It is not the fully animal-looking case, nor the hybrid with an animal face. *Lo nachleku ela* — they only debate the case where the face otherwise appears human, but one eye looks like an animal's eye while the other looks human. Is that partial deviation from human facial appearance sufficient to strip the fetus of its *velad* status?

Rabbi Meir holds that as long as some human appearance (*mitzuras adam*) is present, it is enough. The *chachamim* require complete human appearance (*kol tzuras adam*) — the face as a whole must look human.

A *braita* is then cited that appears to reverse the positions: Rabbi Meir demanding complete appearance and the *chachamim* accepting partial. Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba responds simply: *i tanya tanya* — if that is a received tradition, so be it, even if it differs from his own. These are simply two transmitted versions of the dispute.

### Facial Components

Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba then transmits a further teaching in the name of Rabbi Yochanan specifying which facial features constitute the *tzuras adam* that must be present: *metzach* — the forehead; *hagebinin* — the eyebrows; *ha'einayim* — the eyes; *halistot* — the cheeks; and *gabbot hazakan* — the chin. According to this view, all of these features, *ad she'kulam ke'echad*, must collectively appear human.

It is worth observing what is notably absent from this list: the nose and, especially, the ears. The ears, one might think, are quite distinctively human — other animals have ears that project differently from the skull and lack the characteristic lobular form. Yet the Gemara does not include the ears. This likely reflects something deeper about how the Talmud understands human identity: what we attach to the *face* as a locus of personhood is not simply what is biologically unique, but what we encounter and recognize when we look at another human being. The forehead, the eyes, the cheeks — these are the features through which we read personality and humanity.

### Rava Half-Features

Rava, citing Chasa, offers a different accounting. One need not have all features on both sides of the face. It suffices to have: *metzach* — the forehead, *hagaban* — one eyebrow, *ayin* — one eye, *leset* — one cheek, and *vegabbat hazakan* — one half of the chin, with the requirement that all of these be present together (*ad she'kulam ke'echad*), but only in their singular forms, not their bilateral pairs.

The Gemara notes that Rava and Rabbi Yochanan are not really disputing a principle but simply aligning with the two earlier opinions. Rabbi Yochanan's view — requiring all features bilaterally — corresponds to the position that demands *kol tzuras adam*. Rava's view — requiring all the features but only one of each paired set — corresponds to the position that *mitzuras adam* suffices.

### One Feature Objection

An objection is raised from a *braita*: *tzuras panim she'amru* — when the sages spoke of the appearance of the face as the determining criterion, even *partzuf echad*, a single facial feature, suffices — with the explicit exception of the ear (*chutz min ha'ozen*). This seems to undercut both Rava and Rabbi Yochanan, suggesting that even one feature is sufficient.

Abaye resolves this: *ki tanya hahi le'akev tanya* — that *braita* is teaching not the minimum sufficient for *tumah* but rather the minimum whose absence creates a problem. Missing even one feature is disqualifying — not that one feature alone is sufficient. This aligns with the stricter opinion requiring complete facial appearance. Alternatively, the Gemara suggests reading *echad* not as a single feature but as one from each pair — one of each bilateral set is required, consistent with Rava.

### Missing Limb Position

Rava introduces a related case. If a fetus is born with only one eye and one thigh — not because it resembles an animal, but simply because the other is absent — *min hatzad*, and what is present is in its proper anatomical location, the mother is still *temei'ah*. The single eye is where an eye should be, the single thigh is where a thigh should be. Even a fetus missing paired features, as long as what is there occupies its correct position, carries the status of a *velad*.

### Cyclops Malformation

The situation changes entirely if the eye or the trunk-like limb is located in the center — *be'emtza*. A fetus with a single eye in the middle of its face, like a cyclops, or with a single limb emerging from the center of the torso, *imo tehorah* — the mother is *tehorah*. Despite having human-derived features, the radical displacement from normal human anatomy is sufficient to deprive the fetus of human appearance. What matters is not just the presence of features but their location within the expected human form.

---

## Viability Standard

### Esophagus Viability

The Gemara now shifts its analytical frame. Until this point, the discussion had centered primarily on *appearance* — does the fetus look sufficiently human? A new criterion is introduced: viability. Even granting that a miscarriage confers *tumah*, this holds only if the fetus was developing along a path that could have led to a viable child. If its internal development was fundamentally incompatible with life, the mother is not *temei'ah*.

Rava teaches: *shta nakuv* — if the esophagus had a perforation, the mother is *temei'ah*; *shta atum* — if the esophagus was completely sealed, the mother is *tehorah*. A sealed esophagus means the fetus was developing in a manner that could never have yielded a viable child. The absence of a functional alimentary opening signals not merely deformity but fundamental non-viability, and such a development does not rise to the level of a halachic birth.

This raises a natural question about how such a determination could practically be made in the absence of modern anatomy — whether by palpation, observation at delivery, or some other means available to the Sages. The Gemara does not address this directly.

The broader principle emerging here is important: the Gemara is not asserting that these fetuses are non-human in any philosophical sense. Rather, it is asking a narrow halachic question — was this fetus developing in a way that constituted *velad*, on the trajectory toward a viable child? The framework of before and after forty days of gestation is relevant: only after forty days does a miscarriage confer *tumah* at all; beyond that threshold, certain internal or external conditions can indicate that even a forty-day-plus fetus was not on a viable developmental path.

### Missing Limbs

A *braita* addresses miscarriage of a *guf atum* — a body missing certain limbs. Such a miscarriage does not render the mother *temei'ah leidah*, again because the fetus was developing in a manner incompatible with viability. The Gemara then asks: *v'eizehu guf atum?* — what precisely constitutes a *guf atum*? Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi defines it as missing enough that, had the child been alive, it would have died from this deficiency — *kedei sheyinnatel min hachai vayammut*. The question then becomes: how much must be missing?

### Leg Amputation Debate

At the top of 24b, Rav Zakkai says: *ad ha'arkuvah* — missing up to what appears to be the knee (more precisely, one of the joints of the animal's hind leg, corresponding roughly to the hock). Rabbi Yannai says: *ad lanekevah* — until the genitalia, meaning the entire thigh is absent, not merely the lower leg. Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Yosei ben Yehoshua, extends this further: *ad mekom tiburo* — even up to the navel.

### Eliezer Already Dead

The Gemara identifies the underlying dispute between Rav Zakkai and Rabbi Yannai as turning on a question of *treifa* status: *treifah chayah* — can a *treifah* animal survive? Missing the lower leg renders an animal a *treifah*. If one holds that a *treifah* can nonetheless remain alive for some time, then the lower leg alone is insufficient to establish non-viability; one must require the upper thigh to be missing as well. If one holds that a *treifah* cannot survive, then the lower leg already establishes non-viability.

The debate between Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Yochanan turns on a statement of Rabbi Eliezer: *nittal yarech vechalal shelah* — if the thigh and its socket (the entire hip joint) are removed, *nevelah* — the animal is considered already dead, not merely a *treifah* but in the category of something from which life has already departed. Missing the thigh thus represents a more extreme threshold than mere *treifah* status. Rabbi Yochanan, who goes even further to the navel, apparently rejects that threshold as sufficient and demands a yet greater degree of absence.

It should be emphasized: this entire discussion has nothing to do with appearance. It is purely a question of viability — was this fetus on a developmental path toward a living child?

### Head Defect Priority

Rav Pappa introduces an important asymmetry. The debates just described — Rav Zakkai, Rabbi Yannai, Rabbi Yochanan — all concern deficiencies *milmata lemala*, from the bottom upward. How far from the foot up must be missing before we say the fetus was non-viable? But *milmala lemata* — if something is missing from the head downward — *afilu kol shehu tehorah* — even the slightest deficiency in the head renders the mother *tehorah*. The head is categorically different. Any defect there, however small, is sufficient to establish non-viability.

### Sealed Skull

In keeping with this principle, Rav Giddel in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules: if a woman miscarries a fetus whose skull is sealed — *shegulgolto atuma*, fused or undifferentiated — the mother is *tehorah*. Rashi explains *atuma* here as *chaserah* — lacking, meaning some portion of the skull is absent or improperly formed. The principle of Rav Pappa applies: any cranial deficiency, however partial, disqualifies the fetus from conferring *tumah*.

### Palm Tree Fetus

Rav Giddel also transmits in the name of Rabbi Yochanan a case involving a fetus that resembles *k'min afakta d'dikla* — a palm tree configuration. Rashi describes this as a trunk at the bottom with the limbs emerging from the top, much as a palm tree has its fronds all extending from the crown. The mother in such a case is *tehorah*. The reasoning here appears to rest on viability rather than appearance: such a configuration is presumed incapable of supporting life.

---

## Facial Deformation

### Smushed Face

The Gemara records a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish regarding a fetus whose face is *musmasin* — smushed. The features are present but pressed down or compressed. Rabbi Yochanan holds the mother is *temei'ah*: the face, however distorted, retains enough human appearance. Resh Lakish holds the mother is *tehorah*: even smushed features do not constitute sufficient *tzuras adam*.

### Challenge Logic

Rabbi Yochanan challenges Resh Lakish from a *mishnah* dealing with a case where only a detached limb — a cut-off arm or leg — emerges from the miscarriage without the body. The *mishnah* rules the mother is *temei'ah*, and adds: *v'ein chosheshin shema m'guf atum ba* — we need not be concerned that perhaps the rest of the body was a *guf atum*, a malformed non-viable trunk. The implicit assumption is that we treat the body as normal. Rabbi Yochanan presses: if Resh Lakish is right that a smushed face renders the mother *tehorah*, then the *mishnah* should have added another exemption — we also need not worry that the face was smushed. Its silence on that point suggests no such concern exists, i.e., a smushed face is never a problem, which contradicts Resh Lakish's position.

### Resolution Smushed

Rav Pappi resolves the dispute by redefining its terms. *Musmasin kuli alma lo pligi detmei'ah* — regarding a smushed face, everyone agrees the mother is *temei'ah*. There is no dispute there. The actual debate concerns *panav tuchot* — features that are completely effaced, entirely flattened to the point of erasure, far beyond merely smushed. According to this resolution, Rabbi Yochanan holds the mother is *tehorah* when features are fully effaced; Resh Lakish holds even then the mother is *temei'ah*.

This also dissolves Rabbi Yochanan's challenge to Resh Lakish. The *mishnah*'s silence about the face simply means it need not be mentioned separately: completely effaced facial features are effectively equivalent to a *guf atum*, a body missing limbs. It is the same category — absence of a body part — and is therefore already covered.

---

## Facial Deformation (II)

### Stringency Leniency

The sons of Rabbi Chiya went out to a city and returned to their father reporting a case they had encountered: a fetus was born with *panim tuchot* — completely effaced facial features. They had ruled the mother *temei'ah*, taking what they considered the stringent position, going against the opinion of Rabbi Yochanan who would have declared her *tehorah*.

Rabbi Chiya told them plainly: *tze'u v'taharu mah shetimatem* — go back and reverse your ruling. He then identified their error: *l'chumra? chumra d'ati liyadei kula* — you thought you were being strict? This is a *chumra* that generates a *kula*. By declaring the mother a *yoledet*, they triggered not only the initial period of *tum'at leidah* but also the *yemei tohar* — the following thirty-three or sixty-six days during which bleeding is treated as *tohar blood*, a significant leniency. You cannot play it safe by always ruling *tamei* in childbirth cases; the halachic outcome must be evaluated in full. The *halacha* here follows Rabbi Yochanan: with completely effaced features, the mother is *tehorah*.

This episode encodes a broader principle of the utmost practical importance: *chumrot* do not always produce stringent outcomes. Very often an apparent stringency in one dimension of a halachic framework produces unintended and serious leniencies in another, and the posek must account for the full picture.

---

## Conjoined Twins

### Two Backs Status

The Gemara now introduces a new case: a creature — whether fetus or born animal — that has *shenei gabin ushtei shidra'ot*, two backs and two spinal cords. The question is whether this constitutes a *velad* for a human mother and whether it is permissible as food if born to an animal. The description raises the image of what we would today call conjoined twins fused at the back, though the precise anatomy the Gemara envisions is not entirely clear — the Gemara elsewhere discusses two heads but does not specify that here.

### Rav Non-Viable

Rav rules: *be'ishah eino valad* — by a woman, this is not considered a fetus; the mother is not *temei'ah leidah*. And *bevehemah asurah ba'achilah* — if born from an animal, it is forbidden to eat. The reasoning is not that it looks like an animal or lacks human features in the conventional sense, but rather that it is so fundamentally malformed as to be non-viable.

### Shmuel Viable

Shmuel disagrees: *be'ishah valad* — by a woman, it is a fetus, and the mother is *temei'ah*; *uvevehemah muteret ba'achilah* — and from an animal it is permitted to eat. Shmuel accepts that even a creature with this significant deformity can be viable, and viability is the operative criterion.

The underlying dispute, the Gemara explains, turns on the position of Rabbi Chanin bar Abba. Rabbi Chanin bar Abba identifies the *shasu'ah* mentioned in the Torah among the forbidden animals with precisely this creature — one that has two backs and two spines. Rav understands this to mean: Rav says such a creature *biryah be'alma leita* — does not exist as a viable independent creature. The only place such a thing ever appears is *beme'ei imma* — in the mother's womb. Accordingly, when God taught Moshe that the *shasu'ah* is forbidden, it was referring to the creature in the womb; once born, it is moot because it never survives. For the human mother, it is not a *velad*; for the animal it is forbidden only in the womb on account of that *drasha*.

### Priest Blemish

Rav Shimi bar Chiyya challenges Rav from a Mishnah. The Mishnah in the context of priestly blemishes lists *kol she-yesh lo shenei gavin u-shenei shidra'ot* — a *kohen* with two backs and two spinal cords — as disqualified from Temple service on account of a *mum*. The fact that the Mishnah treats this as a disqualifying blemish presupposes that such a *kohen* exists, functions, and serves. This implies viability, directly contradicting Rav.

---

## Conjoined Twins (II)

### Rav Bent Spine

Rav responds dismissively but with substance: *ach Shimyya* — my dear Shimi — *she-shidrato akuma*, that Mishnah is speaking of a *bent* spine, not a genuinely doubled spine. A kohen with severe spinal curvature, appearing as if he has a double back, is disqualified for his appearance, but this is not the biologically impossible case of true double spines. Rav maintains that a genuine two-spine creature is non-viable and the Mishnah does not contradict this.

### Gestation Periods

The Gemara now cites a *braita* concerning fetal development and the threshold of viability in animals. For a small animal (*dakka*) such as a sheep or goat, whose normal gestation is five months, any fetus born within four months is non-viable. For a large animal (*gassa*) such as a cow, whose normal gestation is nine months, a fetus born within eight months is non-viable. Below those thresholds, the animal is considered not to have reached a stage of development compatible with survival.

The *braita* adds: *yatza mi she-yesh lo shenei gavin u-shenei shidra'ot* — this excludes the case of two backs and two spines. The question is what this exclusion means and how each Amora reads it.

### Rav Reading

Rav explains the *braita* according to his view. The rule that animals born within four or eight months are forbidden applies to those born into the world, *yatza le'avir ha'olam*. But a fetus *bimei immo*, in the mother's womb, is permissible when the mother is slaughtered — a standard rule about fetal animals. The exclusion of the two-spine case means: unlike normal fetuses, the two-spine creature is forbidden *even in the mother's womb*, because it is the *shasu'ah* described by Rabbi Chanin bar Abba, and that prohibition was taught with reference to its in-utero existence. Rav's position thus receives textual support from the *braita*.

### Shmuel Reading

Shmuel reads the *braita* entirely differently. The rule that animals born below the gestation threshold are forbidden applies when their months of development are *not* complete — *she-lo kalu lo chodashav*. If they are fully developed, they are permitted even if premature. The exclusion of the two-spine case means: even when its months are fully complete, once born — *im yatza le'avir ha'olam* — it is forbidden, because it falls under the prohibition of *shasu'ah*. But *bimei immo*, as a fetus in the womb, it is permissible, exactly the reverse of Rav's position.

### Two-Spine Application

The practical consequence for the human case: according to Rav, the two-spine creature is non-viable, never exists independently, and is not a *velad* — the mother is not *temei'ah*. According to Shmuel, such a creature can be viable, and if born it is a *velad* — the mother is *temei'ah*.

### Huna Warning

Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba was inclined to rule like Shmuel in a case that came before him — to declare a woman who miscarried such a creature a *yoledet* and thus *temei'ah*, which would have been the stricter ruling. Rav Huna intervened: *mai da'atach? l'chumra? chumra d'asi lidei kula* — again the same principle. Treating her as a *yoledet* triggers not only the initial *tumah* but the subsequent *yemei tohar*, a significant leniency. Moreover, the standing rule is *halacha keRav be'issurei*, *bein lekula bein lechumra* — in matters of ritual law, we follow Rav whether his ruling is lenient or strict. Rule like Rav: the creature is not viable, and the mother is not a *yoledet*.

---

## Human Animal Gestation

### Human Months

Rava introduces a comparison between the viability standards governing humans and those governing animals. It is established that a human child born in the ninth month is viable, and one born in the seventh month is viable, but one born in the eighth month is not — a physiologically surprising principle that the Gemara nonetheless treats as settled. The question is whether a parallel rule operates for large animals.

### Animal Seven Month

For a large animal such as a cow, we know that a fetus born within eight months — less than the full nine-month gestation — is non-viable. But does the analogy to humans extend further? In humans, both the ninth and seventh months yield viable births. Does this mean a seven-month calf might similarly be viable, in contrast to an eight-month calf?

### Species Distinction

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak directs us to the *braita*: *shemona ulemata asur* — eight months and below is forbidden for a cow. The question is whether this statement refers to cows specifically or to sheep, whose threshold is four months.

### Braita Scope

If the statement refers to cows, it is needed precisely to forestall the analogy to humans: one might have thought that since a seven-month human is viable, a seven-month calf is also viable, and the *braita* corrects this by specifying that for cows, anything less than nine months is problematic. If the statement refers only to sheep, the Gemara asks whether the analogy to seven-month human viability applies to cows after all — and no definitive resolution is offered.

---

## Mythical Creatures

### Lilith Fetus

Rav Yehuda transmits in the name of Shmuel: *hamapelet demus Lilith* — if a woman miscarries a fetus resembling *Lilith*, which Rashi describes as a human form with wings, the mother is *temei'ah leidah*. The wings do not cancel the fundamental human appearance. *Vlada hu ela she-yesh lo knafayim* — it is a fetus, it merely also has wings.

### Simuni Case

A *braita* confirms this ruling. Rabbi Yosi reports that a case arose in Simuni in which a woman gave birth to a *Lilith*-like fetus. When it was brought before the sages, they ruled *vlada hu ela she-yesh lo knafayim* — it is a fetus, with the additional feature of wings. The winged form does not displace human identity.

### Snake Fetus

The Gemara turns to a more challenging case: *hamapelet demus nachash* — a fetus resembling a snake. The difficulty here, which was touched upon earlier in the discussion, is that a snake's eyes have a rounded appearance resembling human eyes, while the rest of the body is entirely unlike a human. Does the eye quality carry sufficient weight?

### Chanania Initial

Chanania ben achi shel Rabbi Yehoshua — Rabbi Yehoshua's nephew — issued a ruling: *imo temei'ah leidah*. The mother is *temei'ah*. The basis of the ruling, as emerges later, was that the eye of the snake-like fetus was round like a human eye, and that was the deciding feature.

### Gamliel Summons

Rabbi Yosi, evidently troubled by this ruling, brought it to Rabban Gamliel's attention. The underlying issue appears to be at least partly one of rabbinic authority: who has the standing to issue an independent halachic ruling of this kind? Rabban Gamliel — who is the *nasi* and whose contentious relationship with Rabbi Yehoshua over questions of rabbinic authority is well documented — sent word to Rabbi Yehoshua: bring your nephew and come before me.

### Daughter-in-law Exchange

As they were on their way, Chanania's daughter-in-law came out to meet them. She addressed Chanania and asked: *hamapelet k'min nachash mahu* — what is the law if the fetus resembles a snake? He answered her: *imo tehorah* — the mother is *tehorah*. He had reversed his ruling. She then pressed him: *v'halo shimcha amra li chamoti* — but your wife told me in your name that the mother is *temei'ah*. Chanania asked what reason his wife had given. The daughter-in-law replied: *ho'il v'galgal eino agol k'shel adam* — because the eye of the snake is round like a human eye.

### Yehoshua Support

This exchange triggered Rabbi Yehoshua's memory. *Nitkar Rabbi Yehoshua* — Rabbi Yehoshua recalled that he himself had once ruled this way, and that Chanania's ruling had in fact been based on his own authority. He sent word to Rabban Gamliel: *mipi horah Chananya* — Chanania's ruling was given on my authority. He should not be in trouble; he was in fact transmitting his uncle's own ruling, which had simply been forgotten.

Whether Chanania was summoned because the ruling was considered incorrect or because the concern was about a junior scholar issuing independent rulings without authorization is itself an interesting question. The resolution — that the ruling was traceable to Rabbi Yehoshua himself — addresses both concerns simultaneously.

### Abyaye Principle

Abyaye derives from this episode a general principle: *tzurba me-rabanan d'amar milta leima b'ta'ameh* — when a Torah scholar issues a ruling, he should state his reasoning alongside it. *D'chi madkru lei midkar* — because if he provides the reason, when someone later reminds him of it, he will remember. If only the conclusion is transmitted — *muttar*, *asur* — the scholar may later be entirely unable to account for the ruling. But if the reason accompanies the ruling, a reminder can restore recollection. This is exactly what happened here: the reasoning transmitted by the daughter-in-law — the round eye — restored Rabbi Yehoshua's memory of his own position and vindicated Chanania entirely.

---

---

# Niddah 25

## Mishnah: Shapir & Gender

### Shapir Definition

The twenty-fifth daf opens with a new *mishnah* at the bottom of 24b, continuing the broader discussion of which types of births and miscarriages render a mother *tme'ah leida* — impure with the impurity of childbirth. The previous *mishnah* had addressed the appearance of the fetus and, as the *gemara* developed, also the question of whether it was in the process of natural development, since even a miscarriage confers *tumah* only if it represents the kind of development that could have led to a viable child.

The key term introduced here is *shapir*. While it is sometimes translated as the embryonic sac, the more precise referent appears to be the developing fetus itself — not the *shilya*, which is the placenta and its membranes, but the thing that is presumably the fetus in formation. The difficulty is that it does not yet have a recognizably human appearance; it is something like a flesh blob, a skin-encased mass of indeterminate status. The very question the *mishnah* is exploring is whether we are prepared to call it a *vlad* — a halachically significant fetus — at all. And as we saw over the preceding days, this breaks down into two related but distinct inquiries: is it a question of appearances, or is it a question of what the thing actually is? Is this a genuine fetus in some stage of development, or is it something else entirely?

### Water/Blood Case

The *mishnah* states: *hamapeles shapir malei mayim, malei dam, malei gnunim, eina chosheshes levlad* — if a woman miscarries a *shapir* filled with water, or with blood, or with various mixed colors, she need not be concerned that it is a *vlad*.

This ruling requires clarification. Does it mean that the *shapir* is not a fetus at all — simply an unidentifiable mass that emerged from her body? Or does it mean that it was once a fetus but never developed along a natural trajectory? After all, a fetus in natural development does contain blood in its system. The distinction being implied here is not that blood is inherently foreign to a fetus, but that a properly developing fetus would not present simply as a container filled with blood or water. Something else must be going on — either it is not a fetus at all, or it developed unnaturally. This is precisely what the *gemara* will explore, but the *mishnah* itself leaves it open.

### Merukam: Stricter Rule

The *mishnah* continues: *ve-im haya merukam, teshev le-zachar u-le-nekevah* — if however the *shapir* is formed, if it actually exhibits some shape of a developing fetus, which the *gemara* will describe in considerable detail later in the *daf*, then she must observe the stricter requirements of both male and female.

What does this mean practically? If the child is male, the mother is *tme'ah* for seven days; if female, for fourteen days — so we assume fourteen days of *tumah*, taking the stricter position. On the other side, if male, she is *tehorah* from day eight through day forty; if female, only from day fifteen through day eighty. The combined stringency therefore means she is *tme'ah* from day one through day fourteen, because it might be female, and *tehorah* from day fifteen through day forty, because it cannot be *tehorah* beyond day forty since it might have been male. That is the practical meaning of *teshev le-zachar u-le-nekevah*.

### Sandal & Placenta

The *mishnah* then addresses two additional cases: *hamapeles sandal* — if the miscarriage is a *sandal*, a flattened fetus — or *shilya*, a placenta. In both cases, the ruling is likewise *teshev le-zachar u-le-nekevah*.

The *shilya* case is more straightforward. As the *gemara* states frequently: *lo she-hashilya vlad, ela she-ein shilya belo vlad* — we are not claiming the placenta is itself the fetus, but a placenta without a fetus is impossible. If there is a placenta, there must have been a fetus. And if there was a fetus, even if it subsequently dissolved and cannot be identified, it may be assumed to have been developing naturally. So the *shapir* discussion concerns cases where we cannot even establish that there was ever a fetus; here, with the *shilya*, that uncertainty is resolved.

The *sandal* — the flattened fetus — appears at first glance to be a simpler case: a fetus that was clearly once developing naturally but became compressed. However, as the *gemara* will clarify, the rabbinic understanding is that a baby becomes a *sandal* by being compressed by another baby in the womb. There is an interesting dispute among the *rishonim* as to whether the *gemara* means to suggest that a woman could become pregnant after she was already pregnant — with the second pregnancy causing the first baby to be flattened — or whether it is simply a matter of twins. But in any event, the *sandal* is understood to imply the likely presence of a second fetus. This is why the ruling of *teshev le-zachar u-le-nekevah* by the *sandal* carries an added dimension beyond mere gender uncertainty: one must also account for the possibility of a second fetus whose presence must be recognized. The *gemara* will address why this matters when the second fetus is not visible and may have dissolved.

---

## Shapir Contents Analysis

### Blood/Water Proof

The *gemara* now analyzes the opening case of the *mishnah*. *Bishlama dam u-mayim, lo khlum hu* — it is understandable that when the *shapir* is filled with water or blood, we say it is nothing, not a *vlad*, because while a fetus does have water and blood in its system, a genuine fetus would not present simply as a container filled with these fluids. That distinction is clear enough.

But the harder case is *gnunim* — the mixed colors, the goopy multicolored contents. Why should that not raise the concern that this was a fetus that dissolved? *Nichush she-vlad hu ve-nimokh* — perhaps we should be concerned that it was indeed a fetus and it dissolved, which would explain the mixture of colors and textures within the sac?

### Abaye: Dissolved Fetus

*Amar Abaye: kama yayin chai shattata immo shel zeh she-nimokh u-vara be-tokh me'eha* — how much raw wine do you think the mother drank that caused the fetus to dissolve inside her womb? This is a striking statement. Abaye is acknowledging that the phenomenon of a dissolved fetus is real — that *yayin chai*, undiluted raw wine, could in extreme cases cause a fetus to dissolve and abort. But he is saying that this is such a rare circumstance, requiring extreme alcohol abuse, that we do not build our default *halacha* around it. Under ordinary circumstances a miscarried fetus does not look like this. So while it is theoretically possible that the mixed colors indicate a dissolved fetus, it is not a realistic concern in the typical case.

### Rava: Not Dissolved

*Rava amar malei tnan* — Rava argues from the language of the *mishnah* itself: it says the *shapir* is *filled* with these mixed contents. *Ve-i ita de-itmuchei itmakh, mikhasar khasar* — if it had truly been a fetus that dissolved on the inside, there would be empty space within the cavity. When a formed thing dissolves, it leaves vacuums, hollows, gaps. The fact that the sac is completely filled is itself proof that it was never a fetus that dissolved; it must have been something else to begin with.

### Rav Adda: Multiple Colors

*Rav Adda bar Abba amar gevanim tnan* — Rav Adda bar Abba focuses on a different aspect of the *mishnah's* language. It says *multiple* colors, not just a single hue. *Ve-i ita de-itmuchei itmakh, kulla be-chad gavna hava ka'ei* — if it were a dissolved fetus, the contents, even if not identifiable as water or blood, would present with a more uniform, consistent color. The wide array of colors is evidence that what is inside is not the product of fetal dissolution.

---

## Abba Shaul: Wine & Bones

### Raw Wine Effects

Since the discussion touched on raw wine, the *gemara* cites a *baraita*: *Abba Shaul omer kover meitim hayiti* — Abba Shaul testified that he was a grave digger by profession. This made sense in the context of the era, when the practice of *likkut atzamot* — the gathering of bones for secondary burial in a niche or cave — meant that grave diggers would regularly encounter skeletal remains after the flesh had decomposed. Abba Shaul therefore had ample opportunity to observe differences in bone condition across many individuals.

His findings: *hashoteh yayin chai atzmotav srufim* — those who had consumed large quantities of raw, undiluted wine had bones that were burnt, consumed, eaten away. This is not merely a rhetorical claim; it reflects a systematic observation from his work.

### Mixed Wine Dosage

By contrast, someone who drank *mazog* — wine that had been properly diluted, as was the convention — fared differently. The *gemara* here reports Rashi's two explanations for the resulting bone condition, *atzmosav shchuyim*: either the bones were blackened, or they were somehow deficient in marrow. This, while not as severe as the damage from raw wine, was still a negative outcome when the drinking was disproportionate. However, if the person drank the proper amount — *karauy*, the right proportion — then *atzmosav meshuchin*, the bones were like anointed with oil, moist and healthy and in genuinely good condition. The *gemara* adds a parallel set of observations: *ve-chol mi she-shtiyaso meruba me-achilaso, atzmosav srufin* — anyone whose drinking exceeds their eating will have burnt bones regardless of the wine's potency. *Achilaso meruba mi-shtiyaso, atzmosav shchuyim* — if eating exceeds drinking, the bones are blackened. And *karauy, atzmosav meshuchin* — with proper balance, the bones are healthy. One must drink neither too much nor too potent a wine, and always in proper proportion to one's food.

### Og's Giant Bones

A second *baraita* is cited, again attributed to Abba Shaul — though the *gemara* notes the alternative attribution *ve-i teima Rabbi Yochanan*, meaning that some attribute this to Rabbi Yochanan, though the identification as a grave digger points more naturally to Abba Shaul. He recounts: *pa'am achas ratzti achar tzvi, ve-nichnasnti be-kulit shel meis* — once while running after a deer, he entered the thigh bone of a corpse. The bone was so vast that the deer could enter it and he could pursue for *shalosh parsa'os* — three parasangs — entirely within the bone, without catching the deer and without reaching the end of the bone. He turned back. *Amru li: shel Og Melech ha-Bashan haysa* — people told him those were the bones of Og, King of Bashan, the biblical giant. The story is embedded here in the text because of the shared context of grave digging and bone examination.

### Absalom's Eye; Stature

Yet another account: *pa'am achas niftacha me'ara tachtai* — a cave opened beneath him, and he found himself standing inside the eye socket of a buried corpse up to his nose. The eye socket was large enough to contain his entire body. When he emerged, *amru li: ayin shel Avshalom haysa* — people told him it was the eye of Absalom. This identification carries its own interest, given Absalom's renowned physical stature and the biblical account of his extraordinary hair.

The *gemara* then addresses a potential objection: *ve-shema tomar Abba Shaul nanos haya* — perhaps one would say that Abba Shaul was himself a small man, a dwarf, and therefore these observations prove nothing about the size of the bones. The *gemara* counters: *Abba Shaul aroch be-dora hava* — Abba Shaul was the tallest of his generation. Indeed, *Rabbi Tarfon magi'ah le-ketefo* — Rabbi Tarfon, himself a tall figure, only reached his shoulders.

### Yeridat Hadorot

This observation about relative stature launches the *gemara* into a striking generational catalog. *Rabbi Tarfon aroch be-dora hava, veRabbi Meir magi'ah le-ketefo* — Rabbi Tarfon was the tallest of his generation, and Rabbi Meir only reached his shoulders. *Rabbi Meir aroch be-dora hava, veRabbi magi'ah le-ketefo* — Rabbi Meir was the tallest of his generation, and Rabbi (Yehudah HaNasi) only reached his shoulders.
