And so it continues: *Rabbi aroch be-dora hava, veRabbi Chiyya magi'ah le-ketefo*; *Rabbi Chiyya aroch be-dora hava, veRav magi'ah le-ketefo*; *Rav aroch be-dora hava, veRav Yehuda magi'ah le-ketefo*. Note that the progression moves from *tanna'im* through the transitional figure of Rabbi Chiyya into the *amora'im*. *Rav Yehuda aroch be-dora hava, ve-Adda Dayyala magi'ah le-ketefo* — and Adda Dayyala, Rashi explains, was the rabbinic assistant (*shamsha de-rabbanan*), already a step removed from the scholarly hierarchy.

At the top of 68a the progression continues further: *Parshavna de-Pumbedita* — an office or a man's name, with Tosafot suggesting it was the governor of Pumbedita — *kailei lei le-Adda Dayyala ad palgei*, only reached half his height. And finally, *ve-chulei alma kailei lei le-Parshavna de-Pumbedita ad chartzei* — the general population only reached the loins of that figure. The subtext is unmistakably *yeridat hadorot* — the decline of generations in stature, greatness, and distinction. Each subsequent generation's tallest figure reaches only the shoulders of the previous one — a pattern that seems to describe far more than physical height, tracking as it does the succession from the greatest *tanna'im* through the *amora'im* and then into mere rabbinic functionaries and the general populace.

One might ask why Rabbi Meir is chosen as the tallest of his generation given that the *halacha* almost never follows his opinion. The *gemara* itself frequently notes that Rabbi Meir was the most brilliant of his generation — so much so that others could not always follow his reasoning. Stature in wisdom and positional authority in *pesak halacha* are not always the same thing. The choice of Rabbi Meir, Rabbi (Yehudah HaNasi), Rabbi Chiyya, and Rav is fairly clear; Rav Yehuda is a major *amora* and defensible. The choices of Abba Shaul, Rabbi Tarfon, and Adda Dayyala are less immediately obvious from the standard hierarchy.

---

## Shapir Meat: R. Yehoshua

### Shapir All Flesh

The *gemara* now takes up a question that was posed before Rabbi (Yehudah HaNasi): *hamapel shapir malei basar mahu* — what is the law if the *shapir* is completely filled with flesh? Not water, not blood, not a mixture of colors, but solid flesh. This, intuitively, seems like it ought to be a fetus — what is a developing fetus if not flesh? Yet it has not yet achieved the state of *merukam*, meaning it has not yet begun to take on identifiable features of a formed fetus. It is a solid flesh blob, but unshapen. Rabbi responded: *lo shamati* — I have no tradition on this matter.

### R. Yishmael: Flesh Case

At that point, *Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yose* spoke up: *kach amar Abba* — here is what my father, Rabbi Yose, said. *Malei dam, tme'ah niddah* — if the *shapir* is filled with blood, she is *tme'ah* as a *niddah*, recalling the earlier discussions about blood that issues in a contained form. *Malei basar, tme'ah leida* — if it is filled with flesh, it is considered a *vlad* and she is *tme'ah* with the impurity of childbirth. So Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yose provided a clear, two-part ruling from his father.

### Rabbi Challenges

Rabbi's response is striking. *Im malei davar chadash amarta lanu mishum avicha, shma'nucha* — had you simply cited your father's ruling as a novel position we had never heard, we would have accepted it without question; your father's authority is unimpeachable. *Achshav, me-ha kamaisa ke-yachida ka'amar* — but now you have revealed too much. Because the first part of the ruling — that the *shapir* filled with blood makes her a *niddah* — is in fact a minority opinion, associated with Rabbi Meir, not the majority view. The majority position, as the *gemara* understands it, is that blood contained entirely within a sac, without ever reaching the vaginal wall, does not confer *niddah* status. So since the first ruling of Rabbi Yose follows a minority view, Rabbi now suspects the second ruling might similarly track a minority position — *shema amar mishum Rabbi Yehoshua* — perhaps he was following Rabbi Yehoshua, who is about to be quoted, and whose ruling is likewise a minority opinion. *Ve-ein halacha ke-Rabbi Yehoshua* — and we would not rule like Rabbi Yehoshua, at least as a *yachid* against the *rabbim*.

### Braita: Formed/Unformed

The *gemara* now cites the relevant *baraita* directly: *hamapel shapir she-eino merukam* — if a woman miscarries a *shapir* that is not yet formed. *Rabbi Yehoshua omer vlad* — Rabbi Yehoshua says it is considered a *vlad*. *Ve-Chachamim omrim eino vlad* — the *Chachamim* say it is not. This is the center of the debate: the *mishnah* spoke of the formed fetus (*merukam*) and the unformed contents (water, blood, colors); the *baraita* now adds the middle case — the unformed flesh blob — and presents the disagreement explicitly.

### RS ben Lakish Debate

Two *amora'im* dispute what exactly is the scope of this disagreement. *Amar Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish mishum Rabbi Yehoshua: machloket be-achur* — Reish Lakish says in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua that the dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and the *Chachamim* applies only when the flesh is *achur*, opaque or dark. Rashi understands this as referring to a flesh that contains cloudy liquid; Tosafot argues the distinction is between flesh that is visually opaque — normal looking flesh with thickness and density — versus flesh that is more translucent. *Aval be-tzalul, divrei ha-kol eino vlad* — but if the flesh is transparent or translucent, everyone agrees it is not a *vlad*.

By contrast, *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi omer: be-tzalul machloket* — Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the opposite, that the debate applies precisely when it is translucent; the dispute is there, not in the opaque case. The *gemara* then asks whether according to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, the *machloket* applies only to the translucent case with the opaque being universally a *vlad*, or whether the dispute applies to both cases. *Teiku* — the *gemara* leaves this question unresolved.

---

## Skin Derasha

### Genesis Verse

The *gemara* now introduces a *derasha* from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya — who is, it should be noted, *stam* Rabbi Yehoshua throughout the *mishnah*, the same Rabbi Yehoshua whose ruling was quoted in the *baraita* above — and presents here his exegetical basis for his position. *Vaya'as Hashem Elokim le-Adam u-le-ishto kasnot or va-yalbishem* — "And God made for Adam and his wife garments of skin and dressed them." The *derasha* reads *or* not as leather but as skin in the literal sense: God clothed Adam and Chava in actual flesh and skin. The verse is then applied to a principle about human development: *melamed she-ein HaKadosh Baruch Hu oseh or la-adam ela im ken nutzar* — God does not form skin for a human being unless that human has been created, meaning unless it was a developing fetus. The implication is that the presence of skin on a *shapir* is proof that it was once a genuine fetus in development.

### Skin Proof Logic

The logic of the *derasha* runs as follows: skin is something that God fashions specifically for a formed human being. Therefore, anything exhibiting skin must, by the verse's implication, have been a developing human. Applied to the case of the *shapir*: if this flesh blob has skin on it — a visible epidermis distinct from mere undifferentiated tissue — that is sufficient proof that it was a *vlad*, regardless of what is found on its interior. The concern about water or blood on the inside would presumably mean that such a *shapir* lacked skin, or that the question about skin was never raised in those cases; here the argument is that once skin is present, the identity as a fetus is established.

### Opaque vs. Transparent

The *gemara* now uses this *derasha* to weigh in on the dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. *Lo shna achur ve-lo shna tzalul* — since the ruling is derived from a verse about skin, it does not matter whether the skin is opaque or transparent; the verse does not differentiate. Now, *ei amarta bishlama be-tzalul machloket* — if you accept the position of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the dispute applies to the translucent case, then there is a good reason Rabbi Yehoshua needed to cite a *pasuk*. One would have thought that transparent skin is insufficient evidence of fetal development — the verse comes to teach us otherwise, that even transparent skin establishes fetal status.

*Ela ei amarta be-achur machloket, lama li kra, svara be-alma hu* — but if you say, as Reish Lakish does, that the dispute is only about opaque skin, then what is the verse accomplishing? Opaque skin as a proof of fetal development is a straightforward logical inference; one does not need a scriptural derivation for it. The very fact that Rabbi Yehoshua found it necessary to cite a *pasuk* suggests he was ruling in a case where logic alone would not have led to that conclusion — namely, the case of transparent skin. *Shema mina be-tzalul machloket. Shema mina.* This supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's position.

The observation that *lama li kra, svara be-alma hu* deserves a brief note. The phrase reflects the *gemara's* recognition of the independent force of logical reasoning (*svara*). Indeed, in more dramatic instances elsewhere, the *gemara* will go so far as to override the plain meaning of a verse because the *svara* compels a different reading — *shavik leih le-kra de-dachik ve-uki anafsheih*, setting aside a verse that strains under the weight of logic and interpreting it in accordance with reason. Such cases illustrate the remarkable authority accorded to *svara* within the *gemara's* halachic methodology. As a related matter, it should be noted that proof from *pesukim* carries relatively little independent weight in *halachic* adjudication; the *gemara* is the operative code for *halacha*, not the *Chumash*, and proofs from *pesukim* function more typically as *asmachta* — support and reinforcement — than as primary *halachic* sources.

---

## Rav Nachman Position

### RN: Opaque Only

Notwithstanding the seemingly strong inference just drawn in favor of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's position, the *gemara* immediately reports: *ve-chein amar Rav Nachman, amar Rabbah bar Avuha: machloket be-achur* — Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha states that the dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and the *Chachamim* applies only in the case of opaque skin. *Aval be-tzalul, divrei ha-kol eino vlad* — but if the skin is transparent, all agree it is not a *vlad*. So despite the *gemara's* inference from the *derasha*, Rav Nachman holds with Reish Lakish. The question remains unresolved as a matter of final ruling.

### Rava: Bechoros Challenge

Rava now challenges Rav Nachman with a *mishnah* from *Bechoros*. The issue there is determining whether a birth counted as a first birth, which affects whether the next offspring is a *bechor*. The *mishnah* states: *siman bi-vehemah dakah, tinuf* — for a small animal, a malodorous discharge is the sign that a fetus had previously passed; *be-gasah, shilya* — for a large animal like a cow, a placenta; *be-ishah, shapir ve-shilya* — for a woman, either a *shapir* or a *shilya*. The question Rava presses is: why does the *mishnah* cite the *shapir* specifically for a woman and not for an animal?

### Shapir for Animals

*De-ilu shapir bi-vehemah lo patar* — the *shapir* does not exempt from *bechor* status in the case of an animal. If we are simply speaking of an opaque, unformed but plausible fetus, the logic that it is a *vlad* should apply equally to animals and humans. Why then is the *shapir* cited only for the human case?

*Ei amarta bishlama be-tzalul machloket* — if we say the dispute (and Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling that it is a *vlad*) applies to the case of transparent skin, then we have a ready explanation: the verse cited by Rabbi Yehoshua — *kasnot or*, God clothing human beings in skin — creates a specific derivation for humans. Transparent skin would be considered a *vlad* for a woman because of that *pasuk*; for an animal, where no such verse applies, it would not be. The asymmetry between human and animal is accounted for by the scriptural basis. *Mishum hachi be-ishah, deribi beih kra, patar bah; be-vehemah, de-lo ribi beih kra, lo patar bah*.

*Ela ei amarta be-achur machloket* — but if you say the debate concerns only opaque skin, the argument rests entirely on *svara*, on logical inference. And if the logic holds, *mai shna ishah u-mai shna behemah* — what distinguishes a woman from an animal? Why should an opaque, unformed but plausible flesh mass count as a *vlad* for a woman and not for an animal? No adequate answer suggests itself.

The *gemara* responds by challenging the premise: *mi savrat Rabbi Yehoshua vadai peshita lei* — do you really think Rabbi Yehoshua held with certainty that these unformed fetuses are definitively a *vlad*? Not necessarily. *Rabbi Yehoshua sfuki me-safeka lei* — perhaps Rabbi Yehoshua was himself in doubt about how to classify these borderline cases. When he said they are a *vlad*, he meant he was ruling stringently out of uncertainty, not that he had a definitive tradition. *Mesafeka lei ve-azil hacha le-chumra ve-hacha le-chumra* — he goes stringently in each direction, and the directions happen to be opposite depending on the context.

*Gabi ishah de-mamona hu* — in the case of a woman and the *bechor* question, the practical consequence for a human *bechor* is monetary: whether the father must give five *shekel* to the *kohen* for *pidyon haben*. Under doubt, *safek mamona le-kula* — monetary uncertainty is resolved leniently. Since the *kohen* is trying to extract money, the doubt favors the father. Therefore, treating the *shapir* as a *vlad* means the next child is not required to undergo *pidyon haben* — a lenient outcome for the father. This is the appropriate way to handle the doubt.

*Gabi behemah de-isura hu* — but for an animal *bechor*, the practical consequence is a prohibition: working the animal, shearing it. *Hatam de-ika gabi giza ve-avoda, safek isura le-chumra* — there the doubt is in the domain of prohibition, and prohibitory doubt is resolved stringently. We must assume the animal might be a *bechor* and treat it accordingly. So the *shapir* does not release the animal from *bechor* status, not because it is definitely not a *vlad*, but because under doubt we are strict about prohibitions. The very same unformed *shapir* generates opposite legal consequences in the two domains, not because its status differs, but because the rules governing doubt differ.

This resolution then also explains Rabbi Yehoshua's position in the context of *tumah* and *tahara* for the woman herself: *hacha nami gabi ishah safek tumah le-chumra* — here too, where we are dealing with the woman's *tumah*, we are stringent, and she is treated as *tme'ah*. As for the clean days of *tahara*, Rabbi Yehoshua would not grant them under this doubt, because that too would be a leniency. Rashi in fact explains the *mishnah* in a way that requires this understanding — that saying it is a *vlad* here means only that she receives the days of *tumah*, not that she receives any days of *tahara*.

### RH: Multiple Views

*Amar lei Rav Chanina bar Shelmia le-Rav* — Rav Chanina bar Shelmia posed the situation to Rav: we now have multiple positions before us. Rabbi (Yehudah HaNasi) said he had no tradition about the unformed flesh *shapir*. Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yose ruled it is *tme'ah leida*. Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi debated whether that ruling applied to opaque or transparent skin. *Mar ke-man sevira lei* — where does Rav himself stand?

### Rav vs. Shmuel

*Amar lei: ani omer echad zeh ve-echad zeh eino chosheshes* — Rav answered that whether the *shapir* is opaque or transparent, if it is unformed it is not a *vlad* and there is no concern. This aligns with the *Chachamim* who argued against Rabbi Yehoshua. *U-Shmuel amar echad zeh ve-echad zeh chosheshes* — Shmuel by contrast says that in either case one must be concerned; it may be a *vlad* and one must be stringent in all directions. Shmuel, then, is the more stringent voice, treating every case of unformed *shapir* — whether opaque or translucent — as a doubtful *vlad* requiring caution.

---

## Shmuel: Nechardea Rule

### Never Tahor

*Ve-azal Shmuel le-ta'amei* — Shmuel consistently applied his own reasoning. *De-chi ata Rav Dimi amar: me'olam lo ishta'kechu shapir be-Nehardea* — when Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael to Bavel he reported that in Nehardea, Shmuel's city, they never treated an unformed *shapir* as *tahor*. Even if it was wholly unformed, even if it was translucent, Shmuel was always concerned that it might have the status of a *vlad*, and the woman was never declared *tahor* on that basis.

### Transparent Exception

There was, however, one exception. *Lebar me-ahu shapira de-asai le-kamei de-Shmuel* — except for a specific case of a *shapir* brought before Shmuel himself. *De-manach lei chuta de-sa'ara me-hai gisa ve-chazei lei me-hai gisa* — he placed a single strand of hair on one side and could see it through from the other side. This was genuinely transparent skin, not merely light in color or thin in texture, but so clear that a hair placed behind it was visible through it. *Amar: im ita de-vlad hava, lo hava zichi kulei hai* — Shmuel declared that if this were truly a fetus, it would not be this transparent. That extreme degree of translucence was itself definitive evidence that the object was not a *vlad*. In that singular case alone Shmuel was prepared to say it was *tahor*.

---

## Fetal Formation Signs

### Eyes Formation

The *mishnah* having established the category of *merukam* — the formed fetus — the *gemara* now turns to the detailed description of what that means in practice. *Tanu rabanan eizehu shapir merukam* — the rabbis taught: what constitutes a formed *shapir*? *Abba Shaul omer techilas briyaso* — Abba Shaul says it is when the fetus is at the beginning of its formation. Some manuscripts read *me-rosho*, meaning formation begins from the head, though other traditions in the *gemara* indicate development begins from the navel; Tosafot notes that some texts read *ke-rashum*, meaning lizard-like, and explains that this refers not to the shape but to the scale — the external limbs are at the size of a lizard's. *U-shtei einav ki-shtei tipin shel zvuv* — its two eyes look like two drops, the two eyes of a fly: extremely small, like dots.

### RChiyya Details

Rabbi Chiyya taught a more detailed *baraita* on the same theme, expanding on the description of fetal formation signs. The two eyes, *meruchakim ze mi-ze* — are spread apart from one another, positioned toward the sides of the head rather than close together as in a fully formed human face. *Shnei chotmin ki-shtei tipin shel zvuv* — the two nostrils are likewise like two tiny drops, each like the eye of a fly in scale. *U-mekuravim ze la-ze* — but unlike the eyes, the nostrils are close to each other. *U-fiv patuach ke-chut ha-sa'ara* — the mouth appears as just a hairline opening, a thin line. *U-geviyato ka-adasha* — and the genital area looks like a lentil bean; this is described specifically for the male, a small round protrusion.

*Ve-im hayta nekevah, nidonah (or nikeret) ki-se'orah le-orkah* — and if it was female, the appearance is like a barley bean lengthwise, and the *gemara* will shortly specify that it appears as a barley bean split down the middle, which is how the beginning of female genital development presents.

### No Digits Yet

*Ve-chituch yadayim ve-raglayim ein lo* — at this stage the fetus does not yet have defined hands and feet. Whether this means there are no limbs at all or that the digits are not yet separated is not entirely certain; it may be that what is being described is the absence of distinct fingers and toes rather than the absence of limb buds entirely. *Ve-al ze meforash ba-kabbala* — on this a verse from *Iyov* is cited: *halo ke-chalav tatchini* — did You not pour me out like milk; *u-ki-gevina takpiani* — You congealed me like cheese; *or u-vasar talbisheni* — You clothed me with skin and flesh; *u-ve-atzamot u-gidim te-sochecheni* — and with bones and sinews You wove me. The verse is read as describing the sequential stages of fetal development, with skin and flesh preceding the full formation of bones and limbs.

### Inspection Methods

*Ve-ein bodkin oto be-mayim* — one does not inspect this fetus in water. *She-ha-mayim azim ve-tordin oto* — water is harsh and will cause the delicate tissue to dissolve or disintegrate. *Ela bodkin oto be-shemen* — instead, one uses oil for inspection, *she-ha-shemen rach u-metzachtzecho* — because oil is gentle and clarifies the surface, allowing one to see the features clearly. *Ve-ein ro'im ela ba-chamma* — and the inspection should be done only in sunlight, not in artificial light or shade. The precision required to identify these minute features — dots for eyes, a hairline for the mouth — makes adequate illumination essential.

### Gender Detection

*Keitzad bodkin oto* — and what specifically are they inspecting for? *Le-da'at im zachar hu im nekevah hi* — to determine whether it is male or female. This is of direct *halachic* consequence: the gender of the fetus determines whether the mother's period of *tum'at leida* is forty days or eighty days. If the *shapir* is confirmed to be *merukam*, she is *tme'ah leida*, but the length of the subsequent *taharah* period depends on the gender. Therefore one wants to inspect the genital area as carefully as possible without disrupting the tissue — hence the use of oil and sunlight.

---

## Stick Test Debate

### Toothpick Method

*Abba Shaul omer* — and some say *Abba Shaul bar Ramash* — describes a practical testing method. *Mevi kisam she-rosho chalak* — one brings a toothpick with a smooth tip, free of splinters. *U-mena'ne'o be-oto makom* — one moves it around in the genital area of the fetus. *Im sachsech, be-yadu'a she-zachar hu* — if the toothpick meets an obstruction, it is known to be male; the resistance comes from a protruding structure, identifiable as the beginning of the male genital. *Ve-im lav, be-yadu'a she-nekevah hi* — and if there is no such obstruction, it is known to be female.

### Vertical Movement Only

*Amar Rav Nachman amar Rabbah bar Avuha: lo shanu ela mi-lemata le-ma'ala* — Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha specifies that this method is valid only when the toothpick is moved vertically, from below upward.

### Side Movement Risk

*Aval min ha-tzedadim, eima kotlei beit ha-rachem ninhu* — if one moves the toothpick from side to side, there is a concern that any resistance encountered might not be from the male genital at all, but from the walls of the uterus (or, as the context suggests, possibly the labia). A false-positive reading of obstruction in the lateral direction could therefore lead to an erroneous gender determination. Only vertical movement provides a reliable result.

---

## Female Genitalia Signs

### Barley Bean Split

*Amar Rabbah bar Abba, tana: im hayta nekevah nidonit ki-se'oret sedukah* — Rabbah bar Abba cited a *baraita*: if it was female, the genital area is judged by its resemblance to a barley bean that is split down the middle. This describes the visible external anatomy of early female fetal development — a small double protrusion divided by a central groove.

### Scrotum Alternative

*Masiv lei Rav Nachman: u-dilma chuta de-veitzim ninhu* — Rav Nachman raised an objection: how do we know that this split protrusion represents female genitalia? Perhaps it is the scrotum of a male fetus, with the central line being the *raphe* — the dividing seam between the two scrotal compartments, visible on the exterior.

### Scrotum Absent

*Amar Abaye: hashta beitzim gufaihu lo yedi'ei* — Abaye responded: at the developmental stage we are discussing, the scrotum itself has not yet descended or developed externally, so it cannot be seen at all. *Chuta de-veitzim yedi'ei* — and you think the dividing line of the scrotum would already be visible? Clearly not. If there is a visible split protrusion at this stage, it must be female genitalia.

---

## Limb Thread Appearance

### RAmram Thickness

*Amar Rav Amram, tana: shetei yerecho teha ki-shnei chutin shel zehorit* — Rav Amram cited a *baraita*: the two thighs of the fetus at this stage of development resemble two strands of red thread. *Ve-amar Rav Amram alah: ke-shel erev* — and Rav Amram added by way of clarification: they are as thick as the *erev*, which is the thicker element of the weave (the woof rather than the warp). *U-shnei zero'oteha ki-shnei chutin shel zehorit* — similarly the two arms look like two threads of the same material. *Ve-amar Rav Amram: lo ke-shel sheti* — and the arms are the thickness of the *sheti*, which is the thinner element of the weave. The arms at this stage are therefore thinner than the thighs.

---

## Hair Test Requirement

### Hair Required

*Amar lei Shmuel le-Rav Yehuda: Shinena* — Shmuel addressed his student Rav Yehuda with the affectionate epithet meaning "sharp one." *Lo ta'avid uvda ad she-yash'ir* — do not render a definitive ruling treating something as a *vlad* until you see hair on it. This is a notably stringent requirement, since fetal hair development occurs relatively late and is not easily visible on a tiny miscarried fetus.

Shmuel's overall approach now becomes apparent in its full scope: from the opposite direction, he had already stated that even an unformed, translucent *shapir* requires concern and must be treated stringently as a possible *vlad*. Now he adds that at no point should one treat it as a *definite* and fully established *vlad* until hair is present. So throughout the entire intermediate range — from formless to clearly formed but before hair — Shmuel holds the status in suspense: *tme'ah* on the *tumah* side, but no *taharah* days.

### Contradiction Noted

*U-mi amar Shmuel hachi? Ve-ha-amar Shmuel echad zeh ve-echad zeh chosheshes* — this raises an apparent contradiction. Shmuel said in the previous discussion that in both cases — whether opaque or translucent — one must be concerned that it is a *vlad*. If he is concerned about even an unformed *shapir*, that seems to indicate he treats it as a *vlad*. But here he says do not call it a *vlad* until there is hair. These two positions seem to pull in opposite directions: one says treat even the formless as a *vlad*, the other says do not call even the formed a *vlad* until it has hair.

### RAmi Resolution

*Amar Rav Ami bar Shmuel* — Rav Ami bar Shmuel resolved this from his own transmission of Shmuel's teaching. *Lei-chosh chosheshes* — yes, one is concerned and treats it as a *vlad* in the stringent direction: she receives the days of *tumah*. *Yemei taharah lo yahavinan lah ad she-yash'ir* — but we do not grant her days of *taharah* until hair is present, meaning we do not treat the *vlad* as fully established in the lenient direction either. From the very beginning, when the *shapir* is still unformed and even translucent, through the point when it begins to take on recognizable features but before hair develops, the entire period is treated as a doubtful *vlad*: the days of *tumah* are observed, but no days of *taharah* are granted. Only once hair is visible does the status shift to a definitively established *vlad* with full accompanying *taharah* days.

---

## Fetus Dating Story

### 41-Day Fetus

The *gemara* concludes with a remarkable story illustrating Shmuel's concern about uncertainty in these judgments — and paradoxically, his extraordinary personal ability to transcend it. *De-hahu shapira de-atai le-kamei de-Mar Shmuel* — a miscarried fetus was brought before Shmuel. He examined it and declared: *arbai bar arbayin ve-chad yoma* — this fetus is 41 days in development.

### 40 Days Calc

*U-vachashi mi-yoma de-azla le-tvila ad hahu yoma, ve-lo havei ela arbayin yoman* — when the relevant party calculated backward from the day the fetus was miscarried to the most recent day the woman had immersed in the *mikveh*, the interval came to only 40 days. Shmuel's count of 41 days of development thus implied that conception had occurred before the immersion, meaning the husband had cohabited with his wife while she was still a *niddah*. *Ve-amar lehu: hai bi-niddah ba'al* — Shmuel declared: this man had relations with his wife while she was a *niddah*. *Ve-odi ve-aktafei* — the husband confessed and Shmuel administered lashes.

### Shmuel Exceptional

*Shani Shmuel de-rav govria* — Shmuel was exceptional; his ability was sui generis. He could look at a fetus and determine its developmental age to the day with a precision that others simply could not match. It is precisely because he understood how difficult this assessment is for ordinary people — and how catastrophic an error in judgment could be — that his rules for everyone else are so stringent. His own extraordinary capacity led him to appreciate rather than underestimate the risks of error. And therefore while he himself could function with confidence, he issued rules for his students and for posterity that demanded caution at every stage.

One final observation is worth noting. The story introduces the 40-to-41-day threshold, which raises a question about the nature of all the preceding discussions. Throughout this *daf*, when the *gemara* discusses unformed or partially formed fetuses, the question has been framed in terms of identification: is this *shapir* really a *vlad* or is it something else? Yet the story of Shmuel's dating suggests an alternative framing: perhaps the concern is not purely one of identification, but also of sufficiency of development — whether the fetus has reached 40 days and thus attained a threshold of *halachic* significance. Both framings may be simultaneously operative. And for those familiar with the first chapter of *Ketubot*, the phrase *shani Shmuel de-rav govria* carries an additional resonance there that provides its own illuminating counterpoint to this passage.

---

---

# Niddah 27

## Placenta & Fetus

### Fetus in Placenta

The daf opens eight lines from the bottom of 26b, where the Gemara had been working through the halachic relationship between a *shilya* (placenta) and the fetus it is presumed to contain. The foundational principle is that a *shilya* is assumed to contain a dissolved fetus, rendering the woman *tme'ah leida* (impure with the impurity of childbirth) and, if the *shilya* is in a house, rendering that house *tamei* with the *tum'ah* of a corpse. The Gemara's preceding discussion addressed the situation where both a fetus and a placenta are present: is the placenta connected to the already-identified fetus, or does it indicate an additional fetus?

The *tanya* had established that when the first birth is a *nefel* (non-viable miscarriage), the placenta is presumed connected only if it emerges within three days; beyond that, one must be concerned that it represents an independent fetus. When the first birth is a live birth, however, no second fetus could have survived alongside it without emerging immediately — and therefore the placenta, however late it appears, is presumed connected to that live birth. The final ruling attributed to the students of Rav added a further distinction: the presumption of connection applies only when the fetus was on a path toward viability. If the fetus was of a kind that could not have been viable, the placenta may be independent.

### Viability & Connection

With this framework established, the Gemara turns to a question posed by Rav Yose ben Shaul to Rebbi: what of a fetus that looks like a raven — one of those anomalous births that bear an animal appearance? Such a fetus does not confer *tumat leida*, since it lacks a human form. Does its placenta follow the same rules? The question carries an inherent ambiguity that the Gemara does not fully resolve: when the text describes a fetus that *looks* like a raven, it may be gesturing at something more essential than mere appearance — that on some level, the Gemara regards such a birth as partaking of the nature of what it resembles.

### Animal Appearance

Rebbi's response is pointed: *ein tolin ela bedavar sheyesh bemino shilya* — one may only ascribe a placenta to a type of creature that actually produces placentas. Mammals have placentas; birds do not. Since this fetus presents as a raven, its placenta cannot logically be attributed to it. Rebbi's reasoning implicitly confirms that the Gemara treats the animal-like appearance as indicative of some underlying essence — the *shilya* simply does not belong to something of avian nature.

### Physical Connection

Rav Yose ben Shaul presses further: what if the placenta is physically intertwined (*keshurah*) with the fetus? Here the physical connection seems to supply direct evidence that they are one. Rebbi dismisses even this question, declaring it a case that simply never occurs (*davar she'eino she'altah*) — implying that his assumption about the avian nature of such a fetus made it inconceivable that a placenta would be present at all, and therefore the question of physical entwinement is moot.

### Multiple Fetuses

A *baraita* then challenges this dismissal. It teaches that if a woman miscarries something that looks like a *behemah*, *chayah*, or *of* (domestic animal, wild animal, or bird), and a placenta accompanies it, then: if the placenta is physically connected (*keshurah*) to the fetus, there is no concern that it represents a separate child — it is treated as one birth. If the placenta is not connected, one must be concerned that it is an independent fetus. The *baraita* further specifies that when there is such concern, the stringencies of two births are imposed — a significant ruling whose practical implications differ depending on whether one follows Rabbi Meir's view (that an animal-appearing fetus does produce *tumat leida*) or that of the *Chachamim* (that it does not).

This *baraita* directly contradicts Rebbi on two counts: it demonstrates both that physical connection *does* occur in such cases, and that it *does* matter halachically. The Gemara accepts this as a *tiyuvta*.

One might ask: if the placenta is not physically connected but the fetus is there, why not simply assume they belong together? The Gemara answers that one must say: *shema nimuach shapir shel shilya* — perhaps the fetus of that placenta dissolved, and separately, the placenta of the unusual fetus dissolved — leaving us with one anomalous-looking fetus and one independent placenta, which happen to be in proximity. Once they are not physically connected and the fetus is of this unusual type, the circumstantial case for connection is overcome by this alternative possibility.

---

## Twin Birth Timing

### Placenta Order

The Gemara next cites a ruling transmitted by Rabba bar Shmuel citing Rav Chisda citing Shmuel: there was a case in which the placenta was attributed as connected to the fetus even ten days after the birth — consistent with the principle that a live birth always retains its connection to the subsequent placenta. The Gemara then specifies a crucial boundary: *velo amru tulin ela beshilya habaa achar havlad* — this entire principle applies only when the placenta follows the fetus. If the placenta emerged before the fetus, it cannot be attributed to it; instead, one must be concerned that it was an independent birth, with a dissolved fetus inside it, and that the fetus which emerged afterward was a separate event entirely. While such a sequence is presumably very rare (hence the term "afterbirth"), the Gemara establishes that when it does occur, the presumption of connection does not apply.

### 33-Day Separation

Rabba bar bar Chana then reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that there was a case where the placenta was attributed to the birth even twenty-three days later. Rav Yosef interjects that when this tradition was transmitted to him, the figure was twenty-four days, not twenty-three — and the Gemara leaves that discrepancy without resolution.

Rav Acha the son of Rav Avira then reports in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak a case of a different kind altogether: not a placenta following a birth, but an actual second birth following the first by thirty-three days — *vlad achar chaveiro lamed gimel yom*. Again Rav Yosef objects that when the report was transmitted to him, the interval was thirty-four days. Here the Gemara sets aside the one-day discrepancy and grapples with the more fundamental puzzle: how is it possible for two viable twin births to be separated by thirty-three (or thirty-four) days?

### Month Viability

The difficulty is rooted in the Gemara's understanding of which gestational months yield viable births. The Gemara assumes that only a seventh-month baby or a full ninth-month baby can be viable. An eighth-month baby, or a ninth-month baby born before the completion of nine months (on one opinion), is not viable.

The Gemara frames this as a dispute: *hanicha leman de'amar yoledes letisha yoledes lekitain* — according to the opinion that viability in the ninth month obtains even if birth occurs partway through the month, the case is straightforward. The first twin was born toward the end of the seventh month, the second was born in the beginning of the ninth month — and both were viable. But according to the stricter opinion, that a ninth-month baby is viable only at the full completion of nine months, the arithmetic creates a problem: if the first twin was born anywhere in the seventh month, thirty-three days later places the second birth somewhere in the ninth month but not necessarily at its end.

### 3-Month Separation

The Gemara resolves the difficulty by reversing (*ipuch shmateta*) the earlier attributions: the thirty-three day interval actually referred to the placenta case, and the twenty-three day interval referred to the second-birth case. With twenty-three days separating two births, and assuming viability anywhere in the seventh month (which the Gemara grants more liberally than it does for the ninth), both twins could have been born in the seventh month.

A further case then extends the discussion dramatically: Avdimi bar Abba (or Rav Adda) cites a report from Rav Menachem of the village of Sharim that a second birth followed the first by three months — and, the Gemara adds, *ve'hareihem yoshvim lefanenu beveit hamidrash*: both children were alive and sitting right there in the *beit midrash*. The Gemara identifies them: Yehuda and Chizkiya, the sons of Rabbi Chiya, who were twins separated by three months of gestation.

### One Drop Split

This prompts an immediate difficulty: the Gemara elsewhere assumes that a woman who conceives cannot conceive again until she gives birth — so how could this be explained as anything other than a second conception three months after the first? The answer, attributed to Abaye, is: *tipa achat hayta venichalka lishnayim* — it was one drop (of seed) that divided into two. Both twins were conceived in the same act; one reached completion of form early (toward the beginning of the seventh month) and the other reached completion of form late (toward the end of the ninth month), and so they were born three months apart.

---

## Placenta Impurity

### Meir vs. Colleagues

Having established the rules about the *shilya*'s connection to a fetus, the Gemara turns to a distinct question: what is the *shilya* itself as a source of *tum'ah*? A *baraita* records the dispute: Rabbi Meir holds that a *shilya* in a house renders the house *tamei*, not because the *shilya* is itself a fetus, but because a *shilya* is never found without a fetus accompanying it — and that fetus has dissolved inside, conferring *tumat met* on the house. His three colleagues — Rabbi Yose, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon — all rule the house is *tahor*.

### Dissolution & Transfer

Rabbi Meir's colleagues challenge him: would he not agree that if the *shilya* were carried in a vessel into an outer chamber, that outer chamber would be *tahor*? The implication is that the act of moving it would cause the dissolved contents to fully dissolve further, eliminating the *tum'ah*. Rabbi Meir replies *aval* — yes, he concedes that point.

The colleagues press: if movement to another room causes full dissolution and thus *taharah*, why should the original room be any different? The jostling of transport would complete the dissolution. The answer is equally interesting: Rabbi Meir says the two cases are not comparable, because there is a difference between something dissolved *once* (*pa'am achas*) and dissolved *twice* (*shtei pe'amim*). In the original room, the fetus has begun to dissolve but retains enough form or integrity to still be legally "present"; transport and the additional agitation cause a second stage of dissolution that removes even that.

### Dissolution Stages

At this point the discussion within the Gemara undergoes a conceptual shift. Initially, the dispute in the Mishnah had appeared to be primarily factual: did the fetus dissolve while still in the womb (in which case it never conferred *tum'ah* upon emerging), or did it dissolve only after emerging (in which case it did)? But the *baraita*'s exchange between Rabbi Meir and his colleagues suggests something more halachic: even granting that the fetus was present when the *shilya* emerged, once dissolution is complete, the *tum'ah* ceases. The debate is not merely about timing but about the legal status of dissolved matter.

This sets the stage for the Gemara's deeper analysis.

Rav Hamnuna was delivering a *shiur* on this matter, and Rav Pappa, seated in the second row behind Rav Bibi, was following along. Rav Hamnuna asked: what is Rabbi Shimon's reason? And he answered: *kasavar kol tum'ah she-nisarvah bah mi-min acher betailah* — Rabbi Shimon holds that any *tum'ah* that becomes mixed with matter of another type is negated. It is not merely that the fetus has dissolved into nothingness; it is that the other liquids present in the *shilya* — the embryonic fluids and other contents of the placental sac — constitute a mixture, and the dissolved fetal matter is negated within that mixture.

---

## Rav Pappa's Lesson

### Three Sages Unite

Rav Pappa speaks up at this point to add a clarification: *hayinu nami ta'ama de-Rabbi Yehuda ve-Rabbi Yose* — this is also the reason of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yose, the other two colleagues who ruled alongside Rabbi Shimon. The *baraita* had listed all three together, so of course they share the same reasoning. The other scholars laughed at him — *achichu alei* — considering it obvious: why state the reason of the other two *tannaim* separately when they had already been cited together with Rabbi Shimon? *Peshita* — self-evident.

### Speak Truth

Rav Pappa's response to being laughed at contains a memorable principle. He said: *afilu ki amilta le-vei inish velo nishka mei-rabbai* — even something that is obvious to others, one must say it, and one must not remain silent before one's *rebbe* out of embarrassment. The point Rav Pappa was making — that the reasoning articulated for Rabbi Shimon applies equally to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yose — was not necessarily self-evident. One might have thought the three sages held identical conclusions for different reasons. By not speaking up, a genuine clarification would have been lost.

Rav Pappa cites the verse: *im navalta be-hitnasei* — if you make yourself lowly in the pursuit of Torah learning, you will be elevated. Conversely, *im zamota yad la-feh* — if you are too proud to speak for fear of appearing foolish, in the end you will be silenced. The principle is the familiar one: *lo ha-bayshan lamed* — the bashful person does not learn. One must not allow concern for one's dignity to suppress genuine Torah clarification, even when the audience may find the point obvious and even when they respond with laughter.

---

## Decomposed Corpse

### Mixed Matter

The Gemara now pivots to an extended discussion of *rekav* — decomposed matter from a corpse — which will ultimately be brought to bear on the case of the dissolved fetus. The foundational *halacha* is that a *melo tarvad* (a full ladle-measure) of *rekav* causes *tum'ah* just as an intact corpse does, but only under extremely narrow and specific conditions. The Gemara is exploring the parallel between external matter mixed into *rekav* and external liquid mixed with a dissolved fetus.

The case: *melo tarvad rekav shenafal letocho afar kol shehu* — the prescribed minimum quantity of *rekav* into which the tiniest amount of external dirt has fallen. The *Rabbanan* rule it is still *tamei*; Rabbi Shimon rules it *tahor*.

Rava reports that he found the scholars of Rav's academy sitting and explaining Rabbi Shimon's position as follows: it is impossible, they argued, that two particles of dirt should not constitute a majority over one particle of *rekav* somewhere in the mixture. That is, if one takes any microscopic cross-section where the dirt is concentrated, the dirt particles outnumber the *rekav* particles at that location, negating a tiny portion of the *rekav* and reducing the total below the required minimum. The logic is subtle: since the *tum'ah* of *rekav* is predicated on having the full minimum amount, even a microscopic deficit caused by *bittul* in one local zone undermines the whole.

Rava, however, rejected this explanation outright: *adaraba* — on the contrary! If one looks at the mixture macroscopically rather than microscopically, the *rekav* will always constitute the majority over any small amount of external dirt. The dirt is negated into the *rekav*, not the other way around. The *rekav* in fact grows, not shrinks. The students' micro-level analysis inverts the normal application of *bittul b'rov*.

It is worth pausing here on the point raised by Tosafot, which illuminates the entire discussion. Normally, *tum'ah* from a corpse is caused by a *kezayit* of flesh, a bone of a certain size, or a limb. None of those categories apply to *rekav*. The only category that can encompass *rekav* is the *tum'ah* of a *meit shalem* — an entire corpse. But that means the *rekav* must be present in its complete minimum quantity. If even a tiny portion is negated — even halachically annulled, not physically removed — one no longer has a "whole corpse" in the relevant sense, and the *tum'ah* does not apply. This is why Tosafot's analysis is so powerful: the same logic will apply to the dissolved fetus, which also cannot be characterized as flesh or bone, only as a whole entity.

Rava then offers the true reason for Rabbi Shimon's position: *sofo ki-techilato* — the end follows the same law as the beginning. The *halacha* of *rekav* is extraordinarily restrictive from the outset: the body must be buried naked, in a marble casket or on a stone floor, with absolutely no external matter present during decomposition. This extreme restriction at the beginning, Rabbi Shimon holds, extends to the end as well: any external matter that becomes mixed in afterward likewise disqualifies the *rekav* from causing *tum'ah*. Just as the presence of a *ganguilon* — any external item (Rashi explains this as something like a belt, derived from a Latin term for a binding band) — at the time of burial prevents the *halacha* of *rekav* from ever taking effect, so too does any external matter mixed in after the fact.

### Marble Casket

The Gemara now cites the *baraita* that defines which corpse gives rise to *rekav* and which does not. A corpse buried naked in a marble casket, or placed naked on a stone floor — that is a corpse whose *rekav* causes *tum'ah*: *zeh meit sheyesh lo rekav*. A corpse buried in its shrouds, or in a wooden casket, or placed on a brick floor — any situation where organic or porous external material was present during decomposition — that is a corpse *she'ein lo rekav*, one that does not have this law.

An additional restriction: *velo amru rekav ela le-meit bilvad* — this *halacha* was stated only for a complete corpse, not for a murder victim. Rashi explains that a murder victim lacks all his blood, and the *halacha* requires the corpse to have been buried whole and complete. Tosafot notes a technical issue — the blood is not what becomes *rekav* in the relevant sense — but the *halacha lemoshe mi-sinai* requires completeness, and any deficiency prevents the law from applying.

The marble casket requirement also serves a practical function beyond the halachic one: it prevents insects and maggots from entering, which is presumably necessary for flesh to decompose into *rekav* rather than being consumed entirely. The question of where *rekav* physically comes from — given that in normal burial, insects consume the flesh and leave only bones — is real, and the requirement of a sealed marble environment addresses it.

### Cemetery Dirt

The second case in this *baraita* is striking: *melo tarvad ve'od afar beit ha-kevarot* — a measure of cemetery dirt, slightly more than the minimum, taken from a gravesite. The *Rabbanan* rule this *tamei*. Rabbi Shimon rules it *tahor*.

The *Rabbanan*'s reasoning: *lefi she'ee efshar le-melo tarvad ve'od afar beit ha-kevarot she'ein bo melo tarvad rekav* — it is impossible that such an amount of cemetery dirt not contain the full minimum measure of *rekav*. This is surprising, as one might ask: given how rare it is to achieve the conditions for valid *rekav* in the first place, how can one assume any random scoop of cemetery dirt contains the required amount? The *Rabbanan*'s position seems to be either a rabbinic extension applied as a fence around the law, or it presupposes a special case — as Tosafot suggests — where one has reason to know that a body buried under these specific conditions decomposed in this particular location. Rabbi Shimon, consistent with his principle, says that the presence of external earth mixed throughout the cemetery dirt disqualifies it from the status of *rekav* entirely.

---

## Fetus Dissolution

### Majority Negates

Having developed the principles around *rekav* and the role of external matter, the Gemara now draws the analogy back to the dissolved fetus in the *shilya*. *Hashta de'amarta ta'ama de-Rabbi Shimon mishum sofo ki-techilato* — now that we have explained Rabbi Shimon's reasoning in the *rekav* case as "the end follows the beginning," we must ask: *gabei shilya mai ta'ama* — what is his reason in the placenta case? The *shilya* is not governed by the special, restrictive *halacha* of *rekav*. Why should mixing with external liquid negate the *tum'ah* of the dissolved fetus?

And indeed, the logic cannot be the same: by our earlier analysis, if anything, the fetus is the majority within the *shilya* — the dissolved fetal matter would negate the other liquids, not the reverse. So one cannot say the fetus is simply nullified by a majority of external matter.

The Gemara therefore attributes to Rabbi Yochanan a distinct rationale: *mishum bittul b'rov nahagu bah* — the ruling follows the principle of *bittul b'rov*, and we must understand Rabbi Shimon as assuming that the majority of the contents of the placental sac consists of other liquids (embryonic fluid and the like), not of the dissolved fetus itself. In that case, the dissolved fetal matter is negated by the majority, loses its halachic identity, and the *tum'ah* does not apply.

### Animal Fetus

Rabbi Yochanan further maintains that Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov are expressing a fundamentally similar principle in different legal contexts — *amru davar echad*. Rabbi Shimon's ruling we have just established. Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov's parallel case is found in a *Mishna* in Bechoros: if a large animal (*behemah gassa*) expelled a mass of blood (*chararas dam*), that mass is buried — because it may have been a miscarried firstborn, which cannot be used for benefit — and the animal is thereby exempted from *bechorah* for its next birth, since this may have been its *peter rechem*. Rabbi Chiya elaborates: the expelled mass does not cause *tum'ah* through contact or carrying.

The Gemara immediately seizes on the internal tension: if it does not cause *tum'ah*, why must it be buried? If it has no halachic status as a birth, there is no prohibition against deriving benefit from it, so burial would be unnecessary. The Gemara answers: *kedei lefarsem she-hi patur min ha-bechorah* — the burial is a public declaration. If the mass is simply discarded or used as fertilizer, people will assume it did not count as a birth, and they will treat the next calf as a firstborn requiring *kedushah*. The burial signals that this was treated as a birth. What we therefore observe is a remarkable halachic situation: the animal is considered to have given birth for purposes of *bechorah* (the next offspring is not a *bechor*), yet the thing it gave birth to has no independent status — it causes no *tum'ah* through contact or carrying.

### Birth Without Status

Rabbi Yochanan explains: *mishum bittul b'rov nahagu bo* — here too, as in the case of the *shilya*, the fetal matter is present but is negated by the majority of surrounding fluid. The birth has occurred — the *rechem* has opened, the *bechorah*-exemption is triggered — but the thing that emerged has lost its status as a fetus because of the majority of external matter surrounding it.

This is, as the Gemara itself makes clear, a genuinely counterintuitive result. A birth has occurred without there being, in halachic terms, anything that was born. The mother (or cow) bears the status of having given birth, but the product of that birth is halachically absent. The *tum'ah* accrues to the mother; nothing accrues to the fetus itself. Rabbi Ami then confirms that Rabbi Shimon himself would acknowledge (*modeh*) that the mother is *tme'ah leida* — precisely the conclusion that Rabbi Yochanan's framework generates.

### Verse Analysis

An elder elaborates on Rabbi Yochanan's position by anchoring it in a verse: *isha ki tazria veyalda zachar* — "if a woman gives forth seed and gives birth to a male." The textual inference is: *afilu lo yalda ela ke'ein she-hizria* — even if what she ultimately produces is only like the seed she emitted, i.e., something entirely liquefied, she is nonetheless *tme'ah leida*. The *tum'ah* of childbirth attaches to the mother based on the process — that a fetus was present and has now emerged, even in dissolved form — regardless of whether the product itself retains halachic substance. This verse-based rationale reinforces Rabbi Yochanan's framework and answers why the dissolution of the fetus does not retroactively eliminate the mother's *tum'ah*, even if it eliminates the independent *tum'ah* of the fetus.

### Form vs. Majority

Resh Lakish offers a different account of why, according to Rabbi Shimon, the dissolved fetus does not confer *tum'ah*. He does not invoke *bittul b'rov* at all. Instead: *shapir she-tarfuhu be-maymav na'asa ke-meit she-nitbalbela tzurato* — a fetus that has been scrambled together with its waters becomes like a corpse whose form has been entirely effaced. The operative concept is not majority but *tzurah* — form and appearance.

This reasoning connects naturally to the discussions earlier in the daf about animal-appearing fetuses, where the Gemara's rulings seemed to turn on whether the thing in question retained recognizable form. Resh Lakish's position is in some ways more intuitive than the majority-based analysis: why does a dissolved fetus not cause *tum'ah*? Because there is simply nothing here that looks like a corpse. The categories of *tum'ah* — flesh, bone, limb — all presuppose identifiable form. Even the category of *meit shalem* (Tosafot's framework) requires some coherent wholeness. When the form is entirely destroyed, none of these categories can apply, and it is not a technical *bittul* calculation but a fundamental loss of identity that produces this result.

### Burned Corpse

Rabbi Yochanan immediately challenges Resh Lakish: from where do we know that a corpse that has lost its form is *tahor*? He begins to introduce the ruling of Rav Shabtai in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak of Magdala (with a reverse attribution also given): *meit she-nisraf ve-shildo kayemet tamei* — if a corpse was burned but its *sheled* (outline or skeletal frame) remains intact, it is *tamei*. The question is what exactly *shildo kayemet* means: whether it refers to a charred body that still holds its general shape, or to a situation where ashes remain in the form of an outline on a surface. In either case, the ruling that form preserved in the aftermath of burning still yields *tum'ah* speaks directly to Resh Lakish's claim that loss of form removes *tum'ah*.

The daf concludes with this debate open: Rabbi Yochanan holds that *bittul b'rov* — the negation of the fetal matter by a majority of surrounding fluid — is the mechanism; Resh Lakish holds that it is the loss of *tzurah*, of identifiable form, that removes the status. The question of what *meit she-nisraf ve-shildo kayemet* proves, and what it implies about the role of form versus majority, will be the opening question of the next daf.

---

---

# Niddah 28

## Dissolved Fetus Debate

### Mishnah Setup

The discussion begins at the bottom of 27b, which provides the necessary context for the opening of 28a. The *mishnah* presents a dispute concerning a woman who miscarries when the embryonic sac — the placenta — is filled with liquid but contains no visible fetus. The *chachamim* rule that this represents a fetus that dissolved: the woman is a *yoledet* and the house is *tamei*, for there had been a dead baby present, even in dissolved form. Rabbi Shimon concedes that the woman is a *yoledet* — clearly a fetus had existed — but maintains that the house is not *tamei*, since the fetus has lost its halakhic status.

### R. Yochanan View

Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Shimon's position through the principle of *batel berov*: within the placenta, the fetus is overwhelmed by a majority of embryonic fluid and other liquids, and therefore loses its distinct identity. Since it is not discernible as a separate entity, it is nullified.

### Reish Lakish View

Reish Lakish goes further. According to his view, *batel berov* is not required at all. The decisive factor is whether the fetus retains its appearance — particularly whether *tzurat panav*, the form of the face, has been eradicated. Once the form has been destroyed, the fetus loses its status as a corpse, regardless of whether it constitutes a majority or minority of the fluid.

### Tosafot Analysis

Tosafot provides the crucial conceptual underpinning for this entire discussion. Ordinarily, even a small quantity of a corpse — a *kezayit* of flesh or a certain measure of bone — generates *tumah*. But that principle does not apply here, because there is no flesh and no bone. What exists is a liquefied mass. The only basis for *tumah* in such a case is not quantity but identity: it must be considered an entire corpse. Reish Lakish therefore reasons that this identity depends on the integrity of the form. If the form — and particularly the face — has been effaced, it can no longer be regarded as a whole *met*, and the *tumah* lapses. One might ask: is this not like a piece of meat, which has no face and yet causes *tumah*? The answer is precisely the point: that rule applies when you have actual flesh. Here there is no flesh, no bone — only the concept of a complete body. And for that concept to generate *tumah*, the body's integrity must remain. If even a significant portion of that form has been disrupted, one can say it is no longer considered a complete corpse.

---

## Burnt Corpse Case

### Burnt Corpse Proof

The *gemara* quotes Reish Lakish's position on 27b: *shepir shetirfuhu be-meimav na'aseh kemet shenitbalbel tzurato* — a fetus that has been scrambled with its waters is analogous to a corpse whose form has been destroyed, and therefore loses its status. Rabbi Yochanan immediately challenges: from where do we know that a *met* whose form is destroyed becomes *tahor*? He anticipates that Reish Lakish will seek support from the following teaching: *met shenisraf* — a corpse that has been burnt — if *shildo kayemes*, its bodily form is still present, it is *tamei*. A burnt corpse occupies a conceptual space distinct from the *rekev* of natural decomposition discussed elsewhere. When a body is charred or burned, it is no longer flesh, no longer bone — yet it derives from an entire body. It is, in that sense, precisely analogous to the dissolved fetus: no *basar*, no *atzamos*, but potentially still recognized as a *met* by virtue of having been a whole body. The question is: what is required to maintain that status?

The teaching says that when the form remains, the burnt corpse is *tamei*. The *gemara* then introduces a striking practical illustration at the top of 28a: *ma'aseh hayah ve-time'u lo petachim gedolim ve-teharu lo petachim ketanim* — in an actual case involving a burnt corpse, they ruled the large doors *tamei* and the small doors *tahor*. To understand this, one must recall two *halachos* of *tumah* in an enclosed space. First, if a window of at least a *tefach al tefach* is open, *tumah* passes through it into an adjacent room. Second, even if all openings are closed, there is a principle of *sof tumah latzeis*: the doorway through which the corpse will most likely be carried out is treated as if already open, and *tumah* exits through it. A corpse will not typically be carried through an opening smaller than a *tefach al tefach*, so only the large doors are treated as likely exit points. Since the burnt corpse retained its form, the small closed windows were ruled *tahor*.

Reish Lakish, Rabbi Yochanan assumes, wishes to infer from this case that the entire basis for *tumah* here is *tzuroto kayemes* — the form is still present — and that without form, the burnt corpse would be *tahor* entirely.

### Doors Analysis

Rabbi Yochanan rejects this inference. The fact that the teaching emphasizes the form does not prove that the form is a prerequisite for *tumah* itself. It may instead explain only why the *tumah* exits through the large doors rather than the small ones. If the form is intact, whoever removes the body will want to preserve it and will therefore carry it out through a large door, not pass it piece by piece through small windows. The presence of form determines the *mode of exit*, not the *existence of tumah*.

### Alternative Logic

Rabbi Yochanan elaborates: *duk mineh lehai gisa* — one could actually read the case in the opposite direction. If the form is present, only the large doors are *tamei*, since that is where the whole body will be carried out. But if the form were gone — if it were merely ashes or dismembered remains — then *petachim ketanim nami teme'im*, even the small openings would be *tamei*, because *dechol chad vechad chazi leappokei eivar eivar* — each small window could serve as a passage for an individual limb or portion. The inference from the burnt corpse case therefore proves nothing about whether a formless *met* retains *tumah* status. It only tells us that form affects which doors are implicated, not whether *tumah* exists at all. This then is the crux of the debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish as applied to the dissolved fetus: when there is no flesh and no bone but the concept of a whole *met*, what is required to dissolve that concept? Rabbi Yochanan requires *batel berov*; Reish Lakish requires only the significant loss of form.

---

## Ashes Tumah

### Ashes Doctrine

The *gemara* now pivots to ask: like whom does Rabbi Yochanan rule? The answer: like Rabbi Eliezer. For we have learned in the *mishnah*: *eifer serufin* — the ashes of burnt corpses — Rabbi Eliezer says their minimum measure to cause *tumah* is a *rova* (a quarter *kav*). Here, then, one has pure ashes: no shape, no form, no flesh, no bone — yet they cause *tumah* provided there is a sufficient quantity. This appears to be a strong support for Rabbi Yochanan's position, and at least potentially for the *chachamim* who disagree with Rabbi Shimon altogether: *tumah* can exist without form, as long as there is a sufficient measure. It also reinforces the underlying conceptual principle: since the basis for *tumah* in these cases is not *basar* or *atzamos* but the identity of an entire *met*, one can maintain that identity even in the form of ashes — at least according to Rabbi Eliezer — as long as a minimum quantity is present.

### Abaye Explanation

The *gemara* now returns to the earlier case of the burnt corpse that retains its form, and asks: how, practically speaking, does a burnt corpse retain its form? Abaye answers: *kagon shesarfo al gabei katafla* — it was burnt on top of a piece of boiled leather. Since fire could not burn through the leather, the charred remains stayed in place upon it. When the body needed to be transported out of the house, one could lift the leather with the form intact. Without such a surface, the act of transport would have scattered and destroyed the form.

### Rava Rashi

Rava offers a different scenario: *kagon shesarfo al gabei apidra* — it was burnt atop a marble surface. The principle is the same: the stable platform preserves the arrangement of the ashes. Rashi adds the detail that such a platform would have low walls around it — *dikulin umechitzos* — preventing the remains from scattering and thereby maintaining the form. Tosafot goes even further, suggesting the possibility that the corpse was placed inside a mold shaped to the human body, *dfus shel adam*, indented to the figure's outline, so that after the burning, the ashes remained fixed within that form. One might wonder whether these scenarios reflect actual historical practice. The *gemara* itself elsewhere imagines a corpse buried naked inside a marble coffin, so it is possible that similar practices occurred, though how common they were is difficult to assess.

### Ravina Position

Ravina offers what is perhaps the most straightforward reading of the case: *kagon de'ichruchi ichruchi* — the corpse was merely charred, not reduced entirely to ashes. It was burnt thoroughly on the outside, completely carbonized, but had not fully disintegrated into ash. In that state, the body retains its shape without requiring any special surface or enclosure. In all of these scenarios, the *tumah* is not generated by flesh or bone but solely by the status of the *met* as a whole — and the question of form remains central to how that status is maintained.

---

## Unknown Birth Timing

### Severed Limb

The *gemara* now introduces a *braisa*: *hamapeles yad chatucha veregel chatucha imo teme'ah leidah* — if a woman miscarries and what emerges is only a severed limb, an arm or a leg, the mother is nonetheless *teme'ah leidah*. One assumes, of course, that a fully forming fetus had been present — it did not develop as merely a limb — and the woman therefore has the *tumah* of a *yoledet*, even though no complete fetus is visible. *Ve'ein chosheshin shema migufo tumah bah* — and we are not concerned that the fetus might have been so abnormally formed as to lack the capacity to generate *tumas leidah*. The assumption is that a normal fetus existed and simply dissolved or came out incompletely.

### No Tahara Days

Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna both rule: *ein notnim lah yemei tohar* — she is not given *yemei tohar*, the days of *tahara* following childbirth. She is considered a *safek yoledet*, a woman who has possibly given birth: she carries the *tumah* of a week or two weeks (since we are uncertain whether the infant was male or female), but she receives no *tahara* days.

### Delayed Birth Fear

The reason: *eima hirchikah leidatah* — perhaps the birth occurred long ago. Clearly a fetus existed, but when did the majority of the body emerge? It is possible that *rubo*, the greater portion of the fetus which halakhically constitutes birth, came out weeks earlier, with only a single limb remaining in the womb until now. If that is the case, the woman is indeed a definite *yoledet* — that is not in question — but the onset of her *yemei tohar* may have begun and even concluded before the limb appeared. We therefore cannot confidently grant her any *tohar* days from this point forward.

This raises a natural question: should we not also be concerned retroactively about the *tumah* she may have transmitted to *terumah* or other objects in the weeks before the limb appeared? The *gemara's* implicit answer is that retroactive *tumah* of this type was treated very leniently from the beginning of the tractate — it is *derabbanan* and applied loosely — and so the concern does not extend that far back. What we can say with certainty is only that we cannot now declare the blood she will see in the coming weeks to be *tahor*.

### Rav Yosef

Rav Yosef challenges this position. The *mishnah* deals with a woman who miscarried and does not know what the fetus was — *hamapelet ve'ein yadu'a mah hi hipilah*. The ruling there is *teshev le-zachar uli-nekeivah*: she observes the stringencies of both male and female, meaning two weeks of *tumah* and *tahara* days extending through day forty. Rav Yosef argues that if the concern is that birth may have occurred at an earlier unknown time — and we therefore deny *tahara* days entirely — then the *mishnah* should have gone further and included the stringency of *niddah* as well. That is: she should be treated as potentially a *niddah* in addition to being potentially a *yoledet*, so that any blood appearing after the first two weeks of *tumah* would be considered *niddas* blood rather than *tohar* blood. If we are already being strict enough to deny *tahara* days, why does the *mishnah* still grant her the framework of boy-or-girl *yoledet*, which implicitly gives her *tahara* up to day forty?

### Abaye Resolution

Abaye resolves this by distinguishing between two layers of the ruling. The *mishnah* does, in fact, reflect the concern that birth timing is uncertain, and accordingly *tahara* days are not granted with confidence. But the *mishnah* frames the ruling as *teshev le-zachar uli-nekeivah* — not as *niddah* — for a deliberate reason: *ei tana le-niddah hava amina meviah korban ve'eino ne'echal* — had the *mishnah* used the language of *niddah*, one might infer that there is doubt whether she is a *yoledet* at all, and if her status as *yoledet* is in doubt, her *korban* would not be eaten. The use of *niddah* language in contrast to *yoledet* language would have cast doubt on her very status as someone who gave birth. But she is unquestionably a *yoledet*: she definitely miscarried. We simply do not know when the majority emerged. The *mishnah* therefore deliberately says boy-or-girl to affirm her *yoledet* status and her right to bring and eat the *korban*, while the practical effect — that she cannot rely on *tahara* days — follows from the underlying uncertainty about timing. *Kamashmalan denachal*: it teaches us that the *korban* is eaten.

---

## Fetal Hand

### Rav Huna

The *gemara* introduces a teaching of Rav Huna: *hotzi ubar yado vehachzira imo teme'ah leidah* — if a fetus extended its hand and then retracted it, the mother acquires the *tumah* of a *yoledet*. This is striking, since the general assumption — which will be confirmed by the next *mishnah* — is that birth is defined by the emergence of the head, or at minimum the majority of the body. How can the momentary protrusion of a hand confer *tumas leidah*? Rav Huna grounds this in a *pasuk*: *vayehi belidta vayiten yad* — and it was when she was giving birth, and he put forth a hand — referring to the narrative of Zarach and Peretz. The *pasuk* uses the language of giving birth (*leidah*) in conjunction with the protrusion of a hand, implying that the hand's emergence already carries halakhic significance.

### Rav Yehuda

Rav Yehuda objects from a *braisa*: *hotzi ubar yado ein imo chosheshet lechol davar* — if a fetus extends its hand, the mother need not be concerned about anything. No *tumah*, no status change of any kind. This appears to directly contradict Rav Huna.

### Doubtful Birth

Rav Nachman resolves the tension: the statement of Rav Huna was explained to him directly by Rav Huna himself. The protrusion of the hand creates *chasusha* — concern, a state of doubt — but not definite birth. *Yemei tohar lo yahavinan lah ad denafik rubei*: she is not given *tahara* days until the majority of the body has emerged. In other words, the protrusion of the hand initiates a period of *tumah* out of concern — *lachush chosheshas* — but does not establish the definite status of *yoledet* with its attendant *tahara* days. That status awaits the emergence of the majority of the body, or, in a normal birth, the forehead.

### Rabbinic Concern

The *gemara* presses further: the *braisa* said she need not be concerned about *anything* — *lechol davar* — which would seem to preclude even this rabbinic-level concern when the hand appears. Abaye resolves this: *einah chosheshet lechol davar midioraisa* — biblically, nothing whatsoever begins when only a hand emerges. The *braisa* speaks at the biblical level. *Aval miderabbanan chosheshet* — but rabbinically, we are concerned. The *gemara* then asks: but Rav Huna quoted a *pasuk* — does that not indicate a biblical basis? Abaye answers: *miderabbanan u'kraya asmakhta be'alma* — the ruling is rabbinic, and the *pasuk* is merely an *asmakhta*, a textual support.

An interesting question remains: what precisely is the nature of this rabbinic *chasusha*? Is it a general precautionary measure, analogous to the way rabbis guard their enactments so that people cannot easily circumvent them? Or is it a specific concern that perhaps the head already emerged and retracted unobserved, and the arm's protrusion is evidence that active birth has begun? This question has practical implications — notably for *bris milah* and similar contexts — though the *gemara* here limits the discussion to the domain of *tumah* and *tahara*. For the purposes of *bris milah* and related matters, the next *mishnah* clearly governs: birth is defined by the crown of the head or the emergence of the majority.

---

## Tumtum Birth

### Mishnah Setup

The *mishnah* introduces a new category of unusual births. *Hamapeles tumtum ve'androgynus* — if a woman gives birth to a *tumtum* or an *androgynus*. A *tumtum* is an infant whose genitalia is covered or concealed — the sex is simply unknown. An *androgynus* (the word carries its Greek derivation transparently) is an infant with both male and female genitalia. In either case, the sex cannot be determined with certainty.

The *mishnah* rules: *teshev le-zachar uli-nekeivah* — the mother observes the stringencies of both male and female. She has two weeks of *tumah* as for a female, but her *tahara* days end at day forty as for a male.

If she gave birth to a *tumtum* and a male twin, or an *androgynus* and a male, the ruling is the same: *teshev le-zachar uli-nekeivah*. The *tumtum* or *androgynus* may be female, and therefore, combined with the definite male, both stringencies apply.

If, however, she gave birth to a *tumtum* and a female, or an *androgynus* and a female, the ruling is *teshev le-nekeivah bilvad* — she observes only the stringencies of a female. The reasoning is that a definite female already brings the maximum *tumah* (fourteen days) and the maximum *tahara* period (sixty-six days). The male's contribution — a shorter *tahara* window — does not diminish the female's grant of sixty-six days of *tahara*. The male gives a thirty-three-day *tohar* period; the female gives sixty-six days. Having the thirty-three does not eliminate the sixty-six. Therefore, the presence of the *tumtum* or *androgynus* is irrelevant: whatever it is, the definite female already gives the longer stringencies in every direction.

---

## Tumtum Birth (II)

### Twin Gender

The *gemara* raises a question about the *mishnah's* case of *tumtum* and a male twin. If a *tumtum* by itself already requires the stringencies of both male and female, and a male by itself certainly requires male stringencies, what new information does the combined case of *tumtum* and male add? One might initially think the answer is obvious — of course the combined case is at least as strict — and that the *mishnah* was simply leading to the more novel case of *tumtum* and female. But the *gemara* presses: why include the *tumtum-and-male* case if it teaches nothing beyond the *tumtum* alone?

### R. Yitzchak

The answer invokes a theory of fetal sex determination attributed to Rabbi Yitzchak: *isha mazra'at techilah yoledet zachar, ish mazria techilah yoledet nekeivah* — if the woman contributes seed first, the child will be male; if the man contributes seed first, the child will be female. Based on this theory, one might reason that in the case of twins, either the woman went first — producing two males — or the man went first — producing two females. Under this view, boy-girl twins would be impossible, because both twins would be conceived from the same sequential act. If so, seeing a *tumtum* together with a definite male, I might assume both are males, and there would be no reason to apply the stringencies of a female.

### Simultaneous Seed

The *gemara* refutes this: *eima sheneihem hizriu bevat achat* — perhaps both husband and wife contributed seed simultaneously, in which case both a male and a female could emerge from the same conception event. Boy-girl twins are therefore possible, and the *mishnah* needed to teach explicitly that even in the case of a *tumtum* and a male, we cannot assume both are male. We must treat the *tumtum* as potentially female, and apply both stringencies accordingly.

---

## Gender Impurity

### Emission Status

Rav Nachman said in the name of Rav: a *tumtum* or *androgynus* who observes a white discharge (*laven*, semen) or a red discharge (*odem*, blood) — *ein chayavin al biat mikdash* — is not liable for entering the *beis hamikdash*, and *ein sorfin aleihem et haterumah* — *terumah* they contact is not burned.

The *safek* for a *tumtum* is clear: we simply do not know whether the person is male or female, so we cannot determine whether a white discharge functions as semen (making him a *ba'al keri*) or whether a red discharge functions as menstrual blood (making her a *niddah*). For the *androgynus*, the case is more initially surprising: the individual visibly has both sets of genitalia, so one might think that semen from the male genitalia definitively creates the status of *ba'al keri*, or blood from the female genitalia definitively creates the status of *niddah*. Nevertheless, the *gemara* rules that this is not so. *Ba'al keri* is a status that applies to men; *niddah* is a status that applies to women. If we cannot assign the person a definitive gender identity, we cannot assign the gender-specific *tumah* that flows from that identity — even when the discharge itself is unambiguous.

### Definite Gender

The reasoning is rooted in the nature of these *tumos*. *Ba'al keri* and *niddah* are not merely about the physical substance — they are about personal status, about what the *gemara* elsewhere calls *ro'eh* rather than *nogea*. It is not that the person touched their semen or blood; it is that their very being is in a state of *tumah* related to their maleness or femaleness.
