If the gender itself is indeterminate, the gender-linked personal *tumah* does not fully attach. One could push further and argue that perhaps these individuals bear no *tumah* at all — but the *gemara* does not go that far, as we will see.

### Mikdash Entry

The *gemara* then asks: what if both discharges occur together? *Ra'u loven ve'odem ke'echad* — they observed both. In that case, regarding *beis hamikdash* entry: *ein chayavin al biat mikdash* — still not liable. Whatever they are, they are definitely *tamei* in some sense. But since we cannot specify the nature of the *tumah* — whether it is the *tumah* of a *ba'al keri* or of a *niddah* — the technical criteria for liability have not been met.

### Terumah Burning

And yet: *aval sorfin aleihem et haterumah* — *terumah* they have contacted must be burned. When both discharges occur, the person is unquestionably *tamei* by one or the other route. The *tumah* is definite; only the category is uncertain. *Terumah* therefore cannot be eaten or preserved — it must be burned. This ruling implicitly clarifies that even the *androgynus* is being treated as either male or female — not as a third gender — since if it were genuinely a third category with no gender *tumah* at all, even the *terumah* burning rule would be questionable.

---

## Gender Language

### Language Usage

The *gemara* turns to the textual basis for excluding *tumtum* and *androgynus* from liability regarding *beis hamikdash* entry. Rav had stated: *mizachar ve'ad nekeivah tishaleichu* — "you shall send out, from male to female" — means *zachar vadai u'nekeivah vadais*, only a definite male and definite female, excluding *tumtum* and *androgynus*. But Ulla challenges: perhaps the *braisa* that excludes them from *mikdash* liability is not based on this verse at all. Perhaps it follows only Rabbi Eliezer's position in an entirely different context — that to be liable for a *korban* for entering the *beis hamikdash* while *tamei*, one must know specifically *how* one became *tamei*. Just as Rabbi Eliezer rules that if one touched either a *sheretz* or a *neveilah* and cannot recall which, one does not bring a *korban* — because *al he'elem sheretz hu chayav* requires specific knowledge of the defiling contact — so too here, a *tumtum* who has both discharges but cannot identify whether the *tumah* is that of a *ba'al keri* or a *niddah* would be exempt from a *korban* on those grounds alone. The exclusion need not flow from *zachar ve-nekeivah* language at all.

### Arachin

This raises a broader question: does *zachar ve-nekeivah* language always exclude *tumtum* and *androgynus*? A counterexample: in the context of *arachin* — the valuations of Leviticus — the *Torah* writes *ha-zachar*, with the definite article *heh*. A *braisa* derives from this: *ha-zachar* — and not *tumtum* and *androgynus*. One might ask: even if they cannot be valued as men, perhaps they should be valued at the lower female rate? The *braisa* links *ha-zachar* with *ve-im nekeivah* to show that only definite male and definite female have fixed *arachin* values; the ambiguous cases are excluded from both. The question, then, is why in *arachin* the exclusion required the emphatic *heh* of *ha-zachar*, while elsewhere the plain language of *zachar ve-nekeivah* is said to suffice.

### Necessary Language

The *gemara* answers by drawing a fundamental distinction. In *arachin*, the *Torah* had no choice but to use the words *zachar* and *nekeivah* — these terms were the necessary vehicle for expressing different valuation rates for men and women. Since the gender language was obligatory for other reasons, the mere use of *zachar* alone could not be taken as a signal to exclude *tumtum* and *androgynus*. It was only the additional *heh* — *ha-zachar*, the male specifically — that served as the excluding device.

### Category Division

By contrast, in our context, the *Torah* could have used the inclusive term *adam* — person — and simply stated that *tamei* individuals must be sent out. The deliberate choice to say *zachar ve-nekeivah* where *adam* would have sufficed conveys that only those who definitively fall into one of these two categories are subject to this ruling. The gender language, being optional here, becomes the excluding device by its very specificity. Rav's reading therefore stands: *mizachar ve'ad nekeivah* requires definite male, definite female — *zachar vadai u'nekeivah vadais* — and excludes *tumtum* and *androgynus* not merely from the *korban* obligation, but from the full liability structure associated with *biat mikdash* when in a state of gender-specific *tumah*.

---

---

# Niddah 29

## Birth Status Determinati…

### Head vs. Majority

The present daf opens with a continuation of the *mishnah*'s discussion of when a fetus is considered halachically born. This question carries practical implications across several areas of *halacha*: the *tumah* of childbirth, the determination of when the day-count for a *bris* begins, and questions of *bechor* status. The *mishnah* had established two basic rules: in a normal birth, the child is considered born once the majority of the head — identified as the forehead — has emerged. In a case where the child is born dismembered or as a breech presentation, however, the head carries no special significance, and the determining criterion is the emergence of the majority of the body.

### Eliezer vs. Yochanan

The *gemara* turns to the precise language of the *mishnah*: *yatza mechutach u-mesuras* — "if it emerged dismembered or reversed." Rabbi Eliezer reads this straightforwardly: even if the head emerges in a dismembered birth, the head has no independent significance, and one must wait for the majority of the body. This is intuitive — in a dismembered birth, the head is detached from the rest of the body and cannot symbolically or practically represent the whole child.

Rabbi Yochanan, however, reads the *mishnah* more narrowly. He maintains that the *mishnah*'s ruling requiring the majority of the body applies only when the head has not yet emerged — whether because the birth is a breech presentation or because the child is dismembered and the head happened not to emerge first. But whenever the head does emerge, regardless of circumstances, Rabbi Yochanan holds that *harei hu ke-yalud* — it is considered as though the child has been born. In his view, the emergence of the head is always the decisive criterion.

### Shmuel's Position

The *gemara* then introduces Shmuel's position: *ein ha-rosh poter bi-nefalim* — the head does not constitute a birth determination in the case of fetuses, meaning stillbirths. According to Shmuel, the head counts as signifying birth only when the child is a live birth. Even a whole, intact stillbirth does not acquire *yalud* status through the emergence of the head alone. The *gemara* therefore asks: are Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yochanan debating the position of Shmuel?

The *gemara* responds with a notable answer. *Bishlama de-chulei alma lo peligi* — the case of a whole but stillborn child is actually not the subject of their dispute. Indeed, contrary to what one might expect, the *gemara* suggests that everyone would disagree with Shmuel in that case: when the child is intact and the head emerges, even if the child is not alive, all would agree the birth is considered to have occurred. The debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yochanan is specifically about the dismembered case.

### Three Birth Scenarios

This analysis yields three distinct positions arranged along a spectrum. Shmuel occupies one extreme, holding that the head matters only in a live, intact birth. Rabbi Eliezer occupies the middle position: in an intact stillbirth the head counts, but in a dismembered birth it does not. Rabbi Yochanan occupies the opposite extreme: even in a dismembered birth, the emergence of the head is sufficient to establish *yalud* status. The *mishnah*'s case of the dismembered birth requiring the majority of the body is, according to Rabbi Yochanan, limited to the scenario where the head has not yet emerged at all.

### Independent Debate

The *gemara* now presents an alternative tradition. *Ika dematni la leha shemata be-apei nafshah* — some transmit this debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yochanan not as a dispute about reading the *mishnah*, but as a freestanding *halachic* dispute. In this version, Rabbi Eliezer says *ein ha-rosh ke-rov evarim* — the head does not count as equivalent to the majority of the limbs — and Rabbi Yochanan says it does.

Since the *mishnah* clearly and unanimously rules that the head determines birth in the case of a normal live delivery, this standalone debate cannot possibly concern a live birth. It must therefore be addressing a miscarriage or stillbirth. In this reading, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yochanan are debating the precise case Shmuel addresses: when a woman miscarries and the fetus is whole but not living, does the emergence of the head constitute a halachic birth? Here the positions are inverted from what the first reading suggested — Rabbi Eliezer holds the head does not count, Rabbi Yochanan holds that it does — and both are now engaged with Shmuel's exact question.

### Rav Papa Analysis

Rav Papa introduces a parallel dispute among *tanna'im* to shed light on the debate. The *mishnah* states that for a dismembered or breech birth, *misheyatza rubo harei hu ke-yalud* — once the majority has emerged it is considered born. Rabbi Yosi adds: *misheyatza ke-tikno* — only when it emerges normally. This statement is initially difficult to parse: surely no one would rule that a breech birth is never considered born regardless of how much of the body emerges.

Rav Papa therefore explains Rabbi Yosi's intent. Reading *mechutach u-mesuras* as "dismembered and reversed" — that is, a conjunctive description of a single compound case rather than two separate cases — the *mishnah*'s majority rule applies only to a birth that is both dismembered and reversed, meaning the head has not emerged. The implicit ruling of the first position is that if the dismembered child emerges in the normal head-first order, *ha-rosh poter* — the head alone suffices. Rabbi Yosi then responds that the head is determinative only *ke-tikno le-chaim* — when the child emerges naturally and is alive. Anything short of a natural live birth renders the head insufficient.

### Rav Zvid Challenge

Rav Zvid objects to the framing of this debate. The way Rav Papa has read it implies that when a breech birth produces a majority of the body, it would not count. But this is untenable — *rubo ke-kulo*, the majority is always treated as the whole, and no authority disputes that the majority of a body counts as born regardless of orientation. The formulation cannot mean that a reversed birth with a majority emerged is not considered born.

Rav Zvid therefore recasts the debate with greater precision. The *mishnah*'s case of *mechutach u-mesuras* — both dismembered and reversed — teaches that when these two conditions combine and the head has not emerged, you go by the majority. The implicit ruling is that if even a dismembered child emerges in the normal head-first order, *ha-rosh poter*, the head exempts. This is the position of Rabbi Yochanan. Rabbi Yosi then counters: *misheyatza ke-tikno le-chaim* — the head matters only when the child comes out naturally and is alive. This aligns Rabbi Yosi's position closely with Shmuel: only a live, natural birth triggers the rule that the head determines the moment of birth.

### Baraita Parallel

A *baraita* confirms this reading. It states that in a case of a dismembered and reversed birth, *misheyatza rubo harei zeh ke-yalud* — once the majority has emerged it is born. The implicit corollary: if it emerged in normal order even though dismembered, *ha-rosh poter*, the head determines birth. Rabbi Yosi adds in the *baraita*: *misheyatza ke-tikno le-chaim* — only when the child emerges naturally and alive does the head serve as the determining criterion. Anything less — stillbirth, dismemberment — and you revert to the majority standard.

### Head Majority Defined

Having established when the head is the relevant criterion, the *gemara* now asks what exactly constitutes the majority of the head. Three opinions are given. Rabbi Yosi says *misheyatza tzida* — when the temples have emerged. *Abba Chanan* in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua says *misheyatza padachata* — when the forehead has come out, which as Rashi notes corresponds to the primary front surface of the head and effectively represents the majority of the face; this is the ruling implicit in the *mishnah* itself. A third view says *misheyatza karnei rosho* — when the "horns" of the head have emerged, which Rashi identifies as the upper and rear slope of the skull, approximately what is meant in medical terminology by crowning. This position appears to represent a threshold somewhat lower than the forehead — a smaller proportion of the head — and is notably more stringent in requiring less to have emerged before birth is considered to have occurred. The ruling for practical *halacha*, particularly for *brit milah*, follows the *stam mishnah*, which identifies the forehead as the critical threshold.

## Unknown Miscarriage (II)

### Mishnah Overview

The *mishnah* now turns to cases where the status of the miscarriage cannot be established through inspection. The first scenario presented is a woman who miscarries but cannot determine whether the fetus was male or female. In such a case, she observes *teshev le-zachar ule-nekevah* — she must adopt the stringencies of both possibilities. She counts fourteen days of *tumah* as required for a female birth, but her *taharah* days end at day forty as required for a male birth, since she cannot assume the longer *tohar* period of a female.

The *mishnah* then escalates to a harder case: the woman cannot determine whether what she expelled was a halachic fetus at all — *eini yoda'at im velad hayah im lav*. She may not have had the opportunity to inspect the discharge, or what she saw gave her no clear indication of fetal status. In this situation, the *mishnah* rules *teshev le-zachar ule-nekevah ule-niddah* — she must observe the stringencies of three possibilities simultaneously. She treats herself as possibly a *yoledet nekevah*, granting herself fourteen days of *tumah*, but she cannot rely on any *taharah* days following that period, because she must also reckon with the possibility that this was not a birth at all, in which case she is simply a *niddah* with no *yemei tohar*. The mention of *zachar* in this formulation might seem superfluous — since the possibility that she is simply a *niddah* already eliminates any reliance on *taharah* days — and the *gemara* will indeed raise this question.

### R. Yehoshua b. Levi

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi addresses the scenario where a pregnant woman miscarries in circumstances that prevent inspection — his paradigm case is a woman who crosses a river and miscarries into it. He rules that she brings a *korban* as a *yoledet*, and moreover that the *korban* is eaten — meaning we treat her as certainly having had a valid halachic birth. His basis is *halacha ke-rov nashim* — we rule according to the majority of women, and the majority of pregnant women, when they miscarry or give birth, produce a fetus that qualifies halachically as a valid birth. Therefore, even without inspection, we do not entertain the possibility that this was a non-fetal discharge.

The question immediately arises: how does this square with the *mishnah*, which explicitly entertains the possibility that the discharge was not a valid fetus, ruling *teshev le-niddah*? The *gemara* resolves this by distinguishing the cases. The *mishnah* addresses a situation where the woman's pregnancy was not definitively established — *beshelo huchzeka ubra*. Perhaps something emerged from her body, but there was no firm prior knowledge of an established pregnancy. In such a case, we cannot invoke *rov nashim*, because we are not even certain she was pregnant. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling applies specifically *ke-shehuchzeka ubra* — when her pregnant status was known and established. In that case, we rely on the majority and do not worry about the possibility of a non-fetal discharge.

### Animal Parallel

The *gemara* tests Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's principle with a parallel case involving animals. A pregnant animal — *behema sheyatza melei'a uvah reikanis* — leaves while pregnant and returns no longer pregnant, without the owner having witnessed the birth or miscarriage and without a live offspring having appeared. The question is whether the next offspring born to this animal is a *bechor*. The ruling is that it is a *bechor mi-safek* — a doubtful firstborn — because we cannot be certain that what previously emerged was a halachic birth. This appears to contradict Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi directly: the animal's pregnancy was established, yet we do not simply apply *rov behemot* to assume it gave birth to a valid fetus.

### Ravina's Answer

Ravina resolves the apparent contradiction. It is true that the majority of pregnant animals give birth or miscarry in a manner that halachically constitutes a birth and would therefore exempt the subsequent offspring from *bechor* status. However, there is a minority of cases where what is discharged does not constitute a halachic fetus — such as a fluid-filled placenta without a recognizable embryo. Normally we would not be concerned about such a minority. But here a specific indicator undermines the application of the majority: *dechol hayoldot mitnapfot* — any animal that carries a true fetus and is about to give birth emits a characteristic odor beforehand, and *vezo ho'il velo tinpa* — this animal displayed no such smell. The absence of this biological sign *itra lei ruba* — weakens the presumption of the majority, and we therefore treat the status of the subsequent offspring as doubtful.

Tosafot add the necessary clarification: this ruling applies only when the animal was not away from its owner's purview long enough to have produced that smell and then miscarried without the owner's knowledge. If the animal had been absent for an extended period, one would simply assume the smell occurred and was missed. The case is therefore a tightly constrained one where the absence of the pre-birth indicator is a meaningful and observable datum.

## Unknown Miscarriage (II)

### Woman in Error Case

*Ki ata Ravin amar* — when Ravin came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he reported that Rabbi Yose the son of Rabbi Chanina had challenged Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's principle from a *baraita* concerning a *to'eh* — a woman who is in error regarding her cycle and her status. Ravin then adds, pointedly, *velo yadana mai tiyuvteih* — and I do not even understand what the challenge was. He does not believe it constituted a valid refutation. The *gemara* proceeds to examine this *baraita* in detail, which concerns a woman who departed while pregnant and returned no longer pregnant, without any knowledge of when the miscarriage occurred. The case is brought as a potential challenge to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi — specifically, the *gemara* will argue that the difficulty in this case might imply we cannot assume the miscarriage was a valid halachic birth — and Ravin's point is that this implication is mistaken.

## Unknown Miscarriage (II)

### Case Setup

The *baraita* describes a woman who left while visibly pregnant and returned in a state that is no longer pregnant, without any knowledge of when the miscarriage occurred. She presents herself to *beit din* asking: what is my status, when do I go to the *mikvah*, and when may I resume relations with my husband? The case is complicated by the fact that she does not know the date of the miscarriage — it could have been that very day, or it could have been weeks prior. Over the following period she is observed to be clean for three full weeks, then bleeding every other week for ten weeks.

### Worst-Case Scenario

To analyze when she may resume relations with her husband, the *gemara* begins by identifying the worst-case scenario in terms of her *tumah* status. The most stringent possible reading is that she gave birth at this very moment, that the child was female — imposing two full weeks of *tumah* — and that she was also a *yoledet be-zova*, meaning that prior to giving birth she had been a *zava*, bleeding for three days outside her normal cycle without accompanying pain. A *zava gedolah* requires seven clean days before she becomes *tehorah*. The intersection of these two statuses creates a complex layering: she needs two weeks of *tumah* for the female birth, then must count seven clean days for the *zava* status. The question of whether *yemei leida she-eina ro'ah bahem* — days of childbirth *tumah* during which she does not bleed — can count toward the seven clean days of the *zava* is a matter of dispute; the *gemara* proceeds on the assumption that they do not.

### Tevilah Timing

A further complicating principle is *tevilah bi-zmanah mitzvah* — it is a *mitzvah* to immerse at the earliest possible permitted moment, not merely to wait until one is certainly *tahor* and go to the *mikvah* then. This principle, disputed between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, drives the *gemara* to calculate not just when she is certainly *tahor*, but every individual day on which she might possibly first become *tahor* — because on each such day she is obligated to immerse. She cannot be permitted to her husband even after immersing on one of these days, since she may not yet be actually *tahor* — but according to Beit Shammai she must immerse nonetheless. This generates an enormous number of required immersions across the full period.

### Structured Scenario

The constructed scenario has the woman presenting herself having not bled at all for three clean weeks, then bleeding the entirety of every other week for a further ten weeks, alternating one week of bleeding with one week clean. The *gemara* determines through analysis that the sole night on which she may actually have relations with her husband in this entire period is the night before day thirty-five. The entire preceding period involves either *tumah* of some kind or unresolvable doubt, and the weeks that follow, as will be established, are complicated by *zava* status and the possibility that seven clean days have been disrupted by nighttime bleeding.

### Days 40 & 80

The *gemara* introduces day forty and day eighty as critical temporal boundaries. Day forty marks the end of the *yemei tohar* — the period of *taharah* blood — for the birth of a male child, while day eighty marks the same endpoint for a female. Since this woman does not know when her birth occurred, she cannot know when her own day forty or day eighty falls. The *gemara* constructs the scenario by assuming the birth occurred on the day she first presented herself, placing day forty and day eighty within the observable ten-week alternating period that follows.

### Weeks 1-2 Analysis

The *gemara* explains why she cannot have relations during either of the first two weeks. The first week falls within the possible *tumah* period of a *yoledet zachar* — if she gave birth to a male, she is *tamei* for seven days. The second week falls within the possible *tumah* period of a *yoledet nekevah* — if she gave birth to a female, she remains *tamei* through the end of the second week. Therefore, even though she is not actively bleeding during these two weeks, she is presumed *tamei* due to the *tumah* of childbirth itself.

### Single Permitted Night

The *gemara* establishes that the sole moment in this entire constructed scenario where marital relations are permitted is the night before day thirty-five. The analysis that leads to this conclusion proceeds as follows. Week three, during which she observes seven clean days, could serve as the seven clean days required of a *zava*. Were this the case, one might expect that she could immerse at the conclusion of week three and resume relations. However, the *gemara* will show that this is precluded — due to nighttime bleeding at the start of week four — and that week four is itself problematic because any one of those days might have been the last day of the forty-day *taharah* period, making the blood of that week's end the first genuine *niddah* blood, extending her *niddah* period all the way to the Friday of week five. The last possible moment at which her *niddah* period could begin in week four is the final day of that week — *Shabbat* — in which case she completes her seven *niddah* days on the Friday of week five, and may immerse and have relations on the night before day thirty-five.

### 95 Immersions

Beit Shammai, applying the principle of *tevilah bi-zmanah mitzvah*, holds that on every day that could conceivably be the precise moment she first becomes *tahor*, she must immerse. Across the full ten-week alternating period, the *gemara* identifies ninety-five such days — each representing one possible configuration of birth timing, *tumah* status, and *zava* count that could make that particular day the earliest permissible moment of *taharah*. Because some of those days are moments of possible *niddah* or *yoledet* status requiring nighttime immersion, while others are moments of possible *zava* status requiring daytime immersion, the ninety-five immersions include a combination of morning and evening immersions across the ten weeks.

### Final Immersion

Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Yehuda dispute the entire framework of Beit Shammai. Their view is expressed in the principle *dayah la-tevilah she-tehei ba-acharonah* — it is sufficient for her to immerse only at the final immersion, meaning only when she is certainly and definitively *tahor*, without any lingering doubt. There is no obligation to immerse at each possible earlier moment of *taharah*; she waits until the one immersion she can perform with full confidence and performs that single immersion. According to this view, the elaborate counting of ninety-five separate immersion opportunities is entirely unnecessary.

### Week 3 Zava Status

The *gemara* examines why week three cannot simply allow relations. Having established that weeks one and two are off-limits due to *tumah* of childbirth, one might assume that week three — which is clean — serves as the seven clean days for a *zava*, and that at the end of week three she is *tahor* and may resume relations. The *gemara* addresses this by raising the possibility that she is a *yoledet nekevah* and also a *zava*, requiring that after the two weeks of *tumah* for the female birth she count seven clean days before immersing. If those seven clean days can only begin after the *tumah* period ends, they would run across week three.

### Yemei Leida Phrase

A critical phrase governs this analysis: *yemei leida she-eina ro'ah bahem einam olim le-sfirat zivasah* — days of childbirth *tumah* during which she does not see blood do not count toward the seven clean days required of a *zava*. The significance of this ruling is that the two weeks of *tumah* for a female birth, even if she is not actively bleeding during them, cannot be credited toward her seven clean days as a *zava*. Therefore, the seven clean days must be counted only after the two *tumah* weeks conclude — which means they fall in week three — and only at the end of week three is she potentially in a position to immerse and have relations.

### Night Bleeding

Even granting that week three serves as the seven clean days of a *zava*, the *gemara* shows that she cannot actually have relations at the conclusion of that week. The reason is that the bleeding of week four begins at night — specifically, on *Shabbat* night at the transition from week three to week four. A *zava gedolah* completes her seven clean days and may immerse on the seventh day during the day, based on the principle of *miktzat ha-yom ke-kulo*. The *gemara* raises whether she could immerse on the seventh day — *Shabbat* — and have relations then. Rabbi Shimon rules that this is prohibited, because going to the *mikvah* on the seventh day and having relations creates a situation of potential retroactive transgression: if she bleeds later that same day, the *miktzat ha-yom ke-kulo* principle is undermined and the immersion is retroactively voided, meaning she would have had relations while still in a state of *tumah*. Therefore she may not have relations on the day of her seventh clean day. And since the bleeding begins *Shabbat* night, she has no opportunity to have relations *Shabbat* night either.

### Week 4 Problem

Even were one to suggest that the blood of week four is *dam tohar* — ritually pure blood that falls within the *yemei tohar* following a valid birth — and therefore she should be permitted to have relations during that week without concern for the bleeding, the *gemara* rejects this reasoning. The problem is that we do not know when the *yemei tohar* began. Any one of the days of week four could be the last day of the forty-day period — meaning the blood on that day, or the day before, or earlier in the week, might be the first genuine *niddah* blood rather than *dam tohar*. We therefore cannot assume on any particular day of week four that we are still within the *yemei tohar*; the worst case scenario must always be entertained.

### Ravin's Defense

This is precisely the point Ravin was making when he said he did not understand Rabbi Yose ben Rabbi Chanina's challenge to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. The difficulty with week four is not that we are uncertain whether the miscarriage was a valid halachic birth. We may fully assume — following Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi — that the birth was valid and that she has *yemei tohar*. The problem is simply that we do not know when those *yemei tohar* begin. *Eimar hirchika leidatah* — perhaps the birth occurred long ago, well before she presented herself, in which case by the time we reach week four the forty days have already elapsed and the blood is ordinary *niddah* blood. The uncertainty is temporal, not categorical, and therefore this case provides no challenge to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's principle.

### Week 3 Saturday

The *gemara* revisits the question of whether any moment in week three allows relations. On *Shabbat* day — the seventh day of the seven clean days — she could in principle immerse in the daytime as a *zava* completing her count. The question is whether she may then have relations on *Shabbat* day itself. Rabbi Shimon's ruling, as described above, is that relations on the seventh day are prohibited because of the risk of retroactive violation if bleeding occurs later that day. And since the bleeding of week four begins *Shabbat* night — at the very transition out of week three — she had no window to have relations *Shabbat* night either. Week three therefore offers no permissible moment.

### Week 1 Immersions

The *gemara* now accounts for the ninety-five immersions required by Beit Shammai. In week one, she immerses seven times — once each night. The reasoning is that any one of the seven nights of week one could be the first night following the end of the *tumah* period of a *yoledet zachar*. If she gave birth seven days before she presented herself, then day seven of her *tumah* as a *yoledet zachar* falls on the first night of this week; if she gave birth six days before, it falls on the second night; and so on through each night of the week. Since on each of those nights she could be crossing from *tumah* to a possible state of *taharah*, she must immerse each night. These are nighttime immersions because *yoledet* and *niddah* status, like that of a *zava*, requires nighttime immersion when the *tumah* period ends in the evening.

### Week 2 Immersions

In week two, she must immerse fourteen times — seven times at night and seven times in the morning. The seven nighttime immersions correspond to the possibility that she gave birth to a female and any of the seven nights of week two marks the conclusion of the fourteen-day *tumah* period of a *yoledet nekevah*. The seven morning immersions correspond to the possibility that she gave birth to a male and was also a *zava*, such that the seven days of week one served as her first clean days following the cessation of *zova* bleeding, and any morning of week two could be the seventh day of her clean days on which she immerses as a *zava*. This accounts for twenty-one immersions across the first two weeks.

### Week 3 Immersions

In week three, she immerses seven times in the morning — on each of the seven days of that clean week. These correspond to the possibility that she gave birth to a female and was also a *zava*, such that the fourteen days of *tumah* as a *yoledet nekevah* precluded counting the clean days of weeks one and two toward her seven clean days, and week three is the first valid week for counting. Any one of the seven days of week three could therefore be the seventh day of her seven clean days as a *zava*, requiring a daytime immersion on each. This brings the running total to twenty-eight, with further weeks — and the remaining sixty-seven immersions — to be accounted for in the continuation of the sugya.

---

---

# Niddah 30

## Unknown Miscarriage Setup

### Scenario Intro

The *daf* begins at the bottom of 27b and continues into a highly specific, constructive scenario: a woman appears before the rabbis having suffered a miscarriage at some point in the recent past, though she cannot determine precisely when it occurred. Because she does not know when the miscarriage took place, she cannot establish her own status. The scenario stipulates that she does not bleed for three weeks, and then bleeds for a full week every other week throughout a fourteen-week period. The Gemara presents this case not as a realistic expectation — God forbid such a situation should occur in practice — but as a vehicle for exploring the outer limits of several key principles.

Two questions drive the analysis. First: when during this period can she be definitively *tehorah*, and when, if ever, can she be with her husband? Second: given the position that *tevilah bizmanah mitzvah* — that one must immerse in the *mikvah* at the earliest possible moment — how many times would this woman be required to immerse? Since we do not know precisely when she became *temeah* or *tehorah*, every moment that might represent the onset of her *tahorah* would trigger an obligation to immerse immediately.

### Day 36 Analysis

The *Beraita* states that the only night during this entire ninety-one-day period that she may be with her husband is the night leading into the thirty-sixth day. The *Beraita* further states that according to *Beit Shammai* she immerses ninety-five times, and according to *Beit Hillel* thirty-five times. It is worth reviewing why the night of day thirty-six is the unique window.

During the first three weeks, even though she has not bled at all, she cannot be with her husband. The reason: she may have given birth, and a birth — if it was a girl — entails two weeks of *tumah*. Moreover, if she was also a *zavah* before the birth, and we apply the ruling that the *tumah* days of *yoledes* status cannot be counted toward the seven clean days required to clear *zavah* status, then those seven clean days have never been observed. Worst case, she had a baby girl and is a *zavah* — a combination requiring the full three weeks to resolve.

Why not immerse and be with her husband on the night that immediately follows the three-week clean period? Because that is precisely when the bleeding resumes. She is clearly a *niddah*. She cannot be with her husband while bleeding. After seven days of *niddah* bleeding, one might think she could immerse on the night of day thirty-five — but that is still the day of bleeding in some scenarios. Then, on the worst-case reading, this bleeding began as *niddah*, and all the preceding weeks were within the *tohar* period of a childbirth — potentially eighty days if it was a girl. That eighty-day period might end precisely at day thirty-five. She is *temeah* through that Friday, immerses Friday night, and the night of day thirty-six — at last — she may be with her husband. But by the following day, she is already bleeding again. And the subsequent non-bleeding week cannot be used for relations either, because that prior bleeding might have been *zavah* bleeding, which requires seven clean days of its own. That is why the entire period yields only a single permissible night.

### Immersion Framework

The question of how many times she must immerse requires careful attention to when a *niddah* immerses versus when a *zavah* immerses, since these occur at different times of day. A *niddah* immerses at night — specifically, the night following the seventh day of her *tumah*. A *zavah*, by contrast, immerses during the day — on the daytime of her seventh clean day. This distinction generates the entire framework of nighttime versus daytime immersions across the three-week period.

In the first week, even though she has not bled during this period, it is impossible to count her as a *zavah*, because a *zavah* requires seven clean days that are *v'safarnu* — counted with awareness. No such counting has been established before she appears. However, any one of these seven days might be the last day of her *yoledes* status, whether as the final day of a one-week *tumah* for a boy or any day within the two-week *tumah* for a girl. Since the night following the last day of *yoledes* status triggers an immersion — analogous to a *niddah*'s nighttime immersion — she must immerse every single night of the first week. That yields seven nighttime immersions. She cannot, however, go during the day as a *zavah*, since no seven clean days have been established.

In the second week, two tracks open simultaneously. On the one hand, any night of the second week could still be the final night of *yoledes* status — since if the miscarriage occurred near the beginning of the scenario, the two-week *tumah* for a girl could extend into the second week. That gives another seven nighttime immersions. On the other hand, the *yoledes* period for a boy might have concluded during the first week, at which point the woman could have begun counting her seven clean days as a *zavah*. Depending on exactly when the *yoledes* period ended, the seventh clean day of *zavah* could fall on any day of the second week. That generates seven daytime immersions as well.

The third week follows the same logic for daytime immersions: the *yoledes* period for a girl might have ended on any day of the second week, pushing the seventh clean day of *zavah* into any day of the third week — seven more daytime immersions. Nighttime immersions, however, belong exclusively to the *yoledes* framework, and since the *tumah* of a boy or girl is complete within two weeks at the latest, the *yoledes* status is definitively over by the end of the second week. The Gemara will go on to explain how one might account for additional nighttime immersions in the third week even after *yoledes tumah* has concluded — but that requires further argumentation.

The running total to this point: seven nights in week one, seven nights and seven days in week two, and seven days in week three — yielding 7 + 14 + 7 = 28 immersions across the first three weeks.

One might ask: why should this woman immerse at all if there is no practical benefit — no permissible marital relations — that results from any given immersion? The short answer is that in the world of the Gemara, where *tumah* and *tahara* remain operative categories, *tevilah bizmanah mitzvah* holds that immersion at the proper time is itself a *mitzvah*, independent of whether it enables marital relations. In contemporary practice, matters stand differently. The *rishonim* observe that women today count seven clean days regardless of whether they are most likely a *niddah* or a *zavah*, meaning that no woman immerses *bizmanah* in the Talmudic sense anyway. The practical reframing is therefore about not unnecessarily delaying the opportunity for husband and wife to be together — with secondary implications for questions such as whether a woman who delayed her immersion may still go to the *mikvah* on *Shabbos*.

---

## Beit Shammai: 95

### Tevul Yom Aroch

To understand how *Beit Shammai* arrives at ninety-five immersions, one must first grasp the concept of *tevul yom aroch*. In the ordinary case, when a woman gives birth she immerses at the end of her first week (for a boy) or two weeks (for a girl). After that immersion she is *tehorah* for the purposes of marital relations, but she is not fully *tehorah* in the sense that would permit entry into the *Beit Hamikdash* or contact with *terumah*. She remains in the status of a *tevul yom* — one who has immersed but whose *tahara* is not yet complete — until the conclusion of the forty or eighty days of *tohar*. In a normal case, *tevul yom* status ends with the onset of night following the immersion. Here, however, the *tevul yom* stretches across thirty-three or sixty-six additional days. *Beit Shammai* holds that this extended *tevul yom aroch* — this prolonged, drawn-out status — requires a separate immersion at its conclusion to formally close out the period.

The practical consequence is significant: according to *Beit Shammai*, the woman must immerse every single night through day eighty, because each night might be the last night of her eighty-day *tohar* period. If she had a girl on any day within the scenario, the eighty-day period could end on any one of those nights, and the *tevul yom aroch* ends with an immersion. So rather than having only a handful of specific nighttime immersions, *Beit Shammai* requires a nighttime immersion every single night for eighty consecutive days.

### 80+14=94

The Gemara works through the arithmetic, though it approaches it from a slightly more complex angle than a simple eighty-plus-fourteen calculation. The Gemara asks: how many days of *tahara* are there? Once the fourteen days of *tumah* are over, sixty-six days of *tahara* remain. We have already accounted for the first three weeks of immersions in our earlier analysis. Subtracting those three weeks from the sixty-six remaining days of *tahara* — or more precisely, taking sixty minus one — yields fifty-nine additional nighttime immersions after the first three weeks. Together with the thirty-five immersions previously calculated (the fourteen nighttime and twenty-one daytime from the first three weeks, plus the later daytime immersions), the Gemara reckons: fifty-nine plus thirty-five equals ninety-four. The Gemara then asks directly: *tishin vachamisha mai avidtaihu* — how do we arrive at ninety-five?

### Night of Arrival +1

The answer is given by Rabbi Yirmeyah of Difti: *yom sheba lefanenu bein hashmashos yahavinan leh tevilah yeseirah* — because when the woman first arrived before the rabbis, she arrived at twilight, at nighttime, on what we count as day one. Rashi explains simply that she could have come at night. Since she arrived at night — at the very first possible moment, the night preceding the first halakhic day of the scenario — the rabbis immediately sent her to the *mikvah*, because this might already be the eightieth night of her *tohar* period. That single additional nighttime immersion, captured at the very moment of her arrival, brings the total from ninety-four to ninety-five.

---

## Beit Hillel: 35

### 7+14+7 Structure

*Beit Hillel* arrives at a dramatically different number: thirty-five. The Gemara asks *lamed-heh mai avidataihu* — how is thirty-five derived? The first twenty-eight, *kaf-chet k'da'amaran*, we have already established: seven nights in the first week, seven nights and seven days in the second week, and seven days in the third week. The remaining seven come from the fifth week of the scenario.

### Fifth Week Cutoff

The fifth week is the week immediately following the first episode of renewed bleeding. Since any one of the days of that bleeding might have been the beginning of *niddah* status, any one of the subsequent nights might be the seventh night from the onset of *niddah* — and therefore the night she may immerse as a *niddah*. This generates seven additional nighttime immersions, bringing the total to thirty-five.

The obvious question is: why stop there? After those seven days of bleeding, the subsequent clean week should generate another seven nights (as a possible *niddah*), and perhaps additional daytime immersions for *zavah*, and so on through the remaining weeks. If *Beit Hillel* were counting the entire period the way *Beit Shammai* does, the total would approach fifty-six or more.

The Gemara's answer is pointed: *Beit Hillel* stops counting after the woman has had her first opportunity to be with her husband. The thirty-five immersions represent everything up through the moment she can reunite with her husband on the night of day thirty-six. *Beit Hillel* does not demand immersions that serve no purpose in bringing husband and wife together — he counts only those immersions that lead up to the first permissible encounter. The contrast with *Beit Shammai*'s ninety-five is therefore less radical than it first appears: *Beit Shammai* counts the entire eighty-day period; *Beit Hillel* counts only through the first permissible union.

---

## Scope: 13 Weeks

### Day 80 Boundary

The Gemara raises a structural question: *yud-gimel shavuon lamma lee* — why was the scenario framed as thirteen weeks? The uncertainty about *yoledes* status extends only to day eighty. After day eighty, the maximum possible *yoledes* period — eighty days of *tohar* following the birth of a girl — has definitively concluded, and the case loses much of its halakhic complexity. Three weeks plus eight and a half more weeks would bring us precisely to day eighty, which is eleven and a half weeks total. So why extend the scenario to thirteen weeks?

### Avoiding Half-Weeks

The Gemara's answer is structural and elegant: *aidi d'tani palga d'shavuah masik leh* — since the calculation would otherwise end mid-week (at eleven and a half weeks), and the scenario operates in units of whole weeks, one rounds up to twelve complete weeks. But the twelfth week is a week of bleeding. Since the scenario has consistently paired a week of bleeding with a week of clean days, *tani nami shavuah tahor* — the thirteenth week of clean days is added for symmetry. In other words, the real halakhic limit is day eighty, but to avoid the awkwardness of a half-week and to maintain the elegant alternating pattern of the hypothetical, the scenario extends to thirteen full weeks.

---

## Yoledet vs. Zavah

### Yoledet B'Zove

Having established the immersion counts for *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai*, the Gemara turns to several complications. One might ask: according to *Beit Shammai*, who is counting every night through day eighty as a potential *tevul yom aroch*, have we forgotten to include the daytime immersions that would be generated by the possibility of *zavah* status arising during those eighty days? There are five episodes of bleeding across the scenario, and after any given episode of bleeding she might be a *zavah*, requiring a daytime immersion on the seventh clean day.

The Gemara initially proposes that *Beit Shammai* might be counting only *yoledes* immersions and not *zavah* immersions. But this cannot be sustained: the very seven daytime immersions already counted in the second and third weeks are explicitly *zavah* immersions — immersions for the *zavah* status that arose concomitant with the *yoledes* status. The Gemara resolves this with the distinction between *yoledes b'zove* and *zavah geridaisa*: immersions for a *zavah* status that arose together with and as part of the *yoledes* episode are counted, because they are part of wrapping up the original event of birth and its associated *zova*. But entirely new *zavah* episodes — *zavah geridaisa*, independent *zavah* bleeding unconnected to the original birth — are not counted. *Beit Shammai*'s ninety-five, and the fourteen daytime immersions within it, represent exclusively the resolution of the original *yoledes-zavah* complex. New independent *zavah* status generated by the subsequent bleedings is a different category and is excluded from the count.

### Singleton Days Exclusion

Another question: in the very first week, before the woman has established any pattern of clean days, could she not have had seven clean days immediately before she appeared — perhaps her clean days began several days prior, and any given day of the first week might be the seventh and final clean day, calling for a daytime *zavah* immersion? This is the question *dilma kol yoma veyoma chamia lei sefurim didah* — perhaps each day of the first week could be the end of her seven clean days?

The Gemara answers by invoking the principle of *Beit Shammai*'s ruling elsewhere: *ha manni Rabbi Akiva hi, de'amar beinan sefurim lefanenu* — this is according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that seven clean days for a *zavah* must be observed *befanenu*, with awareness. If she was not bleeding and was unaware that she was counting clean days, those days do not count toward her *zavah* clearance. Since she had not yet appeared before anyone who could witness her clean days, those prior days cannot be credited.

Even granting Rabbi Akiva's principle, one might push further: at the very end of week one, she has been observed for seven full days. Why not credit those as seven clean days of *zavah* and grant her one daytime immersion at the close of week one? The Gemara answers: *chada bashavua lo kama'irei* — we do not count singleton days. The entire framework here counts by weeks. A single solitary day appearing at the end of a week, disconnected from the structured weekly analysis, is simply not counted in this scenario.

### Shomeret Yom Exception

The Gemara raises one final potential immersion that might have been missed. On the first day the woman appears — let us say Sunday — she might have bled the previous day (Saturday) as a *zava ktana*, a woman who bleeds once during her non-cycle period and requires only a single clean day rather than seven. If so, Sunday itself would be her one required clean day, and she should immerse Sunday morning — a daytime immersion entirely distinct from the *zavah gedolah* framework. This would add at least one additional immersion (Saturday morning for the possible *zavah gedolah* scenario, and Sunday morning for the possible *shomeret yom kineged yom* scenario), giving the first week two immersion opportunities rather than none.

The Gemara responds: *bezava gdola kamairei, bezava ktana lo kamairei* — the scenario concerns itself only with the *zavah gedolah*, the woman who bleeds for three or more consecutive days and requires seven clean days. The *zavah ktana*, who watches only one day opposite one day, is a different and lesser category that this analysis deliberately sets aside. The scenario counts by full weeks and major categories; minor and singleton occurrences are excluded from the tally.

---

## Three Key Lessons

### Tefurim Befanenu

Having completed this intricate analysis, the Gemara declares *shmina tlat* — we learn from all of this three things. The first: *shmina Rabbi Akiva hi d'amar bivinan sefurim lefanenu*. The scenario implicitly assumes the position of Rabbi Akiva, who requires that the seven clean days of a *zavah* be counted with awareness — *befanenu*, in our presence, or at least with some degree of conscious reckoning. Days during which she was not bleeding but was wholly unaware of her clean state do not count. This is a *halacha* with ongoing relevance: questions about whether days during which a woman did not bleed but lacked the awareness or proper observation of her *shiva nekiim* count toward those clean days are adjudicated in light of this principle. The precise parameters of *befanenu* — how much awareness is required, and what evidence suffices — are a subject for further discussion, but the principle itself emerges clearly from this analysis.

### Retroactive Contamination

The second lesson: *shmina Rabbi Shimon hi d'amar aval amru chachamim asur laasot ken shema tavo lidei safek*. The scenario also assumes the position of Rabbi Shimon, that a woman may not have marital relations on the daytime of her seventh clean day as a *zavah* — even after she has immersed that morning — because we fear retroactive contamination. If she has relations during the day and subsequently bleeds, that bleeding would retroactively redefine the entire day as a day of *tumah*, thereby invalidating the *mikvah* immersion that took place within it. This is why, throughout the analysis, the permissible moment for marital relations is always the night following the seventh clean day, never the daytime of that day itself. Rabbi Shimon's concern is not merely an issue of *derech eretz* but a serious *halachic* concern rooted in the possibility of actual retroactive *tumah* — weightier than the various other considerations that may, in special circumstances, permit relations during daylight hours.

### Tevilah Bizmanah Mitzvah

The third lesson: *ushmina tvila bizmanah mitzvah*. The entire elaborate structure of immersions — ninety-five according to *Beit Shammai*, thirty-five according to *Beit Hillel* — demonstrates that at the right time, in the right set of circumstances where *tumah* and *tahara* are operative, there is a *mitzvah* to immerse at the proper moment, even when no immediate practical benefit follows. The woman in this scenario immerses dozens of times with no prospect of marital relations on most of those nights, purely because each immersion may represent the correct moment.

### Rabbi Yose Dissent

*Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai*'s positions both rest on accepting *tevilah bizmanah mitzvah*. The *Beraita* concludes, however, with a dissenting voice: *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda omer daya l'tvila baacharonah* — Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda says it is sufficient to immerse only at the final relevant moment. Rather than ninety-five or thirty-five immersions, he would have her immerse once when she is definitively *tehorah* and ready to be with her husband, and then once more when the full eighty-day period concludes. Go when it is practically necessary; do not immerse repeatedly merely because the timing is theoretically correct. Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda thus rejects the principle of *tevilah bizmanah mitzvah*, holding that the *mitzvah* of immersion is tied to its practical function of enabling marital relations, not to abstract temporal precision.

---

## Fetal Viability: Day 41

### Day 40 vs. 41

The elaborate immersion scenario was introduced in service of a broader question: when a woman miscarries, do we treat it as a halakhic birth? The answer depends entirely on whether the fetus had reached the threshold of viability. The *Mishna* at the bottom of 30a establishes the operative rule. If a woman miscarries on day forty of conception, *ein chosheshet l'valad* — it has no status as a fetus at all. If she miscarries on day forty-one, however, the fetus is halakhically viable, and she must observe *teshev l'zachar u'linekeva u'leniddah* — she must sit as if it might be a male (one week of *tumah*), as if it might be a female (two weeks of *tumah*), and as if it might not have been a fetus at all, meaning she might be merely a *niddah* with no *tohar* days whatsoever.

From when does one count the forty-one days? Rashi reckons from the night of the *mikvah* immersion preceding conception — the night presumed to be when relations occurred. In practice, the reckoning can also proceed from other indicators. The Gemara implicitly acknowledges a certain imprecision: the Sages were aware that semen can remain potent for some period within the body, which in principle could shift the actual moment of conception. This raises genuine uncertainty about whether the forty-one-day boundary can ever be pinpointed with exactness, and the case is treated accordingly as a matter of *safek*.

### Gender & Viability

The reason the *Mishna* includes the possibility of a male is not immediately obvious. If the goal is to maximize *tumah* days, it suffices to say: perhaps it was a female (two weeks of *tumah*) or perhaps it was not a fetus at all (*niddah* status with no *tohar* days). Why add the male possibility, which generates only one week of *tumah* — less than either of the other two options?

The *nafka mina* emerges in a specific case: if the woman bled on day thirty-four and then again on day forty-one. In that scenario, if we knew it was a boy, the day-thirty-four bleeding falls within her *tohar* days (since the boy's forty-day *tohar* period is still running) and is therefore disregarded for *niddah* purposes, while the day-forty-one bleeding makes her a *niddah*. If we knew it was a girl, the thirty-four and the forty-one fall within *tumah* days and *tohar* days differently, leaving her *tehorah* at day forty-one. If we knew it was not a fetus, then both bleedings are independent events: the day-thirty-four bleeding is a *niddah*, and the day-forty-one bleeding — occurring between days eight and eighteen of the previous bleeding — might constitute *zavah* status. The critical point is this: because of the male possibility, we cannot simply resolve the case as *niddah* versus *zavah*; we must also hold open the possibility of *niddah* alone. The combined uncertainty leaves her *mekulkela* — in a state of unresolved confusion — until day forty-eight, when she can accumulate seven clean days, immerse, and start fresh. An analogous case for the female scenario involves bleeding on day seventy-four and again on day eighty-one, leaving her uncertain until day eighty-eight.

### Yishmael: 41 vs. 81

Rabbi Yishmael takes a sharply different position. According to Rabbi Yishmael, if a woman miscarries on day forty-one, she need only be concerned that it was a boy or not a fetus at all — *teshev l'zachar u'leniddah* — but she need not be concerned that it was a girl. A girl, in Rabbi Yishmael's view, does not reach the threshold of halakhic viability until day eighty-one. Only then must she observe *teshev l'zachar u'linekeva u'leniddah* — all three possibilities.

Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning is derived from the *Torah*'s own structure of *tumah* and *tahara* for mother and child. For a boy, the mother has forty days of *tumah* and *tahara* combined; for a girl, eighty days. Rabbi Yishmael infers that these periods of maternal status mirror the stages of fetal development: a male fetus reaches the relevant developmental threshold at forty-one days, a female at eighty-one. The days of maternal *tumah* and *tahara* are thus understood as a halakhic encoding of embryological development. He finds support in the Torah's use of the verb *teileid* — "she shall give birth" — applied an additional time to the female case, implying an extended process.

### Sages: Both Day 41

The *chachamim* reject Rabbi Yishmael's position outright: *echad biyat ha-zachar ve-echad biyat ha-nekeiva, zeh ve-zeh le-mem alef* — whether male or female, the threshold of halakhic viability is day forty-one for both. To Rabbi Yishmael's textual argument, the Sages respond: *ein le-meidin yetzirah mi-tumah* — one cannot derive the stages of fetal formation from the laws of *tumah*. The periods of maternal *tumah* and *tahara* have their own independent logic and carry no implication about embryological development. A structurally elegant *drasha* does not establish a *din* if the two domains being linked are inherently unrelated.

---

## Cleopatra Evidence

### Historical Account

The dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and the Sages does not remain purely textual. The Sages invoke empirical evidence: *maaseh bi-Cleopatra malkas Alexandros* — there is an account involving Cleopatra, the queen of Alexandria. Her maidservants had been sentenced to death for crimes against the state. Before their execution, Cleopatra had them impregnated, then killed and dissected at intervals to determine the state of fetal development. When she examined maidservants carrying both male and female fetuses at day forty-one, she found them equally developed. The clear implication, the Sages argue, is that both male and female reach the same stage of development at day forty-one — supporting the majority position against Rabbi Yishmael's differentiated timeline.

### Scripture Over Empirical

Rabbi Yishmael's response is terse and pointed: *ani meivi lachem rayah min ha-Torah, ve-atem meivim li rayah min ha-shotim* — I am bringing you proof from the *Torah*; you are bringing me proof from fools. The dismissal is not merely rhetorical. Rabbi Yishmael is making an epistemological claim: when he has derivations from *psukim*, an empirical observation — however dramatic — does not override the textual tradition.

### Experimental Flaws

But the Gemara presses further and finds an independent reason why the Cleopatra experiment cannot serve as valid proof, regardless of whether one privileges scriptural over empirical reasoning. *Eima nekeiva kadam ve-ubar arbaim yomin kamei zachar* — perhaps the female fetus was actually forty days older than the male fetus when examined. How would anyone know the precise moment of conception for each maidservant? The experiment lacks the control necessary for its conclusion to follow. Perhaps the maidservant carrying the girl had already been pregnant for forty days before the experiment began. If so, what appeared to be equal development at day forty-one for both would actually represent development at day eighty-one for the girl and day forty-one for the boy — precisely what Rabbi Yishmael's position predicts. The Cleopatra evidence proves nothing.

### Ein Apotropus

The Sages, anticipating this objection, note that Cleopatra took precautions: she had the maidservants drink an abortifacient potion before the experiment began, to ensure that any pre-existing fetus was discharged, and then placed them under guard after the designated conception to ensure that no further sexual activity occurred. All pregnancies were thus controlled from a known starting point. But Rabbi Yishmael's retort is devastating: *ein apotropus l'arayot* — there is no such thing as a reliable chaperone when it comes to sexual matters. No guard can guarantee that nothing occurred. Perhaps the very guard charged with protecting the women was the one who had relations with them. This principle — *ein apotropus l'arayot* — is not merely a rhetorical flourish; it is an established halakhic concept with its own doctrinal weight. You cannot base an empirical proof on conditions that cannot be certified.

### Equal Development Stages

One remaining question: even granting the Sages' claim that the maidservants were monitored and the conception dates were known, how can we be confident that the girl, if examined at eighty-one days, had not already reached the same stage of development forty days earlier? Perhaps that fetal stage was already present at day forty-one for the girl as well, and simply persisted unchanged. In that case, seeing equal development at day eighty-one for the girl and forty-one for the boy tells us nothing about when each first reached that stage.

Abaye resolves this: *besimaneihon shavin* — because the characteristics of the forty-one-day male fetus and the eighty-one-day female fetus were exactly identical, we can conclude they had reached the same developmental stage at the same pace of development. A fetus does not remain static for forty days and then suddenly resume development; if the two were at exactly the same stage, that is evidence they matured in parallel. This is Abaye's resolution, though the Gemara's ambivalence about the entire line of empirical reasoning is palpable throughout the discussion.

The Gemara's treatment of the Cleopatra account is revealing. Rabbi Yishmael's initial dismissal — *rayah min ha-shotim*, proof from fools — might be read as an epistemological rejection of empirical evidence altogether. But the subsequent discussion actually engages with the experiment on its own terms, identifying specific methodological failures: no control for prior pregnancy, no guaranteed chaperonage. This suggests that the Gemara is somewhere between wholesale rejection and full acceptance of empirical proof. It would accept solid experimental evidence in principle, but is rightly skeptical of evidence derived from conditions that cannot be certified.

---

## Consensus: Day 41

### Majority Prevails

The *Gemara* closes the dispute with a note on *pesak*: *ve-chachamim haynu tanna kamma* — the *chachamim* who debated Rabbi Yishmael are simply the *tanna kamma* of the *Mishna*, who established day forty-one for both male and female. One might have thought the *halacha* could follow Rabbi Yishmael, given that his position is supported by at least a textual derivation — *dekamsaya lei kra*, the *pasuk* provides him some grounding — and it offers a coherent explanation for why the *Torah* assigns the mother double the *tumah* and *tahara* days for a girl. Absent Rabbi Yishmael's linkage, why does a girl's birth impose twice as many days of *tumah* and *tahara* on the mother? It is one of the first questions that arises when learning *parashat Tazria*. Rabbi Yishmael's answer is elegant. Nonetheless, *ka mashma lan*: the *halacha* follows the *chachamim*. Majority opinion controls, and the *sages*' categorical rejection — *ein le-meidin yetzirah mi-tumah* — stands. For all halakhic purposes, fetal viability begins at day forty-one for both male and female.

---

## Fetal Aggada

### Posture & Anatomy

The *Gemara* now transitions from the most technically demanding material of the *daf* to some of its most memorable aggadic content. The contrast between 30a and 30b — dense halakhic computation on one side, lyrical *aggadata* on the other — is striking. *Darash Rabbi Simlai: lema havlad domeh bimei immo* — Rabbi Simlai expounded: to what is the infant comparable while it is in its mother's womb? *Le-pinkas shemekupal umunach* — like a ledger, like two stiff boards folded together. The fetus is folded: *yadav al shtei tzad'av* — hands on the temples; *shtei atzilav al shtei arkubotav* — elbows at the knees; *bet ekevav al bet agvotov* — ankles tucked in by the buttocks; *verosho munach lo bein birkav* — and the head between the thighs. The description is a remarkably accurate account of fetal positioning in the womb.

### Nutrition & Waste

*Upiv satum vetiburo patuach* — the mouth is sealed and the navel is open. Through the open navel — the umbilical cord — the fetus receives all its sustenance: *ve'ochel mimmah she'immo ochelet* — it eats what its mother eats; *ve'shoteh mimmah she'immo shotah* — it drinks what its mother drinks. And *ve'eino motzi re'i* — it does not excrete. The reason: *shema yaharog et immo* — lest it kill its mother. Were the fetus to excrete normally, the waste matter would flow back into the mother's bloodstream with lethal consequences. The amniotic environment neutralizes and contains what must be contained, and the system is self-sustaining precisely because of what remains sealed.

### Birth Transformation

*Ve-keivan sheyatza la'avir ha'olam, niftach hasatum, venistam hapatuach* — at the moment of birth, what was closed opens and what was open closes. The mouth, sealed throughout the gestation, opens to the air of the world. The navel, the conduit of all life-giving sustenance, closes. *She'ilmalei ken, eino yachol lichyot afilu sha'ah achat* — were this reversal not to occur, the newborn could not survive for even a single moment. This is the foundation of the blessing of *Asher Yatzar*, which praises the Creator for the precise arrangement of openings and closures in the human body: if any one that should remain open were to close, or any one that should close were to remain open, survival would be impossible.

### Candle & Torah

*Ve-ner daluk lo al rosho* — while in the womb, a candle burns over the fetus's head. This is not understood as a literal flame but as some form of illumination. *Ve-tzofeh umabit missof ha'olam ve'ad sofo* — by its light the fetus can see from one end of the world to the other. This seemingly impossible claim is preemptively defended: one should not be astonished, for a person asleep here can dream of distant lands far beyond the reach of ordinary vision. The faculty operative in the womb is of a similar character.

*U-melamdin oto kol ha-Torah kullah* — and the fetus is taught the entire Torah. The Gemara grounds this in two *psukim*. The first, *be-sod eloka alai oholi* — in the secret of God hovering over my tent — might be dismissed as the words of a prophet speaking of his own adult experience. But the continuation of the verse places it within the context of *yerachei kedem*, the months of old, which the Gemara identifies as the months of the womb: a period measured in months, not years, lasting only nine. The Torah knowledge is complete, absolute, and supernaturally comprehensive.

### Womb Perfection

*Ve-ein lecha yamim she'adam sharui be-tovah yoter me'otan hayamim* — there are no days in which a person dwells in such complete goodness as those days in the womb. The womb is a world of perfection: total knowledge, total sustenance, total vision. Then comes the moment of birth.

*Ba malach u-sataro al piv, u-mashkachu kol ha-Torah kullah* — an angel comes and strikes him on the mouth, and he forgets the entire Torah. *She-neemar l'petach chatat roveitz* — as it is written, sin crouches at the opening. The moment of emergence into the imperfect world is the moment of forgetting. The human being enters the world stripped of the perfect knowledge it possessed in utero, and must spend a lifetime struggling to recover what was once held in complete and effortless wholeness. The image is at once melancholy and galvanizing: we are not learning Torah for the first time; we are remembering what we once knew entirely and have since forgotten.

---

---

# Niddah 31

## Fetus & Torah

### Torah Learning

The *daf* opens in the middle of a beautiful *aggadata* discussing what happens to the fetus while it is in the mother's womb and as it comes into the world. The *Gemara* returns to a passage that was read at the close of the previous *daf*: that while in the womb, the baby learns the entire *Torah*. *V'cheivan sheba l'avir ha'olam* — and when it comes out into the air of the world — *ba malach v'satro al piv, umeshachacho kol hatorah kulah* — an angel comes and strikes it on its mouth, and causes it to forget the entire *Torah*.

The verse adduced is *lapetach chatat rovetz* — "sin crouches at the opening." The precise meaning of *chatat* here is ambiguous: it may refer to the imperfection of the world the infant is entering, a world where *Torah* does not come easily and must be acquired through struggle, or it may refer to the angel itself — though that reading would be unusual. In any case, the image is of a transition from a state of completeness into an imperfect world where *Torah* must be striven for anew.

### Angel's Strike

One might wonder why the *malach* strikes the infant on its mouth rather than on its brain, where the *Torah* presumably resides. This *midrash* does not say. Yet the connection between speech and *Torah* is deep — *v'shinantam l'vanecha v'dibarta bam* — and so the mouth as the locus of *Torah* expression is perhaps not so strange. There is also a possible wordplay in *lapetach*, "at the opening," understood as the *petach* of the mouth. In any event, the *midrash* presents the forgetting not as a deprivation but as a condition of human existence in an imperfect world: *Torah* must now be earned.

### The Oath

The *Gemara* continues: *v'eino yo'tzei misham ad she'mashbi'ino oto* — the fetus does not leave the womb until it is administered an oath. The source is the verse *ki li tichra kol berech tishava kol lashon* — "to Me shall every knee bow, every tongue shall swear." The *Gemara* reads this verse on two registers. *Ki li tichra kol berech* — every knee bows — this refers to *yom hamitah*, the day of death, as in the verse *lifanav yichre'u kol yordei afar*, all who descend to the dust shall bow before Him. *Tishava kol lashon* — every tongue has sworn — this refers to *yom haledah*, the day of birth. Support comes from the verse *neki chapayim u'var levav asher lo nasa lashav nafshi v'lo nishba l'mirmach* — the one of clean hands and pure heart who has not borne My soul in vain and has not sworn deceitfully.

The content of the oath itself is: *tehe tzaddik v'al tehe rasha* — be righteous and do not be wicked. And even if the entire world were to say to you, "you are righteous," you should regard yourself as though you still have far to go — *heye b'einecha k'rasha*. Whether framing this as "regard yourself as wicked" is psychologically helpful may be debated; perhaps it is better rendered as: never assume you have arrived. At the same time, *v'al tehe rasha bifnei atzmecha* — do not be wicked in your own eyes either. The oath is double-edged: it obligates constant striving while prohibiting self-contempt.

### Pure Soul

The passage continues: *she'hakadosh baruch hu tahor u'meshartav tehorim v'neshamah shenatan b'cha tehorah hi* — God is *tahor*, pure, those who attend God are pure, and the soul He has placed within you is pure. This is, of course, the source of the *Elokai neshamah* prayer recited each morning: *Elokai neshamah shenatata bi tehorah hi*. The conditional follows: if you guard that soul in its purity, well and good. If not — *hareni notlah mimcha* — I will take it back from you. Do not assume the soul is yours unconditionally.

### Kohen & Trumah

A *mashal* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: this is comparable to a *kohen* who entrusts his *terumah* to an *am ha'aretz*. The *kohen* says: if you guard it in its purity, good; if not, *harei hi nisrefet l'fanecha* — it will be burned before you. I will not hesitate to destroy it in your presence. The entire human race is here cast in the role of the *am ha'aretz* relative to God — the recipient of something precious and holy that does not inherently belong to them, held in trust under condition of care.

### Sin & Purity

There is a striking tension in this passage that deserves careful attention. The *Gemara* describes God as *tahor* — not *kadosh*, the more typical divine epithet, but *tahor*. This choice seems deliberate. The point appears to be a direct counterstatement to the doctrine of original sin. *Lapetach chatat rovetz* is not ignored — the *Gemara* is aware that sin crouches at the threshold of the world. But entering a world where sin exists, a world of struggle and incompleteness in which the *Torah* one was born knowing must now be laboriously reacquired, is categorically different from being born sinful or impure.

The soul comes from God. God is *tahor*. Therefore the soul is *tahor*. If one were to say that the soul enters the world already stained or corrupted, one would be saying something about God — and that is precisely what this passage refuses to say. The mention of *meshartav tehorim* — God's attendants are likewise pure — may carry an additional implication: it is perhaps a quiet rejoinder to any notion of a sinful or evil divine being, a *satan* who is ontologically corrupt. Everything in the heavenly retinue is pure; the corruption of this world is not traced to some primordial divine evil.

### Being vs. Becoming

This connects to a theme from the week's *parshah*. Korach declares *ki kol ha'edah kulam kedoshim* — all of the congregation is holy. And is that not true? The *Torah* indeed says *v'hayitem li mamlechet kohanim v'goy kadosh*, *kedoshim tihyu*, *anshei kodesh tihyun li* — you shall be, you shall become, a holy people. But every one of those formulations is in the future tense or imperative: you shall become holy, be holy. Korach says: we *are* holy. The difference is enormous. There is a profound distinction between asserting that one has arrived at holiness — that one's existing status renders further striving unnecessary — and recognizing that holiness is an ongoing obligation, a state of perpetual *becoming*. The oath *tehe tzaddik v'al tehe rasha* encodes this very dynamic: it commands continuous striving and warns against the complacency of assuming the work is done.

---

## Fetal Development

### Oath Source

Rav Elazar asks: *mai kra* — what is the verse? The *Gemara* has spoken of an oath taken in the womb, but has not yet identified the biblical locus for where exactly in the womb this occurs. The verse offered is *mi'ma'ai imi atah gozi* — "from my mother's womb You are my *gozi*." The word *gozi* is normally translated as "You who shaped me," but the *Gemara* reads it as a term of oath-taking. The proof that *gozi* can connote an oath is from the verse *gazi nizrech vehashlichi* — a *nazir* takes a vow, *nezirut*, and the word *gazi* is related to that act of vowing.

### Walnut in Water

Rav Elazar offers a second teaching: *lama havlad domeh bimei imo* — what is the fetus like in its mother's womb? *Le'egoz munach bisafal shel mayim* — like a walnut resting in a dish of water. If one presses a finger upon it, the walnut shifts and bobs in every direction, *shokeia lechan u'lechan*, yet remains protected. The image conveys how the fetus, suspended in amniotic fluid, can be moved from the outside while still being sheltered within.

### Three Chambers

The *Baraita* teaches: *shlosha chadashim harishonim velad dar bimador hatachton* — during the first trimester, the fetus resides in the lower chamber of the womb, closest to the birth canal. In the second trimester, it rises to the middle chamber. In the final trimester, it ascends to the upper chamber — *bimador ha'elyon*. This is the reverse of what one might expect intuitively, but the *Gemara* supports it from the verse in Tehillim: *asher asiti baseter rukamti betachtiyot aretz* — "You fashioned me in secret, You wove me in the lowest depths." The word *rukamti*, "You wove me," is used rather than *darti*, "I dwelt," which indicates that the fashioning — the early formation — occurs in the lower chamber. From there the fetus ascends.

### Birth Pangs

When the time arrives for the fetus to emerge — *mitehafech veyotze* — it turns and comes out. This turning, the *Gemara* will explain, is the source of *chevlei isha*, the birth pangs of a woman. A *Baraita* states: *chevlei shel nekeivah merubin mishel zachar* — the birth pangs of giving birth to a girl are greater than those of giving birth to a boy. Rav Elazar asks: *mai kra* — what is the textual basis?

### Girl Birth Pangs

The explanation proceeds from an understanding of how conception shapes fetal orientation. The *Gemara* reasons that during conception the man is typically on top, and the child is formed in the orientation of its parent: *zeh ba k'derech tashmisho v'zeh ba k'derech tashmisho*. A male fetus is fashioned face-down, as the father was, and emerges face-down — which is indeed the normal presentation at birth — without needing to flip. A female fetus, fashioned face-up as the mother was, must turn over in order to be born face-down: *vezehu chevlei isha*, and this turning is what produces the additional birth pangs.
