The *Gemara* states it directly: *ve-ze ofech paneha ve-ze ein ofech paneha* — the female fetus must flip, the male need not.

---

## Sex in Pregnancy

### Trimesters

The *Baraita* addresses the impact of marital relations during pregnancy, broken down by trimester. *Shlosha chodashim harishonim tashmish kasheh l'ishah vegam kasheh lavalad* — in the first trimester, relations are difficult and potentially harmful for both the woman and the fetus. In the second trimester, *kasheh l'ishah v'yafeh lavalad* — they are difficult for the woman but beneficial for the fetus. In the final trimester, *yafeh l'ishah v'yafeh lavalad* — they are beneficial for both. Rashi notes that he is not certain of the underlying reasoning for the effect on the woman, but explains the differential impact on the fetus as follows: since in the first trimester the fetus resides in the lower chamber, it is more directly affected by penetration; as the fetus ascends through the second and third trimesters, it becomes progressively less vulnerable and the semen can even be beneficial. The precise mechanism remains unclear, but this trimester-based framework was, notably, widely accepted not only in Rabbinic literature but in broader medical culture well into the late medieval period.

### Day 90

The *Gemara* adds: *tana hameshammesh mitato l'yom tish'im* — if a husband has relations with his wife on exactly the 90th day of pregnancy — the cusp between the first and second trimesters — *k'ilu shofech damim*, it is as though he has spilled blood, as this is the moment of greatest vulnerability and risk of miscarriage. The practical difficulty is immediately raised: *hashta mana yadei* — how would one know exactly which day is the 90th? Abaye resolves this pragmatically: *meshammesh veholech v'shomer peta'im Hashem* — one should simply proceed, and God watches over the simple. The *Gemara* also assumes that in many cases a woman may not even know she is pregnant during the first trimester, which further renders the concern largely theoretical. It should be noted that the *Gemara* appears to count from the moment of conception, whereas the contemporary convention counts weeks from the last menstruation, adding approximately two weeks to the baseline.

---

## Three Partners

### Father's White

The *Gemara* introduces one of its most celebrated passages: *shlosha shutafim yesh b'adam* — there are three partners in a human being: *HaKadosh Baruch Hu v'aviv v'imo* — God, the father, and the mother. *Aviv mazria haloven* — the father provides the white matter. From this white matter come the bones, the sinews, the fingernails — which are translucent and whitish — the brain, and the white of the eye.

### Mother's Red

*Imo mazra'at odem* — the mother contributes the red matter, associated with her blood and with the menstrual cycle that the Rabbis observed. From this red matter come the skin, the flesh, the blood, the hair, and the black of the eye. The *Gemara* thus maps the visible components of the body onto two color registers: the father's white and the mother's red. One might wonder whether lighter-skinned populations are imagined here, but it is worth noting that this *Baraita* originates in *Eretz Yisrael*.

Of particular interest among God's contributions — which are enumerated next — is the *klaster panim*, the distinctive configuration of the face. Even if a child has the physical eyes of the father and the skin of the mother, the individual character of how those features cohere into a particular human face — what Rashi describes as *ziv*, the radiance or expression — that belongs to the divine contribution.

### God's Gifts

While the father and mother supply the raw materials, none of it functions until God animates it. God contributes *reiyat ha'ayin* — sight, *shemiat haozen* — hearing, *dibur peh* — speech (*mi sam peh l'adam*), *hilukh raglayim* — the ability to walk, and *deah u'vinah v'sechel* — knowledge, understanding, and wisdom. These may correspond to different levels of the soul: what is more purely spiritual (*neshamah*) versus what is shared with the animal world (*ruach*) — a distinction developed extensively in medieval Jewish philosophy, though the *Gemara* does not elaborate on it here. What is clear is that *klaster panim*, appearing among these divine gifts, occupies a peculiar middle position: it is physical in nature, yet it is somehow the most distinctly human aspect of the body, the visible mark of the individual soul.

### Death & Return

*V'kivun she'higia zemano l'ipater min ha'olam* — when the time comes for departure from this world, *HaKadosh Baruch Hu notel chelko* — God takes back His portion, namely the soul, *v'chelek avi v'imo maniakh lifneihem* — and the portions of the father and mother are left below. This echoes the verse in Kohelet: *v'haruach tashuv el ha'Elokim asher netanah* — the spirit returns to God who gave it, while the body returns to the earth from which it came.

Rav Pappa adds a folk saying: *pot milkhakh v'shadi l'visra* — once you remove the salt that preserves the meat, you might as well throw the meat to the dogs. The coarser image drives home the point: it is not merely that the soul animates the body spiritually; the soul is in some sense what preserves the body even physically. Once the soul departs, decomposition begins. The two things are more intertwined than a simple body-soul dualism would suggest.

---

## Miracles

### Pouch Analogy

Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa expounds: *mai dikhtiv oseh gedolot ad ein kheker v'niflaot ad ein mispar* — "Who performs great deeds beyond comprehension and wonders beyond number." *Bo ur'eh shelo k'midat HaKadosh Baruch Hu midat basar vedam* — come and see how God's ways differ from the ways of human beings. A person places a valuable object in a bound leather pouch — *cheimas tzerurah* — with the mouth of the pouch facing upward, and even so it is doubtful whether the contents will remain secure. God, by contrast, fashions the fetus *bimei ishah pesuchah ufia lematah* — in the open womb with the mouth facing downward — and yet *umishtameir* — it remains protected. Rashi emphasizes that the fetus, residing in the lower chamber, is already in closest proximity to the opening, making the miracle of retention all the more striking.

### Scale Rises

A second comparison: a person places objects on a balance scale, and the heavier the load, the further down that side descends — *kol zeman shemachbid yoreid lematah*. But with God, *kol zeman shemachbid havlad oleh lema'alah* — as the fetus grows heavier, it rises higher in the womb. This corresponds to the movement through the three trimesters: the fetus ascends from the lower chamber through the middle to the upper, even as it increases in weight — the inverse of ordinary physical expectation.

### Seeds Merge

Rabbi Yose HaGlili expounds the verse *odkha al kol nora'os niflesi nifla'im ma'asekha venafshi yoda'as me'od* — "I will thank You for the awesome wonders You have done for me; wondrous are Your works and my soul knows it well." *Adam nosein zir'onim be'arugah* — when a person plants seeds in a garden bed, *kol achas ve'achas olah beminah* — each seed grows true to its own kind. Plant a cucumber seed and you get a cucumber; plant a tomato seed and you get a tomato. Even if planted side by side, they remain distinct and do not merge. *Ve'ilu HaKadosh Baruch Hu tzar ubar b'mei ishah vechulam olim lemin echad* — but God fashions the fetus in the mother's womb, and the contribution of the father, the contribution of the mother, and the divine contribution all merge into a single, beautiful, unified human being — something that would never occur if one merely planted the seeds next to one another.

It is worth noting that in this *drasha*, the three components are treated as genuine equals. One could have made the point about divine involvement by simply contrasting the human partners with God, but instead the *drasha* builds a three-way partnership in which all three are necessary and none is dispensable. This is significant in light of where the *sugyah* began: a discussion of viable and non-viable birth, rooted in the recognition that God is a genuine *shutaf* in every human life.

### Dyer's Colors

A final *davar acher*: *tzava noten samanin leyoreh* — a dyer places different colored dyes into a vat, *kulam olim letzeva echad* — and they all merge into one undifferentiated color. But God, *tzar hu bimei ishah*, fashions the fetus in the womb, *kol echad ve'echad oleh lemino* — and each component retains its own character within the whole. The white matter of the father remains distinct as bone and sinew; the red matter of the mother remains distinct as skin and blood; the divine gifts of sight, speech, and *klaster panim* remain distinguishable. They do not homogenize.

This is the salad-bowl model rather than the melting-pot model, to use a contemporary analogy: the component elements cohere into a greater whole while preserving their distinctiveness. And this, as it happens, is precisely how modern genetics understands the situation — maternal and paternal genetic imprints are preserved as such, with dominant and recessive expressions, rather than being fused into a single undifferentiated code.

---

## Divine Oversight

### Yosef Drasha

The *Gemara* shifts slightly from the immediate topic of fetal formation to a series of *drashot* on related themes of divine involvement. The *drasha* attributed to Yosef expounds: *odkha Hashem ki anafta bi yashov apecha utnachameni* — "I will thank You, God, because You were angry with me; Your anger has turned away and You have comforted me." The plain meaning is probably gratitude for the removal of divine anger, but the *Gemara* asks: *bameh hakatuv medaber* — what is this verse speaking about?

The answer is a parable: two people set out together on a business trip. One of them gets a splinter and, unable to travel, is forced to stay behind. He curses and blasphemes — *mecharef umegadef* — furious at his misfortune. Then, days later, he hears that the ship his companion was sailing on has sunk. *Hitchil modeh umeshabeach* — he begins to offer thanks and praise. The bad thing was, in retrospect, the deliverance. *Vekach ne'emar yashov apecha utnachameni* — your anger has turned away and become comfort. One becomes grateful even for what appeared at the time to be a calamity.

There is a genuine theological difficulty in these stories: the gratitude of the one who survived raises uncomfortable questions about the hundreds who did not. The *Gemara* does not resolve that question. But the *gam zu letovah* message — the teaching of Nachum Ish Gam Zu — is present here: that even bad things can ultimately contain hidden good. What is particularly striking is that the figure in the parable is not a righteous man — he is blaspheming God. Yet even such a person can, in the end, arrive at gratitude and recognition. Perhaps that too is part of the point: the capacity to ultimately recognize God's hidden goodness is not reserved for the *tzaddik*.

### Miracles Alone

Rabbi Elazar expounds: *mai d'chsiv oseh niflaot levado uvaruch shem kevodo le'olam* — "Who alone performs wonders, and blessed is His glorious name forever." The word *levado* — alone — means that the miracle is known only to God. *Afilu ba'al haness eino makir benisso* — even the recipient of the miracle does not recognize the miracle that has been done for him. There are moments when great salvations occur, and the very person saved cannot perceive them — perhaps because being at the center of events obscures one's perspective, or because the miracle presents itself under the guise of an ordinary inconvenience, like a splinter. This connects back to the *drasha* of Yosef: the blasphemer does not know, in the moment, that he is the beneficiary of a miracle.

### Winnowing Seed

Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa expounds the verse *orchi veriv'i zerita* — "You have spread out my path and my lying down." The word *riv'i* is read in a sexual register — *rove'a* denotes an act of intercourse — and *zerita* is read as *zoreh*, to winnow. The teaching: *melo notzar adam mikol hatipa ela min habarur shebah* — a person is not created from the entirety of the drop of semen, but from the clearest, most refined part of it.

A *mashal* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: a winnower in a threshing floor removes the food grain and casts aside the chaff — *notel et haohel umeniach et hapsoles*. So too God winnows the semen, taking only the most refined element for the formation of life. This raises an interesting observation: while the earlier teaching assigned the physical components of the body entirely to father and mother, with God contributing only the spiritual gifts, here God is implicated in the fashioning of the physical as well — it is God who selects which element of the seed will form the child.

Rabbi Abahu resolves an apparent contradiction between two verses. One verse uses the form *vatizreni chayil* — "You have winnowed me with strength" — without an *alef*, yielding the sense of winnowing (*zoreh*). Another uses *ha'el hame'azreni chayil* — "God who has girded me with strength" — with an *alef*, yielding the sense of girding. Rabbi Abahu says: David was saying before the Holy One, Blessed be He — *zeritani vezirzatani* — by winnowing the seed that led to my conception, You have thereby girded me with strength. The process of refinement is itself a source of strength.

### God Counts

Rabbi Abahu expounds: *mi manah afar Yaakov umispar et rova Yisrael* — "Who has counted the dust of Yaakov and numbered the *rova* of Israel?" The word *rova* — normally meaning "myriad" — is read through the cognate *rove'a*, an act of sexual intercourse. *Melamed sheHaKadosh Baruch Hu yoshev vesoper et riviosaihem shel Yisrael* — this teaches that God sits and counts the sexual encounters of Israel. Rashi specifies that it is perhaps the *onas tashmishan* — the appointed times of their relations — that is being counted.

The question is: to what end? *Matai tavo tipa shetzadik notzar mimenah* — God is watching for when the conception of a *tzadik* will take place. This requires care: the famous principle states *hakol bidei shamayim chutz miyiras shamayim* — everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven — meaning that righteousness itself is beyond divine predetermination and remains in human control. A related *midrash* observes that while God determines whether a child will be wealthy or wise, it pointedly does not say whether the child will be *tzadik* or *rasha*. What the *Gemara* may mean here, then, is not that God is waiting to predetermine a *tzadik*, but that God is deeply attentive to the moment when someone who will *choose* to become a *tzadik* is conceived.

### Bilam Blind

The punishment of Bilam flows from this very teaching. Bilam, upon hearing that God sits and counts the sexual encounters of Israel in anticipation of righteous conception, was outraged: *mi shehu tahor vekadosh umeshartav tehorim vekdoshim yatzitz bidavar zeh* — He who is holy and pure, whose attendants are holy and pure — this is a fitting preoccupation for Him? *Miyad nismit eino* — immediately one of his eyes was blinded. As the Gemara puts it: you think you see properly? You do not see at all. The verse reads Bilam as *shtum ha'ayin* — of the sealed eye. Tosafot notes that *shtum* in fact means an *open* eye, singular — meaning one eye was open and the other sealed shut.

### Yissachar

Rabbi Yochanan expounds the verse *vayshkav imah balaila hu* — "and he lay with her that night, *hu*." The word *hu* — "he" — is taken as an allusion to God. *Melamed sheHaKadosh Baruch Hu siyaya be'oto ma'aseh* — this teaches that God assisted in that encounter. Leah had acquired the *dudaim* and said to Yaakov: come to me tonight. The *Gemara* adds that the verse *Yissachar chamor garem* — "Yissachar, a bony donkey" — is read as *chamor garam lo l'Yissachar*: the donkey caused it to happen for Yissachar. Rashi explains: Yaakov was traveling home on his donkey, perhaps hesitating, and God caused the donkey to walk toward Leah's tent, so that the encounter — and the conception of Yissachar — took place through divine involvement in the physical circumstances.

This sits in deliberate contrast to anything like a Christian theological reading. The *Gemara* is not saying that God impregnates in any supernatural sense. It is saying that God is genuinely invested in the conception of righteous people, and acts within the natural order — through the direction of a donkey, through the winnowing of seed — to bring such conceptions about. And just as *lapetach chatat rovetz* is met not by denying sin's existence in the world but by insisting on the purity of the soul, so here the response to divine withdrawal from human biology is not adopted but rather rejected: God is present, deeply present, in the most physical aspects of human generation.

---

## Male vs Female

### Ancient Rule

The *Gemara* now records: *amar Rabbi Yitzchak amar Rabbi Ami* — Rabbi Yitzchak said in the name of Rabbi Ami — *ishah mazra'at techilah yoledet zachar* — if the woman gives forth seed first, she gives birth to a male. *Ish mazria techilah yoledet nekevah* — if the man gives forth seed first, she gives birth to a female. The verse is: *ishah ki tazria veyaldah zachar* — "a woman who gives forth seed and gives birth to a male" — meaning: when she does so first, it is a male.

### Tarfon Proof

A *Baraita* elaborates: the ancients taught this rule — *barishonim hayu omrim* — but they did not explain its source, *velo pirshu Chachamim et hadavar*, until Rabbi Tarfon came and explained it. His proof text is not from the verse quoted above but from: *eleh bnei Leah asher yaldah l'Yaakov b'Padan Aram v'et Dinah bito* — "these are the sons of Leah that she bore Yaakov in Padan Aram, and Dinah his daughter." The verse *attaches* the sons to the mother — *talah hazacharim binkevot* — and attaches the daughter to the father — *vehankevot bazacharim*. This demonstrates that when the mother's seed comes first, the result is male, and when the father's seed comes first, the result is female.

### Female Orgasm

It is at this point that the *sugyah* makes explicit what was implicit above: the *Gemara* is referring, in its discussion of *ishah mazra'at*, to something akin to female orgasm or arousal resulting in the release of fluids. The *Gemara* never states this baldly, but no other biological phenomenon is analogous to the male *zera* in a way that the *Gemara* could have observed, and the subsequent discussion makes the point unmistakable.

This understanding has a striking implication in the cultural context the *Gemara* is addressing. The *Gemara* assumes — and states plainly — that male offspring were strongly preferred: sons were valued and the birth of a daughter was, in certain settings, a source of disappointment. Given the typical dynamics of marital relations, in which a husband might seek his own satisfaction without attending to his wife's, this biological teaching — whether accurate or not — creates a powerful incentive for husbands to ensure their wives' satisfaction. The man who seeks sons must, on this model, concern himself with *ishah mazra'at techilah*.

It is a historical fact, documented by scholars such as Laqueur (*The Making of Sex*), that prior to the discovery of the ovum roughly 150 years ago, a widespread belief held that female orgasm was necessary for conception. This belief, whether arising from the two-seed theory or from other reasoning, correlated historically with significant concern for female sexual satisfaction. Once the egg was discovered and it became clear that female arousal played no role in fertilization, interest in the topic sharply declined in medical and popular literature. Whether the *Gemara* means orgasm specifically or something closer to arousal is a question that cannot be resolved with certainty from the text, but the weight of analogy points toward orgasm.

### Archers

The *Gemara* turns to the verse about the sons of Ulam: *u'vnei ulam anashim giborei chayil dorkhei keshet umarbim banim u'vnei banim* — "and the sons of Ulam were men of valor, archers, who had many sons and sons of sons." The question is raised: can one truly control whether one's children will be male? The *Gemara* answers: *ela mitokh she-mash'him atzmam ba-beten kedei she-yazri'u nishoteihem techilah* — because they withheld themselves during intercourse in order that their wives should give forth seed first. The archery metaphor is apt: archers hold the tension of the drawn bow before releasing. *Hainu de-skharam she-yihyu bneihem zakharim* — this is their reward: that their children were male.

There is another dimension here worth noting. If the birth of a daughter can be attributed to a father's failure to ensure his wife's satisfaction, then a girl's birth carries an implicit social criticism of the father — that he acted selfishly. In a society already inclined to prefer sons, this compounds the pressure on husbands to attend to their wives. Whether this framing is fair or generous is another question; but it is the *Gemara*'s framing, and it has real social consequences.

### Rav Katina

Rav Katina declares: *yacholni la'asot kol banai zakharim* — I could ensure that all my children would be male, for I could always withhold until my wife reached satisfaction first. Why did he not? Apparently because he ruled like Beit Hillel: the obligation of *pru u-rvu* requires one to have at least one son and one daughter, and making all children male would preclude fulfilling the female part of that obligation. Rava then offers a more refined strategy: *ha-rotzeh la'asot kol banav zakharim yiv'ol ve-yishneh* — one who wishes all his children to be male should have relations twice in the same night. The reasoning, spelled out by Rashi, is that a man may not always be able to withhold himself on the first occasion; but having achieved satisfaction the first time, on the second he will be less urgently driven, giving his wife the opportunity to reach satisfaction first — *ishah mazra'at techilah* — thus increasing the likelihood of male offspring.

---

## Conception Timing

### Near Period

Rabbi Yitzchak says in the name of Rabbi Ami: *ein ishah mit'aberet ela samukh le-vistah* — a woman becomes pregnant only near the time of her period. The scientific accuracy of this claim is, of course, inverted — fertility is highest at ovulation, which is near the midpoint of the cycle, not near the period. But that is not the direction the *Gemara* is pursuing.

### Cleansing Sin

The verse brought is *hen be-avon cholalti* — "behold, in iniquity I was fashioned." One might read this verse as implying that the sexual act itself is sinful, or that conception carries an inherent moral taint — a reading that would dovetail with certain Christian interpretations of original sin. The *Gemara* firmly rejects this reading. The word *avon* here does not mean moral sin; it refers to the fact that conception occurs near the time of the woman's period, which is when relations carry the risk of *niddah* status. That is the only *issur* in view.

Rabbi Yochanan reads the verse differently and more accurately in practical terms: *samukh l'tvilah* — it is near the time of her immersion in the *mikvah* that conception is most likely. This corresponds much more closely to the actual peak of fertility following the completion of the *niddah* period. The verse he uses is *uv'cheit yechematni immi* — "and in sin my mother heated for me." Here *cheit* is read not as moral transgression but as *cleansing*, cognate with *v'chitteh et habayit* — "he shall cleanse the house" — which appears in the *Torah* as a term of ritual purification. The *Targum* renders that verse *v'idaki yat beita* — he cleansed the house — confirming the lexical point. And the verse *techatani b'eizov v'et'har* — "cleanse me with hyssop and I will be pure" — makes clear that the biblical Hebrew root *chet-tet-alef* carries the meaning of purification and cleansing at least as naturally as it carries the meaning of sin. So the verse is not saying "in sin my mother fashioned me" but "in the cleansing — the *mikvah* — my mother became heated and conceived me." The optimal moment of conception is thus located precisely at the *mikvah*, the moment of tahorah following the *niddah* period.

---

---

# Niddah 32

## Gender & Procreation

### Male & Peace

The *aggadata* of 31b concludes with a teaching of Rabbi Yitzchak in the school of Rabbi Yannai: *kivan sheba zachar l'olam ba shalom l'olam* — when a male comes into the world, peace comes into the world. The proof-text offered is *shilchu kar moshel aretz* ("send out the *kar*, master of the land"), where Rashi reads *zachar* as a contraction of *ze kar* — "this is the gift," the peace-offering, the thing of value that the male brings into the world.

### Male Production, Female…

A second teaching from the same school continues the wordplay: *ba zachar l'olam ba k'reih beyado* — when a male comes into the world, his loaf of bread is in his hands. The word *zachar* is again parsed as *ze kar*, this time in the sense of productive capacity, supported by the verse *vayikra lahem k'ra gedolah* ("he dug for them a great pit"), which is taken to evoke the ability to produce and be productive. By contrast, *nekeivah ein imah klum* — the female comes with nothing. The wordplay here is *nekiyah ba'ah*, she comes empty-handed. The proof-text is *nakvah s'charach alai v'etenah* ("articulate your fee and I will pay it"), Lavan's words to Yaakov, which is read to mean that she must ask — *ad d'amrah mezuni lo yahavu lah* — "until she says, give me my sustenance, they do not give her."

Rashi renders this as a matter of prayer — *sheyeda l'hitpaleil* — turning the formula into a petition to God. But the more natural reading is that it reflects the social realities of the time: women lacked the opportunity and education for independent means of earning a living. Indeed, the *gemara* throughout assumes that the husband bears the obligation of *mezonos* for his wife precisely because the working assumption is that she cannot earn independently, even though the *gemara* certainly knew of counterexamples.

### Essentialist vs. Societal

What makes this *aggadata* more than a sociological observation is that it is framed as an essentialist claim — not merely that women in this society lacked economic opportunity, but that the nature of the male is to produce and the nature of the female is to be without. This raises the question of whether the Rabbis are describing a societal reality or encoding it as a metaphysical truth. The framing in the *gemara* slides toward the latter, which is notable.

There is also, one might add, an implicit anatomical dimension to this framing: ancient and medieval thinkers — the Rabbis perhaps among them — sometimes conceived of the female as a male who lacks something, since the female anatomy is internal and concealed. The imagery of the male arriving with something in hand while the female arrives empty fits naturally into that broader perspective, however uncomfortable it may be from a modern vantage point.

### Shalom Debate

The *shalom* dimension of the opening teaching deserves its own examination. The straightforward reading might be that the birth of a boy brings domestic joy and harmony. But one might equally ask: men are historically the ones who go to war, so in what sense does the arrival of a male bring *shalom*? A more compelling reading is that *shalom* here means protection and security — the male as the protector of the household. The word *shalom* thus carries a sense not of peace in the abstract but of the physical safety and security that a male presence was understood to provide in that cultural context.

---

## Korban & Labor Oath

### Students' Question

The *gemara* turns to a famous piece of *aggadata* in which the students of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai pose the question: *mipnei mah amrah Torah yoledet meviah korban?* — why does a woman who gives birth have to bring a *korban*? This question rests on an implicit assumption that a *chatas* is about sin. As we have studied at length in *Kerisos* and *Shavuos*, a *chatas* is not primarily about sin; rather, it belongs to the category of *mechusrei kapparah*, those whose *tumah* is concluded through the bringing of a *korban* — a *zav*, a *metzora*, a *yoledet*, and similar cases. The *gemara* in *Shavuos* says this explicitly. Yet here the students treat the *chatas* as a response to transgression and want to know what sin was committed.

### Labor Oath Answer

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai answers: *besha'ah shekora'at laleid, kofetzet venishba'at shelo tizakek leva'alah* — at the moment of crouching to give birth, she swears that she will never again have relations with her husband, because of the pain of childbirth. *Lefikach amrah Torah tavi korban* — therefore the Torah said she must bring a *korban*, because she will inevitably go back on that oath when she wishes to resume her marital life. Rashi explains it as the transgression of that *shevuah* that requires atonement.

### Rav Yosef Objects

*Matkif lah Rav Yosef*: Rav Yosef challenges this sharply. *Veha mezidah hi* — but she is a *mezid*, someone who transgresses willingly. She knew she had taken the oath and she knowingly violated it. *Vechi chatas al mezid teiti?* — can a *chatas*, which is for inadvertent sin, apply to an intentional transgression? Furthermore, even if she felt genuine *charatah* and sought release from her oath, the mechanism for that is *hatarat nedarim*, not a *korban chatas*. And if there were a *korban* to bring for an oath, it would be a *korban shevuah*, a specific category of its own. The *gemara* offers no resolution, which effectively signals that the *gemara* was not fully persuaded by Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's answer. The more fundamental answer — that the *korban* is not about sin at all but about concluding the state of *tumah* — remains, as stated elsewhere in the *gemara*, the more solid foundation.

---

## Tumah Periods

### One vs. Two Weeks

The *gemara* proceeds to another question in the same vein: *mipnei mah amrah Torah zachar leshiv'ah unekevah le'arba'ah asar?* — why does the Torah prescribe one week of *tumah* after the birth of a boy and two weeks after the birth of a girl? This is a pointed question, especially given that the physical process of childbirth does not differ so dramatically between the cases, at least not according to all views.

### Joy vs. Sadness

The answer given is rooted in the emotional context of the birth. By a *zachar*, *shehakol smeichim bo mitcharata leshiv'ah* — because everyone is joyous at the birth of a boy, the mother regrets her oath after one week; she is happy enough to return to her husband. By a *nekevah*, *shehakol atzeivim bah mitcharata le'arba'ah asar* — because everyone is saddened, disappointed that it was not a boy, the mother remains in her distress for two weeks before she is willing to go back.

This is a striking passage, reflecting with uncomfortable directness the cultural assumption that the birth of a daughter was received with less joy than the birth of a son. There is, to some degree, an empirical truth embedded here that persists even today: in communities where a son receives a *bris* on the eighth day, the birth of a boy carries a built-in communal celebration that the birth of a girl does not automatically receive. If someone in a *haredi* community announces "so-and-so had a baby," the assumption is often that it was a girl — because if it were a boy they would say so directly.

### Modern Brachot Rulings

This has *halachic* ramifications as well. Classically, the birth of a boy would occasion a *bracha* of *Shehecheyanu* or *HaTov VeHaMeitiv*, while the birth of a girl would not. Contemporary *poskim*, however — not merely the most modern ones but a meaningful range of later authorities — have ruled that since societal attitudes have genuinely shifted and people do celebrate the birth of daughters with real *simcha*, one may and should recite *Shehecheyanu* and *HaTov VeHaMeitiv* for a daughter as well. The *HaTov VeHaMeitiv* is recited over wine, not directly over the child. This evolution in *p'sak* is itself instructive: it acknowledges that the *gemara*'s distinction was rooted in societal norms rather than timeless metaphysics.

The *gemara* also notes that the *bris milah* is performed on the eighth day — which corresponds to the end of the mother's week of *tumah* after a boy — so that the husband and wife can be together at the time of the communal *simcha*. This connection no longer applies in the same way given later developments in *hilchos niddah*.

---

## Niddah Seven Days

### Why Seven Days?

A *Baraisa* is cited in the name of Rabbi Meir: *mipnei mah amrah Torah niddah leshiv'ah?* — why did the Torah prescribe seven days for a *niddah*? The question has force because most bodily *tumos* that are natural — relating to the living body rather than death or animal carcasses — last only a single day. A *ba'al keri*, for instance, is *tamei* for only one day. Why should *niddah* be seven days?

### Familiarity Remedy

The answer is: *mipnei sheragil bah vekatzah bah* — because a husband becomes too accustomed to his wife, and familiarity leads to a kind of boredom or dulling of desire. *Amrah Torah tehei temei'ah shivah yamim* — therefore the Torah said she should be *temei'ah* for seven days, *kedei shetehei chavivah al baalah kesha'at kenisatah lachuppah* — so that she should be as beloved to her husband as at the moment she entered the *chuppah*. The seven-day separation is a mechanism for renewal, for resetting the emotional and physical intimacy of the marriage to something closer to its original freshness.

### Modern Marriage Context

There is genuine psychological truth to this. Statistics on long-term marriages show a consistent pattern of declining frequency of intimate relations, driven precisely by the dynamic the *gemara* describes — everything becoming routine, familiar, undifferentiated. The *gemara*'s answer identifies this tendency and offers the *niddah* cycle as a structural corrective. It is worth noting that this should not be taught with false idealism, as though the *mikvah* night will always be experienced as a wedding night and expectations will always be met. Setting realistic expectations matters. But the core insight — that periodic separation followed by reunion can restore a sense of novelty and desire — is well-founded.

### Rambam Analogy

The Rambam in the *Guide to the Perplexed* offers a related observation about *Beis HaMikdash*: one of the purposes of *tumah* and *taharah* rules is to create periods during which one cannot enter the *Beis HaMikdash*, so that when access is restored, the encounter carries weight and appreciation. The analogy is instructive even if imperfect: the *Beis HaMikdash* is something one wants to experience rarely and at special moments of elevation, whereas marriage is something that should be regular and sustaining. The mechanism is similar — restricted access creates renewed appreciation — but the goal is different in each case.

---

## Gender Dynamics

### Man Pursues Woman

A *Baraisa* from the school of Rabbi Dostai bar Yannai asks: *mipnei mah ish mechazeir al ha-ishah ve-ein ishah mechazeret al ha-ish?* — why is it that the man pursues the woman in courtship and not the reverse? Both need to marry; why is the man generally the more active party?

The answer: *mashal le-adam she-avad lo aveidah* — it is like a person who has lost an object. *Mi mechazeir al mi? Ba'al ha-aveidah mechazeir al aveidato* — who looks for whom? The one who lost the object searches for what he lost; the lost object does not search for its owner. This echoes back to the narrative of *Bereishit*, where *Chavah* is formed from *Adam* — something that was part of him and was taken from him. When he encounters her he says *etzem mi-atzamai u-basar mi-besari* — he has found the part of himself that was missing. He is the one who lacks, and so he is the one who searches.

The metaphor is in one sense beautiful: the man is not pursuing something alien but recovering something that completes him, makes him whole. At the same time, the use of the word *aveidah* — a lost object — is undeniably possessive. The woman here is framed as an object that belongs to someone rather than as a subject who seeks completion herself. A *Rosh Yeshiva* once cited this *gemara* at the opening of a *zman* of *Masechet Kiddushin* and quipped to students who were slow to marry: if you are looking for an *aveidah*, you will find it; if you are looking for a *metziah*, it will take forever.

### Downward/Upward

The *gemara* continues: *mipnei mah ish panav le-mata ve-ishah paneha le-ma'ala?* — why does the man face downward and the woman face upward during marital relations, assuming this to be the standard position? *Zeh mi-makom she-nivra ve-zeh mi-makom she-nivra* — each faces toward the place from which they were created. The man looks down toward the earth, from which he was formed. The woman looks up toward the man, from whom she was formed. One might read this as the man expressing humility before his earthly origins, but the framing also reinforces a sense of the woman orienting herself toward the man as her source, which carries obvious symbolic weight in terms of hierarchy and dependence.

### Appeasement

*Umipnei mah ha'ish mekabel piyus ve'ein ha'ishah mekabeles piyus?* — why is a man easily appeased when angered, while a woman is not? Again, *zeh mi-makom she-nivra ve-zo mi-makom she-nivret*. The man, created from earth, is like earth — pliable, moldable, amenable to tilling and replanting. The woman, created from bone, is harder and less yielding. Rashi glosses this as *no'ach leratzos* — easy to pacify or to win over — and some read *piyus* here specifically in the marital context, noting that a man can more readily be persuaded toward intimacy than a woman, which also rings true.

### Voice Beauty

Finally: *umipnei mah ha'ishah kolah arev ve'ein ha'ish kolo arev?* — why does a woman have a beautiful, pleasing voice while a man does not? Again the same formula: *zeh mi-makom she-nivra ve-zo mi-makom she-nivret*. The man was formed from earth, which produces no melody. The woman was formed from bone, and Rashi notes that bone — when fashioned into an instrument — produces resonant, pleasing sound. The verse *ki kolech arev umarech naveh* ("for your voice is pleasing and your appearance is lovely") is cited as confirmation that women possess beautiful voices, though it serves as proof of the fact rather than explanation of the cause.

---

## Benot Kutim

### Status Overview

With the conclusion of the *aggadata* we turn to the opening of a new *Mishnah* — *benot Kutim niddot me'arisatan*. The daughters of the *Kutim* — the Samaritans — are considered *niddot* from their very cradles, from the moment of birth. *Kutim* were Samaritans, a population that maintained certain Jewish practices but not all, and whose halachic status oscillated between Jewish and non-Jewish. The *gemara* works within the assumption that they are Jewish, but that they do not observe the details of *hilchos niddah* in the same manner.

The *Mishnah* adds that the *Kutim* men themselves — *metamme'im mishkav tachton ke'elyon* — render the lower couch or seat *tamei* like the upper one, the logic being that since their wives are always considered *niddot*, the men are always considered *bo'alei niddot*, and this status renders whatever they sit or lie upon *tamei* in the manner of *mishkav u'moshav*. *Mipnei she'hen bo'alei niddot* — because they are treated as having had relations with *niddot*, they carry the corresponding *tumah*.

There is a significant *Tosafos* here. Elsewhere in the *gemara* (in the tractate of *Shabbat*), these *gezeiros* against *Kutim* are listed among the eighteen things enacted by *Beis Shammai*, many of which involve *tumah* and *taharah* and others of which concern limiting interaction with non-Jews. *Tosafos* reconciles the two sources by noting that even if the motivation behind some of these *gezeiros* was to erect social barriers, a *gezeirah* cannot be entirely a fiction — it must be rooted in some halachic reality. Hence our *gemara* focuses on the actual halachic ground for treating *benot Kutim* as *niddot*.

### Blood Color Indistinction

The reason given is: *ve'hen yoshvot al kol dam va'dam* — they sit upon every type of blood. That is, they do not distinguish between the different colors of blood, some of which render a woman *tamei* and some of which do not. Whatever blood they see, they treat as *niddah* blood. One might think this is a *chumra* — they're being stricter than the law requires. But in fact this is a textbook case of *chumra de'ati lidei kula* — a stringency that produces a leniency.

### Stringency/Leniency Para…

The mechanism works as follows. If a woman begins to bleed with a color that is not actually a *niddah* color — say, a brownish discharge two or three days before the true red flow — and she begins counting her seven days from that non-qualifying blood rather than from the onset of the actual qualifying *niddah* flow, her seven-day count ends too early. She will go to the *mikvah* while she is still technically a *niddah*, and thus never actually becomes *tehorah*. Her *chumra* of counting from the earliest drop, regardless of color, causes her to go to the *mikvah* at the wrong time, and her *tumah* is never resolved. This is the fundamental problem: the stringency of not distinguishing blood colors ends up producing the leniency of never actually achieving *taharah*.

### Safek Status

Despite all this, the *Mishnah* qualifies the consequence: *ve'ein chayavin aleihen bi'at mikdash* — if someone who became *tamei* through contact with a Samaritan woman entered the *Beis HaMikdash*, they are not liable for *karet*, because the *tumah* is a matter of *safek* — we do not know with certainty that this particular woman was indeed a *niddah* at the time. Similarly, *ve'ein sorfin aleihen et ha'terumah* — if a Samaritan woman touches *terumah*, it is not burned, because there remains a possibility that she was in fact *tehorah*. The ruling is: treat them as *tamei* for practical purposes, but since it is never a certainty, the severe consequences reserved for definite *tumah* do not apply.

---

## Infant Emissions

### Actual Bleeding?

The *gemara* opens with the classic *heichi dami* — what exactly is the case? If Samaritan infants actually bleed (*ei de'chazya*), then our infants would also be subject to the same concern — *afilu didan nami*. And if they do not bleed (*ei de'la kachazya*), then *didehu nami lo* — their infants are also not a concern, and the ruling seems to be baseless either way.

### Minority Possibility

Rava, son of Rav Acha bar Rav Huna, citing Rav Sheshet, resolves this: *hacha be'mai askinan be'stama* — we are dealing with a case of uncertainty, where we simply do not know whether a given infant has bled. And *de'keivan de'ika mi'uta de'chazya* — since there is a small minority of infants who do in fact experience some bleeding, we are *chaishinan* — concerned — that it may have occurred. The *gemara* then asks: whose view is this in the *Mishnah*, that we are concerned for a minority? The answer is Rabbi Meir.

### Rabbi Meir Minority

The *gemara* cites a *Braisa*. *Katan ve'ketanah lo choltzin ve'lo meyabemin* — a minor boy or girl cannot perform *chalitzah* or *yibbum*. Rabbi Meir forbids *yibbum* for minors not because there is a formal age requirement, but because *katan shema yimatze saris, ketanah shema timatze aylonit* — there is a minority possibility that the boy will prove to be a *saris* (infertile), or that the girl will prove to be an *aylonit* (infertile). If either is the case, the *mitzvah* of *yibbum* was never present, and the intercourse constituted a forbidden relationship with an *ervah* without the justifying *mitzvah* — *venimtze'u pog'in be'ervah shelo bimkom mitzvah*. The Rabbis respond: *zil batar rubba* — go by the majority. Most minor boys are not *sarisim* and most minor girls are not *ayloniyot*. The debate is thus whether we act on a minority possibility.

The *gemara* then introduces a limiting principle: Rabbi Meir is concerned for a minority when it is *miyuta deshchiach* — a minority that is not exceedingly rare. A minority that is *lo shchiach* — almost never encountered — would not, even by Rabbi Meir, generate a *gezeirah*. The question then is whether infant bleeding falls into the category of *shchiach*. The *gemara* maintains that it does, based on actual reported cases.

### Historical Stories

Three stories are adduced. Rabbi Yosi reports a case in *Ein Bul* where an infant girl was taken to the *mikvah* before her mother — the infant bled shortly after birth, began her seven-day *niddah* count, and reached the end of those seven days before her mother, whose post-partum *tumah* for a girl extended fourteen days. Rabbi (Rebbi) reports a similar case in *Beit She'arim*, and Rav Yosef reports a case in *Pumbedita*.

The *gemara* then notes a discrepancy. One can understand why Rabbi Yosi and Rebbi in *Eretz Yisrael* would bother taking the infant to the *mikvah*: there was *terumah* in *Eretz Yisrael* and one would not want the infant to touch it while *tamei*. But why would Rav Yosef in *Bavel* bother? Shmuel rules that the *terumah* of *chutz la'aretz* is only forbidden to someone whose *tumah* comes from their own body (*mi shetumah yotze'ah miguffo*) — a *ba'al keri*, a *zav*, a *zavah* — which would include a *niddah*. So the girl as a *niddah* is indeed covered by this prohibition. But the concern shifts: an infant cannot eat *terumah* in any case — she is months from eating solid food. And the *gemara* rules that the prohibition of *terumah chutz la'aretz* in this context applies to *achilah* — eating — but not to *negi'ah* — mere touching. So what was the concern?

Mar Zutra answers: *lo nitzrecha ella lesochah* — it was necessary because of *shemen shel terumah*, olive oil from *terumah*, which one wished to rub onto the infant as a lotion or ointment. The principle of *sichah k'shtiyah* — rubbing oil into the skin is halachically equivalent to drinking — renders this equivalent to ingesting the *terumah*, which a *niddah* may not do, even *terumah* of *chutz la'aretz* according to Shmuel's ruling. A *Baraisa* confirms: the verse *velo yichalelu et kodshei benei Yisrael et asher yarimu l'Adonai* teaches that *hasach* — anointing — is included in the prohibition alongside *achilah*, and the verse *vattavo chamayim b'kirbo u'chashemen b'atzmosav* ("it entered like water within him and like oil into his bones") similarly equates oil absorption with drinking. This is why even in *Bavel*, where they would not worry about the infant touching *terumah*, they took her to the *mikvah* — so she could have *terumah* oil applied to her skin.

---

## Our vs. Their Infants

### Drasha from Tanakh

The *gemara* returns to the central question: if infant bleeding is a real if rare phenomenon, why does the ruling apply specifically to *benot Kutim* and not to our own infant daughters? The answer is: *anan dedarshinan ishah v'ishah* — we derive from the Torah (as will be spelled out momentarily) that even underage girls can become *niddot*, all the way down to one day old.

### Our Knowledge vs. Theirs

Because we have this *drasha* and apply it, *d'chi chazi mafreshinan lehu* — when we see that an infant girl has bled, we immediately treat her as *tamei*, separate her from *taharos*, and handle the situation appropriately. We know the *halacha* and we act on it.

### Gezeirah Logic

The *Kutim*, by contrast, *d'lo darshi ishah v'ishah* — do not have this *drasha* and do not accept that underage girls can become *niddot*. Therefore *v'chi chazi lo mafreshi lehu* — even when they see that an infant has bled, they do not separate her or treat her as *tamei*. Because they are systematically unaware of and inattentive to this *halacha*, the Rabbis were compelled to issue a *gezeirah* treating all of their infants as *tamei*. *Gazru behu rabbanan* — the Rabbis decreed. This is the operative logic: it is not that their infants are more likely to bleed than ours; it is that when ours do bleed we respond correctly, and when theirs do, nothing is done about it.

*Tosafos* raises a further question: once you have already declared all *benot Kutim tamei* as infants, why is a separate reason needed for declaring adult *Kutim* women *tamei* — namely, their failure to distinguish blood colors? If the infant *gezeirah* already applies to them, does it not follow through to adulthood? *Tosafos* answers that the infant *gezeirah* was issued specifically because *Kutim* do not recognize that infants can become *niddot*. But once they reach adulthood, one might have thought we could trust them. A separate and independent reason is needed to explain why we cannot trust adult *Kutim* women either — and that reason is their failure to distinguish between qualifying and non-qualifying blood colors.

---

## Extra Vav Niddah

### Infant Girl Niddah

The *gemara* now spells out the *drasha* itself. *Mai ishah v'ishah?* — what is the derivation from the "extra" word? A *Baraisa* teaches: *isha, ein li ela isha* — from the word *isha* ("woman") I know only an adult woman can become *tamei* as a *niddah*. *Tinokes bat yom echad leniddah minayin?* — how do I derive that even an infant girl one day old can become a *niddah*? *Talmud lomar v'isha* — the extra *vav* (i.e., *ve'isha* rather than *isha*) teaches an additional case, including even a one-day-old infant.

### Vav Inclusion

The *gemara* then raises a challenge: if the extra *vav* includes someone as young as one day old when we go below the normal age, why does a different *baraisa* seem to stop at three years old? For the *tumah* of *shichvat zera* — the *tumah* acquired through an act of *bi'ah* — the *Baraisa* states *isha ein li ela isha, tinokes bas shalosh shanim v'yom echad l'bi'ah minayin, talmud lomar v'isha*. Here the extra *vav* brings us down to three years and a day, not to one day old.

Rava resolves this: *hilchata ninhu ve'asmi'chinhu rabbanan akra'ei* — both *shiurim* rest on tradition (*halacha le'Moshe mi'Sinai*), and the Rabbis found scriptural support for each. The question is which *shiur* is the tradition and which is the *pasuk*. Rava concludes: the *shiur* of three years and one day for the definition of an act of *bi'ah* is the transmitted tradition, since no *pasuk* could independently yield such a specific number. The *pasuk* of *v'isha*, once it extends the category below the adult age, naturally extends all the way to the minimum — one day. Conversely, *bas yom echad* for *niddah* is rooted in the *pasuk*, while *bas shalosh shanim v'yom echad* is the tradition.

This leads to a further question: if the *pasuk* of *v'isha* by the *tumah* of *shichvat zera* is not needed for the *shiur* of three years (since that is *halacha le'Moshe mi'Sinai*), and if the one-day-old *niddah* can alternatively be inferred once we know that an infant can become a *zavah* (since there can be no *zivah* without *niddah* preceding it), what function does the *pasuk* of *v'isha* actually serve in each context? The *gemara* answers: *l'mautei ish mi'odem* — to exclude the male from the *tumah* of red blood. By emphasizing *v'isha* — the woman — the Torah underscores that *tumah* through blood or through *shichvat zera* applies to women in these forms and not to men. Specifically, two exclusions are operative: one by *niddah* and one by *shichvat zera*, excluding respectively (a) semen that appears red, and (b) actual blood that emerges from the male organ — neither renders the man *tamei* in the manner of a *niddah*.

### Zavah Question

The *gemara* then examines the parallel by *zavah*: *isha ein li ela isha, bas yud yamim v'zivah minayin?* — I know only an adult woman can become a *zavah*; how do I know that a girl as young as ten days old can become a *zavah*? *Talmud lomar v'isha* — the extra *vav* by *zavah*. The *gemara* asks why this separate derivation is needed; once we know an infant girl can become a *niddah*, why can't we infer that she can become a *zavah* as well?

### Female Exclusivity

The *gemara* answers that neither direction of inference works cleanly on its own. Had the Torah taught only *niddah* for infants, one might have said that *niddah* applies to infants because it is strict — a single day of bleeding generates a seven-day *tumah* — and therefore extends even to infants. But *zivah* is less strict — a single day of bleeding requires only a one-day watch — and one might have thought it would not apply to infants. Conversely, had the Torah taught only *zavah* for infants, one might have argued: *zavah* applies because even *zivah* be'ones — bleeding due to external trauma — creates *tumah* for a woman, making *zivah* strict in its own way, and therefore even infants are included. But one could not then infer *niddah*, since we cannot infer one category from the other in either direction. Both are necessary. The *pasuk*s of *v'isha* by *niddah* and *v'isha* by *zavah* each do independent work and cannot be reduced to each other.

---

## Ish Ish Zav

### Ish Ish Meaning

The *gemara* now turns to the parallel derivation for males. *V'chen b'zcharim* — the same logic of including infants applies to boys. The *Baraisa*: *ish ish* — the double expression of *ish* (*ish ish ki yihyeh zav*) — *mah talmud lomar ish ish? l'rabos tinok ben yom echad she'metamei b'ziva* — the double *ish* serves to include a one-day-old infant boy who is able to become a *zav*. This is in the name of Rabbi Yehudah. The ability of an infant to become a *zav* is already accessible from the first day of life because the requirements for male *zivah* do not include a preceding *niddah* period — three separate sightings of the discharge suffice, potentially even on the same day.

### Yishmael Objection

Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka disagrees: *ein tzarich* — no derivation is necessary. *Harei hu omer l'zachar u'l'nekeivah* — the Torah states explicitly "male or female" in the context of *zivah*. *L'zachar kol she'hu zachar bein gadol bein katan* — "male" means any male, adult or minor. *Ul'nekeivah kol she'hi nekeivah bein gedolah bein ketanah* — and "female" means any female, adult or minor. If so, why does the Torah say *ish ish* at all?

### Divine Language

Rabbi Yishmael's answer: *dibra Torah k'lishon bnei adam* — the Torah speaks in the manner of human language. The doubling of *ish* is simply a stylistic feature of biblical Hebrew, not a hermeneutical signal. Therefore one cannot derive the inclusion of minors from *ish ish*, because that formulation carries no additional legal force — it is simply how people speak.

---

## Both Genders Needed

### Male Zav Strictness

The *gemara* asks why we need both the derivation for underage girls (*v'isha*) and the derivation for underage boys (*ish ish* or *l'zachar u'l'nekeivah*) — why not derive one gender from the other? The answer is that the *tumah* categories differ between male and female in ways that preclude cross-inference. For males, *zivah* is in some respects strict: *mishum demitmu bire'iyot kiveyamim* — a male becomes a *zav* through three sightings of the discharge, which can all occur on the same day, without any requirement that they fall on separate days. Because male *zivah* is such an expansive category in this sense, one might readily assume it extends even to infants.

### Female Zavah Strictness

For females, the *tumah* of *zivah* requires three days of bleeding on three separate days — a more specific and in that sense stricter requirement. One might have thought that because this category is more circumscribed, it would not extend to infants. On the other hand, female *zivah* is strict in a different dimension: *ba'ah be'ones* — bleeding caused by trauma or an external force still creates *tumah* for a woman, whereas the analogous situation for a man — an emission caused by illness or something he ate — does not make him a *zav*. Because each category has its own dimensions of stringency and leniency, no inference from one to the other is valid.

### No Cross-Gender Inference

The conclusion: *tzricha* — both derivations are needed. One cannot derive the inclusion of underage girls from the law governing underage boys, nor vice versa. The differences in the structure of *tumah* between male *zivah* and female *zivah* are too significant to permit the inference to travel in either direction. Both the *pasuk* of *v'isha* by *zavah* and the derivation for males are independently necessary.

---

## Mishnah Tumah Ages

### Girl Tumah Ages

A new *Mishnah* opens with a systematic statement of the ages at which *tumah* takes effect. *Tinoket bat yom echad metama beniddah* — a girl one day old can become *tamei* as a *niddah*. *Bat asara yamim metama bezivah* — a girl ten days old can become a *zavah*. The logic of ten days follows from the structure of the *niddah/zivah* cycle: the first day she can become a *niddah*, her seven-day *niddah* period encompasses days one through seven, and the eleven days of *zivah* begin on day eight. If she bleeds on days eight, nine, and ten, she is a *gedolah zavah* on day ten. Ten days old is thus the earliest she can qualify.

### Boy Tumah Ages

*Tinok ben yom echad metamei bezivah* — a one-day-old boy can already become a *zav*, and *umetamei benega'im* — the infant is also subject to the *tumah* of *nega'im*, the leprosy-like skin afflictions — and *umetamei betumat meit* — and is affected by the *tumah* of contact with a corpse. All of these *tumos* apply from the first day of life.

### Yibum/Terumah

The *Mishnah* then lists civil and personal status consequences of a one-day-old child. *V'zakuk leyibum* — the child is significant for the purpose of *yibbum*: a one-day-old son exempts his mother from *yibbum* should his father die, because the father did not die childless. And under certain circumstances, the child's death and his brother's death could make *yibbum* necessary for a surviving widow. *Ufoteir min hayibum* — and releases from *yibbum*. *Uma'achil biterumah* — if the father was a *kohen* and the mother was not a *kohenet*, the birth of a one-day-old child grants the mother the right to eat *terumah*, since she is now the mother of a *kohen*. *Ufoseil min haterumah* — conversely, if the mother was the daughter of a *kohen* but married a non-*kohen*, the birth of this child disqualifies her from eating *terumah* in her father's house.

### Legal Capacity

*Venocheil umanchil* — a one-day-old child can inherit from his father and can pass on that inheritance. If the child was born and his father died moments later, the child inherits the estate; and if the child then dies, his maternal relatives inherit through him, rather than the estate reverting directly to the father's line. *Vehoreig et hanefesh* — if a one-day-old child kills someone, he is technically a murderer in the eyes of *halacha*, though obviously he cannot be executed. *Harei hu kegadol shaleim lechol devarav* — he is like a complete adult for all these matters. The *Mishnah* presents this as a sweeping and striking statement: on its very first day of life, a newborn child is already a full legal subject, bearing *tumah*, carrying halachic significance for *yibbum* and *terumah*, capable of inheriting, and recognized as a person whose death at another's hand constitutes murder.

---

---

# Niddah 34

## Polelet Shichvat Zera

### Shiva Nekiyim Standard

The daf begins with a brief reprise of the discussion that closed the previous session — specifically, the question of *polelet shichvat zera*: can the days during which semen is expelled from a woman's body after intercourse be counted toward the Torah-mandated days relevant to the status of a *zavah*? While the Gemara will revisit this in fuller detail, the practical upshot is immediately noted: this discussion forms the halachic basis for the contemporary practice — at least among Ashkenazim — of waiting a minimum of five days before beginning the count of *shiva nekiyim*, even in the absence of intercourse. This five-day standard, which developed in the post-Geonic Ashkenazic tradition, flows directly from the Gemara's analysis of how long one must wait before assuming that *polelet shichvat zera* is no longer a concern. It is a profoundly practical matter that will be revisited as the sugya develops.

### Kutim Status

The Gemara then continues from ten lines into amud 2, addressing the status of Kutim with respect to *hilchot niddah*. The Kutim observe *hilchot niddah*, but their practice diverges from rabbinic law in a way that produces a leniency: because they begin counting their days of impurity differently — treating certain non-*tamei* colored blood as the start of the count — they may immerse in the *mikvah* prematurely. Consequently, their women are treated as *safek niddot* and their husbands as *safek ba'alei niddot*. Yet because this status rests on doubt, one who enters the *Beit Hamikdash* after contact with them is not *chayav* for entering in a state of *tumah*, and *terumah* that comes into contact with them is not burned — both because the *tumah* is only a *safek*.

---

## Rav Pappa & Rav Shmuel

### Rav Pappa Arrives

The Gemara introduces a narrative: Rav Pappa came to a place called Tava. Upon arriving, he inquired whether there was a *talmid chacham* in town whom he might greet. An elderly woman informed him that there was indeed a *tzurba me-rabbanan* there — one Rav Shmuel — who was a master of *Mishnayot* and *Baraitot*. This designation is significant: it indicates a scholar who has thoroughly mastered the Tannaitic material but is not necessarily associated with the higher-order work of *amora'im* — the give-and-take of *kashya* and *teretz*, dialectical analysis, and independent reasoning.

There is a subtle irony embedded in what follows. When the woman blesses Rav Pappa with the wish that he should become as great as Rav Shmuel, Rav Pappa's immediate inference is that since she is comparing him to a man who is, by the description given, clearly not his equal in Torah scholarship, the praise must be referring to Rav Shmuel's piety — *shema mina yere shamayim hu*, he concludes: he must be God-fearing. This tells us something about Rav Pappa's assumptions. Implicitly, he is reasoning: the compliment cannot be about his learning, since that obviously cannot exceed mine; therefore it must be about his character. There is, perhaps, a trace of *ga'avah* in this reading — or at least a certain confidence about the hierarchy of scholarly achievement.

### Rav Shmuel's Question

When Rav Pappa arrives, Rav Shmuel welcomes him warmly, serves him a substantial meal, and then proceeds to present him with a contradiction between Mishnayot. The hosting and the challenge are intertwined in the narrative — he served him an ox (*rama lei tora*) and then threw him *mishnayot* (*rama lei matnita ahadadei*), a kind of parallel generosity.

The contradiction Rav Shmuel raises is the following. Our Mishnah states that if someone touches the seat of a Kuti who is a *safek boel niddah* and then enters the *Beit Hamikdash*, he is not *chayav*, and *terumah* that touches that seat is not burned — because the *tumah* is only a *safek*. The operative principle appears to be: in cases of doubt, we do not burn *terumah*. Yet another Mishnah teaches that for six specific doubts, we do burn *terumah* — and among those six is the doubtful status of the garments of an *am ha'aretz* (*safek bigdei am ha'aretz*). The question is not merely a formal tension between two rules regarding doubt. Rashi and Tosafot both observe that the real issue is this: if we are treating a Kuti as insufficiently careful in observance, then the Kuti is, by definition, also in the category of *am ha'aretz*. So why are the garments of a Kuti not subject to the same standard as those of an *am ha'aretz*, for which we burn *terumah*?

Rav Pappa's response is that the Mishnah is speaking of a *Kuti chaver* — a Kuti who is scrupulous in matters of *tumah vetaharah* and thus does not fall into the *am ha'aretz* category. Rav Shmuel immediately pushes back with a sharp counter: *Kuti chaver boel niddah mashkachat lei?* — if the Kuti is considered a *chaver*, meticulous in his observance, how can one simultaneously suspect him of having intercourse with his wife while she is a *niddah*? The categories seem mutually exclusive.

There is, in fact, an obvious answer — one that Tosafot articulates explicitly: it is entirely possible that the Kuti is scrupulous about every law he knows, and even regarding *niddah* he believes himself to be acting correctly, but his interpretation of the law leads him to count from a different starting point. He is *savar la'asot kedat* — he thinks he is fulfilling the law. His violation, if it is one, stems not from negligence but from a sincere but mistaken legal position. This is what Tosafot writes: he is a *chaver* regarding everything that defines the distinction between a *chaver* and an *am ha'aretz*, and even in this particular matter he believes he is acting in accordance with *halacha*. Nonetheless, Rav Shmuel did not accept this answer.

### Departure & Rav Shimi

Rav Pappa left — *shabkieh*. Rashi explains: Rav Pappa left his host's house (*be'ushpizeih*) because he felt embarrassed (*mishum dechasfiah*). Not that Rav Shmuel intentionally embarrassed him — they were engaged in Torah learning — but the effect was that this man, known only as a master of *mishnayot* and *baraitot*, not as someone capable of analytical challenge, had in fact bested Rav Pappa in the exchange. This brings the story's subtext into focus. Rav Pappa had assumed that the woman's blessing could only be referring to Rav Shmuel's piety, not his learning. But it turned out that Rav Shmuel's question was genuinely sharp — sharp enough to send Rav Pappa away without a satisfactory answer. The assumption about the hierarchy, it seems, needed revision.

Rav Pappa then went to Rav Shimi bar Ashi.

### Kuti After Tevilah

Rav Shimi bar Ashi explains the Mishnah by constructing a specific and narrow scenario. He says: the Mishnah is discussing a Kuti who immersed in a *mikvah* (*bekuti shetaval*) and then stepped on the garments of a *chaver*. Here is the logic.

The ordinary concern about an *am ha'aretz* — which leads to his garments being treated as *vadai tamei* with *terumah* burned because of them — stems from his general carelessness with *tumah vetaharah*, not specifically from *niddah* laws. That kind of *tumah* is typically a one-day impurity; immersion in a *mikvah* removes it. So if the Kuti has gone to the *mikvah*, that ordinary *am ha'aretz* concern is resolved. He is no longer in the *am ha'aretz* category in the sense that would render his garments definitively *tamei*.

What remains is only the concern particular to *Kutim*: that his wife may have been a *niddah* and he may have had relations with her before her *mikvah* immersion was halakhically valid, rendering him a *safek boel niddah*. The Kuti, now freshly immersed and naked, then steps on the garments of a *chaver*. Those garments have not been rendered *tamei* as garments of an *am ha'aretz* — he immersed and was not wearing his own clothes. The only possible *tumah* affecting those garments is from his *Kuti* status. And that, Rav Shimi explains, is a *safek sefeika* — a double doubt: perhaps he did not have intercourse with his wife recently; and even if he did, perhaps she had counted correctly after all and the immersion was valid. Because it is a *safek sefeika*, we do not burn *terumah*. That is the case of the Mishnah.

The Gemara then challenges this: surely he stepped on the *chaver*'s garments wearing his sandals, and those sandals are his own clothing — *bigdei am ha'aretz* — which are treated as *vadai tamei*! The answer given is that he stepped on them while naked (*bekusi arum*) — he had just emerged from the *mikvah* and had not yet dressed. The case therefore involves no garments of his own, and the only *tumah* in play is the tenuous Kuti-derived doubt.

The Gemara thus provides two interlocking resolutions to Rav Shmuel's question. First, why isn't the Kuti's garment treated like *bigdei am ha'aretz*? Because he just immersed, removing that *tumah*. Second, even granting the concern of *boel niddah*, why is it treated as a *safek* insufficient to burn *terumah*? Because it is a *safek sefeika* — the doubt is genuinely weak and layered.

It is also worth noting, as the Gemara itself suggests at a later point, that the cleaner answer — attributed to Tosafot and implicit in what is called *Rava's first answer* — is that a Kuti who is a *chaver* in all other respects may simply have a different legal position regarding *niddah*, and the two designations are not contradictory. He is scrupulous; he merely holds differently on this particular question.

---

## Benot Tzaddukim

### Mishna Rules

The Gemara proceeds to the laws governing the daughters of Tzaddukim. The Mishnah states: *benot Tzaddukim bizman she-nahagu lalechet bedarchei avoteihem* — the daughters of Tzaddukim, when they follow the practices of their fathers, are treated like *Kutiyot*. Noteworthy here is that the Mishnah says *avoteihem* — their fathers — even though the discussion concerns *hilchot niddah*, which one might expect to be governed by the practices of the mothers. This reflects the assumption that the religious affiliation of the household is determined by the male line.

If they follow their fathers' Tzadduki practices, they are treated like *Kutiyot* — they may be operating under a different legal standard for when to begin counting *tamei* days, and their *tevilah* may therefore occur too early. If, however, they have separated and follow the practice of Israel (*pirshu lalechet bedarchei Yisrael*), they are treated as Israelite women and are presumed to be observing *halacha* correctly.

Rabbi Yosei holds a more lenient default: *le'olam hen k'Yisraelit* — they are always presumed to be like Israelite women, *ad she'yafrishu lalechet bedarchei avotam* — until they explicitly and actively separate themselves to follow their fathers' ways. His presumption runs in the other direction from the *Tanna Kamma*.

### Default Status

The Gemara asks what the *Tanna Kamma* holds as the default assumption when neither practice can be established. It attempts to infer this from the Mishnah's opening clause (*risha*): if following the fathers' way = *Kutiyot*, then perhaps the unstated default is like Israelite women? But then the closing clause (*seifa*) implies the reverse: if explicitly following Israel = Israelite, then the unstated default might be *Kutiyot*. The Gemara concludes that from the Mishnah itself one cannot resolve the question — *ela me'ha lo tishma*.

The inference is ultimately drawn from Rabbi Yosei's position: since Rabbi Yosei explicitly says the default is Israelite women, *mikhlal de-Tanna Kamma savar stama k'kutyot* — by contrast, the *Tanna Kamma* must hold that the unstated default is to treat them like *Kutiyot*, i.e., as *safek tamei*. This is the position *shema mina*.

### Kohen Gadol Story

To understand why Rabbi Yosei would adopt the opposite presumption, the Gemara introduces a *ma'aseh*: a certain Tzadduki was speaking with the Kohen Gadol in the marketplace — notably, a Kohen Gadol who was a *Perushi*, not a Tzadduki, which was not always the case. In the course of conversation, a stream of spittle (*tzinora*) flew from the Tzadduki's mouth and landed on the Kohen Gadol's garments. The Kohen Gadol's face turned pale (the *Rashash* notes a wordplay: the word *horiku*, from *yarok*, echoes the earlier concern about green-colored blood among the Kutim). He was devastated — having treated the Tzadduki as a *safek boel niddah* like a Kuti, the Tzadduki's spittle was *tamei* and had now *tamei'd* his garments.

He went and reported this incident to his wife. Rashi suggests it was the wife of the Tzadduki, but the contextual reading — and the Maharsha — indicates it was the Kohen Gadol's own wife, since the story would not make sense if he were referring to himself in the third person. She said to him: even though they are the wives of Tzaddukim, *mityarot hen min ha-Perushim* — they are reverent toward the Perushim, and they show their blood to the sages for evaluation.

### Women's Reverence

This is the basis for Rabbi Yosei's position: *baki'in anu bahen yoter min hakol* — we know them better than anyone else, and they are scrupulous about showing their blood to the *chachamim*. He adds one exception: there was one woman in his neighborhood who did not show her blood to the sages — *umeta*, and she died. The implicit point being that the exception proved itself.

The story carries a remarkable subtext. It illustrates that in *hilchot niddah*, it is ultimately the women who determine the communal status — not the men. Whatever the Tzadduki husbands may hold regarding *pesak halacha*, if the women themselves are showing their blood to the *Perushim* sages and following their rulings, then the women's practice governs. The male religious authority of the Tzadduki household, for all its social prominence, does not reach into this domain. This is, as noted, a striking inversion of the usual assumption that the male line defines practice. Furthermore, the word *mityarot* — they are *fearful of* or *reverent toward* — carries an irony. The Tzaddukim were in many respects stricter than the Perushim. But as we saw with the Kutim, strictness can produce leniency: beginning the count earlier leads to an earlier and potentially invalid *tevilah*. The women, in their reverence for the Perushim, actually end up following the standard that produces the correct result.

### Rava's Answer

The Gemara then raises a question parallel to the one asked about the Kuti: *veteipuk lei mishum tzinora d'am ha'aretz* — forget the Tzadduki issue entirely; the spittle of an *am ha'aretz* is treated like that of a *zav*, so the spittle should be *tamei* regardless of the *niddah* consideration!

Abaye answers: he was a *tzadduki chaver* — a Tzadduki who was nonetheless scrupulous in *hilchot tumah vetaharah*, and thus not in the *am ha'aretz* category. Rava rejects this answer with the same challenge that Rav Shmuel posed to Rav Pappa: *tzadduki chaver boel niddah mashkachat lei?* — if he is that scrupulous, how can he be simultaneously suspected of being a *boel niddah*? Rava refuses to accept the *chaver* answer, at least in the form Abaye framed it. (The obvious Tosafot-style rejoinder — that he may be scrupulous yet hold a different legal position — seems to be available here as well, but Rava sets it aside.)

Rava therefore offers a different resolution: *regel havei* — it was one of the three pilgrimage festivals, the *regalim*. On the *regalim*, the rabbis treated the *tumah* of an *am ha'aretz* as if it were *taharah*. The reason: the Torah says *vayei'asef kol ish Yisrael el ha'ir ke'ish echad chaverim* — when all of Israel gathers together as one, the verse itself calls them all *chaverim*. On the *regalim*, when *klal Yisrael* is assembled, all social and halachic distinctions that normally separate *chaverim* from *amei ha'aretz* are suspended in favor of communal unity. Therefore on a *regel*, a Tzadduki's spittle would not carry the *am ha'aretz* *tumah* — only the Tzadduki-specific *safek* would remain, and that *safek* is insufficient to burn *terumah*.

There is no small irony in calling a Tzadduki an *am ha'aretz*. The Tzaddukim were the upper class; they were anything but the hoi polloi. Yet from the perspective of *Perushi* halacha, if a person is not observing the precise laws of *tumah vetaharah* as the *chachamim* define them, he receives the legal category of *am ha'aretz*, whatever his social station.

---

## Dam Ovedet Kochavim

### Blood Status Intro

The Gemara now turns to a new and considerably more intricate Mishnah, treating the question of blood status. By way of introduction: the blood of a *niddah* is an *av ha-tumah* — a primary source of *tumah* — because it is blood that creates her status as a *niddah*. But there is a separate principle: a *niddah*, a *zav*, and a *zavah* also render certain of their *mayanot* — certain bodily fluids such as spit and urine — *tamei* as an *av ha-tumah*. The question that the Mishnah addresses is: what is the status of blood that comes from such a person but is not itself *niddah* blood — either because the person is not Jewish, or because the blood falls within a period in which it would not create *niddah* status? Does such blood share the *tumah* of spit and urine, or does it have no *tumah* status at all?

### Mishna Rules

The Mishnah addresses three cases. First: *dam ovedet kochavim* — the blood of a non-Jewish woman. A non-Jewish woman does not have the halachic status of a *niddah* from the Torah; her blood does not make her a *niddah* in the biblical sense. What then is the status of that blood?

Second: *dam tohar shel metzora'at* — the blood of a woman who is both a *metzora'at* and a *yoledes* (having recently given birth). She is in the *taharah* period following childbirth, during which any uterine blood is not *niddah* blood. However, she remains a *metzora'at*, and the spittle of a *metzora* is *tamei*. The question is whether this blood during the *taharah* period — not *niddah* blood, but still emanating from a *tamei* person — carries the *tumah* of spit.

Third: the blood of a *yoledes* who has not yet immersed after her *taharah* period, i.e., she is past the first or second week after childbirth but has not yet gone to the *mikvah*.

Beit Shammai rules *tahor* for the first two cases — blood that is not *niddah* blood carries no *tumah*, even as a *mayane*-status fluid. Beit Hillel disagrees and rules that it is *tamei ke-roko ukhe-mei raglav* — like spit and urine — and thus *tamei* when wet.

For the third case (the *yoledes* who has not immersed), Beit Shammai says we treat the blood as if it were *spit* — rabbinically *tamei* when wet — because one might confuse day 15 with day 14, and day 14 blood would be *niddah* blood. Beit Hillel goes further: it is *metamei lach ve-yavesh* — it is *tamei* even when dry — treating it as actual *niddah* blood. Beit Hillel's reasoning, as will be explained, is that until she immerses in the *mikvah*, her blood retains its *niddah* status; the *taharah* period changes the halachic categorization of bleeding only once she has completed the process with *tevilah*. Both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that if she was also a *zavah* at the time of childbirth, her blood is *metamei lach ve-yavesh* — genuinely *zavah* blood, *tamei* even dry — since she has not yet undergone *tevilah* as a *zavah*.

### Zavah Status Debate

The Gemara asks: does Beit Shammai not accept the principle that non-Jews, while not *mitamei* from the Torah as *zavim*, were nonetheless decreed upon by the rabbis to have the status of *zavim* in all respects — including for women to have the status of *zavot*?
