If so, why does Beit Shammai say the blood of a non-Jewish woman is entirely *tahor*? If she is treated as a *zavah*, her blood should be *tamei*!

Beit Shammai responds: we face a dilemma. On one hand, if we give her blood the full status of *zav* blood — *tamei lach ve-yavesh* — people will mistake this rabbinic *tumah* for a biblical one, and they will begin burning *terumah* on its basis, which is inappropriate for a rabbinic enactment. On the other hand, if we treat the blood as *tamei* only when wet (like Beit Hillel's position) — essentially treating it like spit — that distinction is too subtle. People will not recognize it as rabbinic; they will think that even for Jewish women, blood is only *tamei* when wet, undermining the law of *niddah* blood being *tamei* even dry.

Beit Shammai therefore concludes: the distinction must be unmistakable. We must say the blood is entirely *tahor*, which will be an obvious signal that the non-Jewish woman's *tumah* is rabbinic and distinct from the *tumah* of a Jewish *niddah*. The subtlety of "wet but not dry" is insufficient as a marker. Beit Hillel accepts the risk of the subtle distinction, treating the blood as *tamei* when wet and *tahor* when dry — following the model of spit — and relying on that distinction to communicate the rabbinic nature of the *tumah*.

### Blood vs. Mayanot

The Gemara asks a further question. If Beit Shammai insists on making an obvious distinction to mark the rabbinic nature of the non-Jewish woman's *tumah*, why not make the obvious distinction with the *spit and urine* rather than with the blood? Say that her spit and urine are *tahor* (making the obvious distinction there) while her blood is *tamei*. This would serve the same purpose.

The Gemara answers: *roka umimei ragleha deshchichi, gazru behu rabbanan* — spit and urine are common occurrences; the rabbis enacted the decree precisely on the common cases. If we are treating a non-Jewish woman like a *zavah*, we must make that practically operative in the ways most commonly encountered. Blood from a non-Jewish woman, by contrast, is not commonly encountered — *dama dela shechichah* — and therefore the rabbis were able to leave the blood outside the decree, using that as the signal of the rabbinic (rather than biblical) nature of the *tumah*. This is the logic: be *machmir* in what is prevalent, and carve out the exception in what is rare. Beit Shammai agrees the common fluids must be *tamei*; it is the blood, as the uncommon and also legally complex case, that serves as the marker of rabbinic status.

It is worth pausing here on an additional point: the entire rabbinic decree treating non-Jews as *zavim* is not driven by a genuine concern about *tumah* in the same way that the Kuti laws were. The Kutim, being treated as Jews, could generate real *tumah*. Non-Jews cannot have biblical *tumah*. The rabbinic decree here serves a social and communal function — maintaining distinctions and barriers between Jews and non-Jews — rather than responding to a direct concern about genuine *tumah* transmission.

### Non-Jewish Man

Rava then addresses the case of a non-Jewish man. He states: *zovo tamei afilu leBeis Shammai* — his *zivah* flow, the discharge that would create *zav* status, is *tamei* even according to Beit Shammai. *Kiryo tahor afilu leBeis Hillel* — his seminal emission, by contrast, is *tahor* even according to Beit Hillel.

The reasoning follows the same structure applied to the woman. Beit Shammai requires making an obvious distinction to signal that the non-Jewish man's *tumah* is rabbinic. For the woman, the obvious distinction was made via the blood (which is *tahor*) while leaving spit and urine as *tamei*. For the man, the distinction is made via the *keri* (seminal emission), which is *tahor*, while the *zivah* discharge remains *tamei*. Why this allocation? *D'ha ika l'mevad heikera b'kiryo* — because the *keri* is available as the place to make the distinction. The *zivah* itself is the basis for treating him as a *zav* in the first place; it would be incoherent to say we treat him like a *zav* yet his *zivah* is *tahor*. So the *keri* is where the distinction is made.

The Gemara raises the reverse question: why not say the *zivah* is *tahor* and the *keri* is *tamei*? The answer: *zovo d'lo tali b'maaseh gazru bei rabbanan* — the *zivah* is not a volitional act and is therefore treated by the rabbis as the primary locus of the decree; *kiryo d'tali b'maaseh lo gazru bei rabbanan* — seminal emission, being more volitional and in some sense more controllable, is the appropriate place to leave *tahor* and thus signal the rabbinic character of the whole regime.

Both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that *keri* of a non-Jewish man must be *tahor*: for Beit Shammai, because it is used as the obvious distinction (analogous to the blood of the non-Jewish woman); for Beit Hillel, because when it comes to a man there is no analogue to the "wet but not dry" distinction that works for blood. Spit and *zivah* do not admit of that subtle distinction in the same way. So Beit Hillel also must identify an entire category to declare *tahor*, and that is the *keri*.

### Semen Status

The Gemara then cites a Mishnah from tractate *Mikvaos* in support. The Mishnah states: *shichvat zera shel Yisrael tmeia b'chol makom* — the semen of a Jewish man is *tamei* in all places, *afilu b'mei ovedet kochavim* — even while inside or emanating from the body of a non-Jewish woman. *Ve-shel ovdei kochavim tehorah b'chol makom* — the semen of a non-Jewish man is *tahor* in all places, *afilu b'mei Yisraelit* — even while inside a Jewish woman. The determining factor is not the woman, but the source of the semen: Jewish semen retains its *tumah* status wherever it is found; non-Jewish semen is *tahor* wherever it is found.

The exception noted by the Mishnah is *chutz mimei raglayim she'bah* — except for the urine. The precise reading here involves some complexity regarding whether it refers to her urine or his. The sense appears to be that the urine of the non-Jewish man is *tamei* — consistent with our ruling that *zivah* and spit and urine of a non-Jewish man carry *tumah* — while his semen alone is *tahor*.

The Gemara initially considers whether the Mishnah's ruling that non-Jewish semen is *tahor* refers only to biblical law, with rabbinic *tumah* still applying. It resolves this by noting that the urine in the same passage is explicitly *tamei*, and that *tumah* is itself only rabbinic (since the non-Jewish man has no biblical *tumah*). If the urine is called *tamei* and the semen is called *tahor* in the same Mishnah, and both statuses can only be rabbinic, then the contrast makes clear that the semen is *tahor* even rabbinically — *shema mina tehorah afilu miderabbanan*.

### Rav Pappa's Question

The Gemara then connects this Mishnah to an unresolved question posed by Rav Pappa. The Mishnah has just stated that the semen of a Jewish man is *tamei* even inside the body of a non-Jewish woman. Could this resolve Rav Pappa's *ba'ya*? Rav Pappa had asked: *shichvat zera shel Yisrael b'mei ovedet kochavim mahu* — what is the status of the semen of a Jewish man that is inside the body of a non-Jewish woman?

The Gemara clarifies: Rav Pappa was not asking about within three days, when obviously the semen retains its status as *tamei*. His question was specifically about *after three days* — after 72 hours — since at that point Jewish semen ordinarily loses its potency and is presumed *tahor*. Does the same apply when the semen is inside a non-Jewish woman?

The Gemara raises two competing theories about what happens inside a non-Jewish woman's body. One theory: *Yisrael de-daige be-mitzvot, chavilei gufaihu u-matriach* — Jews are anxious about their obligations, which causes their bodies to overheat, and this heat causes the semen to spoil and lose potency within 72 hours. Non-Jews, who carry no such burden of anxiety, do not overheat in the same way, and their bodies therefore preserve semen longer. Under this theory, Jewish semen inside a non-Jewish woman might *not* spoil after 72 hours, since her body is cooler. The reverse theory: *de-achli shekatzim uremasim, chavilei gufaihu u-matriach* — non-Jews eat non-kosher food, which heats the body; therefore their bodies *also* cause semen to spoil rapidly. Under this theory, the semen would indeed spoil within 72 hours inside a non-Jewish woman as well. *Teku* — the question remains unresolved.

This is admittedly a striking passage: what appears at first glance to be a formal halachic category question — does the status of semen change depending on whose body it enters — is resolved by the Gemara through a chain of reasoning about the physiology of anxiety, dietary practice, and body temperature. It is notable that Tosafot comments on this, pointing out that the Gemara's framing of Rav Pappa's question as specifically about "after three days" — with the accompanying medical reasoning — is the Gemara's own gloss and elaboration. In other contexts (specifically in tractate Shabbat, in the chapter of Rabbi Akiva), the Gemara treats Rav Pappa's original question as a simpler one: perhaps when semen enters the body of a non-Jewish woman, its halachic status changes categorically, without reference to the three-day threshold at all. Tosafot notes that it is not uncommon for the Gemara to reframe an original statement in a way that adds a layer of interpretation not originally intended by its author.

---

---

# Niddah 35

## Dam Tehorah Shemetzora'at

### Ma'ayanot and Av Hatumah

The daf opens, technically beginning partway through 34b, with a case whose very elegance lies in how precisely it isolates a difficult theoretical question about *tumah*. The governing principle is that the spit, urine, and certain other bodily fluids of a *zav*, *zavah*, and *niddah* carry the status of *av hatumah* — a primary source of impurity. The organizing concept underlying this category is *mit'agel veyotzei*: these are substances that collect within the body and then are expelled, a description that fits urine and saliva quite naturally.

The question arises: what of uterine blood? Ordinarily the question is moot, because uterine blood is itself the very basis of a woman's status as a *niddah* or *zavah*, and is therefore *tamei* by virtue of being the source of *tumah* rather than by virtue of being a bodily fluid. It does not obviously fall into the *mit'agel veyotzei* category — blood does not collect and pool in the way urine does — so under what circumstances could the question become live?

The *Mishnah* constructs precisely that scenario. Consider a woman who has just given birth and is now in her postpartum period — the thirty-three or sixty-six days following the initial week or two during which the blood is designated *dam tehorah*, pure blood. During this window the blood is halachically *tahor* and does not render her a *niddah* or *zavah*. If she has not yet immersed in a *mikvah* following childbirth, the *taharah* of the blood is also technically moot — she is already *tamei* as a *yoledes*. But add a further complication: she is a *metzora'at*, a woman afflicted with *tzara'at*. The halacha governing a *metzora* is that certain bodily fluids of one afflicted with *tzara'at* carry the status of *av hatumah*. The question is therefore this: does her uterine blood during this postpartum period of *dam tehorah* partake of the status of the *ma'ayanot* — the wellspring fluids — of a *metzora'at*?

### Beit Shammai vs. Beit Hi…

*Beit Shammai* rules that this blood is *tahor* and does not have the status of a *metzora'at*'s bodily fluids. *Beit Hillel* rules that it is *tamei* — that the uterine blood does in fact carry the halachic status of such a fluid. The debate between them turns on how to read a verse in *Parashat Zav*.

### Drasha: Lazachar Velanek…

The *Gemara* introduces the position of *Beit Hillel* via a *drasha* transmitted by *Rabbi Yitzchak*. At the conclusion of the *parashah* dealing with *zav* and *zavah*, the verse states: *"Hazav vezovo lazachar velanekevah ule'ish asher tetzei mimenu shichvat zara"* — this is the *tumah* of the flow, for the male and the female, and for a man from whom semen issues. The redundancy is striking: the entire preceding passage has been discussing men and women with flows, so why does the verse now add "for the male and for the female"? *Rabbi Yitzchak* teaches: *lazachar lerabot metzora lema'ayanotav* — the word "male" comes to include the *metzora*, that his bodily fluids likewise carry this elevated status of impurity. Similarly, *velanekevah lerabot metzora'at lema'ayanoteha* — "and female" comes to include the *metzora'at*, that her wellspring fluids are *tamei* as well.

But this still requires a further step to reach the blood. The *Gemara* presses: if *velanekevah* is coming to include the *metzora'at*'s fluids, is it teaching us about her ordinary fluids — spit and urine? That would be unnecessary, because once the *Torah* taught us this about the male *metzora*, we could infer it applies to the female as well. There is no obvious reason to distinguish between them with respect to saliva and urine. Therefore, *ela ledamah* — it must be that the word "female" comes specifically to address something uniquely female, namely her blood: *letammei dam tehorah shelah*, to render *tamei* even the blood that is halachically pure as to its *niddah*/*zavah* status, but which is now treated as the bodily fluid of a *metzora'at*.

### Beit Hillel Reasoning

*Beit Hillel*'s full argument unfolds as follows. The *Torah* could have stated the law of the *metzora'at*'s fluids with reference to the female alone. Had it done so, we could have inferred the male a fortiori: if even a female *metzora'at*, whose obligations of *tzara'at* practice are less severe than a male's — he must let his hair grow wild, rend his garments, and abstain from marital relations, none of which apply to her — even she has her fluids rendered *tamei*, is it not all the more so true of the male *metzora*? Therefore the verse did not need to state it by the male. And since the male formulation is unnecessary, we apply the hermeneutical principle *im eino inyan*: if it has nothing new to teach regarding the male *metzora*'s ordinary fluids, redirect it to teach something novel about the female — specifically, her uterine blood. *Uve'im eino inyan lema'ayanoteha*, and if it is also not needed to teach about her ordinary fluids since those could be derived from the male, redirect it further: *tnehu inyan ledam* — let it teach about her blood.

The underlying reason that blood requires special derivation is precisely because it is not naturally in the *mit'agel veyotzei* category — it is not a fluid that pools and is expelled in the manner of urine or saliva. *Beit Hillel* acknowledges this, but maintains that the extra word in the verse establishes it as though it were in that category.

### Beit Shammai Defense

*Beit Shammai* contests this entire edifice at multiple points. First, they argue that one cannot in fact dispense with *lazachar* by inferring the male from the female, because *de'ika lemifrach* — there is a valid counter-argument: the male *metzora* is in certain respects more stringent than the female, with his requirements of *pri'ah* and *frimah* (disheveled hair and torn garments) and his prohibition from marital relations. Since the female's *tzara'at* obligations are lighter, one might have thought that only she, with her more lenient status, needs a special verse — and therefore the verse about the male was indeed needed and cannot be redirected.

*Beit Hillel* responds: then reverse the argument. State it by the female and let me infer the male — since even the female, with her lighter *tzara'at* obligations, has her fluids rendered *tamei*, the male is surely included. So the verse about the male is indeed superfluous and can be redirected. *Beit Shammai* counters: one cannot so easily dismiss the male formulation, because the female has a stringency of her own in the laws of *zov* and *zava* — namely that a woman can become *tamei* as a *niddah* or *zavah* even when the flow arises from external stimulation (*ones*), whereas for a man, a flow caused by external stimulation does not make him a *zav*. Since the female category is in this respect weightier, you cannot automatically infer the male from the female. *Beit Hillel* rejoins: we are discussing the laws of a *metzora*, not the laws of *zav* and *zavah* — why should stringencies that belong to an entirely different domain of *tumah* affect the inference here? *Beit Shammai* maintains that once a category of *tumah* is in any way weightier, we cannot use it as the source for inference to another category.

Finally, *Beit Shammai* offers an alternative account of what *lazachar* comes to teach. Rather than redirecting the verse to include a new type of fluid, it teaches *kol she-hu zachar bein gadol bein katan* — any male, whether adult or minor. This is the source for the rule that even a one-day-old male can become a *zav*. *Beit Hillel*, by contrast, derives the inclusion of minors from the phrase *zot torat hazav* — "this is the law of the *zav*" — a broad encompassing statement. Since *Beit Hillel* learns the minor's status from *zot torat hazav*, the word *lazachar* remains available to be redirected to teach about the uterine blood of the *metzora'at*. The debate thus comes down, at its core, to competing uses of available textual surplus.

## Rav Yosef on Zav Katan

### Reiyah Rishonah Shel Zav…

The *Gemara* now shifts to a series of related conceptual questions — questions that are, as one might say, more structurally interesting than the *drasha* debate just concluded. *Rav Yosef* reports that whenever *Reish Lakish* would teach the laws of *zav*, he would invariably pose the following question: *re'iyah rishonah shel zav katan mahu shet'tamei bemaga* — does the first flow of a minor *zav* cause impurity through contact?

To appreciate the question, one must recall the basic framework. A man's penile discharge is classified as either *shichvat zera* (semen) or *zov* (the *zav* flow, a non-seminal discharge, pale in color and thinner than semen). Semen makes him a *ba'al keri*, a one-day *tumah*. The *zov* flow: once makes him like a *ba'al keri* in terms of *tumah* status; twice gives him a seven-day *tumah*; three times requires a *korban*. The critical halachic point is that after one *zov* flow, the *tumah* is halachically equivalent to that of *ba'al keri*.

Now the question: can a minor become a *ba'al keri*? No — the laws of *shichvat zera* are tied to an act of marital relations, which halachically is defined as applicable only from age nine and above. Below that age, semen does not generate *tumah*. So if the first *zov* flow carries the same *tumah* as *shichvat zera*, perhaps a minor's first flow also does not generate *tumah* — since he cannot become a *ba'al keri*, perhaps the same logic exempts him. The verse states *zot torat hazav asher tetzei mimenu shichvat zera* — "this is the law of the *zav* from whom semen issues" — from which it is derived: *kol sheshichvat zera shelo metamei re'iyah rishonah shelo metamei* — any person whose semen generates *tumah*, his first *zov* flow likewise generates *tumah*. But a minor's semen does not generate *tumah* — so perhaps his first *zov* flow likewise does not. On the other hand, perhaps we should not press the analogy so far: after all, if the minor has two flows, those will combine to make him a full *zav*. He is already in the process of becoming a *zav* — perhaps that is sufficient to establish that even the first flow generates *tumah*.

### Rava's Proof from Braita

*Rava* resolves the question. The verse *zot torat hazav* is interpreted as a broad statement: *bein gadol bein katan* — whether adult or minor. The *drasha* from the *braita* is: just as an adult's first flow generates *tumah*, so too a minor's first flow generates *tumah*. The answer is thus clear: the analogy to *shichvat zera* does not override the independent rule that a minor can be a *zav*, and even his first flow makes him *tamei*.

### Rav Yosef on Metzora

Having resolved the question about the minor *zav*, *Rav Yosef* poses an analogous question — now about a *metzora*. This question will carry the discussion into the next section.

## Makom Ziva Ma'ayan

### Metzora's First Flow Sta…

The question posed is: *re'iyah rishonah shel metzora mahu shet'titma bemasa* — does the first *zov* flow of a *metzora* render *tamei* through carrying (*masa*)? The conceptual structure here is directly analogous to the question we explored regarding a woman's uterine blood. Normally, a man's *zov* flow poses no question about its fluid status: it is the source of *tumah*, making him a *zav* or at minimum a *ba'al keri*, so of course it is *tamei*. But if the man is already a *metzora*, the question becomes tractable: the *zov* flow does not meaningfully change his *tumah* status, since he is already *tamei* from *tzara'at*. It is at best making him a *ba'al keri* in addition to being a *metzora*, but it is not causing him to become a *zav*. So — is this first flow, which is not generating a new category of *tumah* for him, nevertheless considered one of the *ma'ayanot* of the *metzora*, such that it carries *tumah* through *masa*?

The distinction between *maga* (contact) and *masa* (carrying) matters critically here. The *tumah* of *ba'al keri* — and of the first *zov* flow, which is treated like *ba'al keri* — is transmitted by *maga*, not by *masa*. Only the second *zov* flow, which makes him a full *zav*, generates *tumah* through *masa*. The bodily fluids of a *metzora*, however, are *av hatumah* and carry *tumah* through *masa* as well. The question therefore is: does this first *zov* flow, sitting in the *ba'al keri* category for ordinary purposes, gain the more stringent status of a *metzora*'s *ma'ayan* and thereby generate *tumah* through *masa*?

### Rava: Zov Tamei Hu

*Rava* attempts to resolve the question. The verse states *zovo tamei hu* — "his flow, it is *tamei*." The *Gemara* asks: about what case must the verse speak to tell us something non-obvious? If it is speaking about a simple *zav* whose second flow makes him a full *zav*, there is nothing to prove — of course a flow that makes someone a *zav* is itself *tamei*. *Ela peshita* — so the verse must be addressing the case of a *zav metzora*, where the flow's effect on his *tumah* status is relatively moot. And specifically, the *Gemara* argues, the verse must be speaking about the second *zov* flow of a *metzora* — because by the second flow he genuinely is becoming a *zav*, and yet one might have thought that since he is already *tamei* as a *metzora*, this second flow is also somehow not a true source of *tumah*; the verse therefore tells us it is.

The inference: since the verse was needed to establish that the *second* flow of a *metzora* is *tamei*, we can deduce that the *first* flow, about which no such verse was needed, is *not* considered a *ma'ayan* — *shema mina makom ziva lav ma'ayan hu*. The mere fact of being the site from which *zova* flows is insufficient. It is only when the flow genuinely constitutes a *zov* — i.e., the second flow making him a *zav* — that it has the status of a *ma'ayan*.

### Rav Yehudah's Challenge

*Rav Yehudah of Diskarta* challenges *Rava*'s reasoning. The entire proof rests on the claim that the verse *zovo tamei hu* could not be speaking about a simple *zav* whose second flow makes him a *zav*, because that would be self-evident — a flow that generates *zav* status is of course *tamei*. But is that self-evident? *Rav Yehudah* invokes the *seir hamishtaleach* — the goat sent to Azazel on Yom Kippur, which generates *tumah* in the one who sends it, and yet the goat itself remains *tahor*. This demonstrates that something can cause *tumah* in others without itself being a source of *tumah*. Therefore, it is not obvious that even a flow making a man a *zav* is itself *tamei* — and the verse may indeed have been needed for that ordinary case, leaving nothing to infer about the *metzora* case.

### Rav Yehudah's Challenge

*Abaye* then clarifies the logical structure of the proof. The key is that *Rav Yosef* himself — the one who posed the original question — holds that *lazachar* in the verse is the source for including the *metzora*'s fluids, and *velanekevah* for including the *metzora'at*'s fluids. This was established in the earlier debate between *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai*. Having used *lazachar* for that purpose, it is further available to link the *metzora*'s fluids *lerabot she'af chumrei metzora lezav gamur* — to subject them to the same laws as the full *zav*'s flows.

### Metzora Linked to Zav

The verse's formulation *lazov et zovo lazachar velanekevah* links the fluids of the *metzora* to *lazov et zovo* — to the flows of a genuine *zav*. Just as the second flow of a full *zav* generates *tumah* through *masa*, so too the flows of a *metzora* generate *tumah* through *masa*. The question then is whether this linkage extends to the first flow, which in the ordinary context of a *zav* would not generate *tumah* by *masa* but only by *maga*.

### First Flow Not Ma'ayan

The conclusion that emerges is that the first flow of a *metzora* is not a *ma'ayan* — it does not generate *tumah* through *masa* — while the second flow does. The broader conceptual picture: the analysis of what constitutes a *ma'ayan* depends not merely on the anatomical source of the fluid but on whether in that instance the flow genuinely creates a new *tumah* category. Where it does, as with the second *zov* flow, it is indeed a *ma'ayan*; where it does not, as with the first, it is not.

## First Flow and Ones

### Reiyah Rishonah Be'ones

*Rav Huna* raises yet another dimension of the first *zov* flow question: *re'iyah rishonah shel zav metamei be'ones* — does the first flow of a *zav* generate *tumah* even when caused by external stimulation? This directly parallels the question of how far the analogy to *shichvat zera* extends.

The halacha of *zav* ordinarily requires that one first investigate whether the flow was caused by external factors — eating something unusual, heavy lifting, exertion, and so forth — and if it was, the flow is not counted toward *zav* status. *Shichvat zera*, semen, generates *tumah* even when due to *ones*. Since the first *zov* flow carries the same *tumah* as *shichvat zera*, perhaps it too generates *tumah* even when externally caused. Or perhaps, since it occurs in the context of *zav* physiology, it retains the *zav* rule and is exempt if externally caused.

### Mishnah on Checking Flows

The *Gemara* attempts to resolve this from the *Mishnah*: *ra'ah re'iyah rishonah bodkin oto* — if he has his first flow, they check him for external stimulation. One might think: this checking is to determine whether the flow is *tamei* — implying that if caused externally, it is *not tamei*. The *Gemara* deflects: perhaps the checking is only for purposes of the *korban* — to determine whether this flow can combine with subsequent flows toward a *korban* obligation — but the flow is *tamei* regardless. Then the *Gemara* extends to the second flow: *bishniyah bodkin oto*, you also check the second flow. Why check the second flow? If the intent were only about the *korban*, why check the second — since the *korban* requires three? The answer is that by the second flow, the verse *mibesaro velo machmat onso* establishes that only a flow from within, not from external stimulation, renders him *tamei*. So the checking of the second flow is clearly about *tumah*. And since the *Mishnah* uses the same language for the first and second flows, it seems to follow that checking the first flow is also about *tumah*.

However, the *Gemara* pushes back: *midi irya* — these may simply be independent cases, each governed by its own logic. The second flow's checking is about *tumah*, the first flow's checking may be about whether it can combine toward a *korban*, while the first flow itself is *tamei* regardless.

### Tanna Kamma vs. Rabbi El…

The discussion then turns to the dispute between the *Tanna Kamma* and *Rabbi Elazar* about checking the third flow. *Rabbi Elazar* holds that one checks even the third flow for *ones*, lest it lead to an improper *korban*. The *Tanna Kamma* does not require checking the third flow for *korban* purposes. The *Gemara* suggests this debate may imply that the *Tanna Kamma* requires checking for *tumah* purposes even through the earlier flows, but the *Gemara* rejects this as well: both agree that checking for *korban* purposes is sometimes necessary; they disagree only about whether *ones* matters at flow three for the *korban*, with the *Tanna Kamma* holding it does not (the verse *lazachar velanekevah* equates flow three with the *zavah*, whose *ones* is disregarded), while *Rabbi Elazar* holds that the verse extends the *ones* exemption through flow three. Neither view yields a clear answer about the first flow and *tumah*.

### Rabbi Yitzchak's Solution

*Rabbi Yitzchak* resolves the question with a sharp structural observation. He states: *velo zav bichlal ba'al keri haya* — a *zav* was already included in the category of *ba'al keri*. Why then was the *zav* singled out as a distinct category? *Lehakel alav ulehachmir alav* — both to be lenient with him and to be strict with him. Lenient: *she'ein metamei be'ones* — unlike *ba'al keri*, the *zav* does not generate *tumah* when the flow is externally caused. Strict: *she'hu oseh mishkav umoshav av hatumah* — the *zav* renders the objects he sits or lies upon an *av hatumah*, which *ba'al keri* does not.

The *Gemara* then clarifies what stage is being described. One cannot read this as referring to after the second flow — because then why say the *zav* "was included in the category of *ba'al keri*"? After two flows he is a full *zav*, never having been treated as a *ba'al keri* at that stage. So it must be referring to the first flow — that is when a *zav* carries the status of *ba'al keri*. And the *kal* aspect, the leniency, is that at the stage of the second flow, unlike the first, *ones* does not generate *tumah*. The clear implication — left implicit by the *Gemara* but embedded in the structure — is that the first flow, which is in the *ba'al keri* category, *does* generate *tumah* even through *ones*. The *Gemara* notes that the text does not spell this out entirely, but the reading of the *braita* strongly suggests it. The conclusion that emerges: the first flow is analogous to *shichvat zera* even in this respect, while the second flow departs from the *ba'al keri* category in the lenient direction (no *ones*) as well as the strict direction (seven-day *tumah*, *mishkav umoshav*).

### Zov vs. Zera Description

The *Gemara* closes this section with *Rav Huna*'s physical description of the difference between *zov* and *zera* — since for a woman the distinction between *niddah* and *zavah* is temporal, but for a man it is physiological. *Zov* resembles the water of barley dough — pale and thin. It issues from the non-erect penis. *Shichvat zera* is more viscous, more cohesive, and resembles the white of a fertilized egg, issuing from the erect penis. (Whether *muzeres* here means fertilized or beaten is noted as a matter of some uncertainty — *Rashi* takes it to mean fertilized.)

## Dam Hayoledes Shelo Tavl…

### Beit Hillel's Challenge

The *Gemara* now turns to a case structurally similar to the *metzora'at* question but with a different twist. A woman gave birth, is now in her postpartum period — the thirty-three or sixty-six days of *dam tehorah* — but has not yet immersed in a *mikvah*. She is still *tamei* as a *yoledes*. What is the status of blood she now sees?

This case inverts the earlier one. In the *metzora'at* discussion, the question was whether blood that is not generating *niddah* or *zavah tumah* can nonetheless be classified as a bodily fluid of the *metzora'at*. Here, the question is about the character of the blood itself: is it *dam tehorah* — pure blood — or does the woman's continued *tum'ah* status, by virtue of not having immersed, somehow affect the blood's status?

*Beit Hillel* opens the exchange by challenging *Beit Shammai*: do you not agree that a *niddah* who has completed her seven days but has not yet gone to the *mikvah*, and who then sees blood, is *tamei* — fully *tamei* as *dam niddah* or *dam zavah*, even if the blood dries? If so, why should this *yoledes*, who also has not gone to the *mikvah*, be different?

### Beit Shammai's Response

*Beit Shammai* rejects the analogy. By a *niddah*, even if she immerses and later bleeds, the blood makes her *tamei* again — the blood is always a source of *tumah* when it emerges. By the *yoledes*, however, had she gone to the *mikvah* and then bled during the thirty-three or sixty-six days, that blood would do nothing to her — it is *dam tehorah*. This shows that the blood itself during this period is *tahor*. *Beit Shammai* therefore holds that even without *mikvah* immersion, the blood during the thirty-three or sixty-six days is intrinsically *tahor* — perhaps it has some secondary level of *tumah* by rabbinic enactment, but it is not fundamentally *dam niddah* or *dam zavah*.

### Proof from Zavah Case

*Beit Hillel* responds with a case that both sides agree upon: a *yoledes beza'vah* — a woman who gave birth while she was a *zavah*. Both agree that if she immerses after her seven clean days and then bleeds during the thirty-three or sixty-six days, the blood is *tehorah*. And both agree that if she has not yet completed her seven clean days and bleeds during the thirty-three or sixty-six days, that blood is *tamei* — it prevents her from counting a clean day. So, *Beit Hillel* argues, look at the case where she has completed her seven clean days but has not yet immersed — if she bleeds, should that blood be *tamei* or *tahor*? It is analogous to the *yoledes* who has not immersed: everything is done except the *mikvah*. If *Beit Shammai* agrees that the *zavah* in this position is still *tamei* until she immerses, then why not say the same for the *yoledes*?

### Conditional Agreement

*Beit Shammai*'s response is *hu hadin vehu hateshuvah* — the same answer applies. Whatever we say about the *yoledes*, we say about the *zavah* in that position. A *braita* then confirms that indeed, in the case of a *yoledes beza'vah* who has counted her seven clean days but not yet immersed, the two schools follow their respective positions: *Beit Shammai* to their principle and *Beit Hillel* to theirs. The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction between this and a *Mishnah* that implies they agree: the *Mishnah*'s agreement applies only to a *zavah* who is still in the middle of counting her seven clean days — in that case, both agree that bleeding during the thirty-three or sixty-six days is *tamei*, because she is still counting and the blood interrupts her *sefirah*. Only once the seven clean days are complete does the disagreement arise.

### When Blood Becomes Tahor

The conceptual core of the debate may now be stated clearly. *Beit Shammai* holds that the *Torah* purifies the blood of a *yoledes* automatically upon her reaching day 8 or day 15 — the transition is calendrical. *Beit Hillel* holds that the *Torah* does not purify the blood until after she has immersed in a *mikvah* — the transition requires both the calendar and the act of immersion. Until that point, even though the blood would in ordinary circumstances be *dam tehorah*, it retains its *tamei* character by virtue of her not yet having completed the process of *tahara*.

## Ma'ayan Echad or Shnei

### Rav: One Wellspring

The *Gemara* now introduces a dispute between *Rav* and *Levi* that places the entire preceding debate about the *yoledes* into a broader theoretical framework. *Rav* says: *ma'ayan echad hu* — there is one wellspring. All the uterine blood, throughout the postpartum period, flows from the same physical source. The *Torah* simply assigns different halachic statuses to it: *tamei* during the first seven or fourteen days, *tahor* from day 8 or 15, *tamei* again after day 40 or 80. This is a pure halachic designation, not a physical distinction. *Hatorah timaso vehatorah tiharto* — the *Torah* declared it *tamei* and the *Torah* declared it *tahor*.

### Levi: Two Wellsprings

*Levi* disagrees: *shnei ma'ayanot hein* — they are two distinct wellsprings. The *tumah* source physically closes at the end of day 7 or 14: *nistam hatamei*. A different, *tahor* source then opens: *niftach hatahor*. At day 40 or 80, the *tahor* source closes and the *tamei* source reopens. For *Levi*, the change in halachic status reflects an underlying physiological change in the source of the blood.

### Continuous Flow Cases

The practical difference emerges in cases of continuous flow across the status boundaries. If a woman is bleeding steadily from within day 7 into day 8 — a single uninterrupted flow — does the blood that spans the boundary carry the status of the earlier or the later period? The same question arises at the end: a flow that begins within day 40 and continues into day 41.

### Rav's and Levi's Stringe…

For *Rav*, since there is a single wellspring and the change is purely halachic, the transition is sharp: the moment day 8 begins, the blood is *tahor*, regardless of continuity with the earlier flow. This makes *Rav* lenient at the beginning of the process (*reisha lekula*) — as soon as the calendar turns, the blood changes status. But at the end of the process, the moment day 41 begins, the blood again becomes *tamei*, even if it is a continuation of the same flow that was *tahor* the moment before — making *Rav* strict there (*seifa lechumra*).

*Levi* is the reverse. Since the change in status reflects a physical change of source, a continuous flow from within day 7 into day 8 remains problematic: the source has not yet switched, and so the flow cannot be assumed to have become *tahor* (*reisha lechumra*). But at the end of the process, a continuous flow from within day 40 into day 41 remains *tahor*: the physical *tahor* source has not yet closed, and the blood is still issuing from the same *tahor* wellspring (*seifa lekula*).

### Connection to Beit Hillel

The *Gemara* connects this debate back to the dispute between *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai*. *Beit Hillel*'s position — that blood does not become *dam tehorah* until after the woman has immersed in a *mikvah*, not merely upon reaching day 8 or 15 — fits naturally with the view that there is *one* wellspring: *ma'ayan echad*. If the change were physical, tied to the opening and closing of distinct anatomical sources, the *mikvah* would be irrelevant — the blood would automatically shift character once the new source opened. But if the change is halachic, one can readily add the requirement that the *mikvah* be part of the halachic process by which the status shifts. *Beit Hillel*'s position thus implies that the *Torah*'s *tahara* of the *yoledes*'s blood is not automatic upon the calendar date but requires the act of immersion — a position coherent only if one understands the blood as having a single physical source whose halachic status the *Torah* assigns and reassigns. The *Gemara* closes with this connection, to be continued in the following daf.

# Niddah 36

## Rav vs. Levi

### Maayan Echad Framework

The daf opens in the middle of 35b, approximately ten lines down from the top of the wide lines, with the word *meisivei*. The subject is a focused and clearly defined debate between Rav and Levi concerning the nature of the blood a woman produces during the *yemei tohar* — the 33 or 66 days of ritual purity following childbirth (33 days after a boy, 66 after a girl).

Rav's position is stated as *maayan echad hu hatorah timaso vehatorah tiharato*: it is a single source of blood. The blood during *yemei tohar* comes from the same biological origin as all uterine blood; it is the Torah itself that assigns it a *tahor* status during that period. The *tahor* designation is, on this view, a purely halachic reality — the Torah decrees it, and the decree is what determines its status.

### Shnei Maayanos

Levi disagrees on what he presents as biological grounds. His formulation is *shnei maayanos heim nistam hatamei veniftach hatahor niftach hatahor venistam hatamei*: there are two distinct sources. When a woman transitions from the week or two weeks of *tumah* following childbirth into the *yemei tohar*, what actually occurs, according to Levi, is that the *tamei* source closes and a different, *tahor* source opens. The *tahor* character of the blood during *yemei tohar* is thus grounded in a genuine physiological shift, not merely in a halachic assignment. (The Gemara does not specify what this second source consists of biologically, and that question is left unresolved.)

### Dam Yoledes Case

The Gemara now tests these two positions against a *mishna*. The *mishna* reads: *dam yoledes shelo tavla* — the blood of a woman who has given birth and has not yet immersed in the *mikvah*. What is the status of blood she produces during the *yemei tohar*? Beit Shammai says it has a middle-level *tumah*, comparable to her saliva or urine — the fluids of a *yoledes* — rather than full *dam tamei*. Beit Hillel, however, says it is full *dam tamei*, equivalent to *dam niddah*, because she has not yet gone to the *mikvah*.

The focus here is on Beit Hillel's position: even during the 33 or 66 days, the blood remains fully *tamei* if she has not immersed. This seems to indicate strongly that the *tahor* status of *dam yemei tohar* is a halachic reality contingent on immersion — not a biological fact. The Gemara notes: *bishlama leRav de'amar maayan echad hu*, according to Rav this is coherent; the Torah assigns a *tahor* status to this blood, and the Torah may condition that assignment on her having immersed from the preceding period of *tumah*. Accordingly, Beit Hillel's position that blood during *yemei tohar* is still fully *tamei* without *mikvah* immersion is entirely understandable.

*Ela leLevi de'amar shnei maayanos heim* — but according to Levi, who says the blood is coming from an entirely different biological source, why should Beit Hillel say it is *tamei*? What difference does it make whether she went to the *mikvah* or not? If the source of the blood has physically changed, its origin renders it *tahor* regardless.

### Shofaat Answer

Levi's response is: *hacha bamai askinan beshofaat* — we are dealing with a case of *shofaat*, a continuous flow. If the bleeding carried over without interruption from day 7 into day 8 (or day 14 into day 15), then even according to Levi, we know the blood is still coming from the *tamei* source, because it is visibly flowing from the *tamei* period into the *tahor* period. In such a case, Beit Hillel's stringency is perfectly understandable.

It should be noted, however, that this answer generates its own difficulty: if it is *shofaat* and thus biologically still from the *tamei* source, then it should be *tamei* regardless of whether she has or has not gone to the *mikvah*. The *mishna* speaks specifically about a woman who has *not* gone to the *mikvah*; but on Levi's reading, once it is established as a *shofaat* case, the *mikvah* status becomes irrelevant. This is noted as a very weak answer.

### Beit Shammai Challenge

The Gemara presses Levi further: *ei beshofaat mai taama deBeit Shammai* — if it is a case of *shofaat*, what is Beit Shammai's reasoning? If the blood is flowing continuously from the *tamei* source, how can Beit Shammai say it becomes *tahor* the moment day 8 begins? Levi concedes: *ksavar Beit Shammai maayan echad hu* — Beit Shammai holds the position of one source, i.e., Rav's position. On that view, once the day changes, the Torah's assigned status changes and the blood is automatically *tahor* regardless of flow. Levi must concede that Beit Shammai is against him.

The Gemara then turns this around and asks: *bishlama leLevi haini de'ika bein Beit Shammai leBeit Hillel* — fine, according to Levi's framing of the case as *shofaat*, we can explain the Beit Shammai/Beit Hillel debate as a dispute about whether the source is one or two. Beit Hillel says two sources, so a *shofaat* flow during day 8 is still *tamei*; Beit Shammai says one source, so once the day turns it is *tahor*.

But *ela leRav mai beinaihu* — according to Rav, where everyone agrees it is one source, what exactly is the debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel? The Gemara answers: *ika beinaihu yomei u'tvila* — they are debating a purely halachic question: what does the Torah require in order for the status to shift to *tahor*? Is it sufficient that she enters day 8 (*d'Beit Shammai savri b'yomei tala Rachmana*)? Or does the Torah additionally require immersion (*u'Beit Hillel savri lo b'yomei u'tvila*)? On Rav's reading, this is a clean and natural halachic dispute: does the status-change require only the passage of days, or does it also require *mikvah*?

---

## Yoledet BeZova

### Modim BeYoledet

The Gemara continues: *ta shma*, come and hear — *u'modim b'yoledes b'zova she'hi metama'ah lach v'yavesh*. Both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that when a woman gives birth while she is also a *zava* — that is, she was already in the process of counting *shiva nekiyim* when she gave birth — the blood she produces during *yemei tohar* is fully *tamei*, wet and dry.

The Gemara assumes this case involves a break in the bleeding (*salka datchach hacha nami d'paska*): she gave birth and is now in her *yemei tohar*, but she is simultaneously in a period of counting seven clean days as a *zava*. Blood she sees during this period is deemed *tamei* even though it falls within the 33 or 66 days.

### Zova Overlap Test

The implications are immediate. *Bishlama leRav d'amar maayan echad hu* — according to Rav, who holds it is all one source and the *tahor* status is a Torah-assigned designation, it is perfectly coherent that the Torah would not apply its *tahor* designation when the woman simultaneously bears the status of a *zava* still counting *shiva nekiyim*. The Torah's decree of *tahor* blood was not issued for that situation.

### Levi's Zova Problem

But *ela leLevi d'amar shnei maayanos hen* — according to Levi, the blood during *yemei tohar* comes from a biologically different source. If so, why does it matter that she is also a *zava*? Blood from a different biological source ought to be *tahor* regardless of her *zava* status, just as blood from a cut finger would not affect her *zava* count. *Amai metamei lach v'yavesh?*

### Shofaat with Zova

Levi again responds: *amar lach hacha nami b'shofaat* — again, it is a *shofaat* case. The blood was flowing continuously from before the transition into *yemei tohar*, demonstrating it is still coming from the *tamei* biological source.

The Gemara immediately asks: *ei b'shofaat l'mai itzterich* — if it is *shofaat*, why is the *zava* status even needed to make this *tamei*? It is *tamei* simply because it is flowing from the *tamei* source. The Gemara replies: *leBeit Shammai itzterich* — it is a *chiddush* specifically in relation to Beit Shammai. Since Levi had already conceded that Beit Shammai operates on the principle of one source (*maayan echad*), one might have thought that even according to Beit Shammai, the blood becomes automatically *tahor* upon entering day 8, as it is merely a Torah-assigned status that shifts with the day. The *chiddush* is that even Beit Shammai agrees that when a woman is also a *zava*, the *tahor* designation does not apply — even Beit Shammai holds that the Torah's *tahor* status for *yemei tohar* blood was not intended to override the *zava* counting period.

### Braita on Seven Days

The Gemara introduces a *braita*: the verse *kimei niddas devosah tisma* — "as the days of her *niddah* flow, she shall be *tamei*" — is expounded in several ways, one of which is *l'rabos hayoledes b'zov*, to include the *yoledes b'zov*, a woman who gives birth while a *zava*, and to teach that *she'tzricha shiva neki'im* — she requires seven clean days.

The Gemara presents the now-familiar challenge: *bishlama leRav d'amar maayan echad hu mishum hachi ba'ei shiva yamei neki'im* — according to Rav, we readily understand why she needs seven clean days even during *yemei tohar*, because the Torah's *tahor* designation does not apply when she is simultaneously a *zava* counting her days.

### Status Shift Logic

But the question on Levi remains: if the blood is coming from a biologically different source, why does she need seven clean days at all? The Gemara responds on Levi's behalf: *hachi ka'amar* — the *braita* does not mean she needs seven literally blood-free days. Rather, *tzricha shetifsok mashu sheyalu la l'shiva neki'im* — she needs only that the continuous flow cease for a moment (*mashu*), after which the days can count toward *shiva neki'im* even if she is still bleeding, since once there has been a break, the subsequent bleeding is from the different, *tahor* source and does not disqualify the *nekiyim*.

### Levi on Shiva Nekiyim

This is, as the Gemara acknowledges, a stretched reading of the *braita*. If Levi's position requires only a minimal break (*mashu*) to establish a new biological source, then the requirement articulated in the *braita* — *shiva neki'im* — collapses into something far less demanding than what the words suggest. The straightforward reading of *shiva neki'im* is seven days without blood; Levi is forced to reread it as seven days that can count even with blood, provided there was a brief interruption at some point. This is transparently a difficult position.

---

## Mesulekes Damim

### Months Combine

The Gemara brings another case: *yemei iburah olim la l'yemei minikuta* — the months of pregnancy count toward the months of nursing and vice versa for the purpose of establishing *mesulekes damim* status. This is the principle that a woman who has gone three *onot* without bleeding is considered *mesulekes damim*, meaning that the first time she subsequently bleeds, she need not be concerned retroactively for 24 hours. The Gemara specifies: if she did not bleed for two months during pregnancy and one month during nursing, or two during nursing and one during pregnancy, or one and a half from each — any combination reaching three *onot* establishes the *mesulekes damim* status.

### Rav's Requirement

The Gemara asks: *bishlama leRav d'amar maayan echad hu mishum hachi ba'ei hefsek shalosh onot* — according to Rav, it is clear why these months of non-bleeding are necessary. Even if she is in *yemei tohar* and any bleeding would be halachically *tahor*, the biological source is still active; she has not achieved true biological quiescence. *Mesulekes damim* is a biological concept: the source of blood has closed. If she is bleeding during *yemei tohar*, that bleeding is halachically *tahor* but biologically it still represents an active uterine source. Therefore, to establish *mesulekes damim* status, she genuinely needs to have stopped bleeding even during the *yemei tohar* period. The months that qualify for *mesulekes damim* must be months of actual non-bleeding, not merely months of *tahor* blood.

### Levi on Months

According to Levi, however, the blood during *yemei tohar* comes from a distinct biological source. If that is so, why does a woman need actual non-bleeding to establish *mesulekes damim*? Even if she bleeds during *yemei tohar*, it is coming from a different source — it is as though she never bled from the relevant source at all. She should be considered *mesulekes damim* regardless.

### Break = New Source

The Gemara resolves this in Levi's favor — but again with the same *mashu* formula: *hachi ka'amar*, the requirement is not strictly three months without any blood, but *tzericha shetifsok mashu kedei she-ya'alu lah shalosh onot* — she needs only a minimal break to establish that the subsequent bleeding is from the different *tahor* source. Once that is established, even bleeding during *yemei tohar* counts toward the three *onot* of *mesulekes damim*, because it is biologically from a source other than the one that ordinarily creates retroactive concern. As before, Levi's answer is technically coherent but requires a reading of the requirement that strips it of most of its intuitive force.

---

## Dayah Sha'atah

### Levi's Evidence

The Gemara now turns to what appears to be the one piece of evidence that genuinely supports Levi. *Ve-shavin be-ro'ah achar dam tohar she-dayah sha'atah* — everyone agrees that when a woman sees blood after the *yemei tohar* period (after day 40 for a boy, day 80 for a girl), *dayah sha'atah*: it is sufficient for her concern to begin from the moment of discovery; she need not be concerned retroactively for 24 hours. The case, as Rashi clarifies, is that she begins bleeding after day 40 or 80 — after the *yemei tohar* have concluded — and the question is whether she must be *choshesh* going backward 24 hours.

*Bishlama deLevi* — according to Levi, this is entirely natural. During the 40 or 80 days, the normal uterine source (*maayan*) was closed; the *tahor* blood that flowed during *yemei tohar* came from elsewhere. Therefore, when she bleeds after day 40 or 80, it is as though she is beginning afresh from a source that had been dormant. She is essentially *mesulekes damim* in a biological sense, and consequently there is no basis to assume she was bleeding 24 hours earlier.

### Rav's Challenge

According to Rav, however, this is more difficult. Since Rav holds that it is one source throughout, and that the blood during *yemei tohar* was coming from the same uterine source — merely assigned a *tahor* status by the Torah — she was never biologically *mesulekes damim* during that period. If so, when she bleeds after day 40 or 80, she is simply a woman who has been bleeding all along from the same source. *Tipamei me'et l'et* — she should be required to be concerned 24 hours back, just like any woman who has never had a period of biological quiescence.

### Limited Case

The Gemara answers on Rav's behalf: *deleika shahos* — there is no available span of time to retroactively implicate. The case is specifically that she began bleeding on day 41 or day 81. If she is told to be concerned 24 hours backward, that would carry her back into day 40 or day 80, which is still within *yemei tohar* — a period when even Rav agrees the blood was halachically *tahor*. Since the full 24-hour retroactive window cannot be applied (part of it falls within the *tohar* period), the Rabbinic requirement of retroactive concern simply does not engage at all. The rule is either 24 hours back or nothing; the Gemara does not allow for a partial retroactive concern of, say, 13 hours.

The Gemara then asks: but at minimum, should she not be *choshesh* back to the last time she checked (*mipikida lepikida*)? The Gemara answers: *keivan dem'et l'et leika mipikida lepikida lo* — since the primary concern of 24 hours cannot be applied, the secondary concern of *pekidah* likewise does not apply. They are treated as a single package.

### Rav's Answer

This resolution is, as noted, limited. The *dayah sha'atah* rule applies only because the scenario is specifically day 41 or day 81, not because of any underlying biological principle. The case that seemed to support Levi is thus explained by Rav through a procedural constraint. It is the one piece of evidence that *prima facie* appeared to favor Levi; once explained by Rav, it reduces to a technical limitation of retroactive *tumah* rather than to any statement about the biological reality of the sources.

---

## Pesak Le-Rav

### Yoledet BeZova

The Gemara presents one further case: *yoledes b'zov she-safra v'lo tavla v'ra'asa* — a woman who gave birth while a *zava*, who has counted her *shiva nekiyim* but has not yet immersed in the *mikvah*, and who now sees blood during *yemei tohar*. What is the status of this blood? The Gemara reports that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel each follow their respective positions: Beit Shammai says it is not full *dam tamei* as *niddah* or *yoledes* blood (though it may have a lesser degree of *tumah*), while Beit Hillel says it is fully *tamei*, since she has not immersed.

Again, Beit Hillel's insistence that the blood remains fully *tamei* absent *mikvah* immersion — even during *yemei tohar*, even after seven clean days — seems powerfully to indicate a status-based analysis, not a biological one.

### Status Not Biology

*Bishlama leRav d'amar maayan echad hu mishum hachi mitamei lach v'yavesh* — according to Rav, Beit Hillel's position is entirely coherent. It is one source, and the Torah-assigned *tahor* status has not yet taken effect because she has not gone to the *mikvah*. *Ela leLevi d'amar shenei maayanos hein, amai mitamei lach v'yavesh?* — but for Levi, if it is biologically a different source, why is it *tamei*? She has completed her seven clean days; she is not *shofaat*; the biological shift should have occurred. What grounds remain for treating it as *tamei*?

### Final Concession

Levi's first response is a frank concession: *amar lach Levi ana d'amri k'tanna d'shavyan* — I align myself with the *tanna* whose position supports mine, namely the *braita* about *dayah sha'atah* after day 40 or 80, which seemed to support a biological shift. You have your *braita* (the one from which Beit Hillel's ruling is derived); I have mine.

The Gemara then entertains a second response on Levi's behalf: *v'iba'it eima b'shofaat* — perhaps even here it is a case of *shofaat*. But the Gemara objects: *v'ha safra katani* — the case explicitly states she counted seven clean days; how can it be a continuous flow? The Gemara constructs an elaborate answer: *hacha b'yoledes nekeiva b'zov askinan* — this is the case of a woman who gave birth to a girl (14 days of *tumah*), who was a *zava*, and during the first of those two weeks there was no blood (which counted as her *shiva nekiyim* for the *zava* status — a position contingent on the view that *yemei leidah she'einah roah bahen olin lah lisfirat zivatah*, that days of the childbirth period without blood count toward the *zava* clean-day count). Then, during the second week, she began bleeding continuously into the *yemei tohar*, making her a *shofaat*. In this contrived scenario, she has seven clean days and yet is *shofaat*. This is Levi's last resort.

The discussion of *yemei leidah she'einah roah bahen* carries some contemporary relevance: since today all women follow the stringency of a *zava*, the question of whether *yemei leidah* without blood can count toward *shiva nekiyim* arises in practice particularly after a miscarriage, which halachically constitutes a *leidah*. There are halachic consequences for *harchakot* and other matters even when the couple cannot yet resume relations.

### Ravina and Rav Ashi

Ravina said to Rav Ashi: Rav Shaman from Sachra reported that Mar Zutra came to their place and ruled: *hilchata kevata deRav le-chumra ve-hilchata kevata deLevi le-chumra* — we adopt each position in whatever direction produces stringency, since we do not know how to definitively rule between them. Rav Ashi responded: *hilchata kevata deRav bein le-kula bein le-chumra* — the halacha follows Rav consistently, whether in the lenient or the stringent direction. Mareimar likewise ruled that we follow Rav in both directions.

### Hilchata KeRav

The final ruling is: *ve-hilchata kevata deRav bein le-kula bein le-chumra* — we rule like Rav consistently. This conclusion is well-supported by the Gemara's trajectory: virtually every case that the Gemara examined aligned naturally with Rav's position, while Levi was forced to limit his answers to *shofaat* scenarios that were not mentioned in any of the texts, and the very notion of a separate biological source is difficult to conceptualize. Classical halachic thinking understands these differences as halachic-status shifts decreed by the Torah, not as empirical biological claims.

### Tosafot on Chumrot

One final observation is warranted regarding the approach of Mar Zutra — ruling *le-chumra* in both directions simultaneously. Tosafot raises an objection: *ve-im tomar ha terei chumrei de-satri ahadadi ninhu* — is one not prohibited from adopting two self-contradictory stringencies? The two positions here — one source versus two sources — are mutually exclusive; one cannot simultaneously hold that the blood is halachically shifted in status *and* that it is biologically from a different source, at least not when deriving practical consequences in opposite directions. Tosafot answers: *yesh lomar de-hacha di-mesapka lan paska ke-mar le-hachmir u-ke-mar le-hachmir* — where the ruling in both directions is not a genuine *pesak* endorsing either position as true, but rather reflects uncertainty (*safek*), one may indeed adopt both stringencies even if they are logically contradictory. This resolution, Tosafot acknowledges, characterizes much of practical *pesak halachah* more broadly: when the posek cannot reach a conclusion, he plays it safe in all directions, even inconsistently. The further question of whether this represents genuine *safek* or an unwillingness to take halachic responsibility is left open.

---

## Kisha Pains Exception

### Niddah During Kisha

The *mishnah* now introduces the law of labor pains: *ha-maksheh niddah*. A woman who has labor pains (*kishui*) and bleeds during her *niddah* period is a *niddah*. This requires no elaboration: the general rule is that even *dam machmat ones* — bleeding caused by external forces — does not exempt a woman from *niddah* or *zava* status. Labor pains do not change this for the *niddah* period.

### Kisha Negates Zava

There is, however, one exception to the rule that *ones* does not affect *tumah* status: a woman who bleeds during her *zava* period as a result of continuous labor pains leading up to childbirth is not thereby made a *zava*. The bleeding is attributed to the impending birth rather than to an independent uterine discharge.

### Three Days Rule

The *mishnah* implies (though does not state it in those terms) that if a woman bleeds for three days during her 11-day *zava* period (*betoch yud-alef yom*) while experiencing labor pains, this would ordinarily constitute *zivah*. But if those pains are continuous and connected to the birth, the bleeding is not *dam zivah*.

### Break Determines

The critical variable is whether the labor pains were continuous all the way up to childbirth. *Ve-shafsah me'eis le'eis veyaldah harei zu yoledes bazov* — if there was a 24-hour break (*shafsa me'eis le'eis*) in the pains between the bleeding and the birth, she is a *yoledes bazov*. This is the ruling of Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees: not 24 hours (*me'et le'et*), but a full halachic day — a night-and-day unit as measured like the night and day of Shabbat — is required to constitute an interruption. The difference is that 24 hours is a floating period, while a halachic day is anchored to nightfall; a full halachic day will almost always be longer than 24 hours.

The *mishnah* also specifies: *sheshafsah min hatza'ar velo min hadam* — what constitutes an interruption is a break in the *pains*, not merely a break in the bleeding. This is the operative criterion.

### Duration Dispute

How far back from the birth can the *kishui* pains extend and still be attributed to the birth, thus exempting the bleeding from *zivah* status? Rabbi Meir says there is no limit — even 40 or 50 days of continuous labor pains prior to birth suffice. Rabbi Yehuda says only within the preceding month. Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Shimon say no more than two weeks prior to birth.

The determination is made retroactively: once the child is born, one looks back to see whether the bleeding fell within the operative window and whether the pains were continuous throughout. A woman experiencing bleeding with labor pains during pregnancy would track each day to verify continuous pain, and only after birth can the full picture be assessed.

---

## Status During Labor

### Rav's Position

The Gemara asks: *atu kol hamakshah niddah hi* — is every woman who has labor pains automatically a *niddah*? Surely the *mishnah* cannot mean that labor pains alone, without specifying the period of the cycle, determine status. The question leads into a discussion of what a woman's status is in the interim — before it is known whether the pains will be continuous through the birth or whether there will be a break.

Rav answers: *niddah leyoma* — during the day she bleeds, treat her as a *niddah* (meaning, marital relations are prohibited on that day), but by nightfall relations may resume. On Rav's reading, the presumptive status is that the labor pains are efficacious — we assume continuity — and therefore, while it would be inappropriate to engage in relations on the day of bleeding, by nightfall we already assume the best.

### Shmuel's Position

Shmuel disagrees: *chaishinan shema tishpeh* — we are concerned that there may be a break in the pains. *Tishpeh* means the pains will relax, producing a *shofi* that would interrupt the continuity. Since there is prospective concern that a break may yet occur and she will turn out to have been a *zava*, Shmuel holds we cannot yet permit relations. The debate between Rav and Shmuel is essentially: do we presume continuity and permit, or do we remain concerned about future interruption and prohibit? Rav adopts the presumption of continuity; Shmuel requires demonstrated continuity before permitting.

### Rabbi Yitzchak

Rabbi Yitzchak goes further than Rav: *hamakshah einah klum* — labor pains during pregnancy amount to nothing halachically; even relations on that day itself are permitted. In principle, this is the same direction as Rav — assuming that the pain-induced bleeding is not problematic — but Rabbi Yitzchak does not even maintain the restriction for the day itself.

### Rava's Reading

Rava resolves the *mishnah*'s apparent ambiguity straightforwardly: *bimei niddah niddah bimei ziva tehora* — when the bleeding occurs during her *niddah* period, she is a *niddah* without qualification, and the *koshi* rule is irrelevant. When it occurs during her *ziva* period (the 11 days), she may be *tehora* if the pains are continuous. This clarifies that the *mishnah*'s statement that a woman with labor pains is a *niddah* refers specifically to the *niddah* period; it is not a universal statement about the effect of labor pains on all bleeding.

---

## Pain Patterns

### Ending with Pain

The Gemara introduces a *braita* that analyzes specific combinations of bleeding with and without labor pains. If a woman had one day of pain-accompanied bleeding and two days without pains, or two days with pain and one without, or alternating periods ending with a pain-free period (*shaftah ve-kashtah ve-chazarah ve-shaftah*), she is a *yoledes bazov* — because the final period, immediately preceding birth, was without labor pains.

### Ending with Break

Conversely: if she had one day without pain followed by two with pains, or two without and one with, or the reverse alternating pattern ending with pain (*kashtah ve-shaftah ve-chazarah ve-kashtah*), she is *ein zo yoledes bazov* — not a *yoledes bazov*.

The case of *kashtah ve-shaftah ve-chazarah ve-kashtah* is worth examining carefully. Read straightforwardly: one day with pain, one day without, one day with pain, then birth. In this pattern, the middle day (without pain) creates a break that severs the first pain-day from the sequence, making it potentially *dam zivah*. The second and third pain-days, however, remain connected to the birth. The net effect is that only one or two of the three days of bleeding can be attributed to *zivah*, not three — and without three, she is not a *zava* and therefore not a *yoledes bazov*.

### Koshi Negates

The general principle the *braita* articulates: *koshi samuch le-leidah ein zo yoledes bazov* — any period of labor pains leading immediately up to birth is not *yoledes bazov*.

### Shofi Before

*Shofi samuch le-leidah harei zo yoledes bazov* — conversely, a period without pains immediately preceding birth renders her *yoledes bazov*, because it severs all prior bleeding from attribution to the birth, leaving it potentially as *dam zivah*.

### Halachic Day

Chananya ben achi Rabbi Yehoshua adds: as long as the pains occurred on the third day, even if the entire rest of that day was a *shofi* — a pain-free period — she is not *yoledes bazov*. This position resonates with the earlier view in the *mishnah* that a *halachic day* (night and day together) constitutes the meaningful unit; even a full day of *shofi* does not necessarily sever the connection if the third day itself included some *koshi*, and the birth follows the next day. The principle here is that the halachic day, not a floating 24-hour period, is the operative unit.

---

## Derasha on Damah

### Damah Derasha

The Gemara now asks *mana hani mili* — what is the scriptural source for these rules? The Gemara quotes a *braita* expounding the verse *zov damah* (Vayikra 15:19) — "the flow of her blood." The word *damah* — "her blood," or more precisely, "her flow" — is taken as indicative: it must be *her* discharge, belonging to her as the source. *Damah machmat atzmah v'lo machmat velad* — the *tumah*-producing flow must come from the woman herself, not be attributable to the fetus.

One might have thought the exclusion was broader — perhaps any bleeding caused by external forces (*ones*) should be *tahor*. To exclude this reading, the Gemara notes: *keshehu omer isha ki yazuv zov* — the verse "when a woman flows a flow" is phrased inclusively, and the additional word *damah* following it teaches: *zuv zuv damah harei ones amur* — even an involuntary (*ones*) discharge is included. Thus *ones* in general does not exempt a woman from *niddah* or *zava* status.

### Fetus Exception

What, then, does *damah* exclude? *Damah machmat atzmah v'lo machmat velad* — only bleeding whose cause is specifically the fetus is excluded. That narrower exclusion is what *damah* teaches.

### Other Ones

Why then is the fetus-caused bleeding excluded but not other forms of *ones*? This requires justification, since one has just established that *ones* in general is included.

### Ones Analogy

The Gemara anticipates the question: perhaps we should reason by analogy from a *zav* (a man with abnormal discharge). For a *zav*, external causes — certain foods, physical exertion, and other factors — do exempt him from *zav* status; *ones* by a *zav* is *tahor*. If so, perhaps we should apply the same principle to a *zava* by analogy?

### Subset Logic

The Gemara rejects the analogy from *zav* to *zava*: *hashta maya b'isha kayminan* — we are dealing with the laws of women, not men. *V'ones b'isha lo ashkhachun* — we have found no precedent for *ones* producing *taharah* by a woman, except in the specific context of childbirth. The Torah introduced *yemei tohar* — the 33 and 66 days of *tahor* blood — precisely in connection with childbirth. That Torah-originated concept of *taharah* associated with birth and the fetus is what grounds the exclusion.

Alternatively (*v'i ba'it eima*): even if one wanted to say that *ones* in general is *tahor* and childbirth-related bleeding is *tamei*, this would be logically untenable — *ein lach ones gadol mizeh*, for childbirth is itself a paradigmatic case of *ones*, a prime example of an involuntary external force. One cannot exclude the most obvious member of a category while claiming to include the category. What one *can* say is: childbirth is a specific *ones* that the Torah chose to treat as *tahor*, while all lesser forms of *ones* remain *tamei*. The direction of the exclusion must go from the more severe to the less severe, not the reverse.

---

---

# Niddah 37

## Birth Pains & Zavah

### Intro: Birth Pains

We pick up at the bottom of 36b, dealing with the *halacha* that bleeding resulting from birth pains does not render a woman a *zavah*. It may render her a *niddah*, but not a *zavah*. The *gemara* had already established a *drasha* from the *pasuk* describing the *zavah*: the Torah uses the phrase *zov damah* — her blood — to exclude blood that results from a fetus. A woman who bleeds as a consequence of birth pains cannot thereby become a *zavah*.

### Niddah Question

The *gemara* then raises an obvious challenge: if the same word *zovah* — "her flow" — appears in the context of *niddah* as well, should we not apply the same exclusion there? That is, perhaps a woman cannot become a *niddah* either if the blood results from the fetus. One might reason that *zovah machmas atzmah velo machmas vlad* — her flow must come from herself, not from the fetus — and apply this equally to *niddah*. The *gemara* counters: when the Torah elsewhere says simply *ishah ki tihiyeh zavah*, "if a woman flows," that broader phrase implies that even an external stimulus (*ones*) creates *tumah*. Thus the specific phrase *zovah* — her flow — excluding fetal blood applies only where we have first established that *ones*-induced bleeding does not count, namely by *zavah*, not by *niddah*. The question thus remains: how do we know the exclusion is limited to *zavah* and does not extend to *niddah*?

### Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish offers a proof from a *pasuk* regarding the *yoledet*: *veshishim yom vesheshet yamim teshev al demei taharah* — she shall sit upon blood of purity. The verse teaches that a woman who gives birth has a period during which her blood is *tahor*. Reish Lakish argues: this tells us there is another analogous period of *taharah* — namely, bleeding during the *zivah* days that accompanies birth pains. However, as the *gemara* itself notes, this does not fully resolve the question, since one could equally read the *pasuk* as implying that bleeding during *niddah* days associated with birth pains is also *tahor*. The verse establishes the principle that birth-related blood can be *tahor*, but does not itself specify *zivah* over *niddah*.

### Abuh of Shmuel

The *gemara* therefore abandons the previous approaches and turns to the answer of Abuh of Shmuel. The Torah states, regarding a woman who gives birth to a girl: *vetama shevuayim kenidatah* — she shall be impure two weeks *as a niddah*, and not *as a zavah*. The question is: why does the Torah draw the comparison to *niddah* rather than *zavah*? Even granting that there are differences in the details of their respective *tumos*, the very act of comparison implies something meaningful — that in certain respects the *yoledet* is like a *niddah* and unlike a *zavah*. This yields the inference *michlal dezivatah tahor*: there is a context in which *zivah* blood is *tahor*, namely birth pains during the *zivah* period. Hence birth pains during the *zivah* period do not create *zavah* status.

### Her Flow Principle

The *gemara* then asks: given that we derive the ruling from *kenidatah*, what do we do with the verse of *damah* — her blood — the phrase that had earlier seemed to be the source? The answer is that without *damah*, one might have thought that *zavah* is excluded entirely during pregnancy — that any bleeding whatsoever during pregnancy would never create *zavah* status. This would not be unreasonable: the model of *zavah*, as the Rambam makes clear, is analogous to the *zov* of a man, an unnatural, pathological emission. Pregnancy involves considerable bleeding and spotting, and one might argue that no bleeding during pregnancy can ever qualify as the unnatural flow of a *zavah*. The verse *damah* therefore comes to limit the exclusion: only blood that is directly attributable to the fetus — meaning blood that occurs simultaneously with the birth pains — is excluded from *zavah* status. Bleeding during pregnancy that is not concurrent with birth pains can still render a woman a *zavah*.

---

## Rav vs. Shmuel

### Uncertainty

Having established that birth-pain bleeding is only excluded from *zavah* status when the pains continue uninterrupted up to the birth, the *gemara* turns to the practical question: what is the *halacha* when a woman bleeds together with birth pains and we do not yet know whether the pains will continue or whether there will be a break? Since the exemption depends on continuity of pains through to the birth, a break would retroactively make the bleeding count toward *zavah* status. May she assume she remains *tehorah*, or must she be stringent?

### Rav's Position

Rav and Shmuel disagree on this point. Rav holds that she may essentially assume she is *tehorah* — she should avoid relations that day, but that night she is already permitted, without need to wait to see whether the pains will eventually break. Shmuel holds that she must assume she is *temei'ah* and treat the bleeding as potentially significant.

### Shila's Ruling

Shila bar Avina ruled in practice like Rav. A woman had one day of bleeding accompanying birth pains, and he permitted her to her husband that night, relying on Rav's lenient position.

### Deathbed Reversal

When Rav was dying, he said to Rav Asi — apparently present or nearby — *tzanyei*: conceal what I said, or, in Rashi's reading, tell Shila to reverse himself. Rav was retracting his ruling. Rashi understands *tzanyei* to mean Rav was telling Rav Asi to instruct Shila to reverse his practice. Notably, Rashi understands Rav's reversal as moving toward an even more lenient position — that she would be permitted even on the same day — not toward stringency. This reading is surprising, and cuts against what one might expect from a deathbed reversal accompanied by such urgency.

### Rav Asi's Cherem

Rav Asi, however, misheard Rav's instruction. Rav said *gayreihu* — try to draw him, to persuade him to reverse himself. Rav Asi thought he had heard *gadyeihu* — cut him off, meaning place him in *cherem*. Tosafot notes that both textual variants spell the word *gadye*, differing only in whether the *dalet* carries a *dagesh*, and that this subtle phonetic distinction accounts for the discrepancy in meaning. After Rav's death, Rav Asi approached Shila and said: Rav reversed himself — you must reverse your ruling as well.

---

## Rav's Reversal

### Shila Refuses

Shila refused. He argued: if Rav had indeed reversed himself, he would have told me directly. Rav had issued his ruling to me personally, and if he had changed his position, common sense dictates that he would have communicated this to me first. Since Rav never told me directly, I do not accept that he reversed himself. *Lo tzayit* — he refused to comply. Rav Asi, believing he had heard Rav instruct him to place Shila in *cherem* if he did not comply, proceeded to do so.

### Copper & Iron

The exchange that followed was anything but a halakhic discussion. Shila said to Rav Asi: *velo mistafi mar miguchalta* — are you not afraid of being burnt by my ember? The *gemara* in another context warns that one must be cautious about the honor of sages, lest one be consumed by their fire. Rav Asi replied: I am Issi ben Yehuda, Issi ben Gur Aryeh, Issi ben Gamliel, Issi ben Mahalalel — tracing a long lineage — and I am *asita de-nechasha*, a copper mortar, upon which no rot takes hold.
