I am not afraid of your fire. Shila replied: *va-ana Shila bar Avina, buchna de-parzela* — and I am Shila son of Avina, an iron pestle, *de-mitbar asita de-nechasha*, that can break a copper mortar. The exchange had entirely left the realm of *halacha* and become a contest of personal honor — the mirror image of the very thing Rav had tried to avoid by urging Rav Asi merely to try to persuade Shila. Rav had said: reason with him. Instead, Rav Asi moved immediately to *cherem*, which produced this inflammatory response.

### Rav Asi Dies

Rav Asi fell ill. The Talmud describes the attempts to treat him: they placed him in hot water when he had chills, then in cold water when he had fever, cycling between extremes in a vigorous attempt to heal him — and *nach nafshei de-Rav Asi*, he died.

### Myrtle Vision

When Shila heard of Rav Asi's death, he said to his wife: prepare my burial shrouds. His stated reason was that he feared Rav Asi would ascend to heaven and complain about him to Rav — tell Rav that Shila had refused to listen and had not done the right thing. One senses in this, beneath the somewhat legalistic framing, a genuine recognition that Shila himself bore some responsibility for what had transpired. His wife prepared the shrouds, *nach nafshei de-Shila*, and Shila died.

### Heaven's Peace

Those present then saw *deparcha asa* — a myrtle branch flying *me'hai puraya le'hai puraya*, from one bier to the other. People said: *shema mina avdu rabbanan paisa* — we see from this that the rabbis have made peace. They had ascended, learned Torah together, and been reconciled in heaven. The irony, as one might note, is that we do not actually know the content of Rav's reversal — which direction he reversed — and that remains unknown to us even now, though presumably it is known in heaven. The myrtle vision offers a hopeful symbol: that in the end, both sages recognized they had each erred, and reconciliation was possible.

---

## Interrupting Clean D (II)

### Rava's Question

The *gemara* continues on 37a. Rava poses a new question: *koshi mahu she-tistor be-zivah* — given that birth-pain bleeding does not create *zavah* status, does it nonetheless interrupt a woman's seven clean days? Suppose a woman had bled during pregnancy without birth pains and became a *zavah*, and is now counting her seven clean days; then she bleeds again, this time with birth pains. That birth-pain blood cannot make her a *zavah* — but does it interrupt the count?

The conceptual tension Rava identifies is this: on one hand, *davar ha-metamei soter* — perhaps anything that causes *tumah* can interrupt, and since birth-pain blood can cause *tumah* during the *niddah* period, it has at least potential *tumah*-causing capacity. On the other hand, perhaps the principle is *davar ha-gorem soter* — only blood that can specifically cause *zavah* status can interrupt the seven clean days, since the reason an interruption matters is that the blood reasserts her *zavah* trajectory; blood that can never make her a *zavah* should have no power over the clean days.

### Abaye's Male Zav Proof

Abaye responds: *ones be-zivah yochiach* — let me bring a proof from a male *zav*. We learned previously that a man becomes a *zav* only through flows that are not due to external causes (*ones*); a flow caused by external stimulation does not count toward making him a *zav*. Yet once a man has already completed two flows and is counting his seven clean days, a flow due to *ones* — which cannot make him a *zav* — does interrupt the clean days. This, says Abaye, answers Rava's question: we see that a flow which cannot create *zav* status can nonetheless interrupt the seven clean days.

### Ones & Third Level

The *gemara* pushes back: one cannot prove from the case of *ones* that the flow has no *zav*-creating capacity, because in fact a flow due to *ones* does carry some weight in that regard. A Mishnah teaches: the first flow is examined to rule out external causes; the second is examined similarly; but the third — the flow that completes *zav* status and obligates a *korban* — is not examined at all. A third flow counts even if it was due to *ones*. Hence a flow of *ones* does partially make a man a *zav*, advancing him from two-flow status to full three-flow *zav*, and therefore one cannot use it as an example of a flow that cannot make him a *zav* at all.

### Rabbi Eliezer

At this point the *gemara* introduces the position of Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that even the third flow must be examined — *af bishlishi bodkin oto*. According to Rabbi Eliezer, a flow of *ones* never contributes toward *zav* status at any level. The *gemara* then asks: would Rabbi Eliezer say that such a flow also cannot interrupt the seven clean days? The response is direct: *le-Rabbi Eliezer hachi nami* — yes, according to Rabbi Eliezer, a flow of *ones* would not interrupt the clean days.

The *gemara* then cites a fuller version of that *braita* in which Rabbi Eliezer himself clarifies the matter: when he says that the fourth flow need not be examined, he means this only with respect to the *korban* — the fourth flow is irrelevant to whether a *korban* is brought. But *le-stira* — regarding interruption of the seven clean days — even Rabbi Eliezer agrees that a flow of *ones* can interrupt. Here, then, is an explicit statement that according to Rabbi Eliezer, a flow that cannot make a man a *zav* can nonetheless interrupt his clean days.

### Father of Rabbi Avin

The *gemara* then cites a *braita* taught by the father of Rabbi Avin: *ma garam lo zovo shiva* — what does the *zov* flow cause the man? A seven-day *tumah*. Therefore *soter shiva* — it interrupts all seven clean days. Conversely, a seminal emission (*keri*) causes only a one-day *tumah*, and therefore interrupts only one day, not all seven. The critical observation is the language *ma garam lo* — what does it cause — which links the power of interruption explicitly to the causal capacity of the flow. The *gemara* notes: had the *tanna* simply meant to describe the length of *tumah*, he would have said "his flow causes seven days of *tumah*, therefore it interrupts seven days." The choice of *garam* — causes — signals a conceptual principle: *davar ha-gorem soter*, only that which causes the *tumah* can interrupt it.

### Davar Ha-Gorem

Accordingly, the *gemara* concludes: *davar ha-gorem soter, davar she-eino gorem eino soter* — only a flow that can cause a person to become a *zav* or *zavah* can interrupt the seven clean days; a flow that cannot cause that status cannot interrupt. The ruling regarding the female case now follows directly: birth-pain bleeding, which can never make a woman a *zavah*, cannot interrupt her seven clean days, even though in another context it may cause *tumah* as *niddah* blood. According to Rabbi Eliezer, however — who holds that even a flow of *ones* that cannot create *zav* status can interrupt the clean days — birth-pain bleeding would interrupt. The *gemara* thus resolves that the two positions on interruption by birth-pain blood map onto the broader dispute between the *Rabbanan* and Rabbi Eliezer.

---

## Interrupting Clean D (II)

### Conclusion

Abaye states the conclusion as received *halacha*: *naktinan, ein koshi soter be-zivah* — we hold that birth-pain bleeding does not interrupt the seven clean days, since it cannot make a woman a *zavah*. If one encounters a *tanna* who says it does interrupt, that position follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that even a flow without *gorem*-capacity can interrupt.

It is worth noting in this context an important related *halacha* discussed earlier in the *masechta*: the case of a *poletet shichvat zera* — a woman from whom semen is discharged — and whether this interrupts her counting of the clean days. Rashi's position is that *davar ha-gorem soter* applies only to a full interruption requiring the woman to start her seven days over entirely; a situation where only one day is lost does not need to satisfy that criterion. Some *rishonim* find this distinction difficult, and it bears directly on the well-known *Ashkenazi* practice that women do not begin counting their seven clean days until day six, in part due to concerns about *poletet shichvat zera*.

---

## Childbirth & Interruption

### Rav Merinos

The *gemara* moves to a related topic. A *braita* cites Rav Merinos: *ein leida soteret be-zivah* — the act of giving birth itself does not interrupt a woman's seven clean days. The case is a woman who had bled without birth pains, became a *zavah*, began counting her seven clean days, and then gave birth. Childbirth involves substantial bleeding, but Rav Merinos rules that this is not *dam niddah* in the ordinary sense — it is birth blood, and as such does not interrupt the *zavah* counting. After the birth bleeding ceases, she may resume counting from where she left off.

### Non-Bleeding Days

A further question is then raised: *mahu she-ta'aleh* — may the days of the *leida* period during which she is not bleeding count toward her seven clean days? The *yoledet* has a period of *tumah* of one or two weeks regardless of bleeding. If during that period the bleeding stops, can she count those non-bleeding days toward completing her *shiva nekiyim*?

This question has practical relevance: a woman who miscarries carries *tumah* of *leida* once the fetus is at least forty days old, and that *leida tumah* extends for a week (for a male) or two weeks (for a female). Since every woman today is treated as requiring seven clean days — effectively as a *zavah gedolah* — the question of whether those non-bleeding *leida* days may be counted is significant.

### Abaye's View

Abaye holds: *eina soteret ve-eina olah* — the *leida* days neither interrupt the seven clean days nor count toward them. She is *temei'ah* during that period, and even if she is not bleeding, those days do not advance her count.

### Rava's View

Rava holds: *eina soteret ve-olah* — the *leida* days do not interrupt, and those days during which she does not bleed do count toward the seven clean days, even though the *tumah* of *yoledet* continues.

### Rava's Proof

Rava marshals two proofs. First, the *gemara* cites a *braita*: *v'achar tithar* — "and afterwards she shall be purified" — is interpreted to mean that the seven clean days must form one uninterrupted unit, with no *tumah* breaking them. *Ei amart bishlama olah* — if you say that the non-bleeding *leida* days can count, there is no problem: those days are not a gap in the sequence, since they themselves advance the count. But *ei amart eina olah* — if you say they cannot count, then if she had accumulated three clean days before childbirth and then entered a two-week *leida* period during which no days count, and then resumes counting, how can that be called a single unit of seven? The *leida* period creates an irreparable break in the sequence. The *braita*'s language — that *tumah* should not interrupt *between* the days — implies that *leida* days are not a severing interruption, which supports Rava's view that they can count.

Second, Rava cites a *braita*: *mizovah* — from her flow she may purify herself. Even a woman who is a *metzora'at* can complete her *zavah* counting and immerse without first being purified of her *tzara'at*. And then: *velo milleidatah* — and even if she is a *yoledet*, this does not prevent her from counting and completing her seven clean days. Rashi explains that this does not literally mean she immerses while still a *yoledet*, since the *tumah* of *yoledet* and *zavah* share the same domain and must both be resolved before she is permitted to her husband; rather, it means that her *yoledet* status does not prevent the *leida* days from counting toward completion of the seven clean days. This is an explicit ruling in accordance with Rava.

### Abaye's Counter

Abaye responds to the first proof by reinterpreting the *braita*: *she-lo tehei tumat zivah mafseket beineihem* — the *braita* is saying that *zivah tumah* should not interrupt the seven clean days. Since the woman is not in a state of *zivah tumah* during the *leida* period — she is in *leida tumah*, which is a distinct category — the *braita* simply does not address whether those days count. It only tells us that a *zivah*-type interruption would destroy the continuity; it says nothing about *leida* days.

To the second proof, Abaye simply proposes emending the *braita*: remove the phrase *velo milleidatah*. The *braita* should only contain *mizovah velo minega'ah* — that *metzora'at* status does not prevent completion of *zavah* counting — and not the phrase about *leida*. Rava responds that this reading is untenable: if the *braita* only tells us about *metzora'at*, there was no need to state it, since the same ruling for men — *mizovo velo minega'o* — is already stated elsewhere, and we could derive the female case by extension. The only reason the *braita* adds the female case independently is to teach the novel *halacha* of *leida* — that *yoledet* status does not bar her from counting toward her clean days. The *metzora'at* clause is included incidentally alongside it. Abaye responds that in fact one cannot automatically extend from male *zav* to female *zavah* or vice versa, since each has distinctive stringencies, and therefore the *braita* must spell out both *metzora'at* cases independently. The phrase about *leida* is thus unnecessary and should be removed.

Abaye then advances his own proof: a *braita* teaches *kimei nidasah kach yimei leidatah* — just as her *niddah* days are, so are her *leida* days. The comparison: during the *niddah* period, a woman cannot become a *zavah*, and the *niddah* days do not count toward the seven clean days of a *zavah*. Similarly, the *leida* days should not count. Rava responds that this *braita* reflects the position of Rabbi Eliezer — specifically Rabbi Eliezer's ruling *danin efshar mi-she-ein efshar*, that one may draw a legal inference from a possible situation compared to an impossible one. In ordinary cases one cannot learn from what never occurs, but since the Torah explicitly equates *yoledet* and *niddah* — *kimei nidas devosah titma* — the equation is compelled by the verse itself, even across the *efshar/she-ein efshar* divide. Rav Sheshet (or, in another version, Rav Achdavoi bar Ami in the name of Rav Sheshet) states this point: *al korchach hikishan hakatuv* — the text itself forces the comparison, which justifies the inference. Accordingly, Abaye's proof from the *braita* holds only according to Rabbi Eliezer, but does not compel the conclusion for the *Rabbanan*.

Ultimately, Rashi himself, in a responsum cited by Tosafot, rules that even Abaye concedes in practice that the non-bleeding *leida* days may count toward the seven clean days. Tosafot notes that Rashi writes: *d'Abaye modeh d'yimei leida she-eina ro'ah bahem olim lisfirat zivtah* — that in practice even Abaye agrees these days count. The entire discussion, Rashi indicates, is conducted according to Rav Merinos's position, but the final *halacha* follows Rava.

---

## Break in Pains

### Pains & Bleeding Break

The *gemara* now returns to the main topic of birth pains and raises a new question: *shavta mizeh umizeh mahu* — what is the *halacha* if there is a full cessation of both the pains and the bleeding? We already know that a break in pains alone, while bleeding continues, creates an interruption and undermines the *koshi* exemption. But if both stop entirely — no pains and no bleeding — does that also create a break, or does it actually favor the woman?

The question is genuinely two-sided. On one hand, a complete cessation seems an even clearer break — if even pains alone ceasing creates an interruption, surely the cessation of both must do so. On the other hand, one might argue the opposite: bleeding without pains suggests that the bleeding is at least partly independent of the pains, calling into question whether even the earlier bleeding with pains was truly *koshi*-related. But if both stop together, there is no evidence of bleeding independent of pains, and the earlier bleeding may be attributed entirely to the *koshi*, leaving it *tahor*.

### Rav Chisda

Rav Chisda rules: *temei'ah*. A full cessation creates a break just as a cessation of pains alone does. The bleeding is no longer connected to the *leida* process.

### Rav Chanina

Rav Chanina rules: *tehorah*. When both pains and bleeding stop together, the earlier pains and bleeding remain attributed to the *leida*, and the woman is *tehorah*. He explains with a *mashal*: *mashal le-melech she-yatza ve-chayalotav lefanav* — it is like a king whose troops march in advance before him. Everyone knows that these are the king's troops. The birth pains that preceded the delivery, even with a gap before the actual birth, are the advance troops — they are recognizably connected to the event that follows. They need not march uninterrupted all the way to the last moment.

### Chisda Objects

Rav Chisda objects: *kol sheken deva'ei nafish chayalot tefei* — on the contrary, as the king approaches, the number of troops should increase. If the pains were truly connected to the birth, they would have intensified and continued. A gap in pains, Rav Chisda argues, demonstrates that the pains have discharged their function and are not building continuously toward the birth. The debate thus crystallizes around two conceptual models: according to Rav Chisda, true *koshi* must persist uninterruptedly up to the delivery; according to Rav Chanina, pains that precede delivery and are accompanied by bleeding are inherently connected to the birth, and the only thing that can sever that connection is bleeding without pains — which shows the bleeding is not fully dependent on the pains.

### Mishna Analysis

Rav Chisda then attempts to prove his position from a Mishnah: *kashta shlosha yamim betoch achad asar yom veshavta me'et le'et veyalda harei zu yoledet be-zov* — if a woman had birth pains for three days within the eleven-day *zivah* period, then had a break of a full twenty-four hours, and then gave birth, she is a *yoledet be-zov*. Rav Chisda asks: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the scenario? If it is as literally stated — three days of pain with bleeding, then a full day of nothing, then birth — why was it necessary to give three days of pain? The same conclusion could be reached with two days of pain and bleeding and one day of bleeding without pain: the painless bleeding on day three would itself constitute the break, yielding the same *yoledet be-zov* result. The only reason the Mishnah gives three full days of *koshi* and a separate fourth day of complete cessation must be to teach that a full cessation of both pain and bleeding also constitutes a break — thereby supporting Rav Chisda.

### Chanina Defense

Rav Chanina responds: *lo, le-olam ke-dik-tani* — no, take the Mishnah literally, the scenario is as stated: three days of pain and bleeding. The reason the Mishnah needed to give three days rather than two is to exclude a different ruling — that of a different Rav Chanina mentioned earlier — who had held that if a woman bleeds on the day immediately before giving birth, that bleeding is always considered connected to the birth even if there was a twenty-four-hour break before it. To refute that position, the Mishnah specifically gives the scenario of three full days of *koshi*, then a break, then birth: since the bleeding on day three was followed by a full twenty-four-hour gap with nothing, even though day three's bleeding was the day before the birth, the break is sufficient to create a *yoledet be-zov* status. The Mishnah is thus teaching against that specific position, and its formulation of three days of *koshi* followed by a clean day is not intended to address the question of a complete double cessation at all. The debate between Rav Chisda and Rav Chanina therefore remains unresolved.

---

---

# Niddah 38

## Kishuy Duration

### Kishuy Timeframe

The Gemara on 37b opens with a fundamental question concerning *kishuy*—the phenomenon of childbirth pains accompanying bleeding. Having established the circumstances under which such pains render blood non-problematic, the Gemara now asks: how far back in time can the pains still be attributed to the childbirth? In other words, how many days before birth can we say that bleeding accompanied by pain is related to the impending birth, such that it does not create *dam zivah*?

### Three Opinions

The Mishnah presents three positions. Rabbi Meir says forty or fifty days. Another opinion holds that one month suffices. A third limits it to two weeks.

The Gemara immediately notes a difficulty with Rabbi Meir's formulation: if fifty days is sufficient, is there any question about forty? The phrase "forty or fifty" would normally suggest an open-ended range—as in the first Mishnah in Sukkah, where Rabbi Yehuda says a *sukkah* may be forty or fifty *amot* tall, meaning there is no upper limit at all. Tosafot raises this point. But as the Gemara will demonstrate shortly, Rabbi Meir treats fifty as a precise number, offering an exact count of days. The Gemara therefore asks: if fifty is the precise figure, why does the Mishnah also cite forty?

### Sick vs. Healthy

Rav Chisda resolves this: *kan chola, kan bria*—the distinction turns on whether the woman is sick or healthy. Rashi explains that for a woman with a weaker constitution, bleeding can plausibly be attributed to the fetus at an earlier stage, up to fifty days before birth; for a healthy woman, the connection holds only up to forty days.

### Rabbi Levi

Rabbi Levi introduces a more restrictive principle: *ein hadam metaher ela yamim hare'uyim lihyot bahen zavah*—the *kishuy* renders blood pure only during those days when she is actually fit to become a *zavah*. The critical distinction underlying Rabbi Levi's position is that blood during the *niddah* period is problematic regardless of accompanying pain; *kishuy* operates exclusively to neutralize *dam zivah*. Consequently, only the eleven days of the *zavah* period—and no others—are affected by the *kishuy*.

### Rava's View

Rava extends this framework: *afilu biyamim hare'uyim lisfirat zivah*—the *kishuy* applies even during the days relevant to the *counting* of *zavah* status, not merely during the eleven days themselves. To illustrate: suppose a woman bled at some point during her pregnancy, say on the first of the month, making her a *niddah*. Starting on day eight, any subsequent bleeding would constitute *dam zivah*. Now, had she actually become a *zavah gedolah* during days eight through eighteen, she would have needed seven clean days afterward. Therefore, blood on any of the days running from day eight through day twenty-five is in some sense "related" to a potential *zavah* status—either as the *zavah* period itself or as the seven-day counting period that would follow it. Rava holds that *kishuy* renders blood pure throughout this extended range, through day twenty-five.

### Rav Adda

Rav Adda bar Ahava goes further still, following Rava's logic to its ultimate conclusion. According to Rava's reasoning, the *kishuy* applies not only through day twenty-five but potentially indefinitely. Once she has bled once and entered the *niddah* period, a *zavah* period opens on day eight. If she were to bleed three times during that period, she would become a *zavah gedolah* and would need seven clean days. But if bleeding interrupted those seven days, the count would be reset, and she could theoretically never complete the seven clean days. Thus, from day eight onward, every subsequent day is potentially a day relevant to the *zavah* counting process—an extension of the unresolved *zavah* status. Rav Adda therefore holds that any blood after the first seven days of the initial bleeding is considered potential *dam zivah*, and *kishuy* renders it pure. This is a striking *kula*: once a *niddah* period occurs, virtually any subsequent bleeding—no matter how far removed in time—falls within the scope of *kishuy* leniency.

### Reconciliation

The Gemara now asks how these positions square with Rabbi Meir's statement that *kishuy* applies for forty or fifty days. This formulation implies that for an entire stretch of forty or fifty days, bleeding accompanied by pain is rendered pure—but how is that consistent with Rabbi Levi, who limits *kishuy* to the eleven days of the *zavah* period?

The Gemara answers on behalf of Rabbi Levi: *mi katani tahorah b'kullan?*—the Mishnah never says she is *tehorah* for the entire forty or fifty days. Rather, *biyemei niddah niddah, biyemei zivah tehorah*: during the *niddah* days she remains a *niddah*, and during the *zavah* days she is *tehorah*. The statement that *kishuy* is relevant for forty or fifty days means only that this is the window within which the laws of *kishuy* are operative—the rules apply whenever, within that stretch, she happens to be in a *zavah* period. It does not guarantee that she is *tehorah* throughout.

The Gemara asks further about the second formulation attributed to Rabbi Levi: *ein hadam metaher ela yamim hare'uyim lihyot bahen zavah gedolah*—it renders blood pure only on days when she could become a *zavah gedolah*. Tosafot presents two readings of this stricter formulation. One reading holds that it excludes days one and two of the *zavah* period, since a *zavah gedolah* requires three consecutive days of bleeding and therefore cannot be initiated on those days. The other reading excludes days ten and eleven, since a *zavah gedolah* cannot be completed if the bleeding begins that late. Either way, Tosafot understands Rabbi Levi to be restricting *kishuy* to a subset of the eleven-day period.

Rashi reads the passage differently. In his view, the formulation "*zavah gedolah*" tells us not which days are covered, but what type of *zavah* status is neutralized. *Kishuy* prevents her from becoming a *zavah gedolah*, but it does not prevent her from becoming a *zavah ketanah*. If she bleeds once or twice during the *zavah* period with accompanying pain, she remains a *zavah ketanah* and still requires one clean day. *Kishuy* thus provides immunity only from *zavah gedolah* status, not from all forms of *zavah*.

In the subsequent formulation, *Abba Shaul* citing Rava holds: *afilu yamim hare'uyim lihyot bahen zavah ketanah*—*kishuy* renders blood pure even on days when she could become only a *zavah ketanah*. The *drashah* for *zavah ketanah* status derives from the same verse (*dameha yamim rabim*) used to establish that *kishuy* applies, and therefore the full eleven days are included. Both approaches ultimately limit the operative period to eleven days; the expansive reading of Rav Adda bar Ahava—where *kishuy* applies indefinitely after any initial bleeding—is what accounts for the forty or fifty days mentioned by Rabbi Meir.

---

## Bleeding Calculations

### 150 Days

The Gemara introduces a remarkable calculation in the name of Rabbi Meir: *yesh makshah kuf nun yom ve'ein zavah olah bahen*—there is a case in which a woman can bleed for 150 consecutive days and never become a *zavah*. The Gemara then works through exactly how this is achieved.

### Precise Count

The construction begins with a sequence of bleeding that precedes the fifty-day *kishuy* window. A woman bleeds for two days during the *zavah* period—she is a *zavah ketanah* but not a *zavah gedolah*. Then she bleeds for seven days as a *niddah*. Then she bleeds for two more days in the *zavah* period following the *niddah*—again a *zavah ketanah*, not a *zavah gedolah*. This totals eleven days of bleeding, and she has not yet become a *zavah gedolah*. On the very next day, she would be in the *zavah* period and a third day of bleeding would create *zavah gedolah* status—but this is precisely when the fifty-day *kishuy* period begins. The Gemara notes that this makes clear that Rabbi Meir treats fifty as a precise figure: he is counting exactly.

### Full 150 Count

For the next fifty days, she bleeds continuously, but since it is accompanied by *kishuy*, none of it constitutes *dam zivah*. She then gives birth—to a girl. The birth itself triggers *tumas yoledet*: two weeks of *niddah* status followed by sixty-six days of *toharah*, during which even normal bleeding does not render her a *zavah*. These eighty days of post-birth status add to the total: eleven plus fifty is sixty-one, plus eighty is one hundred forty-one. After the eighty days, she bleeds seven more days as a *niddah*, then two more days in the *zavah* period—again a *zavah ketanah* only. That adds nine more days, bringing the total to one hundred fifty. At no point has she become a *zavah gedolah*.

### Lifetime Bleeding

The Gemara raises a pointed objection: if this reasoning is accepted, one could construct a scenario in which a woman bleeds every single day of her life—continuously cycling through *kishuy* periods, births, and eighty-day post-birth periods—and never become a *zavah*. The scenario involves a woman who repeatedly gives birth, then during her eighty days of *toharah* miscarries, restarting the cycle indefinitely. The implication is that the entire structure of *zavah* law could be circumvented.

### No Kishuy Miscarriage

Rabbi Meir responds: *ein koshi linefalim*. The laws of *kishuy* apply only when the bleeding leads to a live birth. A miscarriage does not trigger the *kishuy* leniency. Therefore, any scenario dependent on miscarriage to extend the cycle will not work: if the birth is a miscarriage, then whatever bleeding preceded it—even if accompanied by pain—does not benefit from *kishuy*, and three days of *zavah*-period bleeding would render her a *zavah gedolah*.

The Gemara notes in passing that one could still construct a scenario of perpetual bleeding without *zavah* status by chaining together multiple live births without invoking *kishuy* at all—simply by becoming pregnant again during the eighty *toharah* days, giving birth, and repeating. But if one wants to include *kishuy* as part of the mechanism, that portion of the argument collapses wherever miscarriage is involved.

---

## 100 Days Baraita

### 100-Day Count

A *beraita* presents a more modest version of the calculation: *yesh ro'ah me'ah yom ve'ein zivah olah bahen*—there is a case in which a woman can bleed for one hundred days without ever becoming a *zavah*. The construction here does not invoke *kishuy* at all and involves only a single birth. She bleeds two days in the *zavah* period, seven days as a *niddah*, and two more in the *zavah* period—eleven days total, still not a *zavah gedolah*. She then gives birth to a girl, and the following eighty days of post-birth *toharah* contribute eighty more days of bleeding. After those eighty days, she bleeds seven days as a *niddah* and two more in the *zavah* period—nine additional days. The total: eleven plus eighty plus nine equals one hundred days of continuous bleeding, without *kishuy* and with a single birth, and she has never been a *zavah gedolah*.

### No Blood Requirement

The Gemara asks: *mai kamashma lan?*—what is the *beraita* teaching us that we do not already know? The answer is that the *beraita* comes to reject the position that *i efshar liftichat hakever belo dam*—it is impossible for the opening of the womb to occur without blood. In the scenario described, the woman bleeds two days as a *zavah ketanah*, then seven as a *niddah*, then two more—and then gives birth. One might suppose that the very process of the child exiting through the womb would itself cause blood to flow before the child had fully emerged, which would be a third day of *zavah*-period bleeding and render her a *zavah gedolah* before the *yoledet* status took hold.

The *beraita* teaches that we do not make that assumption. We do not presume that blood necessarily accompanies the opening of the womb. If blood is seen, it is noted; but absent actual evidence of bleeding, we do not presuppose it. Therefore, the scenario can in principle be completed—a woman exits the *zavah*-period bleeding and enters childbirth without the act of birth itself generating an additional day of *zavah* blood.

Rashi notes an apparent tension: in any real-world case, bleeding during the act of childbirth would be accompanied by the pains of *kishuy* and would thus not constitute *dam zivah* regardless. The scenario requires us to imagine—however hypothetically—that there were no childbirth pains, so that we can speak of the one-hundred-day count as independent of *kishuy*. The theoretical point, however, stands: *ptichat hakever* does not automatically entail blood.

---

## Ninth Month View

### Ninth Month Lenient

Rabbi Yehuda, citing Rabbi Tarfon, holds: *daiyah chodshah*—her month is sufficient. Rather than computing fifty days back or focusing solely on the eleven-day *zavah* period, Rabbi Yehuda focuses on whether the bleeding with pain occurred within the ninth month of pregnancy. A *beraita* elaborates that this position contains both a stringency and a leniency relative to other opinions.

### Eighth Month Strict

The stringent dimension: if a woman bled for two days at the end of the eighth month and one day at the beginning of the ninth, and gave birth even at the very beginning of the ninth month, she is a *yoledet bezov*—she gives birth having been a *zavah*. The reason is that the majority of the three days of potentially *zavah*-producing bleeding occurred in the eighth month. Since Rabbi Yehuda's rule looks to the month in which the bleeding predominantly occurred, the single day in the ninth month is treated as fundamentally belonging to the eighth-month bleeding episode, and *kishuy* provides no relief.

### Ninth Month Always OK

The lenient dimension is striking: if she bled one day at the end of the eighth month and two days at the beginning of the ninth, and gave birth at the very end of the ninth month—even without any continuous pain leading up to the delivery—she is not a *yoledet bezov*. According to Rabbi Yehuda, once the majority of the bleeding occurred within the ninth month, the entire episode is attributed to childbirth, and *kishuy* applies. There is no requirement that the pain be continuous and uninterrupted all the way to the moment of birth. This is a significant leniency beyond all other positions, which generally require the pain to connect the bleeding to the actual birth.

### Calendar Month

Rav Adda bar Ahava draws an inference from Rabbi Yehuda's formulation: *shema minah kasavar Rabbi Yehuda shipura garin*—Rabbi Yehuda holds that it is the *shofar*, the announcement of *Rosh Chodesh*, that is determinative. The "month" in question is not the woman's personal ninth month of pregnancy, counted from conception, but the ninth calendar month as established by *beit din*.

Both Rashi and Tosafot address this inference at length. Tosafot's key argument is as follows: Rabbi Yehuda draws a sharp distinction between two days in the ninth month and one in the eighth versus two in the eighth and one in the ninth. But how could such precision be applied to a personal pregnancy month? The day of conception cannot be known with certainty—semen can remain viable for up to three days, so the actual day of fertilization is unknown. Since Rabbi Yehuda's rule demands exactness about which day belongs to which month, the "month" must be the objective calendar month, not the imprecise personal month of pregnancy. The determination is therefore a formal, *halachic* one based on the calendar sanctified by *beit din*, rather than a purely biological calculation.

---

## Pregnancy Biology

### 271 Days

Shmuel states: *ein ishah mis'aberet veyoledet ela l'masayim veshivim ve'echad yom*—a woman does not conceive and give birth except at two hundred seventy-one days. That is, counting the day of conception as day one, pregnancy lasts through day two hundred seventy and birth occurs on day two hundred seventy-one. The Gemara adds that birth may also occur on day two hundred seventy-two or two hundred seventy-three—not because women vary, but because semen may remain viable for up to three days after intercourse. If fertilization occurs on the day of intercourse, birth will be on day two hundred seventy-one; if not until the second day, on two hundred seventy-two; if not until the third day, on two hundred seventy-three. The pregnancy itself is exactly two hundred seventy days from conception.

This precision appears to conflict with Rabbi Yehuda's view that birth can occur anywhere across the ninth month. The Gemara explains that Shmuel speaks in accordance with the practice of the early *chasidim*.

### Chasidim Wednes

The *beraita* reports: *chasidim harishonim lo hayu meshamshim mitoteihem ela b'revi'i b'Shabbat*—the early pious ones would only engage in marital relations on Wednesday, so that their wives would not be placed in a situation of giving birth on Shabbat and encountering issues associated with that circumstance. Their practice was premised on Shmuel's precise calculation: if the length of pregnancy from the day of intercourse is a fixed number of days, then the day of birth can be predicted from the day of intercourse, and one can choose accordingly.

### Day Calculation

The Gemara asks: why only Wednesday? If it is Wednesday and beyond, what about Thursday, Friday, and Shabbat itself? The Gemara clarifies: *m'revi'i ve'eilach*—from Wednesday onward. The reasoning is as follows. Since two hundred seventy-three is divisible by seven, the day of birth falls on the same weekday as the day of intercourse when 273 days are counted. If intercourse occurred on Sunday and birth is on day 273, she gives birth on Shabbat. If intercourse was on Monday and birth is on day 272, she gives birth on Shabbat. If intercourse was on Tuesday and birth is on day 271, she gives birth on Shabbat. Therefore, intercourse on Sunday, Monday, or Tuesday could result in a Shabbat birth. Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, or Shabbat will not, because none of the three possible day-counts—271, 272, or 273—from those days lands on Shabbat. The *chasidim* therefore restricted themselves to Wednesday onward.

### Gematria 271

The source for Shmuel's figure of 271 is a *drashah*: *vayiten Hashem lah herayon*—"and God gave her a pregnancy" (in the context of Ruth). The word *herayon*, pregnancy, has a *gematria* of two hundred seventy-one. The days of 272 and 273 are derivative of this base figure, accounting for the possible delay between intercourse and fertilization.

### Seventh Month Birth

Mar Zutra adds a distinction: even according to the opinion that a nine-month birth occurs only after a full nine months (*yoledet l'tisha einah yoledet l'mekutain*)—that is, a nine-month baby is always carried to term and born only after complete months—a seven-month birth is different. *Yoledet l'sheva yoledet l'mekutain*: a seven-month baby can be born even at the very beginning of the seventh month. The scriptural basis is the verse regarding Chana: *vayehi litkufat hayamim vatahar Chana vateled ben*—"and it was after the period of days that Chana conceived and bore a son." The Gemara derives: *miut tekufot shtayim*—the minimum number of *tekufot* (seasons of three months each) is two, equaling six months; *miut yamim shnayim*—the minimum number of additional days is two. Six months and two days places the birth at the very beginning of the seventh month, showing that a viable seventh-month birth can occur from the outset of that month.

---

## Two Weeks View

### Two Week Limit

Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Shimon hold the most restrictive position: *ein koshi yoter mi'shtei shabbatot*—*kishuy* applies for no more than two weeks before the birth. Shmuel explains the reasoning behind this view.

### Two Week Verse

The derivation is from the verse regarding the *yoledet*: *v'tam'ah shvuayim k'nidatah*—she shall be *tamei* two weeks like her *niddah*. The analysis proceeds: *k'nidatah v'lo k'zivatah*—only like *niddah* status applies during this period, not *zavah* status. This implies that *zavah* blood during the period around childbirth is *tehorah*—because the verse specifies *niddah* and not *zavah*, we learn that *zavah* blood is set aside during this time. The question then becomes: for how long? The verse itself provides the answer—*shvuayim*, two weeks. The same verse from which we derive the leniency of *kishuy* also specifies its duration: two weeks.

### 25 Days Max

A *beraita* then works through the calculation under this view. A woman can bleed for twenty-five days without becoming a *zavah gedolah*: two days in the *zavah* period (*zavah ketanah*), seven days as a *niddah*, two more days in the *zavah* period (*zavah ketanah* again)—totaling eleven days. Then the two-week *kishuy* window applies, covering fourteen additional days. Eleven plus fourteen equals twenty-five days of bleeding without *zavah gedolah* status.

### 26 Days Zavah

If she were to bleed for twenty-six days before birth, she would inevitably become a *zavah gedolah*. The twenty-sixth day would fall within the *zavah* period and, combined with previous *zavah*-period days, would constitute a third consecutive day of *dam zivah*, making her a *zavah gedolah*. The *beraita* states this as a limit: one cannot have twenty-six days of pre-birth bleeding with *kishuy* and avoid *zavah* status. The Gemara adds the ruling of *ein koshi linefalim*—if there is a miscarriage rather than a live birth, the *kishuy* leniency does not apply at all, and even three days of *zavah*-period bleeding make her a *zavah gedolah* without any offset.

---

## Post-Birth Bleeding

### Two Positions

The Mishnah addresses a case of *hamakshah betoch shemonim shel nekevah kodem sheyeitzei havalad*—a woman who is experiencing *kishuy* during her eighty days of post-birth status following the birth of a girl, before the subsequent child has been born. The sixty-six days following the initial fourteen constitute a period of *toharah* in which even ordinary, painless bleeding does not render her a *niddah* or a *zavah*. The question is: what is the status of bleeding that occurs during these sixty-six days and is accompanied by *kishuy*—that is, pains attributable to a subsequent fetus?

The *tanna kamma* holds that all such blood remains *tahor* until the second birth. Rabbi Eliezer disagrees and rules that it is *tamei*.

### First Argument

The Rabbis confront Rabbi Eliezer with a *kal vachomer*. Before childbirth, the law is strict regarding ordinary bleeding (*dam shofei*)—it can create *zavah* status—and yet lenient regarding *dam koshi*, blood accompanied by childbirth pain. Here, during the sixty-six days of *toharah*, ordinary bleeding is already entirely *tahor*. How much more so, then, should bleeding with *kishuy* be *tahor*? If *kishuy* confers leniency even in a context where ordinary bleeding is *tamei*, surely it should confer leniency in a context where ordinary bleeding is already *tahor*.

### Dayo Principle

Rabbi Eliezer responds: *dayo lavo min hadin lihyot kenidon*—it is sufficient for the conclusion of a *kal vachomer* to be equal to its source, not greater than it. The premise of *kishuy*'s leniency is that it exempts her from *tumas zavah*. That is all. One cannot derive from *kishuy* a broader exemption from *tumas niddah*, because the source of the leniency—*kishuy*—speaks only of *zavah* status. Therefore, even if the *kal vachomer* is accepted, its conclusion is limited: she is not a *zavah*, but she can still be a *niddah* if the bleeding falls during *niddah* days.

The Rabbis' argument thus yields only that she is not a *zavah*—which Rabbi Eliezer does not dispute. He is perfectly willing to concede that *kishuy* exempts her from *zavah* status during these sixty-six days. His position is that the blood may still produce *niddah* status, and since the *kal vachomer* cannot exceed its source (*dayo*), the exemption from *zavah* does not carry over to an exemption from *niddah*.

### Second Argument

The Rabbis then reformulate: *amru lo harei anu meshivim lach lashon acher*—they reframe the *kal vachomer* entirely. Rather than comparing pain before birth to pain after birth, they now compare pain after birth to non-pain after birth. During the sixty-six days, ordinary bleeding—without any *kishuy*—is completely *tahor*, creating no status of *niddah* or *zavah*. Since bleeding with *kishuy* is always treated more leniently than bleeding without, and since bleeding without *kishuy* creates no status here at all, how much more so should bleeding with *kishuy* create no status during this period?

This is a stronger argument. The original *kal vachomer* compared two instances of pain in different contexts; Rabbi Eliezer could deflect it with *dayo*, saying the conclusion of *kishuy* is simply no *zavah*. But the reformulated argument does not compare two instances of *kishuy* at all. It compares *kishuy* after birth to ordinary bleeding after birth. Since ordinary bleeding after birth produces nothing, and since *kishuy* is always the more lenient category, blood with *kishuy* here must also produce nothing.

### Self vs. Fetus

Rabbi Eliezer holds firm: *afilu atem meshivim kol hayom kulo*—you may reformulate this all day long. The *dayo* principle still applies. However the *kal vachomer* is constructed, its premise remains the leniency of *kishuy*, and *kishuy* removes only *zavah* status. Nothing in the *kishuy* framework has ever addressed *niddah* status. Therefore, the conclusion can reach no further than the exemption from *zavah*, leaving *niddah* intact.

### Wellspring Limit

Rava offers a sharper formulation of Rabbi Eliezer's underlying logic. The Rabbis' basis for saying that *kishuy* exempts her from *zavah* is the verse *dameha machmat atzmah v'lo machmat valad*—the bleeding that creates *zavah* status must come from the woman herself, not as a consequence of the fetus. Since *kishuy* indicates that the blood is attributable to the fetus, it is not her own blood, and thus not *dam zivah*. Rava notes that by the same token, the Torah specifies regarding the post-birth *toharah* period: *tahorah mimkor dameha*—she is pure from the source of her blood. This refers to blood that emerges naturally from her own body during those sixty-six days. Blood that flows as a result of a subsequent fetus is *not* from her natural wellspring—it has a different cause—and the Torah's grant of *toharah* does not extend to it. Thus Rabbi Eliezer is on firm textual ground: the *toharah* of the post-birth period covers her own natural bleeding, not bleeding generated by a new fetus.

### No Niddah Either

The Gemara records the Rabbis' final rejoinder. Even granting Rabbi Eliezer's logic—that blood from the subsequent fetus is not covered by the *toharah* of the sixty-six days—the conclusion that she becomes a *niddah* during this period is untenable. *Amar kra teshev yeshiva achat lekulan*: the Torah states that she shall sit her singular sitting covering all cases. The structure of the post-birth *toharah* is unitary and consistent. Since she categorically cannot be a *zavah* during these sixty-six days—even Rabbi Eliezer does not contest this—she equally cannot be a *niddah*. The Torah's decree of *toharah* for the period is all-encompassing: once she is exempt from *zavah* status throughout, she is correspondingly exempt from *niddah* status as well. The two statuses rise and fall together within this period, and Rabbi Eliezer's attempt to maintain *niddah* liability while conceding the absence of *zavah* liability cannot be sustained.

---

---

# Niddah 39

## Fourth Perek & Eleven Da…

### Fourth Perek Context

We begin today at *daf* 39, picking up on the *mishna* found at the very last line of 38. The third *perek* was devoted entirely to *yoledet*. The fourth *perek*, *Bnos Kusim*, opened with women of various statuses — *Tzadukim*, *Kutim*, and a series of special cases — before doubling back to *yoledet* and the discussion of *dam koshi*. It is not entirely obvious what principle of organization governs this *perek*, though some have suggested it is unified by the theme of *dam ziva*, since to some degree every case implicates the status of a *zav* as well. Whatever the theory, the *mishna* before us now brings us back to the foundational *halachos* of *niddah* and away from the more specialized discussions of *yoledet* and *dam koshi*.

### Kol Achas Asar Yom

The *mishna* opens: *kol achas asar yom bechezkas tahara* — for the entire eleven days following *niddah*, a woman is presumed to be in a state of purity. Which eleven days are these? They are the eleven days after *niddah* during which, if a woman bleeds, she would be a *zava* rather than a *niddah*. The underlying logic is that the minimum interval of a normal menstrual cycle is nineteen days. Accordingly, anything less — days eight through eighteen from the previous onset of bleeding — is considered unusual, non-standard, and not menstrual blood. Because these days are not expected to be days of bleeding, she is assumed to be *tehora* during them.

### Eleven Days Logic

What precisely does it mean that she is presumed *tehora* during those eleven days? The *Gemara* will address this shortly, because we may recall the *mishna* earlier — around *daf* 12 — which stated that every woman, without exception, is required to check for *taharos* at regular intervals throughout the year, except perhaps when she is *niddah*, when such checking is irrelevant. Even women who are *mesulakos damim* — whose flow is suspended, such as a pregnant woman, a nursing woman, or a woman past menopause — still carry an obligation to check. So in what way are the eleven days of *zivah* a state of *bechezkas tahara* that excuses her from checking? This question will drive the *Gemara*'s discussion.

---

## Checking Obligations

### Yashva Lo Velo Badka

The *mishna* continues: *yashva lo velo badka* — if a woman who was supposed to check did not do so. This refers to any woman who failed to perform the twice-daily check that was obligatory in a world concerned with *tuma ve-tahara*. Whether she was negligent (*shogega*), compelled (*ones*), or deliberately chose not to (*hizida*), the result is the same: *tehora*. She is presumed pure regardless.

### Higia Zman Vesta

However, the *mishna* introduces a different case: *higia zman vesta velo badka* — the time of her expected period arrived and she did not check. This situation carries a different weight. That day she is assumed to have seen blood unless she can demonstrate otherwise. Accordingly, *harei zu tmeia* — she must consider herself *tmeia*. This principle is the foundational basis for the practice that women check on the day they anticipate their period. The twice-daily checking discussed earlier, which is an obligation within a system of *tuma ve-tahara*, does not carry consequences if left undone; it does not shift her presumptive status. But the day of the *veset* — the expected onset — does. If she fails to check on that day, she is presumed to have bled. This distinction is critical for contemporary practice: the obligation to check at the anticipated time of one's period, and the consequence of not having done so, remains operative today.

### Rabbi Meir - Fear & Hidi…

*Rabbi Meir* introduces an exception: *im haysa bemachvo* — if she was in hiding, fearing for her life, and the time of her *veset* arrived without her having checked, *harei zu tehora* — she is considered pure. The reason given: *mipnei shecharada mesalekes es hadamim* — fear causes the bleeding to be suspended. This overrides the normal assumption that a woman who fails to check at the time of her expected period is presumed *tmeia*.

### Zav & Zavah Status

The *mishna* closes with another category: *aval yemei hazav vehazava veshomeret yom keneged yom* — when it comes to the days of the *zav*, the *zavah*, and the *shomeres yom keneged yom*. If a person has become a *zav*, or a woman has bled during the eleven days and become a *zavah gedolah*, or she bled once and is a *zavah ketanah* — *shomeres yom keneged yom* — needing to observe a clean day, then *harei elu bechezkas tumah*. Because of the concern that the flow may continue, if they fail to check, they are assumed to have had continued bleeding. This anticipates the requirement of checking during the *shiva nekiim* — the seven clean days a woman must count after becoming a *zavah*. The checking during that period carries a different quality: failure to check during the clean days results in a presumption of continued *tumah*.

So in sum, the *mishna* delineates three tiers of checking. First, the standard twice-daily check, which is operative in a world of *tuma ve-tahara* but which, if omitted, does not alter one's status (*b'diavad tehora*); this we no longer practice. Second, checking at the time of the expected *veset*, which if omitted results in a presumption of *tumah*; this we do observe today. Third, checking during the clean days following *zivah* bleeding, which likewise carries a presumption of *tumah* if omitted.

---

## Lemai Hilchata

### Rav Yehuda - No Checking

The *Gemara* now asks: *l'mai hilchata* — for what practical purpose does the *mishna* state that the eleven days are *bechezkas tahara*? *Rav Yehuda* answers: to teach us *she'eina tzricha bedika* — that a woman does not need to check during those days. This seems reasonable on its face.

### Contradiction: Daily Che…

But the *Gemara* immediately raises a difficulty. The *seifa* of the *mishna* — the latter portion — states *yashva velo badka tehora*, implying by implication (*miklal d'lechatchila ba'ei bedika*) that she was in fact required to check beforehand. If the opening line is telling us she is exempt from checking during the eleven days, why does the *mishna* right afterward speak of a woman who failed to check when she was supposed to — as if those are the very same eleven days?

### Seifa Atan L'Yemei Nida

The *Gemara* resolves this by reading the *mishna* as addressing two separate *halachos*. The *seifa* is not a continuation of the opening statement about the eleven days; rather, *seifa atan l'yemei niddah* — the latter portion transitions to a different law, concerning the days of *niddah*. Here is how the *mishna* should be read: *kol yod-alef yom bechezkas tahara v'lo ba'ei bedika* — the eleven days are presumed pure and no checking is required. That is the first *halacha*. Separately, the rest of the *mishna* addresses the other days of the month when a woman could become a *niddah*: during those days she is required to check, but *b'diavad*, if she did not check — whether deliberately, inadvertently, or under compulsion — she remains *tehora*. The exception is when the time of her *veset* arrives: then failure to check results in a presumption of *tumah*.

This is an elegant reading of the *mishna*, though it creates a significant challenge. It now appears that during the eleven days — uniquely — a woman is exempt from the twice-daily checking obligation, while during the rest of the month she remains obligated, even if the failure to check carries no retroactive consequence. This seems to invert what we might have expected, because we have seen that women who are *mesulakos damim* — pregnant, nursing, or pre-menopausal — are still required to check precisely during those periods when they are not expected to bleed. *Tosafos* addresses this tension and arrives at a somewhat counterintuitive conclusion: the temporary states of *mesulekos damim* — pregnancy, nursing, pre-menopause — occur within a woman's general years of active menstrual life, and therefore the checking obligation persists even during those intervals. But the eleven days between *niddah* and *niddah* are structurally different: they are never a time when menstrual bleeding is anticipated, as a matter of the basic calendar of *tumah*. Therefore, unlike the temporary states of *mesulekos damim*, the eleven days are categorically exempt. One might add that the post-menopausal woman presents a difficulty for this analysis since her state is permanent — *Tosafos* grapples with that case as well — but the framework is as described.

---

## Rabbi Meir's Position

### Yotzi Ve-Lo Yachzir

*Rav Hisda* now offers an alternative: the teaching that the eleven days are *bechezkas tahara* is relevant *le-Rabbi Meir*. *Rabbi Meir* had ruled that a woman who lacks a fixed period (*she'ein lah veset*) is forbidden to have relations with her husband, because any day could potentially be the onset of her period — *asurah le-shamesh*. The *bechezkas tahara* of the eleven days comes to limit this prohibition. *Hani milei bimei niddatah* — Rabbi Meir's concern applies to the days when she could become a *niddah*. But *bimei zivatah bechezkas tahara kaima* — during the eleven days of potential *zivah*, she stands in a presumption of purity. The logic is compelling: even *Rabbi Meir*, who fears that the next period may come at any time, must concede that there is a minimum spacing between cycles. Days eight through eighteen cannot be the next period. Therefore, during those eleven days, a woman without a fixed *veset* is permitted to her husband.

### Danger of Transgression

The *Gemara* then asks: if the eleven days are permissible even according to *Rabbi Meir*, why did *Rabbi Meir* rule *yotzi velo yachzir* — that a husband must divorce a wife who lacks a fixed period and may never remarry her? Could he not remain married and simply confine marital relations to days eight through eighteen? The *Gemara* answers: *dilma atei le-akulei bimei niddah* — we are concerned that the *yetzer hara* will prevail. Once a husband becomes accustomed to the limited window of days eight through eighteen, we fear he will overstep and have relations on day nineteen, then day twenty, reasoning that she has not yet bled and has no fixed period, so what difference does it make. Since we cannot rely on him to maintain the restriction, *Rabbi Meir* requires divorce. *Tosafos* raises the question: if divorce is ultimately required, what is the practical relevance of permitting the eleven days? *Tosafos* answers that the permission applies during the period before the couple has gotten around to divorcing — the eleven days are permitted in that interval.

### Kula Rabbi Meir Hi

The *Gemara* then addresses a structural problem with the *mishna*. Because *Rabbi Meir*'s name appears only toward the end of the *mishna* — introducing the *machvo* case about hiding from oppressors — one might infer that the earlier portion of the *mishna* is not *Rabbi Meir*'s opinion. If *Rabbi Meir* is first introduced at the end, then *reisha lav Rabbi Meir* — the opening is a different authority. The *Gemara* rejects this: *kula Rabbi Meir hi* — the entire *mishna* is *Rabbi Meir*. The opening, which establishes eleven days of *bechezkas tahara* and the rule about a woman without a *veset*, is *Rabbi Meir*. His statement about hiding is simply a qualification within his own position: in a normal case, if the time of the *veset* arrived and she did not check, she is *tmeia*; but if she was in hiding, she is *tehora* because fear suspends the bleeding.

Reading the *mishna* this way requires inserting implicit language. The *Gemara* reconstructs it as follows. *Kol yod-alef yom bechezkas tahara u-shraya le-ba'alah* — during the eleven days she is presumed pure and is permitted to her husband. *U-vimei niddatah asurah* — but during the rest of the days when she might become a *niddah*, she is forbidden. *Bameh devarim amurim* — to whom does this apply? *Be-ishah she-ein lah veset* — to a woman without a fixed period. But *aval yesh lah veset* — a woman who does have a fixed period is permitted to her husband at any time that she is *tehora*, without the constraint of the eleven-day window. She does, however, retain an obligation to check on a regular basis. If she did not check, she is *tehora b'diavad*, but once the time of her *veset* arrives and she fails to check, she is *tmeia*. The first line of the *mishna* therefore addresses the woman without a fixed period; the remainder addresses the woman with one. The *Gemara* notes that this reading requires treating the seifa as belonging to *Rabbi Meir* as well — the entire *mishna* is *Rabbi Meir*, with the hiding case as an internal qualification.

One observation worth noting: the *Gemara* operates on the assumption that a fixed *veset* is the standard condition for a woman. In contemporary practice, most women do not have a fully fixed *veset kavua* in the *halachic* sense, which may relate to how *vesotos* are taught and to how attuned we are to the patterns of our own bodies. But the *Gemara* treats *veset kavua* as thoroughly normative.

---

## Purpose Answers

### Metame'ah Me-Et Le-Et

*Rava* now offers a third answer to *l'mai hilchata*. The relevance of the eleven days being *bechezkas tahara* is *lomar she-einah metame'ah me-et le-et* — to teach that a woman who bleeds during this period does not carry retroactive concern twenty-four hours back. This is a very elegant answer. Recall that *mesulakos damim* — women whose flow is suspended, such as pregnant or nursing women — do not need to be concerned retroactively about the twenty-four hours before they discovered the bleeding. This is precisely the practical meaning of *mesulakos damim*. The eleven days, like those periods, represent a time when a woman is not expected to bleed. Therefore, *Rava* suggests, when she does bleed during those days, she likewise need not extend retroactive concern back twenty-four hours. This would align the eleven days neatly with what we already know about *mesulakos damim*.

### Braita Challenge

The *Gemara* challenges this from a *braita*: *ha-niddah ve-ha-zavah ve-ha-shomeres yom keneged yom ve-ha-yoledet, kulam metame'os me-et le-et* — a *niddah*, a *zavah*, a *shomeres yom keneged yom*, and a *yoledet* all carry retroactive concern for twenty-four hours. So it is explicit that a woman who bleeds during the eleven days and becomes a *zavah* is *chosheshes* twenty-four hours back. This is a direct refutation of *Rava*'s answer, and the *Gemara* accepts it as such — *tiyuvta*. The third answer is rejected.

This outcome produces a striking irony that *Tosafos* takes pains to underscore. According to the first answer — *Rav Yehuda*'s — a woman during the eleven days does not need to check. Yet now we have established that if she bleeds during those days she does have retroactive concern twenty-four hours back. This is precisely the inverse of the pregnant woman: the pregnant woman must check twice daily, yet if she bleeds she does not carry retroactive concern. The woman during the eleven days need not check at all, yet if she bleeds she does carry retroactive concern. It is a genuinely counterintuitive asymmetry, but the *Gemara* leaves it in place.

### Eina Kova'as Vest

The fourth answer is offered by *Rav Huna bar Chiya* in the name of *Shmuel*: *lo basi lomar lach she'eina kova'as veses besoch yemei zivasah* — the relevance of the eleven days is that a woman cannot establish a fixed *veset* during those days. This answer flows directly from the conceptual logic of *zivah*: if the reason bleeding during days eight through eighteen constitutes *zivah* rather than *niddah* is precisely because that blood cannot be menstrual, then by definition a cycle shorter than nineteen days cannot be recognized as a normal menstrual period. A woman who bleeds every eighteen days, or every fifteen days, cannot have that pattern recognized as a *veset kavua*, because the very structure of *zivah* denies menstrual status to blood occurring within those days.

---

## Veset Kavua

### Fixed Period Definition

Before proceeding, it is worth pausing to understand why *veset kavua* matters so much. *Rashi* captures the essential point with characteristic brevity. The two principal *nafka minas* of having a *veset kavua* are the following.

### Veset Stringencies

First, there is a stringency: once a woman has established a fixed period, that day remains a day of concern even if her pattern shifts. Should a woman who normally sees on day 30 begin seeing on day 25 for two months running, she cannot yet abandon concern for day 30. A *veset kavua* is not dislodged until it has been reversed three consecutive times. Fewer than three reversals leave the original day still operative, so she must check both on day 25 — based on recent patterns — and on day 30, until the old *veset* has been clearly negated.

Second, and this follows from the general rule about the day of the *veset*: if the day of her *veset kavua* arrives and she does not check, she is presumed *tmeia*. The *veset kavua* transforms that day into a day of heightened concern with real presumptive consequences for failure to check.

There is, of course, a significant leniency on the other side. *Rabbi Meir* held that a woman without any *veset* at all cannot remain married to her husband. A *veset kavua* removes that radical concern: she is permitted to her husband throughout the month except on the days of concern themselves. So while the *veset kavua* heightens concern on its specific day, it simultaneously resolves the broader anxiety about unpredictable bleeding. The importance of establishing a *veset kavua* therefore cuts in both directions. As regards the fourth answer, its halachic implication is clear: any cycle of fewer than nineteen days cannot attain the status of *veset kavua*.

---

## Counting Methods (II)

### Lo Shmi'a Li

*Rav Yosef*, who was a student of *Rav Yehuda*, who in turn was a prominent student of *Shmuel*, responds to the fourth answer by saying: *lo shmi'a li ha shema'ata* — I never heard this teaching. The ruling is being transmitted in the name of *Shmuel*, yet *Rav Yosef*, who was trained in *Shmuel*'s tradition through *Rav Yehuda*, has no recollection of it. This is not an uncommon situation for *Rav Yosef*, who suffered an illness that caused him to forget much of his learning. His *lo shmi'a li* is therefore not simply a denial but an implicit challenge to the tradition's authenticity: had it genuinely come from *Shmuel*, he argues, he would have encountered it.

---

## Veset Kavua (II)

### Day 15 to Day 20

*Abaye* responds to this challenge by invoking a *mishna* that *Rav Yosef* himself had taught them. The *mishna* presents the following case: a woman who regularly saw on day 15 (*haisah lemudah lihayos ro'ah yom tes-vav*) and switched to seeing on day 20 (*veshinsah leyom chaf*) — both days are forbidden (*ze vaze asurin*). One month later, she again sees on day 20 — still both days are forbidden. The rule is that a *veset kavua* must be reversed three consecutive times before the old day is no longer a concern. Accordingly, until she has seen on day 20 three times in a row without seeing on day 15, she remains obligated to be concerned about both days.

---

## Counting Methods (II)

### Abaye's Response

*Abaye* presses further: you, *Rav Yosef*, taught us this *mishna* and explained it to us in the name of *Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Shmuel*. You therefore did in fact transmit *Shmuel*'s position to us, even if you no longer recall having done so.

### Tes-Vav Litvilatah

The specific teaching that *Abaye* attributes to *Rav Yosef* in *Shmuel*'s name is: *lo shanu ela tes-vav litvilasah* — the day 15 in the *mishna* does not mean day 15 from the last time she bled, but day 15 from her *tevilah*, from when she immersed in the *mikvah*. This distinction is critical. A woman immersed at the *mikvah* after the night of the seventh day following the onset of bleeding. Day 15 from the *mikvah* is therefore day 22 from the last time she bled (*shehein chaf-beis lir'iyasah*), which falls squarely within the *niddah* period, not the *zivah* period. Conversely, day 15 from the actual onset of bleeding (*tes-vav lir'iyasah*) would place her in the middle of the *zivah* days — and for that reason, *lo kav'ah* — no fixed *veset* can be established for that day. This is precisely the ruling of *Shmuel* that *Rav Yosef* had claimed never to have heard: bleeding during the *zivah* period cannot constitute a *veset kavua*. *Abaye* demonstrates that *Rav Yosef* not only knew it but transmitted it himself.

---

## Rav Papa's Question

### Michush Mai Denichush

*Rav Papa* reports that he presented this teaching before *Rav Yehuda of Diskarta* and posed the following question: granted that a woman cannot establish a *veset kavua* during the *zivah* days (*mikva lo kav'ah*), must she nevertheless be concerned about those days (*michush mai denichush lah*)? That is: even if the *zivah* period cannot produce a fixed *veset* with all the weight that entails, is it at least enough to require refraining from relations on a day within the *zivah* period on which she has been repeatedly bleeding? This is the distinction between a *veset kavua* — with its full halachic implications — and a *veset einah kavua*, a non-fixed anticipatory concern that still requires caution on any day that recent history suggests may be the onset of bleeding. *Rav Yehuda of Diskarta* was silent and offered no answer.

### Count From Actual

*Rav Papa* then attempted to resolve the question on his own from the same *mishna* discussed above. He reasoned as follows. The *mishna* speaks of a woman who regularly saw on day 22 from her *mikvah* (which the *Gemara* has identified as the corrected reading of "day 15" in the *mishna*), and who then switched to day 27. In the following month, both day 22 and day 27 are forbidden. Now, day 22 in the next month — if counted not from the last time she actually bled (day 27) but from when she *would have* bled based on the old pattern (day 22) — falls within the *zivah* period. And yet the *mishna* says she must be concerned about it. This, *Rav Papa* argued, demonstrates that even within the *zivah* period there is at least a *choshesh* — a concern sufficient to require restraint — even absent a formal *veset kavua*. Moreover, his reading assumed that the counting of "day 22" is done from the virtual prior day 22, not from the actual last bleeding.

*Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua* objected: who says we count from the virtual date? Perhaps we count day 22 from the actual last time she bled, which was day 27. Twenty-two days from day 27 places her concern on day 49 — firmly within the *niddah* period, not the *zivah* period. There goes the proof. And it is furthermore more logical to count from actual bleeding, not from what should have happened.

### Hen Analogy

To demonstrate that we count from actual events, the *Gemara* introduces a striking analogy. Consider a hen that lays an egg every other day. Suppose she lays on days one, three, five, seven — odd days. Then, at some point, she goes two days without laying: she was expected to lay on day seven, but she withheld on both day six and day seven. Then on day eight she lays. When will she lay next — on day nine or day ten? Clearly on day ten: we do not say she will lay on day nine because that is nine days from the last expected laying of day seven. She laid most recently on day eight, and we count from there. The cycle resets from actual occurrence, not from expectation. *Ki hadra nakta l'tamei nakta* — when she returns to laying, she does so based on what she most recently did. So too with a woman's *veset*: we count from the last actual bleeding, not from when she theoretically should have bled.

---

## Reish Lakish & R. Yochan…

### Reish Lakish Position

The *Gemara* now introduces a debate between *Reish Lakish* and *Rabbi Yochanan* that bears on the question of *veset* during the *zivah* period. *Reish Lakish* holds that a woman can establish a *veset* during her *zivah* days — this directly contradicts what *Shmuel* had said and what the *Gemara* has been assuming — but she cannot establish a *veset* during the *niddah* period itself. By "during the *niddah* period itself" he means not simply during the seven days following onset of bleeding, but during the *niddah* days proper: if she bled on day one and became a *niddah*, can a separate bleeding on day five of that same *niddah* period — when she had stopped and restarted — count toward establishing a *veset*? *Reish Lakish* says no: it is all a continuation of the same *niddah* episode.

### Rabbi Yochanan Position

*Rabbi Yochanan* disagrees and holds that a woman can even establish a *veset* during her *niddah* period.

### Rosh Chodesh Example

The *Gemara* asks for the practical case of *Rabbi Yochanan*'s position. The example offered: she saw on *Rosh Chodesh*, on *Rosh Chodesh*, and then on the 25th of the following month and on *Rosh Chodesh*. So she has two instances of *Rosh Chodesh* and three instances of the fifth, with the third fifth coming after the bleeding that began five days earlier on the 25th. According to *Rabbi Yochanan*, if we can use that day five — which falls during the *niddah* period — as a valid data point, then she now has three fives, which suffices to establish a *veset kavua* for the fifth of the month. And since she has seen only twice on *Rosh Chodesh*, not three times, the one instance cancels and she no longer needs to be concerned about *Rosh Chodesh*. *Rabbi Yochanan*'s position thus permits using a bleeding that occurs within the *niddah* period to help constitute a *veset*.

### Tosefet Hi

*Rav Papa* attempted to use this case to prove his earlier point — that we can count from a virtual day rather than from an actual one. His reasoning was that in the *Rabbi Yochanan* case, the fifth of the third month is used even though there was no independent day-one that month; we treated day five as if there had been. The *Gemara* rejects this reading, clarifying what *Rabbi Yochanan*'s position actually is: *hachi amar Rabbi Yochanan* — the case is not one where we imagined a day one. Rather, she bled on *Rosh Chodesh*, *Rosh Chodesh*, the 25th of the month, and then *Rosh Chodesh* again. Given that she has seen on *Rosh Chodesh* twice previously, we are willing to treat the bleeding that began on the 25th as *tosefet* — a precursor or extension — to the *Rosh Chodesh* bleeding, and use the day-one onset as a valid data point for the pattern. The last *Rosh Chodesh* is usable because of the prior pattern, not because we imagined bleeding that did not occur. This is counting from actual bleeding, not from virtual expectation.

### Ravin's Resolution

When *Ravin* and those who traveled from Eretz Yisrael to Bavel came, they reported that *Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua* had stated the same principle: we count from when she actually bled, not from when she theoretically should have bled. This confirms the rejection of *Rav Papa*'s proof and upholds the hen analogy as the operative logic.

---

## Three Possibilities

### Is Veset Kavua

We are thus left without a definitive answer to *Rav Papa*'s original question. The first possibility is that a cycle of fewer than nineteen days — one that falls within the *zivah* days — can in fact establish a *veset kavua* with full halachic weight. This is the position of *Reish Lakish*.

### Must Be Concerned

The second possibility is that such a cycle cannot constitute a *veset kavua*, but there remains at least a *chosheish* — a concern — sufficient to require restraint on those days. This was what *Rav Papa* sought to establish, but could not demonstrate from the *mishna*.

### No Concern

The third possibility is that there is no concern whatsoever; a cycle of fewer than nineteen days is simply irrelevant for *halachic* purposes and requires neither a presumption of fixed period nor even a precautionary restraint. The *Gemara* leaves all three possibilities unresolved. And given the contemporary confluence of *niddah* and *zivah* law into a single unified practice, the theoretical distinction between the *niddah* period and the *zivah* period is largely without practical consequence in any case — which likely renders the question moot for applied *halacha*, even before we reach a determination.

---

---

# Niddah 41

## C-section & Korban

### Mishnah Review

The daf opens with a review of where the previous session left off. The *mishnah* had established that a baby born through C-section — *yotzei dofen* — does not constitute the type of birth the *Torah* contemplates when it establishes the *tum'ah* and *taharah* of a *yoledes*: the week and thirty-three days, or the two weeks and sixty-six days. This is the position of the *Chachamim*. *Rabbi Shimon*, however, maintains that a C-section does constitute childbirth for those categories. The *Gemara* now clarifies that even according to *Rabbi Shimon*, an animal born by C-section cannot be brought as a *korban*. The *Torah* uses the verb *leida* in the context of a woman giving birth — *ki tazria ve'yalda zachar* — and *Rabbi Shimon* reads that as inclusive enough to confer *yoledes* status. But by animals the *Torah* uses the parallel verb *yivaled* — *shor o chesev o ez ki yivaled* — and through a connection to *bechor*, it is established that for animals, only vaginal birth qualifies.

### Braita: Animal Removal

This point is supported by a *braisa* discussed in the previous session: an animal born by C-section and placed on the *mizbeach* must be removed. Most *pasul* offerings may remain on the *mizbeach* once placed there; this animal is so thoroughly outside the relevant category that it must be taken down. This serves as proof that even *Rabbi Shimon* — who is lenient regarding human C-section birth — agrees that for animals the *Torah* requires vaginal birth.

### Bechor vs. Kodashim

The *Gemara* picks up three lines from the top of 41a. *Katani miyas* — from the *braisa* just discussed — *yotzei dofen delo*, an animal born by C-section cannot remain on the *mizbeach*. The *Gemara* asks: *mai lav yotzei dofen de'kodashim* — does this not mean a standard consecrated animal born by C-section is invalid? *Rav Huna brei de'Rav Natan* responds: no, we are talking about a *bechor*. The *Torah*'s language of *peter rechem* — breaching the womb — means exiting the womb naturally, vaginally. So the *pesul* in the *braisa* is simply that this animal is not a *bechor*; it was never sanctified as such. If it had been a regular *korban*, the problem would not exist.

The *Gemara* immediately presses this. If the only issue is *bechor*, the *pesul* is derivable from *peter rechem* itself — you would not need the extra word *zos* in *zos toras ha'olah*, which excludes certain things from remaining on the *mizbeach*. So why does *zos* appear? *Ela mai de'kodashim* — if you want to say we are talking about a standard *korban*, again, the exclusion should be derivable from the *imo* verse: *shivas yamim yihyeh im imo*, which the *Gemara* had linked to both *bechor* and other *korbanos*, teaching that what applies to one applies to the other. So why do you need *zos*?

### Two Pesukim Needed

The *Gemara* resolves this by saying *hai mai* — what kind of question is that? *Ei amart bishlama de'kodashim* — if you say we are discussing regular *korbanos*, *hainu de'itztrichu terei karai* — that is precisely why you need two *pesukim*. One *pasuk* addresses the case where the animal was born by C-section and *then* sanctified — *behemas chullin de'olid derech dofen ve'akdishah*. The other *pasuk* addresses the case where the animal was born of a *korban* — *behemas kodshim d'olidi derech dofen* — meaning the *kedushah* was already present before birth.
