Shmuel applies an essentially parallel principle to women: blood that exits without *hargasha* does not convey *tumah*. That discussion lies ahead, but the grounding is already being established here. Both rulings by Shmuel reframe the question: it is not merely about a fluid exiting the body, but about a real physiological experience accompanying that exit. The locus shifts from purely objective—did the fluid leave?—to substantially subjective: did the appropriate sensation occur?

### Night Emission

A challenge is raised from a ruling about nocturnal emission: if a man had sexual thoughts during the night, and upon waking finds his flesh warm, he is deemed *tamei*, having presumably ejaculated in his sleep—even though he was unconscious and experienced no waking sensation.

The Gemara resolves this through the explanation of Rav Huna: the case concerns one who dreamed that he was engaged in intercourse (*mishamshe mitato bachalomo*). Since it is possible to engage in intercourse in a dream without conscious awareness (*de'efshar leshamesh belo hargasha* in the waking sense), the sensation was in fact present—it was simply incorporated into the dream. The body did experience the appropriate physiological excitation; the dreamer was simply unaware of it as a waking experience. This *okimta* saves Shmuel's position: the *hargasha* requirement is satisfied, even if not consciously perceived, as long as the body underwent the relevant process, which was then reflected in the dream.

The significance of Shmuel's framing is underscored by the parallel to women. The same Shmuel who requires *hargasha* for a man's seminal emission to be *tamei* will require *hargasha* for a woman's blood to render her *teme'ah*. In both cases, Shmuel locates the determinative moment not in the objectified fluid but in the subjective experience of the body through which it passed.

### Arrow Ejection

The Gemara presents an alternative version of Shmuel's ruling: *kol shichvat zera she-eino yoreh kacheitz eino metamei*—any semen that does not exit like an arrow, in a forceful stream, does not convey *tumah*. This version shifts the criterion from bodily sensation to the manner of exit itself. Even if sensation accompanied the process, if the semen did not emerge with sufficient force, it is *tahor*.

This is a still more striking *chiddush*. The first version distinguished between qualitatively different types of semen—semen capable of causing conception versus semen that cannot. The second version distinguishes not by quality of semen but by the mechanics of emission. Even semen that is in principle capable of conception does not convey *tumah* if it does not exit in the requisite manner. As the *Tosafot* clarify: the concern is not that such semen literally cannot impregnate, but that it will not reach where it needs to reach. This version places the emphasis entirely on the process and the act of emission rather than the intrinsic properties of the fluid.

### Process Stages

What precisely is the difference between the two versions? The Gemara argues they are not identical: *ikka beinaihu ne'ekra behargasha veyatza shelo behargasha*—the case where the process was uprooted (the *akirah* began) with sensation, but the semen exited without sensation and without a forceful stream. According to the first version, which focuses on whether sensation accompanied the *akirah* (the beginning of the process), this would be *tamei*, since the *hargasha* was present at the outset. According to the second version, which requires the semen to exit like an arrow, this would be *tahor*, since the exit itself lacked that quality.

Rava, notably, regarded this case as an unresolved question: *ne'ekra behargasha veyatza shelo behargasha—mahu?* The Gemara notes that what Shmuel held as obvious (*pshita leh le-Shmuel*) remained a *she'eilah* for Rava. The Gemara offers an apparent resolution from a Mishnah: a *baal keri* who immersed in a *mikveh* but did not urinate beforehand becomes *tamei* when he later urinates, because the urine carries residual semen. That semen exits without the force of the original emission, yet it is *tamei*. The Gemara deflects: *shani hatam de-ruba behargasha nafik*—it is different there, because the bulk of the emission exited with *hargasha*, and the residual drops are considered part of that prior process. The *tumah* of the residual semen is therefore parasitic on the *hargasha* that attended the original emission. This resolution itself is revealing: the halakhic status of semen is determined not only by what it is at the moment of contact but by the process from which it originated—even if that process occurred the previous day.

A third version of Shmuel's statement is then presented: *kol shichvat zera she-eino yoreh kacheitz eino mazria—mazria hu de-la mazria, ha tamuyei matmei*—semen that does not exit like an arrow does not cause conception, but it does convey *tumah*. This version essentially rejects the halakhic significance of the *arrow* criterion for *tumah*: whatever the quality of the semen, and however it exits, the verse *ki yihyeh becha ish asher lo yihyeh tahor mikreh layla*—"if there is a man who is not *tahor* because of a nocturnal occurrence"—implies that any emission, in any manner, conveys *tumah*.

Three positions thus emerge: one that ties *tumah* to conception-capable semen (first version), one that ties it to forcefulness of ejaculation (second version), and one that rejects these limitations entirely (third version). Nonetheless, at least two of the three give significant weight to the concept of *hargasha* and the process of emission, rather than treating the mere presence of semen as the operative fact.

---

## Conversion Question

### Non-Jew Case

Rava poses a conceptual question: a non-Jew experienced sexual excitement, and the semen was already in the process of being uprooted (*akira*)—fully on its way but not yet exited—when he converted. When the semen subsequently exits, is he *tamei* as a *baal keri*?

The question is framed by the stakes: we have now established that the *akirah*, the beginning of the process, carries halakhic weight. If the *akirah* occurred while he was a non-Jew, it carried no *tumah* significance. Can the exit—now occurring while he is a Jew—nonetheless convey *tumah*? Or is the *akirah* essential to establishing the halakhic process such that, without a valid *akirah*, there is no *tumah* even upon exit?

The Gemara frames it carefully: *im timtza lomar batar akira azlinan*—if we say we follow the *akirah*, then we might distinguish between the case where the *akirah* is used *lechumra* (to be strict—even if the semen dribbles out, as long as the *akirah* was with *hargasha*, it is *tamei*) and the use of the *akirah* *lekula* (to be lenient—where the *akirah* was not halakhically significant, as here, perhaps the exit alone does not suffice). Alternatively, *o dilma lo shana*—perhaps the *akirah* and the exit are independent, and exit alone is determinative regardless. The Gemara concludes: *teiku*. The question remains unresolved.

---

## Women's Urine

### Zavah Urine

Rava poses a parallel question regarding a *zavah*. In general, a *zavah*'s *tumah* attaches while the blood is still within her body—a rule that, on its face, renders questions about the *akirah* less acute for women. However, a *zavah* also conveys *tumah* through her other bodily fluids, including urine (*me'ayanot*), and these presumably attach when the fluid exits. This creates the opening for the same type of question about process stages.

The case: a *zavah* feels the urge to urinate—the urine has, in the Gemara's language, been "uprooted" (*ne'ekru mimei raglehah*)—and she descends and immerses in a *mikveh*. When she later urinates, is that urine *tamei*? The question is whether the *tumah* of a *zavah*'s urine attaches at the moment of *akirah* (when she first feels the need to urinate, while still a *zavah* before immersion) or only at the moment of exit (after immersion, when she is no longer a *zavah*).

The Gemara notes an important asymmetry between this case and the parallel question about semen: *hani milei shichvat zera de-la mitzi naktei*—with semen, once the process is uprooted, it is effectively impossible to hold it back; the *akirah* and the exit are nearly continuous and clearly part of the same process. Urine, by contrast, *matzi nakit lah*—can be held back indefinitely. On a long road trip, one knows exactly how long this can persist. Since urine can be withheld, one might argue that the *akirah* is a more detached and preliminary stage, less integrated into the eventual exit, and therefore less likely to be determinative. Or, *o dilma lo shana*—perhaps the distinction is irrelevant, and we apply the same rule regardless of whether the fluid could have been held back. *Teiku*. The Gemara reaches no conclusion.

One should note an interesting inversion here. A woman's *tumah* of blood is internal—it attaches *bifnim*. A man's *tumah* of semen is external—it attaches only *bachutz*, upon exit. Yet it is in the man's case that *akirah* acquires significant halakhic weight, while for the woman's urine, the parallel question about *akirah* is left unresolved. The conceptual terrain is not as symmetrical as it might appear.

### Non-Jewish Zavah

Rava adds a further layer: a non-Jewish woman who has the status of a *zavah*. By rabbinic decree, all non-Jewish women are treated as *zavaniyot*, and their urine is therefore *tamei* rabbinically. This woman urinated to the point of *akirah* and then immersed in a *mikveh* to convert. When the urine exits, is it *tamei*?

The Gemara identifies yet another variable: even if one were to resolve the prior question and say that for a Jewish *zavah* we follow the *akirah*—meaning the urine is *tamei* from the moment she felt the need to go, and therefore the *mikveh* does not sever the *tumah*—perhaps for a non-Jewish *zavah* the rule is more lenient. Her *zavah* status is only rabbinic, and her urine's *tumah* is therefore rabbinic. Perhaps the rabbis would not apply the *akirah* principle with equal stringency in a case that is only rabbinic to begin with. Or, *o dilma lo shana*—perhaps the rabbinic/biblical distinction is irrelevant here. *Teiku*. Again, no resolution.

---

## Zav Flow Size

### Orifice Filling

The Gemara turns to the last section of the Mishnah, which states that *tumah* of semen and blood conveys *tumah* in any amount (*bechol shehu*). Shmuel, whose voice has been dominant throughout this daf, adds a ruling that appears to stand in tension with that Mishnah: *zav tzarich kechatimat pi ha'amah*—by a *zav*, the flow must be sufficient in quantity to fill the orifice of the penis completely. The source, as Shmuel reads it, is the verse *o hechtim besaro mi-zovo*—"or his flesh is sealed through his flow"—which implies that the flow seals, i.e., fills, the orifice.

### Derivation Debate

The Gemara notes that Shmuel's ruling conflicts with the Mishnah, which includes a *zav* among those who convey *tumah* in any amount. The resolution: Shmuel follows the position of Rabbi Natan citing Rabbi Yishmael, as recorded in a *baraita*: *zav tzarich kechatimat pi ha'amah*—the flow must fill the orifice. The majority of sages do not accept this.

The debate between Rabbi Yishmael and the sages turns on how to read the word *hechtim* in the verse *o hechtim besaro mi-zovo*. Rabbi Yishmael reads *hechtim* as requiring that the flow seal (fill) the orifice. The sages read *hechtim* differently: it refers not to a quantity that fills the hole, but rather to the quality of the flow—that it be a liquid (*lach*), not a solid (*yavesh*). The verse teaches that *tumah* attaches only when the flow is in liquid form; once dried, it no longer conveys *tumah* through the primary mechanism.

Rabbi Yishmael, by contrast, derives the liquid requirement from a different word in the verse: *rar*, which itself denotes a dribbling or liquid quality. If *rar* already tells us the flow must be liquid, then *hechtim* is freed to teach the additional requirement of filling the orifice.

The sages counter: they do not learn the liquid requirement from *rar* alone. They read *rar besaro et zovo* and other phrases as contributing to the count of *re'iyot* (episodes of flow) needed to establish *zav* status—two for the seven-day *tumah* and three for the obligation of a *korban*. The verse *o hechtim besaro mi-zovo*, by contrast, they read as an additional statement of *tumah* applying to a partial flow, i.e., one who has seen fewer than three times is already *tamei* for *mishkav u-moshav* even without the *korban*.

Rabbi Yishmael learns the count of two and three from the method of Rabbi Simai, who derives these numbers from the repetition of the words *tumato* ("his *tumah*") paired with different descriptions of the flow: twice the Torah says there is a flow and calls him *tamei*—those two instances correspond to the two *re'iyot* requiring *tumah*; three such formulations correspond to the three *re'iyot* requiring a *korban*. With the numerical derivation handled separately, *hechtim* is again freed to teach the quantity requirement.

The Gemara further notes that yet another position learns both the count of two and three from a single verse—*zot tihyeh tumato be-zovo*—freeing all remaining verses for other derivations, including the basic rule that the flow must exit the body (*ad sheyetzei mibesaro*), that the flow itself is *tamei* (*zovo tamei*), that the flow must be liquid, and—according to Rabbi Yishmael—that it must fill the orifice.

### Semen vs Touch Size

Rav Chanilai in the name of Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Shimon rules: *shichvat zera laro'eh bechol shehu, lanogea ki-ke'adashah*—when semen exits a man's own body (*ro'eh*), any amount, however small, conveys *tumah*; but when another person touches semen (*nogea*), there is a minimum size requirement of a lentil bean (*ke'adashah*). Rav Chanilai derives the *ke'adashah* for touching from the parallel to *sheretz*, as will be developed in the following section.

---

## Semen Minimum Size

### Mishnah Perspective

The Gemara challenges: does not the Mishnah say *metameim bechol shehu*, the smallest amount causes *tumah*? Does this not include touching? The Gemara answers: no, the Mishnah refers to the *ro'eh* case—when the semen exits the man's own body—not to touching.

### Semen vs Rodent

A *baraita* is then cited that enumerates the ways in which semen is stricter than the *tumah* of a dead rodent (*sheretz*) and the ways in which the rodent is stricter than semen.

The *sheretz* is stricter in that its *tumah* is not divided (*ein chalukah tumato*)—there is no distinction between types of rodents within the eight species that convey *tumah*; a young rodent and an old one are equally *tamei*. Semen, by contrast, is categorically divided: semen from a male under the age of nine years does not convey *tumah*, whereas semen from an adult does. This asymmetry represents the way in which *sheretz* is stricter.

Semen is stricter in that it conveys *tumah* in any amount (*bechol shehu*), whereas the *sheretz* requires the minimum size of a lentil bean (*ke'adashah*). The *baraita* presents this as a direct comparison. The Gemara immediately asks: is this comparison made in the analogous case—touching semen versus touching a *sheretz*? And if so, does this not prove that even touching semen is *bechol shehu*?

The Gemara responds through Rav Adda bar Ahava: the comparison in the *baraita* is not between parallel cases. The *baraita* says *shem sheretz* and *shem shichvat zera*—each in its respective category. When the *baraita* says semen is stricter in being *bechol shehu*, it means in the *ro'eh* context (emission). The comparison with the *sheretz* (which requires *ke'adashah* for touching) is not asserted for the analogous touching case of semen; the *baraita* is comparing a non-analogous situation where, in that situation, semen is stricter.

The Gemara then asks: but is the *sheretz* truly not *bechol shehu* in any case? Does not a Mishnah state that limbs (*evarim*) have no minimum size—so even a fragment of a rodent limb, smaller than a *ke'adashah*, would convey *tumah*? The Gemara answers: a limb is not a case of *bechol shehu* in the relevant sense. When we say a limb conveys *tumah* regardless of size, it is because the limb itself constitutes a qualitative substitute for the *ke'adashah*—it possesses a form of inherent significance that replaces quantitative sufficiency. If any part of the limb is missing, that fragment no longer conveys *tumah*. The *ke'adashah* requirement for a *sheretz* is therefore either quantitative or qualitative; semen, by contrast, conveys *tumah* with genuinely no significance required, *bechol shehu* in the strictest sense.

### Learning Context

Rav Pappa raises a further point: *ketannai*—this dispute about whether touching semen requires a minimum amount is in fact a debate among *Tannaim*. The *baraita* asks: from where do we know that touching semen (*nogea beshichvat zera*) conveys *tumah*? The answer: *talmud lomar o ish*—we learn it from the additional word *o ish* in a verse. The question is: which verse containing the words *o ish*?

Rav Pappa assumes the verse is *o asher yiga bechol sheretz asher yitma lo*—the verse about touching a *sheretz*, where an extra *o ish* is used to include touching semen. If so, a structural debate among *Tannaim* determines the *shiur*: some hold *don minah uminah*—learn from the source and retain its context, meaning the *shiur* of *ke'adashah* from *sheretz* is carried over to semen. Others hold *don minah ve'okei be'asra*—learn from the source but apply it in its natural context, meaning once we have derived that touching semen is *tamei*, we now apply the rules of semen: and semen when it exits the body is *bechol shehu*, so touching it is also *bechol shehu*.

Rav Huna the son of Rav Natan challenges Rav Pappa's assumption: perhaps the verse from which we learn that touching semen is *tamei* is *o ish asher yetzei mimenu shichvat zera*, the verse about *shichvat zera* itself, where the extra word *o ish* teaches an additional form of *tumah* via touching. If that is the source verse, then everybody agrees we apply the context of semen—*bechol shehu*—and there is no *tannaitic* dispute. The question of which *o ish* is meant is then put to the *Tanna'im*, the reciters who had memorized the *baraita*. The answer: some of those who had memorized the *baraita* held it referred to the verse of *sheretz*, and some held it referred to the verse of *shichvat zera*.

The upshot: it is undisputed that when semen exits a man's body, *tumah* attaches in any amount. When another person touches semen, there is a genuine dispute—some hold *bechol shehu*, others hold a minimum size of *ke'adashah* is required—and this dispute may trace back to which verse was the original source for deriving that touching semen conveys *tumah*, and whether the *shiur* of the source verse is carried forward or supplanted.

---

---

# Niddah 44

## Tumah to Development

### Daf Overview

Daf 44 opens with the *mishna* found at the bottom of 43b. Until this point, the *masechet* has been concerned with the details of *tumah* and *tahara*: precisely when *tumah* takes effect, where it originates in the body, and the distinctions between touching and carrying. With the *mishna* before us, the *masechet* pivots to an entirely new subject — the ages of development of boys and girls and the different *halakhot* that apply at different stages of their maturity.

### Niddah Blood

By way of brief clarification before proceeding: concerning the blood of a *niddah*, it is worth noting that *mishkav* of a *niddah* and similar matters convey *tumah* not only through touching but even through carrying. This distinction will not occupy us further here, but it is important to have it correct.

## Infants: Niddah/Zavah

### Female Infant Tumah

The *mishna* states: *tinoket bat yom echad metame'ah be-niddah* — a baby girl even one day old, if she produces uterine bleeding, is considered a *niddah*. We have encountered this *halakha* before, but it bears emphasis here because it goes to the heart of a fundamental question: to what degree is *niddah* a formal legal category, and to what degree is it organically connected to the physiological phenomenon of menstruation? The answer is clearly that it is a formal definition, since a one-day-old infant can acquire the status.

The *mishna* continues: *bat asarah yamim metame'ah be-zivah* — at ten days old she can be a *zavah*. This is because the period of *zivah* begins only on the eighth day after the first bleeding. For a girl to become a *zavah gedolah* she must bleed on three consecutive days — days eight, nine, and ten — meaning the earliest she can attain that status is when she is ten days old.

### Male Infant Zav

Regarding infant boys: *tinok ben yom echad metameh be-zivah* — a one-day-old male infant who produces a penile discharge of the type associated with *zivah* can become a *zav*. However, he cannot be a *ba'al keri*, because the *tumah* of *shikhvat zera* applies only when the emission occurs in the context of what is halakhically recognized as an act of intercourse, which requires the boy to be at least nine years old and a day. Even if what emerges from him is biologically semen, it does not carry the *tumah* of *shikhvat zera*. That is why *shikhvat zera* is not listed among the *tumot* applicable to infants.

### Negaim & Met Tumah

The *mishna* adds that even a one-day-old child can become *tamei* through *tzara'at* and can become *tamei met* — *tamei* through contact with a corpse. These two are listed explicitly, and *Tosafot* explains why.

### Tosafot on Psukim

*Tosafot* notes that by *nega'im* the Torah writes *ish o ishah* — man or woman — which might imply that only adults are subject to *tzara'at*. Similarly, by *tumah* from a corpse the verse writes *ha-ish asher yitma* — the man who becomes *tamei* — which again suggests limitation to adults. The *mishna* therefore specifies that even a one-day-old child is subject to both, and the *Gemara* will derive this from the *pesukim* through alternative textual readings. These two *tumot* are singled out precisely because the language of the verses might have led us to restrict them to adults.

## Birth Threshold

### Yibum & Birth

The *mishna* now turns to a category that works in the opposite direction: here, the novelty is not that an infant is included, but that a fetus is excluded. The *mishna* states that a born child can create the obligation of *yibum* — *zokeket le-yibum* — and can exempt a widow from *yibum* — *poteret min ha-yibum*.

To explain: if a man dies and his brother was already born at the time of death, that surviving brother creates the *mitzva* of *yibum* with the deceased's wife. If, however, the brother was still a fetus at the time of the brother's death, there is no *mitzva* of *yibum*. He must have been born — an actual living person — at the moment the obligation would take effect. This is the reverse of the *chiddush* above: whereas with *tumah* the surprise was that even an infant is included, here the surprise is that a fetus does not yet suffice. Only birth confers the necessary legal standing.

Similarly, regarding *poteret min ha-yibum*: if a surviving wife is pregnant with her dead husband's child, she is not yet exempt from *yibum*. She must wait to see whether the child will be born as a viable living infant. Even if she is pregnant, this does not yet constitute having a child in the halakhic sense that would dissolve the *yibum* obligation. Only once the child is actually born does she become exempt. In the meantime, she cannot remarry, for the child may yet be born and retroactively establish that *yibum* was never required.

One might ask: does the child need to survive for a particular period after birth? The answer is no — even a child who lives only one day suffices, provided there is no indication that it was never viable. Once born, even briefly, it exempts the mother from *yibum*.

### Terumah Via Child

The *mishna* states *uma'akhil ba-terumah* — a born child can enable his mother to eat *terumah*. This refers to the following case: a non-*kohen* woman married to a *kohen* may eat *terumah* by virtue of her marriage. If her husband dies, she may continue to eat *terumah* by virtue of her surviving children. However, if she is merely pregnant and has not yet given birth, she cannot yet eat *terumah* on that basis. Only once the child is born can his existence grant her the right. It is worth noting the halakhic logic here: her right to *terumah* after her husband's death rests not on her own blood connection to *kehuna* — she has none — but on being the mother of children who are *kohanim* or *benot kohen*. Since that status requires an actual born person, the child must be born before she can claim the benefit.

### Pregnant Bas Kohen

The *mishna* then states *uposseil min ha-terumah* — a born child can disqualify his mother from eating *terumah*. This is the reverse case: a *bat kohen* who married a *Yisrael* loses her right to eat *terumah* by virtue of her marriage into a non-*kohen* household. If her *Yisrael* husband dies and she has no children and is not pregnant, she returns to her father's house and resumes eating *terumah*. But if she has a child from her *Yisrael* husband, she remains connected to that household and cannot eat *terumah*.

The *mishna*'s language implies that it is only the *born* child that prevents her return — suggesting that if she were merely pregnant, she could go back. The *Gemara*, however, challenges this reading directly, since the *halakha* is that pregnancy alone also prevents her return. This challenge will be addressed at length below.

### Nachal & Hanchil

The *mishna* states that the child must be born to inherit — *nochal* — and to bequeath — *manchil*. If his father dies while he is still in the womb, he does not yet inherit. Likewise, he cannot bequeath until he is born. The significance of this distinction will be unpacked by the *Gemara*.

### Horgo Chayav

The *mishna* states *ve-hargo chayav* — only once the child is born is killing him considered murder. Prior to birth, the taking of a fetal life is not *categorized* as murder in the sense that would carry the death penalty. This of course opens onto the broader question of abortion, which the *Gemara* and later authorities will discuss.

### Aveilus & Choson

Finally, the *mishna* states: *va-harei hu le-aviv ule-imo ule-khol kerovav ke-chatan shalem* — once he is born, he is to his father, his mother, and all his relatives like a complete *chatan*. The *Gemara* will explain that the halakhic significance of this phrase is with respect to *aveilus*: if the infant dies, the full laws of mourning apply even for a one-day-old child.

## Gemara: Textual Derivati…

### Niddah from Vav

The *Gemara* asks: *mena hanei milei* — from where do we derive that an infant girl can be a *niddah*? A *beraita* is cited: the verse writes *isha* — a woman. I might have thought only an adult woman. How do I know even a one-day-old girl? *Talmud lomar ve-isha* — the *vav* prefixed to the word *isha* extends the category to include any female, even an infant.

### Zavah from Vav

The same derivation applies by *zavah*. There too the verse writes *isha*, and one might think only an adult. The *vav* in *ve-isha* teaches us that any female — even a ten-day-old infant — can become a *zavah*. The two *derashot* are parallel in form but are derived independently: one *ve-isha* by the laws of *niddah*, and one *ve-isha* by the laws of *zavah*.

### Zav from Ish Ish

For a male infant as *zav*, the derivation is different. The verse concerning *zav* uses the doubled formulation *ish ish* — any man. *Mah talmud lomar ish ish?* What does the doubling teach? *Le-rabot ben yom echad* — to include even a one-day-old infant, who can become a *zav*. This is the position of *Rabbi Yehuda*.

### Yishmael: Male/Female

*Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka* disagrees and says one need not derive the inclusion of infants from the doubled *ish ish* at all. Another verse states *ve-ha-zav et zovo la-zachar ve-la-nekevah* — the one who has the flow, whether male or female. *La-zachar kol she-hu* — any type of male being, whether adult or minor; *la-nekevah kol she-hi* — any female, whether adult or minor. This verse explicitly covers any male or female regardless of age, rendering the *drasha* from *ish ish* unnecessary. According to this view, *ish ish* is a case of *dibra Torah ki-leshon benei adam* — the Torah sometimes doubles its language in the manner of ordinary human speech, without intending any specific inclusion.

It should be noted parenthetically that the principle of *dibra Torah ki-leshon benei adam* is characteristically associated with *stam* Rabbi Yishmael. Whether the *Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka* mentioned here is the same authority deserves further investigation.

### Negaim from Adam

How do we know that *tzara'at* applies even to infants, given that the relevant verse says *ish o ishah*? The *Gemara* derives it from a different verse: *adam ki yihye be-or besaro* — a person, when there is in the skin of his flesh... The word *adam* — person — carries no restriction as to age. *Adam kol she-hu* — any type of person, male or female, adult or infant.

### Met Tumah from Nefesh

Similarly, the *tumah* from a corpse is derived from the verse *ve-al ha-nefashot asher hayu sham* — that the ashes of the *parah adumah* are sprinkled upon the souls that were there. *Nefesh kol she-hu* — any soul, with no restriction to adult or male. Thus even a one-day-old infant becomes *tamei* through contact with a corpse.

## Birth Requirement: Yibum

### Achim Yachdav

The *Gemara* now turns to the derivations for the opposite direction — that birth is required. Regarding *zikuk le-yibum*, the verse states *ki yeshvu achim yachdav* — when brothers dwell together and one dies. The phrase *yeshvu yachdav* — dwelling together — means they were both simultaneously alive in the world. *Achim she-haya lahem yeshiva achat ba-olam* — brothers who shared a period of co-existence. If the younger brother was born only after his elder brother had already died, they never co-existed, and therefore there is no *mitzva* of *yibum*.

### Ven Ein Lo

Regarding *poter min ha-yibum* — exemption from *yibum* — the verse states *u-ven ein lo*, that the *yibum* obligation applies only when the deceased has no son. As long as the child has not yet been born, *leit lei* — there is no son. A fetus is a potential son, not yet a son in the halakhic sense. Only once he is born is the widow exempt.

### Pregnant Bas Kohen

The *Gemara* now raises a strong challenge against the *mishna*'s formulation of *posseil min ha-terumah*. The verse states *ve-zera ein lah* — when she has no offspring, the *bat kohen* who was widowed from her *Yisrael* husband can return and eat *terumah*. *Ve-ha issa* — but she does have seed, namely the fetus in her womb. Even a fetus should prevent her return.

### Knuracha Pshat

The *Gemara* presses further: the verse also states *ki-neuracha* — she returns like her youth, as if she could erase her past and go back to the state she was in when she was a young woman in her father's house. *Prat le-muberet* — this excludes a pregnant woman outright. If she is pregnant, she is plainly not returning as she was in her youth. So why does the *mishna* require the child to be born? Pregnancy alone should already prevent her return.

### Why Both Stated?

The *Gemara* answers with *tzarichi* — both formulations are necessary. Had the Torah stated only *ve-zera ein lah*, I might have thought that a child — who is a separate body — creates a profound enough change to prevent her return, since what began as one body has become two. But perhaps pregnancy, where she is still one person carrying something internal, is not a sufficient change. *Eima techal* — maybe she can still go back when pregnant. Therefore the Torah writes *ki-neuracha* — not like her youth — to tell us that even pregnancy prevents her return.

Conversely, had the Torah stated only *ki-neuracha*, I might have thought that pregnancy — which visibly transforms the person, *gufa malya*, a full body as opposed to an empty one — is sufficient to prevent return, but that a child who now lives independently somewhere poses no such obstacle. One might say *gufa srika*, the body is the same as it was, empty, and perhaps the distant child is not enough of a connection. Therefore the Torah states *ve-zera ein lah* — even a born child, even when the mother's body looks as it did before, remains enough of a link to her prior marriage to prevent return.

Thus each formulation teaches what the other cannot, and both are necessary.

### Rav Sheshet Resolution

The *Gemara* then asks: fine, the *pesukim* have been explained. But our *mishna* — why does it specify a *one-day-old* child for *posseil min ha-terumah*? Given the Torah's teaching that even pregnancy prevents return, the *mishna* should have said pregnancy alone prevents her from going back. *Amar Rav Sheshet*: the *mishna* is not speaking about the *bat kohen*'s own status at all. It is addressing an entirely different case.

### Two Wives Case

*Hacha be-mai askinan* — what is the *mishna* actually addressing? A *kohen* who had two wives: one a divorcée (*grusha*) and one a non-divorcée. Children born from the divorcée are *chalalim* and cannot eat *terumah*; children born from the non-divorcée are legitimate *kohanim* or *benot kohen* who can eat *terumah*. Now the *kohen* dies, leaving behind sons from both wives as well as slaves. Those slaves are co-owned by all heirs. A slave who is partly owned by a non-*kohen* cannot eat *terumah*. Since the son of the divorcée is a *chalal*, his ownership of a portion of the slaves disqualifies them from eating *terumah*.

The question is: when does the *chalal* son's ownership begin? Only once he is born — *ben yom echad* — can he inherit. If he was still a fetus when his father died, he could not yet inherit, and therefore his ownership share would not yet exist, and the slaves could eat *terumah*. But once he is born and inherits, the slaves become partly owned by a non-*kohen* and are disqualified.

This reading is explicitly directed against the position of *Rabbi Yosi*, who holds that a fetus can inherit and therefore could disqualify the slaves even before birth. The *mishna* comes to teach us that a fetus does not inherit — *ben yom echad in, ubar lo* — and that inheritance, with all its halakhic consequences, begins only at birth.

## Inheritance Details

### Nochal Umanchil

The *Gemara* returns to the direct language of the *mishna*: *nochal u-manchil* — only once born does the infant inherit from his father and bequeath to others upon his own death.

### Why Inheritance Matters

The *Gemara* asks a probing question: why does it even matter whether the infant inherited and bequeathed? If we take the case of three brothers — *Reuven*, *Shimon*, and *Levi* — and *Levi* is born one day old, inherits from the father, and then dies, his estate passes to *Reuven* and *Shimon*. But had *Levi* never been born, *Reuven* and *Shimon* would have inherited from the father directly. The end result appears identical. In what case does it actually matter whether *Levi* inherited and bequeathed?

### Bechor Reduction

*Mar the son of Rav Yosef* in the name of *Rava* gives the answer: *lomar she-mema'it be-chelek bechora* — the born infant reduces the *bechor*'s double portion. If there are only *Reuven* and *Shimon*, *Reuven* the *bechor* receives a double share — say, four units out of six. With *Levi* present, the estate is divided into four shares, with *Reuven* receiving two and the others one and a half each. When *Levi* dies, his one and a half is divided equally among the remaining brothers, including *Reuven*. *Reuven* ends up with less than the four units he would have received had *Levi* never existed. Thus the born-and-deceased infant's existence materially diminishes the *bechor*'s portion, and the distinction between inheritance by a born infant versus a fetus carries real halakhic consequence.

### Mother's Property Case

The *Gemara* also establishes the case of inheriting the mother's property to pass it on to paternal brothers. Here is where the distinction is starkest. Say a mother — the paradigmatic case is *Rachel* dying in childbirth — dies as her son is born. The newborn son inherits her estate. When he then dies, his paternal brothers inherit from him. As a result, the mother's property passes to her husband's other children, who are her son's paternal brothers. Had the son not been born at all, the mother's property would have reverted to her own blood relatives — her father's family. It is precisely because he was born, inherited, and bequeathed that the maternal property flows to the paternal line. *Nochal be-nichsei ha-em le-hanhil le-achiv min ha-av* — he inherits from his mother in order to pass on to his father's brothers.

## Fetal Viability

### Mother Dies First

Interestingly, the *Gemara* assumes something that goes beyond the simple legal principle. Rather than saying straightforwardly that a fetus lacks legal personhood and therefore cannot inherit, the *Gemara* leaves open the possibility that a fetus *could* inherit in utero. It asks why the infant must be born, and answers: *de-hu mayyit bereisha* — because when a mother dies, the assumption is that the fetus dies first. The mother is not yet dead when the fetus expires. Therefore the fetus cannot inherit from the mother, because by the time the mother's death takes effect, the fetus is already gone. *Ve-ein ha-ben yoresh et imo ba-kever* — a son cannot inherit from his mother once he is already dead.

This is a strikingly unusual reading of the *mishna*. The simple understanding would be that a fetus is simply not yet a legal person and cannot inherit regardless of the sequence of deaths. Our *Gemara*, however, appears to assume that perhaps a fetus *can* inherit — and the reason it does not in this case is purely the biological assumption about the order of death.

### Thrashing & Lizard

The *Gemara* challenges this assumption: *va-ha havi uvda u-firkes ad tlata pirkusei* — was there not an actual incident where a fetus thrashed three times after the mother's death, demonstrating that the fetus survived her? *Mar the son of Rav Ashi* responds: that proves nothing. *Midi de-hava aznav ha-leta'ah* — it is like the tail of a lizard. If you cut off a lizard's tail, the tail continues to thrash. That thrashing does not indicate ongoing life; it is a residual muscular reflex, not a sign of vitality.

### Tosafot: In a Box

*Tosafot* adds a further dimension. Even if we accept the *Gemara*'s position that the fetus typically dies before the mother, *Tosafot* notes the implication: if the mother dies first, the fetus might actually be considered as though already born. *Tosafot* uses the metaphor of a box — *de-ke-munach be-kupsa dami*: once the mother is dead, the fetus is no longer inside a living person but is, as it were, sitting in a container. He has independent viability. In that case, even if we otherwise hold that a fetus cannot inherit, the *Gemara*'s insistence that the fetus dies first may be necessary precisely because if the mother died first, the fetus would be deemed already born and capable of inheriting.

### Tosafot: Abortion Status

This leads *Tosafot* into a discussion that is of major significance for the laws of abortion. *Tosafot* raises the question of whether one who kills a fetus in its mother's womb is guilty of a capital offense. Given the uncertainty about the fetus's legal status — is it a person or not — the question arises on both sides of the ledger. And here *Tosafot* uses language that is striking: *muttar le-horgo be-veten* — it is permissible to kill him in utero.

### Mutar Language

The word *muttar* is stark and has attracted significant attention in the abortion literature. Most authorities understand abortion to be prohibited in some degree — the question is how severely — and *Tosafot*'s use of *muttar* is far more permissive than the consensus. Some later authorities argue that *Tosafot* did not intend this language literally, but the phrase is there and has played a role in the halakhic debate.

### Shabbat Paradox

*Tosafot* himself recognizes the resulting paradox and raises it explicitly. If one could say it is *muttar* to abort a fetus, why then can one violate *Shabbat* to save a fetus? *Amai mechallelin alav et ha-Shabbat?* The basis for *chilul Shabbat* is *pikuach nefesh* — saving a life. If the fetus is not a life, there should be no *pikuach nefesh* to justify *chilul Shabbat*. Yet halakhic practice clearly permits — indeed, requires — violating *Shabbat* to save a fetus in danger.

*Tosafot* answers: *de-mikkol makom mishum pikuach nefesh mechallelin alav et ha-Shabbat, af al gav de-muttar le-horgo* — nevertheless, because of *pikuach nefesh*, one violates *Shabbat* for the fetus even though abortion might be permissible. The two rulings coexist: a choice to end the pregnancy may be permitted, but if the pregnancy is being preserved, one violates *Shabbat* to protect it.

This paradox is not unique to the beginning of life. An analogous tension appears at the end of life, where in certain circumstances a person may have the right to refuse intervention and allow their own death, while at the same time, if they choose to live, every halakhic resource including *chilul Shabbat* is deployed to preserve them. *Tosafot* recognizes this as a genuine and unresolved tension, and the observation remains directly relevant to contemporary halakhic discussions.

## Inheritance Details…

### Born After Death

The *Gemara* returns to the laws of *bechor* and inheritance. *Mar the son of Rav Yosef* in the name of *Rava* teaches: if *Levi* was born after his father's death, his existence does not reduce *Reuven*'s double portion. In such a case, the size of the double portion is calculated based on the children who were alive at the time the father died. *Reuven*'s entitlement is set aside first, calculated as if *Levi* never existed, and then *Levi* inherits from the remainder together with the others.

Conversely, if the *bechor* himself was born after the father's death, he does not receive a double portion at all. *Yakir ba'inan* — the verse requires the father to recognize his firstborn son, meaning the father must have been alive when the son was born. If the *bechor* was born posthumously, the condition of recognition is not met, and the double portion does not apply.

### Halacha: Rav Yosef

The *Gemara* concludes: *ve-hilkheta ke-khol hanei lishnei be-Mar bar Rav Yosef mishemei de-Rava* — the *halakha* follows both rulings transmitted by *Mar the son of Rav Yosef* in the name of *Rava*: a posthumously born *bechor* does not receive a double portion, and a posthumously born ordinary brother does not reduce the *bechor*'s share.

## Horgo Chayav & Aveilus

### Murder Threshold

The *mishna* states *ve-hargo chayav* — only once the child is born does killing him constitute murder. A *pasuk* confirms this: *ve-ish ki yakkeh kol nefesh* — if a man strikes any soul. The phrase *kol nefesh* — any soul — teaches that even an infant is included; the *chiddush* of the *mishna* is not the birth requirement per se but that even a newborn counts as a full life for the purposes of murder. The birth requirement emerges as the other side of the same coin.

## Fetal Viability…

### Rav Moshe: Murder

It should be noted that *Rav Moshe Feinstein* took the position that abortion constitutes an act equivalent to murder, even if the perpetrator is exempt from the death penalty. This view is grounded in an ambiguous *Rambam* which *Rav Moshe* reads in support of that position. Prior to *Rav Moshe*, authorities debated the severity of abortion across a broad spectrum — from the relatively lenient to the very severe — but *Rav Moshe* appears to be the first to articulate explicitly that abortion is structurally equivalent to murder, with only the capital sanction removed.

## Horgo Chayav & Aveilus…

### Kol Nefesh

The verse *ve-ish ki yakkeh kol nefesh* — *kol nefesh* — applies to any soul, confirming that a newborn infant is fully protected under the laws of murder. The *chiddush* is inclusive rather than exclusive: it is telling us not that a fetus is excluded, but that even the youngest born child is included.

### Aveilus Day One

For the halakhic significance of the phrase *ke-chatan shalem* — like a full *chatan* — the *Gemara* states *amar Rav Pappa le-inyan aveilus*: full laws of mourning apply even upon the death of a one-day-old infant. *Shiva* is observed, and all the obligations of *aveilus* apply.

### 30-Day Viability

This ruling, however, is not in accordance with *Rabban Shimon Ben Gamliel*, who holds that only after a child has survived thirty days can we establish that it was viable. If the child dies within thirty days, it is presumed to have been a *nefel* — a non-viable birth — and no *aveilus* is observed. According to *Rabban Shimon Ben Gamliel*, a child who dies before thirty days is a *safek*, and the presumption against *aveilus* prevails.

### Early Viability Signs

The *Gemara* reconciles the ruling of our *mishna* with the position of *Rabban Shimon Ben Gamliel* as follows: *hacha be-mai askinan de-khillu lo chodashav* — the *mishna* is speaking of a case where the full term of gestation was completed and observable. In such circumstances, the physical features and robustness of the infant may allow us to determine viability before thirty days. Even *Rabban Shimon Ben Gamliel* would agree that when full gestation is evident, we do not need to wait the full thirty days before confirming viability and therefore before *aveilus* applies.

*Tosafot* adds a further clarification: the dispute between *Rabban Shimon Ben Gamliel* and the *chakhamim* applies specifically when the infant dies from what appears to be natural weakness. But if the infant died from an external cause — say, a fall — and there was no indication of inherent frailty, the *chakhamim* would require *aveilus* even within thirty days, while *Rabban Shimon Ben Gamliel* would still demand the thirty-day threshold.

## 3 Years 1 Day

### 3-Year Threshold

The *mishna* now moves up the developmental ladder: *bat shalosh shanim ve-yom echad* — a girl three years and a day old. This is the threshold at which an act of sexual intercourse with her is halakhically recognized as an act of *bi'ah*. Below this age, the act is not considered *bi'ah* in the halakhic sense.

Before proceeding to the *mishna*'s list of consequences, it must be said plainly: the entire discussion presupposes the sexual violation of very young children. The *Gemara* treats it with complete legal detachment, noting thresholds and consequences without any remark on the horror of the underlying acts. When this material is studied — whether in *Daf Yomi* or in *yeshivot* — to engage with it without acknowledgment of that horror is itself a serious problem. The legal analysis is what it is; the human dimension cannot be bracketed.

### Kiddushin vs. Bia

A father can give his daughter in *kiddushin* through *kesef* or *shtar* even when she is one day old. But *kiddushin* effected through *bi'ah* — through intercourse — requires that she be three years and a day old, since only then is the act considered a valid act of *bi'ah*. So too, *nisuin* — the consummation of marriage in the full halakhic sense — takes effect only at three years and a day.

### Yibum & Adultery

If she was given in marriage by her father and her husband died without children, the *mitzva* of *yibum* falls on the surviving brother. *Yibum* is effected through intercourse, and therefore *yabam kanah* — the brother-in-law acquires her through the act — only when she is three years and a day old. Similarly, if another man has intercourse with a girl who has been betrothed or married, this constitutes adultery — *eshes ish* — only when she is three years and a day old. Below that threshold, the act does not rise to the level of a recognized sexual act, and the liability of *eshes ish* does not apply.

### Niddah Intercourse

If the girl is a *niddah* and a man has intercourse with her when she is three years and a day old, the man becomes *tamei* in the manner of one who has relations with a *niddah*. The *mishna* specifies *mishkav tachton ke-elyon* — his own *mishkav* takes on a secondary level of *tumah*, equivalent to what is carried above a *zav* rather than the primary *tumah* of the *zav* himself. This specific consequence flows from the act being considered a recognized *bi'ah*, which only applies at three years and a day.

### Wife to Kohen

If she is the wife of a *kohen* through *nesuin* — and again, *nesuin* is only effective once she is three years and a day — she eats *terumah* by virtue of that marriage. *Kiddushin* alone, prior to *nesuin*, does not confer the right to eat *terumah*.

### Pasul Kohen

If a man who is *pasul* to marry a *kohen* — a *chalal*, a *mamzer*, or another *pasul* — has intercourse with a girl who is three years and a day old, she becomes *pesulah min ha-kehunah* — invalid to marry a *kohen*. This disqualification flows from the act being a recognized *bi'ah*. Below three years and a day, no such *bi'ah* is recognized, and therefore no disqualification results.

### Arayos Intercourse

If a man commits one of the forbidden *arayos* with her — a case of incest, for instance — when she is three years and a day old, both parties are subject to the relevant penalties, including death in those cases where the *arayos* carries a capital punishment. The perpetrator is of course fully liable; the girl, being below the age of adulthood, is exempt. The point is that the severity of the *isur* and its consequences apply only once the act is recognized as *bi'ah*, i.e., at three years and a day.

### Under 3 Years

The *mishna* concludes with the formulation for intercourse with a girl below three years and a day: *ke-noten etzba ba-ayin* — it is like putting a finger in an eye. The metaphor apparently points to the following biological assumption underlying the *mishna*: below three years, the hymen is not ruptured permanently, or if ruptured, it grows back. The act therefore leaves no lasting physical change, and on that basis it is not considered a recognized act of *bi'ah*. This seems to be the *mishna*'s understanding of why three years functions as the dividing line — though the analogy is obscure, and the *Gemara*'s discussion of this will continue in the next session.

---

---

# Niddah 45

## Three Years and a Day

### Meir vs. Chachamim

The daf begins near the bottom of 44b, in the midst of a series of *mishnayot* that carry significance not only for *Niddah* but throughout *Shas*, addressing the halakhic significance of various stages of physical development for boys and girls. The *mishna* discussed previously established that once a girl reaches three years and a day, an act of intercourse with her is considered halakhically meaningful — less than that, it is not — and enumerated the practical consequences of this threshold.

The *Gemara* now picks up with a *beraita*: *bat shalosh shanim mitkadeshet be-vi'ah, divrei Rabbi Meir* — a three-year-old girl can acquire *kiddushin* through an act of intercourse, in the view of Rabbi Meir. By way of background: *kiddushin* can be effected through *kesef*, *shtar*, or *bi'ah*. When the girl is a minor, it is the father who provides the necessary consent, and the act of *bi'ah* — with the father's acquiescence — can constitute *kiddushin* once she has reached the relevant age. The *chachamim*, however, say *bat shalosh shanim ve-yom echad* — three years and a day, not merely three years. The *Gemara* asks: *mai beinaihu* — what precisely is the point of dispute?

### Yochanan: Mitzas Hashana

*Amar debei Rabbi Yannai*: the debate concerns *erev hashana* — the eve of the new year of her birth. To illustrate with a concrete case, suppose she was born on Rosh Hashana. Rabbi Meir holds that the final day of her third year — the day before her birthday, still within her third year — suffices. The *chachamim* hold that only the following day, when her fourth year begins, is valid. On this reading, the dispute is literally about a single day.

Rabbi Yochanan, however, understands the disagreement to be far more substantial. He invokes the principle of *mitzas hashana ke-kulah* — part of a year counts as a full year. According to Rabbi Yochanan, when Rabbi Meir says "three years," he does not mean three complete years. Rather, once she is in her third year — even one month into it, at two years and thirty days — that partial year is treated as a full year, and she is considered to have reached the threshold. The *chachamim*, by contrast, require three complete years, and the phrase "and a day" means the day of her actual third birthday, that is, the day her fourth year commences.

### Beraita Challenge

The *Gemara* then raises a challenge from a *beraita*: *bat shalosh shanim va-afilu bat shetei shanim ve-yom echad mitkadeshet be-vi'ah, divrei Rabbi Meir* — three years, or even two years and a day, is sufficient for *kiddushin* through *bi'ah*, according to Rabbi Meir. The *chachamim* in this *beraita* likewise say *bat shalosh shanim ve-yom echad*. The *beraita* thus implies that Rabbi Meir's position allows for as little as two years and one day — even less than two years and a month. The *Gemara* notes that according to Rabbi Yochanan's framework, this is not difficult: there is already a dispute elsewhere about how much of a year must pass for the principle of *mitzas hashana ke-kulah* to apply — some hold that even a single day into a year counts as the whole year, while others require a full month. Both positions share the same conceptual foundation; they differ only in how minimal the partial year must be for it to count as complete.

### Reconciliation

The *Gemara* then considers the difficulty this *beraita* creates for the view of *debei Rabbi Yannai*, which had reduced the dispute to a single day. If the *chachamim* understood Rabbi Meir to require three full years, how can the *beraita* attribute to Rabbi Meir a position that allows two years and a day? The *Gemara* resolves this: *ela, mitzas hashana ke-kulah* — Rabbi Meir, in both the *mishna* and the *beraita*, operates with the principle that a partial year counts as a full year. Whether one applies it as a day or as a month, the conceptual position is the same. The difficulty of reconciling the exact figures with the *chachamim's* counter-position, however, remains — and the *Gemara* leaves it with *kashya*.

---

## Hymenal Formation

### Rupture vs. Formation

The *mishna* had employed the phrase *pachos mi-kan ke-noten etzba ba-ayin* — less than three years is like placing a finger in the eye — to characterize why intercourse with a girl under three is not considered a meaningful act of sex. The implication, drawn by juxtaposition, is that it does not permanently rupture the hymen, or that whatever occurs is reversible. The *Gemara* now asks a precise anatomical question about this: *hanei besulim* — the hymen, when ruptured before the age of three, what exactly is its status? *Meizil azli ve-atu* — does it rupture and then grow back? Or, alternatively, *itzulyei hu d'lo mitzadei* — has it not yet sufficiently formed, so that the reason intercourse under three has no lasting effect is that there was no fully developed hymen to rupture in the first place?

### Nafka Mina: Bleeding Cas…

The *Gemara* asks: *l'mai nafka mina* — what practical difference does this theoretical question make? Either way, the halakhic assumption after the age of three is that the hymen is present. The *Gemara* then constructs a case: a man has intercourse with a girl under three — in a scenario where, for instance, the father had effected a *kiddushin* through *kesef* when she was under three — and there was bleeding. Subsequently, after she turns three, he has intercourse again and there is no bleeding. How do we explain the absence of blood the second time?

If we say the hymen ruptures and grows back — *meizil azli ve-atu* — then we can explain the absence of blood on the second occasion by saying *shehussa lo hava lah*: there was not sufficient time for the hymen to regenerate between the two acts. The lack of blood proves nothing sinister.

If, on the other hand, we say the hymen had not yet formed under three and there was therefore no rupture to begin with, then the blood from the first encounter requires a separate explanation — likely *dam niddah*, menstrual blood. But now the absence of blood after the age of three becomes difficult to explain. The hymen had never been ruptured before, since it did not yet exist. Now that she is three and it has formed, there should be blood. If there is none, the implication is that someone else — *acher ba aleha* — must have had intercourse with her in the interim, rupturing the hymen before this second act. And that conclusion matters: if the husband is a *kohen*, and a man of *pasul* status had intercourse with her in that interval, she becomes *asura* to him.

This discussion proceeds with full awareness — shared by several in the room — of the profound moral horror that underlies it. The *Gemara* deals with these scenarios in an entirely dispassionate, technical register, asking about hymenal formation and the *issur kehunah* consequences without pausing to comment on the acts themselves. The disconnect between the clinical halakhic analysis and the reality of what is being described — sexual acts with girls of two and three years old — is striking, and it bears noting explicitly even if the *Gemara* does not.

### Two Bleeding Cases

Rav Chiya the son of Rav Ika objects: this *nafka mina* does not actually distinguish between the two positions. *U-man leima lan d'maka she-betoch gimmel einah chozeret l'altar* — who says that a rupture before the age of three does not grow back immediately? Perhaps the hymen regenerates at once, in which case the absence of blood after three cannot be attributed to insufficient time for regrowth. Under either theory — rupture and regrowth, or non-formation — the absence of blood after three would suggest that someone else had relations with her, and there would be no *nafka mina* between the two positions.

The *Gemara* therefore reframes the distinguishing case: suppose there was intercourse under three and there was bleeding, and then intercourse after three and there was bleeding again. The question now is what to make of the bleeding *under* three. If we say the hymen ruptures and grows back, then the blood under three is *dam betulin* — hymenal blood, since there was indeed something there to rupture. If we say the hymen had not yet formed by under three, then there was nothing to rupture, and the blood under three must be *dam niddah* — with all the attendant *tumah* implications that follow from that.

### Eye Metaphor

Rav Chisda resolves the underlying question by directing attention back to the language of the *mishna* itself. The *mishna* compared intercourse with a girl under three to *ke-noten etzba ba-ayin* — like placing a finger in an eye. The *Gemara* asks: why deploy that metaphor at all? Simply say "under three it is nothing" — *pachos mi-kan ve-lo klum*. The elaborate comparison must be teaching something specific. *Mah ayin m'dama'as ve-chozeres u-m'dama'as* — just as an eye, when a finger is placed in it, produces tears, and if the finger is withdrawn and reinserted it will produce tears again, so too the *betulin* — *meizal azli ve-atu* — rupture and grow back. The hymen is present from the outset; under three it ruptures but regenerates, just as the eye continues to produce tears each time it is irritated. This resolves the question: the blood under three is *dam betulin*, and the hymen's regrowth, not its absence, is what the *mishna* is describing.

---

## Justinian Story

### Pregnancy Age Question

The *Gemara* introduces a narrative: *ma'aseh be-Yostani bito shel Asaverus ben Antoninos* — a story involving the daughter of Severus the son of Antoninus, likely the Roman emperor Severus, though the exact identification was not confirmed. In any case, this is a non-Jewish woman of high standing — perhaps Justina — who came before Rebbe. She posed two questions. First, *isha be-chama nisnis* — at what age does a woman become capable of an actualized marriage and consummation? Rebbe replied: three years and a day. This response is notable because she was not asking a strictly halakhic question about when *kiddushin* takes effect; she was asking something closer to a biological or universal question. That Rebbe answers with the halakhic threshold underscores the extent to which, in the *Gemara's* framework, the halakhic definition of a meaningful act of intercourse is grounded in an understanding of physical reality — specifically, the rupture of the hymen.

### Six-Year Marriage

She then asked: *u-ve-chama mitaberet* — at what age can she become pregnant? Rebbe replied: twelve years and a day. To this she responded: *ani nisa'ti be-shesh ve-yaladti be-sheva* — I was married at six and gave birth at seven. I became pregnant at the age of six. *Oi le-shalosh shanim she-ibad'ti be-veis aba* — woe to the three years I wasted in my father's house. In other words, if pregnancy is possible from the age of three — from the moment you have declared that intercourse is meaningful — then she lost three years of potential childbearing by not marrying until she was six.

The precise intent of her remark invites scrutiny. One reading is that she is being subversive — challenging the entire rabbinic framework by pointing to her own experience as evidence that pregnancy is possible well before twelve. On this reading, the closing line about wasted years is laced with irony: if what you told me is true, I could have been pregnant three years sooner. Another reading is that the *Gemara* is placing in the mouth of a woman an embrace of early marriage and early childbirth — presenting her as mourning lost years. Either way, the episode is striking. The narrative puts this statement in a woman's voice without any authorial commentary on its content, and it is difficult to read without discomfort — particularly following the earlier discussion in which men's intercourse with girls as young as two was treated as a technical halakhic category.

---

## Moch & Birth Control

### Three Categories

The *Gemara* here introduces a *beraita* taught by Rabbi Bibi before Rav Nachman: *gimel nashim meshameshot be-moch* — three categories of women use a *moch*, a contraceptive barrier device. The *moch* is best understood as something akin to a cervical barrier — closer to what might today be called a female condom or a diaphragm positioned at the cervix — rather than a diaphragm in the modern sense, which sits higher internally and raises fewer concerns about *zera le-vatala*. There is a well-known dispute among the *rishonim* as to whether the *beraita* is prescriptive — these three women *must* use the *moch* — or permissive — these three *may* use it, while all others are forbidden. That dispute carries significant implications for the broader *halacha* of *hashchatat zera* and certain forms of contraception, but this *sugya* is treated at greater length in Yevamot and is mentioned here only in passing.

The three women are: *ketana* — a minor, who uses the *moch* because she might otherwise become pregnant and die; *me'uberet* — a pregnant woman, because a second conception could produce a *sandal*, the flattened, compressed fetus the *Gemara* had discussed earlier; and *menika* — a nursing woman, because a new pregnancy might force premature weaning, endangering the child already born.

### Ages 11-12

The *beraita* then specifies what it means by *ketana* in this context: *mi-bat yod-alef shana ve-yom echad ve-ad yod-bet shana ve-yom echad* — from eleven years and a day until twelve years and a day. This is the year immediately before *bat mitzvah*, and according to the *beraita* it is the window during which pregnancy is physiologically possible but physically dangerous. Below eleven, the concern is that she will not become pregnant at all; above twelve, she has passed the *bat mitzvah* threshold — *meshameshet ve-holekhet*, she may have relations without the device, because the danger of a life-threatening pregnancy no longer applies. The risk of pregnancy combined with mortal danger is concentrated precisely in that single intermediate year.

### Meir vs. Chachamim

This position — that the *moch* must or may be used during this window — is attributed to Rabbi Meir. *Ve-chachamim omrim: achat zo ve-achat zo meshameshet ke-darkah ve-holekhet* — the *chachamim* say that all women, regardless of category, may have relations in their ordinary manner without using the *moch*. Their justification: *u-min ha-shamayim yerachamu*, heaven will have mercy; *she-ne'emar shomer peta'im Hashem*, as it is written, God guards the simple.

This invocation of *shomer peta'im Hashem* raises a serious underlying question about the extent to which *halacha* mandates proactive self-protection. The principle *chamira sakanta me-isura* would suggest that danger to life should be treated with greater stringency than mere prohibitions. Yet at the same time, there are relatively few areas in which *halacha* actively legislates prophylactic health measures when the risk is not absolute. Rav Moshe Feinstein invoked a similar logic when discussing smoking — ruling that it is forbidden to begin but stopping short of obligating those already addicted to quit, implicitly allowing *shomer peta'im Hashem* to do some work. In that context the question is one of legislating individual self-protection; it is more tractable. Here, however, it is not solely the woman's own risk that is at stake — the *chachamim's* position extends to cases involving the nursing infant, and arguably to the minor girl herself, whose life is endangered by the very acts being permitted. The claim that *shomer peta'im* can justify exposing an eleven-year-old girl to mortal danger from pregnancy is, at minimum, a position that demands careful scrutiny, and the *Gemara* does not provide it.

---

## Justinian Story (II)

### Gemara Response

Having established that under eleven, pregnancy does not occur, the *Gemara* returns to the story of Justina and asks: *u-mi me'abra* — could she really have become pregnant at six? The *Gemara* offers two answers. *Iba'it eima*: *asher besar chamorim besaram* — their flesh is the flesh of donkeys, a reference to Ezekiel's characterization of non-Jews as constitutionally different from Jews. On this reading, non-Jews develop differently and may become capable of pregnancy at younger ages; thus no proof can be drawn from Justina's account to challenge the Jewish halakhic standard. *Ve-iba'it eima*: *asher pihem diber shav ve-yiminam yemin shaker* — their mouths speak falsehood and their right hand is a right hand of lying. She was simply not telling the truth.

These two answers sit uncomfortably. The *Gemara* is, in effect, rejecting an empirical claim by saying either that non-Jews are biologically akin to animals or that the woman is lying. This reflects a broader feature of ancient intellectual culture — not unique to the rabbis — in which authoritative texts determined reality, and observed phenomena that conflicted with received wisdom were explained away rather than taken as grounds to revise the theory. Just as a physician trained on Galen would interpret an anomalous body as a deviation from the norm rather than as evidence against Galen, the *Gemara* here subordinates the empirical testimony to the halakhic framework. The specific language used to dismiss her account, however — *besar chamorim besaram* or flat-out lying — carries implications that go well beyond methodological conservatism, and they do not reflect well when read without the filter of apologetics.

---

## Woman & Rabbi Akiva

### Kohen Question

The *Gemara* presents another narrative: *ma'aseh be-isha achat she-ba'as lifnei Rabbi Akiva* — a woman came before Rabbi Akiva. *Nivalti be-toch shalosh shanim* — I had intercourse with a man when I was under three years old. *Mah ani le-kehunah* — what is my status with respect to marrying a *kohen*? The halakhic background: a woman does not become *pesulah le-kehunah* simply by virtue of premarital intercourse. She becomes *pesulah* only if the man involved is someone with whom *kiddushin* cannot take effect — such as a non-Jew — or if he is personally of *pasul* status, such as a *mamzer* or *chalal*. Apparently, the man in question was of such a category. Rabbi Akiva told her: *ke-sheira le-kehunah* — you are fit to marry a *kohen*, because the act occurred before the age of three and is therefore not considered a halakhically meaningful act of intercourse.

### Honey Metaphor

The woman then offered a *mashal*: *l'tinok she-tamnu lo etzba'o be-dvash* — consider an infant whose finger is placed in honey. *Pa'am rishonah u-shniyah go'al bah* — the first and second times, it is repulsive to him. *Shlishit matzetzah* — by the third time, he sucks it and enjoys it. Her point was that although the first encounters were distressing, eventually the experience became pleasurable. How, she asked, can you say it was not an act of sex if it ultimately became a pleasurable and meaningful experience for me, even when I was under three?

The metaphor maps onto something known about the psychology of abuse — that victims can, over time, develop responses that complicate the straightforward characterization of early experiences as simply nothing. The *Gemara* records this without comment. Rabbi Akiva's initial response, however, was sharp: *im kein, pesulah le-kehunah* — if that is your position, then you are indeed *pesulah*, because you are asking that we treat it as an act of sex.

### Halacha Lmoshe

The students were visibly astonished — *talmidim mistaklim zeh ba-zeh* — apparently troubled by the reversal. There then follows a statement — whether from the students back to Rabbi Akiva or from Rabbi Akiva to the students is somewhat unclear from the text, though reading it as a student response better resolves the flow — *ke-sheim she-kol ha-Torah kulah halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai, kach pe-chutah mi-bat shalosh shanim ke-sheira le-kehunah halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*: just as the entire Torah is a tradition from Moses at Sinai, so too the rule that intercourse with a girl under three is not considered an act of sex is *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*. The halakhic threshold is a formal, objective category — a *shiur* — and it does not depend on the subjective experience of the parties involved. What the woman felt, or eventually came to feel, is simply not the relevant criterion. As with all such quantitative thresholds in *halacha*, the line is fixed and not negotiable through personal testimony about inner states.

*Ve-af Rabbi Akiva lo amar ela le-chaded bah et ha-talmidim* — the *Gemara* concludes that even Rabbi Akiva's sharp reversal was intended only to sharpen the students' thinking, not to rule that she was genuinely *pesulah*. The episode thus ends by reasserting the original ruling — she is *ke-sheira le-kehunah* — while using the rhetorical challenge as a pedagogical tool.

---

## Boys: Nine Years

### Nine-Year-Old Boy

The *Gemara* now shifts to boys. *Ben tisha shanim ve-yom echad* — nine years and a day — is the threshold at which a boy's act of intercourse carries halakhic weight. This applies in several distinct domains.

### Kiddushin vs. Yibbum

One area is *yibbum* — levirate marriage. If the boy's brother dies leaving a childless widow, the obligation of *yibbum* applies, and it can be actualized through the act of intercourse. The reason a minor can accomplish *yibbum* through *bi'ah*, even though he cannot effect *kiddushin* until he is an adult at thirteen, lies in the fundamental nature of each institution. *Kiddushin* requires a conscious, deliberate act to create a new halakhic status — and for that, the actor must be a full adult with the legal capacity to perform binding acts. *Yibbum*, by contrast, is not the creation of a new status *ex nihilo*. It is understood as a continuation of the deceased brother's marriage: the surviving brother has an existing, legally recognized *zika* — connection — to the widow, and the act of *bi'ah* merely actualizes that pre-existing relationship. Since it is the actualization of something already present rather than an originating act, the minor's *bi'ah*, once it is considered a meaningful act of sex at nine years and a day, is sufficient to accomplish it.

### Yibbum Consequences

Several halakhic consequences follow from the nine-year-old's act of *yibbum*. *Ve-eino noten get ad she-yagdil* — he cannot issue a *get* until he reaches adulthood, because giving a *get* is an independent legal act requiring full majority. *U-metame be-niddah* — if he has intercourse with a *niddah*, he acquires the status of *boel niddah*: he generates *tumah* such that his *mishkav* — the surface he lies on — is a *rishon le-tumah* rather than an *av ha-tumah*, comparable to what a *zav* would produce rather than a *niddah* herself. This *tumah* status applies once he is nine and a day; younger than that, the act is not considered intercourse and the relevant *tumah* does not attach.

*U-fosel ve-eino machil be-trumah* — if the boy is himself of *pasul* status, such as a *chalal*, then his act of intercourse at nine and a day *fosel* the woman, rendering her *pesulah le-kehunah*. But even after the valid act of *yibbum* has been performed, the *yevamah* — the sister-in-law — cannot yet eat *trumah* by virtue of her marriage to him. There is an important dispute between Rashi and Tosafot about why this is so: the marriage has been effected through *bi'ah*, yet because he is a minor, the marriage is in some sense incomplete. Although *kiddushin* of a girl under three through *bi'ah* is fully valid even for a girl of that age, the question here is whether the minority of the *husband* prevents the marriage from attaining its full legal force — and the inability to eat *trumah* suggests that it does not yet constitute the complete actualized state of marriage.

Similarly, *posel et ha-behemah* — if at nine years and a day the boy has intercourse with an animal, it is considered an act of bestiality. The animal becomes disqualified for use as a *korban* and is subject to *sekilah* — stoning — even though the boy himself is exempt from punishment as a minor.

If a boy of nine years and a day has intercourse with any of the *arayot* enumerated in the Torah — a married woman, his mother, his sister, and the like — *mumassim al yado* — the woman is subject to the death penalty, *ve-hu patur* — and he is exempt, being a minor. This is the precise mirror of the rule established in the prior *mishna*: when a man has intercourse with an underage girl and it is an act of *arayot*, the man is liable and the girl is not. In both cases, only the adult is punishable; the minor is exempt.

---

## Get & Chalitzah

### Maamar Parallel

The *Gemara* now addresses what happens when the nine-year-old, having performed *yibbum*, reaches adulthood. *Get sagi lah* — is a *get* alone sufficient? To understand the question, the *Gemara* introduces the parallel institution of *maamar* — the quasi-*kiddushin* that one of the *yevamim* can perform with the widow as a way of locking in his intention to do *yibbum* before the actual act takes place. A *maamar* is not binding in the full sense — only *bi'ah* can fully actualize *yibbum* — but it has sufficient halakhic weight that reversing it requires both a *get*, to undo the *maamar* itself, and *chalitzah*, to sever the underlying biblical *zika*. The *get* addresses the rabbinic act of *maamar*; the *chalitzah* addresses the real biblical obligation that has not yet been actualized through intercourse.

The *Gemara* then draws the analogy: *af bi'as ben tes ke-maamar be-gadol* — the intercourse of a nine-year-old is halakhically comparable to a *maamar* performed by an adult. Just as *maamar* requires both a *get* and *chalitzah* to unwind, so too the *bi'ah* of the minor *yavam* — if he wishes to dissolve the marriage before reaching adulthood — requires both a *get* for the *bi'ah* itself and *chalitzah* for the residual *zika* that the *bi'ah* has not fully resolved.

### Adult Actualization

Rav explains the *mishna's* statement that a *get* is sufficient: *le-cheshe-yagdil yavo ve-yiten get* — the meaning is that once he grows up, he should first have relations again as an adult, thereby fully actualizing the *yibbum*, and only then give a *get*. Once the adult act has occurred, the *yibbum* is complete in every respect, the *zika* has been fully actualized, and a *get* alone is sufficient to dissolve the marriage. If, however, he seeks to dissolve the marriage while still relying only on the act performed as a minor, the *chalitzah* requirement remains, because the minority of the actor left something incomplete in the actualization of the *yibbum*. The inability to eat *trumah*, noted earlier, is itself evidence that the marriage was not fully actualized — which in turn explains why the *zika* is not fully discharged and *chalitzah* is still needed alongside the *get*.

---

## Mufla & Adulthood

### Ages 11-12-13

The *Gemara* now turns to the age of majority as it pertains to vows and sanctifications. The *mishna* establishes: *bat achas esreh shanah ve-yom echad* — eleven years and a day — *nedareha nivdakim*: if a girl of this age makes a *neder*, her vow is examined to determine whether she understood what she was doing, and if she did, the vow is binding even though she has not yet reached *bat mitzvah*. *Bat sheteim esreh shanah ve-yom echad* — twelve years and a day — *nedareha kayamim*: her vows are binding without examination, because she is now a full adult. The *mishna* adds that throughout the twelfth year — *uvechol sheteim esreh* — one remains prepared to examine her vows at any point, since her understanding may develop over the course of that year. The parallel structure applies to boys: examination at twelve years and a day, full binding force at thirteen years and a day, with the entire thirteenth year treated as a period of ongoing examination.

### Mufla Year

The halakhic status of the year before *bar* or *bat mitzvah* has a formal name: *mufla samuch le-ish* — one who is *mufla*, capable of *hafla'ah* (verbal acts of sanctification or vowing), in close proximity to adulthood. The term *mufla* derives from *hafla'ah*, the class of verbal acts — vows, dedications, sanctifications — that this transitional status governs. There is a tradition, treated as *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*, that precisely in this year, if the minor demonstrates genuine understanding of what he or she is doing, such acts take effect. Outside of this context, the acts of a minor are simply null.

### Pre-Mufla
