So too in *halacha* — her obligations as a *bat mitzvah* are one matter; her capacity to execute certain binding legal acts is another. *Chalitzah* and *yibbum* belong to the latter category.

### Boys & Ben Sorer

The *mishna* then turns to a parallel formulation for young boys: *vekhen tinok she'hevi shtei sa'aros chayav bechol mitzvos ha'amuros batorah*. Interestingly, the *mishna* does not here enumerate examples from marriage law for the boy, nor does it mention *chalitzah* explicitly. Instead, it moves directly to the obligation in all *mitzvos* and highlights one particular matter of personal status: *vera'uy lihyos ben sorer umoreh* — he is fit to be treated as a rebellious son.

The *gemara* in Sanhedrin establishes that *ben sorer umoreh* requires the boy to be an adult — he must be punishable — and yet also still young enough to be called *ben*, a son. Two pubic hairs mark the beginning of this window, but it has an upper limit as well, stated in the *mishna*: *ad sheyakif zakan hatachton* — until the lower beard is surrounded.

### Beard Development

The *mishna* then adds, *velo ha'elyon ela she'dibru chachamim bilshon nekiyah* — not the upper beard, but the rabbis are speaking in euphemistic language. In other words, not the beard on the face, but the pubic hair that surrounds the genital area. Once that region is surrounded — meaning the hair runs from one edge to the other of the pubic area — he is no longer considered a *ben* in the relevant sense.

The *gemara*'s reasoning is that at this later stage of development, he is capable of fathering children. The *gemara* assumes — whether or not this is biologically precise — that the capacity to impregnate is tied to this later stage of physical maturation. Once he can be a father, he can no longer be merely a *ben* in the sense required for *ben sorer umoreh*.

### Mi'un Right

The *mishna* returns to the girl with a distinct and practically important law: *einah yecholah lema'en* — once she has two pubic hairs, she can no longer perform *mi'un*.

*Mi'un* is the halakhic mechanism by which a minor girl, married off not by her father but by her mother or brothers, may refuse the marriage and walk away without requiring a *get*. The institution of allowing a mother or brothers to arrange a marriage was a rabbinic creation, driven by genuine socioeconomic necessity — the need to ensure that girls without fathers would be provided for. But since this marriage is only *miderabbanan*, it carries a corresponding leniency: the girl retains the right of refusal until she becomes an adult.

The *mishna* takes for granted that once she is an adult, the mother and brothers no longer have any authority over her at all. What it addresses is the narrower question of the prior rabbinic marriage: once she is an adult with two pubic hairs, she cannot undo even that rabbinic marriage through *mi'un*. She has crossed the threshold.

*Rabbi Yehuda* dissents: *ad sheyirbe hashachor* — she retains the right of *mi'un* even after two pubic hairs, until the black hair genuinely fills the pubic region. The distinction in language between *yakif* (surrounds, used for the boy) and *yirbe* (fills, used in Rabbi Yehuda's formulation for the girl) appears deliberate — *yakif* suggests a perimeter, while *yirbe* suggests a more substantial covering.

---

## Gemara: Chalitzah

### Michoel's Q

The *gemara* opens with a pointed question: once the *mishna* has stated *chayeves bechol hamitzvos ha'amuros batorah* — she is obligated in all *mitzvos* — why is it necessary to separately state that she performs *chalitzah* or *yibbum*? If she is an adult across the board, her eligibility for *chalitzah* should be implicit.

### Rabbi Yosi

The *gemara* answers: *le'appuki miDe'Rabbi Yosi* — to exclude the position of Rabbi Yosi. Rabbi Yosi held that when the Torah writes *ve'im lo yachpotz ha'ish* in the *parasha* of *chalitzah* in Devarim 25, the word *ish* — man — is the only indicator of an adult requirement, and it appears only in reference to the man performing *chalitzah*. From this, Rabbi Yosi derived that only the *man* performing *chalitzah* must be an adult; the woman, however — *bein gedolah bein ketanah* — whether adult or minor, may perform *chalitzah*. The *mishna* therefore explicitly rejects this position.

### Woman = Man

The *mishna*'s counter-position rests on the principle of *ishah ke'ish* — the woman is parallel to the man in the act of *chalitzah*. Since the man must be an adult, so too must the woman. This parallel is logical given the bilateral nature of the *chalitzah* ceremony, even if the Torah's language does not make it explicit on the woman's side.

### Why Spell Out

A further question is raised: given that the *mishna* already said *vekhen hatinok* — the same applies to the boy — why does it then proceed to spell out that he is obligated in all *mitzvos*? If the *mishna* said "the same," the same should suffice. One might suggest the *mishna* does so in order to build toward the discussion of *ben sorer umoreh* and its upper time limit. But the *gemara* rejects that rationale.

### Already Taught

The *gemara* objects: *tanina hada zimna* — that law has already been taught. The *perek* of *ben sorer umoreh* in Sanhedrin contains a *mishna* that uses precisely the same language — *misheyavi shtei sa'aros ve'ad sheyakif zakan hatachton, velo ha'elyon ela she'dibru chachamim bilshon nekiyah* — word for word. The *mishna* here could simply have said "the same applies to the boy" without repeating anything. Why be so expansive?

The *gemara* concludes: *ein hakhi nami* — you are correct, it was not strictly necessary. *Ela aidi de'perish millei de'tinoket kama perish nami millei de'tinok* — since the *mishna* is spelling out all the details regarding the girl, it decided to spend some time elaborating on the boy as well, even if the material was not strictly necessary here. After all, the thrust of this entire *perek* and *masechet* is overwhelmingly concerned with the girl's stages of development; nevertheless, the *mishna* offers a parallel treatment of the boy, even if briefer and ultimately redundant.

---

## Mi'un & Sex

### Halakha: R. Yehuda

*Rabbi Abbahu* says in the name of *Rabbi Elazar*: *halacha keRabbi Yehuda* — the law follows Rabbi Yehuda. A girl married off by her mother or brothers retains the right of *mi'un* until the later stage of development, beyond two pubic hairs, when the pubic region becomes substantially filled with hair.

### Sex = Binding

However — and this is the important qualification — *umodeh Rabbi Yehuda she'miniv'alah le'achar shehevi'ah shtei sa'aros, shuv einah yecholah lema'en*. Even Rabbi Yehuda concedes that once the girl has had sexual relations with her husband *after* acquiring two pubic hairs, she can no longer perform *mi'un*. The reasoning is that once she is an adult — marked by two pubic hairs — and she has sex within what is nominally a marital context, that act of sex is interpreted as *kiddushei biah*. Sexual relations in a marital context, once she is an adult, constitute a new act of *kiddushin* effected through intercourse. And once that biblical *kiddushin* has been created, *mi'un* — which operates only against a rabbinic marriage — is no longer available.

### Minor vs Adult

This distinction between minor and adult is crucial. Before two pubic hairs, if the girl (who has no father) has sex with this man, no new marital status is created. The rabbinic marriage remains defined by the original act of the mother or brothers, and nothing about the sexual relations changes its nature. But once she is an adult, the legal calculus shifts: sex in a marital context by an adult woman creates *kiddushei biah*, upgrading the marriage from rabbinic to biblical.

### Sex Creates Marriage?

This analysis raises a broader and much-debated question: do we apply the principle of *kol habo'el al da'at kiddushin rishonim bo'el* — that anyone who has sex does so in the context and intent of the original *kiddushin*? This principle addresses cases where the initial act of *kiddushin* was somehow defective — the coin given was later discovered not to be worth a *perutah*, for instance, or a stipulation was not fulfilled. In such a case, the couple may have lived together for years, had children, and conducted themselves in every way as a married couple. The question is whether the ongoing sexual relations throughout that marriage constitute a new act of *kiddushei biah* that independently validates the marriage — or whether all of it remains framed entirely by the original, now-defective, act of *kiddushin*, such that no valid marriage was ever created.

This is not merely an abstract Talmudic debate. It is directly relevant to *agunah* cases today and to situations where a woman cannot obtain a *get* and a *posek* is examining whether the original marriage ceremony was halakhically valid.

### Agunah Cases

If the original ceremony was defective, one approach holds that the subsequent sexual relations — conducted in what the parties understood to be a marital relationship — themselves constitute *kiddushei biah* and create a biblically binding marriage. This was the strong position of Rav Yosef Eliyahu Henkin, who argued that cohabitation and sexual relations in a recognized marital context bind the couple regardless of defects in the original ceremony. A countervailing position holds that when the couple intended their relationship to be governed by the original ceremony, the sexual relations are always understood as occurring *al da'at* that original act — and if that act was void, nothing that follows validates the marriage.

One might try to distinguish between a case where there was *no ceremony at all* and one where there was a ceremony that turned out to be invalid. Where there was no ceremony, one might more readily infer that the parties intended their cohabitation itself to constitute marriage. Where there was a ceremony, however defective, the legal relationship might be understood as defined entirely by that ceremony. These distinctions are debated by the *rishonim* and *acharonim*, and *Tosafot* engages directly with the question.

The present *gemara* is operating in precisely this conceptual space: when a girl's marriage was arranged by her mother — a rabbinic act — and she subsequently has sex with this man as an adult, does that sex constitute a new, independent, biblically binding act of *kiddushei biah*? The *gemara*'s position here is that it does.

---

## R. Yishmael Story

### Chavruhei Ruling

The *gemara* reports that *chavruhei deRav Kahana* — the colleagues of Rav Kahana — *savru lema'avid uvda keRabbi Yehuda* — wished to rule in practice like Rabbi Yehuda in a case where the girl had already had sexual relations as an adult with the man to whom she had been married by her mother. They intended to permit her to perform *mi'un* regardless, taking the position that the sex did not constitute *kiddushei biah* and the marriage remained solely rabbinic.

### Child on Shoulders

Rav Kahana stopped them. *Lo kach haya ma'aseh bevito shel Rabbi Yishmael* — is this not exactly what happened in the case of the daughter of Rabbi Yishmael? Rabbi Yishmael had died, and his wife — the girl's mother — had married the daughter off. The girl came to the *beit midrash* to perform *mi'un* and leave her husband. But she arrived with her child on her shoulders — *uvna murchav al ketayfa*. She had already had a child with this man, which the *gemara* takes as indicating that she had sexual relations with him as an adult, since as a general rule girls do not give birth before reaching the age of *bat mitzvah*.

### Beit Midrash Weeps

That day, the statements of Rabbi Yishmael were quoted in the *beit midrash* — *huskeru devarav shel Rabbi Yishmael beBeit HaMidrash* — and the *beit midrash* erupted in weeping: *ravtsa bechiya gedola beBeit HaMidrash*. The language here is significant — *ravtsa* is not simply "she cried." It suggests a collective, overwhelming outpouring of grief. And they said: *davar she'amar oso hatzadik yikashel bo zaro* — shall the very ruling of that righteous man cause his own daughter to stumble?

To understand this, we must see what Rabbi Yishmael actually ruled.

### Kiddushei Taut

*De'amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel mishum Rabbi Yishmael*: Rabbi Yishmael had taught a principle drawn from the *sota* passage — *vehi lo nitpasa*, "she was not seized," implying that a woman who committed adultery willingly is forbidden to her husband, while one who was raped (*nitpasa*) remains permitted. But Rabbi Yishmael added a further case: *yesh lach acheres she'af al pi she'lo nitpasa, muteres* — there is another category of woman who, even though she willingly had sex with a man who is not her husband, is nonetheless not forbidden.

### Ach'eres Case

What case is this? *She'kidusheha kidushei taut* — a case where the original marriage was a marriage in error. Perhaps the coin used for *kiddushin* was not worth a *perutah*; perhaps a stipulation was not met. In such a case, even if she had sex with another man — even willingly — and even *she'uvna murchav al ketayfa*, even if her child rides on her shoulders — *umeima'enes veholechet la*, she may still refuse the first "husband" and leave. Because the first marriage was never valid, her sexual relations with the other man did not constitute adultery. She needs no *get*, and the sex creates no binding status.

The *gemara* assumes that this principle applies equally to the case of *mi'un*: if the original marriage was arranged by the mother and is only rabbinic, then just as in a *kiddushei taut* the woman can walk away even after having sex and having a child, so too here, the girl can perform *mi'un* even after sex and even after having a child. According to Rabbi Yishmael's position, the daughter of Rabbi Yishmael should have been permitted to perform *mi'un*.

### Yavne Vote

But there was a problem. *Venimnu vegamru* — a vote was taken and it was concluded: *ad matai habat memanet, ad shetavi shtei sa'aros* — a girl may perform *mi'un* only until she produces two pubic hairs. This vote effectively overruled Rabbi Yishmael's position and established that once she is an adult — two pubic hairs — and has had sex in the marital context, she can no longer perform *mi'un*, regardless of whether the original marriage was *kiddushei taut* or a rabbinic marriage by the mother.

The weeping in the *beit midrash* is now intelligible. The daughter of Rabbi Yishmael had come seeking *mi'un* on the basis of her father's ruling — a ruling of a *tzadik* that should have permitted her to leave. Yet that ruling had been overruled. She stood there with her child on her shoulders, seeking release from a man she did not wish to remain with, and the *beit midrash* — relying on the majority vote — denied her. That a righteous man's ruling could leave his own daughter in this position was the source of the collective anguish.

There is an alternative reading of the episode, and it may actually fit the text more precisely. On that reading, the assembled sages were not lamenting that Rabbi Yishmael's ruling had been overruled. Rather, they felt it would be deeply wrong for the daughter to invoke her father's ruling in order to leave this man — the father of her child — and that it would therefore constitute a moral stumbling caused by the father's leniency. Under this reading, *venimnu vegamru* was not a prior vote being recalled to defeat her, but a vote taken in response to her appearance — a vote to overrule Rabbi Yishmael precisely because they found it unconscionable that his ruling would be used to separate a mother from the father of her child. This reading makes the sages less sympathetic to the girl — and arguably, as several in the room noted, less responsive to what may well have been a genuinely desperate situation.

What is not in doubt is that this happens — and happened — with some regularity. A young woman, perhaps trapped in an unwanted marriage, comes before a *beit din* with a valid legal argument, and is refused. The parallel to contemporary *agunah* cases requires little elaboration.

The *gemara* also raises the question of whether *kiddushei taut* and a rabbinic marriage by the mother are truly analogous. *Tosafot* addresses this and notes that the cases may be distinguishable. In a *kiddushei taut*, the original marriage was intended to be biblical but was defective from the outset; in the *mi'un* case, the marriage was always intentionally rabbinic. Whether the status of ongoing sexual relations is identical in both cases is a genuine question, and *Tosafot* discusses opinions that differentiate between them.

One deeper question runs through this entire discussion: is *kiddushei biah* created by the mere fact of sex in a marital context, or does it require a conscious *intent* to effect marriage through the act of sex? If intention is required, then ongoing marital relations — conducted without any deliberate thought of creating new *kiddushin* — may not constitute *kiddushei biah* at all, even when the parties consider themselves married. This consideration bears on how broadly the principle is applied in practice.

### Kahana Silenced

The *gemara* reports: *perash velo avad uvda* — Rav Kahana, having cited the story of Rabbi Yishmael's daughter, withdrew. He did not issue a ruling permitting *mi'un* after sexual relations as an adult. Whether he formally declared it prohibited or simply refrained from permitting it is not entirely clear, but he was effectively silenced by the precedent.

### Dissenting Voices

Nevertheless, *Rabbi Yitzchak vetalmidei Rabbi Chanina avdu uvda keRabbi Yehuda ve'af al gav d'niv'alah* — Rabbi Yitzchak and the students of Rabbi Chanina did in fact rule in practice like Rabbi Yehuda, permitting *mi'un* even after she had had sexual relations as an adult.

### Troops Deployed

*Ve'azal Rav Sheman bar Abba ve'amar kamei deRabbi Yochanan* — Rav Sheman bar Abba went and reported this before Rabbi Yochanan. Rabbi Yochanan in turn brought it before Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'ah — the grandson of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the political head of the community. The response was swift and striking: *shadar bulshafi ve'apkinehu* — he dispatched officers, who removed the woman from the second husband to whom she had gone after performing *mi'un*. A ruling had been issued that permitted her to leave the first husband and remarry; she had done so; and yet the political authority sent troops to forcibly undo that remarriage. It does not state that she was returned to the first husband — only that she was taken from the second. The question of whether she could return to the first, given that she had since had relations with the second, touches on a separate discussion in Yevamot about women who remarry under the assumption their first husband is dead and later discover he is alive, and whether return is possible in such cases.

---

## Hair Criteria

### Two Long Hairs

Now that the volatile discussion of *mi'un* and its limits has concluded, the *gemara* turns to a more technical set of questions: what precisely constitutes the hair-related criteria for the various halakhic thresholds we have been discussing?

*Amar Rav Chisda amar Mar Ukva*: the phrase *yarba hashachor* does not require the entire pubic region to be physically covered with hair. *Lo she'yarba hashachor mamash* — it need not literally be filled. Rather, *kedei sheyihiyu shtei sa'arot shochvot venira'os kemi sheyarba hashachor al halavan* — two hairs suffice, provided they are long enough that if laid flat they would appear to cover the white of the skin beneath, creating the visual impression of black overwhelming white. This is a striking leniency in interpreting the requirement — though precisely how two hairs, however long, can visually fill an area remains somewhat unclear.

### Rava: Surrounding

*Rava amar shtei sa'arot hamakifot misafa lesafa* — Rava defines it as two hairs that surround from edge to edge. Whether this means hairs so long that they traverse the entire region, or a row of hairs that forms a band across the region which when laid flat would fill it, is not entirely clear from the text. It may not be substantially different from the position of Rav Chisda and Mar Ukva in practical terms.

### From Follicles

*Amar Rabbi Chelbo amar Rav Huna*: the two hairs referred to throughout — in the classic threshold for adulthood, not merely for the extended *mi'un* period — *tzarich sheyehei be'ikaran gumot*, must come from follicles. The hair must emerge from actual follicles. This seems obvious — how would a hair exist without a follicle? — but the *gemara* will shortly clarify why this requires statement.

### Follicles Alone

*Rav Malkio amar Rav Adda bar Ahava* takes this a significant step further: *gumot af al pi she'ein sa'arot* — follicles even without hairs are sufficient. The presence of follicles, even before hairs have actually grown from them, is enough to establish the halakhic threshold of adulthood. The question of whether follicles can exist before hair grows from them is left somewhat open, but the answer appears to be yes.

### Two Ravs

The *gemara* then pauses to clarify a point of attribution that has practical significance for *pesak*: the names Rav Malkio and Rav Malkia are easily confused, yet they are two distinct figures whose rulings should not be interchanged. *Rav Chanina berei deRav Ika* offers one sorting principle: *shipud, shefachot, vegumot Rav Malkio; belorit, efer mikleh, vegvinah Rav Malkia*. Three statements about a type of spit, maidservants (a *mishna* in Ketubot), and follicles belong to Rav Malkio; three others concerning a certain pagan haircut, the use of ashes, and cheese of non-Jews belong to Rav Malkia.

*Rav Papa* offers a cleaner mnemonic principle: *matnitin uMatnita Rav Malkio* — anything based on explaining a *mishna* or *baraita* was said by Rav Malkio; *shma'teta* — amoraic teachings — were Rav Malkia's. The mnemonic is *matnitin malchasa* — the *mishna* is the queen, and *malkia* (king/queen) helps you remember that it is Rav Malkia — wait, the logic runs in the other direction: *matnitin* is the queen, which calls to mind the word *malka*, which helps anchor Rav Malkio as the one associated with *mishnas* and *baraitas*. The practical difference this creates in the list concerns the case of *shefachot* — the maidservants ruling is a *mishna* in Ketubot and therefore belongs to Rav Malkio under Rav Papa's system, while *efer mikleh* (ashes), which is amoraic, is moved to Rav Malkia's column.

### Proof from Silence

*Rav Ashi* then reports: *Mar Zutra said to me* that *Rabbi Chanina mi-Sura* was troubled by the ruling that follicles alone constitute adulthood. His challenge was from silence: *lo ishtamit tana ve'ashmi'einan guma* — throughout all of *Shas*, wherever *tannaim* discuss the two-hair criterion, they always say "two hairs." Not once do they say "two follicles." If follicles without hairs were sufficient, surely at least one *tanna* would have mentioned it somewhere. The consistent silence must indicate that follicles alone are not sufficient.

### Two from One

*Rav Ashi* offers a defense. The *tannaim* always spoke about hairs rather than follicles not because follicles are insufficient, but because they wished to teach a further law: *de'afilu shtei sa'aros beguma achas* — that two hairs count toward the threshold even if both emerge from a single follicle. Had the *tannaim* taught about follicles, one might have assumed that you need two hairs *from two separate follicles*. By consistently saying "two hairs," they communicate that even two hairs from one follicle are sufficient — and implicitly preserve the ruling that follicles alone are also sufficient.

### Iyov Midrash

But this immediately prompts a question: *umi ika kai ha'gavna* — is it even possible to have two hairs from one follicle? The *gemara* cites the verse from Iyov: *asher bise'arah yeshufeni*, and notes that *Rava said: Iyov bi'se'arah cheiref* — Iyov used the whirlwind as the vehicle for his complaint. He blasphemed, essentially accusing God of having confused him (*Iyov*) for His enemy (*oyev*) — perhaps, he suggested, God's attention was distracted by a passing whirlwind. *Bise'arah heshivu* — and God answered him from the whirlwind.

The *gemara* presents God's response with remarkable specificity: *shoteh she-ba'olam, harbeh nimin barasi bero'sho shel adam, ulchol nima venima barasi lah guma bifnei atzmah* — you fool, I created many hairs on the human head, and for each and every hair I created its own individual follicle, so that two hairs should not share one follicle. *She'lo yehu shtayim yonkos miguma achas* — and had two hairs grown from one follicle, *makhish ma'or einav shel adam* — it would weaken the sight of a person. *Guma beguma lo nishalef li* — I ensure that not one follicle is confused with another. *Iyov be'oyev nishalef li?* — And you think I confused Iyov for oyev?

The wordplay on *se'arah* — both whirlwind and hair — runs through the entire exchange. God's point is that the perfection of the natural order, down to the unique assignment of each hair to its own follicle, testifies to a level of precision that makes any accusation of divine error absurd.

### Head vs Body

This *midrash*, however, creates a problem: if two hairs cannot share one follicle — as divine design ensures — then the entire reason Rav Ashi gave for why the *tannaim* speak of two hairs (to include the case of two hairs from one follicle) collapses. The *gemara* resolves this with the principle of *lo kashya*: *ha begufah ha bereisha* — the midrashic teaching about God ensuring each hair has its own follicle refers to the hairs of the head. On the body, it may be possible for two hairs to share a single follicle. Rav Ashi's defense therefore remains valid with respect to body hair, which is precisely what is at issue in the question of *shtei sa'aros* for halakhic maturity.

---

## Hair Location

### Different Locations

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel*: the two hairs need not be in the same location. For a young boy, even *achat al hakaf ve'achat al habetzim* — one in the region above the genitals and one at the testicles — the two hairs may be in different places and still combine.

### Girl: Varied Spots

A *baraita* teaches a parallel principle for a young girl: *afillu achat begavah ve'achat bechersa* — even one hair in the area below and one in the pubic area count together. Moreover, *achat al gabei kishrei etzbe'oteha shel yad ve'achat al gabei kishrei etzbe'oteha shel regel* — a hair at the knuckles of the hand and a hair at the knuckles of the foot may also count. The claim is striking: at the age of maturity, hair begins to grow not only in the pubic area but also on the hands and feet, and such hair itself constitutes evidence of — or perhaps even independently establishes — the halakhic threshold.

### R. Shimon's View

*Divrei Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda ish Kefar Akko she'amar mishum Rabbi Shimon*: this lenient position, allowing hair from the hands and feet to count and allowing hairs from different body locations to combine, is the view of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon.

### Same Place Only

The *rabbanan*, cited in the name of *Rav Chisda*, disagree: *ad sheyihyu shtei sa'arot bemakom echad* — the two hairs must be in the same place, and by implication they must be in the pubic area specifically. Hairs from the hands or feet do not count, and hairs cannot be combined across different regions of the body.

---

## Mi'un Duration

### Four Opinions

*Tanu rabbanan* presents a formal enumeration of the competing views on the duration of *mi'un* rights — that is, until what stage of development may a girl married off by her mother or brothers perform *mi'un* and leave without a *get*.

### Meir vs Yehuda

*Rabbi Meir* holds the strictest position: *ad shetavi shtei sa'arot* — only until she produces two pubic hairs. Once she is an adult, *mi'un* is closed. *Rabbi Yehuda*, as we have discussed at length, is considerably more lenient: *ad sheyirbeh shachor* — until the black pubic hair has substantially filled the area, allowing *mi'un* to continue well into what is technically adult status.

### Yosi Middle

*Rabbi Yosi* occupies a middle position: *ad shetakif ha'atarah* — until the crown is surrounded. This appears to mean a ring or perimeter of hair around the pubic region, more than Rabbi Meir's two hairs but less than Rabbi Yehuda's requirement of a full covering.

### Ben Shlakot

*Ben Shlakot* takes the most lenient position of all: *ad shetechalkel* — until *techalkel*, a term whose precise meaning is uncertain. Both Rashi and Tosafot point to a usage elsewhere in the *gemara* suggesting something like a large mop or mass of hair, more substantial even than Rabbi Yehuda's *yarba hashachor*, or at minimum equivalent to it. The exact boundary between the two remains unclear.

### Yavne Testimony

*Rabbi Shimon* reports that he encountered *Chananya ben Chakinai* in Tzidan, who asked him to relay a message to Rabbi Akiva: when you reach him, ask him until when a girl may perform *mi'un*. And if he tells you "until two hairs" — which Chananya presumed was Rabbi Akiva's position — tell him that Ben Shlakot testified before all of you in Yavne that it is until *techalkel*, and you said nothing in response. Silence, in the presence of the assembled sages at Yavne, implies consent. How can Rabbi Akiva now hold to the stricter position?

### Akiva Rejects

Rabbi Shimon reports that when he brought this message to Rabbi Akiva, the response was dismissive: *kalkal zeh eini yodea mahu* — I do not know what *kalkal* even means; *Ben Shlakot eini makir* — I do not recognize who Ben Shlakot is. Rabbi Akiva effectively refused to acknowledge the testimony — whether because he genuinely did not recall it, because he was in disagreement with it, or because he did not consider Ben Shlakot a credible witness is left unstated. His position remained: *ad shetavi shtei sa'arot* — until two pubic hairs only. This, of course, is the strictest ruling, cutting off the girl's right of *mi'un* at the earliest possible moment.

---

## Hair Length Standards

### Two Hairs Analogy

The *gemara* now turns to a different dimension of the two-hair criterion — not where the hairs must be, or how many follicles they require, but how long the hairs themselves must be. And this question, it emerges, is not unique to the context of maturity. *Shtei sa'arot ha'amuros beparah uvnega'im* — the "two hairs" mentioned in the context of the *parah adumah* and in the laws of *nega'im* are governed by the same length standard as the two hairs in the context of maturity. In *parah adumah*, two black hairs disqualify the animal from serving as the *parah adumah*; in *nega'im*, two white hairs within a leprous spot are halakhically significant. The question of minimum hair length thus applies across these domains.

### Bend to Root

*Rabbi Yishmael* establishes the baseline: *kedei lachof roshan le'ikaran* — the hair must be long enough to bend its tip over and touch its own root. This requires a hair of meaningful length — long enough to be folded back on itself.

### Fingernail Length

*Rabbi Eliezer* is more lenient: *kedei likrotz betziporen* — it suffices if the hair can be grasped and pulled out by a fingernail, which is presumably shorter than the length needed to fold back to the root.

### Tweezers Length

*Rabbi Akiva* specifies: *kedei she'yihiyu nitalos bezug* — long enough to be removed with tweezers. Rashi apparently understands this as *longer* than the fingernail standard — perhaps because tweezers require a bit more hair to grip than a fingernail — though this is somewhat counterintuitive and the precise reading is not obvious.

### Strict in All Ways

*Amar Rav Chisda amar Mar Ukva*: *halacha kedivarei kulam lehachmir* — the law follows all of the opinions, in the direction of stringency. We are strict in both directions. From the shortest possible length that satisfies any of the three opinions, we are concerned that the hair may already be sufficient — and therefore, in cases where the presence of sufficient hair is a leniency (such as *mi'un* being closed or *chalitzah* being valid), we take even the smallest qualifying hair seriously. Conversely, until the longest standard is met, we remain uncertain that the threshold has been definitively crossed — and therefore, in cases where the hair would serve as a stringency (such as requiring an additional *get* out of doubt), we hold out until the highest standard is satisfied.

### Back to Niddah

With this ruling, the extended treatment of physical development, maturity criteria, the laws of *mi'un*, and the technical dimensions of the two-hair standard comes to a close. Tomorrow the *masechet* returns to its primary subject: *niddah* proper.

---

---

# Niddah 53

## Ketamim Overview

### Ketamim Definition

The daf begins at the Mishnah towards the bottom of 52b, marking a full return to the discussion of *niddah* and shifting into the area of *ketamim* — stains found on a woman's garment. The historical context is important: at a time when laundry was not done daily and blood was prevalent in the marketplace from slaughtered animals, the question of whether a discovered stain genuinely originated from the woman herself was far from settled. Even when we do attribute the stain to her, we do not do so with certainty, and she is therefore rendered only rabbinically *teme'ah* — not a biblical *niddah* — precisely because of that inherent element of doubt.

### Mishnah Haro'ah Ketem

The Mishnah states: *haro'ah ketem harei zo mekukeles ve-chosheshes le-mishum zov* — if a woman finds a stain on her garment, she is *mekukeles* and must be concerned about *zov*. This is the position of Rabbi Meir.

### Mekukeles Explained

The term *mekukeles* — literally "disrupted" or "thrown into disorder" — refers specifically to the disruption of the woman's menstrual cycle counting. The mechanism is as follows: whether a woman is a *niddah* or a *zavah* depends entirely on when she last saw blood. She is a *niddah* for seven days following any bleeding; during the subsequent eleven days, any bleeding renders her a *zavah*, and three consecutive days of bleeding render her a *zavah gedolah*. It is therefore critical to know precisely when she last bled.

When a woman discovers a stain and cannot determine when it appeared on her garment — it could have been today, yesterday, or two weeks ago, since the last time she laundered — she must assume rabbinically that the stain came from her body. She is thus a rabbinic *niddah*. But now, if she bleeds again, she has no way of knowing whether she is bleeding as a *niddah* or as a *zavah*, because she cannot locate the stain in her cycle. That is the meaning of *mekukeles*: her cycle is completely disoriented, and the only way to restore orientation is to wait eighteen days without any bleeding. Any bleeding in the interim leaves her status indeterminate.

### Rabbi Meir Position

Rabbi Meir goes further, adding that she must also be concerned about *zov* — that is, if the stain is large enough, she must worry that it represents three separate episodes of bleeding, potentially all occurring during her *zavah* period, assuming she has not laundered since then. If so, she may be a *zavah*. This reflects Rabbi Meir's maximally stringent approach: he takes the worst-case interpretation of what the stain could represent.

### Rabbis Counter

The *chakhamim* respond: *ein be-ketamim mishum zov* — stains do not carry the concern of *zov*. Their reasoning is one of proportion. This woman is not even a biblical *niddah*; we cannot be certain the stain is from her at all. Since the entire *tumah* here is rabbinic, it would be an overreach to treat the stain as evidence that she is a *zavah*. The Rabbis do not explicitly address whether they agree with the *mekukeles* consequence, leaving open the question of whether their disagreement is with both aspects or only with the *zavah* concern.

---

## Chanina ben Antignos

### Chanina Identity

The Gemara immediately asks: *man chachamim* — who are these Rabbis who deny the *zavah* concern? The answer is Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos, as established from a *baraita* in which he is cited explicitly.

### 3 Garments Case

Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos states: *ketamim ein bahem mishum zav* — stains do not carry the *zov* concern. However, he concedes that there are circumstances in which stains can indeed lead to *zivah* status. He illustrates: *lavsha gimel chalukos badukos la* — if she wore three garments that had been pre-checked and laundered, confirmed clean before she put them on, and she subsequently found a stain on each of them on three separate days, then there is compelling evidence that each stain came from her on a different day. In that case, she must be concerned that she is a *zavah*, or at least a *safek zavah*.

### 2 Days Bleeding

A second case is presented: if she had two days of direct bodily flow during her *zavah* period — genuine *re'iyos* from her body — and then on the third day found a stain on a pre-checked garment, this is even clearer evidence. The Gemara asks why this second case needed to be stated: if three stained garments on three separate days suffice to create concern, surely two confirmed days of direct bleeding followed by a stained garment would do so as well?

The Gemara answers: one might have thought that given the enormity of the supporting evidence in this second case — two confirmed direct *re'iyos* — we should go further and treat her as a *vadai zavah*, allowing her to bring a *korban* and eat it. The *baraita* therefore teaches that even here she remains only a *safek zavah*. The fact that one of the three *re'iyos* is a *ketem* prevents us from ever treating the full status as certain, even when the evidence is overwhelming. This underscores the consistent halakhic principle: a *ketem*, even a well-supported one, always retains an element of *safek*.

### Rava Assessment

Rava remarks: *be-ha zakinu Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos le-rabbanan* — in this argument, Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos prevailed over the Rabbis. The implicit force of his position is more powerful than it might initially appear.

### 3 Beans Argument

Rava articulates Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos's implicit challenge to the Rabbis' position. The Rabbis, following Rabbi Meir, would treat a stain large enough to be divided into three *gris* sizes as evidence of three separate days of bleeding, and thus a *zavah* concern. Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos presses the question: *mai shna pachos mi-gimel grisin be-makom echad de-lo chaishinan* — why are you not concerned if the stain is smaller than three *grisin* in one location? The answer must be that you say it is only two stains, not three. But then, even if the stain equals three *grisin*, why not say that two and a half came from her body and the remainder is attributable to insects — to the *zuhama*, the discharge, that attracts lice? Once you allow that logic at all, it should apply even to a stain of three sizes.

---

## Gris Measurement

### Gris Definition

The *gris* is a measurement used in the laws of *ketamim* to discount smaller stains. Because lice were prevalent and their blood could appear on garments, any stain smaller than the size of a *gris* — a particular type of bean — is automatically attributed to lice and does not render the woman *teme'ah* at all. Furthermore, the operative threshold is not merely a *gris* but a *gris ve-od* — slightly more than a *gris* — in order for the stain to demand halakhic attention.

### 3 Gris Threshold

The Rabbis (following Rabbi Meir) hold that if a stain is large enough to be divided into three portions each the size of a *gris ve-od*, the woman must be concerned that it represents three separate episodes of bleeding on three separate days. She is therefore treated as a *zavah*, at least rabbinically, even though the stain appears in a single location on the garment.

### Chanina Challenge

Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos challenges this reasoning. His argument, as articulated by Rava, is as follows: *mai shna pachos mi-gimel grisin be-makom echad de-lo chaishinan* — you concede that a stain smaller than three *grisin* in one spot does not require *zavah* concern. Why? Presumably because you say it represents only two separate bleedings, not three. But then *shelosha grisin be-makom echad nami neima* — even when it is the size of three *grisin*, why not say the same? Why not say two and a half portions came from her body, while the remainder — *agav zuma dama* — was attracted by the stench, and the blood of insects contributed the rest? This argument is somewhat unusual in construction, since the simpler objection would be that the entire large stain came from a single episode on one day. The framing as "two and a half from her body plus lice" is admittedly strange, and it is equally strange that the very premise for discounting small stains in the first place is the concern for lice — yet here lice are invoked selectively only for one portion. Nevertheless, Rava presents this as the thrust of Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos's challenge, and he considers it a strong one.

### Rabbis Respond

The Rabbis reply: *kivan de'ika le-miplagei ke-chagris ve-yoter be-chol yoma, lo talinan* — since the stain is large enough that one could allocate a *gris ve-od* per day across three days, we do not attribute any portion to an outside cause. Once it reaches that threshold, we assume three separate *re'iyos* on three separate days, rather than any combination of human blood and insect blood. In other words, the size is itself the deciding factor: once divisible into three minimum-sized portions, the worst-case scenario is invoked and the woman is treated as a potential *zavah*.

---

## Spot Location Debate

### Spot vs. Spots

The Gemara now reframes the entire dispute by distinguishing between a single large stain in one location and stains in three separate locations on the same garment. If Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos's challenge about one large spot carries such force, his implied concession is equally significant: *gimmel grisin be-makom echad lo chaishinan* — if it is all one spot, we should not be concerned it is three separate bleedings. This implies, by contrast, that *ha be-gimel mekomos chaishinan* — if the stains appear in three distinct locations on the garment, he would agree it is a concern.

### Concession Terms

However, this creates a difficulty, because Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos was quoted earlier as saying that only three separate garments worn on three separate days suffice to create concern — not three separate spots on the same garment. The Gemara resolves this: when Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos makes his argument against the Rabbis, he argues *le-divreichem* — according to the Rabbis' own logic. Even by their reasoning, a single large spot should not be treated as three separate bleedings. But as for his own position: *li-didi, gimmel chalukin in* — for me, only three separate garments on separate days constitute sufficient evidence. *Gimmel mekomos lo* — three spots on a single garment, even by me, is not enough.

### Settlement

The final resolution of the dispute is that Rabbi Chanina ben Antignos presses the Rabbis: even granting your own framework of treating stains by size, you must at least concede that a single unified spot cannot be presumed to represent three separate bleedings. The Rabbis decline to concede, maintaining that since the stain is divisible into three *gris ve-od* portions, we invoke the three-day assumption regardless of whether it appears as one spot or multiple. Throughout all of this, it must be emphasized that even Rabbi Meir's stricter view is operating entirely in the realm of *de-rabbanan*: there is always an underlying element of *safek* with *ketamim*, and at most, exceptionally well-supported cases may rise to the level of *safek de-oraita*.

---

## Baraita 3 Gris

### Majority Ruling

The Gemara cites a *baraita*: *ha-ro'ah ketem im yesh bo kedei le-chalek gimel grisin va-od — she-hen ke-gris va-od* — if a woman sees a stain large enough to divide into three portions each of *gris va-od*, she must be concerned that she is a *zavah*. If the stain does not reach that threshold, she need not be concerned. This represents the majority position, aligned with Rabbi Meir, and the *stam* formulation of the *baraita* lends it greater authority — which may explain why the Gemara earlier referred to Rabbi Meir's view as the position of the *rabbanan*.

### Minority Stricter

Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra, citing Rabbi Yosi, states: *achas zu ve-achas zu chosheshes* — in both cases, whether the stain is large or small, she must be concerned. Even a stain that is only the size of two *grisin* — not three — requires concern. This would seem to invoke *zavah gedolah* concern even from what appears to be only two *re'iyos*, which is striking since a *zavah gedolah* requires three.

### Rebbi Analysis

Rabbi Rebbi comments: *nirin divrei Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra be-shelo badkah* — the position of Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra makes sense when the woman did not check. When there was no checking at a particular time, we must be more concerned, and therefore even two apparent *re'iyos* might constitute three. When the woman did check — *ve-divrei chachamim be-she-badkah* — the Rabbis' position, limiting the concern to three-sized stains, applies. The Gemara will now unpack precisely what "checking" and "not checking" mean in this context.

---

## Bein Hashmashos

### Twilight Effect

The mechanism by which two stains can count as three *re'iyos* is now explained. If a woman bleeds during *bein hashmashos* — the twilight period between one day and the next — that single episode counts as two separate days of *re'iyah*: once for the outgoing day and once for the incoming day. If she then sees on the following full day, she has accumulated three *re'iyos* in total, rendering her a *zavah gedolah*, despite only two episodes of visible bleeding.

This is admittedly a surprising ruling, since ordinarily *bein hashmashos* is treated as an unresolved doubt — it is either day or night, but one or the other, not both. One might therefore argue that even if bleeding occurred during *bein hashmashos*, it cannot count as two days simultaneously, since the bleeding itself is of a minimum *gris* size and did not definitively span both sides of the transition. The Gemara does not pause to unpack this assumption but proceeds with it: once we have discounted the lice concern by virtue of the stain's minimum size, we attribute the entire *gris* to her body, and if it can be assumed to have straddled the transition of the day, it counts as two.

This immediately raises the question of what "checking" means in Rabbi Rebbi's formulation. It now emerges that the critical question is: can we eliminate the *bein hashmashos* possibility from the table? If we can, then a stain of only two *grisin* counts as only two *re'iyos* and no *zavah gedolah* concern arises. If we cannot eliminate it, then even two *re'iyos* may in fact be three, and concern is warranted.

### Rava Discussion

Rava reports that he came upon yeshiva students who were framing the debate as follows: *kegon she-badkah atzmah ve-lo badkah chalukah* — she examined herself directly but did not examine her garment. This is the normal *ketem* scenario — there is no direct evidence of bodily flow, only a stain of uncertain origin. The students then specify the precise constructed case: *de-af atzmah lo badkah ela bein hashmashos de-Rabbi Yehuda, u-vein hashmashos de-Rabbi Yosi lo badkah* — she examined herself only during the *bein hashmashos* of Rabbi Yehuda, but not during the *bein hashmashos* of Rabbi Yosi.

### Twilight Periods

The reference here is to the well-known dispute in *Shabbat* about the duration of *bein hashmashos*. Rabbi Yehuda holds that *bein hashmashos* lasts for half a *mil* — approximately nine minutes — beginning from sunset. After those nine minutes, it is definitively night. Rabbi Yosi, by contrast, holds that *bein hashmashos* is *ke-heref ayin* — a split second — and the Gemara here assumes that this split second occurs immediately after Rabbi Yehuda's nine-minute period concludes. So from sunset: nine minutes of Rabbi Yehuda's *bein hashmashos*, and then a single moment of Rabbi Yosi's *bein hashmashos*, after which it is indisputably night.

### Constructed Case

In the constructed case, the woman examined herself throughout Rabbi Yehuda's nine-minute *bein hashmashos*, but not during the moment immediately following. The Rabbis hold that *bein hashmashos de-Rabbi Yosi layla hu* — by Rabbi Yosi's period it is already definitely night, so she has effectively eliminated the *bein hashmashos* possibility entirely. At most she had two *re'iyos*, and no *zavah* concern arises unless the stain is three-sized. Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra in the name of Rabbi Yosi dissents: *bein hashmashos de-Rabbi Yosi safek hu* — that split-second moment is still a genuine doubt, and since she was not checking during it, we cannot rule out that a *re'iyah* occurred then. Therefore even two apparent *re'iyos* must be treated as potentially three.

Rava notes that this framing is itself problematic. The easy version of the debate would simply be: do we care about *bein hashmashos* at all? But the students are saying that everybody agrees *bein hashmashos* is on the table — the only question is whether it can be removed from consideration, and if so, by what means.

### Eliminate Twilight

Rava responds to the students: *de-maliya yadah kol bein hashmashos shafir d'mei* — if she was examining herself continuously for the entire nine-minute *bein hashmashos*, inserting her hand throughout that entire period, then one could argue she has eliminated the *bein hashmashos* possibility. But the students' scenario — checking "during the *bein hashmashos* of Rabbi Yehuda" — might mean only occasional checking during that period, not continuous. In that case, *shema mi-she-asi yadah ra'asah* — perhaps she bled in the moment between one check and the next. That cannot be the scenario being debated, since such a case would always remain unresolved.

The students respond to Rava: *ke-she-nishnis yadah bein eineiha kol bein hashmashos* — yes, she was checking herself continuously throughout the entire nine minutes. The image is striking: continuous self-examination for the duration of that window, analogous to keeping one's finger in one's eye without a break. The Gemara acknowledges that this is a highly constructed scenario, but proceeds on its terms. The debate then is not over whether *bein hashmashos* matters, but over whether a woman who has conclusively eliminated Rabbi Yehuda's nine-minute *bein hashmashos* has also eliminated Rabbi Yosi's single-second *bein hashmashos*, which may or may not fall within the same window.

---

## Rebbi Twilight

### Rebbi Concedes

Rabbi Rebbi states: *nirin divrei Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra be-she-lo badkah* — I acknowledge that the position of Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra is correct when there was no checking. When *bein hashmashos* has not been accounted for, the concern of three *re'iyos* is justified. *Ve-divrei chachamim be-she-badkah* — and the Rabbis' lenient position applies when she did check.

### Conditions

The Gemara presses: *mai lo badkah* — what exactly constitutes "not checking"? If it means she checked during Rabbi Yehuda's nine minutes but not during Rabbi Yosi's single second, *michlal de-Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra savar af al gav de-lo badkah be-travaihu lo chaisha* — it would imply that Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra holds that even without checking either period there is no concern. But *ha lo badkah* — she did not check at all! How can there be no concern? The Gemara concludes that "not checking" must mean she did not check during either period — neither Rabbi Yehuda's nine minutes nor Rabbi Yosi's moment. And "checking" — for purposes of when Rabbi Rebbi concedes to the Rabbis — must mean checking both windows.

### Contradiction Found

With this framing, a difficulty emerges: *kashya de-Rebbi ad Rebbi* — Rabbi Rebbi contradicts himself. When he says he concedes to Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra in the case of "no checking," and to the Rabbis in the case of "checking," it seems that one of his concessions implies a ruling about *bein hashmashos* that conflicts with what the other implies. Specifically, if he concedes to the Rabbis only when both periods were checked, then checking only Rabbi Yehuda's nine minutes would leave him aligned with Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra's concern — meaning Rabbi Rebbi views Rabbi Yosi's *bein hashmashos* as a genuine *safek*. But then, when he says he concedes to Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra only when there was no checking at all, he implies that checking Rabbi Yehuda's nine minutes suffices to resolve the concern — contradicting the previous implication.

### No Checking Agreement

The Gemara resolves this: *hachi ka'amar* — here is the correct reading of Rabbi Rebbi's statement. Rabbi Rebbi is not staking out a middle position between the two disputants; rather, he is clarifying the precise boundaries of their dispute. The Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra disagree only in the case where Rabbi Yehuda's nine minutes were checked but Rabbi Yosi's moment was not. In that constructed case, the Rabbis say *bein hashmashos* is off the table, while Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra says it remains a concern. But when she did not check at all — not even the nine minutes — *af chachamim lo nechleku alav*, even the Rabbis agree with Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra that *bein hashmashos* remains a genuine concern. The entire dispute is confined to that single precise scenario: checked Rabbi Yehuda's window, missed Rabbi Yosi's moment.

---

## Two Versions

### Baraita Conflict

The Gemara now raises a *remiya* — a contradiction from another *baraita*. That *baraita* states: *ha-ro'ah ketem, damyah merubah chosheshes, damyah mu'etes einah chosheshes* — if the stain is large, she must be concerned; if small, she need not be. This is attributed to Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra in the name of Rabbi Yosi. But this directly contradicts the position we have been attributing to Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra — namely, that even a smaller stain (two sizes rather than three) requires concern, because of the *bein hashmashos* possibility.

### Rebbi Small Stain

In that same *baraita*, Rabbi Rebbi states: *ani shamati mimenu she-achas zu ve-achas zu chosheshes* — I heard directly from Rabbi Yosi that in both cases — large stain and small stain alike — she must be concerned. Rabbi Yosi then explained this to him with an analogy: a *niddah* who did not perform a *hefsek tahara* — a bodily examination — toward the end of day seven, from *minchah* onward, cannot assume she is clean and immerse that night. Even if she checked earlier in the week, we assume worst-case and require a fresh examination near day's end, lest she restarted bleeding in the interim. Similarly, a woman who already has evidence of staining should be treated with the same worst-case orientation, and we do not relax the concern for *bein hashmashos* simply because the stain is small.

Rabbi Rebbi then adds: *nirin devarav — ve-nirin dvarav, keshebadkah* — I find his position persuasive, and specifically it applies when she did check. And now the Gemara applies the same analytical pressure that it did before: *mai badkah* — what constitutes checking? If it means checking during Rabbi Yehuda's period but not Rabbi Yosi's, then Rabbi Rebbi's concession would imply that Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra holds there is no concern even without checking Rabbi Yosi's moment. But *ha lo badkah* — she did not check that period. And on the other side, if Rabbi Rebbi says he concedes to the Rabbis when she did check, his concession implies that the Rabbis would hold there is no concern even without any checking — which is equally untenable. The same contradiction recurs. *Kashya de-Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra a-de-Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra* — Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra contradicts himself.

### Two Tannaim

The Gemara resolves: *trei tannai ve-aliba de-Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra* — there are two different Tannaim each transmitting a different version of Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra's ruling.

### Twilight Timing

The two versions reflect a disagreement about the precise temporal relationship between Rabbi Yehuda's *bein hashmashos* and Rabbi Yosi's. One Tanna holds: Rabbi Yosi's moment comes *after* Rabbi Yehuda's nine minutes — it is a distinct period that follows sequentially. Therefore, even if a woman checked the entire nine minutes, she has not covered Rabbi Yosi's *bein hashmashos*, and the concern for a three-count remains. The other Tanna holds: *bein hashmashos de-Rabbi Yosi mishach shaycha be-de-Rabbi Yehuda* — Rabbi Yosi's moment falls *within* Rabbi Yehuda's nine-minute window, not after it. If that is so, then a woman who checked the full nine minutes has covered Rabbi Yosi's moment as well, and *bein hashmashos* is entirely eliminated from consideration. The disagreement between the two versions of Rabbi Yehuda ben Agra's ruling is thus not about the substance of the *zavah* concern, but about this underlying dispute regarding the sequential or overlapping relationship of the two *bein hashmashos* periods.

---

## Retroactive Tumah

### Rabbi Strict

The Gemara transitions to a *baraita* addressing retroactive *tumah* from *ketamim*: how far backward in time does a discovered stain render the woman *teme'ah* with respect to things she may have touched? The general principle for a woman who actually saw blood is twenty-four hours retroactively. But for *ketamim*, because the stain may have been on the garment for an extended period — potentially since the last time she laundered — Rabbi Rebbi holds that she is retroactively *teme'ah* for herself and for *kodashim* going all the way back to the last laundering. This is in one respect *more* strict than a direct *re'iyah*.

### Shimon Lenient

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar disagrees: *shelo yehei ketamah chamur me-reiyatah* — the law of stains should not be more strict than the law of actual seeing. When she actually saw blood, retroactive concern extends only twenty-four hours. For a stain, she should be no more concerned than that.

### Sacrifice Problem

The Gemara challenges: but you yourself, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, acknowledge that *kodashim* she touched are affected going all the way back to the last laundering. That is more strict than the twenty-four-hour rule of actual seeing. You are already conceding a greater stringency.

### Full Correction

The Gemara therefore corrects the text of the *baraita*: *tani hachi* — read it as follows. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says: *af kodashim einah metama'ah, shelo yehei ketamah chamur me-reiyatah le-chol davar* — even *kodashim* she is not required to declare retroactively *teme'ah* beyond what the rules of actual seeing would impose. There is no dimension — not for herself, not for *kodashim* — in which *ketamim* should impose greater strictness than a direct *re'iyah*. Whether Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar would also impose at least twenty-four hours retroactively, or whether his position is even more lenient, remains unresolved.

---

## Stain Connection

### 24 Hour Rule

The Gemara cites another *baraita*: *ra'asah ketem ve-achar kach ra'asah dam, tola ketamah be-reiyatah me-eis le-eis, divrei Rabbi* — if a woman found a stain and then, within twenty-four hours, she saw actual bleeding from her body, she may attribute the stain retroactively to that bleeding episode. This is enormously consequential: rather than worrying that the stain had been on her garment for weeks, she can assume it arrived just now, connected to this *re'iyah*. And further — since we are now confident enough to treat the stain as the beginning of her *niddah* period, her counting of the seven days begins from the time of the stain, not from the time of the direct bleeding. This is an instance where a *ketem* is treated with the weight of genuine *niddah* blood, potentially even on a *de-oraita* level, given how much supporting evidence we have.

### Same Day Stricter

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar disagrees: *yomo* — the stain and the bleeding must occur on the same halakhic day, not merely within twenty-four hours. If she found the stain on Wednesday and bled on Thursday — even if fewer than twenty-four hours elapsed — he does not connect them.

### Rebbi Agrees

Rabbi Rebbi comments: *me-ein dvarav mi-dvarai* — the position of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar makes more sense than my own, *she-hu metaknah va-ani me-avtah* — he is helping her while I am burdening her. Rabbi Rebbi acknowledges that a position more favorable to the woman is preferable.

### Consequences

The Gemara pushes back: how is Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar helping her? By limiting the connection to the same halakhic day, he is actually giving her *less* time to make the attribution — twenty-four hours is more generous than "same day only." Ravina suggests reversing the attributions. Rav Nachman, however, argues that no reversal is necessary: *lo le'olam lo teipach*. There is a dimension in which Rabbi Rebbi's twenty-four-hour rule is in fact more strict than Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's same-day rule, and it concerns the transition from *niddah* to *zavah* status. If the stain is found on Tuesday and bleeding follows on Wednesday, Rabbi Rebbi — who allows a twenty-four-hour connection — will say that her *niddah* counting began Tuesday. If she then bleeds again on the following Tuesday, that falls in her *zavah* period and renders her a *zavah*. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who does not connect across halakhic days in this case, would start her *niddah* count from Wednesday's direct bleeding — meaning the subsequent Tuesday's bleeding falls within her *niddah* period, not her *zavah* period, and she may immerse that night. So *she-hu metakein hilchos niddah li-yedei zivah* — Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar fixes the *niddah* laws in a way that avoids pulling her into *zavah* status, while Rabbi Rebbi's rule can inadvertently do so.

---

## Hefsek Tahara

### Question Asked

Rav Zeira poses a question to Rav Assi: *ketamim tzerichin hefsek tahara o lo* — does a woman who is *teme'ah* by virtue of a stain require a *hefsek tahara* before immersing in the *mikvah*? The issue is significant: for a *niddah*, a *hefsek tahara* — a bodily examination at the end of day seven — is required before immersion. But a woman made *teme'ah* by a *ketem* is only rabbinically *teme'ah*, and since there is always doubt whether the stain genuinely came from her, one might argue she need not perform the examination. Alternatively, since it was not a direct *re'iyah* but only a small stain, perhaps the requirement to actively confirm cessation of bleeding does not apply.

### Silence

Rav Assi was silent and gave no answer.

### Debate Later

On a subsequent occasion, Rav Zeira found Rav Assi engaged in learning and presenting the ruling of Rabbi Rebbi: that a woman who finds a stain and then bleeds within twenty-four hours may retroactively connect the stain to the bleeding. In connection with this, Rav Assi cited the dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan.

### Reish Lakish

Reish Lakish holds: *ve-hu she-badkah* — the ruling that we connect the stain to the subsequent bleeding and begin the *niddah* count from the stain applies only when she checked herself on the night between the stain and the direct *re'iyah*. By performing that check — in preparation, as it were, to immerse — she herself demonstrates that she treats the stain as the beginning of her *niddah* period. Without such a check, she has implicitly indicated that she does not attribute the stain to herself, and therefore the stain cannot retroactively serve as the opening of her *niddah* count.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *af al pi she-lo badkah* — even if she did not check, the objective fact of the stain followed by bleeding within twenty-four hours is sufficient to connect them. Her personal conduct — whether or not she checked — is irrelevant to the objective halakhic determination.

### Recognition

Rav Zeira then said to Rav Assi: from the fact that Reish Lakish requires a checking — *mikhlal de-komi tzricha hefsek tahara* — you can infer that *ketamim* do indeed require a *hefsek tahara*, because the checking that Reish Lakish references *is* the *hefsek tahara*. Rav Assi confirmed: *in* — yes, you are right. Rav Zeira then noted that he had asked Rav Assi this very question many times and received no answer. Rav Assi replied: *agav shitpach asya li* — it arose through the flow of my learning. Caught in the rhythm of the discussion, the answer surfaced in a way it had not before. Whether the *hefsek tahara* required for *ketamim* operates in precisely the same way as for a full *niddah* status — given that in the Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan case there is an actual subsequent *re'iyah*, making it at least partially *de-oraita* — is a question that *Tosafot* takes up separately, but the basic principle is established here: *ketamim* do require a *hefsek tahara*.

---

---

# Niddah 55

## Niddah Blood & Tumah

### Daf Overview

Daf 55a opens a new *perek*, and while the transitions from topic to topic can be difficult to track at first glance, the underlying thematic logic is clear. The discussion has shifted away from the status of the woman as a *niddah* and toward a related but distinct question: the blood she produces, the menstrual blood that renders her a *niddah*, is itself a source of *tumah* for anyone who touches it. From there, the *Gemara* broadens its inquiry to cover other substances that are sources of *tumah*, examining each one with a two-part analysis: first, how do we know the substance is *tamei* at all, and second, in what state must it be in order to transmit *tumah*?

### Mishna Categories

The *Mishna* established that only two substances remain a source of *tumah* even when dried out: the blood of a *niddah* and the flesh of a corpse (*basar hamet*). All other substances on the list are only *tamei* when they are moist, not when they have dried. The *Gemara* proceeds through the list, treating each substance in turn.

---

## Basar Hamet

### Resh Lakish vs R. Yochan…

The *Gemara* begins with *basar hamet* — the flesh of a corpse — and asks: *minalan*, where do we know that the flesh of a dead body is itself *tamei*? The Torah's discussion of a *meit* speaks of the corpse as a whole; it is evident that one who touches a corpse or is under the same roof as one becomes *tamei*. But what is the source that individual portions of the body, specifically the flesh, are *tamei* as well?

Two *Amoraim* offer competing derivations. Resh Lakish cites the verse *l'chol tumato* — "for all of his impurities" — understood to mean that all things which separate from the body of a *meit* are also sources of *tumah*. Rabbi Yochanan, by contrast, derives it from the phrase *etzem adam* — "the bone of a man" — read as an equation: a bone is compared to the man himself. Just as a bone is *tamei* even when dry, so too any part of the body is *tamei* even in a dry state.

Critically, both *Amoraim* are not merely proving that flesh is *tamei*; they are simultaneously proving that it is *tamei* regardless of its state, whether moist or desiccated. Resh Lakish achieves this through the inclusive language of *l'chol tumato*, which encompasses the substance in any condition. Rabbi Yochanan achieves it by analogy to bone, which is inherently dry and yet *tamei*, establishing that dryness is no bar to *tumah*.

### Crumbling Flesh

The *Gemara* then asks: *mai beinaihu*, what practical difference does it make whether we derive the rule from *l'chol tumato* or from the analogy to bone? The answer is a case of *d'afri aprichei* — flesh so desiccated that it will crumble or shatter upon contact. On the one hand, *l'chol tumato* is maximally inclusive and would seem to encompass even such pulverized flesh. On the other hand, such crumbling flesh is no longer analogous to a bone, which is dry but solid; therefore, if one derives the rule solely from the bone analogy, this extreme case would not be *tamei*.

The *Gemara* then raises a challenge from a *Mishna* in *Ohalot*: *basar hamet shehuphrach* — flesh of a corpse that has been so thoroughly dried that it crumbles — is *tahor*. Does this not show that the degree of dryness does matter? The *Gemara* resolves this: the *Mishna* in *Ohalot* refers to flesh that has disintegrated to the point of becoming actual dust (*d'ikmach v'havei afra*). In that case, everyone agrees it is no longer considered flesh at all and is *tahor*. The dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan concerns only an intermediate case: flesh so dry it shatters, but not so far gone as to become dust.

### Body Parts & Intrinsicne…

The *Gemara* next cites a separate *Beraita*: *kol shebames metamei* — everything in a dead body causes *tumah* — *chutz min hashinayim v'hase'ar v'hatzipporen*, with the exception of teeth, hair, and fingernails. However, *b'sha'at chiburan hakol tamei* — while they are still attached, everything is *tamei*; only when separated do these three fail to convey *tumah*.

What makes these three items special? The question is pressing particularly for Resh Lakish, whose source — *l'chol tumato* — is maximally inclusive and should, it would seem, encompass teeth, hair, and fingernails as much as anything else. Even Rabbi Yochanan's more limited derivation from *etzem adam* requires explanation, since one might have included these parts under the general category of body components.

### Gizo Machlif Principle

Rav Adda bar Ahava offers the controlling principle. He explains that even according to the inclusive derivation, there is a limiting criterion derived from the comparison to *etzem* — bone. Bone is *tamei* because it has two properties simultaneously: (1) it is created with the person (*nivra imo*), and (2) it does not replace itself (*ein gizo machlif*). For something to be an intrinsic part of the corpse that conveys *tumah* when separated, it must share both characteristics.

This phrase *gizo machlif* — literally, "its trunk replaces itself" — is familiar from the realm of *berachot*, where the same terminology distinguishes between trees whose trunk survives from year to year (*ein gizo machlif*, and one recites *borei pri ha-etz*) and plants that die back and regrow annually (*gizo machlif*, and one recites *borei pri ha-adamah*). Here, the principle is applied analogously to parts of the human body: a part that will regrow after being cut off is not considered truly intrinsic to the body in the same way that bone is.

Teeth are excluded because they are not created with a person — a newborn has no teeth — satisfying the first criterion for exclusion. But what of hair and fingernails? They are indeed created with a person. The *Gemara* therefore amends Rav Adda bar Ahava's ruling: the exclusion of hair and fingernails rests on the second criterion — *gizo machlif*. Cut hair grows back; cut fingernails grow back. Because they regenerate, they are not considered as integral to the body as bone or flesh, and therefore when separated they do not convey *tumah*.

### Skin's Status

With this principle established, the *Gemara* raises the question of skin (*or*): *de-gizo machlif* — the skin replaces itself, does it not? If you suffer a minor cut, the skin heals over. And yet, a *Mishna* elsewhere states that *or haadam*, the skin of a human being, is *tamei* like flesh. How can this be, if skin regrows and therefore should be classified alongside hair and fingernails as *tahor* when separated?

The *Gemara* marshals evidence from *Ohalot* that skin replaces itself. A *Mishna* regarding *treifot* records a debate about an animal that has been completely flayed (*hagluda*): Rabbi Meir rules it is still kosher (*machshir*), while the Sages rule it is a *treifa* (*poslin*). The *Gemara* initially suggests that even the Sages' ruling that it is a *treifa* does not mean they believe skin cannot regenerate; rather, they hold that while the skin would eventually grow back, the animal would be fatally exposed to the elements in the interim and would die first (*d'adehachi vahachi shalta beih avira u'mait*). Accordingly, everyone may agree that skin regenerates. Yet despite this, a separate *Mishna* includes human skin among things whose *or* is *kivsaran* — like their flesh — in terms of *tumah*. The question therefore stands: why is skin *tamei* if it grows back?

### Ulla on Skin

The *Gemara* cites a statement of Ulla that reframes the entire issue: *devar Torah, or adam tahor* — biblically speaking, the skin of a human being is actually *tahor*. The *Mishna*'s ruling that skin is *tamei* is therefore not a biblical *din* but a rabbinic enactment.

### Skin Gezerah

The reason for this rabbinic measure is startling. The *Gemara* explains: *gezeira shema ya'aseh adam orot aviv v'immo shetichin lachamor* — there was a concern that a person might take the skin of his father and mother and fashion it into a pad for a donkey's saddle. To forestall this grotesque possibility, the Sages declared human skin *tamei*, thereby ensuring that people would keep their distance from it rather than processing it for utilitarian purposes.

This explanation raises a natural question, which *Tosafot* addresses: is one not already prohibited from deriving benefit from a corpse (*issurei hanaah*)? *Tosafot* offers two answers. First, in certain contexts — particularly among *kohanim* and those who were especially rigorous about *tumah va-taharah* — the concern of *tumah* was in practice more effective as a deterrent than other prohibitions. The *Gemara* elsewhere notes similarly that the Sages declared *pigul* to be *tamei* because this was more likely to deter *kohanim* from the violation than the direct biblical prohibition itself; the psychology of *tumah* as a category of taboo carries a practical weight that transcends the formal severity of the prohibition. Second, *Tosafot* suggests that perhaps skin may not be included in the prohibition of deriving benefit from a corpse in the first place — paralleling the very question that is being discussed here about what constitutes an intrinsic part of the body for purposes of *tumah*.

### Skin as Leather

At this point, the *Gemara* clarifies where Ulla's statement was originally made. It was not a freestanding comment about skin's *tumah* status in general; rather, it was said in response to a specific clause at the end of the *Mishna* dealing with different types of skin. That *Mishna* states: *v'kullan she'ibadan o she'hilach bahen*, all those categories of skin that are *tamei* — including human skin — if one were to process them into leather or subject them to the treatment used to convert skin into leather (*kedei avodah*), they become *tahor*, since they have transformed into a new identity as leather. The single exception is *chutz me'or adam* — human skin, which even after processing remains *tamei*.

### Skin Regeneration

It is in this context that Ulla speaks: *devar Torah, or adam ki ibdo tahor* — fundamentally, even human skin, once processed into leather, would be *tahor*, just like any other processed skin. The rabbinic exception — that even processed human skin remains *tamei* — is the *gezeira* against making one's parents' skin into leather goods.

The *Gemara* then presents an alternative version (*ika de'amri*) of the entire preceding discussion that reverses the initial premise. In this version, the *Gemara* begins by assuming that skin does *not* regenerate. How is this established? From the very same *treifa* debate — but now read differently. According to this version, the Sages who rule the flayed animal a *treifa* do so because they genuinely believe the skin will not grow back. And even Rabbi Meir, who rules it is not a *treifa*, does not hold that the skin regenerates; rather, he holds that the exposed flesh itself will toughen and harden (*de-kari bisra ve-chaya*), providing adequate protection for the animal to survive, even without skin regrowth.

If skin does not replace itself, then according to the first criterion it should be *tamei de'oraita* — biblically *tamei* — and the *Mishna*'s ruling presents no difficulty. The difficulty is now with Ulla's statement that skin is biblically *tahor*. The resolution is the same as before: Ulla's statement refers specifically to skin that has been processed into leather. Once converted to leather, human skin is fundamentally *tahor* — this is the biblical rule. Only the rabbinic *gezeira* keeps it *tamei* even after processing, to discourage people from converting their relatives' skin into leather goods. The full legal picture, then, is: untreated human skin is *tamei de'oraita* (since it does not regenerate), while processed human skin is *tahor de'oraita* but *tamei mide'rabbanan* due to the *gezeira*.

The *Gemara*'s willingness to pivot entirely between these two versions based on competing readings of the *treifot* debate is itself striking — empirical certainty about whether skin regenerates is effectively resolved by which way one reads a *tannaitic* dispute, rather than by direct observation, though it is noted that the practical reality likely depends on the extent of the wound: minor abrasions heal without scarring, while large areas of lost skin require grafting.

### Flesh Healing

The *Gemara* finally addresses the last apparent difficulty: flesh (*basar*) itself heals — if you lose a piece of flesh from a cut or wound, does it not grow back, placing it in the same category as hair and fingernails? Mar bar Rav Ashi responds: *basar na'asa mekomo tzaleket* — when flesh heals, the area becomes a scar. Healing and complete regeneration are not the same thing. The flesh does not truly replace itself; it leaves a scar, meaning the original tissue is gone and has not been fully reconstituted. This distinguishes flesh from hair and fingernails, which do fully replace themselves, and confirms that flesh remains in the category of *tamei* even when separated from the corpse.

---

## Zov Tumah

### Zovo Tamei Verse

Having completed the discussion of *basar hamet*, the *Gemara* turns to the second category of the *Mishna*: substances that are only *tamei* when moist, not when dried. The first of these is *hazov* — the penile discharge that renders a man a *zav*. The question is not whether the *zav* himself is *tamei* — that is explicit in the Torah — but whether the discharge itself is a source of *tumah* that makes others who come into contact with it *tamei*.

The *Beraita* cites the verse: *ish ish ki yihyeh zav mibsaro, zovo tamei hu* — "a man, a man who has a flow from his flesh, his flow is *tamei*" (Vayikra 15:2). This appears to state directly that the *zov* itself is *tamei*, not merely the man who experiences it.

### Kal Vachomer & Scapegoat

But the *Beraita* itself raises a prior question: is a verse even necessary? Could one not derive the *tumah* of *zov* through a *kal vachomer*? If the *zov* causes the man to become *tamei*, surely the *zov* itself should be an *av hatumah*.
