The *Beraita* deflects this *kal vachomer* with the case of the *seir hamishtaleach*, the scapegoat sent off the cliff on Yom Kippur: the person who dispatches the goat becomes *tamei*, yet the goat itself is *tahor* to the touch. Here, then, is a case where something causes another to become *tamei* while itself remaining *tahor*. The same might be true of *zov*: the man becomes *tamei* through it, yet the discharge itself might be *tahor*. Hence the explicit verse *zovo tamei hu* is needed to establish that the *zov* is itself a source of *tumah*.

### Zov Tumah Severity

Knowing that *zov* is *tamei* does not yet tell us to what degree it is *tamei*. There are three ascending levels of *tumah* in this domain. At the lowest level, a substance is *tamei* only through touch, and the clothes one is wearing do not become *tamei* — analogous to a *sheretz* (dead rodent). At the middle level, when one carries the substance, both the person and his clothes become *tamei*, but touching it alone does not make one's clothes *tamei* — analogous to a *neveilah* (a carcass of an animal). At the highest level, even touching the substance makes both the person and his clothes *tamei* simultaneously — as is the case with a *zav*, a *zavah*, a *niddah*, and a *meit*.

### Zov vs. Semen

The *Gemara* asks: perhaps *zov* is only *tamei* by touch, like a *sheretz*? Rav Bibi bar Abaye responds: we do not need a verse to establish that touching *zov* makes one *tamei*, because that is already derivable from *shichvat zera* — seminal emission. The Torah explicitly states that semen is *tamei* to the touch. Since the *zov* of a single flow renders the man temporarily equivalent to a *baal keri* (one who has experienced a seminal emission), we know that the *zov* is at least as *tamei* as semen. Therefore the additional verse — *zovo tamei hu* — must be doing more work: it is elevating the *tumah* of *zov* beyond touch alone, to include the category of carrying (*masa*) as well.

But even this may not bring us to the highest level. Perhaps *zov* is in the middle category — *tamei* by *masa* (such that both person and clothes are affected when carrying it), but not by mere touch. That is analogous to the *neveilah*: carrying it makes both person and clothes *tamei*, but touching it only affects the person. How do we know *zov* rises to the highest level?

### Hazav Et Zovo

The *Gemara* cites a *Beraita* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael interpreting the verse: *Hazav et zovo*, "the one who flows his flow." The juxtaposition of the *zav* and his *zov* in this phrase creates a direct equation: just as the *zav* himself transmits *tumah* through both touch and carrying, and in both cases makes both the person and his clothes *tamei*, so too the *zov* is exactly as *tamei* as the *zav* himself. By this equation, *zov* reaches the highest level of *tumah* — an *av hatumah* that makes both person and clothes *tamei* even through touch alone.

### Both Verses Needed

This raises an immediate question: if the verse *Hazav et zovo* already establishes that *zov* is fully equivalent to the *zav* in *tumah*, why is the earlier verse *zovo tamei hu* still needed?

Rav Yehuda of Diskarta answers: without *zovo tamei hu*, one would never have concluded that the *zov* is itself *tamei* in the first place. The *seir hamishtaleach* objection applies: one could maintain that the *zov* makes the *zav tamei* while itself remaining *tahor*. In that case, the verse *Hazav et zovo* would carry an entirely different interpretive burden — it would be read not as a statement about the *tumah* of *zov*, but as the source for determining how many instances of *zov* one must experience and whether *oness* (flow due to external causes) counts. Specifically: *zov* (one flow) — *zovo* (two flows) — *Hazav et zovo l'zachar v'l'nekeivah* provides the basis for distinguishing between the first two flows (where only non-*oness* counts, the "male" standard) and the third flow (which must be brought as a *korban* even if due to *oness*, equated with the "female" standard). The entire verse, in this reading, is about quantifying and qualifying the flows, not about the *tumah* status of the *zov* as a substance.

Therefore *zovo tamei hu* is indispensable: it first establishes that the *zov* is itself *tamei*. Only once that is known can we return to *Hazav et zovo* and apply it to determine the *degree* of *tumah* — that the *zov* is as *tamei* as the *zav* himself. Both verses are necessary and neither is redundant.

No verse is needed to restrict *tumah* of *zov* to its moist state alone; this follows naturally from the description of the substance as a "flow." If there is no liquid flow, there is nothing being described by the verse, and dried residue would simply not be encompassed by the verse's terms.

---

## Spit & Phlegm

### Rok Proof

The *Gemara* now turns to *rok* — the spit of a *zav* — which the *Mishna* lists among the substances that are *tamei* only when moist. As before, the *Gemara* first establishes the source of *rok*'s *tumah* and then its degree. The *Beraita* cites the verse: *vechi yarok hazav batahor vechibes begadav verachatz bamayim vetamei ad ha'arev* — "if the *zav* spits upon a *tahor* person, he shall wash his garments, immerse in water, and be *tamei* until evening" (Vayikra 15:8). This verse makes *rok* the most directly scripturally attested of all the fluids under discussion, since the Torah speaks about spitting explicitly.

### Spitting & Yibuma

One might have thought that the mere act of a *zav* spitting in someone's direction — without the spit actually making contact — renders that person *tamei*, on analogy with the *yibuma* case, where the act of spitting (*yareka b'fanav*, "she shall spit before him") does not require the spit to physically strike the *yavam*. The *Beraita* therefore reads *batahor* — "upon the *tahor*" — to indicate that actual contact is required: *ad sheyiga batahor*, it must touch the *tahor* person. *Tosafot* notes that once we establish from this verse that *rok* must actually make contact to convey *tumah*, one might revisit the *yibuma* case and argue the spit must hit there too — though the *Beraita* accepts the distinction.

### Phlegm Types

The verse teaches that *rok* itself is an *av hatumah*. But what about related secretions? *Keicho* and *niaro* — different types of phlegm (Rashi identifies them as phlegm produced by a deep cough versus a surface cough) — and *mei ha-af* — mucus — are not explicitly mentioned in the verse. The *Beraita* derives their inclusion from the prefix *v'* in *vechi yarok*, a form of expansion: anything similar to spit that fits the description of *mit'agel v'yotzei* (collecting in the body and then coming out) is included.

### Rok Severity

Having established that *rok* is *tamei*, the *Gemara* proceeds through the same three-level analysis used for *zov*. Perhaps *rok* is only *tamei* at the lowest level — touch only, like a *sheretz*?

### Drashot Ladder

Resh Lakish, in the name of the school of Rabbi Yishmael, derives from the word *batahor* in the verse a series of escalating conclusions. First, the verse uses *batahor* rather than *b'adam*, which would have been the natural phrasing if the Torah only meant to say the spit must hit the person directly. The prefix *b-* in *batahor* is read to mean "on something belonging to the *tahor* person" — i.e., something he is holding or carrying. This establishes that even if the spit hits only an object the *tahor* person is carrying, that person becomes *tamei* — moving *rok* to the middle level where *masa* is sufficient.

But the verse goes further: by using the word *batahor* — literally "on the *tahor* one" — it invokes the concept of *taharah* in a context where *tumah* results, signaling that even a case where one would normally be *tahor* is here made *tamei*. The *Gemara* identifies this as the case of *maga neveilah*: normally, touching a *neveilah* makes only the person *tamei*, not his clothes. Here the verse teaches that even this level of contact — mere touching, as opposed to carrying — will make both the person and his clothes *tamei*. This elevates *rok* to the highest level of *tumah*.

The *Gemara* confirms: *mai batahor shma mina tarti* — from *batahor* we derive two things simultaneously: both the *masa* rule (that even carrying an object struck by the spit conveys *tumah*) and the highest-level rule (that even touching makes clothes *tamei*). This is a somewhat compressed derivation, and the *Gemara* resolves the apparent redundancy by noting that these two conclusions are extracted together from the single term.

As with *zov*, the moist-state requirement for *rok* needs no explicit verse; the substance is inherently liquid by definition and the verse would not encompass dried residue.

### Mucus Debate

The *Gemara* pauses on the case of *mei ha-af* — mucus — which appears in the *Beraita* but is conspicuously absent from the *Mishna*'s list of the nine fluids of a *zav*, as will become apparent. Rav limits the *tumah*-conveying status of mucus to a specific circumstance: *b'nigrar derech ha-peh* — when it drains through the mouth, i.e., when nasal secretions drain into the back of the throat and are expelled through the mouth. In that case, Rav explains, it is *tumah*-bearing not because the mucus itself is a *mayan* (wellspring of *tumah*), but because *lefi she-ee efshar l'mei ha-af b'lo tzichtzuchei ha-rok* — mucus that comes out through the mouth cannot come without traces of saliva (*rok*) mixed in. The *tumah* of the mucus in this case is effectively the *tumah* of the *rok* it carries.

### R. Yochanan vs. Rav

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *afilu v'nigran derech ha-chotem* — even when mucus comes out through the nose, it is *tamei*, because *alma kasavar mayan hu* — he holds that mucus is itself a genuine *mayan*, an independent source of *tumah* for a *zav*, not merely a vehicle for *rok*.

### Tears Theory

Given Rav's position, the *Gemara* asks: if Rav's rule is that mucus is *tamei* only when it passes through the mouth (because of admixed *rok*), why does he not also mention tears (*dimat eino*) — tears can also drain through the nasal passages into the mouth? The *Gemara* resolves this by citing Rav's own view: *hai man d'ba'i listmiah le'einei* — Rav believed that poison inserted through the eye could be expelled by draining it out through the mouth. This reflects an assumption that the tear ducts can serve as a channel to the mouth. However, the *Gemara* clarifies: Rav distinguished between foreign substances (like poison) that might be pulled through this channel, and the tears themselves. *Nehi d'zhiri nafik, dimato gufah lo nafik* — while foreign fluids inserted into the eye might be extractable through the mouth, the tears themselves do not flow that way. Therefore Rav did not mention tears: they do not pass through the mouth, they carry no *rok*, and by Rav's reckoning they are not *tamei* as a *mayan*.

---

## Nine Fluids

### Three by Three

The *Gemara* now presents a comprehensive classification of the nine fluids (*tisha mashkin*) of a *zav*, organized into three groups of three based on their *tumah* status. This classification clarifies the full landscape of which bodily fluids are *tamei* and to what degree.

### Non-Mayanot

The first category comprises three fluids that are entirely *tahor*: *haze'a* (sweat), *leicha serucha* (rancid or putrid liquid, identified by some as pus), and *ha-re'i* (excrement, or more liquid discharge). These three are *tehorin miklum* — completely *tahor* — for two independent reasons. First, they are *she'einan mayanot*: they do not collect and then emerge as a concentrated flow; they are not of the type described as *mit'agel v'yotzei*. Second, and independently, they are not considered *mashkin* — liquids — at all in the halachic sense, since drinking and liquids are never associated with these substances in any halachic context. Because they fail on both counts, they convey no *tumah* whatsoever.

### Liquids Not Mayanot

The second category comprises three fluids that are considered *mashkin* (liquids) but are not *mayanot* (wellsprings of *tumah*): *dimat eino* (tears), *dam agpato* (blood from a wound), and *chalav isha* (milk of a nursing woman who is a *zavah*). These convey *tumah* only in the sense that any liquid does when touched by a *zav* or *zavah* — they become a *rishon l'tumah*. Furthermore, this *tumah* applies only when there is a minimum measure of *reviit* (approximately 3.5 ounces). They are not themselves *mayanot* because they do not arise through the process of *mit'agel v'yotzei* — tears flow immediately from the eye, wound blood flows immediately from the wound, and milk, while it does accumulate, is debated; the *Gemara* notes the question without resolving it fully, suggesting that milk perhaps does not flow autonomously in the same way.

### True Mayanot

The third and highest category comprises three fluids that are genuine *mayanot* and are themselves *av hatumah*: *zovo* (the discharge itself), *roko* (his spit), and *mei raglav* (his urine). These three convey *tuma chamura* — the severest form of *tumah* — making both person and clothes *tamei* even through touch alone.

### Spit Subcategories

A careful reader will notice that the list of nine fluids does not include *kicho*, *niaro*, or *mei ha-af* — the phlegm types and mucus discussed earlier in the *Gemara*. The *Gemara* explains: *tana roko v'chol d'asi meiribuiya* — the list says "his spit" and subsumes under that heading everything derived from the expansive *drashot* on the verse about spit. Phlegm (*kicho* and *niaro*) and, according to Rabbi Yochanan, mucus (*mei ha-af*), are halachically subsumed under *rok* by virtue of being derived from the same verse. They are not enumerated separately because they are extensions of the *rok* category, not independent entries.

### Drinking Verses

For the middle category — the three fluids that are *mashkin* but not *mayanot* — the *Gemara* provides the scriptural basis for calling each of them a *mashke* (liquid), since halachically a substance is considered a *mashke* only if it is associated with the act of drinking. Tears: the verse in *Tehillim* speaks of being made to *drink* tears — *v'tashkem bidmaot shalish* — associating tears with drinking. Blood from wounds: the verse says *v'dam chalalim yishteh* — "and the blood of the slain he shall drink" — and since we derive that a wound is comparable to a partial death (*mah li kulei mah li palgei*), wound blood is covered. Milk: the verse in *Shoftim* records Yael giving Sisera milk to drink — *vatiftach et nod ha-chalav vatashkehu* — establishing milk as a *mashke* for this purpose. In each case, an association with drinking in scriptural language is sufficient to place the fluid in the category of *mashke*, even if it is not ordinarily consumed as a beverage.

### Urine Source

Urine (*mei raglav*) belongs to the highest category but requires its own derivation since it is not derived from the verses about *zov* or *rok*. The *Beraita* cites: *zovo tamei v'zot tihiyeh tumato* — "his flow is *tamei*, and this shall be his *tumah*." The phrase *v'zot tihiyeh tumato* adds another category of *tumah* to the *zav* beyond the *zov* itself, and this is interpreted as a reference to urine — the other primary excretion from the same area of the body.

### Urine Kal Vachomer

The *Beraita* raises the question: could one not derive the *tumah* of urine through a *kal vachomer*? Spit, which comes from the mouth — a place of *tahara* — is *tamei*; surely urine, which comes from the same place as the *zov* — an area already associated with *tumah* — should certainly be *tamei*. The *Beraita* deflects this *kal vachomer* with a counter-example: blood that exits from the penis (*dam hayotzei mipi ha'ama*) is *tahor*, despite coming from the same source as *zov*. If blood from that area can be *tahor*, there is no automatic inference that urine must be *tamei* simply by virtue of its origin. Hence the explicit verse *zovo tamei v'zot* is necessary to include urine in the *tumah* of the *zav*.

It is worth noting that this derivational structure — specific verses for *zov*, specific verses for *rok* and its subsets, and a specific verse for urine — raises a broader point. The conceptual framework of *mit'agel v'yotzei* may describe the *character* of the substances that qualify as *mayanot*, but it is not itself the operative halachic mechanism. What places each fluid in the highest category of *tumah* is ultimately its explicit scriptural derivation. The absence of a clear verse for mucus may thus be as significant as any conceptual difference between mucus and the other substances — and may explain why the *Gemara* does not fully resolve the debate between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on that point.

---

---

# Niddah 56

## Zav Fluids

### Dam Ha-Yotzei

The daf opens five lines from the top of 56a, at the words *dam ha-yotzei*. The broader context is the *mishnah* that surveys various substances — primarily, though not exclusively, bodily fluids — that are *tamei*, and addresses whether they convey *tumah* only when moist or even when dried. At this juncture, the *Gemara* is examining the fluids of a *zav*.

The *Torah* mentions spit explicitly as a source of *tumah* conveyed by a *zav*. By means of an additional inclusive word in the *pasuk*, the category is extended to include phlegm and nasal mucus. Urine is then included through an analogical derivation: first phlegm and mucus are compared to spit, and then spit is compared to the primary flow of *zivah* from the penis, thereby drawing urine into the same category. Blood, however, even if it were to emerge from the penis, is excluded and is *tahor*. The *Gemara* now sets out to explain the conceptual basis for these distinctions.

### Inclusion Rules

The *Gemara* asks: how do we know that blood emerging from the mouth or from the penis is *tahor*? A *baraita* provides the answer. One might have thought — *yakhol yehei dam ha-yotzei mi-piv u-mi-pi ha-amah tamei* — that blood from either location should be *tamei*, given that other fluids from those same locations are. The verse therefore specifies: *zovo tamei hu* — *hu*, "it," a limiting particle: only the flow itself is *tamei*, to the exclusion of blood emerging from mouth or penis. That exclusion is established by the word *hu*.

But this immediately raises the inverse question: *ve-eippukh ana* — why not reverse the derivation? Why not say that blood is *tamei* and the other fluids — phlegm, mucus, urine — are *tahor*? How do we know which items to include and which to exclude?

### Blood Exclusion

The *Gemara* cites a principle stated by Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: the operative criterion is *dumya de-rok* — analogy to spit, which the *Torah* explicitly designates as a source of *tumah* for a *zav*. From spit we derive the defining characteristic: *mah rok she-mit'agel ve-yotzei* — spit is a fluid that collects within the body before it exits. Accordingly, *af kol she-mit'agel ve-yotzei* — any fluid that similarly collects before coming out is included. Blood, by contrast, does not operate this way: when the body bleeds, whether internally or from a surface wound, the blood does not gather and pool before emerging. Hence *yatza dam* — blood is excluded.

This is the conceptual framework. The *Torah* explicitly identifies *zivah* and spit as sources of *tumah*, and additional *pesukim* extend the category. But the abstracted criterion — collection prior to emission — is what determines which further substances fall within the category and which fall outside it.

### Spit Analogy

The *Gemara* immediately presses: granted that blood is excluded because it does not collect, what of a nursing woman's milk — *chalav she-be-ishah*? Milk certainly collects before it emerges. Yet we know from an earlier teaching — *ve-amar mar* — that mother's milk does not carry the severe *tumah* of a primary fluid of a *zavah*. It is *tamei* only as a liquid that has received *tumah* from a *zavah* (*tumat mashkin*), but it is not itself an *av ha-tumah* in the manner of spit. The challenge stands: if the criterion is simply *mit'agel ve-yotzei*, milk should be included.

### Milk Problem

Rabbi Yochanan, still citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, accordingly refines the criterion. The analogy to spit is more demanding than first stated. Spit has two defining characteristics: first, it collects before being expelled (*mit'agel ve-yotzei*); and second, it can be swallowed back — *ve-chozer ve-nivla* — it is capable of reabsorption into the body if not expelled. This second criterion is what excludes mother's milk. Although milk collects before it emerges (*she-af al pi she-mit'agel ve-yotzei*), it cannot be reabsorbed back into the body (*eino chozer ve-nivla*). Hence *yatza chalav she-be-ishah* — mother's milk is excluded.

### Two Criteria

This dual criterion — collection and reabsorption — resolves the case of milk, but it seems to create a problem with urine. Urine is included within the category of *tamei* fluids of a *zav*, yet can urine really be said to be reabsorbed if not expelled? Rashi addresses this directly, noting in the narrow column that *silon shel mei raglayim chozer ve-nivla* — the stream of urine can be reabsorbed. The lecturer acknowledges this is difficult to understand physiologically. When urination is interrupted, the urine does not literally return into the body; one simply stops urinating. Nevertheless, the *Gemara* appears to accept this distinction.

The harder conceptual question is why urine is treated differently from milk. The *Gemara* never offers an explicit account of this, and the lecturer notes that the *meiтav* commentary does not resolve the asymmetry either. What the *Gemara* does presuppose is that both criteria — collection and potential reabsorption — apply to urine but not to milk, even if the physiological basis for that distinction is not entirely transparent.

A further question arises about *tzichtzuchei zivah* — drops or secretions associated with the flow. The *Gemara* elsewhere states *ee efshar belo tzichtzuchei zivah* — one cannot have a flow of *zivah* without accompanying droplets. Whether *tzichtzuchei* are themselves considered one of the primary *ma'ayanot* of a *zav* — with the consequence of being *tamei be-masa* and *tamei le-vigadim* — or whether they are *tamei* in a lesser sense only, is left as a question requiring further investigation.

There is also a broader hermeneutic point worth noting. The *Gemara* never returns to discuss nasal mucus with full rigor. Whether mucus is included purely through the abstract category of *mit'agel ve-yotzei*, or whether it requires its own independent *pasuk*, remains somewhat open. The underlying tension is between how much work the abstract criterion can do on its own and how much independent textual support each inclusion requires.

One might further ask: why is "natural secretion" not the defining criterion, rather than collection and reabsorption? Spit, phlegm, and urine are natural; blood from the penis would be pathological; and the very *zivah* that makes one a *zav* is itself unnatural. This observation actually reinforces why the *zivah* itself cannot be used as the model for abstraction — which leads directly to the next sub-discussion.

### Flow Challenge

The *Gemara* raises a pointed objection: *ve-nilef mi-zovo* — why not derive the criterion from the *zivah* itself, the primary flow that makes the person a *zav*? The *zivah* does not possess the characteristic of *mit'agel ve-yotzei* — it does not collect before coming out. If we were to abstract from the *zivah*, we would derive a criterion that is the opposite of the one derived from spit, and we would wind up including things that do not collect. This seems to undermine the entire framework.

### Rava Response

Rava resolves the difficulty decisively: *mi-zovo leika le-meylaf* — there is no valid derivation from the *zivah* flow itself, because *she-kein gorem tumah le-achreim* — the *zivah* is what creates the person's status as a *zav* in the first place. It is a categorically different phenomenon: it is the source of his *tumah* identity, not a fluid he conveys *after* becoming a *zav*. When we ask which fluids an already-established *zav* transmits as an *av ha-tumah*, the model must be spit — the fluid the *Torah* explicitly designates for that purpose — not the *zivah* itself, which operates in a different register entirely.

This resolution, as the lecturer notes, actually lends further support to the question about "natural secretion" as a potential criterion. Once the *zivah* is set aside precisely because it is the act that constitutes the *zav* — not merely a fluid he conveys — we are left with spit as the exclusive model. And spit is a natural secretion. That "natural" is not, in the end, treated as the operative criterion remains something of an open question.

---

## Sheretz Status

### Reish Lakish

The *Gemara* now turns to the case of a dead rodent — *sheretz* — which the *Torah* identifies as a source of *tumah*. The *mishnah*'s point is not simply that it conveys *tumah* but that this applies only when the rodent is moist, not when it has dried out. Against the plain reading of the *mishnah*, Reish Lakish states: *sheretz she-yavesh ve-shildo kayemet tamei* — a rodent that has completely desiccated, if its form is still intact, is still *tamei*.

This position invites a conceptual question. Why should drying remove *tumah* at all? Two frameworks are possible. One might hold that a dried-out substance is simply no longer the same entity — it has lost its identity as a rodent. Alternatively, one might hold that it remains the same entity but loses its *significance* — its halachic weight — once dried. The fact that the *mishnah* uses the test of reconstitution in water (if the substance can be refreshed, it is not considered fully dried) might suggest the first framework: it is a question of identity. But Reish Lakish's ruling — that retaining the *shape* is sufficient even when the substance is desiccated — seems clearly to operate within the second framework. A dried rodent that still looks like a rodent has not lost its significance, even though it has lost moisture. It is not "dirt in the shape of a rodent," but a rodent that has retained enough of its form to retain its halachic weight.

### Whole vs Part

This significance-based framework is reinforced by the *Gemara*'s next step. The *mishnah* is cited: *metamin lachim ve-ein metamin yeveshim* — moist rodents convey *tumah*, dried ones do not. Rabbi Zeira resolves the tension with Reish Lakish: *lo kashya — ha be-kullan, ha be-miktzatan* — there is no contradiction. The distinction turns on whether one has the entire rodent or only a part of it.

The minimum quantity required for a *sheretz* to convey *tumah* is normally *ke-adasha* — the size of a lentil (or bean). If one has only a piece of a dried rodent that meets this minimum, it no longer conveys *tumah*. But if one has the entire rodent, even dried out, it still conveys *tumah* — provided its shape is retained.

This distinction parallels a principle known elsewhere in *hilchot tumah*: a *beriah* — an entire creature — conveys *tumah* even if it is smaller than the standard minimum quantity. The qualitative significance of wholeness can substitute for the quantitative threshold. Here too, the conceptual point is that significance can be conveyed either quantitatively (a piece that meets the minimum size) or qualitatively (the entirety of the creature retaining its shape). When a piece dries out, it loses the quantitative significance it once had — it is now just a small fragment of dried matter. But the whole creature, shape intact, retains the qualitative significance that marks it as a *sheretz*.

### Baraita

A *baraita* lends textual support to this framework. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Rabbi Bisni cites Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: the *Torah* uses two formulations — *bahem* ("in them," meaning the entirety) and *mehem* ("from them," meaning a portion). A *talmud lomar* argument resolves the tension: *kan be-lach, kan be-yavesh* — one verse addresses the moist case (where a minimum-sized piece suffices) and the other addresses the dried case (where the entirety is required). This textual derivation anchors Reish Lakish's ruling in the *Torah* itself.

### Shape Significance

Rava applies the principle concretely. He observes that the *zivugim* of Machuza — a species of rodent common in the Babylonian city where Rava resided, and which apparently were frequently found dried out in public spaces — *ke-shildan kayemet, tme'im*: as long as their form is retained, they are *tamei*. Rava is simply applying the theoretical principle to a practical, everyday case.

### Burned Sheretz

Reish Lakish then extends the ruling in a striking direction: *sheretz she-nisraf, ve-shildon kayemet, tme'im* — a rodent that has been burned, if its form is still recognizable, is still *tamei*. The more natural reading of "burned" here refers to charring rather than complete incineration (which would reduce the object to ash and destroy any recognizable form), but the case is nonetheless arresting. A charred rodent whose skeletal shape remains intact retains its *tumah*.

### Current State

An objection is raised from a *mishnah* in *Taharos*: if a burned rodent is found lying on olives (of *terumah* or other *tahara*-sensitive produce), the olives are *tahor* — *kol ha-tme'im ke-sha'at metzi'atan*, things are assessed according to their state at the time of discovery. Since the rodent is found already burned, we assume it was already burned when it fell, and therefore did not convey *tumah*. Does this not suggest that a burned rodent is *tahor*? Similarly, a tattered garment that was once *tamei* but has deteriorated beyond halachic recognition — *matlis ha-muha* — is treated as *tahor* at the time of discovery.

### Entirety Rule

Rav Zeira resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya — ha be-kulah, ha be-miktzatah* — the same whole-versus-part distinction applies. The *mishnah* in *Taharos* speaks of a burned rodent where only a portion remains, which is insufficient once dried or charred; Reish Lakish speaks of the entire rodent with its shape intact. A *baraita* confirms this by presenting the same *bahem/mehem* textual derivation applied now to *saruf* versus *she-eino saruf* — burned versus unburned — rather than to dried versus moist.

The conceptual unity is clear. Whether the diminishment is drying or burning, the operative question is whether halachic significance is retained. Significance can persist even through drying or charring, but only when the entire creature's form is present. A portion, once dried or charred, is simply insignificant matter — neither quantitatively sufficient nor qualitatively whole.

---

## Freshness Rule

### Torah Sources

The *Gemara* now surveys the textual sources establishing that all these substances — *zav* fluid, spit, rodent, semen — convey *tumah* only when fresh, not when dried out. For the *zav* flow, the verse states *rar besaro* — it flows in his flesh, implying a liquid state. For phlegm and spit, the verse says *ki yarok ha-zav ke-eyn rok* — when the *zav* spits, it must be *ke-eyn rok*, resembling actual spit — that is, in liquid form. For the *sheretz*, the verse says *be-motam* — "in their death" — and the *Gemara* reads this as requiring the substance to be *ke-eyn mitah*, as it is at the moment of death — still relatively fresh.

### Semen Fitness

For semen, the source is the term *shichvat zera* itself, understood as *ha-re'uya le-hazria* — that which is capable of causing conception. Dried semen cannot cause conception, and therefore it is no longer *tamei*. This raises an interesting contemporary question: is dried semen truly incapable of causing conception? The lecturer notes that the *Gemara* did not have knowledge of sperm as a distinct biological entity. The *Gemara* elsewhere considers whether semen that emerges in a powerful stream is presumed more capable of causing conception, and *Tosafot* addresses this, arguing that *ra'uya le-hazria* refers to the intrinsic quality of the substance rather than the manner of its propulsion. The broader point, as the lecturer notes, is one the *Gemara* itself implicitly raises throughout: the selection of defining criteria is always an act of interpretation. The question of which properties of semen make it *ra'uya le-hazria* — for purposes of *tumah* — is exactly the same kind of question as which properties of spit define the category of *zav* fluids.

### Reconstitution

The *mishnah* offers a practical test for determining whether a substance has dried sufficiently to lose *tumah*: if it can be soaked in lukewarm water (*poshrin*) and reconstituted, it is not considered dried. This is the test for semen, *sheretz*, and related substances.

### Lukewarm Duration

A question is posed by Rami bar Chama: must the water remain lukewarm for the entire twenty-four-hour soaking period, or is it sufficient that it began as lukewarm even if it cooled subsequently? The *baraita* resolves this as a *tannaitic* dispute. Yehuda ben Nekusa holds: twenty-four hours is required, but it suffices that the water *began* as lukewarm — *techilato af al pi she-ein sofo*. Rabbi Akiva holds more stringently: the water must remain lukewarm throughout the full twenty-four hours — *tzarich she-yehu poshrin me'et le-et*.

### Corpse Flesh

The *tanna kamma* holds that flesh of a corpse — *basar ha-met* — conveys *tumah* even when dried. Rabbi Yosi dissents, ruling that dried corpse flesh is *tahor*.

### Shmuel's View

Shmuel clarifies Rabbi Yosi's position. Rabbi Yosi does not hold that dried corpse flesh is entirely *tahor* in all respects. Rather, *tahor mil-tamei be-khezayit* — it no longer conveys the standard *tumah* of a *kezayit* of corpse flesh, which is what the *tanna kamma* maintained. But *mitamei tum'at rekev* — it does still convey *tumah* as *rekev*, the specially defined category of decomposed corpse matter, which operates under its own parameters (requiring isolation in a sealed marble casket and measured in a distinct quantity). A *baraita* confirms this reading of Rabbi Yosi: the dried flesh is *tahor mil-tamei be-khezayit, aval mitamei tum'at rekev*.

---

## Stains Overview

### Rodent Timeline

The *Gemara* now pivots to the *mishnah* that will dominate the discussion for some time: the question of stains found on women's garments and the retroactive *tumah* they generate. A parallel case introduces the principle: *sheretz she-nimtza ba-mavoi* — a dead rodent found in an alleyway. If a person passed through and wishes to know whether they became *tamei* by stepping on it, the ruling is *tamei le-mafrea* — *tamei* retroactively. How far back? Until the person can say: *badakti et ha-mavoi ha-zeh ve-lo hayah bo sheretz* — I checked this alleyway and found no rodent — or *ad she-kibbud* — until the last time the alleyway was swept. Either a positive check or an act of sweeping constitutes the terminal point beyond which the rodent is not assumed to have been present.

### Stain Timeline

The parallel rule for stains: *ve-chen ketem she-nimtza be-chaluk* — a stain found on a woman's garment — *metamei le-mafrea* — conveys *tumah* retroactively. The terminal point is either her stating *badakti et ha-chaluk ha-zeh ve-lo hayah bo ketem* — I checked this garment and it was clean — or *ad she-kibbud* — until the last laundering. The *mishnah* was cited earlier in the tractate; here is where it originally appears.

A practical note: these rules raise the difficult question of what precisely becomes *tamei*. The garment itself, anyone who touches it, and, most significantly, the woman herself — who must assume she was a *niddah* from as far back as the terminal point. This retroactive personal status is the gravest consequence of the rule.

### Niddah Blood

The *mishnah* further states: *u-metamei bein lach bein yavesh* — a stain of *niddah* blood conveys *tumah* whether moist or dried. This, as established earlier in the *daf*, is the distinctive rule for *niddah* blood: unlike the other substances surveyed in this *mishnah*, its *tumah* is not conditioned on freshness.

### Rabbi Shimon

Rabbi Shimon offers a compelling qualification: *ha-yavesh metamei le-mafrea, ve-ha-lach eino metamei ella ad sheyehei yakhol lihyot lach* — the dried stain conveys *tumah* retroactively to the full extent; but the fresh (moist) stain conveys *tumah* only as far back as it is plausible that it could still be fresh at the point of discovery. A dried stain could have been sitting there for weeks — back to the last check or laundering. But a fresh stain, by its very freshness, limits the temporal window: it cannot have been there longer than the time during which it could remain fresh. Rabbi Shimon's position is straightforwardly logical: the physical state of the stain itself serves as evidence of timing.

The converse implication is also noted: if a stain appears dried, one might reason that it *could* have been more recent. But this matters less, because even a dried stain from some time ago is still *tamei* — as established, *niddah* blood conveys *tumah* even dried. The *Rashash* clarifies that "dried" in this context does not necessarily mean dried to the extreme point of *taharah*; it simply means no longer fresh.

---

## Check Debate

### Sweep Mechanism

The *Gemara* now analyzes the mechanism behind the rule that sweeping serves as a terminal point. *Ad she-kibbud — chazkato baduk*: why does sweeping establish the endpoint? Two possibilities are raised: either because *chazkato baduk* — we presume that a person conducting a sweep is also actively inspecting; or because *chazkato mitkabed* — the act of sweeping itself naturally dislodges and removes anything in the *mavoi*, irrespective of whether the sweeper was looking.

### Hole Scenario

The practical difference between these two rationales is significant. If someone says *kibbadti ve-lo badakti* — I swept but I was not looking — the outcome depends on which rationale applies. If the terminal point rests on the presumption of active inspection, then an admission of non-inspection eliminates the terminal point, and *tumah* must be assumed retroactively from an earlier time. If the terminal point rests on the mechanical effect of sweeping itself, the admission does not matter.

A second *nafka mina* is the case of *de-ishtakach be-guma* — the rodent was found in a hole or crevice. If the rationale is active inspection (*chazkato baduk*), we presume the inspector checked even the crevices, and finding the rodent there now means it arrived after the sweep. If the rationale is mechanical displacement (*chazkato mitkabed*), a sweeping broom does not reach into a hole — *guma lo mitkabed* — and the rodent in the hole could have been there before the sweep without being dislodged.

### Laundry Mechanism

The identical question is applied to laundering as a terminal point for stains. Does laundering serve as a terminal point because *chazkato baduk* — we presume the woman inspects the garment at the time of laundering — or because *chazkato mitkabes* — the laundering process itself will naturally remove any stain that is present, irrespective of inspection?

### Fold Scenario

Again, two practical differences emerge. First: if the woman says *kibasti ve-lo badakti* — I laundered but did not inspect — does she lose the terminal point? If the rationale is active inspection, yes; if the rationale is automatic removal through laundering, no. Second: *de-ishtakach be-sitra* — if the stain is found in a fold of the garment. If the rationale is inspection (*chazkato baduk*), we presume the inspector checked even the folds — *man de-baduk be-sitra nami baduk* — and a stain found there now must have arrived post-laundering. If the rationale is automatic removal (*chazkato mitkabes*), a fold does not necessarily get laundered through — *be-sitra lo mitkabes* — and the stain could have persisted there through the laundering undetected.

### Rabbi Meir

The *Gemara* resolves the question from a *baraita* citing Rabbi Meir. He asks: *mipnei mah amru ha-sheretz she-nimtza ba-mavoi metamei le-mafrea* — why is it that we declare retroactive *tumah* from the time of the sweep? His answer: *mipnei she-chazkat bnei Yisrael bodkin mavo'oteihen bi-sh'at kibudan* — because Jews, as a matter of established practice (*chazakah*), inspect their courtyards as they sweep. The rationale is explicitly inspection, not mechanical displacement. The same reasoning applies to stains: *mipnei she-chazkat bnot Yisrael bodkot chalukeihen bi-sh'at kibuseihen* — Jewish women inspect their garments at the time of laundering.

### No Checking Loss

The consequence follows directly: *ve-im lo badku hifsidu le-mafrea* — if they concede that they did not inspect during the sweeping or laundering, they forfeit the protection of that terminal point and must consider *tumah* as potentially reaching back indefinitely to the prior check. Rabbi Meir's position is unambiguous: it is the active inspection, not the mechanical act, that creates the terminal point.

---

## Stain Age

### Rav Acha

Even granting that an active inspection must have taken place for the terminal point to apply, the *Gemara* now offers practical tools for assessing a stain's age independent of whether inspection occurred. Rav Acha states: *tachzor ve-tis-chabsenu* — re-launder the garment. *Im nidchah mar'ito* — if the stain fades upon second laundering, *be-yadu'a she-le'achar kibus* — it is established that this is a fresh stain, one that arrived after the last laundering, because a fresh stain will visibly fade when first washed. *Ve-im lav* — if it does not fade further, *be-yadu'a she-lifnei ha-kibus* — it is established that the stain predates the laundering, having already been subjected to laundering once before.

This is a reasonable empirical test. A stain that has already been laundered acquires a characteristically faded, set appearance; further laundering changes it little. A fresh stain, by contrast, will fade noticeably on first washing.

---

## Stain Age (II)

### Rebbi View

Rebbi offers a refinement that does not even require re-laundering. *Eino domeh ketem she-le'achar ha-kibus le-ketem she-lifnei ha-kibus* — a post-laundering stain does not resemble a pre-laundering stain to the trained eye. The distinction: *zeh makdir ve-zeh maglid* — one penetrates into the fabric (a stain that has set through previous laundering is embedded into the fibers); the other forms a crust (*maglid*), sitting on the surface with visible substance. A fresh stain has not yet been worked into the garment and retains surface texture; a previously laundered stain has lost that and appears only as a deep coloring of the fabric.

### Inference

From these testing methods, the *Gemara* draws an inference confirming the earlier resolution: *chazkato baduk — shema mina*. The very existence of methods for distinguishing fresh from previously laundered stains presupposes that the operative reason for laundering serving as a terminal point is inspection (*chazkato baduk*). If the terminal point depended merely on the mechanical act of laundering, there would be no need to distinguish the age of the stain — the act itself would have resolved the matter. The fact that we need to test whether the stain is pre- or post-laundering confirms that the terminal point is grounded in the presumption of active inspection.

---

## Origin Analysis

### Rekem Rule

A new *mishnah* opens the discussion that will dominate this section: *kol ha-ketamim ha-ba'im mi-Rekem tehorim* — all stains originating from Rekem, a particular city in Israel, are *tahor*. Rekem was a city whose population was predominantly non-Jewish, and stains belonging to non-Jews do not carry the *halachic tumah* of *niddah* stains, which applies — both as *Torah* law and rabbinically — to Jewish women. The stains found in Rekem are presumed to come from non-Jews and are therefore *tahor*.

### Yehuda Exception

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *metamei* — the stains are *tamei*. His reasoning: *mipnei she-hen gerim ve-toim* — because they are converts who err. The converts in Rekem are technically Jews but are not sufficiently careful about the laws of *tumah* and *taharah* to put away stained garments properly. Therefore, one cannot presume that all freely circulating stains in that city come from non-Jews; there are careless Jewish converts whose stains may be found. Accordingly, Rabbi Yehuda rules those stains *tamei*.

### General Rule

The general principle underlying the *mishnah*: stains from among non-Jews are *tahor*; stains attributed to Jews are *tamei*. But the determination of which stains one encounters in practice depends on where one finds them and who inhabits the area.

### Mixed Cities

For cities with a mixed population of Jews and non-Jews, the *mishnah* addresses the question of attribution. The general rule is that one follows the majority population, or considers the particular characteristics of the inhabitants. The critical variable, as the *mishnah* frames it, is not merely numerical majority but the *carefulness* of the Jewish residents: Jews who are careful with their stained garments — who put them away and do not allow them to circulate — effectively remove their stains from the pool of stains one might encounter. The presumption that careful Jews have removed their potentially *tamei* stains from public circulation means that stains found in mixed cities can often be attributed to the non-Jewish population.

### Convert Status

The *mishnah*'s closing section addresses Samaritans (*Kutim*). The *Gemara* reconstructs the *mishnah* through a *chisuri mechsara*: the text is incomplete and requires supplement. The full reading: if a stain is known to come from a Jew, it is *tamei*; if it is known to come from a Samaritan, the question depends on the disputed status of Samaritans. Rabbi Meir rules it *tamei* — *d'Kutim gerei emet hein* — Samaritans are genuine converts and therefore Jews in all respects, making their stains *tamei*. The *Chachamim* rule it *tahor* — *d'Kutim gerei arayot hein* — Samaritans converted only out of fear of lions sent by God, not from genuine religious conviction, and are therefore not considered Jews; their stains are *tahor* as the stains of non-Jews.

### Carefulness Rule

The *Gemara* notes that if the dispute were purely about Samaritan legal status — Jew versus non-Jew — the *mishnah*'s phrasing, *she-lo nechshdu al kitmeihen* (they are not suspect of mishandling their stains), would be irrelevant. The question of status and the question of carefulness are distinct. The *Gemara* therefore re-reads the *mishnah*: when the stain is *known* to belong to a Jew or Samaritan, it is *tamei* in either case, since even the *Chachamim* agree Samaritans are *gerei emet* for purposes of establishing identity of ownership. The real question in the latter part of the *mishnah* is about stains *found* in various locations without known attribution. In a Jewish city, even found stains are *tahor* — *she-lo nechshdu al kitmeihen ve-tzni'ei matni lehu* — because Jews are careful with their stains and put them away, so any stain encountered in the street is presumed to come from a non-Jewish passerby or from some non-*niddah* source.

### Samaritans

For stains found in Samaritan cities — *ha-nimtza'im be-arei Kutim* — Rabbi Meir rules *tamei*: *d'nechshdu al kitmeihen* — Samaritans are not careful with their stains and allow *tamei* stains to circulate. The *Chachamim* rule *tahor*: *she-lo nechshdu al kitmeihen* — Samaritans are as careful with their stains as Jews.

The principle that emerges from the entire discussion: the *tumah* of a found stain is not determined solely by the *halachic* status of who produced it (Jew versus non-Jew), but by the combination of status and carefulness. A *tamei* stain must be both from a Jew (or legal equivalent) *and* from someone who would allow such a stain to circulate. Because careful Jews put their stained garments away, one cannot infer from the mere discovery of a stain in a Jewish environment that it comes from a negligent Jewish woman. The special cases — Rekem's converts, Samaritan cities — are the cases where this combination of Jewish status and lack of carefulness may coexist, and those are precisely the cases the *mishnah* singles out for attention.

---

---

# Niddah 57

## Ketamim Overview

### Review & Intro

The present daf picks up with the *mishnah* at the bottom of 56b, launching us squarely into the world of *ketamim* — stains. The previous daf introduced two central questions that arise when a stain is discovered: first, how far back in time must a woman assume the stain was present, with the primary implication being from when she must consider herself a *niddah*; and second, whether the appearance of the garment — whether it looks as though it has been laundered — can serve as evidence to establish at least the latest possible time of origin.

An important preliminary observation governs all that follows: even when we rule that a *ketem* is *tamei*, that ruling is only Rabbinic in force. The *tumah* of stains is never biblical.

### Non-Jew Stains

Among the first leniencies the *mishnah* introduces regarding stains is the rule that stains found on the garments of non-Jewish women present no problem whatsoever. Although we rule Rabbinically that non-Jewish women can be *niddot* and that their *niddah* blood is *tamei*, their *ketamim* — their stains — do not create *tumah* for a Jew who comes into contact with them, nor if such a stain contacts *terumah*.

One might ask: does the prohibition against relations with a non-Jewish woman not derive partly from her *niddah* status? Indeed, Rabbinically she carries a *niddah* designation, but there are in fact five separate Rabbinic statuses applied to non-Jewish women to render such relations forbidden — the mnemonic *nasgaz* captures them: *niddah*, *shifchah*, *goyah*, *zonah*, and so on. The *niddah* status is thus only one thread in a larger web of prohibition.

### City Stains

The practical upshot of these rules is that a random bloodstain found on a garment in the public domain is rarely *tamei*. The *mishnah* at the bottom of 56b states: *kol haketamim hanimtzaim bechol makom tehorim* — stains found in the public domain of Jewish cities are *tahor*, because we assume that Jews are careful with garments bearing *niddah* stains and would not leave them out where others might become *tamei*. There is therefore a presumption that publicly found stains originated from non-Jews, and they are consequently not a problem.

The exception is *ketamim* found in *chadarim* — inner, private rooms — where one would not expect such casual discarding. The precise referent of *cheder* is not entirely clear, but it certainly means something more like a private inner chamber than an open living space. In a private room, the assumption shifts, and we do presume the stain may be *niddah* blood.

---

## Beit HaTme'ot

### Definition

The *mishnah* adds a second exception: *uvisvivot beit hatme'ot* — stains found in the surroundings of the "house of impurity." *Rashi* defines *beit hatme'ot* as a room that women would make use of during their days of *niddah*: *cheder shenashim mishtamshot bo bimei niddotan*.

### Societal Attitudes

This reference is remarkable and deserves attention. Many societies throughout history have maintained menstrual taboos requiring women to physically separate themselves from society during menstruation — to be removed from the household, seen as carrying something dangerous, even possessing some form of demonic or metaphysical power that necessitated isolation. The *Ramban* on the *Torah* alludes to this theme when he explains *Rachel*'s words to *Lavan*, *lo uchal lakum mipanecha ki derech nashim li* — on his reading, she invoked her *niddah* status precisely to create distance, given the perceived metaphysical dangers associated with it.

### Halakhic Treatment

What is striking is that essentially none of this appears in the *Gemara's* halakhic treatment. Quite the opposite: the *halacha* permits a husband and wife to sleep in the same bedroom even when she is a *niddah*, notwithstanding the general rule that a man and a forbidden woman may not be secluded together (*yichud*). The various activities that other societies restricted to *niddot* — including food preparation, which was thought to carry dangerous power — are entirely non-issues in *halacha*. The formal *halacha*, in other words, not only ignores the societal taboo but in certain respects legislates against it.

### Halacha vs Practice

That said, one cannot always assume that the official *halacha* perfectly mirrors the attitudes and practices of the community. There is frequently a gap between what is ruled and what is observed, whether in the direction of additional stringency, leniency, or simply a different set of attitudes that persists despite — or alongside — the official position. The *beit hatme'ot* reference in the *mishnah* offers the faintest hint of this phenomenon: women were somehow using this room specifically during their *niddah* period. Whether this amounts to full seclusion — as practiced, for example, by the Ethiopian Jewish community, where women actually left the household during menstruation — or something less formal, is not entirely clear.

What is clear is that some of these attitudes never fully disappeared, even in communities that had access to normative *halachic* literature. The most obvious contemporary expression is the set of attitudes — rooted in medieval *Ashkenaz* but likely with far older antecedents — regarding women touching *Sifrei Torah* or entering the synagogue while a *niddah*. These practices are not grounded in *halacha* but reflect the persistence of older menstrual taboos alongside it. Shaye Cohen's work on women and the sanctum addresses precisely this phenomenon.

### Samaritan Burial

The *mishnah* adds that the *beit hatme'ot* of Samaritans (*Kutim*) carries an additional concern: *metamim be'ohel*, they create *tumah* even under the same roof, because Samaritans would use those rooms not only as spaces for *niddot* but also as places to bury fetuses. The *mishnah* states: *mipnei shehem kovrim sham et hanefalim* — because they bury there fetuses.

*Rabbi Yehuda* qualifies this: they would not actually bury the fetuses at all, but rather cast them there, whereupon animals would drag them away. Consequently, one need not be concerned that fetal remains causing *tumat ohel* are still present.

The *mishnah* then raises a question that recurs throughout the *Gemara's* treatment of Samaritans: can one believe their testimony on this matter? The specific question is whether they can be believed — *ne'emanim lomar* — to say that they buried a fetus there, or that they did not. The *mishnah* asserts that they can be believed. It then extends this trustworthiness to several additional areas: whether an animal has previously given birth and thus whether the next offspring would be a *bechor*, and whether grave sites have been properly marked.

The *mishnah* equally specifies areas where Samaritans cannot be trusted: regarding *sechachot* (overhanging branches), *peru'ot* (protruding stones), and *beit hapras* (a field plowed over a grave). The organizing principle stated in the *mishnah* is *zeh haklal davar shechashudim bo ein ne'emanim alav* — as a rule, regarding matters in which they themselves are suspect, one cannot trust their testimony.

---

## Samaritan Trust

### Drasha Basis

The *Gemara* opens this section by asking *mai darush* — what *derashah* leads Samaritans to the practice of not burying fetuses properly, or at all? The *Gemara* assumes this derives from a textual source rather than being mere custom. The verse cited is *lo tasig gevul re'acha asher gavlu rishonim benachalatcha* — do not move the boundary marker of your neighbor set by those who came before, in the land you are inheriting.

The Samaritan reading: *kol sheyesh lo nachalah* — anyone who has an inheritance, which requires being a viable newborn to receive, *yesh lo gevul* — has a boundary, understood here as a grave site, a defined place of burial. *Kol she'ein lo nachalah* — anyone who does not inherit, *ein lo gevul* — has no grave, and may be disposed of in any fashion. Since a fetus does not inherit, it need not be given a proper burial.

### Trust Question

The *Gemara* then turns to the trust question raised by the *mishnah* — *ne'emanim lomar kavnu* — are they believed to say whether they buried a fetus there or not? Here the *Gemara* makes a move that fundamentally reframes the *mishnah's* assumption: *velait lehu lifnei iver lo titein michshol* — but they do not subscribe to the prohibition of *lifnei iver*, placing a stumbling block before the blind. They interpret that prohibition only literally and are not concerned with causing others to sin. If so, even if they themselves are personally careful about a given practice, why should one trust their testimony to others about it?

This is a striking move. The *mishnah* assumes that if Samaritans are themselves careful about something, that personal carefulness is grounds for trust. The *Gemara* fundamentally rejects this: no, one cannot trust them even when they are personally careful, because they have no compunction about misleading others.

### Kohen Evidence

If trust cannot be based on their stated care, what can it be based on? *Amar Rabbi Abahu bechohen omed sham* — *Rabbi Abbahu* answers that what we look for is their demonstrated behavior. A Samaritan *kohen* is standing in that space — that is, they are themselves acting in a way that shows they believe it is *tahor*.

But the *Gemara* immediately challenges this: perhaps the *kohen* was already *tamei*, in which case his presence there proves nothing. The *Gemara* responds: *denakat terumah beyado* — he is holding *terumah*. A *tamei* person would not hold *terumah*. But perhaps the *terumah* was already *tamei*? *Deka'achil mineih* — he is eating it. One does not eat *tamei terumah*, so the combination of eating *terumah* in that space establishes that they believe it to be entirely *tahor*.

One might ask: what is the *chidush* of all this? The *Gemara* answers: *mahu deteima lo beki'ei beyetzirah* — one might have thought that even if they believe the space to be *tahor*, they might lack sufficient expertise to know whether a fetus was sufficiently developed to transmit *tumah*. Perhaps they assumed the fetus was under forty days' development when it in fact was not. The *Gemara* therefore teaches — *kamashma lan* — that when their behavior clearly demonstrates they believe all is *tahor*, we trust that they also possess sufficient knowledge of the relevant details and are not simply making an inadvertent mistake.

---

## Gemara Reframe

### Reject Mishnah

The *Gemara's* reframing here represents a clean departure from the *mishnah*. The *mishnah* posited that trust follows from personal carefulness — if Samaritans are themselves careful about a practice, they can be believed about it. The *Gemara* categorically rejects this premise. Even when they are personally careful, one cannot trust their testimony to others, because they feel no obligation regarding *lifnei iver* and are not concerned about causing Jews to transgress.

The implication of this reframing is important: all cases where the *mishnah* permits relying on Samaritans must now be re-explained. It is not sufficient that they care about something for themselves. They must be observed actually behaving in a way that demonstrates their belief that the situation is permitted — and that demonstration must be unambiguous.

### Lifnei Iver

The *Gemara* thus sets up a framework in which Samaritan testimony, standing alone, is inherently unreliable. Whatever the historical realities behind this characterization — and the antagonism between the rabbinic class and the Samaritan community goes back at least to *Ezra* and *Nehemiah* — the *Gemara* treats it as given that they will not scruple to mislead Jews.

One might distinguish between their personal practice and their responsibility to others: some people are personally stringent but care nothing about whether their statements lead others astray, particularly where there is animosity or financial interest involved. It is precisely this split that the *Gemara* attributes to Samaritans. The *mishnah* assumed otherwise — that personal care translates into honest testimony — and the *Gemara* overrides that assumption. Crucially, this is not a question of Samaritans being ignorant of the *halacha*; quite the opposite. The *Gemara* assumes they are fully informed but simply indifferent to the consequences for others. Were ignorance the explanation, things would be even worse: even their demonstrated behavior could not be relied upon, since they might simply be acting from a mistaken belief.

---

## Animal/Grave Trust

### Firstborn Animals

The *mishnah* states that Samaritans are trusted regarding whether an animal has previously given birth — *ne'emanim al habehema im bikra o lo bikra* — which determines whether the next offspring constitutes a *bechor* requiring special treatment. The *Gemara* immediately applies its reframing: *veha leit lehu lifnei iver lo titein michshol* — but they do not care about *lifnei iver*, so why should they be trusted even here, particularly given the potential financial interest?

*Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba* citing *Rabbi Yochanan* answers: *begozez veoved* — they are themselves shearing and working the animal, demonstrating by their own behavior that they consider it not to be a *bechor*.

---

## Gemara Reframe (II)

### Knowledge/Intent

The *Gemara* again raises the *mahu deteima*: perhaps they are simply mistaken about whether a prior discharge constituted a miscarriage. Here, as *Dov* correctly observed, the concern is not a *halachic* disagreement but a knowledge gap — specifically, whether they can correctly identify a discharge as a miscarriage and thus know that the next animal is no longer a *bechor*. The *Gemara* answers *kamashma lan* that we assume they possess this knowledge and will not err on these factual matters, parallel to the resolution in the fetus case above.

---

## Animal/Grave Trust (II)

### Grave Markers

The *mishnah* states Samaritans are trusted regarding the marking of graves — *ne'emanim al tziyun kevarot* — so that *kohanim* know where to avoid. The *Gemara* notes a potential difficulty: this is itself only a Rabbinic practice. Given that the *Gemara* has been distinguishing between biblical and Rabbinic categories — with Samaritans following biblical but not Rabbinic law — why should they be trusted here?

The answer is *keivan dechetiva* — because the obligation to mark graves is rooted in a verse: the verse in *Yechezkel* says *ra'ah etzem adam uvanah etzlo tziyun* — if one sees a human bone, one should erect a marker beside it. Because this traces to a biblical text, Samaritans treat it with the seriousness due biblical law, and one can therefore assume they mark their graves conscientiously.

The practical implication follows: since they mark for their own purposes, they are not creating a situation where you must distrust an absence of a marker. Where there is no marker, a *kohen* may walk without concern. This also explains why the fetal burial issue remains separate — presumably a *nefel* does not receive the same treatment, and there would not be a marker to rely upon.

### Suchot/Trees

The *mishnah* declares that Samaritans cannot be trusted regarding *sechachot* and *peru'ot*. The *Gemara* explains: *sechachot detnan* — as taught in the *mishnah*, these are overhanging objects: *ilan hamaysech al ha'aretz* — a tree spreading its branches over the ground. The concern is Rabbinic.

There are two approaches to what makes this Rabbinic. According to *Tosfos*, the branches and leaves, however widespread, never combine to form a genuine *ohel* — a halachically significant "tent" — since they do not constitute a solid surface of *tefach* by *tefach*. Rabbinically, however, we treat such overhanging as an *ohel* because it could grow into one. According to *Rashi*, the issue is different: a *meis* was buried near a cemetery at nightfall, and those who buried it forgot exactly which tree it lies under. There is therefore an area of doubt, and the Rabbis rule that a *kohen* may not walk under any of those trees. Samaritans do not accept this Rabbinic stringency and let their *kohanim* walk under all such trees without concern. Because they dismiss this Rabbinic restriction, one cannot trust their testimony regarding it.

*Peru'ot* — protruding stones jutting from a wall — involve a similar dynamic: a case where it is unknown beneath which stone a *meis* lies, and Rabbinic concern prohibits certain movement in the vicinity. Samaritans disregard this as well.

The point is not that they are being deceptive; the point is that they themselves do not treat these restrictions as binding and therefore their assurances that a particular space presents no problem carry no weight — they would say the same thing regardless.

### Beit HaPras

The third category in which Samaritans cannot be trusted is *beit hapras* — a field in which a grave has been plowed over, scattering small chips of bone throughout. Because a chip of bone less than an olive's bulk can still transmit *tumah* in certain configurations, the Rabbis declared the entire surrounding area — *melo ma'aneh*, the width of the plow's length, which works out to an area of 100 *amah* by 100 *amah* around the grave — to be a restricted zone.

The *Gemara* cites a ruling of *Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Shmuel*: *menapeiach adam beit hapras vehaloch* — one can blow the ground ahead of one step at a time when traversing a *beit hapras*. By blowing, one moves any bone chip without bodily contact and thus avoids *heiseit* — moving a corpse — which would be a more serious form of *tumah*. It is something like navigating a minefield one step at a time. Additionally, *Rav Yehuda bar Ami* in the name of *Rav Yehuda* rules that a *beit hapras* that has been thoroughly trampled is *tahor*, as all loose bone chips would have been either ground into the earth or displaced.

The *Gemara* further teaches: *hachoresh beit hakevarot harei zeh oseh beit hapras* — one who plows over a gravesite creates a *beit hapras*. The area so created is *melo ma'aneh* — 100 *amah* by 100 *amah*, or *beit arba se'in* — the area needed to plant four *seah* of grain. *Rabbi Yossi* says five *seah*. In any event, it is a very large area.

Samaritans do not accept these restrictions and are therefore unreliable regarding them. However, a *baraita* introduces a nuance: *sadeh she'avad bah kever ne'eman Kuti lomar ein sham kever lefi she'eino me'id ela al gufa shel kever* — if a grave has been lost in a field, a Samaritan can be believed to say there was never a grave there at all, since he is then testifying directly on the existence of the grave itself, which is something he agrees is a biblical problem. Similarly, *ilan shemeisech al ha'aretz, ne'eman lomar ein tachtav kever* — regarding an overhanging tree, he can be trusted to say no grave was ever buried beneath it — again, testifying on a biblical issue he takes seriously.

The *Gemara* then adds that *Rav Yochanan* says this trust applies only when he demonstrates it through his own behavior — *bemehalich ube'afnei kulo* — walking throughout the entire field or under all of the trees. Merely walking through part of the field would not suffice; one might worry that he is avoiding the one spot where he suspects the grave actually lies. The *Gemara's* *chidush* here is that we do not entertain this concern — *ritzua nafka*, that there might be a strip he is avoiding — and we take his demonstrated behavior at face value.

### General Principle

The *mishnah's* closing statement — *zeh haklal, davar shechashudim bo ein ne'emanim alav* — is taken by the *Gemara* to include additional Rabbinic laws such as *techumim* (the two-thousand *amah* Shabbat boundary) and *yayin nesech* (wine touched by a non-Jew). These are Rabbinic prohibitions that Samaritans do not observe, and they therefore cannot be trusted regarding them.

The overall movement of this section is significant. The *mishnah* and certain *baraitot* assumed that personal carefulness generates trustworthiness. The *Gemara* systematically displaced that assumption: Samaritans, even when personally careful, may still be misleading you. Trust must be grounded either in demonstrated behavior or in testimony touching on matters they accept as biblically binding. This, the *Gemara* concludes, is the organizing principle beneath all the individual rulings of the *mishnah*.

---

## Stains Body/Garment

### Body Locations

With *hadran alach dam nida* — the conclusion of the previous *perek* — the *Gemara* opens *perek haroa ketem*, which marks a turning point: from here to the end of the *masechet*, the laws of *ketamim* are treated very much in their application to contemporary *halacha*, and the discussions become highly practical.

The new *mishnah* opens: *haroa ketem al besarah* — a woman who sees a stain on her own body. The fundamental question is whether the stain can be attributed to an external source. If so, there is no problem. Even if it cannot, the *tumah* remains only Rabbinic. If the stain is *keneged beit hatorfa* — opposite the genital area — she is *teme'ah*. If it is elsewhere on her body — *shelo keneged beit hatorfa* — she is *tehorah*. The *mishnah* then elaborates on what "opposite" and "not opposite" mean in practice.

### Heel/Toe

The *mishnah* specifies: *al akeivah ve'al rosh godlah* — a stain on her heel or on the top of her big toe renders her *teme'ah*. These are areas where blood can naturally fall as she walks, given the position of the body relative to the genital area.

### Calf/Foot

*Al shokah ve'al parsoteha mibifnim* — on her calf (*shok* refers to the calf, not the thigh) and on the inner surface of her feet (the surfaces that face one another), she is *teme'ah*, since blood could fall to those inner-facing surfaces. *Mibachutz* — on the outside of her calf, facing away — she is *tehorah*. The distinction, then, is inside versus outside, where "inside" means the surfaces oriented toward the center of the body and where falling blood could plausibly reach, and "outside" means facing away. Front and back — *mikan umikan* — are likewise *tehorah*.

### Garment Belt

Turning to stains on garments: *ra'atah al chalukah min hachagor ul'matah teme'ah* — if the stain appears on her garment below the belt, she is *teme'ah*. *Min hachagor ul'ma'alah* — above the belt — she is *tehorah*, since she can assume that blood did not originate from there.

### Sleeve Stains

Regarding a stain on the sleeve: *im magia keneged beit hatorfa* — if that portion of the sleeve is of a type that could naturally come into direct contact with the genital area, she is *teme'ah*. *Ve'im lav* — if it could not come into direct contact with that area, she is *tehorah*.

### Ein Machzikin

An important principle emerges here: one might think that even if the sleeve could not come into direct contact, it might have touched an intermediate surface — first the blood fell on one part of her body or garment, was transferred to her hand, and from there to the sleeve. The *mishnah* does not entertain this reasoning. The operative principle is *ein machzikin tumah mimakom l'makom* — we do not concern ourselves with indirect transmission of *tumah*. Only if a stain could have gotten to a particular location by direct contact do we treat it as *teme'ah*. Since all of this is in the domain of Rabbinic law, the framework is highly formalized and does not simply follow likelihood of actual contamination.

---

## Blanket/Shawl

### Blanket Rule

A critical qualification: *hayetah pashtato umitkasah bo balailah* — if she removed the garment and used it as a blanket at night, then *kol makom shenimtza bo ketem tme'ah* — wherever on that garment a stain appears, she is *teme'ah*. The reason is *mipnei shehu chozer vechozer* — because it shifts around during sleep and therefore any part of it could have come into direct contact with any part of her body.

### Moving Garments

The same rule applies to *palyot* — a large shawl or head covering that moves about the body — which also could have touched any part of her body directly. In these cases, the location of the stain on the garment does not narrow the analysis in the way it would for a normally worn garment. Of course, the principle of *ein machzikin tumah mimakom l'makom* still applies: we are not concerned that the garment first touched one part of her body and then transferred *tumah* to another surface. The concern is only about the direct contact of the garment itself.

---

## Shmuel/Sensation

### Checked Ground Case

We now arrive at what is perhaps the most consequential passage in this entire section of the *masechet* for contemporary *halacha*. *Shmuel* states: *badkah karka olam ve'yashvah aleha* — a woman checked the ground before sitting on it and confirmed there was no blood; she sat, and upon rising, found blood there. The question is almost rhetorical: where else could the blood have come from? Presumably it came from her. Yet *Shmuel* rules she is *tehorah*.

### Biblical Requirement

The basis for this ruling is the verse *be'vasarah* — in her flesh. *Shmuel* derives from this word: *ad she'targish be'vasarah* — there must be a sensation *within* her flesh. She must experience the blood as it flows from her body. If blood exits without any such sensation, she does not become a biblical *niddah*, regardless of whether we know with certainty that it came from her body.

### Woman as Subject

This ruling has implications at both the conceptual and practical levels. On the conceptual level, *halacha* throughout this *masechet* has to some degree treated the woman as an object — a physical entity from which blood either does or does not flow, with the *halacha* adjudicating based on observable evidence. *Shmuel's* ruling fundamentally shifts that framework. A critical criterion for biblical *niddah* status is now a subjective, first-person experience — her *hargashah*, her sensation — to which the *rabbis* have no direct access. This makes the woman genuinely a subject in the halakhic determination, not merely an object of it.

The consequences of this conceptual shift are also deeply practical: the *posekim* found themselves in the position of having to ask women what this sensation feels like — whether it corresponds to what we would call menstrual cramps, or something else entirely — in order to bridge the gap between *Shmuel's* formulation and the subjective reality of women's experience. The fact that the *rabbis* were consulting women to understand what the *hargashah* is illustrates how the subjective has entered into the halakhic process in an unusual way.

### Rabbinic Category

The practical consequences for contemporary *halacha* are enormous. Prior to *Shmuel*, the entire framework for *ketamim* rested on *doubt*: we could never be entirely certain a stain came from the woman, and it was precisely that uncertainty that kept *ketamim* in the Rabbinic category, allowing various leniencies to apply. But what about cases where there is *no* doubt — where a stain is found on tight-fitting underwear, on toilet paper used to wipe, where the source is definitively the woman's own body? Without *Shmuel*, one would have to treat such cases as biblical *niddah*, outside the lenient framework of *ketamim* entirely.

*Shmuel* changes everything. He says that what creates the *stain* category — as opposed to biblical *niddah* — is not doubt about origin but the *absence of hargashah*. Even when the blood is one hundred percent demonstrably from her body, if there was no sensation, she is not a biblical *niddah*. The practical effect is that it places nearly all stain discoveries, even those where origin is certain, into the Rabbinic framework of *ketamim* with all the associated leniencies. This, the *Gemara* will elaborate, is precisely the intent: *bebe'vasarah velah bishapir velah bachaticha* — the blood must touch her flesh directly, and must be accompanied by sensation, for biblical *niddah* status to be triggered.

---

## Challenge Shmuel

### Within Flesh

The *Gemara* raises a preliminary question about the word *be'vasarah*: is it not needed to teach that blood must be *within* her flesh — that is, directly contacting the vaginal wall and not contained within an embryonic sac or membrane? This is itself an important rule (*be'vasarah velo bishapir velo bachaticha*). The *Gemara* responds: *tarti shma mina* — we learn both from the single word: the requirement of direct contact with the flesh, and *Shmuel's* requirement of *hargashah*.

### Urinating Case

The *Gemara* now subjects *Shmuel's* ruling to a series of challenges. *Ta shema* — come and hear: a woman who is urinating (*oseh tzorcheha*) and sees blood in the urine. *Rabbi Meir* rules: *im omedes teme'ah ve'im yoshevet tehorah* — if she is standing when the blood appears, she is *teme'ah*; if she is sitting and urinating, she is *tehorah*, since then she may assume the blood comes from a non-uterine source.

The *Gemara* challenges: *ei de'argishah* — if she is having a *hargashah*, then why should sitting render her *tehorah*? The sensation should confirm that it is uterine blood. *Ela lav delo argishah* — must it be that she has no *hargashah*? But then, how can she be *teme'ah* even when standing? This seems to contradict *Shmuel*.

### Misidentified Sensation

The *Gemara's* answer: *le'olam de'argishah* — in fact she does have a sensation. *Ve'eima hargashat mei raglayim havei* — but perhaps that sensation is the sensation of urinating. The sensation exists, but it may be misidentified: it might be the ordinary physiological experience of urination rather than the distinctive experience of menstrual flow. Consequently, neither the presence nor the absence of sensation is decisive on its own. We must look to other evidence — her posture — to determine the likelihood of the blood's source. *Hadur mei raglayim lemakor ve'aysei dam* — when standing, the urinary flow may be drawing blood from the uterus; when sitting and urinating normally, there is no reason to assume this.

The *Gemara's* answer here establishes a pattern it will follow throughout this section: there is always a sensation, but the sensation may be ambiguous, misattributed to another bodily experience occurring simultaneously.

### Checking Cloth

*Ta shema*: a checking cloth placed under the pillow — *hanasun tachas hakar* — and examined in the morning. A spot of blood is found. Given that blood of a louse was a common concern, the *mishnah* teaches: *im agol tahor* — if the spot is round, it is *tahor*, as crushed louse blood forms a round mark; *ve'im mashuch tamei* — if elongated, it is *tame'ah*, as that shape results from blood emerging through an internal check.
