Nevertheless, since attributing it to her is more *convenient* and no one loses as a result, we do so. This is an extension of the principle of leniency that underlies the entire category of stain law.

### Who Loses Analysis

One might ask why the Mishnah even mentions the non-Jewish woman — after all, she may not have been menstruating at the time. The answer is precisely the point: it does not matter whether she was actively menstruating. Just as the Jewish woman who finds a stain cannot definitively confirm she bled, so too the non-Jewish woman cannot confirm she did not. The stain could have come from either. Since attributing it to the non-Jewish woman costs her nothing — her status remains unchanged — we do so and the Jewish woman may regard herself as *tehorah*.

This is a broad leniency. The entire logic of *kesamim* is rabbinic, and wherever a basis for leniency presents itself — including the availability of a party who does not lose by attribution — we avail ourselves of it.

---

## Three Women Case

### Mishnah Setup

The Mishnah now addresses a more complex scenario: *gimel nashim shelovshu chaluk echad* — three women shared one garment, passing it among themselves without inspecting it in between — or *sheyashvu al safsal echad* — they sat on one chair without an intervening inspection. A stain is subsequently found. Who is responsible?

### Equal Parties Rule

Since there is no basis to attribute the stain to one woman more than another, and since saying it came from any particular woman would impose a status of *tum'ah* on her without greater justification than the others, one cannot legitimately attribute the stain to any single party. The result: *kulan teme'ot* — they all become *teme'ot*.

This might seem surprising. One might think that since each woman can point to the others as equally plausible sources, perhaps they should all be regarded as *tehorah* — each benefiting individually from the doubt. But this reasoning fails.

### Two Roads Analogy

The classic illustration is the case of two roads, one of which has a corpse buried beneath it. If each traveler came individually to ask, we would rule *tahor* for each based on *chezkat taharah* and the principle that *safek tum'ah b'reshut harabim sefeko tahor*. But if they present themselves simultaneously, it becomes absurd to declare both *tahor*, since we know with certainty that one of them walked over the buried corpse. So too here: even if they do not appear simultaneously, there is a limit to how far attribution can stretch when all parties are equal candidates. When no one woman is a more appropriate candidate than another, attribution to any one of them at the expense of the others cannot be justified, and all lose equally.

### Rabbi Nechemia & Mekabel…

The Mishnah then introduces a different scenario: *yashva al safsal shel even o al istaba shel merchatz* — if the women sat on a stone bench or on a bathhouse bench. These are objects that either because they are stone or because they are attached to the ground and therefore not considered independent vessels, do not receive *tum'ah* — they are *eino mekabel tumah*. In such a case, *Rabbi Nechemia metaher* — Rabbi Nechemia rules the women are *tehorah*, even if it was only one woman sitting there. The reason follows in the next section.

---

## Mekabel Tumah Principle

### Stain Principle

Rabbi Nechemia's position is encapsulated in a foundational principle: *kol davar she'eino mekabel tumah eino mekabel ketamim* — anything that cannot become *tamei* is not subject to the laws of stains. This is a principle of enormous practical importance in *hilchot ketamim*.

### Tosafos Analysis

Tosafos explains what makes this principle structurally significant. One might ask: why should the *tum'ah*-susceptibility of the *object* determine whether the *woman* is *teme'ah*? The woman's status should be the primary concern. Tosafos answers that this reveals something fundamental about the category of *kesamim* itself: the entire framework of stain law was rooted in the world of *tumah v'taharah*. The analysis begins with the status of the stain on the object. If we cannot declare the object *tamei*, we cannot proceed to declare the woman *teme'ah*. The woman's status is derived from the object's status, not assessed independently. When the chain of *tum'ah* cannot begin with the object, it cannot reach the woman.

### Modern Applications

This has direct implications for contemporary *halacha*. The question of whether materials such as plastic, polyester, or nylon are *mekabel tumah* is not merely academic. A stain found on a plastic or synthetic garment would, under Rabbi Nechemia's principle, not render the woman *teme'ah*, provided those materials are not *mekabel tumah* — not even *mekabel tumah derabbanan*, since the accepted ruling follows the stricter standard of requiring *mekabel tumah* even rabbinically.

### Relevance Today

This is why, despite the general practice of not studying *Taharot* in depth given its limited direct applicability today, one cannot fully navigate *hilchot niddah* without recourse to these principles. The laws of *kesamim* require knowing what is *mekabel tumah*. Similarly, related areas — such as the requirement for a *chatzitzah*-free immersion in the *mikveh* and the laws of *sechach* — also hinge on questions drawn from *hilchot kelim* and *mekabel tumah*. These chapters of *Shas* that might seem remote turn out to be essential.

---

## Rav's Restriction

### Rav's Position

The Gemara now turns back to the question of attribution to non-Jewish women. *Amar Rav benachrit hara'ah* — Rav limits the Mishnah's leniency. One cannot attribute a stain to just any non-Jewish woman merely because it is convenient. The non-Jewish woman must be someone who has already previously menstruated. She need not be actively menstruating at the time, but she cannot be someone for whom menstruation would be entirely implausible — a young girl who has never yet had a period. Rav derives this by analogy: *dumya deniddah* — just as when we attribute it to a *niddah* we mean a woman who has been seeing blood, *af nachrit dekahazya* — so too with the non-Jewish woman, she must be in the relevant category of someone who has menstruated.

### Rav Sheshet Critique

*Amar Rav Sheshet Rav namnumi namnem* — Rav Sheshet dismisses Rav's position sharply: Rav must have been dozing when he said this, since it conflicts with an explicit *braita*. The *braita* states: *tola b'nochrit* — you may attribute it to a non-Jewish woman. *Rabbi Meir omer b're'uyah lirot* — Rabbi Meir adds that she must at least be of the appropriate age, i.e., fit to be menstruating. This formulation suggests that the *Rabbanan* require nothing at all, while Rabbi Meir — seemingly the stricter opinion — requires only that she be of menstruating age, not that she have already menstruated. If even Rabbi Meir does not demand prior menstruation, how can Rav make such a demand?

### Rabbi Meir Debate

The Gemara pauses to clarify who is being strict and who is being lenient. *Ve'afillu Rabbi Meir lo ka'amar ella b'ru'uyah lirot* — even Rabbi Meir, who appears strict by requiring age appropriateness, does not go so far as to require actual prior menstruation. So Rav's position seems unsupportable.

### Rav Papa Resolution

*Amar Rav Papa utisbara Rabbi Meir lechumra* — Rav Papa corrects the reading entirely: you have misidentified who is strict and who is lenient. Rabbi Meir is actually the *lenient* opinion. A second *braita* makes this explicit: *ein toleh b'nochrit* — you may not attribute a stain to a non-Jewish woman, as the majority position. *Rabbi Meir omer toleh* — Rabbi Meir says you may. Rabbi Meir is the more permissive voice.

This reframes the debate entirely. The *Rabbanan* hold that attribution to a non-Jewish woman is only valid when she has actually had a prior period — her status must be established, not merely theoretical. Rabbi Meir holds that it suffices that she be of the age at which menstruation is appropriate, even without prior menstruation having occurred. So when the first *braita* reads "Rabbi Meir says she must be of the age to see," this is not Rabbi Meir being stricter than the *Rabbanan* — it is Rabbi Meir being *more lenient*, requiring only age appropriateness where the *Rabbanan* require actual prior menstruation.

Thus Rav's ruling aligns with the *Rabbanan* against Rabbi Meir. The principle underlying this dispute is clear: *tliyah* requires not only that no one loses by attribution, but also that the attribution not be entirely implausible. One cannot attribute a stain to a woman for whom menstruation would be absurd. The question is merely how much of a track record is needed.

---

## Unequal Loss Debate

### Case Setup

The Gemara now addresses the most contested terrain: cases where attribution *does* hurt the other party, but hurts her less than it would hurt the woman attributing. The Gemara cites a *braita*: *toleh b'shomeret yom k'neged yom b'sheni shelah* — you may attribute it to a *shomeret yom k'neged yom* on her second day.

To set up the case: the woman who lent her garment is entirely *tehorah* — she is not a *niddah* and is in the middle of her cycle. The borrower is a *shomeret yom k'neged yom* — a woman who had a *zavah*-type stain one day, and is now on the following day, the "watch day." If she does not bleed today, she may immerse. The garment is returned and a stain is found. If the stain came from the lender, she becomes a *niddah* and must count seven days. If it came from the borrower, the borrower loses her clean "watch day" and must wait one more day. The loss is radically asymmetric: one day versus seven days.

The *braita* also addresses the case of a *soferet shivah she-lo tavlah* — a woman who has completed her seven clean days but has not yet immersed. If the stain came from the lender, the lender becomes a *niddah* with a seven-day count. If it came from the borrower, she must restart her seven-day count entirely. Here the loss is more symmetric — seven days lost either way — but with one crucial distinction: the borrower is still *teme'ah* regardless, since she has not yet immersed. The lender is *tehorah*. There is thus at least a structural asymmetry even where the day-count loss appears equal.

### Rabban Shimon View

*Lefikach hi metukenet v'chaverta mekulkelet, divrei Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — therefore, she is spared and her friend bears the loss. That is the ruling of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. His reasoning is that since one party has less to lose — either fewer days or is already *teme'ah* in any event — there is sufficient basis to attribute the stain to her and spare the other party entirely.

### Rabbi's Position

*Rebi omer eina tola* — Rebi disagrees. Even unequal loss is still loss. Once there is any real cost imposed on the other party by attribution, no matter how much smaller that cost is compared to what the attributing woman would face, Rebi refuses to permit attribution. *Lefikach shteihem mekulkalot* — therefore both women suffer, the lender becoming a *niddah* and the borrower losing her clean day or restarting her count, because the stain cannot be attributed to either one definitively.

### Agreement Cases

Despite their dispute, Rebi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel agree in cases where the attribution costs the other party nothing at all. *Shomeret yom k'neged yom b'rishon shelah* — if the borrower had her staining event today, she is on the first day, and saying the stain is hers costs her nothing, since she stained anyway. *O b'yoshevet al dam tohor* — or if she is in the *dam tohor* period following childbirth, the thirty-three or sixty-six days during which blood does not render her *teme'ah*, then attributing the stain to her has no consequence for her. *O b'vatula shedam'eha tehorim* — or if she is a woman who has recently married and whose bleeding is presumed to be hymenal, then again she loses nothing by attribution.

In all these cases, everyone agrees: where attribution is costless, attribute freely. The debate between Rebi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is only where there is genuine, if asymmetric, loss.

The Gemara then asks why the phrase *lefikach* — "therefore" — appears in both Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling and in Rebi's ruling, since in each case the conclusion would seem to follow obviously from the stated position. The answer is that each *lefikach* serves to exclude a possible alternative rule. One might have thought that even if attribution to the other woman is rejected, one would resolve the stain by applying some independent rule — such as assigning responsibility to whichever woman was in physical possession of the garment at the moment of discovery. The *lefikach* in Rebi's formulation rules this out: once attribution fails, both women are *teme'ot*, and no alternative distributional rule comes into play.

---

## Two Roads Case

### Case Introduction

*Amar Rav Chisda*: the Gemara now revisits the case of two roads — one *tamei*, one *tahor* — but with a new twist. We have one *tamei* person and one *tahor* person, both of whom walked down two paths, one of which contained a buried corpse and one of which did not, and neither remembers which path he walked. The most convenient attribution is that the *tamei* person walked the *tamei* path and the *tahor* person walked the *tahor* path. There are also independent legal grounds for leniency: the *tahor* person has a *chezkat taharah*, and if this is *reshut harabim*, *safek tum'ah b'reshut harabim sefeko tahor* would apply.

Rav Chisda says this is subject to the debate of Rebi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. The *tamei* person is already *tamei*, but if he walked the *tamei* path — that of *tum'at met* — he now faces a lengthier purification process. If he walked the *tahor* path, the attribution to him may cost him additional days of *tum'ah* that he would not otherwise have had to observe. Is that loss enough to preclude attribution under Rebi's view, thereby requiring both men to treat themselves as having walked the *tamei* path?

Rav Chisda holds that this is precisely the Rebi–Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel debate. The *tamei* person is not in the same position as someone who has no loss whatsoever, so attribution to him is not uncontested.

### Rav Adda Challenge

*Matkif lah Rav Adda*: Rav Adda challenges the analogy. He argues that the *shomeret yom* case, which animated the original dispute, is structurally different from the two-roads case. In the *shomeret yom* scenario, one might say Rebi refused attribution not because he was unwilling to impose any loss on the other party, but because the *shomeret yom* was essentially already on the cusp of *taharah* — she only needed to go to the *mikveh* — and therefore was essentially equivalent in status to the *tehorah* woman. If the two parties are effectively equivalent, there is no basis for preferring to attribute to one over the other.

The two-roads case might be genuinely different. The *tamei* person is truly *tamei*, not on the threshold of purity. He has real loss to sustain by having the *tamei* path attributed to him, but his loss is modest compared to the *tahor* person's loss. If Rebi's reasoning was about essential equivalence, not about any loss at all, then Rebi might actually *permit* attribution in the two-roads case, since the parties are genuinely unequal in ways beyond mere day-counts.

### Interpretation Debate

*Rav Chisda* responds: *sof sof itvilah ba'aya* — in the end, the *shomeret yom* still needs to immerse. She is not *tehorah*. Her remaining obligation is real. Rebi's refusal to attribute, therefore, was not premised on her being essentially *tahor*. Rather, it was premised on his unwillingness to impose *any* incremental loss on a party through attribution. On that understanding, the two-roads case is indeed subject to the same debate: Rebi would say no attribution even there, because the *tamei* person would suffer at least some additional days, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel would say attribute because the loss is asymmetric in favor of leniency.

The disagreement between Rav Chisda and Rav Adda is thus a dispute about what animated Rebi's position: was it an absolute rule against imposing *any* loss via attribution, or was it a narrower principle that applies only when the parties are essentially equivalent in status?

---

## Doubtful Tamei Cases

### Talui Case

*Amar Rebbi Yosi berabbi Chanina*: the Gemara introduces yet another variation. What if it is not a *tamei* and *tahor* person on two paths, but a *tahor* person and a *talui* — someone whose status is doubtful, who may or may not be *tamei*? They walk down two paths, one *tamei* and one *tahor*, and we do not know which walked where. Can we attribute the *tamei* path to the doubtful person and the *tahor* path to the clearly *tahor* person?

Rabbi Yosi b'Rabbi Chanina rules: *toleh tamei b'talui v'tahor b'tahor* — yes, attribute the *tamei* path to the *talui* and the *tahor* path to the *tahor*. Moreover, *v'divrei hakol* — this is the unanimous position of all opinions, including Rebi.

### No Additional Loss

The reason is critical: the *talui* must treat himself as *tamei* regardless. His doubtful status already obligates him to observe the restrictions of *tum'ah*. Declaring him to have walked the *tamei* path imposes no additional loss upon him — he was already treating himself as *tamei*. Since he suffers no incremental loss by the attribution, even Rebi would agree it is permitted. This is a precise application of the principle that costless attribution is universally accepted.

This reasoning assumes the case concerns the *first day* — if the *talui* would lose additional days by the attribution, the debate would re-emerge.

### Ketem B'Ketem Query

This leads naturally to a more subtle question: *mahu litlos ketem b'ketem* — may one attribute a stain found on a shared garment to a woman who has herself found a stain on a different garment of hers? On the surface, the answer would seem to be yes: if the other woman already has a stain, she becomes *teme'ah* regardless, so attributing this additional stain to her costs her nothing. But a competing consideration arises: the basis for *tliyah* has always required some meaningful identification of the other woman as a *plausible* source of bleeding. A *niddah* is clearly in the context of bleeding. A woman counted in her *shivah neki'im* is still within the *tum'ah* of prior bleeding. But a woman who merely found a *ketem* — a stain on her own garment — is in a more ambiguous position. The nature of *kesamim* is that we do not say definitively that she bled; we say only that a stain was found and she must be treated accordingly. Can such a woman serve as the basis of attribution for another's stain?

---

## Ketem Attribution

### Yochanan Query

*Ba'ei mineih Rebbi Yochanan meRebbi Yehudah bar Livai*: Rebbi Yochanan formally posed the question to Rebbi Yehudah bar Livai — may one attribute a stain to a woman who found a stain on another garment of hers? The two sides of the question are real. On the one hand, since the woman with the *ketem* is *teme'ah* from her own stain anyway, attributing this garment's stain to her costs her nothing additional, which should satisfy even Rebi's stringent standard. On the other hand, one might argue that without an actual *re'iyah* — a confirmed uterine flow — there is insufficient basis to treat her as a genuine source from whom a stain could have originated.

### Rabbi's Answer

*Amar leih ein toleh* — the answer given is that one may not attribute a stain to a woman who had only a *ketem*. *Mah ta'am* — why? *Lefi she'ein toleh* — the reason given, that "you do not attribute," seems at first glance circular, but the Gemara elaborates through its subsequent discussion.

The underlying logic, as the Gemara frames it through its treatment of the *aliba d'Rebbi* question, is this: According to Rebi, attribution is already highly restricted. If even when a woman is definitively known to be bleeding, Rebi is unwilling to attribute a stain to her when she would suffer any incremental loss — certainly when her bleeding status is itself uncertain, based only on a *ketem* she found, Rebi would not permit attribution. *Hashta mah hatam dikachazya migufah* — now, there where she actually bled from her body, Rebi would still not always allow attribution; *hacha d'alma kachazya*, here where the blood might have come from elsewhere entirely, he certainly would not allow it. So according to Rebi, *ein toleh b'ketem* — definitively.

The more interesting question is according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who is generally more willing to permit attribution. *Ki tibei lach aliba d'Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — the real question is for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position. *Hatam hu dikachazya migufah* — in the normal attribution cases, the woman to whom we attribute at least has a known history of bleeding, so it is not implausible. *Aval hacha d'me'alma kachazya* — here, where the source of the stain on her own garment is also uncertain, perhaps even Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel would say that attribution is impermissible — *lo talya*. Or perhaps it makes no difference — *o dilma lo shana* — and attribution is still permitted since she suffers no incremental loss.

### Braita Conflict

The Gemara raises a *braita* that appears to contradict the ruling: *ein tolin ketem b'ketem* — you do not attribute a stain to a woman with a stain. So far so consistent. But the *braita* continues: *hishila chaluka lenochrit o leyoshevet al hakesem, harei zo tola bah* — if she lent her garment to a non-Jewish woman *or* to a woman who was *yoshevet al ha-ketem* (sitting on a stain, i.e., treating herself as *teme'ah* due to a stain), she may attribute it to her. This directly contradicts the first clause — first the *braita* says you cannot attribute to a woman with a stain, then it says you can. *Ha gufa kashya* — the *braita* itself is internally contradictory.

### Resolutions

*Ha lo kashya* — the Gemara offers a first resolution: the two clauses represent the positions of Rebi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel respectively. The first clause reflects Rebi's view that *ein toleh ketem b'ketem*; the second reflects Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's permissive stance.

*Ika de'amri* — an alternative reading: both clauses reflect Rebi's position, but in different cases. *Ha b'rishon shelah ha b'sheni shelah* — the first clause discusses the second day of the *ketem*-woman's count, when she would lose a day if attribution is made; the second clause discusses the first day, when she loses nothing. According to this reading, Rebi would permit attribution on the first day, when it is costless, but would prohibit it on the second day, when there is loss. Notably, this reading also raises the question of whether Rebi's standard for *ketem b'ketem* attribution tracks his general principle about loss.

### Retroactive Discovery

*Rav Ashi amar*: Rav Ashi offers yet another resolution, attributing both clauses to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: *ha v'ha Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*. The difference lies not in who the opinions are, but in the timing of the second stain's discovery. *Kan lemapre'a kan lehaba* — one clause speaks of retroactive determination, the other of forward-looking assessment.

Tosafos explains this distinction clearly. When the first garment's stain is found, a ruling must be made at that moment. If, at that same moment, the other woman has already found a stain on a second garment of hers, then that pre-existing stain is available as a basis for attribution, and one may attribute the first garment's stain to her — *lemapre'a*. But if the other woman discovered her own stain only *after* the first garment's stain had already been assessed — *lehaba* — that later discovery cannot retroactively revise the earlier ruling. Status determinations are fixed at the moment of assessment; they cannot be revised on the basis of facts that emerge subsequently.

This is a striking principle. It is not about ascertaining physical facts — if it were, later evidence would always be relevant. It reflects the formal character of halachic status determinations: once a ruling is made under the conditions that existed at the time, it is not undone by subsequent discoveries. The rules are formal, not merely evidentiary.

---

## Braita Reinterpretation

### Abaye Reframes

*Amar Abaye lo kashya* — Abaye resolves the internal contradiction in the *braita* by reinterpreting its text entirely. The two cases in the *braita*'s permissive clause are not "a non-Jewish woman" and "a woman sitting on a stain" as two separate parallel cases. Rather, the *braita* should be read as follows: *hishila chaluka lenochrit ba'alat ketem* — she lent her garment to a non-Jewish woman who had a stain, or *leyoshevet al dam tohor* — to a woman who was in her *dam tohor* period (the thirty-three or sixty-six post-childbirth days when blood is not *tamei*). Under this reading, the permissive clause does not involve attribution of a *ketem* to a woman whose only basis is another *ketem*. The non-Jewish woman also has a *ketem*, which is irrelevant since her *tum'ah* status is not governed by Jewish law in the same way; and the *dam tohor* woman has no loss from attribution regardless.

### Principle Maintained

This re-reading preserves the principle *ein tolin ketem b'ketem* intact. The *braita*'s permissive clause, properly understood, does not actually permit attributing a stain to a woman whose only relevant status is having found a stain. In both permitted cases, there is an additional feature — non-Jewish status or *dam tohor* period — that independently justifies attribution. The formal principle that stain-to-stain attribution is impermissible remains undisturbed.

---

## Nechemia Extended

### Scriptural Basis

Returning to Rabbi Nechemia's principle, the Gemara now examines its precise scope and derivation. *Amar Rav Matna mai ta'ama deRebbi Nechemia* — what is the textual basis for Rabbi Nechemia's position? The verse states *v'niketa la'aretz teshev* — she shall be cleansed, and she sits on the ground. If she sat on the ground — ground being paradigmatically *eino mekabel tumah*, as it is not a vessel — and found a stain, *v'niketa* — she is clean. Tosafos adds, as noted earlier, that this reveals the entire framework: the category of *kesamim* was constituted within the architecture of *tumah v'taharah*, and if the object cannot be declared *tamei*, the woman cannot be declared *teme'ah*.

### Pottery Example

*Amar Rav Huna amar Rabbi Chanina*: Rabbi Nechemia's principle applies even to the outer side of a pottery vessel (*achorei kli cheres*). Pottery vessels become *tamei* only through their interior; the outer surface does not become *tamei*. Therefore, a stain found on the outer surface of a pottery vessel does not render the woman *teme'ah*, even though the vessel *as a whole* is in the category of objects that receive *tum'ah*. The relevant question is whether *this specific surface* is *mekabel tumah*, not merely whether the object generically is.

*Peshita* — one might think this is obvious. The Gemara responds: *mahu deteima ligzar gabo atu tocho* — one might have thought to issue a rabbinic decree treating the outer surface as equivalent to the inner surface, lest people become lenient about stains found inside. *Ka mashma lan* — the Gemara informs us that no such decree was issued.

### Rag Size

*Amar Abaye*: Rabbi Nechemia similarly rendered *tahor* a stain found on a rag that was less than three finger-widths by three finger-widths — *matlit she'ein bah shalosha al shalosha*. Such a rag is too small to be considered a usable item — *delo chazi lo le'aniyim v'lo le'ashirim*, it has no utility for poor or rich alike. Since it is too small to be classified as a vessel susceptible to *tum'ah*, a stain found on it does not implicate the woman. This further sharpens the principle: it is not enough that the material is one that *generically* can become *tamei*; the specific object must actually be of sufficient character to *receive tum'ah* under the laws of *kelim*.

---

## Historical Precedent

### Nachman Objection

*Darash Rabbi Chiya bar Rav Mattana mishmeih d'Rav halacha k'Rabbi Nechemiah* — Rav ruled publicly that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Nechemia. Rav Nachman immediately challenged this: *Abba tani ma'aseh ba lifnei chachamim v'tim'um* — my father (as a *tanna*) taught a *braita* in which a similar case came before the Sages and they declared the women *teme'ot*. How can one rule like Rabbi Nechemia if the *chachamim* themselves ruled against him in practice?

### Grinding Case

*De-tanya*: the *braita* describes two women grinding grain at a hand mill — *shte nashim she-hayu tachanot b'rechayim shel yad*. One woman was positioned closer to the millstone (*pnimit*, inner), the other farther away (*chitzonah*, outer), though the outer woman sometimes needed to move inward to place grain or gather the flour.

If blood was found under the inner woman: *shtehen teme'ot* — both are *teme'ot*, because the outer woman also moved into the inner space, making her an equal candidate. If found under the outer woman: *ha-chitzonah teme'ah v'ha-pnimit tehorah* — only the outer one is *teme'ah*, since the inner woman had no occasion to move outward. Here the attribution follows not mere convenience but the logic of physical probability. If found precisely between both women: *shtehen teme'ot* — again both, since neither is a stronger candidate.

### Olive Leaf Case

The *braita* continues with two additional instances. Blood was found on the rim of a bath (*sfata shel ambati*), or on an olive leaf during the heating of an oven — *al aleh shel zayit b'sha'ah she-hisiku et ha-tanur*. In the olive-leaf case, oven-heating leaves were gathered beneath, and blood was found on one of them. *U-va ma'aseh lifnei chachamim v'tim'um* — when such cases came before the Sages, they declared the women *teme'ot*. Yet an olive leaf is presumably not *mekabel tumah*. This seems to contradict ruling like Rabbi Nechemia.

### Resolution

*V'mishni tanna'ei hi* — the Gemara resolves the contradiction: the position of the majority (*chachamim*) is itself a debate among *tanna'im*. Another *braita* explicitly states: *Rabbi Yaakov metamei v'Rabbi Nechemia metaher v'horu chachamim k'Rabbi Nechemia* — Rabbi Yaakov renders *tamei*, Rabbi Nechemia renders *tahor*, and the *chachamim* ruled in accordance with Rabbi Nechemia. Since we have a *braita* in which the majority explicitly aligned with Rabbi Nechemia, the ruling follows Rabbi Nechemia. The earlier instances where *chachamim* rendered *teme'ot* represent a tannaic dispute, and the decisive ruling sides with the lenient position.

---

## Kesamim Criteria

### Three Leniencies

With Rabbi Nechemia's principle now firmly established, the Gemara has effectively articulated three major structural leniencies in the law of *kesamim*. First, there is a minimum size requirement: the stain must be larger than a *geris* (the volume of a louse). Second, it must be found on an object that is *mekabel tumah*. Third — coming up in the Mishnah — it must be on non-colored clothing, since on colored fabric the blood may not be visible or distinguishable.

### Tzara'at Parallel

Each of these leniencies can be explained on its own terms. The *geris* size threshold relates to the louse — a common source of red stains. The *mekabel tumah* requirement follows from the Tosafos analysis of the framework. The colored-clothing criterion follows from the need to visually confirm the stain's character. Yet taken together, these three criteria map precisely onto the three conditions for *tum'at nega'im* — the *tzara'at* stains: a minimum size exceeding a *geris*, occurrence on clothing, and occurrence only on white (non-colored) garments. As Tractate *Nega'im* presents it, those same criteria govern the assessment of stains of *tzara'at*.

### Formal vs. Practical

This convergence raises a fundamental question: are the criteria of *kesamim* independently arrived at through practical halachic reasoning, or are they shaped by a formal structural analogy to *tum'at nega'im*? Opinions in the *mishnayot* are distributed — Rabbi Nechemia articulates the *mekabel tumah* principle, Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus articulates the stain principle elsewhere — suggesting the framework was assembled from multiple voices. Yet the perfect alignment of all three criteria with the *nega'im* framework suggests that something more formal may be operating. The size of a *geris* is also a standard threshold across various areas of *tumah v'taharah*, suggesting again that formal criteria and practical considerations are deeply intertwined in this area of law.

---

## Three in One Bed

### Mishnah Setup

The Gemara moves to the next Mishnah: *shalosh nashim she-hayu yeshenot b'mita achat* — three women who were sleeping in one bed, and blood was found beneath one of them.

### All Become Tmeia

*Kulan teme'ot* — all three are *teme'ot*, because during sleep they presumably moved around, and the blood could have originated from any of them. The position of the stain beneath one of the women does not conclusively identify her as the source, since movement in sleep is assumed. If it were established that they lay rigidly in fixed positions and could not have moved, the analysis would differ, but that is the subject of later Gemara discussion.

### Individual Check

*Badka achat mehen v'nimtzet teme'ah* — if one of the women performed an internal examination after waking and found herself to be a *niddah*, then *hi teme'ah v'shtehen tehorot* — she alone is *teme'ah* and the other two are *tehorot*. The positive identification of one woman as the source of the blood removes the uncertainty and frees the others.

### Attribution Between

*V'tolot zo b'zo* — under other circumstances, which the Gemara will specify, one woman may attribute the stain to another based on differential likelihood. This is the *tolot zo b'zo* principle: when the women are not equal candidates — one pregnant, one not; one postmenopausal, one not; and so on — the woman who is a *less* likely source of the stain may attribute it to the woman who is a *more* likely source.

### Equal Unsuitability

*V'im lo hayu re'uyot lirot* — if none of the women were in a state in which they would be expected to have their cycles, all being pregnant for example, then paradoxically *re'uyot k'ilu hen re'uyot* — they are treated as though they are all equally suitable. Since no one woman is a more likely candidate than another, they cannot attribute to one another, and all remain in the status of *teme'ot*. This is the final clause of the Mishnah and will be revisited at the close of the Gemara's discussion.

---

## Checking Timing

### Instantaneous Check

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: the ability to identify one woman as the source of the blood and thereby exempt the others depends on a critical condition — *v'hu she-badka atzma b'shiur veset* — she must have checked herself *instantaneously*, within the *shiur veset*, the minimal time interval following the moment of discovery. Only if she checks immediately and finds she is *niddah* can we retroactively conclude that she was *niddah* at the time the stain was found. If she delayed her examination, then even if she finds herself to be *niddah*, we cannot conclude she was *niddah* at the relevant moment — she may have become *niddah* after the stain was discovered, and so the stain cannot be attributed to her.

This is not merely an abstract distinction. It goes to the heart of how status determinations work in *hilchot niddah*: a woman's *niddah* status is established at the moment of confirmed *re'iyah*, and attribution of past events depends on whether that status was established at the relevant time.

### Chatat Principle

*Savar lah k'Bar Pada* — Rav Yehuda's ruling follows Bar Pada's framework. *D'amar kol she-ba'alah b'chatat tissaref terumah* — whatever scenario would obligate the husband to bring a *chatat* (sin offering) after relations with his wife who was found to be *niddah* also obligates the burning of *terumah* she handled. The two cases are parallel: the husband's *chatat* obligation and the *terumah*'s *tum'ah* status are determined by the same standard of when the woman's *niddah* status is established.

### Bar Pada Framework

Bar Pada's framework operates in three tiers. If the woman checked *immediately* after relations — within the *shiur veset* — and found she was *niddah*, the husband brings a *chatat*, since we conclude she was *niddah* during relations. Correspondingly, any *terumah* she handled during that same window is burned. If she checked after a slightly longer delay — producing a state of doubt (*safek*) about whether she was already *niddah* during relations — the husband brings an *asham talui*, and the *terumah* or *taharot* she handled are in a suspended (*taluy*) state. If she waited long enough that we simply cannot say she was *niddah* during relations — treating her as having become *niddah* afterward — the husband is entirely exempt, and the things she handled are *tehorot*.

The application to the three-women case is direct: only in the first tier, where the check was truly instantaneous, can we definitively attribute the stain to the woman who found herself *niddah* and thereby exempt the other two.

---

## Blood Prevention

### Yoshia Principle

Rabbi Yoshia's principle provides the physiological basis for why an instantaneous post-coital check can establish *niddah* status *during* relations rather than merely *after* them. The principle: *emar shamash ikvo l'dam* — relations themselves prevented the blood from emerging. The blood was present, but was held back by the physical fact of relations. Upon separation, it emerged immediately. Therefore, finding blood immediately after relations is effectively equivalent to blood having been present *during* relations.

### Child & Elder Mashal

*Amar Rabbi Yirmia mashal d'Rabbi Yoshia l'mai davar domeh* — Rabbi Yirmia offers an analogy. A child and an elder are walking together along a road toward a city. As long as they are walking together on the road, the child walks respectfully beside the elder, matching his pace. *Nichnasu la'ir* — the moment they enter the city and the companionship is dissolved, *yeled memaher lavo* — the child runs off immediately. The restraint was the joint circumstance of the road; its removal triggers immediate, rapid action. So too: the physical circumstance of relations restrained the blood; its cessation brought the blood immediately.

### Eye & Tears Mashal

*V'amar Abaye mashal d'Rabbi Yoshia l'mai davar domeh* — Abaye offers a second analogy. If one presses a finger against the eye, tears will not flow — the pressure prevents their emergence — but the moment the finger is removed, *dim'ah memaheret lavo* — the tears come immediately. Again: the restraint removed, the immediate consequence follows.

### Distinction from Others

This reasoning applies specifically to post-coital checking. In other contexts — such as handling *terumah* — if there is a delay, we cannot invoke this principle. There was no physical impediment holding back the blood; if blood appears now, it appeared now, not earlier. The uniqueness of the sexual context is that the physical act of relations itself creates a documented physiological basis for saying that blood present immediately afterward was already present *during*. Without that basis, even an instantaneous check does not retroactively establish prior *niddah* status. This is why the standards diverge between the husband's *chatat* and other cases, and why Rabbi Oshaya could argue that even if the husband brings a *chatat* — the most stringent tier — the *terumah* she handled may still only be in a state of *safek tum'ah* rather than certain *tum'ah*, since the *terumah* was not handled during an act of relations.

---

## Tolot Criteria

### Pregnant Case

*Tanu Rabbanan keitzad tolot zo b'zo* — the Sages taught: how does the attribution among the women in the bed work? *Ubarah v'she'eina ubarah* — if one woman is pregnant and one is not, *tolah ubarah b'she'eina ubarah* — the pregnant woman may attribute the stain to the non-pregnant one. Pregnancy significantly reduces the likelihood of uterine bleeding, making the non-pregnant woman the more plausible source.

### Nursing Case

*Menika v'she'eina menika* — if one woman is nursing and one is not, *tolah menika b'she'eina menika* — the nursing woman may attribute the stain to the non-nursing woman. Nursing similarly suppresses uterine bleeding, making the non-nursing woman the stronger candidate.

### Age Case

*Zekena v'she'eina zekena* — postmenopausal versus premenopausal: *tolah zekena b'she'eina zekena* — the postmenopausal woman may attribute the stain to the premenopausal woman, since uterine bleeding is no longer expected of the postmenopausal woman.

### Menarche Case

*Besulah v'she'eina besulah* — here the term *besulah* is used in the sense of *mesuleket damim*, a woman who has not yet begun to menstruate, as opposed to one who has already established her cycle. *Tolah besulah b'she'eina besulah* — the pre-menarche woman may attribute the stain to the post-menarche woman.

### Equal Status Rule

*Hayu shteian ubarot, shteian menikot, shteian zekenos, shteian besulot* — if both women share the same status in every relevant category, then *zu hi she-shaninu* — this is the case we stated in the Mishnah: *lo hayu re'uyot lirot, ro'im k'ilu hen re'uyot* — since they are all equally unsuitable candidates in the same way, they are treated as though all equally suitable, and *kulan teme'ot* — all become *teme'ot* with no basis for attribution in any direction.

---

---

# Niddah 62

## Seven Cleansers Intr (II)

### Opening & Context

Today's daf is 62. We begin at the very bottom of 61a — actually the *mishnah* on 61b. In that *mishnah* we had an extended discussion about *tolah*, attributing a stain to another cause. Somewhat unconnected to that discussion, the *mishnah* also presents the major third leniency for *ketamim*: the role of color.

Until now we had seen two such leniencies. The first concerns size — the *gris*, the minimum threshold of a grain. The second concerns the nature of the garment or vessel: one that is not *mekabel tumah*, that cannot become *tamei*, does not generate a stain problem. And on the previous daf we saw the third leniency — that on non-white, colored clothing a stain is not a problem — though without any explicit reason being given in the text. One can speculate that it has to do with the ability to identify the color, though the *mishnah* itself does not say so. Interestingly, it was noted historically that although there was concern about permitting colored clothing in the period following the *Churban* — because it might seem too festive — the Sages specifically allowed it precisely because it would serve as a leniency regarding stains. Notably, all three of these criteria also appear in the laws of *nega'im*, the different system of spotting and staining discussed elsewhere, which is interesting to observe even if the *mishnah* does not explain the connection.

We now continue with our *mishnah* at the bottom of 61b, which turns to the question of how to eliminate a stain. The *mishnah*'s interest here is not in how to restore a garment to a presentable appearance, but in using the removal process as a method for determining what *kind* of stain we are dealing with.

### Seven Substances

The *mishnah* states: *shiv'ah sammanim ma'avirin al ha-ketem* — one passes, meaning one applies and rubs, seven types of cleansing substances over the stain. They are as follows: *rok tafel*, tasteless spit, meaning spit from a person who has not eaten recently; *mei grisin*, water from beans — specifically from the chewing of a certain type of bean whose peel fell off naturally rather than by human hand; *mei raglayim*, urine that has turned rancid; *neter*, a form of lye; *borit*, another classic cleanser; *kammoniya*, a particular substance of uncertain nature; and *ashlag*, similarly obscure.

Regarding *neter*, the *gemara* specifies *neter Alexandri* — the Alexandrian variety — and explicitly excludes *neter Antipatris*. The distinction is significant: Alexandria was a major scientific and commercial center, and its *neter* was prized as the genuine article, while the Antipatris variety, produced in southern Judea — the city named for the father of Herod — was considered an inferior local imitation. The situation is not unlike the difference between a name-brand product and a poor substitute.

### Substance Etymology

*Kammoniya* is a Greek word — *Kimolia* — referring to some kind of white substance or earth, named after the island where it was first used. It may correspond to what is known in Arabic as *al-kali*, possibly saltwort, a group of plants that grow in salt marshes and alkaline soils. *Ashlag* is a Persian word for what appears to be the ashes of grass or plants. The *gemara* records that Shmuel investigated this substance by asking seafarers (*nachutei yamma*) who told him it is called *ashlaga* and is found in the crevices of pearl-forming shells, removable only with an iron instrument — which raises obvious practical questions about accessibility.

As for *neter*, it appears to be sodium carbonate, which functions as a water softener and facilitates cleaning. *Borit* is more complicated. Rav Yehuda identifies it as *ahla*, another classic cleanser mentioned in Tanakh. But the *gemara* immediately challenges this from a *baraita* that lists *borit* and *ahla* as two separate items. So perhaps *borit* is *kavrissa* — sulfur, as Rashi suggests. But that too is challenged: the *mishnah* in *Shevi'it* includes *borit* among substances to which the laws of *shemitah* apply, and only things that grow from the ground are subject to *shemitah*, whereas sulfur is a mineral. The *gemara* therefore returns to identifying *borit* as *ahla* and resolves the apparent duplication by positing that there are two varieties of *ahla*. In any case, all of these substances function as soap-like cleansers, and the *mishnah* employs them not for their cosmetic utility but for their evidentiary value in *halacha*.

## Mishnah Scenario

### Stain Doesn't Remove

How is all of this halachically relevant? The *mishnah* presents the following scenario. A woman found a stain on her garment, and the garment — now rendered *tamei* by the presumed blood — was immersed in a *mikveh*. After immersion, *tehorot* were placed upon it — say, *terumah* grain resting on the garment. Subsequently, the seven cleansers were applied to the stain: *he'evir alav shiv'ah sammanim v'lo avar* — and the stain did not come out. In this case, *harei zeh tzeva* — this is a [non-blood] dye. The fact that the seven cleansers failed to remove the stain is taken as evidence that it is not a bloodstain, because these substances would remove blood but not necessarily other colored matter. Therefore, everything is permitted — *tahorot tahorot* — and there is no need to re-immerse.

### Stain Removes/Pales

If, however, after applying the seven cleansers the stain did come out — *avar* — or even if it merely paled — *she-diheh* — then *harei zeh ketem*, this is indeed a stain. Now a problem emerges. Although the garment was immersed in the *mikveh*, the stain was still present on it at the time of immersion. A stain does not cease to be *tamei* simply because the garment was brought into a *mikveh* — just as a *sheretz* placed in a *mikveh* does not become *tahor*. The proper procedure is to remove the stain *before* immersion and then immerse the now-clean garment. In this case, the stain remained during immersion, and therefore *ve-ha-tahorot teme'ot* — the *terumah* items are *tamei* — and one must now immerse the garment again, now that the stain has been removed.

The *mishnah* operates in the world of *tumah ve-taharah*. This was a lived reality: in the household of a *kohen*, or even for someone who was careful to eat *chullin be-taharah*, any garment or vessel that a *niddah* had contact with would have to be kept separate or immersed before being used in connection with food or *terumah*. Wooden vessels, garments, tables — all could become *tamei* and in principle require *tevilah*, though there are categories of large immovable objects that fall under a different legal framework.

The evidentiary logic is straightforward: whether a stain comes out or not with these particular substances is the test of whether it is blood. If it comes out, we know it was blood, which retroactively shows that the stain was present during immersion and that the immersion was therefore insufficient. If it does not come out, we take that as evidence that it was not blood, and the prior immersion stands.

### Implicit Assumptions

Reading the *mishnah* closely reveals several implicit assumptions worth flagging. The first is that one must remove the stain before immersion — the *mishnah*'s case is built on a scenario where this was not done, which is precisely what generates the problem in the second case. The second assumption, more subtle, is embedded in the language *she-diheh* — that paling counts as a meaningful stage of removal. This raises the question: is it necessary for the stain to disappear entirely, or is there a point at which sufficient paling renders the stain halachically "no longer present"? The *mishnah* implies that even paling is legally significant, and this is something the *gemara* will develop at length.

There is also a third implicit point worth noting. If we read the *mishnah* at face value, the non-removal of the stain by the seven cleansers proves *definitively* that it is not blood. But if that is so, why was immersion necessary at all? If we knew it was not blood even before immersion, the garment should have been permitted without any *mikveh*. One possible reading is that the *mishnah* is simply presenting the extreme version of the second case — emphasizing that even having immersed, one has not helped the situation if the stain was blood. But *Tosafot* raises the deeper question: perhaps the failure of the cleansers is not absolute proof of non-blood status, but only strong evidence. In that reading, the combination of factors — the likelihood that it is not blood, plus the prior immersion — together produces the leniency. This question of whether the cleansers *prove* the stain is not blood or merely *indicate* it will drive much of the *gemara*'s subsequent discussion.

## Seven Cleansers Intr (II)

### Application Method

The *mishnah* now specifies how these substances must be applied: *vetzarich lechacheish shalosh pe'amim lechol echad ve'echad* — one must rub three times with each of the seven substances in sequence. Rashi describes the rubbing motion as *shiruv*, working the two parts of the garment against each other. If the substances were applied out of order — *he'eviran shelo ke-sidran* — or if all seven were applied simultaneously — *she-he'evir shiv'ah sammanim ke'echad* — the process is worthless: *lo asa ve-lo klum*. The application must follow this specific prescribed sequence, each substance applied individually three times.

This level of precision is striking, and one might legitimately question whether this procedure was ever widely followed in practice. The requirement of seven very specific substances, applied in a precise order, three rubbings each, raises practical obstacles. If one did not avail oneself of these cleansers, the garment would presumably remain in its halachically ambiguous state — not that the law was "ignored," but simply that the procedure was difficult enough that it may have remained largely in the theoretical realm.

At this point it is worth returning to a detail from the *mishnah* about *mei grisin* — the bean water. The specification that the bean's peel fell off naturally, *chalukat nefesh*, rather than being removed by a person, and that the bean itself be of a particular variety, reflects the high degree of specificity governing these substances. Similarly, *mei raglayim* must be rancid — *she-hechmitzu* — rather than fresh urine.

The *gemara* also revisits the identification of *borit*. As noted, *Rav Yehuda* says it is *ahla*, and the *gemara* reconciles the apparent conflict with the *baraita* that lists them separately by positing two varieties of *ahla* — *trei gavnei ahla*. This taxonomic exercise reflects the general pattern here: the Sages were working to identify substances that were known in practice but described in the *mishnah* only by traditional names, some of Greek or Persian origin, whose precise identification had become uncertain.

The broader question of whether this procedure ever had widespread practical application is worth holding. In a world where one needed seven specific substances, applied in a particular order, with three rubbings each — and where failure to follow the procedure exactly rendered it void — it seems likely that many households simply could not access or prepare all seven in the proper form. The halakhic principle was articulated, its procedure codified, but its real-world implementation may have been limited.

## Tsafon & Proofs

### Tsafon Problem

A *baraita* now introduces the substance *tsafon*, which was apparently a particularly powerful cleanser. The case: the seven cleansers were applied, the stain did not come out, and then *tsafon* was applied and it *did* come out. What is the halachic status?

One might think that if the stain came out with *tsafon*, this proves it was blood — the *tsafon* revealed what the seven substances could not. The *gemara* rejects this reasoning: *tsafon nami ma'avar* — *tsafon* removes non-blood stains as well. Because *tsafon* is so powerful, the fact that it removed the stain cannot serve as evidence that the stain was blood. It would remove anything.

The *gemara* therefore reframes the *baraita*. The case is not that all seven were applied and then *tsafon* was added as an eighth. Rather: six of the seven were applied and the stain did not come out; then *tsafon* was used in place of the seventh substance, and it came out. In this scenario, one cannot claim that the failure of the first six proves it is not blood — perhaps had the proper seventh substance been used, the stain would have come out. And the fact that *tsafon* removed it proves nothing, since *tsafon* would remove anything. Therefore the status remains *tamei*, because the seven-substance procedure was never properly completed.

### Second Application

A second *baraita* addresses a different scenario: the seven cleansers were applied and the stain did not come out — at which point, as we have learned, this is evidence that it is not blood. The substances were then applied a second time — *shanan ve-avar* — and this time the stain did come out. Does this retroactively problematize what was done between the first and second application?

The *baraita* rules: *tahorotav tehorot* — everything remains permitted. The fact that the stain did not come out the first time constitutes sufficient evidence that it is not blood, and the subsequent removal on the second attempt does not undermine that initial determination.

## Kfida/Concern

### First Laundering

Rabbi Zeira now introduces a significant qualification that adds a new dimension to this analysis. The ruling that *tahorotav tehorot* applies only to *tehorot* that were used between the first laundering and the second — that is, during the window after the first application of cleansers failed and before the second application was attempted. If the first laundering did not remove the stain, the woman used the garment for *tahor* purposes, and only then laundered it again — all is well for the period of use between the two launderings.

### Second Laundering

However, if *tehorot* were prepared *after* the second laundering — after the stain had already been removed — *tahorotav teme'ot*. This seems almost paradoxical: the stain is now gone, yet the items are *tamei*. Why? *She-harei hikpid alav ve-avar* — the fact that she laundered it a second time demonstrates that she was concerned about the stain, that she regarded it as still present. The very act of attempting to remove it a second time shows that she treated it as an existing, problematic stain.

This introduces an entirely new halakhic category: *makpid* — being concerned about, investing effort to remove — as distinct from *mevatel* — effectively nullifying the stain by no longer treating it as something that exists. Whether one is *makpid* or *mevatel* now emerges as an independent factor, separate from the question of whether it is blood or not blood.

### Status Paradox

The most striking aspect of Rabbi Zeira's ruling is the apparent on-and-off nature of the stain's halakhic status. Between the first and second launderings, the stain was treated as non-present — the evidence of the first failed laundering rendered it presumably not blood, and the woman did not concern herself with it. During that period, things were *tahor*. Then she laundered a second time, showed renewed *kfida*, and the stain came out — retroactively restoring it, it seems, to the status of a problematic stain from that point forward.

The question is genuinely troubling: if the garment had already achieved *tahor* status based on the first laundering's failure, how can a subsequent act of concern transform something that was *tahor* back into something *tamei*? The *gemara* seems to be saying that the stain ceased to have halakhic reality during the period of non-concern, but as soon as renewed concern was demonstrated — as soon as the woman showed she still regarded it as a stain by laundering again — it regained its identity as a stain from that point forward, requiring a renewed *tevilah* now that it has been removed. This is an extremely unusual mode of halakhic reasoning, and the *gemara* acknowledges its counterintuitive nature.

## Definite Blood

### Rabbi Chiyya

Rabbi Abba asks Rav Ashi: can it really be that the determination depends entirely on *kfida* — on what one happens to care about? Rav Ashi responds affirmatively, citing a *baraita* of Rabbi Chiyya. Rabbi Chiyya's teaching is this: *dam ha-niddah vadai* — even if the blood is definitively identified as *niddah* blood — if the seven cleansers are applied and it is rendered pale, and the woman is *mevatel* it — is not concerned about it — then it loses its halakhic status.

This is a remarkable extension. Until this point, the whole framework of the seven cleansers was understood as a mechanism for determining whether a stain *is* blood or not. Here, Rabbi Chiyya says that even when there is no doubt that it *is* blood — *vadai* — the combination of making it pale and not being concerned about it causes it to cease being halachically considered as blood.

It is important to note that the *mevatel* process is not purely subjective. It is not that any subjective attitude transforms the status. The stain must have been worked on with the seven substances, brought to a sufficiently pale state, and only then — at that point — the additional factor of *bitul*, of non-concern, comes into play.

### Two Issues

The *gemara* has now clarified that there are in fact two distinct issues at work in this entire sugya, and they must be carefully distinguished. The first issue is evidentiary: can we prove from the behavior of the stain under these cleansers that it is not blood at all? This was the framework of the *mishnah*, which presented the seven cleansers as a test for the nature of the substance. The second issue — introduced through Rabbi Zeira and now made explicit by Rabbi Chiyya — is independent of that evidentiary question: even granted that it *is* blood, can the combination of paling and non-concern remove its halakhic status?

These two issues produce different analyses. The first is about identification of the substance; the second is about the threshold at which an identified substance stops being considered halachically "present." The rest of the *gemara* turns on precisely this distinction.

## Reish Lakish Question

### Pottery Vessel Case

The *gemara* now brings a *mishnah* from *Kelim* regarding pottery vessels — *charasin* — that were used by a *zav* and absorbed his bodily fluids, which are an *av ha-tumah*. These vessels then fell into the airspace of an oven — *naflu la-avir ha-tanur* — and the oven was subsequently heated. The fluids are no longer visibly present in the vessels; they have been absorbed into the pottery walls. The *mishnah* rules: *ha-tanur tamei* — the oven is *tamei* — because *sof mashkeh la-tzet* — the absorbed fluids will ultimately come out when the oven is heated, at which point they will render the oven's airspace *tamei*.

### Reish Lakish Position

Reish Lakish analyzes this ruling with an important distinction. The rule applies, he says, only when the fluids involved are *mashkin kalim* — lighter fluids, meaning those that carry only a first-degree (*rishon*) impurity rather than being an *av ha-tumah* themselves, such as blood or breast milk that came into contact with a *zav* or *zavah*. In that case, the oven's *tumah* is only *de-rabbanan*, since a *rishon* cannot Biblically render a vessel *tamei* — only an *av* can do so. For such *mashkin kalim*, one waits for them to actually emerge before treating the oven as *tamei*. But for *mashkin chamurim* — the primary fluids of the *zav* such as urine or spit, which are themselves an *av ha-tumah* — *af al pi she-lo husak ha-tanur* — even if the oven was not fired up and the fluids have not emerged — the oven is already *tamei*. Reish Lakish's position is that fluids absorbed in the walls of a vessel are considered "present" as long as they are capable of emerging. Even while still embedded in the pottery, they constitute an *av ha-tumah* in the airspace of the oven.

## R. Yochanan Response

### Light vs. Heavy

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees. He does not accept Reish Lakish's distinction between *mashkin kalim* and *mashkin chamurim*. According to Rabbi Yochanan, the rule is the same for both: *im husak ha-tanur hen, ve-im lav lav* — if the oven was fired up and the fluids are on their way out, yes; if not, no. The absorbed state, regardless of the Biblical severity of the fluids, does not constitute "presence" in the halakhic sense. For Rabbi Yochanan, the absorbed fluids do not render the oven *tamei* until they actually emerge.

### Heated Vessel

The debate, then, is whether absorption in the walls of a vessel constitutes halakhic "presence" of the substance. Reish Lakish holds that if the fluids are Biblically significant and capable of emerging, they are considered present even while absorbed. Rabbi Yochanan holds that actual emergence — or at least imminent emergence under heating — is required before they are considered present.

### Mishna vs. Baraita

Rabbi Yochanan then challenges Reish Lakish from our *mishnah*: the case where the seven cleansers were applied, the stain did not come out, and the *tehorot* are permitted. If we accept Reish Lakish's position — that absorbed substances remain "present" — how can this *mishnah* permit? The stain is still in the garment; it simply did not respond to the cleansers. According to Reish Lakish, it should still be considered present and problematic.

The *gemara* answers on behalf of Reish Lakish: *hanicha li-ketamim de-rabbanan* — this is only *ketamim*, which are Rabbinic in nature, and for *de-rabbanan* matters one may be lenient. This answer raises the deeper question of what the *mishnah*'s permission is actually based on. Is it based on the certainty that the stain is not blood? Or is it based on the combination of uncertainty (maybe not blood) and non-emergence (what is there is not coming out)? The *gemara* at this point suggests that even for Rabbi Yochanan, the *mishnah*'s leniency may rest partly on the Rabbinic status of *ketamim*, not solely on the evidentiary value of the cleansers.

This is precisely the question that *Tosafot* grapples with at length. The *mishnah* may not be asserting that non-removal definitively proves non-blood status. Rather, it may be that the combination of the likelihood that it is not blood, together with the principle that what is not emerging is not considered present — at least at the Rabbinic level — produces the leniency.

## Rashi Dual Argument

### Not Blood Proof

Rashi offers a two-pronged account of why the *mishnah* permits in the case where the stain did not come out. The first argument is straightforward: the failure of the seven cleansers to remove the stain indicates that it is probably not blood. Blood responds to these cleansers; a different substance might not. So the non-removal constitutes evidence, perhaps strong evidence, that what we are dealing with is not blood at all.

### Not Present Argument

Rashi's second argument is distinct and more subtle. Even if the stain *is* blood, the fact that it could not be removed by the seven cleansers demonstrates that whatever remains in the garment is not emerging — it is deeply embedded, inaccessible through normal cleansing efforts. And if it is not coming out, it is not considered halachically "present." This second argument mirrors the broader debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish about absorbed substances: Rabbi Yochanan's position is that what cannot emerge is not considered present, and Rashi applies that principle here to explain the *mishnah*'s leniency.

The two arguments thus operate on different levels. The first says: the cleansers tell us something about what the substance *is*. The second says: the cleansers tell us something about the substance's *accessibility*, which determines its halachic status regardless of what it is. Rashi is in effect offering both as complementary grounds for the *mishnah*'s ruling.

This double argument creates the structure through which to understand the Rabbi Yochanan–Reish Lakish debate. The *mishnah* works, according to Rabbi Yochanan, because either or both of these factors apply: the stain may not be blood, and/or what remains is not considered present. Reish Lakish, by contrast, maintains that for a Biblically significant substance, absorbed status does not negate presence — the substance is still there, still capable of emerging under sufficient conditions, and therefore still a problem. The *mishnah*'s leniency, on his account, must be limited to the Rabbinic realm of *ketamim*.

The further question raised by all of this is about the intermediate cases — what if some of the stain came out and some did not, or what if it paled but did not disappear? The *mishnah* explicitly contrasts the case of no change with the case of coming out or paling, which implies that the first case involves no change whatsoever. If nothing at all changed — the stain neither came out nor paled — then one can argue either that it is not blood (since blood responds to these cleansers) or that whatever is there is deeply embedded and not coming out. But if there was some change — even paling — the stain showed a response to the cleansers, which is evidence that it is blood, and one cannot rely on the "not present" argument either, since some portion of it was mobile enough to respond.

## Presence Debate

### Blood in House

The *gemara* now brings another case to probe the debate: *revi'is dam she-nivle'ah ba-bayit* — a *revi'is* (approximately three and a half fluid ounces) of blood that was absorbed into a house. This is the quantity of blood from a corpse that causes *tumas ohel* — the impurity of overhanging. If this blood is absorbed into, say, the floorboards of a house, is the house *tamei*? One version says yes — *ha-bayit tamei*; another version says no — *ha-bayit tahor*.

### Temporal Resolution

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction with a temporal distinction: *ha bi-kheilim de-me'ikara ha bi-kheilim de-vasof* — the two rulings refer to different stages in time. The ruling that the house is *tamei* refers to vessels or items that were in the house before the blood was fully absorbed — they were exposed to the blood while it was still in the open, and they are indeed *tamei*. The ruling that the house is *tahor* refers to items brought into the house after the blood was already absorbed into the floor — at that point, since the blood is no longer in the open airspace, new items brought in are not affected. This resolution supports Rabbi Yochanan's position: once the blood is absorbed, it is no longer "present" for the purpose of affecting subsequently introduced items.

### Blood in Garment

The *gemara* then cites a related case: blood absorbed in a garment — *nivle'ah bi-khsut*. The rule stated is: *im mitkabeset ve-yotzei mimmenah revi'is dam teme'ah* — if a normal laundering would cause a *revi'is* of blood to emerge from the garment, the garment is *tamei*; *ve-im lav tehorah* — if not, it is *tahor*. At first glance, this seems to support Reish Lakish: the fact that the blood *could* come out — even before it actually does — renders the garment *tamei*.

### Easy vs. Difficult

The *Rosh* resolves this in favor of Rabbi Yochanan by focusing on the word *mitkabeset* — normal laundering. The case refers to blood that would come out through an ordinary, easy laundering process. In such a case, even Rabbi Yochanan agrees that the blood is still considered present — it is readily accessible and not deeply embedded. Rabbi Yochanan's leniency applies specifically to substances that only emerge under conditions of great difficulty — such as firing an oven, or using the extraordinary cleanser *tsafon*, or extensive rigorous treatment. In such cases, Rabbi Yochanan holds the substance is not considered present. But blood that a simple laundering would release — that is considered present by everyone, since it is effectively still "surface-accessible."

The Reish Lakish–Rabbi Yochanan debate, properly understood, concerns only the middle category: substances that have been absorbed deeply enough that simple methods will not remove them, yet remain theoretically extractable through more intensive means. Does that theoretical extractability constitute "presence"? Reish Lakish says yes; Rabbi Yochanan says no — at least when the Biblical status is not fully at stake.

The garment case is then explained as *de-rabbanan* as well — the blood in question is *dam tevusah*, the blood that emerges during the dying process, which may have exited the body while the person was still alive. Since its status as *metamei be-ohel* is only Rabbinic, the leniency of "easy laundering" as the threshold is calibrated for the Rabbinic realm, not necessarily for fully Biblical impurity.

## Rav Papa Formula

### Cannot Emerge

Rav Papa now synthesizes the debate into a clean three-part formula. The first case: the substance cannot come out and one is not concerned about it — *eino yakhol la-tzet ve-lo hikpid alav*. In this case, *divrei ha-kol tahor* — everyone, including Reish Lakish, agrees that it is *tahor*. Even Reish Lakish only argued that absorbed substances are "present" when they are at least theoretically capable of emerging. If emergence is not possible even in principle, there is nothing to debate.

### Can Emerge & Concerned

The second case: the substance can come out, and one *is* concerned about it — *yakhol la-tzet ve-hikpid alav*. Here too, *divrei ha-kol tamei* — everyone agrees it is *tamei*. If the substance is accessible enough to emerge and the owner is actively trying to get it out — demonstrating through their own conduct that they regard it as present and significant — then there is no basis for leniency.

### Can Emerge & Not Concern…

The third and contested case: the substance can come out — but only through difficult extraction — and one is *not* concerned about it, is *mevatel* it. This is where Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan part ways. Reish Lakish holds: *keivan de-yakhol la-tzet af al gav de-lo hikpid alav* — since there is a way to extract it, regardless of the owner's indifference, it remains physically considered present, and the garment remains *tamei*. Rabbi Yochanan holds: *af al gav de-yakhol la-tzet, im hikpid alav in, i lo lo* — even if it can come out, only if one is concerned about it does it count; if one is not concerned, it does not.

This final formulation reconnects to the teaching of Rabbi Chiyya that was introduced earlier. According to Rabbi Yochanan's position, even definitively identified *niddah* blood, once it has been brought to a sufficiently pale state through the seven cleansers and one no longer regards it as a present stain — *mevatel* it — ceases to be considered a halachically existing substance. It is at that point, once extraction would require great effort and the owner is indifferent to the effort, that Rabbi Yochanan holds the substance is no longer "there" in any meaningful halakhic sense, and the garment or vessel is *tahor*.

---

# Niddah 63

## Rok Tafal

### Definition of Tasteless…

The daf opens at the top of 63a, where the Gemara continues its treatment of the various cleansers used to remove or examine blood stains. Among these cleansers is *rok tafal* — tasteless spit. The Mishnah describes it simply as spit from one who has not tasted anything since the evening (*kol she-lo ta'am klum me-ha-erev*), but this formulation requires further precision.

### Rava's Requirements

Rav Pappa, learning this passage in front of Rava, initially understood the criterion to mean that one had not eaten anything the entire previous night — like a patient told by a doctor not to eat anything before a test, meaning no dinner. Rava rejected this reading. The text does not say *ba-erev*, "at night," but *me-ha-erev*, "since it became night." Rava explains: *le-afokei heicha d'kadmu ve-achil* — to exclude the case where one rose early in the morning and ate before the day properly began. The point is not that dinner is prohibited; one may have had dinner the night before. What disqualifies the spit is eating after one has gone to sleep and then woken up — eating in the early morning hours before the appropriate time. This is closer to the medical instruction not to eat or drink from the time you go to sleep until the test is administered.

### Rabbi Yochanan's View

Rabbah bar bar Chana then cites Rabbi Yochanan's more precise formulation: *rok tafal* is spit that has passed through midnight while one is asleep (*kol she-avar alav chatzot layla bi-sheina*). One need not sleep the entire night; the requirement is that one slept and that midnight has since passed. Dinner the prior evening remains permissible.

The Gemara then challenges this: does the criterion truly depend on sleep? The Beraita states that one who sleeps the entire day does not produce *rok tafal*, and one who stays awake the entire night (*ne'or kol ha-layla*) does produce *rok tafal*. The second case seems to indicate that sleep is not required. The Gemara responds: *hasam b'misnamnem* — "awake the whole night" in this Beraita does not mean fully awake; it means dozing.

### Misnamnem Status

The Gemara then defines this state of *misnamnem* — dozing — a phrase that appears in this precise formulation in several places throughout *Shas*. Rav Ashi explains: *num velo num, teir velo teir* — asleep but not really asleep, awake but not fully awake. If you call to such a person, he will respond, but he cannot reason or articulate any coherent thought. If you remind him of something, he can confirm it — but he cannot independently produce a logical argument. This is a state of half-awareness: one can hear and minimally respond, but cannot engage intellectually.

This description likely reflects something physiologically real about how sleep affects the quality of saliva. When one is fully awake at night, the mouth remains active. When one sleeps, even during the day, the stagnation of the mouth produces the particular staleness characteristic of *rok tafal*. The Gemara thus combines both elements — nighttime and sleep (or at minimum dozing) — as necessary conditions.

### Eating & Speaking

A Tanna adds a further ruling: if one rose early and reviewed one's chapter (*hishkim ve-shana pirko*), that too disqualifies the spit and it is no longer *rok tafal*. The implication is that talking — or at least a certain amount of purposeful speech — changes the character of the saliva, just as eating does.

### Three-Hour Speech

The Gemara then quantifies the speech threshold. Rav Yehuda bar Shila, citing Rav Assi citing Rabbi Eliezer, rules: *kol she-hotzi et rov diburo shel shalosh sha'ot* — if one has spoken the majority of the amount one would typically speak over the course of three hours. Once that threshold is crossed, the spit is no longer *rok tafal*. The underlying intuition is that the oral activity of speaking has sufficiently altered the saliva's character. The cumulative picture is thus: one slept, it was nighttime and past midnight, and since waking one has neither eaten nor spoken excessively. All these criteria together are required.

---

## Cleansers & Methods

### Mei Grisin

The Gemara turns to *mei grisin* — water or paste made from ground beans (not barley, as the Aramaic might suggest at first hearing). The question is raised whether this supports the view of Reish Lakish, who held that *rok tafal* must accompany each of the other cleansers as well — meaning that tasteless spit is not merely its own standalone cleanser but must be mixed into all the others. The connection to *mei grisin* is that the beans are chewed in the mouth, thus introducing saliva into the paste. The Gemara, however, deflects: *dilma havla d'fuma ma'ali* — perhaps it is not the spit itself that matters but the humidity of the mouth, the particular quality introduced by having the substance processed in the oral cavity. The question of Reish Lakish's position thus remains open.

### Rabbi Yehuda & Salt

The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's formulation does not accord with Rabbi Yehuda. The Beraita cites Rabbi Yehuda's view that the *mei grisin* must be boiling (*rotei'ach*) and must be used *over* (before) salt is added — meaning the bean paste at the stage of cooking before any salt has been introduced. This formulation differs from the Mishnah on two counts: it specifies boiling and specifies the timing relative to salting.

### Etymology of Over

The Gemara pauses to ask: what is the semantic basis for reading the word *over* to mean "before"? One might have expected the text to use *kodem*. This question arises in multiple contexts throughout *Shas*, most famously in the rule that blessings must be recited *over la-asiyatan* — before the performance of a commandment. The Gemara establishes the usage through scriptural proof. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites the verse: *va-yarotz Achima'atz derekh ha-kikar va-ya'avor et ha-Kushi* — Achima'atz ran through the valley and passed ahead of the Cushite (2 Samuel 18:23), where *va-ya'avor* implies passing in front of. Abaye cites *ve-hu avar lifneihem* (Genesis 33:3) and *va-ya'avor malkam lifneihem* (Micah 2:13). In all these cases, the word *over* combined with the sense of *lifneihem* — in front of — establishes that the term can denote priority of position or time.
